subject.title: Nature and the Economy
subject.description: How nature supports the economy and how economics can protect nature: ecosystems and the services they provide, the economics needed to reason about them (taught from zero, no prior economics assumed), how nature is valued and accounted for, the policies and markets that put a price on pollution and pay for conservation, natural resource economics, nature-based solutions, climate economics, ecological economics and the governance and justice questions that run through all of it. Ordered from foundational to advanced, sourced from Wikipedia.

outline.title: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
National and corporate natural capital accounts

openers.acct: GDP adds up what a country produces, but it does not ask what that production costs in health, happiness or nature. This part of the course is about measuring wealth and progress more honestly. Some measures widen the lens to people's lives: {{ref:nature-acct-003}} scores life expectancy, schooling and income, and Bhutan's {{ref:nature-acct-018}} sets out to measure collective happiness. Others put nature on the books: {{ref:nature-acct-010}} subtracts environmental damage from GDP, and {{ref:nature-acct-012}} counts natural capital alongside human and social capital. Together they ask whether an economy is truly growing richer or simply spending down what it owns.
openers.beyond-gdp: In 2008 the French government set up an inquiry, {{ref:nature-acct-015}}, into how a nation's progress should be measured. It joined a broad push known as {{ref:nature-acct-007}}. Some answers measure people's lives directly: {{ref:nature-acct-019}} studies life satisfaction, while {{ref:nature-acct-022}} and {{ref:nature-acct-023}} track many social and environmental outcomes at once. Others adjust the accounts: {{ref:nature-acct-026}} subtracts resource depletion and environmental damage from what a nation saves. A {{ref:nature-acct-013}} goes furthest, designing policy itself around health, fairness and nature.
openers.national-and-corporate-natural-capital-a: A firm's books record what it owns or controls, its {{ref:nature-acct-105}}, yet many effects of its activity on nature stay hidden from them. This chapter follows the efforts to change that. {{ref:nature-acct-089}} measures and reports environmental impacts, in money and in physical units, for firms and for whole nations. {{ref:nature-acct-096}} adds up the stocks and flows of natural resources and services in a region, and the UN's {{ref:nature-acct-101}} gives ecosystem accounts a consistent method. Companies, meanwhile, have tried {{ref:nature-acct-114}}, {{ref:nature-acct-103}} and {{ref:nature-acct-110}}, each a way of setting nature's costs beside the profits.
openers.footprints-and-indicators: Every product has a history of energy, water and emissions behind it, and every person and country draws on nature to live. This chapter is about the tools that make that demand visible. {{ref:nature-acct-050}} adds up a product's impacts from raw materials to disposal. {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, {{ref:nature-acct-031}} and {{ref:nature-acct-044}} each turn a way of life into a comparable number, to be set against what ecosystems can supply, their {{ref:nature-acct-047}}. Indicators such as {{ref:nature-acct-076}} track the state of nature itself, and {{ref:nature-acct-043}} marks the date each year when humanity's use of resources passes what Earth can regenerate.
openers.clim: Emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide does damage that economists try to price in dollars. This part of the course follows that effort, from estimates of how large climate damages are and who bears them to the chance that climate change will harm societies and ecosystems. It meets the tools involved: plausible pictures of the future, models that join the economy to the atmosphere, and methods for counting what an organization emits. It also asks who is responsible, because emissions added up over long periods, and the gap between rich and poor emitters, tell an uneven story.
openers.the-economics-of-climate-change: In October 2006 the economist Nicholas Stern released a 700-page review of the economics of climate change for the UK government. This chapter takes up the questions it made famous. How much damage does one more ton of carbon dioxide cause, and what does it cost to cut pollution by one more unit? Economists answer with scenarios of how society and the economy might change up to 2100, and with models that link the economy to the biosphere and atmosphere. Their answers keep returning to responsibility, since rich people and long-industrialized countries have emitted far more than the poor.
openers.energy-economics: Every economy runs on energy, and this chapter studies how societies supply and use it and what it is worth. One benchmark, the spot price of a barrel of crude oil, is watched around the world, and a nation's security hangs on reliable supplies. Using less energy for the same services sounds simple, yet efficiency gains can make energy cheaper and so invite more use. Meanwhile wind and solar power rise and fall with the weather, so grids need storage and customers who shift their demand. Not everyone shares the benefits: many homes still lack electricity and clean cooking fuel.
openers.mitigation-and-carbon-removal: Limiting the greenhouse gases that cause climate change, often called decarbonization, means two kinds of work. One is cutting emissions, sector by sector across buildings, transport, industry and land, and by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them. The other is storing carbon: in forests and other natural sinks, as charcoal in soil, or as captured carbon dioxide pumped deep underground. A carbon budget sets the stakes, the total humanity can still emit while keeping warming below a chosen limit. Cutting emissions also brings side benefits, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security.
openers.adaptation-and-resilience: Cutting emissions limits how much the climate changes, but some change is already locked in. The oceans are rising, and faster than before, as warmer seawater expands and land ice melts. This chapter is about living with that: adjusting to climate change, coping with its floods and droughts, and bouncing back afterward. It asks what makes some people more open to harm than others, what adapting costs, who pays for it, and why private investors hold back. It ends where adaptation runs out, at the limits beyond which no adjustment can protect people or ecosystems.
openers.climate-finance-and-agreements: No country can stop climate change alone, so the world has tried to do it by treaty. At the center sits a UN convention whose stated goal is to keep greenhouse gases below the level that would dangerously disturb the climate. Each year its member countries meet at a conference to negotiate, and from those meetings came two landmark treaties, one in Kyoto and one in Paris. Under the second, every country writes its own pledge for cutting emissions and adapting. Behind every pledge sits a question of money: who pays to cut emissions, adapt and build resilience, and whether investors should pull their money out of fossil fuels.
openers.eco: Beneath every economy lies a living one. Soil, a mix of minerals, organic matter, water, air and organisms, supports the plants that people and animals eat, and its power to give steady harvests can rise or fall. On land, and in the sunlit surface of oceans and lakes, plants and tiny drifting organisms turn carbon dioxide into the organic matter that almost everything else feeds on. This part of the course follows how that living matter is made, weighed and passed along, and how groups of each species grow, shrink and interact. It also meets the movement that grew up to protect it all.
openers.ecosystem-structure-and-function: An ecosystem has parts, and it does work. Some parts are alive: plants and algae that make their own food from sunlight, and the animals, fungi and microbes that must get their carbon from others. Other parts are not alive at all, such as water, light, temperature and the soil, a mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms. The work is the steady making of new living matter, measured by how much mass an area holds and how fast it adds more. This chapter starts with the soil underfoot and the drifting organisms of the sea, then follows how groups of one species change through births, deaths and movement.
openers.populations-and-communities: Populations rarely stand still. Their size and age make-up change as individuals are born, die, arrive and leave, and mathematics can follow those changes over time. This chapter follows those models: how fast a population would grow if nothing held it back, how predator and prey numbers rise and fall together, and how species competing for one resource fare. It also asks the questions conservation depends on, such as how small a population can get before chance events wipe it out, and why larger areas hold more species. Some of the same curves even describe how new inventions spread through a society.
openers.cycles-of-carbon-water-and-nutrients: Nothing in the living world is ever truly used up. The carbon, water and nitrogen in a leaf or a fish have passed through air, rock, soil and sea before, and they will again. This chapter follows those loops, the biogeochemical cycles that move elements between living things, the air and the Earth's crust. It starts with photosynthesis, which turns sunlight into chemical energy, and cellular respiration, which releases it again. Then it traces rain that soaks in, runs off and carries soil away, the carbon stored in soils, and the human hand on the nitrogen cycle, from the Haber process that makes ammonia out of air onward.
openers.climate-science-essentials: Without the gases that trap heat in its air, Earth's surface would average −18 °C instead of about 15 °C. This chapter explains that greenhouse effect, the gases behind it, and how human emissions of those gases, above all carbon dioxide, are strengthening it. It follows the rise in average temperature measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850, along with the extreme weather and wider effects that come with it. Along the way it introduces the yardsticks scientists use to compare causes: radiative forcing, global warming potential, and the feedbacks that amplify or dampen an initial warming.
openers.biodiversity-and-its-loss: Every change people make to land and water reaches the living things that depend on it. This chapter follows those changes, from forests cleared for farms, ranches and towns to habitats broken into small, isolated patches. It traces how fertile land wears out, how dry regions slide toward desert, and how fish, forests and groundwater are taken faster than they can renew. The end point is loss: species that fade from one area, and species that vanish when their last member dies. Against this stands nature conservation, the movement to save species, restore habitats and protect the variety of life.
openers.resilience-thresholds-and-limits: Every environment has a ceiling: the largest population of a species it can keep going on its food, water and habitat. This chapter is about what happens near such limits. When conditions change sharply, many ecosystems resist the damage and recover. Yet a fairly small change in outside conditions can sometimes set off a rapid change, and a system's state can depend on its history as much as on the present. Making sense of this means looking at wholes and at loops of cause and effect, and the same questions reach people: how many of us can the Earth support?
openers.key-ecosystems: Forests, wetlands, grasslands and peatlands are not interchangeable patches of green. A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees; a grassland is one dominated by grasses; a wetland is ground flooded or soaked with water for all or part of the year. Some of these places hide their importance underground or underwater, like the peat that builds up in a bog from dead moss. Each kind works differently, and each gives people different benefits, such as the water that wetlands store and clean. This chapter tours the main kinds, from tropical rainforest and northern taiga to mangrove coasts, and asks what each one does and what happens when it is lost.
openers.econ: Economics begins with a person choosing. Economists measure how satisfied that person is with a state of the world and call it utility, and they call anything that gives welfare or satisfaction a good. Microeconomics then asks how individuals and firms decide to use scarce resources, and how their choices interact. This part builds that toolkit from the ground up, because every later question about what nature is worth depends on what economists mean by value.
openers.choices-scarcity-and-value: Why does anyone choose one thing over another? Economists answer with the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, and with utility, a measure of how satisfied each option leaves them. To study one change at a time, they build models, simplified pictures of an economic process, and assume everything else stays equal. This chapter also separates two kinds of claim: statements about how the economy works, and judgments about what people or societies ought to do.
openers.markets-prices-and-surplus: A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information, and a price is the sum both sides will accept. On one side stands demand, the quantity people are willing and able to buy at various prices. On the other stands supply, the amount sellers are willing and able to offer. The basic model of supply and demand says the price moves until those two amounts match, a balance economists call equilibrium. This chapter follows that model from the law of demand to elasticity, rivalry among sellers and the free market.
openers.firms-costs-and-market-structure: Every business faces the same puzzle: what price to charge, which inputs to use and how much to make. Economists call the answer profit maximization, the choice that gives the highest possible total profit. This chapter takes that puzzle apart, starting with the technical link between inputs and output and the extra output each added worker brings. It then sorts costs into overhead that stays put and costs that rise with every unit made, and shows how time decides which is which. Along the way it asks why firms exist at all, why some band together to stop competing, and how new technology keeps shifting what can be made.
openers.efficiency-and-welfare: Is an economy doing well? Economists answer with two questions that sound alike but are not: is it efficient, and is it fair? An economy is efficient when it gets the most of what people want out of the resources it has, and Pareto efficient when no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. Welfare economics uses those ideas to judge how well off a society is as a whole, resting on two results that link competitive markets to efficiency. Fairness is harder, because deciding how output, income and wealth should be shared draws on ethics, from utilitarianism to theories of justice, and this chapter follows both threads.
openers.externalities-pigou-and-coase: A smoking chimney or a loud noise can harm people who had no say in it, and the law calls such harm a nuisance. Courts deal with a nuisance in two ways, by ordering damages or issuing an injunction, and some legal rules make people pay for harm even when they were not at fault. In 1960 Coase's article The Problem of Social Cost recast all this as the economic problem of externalities. This chapter follows that thread: measuring the extra harm from each unit of pollution, making polluters bear it, and deciding who should be liable when bargaining is hard, even when pollution crosses borders.
openers.public-goods-commons-and-property: Some goods can be fenced off and get used up; others can be kept from no one and leave just as much for the next user. Economists sort every good by those two questions: whether people can be kept from using it, and whether one person's use leaves less for others. The answers explain why goods open to all are usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes, why people who benefit from shared resources tend to pay too little, and why resources such as fishing grounds and irrigation systems get used up. This chapter follows those problems and the remedies people have tried, from public provision to systems of property rights, along with the costs of making a trade that shape them all.
openers.information-incentives-and-contracts: Every deal has two sides, and they rarely know the same things. A used-car seller knows the car's condition; a job seeker knows her own ability; the person acting on your behalf knows whether they are really serving you. This chapter is about what happens when one side knows more than the other, and when someone may take more risk because others will bear the cost. It follows the tools people have built to narrow these gaps: rules that force disclosure, credentials that show hidden ability believably, menus of choices that draw out private information, and contracts that can never spell out every case.
openers.time-risk-and-discounting: A dollar today is not the same as a dollar next year. Rising prices make each unit of money buy less, borrowers pay lenders extra for the use of their money, and most people simply value getting something sooner rather than later. This chapter builds the tools for comparing money across time, ending with the worth today of payments still to come. It also takes on uncertainty, the many situations where information is imperfect or unknown, and the idea of averaging possible outcomes by how likely each one is. Together these tools shape how people judge any choice whose costs and benefits are spread across years.
openers.measuring-an-economy: Before anyone can say whether an economy is doing well, someone has to decide what to count. This chapter gathers the measuring tools. Some describe things that exist at one moment, like a nation's machines or the skills and health of its workers, while others describe things that happen over time, like a year's output. Some boil the movement of many prices down to a single number. And some reach past the economy to the environment, which supplies materials and absorbs the waste that comes back.
openers.behavior-and-decisions: Economic models long pictured people as an 'economic man', always rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing their goals in the best possible way. This chapter tests that view against how people really decide. Their rationality is limited, so they lean on mental shortcuts, settle for an option that is good enough, and often grab a smaller reward now over a larger one later. Controlled experiments, from games of betrayal to a shared pot of tokens, show when people cooperate and when individual interest pulls against the group. Shared standards of behavior steer choices too, and that matters for every problem in which everyone would gain from acting together.
openers.strategic-interaction-and-game-theory: In every situation in this chapter, what is best for one player depends on what the others do. Game theory gives each player a strategy, a complete plan for every situation, and lays games out either as a table of payoffs or as a tree of moves. Some games are pure contests, where one side's gain is exactly the other's loss; others reward players who make the same choice, or who trust each other enough to aim high together. A central idea is the resting point where no one could do better by changing only their own choice. The chapter also follows what happens when the same game is played over and over, and how people split a surplus they can only create together, from bargaining tables to auctions.
openers.mathematical-tools-for-economics: Economics is the science of choosing well under limits, and mathematics gives that choosing a precise language. At its heart lies optimization: picking the best option, judged by some criterion, from the alternatives available, often while obeying constraints such as a cost or a budget. Calculus supplies the basic instrument, a measure of how sensitive an output is to a small change in an input, and equations built from these rates of change describe systems that evolve over time. Some quantities grow at a rate proportional to their size, so the bigger they get, the faster they grow, while others settle into a state where nothing changes. This chapter gathers these tools, from simple linear planning models to whole-economy models that use real data to estimate how policy changes ripple outward.
openers.empirical-methods-and-econometrics: Economists cannot rerun history, so they must learn from data, and this chapter covers the methods for doing that well. A statistical hypothesis test starts from a default claim that an effect is zero, then asks how probable a result at least as extreme as the one observed would be if that claim were true. The deeper challenge is cause: two things moving together does not, on its own, show that one causes the other. Causal inference works to isolate the real, separate effect of one thing inside a larger system, with help from planned experiments, data that follow the same subjects over time, and estimation methods that pick the values making the observed data most probable. Repeated random sampling on computers, sensitivity analysis and Bayesian updating help show how much confidence the answers deserve.
openers.eecon: What if the economy is not the whole picture, but one part of a larger living system? Ecological economics starts from that question, studying how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together. It sits among the heterodox schools, the economic traditions outside the mainstream, and borrows from ecology and physics alike. The laws of energy and of entropy, the measure of how spread out energy is, set hard limits on what any economy can do. From there come sharp arguments: that growth can make life worse, that businesses shift their costs onto others, and that Earth is a spaceship with limited supplies.
openers.ecological-economics: This chapter builds a way of seeing the economy as a subsystem of nature. It starts with the field of ecological economics, its history since the 19th century, and its place among schools outside the mainstream. Then it turns to physics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, and entropy, the spreading out of energy, always tends to rise. Those laws rule out a perpetual motion economy. They also give ecological economists their sharpest claims, from the gap between growth and real development to the idea of Earth as a spaceship whose crew must share limited supplies.
openers.strong-and-weak-sustainability: Can a factory make up for a lost forest? That question divides weak sustainability from strong sustainability, two opposing approaches that differ on whether natural capital can be replaced by human-made capital. This chapter starts with the economist's tools for the question, such as the elasticity of substitution, which measures how easily one input can be swapped for another. It then follows sustainable development, the goal of meeting present needs without compromising future generations, from the Brundtland Commission to today's debates. Along the way come the three dimensions of sustainability, environmental, social and economic, and the barriers that make a sustainability transition so hard.
openers.growth-theory-and-the-environment: How do economies grow, and how do populations? This chapter sets the two side by side. Population growth is simply the increase in the number of people, and logistic models show it slowing as it nears the carrying capacity, the largest population an environment can sustain. Economists explain long-run growth with the Solow–Swan model, built on saving, more workers and technological progress. Its later versions add education, and its leftover, the part of growth nothing else explains, has become a measure of productivity itself.
openers.growth-decoupling-and-limits: Can the economy keep growing on a planet with finite resources? A 1972 report, The Limits to Growth, simulated the question and warned of overshoot. Since then the debate has split into camps: some trust decoupling, growth without a matching rise in pressure on the environment, and call for green growth. Others warn that efficiency backfires through the rebound effect, or argue for degrowth, a planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption. Between them sit new pictures of a good economy, such as the doughnut, which joins planetary limits with a floor of basic human needs.
openers.circular-and-bio-based-economies: Most things people buy follow a one-way road: dug up, made, used and thrown away. This chapter is about the alternatives, starting with recycling, which turns waste materials into new materials and objects. From there the ideas widen into whole systems: an economy that keeps products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible, and a ranking of ways to deal with waste, usually drawn as a pyramid. Some of the answers are about firms and habits, such as sharing goods through online platforms or making more with less material. Others are about doubt, because critics ask whether recycling pays and whether keeping materials in loops leaves growth itself unquestioned.
openers.es: In 1997 Gretchen Daily's edited book Nature's Services laid out a framework for something people had long taken for granted: the economic benefits that flow from the natural workings of ecosystems. In 2005 a United Nations-backed study, the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, carried that idea around the world. This part follows ecosystem services from their roots to their hardest questions. What is nature's work worth, who gains from it, and what happens when boosting one service drains another? Along the way it meets nature's own recycling system, the cycles that keep matter moving back into new life.
openers.the-ecosystem-services-idea: The notion that ecosystems serve people began as ancient observation and became a standard scientific term. Gretchen Daily's 1997 book gave it a framework, and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, launched in 2001, made it famous. This chapter asks what the idea means and who benefits, whether they live beside an ecosystem or feel its effects from far away. It follows economists trying to express services in money so they can be weighed in decisions. It also meets the hard parts: services that rise only at another's expense, land-use choices that juggle ecology and economics, and a newer name from IPBES, {{ref:nature-es-123}}.
openers.provisioning-and-regulating-services: Nature's recycling system moves matter from dead things back into new life, and much of the economy rests on it. This chapter looks at the working services: animals moving pollen so plants can make seeds, rain and snowmelt sinking down to refill underground water, and living organisms keeping pests in check. It also covers what those services deliver, from water fit to drink and medicinal plants to the slow making of soil. Some services guard against disaster, such as coastal defenses against a storm surge, seawater pushed ashore by a storm. And some are faltering: insect and other pollinators have been declining in many ecosystems since the end of the 20th century.
openers.cultural-services-and-human-wellbeing: Not every gift from nature can be eaten, drunk or burned. This chapter turns to the services that work on the mind: recreation done for pleasure, outdoor pursuits in wild settings, and the beauty that philosophers of nature have studied for centuries. It asks whether humans carry an inborn urge to connect with living things, and how far people count nature as part of who they are. Behind it all sits one question: what makes a life go well, judged both by philosophers and by people themselves? The chapter also follows the money into nature tourism and ecotourism, and asks who really keeps the gains when multinational companies run the show.
openers.mapping-and-modeling-services: A service cannot be protected until someone knows where it is and how it might change. This chapter is about the tools that answer those questions. Satellites and aircraft gather information about the land from a distance, and a GIS, computer hardware and software for geographic data, stores and displays it. Simple numbers calculated from sensor readings reveal how dense and healthy vegetation is, and models represent everything from one population to a whole biome. Other tools look ahead, simulating individual agents, projecting how land use and land cover will change, predicting where species will live, and imagining several plausible futures so plans can bend rather than break.
openers.found: Every economy rests on a stock it did not build: rocks, soils, air, water and all living things. That stock is called natural capital, and the many benefits people draw from it are called ecosystem services. This part begins with the basics: what an ecosystem is, how varied life is, and how nature's benefits are sorted. It then asks why that foundation is wearing down, in an age when humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.
openers.nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation: Life on Earth fills a thin zone, the biosphere, built from countless ecosystems. Each one links living things to their non-living surroundings through flows of energy and nutrients. People draw benefits from them all the time, from food and clean water to beauty and spiritual meaning. This chapter names those benefits, counts the stock that yields them, and asks what it would take to keep both going long into the future.
openers.why-markets-miss-nature: Economics studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used, against the basic fact that resources are limited. Markets do much of that sharing, but sometimes they fail, and economic value is lost. Often the cause is an externality: a cost or benefit that lands on a third party and never shows up in the market price. Pollution is the textbook case, and this chapter follows it from definitions and diagrams to the argument over putting an economic value on nature.
openers.gov: Every rule about nature is really a rule about people. Governance is how societies decide what they may take from the environment, and who gets a say in those decisions: governments, businesses and ordinary citizens. Some of those decisions are written into treaties between countries, meant to bind them all. Others come from looser plans, like the action plan and the 27 principles that came out of the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. This part follows how those choices are made, and how fairly their costs and benefits are shared.
openers.environmental-governance: Nobody manages a river or a forest directly. What gets managed is people: how they fish, farm, build and dump. This chapter looks at the machinery for that, from national parks and local plans to treaties among countries and the institutions that help nations cooperate across borders. It also traces a shift in thinking, away from managing single resources and toward managing whole ecosystems, humans included, while learning from monitoring as decisions go.
openers.biodiversity-agreements-and-targets: In 2015 every member of the United Nations signed up to 17 shared goals, three of them about climate, oceans and land. Behind those goals stands a web of treaties: one to conserve the variety of life, one to fight desertification, one for the oceans, one for places of outstanding value to humanity. Many of them work by protecting places, limiting what people may take from them. Others decide who may use the genes of plants, animals and microbes, and who gets paid when they do. This chapter follows those agreements and targets, and asks how well they have worked.
openers.justice-rights-and-indigenous-knowledge: Environmental harm rarely lands evenly. Poor and marginalized communities often live beside the waste dumps, mines and polluting plants whose benefits flow elsewhere, and that grievance grew into a movement for environmental justice. Indigenous peoples sit at the center of this story: their lands are often where resources are pulled out for export, their knowledge of nature has been taken without permission, and they feel climate change more than most. Yet the same peoples, when their hold on land is secure, care for it in ways that benefit everyone. This chapter looks at who bears environmental costs, who gains, and what rights and laws people have used to fight back.
openers.poverty-development-and-the-environment: Most of the world's people live on less than $10 a day, and the poorest depend most directly on land, water and forests. When that land degrades, food and income fall, and families can sink into a cycle of poverty that later generations cannot escape. Whole countries can be stuck the same way, held back by degraded land, disease, war and poor infrastructure. This short chapter looks at how poverty and environmental damage reinforce each other, and at ways of thinking about livelihoods that last.
openers.business-and-nature: Firms make most of the goods people buy, and most of the harm that comes with them. This chapter asks what a business owes to nature and to the people around it. Some answers are voluntary, like corporate social responsibility, where companies run their main business so its overall effect on society is positive. Others are tools and rules: management systems, audits, emissions standards and an EU list of activities that count as sustainable. Buyers push too, choosing what to buy and what to boycott by how products affect people, animals and the environment.
openers.hist: In 1972 delegates from around the world met in Stockholm for the first global conference on environmental issues. The ideas they argued over were much older. In 18th-century France the physiocrats held that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land, and the British classical economists who followed thought hard about land, labor and limits. This last part of the course traces how those threads came together: in books like Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, in the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development, and in the summits from Rio de Janeiro to Johannesburg. It also meets the people and institutions, from the Club of Rome to the TEEB study, who tried to put a price on what nature does for us.
openers.how-the-field-developed: Economists were thinking about nature long before anyone spoke of an environmental movement. Physiocracy, whose name means 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French theory that all wealth comes from land and farming. Two centuries later, the conservation movement, Silent Spring in 1962 and the first Earth Day in 1970 pushed nature onto the political agenda. The 1972 Stockholm conference, the 1987 Brundtland Report and the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio turned that pressure into a global project. This chapter follows that path, from the ideas of Adam Smith's era to the TEEB study's effort to show what losing biodiversity costs.
openers.people-who-shaped-the-field: Some were economists, like Arthur Cecil Pigou, who proposed taxing activities that harm others, and Ronald Coase, who asked whether such taxes were needed at all. Others were ecologists, like Garrett Hardin with his tragedy of the commons and Howard T. Odum with his maps of energy flowing through ecosystems. Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can manage shared resources themselves, and Herman Daly made the case for an economy that stops growing. This chapter meets them one by one, from William Stanley Jevons and his worries about coal to William Nordhaus and his models of climate change.
openers.institutions-and-initiatives: Ideas need organizations to carry them into the world. The United Nations Environment Programme coordinates the UN's response to environmental problems, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature brings governments and conservation groups together. Researchers gather in the International Society for Ecological Economics and in the World Resources Institute, founded in 1982. Newer bodies, such as the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market and its Core Carbon Principles, try to set standards for carbon credits. This final chapter also looks at plans that help the poorest countries adapt to climate change, and at the toll climate change can take on people's minds.
openers.mkt: In 1997 Costa Rica became the first country to run a national program that pays landowners for the services their land provides. This part of the course follows that idea: paying farmers and landowners to manage land so that it delivers clean water, stored carbon or thriving wildlife. China, the United States and the mineral-water brand Vittel have all tried versions of it, and Uganda tested one as a randomized controlled trial. Every scheme meets the same hard question. Did the payment cause an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a prediction of what would have happened without it?
openers.payments-for-ecosystem-services: A payment for ecosystem services offers farmers or landowners money to manage their land so that it keeps providing a service from nature. The US Conservation Reserve Program pays farmers to plant grass, trees or buffer strips on cropland. China's Grain for Green, launched in 1999, pays them to turn eroding farmland back into vegetation. This chapter looks at how such schemes are designed, from auctions in which sellers underbid one another to the rule that money flows only when the service is delivered. It also asks how anyone can tell whether a payment made a difference at all.
openers.offsets-and-banking: Not every harm a development does can be avoided. Offsetting answers with a promise to make up the loss elsewhere, by restoring, creating or protecting habitat. This chapter follows that promise from its logic, a set order of steps that runs avoid, minimize, restore and only then offset, to its markets. In the United States, developers buy credits from restored wetlands and from banks of land kept for endangered species, and newer credits aim to cut the global risk of extinction. Running through all of it is one aim, to balance losses with gains, and one dispute: whether nature lost in one place can truly be replaced in another.
openers.forest-carbon-and-redd: A carbon credit is a tradable certificate claiming that greenhouse gases were kept out of the air or taken back out of it. Forests sit at the center of that trade. A UN framework called REDD+ pays developing countries to cut emissions from losing and degrading their forests, and private standards such as Verra's certify forest credits for companies that buy them voluntarily. This chapter follows how such credits are made, counted and checked, and why that is hard. Protecting one forest can push clearing somewhere else, and critics argue that offsets let polluters carry on instead of cutting their own emissions.
openers.finance-for-conservation: Protecting land, water and wildlife costs money, and conservation finance is the business of raising and managing it. This chapter starts with the basic tools of finance: bonds, which are loans in tradable form, shares of company stock, and return on investment, the profit an investment earns against its cost. It then follows how those tools, along with foreign aid, are bent toward nature. Debt-for-nature swaps cancel part of a poor country's foreign debt in return for local conservation. Blended finance uses public and charitable money to draw private investors in, and every investor is told to spread money across many assets so that no single loss does too much harm.
openers.economics-of-conservation: Conservation is also a set of economic choices about trade, land and limited budgets. CITES, a treaty, tries to protect endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade, and the long fight over the ivory trade shows how hard that is. Closer to the ground, people and wild animals clash over crops, livestock and space, and projects try to make protecting nature pay for local people. Planners must decide where reserves go and how big they are, sometimes with software that finds networks of sites at low cost. Some protected areas exist only on paper, and conservationists must face the hard idea that not every species can be saved.
openers.nbs: Some of the most useful infrastructure on Earth was never poured from concrete. Nature-based solutions are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle problems people face, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. This part follows that idea from rain falling on a city street to the work of controlling floods and storing carbon. It meets the engineers who design with ecology, the hybrids that pair living systems with concrete, and the people who use ecosystems to adapt to climate change and reduce disasters. It also meets the critics, who warn that nature-based solutions can become greenwashing and a distraction from cutting emissions.
openers.what-nature-based-solutions-are: Can a restored ecosystem do a job usually given to engineers? Nature-based solutions say yes: they protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while helping both people and biodiversity. Around that idea sit several close cousins, from ecological engineering to ecosystem-based adaptation, reducing disaster risk and natural climate solutions. This chapter sorts them out and shows why living and built defenses work best together. It also weighs the critics, who see greenwashing and an uneven evidence base.
openers.water-and-flood-solutions: When rain falls on a city, it has to go somewhere. Stormwater, the water from rain and melted hail and snow, can overwhelm storm sewers and flood a built-up area. This chapter follows the ways people reduce that harm, from classic flood control to green infrastructure, a network of nature-like features that builds with nature. It meets planted channels, shallow hollows that let rain soak in, porous paving and artificial wetlands that clean dirty water. It also meets the many names for one big idea, SuDS, WSUD and LID among them, which all make city drainage work with natural water processes.
openers.coastal-solutions: Where land meets sea, waves, currents, tides and storms carry sediment and rock away, and the shoreline retreats. People have long answered with hard defenses such as seawalls, but there are other choices: retreating, rebuilding beaches with sand, or stabilizing dunes. This chapter weighs them all, from managed retreat to deliberately breaching old sea defenses so salt marsh can return. It also meets the living defenders, oyster reefs and coastal plants, and the people who rebuild them. And it follows blue carbon, the carbon that coastal ecosystems take up and store in ways people can manage.
openers.cities-and-green-space: Cities run noticeably hotter than the countryside around them, and that heat falls hardest on poorer and minority neighborhoods, which often have fewer parks and trees. This chapter is about the green answers: parks, city forests, street trees, roofs and walls covered with plants, food grown in town, and belts of open land around the edges. The World Health Organization treats such green space as important to mental and physical health. Urban ecology, the study of how living things fare in cities, shows what each of these spaces can do.
openers.restoring-land-and-forests: Since 2021 the United Nations has run a campaign to repair the world's degraded ecosystems. This chapter asks how that repair works and who pays for it. Some projects bring back lost forests, some plant trees where none recently grew, and some step back so natural processes can return. Payments, credits and tax breaks reward replanting, while Africa's {{ref:nature-nbs-126}}, adopted in 2007, shows both the ambition and the difficulty. Running through it all is a debate over whether repairing nature can stand in for quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions.
openers.working-lands: Food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions, so how land is farmed shapes the planet. This chapter turns from wild places to working ones: fields, pastures and orchards. Farming leaves by-products that pollute water, air and soil, and it can strip topsoil and fertility. A family of approaches tries to do better, from changing crops season by season and leaving soil unplowed to growing plants just to cover the ground. Some aim only to sustain the land, while others aim to rebuild its soil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.
openers.evidence-risks-and-greenwashing: Not every green promise holds up. This chapter looks at the gap between claim and reality, starting with advertising meant to make products, goals or policies look good for the environment. It turns to farming and forestry that grow a single species at a time, and to the trees planted to pull carbon dioxide from the air. A subtle physical effect complicates that hope: dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling that stored carbon brings. Rules on what businesses may claim, and lists of common deceptions, are the tools for telling real benefit from spin.
openers.pol: Some of the costliest things an economy makes are never sold. Microscopic particles drift through city air, acidic rain falls on forests and lakes, and everyday rubbish needs somewhere to go. Breathing fine particles is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths. This part of the course follows those unwanted by-products and the tools societies use to limit them. It begins with the harm itself, and with the ways economists try to put a money value on the damage an environmental change causes.
openers.pollution-economics-and-environmental-he: Pollution is what happens when the costs of making and using things spill onto people who never agreed to bear them. Particles too small to see drift through the air, and rain turns unusually acidic. Waste piles up as household rubbish, as dangerous chemical leftovers, and as old factory land left behind. Some contamination has no single source at all, gathering in small amounts from whole landscapes. This chapter looks at each of these harms in turn, what they do to health and ecosystems, and what has worked to reduce them.
openers.regulation-and-standards: Before economists offered prices, governments wrote rules. This chapter covers the body of law built to protect the environment, from international treaties and national statutes down to local zoning. It looks at how societies study a project's likely effects before deciding to go ahead, and at the US law of 1973 meant to stop extinctions caused by growth that ignored conservation. Strict rules have side effects too: protecting a species can make it a financial burden for the landowner who hosts it. Running through it all is a set of guiding ideas, such as prevention and equity, that not everyone accepts.
openers.pollution-taxes-and-charges: Rules tell polluters what they may not do; a tax tells them what it will cost. This chapter turns to prices as a tool for nature. A Pigouvian tax charges a market activity for the costs it imposes on third parties, and environmental taxes, from carbon and fuel taxes to charges on crowded roads, apply that idea in practice. Behind them sits the principle that whoever causes pollution should pay for the damage. The chapter also asks who bears these taxes, since some fall hardest on poorer people, and how border charges on imports try to keep the playing field level.
openers.tradable-permits-and-carbon-markets: Since 2005, every ton of carbon dioxide released by a covered European power plant or factory has needed a permit. That rule is the heart of {{ref:nature-pol-253}}: a government caps total emissions, issues permits, and lets polluters buy and sell them. Trading is meant to make cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. This chapter follows the idea from theory to working markets in Europe and China, and weighs it against a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, which fixes the price instead of the amount. It also hears the critics, who call carbon trading ineffective, unfair or open to abuse, and who warn that cuts in one country can raise emissions in another.
openers.subsidies-information-and-voluntary-appr: Governments do not only tax polluters and cap their emissions; they also pay, inform and persuade. A {{ref:nature-pol-205}} passes taxpayers' money to people or firms to support them or encourage some activity, and support for coal, oil and gas is among the largest. Other tools work through information: an {{ref:nature-pol-186}} tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact, and voluntary standards let producers show good practice. Nudges change how choices are presented, steering behavior without forcing it. Behind many of these tools sits a question of caution: how to act on possible harm when scientific knowledge is still incomplete.
openers.choosing-among-instruments: Environmental policy is a government's commitment to deal with environmental problems, but commitment is only the start: it must pick its tools. They come in families: regulation, economic instruments that use prices and markets, and persuasion. Analysts still debate which works best, and whether a pollution tax, fixing the cost of cuts, beats a permit system, fixing the total. Rising costs can even spur firms to invent ways of using less of a costly input. Public choice adds a warning, studying politicians, officials and voters as self-interested actors, some of whom sensibly stay uninformed.
openers.political-economy-of-environmental-polic: Environmental rules are made by people, and people have interests. Lobbying tries to influence lawmakers and regulators, and the fossil fuels lobby is among the best funded. Small groups with concentrated interests often beat large groups with diffuse ones, and a regulator can be captured by the industry it oversees. Elections pull candidates toward the median voter, while past decisions constrain later ones, so history matters. This chapter explains why good policy on paper can be hard to pass, and harder still to keep.
openers.trade-and-the-environment: In 2025 world trade was worth 80,733 billion US dollars, and it carries environmental costs and choices across borders. The World Trade Organization, formed in 1995, sets the rules, and lets countries restrict trade to protect the environment and health as long as the measures are not disguised protectionism. Standards and labels can protect people yet also keep out foreign goods. Some fear firms move to countries with weak rules, turning them into havens for pollution. And waste itself is traded, often from rich countries to poor ones, a practice a 1991 memo by Lawrence Summers famously defended.
openers.res: Every economy runs on things taken from nature, from sunlight and water to minerals, plants and wildlife. Some of these renew themselves within a human lifetime; others, once used, are gone for good. Natural resource economics studies how such resources are supplied, demanded and shared out, and why owning them can enrich a country or, surprisingly often, hold it back. This part follows that thread from minerals and fish to the payments that flow to whoever owns scarce land and ore.
openers.renewable-and-non-renewable-resources: Some resources come back and some do not. Forests, fish and other living things can replace what is taken within a human lifetime, while minerals, once used, are gone. This chapter follows that dividing line and what happens when people draw down a resource faster than it can recover. Along the way it meets the old fear that population will outrun food, the bell-shaped curve that tracks a resource's rise and fall, and the puzzle of why mineral wealth so often fails the countries that hold it.
openers.fisheries: About 500 million people depend on fisheries for their living, and fish feed billions more. Fish stocks are renewable, but only while they are caught no faster than they can breed, and many are not. This chapter follows the science and economics of fishing: how a stock grows, how much can be taken year after year, and why open access drives fleets to take too much. It then turns to the tools that answer that pressure, from catch limits and reserves at sea to exclusive zones at sea and quotas that fishers can own.
openers.forests-land-and-water: Every piece of land does a job, whether it grows timber, raises crops or catches the rain that drains toward a river. Land use is the word for what happens on a piece of land: the benefits people take from it and the work they do there. This chapter follows those choices through forests, farms and water, starting with forestry, the craft of growing, using and repairing forests. It then goes underground, to the water held in the pores of soil and rock, and asks why so many regions lack the fresh water they need. Along the way it meets farms that squeeze ever more from each unit of land, and the web of people and institutions that feeds a population.
openers.managing-the-commons: Air, water and a habitable Earth belong to everyone, which raises an old question: who should look after them? Natural resource management is the work of caring for land, water, soil, plants and animals with an eye on people now and in the future. This chapter sorts resources by who holds the rights over them, the state, a private owner, a group or no one at all. It follows the commons from English common land, fenced off by enclosure, to community forests and the high seas beyond any nation's reach. Along the way it meets Elinor Ostrom, who found the rules that let shared resources thrive.
openers.val: Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost far more. That old puzzle opens this part of the course, which asks what it means to say nature has value. Economists separate a thing's usefulness from the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Philosophers ask a different question: is nature good only as a means to human ends, or good in itself? Between the belief that humans are the most important beings on the planet and the view that every living thing has equal worth lies a wide range of positions, and societies turn out to value the non-human world in several ways at once.
openers.kinds-of-value: Some things are very useful and trade for little; others are nearly useless and trade for a fortune. This chapter starts with that gap between usefulness and exchange. It then turns to philosophy, which separates what is good as a means from what is good as an end in itself. From there come rival views of humanity's place: one centered on people, one on all living things, one on nature as a whole, and one that trusts technology to solve environmental problems. Along the way the chapter sorts the ways societies see importance in the non-human world, as useful, as valuable in itself, and through relationships with it.
openers.valuation-methods: Nobody sells a forest or a beach, so putting a number on one takes ingenuity. Economists have two broad routes. One reads value from the choices people actually make, such as the time and money they spend reaching a national park, or the price of a house broken down into its features. The other asks people directly in surveys, an approach important enough that a US panel chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow was convened to judge whether it could be trusted. Between them sit cheaper shortcuts, such as borrowing results from earlier studies or pricing what it would cost to replace something.
openers.valuation-econometrics: Survey answers and observed choices are messy data, and turning them into values takes statistics. This chapter gathers the tools. Some treat choices as partly random; others sort people into hidden groups, or combine findings from many studies. The chapter also meets the traps: values that do not grow with the size of a problem, and distorted answers about goods nobody actually has to pay for. A 1989 disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, shows how much can ride on the numbers.
openers.cost-benefit-analysis: Should a new regulation go ahead, or a project be built? The standard way to answer is to estimate the benefits and the costs, convert those at different times into present values with a discount rate, and compare them. The method reaches into hard places: it needs a money value for avoiding one death on average, and money values for things no market trades. Health economists use measures that count years in perfect health, or years of healthy life lost. Critics object that the method ignores who gains and who loses, discounts the future too heavily and leaves out what cannot be priced.
openers.debates-about-pricing-nature: This chapter takes on the arguments over whether nature should have a price at all. One side holds that environmental damage comes from nature lacking prices, and that markets can fix it. Critics answer that turning nature into commodities raises practical, moral and consequential problems, and that some values share no common measure. Karl Polanyi pointed out that land, labor and money are treated as commodities though none was made for sale. Philosophy asks what arguments can be made for protecting nature, whether animals have moral worth of their own, and how people should regard the land.

reviews.beyond-gdp: The measures in this chapter share one complaint: GDP counts output but not what output costs. Some widen the view to people's lives, from the HDI's mix of life expectancy, schooling and income to Bhutan's Gross National Happiness and the surveys of happiness economics. Others put nature into the accounts: green GDP, the ISEW and the GPI subtract pollution and depletion, while adjusted net saving and inclusive wealth ask whether a nation's stock of capital is shrinking. Sustainable national income goes furthest, and two rough estimates put it at about half of actual output. China's abandoned green GDP and New Zealand's dropped Wellbeing Budget show that a better measure is easier to design than to keep.
reviews.national-and-corporate-natural-capital-a: Every account in this chapter tries to move nature onto the books. Firms do it inward, through environmental management accounting, and outward, through sustainability accounting, integrated reports and environmental profit and loss accounts like Puma's. Nations do it through natural capital accounting, which SEEA Ecosystem Accounting and SEEA-Water standardise, and through depletion adjustments like Repetto's for Indonesia, where conventional accounts overstated income. The hidden costs uncovered can be enormous: the FAO put those of the world's agrifood systems at USD 12.7 trillion. Yet the methods remain contested, from the arbitrariness of valuing externalities to whether the triple bottom line works in practice.
reviews.footprints-and-indicators: The tools in this chapter turn human demand on nature into numbers that can be compared. Life-cycle assessment and input–output analysis trace impacts through supply chains, from a single product to whole economies, and reveal how much carbon is embedded in trade. Footprints then set demand against supply: humanity's ecological footprint ran at 1.71 Earths in 2023, which is why Earth Overshoot Day falls before the year is out. Indicators such as the Living Planet Index and the Red Lists record the result in nature itself. Every tool has blind spots too, from the money-based assumptions of input–output tables to critics who say the footprint mostly measures carbon.
reviews.the-economics-of-climate-change: Climate economics starts by putting a money value on harm, from the social cost of one more ton of carbon dioxide to damages that could cut global GDP by 10–23% by 2100. Integrated assessment models such as DICE, FUND and PAGE produce those values, but their answers swing with a few assumptions, above all the discount rate. Critics add that they miss tipping points, fat tails and deep uncertainty. Scenarios frame the futures these models explore, while carbon accounting, the Kaya identity and marginal abatement cost curves show where cuts can come from and what they cost. Running through it all is fairness: the rich caused most emissions, the poor face most harm, and economics cannot say which path to choose.
reviews.energy-economics: Energy economics weighs the cost and value of energy services, from a barrel of oil to a megawatt-hour on the grid. Efficiency is called the first fuel, but the rebound effect shows that cheaper energy services invite more use. Experience curves cut the cost of wind, solar and batteries, so new wind and solar now beat fossil fuels on levelized cost and push expensive plants out of the merit order. Their variability, though, makes storage, demand response and reserves central to running a grid. Security and fairness frame it all, from the oil crises of the 1970s to the millions of people still living in energy poverty.
reviews.mitigation-and-carbon-removal: Mitigation starts from a carbon budget: warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative CO2, so only so much more can be emitted. Most of the work is cutting emissions, by phasing out fossil fuels, electrifying transport and heat, and building on wind, solar and batteries whose costs fell 55–85% in a decade. Net zero then needs carbon dioxide removal for what remains, from forests and biochar to direct air capture, though storage permanence, cost and the risk of delaying cuts are all disputed. Throughout, fairness decides who cuts and who pays, from splitting carbon budgets among nations to a just transition for workers and the energy poor.
reviews.adaptation-and-resilience: Climate risk comes from three ingredients together: a hazard, the people and assets exposed to it, and their vulnerability. Adaptation works on the last two, through seawalls and retreat, early warning, insurance, new planting times and protected mangroves. Yet the money falls far short: developing countries need 10–18 times the international public money for adaptation they receive, described in {{ref:nature-clim-044}}, and private investors shy away because adaptation rarely earns a clear income. Poorly chosen measures can even backfire as maladaptation. Where adaptation reaches its limits, what remains is loss and damage, and the fight over who should pay for it is still unresolved.
reviews.climate-finance-and-agreements: The climate treaties moved from one design to another. Kyoto imposed binding cuts on industrialised countries only. Paris asks every country for its own pledge and relies on regular review to ratchet ambition up. Money runs through both: rich countries promised $100 billion a year, missed the date, and at COP29 agreed $300 billion a year by 2035, which poorer nations called insufficient. Arguments over fairness, from common but differentiated responsibilities to climate debt and reparations, shape every negotiation. Results so far are mixed: projected warming has fallen, yet most experts judge current pledges insufficient for 1.5 °C.
reviews.ecosystem-structure-and-function: Every ecosystem runs on producers, which capture sunlight or chemical energy and build the biomass that all other organisms depend on. Only about ten percent of that energy passes from one trophic level to the next, which keeps food chains short and lets a few species, such as keystone predators and ecosystem engineers, reshape whole communities. Species share their habitats by occupying different niches, and their interactions run from competition and predation to mutualism. Underfoot, decomposers and soil organisms turn the dead back into the nutrients and organic matter that keep soil fertile, closing the loop that primary production began.
reviews.populations-and-communities: Population models start simply, with births, deaths, arrivals and departures, and a growth rate r that would run unchecked if nothing held numbers back. Real populations meet limits: a ceiling set by resources in the logistic equation, predators in the Lotka–Volterra cycles, and rivals in the competitive version of those equations. At low numbers new dangers appear, as Allee effects and random events push small populations below their minimum viable size. Dispersal links populations across a landscape, and larger areas hold more species, so the size and connection of habitat shape what survives.
reviews.cycles-of-carbon-water-and-nutrients: Photosynthesis captures sunlight and carbon, respiration releases them, and the matter of life moves in loops while energy passes through only once. The carbon, water, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur cycles all run through living things, air, soil, rock and sea, some within years and some over millions of years. People now push hard on every one of them: fossil fuels move carbon from rock to air, fertilizer factories and legumes have more than doubled the nitrogen made usable each year, and phosphorus is mined faster than geology can replace it. The surplus shows up downstream, where runoff feeds algal blooms, hypoxia and dead zones, and the ocean absorbs carbon and grows more acidic. Forests, soils and seas still soak up much of the extra carbon, but how well they do so depends on how people manage land and water.
reviews.climate-science-essentials: Sunlight warms Earth's surface, and greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide hold in part of the heat it gives off. Burning coal, oil and gas has raised carbon dioxide by roughly half, strengthening that effect, and thermometers show the result as a rise of around 0.2 °C per decade. Scientists compare causes with tools such as radiative forcing, global warming potential and carbon dioxide equivalent, and they weigh how feedbacks and climate sensitivity amplify the push. The effects reach from melting ice sheets and extreme weather to farming, fisheries, energy, health and the wider economy, and they fall hardest on the poorest people, who emitted least.
reviews.biodiversity-and-its-loss: Habitat destruction, much of it forest cleared for farming, is the leading cause of biodiversity loss, and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change add to it. The result is a decline estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background rate, with about one million species at risk within decades. Scientists track the damage with species richness, evenness, diversity indices and the IUCN Red List, and they still debate whether it already counts as a sixth mass extinction. Part of the cause is economic: many forest benefits have no market, so owners profit more by clearing than by keeping. Responses range from reserves, corridors and seed banks to land rights for Indigenous communities and curbs on the wildlife trade.
reviews.resilience-thresholds-and-limits: Every environment has a carrying capacity, and a population that overshoots it, like the reindeer of St. Matthew Island, can crash. Ecosystems absorb disturbances through resistance and resilience, while feedbacks hold each regime in place, but only up to a threshold. Past it, a small push can trigger a regime shift that hysteresis makes hard to reverse. The same logic scales up to climate tipping points, ecosystem collapse and the nine planetary boundaries, while researchers increasingly study people and nature as one coupled, complex adaptive system. Much remains contested, from what stability means to how many people the Earth can support.
reviews.key-ecosystems: Every ecosystem in this chapter turns on the same few forces: water, carbon, disturbance and people. Waterlogging slows decay, so peat wetlands and peat swamp forests pile up carbon, and draining them releases it, as tropical peat fires and palm oil plantations show. Coastal mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass meadows and coral reefs calm waves, shelter young fish and bury carbon, yet shrimp farming, nutrient pollution and warming seas are stripping them away. On land, forests hold most plant biomass while grasslands and drylands hide their value underground or in the herds and people they support. Across all of them, the services people depend on, from flood control to fisheries, last only as long as the ecosystem does, which is why conservation and restoration recur in every section.
reviews.choices-scarcity-and-value: This chapter began with one person ranking options and ended with the tools economists use to describe a whole economy. Utility measures satisfaction, preferences rank the options, and a budget constraint marks what a person can afford; the best choice sits where an indifference curve just touches the budget line. Opportunity cost ties it all together, because scarcity means every choice gives up a best alternative, whether an hour of work or the land, labor and capital that make other goods. Thinking at the margin explained why diamonds cost more than water, and the Marginal Revolution of the 1870s moved the source of value from labor to utility. The chapter also showed the cracks: critics doubt that people are rational and fully informed, and many neoclassical theories give no economic value to anything without a market, a gap that matters greatly for nature.
reviews.markets-prices-and-surplus: Markets use prices to pass information, and this chapter showed how. Demand slopes down, supply slopes up, and the price settles where the two meet, an equilibrium that shifts whenever tastes, costs or incomes change. Elasticity measures how strongly buyers and sellers respond, which decides who bears a tax and how far a firm can mark up its price. Perfect competition drives price down to marginal cost and makes economic surplus as large as it can be, while monopoly, price controls and taxes open a deadweight loss that no one regains. Yet an equilibrium is not automatically good: a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve, and with externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution.
reviews.firms-costs-and-market-structure: Every idea in this chapter traces back to one choice: the price, inputs and output that make profit as large as possible. The production function sets what is physically possible, while marginal product and returns to scale describe how output responds as inputs grow. Costs turn that into money: fixed and variable costs add up to total cost, average cost traces a U, and in the long run every cost can change and economies of scale can make bigger firms cheaper. Market structure decides how far firms can push prices, from monopolistic competition to Cournot's quantity-setting rivals and outright cartels. Theories of the firm explain why firms exist at all, while technological change keeps moving the frontier of what can be made.
reviews.efficiency-and-welfare: This chapter has circled one question: when is an economy doing as well as it can, and for whom? Pareto efficiency marks outcomes where no one can gain without someone losing, and the welfare theorems show competitive markets can reach them, but only without the distortions, missing markets and hidden information that fill real economies. Because almost every real change creates losers, economists lean on the Kaldor–Hicks test and the compensation principle, while critics ask why compensation never paid should count. Efficiency says nothing about fairness, so social welfare functions, utilitarianism, Rawls's justice as fairness and the capability approach each offer a way to weigh who gets what. Arrow's impossibility theorem warns that no ranked way of combining preferences is perfect, and the taxes used to redistribute carry their own excess burden.
reviews.externalities-pigou-and-coase: Nuisance law was the first answer to harm that spills across a property line, through damages, injunctions and, for dangerous activities, strict liability. Coase's article The Problem of Social Cost recast the problem: if deals were free, bargaining would reach the efficient outcome whatever the law said, so legal rules matter because real deals are costly. When bargaining is hard, the law can place liability on the cheapest cost avoider, or let a polluter pay damages under a liability rule, as the Atlantic Cement court did. Pigou's approach measures the marginal damage of each unit and taxes it, internalizing the externality so private costs match social ones. Pollution that crosses borders, such as acid rain and haze, shows how far these questions now reach.
reviews.public-goods-commons-and-property: Two questions, whether people can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others, sort goods into private goods, club goods, common-pool resources and public goods, and each type brings its own trouble. Public goods invite free riding, so they tend to be under-supplied unless governments, nonprofits, assurance contracts or Lindahl taxes step in, while common-pool resources invite the overuse Hardin called the tragedy of the commons. Property rights offer one answer, and if transaction costs are low enough the Coase theorem says bargaining can fix a harm whoever holds the rights, though holdouts, free riders and anger often block the deal. Ostrom showed another way, in which communities write, watch and enforce their own rules for shared resources. Old legal ideas such as res communis, the public trust doctrine and usufruct carry the same question into law: who may use nature, and on what terms.
reviews.information-incentives-and-contracts: Every entry in this chapter grows from one gap: one side of a deal knows more than the other. Hidden information before a deal produces adverse selection, as in Akerlof's used cars, while hidden actions after it produce moral hazard, as when insured people take more risk. The informed side can narrow the gap by signalling, through diplomas or brands, and the uninformed side by screening with menus of choices. Contract theory and mechanism design turn these ideas into tools, from pay tied to output to Vickrey's second-price sale, where telling the truth is always the best move. The limits are real too, from contracts that cannot foresee every situation to theorems showing that some honest, efficient arrangements are impossible.
reviews.time-risk-and-discounting: This chapter has followed one thread: a sum of money is worth different amounts depending on when it arrives and how sure it is. Interest pays lenders for waiting, compounding makes it grow on itself, and discounting runs the arithmetic backwards to give present value, the basis of discounted cash flow and the social discount rate. Expected value and expected utility put numbers on risk, insurance and risk pooling spread it, and Knightian and radical uncertainty mark where probabilities run out. Real people depart from the tidy models, discounting hyperbolically and shunning ambiguity. Those gaps matter most for climate policy, where the choice of discount rate, as the Stern–Nordhaus exchange showed, can decide how much the present should do for the future.
reviews.measuring-an-economy: This chapter built a toolkit for measuring an economy, and the distinction between stocks and flows runs through all of it. GDP measures a flow of output, while capital, wealth and natural capital are stocks that investment builds up and depreciation runs down. Price indexes such as the CPI and the GDP deflator separate real change from mere price change, though no index is ever perfect. Governments and central banks lean on these numbers when they steer the economy with fiscal and monetary policy. Yet GDP leaves out unpaid work, inequality and the environment's role as source and sink, which is why green national accounting and SNA 2025 try to count nature in.
reviews.behavior-and-decisions: This chapter swapped homo economicus for a more realistic person. Limited minds lean on heuristics and satisficing, and they are pulled by anchors, frames, defaults and a dread of losses, which prospect theory places at the center of how people weigh risk. Yet people are not narrowly selfish either: in ultimatum, dictator, trust and public goods games they share, return kindness and punish free riders, while social norms steer them further. Those findings matter for nature, because the great environmental crises are collective action problems with the shape of a prisoner's dilemma. Choice architecture shows how the new picture can be put to work, as when more consumers pick renewable electricity once it is the default, though critics question how long nudges last.
reviews.strategic-interaction-and-game-theory: Game theory turns interactions into strategies and payoffs, drawn as tables or trees, and the Nash equilibrium marks where no one gains by changing alone, even when everyone could be better off. Different games capture different troubles: the prisoner's dilemma makes cooperation hard, Chicken makes conflict likely, and the stag hunt shows that the best joint outcome may simply need trust. Repetition changes the picture, because strategies such as tit for tat and the threat of punishment can sustain cooperation among patient players, as the folk theorem shows. Evolutionary game theory carries the same logic into nature, from hawk–dove contests to the reciprocal altruism of guppies inspecting predators. Cooperative game theory, bargaining and auctions ask the final question: how to divide what players can only create together.
reviews.mathematical-tools-for-economics: Every tool in this chapter serves one aim: choosing the best option from those available, judged by some criterion. The derivative measures how sensitive an output is to its inputs, setting it to zero locates candidate optima, and convexity guarantees that a local minimum is also the global one. Constraints turn the hunt into constrained optimization, where Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions put a value on each limit, and linear programming handles the case where every relationship is a straight line. Time adds another layer, as differential and difference equations describe systems that grow exponentially, level off logistically, or settle into steady states that may be stable or unstable. Optimal control, the maximum principle and dynamic programming then steer such systems over time, the machinery economists use for problems of saving, extraction and growth.
reviews.empirical-methods-and-econometrics: The methods in this chapter share one goal: telling real causes from mere correlation. Hypothesis tests ask whether chance alone could explain a result, though p-values, the two kinds of testing error and publication bias show how easily that question is misread. Random assignment balances hidden confounders, which is why randomized trials are so trusted, while natural experiments, difference in differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and matching approximate the unseen counterfactual when experiments are impossible. Regression ties much of this together by isolating one variable's effect while holding others constant, but only when its assumptions hold and problems such as endogeneity, omitted variables and selection bias are handled.
