Sensitivity analysis, systematic reviews and meta-analysis then ask how far any single conclusion can be trusted.
reviews.ecological-economics: The chapter's thread is physics. Because energy is conserved and {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} always tends to rise, every economy is a {{ref:nature-eecon-136}} of matter and energy: low-entropy resources in, high-entropy waste out. That is why ecological economists count {{ref:nature-eecon-095}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-110}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-102}}, and why falling energy returns worry them. It is also why they separate growth from development, warn of {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}, and propose a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} that holds capital and population constant. Critics answer that technology and substitution have kept growth going, and debates over degrowth, valuation and unequal exchange remain open.
reviews.strong-and-weak-sustainability: Everything in this chapter turns on one number: how easily nature can be swapped for machines, the {{ref:nature-eecon-227}}. Weak sustainability assumes the swap is easy, so Hartwick's rule and genuine savings say a nation is sustainable if it reinvests its resource rents. Strong sustainability says some assets, such as clean air, fertile soils and the ozone layer, are critical natural capital that nothing can replace. Both sides claim to serve intergenerational equity, the fairness that the Brundtland Commission put at the heart of sustainable development. Where they differ is in what one generation owes the next.
reviews.growth-theory-and-the-environment: Growth theory and population science share a shape. A population following a logistic path slows as it nears carrying capacity, and in the {{ref:nature-eecon-204}} capital meets diminishing returns, so growth from saving alone fades away. Only technological progress, measured by the {{ref:nature-eecon-205}}, keeps income per person rising. Later models added human capital to explain why poor countries fall behind, and the AK model dropped diminishing returns altogether. None of them includes nature's limits, which is the gap the next chapter takes up.
reviews.growth-decoupling-and-limits: Since {{ref:nature-eecon-154}} warned of overshoot, the evidence has gathered on both sides. Ecological footprint accounts show humanity in overshoot every year since 1970, while some local pollutants have fallen as incomes rose. Efficiency alone keeps disappointing, because the {{ref:nature-eecon-159}} hands part of every saving back to consumption. That leaves a menu of strategies, from green growth and ecomodernism through agrowth to sufficiency and degrowth. Researchers remain split on whether decoupling can be fast and deep enough, which is why the choice among them is still argued.
reviews.circular-and-bio-based-economies: The chapter began with recycling and ended far beyond it, with whole systems that keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value. The waste hierarchy and its R-hierarchy cousins rank the options: refusing and reducing at the top, then reuse, repair and remanufacturing, with recycling and energy recovery near the bottom. Industrial ecology, industrial symbiosis and material flow analysis treat factories like ecosystems, where one firm's waste becomes another's input. New business models sell light instead of lamps and share cars that sit idle 95% of the time, while the bioeconomy draws on renewable living resources. Yet physics and economics set limits: recovery can never be 100%, virgin plastic is often cheaper than recycled, and critics ask whether efficiency gains have ever cut total resource use.
reviews.the-ecosystem-services-idea: Plato's worry about vanishing springs grew, over many centuries, into a standard term carried by Gretchen Daily's 1997 book and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. That assessment found humans had changed ecosystems faster than ever, buying real gains at the cost of degraded services and deeper poverty for some. Economists answered by expressing services in money, from replacement costs to fishers' rising incomes, though some argue nature's total value is infinite. Every choice has winners and losers, as Midwest fertilizer feeding crops while degrading Gulf fisheries shows. Protecting services means weighing ecology and economics under uncertainty, with laws and markets that still lag behind.
reviews.provisioning-and-regulating-services: Nutrients cycle, pollen travels, water sinks into underground stores and soil builds at a fraction of a millimeter a year, and the economy draws on every step. These services feed people, purify water, temper local climates and supply medicines, firewood and fish raised in mangrove nurseries. Many are priced only indirectly: almond growers rent bees, Orange County injects cleaned water underground, and payment schemes reward healthy watersheds. Others show up only when they fail, as when farm erosion outruns soil formation, cane toads turn on native wildlife, or pollinators decline while demand for their crops triples. Seen together, provisioning and regulating services are less a list of gifts than a working system that people can strengthen or wear down.
reviews.cultural-services-and-human-wellbeing: Cultural services are the ones felt rather than harvested: recreation, beauty, a sense of place and the spiritual meaning of a sacred grove. The evidence that they shape well-being keeps growing, from Danish children raised among green space to students who erred less after glimpsing a flowering roof for 40 seconds. Theories compete to explain why, through restored attention, recovery from stress or an inborn love of living things. These benefits also carry a price tag, with outdoor recreation alone worth 2.4 percent of US GDP, and tourism turns them into a business that can protect places or wear them out. Carrying capacities, certification labels and the limits of acceptable change are attempts to keep enjoyment of nature from destroying what people came to enjoy.
reviews.mapping-and-modeling-services: Mapping nature's services starts with seeing: satellites, lidar and NDVI turn reflected light into maps of forests, crops and hedgerows. A GIS ties those observations together by location, and spatial analysis, overlays and interpolation squeeze meaning from them, while warning of traps such as the modifiable areal unit problem. Models then ask what happens next, from Lotka and Volterra's predator and prey equations to agent-based simulations, system dynamics and land change projections whose uncertainty grows the further they look. Tools such as InVEST and i-Tree put those results into the language of value, so managers can weigh trade-offs and steer investment. None of it is certain, which is why validation and scenario planning sit beside every forecast.
reviews.nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation: Ecosystems, joined together in the biosphere, make up the stock called natural capital. That stock yields ecosystem services, sorted into provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting groups, and a rich variety of life often helps keep them steady. Yet people have altered about 70% of Earth's land, fresh water is running short, and pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss feed one another. Efforts to count nature, from the Natural Capital Protocol to national environmental accounts, run into a hard question: whether nature should carry a money value at all. Short-term thinking makes the long-term goal of sustainability harder still.
reviews.why-markets-miss-nature: Markets share out scarce resources through prices, but prices leave out costs that land on others. Those externalities, from car exhaust to a neighbour's late-night music, lead markets to make too much of what harms and too little of what helps. Pollution shows the stakes: air pollution kills millions of people a year and costs the world economy over $8 trillion. Economists answer with taxes, valuation and standards, while critics warn that governments fail too and that firms shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit. Ecological economists go further, arguing that today's prices cannot speak for people not yet born.
reviews.environmental-governance: The chapter's big shift is from managing single resources to managing the people who use whole ecosystems, learning by monitoring as they go. Countries tie themselves together through treaties, from the 1857 Lake Constance deal to conventions on ozone, hazardous waste, air pollution and the sea, yet no country can be forced to join, and free riders weaken every deal. Power is spread across levels and centers, from the EU and UN bodies down to towns writing their own local plans and fishing communities sharing rules with government. Ostrom's work showed that communities can govern shared resources well, while critics warn that participation and collaboration can favor the already powerful. Courts, citizens' rights to information and new research on whole-planet governance all push in the same direction: people affected by environmental decisions want a say in them.
reviews.biodiversity-agreements-and-targets: The world has written many promises for nature, from the 1971 Ramsar wetlands treaty and the Biodiversity Convention to 17 SDGs and the Kunming-Montreal framework's 23 targets for 2030. Most bind no one, and the record shows it: the 2010 target and the Aichi targets were missed, and in 2024 only 17% of SDG targets were on track. Protected areas are the main tool, and inside them vertebrates decline more slowly, but many are paper parks, and the push for 30 by 30 raises fears of evictions. A second thread runs through the chapter: who owns the genes of living things, first common heritage, then national property under the Nagoya Protocol, and now open data in the Cali Fund era.
reviews.justice-rights-and-indigenous-knowledge: The chapter's central fact is a mismatch: those who did least to cause environmental harm often bear the most of it, from Warren County's landfill and Cancer Alley to Pakistan's floods. Indigenous peoples stand at the sharp end, as their lands are mined for export, their knowledge patented, and their homes cleared for parks that make conservation refugees. Yet when their hold on land is secure, through recognized title or territories of life, forests fare better than under fortress conservation. Movements have answered with new tools: consent before development, benefit-sharing for genes, rights to a healthy environment, and even legal personhood for rivers. Each rests on two kinds of fairness, a fair share of costs and benefits and a fair say in how decisions are made.
reviews.poverty-development-and-the-environment: Poverty and environmental damage feed each other. Degraded land cuts harvests and income, and families caught in a poverty trap cannot afford to let land and resources recover. The Brundtland Report blamed poverty for degradation, while others see the poor as a leading force for sustainability, and both sides agree the poor suffer first. Even well-meant help can miss them, as water subsidies flow to richer connected homes. Approaches built on livelihoods and the five kinds of capital, natural capital among them, try to help people support themselves in ways that last.
reviews.business-and-nature: This chapter traced how a business can answer for more than profit. Ideas like corporate social responsibility and stakeholder theory widened a firm's duties to workers, communities and nature, while Friedman held that profit within the law is enough. Tools turned those duties into practice: management systems and audits, the Greenhouse Gas Protocol with its hard-to-measure Scope 3, science-based targets and reporting rules from the TCFD to the EU's CSRD. Much stays contested, from whether going green pays to whether CSR is window-dressing and whether gas and nuclear belong in the EU taxonomy. The newest goal, nature-positive, asks firms to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 across their whole value chains.
reviews.how-the-field-developed: The story of this chapter runs on two tracks that slowly converge. On one, economists from the physiocrats and Malthus to Pigou and Krutilla asked how land, population, side effects and wild places fit into the economy. On the other, writers and activists, from Leopold and Carson to the Ehrlichs and Schumacher, warned that growth was eating into nature's limits. The two tracks met in Stockholm in 1972, where governments agreed that Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be kept. From there, the Brundtland Report, the Rio summits and the TEEB and Dasgupta studies tried to make nature count in the language economists and governments use, while critics kept asking whether a price can ever say what nature is worth.
reviews.people-who-shaped-the-field: Read together, these lives show one long argument with two sides. Pigou, Coase, Hotelling, Krutilla, Kneese and Pearce worked inside mainstream economics, looking for ways to price harm, value wild places and manage resources that run out. Georgescu-Roegen, Daly, Boulding, Odum, Costanza and Martinez Alier insisted that the economy is part of a finite biosphere and obeys the laws of energy, so growth itself has limits. Between them, people such as Ostrom, Holling, Daily and Dasgupta built tools for understanding commons, resilience and natural capital. The disputes never fully closed, from Hardin's commons to Nordhaus's discount rates, and that open argument is the field's living core.
reviews.institutions-and-initiatives: The institutions in this chapter grew out of the summits and ideas that came before them. UNEP was born at Stockholm in 1972, and IUCN's 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report with a chapter on sustainable development. Research bodies such as the International Society for Ecological Economics and the World Resources Institute supplied the measurements, from material flow accounts to satellite maps of forests. Newer efforts like the Core Carbon Principles and national adaptation plans show the same pattern at work today: rules and money meant to turn good intentions into results, and critics checking whether they do.
reviews.payments-for-ecosystem-services: Every scheme in this chapter shares one design: pay landowners to manage land for services others enjoy, and pay only when the service is delivered. The examples run from national programs in Costa Rica, the United States and China to Vittel's private deal with nearby farmers. New York City shows the logic most sharply, guarding upstate watersheds instead of spending more than $10 billion on a filtration plant. Design decides how much nature each dollar buys: reverse auctions reveal landowners' costs, while flat rates leave high-value land unenrolled. Underneath it all sits additionality, judged against a baseline no one can observe, which is why Uganda's randomized trial stands out.
reviews.offsets-and-banking: This chapter traced one chain of logic from a principle to a market. Environmental mitigation and its hierarchy put offsetting last, after harm has been avoided, minimized and restored, and no net loss sets the goal of balancing what remains. Banking turns that goal into tradable credits, from more than 1200 US wetland mitigation banks to conservation banks for endangered species and credits aimed at extinction risk. Each step depends on hard measurement: a unit of exchange, equivalent debits and credits, ratios to cover uncertainty, and proof of additionality. The record so far is mixed, from US wetland banking that produced a net loss of area to the critics' charge that offsetting is a license to trash.
reviews.forest-carbon-and-redd: Every idea in this chapter grows from one claim: that a tonne of carbon kept out of the air in one place can stand in for a tonne cut somewhere else. The Clean Development Mechanism, REDD+ and the voluntary market all turned that claim into credits, and forests became their largest source. Each credit rests on a baseline that cannot be observed, which is why reference levels, monitoring systems, inventories and safeguards matter so much. The weak points recur, from HFC-23 windfalls to leakage, inflated baselines and phantom rainforest credits. Evaluations of REDD+ find real but modest gains, and the dispute over whether offsets delay or accompany real cuts remains open.
reviews.finance-for-conservation: This chapter laid out the tools of finance, from bonds and shares to return on investment and diversification, and then followed them into conservation. Older routes such as foreign aid, debt-for-nature swaps and land trusts still matter, but the gap between needs and actual flows has pushed the field toward private capital. Blended finance, green and blue bonds, impact investing and catastrophe bonds all try to make protecting nature pay investors a return. The same questions follow every tool: whether results are additional and lasting, whether labels are honest, and whether ESG scores that agree only 60% of the time can guide anyone. Behind it all sits a plain economic fact: activities that harm biodiversity usually earn profits, while conservation must find its money.
reviews.economics-of-conservation: Every entry in this chapter turns on a conflict between protecting nature and the economic forces pressing on it. CITES controls trade across borders, yet the ivory fight showed states split over whether a total ban or regulated sales best protect elephants. On the ground, crop-raiding elephants and livestock-killing predators make conservation costly for local people, which is why integrated projects, guard dogs and compensation try to share the gains and losses. Planners must place reserves where they protect most for the money, with tools like Marxan, and avoid parks that exist only on paper. With extinction threats estimated at 15 to 37 percent of species by 2050, the idea of triage forces the hardest choice of all.
reviews.what-nature-based-solutions-are: Nature-based solutions share one idea: protect, manage or restore ecosystems so they tackle human problems while helping biodiversity. Ecological engineering supplies the design craft, ecosystem-based adaptation and Eco-DRR aim it at climate harms and disasters, and natural climate solutions aim it at carbon. The typology shows a trade-off, since a solution that serves many groups cannot maximize any one of them. The best results come when living systems work alongside concrete rather than replacing it. Critics and barriers keep the picture honest: these solutions cannot replace emission cuts, and their evidence and finance remain uneven.
reviews.water-and-flood-solutions: Cities turn rain into a hazard, because hard surfaces stop it soaking in and drains rush it toward rivers, carrying pollution and flooding streets. The old answer was conventional built infrastructure: pipes, walls and reservoirs that fight water and grow less effective as floods intensify. The newer answer copies nature, with rain gardens, bioswales, permeable paving, constructed wetlands, sponge cities and rivers given room to spread, as at Nijmegen and across the Netherlands. The money often favors green, as Philadelphia's plan showed, though new parks can price out poorer residents. Restored floodplains handle frequent floods well, while the extreme ones still call for barriers and walls, so the best results come from mixing the two.
reviews.coastal-solutions: Coasts are eroding, seas are rising, and hard defenses such as seawalls and groynes protect one stretch while pushing the damage onto the next. Soft engineering offers another path: beach nourishment, dune planting, living shorelines, oyster reefs and restored mangroves that damp waves and still feed fish. Those same marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows store blue carbon, so losing them releases it. Where defense costs too much, managed retreat, realignment and buyouts move people back, from Abbott's Hall Farm to Isle de Jean Charles. Throughout, success hinges on local communities, from shrimp farmers paid to keep mangroves to the stewards of community-managed forests.
reviews.cities-and-green-space: Cities trap heat, and green is the most cited remedy: trees, parks, green roofs and green walls shade surfaces and cool the air through evapotranspiration. The same plants soak up stormwater, clean the air, shelter wildlife and, as studies of health show, ease stress and protect hearts. The benefits are unevenly shared, with poorer and minority neighborhoods left hotter and less green, and food deserts showing the same pattern. Ideas from biophilic design to green urbanism try to build nature into the city for everyone, while debates over green belts and pocket forests show that greening still carries costs and trade-offs.
reviews.restoring-land-and-forests: Repairing nature takes many forms, from replanting lost forests and helping seedlings regrow to stepping back and letting wild processes return. The money can add up: restoration benefits are estimated to exceed the investment tenfold, and repair work creates local jobs. Yet up to 90% of planted seedlings often fail, plantations of one or two species lack the wildlife of natural forest, and pledges like the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}} often hide land set aside for wood. Carbon stored in new forests can return to the air through fire or harvest. Above all, restoration is too slow to make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions.
reviews.working-lands: Farming carries a heavy footprint, from fertilizer runoff and plastic waste to the 13%–21% of global emissions from agriculture, forestry and land use. The practices in this chapter answer it in different ways: rotating crops, covering soil, plowing less, and weaving trees, hedges and buffers into farmland. Many save money as well as soil, yet evidence on profits and carbon is often limited or disputed, as with grazing claims and organic yields. A deeper argument runs underneath, over whether to farm intensively and spare wild land or to share farmland with wildlife. Payments such as agri-environment schemes try to make greener farming pay for the farmer.
reviews.evidence-risks-and-greenwashing: Green claims are everywhere, and many do not survive scrutiny: by 2010 about 95% of U.S. products claiming to be green committed at least one of the seven sins. Tree planting shows how a real benefit can be oversold. Single-species plantations, often of introduced trees, store less carbon and hold less wildlife than mixed or natural forests. Dark canopies absorb sunlight, so new forests in snowy regions may help the climate little or even warm it. Rules on green claims and careful reviews of evidence are the tools for separating genuine benefit from spin.
reviews.pollution-economics-and-environmental-he: Pollution takes many forms, but the same pattern runs through this chapter. Fine particles that reach deep into the lungs are the leading environmental risk factor for early death, while acid rain, landfill gas and leachate, hazardous waste and diffuse farm runoff each damage air, water and soil in their own way. The burdens fall hardest on poorer people and minorities who live near polluting sites. Yet policy works: US emissions of the main pollutants fell 79% after 1970, EU deaths from PM2.5 fell 57%, and scrubbers, treaties and emissions trading cut acid rain. Economists weigh such choices with damage functions, though critics warn these miss major risks.
reviews.regulation-and-standards: Environmental law grew from the weak protection of private nuisance suits into a vast body of rules. Its workhorse has been command and control: emission standards, technology standards such as best available technology, and laws like the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act, which worked well for point sources but struggled with diffuse pollution. Assessments bring environmental effects into decisions before they are made, while liability laws such as Superfund make polluters pay afterwards. Every tool has drawn dispute, from the perverse incentives of species protection to the delays of NEPA reviews. Underneath sits one long argument: whether direct rules or economic incentives protect the environment more cheaply.
reviews.pollution-taxes-and-charges: One idea runs through this chapter: make the price of an activity include the harm it does to others. Pigou's tax, the polluter pays principle and environmental taxes on energy, transport, pollution and resources all put that idea into practice, from carbon and fuel taxes to landfill taxes, deposit-refund systems and congestion charges. The hard parts are measuring the true social cost, deciding whether to fix the price or the quantity of pollution, and choosing what to do with the revenue. Returning the money through tax cuts or dividends can ease the burden on poorer households, as British Columbia's revenue-neutral carbon tax tried to do. Whether such swaps yield a second dividend, a more efficient tax system, remains disputed.
reviews.tradable-permits-and-carbon-markets: Every scheme in this chapter starts from one move: cap a pollutant, issue permits, and let trading put the cheapest cuts first. The Acid Rain Program proved the idea in the United States, and the EU Emissions Trading System and China's national scheme carried it to carbon. Their records show which design choices matter: free permits or auctions, too many permits or too few, and price limits such as the safety valve. Critics answer that trading can push emissions abroad, leave pollution near poor communities and reward gaming of credits. Meanwhile the same logic has spread beyond carbon, to water rights, energy savings, renewable power and building rights.
reviews.subsidies-information-and-voluntary-appr: Besides taxes and caps, governments steer the economy by paying, informing and persuading. Subsidies pass money to favored activities, but fossil fuel, fishing and farm subsidies show how support can turn perverse, harming budgets and the environment at once. Information tools, from ecolabels and energy labels to pollution registers, let shoppers and neighbors judge for themselves. Voluntary standards, certification and agreements let firms go beyond the rules, though usually only the best performers take part. Beneath many of these tools lies the precautionary principle, the case for caution when science is incomplete, which remains as contested as the tools themselves.
reviews.choosing-among-instruments: Environmental policy can rely on rules, prices or persuasion, and this chapter showed that none wins every time. Market instruments promise flexibility and lower costs, yet studies find regulation can match them and sometimes spur more radical innovation. Taxes give certainty about cost, permits certainty about quantity, and implicit prices such as fuel taxes add a hidden layer to both. Because problems have many aspects, governments combine tools in a policy mix. Public choice reminds the reader that the people choosing these tools have interests of their own.
reviews.political-economy-of-environmental-polic: The theories in this chapter explain why environmental policy is shaped by more than evidence. Rent-seeking and lobbying let concentrated interests buy favors cheaply, as the Tullock paradox notes, while the logic of collective action leaves the diffuse public poorly organized. Captured regulators, whether by money or by mindset, can serve the industries they watch. Path dependence and critical junctures explain why choices, once made, are hard to reverse. Yet unlikely coalitions of bootleggers and Baptists show that rules can still pass when moral and money interests align.
reviews.trade-and-the-environment: Trade links every country to environments far away, and the rules of the World Trade Organization decide how far governments may restrict it for health and nature. Green standards and other barriers sit on a thin line between protection and protectionism, and fixed compliance costs can favor large firms over small exporters. Stricter rules at home may push pollution abroad, as lead batteries sent to Mexico showed. The waste trade makes the pattern plain: hazardous waste, e-waste, plastics and old ships flow to poorer countries, defended as rational development and condemned as toxic colonialism.
reviews.renewable-and-non-renewable-resources: Every man-made product starts as a natural resource, and the key divide is between resources that regrow and those that can be extracted only once. Using either faster than it is replaced is depletion, a fear as old as Malthus and as fresh as forecasts of peak oil and the Simon–Ehrlich wager over metal prices. Economists watch the money as well as the stock: scarce, unevenly spread land, oil and ore earn rent, and Hotelling showed why a finite resource's net price should rise over time. Those rents can curse as well as bless, through swinging revenues, Dutch disease and conflict. Sovereign wealth funds, severance taxes and resource rent taxes are the tools governments use to turn a passing windfall into lasting wealth.
reviews.fisheries: Fish stocks regrow, but only when the catch stays within what breeding and growth add, and the share of stocks fished within sustainable levels has fallen from 90% in 1974. Open access is the root problem: under the rule of capture each boat races to land fish before others do, fleets overbuild, and the resource rent is wiped out. Science supplies the yardsticks, from logistic models and maximum sustainable yield to stock assessments, though critics warn that MSY itself has helped empty the sea. Managers answer with input and output controls, exclusive economic zones, marine reserves, quotas that fishers can own and trade, and community fishing rights. Each tool trades off biology, profit and fairness, which is why fights over bycatch, subsidies and quota auctions never quite end.
reviews.forests-land-and-water: Land, forests and water turn out to be one system. How land is used decides how much rain soaks into the ground, how fast rivers flood and how much carbon stays in trees. Groundwater supplies about half of the world's drinking water and 40% of irrigation water, yet pumping it faster than it refills sinks land, salts aquifers and leaves small farmers paying for deeper wells. The rules people choose shape the outcome, from prior appropriation and riparian rights to water prices, land taxes and the sustainable management of forests. Across all of it runs the same tension: the planet holds plenty of water and land, but not always where and when people need them.
reviews.managing-the-commons: Who holds the rights to a resource shapes how it fares, and open-access resources that no one owns tend to be the most exploited. Hardin's 1968 article made the commons sound doomed, yet Ostrom found farmers in the Swiss Alps running grazing land for hundreds of years with clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions. Mongolia's shared pastures and Nepal's community forests showed the same pattern. England's enclosure moved the other way, turning common land into private fields and stripping commoners of their rights. At every scale, from customary land and urban commons to the atmosphere, the lesson is that rules made and enforced by users can keep a shared resource alive.
reviews.kinds-of-value: The chapter began with water and diamonds, a puzzle showing that usefulness and exchange value need not line up. Philosophy added a second split, between what is good as a means and what is good in itself, and anthropocentrism, biocentrism and ecocentrism each draw that line in a different place. Economists built their own ladder, from direct and indirect use through option, bequest and existence values, which together make up total economic value. Many of these values belong to non-market goods, so they must be estimated with surveys rather than read from sales. Relational values complete the picture: people also value nature through their ties to it.
reviews.valuation-methods: Every method in this chapter answers one question: how can a value be found for something nobody sells? Revealed preference methods watch behavior, reading the worth of a park from house prices or travel costs. Stated preference methods such as contingent valuation simply ask, and the NOAA panel set rules for doing it well. Surveys have known weak spots, from the embedding effect to the gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay. Choice modeling refines the asking by making people weigh trade-offs, and all of these feed ecosystem valuation, which puts services such as flood control into numbers policy-makers can compare.
reviews.valuation-econometrics: The chapter's tools start from one idea: people's choices look partly random, so value must be inferred from patterns. Random utility models give that idea shape, and multinomial logit, probit, mixed logit and best–worst scaling turn it into estimates. Latent class models find hidden groups, and meta-regression pools findings across many studies. Yet the data come from people, with scope neglect and hypothetical bias distorting what they say. The Exxon Valdez spill, the first case where contingent valuation surveys priced damages, showed how much can ride on these numbers.
reviews.cost-benefit-analysis: Cost–benefit analysis turns a decision into arithmetic: put gains and losses in money, discount them to today and sum them into a net present value. Shadow prices and the value of a statistical life supply money figures where markets give none. Every step invites dispute, from the discount rate to the way unweighted willingness to pay favors the rich. Where pricing an outcome seems wrong, cost-effectiveness analysis counts health gains in QALYs or DALYs, and multiple-criteria analysis weighs conflicting goals without a single money scale. Since 1981, major US federal rules have faced this kind of review through regulatory impact analyses.
reviews.debates-about-pricing-nature: The chapter circles one question: can everything that matters about nature be put into money? Market environmentalism says yes, and that pricing nature is how to save it. Critics, drawing on Polanyi's fictitious commodities and O'Connor's second contradiction, answer that commodification makes different things commensurable and misses cultural, moral and ecological worth. Value pluralism, lexicographic preferences and the small-improvement argument all suggest some values cannot be traded against others. Environmental ethics, from Leopold's land ethic to animal rights, offers reasons to protect nature that do not rest on price.

entries.title: The ecosystem, from a rock's surface to the whole planet

definition.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients.

facts.text: Living (biotic) parts are things like plants; non-living (abiotic) parts are things like soil.
Plants bring energy in through photosynthesis; animals move matter and energy by eating plants and each other; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients.
Outside factors such as climate shape an ecosystem's structure without being affected by it, while inside factors such as decomposition and the species present both shape and respond to it.
Ecosystems are always recovering from past disturbances; the ability to absorb a shock and keep the same basic function is called ecological resilience.
They can range in size over ten orders of magnitude, from the surface of a rock to the surface of the planet.
The term was first used in 1935 by British ecologist Arthur Tansley; Arthur Roy Clapham coined the word at his request.
Ecosystems provide goods such as water, food, fuel and medicinal plants, and services such as clean air and water, oxygen and crop pollination.
Many are degraded by soil loss, pollution, habitat fragmentation and invasive species; one that has lost its defining features is called collapsed.

entries.text: An ecosystem can be as small as the surface of a single rock or as large as the surface of the planet. That is a span of ten orders of magnitude, and one idea covers all of it. An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients. Plants are living, or biotic, parts; soil is a non-living, or abiotic, part. Energy enters when plants capture sunlight, a process traced in {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. Animals carry matter and energy onward by eating plants and one another. Other organisms break down dead matter and return its nutrients to the system. Some forces act from outside: climate shapes an ecosystem without being changed by it. Others act from within, such as the breakdown of dead matter and the mix of species present, which both shape the system and respond to it. No ecosystem stands still. Each is always recovering from past upsets, and its ability to absorb a shock and keep working is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-603}}. The word itself is young. British ecologist Arthur Tansley first used it in 1935; Arthur Roy Clapham coined it at his request. Ecosystems matter to the economy because they supply goods, such as water, food, fuel and medicinal plants. They also supply services, such as clean air and water, oxygen and crop pollination. Many are now degraded by soil loss, pollution, invading species and habitats broken into fragments. One that has lost its defining features is called collapsed.

entries.title: Biodiversity: the variety of life, and where it crowds

definition.text: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It can be measured at several levels, such as the variety of genes, of species and of whole ecosystems.
Biologists most often describe it as the totality of genes, species and ecosystems of a region.
Life is not spread evenly: there is more diversity in the tropics, helped by the warm climate and high plant growth near the equator.
Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species.
Estimates by Mora et al. (2011) put the number of species at about 8.7 million on land and 2.2 million in the ocean.
Human activities are causing ongoing biodiversity loss, often called the Holocene or sixth mass extinction; clearing habitat for farming is a key cause.
Many studies link greater plant species diversity to useful results such as higher fodder and crop yields.
In 2019 the IPBES Global Assessment stated that the state of nature had deteriorated at an unprecedented and accelerating rate.

entries.text: Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land, yet they hold about 50% of the world's species. Life, in other words, is not spread evenly. Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth. Biologists most often describe it as the totality of genes, species and ecosystems of a region, and it can be measured at each of those levels. The tropics are richest, helped by the warm climate and high plant growth near the equator. How much life is there? Estimates by Mora and colleagues in 2011 put the count at about 8.7 million species on land and 2.2 million in the ocean. That variety does useful work. Many studies link more plant species to higher fodder and crop yields. It is also shrinking. Human activities are causing ongoing biodiversity loss, often called the Holocene or sixth mass extinction, and clearing habitat for farming is a key cause. In 2019 a global assessment by an intergovernmental science panel, described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}}, stated that the state of nature had deteriorated at an unprecedented and accelerating rate.

entries.title: Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people

definition.text: Ecosystem services are the many benefits people get from ecosystems.

facts.text: Examples include pollination of crops, clean air and water, breakdown of wastes and flood control.
They are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and climate regulation.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, a United Nations initiative of the early 2000s, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural.
New York City restored its Catskill watershed for an estimated $1–1.5 billion instead of building a filtration plant estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run.
Economists value these services in money using methods such as avoided cost, replacement cost, travel cost, hedonic pricing and contingent valuation.
A 1997 study estimated the value of the world's ecosystem services and natural capital at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion.
Payments for ecosystem services reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.
The term 'environmental services' appeared in a 1970 report; later 'ecosystem services' became the standard term in the scientific literature.

entries.text: New York City had two ways to keep its water clean. It could build a filtration plant, estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run. Or it could restore its Catskill watershed, the land whose streams feed the city's supply, for an estimated $1–1.5 billion. The city chose the land, and the land did the plant's job for a fraction of the cost. That job is an ecosystem service: one of the many benefits people get from ecosystems. Others include pollination of crops, clean air, the breakdown of wastes and flood control. These services are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and a steady climate. The term "environmental services" appeared in a 1970 report, and "ecosystem services" later became the standard term in science. In the early 2000s a United Nations initiative, covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Economists value these services in money using methods such as avoided cost, the cost of replacing a service, travel cost and surveys of what people would pay. A 1997 study put the value of the world's ecosystem services and the natural stocks behind them at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion. Some schemes now reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it keeps providing a service, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

entries.title: Natural capital: nature as the stock behind the economy

definition.text: Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things.

facts.text: It stretches the economic idea of capital, meaning resources that let you produce more resources, to the goods and services nature provides.
A well-kept forest or river can supply new trees or fish indefinitely, while overuse can permanently shrink timber or fish stocks.
Some natural capital assets give people free goods and services, often called ecosystem services, which underpin the economy and society.
Older economics classed nature as 'land' with a fixed supply, but natural capital can be improved or degraded by people over time.
The term was first used in 1973 by E. F. Schumacher in Small Is Beautiful and developed by founders of ecological economics such as Herman Daly and Robert Costanza.
Its values are not counted in national income accounts or GDP and have no prices, because they lie mostly outside markets.
The OECD sees natural capital as three main categories: natural resource stocks, land and ecosystems.
When businesses or people damage nature without being held to account, the harmed nature is called unpriced natural capital.

entries.text: A well-kept forest or river can supply new trees or fish indefinitely. Overuse can shrink the timber or fish on offer for good. That difference sits at the heart of natural capital: the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things. The term stretches an economic idea. Capital means resources that let you produce more resources, and natural capital applies that idea to the goods and services nature provides. Some of these assets give people goods and services at no charge, the ecosystem services that underpin the economy and society. Older economic thinking filed nature under "land", a factor with a fixed supply. Natural capital is different, because people can improve it or degrade it over time. E. F. Schumacher first used the term in 1973, in his book Small Is Beautiful. Herman Daly, Robert Costanza and other founders of a newer school, one that treats the economy as part of the ecosystem, developed it further. The OECD sees three main categories: natural resource stocks, land and ecosystems. Here is the catch. Natural capital's values are not counted in national income accounts or in GDP, the standard measure of a country's output. They have no prices, because they lie mostly outside markets. When businesses or people damage nature without being held to account, the harmed nature is called unpriced natural capital.

entries.title: Sustainability and the hard question of what to keep

definition.text: Sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time; today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future.

facts.text: The word comes from the Latin sustinere; 'to sustain' can mean to maintain, support, uphold or endure.
It is a normative concept: it rests on what people value and want for the future.
Many definitions stress the environmental side, including tackling climate change and biodiversity loss.
The economic side is controversial, and scholars debate it as weak versus strong sustainability.
Sustainability is hard to measure because it is complex, contextual and dynamic, and there is no fixed set of indicators.
Critics call the idea vague, a mere buzzword, or an impossible goal.
UNESCO frames sustainability as the long-term goal and sustainable development as the pathways to reach it.
Scholars usually split it into three dimensions: environmental, social and economic.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the concept is too vague to guide action and may be an impossible goal.
entries.text: The word comes from the Latin sustinere, and "to sustain" can mean to maintain, support, uphold or endure. In its plainest sense, sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time. Today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future. Scholars usually split it along those lines into three dimensions: environmental, social and economic. Many definitions stress the environmental side, including tackling climate change and biodiversity loss. The economic side is controversial, and scholars debate it as a contest between weak and strong versions, explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-216}}. Sustainability is also a normative concept: it rests on what people value and want for the future. That makes it hard to measure. It is complex, it depends on context and it changes over time, and no fixed set of indicators exists. Critics call the idea vague, a mere buzzword, or an impossible goal, too loose to guide action. That charge has not been settled. UNESCO draws a useful line: sustainability is the long-term goal, and the pathways that reach it are a separate idea, covered in {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}.

entries.title: Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered

definition.text: Environmental degradation is the worsening of the environment through loss of resources such as clean air, water and soil, destruction of ecosystems and habitats, extinction of wildlife, and pollution.

facts.text: The UN disaster-reduction body defines it as reducing the environment's capacity to meet social and ecological needs.
Some degradation is plainly visible, like deforestation; some builds slowly, like plastic pollution or greenhouse gases pushing the climate toward tipping points.
Since farming began over 11,000 years ago, people have altered about 70% of Earth's land surface and halved the global mass of vegetation.
A 2021 study found just 3% of Earth's land is ecologically and faunally intact.
Its scale depends not only on population growth but also on consumption patterns and how efficiently resources are used.
Industrialised nations, with higher consumption per person, often have a disproportionately large environmental footprint.
Women's livelihoods, health, food security and access to water and energy are disproportionately hurt by it.

entries.text: Since farming began over 11,000 years ago, people have altered about 70% of Earth's land surface. Along the way they have halved the global mass of vegetation. A 2021 study found that just 3% of Earth's land is still ecologically and faunally intact, with its ecosystems and animal life whole. This is environmental degradation: the worsening of the environment through lost resources such as clean air, water and soil, destroyed ecosystems and habitats, extinct wildlife, and pollution. A UN disaster-reduction body puts it more briefly, as a cut in the environment's capacity to meet social and ecological needs. Degradation runs down the natural capital that ecosystems hold. Some of it is plain to see, like deforestation. Some builds slowly, like plastic pollution, or heat-trapping gases pushing the climate toward tipping points. Its scale depends on more than the number of people. Consumption patterns matter, and so does how efficiently resources are used. Industrialised nations, consuming more per person, often leave a disproportionately large environmental footprint. The harm is not shared evenly either. Women's livelihoods, health, access to food, and access to water and energy are disproportionately hurt.

entries.title: The biosphere, from 19 km underground to 64 km up

definition.text: The biosphere is the sum of all the world's ecosystems: the zone of life on Earth.

facts.text: For matter it is almost a closed system, but for energy it is open, with photosynthesis capturing sunlight at around 100 terawatts.
It integrates all living things and their links with rock, ice, water and air.
Life is found everywhere from the polar ice caps to the equator, including at least 19 km underground and at least 64 km up in the atmosphere.
The term was coined in 1875 by geologist Eduard Suess; Vladimir Vernadsky gave it its ecological meaning in the 1920s.
Earth's biosphere is divided into biomes; most of the richest ones lie near the equator.

entries.text: Life turns up at least 19 km underground and at least 64 km up in the atmosphere. It spreads from the polar ice caps to the equator. All of it together makes the biosphere: the sum of all the world's ecosystems, the zone of life on Earth. The biosphere joins every living thing with the rock, ice, water and air around it. For matter, it is almost a closed system, with little arriving or leaving. For energy, it is open. Living things that capture sunlight take in energy at around 100 terawatts. Geologist Eduard Suess coined the term in 1875, and Vladimir Vernadsky gave it its ecological meaning in the 1920s. Earth's biosphere is divided into large regions of similar life, and most of the richest lie near the equator.

entries.title: The Anthropocene: naming the human age

definition.text: The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.

facts.text: It was proposed as a new geological epoch after the Holocene but was rejected as such in 2024 by the ICS and IUGS.
The vote failed not because human impact was dismissed but because the epoch could not be pinned down geologically; the 1950 start date was judged prone to recency bias.
Proposed start dates range from the Neolithic Revolution, 12,000–15,000 years ago, to as recently as the 1960s.
Eugene F. Stoermer first used the term informally in the 1980s; Paul J. Crutzen popularised it.
Human effects on biodiversity are a main feature; extinction rates may be 100 to 1000 times the normal background rate, though the exact rate is disputed.
Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, is one geological sign of human activity.
The name joins Greek words meaning 'human' and 'new'.

entries.contested_note: Whether the Anthropocene is a valid formal geological unit is disputed, and it was voted down as an epoch in 2024.
entries.text: The name joins Greek words meaning "human" and "new". The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet. Eugene F. Stoermer first used the term informally in the 1980s, and Paul J. Crutzen popularised it. The signs are real. Rising carbon dioxide in the air, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, is one geological mark of human activity. Human effects on biodiversity are another: extinction rates may run 100 to 1000 times the normal background rate, though the exact rate is disputed. Yet in 2024 the ICS and IUGS, the bodies that rule on geological time, rejected it as a formal new epoch after the Holocene. The vote did not dismiss human impact. It found that the epoch could not be pinned down geologically, and that the 1950 start date was prone to recency bias. Whether it is a valid formal unit remains disputed.

entries.title: Four kinds of help: sorting ecosystem services

definition.text: The ways ecosystem services are sorted into groups, most famously the four groups of the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment uses regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting services, with supporting services the base for the other three.
An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them.
Some services touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food, while others act through general conditions, like climate or erosion regulation.
To avoid counting the same benefit twice, The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity replaced supporting services with habitat services.
The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps cultural and provisioning services but merges regulating and habitat services into regulation and maintenance services.
Provisioning services are the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel.
Regulating services are benefits from the regulation of ecosystem processes, such as climate control, carbon sequestration, flood control and disease regulation.
Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling, primary production and soil formation, allow the other services to exist.

entries.text: Not every benefit from nature works the same way. Some touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food. Others act through general conditions, like a steady climate or soil held in place against erosion. To keep track, scientists sort ecosystem services into groups. The best-known scheme, from a United Nations assessment, uses four: regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting. The provisioning group holds the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel. The regulating group comes from nature keeping its processes in check, through climate control, carbon storage, flood control and disease regulation. The supporting group, such as nutrient cycling and the making of soil, allows the other three to exist; it is the base on which the rest stand. Each group gets its own entry, beginning with {{ref:nature-found-009}}. An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them. Other schemes redraw the lines. To avoid counting the same benefit twice, a later study, covered in {{ref:nature-hist-001}}, replaced the base layer with habitat services. The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps the cultural and provisioning groups. It merges regulating and habitat services into one group, regulation and maintenance services.

The best-known scheme, from a United Nations assessment, uses four: regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting. The provisioning group holds the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel. The regulating group comes from nature keeping its processes in check, through climate control, carbon storage, flood control and disease regulation. The supporting group, such as nutrient cycling and the making of soil, allows the other three to exist; it is the base on which the rest stand. Each group gets its own entry, beginning with Cultural services: beauty, belief and a day outdoors. An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them. Other schemes redraw the lines. To avoid counting the same benefit twice, a later study, covered in TEEB: putting a price on the loss of nature, replaced the base layer with habitat services. The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps the cultural and provisioning groups. It merges regulating and habitat services into one group, regulation and maintenance services.

entries.title: When more kinds of life mean more benefits

definition.text: The link between how varied life is in a place and the benefits that place gives people.

facts.text: Many claims have been made about biodiversity boosting ecosystem services; some are validated, some are wrong and some lack enough evidence.
Biodiversity supports regulating services that make ecosystems more stable, functional and adaptable.
Different plants living together can play complementary roles, such as cycling nutrients and regulating water, which steadies ecosystems under climate stress; this is called niche complementarity.

entries.text: Does a richer mix of life give people more? Many claims say so; some have been validated, some are wrong and some lack enough evidence. The firmest link runs through the services that keep nature's processes in check. Biodiversity supports those services, making ecosystems more stable, functional and adaptable. Different plants living together can play complementary roles, such as cycling nutrients and regulating water. This sharing of work, called niche complementarity, steadies ecosystems under climate stress.

entries.title: Why life crowds toward the equator

definition.text: The pattern in which the number of species rises from the poles toward the tropics.

facts.text: Places at lower latitudes generally hold more species than places at higher latitudes.
Several factors may contribute, but the underlying one behind many of them is the higher average temperature at the equator.
The rule has exceptions: parasites do not seem to follow it, and soil bacterial diversity peaks in temperate zones.

entries.text: Travel from the poles toward the tropics, and the number of species rises. This pattern is the latitudinal diversity gradient. Places at lower latitudes, nearer the equator, generally hold more species than places at higher latitudes. Several factors may contribute. Behind many of them lies one underlying cause: the higher average temperature at the equator. The rule has exceptions. Parasites do not seem to follow it, and soil bacteria are most diverse in temperate zones.

entries.title: Cultural services: beauty, belief and a day outdoors

definition.text: The non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning.

facts.text: They are hard to put in money terms.
They include ecotourism and outdoor sports, the use of nature in art and national symbols, and its religious or heritage value.
Critics argue that cultural values attach to unique landscapes and ways of seeing, not to measurable ecosystem properties.

entries.contested_note: Scholars disagree over whether cultural values can be fitted into the ecosystem services approach at all.
entries.text: Some of nature's gifts cannot be eaten or burned. Cultural services are the non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning. They include nature-based tourism and outdoor sports, nature's place in art and national symbols, and its religious or heritage value. They are hard to put in money terms. Critics go further, arguing that cultural values attach to unique landscapes and ways of seeing, not to measurable properties of ecosystems. Scholars still disagree over whether such values fit the ecosystem services approach at all.

entries.title: Provisioning services: food, timber and fuel from the wild

definition.text: The products people obtain from ecosystems, also called ecosystem goods.

facts.text: They include food such as crops, seafood, game and spices.
They also include raw materials such as lumber, skins, fuelwood, fodder and fertilizer.
Global production and trade of all major wood-based products reached their highest recorded values in 2018.

They also include raw materials such as lumber, skins, fuelwood, fodder for animals and fertilizer.

entries.title: Ecosystem goods: the material harvest of nature

definition.text: The tangible, material products of ecosystems, such as water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants.

facts.text: They also include less tangible items like tourism and recreation, and wild genes used to improve domestic species.
They are set apart from ecosystem services, which are improvements in the condition or location of things of value.

entries.text: Water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants are all ecosystem goods: the tangible, material products of ecosystems. The category stretches further than it first seems. It also takes in less tangible items like tourism and recreation. It even includes wild genes used to improve domesticated plants and animals. Ecosystem goods overlap with provisioning services, but they are set apart from ecosystem services. In this view, services are improvements in the condition or location of things of value.

entries.title: Regulating services: bees, wetlands and coastal forests at work

definition.text: The benefits people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests.

facts.text: Examples are carbon sequestration, breaking down and detoxifying wastes, and controlling pests and diseases.
Bee pollination is needed for 15–30% of U.S. food production.
Wetlands hold large amounts of water and release it slowly, making floods less likely; mangroves protect shorelines from erosion.

entries.text: Bee pollination is needed for 15–30% of U.S. food production. Other examples are locking carbon away from the air, breaking down and detoxifying wastes and controlling pests and diseases.

entries.title: Supporting services: the slow work beneath everything else

definition.text: The background services, such as nutrient cycling and soil formation, that make all other ecosystem services possible.

facts.text: Their effects on people are indirect and play out over long periods.
They include nutrient cycling, primary production, soil formation and providing habitat.
Primary production makes the organic matter that forms the base of all food webs and also releases oxygen.

entries.text: Every meal and every breath of oxygen traces back to processes few people notice. Supporting services are the background services, such as nutrient cycling and the slow making of soil, that make all other ecosystem services possible. They also include providing habitat, and the growth of new organic matter that forms the base of every chain of who eats whom. That growth, traced in {{ref:nature-eco-302}}, releases oxygen too. The effects of supporting services on people are indirect and play out over long periods.

entries.title: Freshwater depletion: a sliver of Earth's water, running short

definition.text: The using up and spoiling of Earth's limited fresh water, a major part of environmental degradation.

facts.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and only 30% of that is available for use, since 69% is frozen in ice caps.
About 85% of freshwater consumption goes to irrigation of farmland, golf courses and parks.
An estimated one in three people worldwide already face water shortages.

entries.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh. Of that, 69% is frozen in ice caps, and only 30% is available for use. Freshwater depletion is the using up and spoiling of this limited supply, a major part of environmental degradation. About 85% of freshwater consumption goes to irrigation of farmland, golf courses and parks. An estimated one in three people worldwide already struggle with too little water.

entries.title: The Natural Capital Protocol: a common rulebook for business

definition.text: A standard framework, released in 2016, that helps organisations identify, measure and value their impacts and dependencies on natural capital.

facts.text: It was released in July 2016 by the Natural Capital Coalition, now the Capitals Coalition.
It brings existing tools together so organisations can include nature in strategic and operational decisions.
It was developed by 38 organisations and is free to use under a Creative Commons licence.

It brings existing tools together so that nature can enter strategic and operational decisions. It was developed by 38 organisations and is free to use under a Creative Commons licence.

entries.title: Finance chiefs pledge to count nature at Rio+20

definition.text: A 2012 pledge by finance-sector leaders to build natural capital into their products and reporting.

facts.text: It was launched at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil in June 2012.
Signed by 40 CEOs, it aimed to include natural capital in loans, equity, fixed income and insurance, and in accounting and reporting.
One aim was to increase understanding of how businesses depend on natural capital assets.

entries.text: In June 2012, at the Rio+20 summit in Brazil, 40 chief executives from the finance sector signed the Natural Capital Declaration. They pledged to build natural capital into their products: loans, equity and fixed-income investments, and insurance. They also promised to bring it into accounting and reporting. One aim was to deepen understanding of how businesses depend on natural capital assets.

entries.title: Should nature carry a price tag

definition.text: The argument over whether nature and its free services should be given a money value.

facts.text: Measuring the parts of natural capital is fairly straightforward, but putting a money value on them has proved contentious.
Columnist George Monbiot derided valuation as trying to compare things that cannot be compared, calling the figures 'marmalade'.
Critics add that cultural values cannot carry a dollar amount, so valuation leaves parts of nature out.
Defenders say valuation puts the environment on a fairer footing against commercial pressures and is not the same as turning nature into money.

entries.contested_note: Critics reject monetary valuation of nature while defenders say it gives the environment fairer weight in decisions.

Critics add that cultural values cannot carry a dollar amount, so valuation leaves parts of nature out. Defenders reply that valuation puts the environment on a fairer footing against commercial pressures. Valuing nature, they say, is not the same as turning it into money.

entries.title: SEEA: keeping national books on nature

definition.text: The international statistical standard (SEEA) for measuring the environment and how it relates to the economy.

facts.text: Environmental-economic accounts track both the economy's impacts on the environment and the environment's contribution to the economy.
The SEEA Central Framework was published in its final form in February 2014.
In March 2021 the UN Statistical Commission adopted the SEEA Ecosystem Accounting standard, covering ecosystem extent, condition and services in physical and money terms.
It is a satellite system of the UN System of National Accounts, so it uses the SNA's definitions and rules and the two sets of figures share boundaries.

sources.title: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting

entries.text: Can a country keep books on its environment as it does on its economy? The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, is the international statistical standard for doing so. It tracks both the economy's impacts on the environment and the environment's contribution to the economy. The SEEA Central Framework reached its final form in February 2014. In March 2021 the UN Statistical Commission adopted a standard for ecosystem accounting, covering the extent, condition and services of ecosystems in physical and money terms. SEEA is a satellite of the UN's main system for measuring economies, described in {{ref:nature-econ-596}}, and shares its definitions, rules and boundaries.

entries.title: Eco-capitalism: putting markets to work for nature

definition.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, is the view that nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends, so markets should be used to solve environmental problems.

facts.text: It argues governments should use market-based tools such as a carbon tax.
A central aim is to correct the market failure in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause.
Critics such as eco-socialists say growth and the commodification of nature cannot easily be reconciled with sustainability.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue that commodifying nature and pursuing growth cannot easily coexist with sustainability.
entries.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, starts from a claim: nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends. If that is true, markets should be used to solve environmental problems. Its supporters want governments to use market-based tools, such as a tax on carbon. A central aim is to correct a basic flaw in markets, in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause. Critics, including eco-socialists, doubt the approach. They argue that growth, and turning nature into a commodity, cannot easily be reconciled with sustainability.

entries.title: When did the human age begin

definition.text: The disagreement over when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began.

facts.text: Crutzen proposed the Industrial Revolution; Lovelock proposed the first Newcomen steam engine in 1712.
In 2019 the Anthropocene Working Group proposed the mid-20th century, when population, industry and farm chemicals surged and atomic tests left radioactive debris in sediments.
William Ruddiman argued it began about 8,000 years ago with farming and settled cultures.
Some place it near the start of the Holocene, as early peoples cleared forests, hunted megafauna to extinction and spread invasive species.

entries.contested_note: Researchers propose start dates ranging from early farming to the 1950s.
entries.text: Researchers cannot agree on when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began, and the candidates span thousands of years. William Ruddiman argued it began about 8,000 years ago, with farming and settled cultures. Others place it near the start of the Holocene, the present geological epoch, as early peoples cleared forests, hunted giant animals to extinction and spread invading species. entries.title: The Homogenocene: a world growing more alike

definition.text: A name for the present age in which ecosystems worldwide grow more alike, mainly because people move species around the globe.

facts.text: Species are spread on purpose, as crops and livestock, or by accident.
The term was first used by Michael Samways in 1999.

entries.text: Ecosystems around the world are growing more alike, mainly because people move species across the globe. Some species travel on purpose, as crops and livestock. Others travel by accident. Michael Samways first used a name for this age in 1999: the Homogenocene. It describes one face of the Anthropocene, the sameness that spreads when living things ride along with people.

entries.title: Assimilative capacity: how much waste nature can absorb

definition.text: Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it.

facts.text: Nature absorbs pollutants by diluting and dispersing them and removing them through chemical or biological processes.
A pollutant actually causes pollution once the assimilative capacity is exceeded.
Fast-moving or large bodies of water can absorb more than a slow stream, because dilution is the main way water lowers contaminant levels.
If an irrigation standard for salt is 450 mg/L, a water body's assimilative capacity is the salt that can be added before that level is passed.
Governments use it as a guide for sustainable growth of city regions and to judge how much pressure a region is under.
It is criticised for a vague definition and for wrongly implying that small amounts of pollution do no harm.

entries.text: A big, fast river can absorb more waste than a slow stream, because water lowers contaminant levels mainly by diluting them. That limit has a name. Governments use the idea to guide the sustainable growth of city regions and to judge how much pressure a region is under. Critics call its definition vague. They also say it wrongly implies that small amounts of pollution do no harm.

entries.title: Short-termism: the pull of the quick payoff

definition.text: Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action.

facts.text: It is linked to present bias, a thinking habit that prefers short-term payoffs to long-term rewards.
It can undermine actions whose results take longer than one government's term to appear.
Short-termism and consumerism are named among the barriers to sustainability.

entries.title: The triple planetary crisis: pollution, climate and vanishing species

definition.text: A UN term for three linked global environmental crises: pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss.

facts.text: The three crises feed one another, raising environmental risks and causing global economic loss.
Pollution is the leading environmental cause of disease and death; an estimated 9 million premature deaths in 2015 were linked to it.
The climate crisis comes from too much greenhouse gas in the atmosphere and brings rising temperatures, sea-level rise and extreme weather.
Up to one million plant and animal species face extinction, weakening ecosystems' ability to function and adapt.
Over half of global GDP depends on nature, and over 1 billion people's livelihoods are tied to forests.
The framework resembles other broad views of human impact, such as planetary boundaries.

entries.text: Over half of the world's economic output, measured as GDP, depends on nature, and over 1 billion people's livelihoods are tied to forests. That is why the UN warns of a triple planetary crisis: three linked global crises of pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss. Each is severe on its own. Pollution is the leading environmental cause of disease and death, linked to an estimated 9 million premature deaths in 2015. The climate crisis comes from too much heat-trapping gas in the atmosphere, bringing rising temperatures, sea-level rise and extreme weather. Up to one million plant and animal species face extinction, weakening ecosystems' ability to function and adapt. The three crises feed one another, raising environmental risks and causing global economic loss. The framework resembles other broad views of human impact, such as the limits mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}.

entries.title: Managing the planet's land, water and air for the long run

definition.text: Managing the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale according to sustainability principles.

facts.text: Changes in how land is split between cities, farms, forest and pasture strongly affect the global water, carbon and nitrogen cycles.
Biodiversity loss stems largely from habitat loss as natural capital is converted into man-made capital.
Since the Neolithic Revolution, human consumption has cut the world's forest cover by about 47%.
Feeding humanity takes about 38% of Earth's land surface and about 20% of its net primary productivity.

entries.title: Accommodative capacity: a sharper measure of what water can take

definition.text: The rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

facts.text: It was proposed as a less ambiguous alternative to assimilative capacity because its uses are defined more in numbers.
Inconsistency in assimilative capacity led NOAA and the EPA to restrict that term.

entries.text: Assimilative capacity proved too slippery for some regulators. Inconsistency in how it was used led NOAA and the EPA, two US government agencies, to restrict the term. Accommodative capacity was proposed as a less ambiguous alternative, because its uses are defined more in numbers. It is the rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.
