entries.title: Economics: the science of running the world's household

definition.text: The social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used.

facts.text: It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how economies work.
Microeconomics studies individual agents and markets; macroeconomics studies whole economies, including growth, inflation and unemployment.
A widely accepted definition, from Lionel Robbins in 1932, calls it the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses.
The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household; the field was earlier called political economy.
It separates positive economics, describing what is, from normative economics, arguing for what ought to be.
Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations of 1776 is described as the birth of economics as a separate discipline; it named land, labour and capital as the factors of production.
Because controlled experiments are hard in economics, theories are mostly tested on observed data using econometrics.
Economic analysis is applied far beyond business, including to law, politics and the environment.

entries.text: The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household. Economics is the social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used. It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how whole economies work. The field was once called political economy. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, is described as the birth of economics as a separate discipline. Smith named land, labour and capital as the basic inputs of production, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-086}}. A widely accepted definition came from Lionel Robbins in 1932. He called economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Economists divide their field in two ways. One split is by scale: the study of individual agents and markets, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-134}}, versus the study of whole economies, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-541}}. The second includes growth, inflation and unemployment. The other separates positive economics, which describes what is, from normative economics, which argues for what ought to be. Controlled experiments are hard in economics, so theories are mostly tested on observed data, using statistical methods called econometrics. Economic analysis now reaches far beyond business, into law, politics and the environment.
entries.text_plain: The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household. Economics is the social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used. It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how whole economies work. The field was once called political economy. entries.title: Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else

definition.text: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it.

facts.text: Externalities are parts of production or consumption that carry no price.
Air pollution from cars is one: neither car makers nor drivers pay its cost to society.
Pollution of the environment is the textbook example of a negative externality.
Because the market price does not reflect the true cost or benefit to society, resources could be better allocated, so externalities are a kind of market failure.
Alfred Marshall first developed the idea in the 1890s, and Arthur Pigou brought it wider attention in the 1920s.
Governments often try to 'internalize' externalities so that prices include all the costs and benefits, most often by taxing whoever causes them.
Setting the right tax is hard because regulators rarely have full information about the externality.
The idea is now used beyond economics, in environmental science, public health and urban planning.

entries.text: Every car on the road pollutes the air, yet neither car makers nor drivers pay that cost to society. Economists call this an externality: a cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it. Externalities are the parts of production or consumption that carry no price. Pollution of the environment is the textbook example of a negative, or harmful, one. Because the market price does not reflect the true cost or benefit to society, resources could be better allocated. That makes externalities one cause of the problem explored in {{ref:nature-found-045}}, where a market loses value. Alfred Marshall first developed the idea in the 1890s, and Arthur Pigou brought it wider attention in the 1920s. Governments often try to "internalize" externalities, so that prices include all the costs and benefits. The most common tool is a tax on whoever causes them. Setting the right tax is hard, because regulators rarely have full information about the externality. The idea has spread beyond economics, into environmental science, public health and urban planning.

entries.title: Market failure: when free markets waste value

definition.text: A situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost.

facts.text: Mainstream economics lists several causes: monopoly power, externalities, public goods, missing or unequal information, unequal bargaining power, irrational behaviour, and unemployment or inflation.
Environmental economics deals mostly with externalities, also called 'public bads'.
Remedies include rules based on cost–benefit analysis or market tools that change incentives, such as emission fees or redefined property rights.
Governments often tax or restrict goods with negative externalities and subsidise goods with positive ones.
Most mainstream economists think government can sometimes improve the outcome, as with building codes or endangered species laws.
But government interventions can themselves misallocate resources, which is called government failure.
The term was first used by economists in 1958, though the idea is traced back to John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

entries.text: Mainstream economics keeps a list of the ways free markets go wrong. Market failure is a situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost. The causes on the list include the power of a single dominant seller, externalities, and missing or unequal information. Others are one side's greater power to bargain, irrational behaviour, and unemployment or inflation. Another cause is goods that no one can be kept from enjoying, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-633}}. Economists who study the environment deal mostly with externalities. Governments respond in several ways. They often tax or restrict goods with negative externalities and subsidise goods with positive ones. Other remedies include rules based on weighing costs against benefits, or market tools that change incentives, such as emission fees or redefined rights of ownership. Most mainstream economists think government can sometimes improve the outcome, as with building codes or endangered species laws. But government interventions can themselves misallocate resources, a problem explored in {{ref:nature-found-064}}. Economists first used the term in 1958, though the idea is traced back to John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

entries.title: Environmental economics: weighing what markets leave out

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them.

facts.text: It weighs the costs and benefits of different policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid waste and global warming.
Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre.
Most environmental economists are trained as economists and use economic tools on problems where the market's 'invisible hand' cannot be relied on.
Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all.
The name became popular in the 1960s, but links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo.
Ronald Coase's economic solution to environmental problems is credited with settling it as a sub-field of economics.
It was once separate from natural resource economics, but the two are now hard to tell apart.
Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

entries.text: Markets are often trusted to steer resources to good uses with no one in charge, through the combined effect of many self-interested choices. Environmental economists work where that steering cannot be relied on. Environmental economics is the branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them. Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre. The field weighs the costs and benefits of policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid waste and global warming. Most environmental economists are trained as economists and bring economic tools to these problems. Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all. The name became popular in the 1960s. Yet links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo. An economic solution to environmental problems proposed by Ronald Coase is credited with settling the field as a sub-field of economics. It was once separate from the economics of natural resources, but the two are now hard to tell apart. Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

entries.title: Scarcity: why there is never enough

definition.text: The basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit.

facts.text: Scarcity is central to economic theory and is said to be essential to a proper definition of economics itself.
There is never enough of something to satisfy every human want, even with advanced technology.
Scarcity forces sacrifice: getting more of one thing means giving something else up, a trade-off.
Market prices are one way to share out scarce resources.
Air matters more to us than gold yet is less scarce, because producing air costs nothing while gold must be found and processed.
A scarce good is one where more is wanted than is available at a price of zero.
Monopolies and stockpiling can create artificial scarcity, and panic buying can cause temporary scarcity.
Some argue that economic scarcity comes not only from limited resources but also from human activity and the way societies provide for themselves.

entries.text: Air matters more to people than gold, yet gold is the scarce one. Producing air costs nothing, while gold must be found and processed. Scarcity is the basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit. There is never enough of something to satisfy every human want, even with advanced technology. Economists call a good scarce when more of it is wanted than is available at a price of zero. Monopolies and stockpiling can create artificial scarcity, and panic buying can cause temporary scarcity. Some thinkers go further. They argue that scarcity comes not only from limited resources but also from human activity and the way societies provide for themselves.

entries.title: Negative externalities: the harm nobody pays for

definition.text: A harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party and is not counted in the market price.

facts.text: It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy, and can arise in either production or consumption.
Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society.
Air pollution from burning fossil fuels damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health.
A neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a consumption example.
Because they are Pareto inefficient, negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones.

entries.text: A neighbour's loud late-night music costs someone else a night's sleep. That lost sleep is a negative externality: a harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party. Its cost is not counted in the market price. It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy. Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society. The music is a consumption example, but production causes them too. Air pollution from burning fossil fuels damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health. Negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones. The reason is that they are inefficient in a strict sense: someone could be made better off without anyone being made worse off. That test of efficiency is explained in {{ref:nature-econ-168}}.

entries.title: Social cost: the full bill for an activity

definition.text: The full cost of an activity to society: the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated.

facts.text: Private costs are the direct costs to the producer of making a good or service.
Driving's social costs include wear and tear, congestion and the pollution it causes others.
When social costs exceed private costs, relying on private markets alone gives an inefficient result.
The idea underlies the social cost of carbon, used to judge policies such as a carbon tax.
Pigou argued government should tax each unit by the marginal damage it causes; Coase argued affected parties could instead bargain.

entries.contested_note: Whether government should intervene to correct social costs or leave it to bargaining is hotly debated.
entries.text: A driver pays the direct costs of a trip. Other people pay for the wear and tear, the congestion and the pollution the trip causes. Add the two together and you get social cost: the full cost of an activity to society. It is the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated. Private costs are the direct costs to the producer of making a good or service. When social costs exceed private costs, relying on private markets alone gives an inefficient result. The idea underlies efforts to price the harm from carbon emissions, explored in {{ref:nature-clim-241}}, which help judge policies such as a tax on carbon. How to close the gap is hotly debated. Pigou argued that government should tax each unit by the harm that one extra unit causes. Coase argued that the affected parties could bargain instead.

entries.title: Drawing an externality on a supply and demand graph

definition.text: A standard supply and demand graph with an extra curve added to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society.

facts.text: For pollution, the private cost of making a good sits below its social cost by the amount of the external cost.
Buyers counting only private cost end up at a lower price and higher quantity than the efficient one.
Efficiency requires producing only while the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.
In the steel example, people buy and use too much steel, and society would be better off if the extra units were never made.
With an external benefit such as vaccination, the private benefit falls short of the social benefit.
The gap is not fixed by competitive markets; some collective answer is needed, such as courts, bans or green taxes.

entries.text: Economists like to draw their problems. On the standard graph, one curve shows how much buyers want at each price and another shows how much sellers offer. The externality diagram adds an extra curve, to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society. Take pollution from making steel. The private cost of making steel sits below its social cost, by the amount of the external cost. Buyers who count only private cost end up at a lower price and a higher quantity than the efficient one. People buy and use too much steel, and society would be better off if the extra units were never made. Efficiency requires producing only while the marginal social benefit, the gain to society from one more unit, exceeds the cost to society of that unit. An external benefit, such as vaccination, works the other way: the private benefit falls short of the social benefit. Competitive markets do not fix the gap. Some collective answer is needed, such as courts, bans or green taxes.

entries.title: Positive externalities: the bees that pollinate the neighbours

definition.text: A beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it.

facts.text: It is also called an external benefit or external economy, and like a negative one can come from production or consumption.
A beekeeper's bees pollinate the crops around them as a side effect of honey production.
Planting trees makes nearby properties look nicer and cleans the surrounding area.
Even positive externalities are a market failure, because the good ends up produced below the best amount.
They invite free riding: a neighbour enjoying the bees for free has no reason to buy bees himself.

entries.text: A beekeeper keeps bees for honey. As a side effect, the bees pollinate the crops around them. That is a positive externality: a beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it. It is also called an external benefit or external economy, and it can come from production or consumption. Planting trees is another example: it makes nearby properties look nicer and cleans the surrounding area. Surprisingly, even positive externalities are a market failure, because the good ends up produced below the best amount. They invite free riding. A neighbour enjoying the bees for free has no reason to buy bees himself.

entries.title: Environmental valuation: reading nature's worth from behaviour and surveys

definition.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

facts.text: When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in.
Non-use values include existence value, option value and bequest value, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children.
Use values can be read from behaviour, such as the cost of recreational trips or house prices in hedonic methods.
Non-use values are usually estimated with surveys such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.
Contingent valuation asks people what they would pay for an environmental good, or accept for its loss.

entries.text: When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in. Environmental valuation tries to correct this by putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price. Economists split these values in two. One kind comes from using nature, and it can be read from behaviour. The cost of recreational trips is one clue; house prices, in what are called hedonic methods, are another. The other kind comes from nature even when no one uses it. It includes the value of knowing nature exists and of keeping the option to use it later. It also includes the value of passing nature on, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children. These values are usually estimated with surveys. One survey method asks people what they would pay for an environmental benefit, or accept for its loss.

entries.title: Two schools: environmental and ecological economics

definition.text: The contrast between environmental economics, which applies standard economics to the environment, and ecological economics, which treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem.

facts.text: Ecological economists stress 'strong' sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
Most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists.
Ecological economics is described as more pluralistic and more focused on long-term sustainability and scale.
Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system, ecological economics as more realistic about factors outside it.

entries.contested_note: The two schools hold conflicting views traced to different philosophical foundations.
entries.text: Two schools study the same planet and often reach different conclusions. Environmental economics applies standard economics to the environment. The other, ecological economics, treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem. The split starts with training: most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists. Ecological economists stress a "strong" form of sustainability. They reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital. Their field is described as more pluralistic, open to many methods, and more focused on long-term sustainability and the scale of the economy. Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system. The ecological school, by this account, is more realistic about factors outside it. The two schools hold conflicting views that trace back to different philosophical foundations, and the disagreement is unresolved.

entries.title: Ecological market failure: when the economy outruns nature

definition.text: A market failure in which economic activity exhausts vital non-renewable resources, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste.

facts.text: Ecological economists argue that firms routinely shift social and ecological costs onto others, including future generations, so the market cannot exist without 'failing'.
Today's prices cannot reflect the wishes of people not yet born, so finite minerals are not shared fairly over time, an issue called intergenerational fairness.
Renewable resources with poorly defined property rights get overused, as in overfishing and overgrazing: the tragedy of the commons.
Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common with no clear property rights.
'Uneconomic growth' names the case where the ecological costs of more growth exceed its social benefits.
Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity.

entries.contested_note: Ecological economists say most mainstream economists overlook these failures because Pareto efficiency ignores time.
entries.text: Ecological economists make a bolder claim than most: the market cannot exist without "failing". Firms, they argue, routinely shift social and ecological costs onto others, including future generations. An ecological market failure is one in which economic activity exhausts vital resources that cannot be replaced, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste. Today's prices cannot reflect the wishes of people not yet born, so finite minerals are not shared fairly over time, an issue called intergenerational fairness. Resources that renew themselves but that no one clearly owns get overused, as in too much fishing and grazing, a pattern explored in {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common that no one owns. Growth becomes uneconomic when its ecological costs exceed its social benefits, a case explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}. Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity. Ecological economists say most mainstream economists overlook these failures, because the standard test of efficiency ignores time.

Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common that no one owns. Growth becomes uneconomic when its ecological costs exceed its social benefits, a case explored in Uneconomic growth: when getting bigger makes life worse. Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity. entries.title: Government failure: when the fix falls short

definition.text: Economic waste caused by government action, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative.

facts.text: It is the counterpart to market failure: government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short.
It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none.
It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses: simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure.
It can come from any form of intervention: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation.
Common mechanisms include regulatory capture, unintended consequences, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones.
The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s; Ronald Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures.
Public choice economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.
A small, well-organized interest group can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole.

entries.text: Government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short. Government failure is the economic waste that results, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative. It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none. It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses; simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure. Any form of intervention can fail: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation. Common mechanisms include regulators coming to serve the industries they oversee, unintended consequences, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones. A small, well-organized interest group, for instance, can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole. The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s. Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures. Some economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.
entries.text_plain: Government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short. Government failure is the economic waste that results, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative. It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none. It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses; simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure. Any form of intervention can fail: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation. Common mechanisms include regulators coming to serve the industries they oversee, unintended consequences, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones. A small, well-organized interest group, for instance, can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole. The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s. Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures. Some economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.

entries.title: Does market failure even exist

definition.text: Arguments from several schools of thought that the idea of market failure is misleading, too narrow or does not justify government action.

facts.text: Public choice economists such as Milton Friedman argue that government failure may cost more than the market failure it tries to fix.
Some Austrian School economists deny that market failure exists, saying entrepreneurs seeking profit remove inefficiencies.
Marxian economists see inefficient outcomes as built into capitalism, not as rare exceptions.
High inequality is often called a market failure in everyday speech, but mainstream economics does not count it as one because it is not Pareto inefficient.
Zerbe and McCurdy note that, given transaction costs, market failure describes a situation that exists everywhere.

entries.contested_note: Schools of economics disagree about whether market failure exists and whether it justifies government intervention.

Once the costs of making a trade are counted, market failure describes a situation that exists everywhere. The schools still disagree about whether market failure exists and whether it justifies government intervention.

entries.title: Absolute scarcity: Malthus and the limits of food

definition.text: A condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available, linked to the ideas of Thomas Malthus.

facts.text: In his 1798 Essay on the Principle of Population, Malthus argued that more food raises well-being only for a while, because population then grows.
Malthusianism holds that population can grow exponentially while food supply grows only linearly.
Herman Daly describes absolute scarcity as the scarcity of resources in general, which rises as population and consumption approach the biosphere's carrying capacity.
Substituting one resource for another eases absolute scarcity but cannot remove it, according to Daly.

entries.contested_note: Malthus's view on population and food has dominated debate on hunger for two centuries and remains disputed.
entries.text: In 1798 Thomas Malthus published his Essay on the Principle of Population. He argued that more food raises well-being only for a while, because population then grows. This view holds that population can grow exponentially, by multiplying, while food supply grows only linearly, by fixed steps. It is the root of absolute scarcity: a condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available. The economist Herman Daly describes absolute scarcity as the scarcity of resources in general. It rises as population and consumption approach the limit of what the biosphere can support. Substituting one resource for another eases absolute scarcity but cannot remove it, according to Daly. Malthus's view has dominated debate on hunger for two centuries, and it remains disputed.

entries.title: Relative scarcity: the reason economics exists

definition.text: A condition in which many different wants exceed the available means, which can be put to alternative uses, so people must choose.

facts.text: Mainstream economic theory stresses that it is relative scarcity that defines economics.
Lionel Robbins argued that when time and means are limited and ends can be ranked, behaviour necessarily takes the form of choice.
Every use of scarce means for one end gives up their use for another.
Paul Samuelson tied it to economic goods: without scarcity there would be no economic goods at all.

entries.title: Why externalities happen: ownership and the cost of trading

definition.text: The view that externalities come mainly from poorly defined property rights and from the costs of making trades.

facts.text: Land and money are easy to own, but air, water and wild animals cross borders freely, so people use them without paying the full cost.
A person who gets a flu shot cannot own a share of the herd immunity it creates, so may skip it.
Transaction costs, the costs of making a trade, block some worthwhile exchanges; without them people could bargain away every externality.

entries.title: Is environmental harm really an exception

definition.text: The argument from ecological and heterodox economists that treating environmental harm as an occasional 'externality' misreads how the economy works.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp called the term a misnomer, arguing that businesses shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit.
Clive Spash argues that fixing the odd externality leaves the deeper, system-wide problem untouched.
Future generations, not yet born, cannot influence today's prices at all.
Heterodox economists instead argue for a theory of social costs that prevents harm through the precautionary principle.

entries.contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that internalizing externalities can correct environmental harm.

These critics argue instead for a theory of social costs that prevents harm through precaution, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-pol-201}}. They dispute the mainstream view that pricing in externalities can correct environmental harm.

entries.title: Inframarginal externalities: side effects that change nothing

definition.text: An externality that does not affect the marginal consumer, so it causes no market inefficiency.

facts.text: James Buchanan and Craig Stubblebine introduced the idea in 1962.
Because it acts only away from where the market clears, it does not misallocate resources and needs no policy action.

entries.text: Not every side effect distorts a market. An inframarginal externality is one that does not affect the marginal consumer, the buyer on the edge of deciding whether to buy at all. It causes no market inefficiency and needs no policy action.

entries.title: Positional externalities: keeping up with the neighbours

definition.text: A side effect in which one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own.

facts.text: It grows from the ideas of conspicuous consumption, buying to show off status, and positional goods, whose value depends on comparison with what others own.
When one member of a group buys a luxury car, others may feel they must upgrade too, wasting resources and widening inequality.
It can trigger a cascade of overconsumption as people spend to keep their relative standing.

entries.text: When one member of a group buys a luxury car, the others may feel they must upgrade too. That pressure is a positional externality. Positional goods are things whose value depends on comparison with what others own. The result can be a cascade of buying more than anyone needs, as people spend to keep their relative standing, wasting resources and widening inequality.

entries.title: Marginal social cost: the true cost of one more unit

definition.text: The total cost to society of producing one more unit of a good: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.

facts.text: With a negative production externality such as steel pollution, marginal social cost is greater than marginal private cost.
Firms in a free market produce where marginal private cost meets marginal benefit, so they overproduce, creating a deadweight loss.
A tax equal to marginal damage raises private cost to match social cost.
With a positive externality, such as research and development, there is underproduction, which a Pigouvian subsidy can correct.
It is written MSC = MPC + MEC: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.
Marginal private cost is the cost borne by the firm itself, and it is what businesses use when deciding how much to produce.
When marginal social cost exceeds private cost there is a negative externality; when it is lower, a positive one.
Production should rise only as long as the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.

definition.text: Government payments that reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them.

facts.text: The damage these subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year.
The largest support the fossil fuel, agriculture and water sectors.

entries.title: The $7.3 trillion that industry never pays

definition.text: The value of nature that industries use up without paying for it, which would change their profits if it were priced.

entries.title: Failure of competition: when one firm holds the cards

definition.text: A market failure in which a firm or small group gains enough market power to block trades that would benefit both sides.

facts.text: It takes forms such as monopoly, monopsony and monopolistic competition.
Monopolies can last where barriers to entry keep other firms out.
Natural monopoly, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, is an extreme case.

entries.text: In a failure of market rivalry ({{ref:nature-econ-363}}), a firm or small group gains enough power over a market to block trades that would benefit both sides. This kind of market failure takes several forms: a market with a single seller, one with a single buyer, and markets where sellers compete with slightly different products. Such power can last where barriers to entry keep other firms out. An extreme case is a natural sole-seller market, a form of what {{ref:nature-econ-349}} describes, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, the cost advantages that come with sheer size.

entries.title: Unemployment and inflation as market failures

definition.text: Unemployment, inflation and disequilibrium seen as market failures at the level of the whole economy.

facts.text: They can follow a financial crash, recession or depression, and show up as an economy producing below its capacity for a long time.
Business cycles of downswings and upswings are said to call for some government intervention.

entries.title: Unequal bargaining power: when one side can wait longer

definition.text: A market failure in which one side of a deal, such as an employer, can hold out longer than the other and so sets the terms.

facts.text: It has been used since the early 20th century to justify rules protecting workers, consumers and tenants.
Coase argued it only shifts income, but behavioural evidence shows unfair exchange lowers motivation to work, making it a real market failure.

entries.title: Three kinds of scarcity, and which ones cause conflict

definition.text: The division of scarcity into demand-induced, supply-induced and structural kinds.

facts.text: Demand-induced scarcity comes when demand for a resource rises while supply stays the same.
Supply-induced scarcity, mostly caused by environmental degradation such as deforestation and drought, comes when supply is very low compared with demand.
Structural scarcity arises when part of a population lacks equal access to resources because of political conflict or location.
Supply-induced and structural scarcity cause the most conflict within a country.

entries.title: Kapp's charge: capitalism as cost shifting

definition.text: K. William Kapp's heterodox view that social costs are the share of production costs businesses shift onto society to raise profits.

facts.text: Kapp blames capitalist accounting laws that let producers leave these costs unpaid.
On this view capitalism is essentially a system of cost shifting, and legal cost shifting is a main source of profit.

entries.title: Why social costs are so hard to count

definition.text: The difficulty of putting numbers on social costs, especially future, environmental and long-range harms.

facts.text: Environmental, social and political harms that span long periods are hard to predict and quantify, so hard to include in cost–benefit analysis.
Pricing carbon requires tracing a ton of greenhouse gas through temperature to crops, health, floods and ecosystems.
Costs from one firm in China can affect people's health in the United States, adding to the complexity.

entries.title: Pecuniary externalities: side effects that work through prices

definition.text: A side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others.

facts.text: City-dwellers buying second homes in the countryside can push up house prices for local young people.
It contrasts with technological or real externalities, such as factory pollution, which harm others directly.
In complete markets, buyers' losses from a price rise exactly match sellers' gains, so efficiency is kept; some economists say these are not really externalities.
When markets are incomplete or people face borrowing limits, they can matter for efficiency, which helps justify macroprudential regulation.

entries.title: The tyranny of small decisions: how marshes vanish plot by plot

definition.text: The way many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted.

facts.text: Economist Alfred E. Kahn introduced the idea in a 1966 essay and described it as a common route to market failure.
Kahn's example was Ithaca's passenger railway, withdrawn because travellers' trip-by-trip choices did not cover its costs, though many would have paid to keep it.
Each choice of one option over another is also a vote to remove the other option, which may then disappear.

In 1982 ecologist William Odum applied it to the environment: almost 50 percent of the coastal marshlands of Connecticut and Massachusetts were lost between 1950 and 1970 through hundreds of small conversions.
Lake eutrophication, desertification and the plight of most endangered species are said to stem from series of small decisions.
A way to avoid it is to build and protect higher levels of decision-making, local to global, though these can push decisions back down.

entries.title: Why government fixes go wrong

definition.text: The main reasons government interventions go wrong, such as missing information, political pressure and short-term thinking.

facts.text: Governments find it hard to learn things such as production costs, so they may set quantities too high or too low.
Special interest groups can push politicians toward short-term gains.
Critics say politicians favour quick, visible fixes over lasting long-term solutions, called policy myopia.
Regulators who meet industry representatives often grow sympathetic and write rules that favour producers over society.

Politics is another. Special interest groups can push politicians toward short-term gains. Critics say politicians favour quick, visible fixes over lasting long-term solutions, a political form of short-termism called policy myopia. entries.title: How taxes, subsidies and price controls bend markets

definition.text: The way taxes, subsidies and price controls can change prices artificially and disturb how markets share out scarce resources.

facts.text: Subsidies can waste scarce resources by shielding inefficient firms from market forces.
A price floor set above the market price, such as a minimum wage, can cause unemployment; a price ceiling set below it, such as rent control, causes shortages.
Taxes give people a reason to evade them.

entries.title: Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill

definition.text: The release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm.

facts.text: It can be any substance, solid, liquid or gas, or energy such as heat, sound, light or radioactivity.
The word usually means contaminants from human sources such as manufacturing, mining, poor waste management, transport or farming.
It is classed as point source, from one concentrated site such as a factory, or nonpoint source, from widespread sources such as farm runoff.
In 2019 pollution killed about nine million people, about one in six deaths, roughly three-quarters of them from air pollution.
Polluting industries and waste sites are often placed near vulnerable and marginalized communities, a core reason for the environmental justice movement.
Economists treat pollution from manufacturing as a negative production externality, imposing health and clean-up costs on all of society.
Goods that pollute tend to be overproduced and underpriced because the harm is not priced into the market.
Many pollution sources went unregulated during industrialization until environmental regulation emerged in the later 20th century.

entries.title: Pollutants: when a substance becomes a problem

definition.text: A substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful.

facts.text: Pollutants may occur naturally, such as oil, or be made by people, such as manufactured materials and by-products.
They become pollution or a health concern once their concentration is high enough to do significant harm.
They can damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values.
Some break down naturally, but the breakdown products of others, such as DDT, are themselves pollutants.
Seen through planetary boundaries, people have released novel entities well beyond safe levels.
Because pollutants cross borders, international rules such as the 2004 Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants are needed.

entries.text: Oil occurs naturally, yet it can still be a pollutant. A pollutant is a substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful. A pollutant becomes pollution, or a health concern, once its concentration is high enough to do significant harm. It can then damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values. Some pollutants break down naturally. Others, such as the insecticide DDT, break down into products that are themselves pollutants. Measured against the planet's safe limits, mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}, people have released novel entities, new kinds of substance, well beyond safe levels. Because pollutants cross borders, international rules are needed, such as the 2004 Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants.

entries.title: Air pollution: 7 to 8 million deaths a year

definition.text: The presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment.

facts.text: Pollutants may be gases such as ozone or nitrogen oxides, or small particles such as soot and dust, both outdoors and indoors.

Outdoor air pollution comes from burning fossil fuels for power and transport, wildfires, industry, waste, demolition and farming; indoor pollution often comes from burning wood or crop waste for cooking and heating.
It kills 7 to 8 million people each year, and particulate matter is its deadliest form.
The World Bank estimates its welfare and productivity losses cost the world economy over $8 trillion per year.
Many sources of local air pollution, especially fossil fuels, also release the greenhouse gases that cause global warming.
National laws such as Britain's 1956 Clean Air Act and the 1963 US Clean Air Act have often worked.
It is a standard example of an externality: neither makers nor users of cars pay its cost to society.

entries.title: Noise pollution: a hazard as old as ancient Rome

definition.text: Sound that can harm the health of people and animals.

facts.text: Machines and transport are the main sources of outdoor noise worldwide.
Poor urban planning, such as industrial zones next to homes, can cause noise pollution in residential areas.
In the United States, noise is highest in low-income and racial minority neighbourhoods.
In animals, noise can raise the risk of death by disrupting how they detect predators or prey, and can interfere with breeding and navigation.
A neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a textbook negative consumption externality.
Problems with urban noise are recorded as far back as ancient Rome.

entries.title: The economic bill for dirty air

definition.text: The losses air pollution causes to economies through ill health, lost work, lower crop yields and other damage.

facts.text: It also harms tourism, biodiversity, forestry and water quality.
A World Bank study found PM2.5 pollution in 2019 cost the world economy over $8 trillion in health welfare costs; in India and China the loss was over 10% of GDP.
About 85% of that loss came from lives lost, priced using the value of a statistical life.
The OECD expects direct market costs from lost productivity, healthcare and crop losses to rise to 1% of GDP by 2060.
It even cuts solar power, by blocking sunlight and dirtying panels.

entries.title: Air pollution and the body: 8.1 million deaths in a year

definition.text: The diseases and early deaths caused by breathing polluted air.

facts.text: It raises the risk of COPD, stroke, heart disease, lung cancer and pneumonia.
The 2024 Global Burden of Disease Study estimates it contributed to 8.1 million deaths in 2021, more than 1 in 8 deaths.
Outdoor fine particulate pollution caused the most of these deaths (4.7 million), followed by indoor particulate pollution (3.1 million) and ozone (0.5 million).
Burning fossil fuels is the largest source of air pollution deaths.
Global average life expectancy loss from air pollution in 2015 was 2.9 years, against 0.3 years from all direct violence.
Exposure in pregnancy makes stillbirth, miscarriage, birth defects and low birth weight more likely.

entries.title: Particulate pollution: no known safe dose

definition.text: Pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space.

facts.text: Its three main forms are atmospheric particulate matter, marine debris and space debris.
Some particles are released directly and others form by chemical reactions in the air, from natural or human sources.
Sources include farming, cars, construction, forest fires and power plants.
There is no known safe level of exposure.
About 4.2 million premature deaths in 2016 were due to airborne particulate pollution, 91% of them in low and middle income countries.
US annual PM2.5 averages fell from 13.5 μg/m3 to 8.02 μg/m3 between 2000 and 2017 after tighter standards.

entries.text: There is no known safe level of exposure to particulate pollution: pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space. entries.title: Stock and fund pollutants: what builds up and what fades
entries.article: Pollutant#Different types of pollutants in the environment

definition.text: The division of pollutants by how well the environment can absorb them: stock pollutants build up, fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough.

facts.text: A pollutant only causes pollution once the environment's assimilative, or absorptive, capacity is exceeded.
Stock pollutants, such as PCBs, non-biodegradable plastics and heavy metals, accumulate over time, so damage grows and persists.
Stock pollutants burden future generations, with damage lasting long after the benefits are forgotten.
Fund pollutants, such as carbon dioxide absorbed by plants and oceans, cause harm only when emissions outpace absorption.
Fund pollutants are converted into less harmful substances or diluted, not destroyed.

entries.text: Some pollution fades if emissions stay low enough, while some keeps piling up. A pollutant only causes pollution once the environment's assimilative, or absorptive, capacity is exceeded. That idea splits pollutants into two kinds. They burden future generations, with harm lasting long after the benefits are forgotten. Fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough. Carbon dioxide, taken up by plants and oceans, is one example. Fund pollutants cause harm only when emissions outpace absorption. Even then they are not destroyed, but converted into less harmful substances or diluted.

entries.title: From ancient metalworking to London's Great Stink

definition.text: How pollution grew from prehistoric fires to the industrial age and how societies began to respond.

facts.text: Greenland ice cores show pollution rising with Greek, Roman and Chinese metal production.
The Industrial Revolution created pollution as we know it today.
London's Great Stink on the Thames in 1858 led to the building of its sewer system.
Chicago and Cincinnati were the first American cities to pass clean air laws, in 1881.

entries.title: Pollution control: better to prevent than to clean up

definition.text: The management of emissions and effluents released into air, water or soil.

facts.text: Without it, waste from farming, mining, manufacturing, transport and other activities would degrade the environment.
In the hierarchy of controls, preventing pollution and minimizing waste are preferred to controlling it afterwards.
Devices include wastewater biotreaters and constructed wetlands.

entries.text: Without pollution control, waste from farming, mining, manufacturing, transport and other activities would degrade the environment. Pollution control is the management of waste gases, liquids and other emissions released into air, water or soil. Its hierarchy of controls ranks the options. Preventing pollution and minimizing waste are preferred to controlling pollution afterwards. Devices include wastewater biotreaters, which use living organisms to clean water, and constructed wetlands.

entries.title: What it costs to cut pollution

definition.text: What it costs a firm to cut the pollution it produces, called marginal abatement cost when measured per extra unit cut.

facts.text: Firms cut pollution by choice or because regulation forces them to.
In 2005 US pollution abatement capital and operating costs came to nearly $27 billion.

Firms cut pollution by choice, or because regulation forces them to.

entries.title: Why the best amount of pollution is not zero

definition.text: The amount of pollution at which society's welfare is greatest, where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it.

facts.text: Society gets some indirect benefit from pollution, through polluting goods and lower prices; otherwise no one would pollute.
Policymakers must balance those benefits against pollution's costs to reach an efficient outcome.
Because the free market ignores pollution's cost to society, the true supply curve sits higher than the market one.
At the social optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure.
The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as tariffs, Pigouvian taxes like a carbon tax, and cap and trade.
It lies where the social marginal cost curve meets market demand.
Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.
A corrective tax proportional to marginal damages yields the efficient level of pollution reduction.

entries.text: Society gets something from pollution: the polluting goods themselves, and lower prices. Otherwise no one would pollute. So the aim is not zero pollution but the socially optimal level, the amount at which society's welfare is greatest. That is where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it. The free market misses this point, because it ignores pollution's cost to society. The true supply curve sits higher than the market one, and the optimum lies where the curve of marginal social cost meets market demand. At that optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure. A corrective tax proportional to the damage of each extra unit yields the efficient level of pollution reduction. The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as tariffs, taxes on the damage like a carbon levy, and cap and trade. Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.

entries.title: Air pollution laws: gaps around the world

definition.text: Laws that set limits on pollutant concentrations in the air or on emissions from sources such as vehicles.

facts.text: 43% of countries lack a legal definition of air pollution, 34% lack outdoor air quality standards, and just 31% have laws on pollution from beyond their borders.
Few countries set limits as strict as the World Health Organization's recommendations, which are guidance rather than binding rules.
The Montreal Protocol, ratified worldwide, succeeded internationally, while climate action has been less successful.

entries.title: From black smoke as prosperity to cleaner air
entries.article: Air pollution#Anti-smoke action and modern protections

definition.text: The story of how societies came to regulate air pollution, from early anti-smoke groups to international treaties.

facts.text: During the Industrial Revolution coal burning raised outdoor pollution sharply, yet city leaders saw black smoke as a sign of prosperity.
Early laws against pollution were weak because they were seen to clash with industrial interests.
The 1952 Great Smog of London killed some 12,000 people and led to the Clean Air Act 1956.
Acid rain spread across borders and needed international cooperation; ozone-damaging chemicals were later phased out by negotiation.

entries.title: Primary and secondary pollutants: emitted or made in the air

definition.text: The division of air pollutants into those released directly by a source and those that form in the air from other pollutants.

facts.text: Carbon monoxide from car exhausts and sulfur dioxide from factories are primary pollutants.
Secondary pollutants form when primary pollutants react with each other or the atmosphere; ground-level ozone is one.
Some pollutants are both emitted directly and formed from others.

Secondary pollutants form in the air, when primary pollutants react with each other or with the atmosphere. Ozone near the ground is one. Some pollutants are both, emitted directly and also formed from others.

entries.title: Ground-level ozone: the smog of hot afternoons

definition.text: Ozone near the ground, formed mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

facts.text: It is the main gas in photochemical smog and peaks on hot summer afternoons.
It harms human health, materials, forests and crops, and reduces photosynthesis.
One study estimated that a 1% rise in ozone concentrations would cause a global economic loss of $10 billion each year.

entries.title: Who breathes the dirtiest air

definition.text: The pattern in which poorer groups and some racial groups breathe more polluted air than others.

facts.text: Polluting industries and roads are more often placed in poorer communities, whose residents also more often work outdoors.
Low-income public housing residents who cannot easily move are heavily affected by nearby refineries and chemical plants.

facts.text: It is linked to heart and circulation problems, high blood pressure, stress, tinnitus, hearing loss and disturbed sleep.

Occupational hearing loss is one of the most common work-related illnesses in the US and worldwide.

entries.title: Measuring noise in decibels

definition.text: Quantifying noise exposure as sound pressure levels in decibels, a logarithmic scale linked to how people hear.

facts.text: Road traffic and construction typically range from about 70 to over 100 dB, and repeated exposure above about 85 dB raises the risk of hearing damage.
Long-term community exposure is described with averaged measures such as the equivalent continuous sound level and the day–night average sound level.
Noise is measured with sound level meters, or with dosimeters worn by workers through a shift.

entries.title: Noise control: from nuisance to national policy

definition.text: The rules and methods governments and communities use to limit harmful noise exposure.

facts.text: Building codes and local ordinances may set maximum noise levels for homes, businesses and industry.
Noise barriers, speed limits, road surfaces and better planning reduce road noise.
Until the 1970s governments tended to treat noise as a nuisance rather than an environmental problem, and many disputes are still settled by negotiation between the noise maker and the hearer.
The US Noise Control Act of 1972 set a national policy against noise that endangers health and welfare.

definition.text: The ways human-made noise disrupts animals that rely on sound to communicate, find mates, navigate and avoid predators.

Marine noise affects at least 55 marine species, and human-made ocean noise is doubling every decade.
Whales have changed migration routes and calls to avoid human-made noise.
Noise is now a prominent stressor on coral reefs, which communities depend on for fishing and tourism.

entries.title: PM10 and PM2.5: sizing up deadly dust

entries.title: Utility: the economist's yardstick for satisfaction

definition.text: In economics, utility is a measure of how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world.

facts.text: Normatively, utility is a goal to maximise, close to the utilitarian idea of Bentham and Mill; descriptively, it is what people's choices reveal they are pursuing.
A utility function gives each option a number so that preferred options always get higher numbers.
Because utility cannot be observed directly, economists infer it from choices, for example from willingness to pay; Paul Samuelson called these revealed preferences.
Economists separate total utility, the utility of a whole bundle, from marginal utility, the change from one more unit of a good.
Indifference curves plot combinations of goods that give the same satisfaction, and combined with a budget constraint they yield demand curves.
Joan Robinson called utility circular: goods have utility because people want them, and people wanting them shows they have utility.

entries.contested_note: Economists and ethicists disagree about how the normative and descriptive meanings of utility relate, and critics such as Joan Robinson call the concept circular.
entries.text: Nobody can see satisfaction, yet much of economics is built on measuring it. Utility is the economist's word for how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world. The idea carries two meanings at once. Normatively, it is a goal to maximize, close to the utilitarian thinking of Bentham and Mill. Descriptively, it is whatever people's choices reveal they are pursuing. A utility function makes this precise by giving each option a number, so that preferred options always score higher. Because utility cannot be observed directly, economists infer it from behavior, for example from how much someone is willing to pay. Paul Samuelson gave these inferred rankings a name, taken up in {{ref:nature-val-094}}. Economists also separate total utility, the satisfaction from a whole bundle of things, from the change that one more unit brings, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-091}}. Maps of equal satisfaction, combined with a spending limit, let economists work out how much people buy at each price. Not everyone is convinced. Joan Robinson called the concept circular: things have utility because people want them, and people wanting them is taken as proof they have utility. Economists and ethicists still disagree about how the normative and descriptive meanings fit together.

entries.title: Goods: anything that gives satisfaction

definition.text: In economics, goods are things that give someone welfare or satisfaction.

facts.text: Economics studies economic goods, which are scarce because making them takes effort or resources, unlike free goods such as air.
The Earth's atmosphere and seawater are useful but not scarce enough to have a money value.
Final goods are consumed, while intermediate goods, like transistors, are used to make other goods.
Durable goods used to produce further goods, such as machinery, human skills or ecosystems, are capital goods.
Goods are commonly assumed to have diminishing marginal utility.
An elastic good has close substitutes, so a small price change moves demand a lot; an inelastic good, like insulin, has few or none.

entries.title: Microeconomics: how people and firms choose

definition.text: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how they interact.

facts.text: It studies individual markets, sectors and industries, while macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as growth, inflation and unemployment.
One goal is to explain how markets set relative prices and share out limited resources among different uses.
It shows when free markets lead to desirable outcomes and also analyses market failure, when markets fail to produce efficient outcomes.
Its theory usually starts from a single rational individual trying to maximize utility, where rational means having stable, complete and consistent preferences.
It is also called price theory, because prices, set by the actions of buyers and sellers, are central to it.
The micro–macro distinction was likely introduced in 1933 by Ragnar Frisch; the word 'microeconomics' first appeared in print in 1941, from Pieter de Wolff.

entries.text: Economics can be studied one decision at a time. Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how their choices interact. It looks at single markets, sectors and industries, while its counterpart, {{ref:nature-econ-541}}, studies the economy as a whole: growth, inflation and unemployment. One goal is to explain how markets set relative prices and share limited resources among competing uses. It shows when markets left to themselves produce desirable outcomes. It also analyzes market failure, when markets fail to deliver efficient results. Its theory usually starts from one rational individual trying to get as much utility as possible. Ragnar Frisch likely introduced the split between micro and macro in 1933. The word "microeconomics" first appeared in print in 1941, from Pieter de Wolff.

entries.title: Economic value: what something is worth to someone

definition.text: Economic value is a measure of the benefit a good or service gives to a person, firm or other economic agent.

facts.text: It is usually measured in money, as the most a person is willing and able to pay for a good or service.
Value is how much of one wanted thing a person would give up to get another.
Early economists split value into value in use and value in exchange; value links to price through exchange.
Rival schools hold different theories of value: the labour theory ties it to labour needed for production, while the subjective theory ties it to buyers' marginal utility.
Many neoclassical theories equate value with market price, so something with no market to set a price has no economic value.
Biodiversity is increasingly seen as having economic value because of ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, flood defence and pollination.

entries.contested_note: Different schools of economics disagree about what determines value, and value theories are a major source of their disagreements.
entries.text: Clean air, pollination and flood defense have never carried price tags, yet economists increasingly say they have economic value. Economic value measures the benefit a good or service gives a person, firm or other economic agent. It is usually counted in money, as the most a person is willing and able to pay. That is why biodiversity's growing economic standing rests on ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, flood defense and pollination.

entries.title: Incentives: what moves people to act

definition.text: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organisation to change their behaviour toward a desired outcome.

facts.text: Disincentives work the other way, discouraging certain actions.
Governments, businesses and other organisations commonly use incentives to encourage particular behaviour.
Incentives are often split into intrinsic ones, driven by personal interest or enjoyment, and extrinsic ones, such as pay, recognition or the threat of punishment.
One scheme sorts incentives into financial (material rewards), moral (doing what is seen as right) and coercive (threat of force).
A misaligned incentive arises when parties' goals conflict, which happens in firms and also in environmental policy.
Incentives can produce unintended outcomes.
A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 experiments found that financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

entries.title: Ceteris paribus: holding everything else still

definition.text: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'other things being equal', used to study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same.

facts.text: A standard example: if the price of milk falls, ceteris paribus, people will buy more milk.
The clause does not claim nothing else changes; it isolates the effect of one change.
Alfred Marshall popularised it in the 19th century, describing it as a 'pound' where disturbing causes are set aside for a time.
Because economic variables can only be isolated in theory, ceteris paribus can only reveal tendencies, not absolutes.
Marshall warned that the narrower the question, the less closely it matches real life, as in assuming hydrocarbon fuels are infinite.
In highly interconnected systems, changing one variable changes all the others, so holding everything else constant is not possible in reality.

entries.title: Economic models: simple maps of a messy economy

definition.text: An economic model is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them.

facts.text: Simplifying matters because economies are shaped by many things at once, including decisions, resource limits, environmental and geographical constraints, laws and chance.
Models are used to forecast economic activity, propose and justify policy, and plan in firms and centrally planned economies.
Some models only predict the direction of change, such as demand falling when a price rises, and are often drawn as two-dimensional graphs.
Most models rest on unrealistic assumptions, such as perfect information or frictionless markets, and may leave out important issues such as externalities.
In the late 1980s the Brookings Institution compared 12 leading macroeconomic models and found they gave significantly different answers to the same shocks.
Like weather forecasts, economic forecasts fail because models cannot capture full detail and are sensitive to small changes in their equations.

entries.title: Preferences: how people rank their options

definition.text: In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted.

facts.text: Preferences come from taste and need, as opposed to price, availability or income.
Transitivity, preferring A to C whenever one prefers A to B and B to C, is a basic principle shared by most models of decision-making.
A preference order that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents.
Real preferences are not always transitive, because people are not always rational and preferences can form cycles with no best choice.
Most economic models assume stable preferences, an assumption long disputed outside neoclassical economics.
Preferences can change through new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices.
In 1926 Ragnar Frisch first built a mathematical model of preferences for demand and utility theory.

entries.text: Taste and need, not price, availability or income, decide what a person wants most. In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted. Most models of decision-making share one basic principle, transitivity: anyone who prefers A to B and B to C should prefer A to C. An ordering that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents. Real people do not always behave this way. Their preferences can form cycles with no best choice. Most economic models assume preferences stay stable, an assumption long disputed outside the school described in {{ref:nature-hist-023}}. In fact preferences shift with new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices. Ragnar Frisch built the first mathematical model of preferences for demand and utility theory in 1926.
entries.text_plain: Taste and need, not price, availability or income, decide what a person wants most. entries.title: Indifference curves: mapping equal satisfaction

definition.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining all the combinations of two goods that a consumer likes equally well.

facts.text: A set of indifference curves for one person is an indifference map, read like contour lines: curves further out mean more satisfaction.
The slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution, the rate at which a consumer will give up one good for more of the other.
Curves are usually bowed toward the origin, and their downward slope expresses a willingness to make trade-offs.
The best affordable choice is where an indifference curve touches the budget line; varying the price traces out a demand curve.
Edgeworth set out the mathematics in 1881, Pareto first drew the curves in 1906, and Hicks and Allen popularised them in the 1930s.
Hovenkamp argued that the endowment effect means people have no indifference curve, so courts should use willingness to accept as the measure of value.

entries.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining every combination of two goods that a consumer likes equally well. A set of these curves for one person is an indifference map, read like contour lines: curves further out mean more satisfaction. Their downward slope expresses a willingness to give up some of one good for more of the other. They usually bow in toward the origin, the corner of the graph where both amounts are zero. The slope at any point is the rate at which the consumer will make that swap (see {{ref:nature-econ-129}}). The best affordable choice lies where an indifference curve just touches the line of what the consumer can afford. Edgeworth set out the mathematics in 1881, Pareto first drew the curves in 1906, and Hicks and Allen popularized them in the 1930s. Not everyone accepts them. Hovenkamp argued that people value what they own more than what they could buy, so they have no indifference curve at all. Courts, he said, should ask what people would accept to give something up.

entries.title: Complementary goods: things that go together

definition.text: Complementary goods are goods used together, so that one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular.

facts.text: Demand for a complement rises when the price of the other good falls, giving a negative cross elasticity of demand.
Cars and petrol, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are examples.
Razors have been sold cheaply as loss leaders to raise demand for the blades.
A perfect complement must be consumed with the other good, like left and right shoes; its indifference curve forms a right angle.
Complementarity need not be mutual: a game needs a console, but a console does not need that game.

Cars and gasoline, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are everyday pairs. When the price of one falls, people want more of its partner, a link measured by {{ref:nature-econ-368}}, which is negative for such pairs. A perfect complement must be used with its partner, like left and right shoes, and its indifference curve forms a right angle. The bond need not run both ways. A game needs a console, but a console does not need that particular game.

entries.title: Ordinal utility: ranking without measuring

definition.text: Ordinal utility ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much.

facts.text: If George prefers A to B and B to C, any numbers that keep that order describe his preferences equally well; the numbers themselves mean nothing.
All of the theory of consumer choice under certainty can be, and usually is, written in terms of ordinal utility.
Cardinal utility differs by treating the size of the differences between options as meaningful too.
Vilfredo Pareto first introduced the ordinal utility concept in 1906.
Preferences can be drawn as indifference curves; curves further from the origin mean higher utility.
For a utility function to exist, preferences must be complete (any two options can be compared) and transitive (if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C).

entries.text: If George prefers A to B and B to C, any set of numbers that keeps that order describes his preferences equally well. The numbers themselves mean nothing. The alternative, {{ref:nature-econ-101}}, treats the size of the gaps between options as meaningful too. Vilfredo Pareto introduced the ordinal concept in 1906. It turned out to be enough. For a utility function to exist at all, preferences must be complete, so that any two options can be compared. They must also be transitive: if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C.
