entries.title: The income effect: richer or poorer, you buy differently

definition.text: The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes.

facts.text: With prices fixed, a change in income shifts the budget line in parallel: outward when income rises, inward when it falls.
A good bought more as income rises is a normal good; one bought less is an inferior good.
Together with the substitution effect, it makes up the full effect of a price change.
When a good gets cheaper, purchasing power rises, so the consumer can buy more of it or of other goods, depending on whether it is a normal or an inferior good.

entries.text: When a good gets cheaper, its buyers become a little richer. The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes. With prices fixed, a change in income shifts the budget line in parallel: outward when income rises, inward when it falls. People buy more of a normal good as income rises and less of an inferior good. So a price cut lets the consumer buy more of that good or of others, depending on which kind it is. Together with the substitution effect, the income effect makes up the full effect of a price change.

entries.title: Giffen goods: when a higher price means buying more

definition.text: A Giffen good is a rare kind of inferior good that people buy more of when its price rises, breaking the usual law of demand.

facts.text: It must take up so much of a person's spending that a price rise makes them poorer and pushes them to buy even more of it.
The idea is named after Sir Robert Giffen and usually linked to rising potato prices in 19th-century Ireland.
Potatoes were not in fact Giffen goods during the Great Famine in Ireland, and Marshall explained the paradox using bread.
Potatoes in the Irish Great Famine are a classic example: as their price rose, people cut back on meat and vegetables and bought more potatoes.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree on whether Giffen goods exist in real markets.

entries.title: The Slutsky equation: splitting a price change in two

definition.text: The Slutsky equation splits the change in demand caused by a price change into a substitution effect and an income effect.

facts.text: It links ordinary (Marshallian) demand to compensated (Hicksian) demand, which holds the consumer's utility fixed.
The substitution effect is always negative because indifference curves slope downward; the sign of the income effect depends on the good.
Since utility cannot be observed, the substitution effect cannot be seen directly but can be calculated from the two observable terms.
It explains why the law of demand fails for Giffen goods, where a strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

entries.title: Markets: where buyers meet sellers

definition.text: Any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information.

facts.text: An exchange of goods or services, with or without money, is called a transaction.
Markets let tradeable things be valued and priced, which is how they spread resources around a society.
Economists see a market as a coordinating mechanism that uses prices to pass information among firms, households and individuals; using prices this way is its defining feature.
A market can arise more or less on its own or be built on purpose, and most rely on sellers swapping goods or labour for buyers' money rather than barter.
Markets range from one building's food market to a city's housing market, a whole country, or worldwide trades such as diamonds.
Some markets are created by regulation to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits.
When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too.
Prices can be distorted by a seller with monopoly power or a buyer with monopsony power, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

Some markets are even created by regulation to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits. Markets can also go wrong. When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too. A seller or buyer with the power to sway prices ({{ref:nature-econ-397}}) can distort them, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

entries.title: Price: where buyers and sellers agree

definition.text: The amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service and that sellers are willing to accept.

facts.text: Prices are shaped by production costs, by supply and by demand, and may be set by a monopolist or imposed by market conditions.
Price theory says that in a free market the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.
Milton Friedman named five functions of prices, including passing on information, giving incentives to produce what is valued, and rationing fixed supplies among consumers.
Price is what the buyer pays; cost of production is the seller's own spending on making the product, and the two are different things.
Adam Smith's diamond–water paradox asks why diamonds cost more than water, though water is essential to life and diamonds are mere ornament.
Carl Menger's theory of marginal utility was offered as one answer to that paradox.
In April 2020 the price of West Texas Intermediate crude for May delivery turned negative for the first time, at -$37.63 a barrel.

entries.title: Willingness to pay: the most you would hand over

definition.text: The highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something.

facts.text: It matches the standard economic idea of a consumer's reservation price, though some researchers treat it as a range.
It depends on context: people will pay more for a soft drink at a luxury resort than at a beach bar or a local shop.
Jules Dupuit argued that adding up each user's willingness to pay measures the social benefit of a bridge, road or canal.
Cost–benefit analysis turns hard-to-price impacts into money using willingness to pay, though these are often hard to estimate.
Stated-preference methods such as contingent valuation ask people directly what they would pay for an ecosystem or one of its services.
The value of a statistical life tries to estimate how much people would pay to lower their risk of dying, and is used to cost deaths from air pollution.
People's maximum willingness to pay for an object is typically lower than the least they would accept to give it up once they own it.

entries.text: People will pay more for the same soft drink at a luxury resort than at a beach bar or a local shop. Willingness to pay is the highest price at which a person will definitely buy one unit of something, and as the soft drink shows, it depends on context. It matches the standard economic idea of a consumer's reservation price, though some researchers treat it as a range. The idea has a long public history. Jules Dupuit argued that a bridge, road or canal is worth the sum of what its users would pay. Adding up their willingness to pay, he said, measures its social benefit. Today, {{ref:nature-val-001}} does the same, turning hard-to-price impacts into money, though the amounts are often hard to estimate. For nature, survey methods such as {{ref:nature-val-085}} simply ask people what they would pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. A related measure, {{ref:nature-val-019}}, estimates how much people would pay to lower their risk of dying, and is used to cost deaths from air pollution. One wrinkle runs through all of this. People's maximum willingness to pay for an object is typically lower than the least they would accept to give it up once they own it.

entries.title: Demand: wanting something and being able to pay

definition.text: The quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period.

facts.text: Demand is not the same as desire: it means both wanting something and being able to pay for it.
It is a flow, measured per unit of time, not a single purchase.
The most important influence is the good's own price: normally, the lower the price, the more people buy.
Demand also depends on the prices of complements and substitutes, income, tastes, expectations, population size, climate and government policy.
If consumers expect a price rise, they buy more now to avoid paying more later.
Goods with no substitutes, such as insulin, have nearly perfectly inelastic demand: price barely changes how much is bought.
E. F. Schumacher challenged the assumption that meeting demand is the purpose of economic activity, distinguishing wise demands for genuine needs from unwise ones.

entries.title: Supply: what sellers will offer

definition.text: The amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale.

facts.text: Supply is usually drawn as a supply curve, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, for one seller or the whole market.
Supply depends on the good's own price, the prices of related goods, production costs, technology and sellers' expectations.
A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve; a change in anything else shifts the whole curve, as when a costlier ingredient shifts it left.
A firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve above the point where it would shut down.
The market supply curve adds up the quantities all firms would supply at each price.
A supply curve exists only under perfect competition; a monopoly has none, because it picks price and quantity together.
Where there are no externalities, the supply curve shows the social cost of each extra unit.

entries.text: Farmers, factories and workers looking for jobs all answer the same question: how much will they offer at a given price? Supply is the amount of something that producers, workers or other sellers are willing and able to offer for sale. It is usually drawn as a supply curve, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, for one seller or a whole market. Supply depends on the good's own price, the prices of related goods, production costs, technology and sellers' expectations. These work in two different ways. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the curve. A change in anything else shifts the whole curve, as when a costlier ingredient shifts it left. Behind the curve sits cost. A firm's short-run supply curve traces its extra cost per unit ({{ref:nature-econ-347}}) above the point where it would shut down. The market supply curve adds up what all firms would supply at each price. Where there are no externalities, the curve shows the social cost of each extra unit. It has limits, too. A supply curve exists only under {{ref:nature-econ-353}}. A lone seller has none, because it picks price and quantity together.

entries.title: Supply and demand: the model behind prices

definition.text: The basic economic model of how a market sets prices: the price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

facts.text: The idea of supply and demand is the theoretical foundation of modern economics.
The equilibrium is the price and quantity where the demand and supply curves cross.
Under perfect competition supply follows marginal cost: firms produce more as long as the extra cost is below the market price.
Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the demand curve slopes downward.
Augustin Cournot first drew demand curves in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added supply curves in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890.
The fourteenth-century scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises.
The model also explains wages: workers supply labour, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate.
Where a seller or buyer has market power, models such as oligopoly or monopsony fit better.

entries.contested_note: Sraffa questioned the consistency of partial-equilibrium supply curves, and Post-Keynesians argue the model fails to explain prices that firms set by mark-up.
entries.text: In the fourteenth century the scholar Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that when desire for goods rises while availability falls, the price rises. Modern economics made that insight its theoretical foundation: the model of supply and demand. It explains how a market sets prices. The price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer, and the equilibrium is the price and quantity where the two curves cross. Each curve has a logic. Consumers buy another unit as long as its value to them is more than its price, so the buyers' curve slopes downward. When many small firms compete, supply follows the extra cost of each unit: firms produce more as long as that cost is below the market price. Augustin Cournot first drew the buyers' curve in 1838, Fleeming Jenkin added the sellers' curve in 1870, and Alfred Marshall popularized both in 1890. The model reaches beyond goods. Workers supply labor, businesses demand it, and the equilibrium price is the wage rate. Where a single seller or buyer can sway prices, other models fit better. Critics question the model itself. Sraffa doubted the consistency of supply curves drawn for a single market. Post-Keynesians argue it fails to explain prices that firms set by adding a mark-up to their costs.

entries.title: Equilibrium: when the market stops moving

definition.text: A state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so that prices and quantities stop changing.

facts.text: In a market equilibrium, competition sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce.
That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes.
The idea was borrowed from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes.
Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behaviour is consistent, no agent wants to change its behaviour, and the equilibrium results from a stable dynamic process.
A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down; a price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up.
When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium price and quantity change too.
Economists such as Paul Samuelson warn that an equilibrium price is not automatically good: a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve.
During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford.

entries.contested_note: The classical view that free markets always clear on their own has been challenged by economists who point to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.
entries.text: Economists borrowed equilibrium from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes. Economic equilibrium is a state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so prices and quantities stop changing. In a market equilibrium, rivalry among sellers sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce. That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes. Pull the price away and forces push it back. A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down. A price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up. When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium moves. Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behavior is consistent, no agent wants to change its behavior, and the outcome comes from a stable dynamic process. Balance is not the same as good. Paul Samuelson and others warn that a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve. During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved, because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford. Some economists also challenge the classical view that markets left alone always clear, pointing to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.
entries.text_plain: Economists borrowed equilibrium from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes. Economic equilibrium is a state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so prices and quantities stop changing. In a market equilibrium, rivalry among sellers sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce. That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes. Pull the price away and forces push it back. A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down. A price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up. When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium moves. Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behavior is consistent, no agent wants to change its behavior, and the outcome comes from a stable dynamic process. Balance is not the same as good. Paul Samuelson and others warn that a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve. During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved, because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford. Some economists also challenge the classical view that markets left alone always clear, pointing to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.

entries.title: The law of demand: higher price, fewer buyers

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls.

facts.text: It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much.
It is drawn as the demand curve, with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, which slopes downward.
A price change moves buyers along the demand curve; changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve.
Charles Davenant first stated it in 1699, and Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics (1890).
Together with the law of supply, it fixes the equilibrium price and quantity.
Exceptions include Giffen goods, Veblen goods, necessities and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

entries.text: Charles Davenant stated it in 1699: all else being equal, people buy less of a good when its price rises and more when it falls. This is the law of demand. It says only which way quantity moves when price changes, not by how much. Alfred Marshall drew it as a graph and joined it with supply in his Principles of Economics in 1890. The graph, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-371}}, puts quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical, and it slopes downward. A price change moves buyers along that curve. Changes in the number of buyers, income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations shift the whole curve. Together with its partner on the sellers' side ({{ref:nature-econ-391}}), the law fixes the equilibrium price and quantity. It has exceptions: Giffen goods, status goods ({{ref:nature-econ-390}}), necessities, and cases where buyers expect prices to keep changing.

entries.title: Free markets: prices without government steering

definition.text: An economic system in which the prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers, without government steering.

facts.text: Supporters of the free market contrast it with a regulated market, where government steps into supply and demand through taxes or rules.
In practice governments usually step in to cut harms such as greenhouse gas emissions, sometimes by using markets, as in carbon emissions trading.
Free markets are usually linked with capitalism, but they have also featured in some forms of market socialism.
To classical economists such as Adam Smith, a free market meant one free of privilege, monopolies and artificial scarcities.
A free market does not demand competition as such, but it does demand that new sellers be free to enter.
Critics say real free markets drift toward price-fixing monopolies and unequal bargaining power, which led to measures such as US antitrust law.
Coase, Friedman, von Mises and Hayek replied that markets can absorb or adjust to supposed market failures.

entries.contested_note: Supporters say free markets create healthy competition and fair prices, while critics say they slide into monopoly and need government intervention to work.
entries.text: To classical economists such as Adam Smith, a free market meant one free of privilege, exclusive selling rights and artificial scarcities. Today the term means an economic system without government steering. Prices of goods and services are set by the supply and demand of buyers and sellers. Its supporters contrast it with a regulated market, where government steps into supply and demand through taxes or rules. A free market does not demand rivalry among sellers as such, but it does demand that new sellers be free to enter. Free markets are usually linked with capitalism, but they have also featured in some forms of market socialism. In practice governments usually step in to cut harms such as planet-warming emissions, sometimes by using markets, as in carbon trading. The arguments run both ways. Critics say real free markets drift toward price-fixing and dominant single sellers, and unequal bargaining power, which led to measures such as US antitrust law. Coase, Friedman, von Mises and Hayek replied that markets can absorb or adjust to supposed market failures.

entries.title: Elasticity: how strongly one thing responds to another

definition.text: A measure of how much one economic variable responds to a change in another, given as the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other.

facts.text: If a good's price elasticity of demand is −2, a 10% price rise cuts the quantity demanded by 20%.
The main kinds include price elasticity of demand and of supply, income elasticity of demand and cross-price elasticity of demand.
Elasticity helps explain who bears indirect taxes and how welfare is split among consumer, producer and government surplus.
Seller revenue is highest at unit elasticity: a firm should raise its price when demand is inelastic and cut it when demand is elastic.
Supply of goods made from scarce natural resources such as petrol responds poorly to demand, so rising demand drives prices up.
Time is arguably the biggest influence on supply elasticity: the longer suppliers have to respond, the more supply changes.
Alfred Marshall first described price elasticity informally in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

entries.text: If buyers' elasticity for a good is −2, a 10% price rise cuts the quantity they buy by 20%. Elasticity measures how much one economic variable responds to a change in another: the percentage change in one divided by the percentage change in the other. The main kinds track how buying responds to price and to income, how selling responds to price, and how buying one good responds to another good's price. Elasticity helps explain who bears indirect taxes and how welfare is split among consumers, producers and government. It also guides pricing. Seller revenue is highest at unit elasticity, so a firm should raise its price when demand is inelastic and cut it when demand is elastic. Time is arguably the biggest influence on supply: the longer suppliers have to respond, the more supply changes. Goods made from scarce resources from nature, such as gasoline, respond poorly, so rising demand drives their prices up. Alfred Marshall first described price elasticity informally in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

entries.title: The demand curve: buying at every price

definition.text: A graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.

facts.text: It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, the whole market's demand.
It normally slopes down because of the law of demand; exceptions include Veblen goods, Giffen goods and speculative bubbles.
A price change moves buyers along the curve; a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve.
When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out while demand for inferior goods shifts in.
If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken (a substitute) shifts out and demand for ketchup (a complement) shifts in.
Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, but only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

entries.text: A demand curve is a graph showing how much of a good people will buy at each price. Price goes on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal. It can show one consumer's demand or, added up across everyone, a whole market's. It normally slopes down because of the law of demand. Exceptions include status goods ({{ref:nature-econ-390}}), Giffen goods and speculative bubbles. The curve moves in two ways. A price change moves buyers along it, while a change in anything else, such as income, related goods' prices, population or expectations, shifts the whole curve. When incomes rise, demand for normal goods shifts out and demand for inferior goods shifts in. If hamburgers get dearer, demand for chicken, a substitute, shifts out, while demand for ketchup, a complement, shifts in. One practical snag remains. Demand curves are estimated statistically from past data, yet only one point on the curve can be observed at any one time.

entries.title: Competition: the contest for customers

definition.text: Rivalry among firms for customers and limited resources, using price, product, promotion and place.

facts.text: Classical economists held that competition pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods.
More choice usually means lower prices than under monopoly or oligopoly.
How much competition exists depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information, and access to resources.
Competition arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want.
In 1776 Adam Smith described it as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency.
Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market.
Competition duplicates fixed costs, so for a few goods having many firms is itself inefficient: these are natural monopolies.

entries.contested_note: Economists debate how relevant perfect competition is to real markets and whether it should serve as the benchmark.
entries.text: In 1776 Adam Smith described competition as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency. Competition is the contest among firms for customers and limited resources, fought with price, product, promotion and place. It arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want. Classical economists held that it pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods. More choice usually means lower prices than when one or a few firms dominate. How much competition a market has depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information and access to resources. Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market. For a few goods, having many firms is itself inefficient, because competition duplicates costs that do not vary with output; {{ref:nature-econ-350}} covers these cases. Economists still debate how relevant the textbook ideal of {{ref:nature-econ-353}} is to real markets, and whether it should serve as the benchmark.

entries.title: Price elasticity of demand: how buyers react to price

definition.text: A measure of how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in its price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price.

facts.text: An elasticity of −2 means a one percent price rise cuts the quantity demanded by two percent.
If quantity falls 20 tons from 200 tons after the price rises $5 from $100, quantity drops 10% and price rises 5%, giving an elasticity of −2.
Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one.
Demand is more elastic when close substitutes exist, and less elastic for necessities such as insulin or for broad categories such as food in general.
Elasticity grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport.
For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue; for elastic goods it lowers revenue, and revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one.
Elasticity predicts who bears a tax: with perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it, with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it.
Alfred Marshall is credited with defining elasticity of demand in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

entries.text: Suppose a price rises $5 from $100 and sales fall 20 tons from 200 tons. Quantity drops 10% while price rises 5%, so the price elasticity of demand is −2. That number measures how strongly the quantity people buy responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity for a one percent change in price. Demand is inelastic when the elasticity is below one in absolute value and elastic when it is above one. Close substitutes make demand more elastic. Necessities such as insulin, and broad categories such as food in general, are less elastic. Elasticity also grows with time: after a lasting fuel price rise, more people switch to carpooling or public transport. For inelastic goods a price rise increases revenue, while for elastic goods it lowers revenue. Revenue peaks where elasticity is exactly one. The measure also predicts who bears a tax. With perfectly inelastic demand consumers pay all of it; with perfectly elastic demand firms pay all of it. Alfred Marshall is credited with defining it in his Principles of Economics of 1890.

entries.title: The invisible hand: self-interest serving the public

definition.text: Adam Smith's metaphor for the way free markets can lead self-interested people to serve the public good without meaning to.

facts.text: Smith used the phrase only once each in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and The Wealth of Nations, and spoke of 'an' invisible hand, never 'the'.
In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade.
Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularised the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve.
The idea that market exchange channels self-interest toward social good is a central justification for laissez-faire thinking behind neoclassical economics.
Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there: with externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution.
Environmental economics deals largely with market failures, where the invisible hand is unreliable.

entries.contested_note: Economists such as Stiglitz and Piketty argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good, and scholars disagree about what Smith himself meant.
entries.text: Adam Smith used the phrase just once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and once in The Wealth of Nations. He wrote of "an" invisible hand, never "the." It became his most famous metaphor: the way free markets can lead self-interested people to benefit the public without meaning to. In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about free trade. Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularized the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve. The idea is a central justification for the hands-off thinking behind neoclassical economics. Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there. With externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution, which is why environmental economics deals largely with market failures. Stiglitz, Piketty and others argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good. Scholars also disagree about what Smith himself meant.

entries.title: Income elasticity of demand: what richer people buy

definition.text: How strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income.

facts.text: It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income: if a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0.
Normal goods have positive income elasticity and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury.
Food as a whole has an income elasticity between zero and one, so spending on food grows more slowly than income, an observation called Engel's law.
Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26.
Income elasticities for food and energy tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States.
As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce.
Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

entries.text: As people grow richer, their spending on food grows more slowly than their income, an observation called Engel's law. Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

entries.title: Comparative statics: before-and-after snapshots

definition.text: Comparing two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium.

facts.text: It compares the two equilibria but does not study the path or process of change between them.
It is used to study shifts in supply and demand in one market, and changes in monetary or fiscal policy for a whole economy.
John R. Hicks (1939) and Paul A. Samuelson (1947) formalized it, though it had been drawn in graphs since at least the 1870s.
Results usually come from a linear approximation of the equilibrium equations, which assumes the equilibrium is stable.
Because of that approximation, its results hold only for very small changes in the outside variables.
For models of steady growth, the counterpart is comparative dynamics.
The envelope theorem describes how the value of an optimal solution changes with a parameter.
Claude Berge's 1963 maximum theorem describes when the optimal solution varies continuously with the parameters.

entries.text: Comparative statics compares two economic outcomes, one before and one after a change in some outside factor, once the economy has settled into its new equilibrium. It compares the two snapshots but does not study the path between them. Economists use it to study changes in supply and demand in one market, and changes in government taxing, spending or money policy for a whole economy. The method had been drawn in graphs since at least the 1870s; John R. Hicks (1939) and Paul A. Samuelson (1947) formalized it. Results usually come from a linear approximation of the equilibrium equations, which assumes the equilibrium is stable. Because of that approximation, they hold only for very small changes. For models of steady growth, the counterpart is comparative dynamics. Two mathematical results support the method. The envelope theorem describes how the value of an optimal solution changes with a parameter. Claude Berge's 1963 maximum theorem describes when the optimal solution varies continuously with the parameters.

entries.title: Price signals: what a price tells people

definition.text: The information a price carries to buyers and sellers, telling them to supply or demand more or less of something.

facts.text: When a product runs short and its price rises, people pay more attention to it and produce more of it.
Prices coordinate what is produced, how it is produced and what resources are used.
Friedrich Hayek argued that prices let people share knowledge spread among many others and coordinate their separate actions.
Monopolies, cartels and monopsonies can set prices that do not reflect production costs, weakening the signal.
Credit bubbles and speculation can distort price signals, leading to waste and financial crises.
Fuel taxes send price signals that make consumers aware of hidden costs such as greenhouse gases and other pollution.
Electricity users react little to price in the short run because they do not face the actual cost of production at each moment.

entries.text: When a product runs short and its price rises, people pay more attention to it and produce more of it. That is a price signal at work: the information a price carries to buyers and sellers, telling them to supply or demand more or less of something. Prices coordinate what is produced, how it is produced and what resources are used. Friedrich Hayek argued that prices let people share knowledge spread among many others and coordinate their separate actions. Signals can be weakened. Dominant single sellers, price-fixing groups and dominant single buyers can set prices that do not reflect production costs. Credit bubbles and speculation can distort signals, leading to waste and financial crises. Signals can also be added. Taxes on fuel make consumers aware of hidden costs such as planet-warming gases and other pollution. Where signals are missing, behavior barely responds. Electricity users react little to price in the short run because they do not face the actual cost of production at each moment.

entries.title: Market economies: letting prices guide production

definition.text: An economic system in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand.

facts.text: Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones where governments correct market failures and promote welfare.
They need clearly defined, enforceable property rights, though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets.
A price system signals people to adjust what they produce and invest; strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production.
Governments can set price ceilings or floors, such as minimum wages, or use Pigovian taxes to deal with externalities.
Joseph Stiglitz argues markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures.
A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax incentives, carbon trading and environmental rules.

entries.text: In a market economy, strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production. That price system is the heart of the definition. A market economy is one in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand. Prices signal people to adjust what they produce and invest. Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones, where governments correct market failures and promote welfare. All of them need clearly defined, enforceable rules of ownership ({{ref:nature-econ-621}}), though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets. Governments have several tools. They can set maximum or minimum prices, such as a lowest legal wage, or use taxes on harmful side effects ({{ref:nature-pol-088}}) to deal with externalities. Joseph Stiglitz argues that markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures. A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax breaks, carbon trading and environmental rules.
entries.text_plain: In a market economy, strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production. That price system is the heart of the definition. A market economy is one in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand. Prices signal people to adjust what they produce and invest. Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones, where governments correct market failures and promote welfare. All of them need clearly defined, enforceable rules of ownership (Property rights: the rules of who owns what), though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets. Governments have several tools. They can set maximum or minimum prices, such as a lowest legal wage, or use taxes on harmful side effects (Pigouvian taxes: charging for harm done to others) to deal with externalities. Joseph Stiglitz argues that markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures. A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax breaks, carbon trading and environmental rules.

entries.title: Price controls: when governments set prices

definition.text: Government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services in a market.

facts.text: There are two main kinds: a price ceiling sets the most that may be charged and a price floor the least; rent control and the minimum wage are well-known examples.
They aim to keep goods affordable during shortages, slow inflation, or guarantee a minimum income to some providers.
Price controls are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders, and Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success.
Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, causing shortages, and shortages feed black markets with higher prices.
During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry.
Western economists generally hold that consumer price controls fail, though since the 1990s minimum wages have won strong support among some economists.
Price controls are one of the indirect ways governments subsidise energy.

entries.contested_note: Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, while some support minimum wages and other price caps.

entries.title: Shifts in supply and demand: when the whole curve moves
entries.article: Supply and demand#Changes in market equilibrium

definition.text: Changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole supply or demand curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity.

facts.text: A movement along a curve is a 'change in quantity demanded', while a shift of the whole curve is a 'change in demand'.
Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers; a rise lifts both equilibrium price and quantity.
A cheaper way of growing wheat shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold.
A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.

entries.text: A cheaper way of growing wheat does something a change in the price of wheat cannot: it moves the entire supply curve. Shifts in supply and demand are changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity. Economists guard the language carefully. A movement along a curve is a "change in quantity demanded," while a shift of the whole curve is a "change in demand." Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers. A rise in demand lifts both the equilibrium price and the quantity. Supply shifts work in either direction. The cheaper wheat-growing method shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold. A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.

entries.title: The price mechanism: how prices share out resources

definition.text: The way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded.

facts.text: Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources.
At competitive equilibrium, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, which is allocative efficiency.
The 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, prompting several countries to start producing their own oil.
Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as biodiesel and electric cars.
An auction is a price mechanism in which bidders compete and the highest bid wins.
Greenhouse gas cap-and-trade applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog.
Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

entries.text: When the 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, several countries started producing their own oil. That response is the price mechanism at work: the way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded. Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources. The mechanism can be slow. Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as biodiesel and electric cars. Once competition settles into balance, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, an ideal explored in {{ref:nature-econ-178}}. The mechanism takes many forms. In the form covered in {{ref:nature-econ-671}}, bidders compete and the highest bid wins. Cap-and-trade for planet-warming gases applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog. Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

entries.title: Total cost: the full bill for making output

definition.text: The lowest cost of producing a given amount of output, made up of variable costs plus fixed costs.

facts.text: Variable costs, such as labour and raw materials, change with output; fixed costs, such as buildings and machinery, do not in the short term.
In economics it includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use.
The extra total cost of one more unit is the marginal cost.
Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.

entries.text: Total cost is the lowest cost of producing a given amount of output. It is made up of costs that vary with output plus costs that do not. Labor and raw materials change with output; buildings and machinery do not, in the short term. In economics, total cost includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use. The extra total cost of one more unit gets its own entry, {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. Given time, the bill can shrink. Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.
entries.text_plain: Total cost is the lowest cost of producing a given amount of output. It is made up of costs that vary with output plus costs that do not. Labor and raw materials change with output; buildings and machinery do not, in the short term. In economics, total cost includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use. The extra total cost of one more unit gets its own entry, Marginal cost: the price of one more unit. Given time, the bill can shrink. Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.

entries.title: Marginal cost: the price of one more unit

definition.text: The extra total cost of producing one more unit of output.

facts.text: It differs from average cost, which is total cost divided by the number of units made.
It counts only costs that change with output: for one more car, the labour and parts, but not the factory building.
Because fixed costs do not change with output, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged.
In the short run it eventually rises, as more labour and materials press against a fixed building and machinery.
A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds the marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal.
The marginal cost curve crosses the average total cost and average variable cost curves at their lowest points.
With economies of scale, pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy.
In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell.

entries.contested_note: Textbook models assume marginal cost rises with output, but many empirical studies find it constant or falling for most firms.
entries.text: To make one more car, a carmaker needs more labor and parts, but not a new factory building. Marginal cost is that extra total cost of producing one more unit of output. It counts only costs that change with output. It differs from the cost per unit on average, which is total cost divided by the number of units made. Because costs that do not vary with output stay put, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged. Textbooks expect marginal cost to rise in the short run, as more labor and materials press against a fixed building and machinery. A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal. On a graph, the line for marginal cost crosses the lines for cost per unit at their lowest points. Where growing bigger cuts unit costs ({{ref:nature-econ-303}}), pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy. The textbook picture is disputed. In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell. Many empirical studies likewise find marginal cost constant or falling for most firms.

entries.title: Profit: what is left after every cost

definition.text: What a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs.

facts.text: Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books; economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller.
Normal profit is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry.
In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run.
Economic profit lasts in uncompetitive markets such as monopolies and oligopolies, protected by barriers to entry like patents, land rights and zoning laws.
Economists usually assume firms try to maximise profit, which happens where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
A firm's social profit is its accounting profit plus or minus the externalities, such as pollution, and consumer surplus its activity creates.
Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to entry to protect their profits.

entries.text: Economists usually assume firms try to maximize profit, so they define it carefully. Profit is what a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs. Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller. The break-even case ({{ref:nature-econ-354}}) is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry. Competition erodes anything more. In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run. Profit lasts only in markets with one or a few dominant sellers. Barriers to entry protect it: patents, rights to land and rules on how land is used. Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to protect their profits. Profit is greatest where the revenue from one more unit equals its marginal cost. A wider measure, social profit, adds or subtracts the externalities, such as pollution, and the gains to buyers that a firm's activity creates.

entries.title: Monopoly: the market with one seller

definition.text: A market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service.

facts.text: A monopoly lacks competition and close substitutes, so it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits.
Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market.
Monopolies get their power from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate.
A monopolist picks the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, aiming at the largest total profit rather than the highest price.
Compared with perfect competition it sells less at a higher price, and the trades it forgoes create a deadweight loss.
Contestable-market theory says a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low.
Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behaviour.
The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses.

entries.text: The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses. A monopoly is a market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service. With no competition and no close substitutes, it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits. Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market. Its power comes from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate. A monopolist does not simply charge the highest price. It picks the output where the revenue from one more sale equals the cost of making it, aiming at the largest total profit. Compared with a market of many small competitors it sells less at a higher price. The trades it forgoes are a pure loss to society ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). Contestable-market theory adds that a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low. Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behavior.
entries.text_plain: The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses. With no competition and no close substitutes, it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits. Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market. Its power comes from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate. A monopolist does not simply charge the highest price. It picks the output where the revenue from one more sale equals the cost of making it, aiming at the largest total profit. Compared with a market of many small competitors it sells less at a higher price. The trades it forgoes are a pure loss to society (Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets). Contestable-market theory adds that a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low. Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behavior.

entries.title: Perfect competition: the textbook ideal market

definition.text: An idealized market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price.

facts.text: Under its conditions a market reaches an equilibrium where supply equals demand for every product, including labour, and this equilibrium is Pareto optimal.
Every profit-maximizing firm ends up charging a price equal to its marginal cost, which makes the market allocatively efficient.
Without externalities and public goods, such equilibria are Pareto-efficient: a result called the First Theorem of Welfare Economics.
Each firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve, so it must take the market price.
In the long run no firm earns economic profit, because any profit draws in new firms until the price falls to average cost.
Real markets come close to it mainly for farm products and raw materials sold by many sellers to many buyers.
Critics say it treats firms as passive, ignoring price-cutting, product design, advertising and innovation, and leaves unclear who actually sets prices.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute the realism of its assumptions and whether a model of price-takers can describe a decentralized market at all.
entries.text: Real markets come close to it mainly for farm products and raw materials sold by many sellers to many buyers. Perfect competition is the idealized version: a market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price. Each firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve and must take the market price. Every profit-maximizing firm ends up charging a price equal to its marginal cost, which makes the market allocatively efficient. In the long run no firm earns economic profit, because any profit draws in new firms until the price falls to the cost per unit. Under these conditions a market reaches an equilibrium where supply equals demand for every product, including labor. Without externalities and {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, such equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. This is the first of the theorems in {{ref:nature-econ-191}}. Critics say the model treats firms as passive. It ignores price-cutting, product design, advertising and innovation, and leaves unclear who actually sets prices. They dispute both the realism of its assumptions and whether a model of price-takers can describe a decentralized market at all.

entries.title: Market power: the ability to set your own price

definition.text: A firm's ability to raise the price of what it sells above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers.

facts.text: Firms with no market power, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers.
How much power firms have depends on market structure: perfect competition and monopoly are the extremes, with monopolistic competition and oligopoly in between.
Power lasts only behind barriers to entry, such as control of scarce resources, economies of scale, better technology or government rules; OPEC's power comes from controlling oil.
It is measured by markups, or more often by concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which need only revenue data.
The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost.
Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses measures of market power to judge whether a firm has abused it.
Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analysing market power and regulation.

entries.text: Some sellers can name their price. Market power is a firm's ability to raise its price above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers. Firms with none, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers. How much power firms have depends on market structure. Perfect competition and a lone seller are the extremes. In between sit {{ref:nature-econ-311}} and markets run by a few firms. Power lasts only behind barriers to entry, such as control of scarce resources, advantages of size, better technology or government rules; OPEC's rests on oil. The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost. Economists measure it by markups or, more often, by the market shares of the biggest firms ({{ref:nature-econ-398}} and {{ref:nature-econ-384}}). Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses these measures to judge whether a firm has abused its power. Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analyzing market power and regulation.

entries.title: Oligopoly: a market run by a few

definition.text: A market in which a few sellers control pricing.

facts.text: Each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions, so the firms are mutually interdependent.
Oligopolists often collude to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming cartels that keep new firms out.
Competition laws mostly catch formal collusion such as cartels, so firms can escape through tacit collusion.
A duopoly is an oligopoly of only two firms.
Industries cited as oligopolistic include civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper.

entries.text: Civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper have all been cited as oligopolies: markets in which a few sellers control pricing. A duopoly is the smallest case, an oligopoly of only two firms. In such markets each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions, so the firms are mutually interdependent. That makes cooperation tempting. Oligopolists often collude to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming price-fixing groups ({{ref:nature-econ-301}}) that keep new firms out. Competition laws mostly catch formal agreements to collude, so firms can escape through tacit collusion, coordinating without any explicit deal.
entries.text_plain: Civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper have all been cited as oligopolies: markets in which a few sellers control pricing. That makes cooperation tempting. Oligopolists often collude to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming price-fixing groups (Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete) that keep new firms out. Competition laws mostly catch formal agreements to collude, so firms can escape through tacit collusion, coordinating without any explicit deal.

entries.title: Competitive equilibrium: economics' benchmark of efficiency

definition.text: An equilibrium of a market with flexible prices and many traders, each too small to move prices, in which every trader gets the best bundle they can afford and supply equals demand; also called Walrasian equilibrium.

facts.text: Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu introduced the concept in 1951, and it serves as economics' benchmark of efficiency.
If Alice values her car at 10 and Bob at 20, any price between 10 and 20 is an equilibrium price at which Bob buys the car.
The Arrow–Debreu model shows such an equilibrium exists in any exchange economy with divisible goods when everyone's preferences are strictly convex.
By the welfare theorems, every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient, and every efficient allocation can be reached by one.
At this equilibrium the value society puts on a good equals the value of resources used to make it: marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
Efficiency here says nothing about fairness: an allocation where one person has everything can still be efficient.

Every trader gets the best bundle they can afford, and supply equals demand. Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu introduced the concept in 1951, and it serves as economics' benchmark of efficiency. Their model shows such an equilibrium exists in any exchange economy with divisible goods when everyone's preferences are strictly convex. The welfare theorems add that every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient, and every efficient allocation can be reached by one. At this equilibrium marginal benefit equals marginal cost: the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it. Efficiency, though, says nothing about fairness. An allocation in which one person has everything can still be efficient.

entries.title: Imperfect competition: where real markets fall short

definition.text: Any market that falls short of at least one of the conditions of a perfectly competitive market.

facts.text: Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure.
A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ.
The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces.
The broad imperfect market structures include monopolistic competition, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others.
A firm in an imperfect market faces a downward-sloping demand curve, unlike the flat demand curve facing a perfectly competitive firm.
Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition.

entries.contested_note: Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.
entries.text: Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition. Imperfect competition covers every market that falls short of at least one of them. A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ. The broad imperfect structures include {{ref:nature-econ-311}}, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others. A perfectly competitive firm faces a flat demand curve. A firm in an imperfect market faces one that slopes down. Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure. The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces. Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.
entries.text_plain: Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition. Imperfect competition covers every market that falls short of at least one of them. A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ. The broad imperfect structures include Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others. A perfectly competitive firm faces a flat demand curve. A firm in an imperfect market faces one that slopes down. Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure. The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces. Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.

entries.title: Marginal revenue: what one more sale brings in

definition.text: The extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit of its product.

facts.text: In a perfectly competitive market a firm gets the same price for every unit, so its marginal revenue equals the price.
A monopoly must cut its price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue is always below the price.
Example: selling 20 books at $50 brings $1000, and 21 books at $49 brings $1029, so the 21st book adds $29.
A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; it is making money on extra units while marginal revenue is higher.
When demand is inelastic, selling more forces a price cut on every unit and marginal revenue turns negative.
Under perfect competition the marginal revenue curve is a flat line at the market price; for a monopoly it slopes down and lies below the demand curve.

entries.text: A seller can sell 20 books at $50 each, bringing in $1000. To sell 21, it must cut the price to $49, which brings in $1029. The 21st book adds just $29. That $29 is marginal revenue: the extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit. In a perfectly competitive market a firm gets the same price for every unit. Its marginal revenue equals the price, and its marginal revenue curve is a flat line at the market price. A monopoly must cut its price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue is always below the price. Its curve slopes down and lies below the demand curve. When demand is inelastic, selling more forces a price cut on every unit, and marginal revenue turns negative. The rule for profit follows. A firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; while marginal revenue is higher, extra units still make money.

entries.title: Cost curves: drawing what production costs

definition.text: A graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces.

facts.text: Profit-maximizing firms use cost curves to decide how much to produce.
There are total, average, marginal, fixed and variable cost curves, some for the short run and some for the long run.
Fixed cost is a flat line, while average fixed cost falls as output grows because the same cost is spread over more units.
Short-run marginal cost first falls and then rises because of diminishing marginal returns; the long-run curve is shaped by returns to scale.
When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost falls; when above, it rises; where they are equal, average cost is lowest.
In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

entries.contested_note: Textbooks draw U-shaped cost curves, but surveys of firms suggest most face constant or falling costs.
entries.text: A cost curve is a graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces. Profit-maximizing firms use these curves to decide how much to produce. There are curves for total, average and marginal costs and for costs that stay the same ({{ref:nature-econ-307}}) and costs that change with output ({{ref:nature-econ-328}}), some for the short run and some for the long run. Costs that do not vary with output draw a flat line, while the same cost spread per unit falls as output grows. Short-run marginal cost first falls and then rises, because of diminishing marginal returns. The long-run curve is shaped by {{ref:nature-econ-317}}. One rule links the curves. When marginal cost is below the cost per unit, the cost per unit falls; when above, it rises; where they are equal, the cost per unit is lowest. That gives the textbook U-shape. Real firms may not follow it. In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

That gives the textbook U-shape. Real firms may not follow it. In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

entries.title: Natural monopoly: when one supplier is cheapest

definition.text: A firm whose average cost of production keeps falling across the whole range of market demand, so one large supplier is cheaper than several small ones.

facts.text: Such markets, left alone, tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals.
J.S. Mill first called monopolies 'natural' in 1848, citing gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways.
Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use regulation and public ownership.
Regulators often impose average-cost pricing, which removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

entries.text: In 1848 J.S. Mill first called some monopolies "natural," pointing to gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways. A natural monopoly is a firm whose cost per unit keeps falling across the whole range of market demand. One large supplier is then cheaper than several small ones. Left alone, such markets tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals. Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use regulation and public ownership. Regulators often impose average-cost pricing. It removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

entries.title: The law of supply: higher price, more for sale

definition.text: The basic rule that, all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good.

facts.text: Producers offer more at higher prices because producing more is a way to make more profit; this is why the supply curve slopes upward.
A job paying £20 an hour draws more interest than one paying £15 an hour.
Things other than price shift the supply curve: production costs, the number of suppliers, subsidies, taxes and, in farming, the weather.
If buyers want more than sellers offer, the price rises, cutting demand and raising supply until the two match.
Some heterodox economists, such as Steve Keen, argue the supply curve for mass-produced goods often slopes downward.

entries.contested_note: Some heterodox economists dispute the law of supply for mass-produced goods, whose unit prices may fall as output grows.
entries.text: A job paying £20 an hour draws more interest than one paying £15. The same logic runs through every market: all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good. Other things shift the whole curve: production costs, the number of suppliers, subsidies, taxes and, in farming, the weather. The law works together with demand. Their unit prices may fall as output grows, so the supply curve often slopes downward.

entries.title: Price elasticity of supply: how sellers react to price

definition.text: How strongly the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price.

facts.text: Supply is inelastic below 1, elastic above 1, unit-elastic at exactly 1, and fixed at zero, when quantity does not respond at all.
Unlike demand elasticities, supply elasticities are usually positive, because a higher price encourages more production.
Some goods barely respond to price: a country's gold output may be capped by availability, and no price will produce more Van Gogh paintings.
Supply is usually more elastic in the long run, when all inputs can be expanded, than in the short run.
Spare capacity makes supply more elastic; once capacity is full, more output needs new investment, so supply becomes less elastic.
The more elastic housing supply is, the smaller the rent rise needed to clear a shortage after demand grows.
Land is the classic example of a factor whose supply is inelastic.

entries.text: No price will produce more Van Gogh paintings, and a country's gold output may be capped by availability. These are extreme cases of price elasticity of supply. It measures how strongly the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price. Supply is inelastic below 1, elastic above 1, unit-elastic at exactly 1, and fixed at zero, when quantity does not respond at all. Unlike demand elasticities, supply elasticities are usually positive, because a higher price encourages more production. Time matters. Supply is usually more elastic in the long run, when all inputs can be expanded, than in the short run. So does spare capacity: once capacity is full, more output needs new investment, so supply becomes less elastic. The stakes are real. The more elastic housing supply is, the smaller the rent rise needed to clear a shortage after demand grows. Land is the classic example of a factor whose supply is inelastic.

entries.title: Cross elasticity of demand: how one price moves another good

definition.text: A measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good.

facts.text: A positive value means the goods are substitutes; a negative value means they are complements; zero means they are unrelated.
The cross elasticity of butter with respect to margarine is 0.81: a 1% rise in margarine's price raises butter demand by 0.81%.
Fuel and new cars are complements, so a rise in fuel prices lowers demand for cars.
Governments use cross elasticities between drinks when setting alcohol taxes and minimum prices to reduce harmful drinking.

A positive value means the goods are substitutes, a negative value means they are complements, and zero means they are unrelated. Fuel and new cars are complements, so dearer fuel lowers demand for cars. Governments use cross elasticities between drinks when setting alcohol taxes and minimum prices to reduce harmful drinking.

entries.title: The inverse demand function: price from quantity

definition.text: A formula that gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, so it is also called a price function.

facts.text: Its value is the highest price that could be charged while still selling that quantity; it equals the average revenue function.
It is found by solving the demand function for price: if Q = 240 − 2P, then P = 120 − Q/2.
For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is MR = a − 2bQ: the same starting height and twice the slope.
It is used to find the profit-maximising output, where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and then the price to charge.

entries.text: An inverse demand function flips the usual question. Instead of quantity from price, it gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, which is why it is also called a price function. Its value is the highest price that still sells that quantity. It is found by solving the demand function for price: if Q = 240 − 2P, then P = 120 − Q/2. For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ: the same starting height and twice the slope. Firms use it to find the most profitable output and then the price to charge.

entries.title: Market size: counting buyers or money

definition.text: How big a market is, measured either by its number of buyers and sellers or by the money exchanged in it, usually per year.

facts.text: Measured in money, market size is often called market value.
The same goods can have different, usually rising, market values at the production, wholesale and retail levels.

entries.text: Market size measures how big a market is, either by its number of buyers and sellers or by the money exchanged in it, usually per year. Measured in money, it is often called market value. The same goods can have different market values at each stage, usually rising from production to wholesale to retail.
