entries.title: Negative prices: paying someone to take it

definition.text: A price below zero, where the owner or producer pays the 'buyer' to take an item away.

facts.text: In April 2020 oil for May delivery fell to -$37.63 a barrel, a one-day drop of $55.90, because holders feared there was nowhere left to store it.
Negative interest rates are a similar idea.

entries.title: Disequilibrium: when markets are out of balance

definition.text: The condition of a market that is not in equilibrium, where the amounts supplied and demanded are out of balance.

facts.text: Disequilibrium can last only a moment or persist for a long time.
Many economists see labour markets as stuck in excess supply over long periods.
Some goods' prices adjust slowly because of menu costs and long-term contracts, but they do not stay out of balance forever.

entries.text: Markets are not always in balance. Disequilibrium is the condition of a market in which the amounts supplied and demanded do not match. It can last only a moment or persist for a long time. Many economists see labor markets as stuck for long periods with more workers offering labor than employers want. Some goods' prices adjust slowly, because of the cost of changing prices and because of long-term contracts. Even so, they do not stay out of balance forever.

entries.title: Dynamic equilibrium: growing in step

definition.text: An equilibrium in which several quantities keep growing at the same rate, so that the ratios between them stay fixed.

facts.text: In the neoclassical growth model, output and capital grow at the same rate as the workforce, leaving output per worker unchanged.
Comparing two dynamic equilibria is called comparative dynamics.
In that model a permanently higher saving rate raises capital per worker but leaves the growth rate of output unchanged.

entries.title: Government-granted monopolies: exclusive by law

definition.text: A monopoly created when a government gives one person or company the exclusive right to supply something.

facts.text: It can be granted by a law that excludes rivals, or indirectly through patents, trademarks and copyright.
States grant them to reward risky investment or to enrich a domestic interest group.
A publisher can use its copyright monopoly to charge American students more than Ethiopian students for the same textbook.

entries.title: The inverse elasticity rule: markups and sensitive buyers

definition.text: The rule that a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces.

facts.text: The markup is measured by the Lerner index: price minus marginal cost, divided by price, equals minus one over the elasticity of demand.
Perfectly competitive firms have zero market power and simply take the market price.

entries.text: The less buyers respond to price, the more a monopoly can mark up. The inverse elasticity rule states this exactly: a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces. The markup is measured by {{ref:nature-econ-393}}: price minus marginal cost, divided by price, equals minus one over the elasticity of demand. Perfectly competitive firms sit at the other end, with zero market power, simply taking the market price.

entries.title: Normal profit: just enough to stay in business

definition.text: The return that just makes running a business worthwhile, equal to what the owner's time and capital could earn in their next best use.

facts.text: Economists count normal profit as a cost, not as part of business profit.
It varies within and across industries in line with how risky each kind of investment is.
Under perfect competition only normal profits survive in the long run, so firms have no reason to enter or leave the industry.
Profits above normal persist only where barriers to entry stop new firms from coming in, as in monopoly or oligopoly.

Profits above normal persist only where barriers to entry keep new firms out, as in monopoly or oligopoly.

entries.title: The shutdown point: when to stop producing

definition.text: The price below which a loss-making firm does better to stop producing in the short run: the point where price falls under average variable cost.

facts.text: Shutting down avoids variable costs but not fixed costs, which must be paid anyway and so are ignored in the decision.
A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve at and above the shutdown point.

entries.text: A loss-making firm faces a short-run question: keep going or stop? The shutdown point is the price below which it does better to stop, where price falls under the per-unit cost of inputs that change with output. Shutting down avoids the costs that vary with output, but not those that must be paid anyway, so those are ignored in the decision. A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve at and above the shutdown point.

entries.title: Partial equilibrium: one market at a time

definition.text: An analysis of equilibrium in a single market that holds everything else constant except the one change being studied.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall's supply and demand model is the classic partial equilibrium model.
It treats the prices of substitutes and complements and buyers' incomes as given, which makes it much simpler than general equilibrium.
A tariff on French wine raises its price; partial equilibrium ignores the knock-on rise in demand for domestic wine that feeds back and pushes the price higher still.
Such feedback usually changes the size of a price change but not its direction.

entries.title: General equilibrium theory: all markets at once

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies supply, demand and prices across a whole economy of many linked markets, seeking to show that together they reach an overall equilibrium.

facts.text: It contrasts with partial equilibrium, which studies one part of the economy while holding everything else fixed.
It goes back to Léon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics of 1874 and took its modern form in the 1950s with Arrow, Debreu and McKenzie.
The first welfare theorem says market equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
The first welfare theorem quietly assumes complete markets and perfect information.

The second welfare theorem says any efficient outcome can be reached by redistributing starting endowments and then leaving the market alone, suggesting efficiency and fairness can be handled separately.
From the 1970s, faster computers and input–output tables let economists solve general equilibrium models of real national and world economies numerically.
Computable general equilibrium models use real economic data to estimate how an economy might respond to changes in policy or technology.
Keynesian and Post-Keynesian economists reject the theory as misleading, arguing that real economies are not in equilibrium.

entries.contested_note: General equilibrium theory is a central dispute between neoclassical economists and other schools, some of which call it misleading and useless.

entries.title: Laissez-faire: leave prices alone

definition.text: The principle that prices and wages should be free of non-market pressure such as government taxes, subsidies, tariffs, regulations or granted monopolies.

facts.text: Hayek argued that the point of laissez-faire is to keep the unique information that a price carries.
Karl Popper called the idea of the free market paradoxical, since it needs interventions to prevent interventions.

entries.title: Spontaneous order: order nobody designed

definition.text: The idea, popularised by Friedrich Hayek, that market economies create order through networks no one designed, which arise from many separate individual decisions.

facts.text: Hayek held that this order shares out a society's resources better than any design could.
The idea builds on Adam Smith's invisible hand from The Wealth of Nations.

entries.text: No one designed the networks that coordinate a market economy. Friedrich Hayek popularized this idea of spontaneous order: market economies create order through networks that arise from many separate individual decisions. He held that such order shares out a society's resources better than any design could. The idea builds on Adam Smith's invisible hand from The Wealth of Nations.

entries.title: Residual demand: what is left for one firm

definition.text: The demand facing one particular firm: the market demand left unmet by other firms at each price.

facts.text: It equals market demand minus the supply of the other firms at each price.
With many firms, each firm's demand is extremely elastic and nearly flat, though not perfectly flat as textbooks draw it.

entries.text: A single firm does not face the whole market's demand, only what other firms leave unmet. That leftover is its residual demand curve: market demand minus the supply of the other firms at each price. With many firms, each firm's residual demand is extremely elastic and nearly flat, though not perfectly flat as textbooks draw it.

entries.title: How taxes and subsidies change prices
entries.article: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price

definition.text: How taxes and subsidies change the prices buyers pay and sellers receive, and so the quantity bought and sold.

facts.text: A tax moves the market to a new equilibrium where buyers pay more and sellers keep less.
Who legally pays the tax does not matter: a tax on sellers is largely passed on to buyers through higher prices.
Most of the burden falls on the less elastic side of the market, which is less able to change how much it buys or sells.
A specific tax shifts the supply curve up by the tax amount; an ad valorem tax, a percentage of price, also pivots it.
In one example a $0.50 tax raises the buyers' price from $3.00 to $3.30, sellers keep $2.80, and sales fall from 100 to 80.
A subsidy gives the same lower buyer price and higher seller price whether it is paid to producers or to consumers.
Tobacco taxes cut smoking: most studies find an elasticity of 0.4 to 0.5, so a 10% price rise reduces consumption by 4% to 5%.

sources.title: Effect of taxes and subsidies on price

entries.text: Put a $0.50 tax on a good that sells for $3.00, and buyers do not pay the full $0.50 extra. Who legally pays the tax does not matter: a tax on sellers is largely passed on to buyers through higher prices. Most of the burden falls on the less elastic side of the market, the side less able to change how much it buys or sells. Taxes come in two forms. A specific tax, a fixed amount per unit, shifts the supply curve up by that amount. An ad valorem tax, a percentage of price, also pivots it. Subsidies run the logic in reverse. They give the same lower buyer price and higher seller price whether paid to producers or to consumers. Real taxes behave as predicted. Tobacco taxes cut smoking: most studies find an elasticity of 0.4 to 0.5, so a 10% price rise reduces consumption by 4% to 5%.

entries.title: Arc elasticity: measuring between two points

definition.text: An elasticity measured between two points on a demand curve, using the average of the two prices and the two quantities as the base.

facts.text: It removes the problem that an ordinary elasticity depends on which point is treated as the starting one, and gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve.
Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on.
Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but needs the demand formula to be known.

entries.text: An ordinary elasticity gives different answers depending on which of two points is treated as the start. Arc elasticity removes that problem. It measures elasticity between two points on a demand curve. The base is the average of the two prices and of the two quantities, which gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve. Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on. Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but it needs the demand formula to be known.

entries.title: Concentration ratios: how much the biggest firms hold

definition.text: The combined market share of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four.

facts.text: The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition.
Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly.
Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

entries.text: Add up the market shares of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four, and you have a concentration ratio. The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition. Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly. Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power, because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

entries.title: The Walrasian auction: finding prices by bidding

definition.text: An ascending auction that finds a competitive equilibrium by raising the price of any item more than one buyer wants until each item is wanted by at most one buyer.

facts.text: The auctioneer starts all prices at zero and buyers name their favourite bundle at each round of prices.
Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement or English auctions.

entries.text: This bidding process, named for Walras, finds a competitive equilibrium by steadily raising prices. The auctioneer starts all prices at zero, and at each round buyers name their favorite bundle. Any item wanted by more than one buyer has its price raised, until each item is wanted by at most one buyer. Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement, or English versions of the sales by bidding described in {{ref:nature-econ-671}}.
entries.text_plain: This bidding process, named for Walras, finds a competitive equilibrium by steadily raising prices. The auctioneer starts all prices at zero, and at each round buyers name their favorite bundle. Any item wanted by more than one buyer has its price raised, until each item is wanted by at most one buyer. Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement, or English versions of the sales by bidding described in Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price.

entries.title: The Herfindahl index: weighing market concentration

definition.text: A measure of how concentrated a market is, found by adding up the squares of every firm's market share.

facts.text: It gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does.
It runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms; the more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

entries.text: Square every firm's market share and add them up: the result is the Herfindahl index, a measure of how concentrated a market is. Squaring gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does. The index runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms. The more concentrated the market, the higher the value.
entries.text_plain: Square every firm's market share and add them up: the result is the Herfindahl index, a measure of how concentrated a market is. Squaring gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does. The index runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms. The more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

entries.title: Excess supply: more for sale than buyers want

definition.text: A situation where sellers want to sell more of a good than buyers want to buy, because the price is above its equilibrium level; also called a market surplus or glut.

facts.text: It is the opposite of a shortage, and the two are the two kinds of disequilibrium in a competitive market.
If 1000 televisions are offered at $600 but buyers want only 300, the excess supply of 700 pushes sellers to cut the price until the market balances.
Unemployment is excess supply in the labour market, and it lowers workers' demand for goods in other markets.
Farmers face it often: a good harvest brings perishable surpluses, and governments may step in to buy them up.

entries.text: If 1000 televisions are offered at $600 but buyers want only 300, the 700 left over push sellers to cut the price until the market balances. That leftover is excess supply, also called a market surplus or glut. Sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy, because the price sits above its equilibrium level. It is the opposite of a shortage, and the two are the two kinds of disequilibrium in a competitive market. Unemployment is excess supply in the labor market. Farmers face it after a good harvest, and governments may step in to buy up the perishable surplus.

entries.title: Price floors: a legal minimum price

definition.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service.

facts.text: A floor only bites if it is set above the equilibrium price; set below it, it has no practical effect.
Common examples are minimum wage laws, supply management in Canadian farming, US airfares before 1978 and minimum prices for alcohol.
A binding floor makes buyers buy less while sellers want to sell more, leaving a lasting surplus.
It shifts some consumer surplus to producers and creates a deadweight loss.
EU support buying to hold farm prices at an intervention price has sometimes left 'butter mountains' of surplus in warehouses.
Hybrid cap-and-trade schemes add floor and ceiling prices to steady the carbon price.
Before deregulation in 1978, US airfare floors kept flying so costly that in 1965 more than 80% of Americans had never flown on a jet.

entries.text: Before US airfares were deregulated in 1978, price floors kept flying so costly that in 1965 more than 80% of Americans had never flown on a jet. A price floor is a limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service. It only bites if it is set above the equilibrium price; set below, it has no practical effect. Common examples are laws setting the lowest legal wage, supply management in Canadian farming, US airfares before 1978 and minimum prices for alcohol. A binding floor makes buyers buy less while sellers want to sell more, leaving a lasting surplus. It shifts some of the buyers' gains to producers and creates a pure loss to society ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). EU support buying to hold farm prices at an intervention price has sometimes left "butter mountains" of surplus in warehouses. Floors can also steady a market. Hybrid cap-and-trade schemes add floor and ceiling prices to steady the carbon price.

entries.title: Factor markets: buying land, labor and capital

definition.text: A market where the inputs to production, such as land, labour and capital, are bought and sold.

facts.text: Factor markets share out land, labour and capital among firms and pay income to their owners as wages, rents and the like.
Firms buy inputs in factor markets and sell the goods they make in product markets; both kinds of market work in much the same way.
A firm hires another worker when the extra revenue that worker brings in, the marginal revenue product of labour, exceeds the extra cost.
A factor in scarce supply earns a high price and an abundant one a low price, so when a factor's supply falls its equilibrium price rises.

entries.text: Firms sell what they make in product markets, but they buy their inputs in factor markets, where land, labor and capital are bought and sold. Both kinds of market work in much the same way. Factor markets share out land, labor and capital among firms and pay income to their owners as wages, rents and the like. A factor in scarce supply earns a high price and an abundant one a low price, so when a factor's supply falls, its equilibrium price rises. Firms hire at the margin. A firm takes on another worker when the extra revenue that worker brings in exceeds the extra cost.

entries.title: Monopsony: the market with one buyer

definition.text: A market with a single dominant buyer, the buying-side mirror of a monopoly; an oligopsony has a few dominant buyers.

facts.text: A monopsonist sets the price it pays for an input instead of taking it from the market, choosing a point on the input's supply curve.
Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labour.

entries.text: A monopsony is the buying-side mirror of a monopoly: a market with a single dominant buyer. An oligopsony has a few. Instead of taking the price of an input from the market, a monopsonist sets it, choosing a point on the input's supply curve. Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labor.

Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labor.

entries.title: Derived demand: wanting inputs because people want products

definition.text: Demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make.

facts.text: An intermediate good is one used to make another, final good.
The link is direct and positive: more demand for a final product raises demand for the inputs used to make it.
If shoppers want more new cars, carmakers respond by wanting more of the inputs used to build them.
A firm's demand for labour slopes downward: when the wage rises, the quantity of labour wanted falls.

entries.text: If shoppers want more new cars, carmakers want more of the inputs used to build them. That is derived demand: demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make. The link is direct and positive. A good used to make another, final good is called an intermediate good. Labor works the same way, and a firm's demand for it slopes downward: when the wage rises, the quantity of labor wanted falls.

entries.title: The Lerner index: measuring the markup

definition.text: A measure of market power: the gap between price and marginal cost as a share of price, named after economist Abba Lerner.

facts.text: At the profit-maximising point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.
It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1; the closer to 1, the bigger the gap between price and marginal cost.

entries.text: Named after the economist Abba Lerner, the Lerner index measures market power as the gap between price and marginal cost, taken as a share of price. It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1. The closer to 1, the bigger the gap. At the profit-maximizing point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.

At the profit-maximizing point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.

entries.title: Veblen goods: when a high price is the point

definition.text: A luxury good whose demand rises as its price rises, because a high price signals status.

facts.text: Examples include diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques.
Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than extra usefulness.

entries.text: Diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques can become more wanted as they get dearer. These are Veblen goods: luxuries whose demand rises with their price, because a high price signals status. Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than for extra usefulness.
entries.text_plain: Diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques can become more wanted as they get dearer. These are Veblen goods: luxuries whose demand rises with their price, because a high price signals status. Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than for extra usefulness.

entries.title: The minimum wage: a price floor for labor

definition.text: A price floor for labour: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay.

facts.text: Set above the market wage for low-skilled work, it leads employers to hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines.
The higher wage also draws more people into the labour market, producing a surplus of labour.
Since the credibility revolution of the 1990s, minimum wages have often won strong support among economists.

entries.contested_note: Standard theory predicts a minimum wage above the market wage cuts jobs, yet since the 1990s many economists have strongly supported minimum wages.
entries.text: A minimum wage is a price floor for labor: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay. Standard theory predicts trouble if it is set above the market wage for low-skilled work. Employers hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines. The higher wage also draws more people into the labor market, producing a surplus of labor. Yet since the credibility revolution of the 1990s, minimum wages have often won strong support among economists, so the question remains contested.

entries.title: The market mechanism: prices doing the sharing

definition.text: The way buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tends to share out goods and services well.

facts.text: Prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met.
The market mechanism often cannot provide public goods well, because of problems such as the tragedy of the commons; highways needed government planning.
Free market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

entries.text: Buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tend to share out goods and services well. That is the market mechanism. Its quality depends on information: prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met. The mechanism has limits. It often cannot provide shared goods ({{ref:nature-econ-633}}) well, because of problems such as the one in {{ref:nature-econ-606}}, so highways needed government planning. Free-market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.
entries.text_plain: Buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tend to share out goods and services well. That is the market mechanism. Its quality depends on information: prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met. The mechanism has limits. It often cannot provide shared goods (Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few) well, because of problems such as the one in The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused, so highways needed government planning. Free-market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

entries.title: The zero-profit condition: competition erases profit

definition.text: The state an industry reaches when firms can enter or leave it almost freely, so that competition pushes each firm's economic profit to zero.

facts.text: If firms earn positive economic profit, newcomers join until it is gone; if they make losses, firms leave until profit rises back to zero.
The zero-profit situation is called the industry's long run and is close to perfect competition.
In gold rushes few prospectors got rich, but many people built successful businesses selling shovels.
In neoclassical models, a market economy of profit-seeking firms is compatible with zero growth because of this condition.

entries.text: In gold rushes few prospectors got rich, but many people built successful businesses selling shovels. The zero-profit condition describes where competition leads: when firms can enter or leave an industry almost freely, each firm's economic profit is pushed to zero. If firms earn positive economic profit, newcomers join until it is gone. If they make losses, firms leave until profit rises back to zero. This settled state is called the industry's long run, and it is close to perfect competition. In neoclassical models, the condition also makes a market economy of profit-seeking firms compatible with zero growth.

entries.title: Economic surplus: the gains from trading

definition.text: The total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market, made up of consumer surplus and producer surplus; also called total or social welfare.

facts.text: The sum of consumer and producer surplus is called social or total surplus, and a fall in that total caused by inefficiency is called deadweight loss.
The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous.
It is also called Marshallian surplus, after Alfred Marshall.
On a supply and demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area above the price and below the demand curve, and producer surplus the area below the price and above the supply curve.
Early writers used surplus to study food: farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs.

entries.text: Early writers used the idea of surplus to study food. Farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs. Today economic surplus means the total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market. The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous, so it is also called Marshallian surplus. It has two parts. The buyers' share, {{ref:nature-econ-339}}, is the area above the price and below the demand curve on a supply and demand diagram. The sellers' share, {{ref:nature-econ-340}}, is the area below the price and above the supply curve. Their sum is called social or total surplus, or total welfare. When inefficiency shrinks that total, the lost part is called {{ref:nature-econ-345}}.
entries.text_plain: Early writers used the idea of surplus to study food. Farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs. The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous, so it is also called Marshallian surplus. It has two parts. The buyers' share, Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get, is the area above the price and below the demand curve on a supply and demand diagram. The sellers' share, Producer surplus: the sellers' gain, is the area below the price and above the supply curve. Their sum is called social or total surplus, or total welfare. When inefficiency shrinks that total, the lost part is called Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets.

entries.title: Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets

definition.text: The loss of society's welfare when a good is produced or consumed at a quantity where its benefit to society does not equal its cost to society.

facts.text: It is the net benefit nobody gets: either goods are made that cost more than they are worth, or worthwhile goods are not made.
Unlike most losses, which are someone else's gain, deadweight loss is regained by no one.
It can come from monopoly pricing, externalities, taxes or subsidies, or binding price ceilings and floors such as a minimum wage.
If nails cost $0.10 to make and a monopolist charges $0.60, buyers who value a nail between those prices are shut out, and their lost benefit is the deadweight loss.
A $0.03 subsidy on that nail lowers its price to $0.07, so people who value it below its true $0.10 cost buy it, which also wastes resources.
In a cleaning deal worth $40 of total surplus, a $50 tax stops the trade entirely; the lost $40 is the deadweight loss, and the government collects nothing.
The more elastic supply and demand are, the bigger the deadweight loss from a tax.
Deadweight loss grows with the square of a tax: doubling the tax multiplies the loss by 4.

entries.text: Suppose a cleaning deal would create $40 of total surplus, and a $50 tax is imposed on it. The trade never happens. The government collects nothing, and the $40 simply vanishes. Externalities, taxes, and binding caps and floors on prices, such as a minimum wage, cause it too. The more elastic supply and demand are, the bigger the loss from a tax. It also grows with the square of the tax: doubling the tax multiplies the loss by 4.

entries.title: Gains from trade: why exchange pays

definition.text: The net benefits people or economies get when they are allowed to trade more freely with each other.

facts.text: Technically, they are the rise in consumer surplus plus producer surplus from lower tariffs or freer trade.
They come from specialisation, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly.
Prices draw labour and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost.

Free trade is not always best for everyone: a large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense.
Market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

entries.text: Gains from trade are the net benefits people or economies get when they can trade more freely with each other. David Ricardo first clearly stated and proved comparative advantage in 1817, and it remains the basic explanation for where they come from. Technically, they are the rise in buyers' and sellers' combined surplus that comes from lower tariffs or freer trade. They come from specialization, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly. Prices do the steering. They draw labor and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost. Freer trade is not always best for everyone. A large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense, and market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

entries.title: Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get

definition.text: The gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay.

facts.text: Drinking water usually carries a large consumer surplus: people would pay very high prices for it because they need it to survive.
The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters.
Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit, which is where the surplus comes from.
It equals the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle, otherwise it is found by integration.
A positive change in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in the person's welfare, a negative change as a loss.
When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought and new buyers enter and gain too.

entries.title: Price discrimination: different buyers, different prices

definition.text: A pricing strategy in which the same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to.

facts.text: It works by exploiting differences in buyers' willingness to pay and in how sensitive they are to price.
The seller needs market power; otherwise buyers would switch sellers or resell cheap units to those charged more.
In first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination each buyer pays their maximum, so the seller captures all consumer surplus.
Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought; third-degree charges different groups different prices, as with student and senior discounts.
The aim is to raise profit by shifting consumer surplus to the seller.
Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries; antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.
The first-, second- and third-degree categories are attributed to Pigou.

entries.text: Student and senior discounts are a form of price discrimination. Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought, and third-degree charges different groups different prices. Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries, and antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.

entries.title: Producer surplus: the sellers' gain

definition.text: The gain sellers get when the market price is higher than the least they would accept to supply a good.

facts.text: It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss.
It is shown as the area below the market price line and above the supply curve.
Higher market prices raise it; higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it.
It is used to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

entries.text: Every seller has a lowest price they would accept. Producer surplus is the gain sellers get when the market price is higher than that. It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss. On a graph it is the area below the market price line and above the supply curve. Higher market prices raise it, while higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it. Economists use it to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

entries.title: The rule of one-half: a shortcut for surplus

definition.text: A shortcut that estimates the change in consumer surplus from a small change in supply when the demand curve stays the same.

facts.text: With straight-line demand, the change in surplus is a trapezoid whose height is the price change and whose middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.

entries.text: When supply changes a little and the demand curve stays put, how much do buyers gain? The rule of one-half gives a quick estimate of the change in consumer surplus. With straight-line demand, the change is a trapezoid. Its height is the price change, and its middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.

entries.title: Harberger's triangle: the shape of lost surplus

definition.text: The triangle on a supply and demand graph that shows the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market.

facts.text: It is generally credited to Arnold Harberger, and the interventions include price floors, caps, taxes, tariffs and quotas.
It also measures the loss from a government's failure to step into a market with externalities.
A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, and the triangle's area is the surplus lost for good.
Martin Feldstein holds these losses can drag down long-run growth, while James Tobin argued their effect on the economy is small.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree on whether these triangles seriously harm long-run growth (Feldstein) or matter little (Tobin).

entries.title: Market clearing: no surplus, no shortage

definition.text: The process by which a market's price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage.

facts.text: The market-clearing price, also called the equilibrium price, is the one at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
A price above it builds up unsold stock; a price below it leaves buyers short, sometimes unable to find the product at any price.
After an earthquake destroys homes, a housing shortage pushes prices up, builders build more, and supply rises until it meets the new demand.
Shops discount leftover Christmas decorations after Christmas until shoppers buy the excess supply.
From about 1785 to 1935 most economists took market clearing for granted, until the Great Depression's long mass unemployment led Keynes and others to doubt it.
Most economists now see continuous market clearing as unrealistic but useful for long-run analysis.

entries.contested_note: Since the Great Depression economists have disagreed over whether prices adjust quickly enough for markets to clear, with some blaming sticky prices and others blaming unions or government policy.

entries.title: Shortages: when buyers want more than there is

definition.text: A situation in which people want to buy more of a product than is available at the going price; also called excess demand.

facts.text: It is the opposite of an excess supply, or surplus.
In a simple market, excess demand pushes the price up until demand matches supply; a shortage persists only when something stops the price rising.
Then something other than price, such as first come first served or a lottery, decides who gets the good.
Causes include price ceilings, bans on selling a product and suppliers choosing not to raise prices.
Shortages bring black markets, queues and rationing, more demand for substitutes, and wasted time that lowers overall wealth.
In the 1980s Soviet Union, prices fixed artificially low left people queuing for cars, apartments and clothing.
Economists and historians note that lasting shortages and famines have mostly been caused by war, price controls and repressive regimes rather than overpopulation.

entries.title: Price ceilings: a legal maximum price

definition.text: A limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service.

facts.text: Governments set price ceilings to protect consumers from goods becoming too expensive.
Economists generally agree that consumer price controls fail at their aims, and many advise against them.
A ceiling set below the market equilibrium price leads to a shortage of supply.
Ceilings can even raise prices by giving competing firms a shared target to collude on; US states with an 18 percent interest cap saw rates just below it.
Ceilings on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and mean flats do not go to those who value them most.
Venezuela's food price ceilings from 2003 caused shortages and hoarding.
Some economists, such as Isabella Weber, argue for price caps to fight sellers' inflation, and Paul Krugman became open to them.

entries.contested_note: Most economists say price ceilings backfire, but some, such as Isabella Weber and later Paul Krugman, support price caps against inflation.

entries.title: Rent control: a ceiling on housing costs

definition.text: A price ceiling on housing rents, such as the US rent controls of the 1940s brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration.

facts.text: As economic models predicted, the US controls cut the supply of rental homes available to returning veterans.
Homeownership and homes for sale rose at the same time, likely because landlords turned rentals into homes for sale.

entries.title: Profit maximization: where the next unit stops paying

definition.text: The process by which a firm chooses the price, inputs and output that give it the highest possible total profit.

facts.text: Mainstream economics assumes the firm is a rational agent that wants to maximise profit, total revenue minus total cost.
Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit; marginal cost is the extra cost of making it.
Profit is highest where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; if marginal revenue is larger, producing more adds profit.
Under perfect competition the firm's demand curve is its marginal revenue curve, a horizontal line at the market price.
In the short run a change in fixed costs does not change the profit-maximising output or price, because fixed costs are treated as sunk.
Where extra customers cost almost nothing, such as seats on a scheduled flight, maximising profit means maximising revenue.
Some profit-maximising behaviour harms consumers and is regulated by competition law.
Behavioural economics replaces strict profit maximisation with bounded rationality in its models.

entries.text: Every firm in a standard textbook wants one thing. Mainstream economics treats the firm as a rational agent that seeks the most profit, meaning total revenue minus total cost. Profit maximization is the process of choosing the price, inputs and output that reach that peak. The answer lies at the margin. Marginal revenue is the extra money from selling one more unit, and marginal cost is the extra cost of making it. As long as marginal revenue is larger, producing more adds profit. Profit peaks where the two are equal. Under perfect competition the firm's demand curve is its marginal revenue curve, a flat line at the market price. Some costs do not change the decision at all. In the short run, a change in overhead such as rent, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-307}}, leaves the best output and price untouched, because those costs are treated as sunk. Where an extra customer costs almost nothing, as with a seat on a scheduled flight, maximizing profit simply means maximizing revenue. The pursuit has limits. Some profit-maximizing behavior harms consumers, and competition law regulates it. And the newer field of {{ref:nature-econ-021}} replaces strict profit maximization with a more limited kind of rationality in its models.

entries.title: The production function: from inputs to output

definition.text: A technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs.

facts.text: It is usually taken to give the maximum output obtainable from each combination of inputs, so it traces a frontier.
It links physical inputs to physical outputs; prices and costs are not part of it.
Written Q = f(X1, ..., Xn), its inputs are factors such as capital, labour, land or raw materials, and no inputs means no output.
It is used to define marginal product and to study allocative efficiency.
A production function homogeneous of degree above 1 shows increasing returns to scale, below 1 decreasing, and exactly 1 constant returns.
In macroeconomics, aggregate production functions split growth into the part from more capital and the part from better technology.
The Cobb–Douglas form, first developed in 1927, was the first aggregate production function to be estimated and presented to economists.
Some economists reject aggregate production functions, and a 1950s-1970s debate begun by Joan Robinson questioned how capital is measured.

entries.contested_note: Economists have long debated whether aggregate production functions and the measurement of capital in them are valid.
entries.text: Give a workshop more workers and more machines, and how much more will it make? A production function answers that question. It is a technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs. It is usually read as the maximum output each combination of inputs can give, so it traces a frontier of the possible. Economists write it as Q = f(X1, ..., Xn), where Q is output and the Xs are inputs such as capital, labor, land or raw materials. No inputs means no output. Prices and costs play no part; the function links physical things to physical things. From it economists define the extra output from one more unit of an input, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-310}}. It also shows how output responds when every input grows together, which {{ref:nature-econ-317}} explores. For whole economies, aggregate production functions split growth into the part that comes from more capital and the part that comes from better technology. The Cobb–Douglas form, first developed in 1927, was the first aggregate production function to be estimated and presented to economists. Not everyone accepts these tools. Some economists reject aggregate production functions outright. A debate from the 1950s to the 1970s, begun by Joan Robinson, questioned how capital can be measured at all. Economists have long argued over whether such functions are valid.

entries.title: Fixed costs: the bills that arrive regardless

definition.text: A business cost, also called overhead, that does not change with how much the business produces.

facts.text: Fixed costs tend to recur, like monthly rent or interest, and are often capital costs.
For a bakery, rent and the phone line are fixed costs, while wages are variable because more output needs more workers.
They are fixed only for a period by contract, and in the long run there are no fixed costs because all inputs can change.
Fixed costs act as an entry barrier for new businesses.
Some costs are mixed or semi-variable, such as a phone bill with a fixed charge plus calls.
Accounting and economics use the terms differently, and in recent years fixed costs have come to exceed variable costs at many companies.

entries.text: A bakery pays the same rent whether its ovens run all day or sit cold. That rent is a fixed cost, also called overhead: a business cost that does not change with how much the business produces. Fixed costs tend to recur, like monthly rent or interest, and are often capital costs. The bakery's phone line is another. Its wages are not, because more bread needs more workers. 'Fixed' has a time limit. Costs stay fixed only for the period a contract sets, and in the long run there are none, because every input can change. Some costs are mixed, such as a phone bill with a fixed charge plus calls. Fixed costs also act as a barrier that keeps new businesses out. Accounting and economics use the terms differently, and in recent years fixed costs have come to exceed the costs that rise with output at many companies.

entries.title: The short run and the long run: time in economics

definition.text: In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully.

facts.text: In microeconomics the long run has no fixed inputs, so firms can change their capital or enter and leave industries; in the short run some inputs are fixed.
In macroeconomics the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted.
Alfred Marshall introduced the distinction in his 1890 Principles of Economics; there is no hard rule for how long each period is.
In the long run firms enter, exit or resize their plants in response to profits and losses, moving toward minimum long-run average cost.
All actual production happens in the short run, where only variable inputs such as labour and raw materials can change output.
In the short run a profit-maximising firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts it when above.
Keynes criticised neglect of the short run with the remark 'In the long run, we are all dead'.

entries.text: Time changes what a business can do. In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully. Alfred Marshall introduced the distinction in his 1890 Principles of Economics. There is still no hard rule for how long either period lasts. In the short run some inputs are fixed, so only variable inputs such as labor and raw materials can change output. All actual production happens here. A profit-maximizing firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts back when it is above. In the long run nothing is fixed. Firms can change their capital, resize their plants, or enter and leave industries in response to profits and losses. That movement pushes them toward the lowest possible cost per unit. Economists who study whole economies use the terms a little differently. For them the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted. Keynes thought economists neglected the short run in favor of that distant horizon. 'In the long run,' he remarked, 'we are all dead.'

In the short run some inputs are fixed, so only variable inputs such as labor and raw materials can change output. All actual production happens here. A profit-maximizing firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts back when it is above. In the long run nothing is fixed. Firms can change their capital, resize their plants, or enter and leave industries in response to profits and losses. That movement pushes them toward the lowest possible cost per unit. Economists who study whole economies use the terms a little differently. For them the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted. Keynes thought economists neglected the short run in favor of that distant horizon. 'In the long run,' he remarked, 'we are all dead.'

entries.title: Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything

definition.text: How much a firm's output rises, in proportion, when it increases all its inputs together in the long run.

facts.text: Constant returns: doubling all inputs doubles output; decreasing returns: output less than doubles; increasing returns: output more than doubles.
Decreasing returns come mainly from harder management and coordination as scale grows; increasing returns from efficiency gains of larger scale.
A firm may have increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output.
In mainstream theory returns to scale are set purely by technology, not by market conditions.
With fixed input prices, constant, decreasing and increasing returns mean constant, rising and falling long-run average costs.
For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if 1, and decreasing if less.
Path-dependent increasing returns to scale help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel energy systems.

entries.text: Double every worker and machine a firm uses, and what happens to output? Returns to scale is the answer: how much output rises, in proportion, when all inputs grow together in the long run. Constant returns mean output doubles too. Decreasing returns mean it less than doubles, mainly because management and coordination get harder as scale grows. Increasing returns mean it more than doubles, thanks to the efficiency gains of size. One firm can show all three, with increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output. Mainstream theory holds that technology alone sets the pattern, not market conditions. With fixed input prices, constant returns mean flat long-run costs per unit, decreasing returns mean rising ones and increasing returns mean falling ones. For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if they sum to 1, and decreasing if less. Increasing returns can also trap whole economies. Path-dependent increasing returns help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel energy systems.

entries.title: Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different

definition.text: A market with many producers selling products that are differentiated, for example by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes.

facts.text: Textbook examples include restaurants, cereals, clothing, shoes and city service industries.
Products differ in real or perceived ways such as style, reputation or location, but remain close substitutes.
Each firm has a little market power, facing a downward-sloping demand curve, so it can raise its price without losing all customers.
Entry and exit are free, so economic profit can be positive in the short run but approaches zero in the long run.
It is inefficient: firms charge more than marginal cost and operate with excess capacity, below the output of minimum average cost.
Product variety can raise total utility by better meeting people's wants, while heavy advertising is a common concern.
Edward Chamberlin pioneered the theory in his 1933 book, alongside Joan Robinson's work on imperfect competition.

entries.text: A street of restaurants is a lesson in economics. Each offers something slightly different, yet each can stand in for the others. This is monopolistic competition: many producers selling products that differ, by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes. Differences may be real or perceived, in style, reputation or location. Cereals, clothing, shoes and city service industries are other textbook cases. Each firm has a little market power. Its demand curve slopes down, so it can raise its price without losing every customer. Entry and exit are free, so any economic profit in the short run shrinks toward zero in the long run. The result is inefficient. Firms charge more than marginal cost and run with spare capacity, below the output where cost per unit is lowest. Variety can raise total utility by meeting people's wants better, while heavy advertising is a common concern. Edward Chamberlin pioneered the theory in his 1933 book, alongside Joan Robinson's work on imperfect competition.

entries.title: Marginal product: what one more worker adds

definition.text: The extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same.

facts.text: With divisible inputs it is the derivative of the production function with respect to that input.
As more of one input is added to a fixed amount of another, marginal product first rises, then falls, and can finally turn negative.
When total product reaches its maximum, marginal product is zero.
The marginal product of labour is the slope of the total product curve.
In neoclassical theory of competitive markets the marginal product of labour equals the real wage.
Output is usually measured ignoring external costs and benefits.
The Cambridge capital controversy showed the claim that capital's marginal product equals its return cannot generally hold in multi-good models.

entries.contested_note: The Cambridge capital controversy disputed whether the marginal product of capital equals its rate of return outside one-good models.
entries.text: Add workers to a kitchen of fixed size and output first climbs, then slows, and can finally fall. Each step measures the marginal product. It is the extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same. The rise-then-fall pattern is general. As more of one input is added to a fixed amount of another, marginal product first rises, then falls, and can turn negative. When total output reaches its peak, marginal product is zero. With inputs that can be divided finely, it is the derivative, or rate of change, of the production function. For labor it is the slope of the total product curve. Neoclassical theory says that in competitive markets the marginal product of labor equals the real wage. Output here is usually measured ignoring external costs and benefits. For capital the idea is disputed. The Cambridge capital controversy showed that capital's marginal product cannot generally equal its return once a model has more than one good.

entries.title: The theory of the firm: why businesses exist

definition.text: A set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations.

facts.text: The nature of the firm covers its origin, survival, behaviour, structure and relation to the market.
It asks why not every transaction goes through the market, and where the boundary between firm and market lies.
Around the First World War economists shifted from industry-level to firm-level analysis as perfect competition no longer described how firms behaved.
Its main frameworks include transaction cost theory, managerial economics, behavioural theory, the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities.
Managerial theories by Baumol, Marris and Williamson suggest managers pursue their own utility, for example maximising sales once profit satisfies shareholders.
Agency theory explains the governance problems that come from separating ownership and control.

entries.text: If markets coordinate so well, why do businesses exist at all? The theory of the firm is the set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations. It covers their origin, survival, behavior, structure and relation to the market. Its central puzzle is why not every transaction goes through the market, and where the boundary between firm and market lies. The field took shape around the First World War. Economists then shifted from studying whole industries to single firms, because perfect competition no longer described how firms behaved. Its main frameworks look at the costs of using markets, managerial economics, behavioral theory, the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities. Managerial theories by Baumol, Marris and Williamson suggest managers pursue their own goals, for example maximizing sales once profit satisfies shareholders. Agency theory explains the governance problems that arise when ownership and control are separated.

entries.title: Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete

definition.text: A group of independent firms that agree not to compete with each other so as to raise their profits and dominate a market.

facts.text: Cartels fix and raise prices by creating artificial shortages through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas.
They are inherently unstable because each member is tempted to cheat, selling below the agreed price or above its quota.
Outsiders often respond to the shortage by producing more, using the good more efficiently or investing in substitutes.
A survey of studies found the median cartel price increase over the last 200 years was about 23 percent, 28 percent for international and 18 percent for domestic cartels.
Discovered 20th-century cartels lasted on average 5 to 8 years.
The US Sherman Act of 1890 was the first enforced law against cartels; price fixing is now illegal in more than 140 countries.
Oligopolies may form cartels; OPEC is one of the best-known international cartels.
Adam Smith argued cartels were undesirable because they could limit production and the quality of goods.

entries.text: Rivals who agree to stop competing can make a lot of money, for a while. A cartel is a group of independent firms that agree not to compete so as to raise their profits and dominate a market. Cartels raise prices by creating artificial shortages, through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas. A survey of studies put the median cartel price increase over the last 200 years at about 23 percent. International cartels reached 28 percent and domestic ones 18 percent. Yet cartels are inherently unstable. Each member is tempted to cheat, selling below the agreed price or above its quota. Outsiders respond too, producing more, using the good more efficiently or investing in substitutes. Discovered 20th-century cartels lasted on average 5 to 8 years. Oligopolies may form cartels, and OPEC is one of the best-known international ones. Adam Smith thought cartels undesirable because they could limit production and the quality of goods. The US Sherman Act of 1890 was the first enforced law against them. Price fixing is now illegal in more than 140 countries.

entries.title: Variable costs: the costs that grow with every unit

definition.text: A cost that changes as the quantity a business produces changes.

facts.text: Variable costs equal the sum of marginal costs over all units produced; with fixed costs they make up total cost.
Common examples are sales commission, labour and raw materials, such as the cloth and labour in each shirt a clothing maker produces.
Some costs are semi-variable, like electricity with a fixed standing charge plus a usage charge.
Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on the time horizon: over five years all costs can become variable.
Not all variable costs are direct costs; variable manufacturing overhead is indirect.

entries.text: Every shirt a clothing maker produces needs its own cloth and its own labor. Those are variable costs: costs that change as the quantity a business produces changes. Sales commission, labor and raw materials are the common examples. Add up the marginal cost of every unit made and the total is the variable cost. Add fixed costs to that and the result is total cost. Some costs straddle the line. Electricity often comes as a fixed standing charge plus a charge for use, which makes it semi-variable. The time horizon matters too. Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on how far ahead one looks, and over five years all costs can become variable. Nor is every variable cost a direct cost: variable manufacturing overhead is indirect.

entries.title: Average cost: what each unit really costs

definition.text: Average cost, or unit cost, is total cost divided by the number of units produced.

facts.text: It is an important factor in how businesses decide what price to charge.
A typical short-run average cost curve is U-shaped: fixed costs are spread over more units at first, then rising marginal costs from diminishing returns push it up.
When marginal cost is below average cost, average cost falls; when above, it rises; the rising marginal cost curve crosses average cost at its lowest point.
A factory built for a set output has high average cost below it from idle equipment and above it from bottlenecks.
Average fixed cost keeps falling toward zero as output grows, and the gap between average cost and average variable cost equals average fixed cost.
With high fixed costs and constant marginal cost, as in hydroelectric generation, average cost slopes down continuously toward marginal cost.
Productive efficiency means goods are supplied at the lowest possible average total cost.

entries.text: A factory built for a set output is cheapest to run at that output. Below it, equipment sits idle; above it, bottlenecks build. The measure behind that pattern is average cost, or unit cost: total cost divided by the number of units produced. It weighs heavily in how businesses decide what price to charge. A typical short-run average cost curve is shaped like a U. At first, fixed costs are spread over more units, so the average falls. Then diminishing returns push marginal costs up and drag the average with them. The rule linking the two is simple. When marginal cost is below average cost, the average falls; when it is above, the average rises. So the rising marginal cost curve crosses average cost at its lowest point. Average fixed cost keeps falling toward zero as output grows. Where fixed costs are high and marginal cost is constant, as in hydroelectric generation, average cost slopes down continuously toward marginal cost. Supplying goods at the lowest possible average total cost is the mark of {{ref:nature-econ-200}}.

entries.title: Technological change: how new ways of making things spread

definition.text: The overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes.

facts.text: It covers invention, commercialisation, research and development, continual improvement and diffusion through industry or society.
The old linear model of innovation has largely given way to one with innovation at every stage of research, development, diffusion and use.
Improvement is often modelled as a learning curve of falling costs, as with fuel cells becoming cheaper every year.
Models such as climate models once treated it as external but now more often treat it as something policy can influence.
In economics it is a change in the set of feasible production possibilities.
In market economies profit is a powerful driver, so technologies that meet social needs but promise little profit may never reach market.
By the Jevons paradox, efficiency improvements can raise rather than lower total use of a resource.

entries.text: Fuel cells get cheaper every year. That steady decline is technological change at work: the overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes. It covers invention, commercialization, research and development, continual improvement and diffusion through industry or society. Economists put it more narrowly, as a change in the set of feasible production possibilities. The old picture was a straight line from laboratory to market. That linear model has largely given way to one with innovation at every stage of research, development, diffusion and use. Improvement is often modeled as a learning curve of falling costs. How models treat it has shifted too. Models of the climate and other systems once treated technological change as coming from outside; now they more often treat it as something policy can influence. Markets give it direction. In market economies profit is a powerful driver, so technologies that meet social needs but promise little profit may never reach the market. And efficiency does not always save resources. As {{ref:nature-eecon-163}} explains, efficiency improvements can raise rather than lower total use of a resource.

entries.title: Cournot competition: rivals choosing how much to make

definition.text: An economic model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce.

facts.text: Firms sell an identical product, each firm's output affects the price, and each seeks the most profit given rivals' output.
Each firm takes rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on it.
The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce.
Antoine Augustin Cournot set it out in 1838 to describe a spring-water market with two suppliers.
Its equilibrium, where no firm wants to change output, was the first use of what is now called a Nash equilibrium.
Prices are lower and quantities higher under duopoly than under monopoly.
As the number of firms grows the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many.
Joseph Bertrand criticised it, arguing that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.

entries.text: In 1838 Antoine Augustin Cournot described a market with just two suppliers of spring water. His model became Cournot competition: a model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce. The firms sell an identical product, and each firm's output affects the price. Each takes its rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on that remainder. The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce. The resting point, where no firm wants to change its output, was the first use of an idea now known as {{ref:nature-econ-718}}. Prices are lower and quantities higher with two firms than under monopoly. As the number of firms grows, the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many. Joseph Bertrand objected that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.
entries.text_plain: In 1838 Antoine Augustin Cournot described a market with just two suppliers of spring water. The firms sell an identical product, and each firm's output affects the price. Each takes its rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on that remainder. The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce. The resting point, where no firm wants to change its output, was the first use of an idea now known as Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone. Prices are lower and quantities higher with two firms than under monopoly. As the number of firms grows, the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many. Joseph Bertrand objected that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.

entries.title: Can machines replace nature? Resources in production functions

definition.text: The debate over how, or whether, standard production functions should include natural resources such as energy.

facts.text: Natural resources are usually left out of production functions.
Solow and Stiglitz added natural resources in a way that let man-made capital fully substitute for them.
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called this a 'conjuring trick' because it ignored the laws of thermodynamics; neither Solow nor Stiglitz replied.
Treating energy as an independent input gives a form like Q = A L^β K^α E^χ, which later work says misrepresents how energy affects production.
An alternative makes labour and capital themselves depend on energy, Q = f(L(E), K(E)).
If a region cannot get the resources needed to build or maintain machines, their output eventually falls to near zero.

entries.contested_note: Georgescu-Roegen disputed Solow and Stiglitz's assumption that man-made capital can fully substitute for natural resources.
entries.text: Standard production functions usually leave natural resources out. Labor and capital go in; the energy and materials that feed them often do not. This debate asks how, or whether, they should be included. Solow and Stiglitz added natural resources, but in a way that let man-made capital fully substitute for them. In that model, enough machines could always make up for lost resources. The economist Georgescu-Roegen called this a 'conjuring trick', because it ignored the physical limits described in {{ref:nature-eecon-118}}. Neither Solow nor Stiglitz replied. Others have tried to put energy in directly. Treating energy as an independent input gives a form like Q = A L^β K^α E^χ, where L is labor, K is capital and E is energy. Later work says this misrepresents how energy affects production. An alternative makes labor and capital themselves depend on energy, written Q = f(L(E), K(E)). The point is physical. If a region cannot get the resources needed to build or maintain its machines, their output eventually falls to near zero. Whether man-made capital can fully replace natural resources remains disputed, with Georgescu-Roegen's challenge still at the heart of the argument.

entries.title: Isoquants: many routes to the same output

definition.text: A curve joining all the combinations of two or more inputs that produce the same quantity of output.

facts.text: Its axes are two inputs such as labour and capital, and it is a level set of the production function.
It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, but output on it can be measured exactly in physical units.
Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other; because this diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin.
Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio.
The least-cost input mix is where an isoquant touches an isocost line, so the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices.
On an isoquant map, isoquants spreading further apart as output rises signal decreasing returns to scale, and closer together increasing returns.
Two isoquants can never cross.

entries.text: A factory can make the same output with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines. An isoquant is the curve joining all the combinations of inputs that produce the same quantity of output. Drawn with two inputs such as labor and capital on its axes, it is a level set of the production function, a slice taken at one output. It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, except that output can be measured exactly in physical units. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other. Because that rate diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin. Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio. The cheapest input mix lies where an isoquant touches an isocost line, a line of equal spending. There the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices. Two isoquants never cross.
entries.text_plain: A factory can make the same output with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines. It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, except that output can be measured exactly in physical units. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other. Because that rate diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin. The cheapest input mix lies where an isoquant touches an isocost line, a line of equal spending. There the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices. Two isoquants never cross.

entries.title: Why firms exist: Coase's answer
entries.article: Theory of the firm#Transaction cost theory

definition.text: Ronald Coase's explanation that firms exist because organising some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange.

facts.text: Coase set out the theory in his 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm', one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market.
It explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale rather than relying on increasing returns.
Coase asked why all production is not carried on by one big firm, the starting point for the economics of outsourcing.
Later economists note the line between within-firm and between-firm transactions is blurred by intermediate forms such as inter-firm cooperation.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm
entries.text: In his 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm', Coase asked a deceptively simple question. Why is all production not carried on by one big firm? His answer was that firms exist because organizing some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange. The costs of using markets, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-641}}, set where a firm ends and the market begins. The essay was one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market. It became the starting point for the economics of outsourcing. It also explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale, rather than relying on increasing returns. Later economists note that the line between dealings inside a firm and dealings between firms is blurred by in-between forms, such as cooperation between firms.
