The essay was one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market. It became the starting point for the economics of outsourcing. It also explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale, rather than relying on increasing returns. Later economists note that the line between dealings inside a firm and dealings between firms is blurred by in-between forms, such as cooperation between firms.

entries.title: Long-run average cost: unit cost when everything can change

definition.text: The unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed.

facts.text: The firm is assumed to pick the cheapest mix of inputs for each output level.
The curve is most often U-shaped, sloping down where there are economies of scale and up where there are diseconomies of scale.
If input prices do not change with the firm's purchases, economies of scale arise exactly when the production function has increasing returns to scale.
Under perfect competition, long-run equilibrium has every firm producing at the lowest point of this curve.
Where it keeps falling indefinitely, the biggest firm has a cost advantage and the industry tends to become a natural monopoly, as in water and electricity supply.

entries.text: Given enough time, a firm can rebuild itself around any output it chooses. Long-run average cost is the unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed. The firm is assumed to pick the cheapest mix of inputs for each output level. The curve is most often U-shaped. It slopes down where growing bigger cuts unit costs and up where it raises them, effects explored in {{ref:nature-econ-303}}. If input prices do not change with the firm's purchases, falling unit costs come exactly when the production function has increasing returns to scale. Under perfect competition, long-run equilibrium has every firm producing at the curve's lowest point. Sometimes the curve keeps falling indefinitely. Then the biggest firm has a cost advantage, and the industry tends to become a natural monopoly, as in water and electricity supply.

entries.title: Economies of scale: why bigger can be cheaper

definition.text: The cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less.

facts.text: They occur when average costs fall as output increases.
Common sources are bulk buying, specialised managers, cheaper borrowing, spreading advertising costs and returns to scale in production.
Some have a physical basis: by the square–cube law a vessel's surface grows with the square of its size but its volume with the cube.
A rough engineering rule says capital cost changes with the 0.6 power of the capacity ratio.
They help explain why firms grow large in some industries and patterns in international trade.
Economies of scale concern a firm's costs, while returns to scale describe how outputs respond to inputs in the production function.
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) gave the first systematic analysis, through the division of labour.
Economies of scale and learning-by-doing can lower the costs of climate technologies over time.

entries.text: Make a vessel bigger and its surface grows with the square of its size, but its volume grows with the cube. That rule, the square–cube law, is one physical root of economies of scale. These are the cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less. Put simply, they occur when average costs fall as output increases. Most sources are not physical. Large firms buy in bulk, hire specialized managers, borrow more cheaply and spread advertising costs over more sales. Returns to scale in production add to the effect. Engineers even use a rough rule: capital cost changes with the 0.6 power of the capacity ratio, so a plant with more capacity costs proportionally less to build. The two ideas are easy to confuse. Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) gave the first systematic analysis, through the division of labor. Economies of scale help explain why firms grow large in some industries, and they shape patterns in trade between countries, described in {{ref:nature-pol-001}}. They matter for the climate too. Together with learning by doing, they can lower the costs of climate technologies over time.

entries.title: Cournot's dilemma: why scale does not always breed monopoly
entries.article: Economies of scale#Economies of scale and the tendency towards monopoly: "Cournot's dilemma"

definition.text: The puzzle that strong economies of scale should logically lead to monopoly, yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes.

facts.text: Marshall noted Cournot's premises implied the first firm to get a good start would monopolise its trade, and named factors such as founders' deaths that limit this.
Morroni argues that once knowledge and the organisation of transactions are included, economies of scale do not always lead to monopoly.

entries.text: If bigger always means cheaper, the first firm to get a good start should swallow its whole trade. Alfred Marshall saw that Cournot's premises implied exactly that. Yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes. The puzzle is Cournot's dilemma. Marshall named factors that limit the runaway, such as the deaths of founders. Morroni argues that once knowledge and the organization of transactions are counted, economies of scale do not always lead to monopoly.

entries.title: External economies of scale: savings shared by an industry
entries.article: Economies of scale#External economies of scale

definition.text: Cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one.

facts.text: They tend to be more common than internal economies of scale.
The entry of new firms lowers average cost for all firms, while internal economies help only the single firm.
Sraffa argued such economies are rarely met with and that, under perfect competition, economies of scale should be excluded.

entries.text: Sometimes a firm gets cheaper because its whole industry grows. External economies of scale are cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one. When new firms enter, average cost falls for all of them, while internal economies help only the single firm that grows. External economies tend to be more common than internal ones. Sraffa disagreed: he argued such economies are rarely met with, and that under perfect competition economies of scale should be excluded.

entries.title: Learning and growth economies: getting cheaper with experience
entries.article: Economies of scale#Learning and growth economies

definition.text: Dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from experience, rather than from size itself.

facts.text: Learning by doing improves skills and brings small innovations that steadily lower average costs.
Learning economies rise with cumulative production, the experience curve.
Growth economies arise when expanding lets a firm use resources or skills it had not fully used.

entries.text: Experience cuts costs. Learning and growth economies are dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from practice, rather than from size itself. Learning by doing improves skills and brings small innovations that steadily lower average costs. These learning economies rise with cumulative production, a pattern called the experience curve. Growth economies are different. They arise when expanding lets a firm use resources or skills it had not fully used.

entries.title: The marginal revenue product rule: when to hire one more
entries.article: Profit maximization#Marginal product of labor, marginal revenue product of labor, and profit maximization

definition.text: The rule that a firm maximises profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost.

facts.text: For labour the rule is MRP_L = MC_L.
The marginal revenue product is the change in total revenue per unit change in the input.

entries.text: Should a firm hire one more worker? The marginal revenue product rule says yes, as long as that worker brings in at least what they cost. Formally, a firm maximizes profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost. The marginal revenue product is the change in total revenue for each unit change in the input. For labor the rule is written MRP_L = MC_L: the marginal revenue product of labor equals its marginal cost.

entries.title: Stages of production: the phases of adding inputs

definition.text: The three ranges into which a production function is divided according to how output per unit of the variable input changes.

facts.text: In stage 1 output per unit of the variable input rises to a peak, so a price-taking firm always produces beyond it.
In stage 2 output still rises but at a decreasing rate, with average and marginal product both falling.

entries.text: Adding more of one input to a fixed plant passes through distinct phases. Economists divide a production function into three stages, according to how output per unit of the variable input changes. In stage 1, output per unit of the variable input rises to a peak. A price-taking firm, one too small to move the market price, always produces beyond this stage. In stage 2 output still rises, but at a decreasing rate, with average and marginal product both falling.

entries.title: Asset specificity: when assets are tied together

definition.text: Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use.

facts.text: If such assets are owned by different firms, the parties get locked in and bargain at length over the gains from trade.
Repeated or long transactions need renegotiation, raising transaction costs further.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm
Property rights theory of the firm
entries.text: Some assets are valuable together and worth far less apart. Asset specificity is Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use. If such assets are owned by different firms, the parties get locked in and bargain at length over the gains from trade. Repeated or long transactions need renegotiating, which raises the costs of dealing further. Bringing the assets into one firm is the way out.

entries.title: The behavioral theory of the firm: good enough, not best

definition.text: An approach, developed by Cyert and March, that explains how decisions are actually made inside firms, going beyond neoclassical economics.

facts.text: It builds on Herbert Simon's idea that limited cognitive ability allows only bounded rationality in complex, uncertain situations.
People and groups therefore 'satisfice', aiming for realistic goals rather than maximum utility or profit.
The neoclassical theory of the firm was not seriously challenged by managerial and behavioural alternatives until the 1960s.

entries.title: Ownership and the hold-up problem: who should own the assets

definition.text: The approach of Grossman, Hart and Moore that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete.

facts.text: In modern contract theory the theory of the firm is often identified with this property rights approach.
Its seminal works, Grossman and Hart (1986), Hart and Moore (1990) and Hart (1995), built the incomplete contracting paradigm.
Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment and so invests too little, the hold-up problem.
The approach explains the pros and cons of merging firms and has also been applied to public good provision and privatization.

entries.title: The resource-based view: advantage from rare resources
entries.article: Theory of the firm#The resource-based and knowledge-based theories

definition.text: The view that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

facts.text: It grew from Edith Penrose's 1959 argument that a firm is a collection of productive resources whose growth depends on managers finding new uses for idle ones.
Wernerfelt (1984) and Barney (1991) developed the resource-based view.

distinct_from: Transaction cost theory of the firm

entries.text: In 1959 Edith Penrose described a firm as a collection of productive resources. Its growth, she argued, depends on managers finding new uses for resources lying idle. From that argument grew the resource-based view of the firm, developed by Wernerfelt (1984) and Barney (1991). It holds that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

entries.title: The shutdown rule: when to keep losing money

definition.text: The short-run rule that a firm should keep producing as long as its revenue covers its variable costs, and shut down if it does not.

facts.text: A firm earning more than variable cost but less than total cost keeps operating while making an economic loss.
In the short run fixed costs are paid even at zero output, so they do not affect the decision.

entries.text: A firm can lose money and still be right to stay open. The shutdown rule says that in the short run a firm should keep producing while its revenue covers its variable costs. If revenue falls short, it should shut down. Fixed costs drop out of the decision, because in the short run they must be paid even at zero output. So a firm earning more than its variable cost but less than its total cost keeps operating. It makes an economic loss, but a smaller one than closing would bring.

entries.title: Induced technological change: steering invention with prices

definition.text: The hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices.

facts.text: Climate policy that makes fossil energy relatively more expensive is the standard example.
Empirical evidence that policy induces innovation is still lacking, partly because of long-term policy uncertainty.
The related idea of directed technical change stresses price-driven direction rather than policy-driven scale.

entries.text: Make fossil energy relatively more expensive, and invention may turn toward other kinds of energy. Induced technological change is the hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices. Climate policy is the standard example. Yet evidence that policy actually induces innovation is still lacking, partly because of long-term policy uncertainty. A related idea, directed technical change, stresses price-driven direction rather than policy-driven scale.

entries.title: Neutral technical change: which input does progress favor

definition.text: Ways of classifying technical progress by which input's productivity it raises.

facts.text: Hicks-neutral change, after John Hicks (1932), leaves the ratio of capital's and labour's marginal products unchanged at a given capital-labour ratio.
Harrod-neutral change is labour-augmenting and Solow-neutral change is capital-augmenting.

entries.text: Progress does not lift every input equally. Economists classify technical change by which input's productivity it raises. Hicks-neutral change, named after John Hicks (1932), leaves the ratio of capital's and labor's marginal products unchanged at a given mix of capital and labor. Harrod-neutral change is labor-augmenting, making each worker effectively count for more. Solow-neutral change is capital-augmenting, doing the same for machines.

entries.title: Technology diffusion: the S-curve of adoption

definition.text: The spread of a technology through a society or industry.

facts.text: Adoption usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then rapid, then levelling off as the market saturates.
Everett Rogers named five attributes that speed acceptance: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability.
Mass media mostly build awareness, while face-to-face contact mostly reduces the uncertainty that blocks adoption.

entries.title: Economic efficiency: getting the most from what we have

definition.text: An economy or market is efficient when it gets the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources it has; economists usually mean allocative (Pareto) or productive efficiency.

facts.text: Allocative or Pareto efficiency means no change could help one person without harming another; productive efficiency means no more of one good can be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost.
The two ideas are not the same: a market can be allocatively efficient without being productively efficient, or the other way round.
Because productive resources are scarce, they must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets produced.
One school of thought stresses the distortions that governments create; another stresses the distortions that markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them.
The first welfare theorem says a perfectly competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient, but this only holds without market imperfections, which are significant in real markets.
Efficiency in the Pareto sense says nothing about equality or the overall well-being of a society.
Removing one market distortion does not always raise efficiency: if another distortion cannot be removed, the theory of the second best says efficiency may even fall.
Many economists consider carbon pricing the most economically efficient way to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

entries.text: An economy can be efficient and still deeply unequal. Economic efficiency means getting the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources available. Economists usually mean one of two things by it. The first asks whether any change could help one person without harming another; it is named after Vilfredo Pareto and explored in {{ref:nature-econ-178}}. The second asks whether more of one good could be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-200}}. The two need not go together. A market can pass one test and fail the other. Both matter because productive resources are scarce. They must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets made. Theory says a perfectly competitive equilibrium passes the first test, but only without market imperfections, and these are significant in real markets. Efficiency in this sense says nothing about equality or a society's overall well-being. Removing one distortion does not always help either: if another cannot be removed, efficiency may even fall. Economists also split over who distorts more. One school stresses the distortions governments create; another stresses those markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them. Many economists consider putting a price on carbon, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-239}}, the most efficient way to cut the release of heat-trapping gases, described in {{ref:nature-eco-163}}.

entries.title: Pareto efficiency: when no one can gain without someone losing

definition.text: A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off.

facts.text: A Pareto improvement is a change that leaves at least one person better off and nobody worse off; Pareto efficiency is reached once no such change is left.
Example: if Smith owns an apple but wants an orange, and Jones owns an orange but wants an apple, the situation is inefficient because trading makes both better off.
It is named after Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and income distribution.
Pareto called it 'optimal', but it does not pick one best outcome; it only marks out a set of outcomes, which is why 'efficiency' fits better.
Pareto efficiency does not mean fairness: an economy where a wealthy few hold most resources can still be Pareto efficient.
Market failure is a case where markets do not produce an efficient allocation, so a Pareto improvement is possible.
In social choice theory the same idea is called the unanimity principle: if everyone prefers A to B, society should too.

Because asymmetric information, adverse selection and moral hazard make Pareto efficiency hard to judge in practice, most people do not take the welfare theorems as accurate descriptions of the real world.

entries.text: Smith owns an apple but wants an orange. Jones owns an orange but wants an apple. A swap makes both better off, so the starting point was wasteful. That small scene captures Pareto efficiency. A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off. A change that helps at least one person and harms nobody is a Pareto improvement, and efficiency is reached once no such change is left. The idea is named after Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and how income is shared. He called it 'optimal', but it does not pick out one best outcome. It marks out a whole set of outcomes, which is why 'efficiency' fits better. Nor does it mean fairness. An economy where a wealthy few hold most resources can still be Pareto efficient. Market failure, in these terms, is a case where markets miss an efficient allocation, so a Pareto improvement is possible. In {{ref:nature-econ-202}} the same idea is called the unanimity principle: if everyone prefers A to B, society should too. In practice, hidden information and the problems it causes make Pareto efficiency hard to judge. So most people do not take the welfare theorems as accurate descriptions of the real world.

entries.title: Welfare economics: judging how well off a society is

definition.text: The branch of economics that uses the tools of microeconomics to judge how well off a society is as a whole.

facts.text: Welfare economics guides public economics, which studies how government action can improve social welfare, and it is the theoretical basis of cost–benefit analysis.
Its first fundamental theorem says competitive markets, under certain assumptions, give Pareto efficient outcomes, an idea sometimes linked to Adam Smith's invisible hand.
Its second theorem says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached through a competitive market if a planner first makes lump-sum transfers.
Arrow's impossibility theorem is sometimes counted as a third fundamental theorem of welfare economics.
The early neoclassical approach was built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou; the later 'new welfare economics' rests on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky.
The idea of an externality, developed by Pigou, remains central to modern welfare economics and to environmental economics.
Amartya Sen urged welfare research to use a wider range of data and to discuss ethics and morality openly.
Austrian school economists reject both cardinal and ordinal welfare economics because they rely on comparing different people's utility.

entries.text: How can anyone judge whether a whole society is better or worse off? Welfare economics is the branch of economics that tries, using the tools of microeconomics. It guides the study of how government action can improve social welfare, and it supplies the theory behind {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Two results anchor it. The first fundamental theorem says competitive markets, under certain assumptions, give Pareto efficient outcomes, an idea sometimes linked to Adam Smith's invisible hand. The second says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached through a competitive market. A planner first makes lump-sum transfers, one-off payments that do not depend on what anyone does. Some count {{ref:nature-econ-179}} as a third. The field has had two eras. Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou built the early neoclassical approach. The later approach, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-167}}, rests on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky. Pigou's idea of an externality remains central, both here and in environmental economics. Critics push from different sides. Amartya Sen urged welfare research to use a wider range of data and to discuss ethics and morality openly. Austrian school economists reject welfare economics outright, cardinal and ordinal alike, because it relies on comparing different people's utility.

entries.title: Utilitarianism: the greatest good for everyone affected

definition.text: A family of ethical theories holding that the right action is the one that produces the most happiness and well-being for everyone affected.

facts.text: Jeremy Bentham founded it; his successor John Stuart Mill reshaped it and popularized the word 'utilitarianism'.
Bentham proposed measuring pleasures and pains by their intensity, duration, certainty and nearness, a method called the hedonic calculus.
Mill rejected a purely quantitative measure, arguing some kinds of pleasure are more valuable than others.
Its ideas have been applied to welfare economics, justice, global poverty, the ethics of raising animals for food and existential risks.
In social choice, the utilitarian rule picks the option that maximizes the sum of everyone's utilities.
Wealth maximization, an offshoot tied to Kaldor–Hicks efficiency, allows changes that raise total surplus even if some lose, as long as winners could compensate losers.
Critics object that well-being cannot be measured or compared, and Rawls argued it ignores the distinction between persons.
Utilitarian thinking underlies one of the two main approaches to animal ethics, most associated with Peter Singer.

entries.text: What is the right thing to do? Utilitarianism gives one answer: whatever produces the most happiness and well-being for everyone affected. Jeremy Bentham founded it. An offshoot, wealth maximization, allows changes that raise total surplus even if some lose, as long as winners could compensate losers. Its ideas reach welfare economics, justice, global poverty, the ethics of raising animals for food and existential risks, and they underlie Peter Singer's approach to animal ethics. Critics object that well-being cannot be measured or compared. In 1971 Rawls argued that it ignores the distinction between persons.

entries.title: Social welfare functions: ranking states of society

definition.text: A rule that ranks possible states of society from more to less desirable by combining the preferences of everyone in it.

facts.text: Economists use social welfare functions to decide which of two outcomes, such as two income distributions, is better for society as a whole.
Unlike one consumer's utility function, it maps many people's utility functions onto a single result.
Ordinal versions use only whether one option is better than another; cardinal versions also use how much better it is.
Abram Bergson introduced the term in a 1938 article to state precisely the value judgements needed to define maximum economic welfare.
In 1935 Lionel Robbins argued that changes in different people's utilities cannot be compared by any empirical test.
Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that, unlike a single consumer, a society cannot build a fully consistent decision rule from ranked preferences alone.

entries.text: A single shopper can rank two baskets of groceries. Can a whole society rank two ways of sharing out its income? A social welfare function tries to. entries.title: Social choice theory: turning many wishes into one decision

definition.text: The branch of welfare economics that studies how individual preferences can be combined into good collective decisions.

facts.text: It is normative, asking how a society should decide, unlike political science, which describes how societies actually decide.
Constitutions, parliamentary voting procedures and electoral systems are real-world social choice rules, so the field is sometimes called voting theory.
It began with the Marquis de Condorcet; Kenneth Arrow's book Social Choice and Individual Values opened its modern era.
Two classic rules are the utilitarian rule, which maximizes the sum of utilities, and the egalitarian or Rawlsian rule, which maximizes the smallest utility.
Gibbard's theorem shows that with three or more outcomes no voting rule can always make honest voting the best strategy.
In 1970 Amartya Sen's Collective Choice and Social Welfare brought comparisons between people and the idea of capability into the field.
Later work extended social choice to fair division, legal compensation and natural resources, among other topics.

entries.title: Market distortions: when prices stop telling the truth

definition.text: Any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one, so that people pursuing their own good no longer maximize society's welfare.

facts.text: A distortion can be measured as the gap between a good's market price and its marginal social cost.

Sources include regulation, monopoly, tariffs and import quotas, uncorrected externalities, unequal tax rates, inflation and incomplete information, each of which can cause a net loss of social surplus.
A proportional tax on wages is distorting because it discourages work; a lump-sum tax is not.
Distortions are often responses to market failures, the circumstances that prevent perfect competition.
Revenue from emissions trading could be used to cut distorting taxes, improving the efficiency of climate policy.

entries.text: A tax on wages discourages some people from working. That push is a market distortion. The term covers any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one. People pursuing their own good then no longer maximize society's welfare. A distortion can be measured as the gap between a good's market price and its marginal social cost. Sources include regulation, monopoly, tariffs and limits on imports, uncorrected externalities, unequal tax rates, inflation and incomplete information. Each can cause a net loss of social surplus. Not every tax distorts. A proportional tax on wages does, because it discourages work; a fixed charge that nothing can change, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-119}}, does not. Distortions are often responses to market failures, the circumstances that prevent perfect competition. They can also be reduced on purpose. Revenue from {{ref:nature-pol-253}} could be used to cut distorting taxes, making climate policy more efficient.

entries.title: Distributive justice: who should get what

definition.text: The question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members.

facts.text: Distributive justice looks at outcomes, in contrast with fair process and formal equal opportunity.
Most modern theories of distributive justice start from the fact that material resources are scarce.
Leading theories include Rawls's justice as fairness, utilitarianism, egalitarianism and Marxism's 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'.
In an environmental setting it means sharing a society's environmental risks, harms and benefits fairly; such burdens fall mostly on the Global South while benefits go mainly to the Global North.
In climate justice, distributive justice asks who bears the costs of climate change and of the actions taken against it.
Friedrich von Hayek called distributive justice meaningless in a market system, where outcomes arise spontaneously rather than by anyone's design.
Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that the term is not neutral, because no central distributor hands out shares.

entries.contested_note: Theorists hold widely different conceptions of distributive justice, and libertarians such as Hayek and Nozick reject the idea itself.
entries.text: Who should get what? Distributive justice is the question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members. Most modern theories start from scarcity: material resources are limited. Their answers differ sharply. Rawls offered one, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-175}}. Others include utilitarianism, the push for equal treatment covered in {{ref:nature-econ-176}}, and the Marxist rule 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'. entries.title: Allocative efficiency: making the goods people want

definition.text: A state of the economy in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so that society's welfare is as high as it can be.

facts.text: It is reached when each good's marginal benefit to consumers is at least the marginal cost of producing it; for a firm in a perfect market this means price equals marginal cost.
With no externalities, the market equilibrium is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so net social benefit is maximized.
At that point social surplus is maximized and there is no deadweight loss.
Example: at an output of 40 the marginal cost is $6 but buyers would pay $15, so the good is under-consumed; the efficient output is 70, where marginal cost equals marginal utility.
A monopoly can set price above marginal cost, making the allocation inefficient and causing a deadweight welfare loss.
When a market fails to allocate resources efficiently, through imperfect knowledge, market power or externalities, there is market failure.
Pareto efficiency is possible without allocative efficiency, when no one can gain without someone losing but gainers could gain more than losers lose.

entries.text: Suppose a firm makes 40 units of a good. The 40th costs $6 to make, yet buyers would pay $15 for it. Society would gain from more. Allocative efficiency is the state in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so society's welfare is as high as it can be. In that example it is reached at 70 units, where marginal cost equals marginal utility. In general, each good's marginal benefit to consumers must be at least its marginal cost; for a firm in a perfect market, price equals marginal cost. With no externalities, the market equilibrium lands where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. Social surplus is then as large as possible and there is no deadweight loss. A monopoly can set its price above marginal cost, making the allocation inefficient. When imperfect knowledge, market power or externalities stop a market allocating resources efficiently, there is market failure. Allocative efficiency is the stricter test: an outcome can be Pareto efficient without it.

entries.title: The fundamental theorems of welfare economics

definition.text: Two results linking markets and efficiency: competitive markets reach a Pareto efficient outcome, and any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached by a competitive market from suitable starting endowments.

facts.text: The first theorem needs complete markets, complete information and perfect competition, in which firms and consumers take prices as given.
It is often seen as a formal confirmation of Adam Smith's 'invisible hand'; Kaushik Basu called it the Invisible Hand Theorem.
The market outcome need not be fair: many Pareto efficient allocations exist, including one where one person owns everything.
The second theorem needs stronger conditions, such as convex preferences and convex production sets.
Samuelson, building on Bergson, concluded that any desired ethical goal could be reached through lump-sum taxes or bounties.
Externalities, prominently pollution and climate, often break the theorems' assumptions; in some cases a Pigouvian tax can restore efficiency.
Oskar Lange's 1942 paper set up the now-traditional pair of theorems, one about markets and one about distribution.
The theorems do not generally guarantee that an equilibrium exists or is unique.

The outcome need not be fair: many efficient allocations exist, including one where one person owns everything. Externalities, above all pollution and climate, often break their assumptions. Sometimes a tax on the harm itself, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-088}}, can restore efficiency.

entries.title: Distribution: how output and income are shared out

definition.text: The way an economy's total output, income or wealth is shared out among people or among the factors of production such as labour, land and capital.

facts.text: Studies of household income often look at the share going to the top or bottom slices, such as fifths, of households and at what drives those shares.
Distribution has been central to political economy since the 19th century, in the work of Adam Smith, David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill.
Welfare economics separates how much output is possible from how the resulting income is distributed.
In neoclassical theory, supply and demand in factor markets set equilibrium output, income and its distribution.
Vilfredo Pareto proposed that income follows a power law, now called the Pareto distribution.
Ecological economics treats fair distribution as a goal alongside efficient allocation and a sustainable scale of the economy.

entries.text: An economy's output has to end up in someone's hands. Distribution is the way total output, income or wealth is shared out among people, or among the factors of production such as labor, land and capital. Studies of household income often look at the share going to the top or bottom fifth of households, and at what drives those shares. Distribution has been central to political economy since the 19th century, in the work of Adam Smith, David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill. Welfare economics separates how much output is possible from how the resulting income is shared. In neoclassical theory, supply and demand in the markets for labor, land and capital set equilibrium output, income and its distribution. entries.title: Equity: fairness in economics

definition.text: Fairness in economics: the idea of justice in how wealth, resources and taxes are shared within a society.

facts.text: Equity means economic processes and outcomes do not unduly favour or disadvantage any group or person.
Equity is judged separately from economic efficiency when assessing social welfare, and is often measured with tools such as the Gini index.
It is hard to define because it depends on social values and would require comparing different people's utility.
Peter Corning names three kinds of fairness, equality, equity and reciprocity, that must be balanced for a truly fair society.
Experimental economics studies equity as inequity aversion.
For the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, economists argued that equity could be separated from efficiency, handled for example through how emission rights are allocated between countries.

entries.text: Fair is not always the same as equal. In economics, equity means fairness: the idea of justice in how wealth, resources and taxes are shared within a society. Economic processes and outcomes should not unduly favor or disadvantage any group or person. Equity is judged separately from efficiency when assessing social welfare, and it is often measured with tools such as the Gini index. It is hard to define, because it depends on social values and would require comparing different people's utility. Peter Corning names three kinds of fairness, equality, equity and the return of like for like described in {{ref:nature-econ-077}}, that must be balanced for a truly fair society. Economists who run experiments study equity as a dislike of unfair outcomes, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-193}}. Climate policy has tested the idea. Under an early climate treaty, {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, economists argued that equity could be separated from efficiency. It could be handled, for example, through how emission rights are allocated between countries.

entries.title: Productive efficiency: no waste on the production line

definition.text: A situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another.

facts.text: Every point on the production possibility frontier is productively efficient.
An economy is productively inefficient, inside its frontier, when capital or labour sit idle or are put into the wrong industries.
In long-run perfect competition, each good is made at the lowest point of the average total cost curve, where marginal cost equals average total cost.
Productive efficiency says nothing about making the right mix of goods; misapplied, it can produce the wrong basket faster and cheaper.
Monopolies may be productively inefficient through X-inefficiency, though economies of scale can sometimes let them charge less than competitive firms.
Better technology and management can push the production possibility frontier outward.
Data envelopment analysis and stochastic frontier analysis are the most popular ways to estimate it.

entries.text: An economy can make things cheaply and still make the wrong things. Productive efficiency is a situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another. Every point on the production possibility frontier meets the test. An economy falls inside its frontier when capital or labor sit idle or are put into the wrong industries. In long-run perfect competition, each good is made at the lowest point of its average total cost curve, where marginal cost equals average total cost. Productive efficiency says nothing about making the right mix of goods; misapplied, it can produce the wrong basket faster and cheaper. Monopolies may fall short through what economists call X-inefficiency, though economies of scale can sometimes let them charge less than competitive firms. Better technology and management can push the frontier outward. Data envelopment analysis and stochastic frontier analysis are the most popular ways to estimate it.

entries.title: Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: could the winners pay off the losers

definition.text: A change counts as a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if the people who gain could, in principle, fully compensate the people who lose, even if they never actually do.

facts.text: It is a looser test than a Pareto improvement, useful because almost any real policy change makes at least one person worse off.
Every Pareto improvement is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement, but most Kaldor–Hicks improvements are not Pareto improvements.
Example: a deal that causes pollution is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if buyers and sellers would still go ahead while fully compensating the pollution's victims.
The Kaldor test asks whether gainers would pay enough to win losers' consent; the Hicks test asks whether losers could not afford to bribe gainers to drop the change.
It is named after the twentieth-century economists Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks.
It underpins cost–benefit analysis: approving a project when benefits exceed costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers.
Critics ask why the mere ability to compensate losers should matter morally if compensation is never paid, and note that it ignores income distribution.
The Kaldor–Hicks compensation principle is the standard criterion in cost–benefit analysis of climate change.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute why hypothetical compensation that is never paid should carry moral weight in deciding policy.

Every Pareto improvement passes, but most Kaldor–Hicks improvements are not Pareto improvements. Take a deal that causes pollution. It passes if buyers and sellers would still go ahead while fully compensating the pollution's victims. The Kaldor test asks whether gainers would pay enough to win losers' consent. Approving a project whose benefits exceed its costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers. It is also the standard criterion when the costs and benefits of climate change are weighed. Named after the twentieth-century economists Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks, the test underpins Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses. Approving a project whose benefits exceed its costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers. It is also the standard criterion when the costs and benefits of climate change are weighed. Critics dispute why compensation that is never paid should carry moral weight, and note that the test ignores how income is shared.

entries.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem: no perfect way to vote

definition.text: Kenneth Arrow's proof that no way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice.

facts.text: In particular, no such rule can satisfy independence of irrelevant alternatives, so in voting no ranked system can fully avoid the spoiler effect.
Arrow proved the theorem in 1950, founding modern social choice theory, a branch of welfare economics that studies how to combine preferences across a society.
It generalizes Condorcet's voting paradox: with three voters and three options, the majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A even though each voter is consistent.
Arrow remarked that most voting systems do not work badly all the time; he only proved that all can work badly at times.
Black's median voter theorem showed that if voters and candidates lie along a single left-right spectrum, Arrow's conditions can all be met by majority rule.
The theorem depends on people giving rankings; rated voting systems that ask for scores, such as 0–10, can escape it.
By the 1950s some economists claimed the theorem proved that any attempt to build normative standards in economics was doomed.

entries.text: Three voters face three options, and each voter is perfectly consistent. Yet the majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A. No way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice. In particular, no such rule can satisfy the principle explored in {{ref:nature-econ-180}}, so no ranked voting system can fully avoid the spoiler effect. Black showed that if voters and candidates lie along a single left-right spectrum, majority rule can meet all of Arrow's conditions. Rated systems that ask for scores, such as 0–10, escape the theorem by not asking for rankings.

entries.title: The capability approach: what people can actually do and be

definition.text: A way of judging human welfare by what people are actually able to do and be in leading lives they value, not just by their rights or income.

facts.text: Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed it in the 1980s as an alternative to traditional welfare economics.
'Functionings' are the beings and doings that make up a life, such as being healthy or safe; 'capabilities' are the combinations of functionings a person can really achieve.
Sen argues that utility-based welfare economics ignores how welfare is distributed, neglects rights and freedoms, and is misled by people adapting to bad conditions.
Resource- or income-based measures struggle because people differ in their ability to turn resources into valuable activities.
Nussbaum lists 10 central capabilities and holds that a decent political order must secure at least a threshold level of each for everyone.
The approach led to the UN's Human Development Index, first published in 1990, which equally weighted health, education and income.
It looks at the capabilities people enjoy within a country rather than total GDP, and is closely linked to sustainability within a generation.

entries.title: The second best: when fixing one flaw makes things worse

definition.text: The result that when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met, the best remaining option may require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too.

facts.text: Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster showed this in 1956.
If one market distortion cannot be removed, adding another distortion in a linked market may partly offset it and raise efficiency.
Fixing a market failure in one sector while an uncorrectable failure remains in a related sector can lower overall efficiency.
A common error, the 'fallacy of exhaustive effort', assumes meeting as many remaining ideal conditions as possible gives the second-best result.
Example: liberalising trade while ignoring an environmental externality, because 'free trade is good', can leave welfare lower than doing nothing.
When the externality itself cannot be taxed, taxing a related product can be the second-best Pigouvian solution.

entries.title: The equity–efficiency trade-off: fairness has a price

definition.text: The conflict that arises because policies making the economy fairer usually cost some efficiency, so society must choose between the two.

facts.text: Redistributing income is costly, so there is a built-in choice between more efficiency and more equity.
Much economic research therefore measures the efficiency losses of tax and transfer programmes, which redistribute by their nature.
The trade-off is at the heart of many debates about tax policy; its formal study was begun by James Mirrlees in 1971.
Because real markets are imperfect, emissions trading may also involve a trade-off between equity and efficiency.

entries.title: The excess burden of taxation: the hidden cost of taxes

definition.text: The economic loss a society suffers, beyond the money collected, because taxes or subsidies change how people behave; also called the deadweight loss of taxation.

facts.text: Adam Smith first discussed excess burdens; subsidies, which act as negative taxes, cause the same kind of inefficiency.
Estimates of losses from taxes range from 2.5 cents to 30 cents per dollar of revenue on average, and much higher at the margin.
As a rule of thumb, the excess burden of a tax rises with the square of the tax rate.
It is measured by the average cost of funds (total distortion over total revenue) or the marginal cost of funds (the distortion from the last unit of revenue).
A sales tax discourages buying the taxed goods and an income tax discourages earning taxed income; some people leave work or move into the black economy.
Pigouvian taxes distort on purpose to correct externalities, and so have a negative marginal cost of funds.
'Sin taxes' on alcohol, tobacco and pollution ideally raise the price to what it would be if the external costs were included.

entries.text: A tax costs society more than the money it raises. The extra is the excess burden of taxation, or deadweight loss of taxation. It is the loss a society suffers, beyond the money collected, because taxes or subsidies change how people behave. A sales tax discourages buying the taxed goods. An income tax discourages earning taxed income, and some people leave work or move into the black economy. Subsidies, acting as negative taxes, cause the same waste. Adam Smith first discussed such burdens. Estimates range from 2.5 cents to 30 cents per dollar of revenue on average, and much higher at the margin. As a rule of thumb, the excess burden rises with the square of the tax rate. It can be measured per average dollar raised or for the last dollar raised, the marginal cost of funds. Some taxes distort on purpose. Taxes on alcohol, tobacco and pollution ideally raise the price to include external costs, and such corrective taxes have a negative marginal cost of funds.

entries.title: Cardinal social welfare functions: adding up well-being

definition.text: A social welfare function that takes numerical measures of each person's well-being, often income, and turns them into one number for the whole society's welfare.

facts.text: The utilitarian or Benthamite version adds up individual utilities, so it maximizes total income without caring how that income is shared.
Under the utilitarian version, society should accept a transfer from poor to rich if the rich gain more utility than the poor lose.
The max-min or Rawlsian version, based on John Rawls, judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member alone.
The max-min function can be read as society showing an extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face.
In 1973 Amartya Sen proposed a welfare function equal to average income multiplied by one minus the Gini index.

entries.text: Should society take money from the poor and give it to the rich? One kind of social welfare function says yes, if the rich gain more utility than the poor lose. The max-min or Rawlsian version, based on John Rawls, judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member alone. It can be read as society showing an extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face. In 1973 Amartya Sen proposed another: average income multiplied by one minus the Gini index.

entries.title: Constrained Pareto efficiency: a planner with the same blind spots

definition.text: A weaker form of Pareto efficiency that recognises a planner such as a government may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome because it faces the same limits as everyone else.

facts.text: It matters when people hold private information, such as a worker's own productivity or a used car's quality, leading to moral hazard or adverse selection.
A planner usually has no more information than market participants, so it can only use anonymous rules or rules based on observable behaviour.
If no allowed rule can improve on the market outcome, that outcome is called constrained Pareto optimal.

entries.text: A government cannot fix what it cannot see. Constrained Pareto efficiency is a weaker form of Pareto efficiency. It recognizes that a planner may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome, because it faces the same limits as everyone else. It matters when people hold private information, such as a worker's own productivity or a used car's quality. A planner usually has no more information than market participants. So it can only use anonymous rules or rules based on behavior it can observe. If no allowed rule improves on the market outcome, that outcome is called constrained Pareto optimal.

entries.title: Pareto efficiency and welfare maximization: two views of one set

definition.text: The link showing that maximizing a weighted sum of everyone's utility, with positive weights, always gives a Pareto efficient allocation, and under some assumptions every efficient allocation can be found that way.

facts.text: An allocation that maximizes a positively weighted sum of utilities must be Pareto efficient, since any Pareto improvement would raise the sum.
Takashi Negishi proved that, under certain assumptions, every Pareto efficient allocation maximizes such a weighted sum for some set of positive weights.

entries.text: Give every person's utility a positive weight, add the weighted utilities up, and make the total as large as possible. The result is always Pareto efficient, because any Pareto improvement would raise the sum. The link can also run the other way. Takashi Negishi proved that, under certain assumptions, every Pareto efficient allocation maximizes such a weighted sum for some set of positive weights. Choosing the weights then amounts to choosing which efficient outcome to aim for.

entries.title: Weak Pareto efficiency: when no one-for-all gain remains

definition.text: A situation is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off.

facts.text: A strong Pareto improvement makes all agents strictly better off, while an ordinary Pareto improvement needs only one strictly better off and the rest no worse.
Every strong Pareto improvement is also a weak one, but not the reverse, so a weakly efficient outcome may not be fully Pareto efficient.

entries.text: An outcome is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off. That is a lower bar than the ordinary test. A strong Pareto improvement makes all people strictly better off, while an ordinary Pareto improvement needs only one person strictly better off and the rest no worse. Every strong improvement is also an ordinary one, but not the reverse. So a weakly efficient outcome may still leave room for an ordinary improvement, and may not be fully Pareto efficient.

entries.title: The Edgeworth box: a market drawn as a rectangle

definition.text: A diagram of a tiny market with just two goods and two consumers, where each point in the box is one way of splitting the goods between them.

facts.text: The box's sides equal the total amounts of the two goods; each consumer's holdings are measured from opposite corners, and their indifference curves show what they prefer.
It is named after Francis Ysidro Edgeworth, who presented it in 1881; Pareto turned it into the familiar box in 1906 and Bowley popularized it.
Points where the two consumers' indifference curves touch are Pareto optima; together they form the Pareto set or efficient locus.
Market equilibria are where both indifference curves touch a common price line, so the equilibria are exactly the Pareto optima: the first welfare theorem in pictures.
For the second welfare theorem, a government need not hand out the exact desired allocation; it can shift resources onto the right price line and let the market finish the job.

entries.title: Causes of economic inefficiency: why economies fall short

definition.text: The conditions, such as monopoly, hidden information or poorly designed regulation, that keep an economy from reaching Pareto efficiency.

facts.text: Imperfect market structures such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition cause inefficiency.
Asymmetric information, including principal–agent problems, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly also cause inefficiency.
Government limits on prices and quantities and other regulation arising from government failure can also make an economy inefficient.
One inefficiency can offset another: if pollution leads to too many tyres being made, a tax on tyres might restore the efficient amount.

entries.text: Economies fall short of Pareto efficiency for many reasons. Imperfect market structures, such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition, cause inefficiency. So do hidden information, including problems that arise when one party acts for another, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly. Governments add their own: limits on prices and quantities, and regulation arising from government failure. One inefficiency can offset another. If pollution leads to too many tires being made, a tax on tires might restore the efficient amount.

entries.title: The four marginal conditions for Pareto efficiency

definition.text: The four marginal conditions on consumption and production that must all hold for an economy to be Pareto efficient.

facts.text: Every consumer must have the same marginal rate of substitution between any two goods, so no swap between consumers can make both happier.
Every producer must have the same marginal rate of transformation between two goods, so shifting production between producers cannot raise total output.
A factor such as labour must have the same marginal product at every producer of a good, so moving production cannot cut its cost.
Consumers' marginal rates of substitution must equal producers' marginal rates of transformation, so changing the product mix cannot make consumers happier.

entries.text: Pareto efficiency requires four marginal conditions to hold at once. Every consumer must have the same marginal rate of substitution between any two goods, so no swap between consumers can make both happier. Every producer must have the same marginal rate of transformation between two goods, so shifting production between producers cannot raise total output. A factor such as labor must have the same marginal product at every producer of a good, so moving production cannot cut its cost. Finally, consumers' marginal rates of substitution must equal producers' marginal rates of transformation, so changing the product mix cannot make consumers happier.

entries.title: Old welfare economics: when utility could be added up

definition.text: The early neoclassical approach to welfare, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, which treated utility as measurable and added it up across people.

facts.text: It assumed utility can be measured on a scale, that preferences are fixed and stable, and that each extra unit consumed adds less and less utility.
With those assumptions a social welfare function is simply the sum of all individual utility functions, in the tradition of Bentham.
It was often inferred that moving income from a rich person to a poor person tends to raise total utility.

entries.text: The first welfare economists believed utility could be measured and summed. This early neoclassical approach, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, treated utility as measurable and added it up across people. It assumed utility can be measured on a scale, that preferences are fixed and stable, and that each extra unit consumed adds less and less utility. On those assumptions a social welfare function is simply the sum of everyone's utility functions, in Bentham's tradition. It was often inferred that moving income from a rich person to a poor person tends to raise total utility.

entries.title: New welfare economics: efficiency without measuring happiness

definition.text: The ordinal approach to welfare, based on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky, which judges efficiency without measuring or comparing people's utility.

facts.text: It treats efficiency and distribution separately: efficiency is judged by Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks criteria, distribution by the choice of social welfare function.
It replaces measurable utility with ordinal utility, which only ranks bundles of goods, for example on an indifference-curve map.
The consensus behind it largely collapsed after Arrow's impossibility theorem and utility representation theorems showed such approaches to be self-contradictory.
Murray Rothbard proposed rebuilding welfare economics on 'demonstrated preference', under which only voluntary market exchanges clearly raise welfare.

entries.title: The compensation principle: gains that could cover the losses

definition.text: A rule in welfare economics that favours a change if those who gain from it could compensate those who lose and still leave nobody worse off.

facts.text: The Pareto criterion is a strict form in which compensation must actually happen, not just be possible.
The principle is controversial when full compensation is possible but not paid, leaving some people as losers.
Many neoclassical economists judge an intervention good if total gains exceed total losses, even if losers are not compensated in practice.
In cost–benefit analysis of climate policy, a project that benefits some, compensates losers and still leaves something over is an unambiguous welfare gain.

entries.contested_note: Its use is disputed where compensation is feasible but not actually paid.
entries.text: The compensation principle favors a change if those who gain could compensate those who lose and still leave nobody worse off. The Pareto criterion is a strict form, in which compensation must actually happen, not just be possible. Many neoclassical economists accept an intervention whenever total gains exceed total losses, paid or not. That is the controversy: when compensation is possible but not paid, some people are simply left as losers. In weighing climate policy, a project that benefits some, compensates the losers and still has something left over is an unambiguous welfare gain.

That is the controversy: when compensation is possible but not paid, some people are simply left as losers. entries.title: Lump-sum taxes: the efficient tax almost nobody uses

definition.text: A tax of a fixed amount that does not depend on the taxpayer's circumstances, so nothing they do can change what they owe.

facts.text: Because people cannot change their behaviour to reduce it, a lump-sum tax creates no deadweight loss.
It is regressive: the lower someone's income, the larger the share of it the tax takes; a per-person version is called a poll tax.
It is rarely used because charging low-income people very large sums relative to income would be politically unacceptable; Switzerland still uses it for some rich foreign residents.
It matters in theory: the second welfare theorem relies on lump-sum transfers to reach a desired efficient outcome.

It is rare, because charging poor people such large sums would be politically unacceptable. Switzerland still uses it for some rich foreign residents.

Because people cannot change their behavior to reduce it, it creates no deadweight loss. The second welfare theorem relies on such lump-sum transfers. The catch is fairness. The tax is regressive: the lower someone's income, the larger the share it takes. A per-person version is called a poll tax. It is rare, because charging poor people such large sums would be politically unacceptable. Switzerland still uses it for some rich foreign residents.

entries.title: Missing markets: trades that would help but never happen

definition.text: A situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet no such market exists.

facts.text: Pollution is the classic case: a factory dumping waste into a river harms people downstream, but has no incentive to count that harm, so no market for pollution forms.
Markets can also be missing because of coordination failures such as the free-rider problem, difficulty monitoring who causes harm, high transaction costs, or lack of trust and information.
Alternative fuels show the chicken-and-egg problem: stations won't sell a fuel until such cars exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist.
Governments can create the missing conditions; for pollution, a popular solution is assigning property rights so the parties can bargain, as in the Coase theorem.
Economists may try to avoid waste by creating missing markets so that efficient trading can happen where none existed before.

entries.text: A factory dumps waste into a river and people downstream are harmed. The factory has no reason to count that harm, so no market for pollution forms. That is a missing market: a situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet none exists. Markets go missing for other reasons too, including free riding, difficulty monitoring who causes harm, high costs of making deals, and lack of trust and information. Alternative fuels show the chicken-and-egg version. Stations won't sell a fuel until cars that use it exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist. Governments can create the missing conditions. For pollution, a popular fix is assigning clear ownership so the parties can bargain, as in {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. More broadly, economists may try to create missing markets so that efficient trading can happen where none existed before.

entries.title: The contract curve: where mutually helpful trading ends

definition.text: The set of final splits of two goods between two people that they could reach by trading to mutual benefit from their starting holdings; every point on it is Pareto efficient.

facts.text: It is drawn in an Edgeworth box, with each person's holdings measured from opposite corners.
The two people keep trading as long as their marginal rates of substitution differ; on the curve their indifference curves just touch and the rates are equal.
The analysis cannot say where on the curve they end up; that depends on their bargaining skills.
Any Walrasian (competitive) equilibrium lies on the contract curve.

entries.text: Two traders keep swapping as long as they value the goods differently at the margin. The contract curve shows where they could end up. It is the set of final splits of two goods that two people could reach by trading to mutual benefit. Every point on it is Pareto efficient. Drawn in an Edgeworth box, it marks where the two indifference curves just touch and the marginal rates of substitution are equal. Any competitive equilibrium lies on it. Where on the curve they land depends on their bargaining skills.

entries.title: Inequity aversion: paying to punish unfairness

definition.text: People's preference for fairness and their dislike of unequal outcomes, even when it costs them.

facts.text: In 1999 Fehr and Schmidt modelled people as disliking both being behind others and being ahead of them.
In the ultimatum game, people usually reject low offers, preferring nothing to a small share and in effect paying to punish the proposer.
Willingness to punish those who earn more helps keep cooperation stable, since free riders who earn more get punished.
Capuchin monkeys refused rewards that were handed out unequally in favour of another monkey.

entries.contested_note: Binmore and Shaked attacked Fehr and Schmidt's model for free parameters and unjustified assumptions, and later estimates have contradicted some of its parameters.
entries.text: People will pay to punish unfairness. Inequity aversion is people's preference for fairness and their dislike of unequal outcomes, even when it costs them. In the bargaining experiment known as {{ref:nature-econ-035}}, people usually reject low offers, preferring nothing to a small share. In 1999 Fehr and Schmidt modeled people as disliking both being behind others and being ahead of them. Such willingness to punish helps keep cooperation stable, since free riders who earn more get punished. Capuchin monkeys refused rewards handed out unequally in favor of another monkey. The model is disputed: Binmore and Shaked attacked its free parameters and assumptions, and later estimates contradict some of them.

entries.title: Harsanyi's utilitarian theorem: rational choice points to adding up

definition.text: The result that if society's choices follow the rules of rational choice under risk, the social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities.

facts.text: By the theorem, any non-utilitarian rule is incoherent: it will accept some bets that every member of society opposes.
With a weaker condition, that rankings do not depend on the unit (cents or dollars), the welfare function must belong to the isoelastic family.
In that family, one parameter value gives the Nash bargaining solution (maximizing the product of utilities) and another gives the utilitarian sum.
Requiring the Pigou–Dalton principle, that inequality is not a good thing, limits the parameter to at most 1.

entries.text: If a society makes choices the way a rational person handles risk, its social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities. That is Harsanyi's utilitarian theorem. By it, any non-utilitarian rule is incoherent: it will accept some bets that every member of society opposes. A weaker condition, that rankings do not depend on the unit, cents or dollars, allows a wider family of welfare functions, the isoelastic family. One setting within it gives the utilitarian sum; another maximizes the product of utilities, as in {{ref:nature-econ-689}}. Requiring the Pigou–Dalton principle, that inequality is not a good thing, limits the parameter to at most 1.

entries.title: The Condorcet paradox: when majorities go in circles

definition.text: The finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle: A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A.

facts.text: It shows democracy cannot simply equal majority rule, which becomes self-contradictory with three or more options.
With only two options, May's theorem shows simple majority is the best rule.
A review of 37 studies covering 265 real elections found 25 cases of the paradox, a likelihood of 9.4%.

entries.text: Majority rule can chase its own tail. The Condorcet paradox is the finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle. A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A. Democracy therefore cannot simply equal majority rule, which becomes self-contradictory with three or more options. With only two options, May's theorem shows simple majority is the best rule. How often does the circle appear? A review of 37 studies covering 265 real elections found 25 cases, a likelihood of 9.4%.

entries.title: Comparing well-being across people: a long-running dispute

definition.text: The disputed question of whether one person's gain or loss in well-being can be measured and weighed against another's.

facts.text: Following Bentham, utilitarians argue utilities can be compared and added up into a total for society to maximize.
Diminishing marginal utility has been used to justify transfers from rich to poor, since the poor gain more from an extra unit of income.
Lionel Robbins argued such comparisons are unscientific and cannot be tested.
Harsanyi and Sen reply that at least partial comparisons are possible, so social choice should proceed on that basis.

entries.contested_note: Robbins and his followers deny that utility can be compared across people, while Harsanyi and Sen argue partial comparison is possible.
entries.text: Does an extra dollar mean more to a poor person than to a rich one? Following Bentham, utilitarians argue that utilities can be compared and added up into a total for society to maximize. Diminishing marginal utility has been used to justify transfers from rich to poor, since the poor gain more from an extra unit of income. Lionel Robbins answered that such interpersonal comparisons are unscientific and cannot be tested. Harsanyi and Sen reply that at least partial comparisons are possible, so social choice should proceed on that basis. The dispute remains open.

entries.title: Distributive norms: rules for sharing rewards and costs

definition.text: The different rules a group can use to share out rewards and costs, such as equal shares, shares by contribution, or shares by need.

facts.text: Donelson R. Forsyth defines five norms: equality, equity, power, need and responsibility.
Under equality everyone gets the same share whatever they put in; under equity people who contribute more receive more.
Members of large groups prefer to share rewards and costs according to equity.
Under the need norm, those in greatest need get more resources regardless of what they contributed.

Forsyth defines five: equality, equity, power, need and responsibility. Under equality everyone gets the same share, whatever they put in. Under equity, people who contribute more receive more, and members of large groups prefer this rule. Under need, those in greatest need get more resources, regardless of what they contributed.

entries.title: Egalitarianism: treating people as equals

definition.text: The view, based on the equal worth of all people, that citizens should be treated equally in respect and concern by the state and by one another.

facts.text: Egalitarianism focuses on unchosen circumstances that hold people back, and its central problem is deciding which kind of equality to pursue.
Strict egalitarianism insists on equal shares even when an unequal split would make everyone better off, so it can produce Pareto-inefficient outcomes.
Equality of welfare concerns outcomes; critics favour equality of prospects instead, such as equality of opportunity.

entries.text: Should everyone get equal shares, even when unequal shares would leave everyone better off? Strict egalitarians say yes, so their rule can produce Pareto-inefficient outcomes. Egalitarianism starts from the equal worth of all people: citizens should be treated with equal respect and concern by the state and by one another. It focuses on unchosen circumstances that hold people back. Its central problem is deciding which kind of equality to pursue. Equality of welfare concerns outcomes; critics favor equality of prospects instead, such as equality of opportunity.

entries.title: Justice as fairness: Rawls's two principles

definition.text: John Rawls's theory, set out in A Theory of Justice, that a just society gives equal rights and liberties, equal opportunity, and arranges inequalities to benefit the least advantaged.

facts.text: Rawls roots justice in society's 'basic structure', the fundamental rules that shape its institutions and so its citizens' life chances.
The first principle, the liberty principle, gives everyone equal access to basic rights and liberties.
The second principle, the difference principle, allows inequalities only if they bring the greatest benefit to the least advantaged and positions stay open to all.

Its second, the difference principle, allows inequalities only if they bring the greatest benefit to the least advantaged, and only if positions stay open to all.

entries.title: The Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem: when markets miss easy gains
entries.article: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics#Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem

definition.text: Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz's 1986 result that the welfare theorems fail when markets are incomplete or information is imperfect.

facts.text: With asymmetric information, a competitive equilibrium is generally not even constrained Pareto efficient.
So a government with no better information than private individuals can still find policies that make someone better off and no one worse off.
Example: because of moral hazard, an alcohol tax may be a Pareto improvement by reducing car accidents.

entries.text: In 1986 Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz showed that the welfare theorems fail when markets are incomplete or information is imperfect. When one side knows more than the other, a competitive equilibrium is generally not even constrained Pareto efficient. So a government with no better information than private individuals can still find policies that make someone better off and no one worse off. One example involves the problem explored in {{ref:nature-econ-004}}: because of it, an alcohol tax may be a Pareto improvement by reducing car accidents.

entries.title: Horizontal and vertical equity: two tests of a fair tax

definition.text: Two fairness principles for taxes and public services: treat people in similar situations alike (horizontal), and treat people with more ability to pay differently (vertical).

facts.text: Horizontal equity says people with similar incomes should carry similar tax burdens; it links to tax neutrality.
Vertical equity says the better-off should pay more, supporting progressive taxes whose rates rise with income or wealth.
A tax taking the same share from all is proportional; one taking a rising share from the rich is progressive, a main tool for reducing inequality.
Both are hard to apply: defining similar situations is subjective, and vertical equity runs into problems of comparing utility across people.

entries.text: A fair tax must pass two tests. Horizontal equity says people in similar situations, such as similar incomes, should carry similar tax burdens; it links to tax neutrality. Vertical equity says the better-off should pay more, which supports progressive taxes whose rates rise with income or wealth. A tax taking the same share from all is proportional. One taking a rising share from the rich is progressive, a main tool for reducing inequality. Both tests are hard to apply. Defining similar situations is subjective, and vertical equity runs into the problem of comparing utility across people.
