entries.title: The social planner: an imaginary decision-maker

definition.text: An imaginary decision-maker used in economic models who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function.

facts.text: The planner's problem is a constrained optimization; solving it for every set of weights on people yields all Pareto efficient allocations.
Solving it would require knowing everyone's preferences and every resource limit, so economists ask whether decentralized markets can reach the same outcomes; the welfare theorems answer this.
Ramsey first framed his growth model as a social planner maximizing total consumption across generations.

entries.text: Economists often build their models around a decision-maker who does not exist. The social planner is an imaginary figure who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function. The planner's problem is one of maximizing under limits, and solving it for every set of weights on people yields all the Pareto efficient allocations. No real planner could solve it, since that would require knowing everyone's preferences and every resource limit. So economists ask whether decentralized markets can reach the same outcomes, and the welfare theorems answer that question. Ramsey first framed his growth model as a social planner maximizing total consumption across generations.

entries.title: Dynamic efficiency: can an economy save too much

definition.text: An economy is dynamically efficient when it invests less than the return to capital, so that no generation can be made better off without making another worse off.

facts.text: In the Solow growth model, saving above the Golden Rule rate is dynamically inefficient: the economy could be better off today and tomorrow by saving less.
In overlapping-generations models people may save more than is socially optimal, causing dynamic inefficiency.
A 1989 study by Abel, Mankiw, Summers and Zeckhauser suggested the United States and other OECD countries are dynamically efficient.
In industrial economics, some argue that business concentration or monopolies can promote dynamic efficiency.

entries.text: An economy can save too much. It is dynamically efficient when it invests less than the return to capital, so that no generation can be made better off without making another worse off. In the Solow growth model, saving above the rate explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-201}} is dynamically inefficient: the economy could be better off today and tomorrow by saving less. In models of overlapping generations, people may save more than is socially optimal. A 1989 study by Abel, Mankiw, Summers and Zeckhauser suggested the United States and other OECD countries are dynamically efficient. In industrial economics, some argue that business concentration or monopolies can promote dynamic efficiency.

entries.title: Prioritarianism: extra weight for the worse off

definition.text: The ethical view that judgements of social welfare should give extra weight to benefits for people who are worse off.

facts.text: Like utilitarianism it adds up consequences, but it weights each gain more heavily the worse off the person receiving it is.
Unlike egalitarianism it places no value on equality itself, and unlike maximin it does not look only at the worst-off person.
A main objection is how much extra weight the worse off should get, which risks arbitrariness.
It offers one ethical argument for a high discount rate in climate economics: if future people will be richer, benefits to people today count for more.

entries.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: no spoilers allowed

definition.text: The principle that a choice between two options, A and B, should not depend on how anyone feels about some third, unrelated option C.

facts.text: For a voting rule, it means society's ranking of A against B should not flip just because voters change their view of A against C.
It is equivalent to saying an election should be free of spoiler candidates.
Behavioural economists have found that individuals themselves violate it, for example through decoy effects.

entries.text: A choice between A and B should not depend on how anyone feels about some unrelated option C. That is the principle of independence of irrelevant alternatives. For a voting rule, it means society's ranking of A against B should not flip just because voters change their view of A against C. Put another way, an election should be free of spoiler candidates. It sounds obvious, yet individuals break it themselves. Behavioral economists have found violations through decoys, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-042}}.

entries.title: The Scitovsky paradox: a test that contradicts itself

definition.text: The finding that the Kaldor compensation test can judge allocation A better than B and also, by the same test, B better than A.

facts.text: It arises when gainers could compensate losers for a change, yet losers could then compensate gainers for switching back.
It is named after the Hungarian-born American economist Tibor Scitovsky, who set out his double criterion in a 1941 paper.
Combining the Kaldor and Hicks tests removes this flaw, but the combined criterion may still not be transitive.

entries.text: A test that ranks A above B and also B above A is a broken test. The Scitovsky paradox shows that the Kaldor compensation test can do exactly that. It arises when gainers could compensate losers for a change, yet losers could then compensate gainers for switching back. The Hungarian-born American economist Tibor Scitovsky set out his double criterion in a 1941 paper. Combining the Kaldor and Hicks tests removes this flaw, but the combined criterion may still not be transitive, so its rankings need not line up consistently.

entries.title: The original position: choosing rules behind a veil of ignorance

definition.text: A thought experiment in which people choose the rules of their society from behind a 'veil of ignorance', not knowing what place they will occupy in it.

facts.text: The veil hides each person's ethnicity, social status, gender and idea of a good life, so they must choose impartially; the idea is central to Rawls's 1971 A Theory of Justice.
Rawls argued people would use the maximin rule, judging options by the outcome for the least advantaged.
Vickrey and Harsanyi had earlier used the same thought experiment to show a rational chooser would adopt utilitarianism, maximizing expected well-being.
In a 1987 study, students in a simulated original position preferred maximizing the average with a floor for the worst-off; Rawls's principle was chosen by under 5%.

entries.contested_note: Nozick, Sandel and others dispute Rawls's use of the veil, especially the extreme risk aversion of the maximin rule.

entries.title: The tax wedge: the gap between what buyers pay and sellers get

definition.text: The gap a tax opens between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive for a good.

facts.text: With a tax, consumers pay more, suppliers receive less, and the quantity traded falls; the price gap equals the per-unit tax.
The wedge-shaped area on a supply-and-demand diagram equals the deadweight loss of the tax, one half times the tax times the fall in quantity.
A monopoly pricing above marginal cost drives a similar wedge between what consumers pay and what it costs to supply.

entries.text: Tax a good and two prices appear: the one buyers pay and the one sellers receive. The tax wedge is the gap between them, and it equals the per-unit tax. Consumers pay more, suppliers receive less, and the quantity traded falls. On a supply-and-demand diagram, the wedge-shaped area equals the deadweight loss of the tax: one half times the tax times the fall in quantity. A monopoly pricing above marginal cost drives a similar wedge between what consumers pay and what supply costs.

entries.title: The Atkinson index: inequality measured by how much you care

definition.text: A measure of income inequality, developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, that lets the user choose how much to care about inequality.

facts.text: Its parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level, makes the index more sensitive to the bottom of the income distribution as it rises.
The index gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal.
It runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are the same; with ε = 0 (no aversion to inequality) it is always zero.
It is tied to a generalized entropy index, so overall inequality can be broken down by groups, which the Gini index cannot do.

entries.text: How much does inequality matter? The Atkinson index lets its user decide. Developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, it measures inequality of income using a parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level. The higher ε is, the more the index responds to the bottom of the income distribution. The index runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are equal, or when ε = 0. It gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal. Unlike the Gini index, it lets overall inequality be broken down by groups.
entries.text_plain: How much does inequality matter? The Atkinson index lets its user decide. Developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, it measures inequality of income using a parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level. The higher ε is, the more the index responds to the bottom of the income distribution. The index runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are equal, or when ε = 0. It gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal. Unlike the Gini index, it lets overall inequality be broken down by groups.

entries.title: The marginal cost of public funds: what each tax dollar really costs

definition.text: A measure of how much society loses, because taxes distort behaviour, for each extra unit of money the government raises.

facts.text: It is used in the rule for how many public goods to provide, in setting corrective taxes on externalities, and in social cost–benefit analysis.
Pigou (1947) is generally credited with first stating the problem.
In practice it can be calculated from the tax rate and the elasticities of demand and supply.
A common view is that costs of any tax-funded project in a cost–benefit analysis should be scaled up by the marginal cost of funds.

entries.text: Raising money through taxes costs society more than the money itself, because taxes distort behavior. entries.title: Non-convexity: when half of each is worse than all of one

definition.text: A breach of the convexity assumptions of basic economics, such as consumers preferring extremes over mixtures or firms with increasing returns to scale.

facts.text: When convexity fails, competitive markets lose many of their good properties: supply and demand may not match, or equilibria may be inefficient.
Example: a zoo that can afford one lion or one eagle wants either whole animal, not half of each, so its preferences are non-convex.
Non-convexities arise with environmental goods and other externalities, as well as in public economics.
The Shapley–Folkman lemma shows that non-convexities still allow approximate equilibria in markets with many consumers.

entries.title: The utility–possibility frontier: the limits of everyone's welfare

definition.text: A curve showing the most utility one person can have for each level of utility the others have, given society's resources; the welfare counterpart of the production possibility frontier.

facts.text: Every point on the frontier is Pareto efficient; points inside it are not, and points beyond it cannot be reached.
Its slope shows how much one person's utility must fall for another's to rise.
It is derived from the contract curve, re-drawn in terms of utilities instead of goods.
Choosing among its points needs a social welfare function; the best is where it touches society's highest indifference curve, called the 'point of bliss'.

entries.title: Tax incidence: who really pays a tax

definition.text: Who actually bears the cost of a tax, which may differ from who legally hands the money to the government.

facts.text: Statutory incidence falls on whoever pays the government; economic incidence falls on whoever really bears the cost, and the first does not determine the second.
Economic incidence depends entirely on the elasticities of supply and demand: the side less able to adjust bears more.
Smokers bear most of a tobacco tax because their demand barely responds to price, while owners of beachfront hotels bear most of a hotel tax because supply cannot change.
In the long run supply and demand become more elastic, so the split of the burden can shift.

entries.contested_note: Public finance economists disagree greatly on how far market forces shift the burden of particular taxes.

entries.title: Nuisance: when your neighbor's activity becomes your problem

definition.text: A common-law wrong where someone's activity causes offence, annoyance or harm to others, such as a smoking chimney or loud noise.

facts.text: A nuisance is public when it interferes with rights shared by everyone, such as public health and safety, and private when it affects specific people.
Landholders are entitled to quiet enjoyment of their land; a neighbour's smells, sounds or pollution crossing the boundary can ground a nuisance claim.
Nuisance is one of the oldest causes of action in the common law.
As nuisance suits became costly to settle, most places adopted zoning to say which activities are allowed where.
Modern environmental laws adapt the nuisance idea to harms that reach people far from the source.
Noise, water and light pollution are among the environmental harms treated as nuisances in law.

entries.title: The Problem of Social Cost: Coase's article on harm and bargaining

definition.text: Ronald Coase's 1960 law review article on the economic problem of externalities, such as pollution harming neighbours.

facts.text: Coase argued that with no costs of making deals, people would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources whatever the starting legal rights.
Because real bargaining and information are costly, legal rules matter insofar as they give rights to whoever values them most.
Many useful deals never happen because of these transaction costs, such as sorting genuine claims from many neighbours or holdouts demanding too much.
Its lesson was that the burden should be on governments to show their interventions do more good than harm.
Its argument became the basis of what George Stigler labelled the Coase theorem.
It showed the Pigouvian tax is not the only path to dealing with externalities.
It founded the field of law and economics, is the most frequently cited work in legal scholarship, and was cited in Coase's 1991 Nobel Prize.

entries.text: The most frequently cited work in legal scholarship is an economics article about neighbors. The Problem of Social Cost is Coase's 1960 law review article on externalities, such as pollution harming people next door. Its central claim was bold. If making deals cost nothing, people would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources, whatever legal rights they started with. Real bargaining and information are costly, though. Many useful deals never happen because of these costs, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-641}}: sorting genuine claims from many neighbors, say, or facing holdouts who demand too much. So legal rules matter insofar as they give rights to whoever values them most. The article showed that a tax on the harm, the remedy explored in {{ref:nature-pol-088}}, is not the only path. Its lesson was that governments should have to show their interventions do more good than harm. George Stigler later gave its argument a name, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. It founded the field of law and economics and was cited in Coase's 1991 Nobel Prize.

entries.title: Strict liability: paying for harm without being at fault

definition.text: A legal rule that makes a person responsible for harm caused by their activity even when they were not at fault.

facts.text: Someone who keeps something inherently dangerous is liable for resulting damage no matter how carefully it was guarded.
US courts have treated storing large amounts of flammable liquid in a city, noxious factory fumes in settled areas, and oil wells in populated places as ultrahazardous.
By making defendants pay regardless of fault, it pushes them to take every possible precaution.
An early example is Rylands v Fletcher: whoever keeps something on their land likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage.
After an environmental impact assessment, the polluter pays principle may be used to require strict liability or insurance for a project.
Strict liability in US aviation helped push small-aircraft production from 18,000 units a year in 1978 to a few hundred by 1993.

entries.text: Keep something dangerous and you pay for any damage it does, no matter how carefully you guarded it. That is strict liability: a legal rule making a person responsible for harm caused by their activity even when they were not at fault. An early example is Rylands v Fletcher. Whoever keeps something on their land that is likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage. Because defendants pay regardless of fault, the rule pushes them to take every possible precaution. It can push hard. Strict liability in US aviation helped cut small-aircraft production from 18,000 units a year in 1978 to a few hundred by 1993. Once a project's environmental effects have been assessed, the principle explored in {{ref:nature-pol-095}} may be used to require strict liability or insurance.

entries.title: The cheapest cost avoider: who can prevent harm most cheaply
entries.article: The Problem of Social Cost#Theoretical challenges

definition.text: The party able to prevent a harm at the lowest cost, to whom liability can efficiently be assigned when bargaining is hard.

facts.text: Guido Calabresi argued in The Costs of Accidents (1970) that it can still be efficient to hold wealth-producing companies liable.
When one factory's smoke harms many farms, the farmers struggle to organize, and some may free ride rather than pay their share.
The factory may know best how to cut harm, making it the cheapest avoider.

entries.text: When one factory's smoke harms many farms, who should fix it? The farmers struggle to organize, and some may free ride rather than pay their share. The factory, meanwhile, may know best how to cut the harm. That makes it the cheapest cost avoider, the party able to prevent a harm at the lowest cost. Liability can efficiently be assigned to it when bargaining is hard. Guido Calabresi made the case in The Costs of Accidents (1970), arguing that it can still be efficient to hold wealth-producing companies liable.

entries.title: Coming to the nuisance: can newcomers complain

definition.text: The question of whether someone who moves next to an existing nuisance can still complain about it.

facts.text: In English law, unlike US law, coming to the nuisance is no defence; the 1879 case Sturges v Bridgman still stands.
Many US states limit nuisance claims, for example with right-to-farm rules protecting agriculture from newcomers' complaints about smells.
Coase used Sturges v Bridgman, a noisy sweet-maker next to a quiet doctor, to illustrate his argument.

entries.title: Damages or injunction: how courts handle a nuisance

definition.text: The two ways courts deal with a nuisance: ordering payment of damages, or issuing an injunction to stop the activity.

facts.text: Under the old common law, damages were the only remedy; courts of equity later added the injunction.
The law and economics movement analyses which remedy is most efficient in each case.
In the Atlantic Cement case, a New York court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of obeying an injunction, since compliance would cost far more than the neighbours' harm.
In theory, permanent damages should equal the net present value of all future harm to the plaintiff.

entries.text: A court facing a nuisance has two tools. It can order the offender to pay damages, or it can issue an injunction to stop the activity. Under the old common law, damages were the only remedy; courts of equity later added the injunction. The law and economics movement asks which remedy is most efficient in each case. In the Atlantic Cement case, a New York court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of obeying an injunction. Compliance would have cost far more than the neighbors' harm. In theory, permanent damages should equal the value today of all future harm to the plaintiff.

entries.title: Marginal damage: the harm from one more unit of pollution

definition.text: The extra harm done to others by one more unit of a polluting activity, also called the marginal external cost.

facts.text: Steel production causes marginal damages through pollution and other environmental effects.
Pigou argued for a tax equal to the marginal damage per unit to correct the externality.
A tax around 50% higher or lower than marginal damages still captures around three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more than precise measurement.
Weitzman showed that if marginal damages rise more steeply than abatement costs, quantity controls work better than price controls.

entries.text: Marginal damage, or marginal external cost, is the extra harm to others from one more unit of a polluting activity, such as making steel. Pigou argued for a tax equal to the marginal damage per unit, to correct the externality. Precision matters little. A tax around 50% higher or lower than marginal damages still captures around three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more. Weitzman showed that if marginal damages rise more steeply than the costs of cutting pollution, quantity controls work better than price controls.

entries.title: Internalizing externalities: making polluters face the full cost

definition.text: Making those who cause an external cost bear it themselves, so their private costs line up with the costs to society.

facts.text: Pigou proposed corrective taxes aimed at internalizing externalities by aligning private and social costs.
A corrective tax is one of the public remedies for internalizing externalities.
Carbon trading is a prime example of a shift toward internalizing externalities.
Pricing an externality at its marginal damage lets producers and consumers choose the cheapest way to cut emissions.
An older ecological economics critique questions whether internalizing externalities can really correct the current system.

entries.contested_note: Ecological economists question whether internalizing externalities can correct market systems, while mainstream economists favour it.
entries.text: A polluter who pays nothing for the harm it causes is working with the wrong prices. Internalizing an externality means making those who cause an external cost bear it themselves, so their private costs line up with the costs to society. Pigou proposed corrective taxes for exactly this purpose, and such a tax remains one of the main public remedies. Pricing an externality at its marginal damage lets producers and consumers choose the cheapest way to cut emissions. Carbon trading is a prime example of the shift toward internalizing externalities. Not everyone is convinced. Mainstream economists favor the approach, but an older critique from {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} questions whether internalizing externalities can really correct the current system.

entries.title: Liability rules: take now, pay later

definition.text: Legal rules, described by Calabresi and Melamed, under which a liability rule is a form of legalized private expropriation that can be used when transaction costs block voluntary trade.

facts.text: Calabresi and Melamed argue such liability rules can increase welfare when transaction costs are large.
In the Atlantic Cement nuisance case, a court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of being stopped by injunction.

entries.text: Sometimes the law lets one party take another's right and pay for it afterward. Calabresi and Melamed described such liability rules as a form of legalized private expropriation, useful when the costs of making deals block voluntary trade. They argue these rules can increase welfare when those costs are large. The Atlantic Cement nuisance case is an example. A court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of being stopped by an injunction.

entries.title: Transboundary pollution: when dirty air crosses borders

definition.text: Pollution produced in one country that crosses borders and harms other places.

facts.text: Acid rain from sulfur dioxide became a major issue as it spread across borders.
Some countries pass their pollution to other places to clean up, prompting laws on holding countries liable for damage.
ASEAN ministers called in 1990 for harmonized transboundary pollution prevention, leading to a 2002 agreement on haze.

sources.title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution

entries.text: Smoke and dirty water do not stop at borders. Transboundary pollution is pollution produced in one country that crosses borders and harms other places. Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-046}}, became a major issue as it spread across borders. Some countries pass their pollution to other places to clean up, which has prompted laws on holding countries liable for damage. ASEAN ministers called in 1990 for harmonized prevention of transboundary pollution, leading to a 2002 agreement on haze.

entries.title: Transaction costs: the price of making a deal

definition.text: A cost of making a trade in a market, over and above the price of the thing traded.

facts.text: They fall into three groups: search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs.
Douglass North argued that a society's rules, its institutions, largely set transaction costs, and institutions that keep them low can boost economic growth.
The term is often wrongly credited to Ronald Coase, though his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm discussed the 'costs of using the price mechanism'.
John R. Commons introduced the idea in 1931 that transactions are the basis of economic thinking.
High transaction costs, such as proving additionality, have been a known difficulty of carbon offset schemes like the Clean Development Mechanism.

entries.text: Every trade costs more than its price. A transaction cost is any cost of making a trade in a market, over and above the price of the thing traded. Economists sort these costs into three groups: search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs. John R. Commons introduced the idea in 1931 that transactions are the basis of economic thinking. The term is often wrongly credited to Coase, though his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm did discuss the 'costs of using the price mechanism'. Douglass North argued that a society's rules, its institutions, largely set transaction costs, and that institutions keeping them low can help an economy grow. The costs bite in environmental markets too. High transaction costs, such as proving that a project would not have happened anyway, have long troubled carbon offset schemes like {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}.

entries.title: Excludability: can non-payers be kept out

definition.text: How far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it.

facts.text: Economists describe every good by two traits: how excludable it is and how rival it is.
A cinema film is excludable: ushers check tickets, so non-payers cannot see it.
A lighthouse is non-excludable, because any ship at sea can use its light.
Paul Samuelson proposed the idea in 1954 as a yes-or-no trait; Elinor Ostrom in 1990 recast it as a scale from fully excludable to fully non-excludable.
Music, films and software are semi-excludable: they have a price, but piracy lets many non-payers use them.
Because producers cannot profit from goods people get free, non-excludable goods tend to be under-supplied without government help.

entries.text: A cinema can check tickets at the door. A lighthouse cannot stop a passing ship from using its light. That difference is excludability: how far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it. Economists describe every good by two traits, how excludable it is and how rival it is. Paul Samuelson proposed the idea in 1954 as a yes-or-no trait. Ostrom recast it in 1990 as a scale, from fully excludable to fully non-excludable. Music, films and software sit in between: they have a price, but piracy lets many non-payers use them. The trait matters because producers cannot profit from goods people get free. Without government help, non-excludable goods therefore tend to be under-supplied.

entries.title: Rivalry: does my use leave less for you

definition.text: A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use of it at the same time.

facts.text: An apple is rival: once one person eats it, no one else can.
A good is non-rival when serving one more person costs nothing extra; a TV broadcast, a scenic view, clean air and street lights are examples.
Non-rivalry does not mean a good is cheap to provide in total, only that the cost of one more user is zero.
Roads, the internet and courts are non-rival only up to a point, after which congestion slows everyone, so economists now treat rivalry as a scale rather than a yes-or-no.
Paul Samuelson introduced non-rival consumption in 1954 to tell private from public goods, and Richard Musgrave later added rivalry and excludability as criteria.

entries.text: Once someone eats an apple, no one else can. A TV broadcast is different: one more viewer takes nothing from the rest. A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use at the same time. It is non-rival when serving one more person costs nothing extra, as with a scenic view, clean air or street lights. Non-rival does not mean cheap. The total cost of providing the good can be large; only the cost of one more user is zero. Many goods are non-rival only up to a point. Roads, the internet and courts slow everyone down once congestion sets in, so economists now treat rivalry as a scale rather than a yes-or-no. Paul Samuelson introduced non-rival consumption in 1954 to separate goods shared by all, {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, from ordinary goods. Richard Musgrave later added rivalry and excludability as criteria.

entries.title: Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few

definition.text: A good or service that no one can be kept from using and that one person's use does not reduce for others, usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes.

facts.text: Examples include knowledge, official statistics, national security, flood control systems, aids to navigation and street lighting.
Clean air and other environmental goods are common examples of public goods.
Because people who do not pay can still use them, public goods may be under-produced, overused or degraded: the free-rider problem.
Without government provision, such goods might be produced only in small amounts or not at all, since they are not profitable enough for private firms.
Paul Samuelson set out the modern theory in his 1954 paper The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure, building on Wicksell and Lindahl.
It is a misconception that public goods must come from the public sector: they can occur naturally or be produced by individuals, firms or community groups.
Pure public goods are rare, and economists debate how to define public goods and how serious the problems they cause are.
Technology can change a good's status: encryption lets broadcasters sell access, and cheaper road pricing allows charging by actual use.

entries.contested_note: Economists debate whether 'public goods' form a real category at all, and how to define and measure public goods problems.

entries.title: Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to deplete

definition.text: A natural or human-made resource system, such as fishing grounds or an irrigation system, that is costly but not impossible to keep people from using.

facts.text: Unlike pure public goods, common-pool resources get crowded or overused because what one user takes is no longer there for others.
Examples include forests, irrigation systems, fishing grounds, groundwater basins, pastures and the atmosphere.
Without management, each fisher has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does, so fish stocks soon run down.
They may be owned by governments as public goods, by communities as common property, or by individuals and firms as private goods; when no one owns them they are open access.
Elinor Ostrom found many such resources run by local self-managing communities, contradicting the claim that they must be privatized or be destroyed.
In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

entries.title: The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused

definition.text: The idea that when people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each person has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up.

facts.text: English economist William Forster Lloyd described the problem in an 1833 pamphlet about herders sharing a common pasture, where adding extra cattle could lead to overgrazing.
The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by ecologist Garrett Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet.
Hardin's main worry was human overpopulation, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'.
The commons problem is used as a model for many resource problems today, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal.
Climate change has been described as a huge example of the tragedy, with the Earth treated as a commons whose resources are depleted without regard to the harm done to others.
Proposed government fixes include privatization, regulation such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause.

Elinor Ostrom and colleagues found the tragedy less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules; a Swiss Alpine commons has been run by farmers since 1517.
Critics note that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

entries.contested_note: Scholars dispute whether overuse is inevitable: Ostrom's work is seen by some economists as refuting Hardin, and others say open, unregulated common land never really existed.

entries.title: The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying

definition.text: A market failure that happens when people who benefit from a shared resource or public good pay nothing, or too little, for it.

facts.text: A coastal town's lighthouse helps ships from many countries, even though those ships pay nothing toward its costs.
Because no one can be kept from using a public good, each person has little reason to help pay for it.
Free riding leads to too little of a good being produced or too much being used up, which is wasteful for society.
When asked how much money they would pay for a public good, people tend to understate how much they value it.
Even though people tend to cooperate by nature, the presence of free riders has been shown to make cooperation break down.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: every country gains from others cutting emissions, but each would lose by switching to a low-carbon economy itself.
Shown as a prisoner's dilemma, if two people should share the cost of a fire station and both refuse to pay, society gets nothing.
Low-cost pooling of contributions, as in internet crowdfunding where no money changes hands until a goal is met, is one way around the problem.

entries.title: Private goods: yours to keep, and gone once used

definition.text: A useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others.

facts.text: Bread is a private good: a loaf one person eats cannot be eaten by another, and a baker can refuse to sell it.
Private goods are scarce, which can create competition for them.
Unlike public goods such as clean air, private goods rarely suffer from free riding.
Market demand for a private good is found by adding up how much each person will buy at each price (horizontal summation), unlike public goods, whose individual demands are summed vertically.

entries.text: A loaf of bread is the model of a private good. Once one person eats it no one else can, and a baker can refuse to sell it. A private good is a useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others. Private goods are scarce, which can create competition for them. Unlike public goods such as clean air, they rarely suffer from free riding. Their market demand is found by adding up how much each person will buy at each price, a method called horizontal summation. Public goods, enjoyed by everyone at once, have their individual demands summed vertically instead.

entries.title: Public economics: when should government step in

definition.text: The study of government policy in terms of efficiency and fairness, asking whether and how far government should take part in markets.

facts.text: It builds on welfare economics and aims to improve social welfare.
It focuses on market failures such as public goods, externalities and imperfect competition, and on taxes and government spending.
Government examples include providing defense, regulating pollution and dealing with unequal information between buyers and sellers.
A.C. Pigou proposed taxes to correct externalities, such as an emissions tax; in 1960 Ronald Coase proposed instead assigning property rights and letting people negotiate.
Much of cost-benefit analysis was developed in the United States from the problems of water-resource projects.

entries.text: When should government step into markets, and how far? Public economics studies government policy in terms of efficiency and fairness to answer that question. entries.title: Four types of goods: a grid for every good

definition.text: A grid that sorts goods by two questions, whether people can be kept from using them and whether one person's use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Goods that can be withheld and are used up, such as food, clothing and parking spaces, are private goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld but are used up, such as fish stocks and timber, are common-pool resources.
Goods that can be withheld but are not used up, such as cinemas, software and private parks, are club goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld and are not used up, such as free-to-air television, air and national defense, are public goods.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
entries.text: Two questions sort every good in the economy. Can people be kept from using it? And does one person's use leave less for others? The answers give a grid of four types. Goods that can be withheld and are used up are private goods, such as food, clothing and parking spaces. Goods that cannot be withheld but are used up are common-pool resources, such as fish stocks and timber. Goods that can be withheld but are not used up are the kind explored in {{ref:nature-econ-627}}, such as cinemas, software and private parks. Goods that cannot be withheld and are not used up are public goods, such as free-to-air television, air and national defense. The grid shows where trouble lies. Common-pool resources invite overuse because no one can be kept out, and public goods invite free riding for the same reason. Private goods rarely face either problem.

entries.title: Club goods: members only, but no one else loses

definition.text: A good that people can be kept from using, usually by charging them, but that one person's use does not reduce for others until it gets crowded.

facts.text: Examples include cinemas, cable television, software as a service, and gym, golf club or swimming pool memberships.
Serving one more user costs almost nothing, so club goods are often supplied by natural monopolies and are kept artificially scarce.
Providers exclude non-payers either to cover fixed costs, as nonprofits do, or to make a profit.
Controlling access nearly always causes a deadweight loss, such as the cost of tollbooths or digital rights management.
The European Union has been treated as a club good: its services can be withheld from non-members, while adding members to the Schengen Area does not make travel harder for existing ones.

entries.title: Property: rights over things, and the things themselves

definition.text: A system of rights that gives people legal control over valuable things, and also the valuable things themselves.

facts.text: Depending on the thing, an owner may use, change, share, rent, sell, give away or destroy it, and keep others from doing so.
Economics recognizes four broad forms: private, public, collective and common property.
Legal systems usually separate land and buildings (real property) from movable things (personal property), and tangible from intangible property.
One view holds that things become property only when they are scarce: hunter-gatherers did not treat land as property because there was no shortage of it.
Aristotle favored private property, arguing that self-interest leads people to neglect the commons.

entries.text: Property means two things at once: a system of rights giving people legal control over valuable things, and the valuable things themselves. Depending on the thing, an owner may use, change, share, rent, sell, give away or destroy it, and keep others from doing so. Economics recognizes four broad forms: private, public, collective and common. Legal systems separate land and buildings, real property, from movable personal property. One view holds that things become property only when scarce: hunter-gatherers did not treat land as property, because there was no shortage of it. Aristotle favored private ownership, arguing that self-interest leads people to neglect the commons.

entries.title: Property rights: the rules of who owns what

definition.text: The rules that decide who owns a resource or good and how it may be used.

facts.text: Resources can be owned by individuals, associations, collectives or governments.
Property rights have three parts: the right to use a good, the right to earn income from it, and the right to sell, change, abandon or destroy it.
Well-enforced property rights give people reasons to invest, innovate and trade, which makes markets work better.
Governments can create property rights through direct rules such as discharge limits, or through market tools such as taxes and tradable permits.
An emissions trading scheme works by setting up property rights for the atmosphere.
Secure rights make resources harder to exploit, so people are less likely to use them unsustainably.
Studying former European colonies, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found strong evidence that institutions giving secure property rights lead to prosperity.

entries.text: Can anyone own the air? Some climate policies work by setting up property rights for the atmosphere. The rights come in three parts. There is the right to use a good, the right to earn income from it, and the right to sell, change, abandon or destroy it. Well-enforced rights give people reasons to invest, innovate and trade, which makes markets work better. Governments can create property rights directly, through rules such as limits on discharges, or through market tools such as taxes and tradable permits. A scheme that trades permits to emit, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-253}}, creates exactly such rights over the atmosphere. The stakes are large. Studying former European colonies, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found strong evidence that institutions giving secure property rights lead to prosperity.

entries.title: Land tenure: who may use land, and on what terms

definition.text: The system that decides who may use land, for how long and on what conditions.

facts.text: Tenure can rest on official laws and policies or on informal local customs.
It sets out the holder's rights and responsibilities toward the land.
Forms include fee simple, the most complete ownership in common law, as well as leasehold, life estates, common land rights, sharecropping and easements.
Land tenure and forest governance were named among the issues national REDD+ forest strategies must address.
Tradeable individual ownership of land was often introduced through colonialism.

entries.text: Who may farm a field, for how long, and on what terms? Land tenure is the system that decides. It can rest on official laws and policies or on informal local customs, and it sets out the holder's rights and responsibilities toward the land. Its forms range widely. Fee simple, the most complete ownership in common law, sits alongside leasehold, life estates, shared rights to common land, sharecropping and easements. Tradeable individual ownership of land was often introduced through colonialism. Tenure matters for nature too. Land tenure and forest governance were named among the issues that national forest strategies under {{ref:nature-mkt-092}} must address.

entries.title: Private property: ownership outside the state

definition.text: Ownership of property by people or organizations other than the government.

facts.text: It differs from public property, owned by the state, and from collective or cooperative property.
Private property is a legal idea defined and enforced by each country's legal and political institutions, and it is the foundation of capitalism.
John Locke's chief argument for owning land privately was that it led to better land management and farming than common land.
Supporters say private ownership puts land to productive use, protects its value, and lets it be traded or used as collateral.
Owners' rights usually come with limits, such as building codes or bans on demolishing historic buildings.
Socialists criticize private ownership of the means of production, and critics also call property law a tool of empire that ignored Indigenous common ownership of land.

entries.contested_note: Economic liberals see private property as essential to prosperity, while socialists and other critics see it as a source of exploitation, inequality and land appropriation.
entries.text: Private property is the foundation of capitalism, and one of its most contested ideas. It means ownership by people or organizations other than the government, as distinct from public property owned by the state and from collective or cooperative property. It is a legal idea, defined and enforced by each country's legal and political institutions. John Locke's chief argument for owning land privately was that it led to better land management and farming than common land. Supporters say private ownership puts land to productive use, protects its value, and lets it be traded or used as collateral. Owners' rights usually come with limits, such as building codes or bans on demolishing historic buildings. Economic liberals see private property as essential to prosperity. Socialists criticize private ownership of the means of production, and other critics call property law a tool of empire that ignored Indigenous communities' shared holding of land.

entries.title: Georgism: keep what you make, share what nature gives

definition.text: The economic idea that people should own what they produce, but the income that comes from land and natural resources should belong equally to everyone in society.

facts.text: It grew from the writings of American economist Henry George, whose first book, Progress and Poverty (1879), argued for raising public money mainly from land and natural resources.
Its main policy is a land value tax, whose revenue could cut or replace taxes on income, trade and purchases.
In economics, 'land' means everything in nature that exists without human effort; George included climate, soil, waterways, minerals, forests, oceans, air and solar energy.
Milton Friedman called a tax on unimproved land value the 'least bad tax', because it does not hold back economic activity the way other taxes do.
Some Georgists want surplus revenue returned to people as a basic income or citizen's dividend.
George blamed private capture of land rent for persistent poverty despite technological progress, and for boom-and-bust cycles.

entries.title: Common property regimes: communities that manage their own commons

definition.text: A social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used.

facts.text: It is not the same thing as a common-pool resource, since such resources are not always governed as common property.
Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the total benefit of the resource, and they protect the core resource while sharing out what can be harvested.
Community members have monitored access, while outsiders can be kept out, so the resource looks private to outsiders and common to insiders.
Rules must limit the amount, timing and technology of harvesting: limits set too high destroy the resource, and limits set too low waste benefits.
It differs from open access: in a common property system access is not free, so the resource looks private to outsiders and common to insiders.
Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the resource's total benefit, and usually work locally to prevent overexploitation.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons was criticized for not distinguishing common property from open-access resources.
Members' local knowledge often lets these regimes outperform rules designed by outside experts, and results are best when they also consult governments and experts.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
entries.text: To outsiders a community-run resource looks private; to its members it is common. That double face marks a common property regime: a social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used. Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the resource's total benefit. They protect the central resource while sharing out what can be harvested, usually working locally to prevent overuse. Members have monitored access, and outsiders can be kept out. The rules must limit the amount, timing and technology of harvesting. Limits set too high destroy the resource; limits set too low waste its benefits. Such a regime is not the same as a common-pool resource, which is not always governed as common property. Nor is it open access, where entry is free. Hardin's tragedy of the commons was criticized for blurring that line. Members' local knowledge often lets these regimes outperform rules designed by outside experts, and results are best when they also consult governments and experts.

entries.title: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons: from owners to communities

definition.text: The range of ways, from local self-organized rules to government action, proposed for stopping people from overusing a shared resource.

facts.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons is counted among the main problems of political philosophy.
Turning a common resource into private property gives the new owner a reason to keep it productive, an idea linked to Coase in 1960.
Privatization works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource.
Governments can cap how much of a shared resource any one person may use, for example through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging.
Government solutions are used when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together.
A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power.
Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

entries.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons counts among the main problems of political philosophy. The proposals run from local, self-organized rules to government action. It works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource. Another is a government cap on how much any one person may use, through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging. Governments step in when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together. A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power. Cooperation can also come from below. Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

entries.title: Open access resources: first come, first served

definition.text: A resource that no one owns and that anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open access goods need little oversight or are hard to restrict, and because they are first come, first served, they are prone to the tragedy of the commons.
In an open fishery, profits draw in more fishers, leaving fewer fish; scarcer fish raise prices, which draws in still more fishers.
Hardin's work has been criticized for failing to tell common-pool resources apart from open access resources.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
entries.text: In an open fishery, profits draw in more fishers. More fishers leave fewer fish, scarcer fish fetch higher prices, and higher prices draw in still more fishers. That spiral is the danger of an open access resource: one that no one owns and anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others. Such resources need little oversight or are hard to restrict. Because they are first come, first served, they are prone to the tragedy of the commons. The distinction from managed commons matters. Hardin's work has been criticized for failing to tell common-pool resources apart from open access resources.

entries.title: Ostrom's design principles: what long-lived commons share

definition.text: Eight conditions that Elinor Ostrom found in long-lasting community arrangements for managing shared resources.

facts.text: The first principles are clearly defined boundaries, and rules for taking and supplying the resource that fit local conditions.
Most users should take part in making the rules, and monitors should be users themselves or answer to them.
Rule-breakers face sanctions that grow step by step, and conflicts can be settled cheaply and easily.
Authorities such as the government must at least recognize the users' right to organize, and large resources are run as layers of nested groups with small local ones at the base.
Ostrom set out this work in Governing the Commons (1990), showing that communities around the world have managed shared resources successfully through local governance.

entries.text: Ostrom did not just argue that communities could manage shared resources; she showed how. In her 1990 book, {{ref:nature-res-197}}, she reported that communities around the world had managed shared resources successfully through local governance. From the long-lasting cases she drew eight conditions. The first are clearly defined boundaries, and rules for taking and supplying the resource that fit local conditions. Most users should take part in making the rules. Monitors should be users themselves or answer to them. Rule-breakers face sanctions that grow step by step, and conflicts can be settled cheaply and easily. Authorities such as the government must at least recognize the users' right to organize. Large resources are run as layers of nested groups, with small local ones at the base. Together the principles describe arrangements in which the users themselves make, watch and enforce the rules.

entries.title: Types of property regimes: four ways to hold a resource

definition.text: The main ways a resource can be held, open access, public, private or common property, sorted by whether others can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open-access property is owned by nobody, nobody manages it and access is not controlled; an unregulated forest is an example.
Open access can exist because ownership was never set up in law, or because keeping people out costs more than it is worth.
Public or state property is owned by the public, with access and use controlled by a government agency.
Private property is controlled by its owner or owners; a cellphone is an example because only one person can use it and it must be bought.
Common or collective property in the legal sense is owned by a group whose members jointly control access, use and exclusion.

entries.title: Bargaining: haggling over the terms of a deal

definition.text: A kind of negotiation in which a buyer and a seller argue over the price or terms of a deal.

facts.text: If the two sides agree on terms, the trade goes ahead.
Bargaining has largely disappeared where fixed-price shops dominate, but remains common for expensive goods such as homes, cars and jewellery.
Emotions, mental biases and a sense of fairness strongly affect bargaining; the endowment effect makes sellers ask more than buyers will pay.
Coase argued that without transaction costs, people would bargain their way to the same use of resources however a court ruled in a property dispute.

entries.title: The Coase theorem: bargaining your way out of harm

definition.text: The claim that when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain their way to an efficient outcome, whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough.

facts.text: If true, the theorem would let private individuals solve externality problems by themselves.
Coase developed it while thinking about radio stations interfering with each other: the station that gained more from broadcasting would pay the other not to interfere.
If fencing the farm is cheaper than fencing the cattle, bargaining should produce a fence around the farm whether the farmer or the rancher holds the rights.
In his 1960 paper Coase himself argued that real transaction costs are rarely low enough for efficient bargaining.
Imperfect information and poorly defined property rights can also block the bargain.
In Danish talks between waterworks and farmers, farmers used their information advantage to seek over-compensation and drag out talks, showing how sensitive the theorem is to transaction costs.
Behavioral economist Richard Thaler found that people care about fairness when bargaining over their own property, so they may reject efficient but unfair deals.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the theorem rarely applies in practice, and Duncan Kennedy argues that the starting allocation of rights always matters.
distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

entries.title: Environmental goods: valuable, unpriced and hard to protect

definition.text: A usually unpriced good from nature or green infrastructure, such as clean air and water, landscapes, parks, rivers, forests and beaches.

facts.text: Environmental goods are a sub-category of public goods.
They are hard to protect because users pay nothing up front and pollution can damage them indefinitely.
There is no agreed method for putting an economic value on them; obstacles include free riding, unclear ownership and the fact that they cannot be divided up.
Economists try to value them by asking people's willingness to pay, sometimes with simulated markets and contingent valuation, but critics cite framing effects and biases.
Alternative measures of progress, such as the Genuine Progress Indicator and Gross National Happiness, count environmental damage and resource depletion.

entries.text: Nobody pays at a gate to breathe clean air or walk a beach, and that is part of the problem. entries.title: Public bads: harms no one can escape

definition.text: The mirror image of a public good: something harmful that no one can avoid and that harms everyone at once, such as air pollution.

facts.text: While markets supply too little of a public good, they supply too much of a public bad, because those causing it ignore the harm to others.
One way to reduce a public bad is for a third party, usually the state, to step in.
Deforestation, excess water use and pesticide use can be seen as public bads that push harm onto present and future generations.
Much of environmental economics is about externalities or 'public bads'.
Green economists suggest judging such impacts as far ahead as the seventh generation.

entries.title: Global public goods: benefits that know no borders

definition.text: A public good available more or less worldwide, which no one can be kept from and whose use by one does not reduce it for others.

facts.text: The idea extends Paul Samuelson's notion of public goods to the global economy.
Knowledge is the classic example, including freely released projects such as free software and Wikipedia.
Kaul and colleagues (2003) note that some goods are public only by default, such as the ozone layer before anyone understood the damage from CFCs.
Climate change mitigation, financial stability, security, knowledge and global public health need international or supranational bodies to manage them, since national laws stop at borders.
A firm that saves money by polluting shared air or water becomes a corporate free rider, raising the cost of these often transnational public goods.
Because water crosses political borders, it cannot be managed by local or national authorities alone, and leaving it to the market would hurt those most in need.

entries.title: Digital public goods: open code and data for all

definition.text: Open-source software, data sets, AI models, standards and content that anyone can use, treated as public goods.

facts.text: The UN Secretary-General's Roadmap for Digital Cooperation defines them as open resources that follow privacy laws, do no harm and help reach the Sustainable Development Goals.
A small group of maintainers often keeps such projects going while many more users benefit, raising worries about burnout and underfunding.

entries.title: Local public goods: benefits that stay close to home

definition.text: Public goods whose benefits fall mainly on the people nearby, such as a clean office or a neighborhood crime watch, rather than equally on everyone.

facts.text: Overlapping neighborhoods are often modeled as a network; when neighborhoods do not overlap, the standard model is the Tiebout model.
A 2019 theory of public goods in networks found voluntary provision usually falls short of the efficient level, with a few people contributing heavily and their neighbors free riding.

entries.title: Lotteries for public goods: funding by raffle

definition.text: Funding a public good by selling lottery tickets, with all ticket money going to the good and the prize paid from outside funds.

facts.text: Lotteries are approximately efficient, and funding approaches the optimal level as the prize grows.
In very large populations, contributions through a lottery shrink toward those of plain voluntary giving and should fall to zero.

entries.text: Sell lottery tickets, put all the ticket money into a public good, and pay the prize from outside funds. That is the idea of funding public goods by lottery. The scheme is approximately efficient, and funding approaches the optimal level as the prize grows. It has a limit, though. In very large populations, contributions through a lottery shrink toward those of plain voluntary giving, and should fall to zero.
entries.text_plain: Sell lottery tickets, put all the ticket money into a public good, and pay the prize from outside funds. That is the idea of funding public goods by lottery. The scheme is approximately efficient, and funding approaches the optimal level as the prize grows. It has a limit, though. In very large populations, contributions through a lottery shrink toward those of plain voluntary giving, and should fall to zero.

entries.title: Nonprofits and public goods: filling the gap government leaves

definition.text: The Weisbrod model's idea that nonprofit organizations supply public goods that government leaves unprovided.

facts.text: Government supplies what the median voter wants, which is less than citizens with stronger demand would like.
Nonprofits funded by donations from those citizens fill the gap.

entries.text: Why do nonprofits supply goods that government could provide? The Weisbrod model answers that government supplies what the median voter wants. That is less than citizens with stronger demand would like. Nonprofit organizations, funded by donations from those citizens, fill the gap with the public goods government leaves unprovided.

entries.title: Quasi-public goods: why goods get misclassified

definition.text: Goods such as streets, libraries and education that share some traits of public goods but from which people can be excluded, and are therefore often misclassified.

facts.text: The lighthouse is the textbook public good, but Ronald Coase argued its costs could be profitably bundled into port fees, which has funded real lighthouses.
A community soccer field is a mixed case: the field is shared, but players bring their own gear and pay a rental fee.
Some goods, such as orphan drugs, need government incentives to be made yet are not public goods.

entries.title: Common goods: open to all, but used up

definition.text: In economics, a good that is rival (one person's use leaves less for others) but non-excludable (people cannot be kept from using it).

facts.text: Because anyone can use them, common goods risk being overexploited when people act in their own interest.
A road is a public good when empty, but once congested each extra driver slows others, turning it into a common good.
Fish stocks in international waters, among the least regulated common resources, are likely to be depleted if fish are taken without limits.
Aristotle already observed that 'what is common to many is taken least care of'.

entries.text: An empty road is a public good. Add traffic until each extra driver slows the others, and it becomes a common good. Because anyone can use them, common goods risk overuse when people act in their own interest. Fish stocks in international waters, among the least regulated common resources, are likely to be depleted if fish are taken without limits. Aristotle had already observed that 'what is common to many is taken least care of'.

entries.title: New institutional economics: the rules behind the market

definition.text: A school of economics that studies the institutions, meaning the legal rules and social norms, that underlie economic activity.

facts.text: It assumes people are rational but have limited minds and information and find agreements hard to enforce, so institutions arise largely to cut transaction costs.
It grew from Ronald Coase's papers 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937) and 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960); Oliver Williamson coined the name in 1975.
Following Douglass North, institutions are 'the rules of the game', formal laws and informal norms, while organizations are the teams that play.
Associated Nobel laureates include Daron Acemoglu, Ronald Coase, Douglass North, Elinor Ostrom and Oliver Williamson.
Critics say it overlooks the coercion and power politics involved in creating and keeping institutions.

conflicts.text: In 1972 Harold Demsetz and Armen Alchian published the work described as founding New Institutional Economics.
conflicts.note: The NIE page dates the name to Williamson in 1975; this is a founding claim rather than the coining, so not strictly the same quantity.

entries.title: Adaptive governance: managing commons that keep changing

definition.text: A way of managing shared resources that Ostrom recommended for problems that are complex, uncertain and fragmented.

facts.text: Because management depends on the type of resource, a strategy that works in one place may not suit another.
Ostrom's five requirements are good timely information, ways to handle conflict, users who help monitor rule-keeping, flexible infrastructure, and readiness to adapt and fix errors.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

For problems that are complex, uncertain and fragmented, Ostrom recommended governance that can adapt. Her approach has five requirements: good, timely information; ways to handle conflict; users who help monitor rule-keeping; flexible infrastructure; and readiness to adapt and fix errors.

entries.title: Stock and flow: living off a resource's interest

definition.text: The split of a shared resource into a core stock that must be protected and a flow of units, such as fish or grass, that can be harvested from it.

facts.text: As long as the stock is not harmed, it keeps regrowing the flow, so careful use can continue indefinitely.
Taking more than the flow shrinks the stock, which in turn shrinks future flows; sometimes the loss cannot be undone.
A pasture can be grazed a certain amount each year without harm, but overgrazing makes it prone to erosion and less useful.

entries.title: Transaction cost economics: firms as ways of governing deals

definition.text: Oliver Williamson's approach that studies the transaction itself and treats firms as structures for governing deals rather than just production machines.

facts.text: Unlike standard microeconomics, it assumes people have bounded rationality and treats property rights and contracts as problematic rather than costless to enforce.
Williamson named frequency, asset specificity, uncertainty, limited rationality and opportunism as what drives transaction costs.
Specialized investments cannot be redeployed if a contract ends, so ending such a deal causes significant loss.
Williamson was awarded the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics.

entries.title: The Samuelson condition: how much of a public good to provide

definition.text: Paul Samuelson's rule for the best amount of a public good: provide more as long as the total of everyone's extra benefit is at least the extra cost of providing it.

facts.text: Formally, the sum of all consumers' marginal rates of substitution equals the economy's marginal rate of transformation between the public good and a private good.
For a private good, by contrast, each consumer's own valuation is set equal to the cost of producing one more unit.
Because everyone enjoys a public good at once, individual demands are added together vertically, so the rule extends supply and demand from private to public goods.
If two people would pay $200 and $100 for a park costing $225, its $300 total value leaves a $75 surplus, so it should be built.
Samuelson stressed that people have reasons to understate their valuations, which makes applying the rule hard in practice.

entries.title: Assurance contracts: pledges that pay only if enough join

definition.text: An agreement in which people pledge money toward a public good only if enough others also pledge; otherwise the good is not built and the money is returned.

facts.text: In a dominant assurance contract, an entrepreneur refunds pledges plus an extra sum if the target is missed, and earns a fee if it is met.
This makes pledging the best move for each person whatever others do, which game theory calls a dominant strategy.
First proposed by Bagnoli and Lipman in 1989, they work best in small groups of easily identified people, and crowdfunding sites such as Kickstarter use them.

distinct_from: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism
entries.text: Pledge money toward a public good, and you get it back if too few others pledge. That is an assurance contract: the good is built only if enough people sign up. Such contracts work best in small groups of easily identified people, and crowdfunding sites such as Kickstarter use them.

entries.title: Intellectual property: fencing off ideas
entries.article: Free-rider problem#Introducing an exclusion mechanism (club goods)

definition.text: Using laws such as copyright and patents to stop people copying an information good, turning a public good into a club good.

facts.text: These laws can solve free riding, but they give owners monopoly power, so the result is not fully efficient.
In the United States, patent rights encourage drug companies to charge prices above the cost of making one more dose.

entries.title: Social sanctions: how groups punish free riders
entries.article: Free-rider problem#Non-altruistic social sanctions (common property regimes)

definition.text: Punishments that group members impose on those who use a shared resource without contributing, as a way to keep cooperation going without the state.

facts.text: Punishing costs the punisher, so groups often reward members who sanction free riders.
Paying for enforcement is not perfectly efficient, but it is often cheaper than letting the resource run down.
People sometimes punish free riders even without any reward, though whether such costly punishment explains cooperation is disputed.

entries.contested_note: Researchers dispute whether costly punishment of free riders can explain cooperation.

entries.title: Traditional land tenure: holding land through care

definition.text: Indigenous ways of holding land, which in North America rested on stewardship rather than the control at the heart of European ownership.

facts.text: European settlers in North America sometimes ignored traditional tenure and seized land, and sometimes recognized it as aboriginal title.
Traditional communities in Brazil, such as fundos de pasto and faxinais, still practice communal land use.

entries.title: Why Coasean bargains fail in practice
entries.article: Coase theorem#Criticisms of the applicability of the theorem

definition.text: The practical reasons why private bargaining over harms such as pollution often fails to reach the efficient outcome the Coase theorem predicts.

facts.text: The assignment problem: with a polluted river it is hard to tell which factories caused the harm and who was hurt, and victims tend to overstate their losses.
The holdout problem: when many people hold rights, the last one can demand more, so everyone has a reason to demand more and bargaining unravels.
When many parties benefit equally from a deal, each has a reason to free ride by withholding payment.
In twenty legal nuisance cases studied by Ward Farnsworth, no party tried Coasean bargaining, out of anger at the unfairness of having to bargain.

distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem
entries.text: The bargain Coase described often never happens. With a polluted river, it is hard to tell which factories caused the harm and who was hurt, and victims tend to overstate their losses: the assignment problem. When many people hold rights, the last one can demand more, so everyone has a reason to hold out and bargaining unravels. When many parties benefit equally from a deal, each has a reason to free ride by withholding payment. Emotion matters too. In twenty legal nuisance cases studied by Ward Farnsworth, no party tried Coasean bargaining, out of anger at the unfairness of having to bargain.

entries.title: Two claims inside the Coase theorem: efficiency and invariance

definition.text: The two separate claims inside the Coase theorem: that bargaining gives an efficient result, and that it gives the same result whoever starts with the rights.

facts.text: Coase did not set out a single formal theorem; others built the loose formulation from his work.
Later authors showed the invariance claim is not generally true, because who bears liability changes wealth, which in turn changes demand and prices.
Steven Cheung extended it in 1969: without transaction costs, contracts, markets and corrective taxes can all reach the same efficient result.

entries.title: Anti-rival goods: better the more people use them

definition.text: A good that becomes more valuable to each user the more other people use it.

facts.text: Steven Weber introduced the idea in 2004, noting that free and open-source software gets better for everyone as more people use it.
Any natural language is anti-rival, because it is more useful the more people speak it.
Efforts against climate change are perversely anti-rival: a free-riding country still gains from others' efforts.

entries.title: The comedy of the commons: the more the merrier
entries.article: Tragedy of the commons#Comedy of the commons

definition.text: The case where a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it, so 'the more the merrier'.

facts.text: Legal scholar Carol M. Rose described the idea in a 1986 article, giving commerce and group recreation as examples.
Rose argued that such 'comedic' public resources are more likely to suffer from too little investment than from overuse.

distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons
entries.text: Not every commons ends in tragedy. In a 1986 article the legal scholar Carol M. Rose described the opposite case, the comedy of the commons. Here a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it: 'the more the merrier'. Her examples were commerce and group recreation. Rose argued that such resources are more likely to suffer from too little investment than from overuse.

entries.title: Social traps: short-term gain, long-term loss

definition.text: A situation where people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off.

facts.text: John Platt introduced the term in a 1973 paper, applying behavioral psychology to Hardin's tragedy of the commons.
Social traps are blamed for overfishing, overgrazing in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change.
Choosing a car over public transport is a social trap: comfort now, more greenhouse gas emissions later.
Platt proposed rewards for green behavior and penalties such as pollution taxes as ways out.

entries.text: Taking the car instead of public transport buys comfort now and more heat-trapping gas released later. Social traps are blamed for taking too many fish, overgrazing in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change. Platt proposed ways out: rewards for green behavior, and penalties such as pollution taxes.
