entries.title: Locke's labor theory of property: mixing work with nature

definition.text: John Locke's idea that a person who mixes their labor with an unowned resource comes to own the result, as long as enough of as good quality is left for others.

facts.text: Locke set out the theory in his Second Treatise of Government (1689), starting from the claim that each person owns their own self.
The condition that 'enough and as good' must remain for others is called the Lockean proviso.
Libertarians cite the tragedy of the commons as what happens when governments forbid people to claim resources in the Lockean way.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm
entries.text: Mix your labor with something no one owns, and the result becomes yours. That is John Locke's labor theory of property, set out in his Second Treatise of Government (1689). Libertarians cite the tragedy of the commons as what happens when governments forbid people to claim resources in the Lockean way.

entries.title: Georgism and the environment: pollution as a taking from the commons

definition.text: The Georgist view that pollution is a taking from the commons, so its value should be captured for the public through taxes or quotas.

facts.text: Henry George partly inspired the early conservation movement of the Progressive Era.
Some ecological economists back a land value tax as a way to free up unused land for rewilding and to curb urban sprawl.
Georgists and ecological economists both favor market-based limits on pollution, but Georgists stress that the resulting income should not go to polluters.
'Cap and share', the Georgist version of cap and trade, would auction temporary pollution permits and give the proceeds to the public instead of handing permits free to polluters.

Their 'cap and share' would sell temporary pollution permits by bidding and give the proceeds to the public, instead of handing permits free to polluters. Some ecological economists also back a tax on land values, to free unused land for nature and curb urban sprawl.

entries.title: The Diamond–Mirrlees theorem: keep production efficient

definition.text: The 1971 result by Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees that production efficiency is still desirable even when a government cannot use lump-sum taxes.

facts.text: It is credited with modernizing Ramsey's analysis of taxation by considering income distribution together with raising revenue.
Joseph Stiglitz and Partha Dasgupta (1971) argued it is not robust if some tax tools cannot be used.

entries.text: Even a government that cannot use lump-sum taxes should not waste resources in production. That was the 1971 result of Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees: production efficiency stays desirable without lump-sum taxes. It is credited with modernizing Ramsey's analysis of taxation by considering how income is distributed together with raising revenue. Stiglitz and Dasgupta (1971) argued it is not robust if some tax tools cannot be used.

entries.title: The Nash bargaining solution: splitting the gains from agreement

definition.text: John Nash's answer to how two parties should split the gains from agreeing: the deal that maximizes the product of what each gains over failing to agree.

facts.text: Nash (1950) defined a bargaining problem as the set of possible agreements plus a disagreement point, what each gets if talks fail.
Bargaining solutions are usually built from axioms such as efficiency, symmetry and independence of irrelevant alternatives.
The Nash solution handles only the simplest structure and does not show how efficient outcomes are reached over time.
It picks the agreement that maximizes the product of each player's gain over the disagreement point, called the Nash product.

entries.text: Two parties can gain by agreeing, but how should they split the gains? It handles only the simplest structure, though, and does not show how efficient outcomes are reached over time.

entries.title: The Lindahl tax: each pays what the good is worth to them

definition.text: A tax, proposed by Swedish economist Erik Lindahl, in which each person pays for a public good according to the extra benefit they get from one more unit of it.

facts.text: Lindahl put forward the idea in 1919, influenced by his teacher Knut Wicksell, to show that agreement on public spending is possible.
If each person's tax price equals their own marginal benefit at the ideal level, everyone is better off and may agree to that level of provision.
In a worked example, a park costs $15 per acre; Sarah and Tom together will pay $15 at the 60th acre, so Sarah pays $5 and Tom $10 for each of 60 acres.
In theory it provides public goods efficiently, but it needs each person's demand, which is hard to know in practice.
People may understate their benefits to pay less, may not know their own valuation (for national defense, say), and government may struggle to add valuations up.

entries.title: Club theory: how big should a club be

definition.text: The branch of economics, founded by James M. Buchanan in 1965, that studies how big a group sharing a good should be and how it should share the costs.

facts.text: Buchanan saw a gap between purely private and purely public goods: excludable goods shared by more people than a private good but fewer than a public one.
Each new member lowers the cost per head but adds congestion, so there is an optimal club size that gives members the most benefit.
Cornes and Sandler's conditions lead to two-part pricing: a fixed membership fee plus a charge per use.
Olson and Zeckhauser (1967) applied the theory to cost-sharing in NATO, asking whether some members were free riding.

entries.title: Social dilemmas: when selfishness pays but cooperation pays more

definition.text: A situation where each person does better by acting selfishly whatever others do, yet everyone would do best if all cooperated.

facts.text: Robyn Dawes coined the term a few years after Platt, to cover both social traps and commons dilemmas.
There are three main kinds: large-scale dilemmas, commons (resource) dilemmas and public goods dilemmas.
Uncertainty about others' actions or about the resource discourages cooperation, but a trustworthy leader who manages the resource fairly can restore it.

entries.title: The commons dilemma: self-interest against the group

definition.text: A kind of social dilemma in which people's short-term selfish interests clash with the long-term interests of the group and the common good.

facts.text: Researchers study, in the laboratory and the field, when groups under- or over-harvest common resources.
When people harvest in a fixed order, those who go first take more than those who follow.
People take less from a common pool when others can see them than when they act anonymously.
Selective punishments for overuse, such as installing water and electricity meters in houses, can encourage conservation.

entries.title: Res communis: things that belong to everyone

definition.text: A Roman law idea of things common to all humankind, such as air, running water, the sea and its shores, that came before modern ideas of the commons.

facts.text: The Institutes of Justinian codified it in the 6th century.
It differs from res publica, public property managed by government, since common things are for everyone to use and enjoy.
In environmental law it means the state is trustee of shared natural resources and cannot sell them into private hands.
Fish and mammals on the high seas are examples, and the rules for Antarctica and for space law were built on it.

entries.text: Roman law held that some things belong to all humankind: air, running water, the sea and its shores. In laws protecting the environment, it means the state is trustee of shared natural resources and cannot sell them into private hands. Fish and mammals on the high seas are examples, and the rules for Antarctica and for space law were built on it.

entries.title: The public trust doctrine: resources the state holds for all

definition.text: The principle that the state holds certain resources, such as the shore between high and low tide, in trust for public use, whoever owns the land beside them.

facts.text: It goes back to Roman law, which held air, flowing water, the sea and the seashore to be common to all and not open to ownership.
It passed into English law and later into the common law of the United States, where it covers tidal and navigable waters and the minerals and animals in them.
It has been used to claim public interest in oil under tidal lands and to stop private ownership of fish stocks and shellfish beds.
Some countries have used it to protect natural resources as a human right, and protections are spreading to a global scale.

entries.title: The bundle of rights: ownership as a set of sticks

definition.text: A way of picturing property ownership as a set of separate rights, like sticks in a bundle, that can be split among different people and put back together.

facts.text: The idea began with Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld in 1913, though he never used the phrase.
The five traditional rights are possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment (use, including resource extraction) and disposition (transfer).
Parts of a right can be held separately: a tenant may live on land while someone else owns the minerals or water beneath it.
Governments keep rights such as environmental regulation, zoning and eminent domain, and third parties may hold rights such as conservation easements.

entries.title: Usufruct: the right to use without owning

definition.text: The right to use someone else's property, often land, and to take its fruits or profits, without owning it or being allowed to damage it.

facts.text: It combines usus, the right to use a thing, and fructus, the right to profit from it, such as by selling crops; full ownership adds abusus, the right to sell or destroy it.
In some customary law systems of Indigenous peoples of the Americas, all land was publicly owned and people gained rights to use areas, without damaging the land's future productivity.
Thomas Jefferson wrote in 1789 that 'Earth belongs in usufruct to the living', meaning each generation may use the earth but must not impoverish it for those to come.
Western US water rights are usufruct rights that can be forfeited if the holder does not put their full allocation to beneficial use.

It combines usus, the right to use, and fructus, the right to profit; full ownership adds abusus, the right to sell or destroy. In the western United States, rights to water are usufruct rights, lost if not put to full beneficial use.

entries.title: Preference revelation: getting honest answers about public goods

definition.text: The problem of finding out how much the public really wants a public good, when there is no market to make people show what it is worth to them.

facts.text: Without full knowledge of people's preferences, government planners are likely to supply too much or too little of a public good.
Since only individuals know their own benefit, they have a reason to understate it, a form of free riding.
Mechanisms such as Vickrey-Clarke-Groves aim to draw out true values, but none has fully solved the problem, and asking a large population is costly in money and time.

entries.text: How much would you pay for a public good you can enjoy for free? Honest answers are hard to get, and there is no market to make people show what the good is worth. That is the problem of preference revelation. Only individuals know their own benefit, and they have a reason to understate it, a form of free riding. Without full knowledge of preferences, government planners are likely to supply too much or too little. entries.title: The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism: making honesty pay

definition.text: One of the best-studied procedures for deciding how much of a public good to fund and who pays, based on what each person reports it is worth to them.

facts.text: Most work uses the Clarke pivot rule, which makes sure everyone pays in and no one is worse off for taking part.
It needs a great deal of information from each user, which, among other problems, has kept it from being used in practice.
Mechanisms like it were developed to draw out people's true valuations, since people have reasons to understate how much they value public goods.
Each participant is paid the total value of everyone else, so its own welfare matches society's and telling the truth is its best strategy.

entries.title: Quadratic funding: small gifts, big matching

definition.text: A recent way to fund public goods, developed by Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl from quadratic voting, in which each contributor gives a single amount and a subsidy tops up the total.

facts.text: Like the VCG mechanism it needs a subsidy, and there is always a deficit the designer must cover.
It is vulnerable to collusion between contributors and to fake identities (sybil attacks).

entries.title: The Environmental Goods Agreement: trade talks that collapsed

definition.text: Talks among 18 World Trade Organization members, begun in 2015, to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment.

facts.text: In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means products used to protect the environment, such as renewable energy technology and pollution control systems.
The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, renewable energy, monitoring and energy efficiency.
The negotiations collapsed in 2016.

entries.title: Impure public goods: partly shared, partly not

definition.text: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable only partly or only some of the time.

facts.text: Some parts of cybersecurity, such as sharing threat information and protecting critical infrastructure and election integrity, behave like impure public goods.
Public property is sometimes treated as a public good, usually an impure one.
Since pure public goods are rare, most goods called public are impure in practice.

entries.title: The tragedy of the anticommons: too many owners, too little use

definition.text: The mirror image of the tragedy of the commons: when a resource has many owners who can each block its use, it ends up underused.

facts.text: Michael Heller introduced the term in a 1998 article, after seeing empty shops in post-communist Eastern European cities where too many parties held rights over each space.
Early aviation patents held by the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss blocked each other until the government created a patent pool in World War I.
Housing shortages in many western cities have been described this way, since zoning lets many stakeholders block new homes.
Remedies include eminent domain and patent pools or other licensing bodies.

entries.title: When one side of a deal knows more

definition.text: A situation in which one side of a deal has more or better information than the other.

facts.text: It gives one side more power in a deal and can make trades inefficient, in the worst case causing market failure.
A used-car seller usually knows the car's condition far better than the buyer.
Its main forms are adverse selection, moral hazard and monopolies of knowledge.
It contrasts with perfect information, a key assumption of neoclassical economics.
Firms know better than regulators what they would do without regulation, which can weaken the rules.
Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for analysing markets with asymmetric information.
Distrust between buyers and sellers can lead to opportunistic behaviour and even to a market breaking down.

entries.text: The person selling a used car usually knows its condition far better than the person buying it. Economists call this information asymmetry: one side of a deal has more or better information than the other. The gap hands the better-informed side extra power, and it can make trades inefficient. Distrust breeds opportunistic behavior, and in the worst case the market breaks down entirely, a form of {{ref:nature-found-045}}. The idea cuts against perfect information, a key assumption of neoclassical economics. Regulation suffers too: firms know better than regulators what they would do without the rules, which can weaken them. The main forms are {{ref:nature-econ-001}}, {{ref:nature-econ-004}} and monopolies of knowledge. George Akerlof, Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for analyzing markets with this kind of gap.

entries.title: Moral hazard: taking risks someone else pays for

definition.text: A situation in which someone has a reason to take more risk because they will not bear the full cost if things go wrong.

facts.text: An insured firm may take on more risk knowing its insurer will pay; someone with theft insurance may be less careful about locking their car.
It arises from hidden actions after a deal is made, while adverse selection comes from hidden information before it.
The term goes back to the 17th century in insurance; from the 1960s, starting with Ken Arrow, economists used it without any suggestion of fraud.
If health care costs $10 a unit and demand is Q = 20 − P, a person buys 10 units; with free insurance they use 20, and the insurer pays.
Bailouts can encourage future risky lending if lenders believe they will not carry the full losses.
Many argue moral hazard helped cause the 2008 financial crisis, through fund managers, mortgage originators and banks seen as 'too big to fail'.
Firms reduce it with performance-based pay, monitoring and screening.

entries.title: When the person acting for you has goals of their own

definition.text: The clash of interests that arises when one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and may pursue its own goals instead.

facts.text: Familiar pairs are managers and shareholders, elected officials and citizens, and brokers and the buyers and sellers they serve.
The problem worsens the more the two sides' interests and information differ and the less the principal can punish the agent.
The losses from an agent straying from the principal's interest are called agency costs.
Principal–agent models study either moral hazard, from hidden actions, or adverse selection, from hidden information.
The theory emerged in the 1970s from economics and institutional theory.
Contracts try to tie pay to performance through piece rates, share options, bonuses, promotions and profit sharing; switching from salary to piece rates raised productivity by 44% in one study.
Jaffe and Stavins in 1994 described the landlord–tenant problem as a principal–agent barrier to adopting cost-effective energy efficiency.
Common property regimes can avoid the principal–agent problem, one reason their local knowledge often beats rules designed by outside experts.

entries.text: Shareholders hire managers, citizens elect officials, and buyers and sellers rely on brokers. In each pair one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and may pursue its own goals instead. This clash is the principal–agent problem. It worsens as the two sides' goals and information drift apart, and as the principal's power to punish the agent shrinks. The losses are called agency costs. The theory emerged in the 1970s from economics and institutional theory. Its models study either moral hazard, from hidden actions, or {{ref:nature-econ-001}}, from hidden information. Contracts try to tie pay to performance through piece rates, which pay per item produced, and through share options, bonuses, promotions and profit sharing. In one study, switching from salary to piece rates raised output per worker by 44%. The problem reaches the environment too. In 1994 Jaffe and Stavins described the split between landlords and tenants as a principal–agent barrier to cost-effective energy efficiency. Common property regimes can avoid the problem, one reason their local knowledge often beats rules designed by outside experts.

It worsens as the two sides' goals and information drift apart, and as the principal's power to punish the agent shrinks. The losses are called agency costs. The theory emerged in the 1970s from economics and institutional theory. Its models study either moral hazard, from hidden actions, or Adverse selection: when hidden knowledge drives buyers away, from hidden information. Contracts try to tie pay to performance through piece rates, which pay per item produced, and through share options, bonuses, promotions and profit sharing. In one study, switching from salary to piece rates raised output per worker by 44%. The problem reaches the environment too. In 1994 Jaffe and Stavins described the split between landlords and tenants as a principal–agent barrier to cost-effective energy efficiency. Common property regimes can avoid the problem, one reason their local knowledge often beats rules designed by outside experts.

entries.title: Adverse selection: when hidden knowledge drives buyers away

definition.text: A market problem in which one side of a deal knows something the other does not, and uses that hidden information to get a better bargain.

facts.text: The less-informed side may protect itself by pulling out, demanding different prices or staying away, which shrinks trade and competition.
George Akerlof's 1970 paper 'The Market for Lemons' showed how hidden flaws in used cars can make such a market collapse.
It was first described for life insurance: if smokers pay the same premium as non-smokers, smokers buy more cover, raising the insurer's claims.
In contract theory, adverse selection means the agent holds private information before the contract is signed; moral hazard arises after.
Remedies include reputation systems such as eBay's ratings, screening by the uninformed side, warranties and lemon laws.
Voluntary green labelling of bonds is seen as open to greenwashing and adverse selection because of weak oversight.
Fixing one problem can worsen another: mandatory insurance against adverse selection may add to moral hazard.
In health insurance, healthy people may skip cover while those with existing conditions buy it, pushing premiums up for everyone left.

entries.text: Life insurers were the first to meet the problem. If smokers pay the same premium as non-smokers, smokers buy more cover, and the insurer's claims rise. This is adverse selection: one side of a deal knows something the other does not and uses that hidden knowledge to get a better bargain. In {{ref:nature-econ-012}}, the hidden information exists before the contract is signed; moral hazard arises after. Health cover shows the spiral. Healthy people skip it, people with existing conditions buy it, and premiums rise for everyone left. The less-informed side protects itself by pulling out, demanding different prices or staying away, so trade and competition shrink. George Akerlof's 1970 paper on used cars showed that hidden flaws can make such a market collapse. Remedies include reputation systems such as eBay's ratings, {{ref:nature-econ-333}}, warranties and lemon laws. Yet one fix can worsen another: mandatory cover against adverse selection may add to moral hazard. Even a {{ref:nature-mkt-065}} sold under a voluntary green label is exposed, since weak oversight leaves such labels open to {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}.

entries.title: Contract theory: designing deals when one side knows more

definition.text: The study of how people and firms design agreements with each other, usually when one side knows more than the other.

facts.text: Its classic problems are moral hazard, adverse selection and signalling, and it looks for ways to motivate agents to act well.
A leading application is designing the best pay schemes for managers.
It began with Ronald Coase's 1937 article 'The Nature of the Firm'; Kenneth Arrow gave the first formal economic treatment in the 1960s.
Complete contract theory treats firms and markets alike as contracts in which both sides foresee every future situation; it is equivalent to principal–agent theory.
Oliver Hart and Bengt Holmström won the 2016 Nobel prize for it: Holmström on incentives and risk, Hart on gaps in contracts left by an unpredictable future.
Its models usually treat people as maximizing expected utility and solve for the best decisions mathematically.

entries.title: Forcing the better-informed side to speak up

definition.text: Rules that require the better-informed party to reveal information, used when voluntary disclosure does not happen.

facts.text: The US Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Fair Disclosure requires companies to disclose material information to investors.
That rule reduced information asymmetry, as seen in lower trading costs.

entries.text: Sometimes the side that knows more will not share it voluntarily. Mandatory information disclosure rules then require it to. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Fair Disclosure requires companies to reveal material information, the facts that could sway an investor, to all investors. The rule narrowed the information gap, and the evidence showed up in lower trading costs.

entries.title: Signalling: showing what you know in a believable way

definition.text: A way for the better-informed side to show its type believably to the other side and so reduce an information gap.

facts.text: Michael Spence first proposed it and coined the term.
Spence's example: finishing college can signal an ability to learn to employers.

entries.text: A college diploma can say something a job interview cannot. Michael Spence first proposed the idea and coined its name: signalling. It is a way for the better-informed side to show its type believably to the other side, and so shrink an information gap. In Spence's example, finishing college signals to employers an ability to learn. The degree vouches for a quality the employer has no direct way to see.

entries.title: Why a diploma can pay even if it teaches nothing

definition.text: Michael Spence's model in which job seekers show employers their hidden ability by earning education credentials.

facts.text: Employers cannot observe a candidate's ability, so there is an information gap that credentials can narrow.
Signals are credible when they cost low-quality senders more to produce or imitate than high-quality ones.
Spence's key assumption is that able workers pay less, in effort, time and stress as well as money, for each unit of education.
Spence found education can be valuable as a signal even if it adds nothing to a worker's productivity.
Many equilibria are possible, and without signalling everyone would be paid the average product, so low-ability workers lose when signalling exists.
The 'sheepskin effect' is the wage gain from holding a diploma beyond the return to the extra year of study, seen when comparing drop-outs and completers.
Studies find signalling a statistically significant influence on wages, alongside factors such as age, sex and geography.

entries.text: An employer cannot see a candidate's ability. Michael Spence's model shows how job seekers narrow that gap by earning education credentials. A signal is believable only when it costs low-quality senders more to produce or imitate than high-quality ones. Studies find signalling a statistically significant influence on wages, alongside age, sex and geography.

entries.title: Screening: getting the other side to reveal itself

definition.text: A way for the less-informed side to get the other side to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices.

facts.text: Joseph Stiglitz pioneered the theory of screening.
Signalling and screening both resemble voluntary disclosure of information.

entries.text: Signalling lets the informed side speak first. Screening flips the roles: the less-informed side gets the other to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices and watching which one is picked. Joseph Stiglitz pioneered the theory of screening. Both screening and signalling resemble voluntary disclosure of information.

Screening flips the roles: the less-informed side gets the other to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices and watching which one is picked. Joseph Stiglitz pioneered the theory of screening. Both screening and signalling resemble voluntary disclosure of information.

entries.title: Akerlof's lemons: used cars and hidden flaws

definition.text: George Akerlof's 1970 paper showing how markets behave when buyers cannot judge quality, using the used-car market.

facts.text: In the model the seller knows a car's exact quality, while the buyer only knows the chance it is a bad car, a 'lemon'.
It brought information problems to the forefront of economic theory.
It arises when buyers cannot judge quality before buying, sellers gain by passing off bad goods as good, and sellers have no credible way to prove quality.
A lack of reputation, regulation, guarantees or warranties to assure quality also helps produce it.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether a lemons market actually exists in used vehicles (S:29ec2fbd1b20).
entries.text: In 1970 George Akerlof published a paper about used cars that brought information problems to the forefront of economic theory. In his model the seller knows a car's exact quality. The buyer knows only the chance that it is a bad car, a 'lemon'. A lemons market needs three things. Buyers cannot judge quality before buying, sellers gain by passing off bad goods as good, and sellers have no credible way to prove quality. A lack of reputation, regulation, guarantees or warranties helps produce it. Researchers still disagree on whether a lemons market actually exists in used vehicles.

entries.title: Paying by results or by rank
entries.article: Contract theory#Rewards on Absolute Performance and Relative Performance

definition.text: Two ways to reward workers: in proportion to what each achieves (absolute) or by ranking workers against each other (relative).

facts.text: Absolute performance pay is widely used, but it invites cheating and is exposed to recessions or sudden growth.
Rewarding a whole group for its performance lets some members slack while others work hard.

entries.text: A firm can reward each worker for what she achieves, or for how she ranks against her colleagues. The first is absolute performance pay; the second is relative. Absolute pay is widely used, but it invites cheating and leaves earnings exposed to recessions or sudden growth. Rewarding a whole group has its own flaw: some members slack while others work hard.
entries.text_plain: A firm can reward each worker for what she achieves, or for how she ranks against her colleagues. The first is absolute performance pay; the second is relative. Absolute pay is widely used, but it invites cheating and leaves earnings exposed to recessions or sudden growth. Rewarding a whole group has its own flaw: some members slack while others work hard.

entries.title: Why no contract can foresee everything

definition.text: Contracts that cannot spell out what happens in every possible situation, because writing a complete one would be too hard or too costly.

facts.text: A complete contract would set the legal consequences of every possible state of the world.
Oliver Hart and coauthors pioneered the theory, which studies how this inability affects incentives, for example for relationship-specific investments.
A leading application is the Grossman–Hart–Moore property rights theory of the firm.
The law supplies default rules to fill the gaps that parties leave.

entries.text: A complete contract would set the legal consequences of every possible state of the world. Real contracts never do, because writing one would be too hard or too costly. Oliver Hart and coauthors pioneered the theory of incomplete contracts. It studies how these gaps affect incentives, for example the incentive to spend on things that pay off only within one particular relationship. A leading application is the Grossman–Hart–Moore version of the {{ref:nature-econ-623}}. Where the parties leave gaps, the law supplies default rules to fill them.

entries.title: Brands as a promise of quality

definition.text: The use of brand reputation by firms to signal quality and reliability to buyers who cannot judge them directly.

facts.text: A study found that information websites raised visits to unbranded sellers and cut visits to branded ones, suggesting better information weakens brand spending.
Certifications and third-party endorsements can add credibility to brand claims.

entries.text: A buyer who cannot judge quality directly may trust a name instead. Firms use brand reputation to signal quality and reliability to such buyers. Certifications and third-party endorsements can make those brand claims more credible. Better information cuts the other way. One study found that information websites raised visits to unbranded sellers and cut visits to branded ones, suggesting that better information weakens the payoff from brand spending.

entries.title: How insurers sort the careful from the risky

definition.text: Insurers' efforts to find out how risky each customer is, and so how likely a claim is, before offering cover.

facts.text: Rothschild and Stiglitz showed how an uninformed insurer can draw out customers' risk levels by offering incentives to reveal them.
This lets insurers sort customers into risk classes and offer choices such as higher deductibles for lower premiums.
Tools include background checks and demographic data; a young man, for example, is likelier to crash a car than a middle-aged woman.

entries.title: Menus of contracts that make types sort themselves

definition.text: Models in which a principal, facing an agent with private information about its type, offers a menu of contracts designed so different types pick different ones.

facts.text: The best type usually trades as much as it would with full information ('no distortion at the top'), while other types trade less.
Optimal auction design is a many-agent version of the basic screening model; Roger Myerson and Eric Maskin pioneered these models.
Applications include regulation, public procurement and price discrimination, and the models have been tested in laboratory and field data.

entries.title: Mechanism design: game theory run in reverse

definition.text: A branch of economics and game theory that designs rules, called mechanisms, so that good outcomes result even when the designer cannot see people's true preferences or information.

facts.text: It works backwards from a desired result to a game that produces it, so it is sometimes called reverse game theory.
Example: a buyer wants to know a used car's true quality but cannot just ask, since the seller gains by lying; the buyer can instead set rules that shape the seller's behaviour.
Each player has private information, called its type, and may misreport it; the designer commits to rules that turn reports into an allocation of goods and money transfers.
Thanks to the revelation principle, the designer need only consider mechanisms in which people truthfully report their private information.
Uses include market design, voting theory, internet routing, e-commerce and the advertising auctions of Facebook and Google.
Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson won the 2007 Nobel prize for founding the theory; William Vickrey's related work earned the 1996 prize.

entries.title: Rules under which honesty pays

definition.text: A property of a mechanism or set of rules under which every participant does best for themselves by reporting their true preferences.

facts.text: Example: if an insurer sells discounted cover only to high-risk clients, the scheme is incentive-compatible when high-risk clients gain by admitting their risk and low-risk clients lose by pretending.
The concept is credited to the economist Leonid Hurwicz.
In the strong form, truth-telling is best whatever others do, as in a second-price auction; in the weaker form, it is best if everyone else is truthful.
Lindahl taxes based on surveys are not incentive-compatible, because people gain by misreporting how much they value a public good.

entries.text: Suppose an insurer sells discounted cover only to high-risk clients. The scheme works only if high-risk clients gain by admitting their risk and low-risk clients lose by pretending. That property is incentive compatibility: under the rules, every participant does best for themselves by reporting their true preferences. The concept is credited to the economist Leonid Hurwicz. In its strong form, telling the truth is best whatever others do, as in a second-price sale by sealed bids. In the weaker form, it is best if everyone else is truthful. Lindahl taxes based on surveys fail the test, because people gain by misreporting how much they value a public good.

entries.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite: why truthful rules turn dictatorial

definition.text: An impossibility result showing that, with three or more options, any rule that makes truthful reporting always worthwhile must be dictatorial.

facts.text: A rule is dictatorial when one person always gets their most-favoured outcome.
Mechanism design can be seen as a search for ways around it, by changing the model to allow a wider range of mechanisms.

entries.text: Give people three or more options, and any rule that always makes truthful reporting worthwhile must be dictatorial. A rule is dictatorial when one person always gets their most-favored outcome. This is the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem, an impossibility result from {{ref:nature-econ-202}}. Mechanism design can be seen as a search for ways around it, by changing the model to allow a wider range of mechanisms.

entries.title: Myerson–Satterthwaite: when private values block efficient trade

definition.text: The 1983 result that two parties who each privately know how much a good is worth to them cannot always trade it efficiently without risking a loss for one side.

facts.text: It is among the most striking negative results in economics, a kind of mirror image of the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.

The Myerson–Satterthwaite theorem, a 1983 result, shows that they cannot always trade it efficiently without risking a loss for one side. The result ranks among the most striking negative results in economics. It is a kind of mirror image of the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.

entries.title: Revenue equivalence: when the auction format does not matter

definition.text: Vickrey's 1961 result that, under certain conditions, a large class of auctions all give the seller the same expected revenue, the best the seller can get.

facts.text: It needs buyers with independent types from a continuous distribution and an auction that sells to the buyer who values the good most.
To earn more, a seller must risk giving the item to a lower-valuing buyer, which usually means risking not selling it at all.

entries.text: Under certain conditions, a seller can stop worrying about which kind of {{ref:nature-econ-671}} to run. Buyers must have independent types drawn from a continuous distribution, and the sale must go to the buyer who values the good most. entries.title: The standard moral hazard model: paying for output you can see

definition.text: The basic contract-theory model in which a principal who cannot observe an agent's effort chooses a pay scheme tied to output to maximize expected profit.

facts.text: Pay must satisfy a participation constraint, so the agent accepts the deal, and an incentive-compatibility constraint, so the agent prefers the intended effort.
Pay tied to observable output gives the agent incentives to act in the principal's interest.
With a risk-averse agent such contracts are only second-best, because strong incentives rule out full insurance.

entries.text: A principal cannot observe how hard an agent works, but can see what the agent produces. The standard moral hazard model starts there: the principal chooses a pay scheme tied to output to maximize expected profit. Such pay gives the agent incentives to act as the principal would wish. It must clear two hurdles. A participation constraint makes sure the agent accepts the deal at all. An incentive-compatibility constraint makes sure the agent prefers the intended effort. If the agent dislikes risk, such contracts are only second-best, because strong incentives rule out shielding the agent fully from risk.

entries.title: The revelation principle: you only need truthful rules

definition.text: The result that any outcome that can be achieved by some strategic mechanism can also be achieved by an incentive-compatible one, in which everyone simply tells the truth.

facts.text: It comes in two versions, matching the dominant-strategy and Bayesian–Nash forms of incentive compatibility.
It means a mechanism designer need only consider games in which people truthfully report their private information.

entries.text: Designing rules for people who might lie sounds endlessly complicated. The revelation principle cuts the task down. It says that any outcome some strategic mechanism can achieve can also be achieved by an incentive-compatible one, in which everyone simply tells the truth. So a mechanism designer need only consider games in which people truthfully report their private information. The principle comes in two versions, matching the two forms of incentive compatibility, known as dominant-strategy and Bayesian–Nash.

So a mechanism designer need only consider games in which people truthfully report their private information. The principle comes in two versions, matching the two forms of incentive compatibility, known as dominant-strategy and Bayesian–Nash.

entries.title: The Vickrey auction: win with the top bid, pay the second

definition.text: A sealed-bid auction for a single item in which the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid.

facts.text: It is a special case of the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism, and losers pay nothing.
Second-price auctions are a typical example of mechanisms where telling the truth is a dominant strategy.

Second-price sales are a typical example of mechanisms in which telling the truth is dominant: it is the best move whatever anyone else does. entries.title: Inflation: why money buys a little less each year

definition.text: Inflation is a rise in the average price of goods and services measured in money, which means each unit of money buys less.

facts.text: It is measured with a price index, usually a consumer price index, and the inflation rate is the yearly percentage change in that index.
Its opposite, a fall in the general price level, is deflation.
Inflation refers to the general trend of prices, not a change in any single price.
Causes include growth in the money supply, demand shocks, supply shocks such as energy crises, interest-rate cuts and changing expectations.
High or unpredictable inflation harms an economy: it makes long-term planning hard and uncertainty about money's future value discourages saving and investment.
It shifts buying power away from people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners whose pensions are not indexed to prices.
Most economists today favour a low and steady inflation rate, a task usually given to central banks.
Since the Great Depression of the 1930s, prices have generally risen every year.

entries.title: Uncertainty: deciding without knowing

definition.text: Uncertainty describes situations where information is imperfect or unknown.

facts.text: It applies to predictions of future events, to measurements already made and to the unknown, and matters especially for decision-making.
It arises in partly observable, random, complex or changing environments, and from ignorance.
It is a state of limited knowledge in which the possible future states, their probabilities or their values cannot all be fully described.
Uncertainty can be measured only when treated as risk, by assigning probabilities to each possible outcome.
Adaptive management is an iterative way of deciding under uncertainty that aims to reduce it over time through monitoring.

entries.text: Predictions of the future, measurements already taken and the plain unknown all share one trait. Each carries uncertainty, which describes any situation where information is imperfect or unknown. It matters most when someone has to make a decision. Uncertainty arises in environments that are partly observable, random, complex or changing, and from simple ignorance. More precisely, it is a state of limited knowledge in which the possible future states, their probabilities or their values cannot all be fully described. That limits what can be measured. Uncertainty can be measured only when it is treated as risk, by assigning a probability to each possible outcome. One practical response is {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}, a step-by-step way of deciding under uncertainty that aims to shrink it over time through monitoring.

entries.title: Expected value: the average of what might happen

definition.text: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the average of its possible values, each weighted by how likely it is.

facts.text: It can be read as the long-run average result of repeating the same random experiment many times, as the law of large numbers shows.
For a fair six-sided die, whose faces 1 to 6 each have probability 1/6, the expected value is 3.5.
When all outcomes are equally likely, the expected value is simply the ordinary average.
It is usually written E(X), E[X] or EX; the letter E goes back to W. A. Whitworth in 1901.
The idea arose in the mid-17th century from the problem of points: how to split stakes fairly when a game ends early.
Pascal and Fermat solved it on the principle that a future gain is worth an amount proportional to the chance of getting it.
Christiaan Huygens published the first treatise on it in 1657, often seen as the first foundation of probability theory.
In decision theory, a person choosing under incomplete information is often assumed to maximise the expected value of their utility.

entries.title: Expected utility: weighing outcomes by what they mean to you

definition.text: The expected utility hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome.

facts.text: It is a foundational assumption of mathematical economics about decisions under uncertainty, and rational choice theory builds on it.
Expected utility is the sum over outcomes of each payoff's utility times its probability.
The curve of the utility function captures risk attitude: linear for risk-neutral, convex for risk-seeking and concave for risk-averse people.
Bernoulli's version was the first formal statement of marginal utility: an extra sum is worth less to a rich person than a poor one.
Von Neumann and Morgenstern defined a rational decision-maker by four axioms: completeness, transitivity, independence and continuity.
Psychologists have found systematic violations, and behavioural finance has produced generalised theories such as prospect theory to account for them.
Such deviations are called irrational because they depend on how a problem is presented, not on its costs, rewards or probabilities.

entries.text: An extra sum of money is worth less to a rich person than to a poor one. The hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome. Expected utility is the sum over outcomes of each payoff's utility times its probability. The shape of the utility curve captures a person's attitude to risk. It is a straight line for someone risk-neutral, convex, bending upward, for a risk-seeker, and concave, bending downward, for someone who shuns risk. Researchers have produced broader theories, such as {{ref:nature-econ-067}}, to account for them. These departures are called irrational because they depend on how a problem is presented, not on its costs, rewards or probabilities.

entries.title: Interest: the price of waiting for your money

definition.text: Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender, on top of paying back the amount borrowed, at a set rate.

facts.text: A bank customer usually pays interest to borrow, paying back more than was lent, and earns interest on savings, withdrawing more than was deposited.
Unlike a dividend, which a company shares out from profit, interest is paid at a rate fixed beforehand.
In economics the interest rate is the price of credit and acts as the cost of capital.
One explanation for interest rates usually being above zero is that loanable funds are scarce.
In the sixteenth century Martín de Azpilcueta argued that a good now is better than the same good later, so interest pays the lender for giving up spending in the meantime.
Sumerian documents from 3000 BC show systematic lending of grain and metals, and interest seems to have been well established by then.
Jacob Bernoulli is thought to have discovered the constant e by studying what happens as interest is compounded more and more often.

entries.title: Interest rates: the cost of money now instead of later

definition.text: An interest rate is the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed.

facts.text: Rates are normally quoted per year.
Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, how often interest compounds and the length of time.
Interest rates reflect a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future.
Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the interest rate.
Riskier investments such as shares and junk bonds normally have to promise higher returns than safer government bonds.
Changing interest rates raises or lowers the opportunity cost of investing for firms.
The spread is the lending rate minus the deposit rate, and it covers banks' operating costs.

entries.text: Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the cost of the loan. That cost is set by the interest rate: the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed. Rates are normally quoted per year. Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, the sum originally lent, and on how often interest compounds and for how long. At heart, a rate reflects a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future. When rates change, the opportunity cost of funding new projects rises or falls for firms. Risk matters too. Riskier choices such as shares and high-risk 'junk' debt normally have to promise higher returns than safer government debt. Banks themselves live on the spread, the lending rate minus the deposit rate, which covers their operating costs.

entries.title: Real versus nominal: counting money or counting what it buys

definition.text: A nominal value is measured in plain money amounts, while a real value is measured by the goods and services that money can actually buy.

facts.text: Real value allows for inflation and reflects purchasing power.
Real values are found by dividing the nominal value by the growth factor of a price index, giving values in, for example, constant 1992 dollars.
Real GDP removes inflation from growth figures to show how much an economy actually grows; nominal GDP includes inflation and is higher.
Real wages, the buying power of wages, are the after-tax nominal wage divided by the growth factor of the consumer price index.
In one example the real wage rose 20 percent, so an hour's wage bought 20% more goods in year 2 than in year 1.
Output from different regions can be compared by repricing their goods at common or average prices.

entries.title: Time preference: why sooner beats later

definition.text: Time preference, also called time or delay discounting, is how much more a person values getting something sooner rather than later.

facts.text: The higher the time preference, the more future returns or costs are discounted.
It shows in choices like $100 today versus $110 in a month: taking the $100 implies an annual discount rate of at least 10%.
It is captured by the discount function; the main models are exponential, hyperbolic and quasi-hyperbolic.
John Rae began the study, arguing that wealth differs across nations because of differences in saving, driven by willingness to delay gratification.
In Irving Fisher's neoclassical theory, the rate of time preference underlies the real rate of interest.
Thomas Schelling framed climate change as an intergenerational discounting problem: how to share well-being between present and future generations.
The Stern Review set δ = .1%, η = 1 and g = 1.3%, giving a 1.4% discount rate; William Nordhaus objected that this near-zero time preference drove its conclusions.
There is still no consensus on the climate discount rate; revealed environmental discount rates of countries span 1%-10%.

entries.title: Why a dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow

definition.text: The time value of money is the idea that receiving a sum of money now is generally better than receiving the same sum later.

facts.text: Money held today can be invested to earn a return, so a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future.
It is one reason interest exists: interest compensates a depositor or lender for losing the use of their money.
It compares cash flows at different dates by converting them all to one valuation date, often called time 0.
An amount PV invested at rate i grows to PV(1 + i)^n after n periods; discounting reverses this to find present value.
The present value formula is the core formula, and the others, such as the annuity formula, are built from it.
It is weighed when judging the opportunity cost of spending rather than saving or investing.
Compound interest was used in business from the Middle Ages, and pricing annuities was a key setting for developing present-value methods.
Cost–benefit analysis adjusts all costs and benefits for the time value of money, expressing them as a net present value.

entries.title: Present value: what future money is worth today

definition.text: Present value is what a stream of expected future payments is worth as of today.

facts.text: Present value is usually below future value because money held now can earn interest, which is called the time value of money.
Put simply, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, since today's dollar can be invested and earn a day's interest.
If a zero-coupon $100 note payable in one year sells for $80 now, $80 is its present value.
Working out what money today will be worth later is called capitalization; the reverse, valuing future money today, is discounting.
The usual model uses compound interest, and (1 + i) to the power −n is called the present value factor.
The net present value of a stream of cash flows discounts each flow to the present and adds them up.
A risk-free interest rate is used for riskless projects; for risky ones a risk premium is added, judged from projects with similar risks.
When both timing and size of cash flows are uncertain, an expected present value approach weighs several scenarios by their probabilities.

entries.title: Discounting: paying to put off a payment

definition.text: Discounting is the arrangement in which someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time.

facts.text: The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt.
Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects.
A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest.
The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for the income the money could have earned by being invested meanwhile.
Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn in other assets of similar risk over the same period.
Discounting is tied to the time value of money: a payment has a different future value and present value.
Discounting turns a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value.

entries.text: Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects, the pull of what is vivid and close at hand. Discounting builds that preference into a deal. Someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time. The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt. Why should a delay cost anything? A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest. The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for what the money could have earned meanwhile. Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn elsewhere, at similar risk, over the same period. Discounting also runs the other way, turning a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value. Either way it rests on the time value of money: the same payment is worth one amount in the future and another today.
entries.text_plain: Most people prefer money now to money later, because of mortality, impatience and salience effects, the pull of what is vivid and close at hand. Discounting builds that preference into a deal. Someone who owes money pays a charge for the right to delay the payment for a set time. The discount is the gap between what is owed today and the larger amount that must be paid later to settle the debt. Why should a delay cost anything? A payment made in the future is worth less than the same payment today, because money in hand now could be banked to earn interest. The debtor who delays is in effect compensating the creditor for what the money could have earned meanwhile. Most models assume the discount yield equals the return the money could earn elsewhere, at similar risk, over the same period. Discounting also runs the other way, turning a future payment into its present value, also called its discounted value. Either way it rests on the time value of money: the same payment is worth one amount in the future and another today.

entries.title: Decision theory: the logic of choosing under uncertainty

definition.text: Decision theory, or the theory of rational choice, uses expected utility and probability to model how people would act rationally under uncertainty.

facts.text: It is mainly prescriptive, identifying optimal decisions for a rational agent rather than describing how people actually choose.
Its roots lie in 17th-century probability theory from Pascal and Fermat, refined by Huygens.
Daniel Bernoulli introduced expected utility in the 18th century; von Neumann and Morgenstern formalised it in the 1940s.
Choice under uncertainty is the heart of decision theory.
Allais and Ellsberg showed systematic departures from expected-utility maximisation, and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory renewed empirical study.
Kahneman and Tversky found that losses loom larger than gains, people focus on changes rather than levels, and probability estimates are biased by anchoring.
It also covers intertemporal choice, where actions lead to outcomes at different times, such as spending a windfall now or saving it for a pension.

entries.title: Compound interest: earning interest on interest

definition.text: Compound interest is interest earned on both the original sum and on interest already added to it.

facts.text: It differs from simple interest, where past interest is not added to the principal.
$1,000 at 5% a year grows to $1,050 after one year and $1,102.50 after two, because the second year's interest is on the new total.
The compounding frequency can be yearly, monthly, daily, continuous or not at all until maturity.
Compound interest at a constant rate gives exponential growth of capital.
Luca Pacioli's Rule of 72 (1494) says the years for money to double is roughly 72 divided by the interest rate.
Lenders charging compound interest were once condemned as the worst kind of usury under Roman law.
Garrett Hardin argued any economy based on long-term compound interest must fail, since exponential growth is impossible on a finite planet.

entries.text: Put $1,000 in an account at 5% a year. After one year it holds $1,050; after two, $1,102.50, because the second year's interest is paid on the new total. That is compound interest: interest earned both on the original sum and on interest already added to it. It differs from {{ref:nature-econ-812}}, where past interest is not added to the principal. Compounding can happen yearly, monthly, daily, continuously, or not at all until the loan matures. At a constant rate it makes capital grow exponentially, by the same proportion each period. Luca Pacioli's rule from 1494 says the years for money to double is roughly 72 divided by the interest rate. Not everyone admired the arithmetic. Under Roman law, lenders charging compound interest were condemned as the worst kind of usury, or extortionate lending. The ecologist {{ref:nature-hist-052}} argued that any economy based on long-term compound interest must fail, since growth of that kind is impossible on a finite planet.

entries.title: Von Neumann and Morgenstern: rational choice as expected utility

definition.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern theorem shows that rational choice under uncertainty amounts to maximising the expected value of some utility function.

facts.text: In 1947 John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern proved that anyone whose preferences meet four axioms acts as if maximising expected utility.
The four axioms are completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence.
Choices are framed as lotteries: sets of outcomes, each with a probability, the probabilities summing to one.
The theorem forms the foundation of expected utility theory, though it claims only that such a utility function exists, not that people consciously maximise it.
Risk aversion is built in automatically, since utility need not rise in step with money.
Its utilities cannot be compared or added across people, so 'total' or 'average' utility of a population is not meaningful without extra assumptions.
Lab experiments such as the Allais paradox show expected utility predicts imperfectly; most generalised theories drop or relax the independence axiom.

The theorem shows that rational choice under uncertainty amounts to maximizing the expected value of some utility function. Its utilities cannot be compared or added across people, so a group's 'total' or 'average' utility means nothing without extra assumptions. entries.title: Intertemporal choice: trading today against tomorrow

definition.text: Intertemporal choice is the study of how people value payoffs that arrive at different times, usually simplified to now versus some future date.

facts.text: John Rae introduced the idea in 1834; Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1889 and Irving Fisher in 1930 developed the model further.
Consuming something today means it cannot be consumed in the future, so choices trade present against future consumption.
Diminishing marginal utility is a key idea used to analyse intertemporal choice, along with choice under uncertainty and social welfare.
Uncertain fuel prices and high discount rates for running costs make energy-efficiency investments look riskier to many decision makers.

entries.title: Minimax: choosing the least bad worst case

definition.text: Minimax is a decision rule that picks the option whose worst possible outcome is least bad; for gains it is called maximin, maximising the minimum gain.

facts.text: It was first formulated for zero-sum games between players and later extended to general decisions under uncertainty.
A player's maximin value is the most they can be sure of getting without knowing what the other players will do.
In two-player zero-sum games the minimax solution is the same as the Nash equilibrium.
Minimax values are central to the theory of repeated games, including the folk theorem.
It suits cases without good probability models but can overweight very unlikely, costly events.

entries.text: A cautious chooser can set probabilities aside and ask a single question: what is the worst that could happen? entries.title: Risk: uncertainty with numbers attached

definition.text: Risk is uncertainty that has been quantified: the possible outcomes have known probabilities and some of them involve losses.

facts.text: Not knowing whether it will rain tomorrow is uncertainty; giving it a probability, say from a weather forecast, quantifies the risk.
If a business event loses $100,000 when it rains and rain has a 10% chance, the risk is a 10% chance of losing $100,000.
The expected opportunity loss multiplies the chance of loss by its size, here $10,000, which suits only a risk-neutral decision-maker.
Most people would pay a premium to avoid the loss, so insurers charge more than the expected loss.
Risk differs from variability: risk concerns one uncertain future value, variability the spread of many observed values.

entries.title: Insurance: a small sure cost against a large uncertain one

definition.text: Insurance is protection from financial loss: for a fee, one party promises to pay another if a particular loss, damage or injury happens.

facts.text: It is a form of risk management, used mainly to guard against a loss that may or may not happen.
The buyer accepts a certain, known and fairly small loss, the premium, in exchange for the insurer's promise to pay if a covered loss occurs.
A deductible (or excess) is the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim.
Insurance transfers the financial burden of a chance event to a bigger entity; it does not lower the chance that the event happens.
Needing an insurable interest, a real stake in the loss, is what separates insurance from gambling.
Chinese and Indian traders spread risk as early as the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC; Chinese merchants split cargo across many boats so one capsizing lost little.
Economists and consumer advocates in the United States generally see insurance as worthwhile for rare, catastrophic losses but not for likely, small ones.
Insurance can help households and societies prepare for and soften catastrophes, but it can also raise fraud and careless behaviour.

entries.title: Risk aversion: why a sure thing often wins

definition.text: Risk aversion is the tendency to prefer a more certain outcome to a riskier one, even when the risky option pays the same or more on average.

facts.text: A risk-averse investor may choose a bank account with a low guaranteed rate over shares that could pay more but might lose value.
Offered a sure $50 or a coin flip for $100 or nothing, a risk-averse person would accept a sure amount below $50, such as $40.
A risk-neutral person is indifferent between the bet and a sure $50; a risk-loving person takes the bet even against a sure $60.
The certainty equivalent is the smallest sure amount a person would accept instead of a gamble; it is a measure of risk aversion.
The risk premium is the gap between a gamble's expected value and its certainty equivalent, positive for the risk-averse.
In expected utility theory a person is risk-averse exactly when their utility function is concave.
On average, higher earners are less risk-averse than lower earners.

entries.title: The risk premium: the extra return that pays for risk

definition.text: A risk premium is the extra return a person demands to accept more risk, generally the expected risky return minus the risk-free return.

facts.text: Choosing a risky share over a 3% risk-free treasury bond, an investor might demand 8%, a risk premium of 5%.
Risk premiums are larger during economic downturns and periods of heightened uncertainty.
The more risk averse a person or firm, the larger the premium they will pay to avoid a risk; it usually falls as wealth rises.
For bonds the risk premium is called the credit spread: the extra yield over a risk-free treasury bond.
Schroeder estimated stock market risk premiums of 4.83 to 7.75 percent in the UK and EU, mostly between 6.3 and 7.2 percent.
In some models, the option value of investing in invasive species quarantine or management is a risk premium.
When a multiply-resistant wheat cultivar was released in 2000, it sharply cut the risk premium farmers bore against Fusarium head blight.

entries.title: Cost of capital: the bar every project must clear

definition.text: The cost of capital is what a company pays for its funds, both borrowed and from shareholders, or the return investors require for providing them.

facts.text: It is the minimum return investors expect, so it sets the benchmark a new project must beat.
An investment is worthwhile only if its expected return on capital exceeds the cost of capital.
It equals what the money could earn in the best alternative investment of similar risk: the opportunity cost of capital.
For projects outside a firm's core business, its usual cost of capital may be the wrong yardstick, since the risks differ.
Finding it means estimating both the cost of debt and the cost of equity, and both must look forward to expected future risk and return.
The discount rate used in financial calculations is usually set equal to the cost of capital.

entries.title: Discounted cash flow: valuing a project by its future payments

definition.text: Discounted cash flow analysis values a security, project, company or asset by allowing for the time value of money in its expected cash flows.

facts.text: All future cash flows are estimated and discounted, usually at the cost of capital, and their sum is the net present value.
The discount rate combines the time value of money (the risk-free rate) with a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive.
Run in reverse, taking a known price and solving for the rate, it gives the internal rate of return or a bond's yield.
It is widely used in investment finance, real estate development, corporate finance, actuarial science and patent valuation.
It has been used in the UK coal industry since 1801 and was first set out in modern terms by Irving Fisher (1930) and John Burr Williams (1938).
Its forecasts assume the future resembles the past, and small input changes, especially to terminal value, can swing the result greatly.
Traditional DCF counts only financial costs and benefits, leaving out environmental, social and governance performance.

entries.title: Internal rate of return: a project's break-even rate

definition.text: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the yearly rate of return at which the net present value of all of an investment's cash flows equals zero.

facts.text: It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk.
Used before the fact it estimates a future annual return; used afterwards it measures the return actually achieved.
A project whose estimated IRR exceeds the firm's cost of capital for it is profitable.
IRR measures an investment's profitability or efficiency, while net present value measures how much value it adds.
For cash flows of -123,400, then 36,200, 54,800 and 48,100 over three years, the IRR is 5.96%.
In savings and loans the IRR is also called the effective interest rate.
A project with a negative net present value is not necessarily loss-making; it means its internal rate of return is below the required rate.
The modified internal rate of return was developed to fix some problems with it and to rank investments of unequal size.

distinct_from: Problems with the internal rate of return
entries.text: Suppose a project costs 123,400 up front and then returns 36,200, 54,800 and 48,100 over three years. Its internal rate of return, or IRR, is 5.96%. That is the yearly rate at which the {{ref:nature-val-014}}, or NPV, of all its cash flows equals zero. It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk. Estimated in advance, it predicts a future annual return; measured afterwards, it shows the return actually achieved. A project whose estimated IRR beats the firm's cost of capital for it is profitable. IRR measures a project's profitability or efficiency, while NPV measures how much value it adds. A negative NPV does not necessarily mean a loss. It means the IRR falls below the required rate. For loans and deposits, the IRR is also called the effective interest rate. The modified internal rate of return was developed to fix some of its problems and to rank projects of unequal size.

It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk. entries.title: The real interest rate: what a loan earns after inflation

definition.text: The real interest rate is the interest rate after allowing for inflation, while the nominal rate is the rate before that adjustment.

facts.text: Real rates measure what is repaid against the buying power the money had when it was lent or invested.
If inflation equals the nominal rate, the real rate is zero.
The Fisher equation links real rates, nominal rates and the inflation rate; it can be used with projected (ex ante) or historical (ex post) rates.
Lenders and borrowers accept a nominal rate made up of the real rate they require plus the inflation they expect.
Real rates can be negative when nominal rates are below inflation.

So lenders and borrowers accept a nominal rate made up of the real rate they require plus the inflation they expect. When nominal rates sit below inflation, real rates turn negative. entries.title: Risk pooling: many pay so that a few are made whole

definition.text: Risk pooling is gathering money from many insured people or firms so that it can pay the losses that only some of them will suffer.

facts.text: Each member is protected for a fee, and the fee depends on how often and how badly the insured event tends to happen.
Because policies cover members of large classes, insurers can rely on the law of large numbers, under which predicted losses come close to actual losses.
Instead of joining a pool, a person or firm can self-insure by saving money for possible future losses.
Some communities, including the Amish and some Muslim groups, rely on mutual support from their community when disaster strikes rather than on insurance contracts.

entries.title: Annuities: equal payments at regular intervals

definition.text: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals, usually for a limited term.

facts.text: Life insurers commonly sell annuities: a person pays a lump sum or premiums in return for regular income, often for retirement.
Everyday examples include regular savings deposits, monthly mortgage payments, insurance premiums and pension payments.
Its value is expressed as a present or future value by discounting or accumulating the payments at a stated interest rate.
An annuity-immediate pays at the end of each period, like mortgage repayments; an annuity-due pays at the start, like rent.
An annuity that continues indefinitely is a perpetuity.
In medieval and early modern Europe, annuities let lenders provide credit where direct interest-bearing loans were restricted.
By the 16th and 17th centuries governments in the Dutch Republic, France and England sold annuities to raise money.

entries.title: What sets the interest rate on a loan

definition.text: Market interest rates are set in markets such as the money market, bond market and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors.

facts.text: Lenders weigh opportunity cost, the other uses of their money, including the return from competing investments.
A lender putting off consumption wants at least enough to cover price rises from inflation; nominal interest is roughly the real rate plus inflation.
A risk premium covers the chance of default, so loans to developing countries carry higher premiums than loans to the US government.
Shorter loans usually carry less default and inflation risk, so short-term rates are often below long-term rates, an upward sloping yield curve.
Investors want a higher return on an asset that is hard to resell quickly at a fair price than on a liquid one.
Central banks strongly influence short-term rates, one of the main tools of monetary policy.

entries.title: Knightian uncertainty: the risks no one can put odds on

definition.text: Knightian uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be measured or turned into probabilities, as distinct from measurable risk.

facts.text: Frank Knight drew the distinction in 1921, in Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit.
To Knight, risk can in principle be insured, but true uncertainty cannot.
Known risks can be insured because they have a defined probability distribution; uncertainties lack one and can lead to extreme outcomes.
Knight called those who bear uncertainty entrepreneurs, so entrepreneurship research studies how uncertainty creates opportunities.
It is named after Frank Knight, who separated risk from uncertainty in his 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit.
Knight held that measurable uncertainty, risk proper, is so different from unmeasurable uncertainty that it is not really uncertainty at all.
The concept admits a basic limit to knowledge and an essential unpredictability of future events.
It remains largely informal: there is no single best formal system of probability and belief to represent it.

It remains largely informal: there is no single best formal system of probability and belief to represent it.

entries.title: Ambiguity aversion: preferring the odds you know

definition.text: Ambiguity aversion is a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown.

facts.text: It was first shown by the Ellsberg paradox: people prefer betting on an urn of 50 red and 50 black balls over one of 100 balls in an unknown mix.
Risk aversion concerns a gamble against its expected value when odds are known; ambiguity aversion concerns known odds against unknown odds.
Unlike risk aversion, mainly put down to diminishing marginal utility, ambiguity aversion has no widely accepted main cause.
It has been used to explain incomplete contracts, stock-market volatility and selective abstention in elections.
Greater ambiguity aversion raises demand for insurance, as people dislike unknown events affecting their lives and property.
Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behaviour in another.

Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behavior in another.
