entries.title: Keynes's consumption function: spending tied to today's income

definition.text: Keynes's idea, also called the absolute income hypothesis, that consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income.

facts.text: Keynes introduced the consumption function in his 1936 General Theory.
He held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run.
Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing.
Because it ignores future income, its critics developed the permanent income and life-cycle hypotheses.

entries.text: In his 1936 General Theory, Keynes proposed a simple rule: consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income, the income left after taxes. This consumption function is also called the absolute income hypothesis. Keynes held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run. There is also a floor. Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing. The rule has a blind spot: it ignores future income. Its critics developed {{ref:nature-econ-513}} and {{ref:nature-econ-514}} in response.
entries.text_plain: In his 1936 General Theory, Keynes proposed a simple rule: consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income, the income left after taxes. This consumption function is also called the absolute income hypothesis. Keynes held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run. There is also a floor. Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing. The rule has a blind spot: it ignores future income. Its critics developed The permanent income hypothesis: spending on long-run income and The life-cycle hypothesis: spending over a whole lifetime in response.

entries.title: The circular flow: money and goods going round

definition.text: A model of the economy showing the main exchanges as flows of money, goods and services between economic actors.

facts.text: Money and goods flow around a closed circuit in matching amounts but opposite directions.
In its simplest form, households supply labor to businesses and spend the income they earn on the goods and services businesses produce.
Circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts and so of macroeconomics.
Richard Cantillon described the idea in 1730, and François Quesnay first visualized it in his 1758 Tableau économique.
Frank Knight drew the first modern circular flow diagram in 1933.
It shows that activities depend on one another: without consumption there is no demand, which limits production and income.

entries.text: In 1758 François Quesnay drew the economy as a circuit in the chart described in {{ref:nature-hist-018}}, picturing an idea Richard Cantillon had described in 1730. The circular flow of income is a model showing the main exchanges in an economy as flows of money, goods and services between economic actors. Money and goods travel around a closed circuit in matching amounts but opposite directions. In the simplest version, households supply labour to businesses and spend the income they earn on the goods and services businesses produce. The model shows how activities depend on one another: without consumption there is no demand, which limits production and income. Frank Knight drew the first modern circular flow diagram in 1933. Circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts, and so of macroeconomics.

entries.title: Wealth versus income: the orchard and its apples

definition.text: The distinction between wealth, a stock measured at a point in time, and income, a flow measured per unit of time.

facts.text: Wealth is like the value of an orchard on December 31 minus the debt owed on it.
Income is like the value of apples the orchard yields each year; measuring it per unit of time makes it a flow.
For national wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world.
The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

entries.text: Picture an orchard. Wealth is like the value of the orchard on December 31, minus the debt owed on it. Income is like the value of the apples it yields each year. The first is a stock, measured at a point in time. The second is a flow, measured per unit of time. For a nation's wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world. The two are linked by behaviour. The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

entries.title: Economic depreciation: the shrinking value of capital

definition.text: The gradual loss in economic value of the capital stock of a firm or nation through physical wear, obsolescence or falling demand for what the capital provides.

facts.text: Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation.
Gross investment minus depreciation is net investment, the net addition to the capital stock.
Economic depreciation is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future.
An asset's value can rise instead, for example if the price of its services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls.
In national accounts it is called consumption of fixed capital, equal to the gap between gross and net fixed capital formation.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, a steady state occurs when gross investment equals depreciation.

entries.text: Accountants depreciate an asset by spreading out its cost. Economists ask a different question: how much less are the asset's future services worth today? Economic depreciation is the gradual loss in value of a firm's or nation's capital stock through physical wear, obsolescence, or falling demand for what the capital provides. Formally, it is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future. The bookkeeping is simple. Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation, and gross investment minus depreciation is net investment. In national accounts it is called {{ref:nature-econ-517}}. Value can also rise, for example if the price of an asset's services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls. In the growth model of {{ref:nature-eecon-204}}, the capital stock stops changing when gross investment equals depreciation.
entries.text_plain: Accountants depreciate an asset by spreading out its cost. Economists ask a different question: how much less are the asset's future services worth today? Economic depreciation is the gradual loss in value of a firm's or nation's capital stock through physical wear, obsolescence, or falling demand for what the capital provides. Formally, it is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future. The bookkeeping is simple. Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation, and gross investment minus depreciation is net investment. In national accounts it is called Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts. Value can also rise, for example if the price of an asset's services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls. In the growth model of The Solow–Swan model: where long-run growth comes from, the capital stock stops changing when gross investment equals depreciation.

entries.title: Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts

definition.text: The national-accounts term for the depreciation of fixed assets: the fall in their current value over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage.

facts.text: It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation.
The UN manual says it may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP.
Net measures such as net domestic product and net national income are found by deducting it from GDP and GNI.
Net national income shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, making it a better measure of economic welfare than GDP.
It excludes the depletion or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas.
It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters.
Critics note that its 'economic' valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

entries.text: A large cost hides inside every GDP figure. The UN manual says this cost, consumption of fixed capital, may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP. It is the national-accounts term for depreciation: the fall in the current value of fixed assets over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage. It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation. Subtracting it from GDP gives net domestic product, and subtracting it from {{ref:nature-econ-530}} gives {{ref:nature-econ-571}}. That net figure shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, which makes it a better gauge of economic welfare than GDP. Some losses are left out. entries.title: Income inequality: how unevenly income is shared

definition.text: The extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population.

facts.text: It can be measured with tools such as the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient.
Many economists argue some inequality is necessary but excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality.
Globalization tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

entries.title: The Gini coefficient: inequality in a single number

definition.text: A measure of how unequally income, wealth or consumption is spread across a nation or group, from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality.

facts.text: Corrado Gini published it in 1912, building on Max Lorenz's work.
It is usually defined from the Lorenz curve, which plots the share of total income earned by the bottom share of the population; the 45-degree line is perfect equality.
With just two income groups, if the high earners are a share u of people and earn a share f of income, the Gini is f − u.
It can be calculated on market income, before taxes and transfers, or on disposable income.
In ecology it has been used to measure biodiversity, plotting the cumulative share of species against the cumulative share of individuals.
UNICEF put Latin America and the Caribbean's net income Gini at 48.3 in 2008, the highest of any region.

entries.title: What GDP leaves out

definition.text: The criticisms that GDP leaves out much of what shapes living standards, such as pollution, unpaid work, health and how income is shared.

facts.text: GDP ignores negative externalities: industrial output may raise GDP while the pollution it causes is not counted.
It excludes non-market activity such as household production, barter and volunteer work.
Estimates of unpaid work's value range from about 15% of GDP in Canada to nearly 70% in the United Kingdom.
Kuznets warned in 1937 that a nation's welfare can scarcely be inferred from national income.
GDP counts spending that would shrink if problems were solved, such as medical care and crime-fighting.
Robert F. Kennedy said GNP measures everything except that which makes life worthwhile.
The parable of the broken window notes that GDP treats spending on repairs as a net benefit, ignoring the original destruction.

entries.text: Robert F. Kennedy said GNP, a close cousin of GDP, measures everything except that which makes life worthwhile. Critics of GDP have a long list of reasons. It ignores negative externalities: industrial output may raise GDP while the pollution it causes goes uncounted. It excludes non-market activity such as unpaid work at home, barter and volunteer work. Estimates of unpaid work's value range from about 15% of GDP in Canada to nearly 70% in the United Kingdom. GDP also counts spending that would shrink if problems were solved, such as medical care and crime-fighting. The parable of the broken window makes the point sharply: GDP treats spending on repairs as a net benefit and ignores the original destruction. entries.title: Why GDP looks good when nature suffers

definition.text: The criticism that GDP rewards activities that harm the environment and fails to show natural capital being used up.

facts.text: A traffic jam can raise GDP through extra fuel use while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted.
GDP may not show how much natural capital an economy is building or protecting.
The UK's Natural Capital Committee said in 2013 that GDP focuses on flows, not stocks, so an economy can run down its assets while recording high growth.
Deforestation, strip mining and overfishing are counted as activity in GDP despite long-term harm.
In 1989 John Cobb and Herman Daly introduced the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, which subtracts environmental degradation and natural capital depreciation.
China launched Gross Ecosystem Product in 2020 to measure ecosystems' contribution to the economy, including climate regulation.

entries.text: A traffic jam is good for GDP. Stuck cars burn extra fuel, which counts as economic activity, while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted. That is the heart of the criticism: GDP rewards activities that harm the environment and fails to show natural capital being used up. Clearing forests, strip mining and taking too many fish all count as activity despite their long-term harm. GDP may not show how much natural capital an economy is building or protecting. The UK's Natural Capital Committee put it plainly in 2013. GDP focuses on flows, not stocks, so an economy can run down its assets while recording high growth. Alternatives have followed. In 1989 John Cobb and {{ref:nature-hist-040}} introduced {{ref:nature-acct-001}}, which subtracts environmental degradation and the depreciation of natural capital. In 2020 China launched {{ref:nature-acct-109}} to measure ecosystems' contribution to the economy, including its role in steadying the climate.

entries.title: The threshold hypothesis: when more growth stops helping

definition.text: The idea that economic growth improves quality of life only up to a threshold point, after which further growth can make it worse.

facts.text: The idea produces an upside-down U-shaped curve whose peak marks the level of growth to aim for.
Happiness has been shown to rise with GDP per person at least up to $15,000 per person.
Health, education and political freedoms sometimes fail to improve as an economy grows.

entries.text: Does more growth always mean a better life? The threshold hypothesis says no. Growth improves quality of life only up to a threshold point, after which further growth can make it worse. Plotted, the idea forms an upside-down U, whose peak marks the level of growth to aim for. Happiness has been shown to rise with GDP per person at least up to $15,000 per person. Yet health, education and political freedoms sometimes fail to improve as an economy grows.

entries.title: Crowding out: when public spending displaces private

definition.text: The reduction of private activity when government spending uses resources or raises interest rates, limiting fiscal policy's effect.

facts.text: Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it.
Government spending that raises interest rates can also cut private investment.

entries.text: Government spending does not always add to an economy. Sometimes it just takes the place of private activity, an effect called crowding out. Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it. A subtler route runs through interest rates. Government spending that raises interest rates can cut private investment, limiting what fiscal policy achieves.

entries.title: Heterodox macroeconomics: the dissenting schools

definition.text: Branches of macroeconomics that reject mainstream theory, including ecological economics, modern monetary theory and Marxian economics.

facts.text: Heterodox economists see price flexibility, not price stickiness, as the source of instability, so they build models with different assumptions.

entries.title: Monetarism: Milton Friedman's case for steady money

definition.text: Milton Friedman's school of macroeconomics, which updated the quantity theory of money and stressed money's role in the economy.

facts.text: Friedman argued monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but favoured steady money-supply growth over frequent intervention.
Friedman and Edmund Phelps denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view supported by the 1970s oil shocks.
It was influential in the early 1980s but faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

Friedman argued that monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but he favoured steady growth of the money supply over frequent intervention. With Edmund Phelps, he denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view the 1970s oil shocks supported. Monetarism was influential in the early 1980s. It faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

entries.title: Rational expectations: people look ahead, not just back

definition.text: The assumption, brought into macroeconomics by Robert Lucas, that people form forecasts using all current information about policy and conditions rather than just recent past trends.

facts.text: Before Lucas, economists used adaptive expectations, where people look only at the recent past.
In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect.
The Lucas critique argued that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes, and called for models with microeconomic foundations.

entries.text: Before Robert Lucas, economists mostly assumed adaptive expectations: people forecast by looking only at the recent past. Lucas brought in rational expectations, the assumption that people use all current information about policy and conditions. The consequences were large. In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect. The Lucas critique added that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes. It called for models with microeconomic foundations instead.

entries.title: New Keynesian economics: sticky prices bring policy back

definition.text: A macroeconomic school that accepts rational expectations but shows how sticky prices and wages let monetary and fiscal policy affect real output.

facts.text: It traces sticky prices and wages to imperfect competition, so monetary policy changes quantities rather than only prices.
Stanley Fischer and John B. Taylor showed monetary policy could work even under rational expectations when contracts fix wages.

entries.title: How consumption shapes the environment

definition.text: The link between what and how much people consume and their impact on the environment.

facts.text: What people eat and wear, the homes they live in and where they shop all affect the environment.
Consumption patterns changed drastically with the Industrial Revolution, as cheap mass-produced goods met rising wages.
Overconsumption, pollution and climate change can devastate biodiversity.
Researchers have found affluence to be the key driver of carbon emissions.

entries.title: Household production: the economy inside the home

definition.text: The idea, from the New Home Economics, that market consumption must be studied alongside the goods and services households produce for themselves.

facts.text: The opportunity cost of time changes the cost of home-made substitutes and so the demand for bought goods and services.
GDP excludes household production such as unpaid childcare.

entries.text: Households do not only buy things; they also make them. The New Home Economics holds that market consumption must be studied alongside the goods and services households produce for themselves. Time is the hinge. The opportunity cost of time changes the cost of home-made substitutes, and so changes the demand for bought goods and services. This home production is largely invisible in the statistics, since GDP excludes it, including unpaid childcare.

entries.title: The life-cycle hypothesis: spending over a whole lifetime

definition.text: Franco Modigliani's theory that people plan consumption using past, current and expected future income, spreading it over their lifetime.

facts.text: The source dates its publication by Modigliani to 1966.
It grew out of criticism that the Keynesian consumption function ignores future income.

entries.title: The permanent income hypothesis: spending on long-run income

definition.text: Milton Friedman's theory that consumption depends on a person's long-run permanent income rather than temporary swings in income.

facts.text: Friedman set it out in the 1950s in A Theory of the Consumption Function.
Income is split into transitory and permanent parts, and changes in each affect consumption differently.
A change in permanent income changes consumption by the marginal propensity to consume times that change.

A change in permanent income changes consumption by the marginal propensity to consume, the share of extra income that is spent, times that change.

entries.title: The relative income hypothesis: keeping up with others

definition.text: James Duesenberry's 1949 theory that people's consumption depends on their income relative to others, not only on its level.

facts.text: It assumes people's consumption choices are not independent of one another.
Two people with the same income but different positions in the income distribution will consume differently.

So two people with the same income, but different positions in the income distribution, will consume differently.

entries.title: Does school build skills or just signal them?

definition.text: The challenge to human capital theory from signaling theory, which says education may mark existing ability rather than create skills.

facts.text: Some labor economists criticize the Chicago-school theory for trying to explain all wage differences by human capital.
In Spence and Stiglitz's signaling theory, education lets able workers signal their ability to employers and earn higher wages.
Studies find wages also vary with gender, nativity, workplace discrimination and socioeconomic status.

entries.title: The circular flow ignores the energy that drives it
entries.article: Circular flow of income#Circular flow diagram as a subsystem of the environment

definition.text: The critique that the circular flow model treats the economy as self-sustaining, when it really depends on a one-way throughput of matter and energy from the environment.

facts.text: The model implies the economy runs like a perpetual motion machine, which the laws of thermodynamics rule out.
No economy can recycle its own waste without new energy, so it must operate as a subsystem of a larger ecosystem.
Low-entropy matter and energy enter from natural capital such as solar energy, oil wells, fisheries and mines, and leave as high-entropy waste.
Because these inputs and the capacity to absorb waste are finite, there is a sustainable limit to the economy's growth.
Ecological economics replaces the simple circular flow with a diagram that includes solar energy and the natural inputs and services it sustains.

entries.title: Who owns the world's wealth

definition.text: How a society's or the world's total wealth is shared among people and regions.

facts.text: The Kuznets curve holds that inequality of wealth and income rises in early development, stabilizes, then falls.
In 2008 about 1% of adults were estimated to hold 40% of world wealth, or 32% adjusted for purchasing power parity.
In 2013, 1% of adults were estimated to hold 46% of world wealth.
Some adults have negative net worth, with debts larger than assets.

entries.title: Does inequality help or hurt growth?

definition.text: The question of whether unequal income and wealth help or hinder a country's economic growth.

facts.text: The classical view, from Adam Smith, held that inequality boosts saving by the wealthy and so speeds capital accumulation and growth.
Galor and Zeira argued that with imperfect credit markets inequality harms investment in skills and slows growth, except in very poor economies.
Galor and Moav suggest inequality helped early industrial growth but became harmful once human capital replaced physical capital as the main engine.
Thomas Piketty argued in 2013 that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of output, inequality rises.

entries.title: Tobin's q: when buying new machines pays

definition.text: The ratio between a physical asset's market value and the cost of replacing it, used to explain investment.

facts.text: When the ratio is above 1, a machine can be bought for less than the output it generates is worth, so firms gain by investing.

entries.title: Factor income: rent, wages, interest and profit

definition.text: The income earned from the factors of production: rent from land, wages from labor, interest from capital and profit from enterprise.

facts.text: In consumer theory, income is the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.
National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market.

entries.text: Each factor of production earns its own kind of income: rent from land, wages from labour, interest from capital and profit from enterprise. Together these make up factor income. National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market. In consumer theory, income takes a narrower meaning: the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.

entries.title: Gross national income: counting by ownership, not location

definition.text: The total factor income earned by a country's residents, formerly called gross national product (GNP).

facts.text: GNI equals GDP plus factor income residents receive from abroad, minus factor income paid to non-residents.
GDP defines its scope by location, GNI by ownership; for the whole world the two are the same.
Unlike GDP, GNI is a concept of income rather than of value added.
Net national income is GNI minus depreciation.
The 1993 revision of the System of National Accounts renamed GNP as GNI.
The United States used GNP as its main measure until 1991, when it switched to GDP.
It includes wages of cross-border and seasonal workers abroad but not remittances sent home, which is why France's GNI exceeds its GDP.
Ireland's GDP became so distorted by multinational profit shifting that in 2017 its central bank adopted a modified GNI measure.

entries.title: Net national income: allowing for wear and tear

definition.text: Gross national income minus depreciation.

facts.text: It covers the income of households, businesses and government.
It equals GDP plus net wages, salaries and property income from abroad, minus wear and tear of buildings, machinery, equipment and infrastructure.
By the expenditure method it is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, plus net foreign factor income, minus indirect taxes and depreciation of manufactured capital.

entries.text: Machines, buildings and roads wear out, and gross national income ignores that loss. Net national income subtracts it: it is gross national income minus depreciation. It covers the income of households, businesses and government. Put another way, it equals GDP plus net wages, salaries and property income from abroad, minus wear and tear of buildings, machinery, equipment and infrastructure. By the expenditure method, it is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, plus net foreign factor income, minus indirect taxes and depreciation of manufactured capital.

entries.title: Haig–Simons income: consumption plus change in net worth

definition.text: A widely used economic definition of income as consumption plus the change in a person's net worth.

facts.text: The definition dates from 1938 and counts both what is consumed and the change in the value of property held.
Taxable income is usually lower than Haig–Simons income, since unrealized gains such as a rise in share prices are economic but not taxable income.
'Full income' adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income, but it cannot be observed, forcing reliance on money income.

entries.text: A widely used economic definition of income dates from 1938. Taxable income is typically lower, because unrealized gains, such as a rise in share prices, are economic income but not taxable income. A broader idea, full income, adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income. It cannot be observed, so economists must rely on money income.

entries.title: The unpaid work the national accounts ignore

definition.text: The exclusion of unpaid work, such as household work, from every category of the national accounts and from GDP.

facts.text: An Australian study put the value of this uncounted work at about 50% of GDP.
Because GDP is tied to the national accounts, the omission may distort the picture they give.
Feminist economists such as Marilyn Waring and Nancy Folbre call the SNA biased for valuing no unpaid housework, though GDP imputes rent for owner-occupied homes.
Unpaid housework falls outside the SNA production boundary, which critics say hides how much market production depends on non-market labour.

entries.contested_note: Feminist economists criticise the exclusion of unpaid work, while statisticians question whether valuing it is feasible.

entries.title: The marginal propensity to save

definition.text: The share of an extra unit of income that is saved; the share of total income saved is the average propensity to save.

facts.text: The saving rate is directly affected by the general level of interest rates.

entries.text: Of each extra unit of income, a household spends some and saves the rest. The share saved is the marginal propensity to save. The share of total income saved, by contrast, is the average propensity to save. The general level of interest rates directly affects the saving rate.

entries.title: The multiplier: how spending ripples through an economy

definition.text: The way a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, raising or lowering total output by more than the original change.

facts.text: Keynes explained how a small fall in consumption or investment could be magnified into declines across the economy.
A government-paid bridge adds its own value to output and also lets the workers spend and invest more, helping close an output gap.

entries.text: A government pays for a bridge. The bridge adds its own value to output, and the workers who built it can then spend and invest more. This is the multiplier effect: a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, moving total output by more than the original change. Such spending can help close an output gap, the shortfall of output below its potential. Keynes showed that the logic also runs in reverse. A small fall in consumption or investment can be magnified into declines across the economy.

entries.title: Does fiscal stimulus work?

definition.text: The question of how government spending increases and tax cuts change demand, prices, interest rates and output.

facts.text: Keynesians argue expansionary fiscal policy in recessions builds the base for growth and full employment, with deficits repaid by the later expansion.
In the IS-LM model, fiscal expansion raises the price level and real interest rates in the long run.
The AD-AS model lets the price level vary, making it better for long-run analysis.
Economists still debate how effective fiscal stimulus is.

entries.contested_note: The sources say economists still debate the effectiveness of fiscal stimulus.

entries.title: Do interest rates keep saving and investment equal?

definition.text: The question of whether interest rates automatically keep a nation's saving equal to its investment.

facts.text: Classical economics held that a rise in saving would lower interest rates and stimulate investment, so the two would always match.
Keynes argued both are insensitive to interest rates, so saving could exceed investment for long periods, causing a general glut and recession.
Keynes argued that savings withheld from investment cut total spending, incomes and jobs, which in turn reduces savings again.

entries.contested_note: Classical economists and Keynes disagreed on whether interest rates keep saving and investment equal.
entries.text: Classical economists believed saving and investment would always match. If saving rose, interest rates would fall, and cheaper funds would stimulate investment. Keynes disagreed. He argued that both are insensitive to interest rates, so saving could exceed investment for long periods, causing a general glut and recession. Savings withheld from investment cut total spending, incomes and jobs, which in turn reduces savings again. The two camps remain divided on whether interest rates keep saving and investment equal.

entries.title: The IS–LM model: two markets in balance

definition.text: A model invented by John Hicks in 1936 showing the interest rates and output levels at which both the goods market and the money market are in balance.

facts.text: The goods market balances investment against saving (IS) and the money market balances money supply against money demand (LM).
It underpins the idea of aggregate demand by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

entries.text: John Hicks invented the IS–LM model in 1936. It finds the interest rates and output levels at which two markets are in balance at once. In the goods market, investment must balance saving, which gives the IS part of the name. In the money market, money supply must balance money demand, which gives the LM part. The model underpins the idea of aggregate demand, by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

entries.title: Gross or net, domestic or national: decoding the names
entries.article: Measures of national income and output#Expenditure

definition.text: The naming scheme of national income measures, combining gross or net, national or domestic, and product, income or expenditure.

facts.text: 'Gross' means total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital.
'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders; 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere.
A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but France's national figures.
Net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital.

distinct_from: Measures of national income and output

sources.title: Measures of national income and output

entries.text: A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but in France's national figures. That example captures half of a naming scheme. 'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders, while 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere. The other half is gross versus net. 'Gross' means the total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital. So net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital. Each measure can also be framed as product, income or expenditure.

entries.title: Is national income a good measure of welfare?
entries.article: Measures of national income and output#National income and welfare

definition.text: The question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare, given what it leaves out.

facts.text: Countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures such as life expectancy.
A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not.
Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches is not measured.
Alternatives include the Human Development Index, Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, Genuine Progress Indicator and sustainable national income.

distinct_from: Measures of national income and output

entries.text: Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches goes unmeasured. A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not. Still, alternatives exist, including {{ref:nature-acct-003}}, indexes of sustainable economic welfare and genuine progress, and a sustainable version of national income.

entries.title: Two centuries of global income inequality
entries.article: Gini coefficient#World income Gini index since 1800s

definition.text: The long-run trend in income inequality among all the world's people.

facts.text: The global income Gini rose steadily from 1820 to 2002, with a sharp increase between 1980 and 2002.
The trend appears to have peaked and started to reverse with rapid growth in emerging economies such as the BRIC countries.

entries.title: Where the Gini coefficient falls short

definition.text: The weaknesses of the Gini coefficient as a measure of inequality.

facts.text: It is a relative measure, so it can rise even while the number of people in absolute poverty falls.
It is not additive, and different income distributions can share the same value.
A population can have a very low income Gini and a very high wealth Gini at once.
Small populations with less varied economies tend to report lower values.

entries.title: Weighting the CPI: why housing counts most

definition.text: The way a consumer price index combines price changes for different goods, giving each a weight that reflects its share of consumer spending.

facts.text: In one example, housing carries 41.4% of the weight, food and beverages 17.4% and transport 17.0%.
Weights should ideally reflect current spending but in practice use the most recent past data.
Infrequent reweighting saves money but delays new kinds of spending, such as Internet subscriptions, from entering the index.

entries.text: In one example of a consumer price index, housing carries 41.4% of the weight, food and beverages 17.4% and transport 17.0%. Each weight reflects that item's share of consumer spending, so a price change in housing moves the index more than the same change in a smaller category. Ideally the weights would reflect current spending, but in practice they use the most recent past data. Updating the weights only now and then saves money, but it delays new kinds of spending, such as Internet subscriptions, from entering the index.

entries.title: Adjusted net national income: subtracting nature's losses

definition.text: Net national income further reduced to account for the depletion of natural resources.

facts.text: The natural resources deducted are non-critical natural capital such as minerals.
It does not account for critical natural capital such as air and water.
Capital is split into manufactured capital, non-critical natural capital and critical natural capital, among other categories.
The European Environment Agency proposed using consumption of ecosystem capital to create an adjusted net national income.

entries.text: Net national income allows for machines wearing out, but not for minerals dug up and gone. Adjusted net national income makes that further correction, subtracting the running down of resources taken from nature. Economists divide capital into categories, among them manufactured capital and two kinds of natural capital. The non-critical kind includes minerals, and that is what gets deducted. The critical kind, such as air and water, is not accounted for; {{ref:nature-eecon-229}} returns to it. The European Environment Agency has proposed using the consumption of ecosystem capital to create an adjusted net national income.

entries.title: From two sectors to five: building up the circular flow
entries.article: Circular flow of income#Types of models

definition.text: The versions of the circular flow model with two to five sectors, built up by adding government, the rest of the world and finance to households and firms.

facts.text: The two-sector model has only households and firms, with households spending all their income on firms' output.
The three-sector model adds government; the four-sector model adds foreign trade and capital flows.
The five-sector model adds banks and other intermediaries that borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

entries.text: The simplest circular flow has just two sectors: households and firms, with households spending all their income on firms' output. Each added sector brings the model closer to a real economy. The three-sector model adds government. The four-sector model adds foreign trade and capital flows. The five-sector model adds banks and other intermediaries, which borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

entries.title: Leakages and injections: money leaving and entering the flow
entries.article: Circular flow of income#Leakages and injection

definition.text: Leakages are money withdrawn from the circular flow, such as savings, taxes and imports; injections are money added, such as investment, government spending and exports.

facts.text: Saved money is a leakage because it is not spent, so not all output gets bought.
Taxes are a leakage; government spending on services and welfare payments is the matching injection.
Equilibrium in the five-sector model comes when total leakages equal total injections: savings + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports.

entries.text: Not all income flows straight back into spending. Saved money is a leakage: it is not spent, so not all output gets bought. Taxes are a leakage too, and imports a third. Injections add money back in: investment, government spending on services and welfare payments, and exports. In the five-sector model, the economy is in equilibrium when total leakages equal total injections. Savings plus taxes plus imports must equal investment plus government spending plus exports.

entries.title: The capital consumption allowance: running to stand still
entries.article: Consumption of fixed capital#Capital Consumption Allowance

definition.text: The part of GDP due to depreciation, measuring what a country must spend just to maintain, rather than grow, its productive capacity.

facts.text: It covers wear and tear on physical capital plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees.
GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

entries.text: Part of every year's GDP buys no growth at all. It simply keeps the country's productive capacity from shrinking. This is the capital consumption allowance, the part of GDP due to depreciation. It covers wear and tear on physical capital, plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees. GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

entries.title: Net national product: output after depreciation

definition.text: Gross national product minus depreciation; net domestic product is likewise GDP minus depreciation.

facts.text: Depreciation is the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear in production.
Economics research usually uses gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed.
It features in environmental economics as an indicator of sustainability and in models of natural resource depletion.
Research has studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

Net domestic product is, likewise, GDP minus depreciation. Economics research usually uses the gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed. The net measures matter for the environment. Net national product serves as an indicator of sustainability in environmental economics and appears in models of resources running out. Research has also studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

entries.title: Value added: what each producer contributes

definition.text: The difference between the market value of a product or service and the value of the inputs used to make it.

facts.text: A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus intermediate consumption.
It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital.
In macroeconomics, it is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them.
In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus intermediate consumption, which equals net output.
Net value added deducts depreciation from gross value added.
For the whole economy at market prices, gross value added equals GDP.

entries.text: A firm buys in materials and services, works on them, and sells the result. The difference between the market value of what it sells and the value of what it used is its value added. A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus {{ref:nature-econ-536}}, the inputs it uses up. It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital. In macroeconomics, value added is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them. In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus those used-up inputs, which equals net output. Net value added deducts depreciation from it. Add up gross value added across the whole economy at market prices and you get GDP.

The difference between the market value of what it sells and the value of what it used is its value added. A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus Intermediate consumption: inputs used up in production, the inputs it uses up. It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital. In macroeconomics, value added is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them. In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus those used-up inputs, which equals net output. Net value added deducts depreciation from it. Add up gross value added across the whole economy at market prices and you get GDP.

entries.title: Intermediate consumption: inputs used up in production

definition.text: The total value of goods and services that businesses use up as inputs while producing, such as raw materials, services and other running costs.

facts.text: It equals the gap between gross output (roughly total sales value) and net output, that is gross value added or GDP.
Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP, how it is defined and estimated strongly affects the size of the GDP figure.
In the US economy, intermediate consumption is about 45% of gross output.
Inputs may be changed in form, like bulk sugar, or used up completely, like electric power.
Depreciation of fixed assets and major renovations that extend an asset's life are excluded; ordinary maintenance, repairs and research and development spending are included.
Buying a service from another firm instead of doing it in-house raises a firm's intermediate consumption and lowers its own value added.
If businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

It equals the gap between gross output, roughly total sales value, and net output, which is gross value added or GDP. And when businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

Ordinary maintenance, repairs and research and development spending count as intermediate consumption. Depreciation of fixed assets and major renovations that extend an asset's life do not. Some odd results follow. Buying a service from another firm instead of doing it in-house raises a firm's intermediate consumption and lowers its own value added. And when businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

entries.title: Three ways to measure GDP
entries.article: Gross domestic product#Determining gross domestic product (GDP)

definition.text: The production, income and expenditure approaches, three ways of measuring GDP that should in theory give the same total.

facts.text: The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise.
Also called the value-added approach, it counts how much value is contributed at each stage of production.
The income approach sums the primary incomes paid out by producers; measured this way it is called gross domestic income.
The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption.
Within each country GDP is normally measured by a national statistical agency.

entries.text: GDP can be measured three ways, and in theory all three give the same total. The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise. It is also called the value-added approach, because it counts how much value is contributed at each stage of production. The income approach sums the primary incomes paid out by producers; measured this way, the total is called {{ref:nature-econ-490}}. The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption. Within each country, a national statistical agency normally does the measuring.
entries.text_plain: GDP can be measured three ways, and in theory all three give the same total. The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise. The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption. Within each country, a national statistical agency normally does the measuring.

entries.title: Labour productivity: output per hour of work

definition.text: Output volume, such as GDP or gross value added, divided by labour input, such as total hours worked or total employment.

facts.text: Output is usually measured as value added, the value of outputs minus intermediate inputs, to avoid double counting.
Total hours worked is generally preferred to a headcount, which can hide changes in average hours.
It is a key indicator of economic growth, competitiveness and living standards.
A country's ability to raise its living standards over time is said to depend almost entirely on raising output per worker.
Productivity can decouple from wages.

entries.text: A country's ability to raise its living standards over time is said to depend almost entirely on raising output per worker. Labour productivity measures exactly that: output volume, such as GDP or gross value added, divided by labour input, such as total hours worked or total employment. Output is usually measured as value added, the value of outputs minus intermediate inputs, to avoid double counting. Total hours worked is generally preferred to a headcount, which can hide changes in average hours. Labour productivity is a key indicator of growth, competitiveness and living standards. Yet productivity and wages do not always move together. They can decouple.

entries.title: Gross domestic income: GDP counted from the income side

definition.text: GDP measured by adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country.

facts.text: Gross domestic income should give the same total as the expenditure method.

entries.text: Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, so GDP can also be counted from the income side. Gross domestic income does exactly that, adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country. It should give the same total as the expenditure method.
entries.text_plain: Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, so GDP can also be counted from the income side. Gross domestic income does exactly that, adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country. It should give the same total as the expenditure method.

entries.title: The linked accounts that make up a nation's books

definition.text: The standard set of linked accounts that make up a nation's accounts: production, income, expenditure, capital and financial accounts, plus balance sheets.

facts.text: Each account has a balancing item: value added (equal to GDP for the whole economy), disposable income, saving, net lending or borrowing, and net worth.
Balance sheets record the stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time.
Accounts can be gross or net of consumption of fixed capital, the national-accounts version of depreciation.

entries.text: A nation's accounts are not one ledger but a linked set: production, income, expenditure, capital and financial accounts, plus balance sheets. Each account has a balancing item. These include value added, which equals GDP for the whole economy, along with disposable income, saving, net lending or borrowing, and net worth. Balance sheets record the stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time. Accounts can be shown gross or net of consumption of fixed capital, the national-accounts version of depreciation.

entries.title: Avoiding double counting: the meat that is counted once
entries.article: Measures of national income and output#Output

definition.text: The rule that national output counts only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain.

facts.text: If meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket, $60 enters national output, not the $100 sum.
The values added at each stage, $10, $20 and $30, sum to the same final value.
GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

entries.text: Meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket. Adding the three sales gives $100, but only $60 enters national output. The rule is to count only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain. Here the values added are $10, $20 and $30, which sum to the same final value. In general, GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

entries.title: Value-added tax: taxing each stage of production

definition.text: A tax on sales that is charged at each stage of production on the value that stage adds.

facts.text: It is assessed step by step on a product or service, taxing each stage's unit value added.

entries.text: A value-added tax is a tax on sales that is charged at each stage of production, but only on the value that stage adds. It is assessed step by step on a product or service, so each stage is taxed on its own unit value added.

entries.title: Imputed rent: the rent homeowners pay themselves

definition.text: The market rent that owner-occupiers would receive if their homes were rented out, which national accounts add to value added.

facts.text: Critics call this addition to GDP largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.
The imputation rests on the idea that a dwelling provides its owner with a service.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the imputed rent added to GDP is largely fictitious.
entries.text: Homeowners who live in their own houses pay no rent, yet national accounts record one for them. The imputed rent of owner-occupied housing is the market rent owner-occupiers would receive if they rented their homes out. National accounts add it to value added, and so to GDP. The idea is that a dwelling provides its owner with a service, whether or not anyone pays for it. Critics call this addition largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.

entries.title: Owner-occupied housing: the CPI's long-running puzzle
entries.article: Consumer price index#Owner-occupiers and the price index

definition.text: The long-running controversy over how a consumer price index should count the cost of living in a home one owns.

facts.text: Many economists argue the index should include the opportunity cost of living in one's own home.
A spending approach would count repairs, maintenance and also mortgage interest.
A transaction-price approach would count only purchases of new dwellings, like other durable goods.

entries.contested_note: Statisticians and economists disagree on which of the competing methods should be used.
entries.text: What does it cost to live in a home you own? Statisticians and economists have long disagreed over how a consumer price index should count it. Many economists argue the index should include the opportunity cost of living in one's own home. A spending approach would count repairs, maintenance and also mortgage interest. A transaction-price approach would count only purchases of new dwellings, treating them like other durable goods. No single method has won agreement.
entries.text_plain: What does it cost to live in a home you own? Statisticians and economists have long disagreed over how a consumer price index should count it. entries.title: Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game

definition.text: The branch of applied mathematics that models interactions between several decision-makers as games of strategy between players.

facts.text: It describes, predicts and evaluates choices, often assuming each player tries to maximise their payoff.
A game captures the choices available to each player and the payoffs that result.
A game is cooperative if players can make binding, externally enforced commitments, and non-cooperative if agreements must enforce themselves.
Players are usually assumed to be rational, with consistent preferences and unlimited capacity to calculate the best payoff.
In a Nash equilibrium each player's choice is a best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone.
The field began with von Neumann and Morgenstern's 1944 book Theory of Games and Economic Behavior.
John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten won the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering game theory.
It is a major method in economics for modelling competing agents, and is also used in biology, political science and the study of vaccination decisions.

entries.text: Game theory began with a single book: von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, published in 1944. It is the branch of applied mathematics that treats interactions between several decision-makers as strategic games. A game spells out the choices open to each player and the payoffs that result. Players are usually assumed rational in the sense of the {{ref:nature-econ-098}}. They have consistent preferences, unlimited capacity to calculate, and each tries to maximize their payoff. Games come in two families. In a cooperative game, players can make binding promises that someone outside enforces. In a non-cooperative game, any agreement has to enforce itself. A central idea is the {{ref:nature-econ-718}}, a situation where each player's choice is the best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone. John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering the field. Game theory now describes, predicts and evaluates choices far beyond markets. It is a major method for modelling competing agents in economics. It is also used in biology, political science and the study of how people decide whether to be vaccinated.
entries.text_plain: Game theory began with a single book: von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, published in 1944. It is the branch of applied mathematics that treats interactions between several decision-makers as strategic games. A game spells out the choices open to each player and the payoffs that result. Players are usually assumed rational in the sense of the Rational choice: people as careful calculators. They have consistent preferences, unlimited capacity to calculate, and each tries to maximize their payoff. Games come in two families. In a cooperative game, players can make binding promises that someone outside enforces. In a non-cooperative game, any agreement has to enforce itself. A central idea is the Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone, a situation where each player's choice is the best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone. John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering the field. Game theory now describes, predicts and evaluates choices far beyond markets. It is a major method for modelling competing agents in economics. It is also used in biology, political science and the study of how people decide whether to be vaccinated.

entries.title: Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'

definition.text: The 'economic man' of economic models: a picture of people as always rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing their own goals in the best possible way.

facts.text: The model assumes people maximize their satisfaction (utility) as consumers and profit as producers, and can think through every possible outcome to pick the best.
Its 'rationality' only means reaching one's own goals at least cost; it does not judge whether those goals are rational in an ethical or social sense.
The term 'economic man' was first used in the late nineteenth century by critics of John Stuart Mill's political economy.
Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the butcher's or baker's kindness but from their regard to their own interest.
It contrasts with behavioral economics, which studies biases, and with bounded rationality, which stresses limits of mind and time.
Its preferences need not be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation.
Advanced economic theory now uses modified models, such as agents with bounded rationality or envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

entries.text: Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the kindness of the butcher or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest. Economic models turned that remark into a character: homo economicus, or 'economic man'. This imagined person is always rational and narrowly self-interested. As a consumer he maximizes his satisfaction, or {{ref:nature-econ-100}}. As a producer he maximizes profit. And he can think through every possible outcome to pick the best. The name came from his critics, who used it in the late nineteenth century to attack John Stuart Mill's political economy. 'Rational' here has a narrow meaning. It only means reaching one's own goals at least cost, and says nothing about whether those goals are wise in an ethical or social sense. Nor must the goals be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation. Two later ideas push against this view: {{ref:nature-econ-021}}, which studies biases, and {{ref:nature-econ-022}}, which stresses limits of mind and time. Advanced theory now often uses modified agents, with limited rationality or even envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.
entries.text_plain: Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the kindness of the butcher or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest. Economic models turned that remark into a character: homo economicus, or 'economic man'. This imagined person is always rational and narrowly self-interested. As a consumer he maximizes his satisfaction, or Utility: the economist's yardstick for satisfaction. As a producer he maximizes profit. And he can think through every possible outcome to pick the best. The name came from his critics, who used it in the late nineteenth century to attack John Stuart Mill's political economy. 'Rational' here has a narrow meaning. It only means reaching one's own goals at least cost, and says nothing about whether those goals are wise in an ethical or social sense. Nor must the goals be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation. Two later ideas push against this view: Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics, which studies biases, and Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough, which stresses limits of mind and time. Advanced theory now often uses modified agents, with limited rationality or even envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

entries.title: Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough

definition.text: The idea that people's rationality is limited when they decide, so they pick an option that is good enough rather than the best one.

facts.text: The limits are how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time is available.
People therefore act as satisficers and do not carry out a full cost-benefit analysis; they take an option that meets their standard of adequacy.
Herbert A. Simon coined the term as an alternative to modelling decision-makers as perfectly rational.
Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors: one blade is human cognitive limits, the other the structure of the environment.
Simon argued that decision-makers use heuristics, or rules of thumb, instead of strict optimisation because situations are complex.
Gerd Gigerenzer showed that simple heuristics often give better decisions than theoretically optimal procedures.
Nudges are designed to help people get around the limits and biases that bounded rationality creates.
Kahneman and Tversky's work on heuristics, risky choice and framing extended Simon's ideas into a map of bounded rationality.

entries.contested_note: Bounded rationality remains debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.
entries.text: Herbert A. Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors. One blade is the limits of the human mind; the other is the structure of the environment the mind faces. Simon coined the term bounded rationality as an alternative to modelling people as perfectly rational, like {{ref:nature-econ-059}}. Three limits bind every decision: how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time there is. So people skip the full weighing of costs and benefits. They take an option that meets their standard of adequacy, a habit explored in {{ref:nature-econ-071}}, and they lean on rules of thumb instead of strict optimization. Gerd Gigerenzer later showed that simple rules often beat theoretically optimal procedures. Kahneman and Tversky extended Simon's ideas into a map of these limits. The idea is still debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.
entries.text_plain: Herbert A. Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors. One blade is the limits of the human mind; the other is the structure of the environment the mind faces. Simon coined the term bounded rationality as an alternative to modelling people as perfectly rational, like Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'. Three limits bind every decision: how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time there is. So people skip the full weighing of costs and benefits. They take an option that meets their standard of adequacy, a habit explored in Satisficing: stopping at good enough, and they lean on rules of thumb instead of strict optimization. Gerd Gigerenzer later showed that simple rules often beat theoretically optimal procedures. Kahneman and Tversky extended Simon's ideas into a map of these limits. The idea is still debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.

entries.title: Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics

definition.text: The study of how psychological factors shape the decisions of people and institutions, and how those decisions differ from what traditional economic theory predicts.

facts.text: Its main concern is the limits on how rational people's economic choices really are.
It studies where the standard assumptions that people are rational and selfish break down, looking at biases, tendencies and mental shortcuts.
It helps judge whether people choose well and whether they could be helped to choose better.
Its models combine psychology, neuroscience and microeconomic theory.
It became a distinct field in the 1970s and 1980s, though ideas such as loss aversion appear as early as Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments.
In the early 1900s economists pushed psychology out of economics and modelled people as purely rational, self-interested decision makers.
The field spread widely after Kahneman and Tversky's work, through the 1990s and 2000s.
Nobel prizes went to Herbert Simon in 1978, Daniel Kahneman and Vernon Smith in 2002, and Richard Thaler in 2017.

entries.text: In the early 1900s economists pushed psychology out of their discipline. From then on, models treated people as purely rational, self-interested decision makers, the {{ref:nature-econ-059}} of the textbooks. Behavioral economics brings the psychology back. It studies how psychological factors shape the decisions of people and institutions, and how those decisions differ from what traditional theory predicts. Its main concern is the limits on how rational economic choices really are. It looks for the places where the standard assumptions of rational, selfish people break down, cataloguing biases, tendencies and mental shortcuts. That work has a practical edge: it helps judge whether people choose well and whether they could be helped to choose better. Its models combine psychology, neuroscience and microeconomic theory. Some of its ideas are old. The notion that losses weigh more than gains appears as early as Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments. Yet the field only became distinct in the 1970s and 1980s, and it spread widely after the work of Kahneman and Tversky, through the 1990s and 2000s. Nobel prizes mark its rise: Herbert Simon in 1978, Daniel Kahneman and Vernon Smith in 2002, and Richard Thaler in 2017.

entries.title: The prisoner's dilemma: when betrayal is rational

definition.text: A thought experiment in which two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain.

facts.text: Betraying is the rational choice for each player, yet both would get a higher payoff by cooperating.
Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher designed the puzzle in 1950 at the RAND Corporation.
It is the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, showing how individual interests can conflict with the group's.
Climate change fits it: every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions.
Unlike the textbook game, climate politics has uncertain payoffs, which suggests states will cooperate even less.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be seen as a many-player version, in which widespread defection destroys the commons.
It has been called the E. coli of social psychology, used to study topics such as oligopoly and collective action.

entries.text: In 1950 Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, working at the RAND Corporation, designed a puzzle that still troubles economists. Two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain. Betrayal is the rational choice for each, yet both would get a higher payoff if both cooperated. This is the prisoner's dilemma, the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, where individual interest pulls against the group's. {{ref:nature-hist-007}} fits the pattern closely. Every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions. Real climate politics is worse than the textbook game, because its payoffs are uncertain, which suggests states will cooperate even less. Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be read as a many-player version, in which widespread betrayal destroys a shared resource. The game has been called the E. coli of social psychology, a standard test case for studying oligopoly and collective action.

This is the prisoner's dilemma, the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, where individual interest pulls against the group's. Climate change: a warming world and why it matters fits the pattern closely. Every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions. entries.title: Experimental economics takes theory into the laboratory

definition.text: The use of controlled experiments, analysed with statistical and computational tools, to study economic questions.

facts.text: Experimental data are used to estimate effect sizes, test economic theories and shed light on how markets work.
Experiments usually pay subjects in cash to mimic real-world incentives.
Vernon L. Smith shared the 2002 Nobel prize for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool of economic analysis.
Prominent behavioural and experimental economists tend to share techniques, though some see a schism between the two fields.

entries.text: How do you test an economic theory? One answer is to run it as an experiment, with real people and real money. Experimental economics uses controlled experiments to study economic questions, and analyses the results with statistical and computational tools. The data are used to estimate the size of effects, to test theories and to shed light on how markets work. Subjects are usually paid in cash, so the incentives in the lab mimic those of the real world. Vernon L. Smith shared the 2002 Nobel prize for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool of economic analysis. The field sits close to {{ref:nature-econ-021}}. Leading researchers in the two tend to share techniques, though some see a schism between them.

entries.title: Social norms: the unwritten rules a group shares

definition.text: A standard of acceptable behavior shared by a group.

facts.text: Norms can be informal understandings or be written into rules and laws, and institutions are made up of many norms.
Unlike private ideas, attitudes or values, norms are shared beliefs about behavior, and they depend on context, group and history.
Many norms evolve without top-down design, through repeated interactions between individuals.
Breaking an informal norm brings reprimands, warnings or exclusion rather than legal penalties, and people who break norms are labelled deviants.
A norm's life cycle runs from emergence, pushed by norm entrepreneurs, to a cascade of broad acceptance, to internalization, when it is taken for granted.
Game theory can treat a norm as a rule of thumb that a rational person follows only when it benefits them, often modelled with a repeated game.
Social norms affect free riding on voluntarily provided public goods, an effect economic models often underestimate.

entries.text: Many of the rules people live by were never designed by anyone. They evolved through repeated interactions between individuals. A social norm is a standard of acceptable behavior shared by a group. Some norms stay informal understandings; others are written into rules and laws, and institutions are built from many of them. Norms differ from private ideas, attitudes or values because they are shared beliefs about behavior, and they depend on context, group and history. Breaking an informal norm brings reprimands, warnings or exclusion rather than legal penalties, and the rule-breaker is labelled a deviant. A norm's life cycle runs from emergence, pushed by norm entrepreneurs, through a cascade of broad acceptance to internalization, when it is simply taken for granted. Norms also curb free riding on voluntarily provided public goods, an effect economic models often underestimate.
