entries.title: Collective action problems: when acting alone defeats everyone

definition.text: A situation, also called a social dilemma, in which everyone would be better off cooperating but people fail to because their individual interests pull against joint action.

facts.text: Trouble arises when too many members chase individual, immediate gain instead of the group's long-term interest.
Resource depletion and low voter turnout are both explained as social dilemmas.
Climate change, biodiversity loss and waste build-up can all be described as collective action problems.
Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves non-renewable resources.
Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action argued that rational individuals do not automatically make a rational group.
Olson argued that for a pure public good, one contributor tends to give less as others give more.
It is analysed with game theory and the free-rider problem that arises in providing public goods.
David Hume described the problem in 1738 through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow.

entries.text: In 1738 David Hume described a puzzle through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow. Economists now call it a collective action problem, or social dilemma. Everyone would be better off cooperating, but people fail to, because their individual interests pull against joint action. Trouble comes when too many members chase immediate, personal gain instead of the group's long-term interest. The pattern explains things as different as the running down of resources and low voter turnout. It also describes the environmental crises at the center of this course: {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, {{ref:nature-eco-035}} and the build-up of waste. Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves resources that cannot be replaced. In a 1965 book, Mancur Olson argued that rational individuals do not automatically add up to a rational group, a claim explored in {{ref:nature-pol-044}}. For a pure {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, he argued, each contributor tends to give less as others give more. The problem is analysed with {{ref:nature-econ-034}} and through the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}, which arises whenever public goods must be paid for.
entries.text_plain: In 1738 David Hume described a puzzle through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow. Economists now call it a collective action problem, or social dilemma. Everyone would be better off cooperating, but people fail to, because their individual interests pull against joint action. Trouble comes when too many members chase immediate, personal gain instead of the group's long-term interest. The pattern explains things as different as the running down of resources and low voter turnout. It also describes the environmental crises at the center of this course: Climate change: a warming world and why it matters, Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace and the build-up of waste. Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves resources that cannot be replaced. In a 1965 book, Mancur Olson argued that rational individuals do not automatically add up to a rational group, a claim explored in The logic of collective action: why small groups win. For a pure Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, he argued, each contributor tends to give less as others give more. The problem is analysed with Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game and through the The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying, which arises whenever public goods must be paid for.

entries.title: Heuristics: the mind's shortcuts

definition.text: Mental shortcuts people use to reach judgments and decisions quickly.

facts.text: Humans, animals, organizations and even machines use simple strategies to form judgments and solve complex problems fast.
Heuristic answers are good enough for a pressing need when information is incomplete, but they are not always right and can differ from what logic and probability give.
Herbert A. Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his satisficing rule was one of the first models of a heuristic.
In the 1970s Tversky and Kahneman linked heuristics to cognitive bias, first proposing availability, representativeness, and anchoring and adjustment.
Theories differ on whether heuristics are irrational: one view treats them as unavoidable shortcuts for a limited brain, another as fast methods that do as well as complex ones with less information.
In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his rule of settling for the first adequate option was one of the first models of a heuristic. In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

entries.title: Satisficing: stopping at good enough

definition.text: A decision strategy of looking through options until one is good enough, rather than searching for the very best.

facts.text: Herbert A. Simon introduced the word, a blend of 'satisfy' and 'suffice', in 1956, though the idea first appeared in his 1947 book Administrative Behavior.
Simon used it for problems where the best answer cannot be found because the calculation is too hard or information is lacking.
A satisficer sets an aspiration level, takes the first option that meets it, and lowers the level if nothing meets it in time.
Of 628 used-car dealers studied, 97% used a form of satisficing, typically cutting a car's price by about 3% if it was unsold after 24 days.
The behavioral theory of the firm treats profit as a level to reach rather than something to maximize, after which firms pursue other goals.
Maximizers search more options than satisficers, yet tend to be less happy and more regretful about their choices.

entries.title: The public goods game: tokens in a shared pot

definition.text: A standard economics experiment in which players secretly decide how many of their tokens to put into a shared pot that is multiplied and split among everyone.

facts.text: Each player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the multiplied pot, so it is used to study altruism, cooperation and free riding.
If players are purely selfish, the Nash equilibrium is that nobody contributes.
It tests the theory that public goods, such as street lighting that no one can be excluded from, are under-provided because no one has a private motive to pay.
In repeated play contributions usually decline as generous players see others give less, but they rarely reach zero because a hard core of givers remains.
Players will punish non-contributors even at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises group cooperation.
With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 leads almost everyone to stop giving, while a multiplier of 1.3 keeps average contributions around 50%.
Framing the same game as a climate negotiation rather than neutrally can change how players behave.
Contributions tend to be lower when players start with unequal endowments.

entries.text: In the public goods game, each player secretly decides how many tokens to put into a shared pot. The pot is then multiplied and split among everyone. A player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the pot, so the game measures altruism, cooperation and free riding. It tests a theory about a {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, such as street lighting that no one can be kept from using. The theory says such goods are under-provided, because no one has a private motive to pay. If everyone were purely selfish, the stable outcome would be that nobody gives. Real players do give. In repeated rounds contributions usually slide as generous players see others hold back, but a stubborn group of givers keeps them above zero. Players will also punish non-contributors at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises cooperation. Details matter. With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 makes almost everyone stop giving, while 1.3 keeps average contributions near 50%. Unequal starting endowments lower contributions, and presenting the game as a climate negotiation can change behavior.

entries.title: Present bias: why now beats later

definition.text: The tendency to take a smaller reward now rather than wait for a larger one later.

facts.text: It means overvaluing immediate rewards and giving too little weight to long-term consequences.
Early models assumed people discount the future at a steady rate, but research showed they discount sharply over short delays and less over longer ones, so their preferences are time-inconsistent.
Phelps and Pollak introduced the quasi-hyperbolic discounting model in 1968 to capture this.
Present-biased preferences often lead to procrastination, especially when actions bring immediate costs.
It discourages unpleasant actions for health, such as dieting, quitting smoking or regular check-ups, whose benefits come only later.
It is linked to strong desires to spend money and failure to stick to a saving plan.
Short-termism has been linked to present bias, which favours short-term payoffs over long-term rewards.

entries.text: Present bias is the pull of a smaller reward now over a larger reward later. It means overvaluing what is immediate and giving too little weight to long-term consequences. Early models assumed people discount the future at a steady rate, a fixed form of {{ref:nature-econ-839}}. Research showed instead that people discount sharply over short delays and less over longer ones. Their preferences are time-inconsistent: what they plan for later is not what they choose when later arrives. Phelps and Pollak captured this in 1968 with the quasi-hyperbolic discounting model. The consequences are familiar. Present bias feeds procrastination, especially when acting brings immediate costs. It discourages dieting, quitting smoking and regular check-ups, whose benefits come only later. It is linked to strong urges to spend and to failed saving plans, and short-termism in general has been tied to it.

entries.title: Anchoring: how an arbitrary number pulls a guess

definition.text: The tendency for judgments to be pulled toward a reference point, or anchor, even one that is completely irrelevant.

facts.text: Tversky and Kahneman described anchoring in 1974 as a heuristic for estimating under uncertainty.
People asked to estimate 1 x 2 x ... x 8 quickly gave a median of 512; those shown 8 x 7 x ... x 1 gave 2,250.
The usual explanation is that people adjust away from the anchor too little.
Anchoring is hard to avoid: even obviously wrong anchors about Gandhi's age at death shifted guesses to averages of 50 versus 67.
It appears in legal sentencing, shopping, salary negotiations and forecasting, and even experts are susceptible.
In negotiation, the first price offer sets the anchor for what follows.

entries.contested_note: Scholars agree anchoring is easy to demonstrate but do not agree on what causes it.
entries.text: People asked to estimate 1 x 2 x ... x 8 quickly gave a median answer of 512. People shown 8 x 7 x ... x 1 gave 2,250. The first numbers they saw set an anchor, a reference point that pulls judgment toward it even when it is irrelevant. The usual explanation is that people adjust away from the anchor too little. Scholars agree the effect is easy to demonstrate, but they still disagree about what causes it. It is also hard to escape. entries.title: Choice architecture: designing how options are presented

definition.text: The design of the ways choices are presented to people, and the effect that presentation has on what they decide.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term in their 2008 book Nudge.
Advocates use it to nudge people toward saving for retirement, healthier food or organ donation, compensating for decision biases.
Its tools include defaults, expecting error, feedback, structuring complex choices and incentives.
It can translate metrics into what people care about, such as turning energy use into greenhouse gas emissions.
It led to the UK's Behavioural Insights Team and a White House Nudge Unit.
Critics say it can limit choice, undermine autonomy, or raise firm profits at consumers' expense through dark patterns.
Responses differ by person; liberals and conservatives react differently to information about the environmental effects of energy use.

entries.contested_note: Critics of libertarian paternalism argue choice architecture can impose costs on rational people and undermine autonomy, while its advocates say no presentation is neutral.
entries.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term choice architecture in a 2008 book. It means the design of the ways choices are presented, and the effect that presentation has on what people decide. Its tools include defaults, planning for error, information about results, structuring complex choices and incentives. It can also translate metrics into what people care about, for instance turning energy use into the emissions it causes. entries.title: Nudges: steering choices without forbidding any

definition.text: A change in how choices are presented, designed to steer people's decisions without restricting their freedom to choose.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge.
Nudges can simplify complex decisions by presenting information clearly, reducing mental effort.
Making organ donation the default with an opt-out has, alongside other policies, raised actual donation rates.
Showing calorie counts on menus is a nudge that supplies missing information for healthier choices.
Critics say nudges can be manipulative, diminish autonomy or lack scientific credibility; Sunstein has defended them at length.
A 2024 review reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments keep a long-term effect when re-tested.

entries.contested_note: Critics charge that nudges are manipulative or scientifically weak, and defenders such as Sunstein dispute these charges.
entries.text: A calorie count on a menu forbids nothing. It simply supplies missing information for healthier choices. That is a nudge: a change in how choices are presented, designed to steer decisions without restricting anyone's freedom to choose. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge, building on {{ref:nature-econ-045}}. Nudges work with the limits of bounded rationality rather than against them. They can simplify complex decisions by presenting information clearly, cutting the mental effort required. Making organ donation the default, with an opt-out, has helped raise actual donation rates alongside other policies. Nudges have critics, who call them manipulative, a threat to autonomy or scientifically weak. Sunstein has defended them at length. The evidence on staying power is sobering: a 2024 review reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments keep a long-term effect when re-tested.

entries.title: Field experiments: testing ideas in the real world

definition.text: An experiment carried out in a real-world setting rather than a laboratory.

facts.text: Researchers randomly assign subjects to treatment or control groups so that later differences reflect the treatment, not pre-existing differences.
Unlike natural experiments, the researchers themselves control the randomisation and how the treatment is delivered.
They offer higher external validity and can test people who do not know they are being studied.
Economists use them to study discrimination, health programmes, charitable fundraising, education and microfinance.
Spillovers to untreated groups, noncompliance and attrition can bias results, and they can be costly, hard to replicate and ethically fraught.
Behavioural economists turned to field studies partly in response to criticism of lab experiments.

entries.text: A field experiment takes the method of the laboratory out into a real-world setting. Researchers randomly assign people to a treatment group or a control group. Any later difference then reflects the treatment rather than differences that were already there. Unlike a {{ref:nature-econ-243}}, a field experiment lets the researchers themselves control the randomization and how the treatment is delivered. The gain is realism. Field experiments have higher external validity, meaning their results carry over better to everyday life, and they can test people who do not know they are being studied. Economists use them to study discrimination, health programmes, charitable fundraising, education and microfinance. Behavioural economists turned to them partly in response to criticism of lab experiments. They have weaknesses too. Spillovers to untreated groups, people who do not comply and people who drop out can all bias results. Such studies can also be costly, hard to replicate and ethically fraught.

entries.title: Motivation crowding: when paying people backfires

definition.text: The theory that outside rewards for a behavior, such as payment for a task, can sometimes weaken people's inner motivation to do it.

facts.text: Against the predictions of standard economics, the lowered motivation can reduce total performance.
Richard Titmuss argued in 1970 that paying for some behaviors could reduce them; Bruno Frey coined the term 'crowding out' in 1997.
In Edward Deci's classic study, people paid per puzzle solved did fewer unpaid puzzles in free time and reported less interest than people paid just for showing up.
Paying people a token amount to collect money for charity led them to collect less than unpaid volunteers.
Crowding out has been found in teachers' performance pay, commission pay, charitable giving and student performance, prompting calls to rethink incentives for volunteers.
Rewards seen as controlling are argued to replace inner motivation, while rewards seen as a mark of status or achievement can raise effort without crowding it out.
Crowding out is stronger when the reward is publicly known, since people who care about appearing altruistic avoid looking paid.
A 2020 review of over 100 tests found that paying for enjoyable tasks boosts performance, but removing an expected payment can leave people worse than if never paid.

entries.contested_note: Some meta-analyses found mixed or null effects of rewards on inner motivation, while others found a robust effect for certain rewards once moderating factors are controlled.
entries.text: In Edward Deci's classic study, some people were paid for each puzzle they solved and others just for showing up. Later, in their free time, the per-puzzle group did fewer unpaid puzzles and reported less interest. Against the predictions of standard economics, the drop in motivation can lower total performance. It is stronger when the reward is publicly known, since people who care about looking altruistic avoid looking paid. The evidence is mixed. A 2020 review of over 100 tests found that paying for enjoyable tasks boosts performance. But removing an expected payment can leave people worse off than if they had never been paid.

entries.title: The energy efficiency gap: savings left untaken

definition.text: The difference between the cost-minimising level of energy efficiency and the level people and firms actually achieve.

facts.text: Its existence suggests society passes up cost-effective investments that could cut energy use at low cost.
Eric Hirst and Marilyn Brown coined the term in a 1990 paper.
Hirst and Brown split its causes into structural barriers, such as fuel prices that leave out social and environmental costs, and behavioural barriers in users' decisions.
High up-front costs, high discount rates, uncertain fuel prices and lack of information all hold back efficiency investments.
Jaffe and Stavins attribute it to both market failures, such as imperfect information, and non-market failures such as consumer inertia.
Remedies include subsidies and cheap loans, minimum building and equipment standards, information and labelling programmes, and government procurement.
It implies society forgoes cost-effective efficiency investments that could cut energy use substantially.
It exists because of market failures: fuel prices leave out social and environmental costs, future prices are uncertain, and upfront costs and capital limits deter buyers.

entries.text: Society passes up investments that could cut energy use substantially and at low cost. The energy efficiency gap measures that shortfall: the difference between the cost-minimising level of energy efficiency and the level people and firms actually achieve. Eric Hirst and Marilyn Brown coined the term in a 1990 paper. They split its causes into two kinds. Structural barriers include fuel prices that leave out social and environmental costs, a classic externality. Behavioural barriers lie in users' own decisions, shaped by {{ref:nature-econ-022}}. High up-front costs, high discount rates, uncertain fuel prices and missing information all hold investment back. Jaffe and Stavins blame both market failures, such as imperfect information, and non-market failures such as consumer inertia. Remedies include subsidies and cheap loans, minimum standards for buildings and equipment, information and labelling programmes, and government procurement.

entries.title: The trust game: send money and hope for a return

definition.text: An experiment that measures trust: an investor sends money to a trustee, the amount is tripled, and the trustee decides how much to return.

facts.text: It was designed by Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe in 1995.
A purely self-interested trustee would return nothing, but in experiments people do place trust, expecting reciprocity.

entries.text: In the trust game, designed by Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe in 1995, an investor sends money to a trustee. The amount is tripled, and the trustee decides how much to send back. A purely self-interested trustee would return nothing, so a purely self-interested investor would never send anything. Yet in experiments people do place trust, expecting the favor to be returned. The game turns that trust into something a researcher can measure.

entries.title: The ultimatum game: take it or leave it

definition.text: An economic experiment in which one player proposes how to split a sum of money and the other can accept, or reject so that both get nothing.

facts.text: It has become a popular tool of economic experiments, first described by John Harsanyi in 1961.
It shows how fairness, generosity and social acceptance shape players' decisions.

entries.text: One player proposes how to split a sum of money. The other can accept the split, or reject it so that both get nothing. That is the whole of the ultimatum game, first described by John Harsanyi in 1961. Its simplicity is its strength. It has become a popular tool of economic experiments because it shows how fairness, generosity and social acceptance shape real decisions, not just the drive for money.

entries.title: Behavioral finance: the psychology of investors

definition.text: The study of how psychology influences the behaviour of investors and financial analysts.

facts.text: It assumes investors are not always rational, have limited self-control and are swayed by biases.
Its central question is why market participants make systematic errors, which affect prices and returns and make markets inefficient.

entries.text: Behavioral finance studies how psychology influences the behavior of investors and financial analysts. It assumes they are not always rational, have limited self-control and are swayed by biases. Its central question is why market participants make systematic errors. Those errors matter beyond the individual investor. They affect prices and returns, and they make whole markets inefficient.

entries.title: Behavioral game theory: testing strategy on real players

definition.text: The study of strategic decisions between people using game theory together with experiments from economics and psychology.

facts.text: Colin Camerer invented it.
Its experiments test departures from standard theory, such as the neglect of altruism, fairness and framing effects.
It has been applied to interactive learning and social preferences.

entries.text: Game theory usually assumes players who calculate perfectly. Behavioral game theory, invented by Colin Camerer, checks that assumption against real people. It joins game theory with experiments from economics and psychology to study strategic decisions. Its experiments test departures from standard theory, such as its neglect of altruism, fairness and the effect of how options are worded. It has been applied to interactive learning and to {{ref:nature-econ-076}}.
entries.text_plain: Game theory usually assumes players who calculate perfectly. Behavioral game theory, invented by Colin Camerer, checks that assumption against real people. It joins game theory with experiments from economics and psychology to study strategic decisions. Its experiments test departures from standard theory, such as its neglect of altruism, fairness and the effect of how options are worded. It has been applied to interactive learning and to Social preferences: caring about what others get.

entries.title: Does behavioral economics hold up?

definition.text: The debate over whether behavioural findings undermine standard economic analysis and whether they hold up outside the laboratory.

facts.text: Papers by Armen Alchian in 1950 and Gary Becker in 1962 argued that standard neoclassical analysis works even without assuming fully rational individuals.
Many behavioural studies fail to reproduce when repeated, part of the replicability crisis.
Behavioural economists responded by turning from lab experiments to field studies.
Matthew Rabin counters that results tend to be consistent across many situations and places.

entries.contested_note: Critics question the replicability and real-world validity of behavioural findings, while behavioural economists such as Rabin defend them.

entries.title: Neuroeconomics: looking inside the deciding brain

definition.text: An interdisciplinary field that explains how people make decisions by combining neuroscience with economics and psychology.

facts.text: It asks both how economic behaviour informs our understanding of the brain and how brain research can constrain economic models.

entries.text: Neuroeconomics combines neuroscience with economics and psychology to explain how people make decisions. The traffic between the fields runs both ways. It asks how economic behavior can inform our understanding of the brain. It also asks how brain research can constrain economic models, such as the {{ref:nature-econ-098}}.

entries.title: Three ways out of a social dilemma
entries.article: Collective action problem#Factors promoting cooperation in social dilemmas

definition.text: The three broad ways of getting people to cooperate in a social dilemma: motivational, strategic and structural solutions.

facts.text: Motivational solutions assume people care about others; research finds people have stable preferences for how much they weigh others' outcomes against their own.
Strategic solutions include tit for tat in repeated interactions: cooperate first, then copy the partner's last move.
Structural solutions change the rules of the game or remove the dilemma; monetary rewards have cut household water and electricity use.
Cooperation is more likely when people can monitor, sanction defectors, communicate, know one another and manage resources with clear boundaries.
Sanction systems are costly and are themselves public goods, and rewards can crowd out people's voluntary cooperation.
Graduated sanctions, which start mild and let violators regain trust, support collective resource management.

entries.text: If a collective action problem traps people, what frees them? Researchers group the answers into three kinds. Motivational solutions rely on people caring about others, and research finds stable individual preferences for how much people weigh others' outcomes against their own. Strategic solutions work in repeated interactions; the best known is {{ref:nature-econ-737}}, which cooperates first and then copies the partner's last move. Structural solutions change the rules of the game or remove the dilemma, as when money rewards have cut household water and electricity use. Cooperation is likelier when people can monitor each other, sanction defectors, communicate, know one another and manage resources with clear boundaries. Graduated sanctions, which start mild and let violators regain trust, support shared resource management. Yet sanction systems are costly and are themselves public goods, and rewards can crowd out voluntary cooperation.

entries.title: Bounded willpower and bounded selfishness

definition.text: Two companions of bounded rationality: people have limited self-control over long-term plans, and their concern for others is real but limited.

facts.text: Bounded willpower helps explain procrastination, impulsive spending and unhealthy lifestyle choices.
Bounded willpower is closely linked to hyperbolic discounting, the tendency to value immediate rewards more than future ones.
Bounded selfishness means people also care about fairness, reciprocity and others' well-being, which helps explain charitable giving, cooperation and social norms.

Bounded selfishness means people's concern for others is real but limited. They care about fairness, returning kindness and how others fare, which helps explain charitable giving, cooperation and social norms.

entries.title: Playing the prisoner's dilemma again and again

definition.text: The prisoner's dilemma played repeatedly, with players remembering past moves and able to change strategy.

facts.text: It underlies some theories of human cooperation and trust.
If both players know the number of rounds is fixed, the equilibrium is to defect in every round.
In Robert Axelrod's 1984 computer tournaments, greedy strategies did poorly over time and more altruistic ones did better.
The winner was tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's previous move.

entries.title: The case against economic man

definition.text: Arguments from economists, psychologists, anthropologists, sociologists and feminist scholars that the purely rational, self-interested model of people is unrealistic or one-sided.

facts.text: Economists such as Veblen, Keynes and Simon stressed uncertainty and bounded rationality, arguing perfect knowledge never exists.
Anthropologists found that in traditional societies production and exchange follow patterns of reciprocity, called a gift economy, rather than the model's predictions.
Bruno Frey criticised its stress on outside rewards and punishments over intrinsic motivation.
Feminist economists argue it undervalues unpaid care work such as caregiving and domestic labour.

entries.text: The perfectly rational, self-interested person of homo economicus has drawn fire from many directions. Bruno Frey criticised its stress on outside rewards and punishments over inner motivation. Feminist economists argue it undervalues unpaid care work such as caregiving and domestic labor.

entries.title: The availability heuristic: what comes to mind seems common

definition.text: A mental shortcut that judges how likely or important something is by how easily examples come to mind.

facts.text: The easier the consequences of something are to recall, the bigger they tend to seem.
Tversky and Kahneman first studied and named it in 1973.
Wide media coverage of rare, vivid events such as homicides or airline accidents makes people overrate them compared with common diseases or car accidents.
Because recall is affected by more than real frequency, relying on it produces systematic biases.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue that ease of recall, not the number of examples recalled, drives the effect, and that the classic studies are too vague about mental processes.

entries.title: The dictator game: giving when no one can refuse

definition.text: An economic experiment in which one player, the dictator, decides how to split a sum of money with a passive second player.

facts.text: It is a simplified version of the ultimatum game: the recipient cannot reject the offer.
Most dictators send some money, which shows the role of fairness and norms and undermines the assumption of narrow self-interest.
A wide cross-cultural study by Henrich and colleagues found dictators give a non-zero share everywhere.
Removing full anonymity raised giving from 18.3% to 27.2%, and dictators give less when they feel they earned the money.

entries.contested_note: Some authors argue giving reflects a wish not to look greedy rather than altruism, and tests of this idea give mixed results.

entries.title: Social preferences: caring about what others get

definition.text: People's tendency to care not only about their own material payoff but also about others' payoffs and the intentions behind them.

facts.text: They include altruism, fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion.
Research began with lab experiments around 1980, when players in games such as the ultimatum and dictator games departed systematically from pure self-interest.
In the ultimatum game proposers typically offer 25%-50% and responders tend to reject splits below 20%; in the dictator game the average gift falls to 20%, yet over 60% still give something.
Models divide them into distributive preferences, about how payoffs are shared, and reciprocal preferences, about the intentions behind others' actions.
Reciprocal and fairness-minded people can cooperate when they expect others to cooperate and can punish free riders, which matters for solving free-riding problems.
Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler found that concern for fairness restrains firms from, for example, raising prices after demand rises.
Without such preferences, society would be unlikely to reach desirable allocations because of self-interest and free riding.

Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler found that fairness concerns stop firms from, for instance, raising prices after demand rises. Without such preferences, self-interest and free riding would make good shared outcomes unlikely.

entries.title: Descriptive and injunctive norms: what people do and what they should

definition.text: Two kinds of social norm: descriptive norms show what people commonly do, while injunctive norms say what people ought to do.

facts.text: A parking lot with no litter on the ground signals the descriptive norm that most people there do not litter.
Seeing someone pick up trash and throw it away conveys the injunctive norm that one ought not to litter.
Voters in a US field experiment were more motivated to vote when told many people around them were voting, evidence that descriptive norms matter.

Both kinds of social norm shape behavior. In a US field experiment, voters were more motivated to vote when told many people around them were voting, evidence that descriptive norms matter.

entries.title: Attribute substitution: quietly answering an easier question

definition.text: An unnoticed mental process in which a hard question is answered by replacing it with an easier, related one.

facts.text: Daniel Kahneman and Shane Frederick proposed it in 2002.
It explains why people can be unaware of their own biases and why biases persist even after people are told about them.
In the bat-and-ball puzzle many people wrongly answer $0.10, splitting $1.10 into a big and a small amount instead of working out the sum.
Travellers paid more for insurance against death in a terrorist attack than for insurance covering death of any kind, as fear stood in for a judgment of total risk.

The swap goes unnoticed, which is why people can be unaware of their biases, and why biases persist even after people are told about them. entries.title: Fast and frugal heuristics: when less is more

definition.text: The view, argued by Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues, that simple rules of thumb can give judgments as accurate as complicated procedures.

facts.text: This approach holds that heuristics perform as well as complex methods, but faster and with less information.
A fast-and-frugal tree makes a classification, such as whether chest pain signals a heart attack, by asking a short sequence of questions on few cues.
Some theories argue that a heuristic can be more accurate than weighing every known factor, the so-called less-is-more effect.

Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues argue that simple rules of thumb like this can be as accurate as complicated procedures, while being faster and needing less information. Some theories go further. A heuristic, they argue, can be more accurate than weighing every known factor, the so-called less-is-more effect. On this view, shortcuts are good tools in their own right, not mere patches for a limited mind.

entries.title: The representativeness heuristic: judging by resemblance

definition.text: Judging how likely something is by how closely it resembles a typical member of a category.

facts.text: It attends to an individual's traits while ignoring how common each category is in the population, which leads to the base rate fallacy.
Asked about a woman named Linda, people rated 'bank teller and active feminist' as likelier than 'bank teller', though a combination can never be more probable than one part of it.
Tversky and Kahneman argued it underlies the gambler's fallacy, the expectation that random outcomes even out over the short run.

entries.title: Pro-environmental behavior: choosing to do less harm

definition.text: Behaviour people consciously choose to reduce the harm their actions do to the environment.

facts.text: Green consumption, buying in ways that harm the environment as little as possible, is one form of it.
Money incentives, costs, regulations and policy norms, along with how much time, money and power people feel they have, shape it through their attitudes.
Barriers to it can be psychological, social or cultural, financial, or structural, such as a home location that forces car dependency.
A meta-analysis confirmed a strong correlation between nature connectedness and pro-environmental behaviour, but found a weaker causal role than assumed.
Climate change narratives told as stories were better at inspiring it in a 2019 study.
Environmental psychology studies the psychological factors behind it and how to encourage it to mitigate climate change and biodiversity loss.

entries.title: Environmental policy for real, limited minds
entries.article: Bounded rationality in environmental decision making

definition.text: The application of bounded rationality to how environmental policy decisions are made.

facts.text: Established environmental policy theory assumes homo economicus: fully rational, self-regarding people.
That assumption is troublesome because policymakers often have only an incomplete picture of an environmental problem.
All environmental actors are human, with limited cognitive abilities and incomplete information.
The more actors involved in an environmental decision, the more complex it becomes and the less predictable its outcome.
A green strategy, in line with the Porter hypothesis, uses strict rules expected to spur cleaner innovation; eco-dumping weakens rules to boost resource exports.
These two extremes try to solve many-sided wicked problems with one-sided policies.

entries.title: Warm glow: the pleasure of doing your part

definition.text: An economic theory of the emotional reward people get from giving to others.

facts.text: In James Andreoni's original model (1989, 1990), people enjoy 'doing their part' whatever the actual impact of their gift.
It describes impure altruism, a mix of altruistic and selfish motives for giving.
Under pure altruism, government grants should fully crowd out private donations; warm glow helps explain why they do not.

Because outside rewards and punishments have often failed to bring lasting green behavior, environmental policy increasingly targets warm glow, with promising results for green energy, recycling and carpooling.
Sustainable investors may get satisfaction from the act itself rather than its impact, so their utility does not rise in line with impact.
A meta-analysis of 36 brain-imaging studies found the brain's reward networks consistently active when people choose to give.
Andreoni himself called adding warm glow to the model 'an admittedly ad hoc fix'.

entries.title: Survey satisficing: good-enough answers to questionnaires

definition.text: Jon Krosnick's theory that survey respondents cut down the mental effort of answering well by giving merely acceptable answers.

facts.text: In weak satisficing respondents go through every step but less thoroughly; in strong satisficing they give plausible answers without searching memory at all.
It shows up as 'don't know' answers, giving the same rating to every item, agreeing with any statement, or picking the first reasonable option.
It is more likely when respondents have less ability or motivation and when the task is hard.

Telltale signs include 'don't know' answers, the same rating for every item, agreeing with any statement and picking the first reasonable option. It is likelier when respondents have less ability or motivation.

entries.title: The marshmallow test and the power of waiting

definition.text: The ability to resist an immediate reward in order to gain a more valuable reward later.

facts.text: In the Stanford marshmallow experiments, begun by Walter Mischel and Ebbe B. Ebbesen in 1970, children were promised a second treat if they waited about 15 minutes without eating the first.
Older children were better at waiting, and the ability to wait as a child correlated with success in follow-up studies years later.
People who are more patient about future political change are more willing to vote in elections.

Ebbesen in 1970, children were promised a second treat if they waited about 15 minutes without eating the first. entries.title: Choice overload: when more options mean less

definition.text: The finding that offering many options can lower people's motivation to choose and their satisfaction with the choice.

facts.text: Classical economics predicts more options leave people at least as well off, but each option costs time and effort to evaluate.
How much it matters varies a lot between situations.
Choice architects can limit options or give decision support tools, though limiting options can reduce welfare.

entries.title: The decoy effect: an option designed to lose

definition.text: A shift in preference between two options when a third, usually inferior, option is added.

facts.text: The decoy might cost more than one option while being lower in quality than the other.
Restaurants pricing meal components separately next to a set meal use the decoy to raise willingness to pay for the set.
Decoy effects show individual irrationality that violates a standard axiom of choice.

The decoy might cost more than one option while being lower in quality than the other. Restaurants use it when they price meal components separately next to a set meal, which raises willingness to pay for the set. entries.title: Reciprocity: kindness for kindness

definition.text: The motivation to answer kind behavior with kindness and unfair behavior with unkindness.

facts.text: Rabin's 1993 model, one of the earliest, has people judge another's kindness by comparing what they receive with a fair payoff.
In the trust game, first movers typically pass on about 50% of their endowment, and the amount returned grows with the amount sent.
Reciprocal altruism may evolve from expecting future kindness in return; tit-for-tat in the prisoner's dilemma is an example.

entries.title: The social norms approach: correcting what people think peers do

definition.text: A campaign strategy, also called social norms marketing, that changes behavior by correcting people's mistaken beliefs about what their peers do.

facts.text: In the mid-1980s H.W. Perkins and A.D. Berkowitz found that college students greatly overestimated how much other students drank.
It rests on pluralistic ignorance: people wrongly believe others' attitudes or behavior differ from their own, often because extreme behavior is the most memorable.
Campaigns survey actual and perceived norms, broadcast messages such as 'Most students drink 0–4 drinks when they party', then evaluate and revise.
It has been used against smoking, drink driving and HIV risk, and to raise seat belt use.

entries.contested_note: Some scholars question its assumptions and methods, and one nationwide study found no fall in drinking at colleges that used it.

entries.title: Construal level theory: distant things look abstract

definition.text: A social-psychology theory that the more psychologically distant something is, the more abstractly people think about it, and the closer it is, the more concretely.

facts.text: The main kinds of psychological distance are distance in time, in space, in social terms, and in how likely an event is.
Nira Liberman and Yaacov Trope developed the theory.
Trope and Liberman argue it offers a framework for understanding time discounting, the lower value placed on future outcomes.
Psychological distance leads people to discount future risks and focus on immediate daily concerns, a barrier to pro-environmental behaviour.

entries.contested_note: Social psychologists debate whether further dimensions of distance, such as informational or experiential distance, belong in the theory.
entries.text: Construal level theory, developed by Nira Liberman and Yaacov Trope, explains why future risks feel less pressing than daily concerns. The more psychologically distant something is, the more abstractly people think about it; the closer it is, the more concretely. Distance comes in four main kinds: in time, in space, in social terms and in how likely an event is. entries.title: Prospect theory: how people really weigh risk

definition.text: A theory of how people actually make choices under risk, developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979.

facts.text: Unlike expected utility theory, which models what perfectly rational agents would do, it aims to describe real behavior.
People judge gains and losses relative to a reference point, their current situation, rather than by absolute wealth.
Losses are felt more sharply than equal gains: for some people the pain of losing $1,000 is only made up by the pleasure of gaining $2,000.
Its value function is concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses, so people avoid risk over gains and seek risk over losses.
Choices pass through an editing phase, where a reference point is set and outcomes are coded as gains or losses, before they are evaluated.
It was cited when Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, and Tversky and Kahneman's work largely launched behavioral economics.
Jeffrey Berejikian used it to analyse how the Montreal Protocol, a landmark environmental agreement, came about.
Critics note that the reference point is hard to pin down, since many outside factors shape what counts as a gain or a loss.

entries.text: For some people, the pain of losing $1,000 is only made up by the pleasure of gaining $2,000. That lopsided feeling sits at the heart of prospect theory, developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979. The older standard, the {{ref:nature-econ-797}}, models what perfectly rational agents would do. Prospect theory instead aims to describe what real people do when choices involve risk. Its first insight is that people judge outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, their current situation, not by their total wealth. Choices pass through an editing phase, where the reference point is set and outcomes are coded as gains or losses, before they are evaluated. Its second insight is the shape of the value function, the curve linking outcomes to how they feel. It is concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses. In plain terms, people play safe when facing gains, gamble when facing losses, and feel losses more sharply than equal gains. It reaches into environmental politics too. Jeffrey Berejikian used it to analyse how the {{ref:nature-clim-094}}, a landmark environmental agreement, came about. Critics point to one weakness: the reference point is hard to pin down, because many outside factors shape what counts as a gain or a loss.

entries.title: Cumulative prospect theory: repairing the original

definition.text: A revised version of prospect theory that weights probabilities by rank, fixing flaws in the original version.

facts.text: The original version could prefer one prospect over another even when the other was at least as good at every outcome level, violating first-order stochastic dominance.
The cumulative version borrows its probability weighting from rank-dependent expected utility theory and also works for continuous outcomes.

entries.text: The original prospect theory had a flaw. It could prefer one prospect over another even when the other was at least as good at every outcome level, breaking a basic rule called first-order stochastic dominance. Cumulative prospect theory repairs this by weighting probabilities by rank, a method borrowed from rank-dependent expected utility theory. The revised version also works when outcomes are continuous rather than a few separate values.

entries.title: The framing effect: same choice, different words

definition.text: A bias in which people's choices change with the way the same options are worded, even when the options are logically identical.

facts.text: When choices are worded as gains, most people prefer a sure gain to a chance of gain; worded as losses, people tend to pick a gamble over a sure loss.
In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 disease problem, a sure treatment was chosen by 72% when described as saving 200 lives, but 78% chose the risky one when outcomes were described as deaths.
Standard logic says a decision should not depend on how the problem is described; deciding on such irrelevant wording is called an extensionality violation.
93% of PhD students registered early when a late penalty fee was stressed, but only 67% when the same terms were shown as an early discount.
Framing shapes decisions in public health, education, politics, law and economics, and is counted among the largest biases in decision making.
People are more open to framing when they rely on fast, intuitive thinking rather than slow, deliberate thinking.
The effect seems to weaken when a decision is made in a foreign language, perhaps because it brings more distance and deliberation.
Valuation surveys of environmental goods have been criticised for bringing in framing effects.

entries.title: Loss aversion: why losses loom larger than gains

definition.text: A bias in which the same situation feels worse when it is framed as a loss than when it is framed as a gain.

facts.text: Empirically, a loss tends to be treated as about twice as large as an equal gain.
Kahneman and Tversky coined the term in 1979 as part of prospect theory.
It differs from risk aversion, which is the rational valuing of an uncertain outcome below its expected value.
Losses are measured against a reference point, such as what a person already owns.
It was first proposed as the explanation for the endowment effect, and the two together break the Coase theorem.
Framing the same price change as a $5 discount or as a $5 surcharge avoided changes consumer behaviour significantly.
Expectations can also set the reference point, so missing an expected purchase feels like a loss.
One explanation is evolutionary: for an organism near the edge of survival, losing a day's food could be fatal while an extra day's food adds little.

entries.title: The endowment effect: why owning something raises its value

definition.text: The finding that people value something more once they own it, so they are more likely to keep an object than to acquire the same object.

facts.text: People's maximum willingness to pay for an item is typically lower than the least they will accept to give it up, even for something owned only minutes.
In the classic Cornell mug study, owners asked about twice as much to sell a mug as buyers would pay for it.
Richard Thaler coined the term in 1980.
The leading explanation is loss aversion: giving up an owned item feels like a loss.
It contradicts the standard theory that willingness to pay and willingness to accept should be equal, and it undermines the Coase theorem.
Hanemann noted that the two need only be equal for close substitutes, so gaps for environmental resources and health can arise without an endowment effect.
Shogren and colleagues found little effect for goods with substitutes but accepted it for goods without them, such as non-renewable Earth resources.
Businesses exploit it with free trials, which give consumers a sense of ownership that makes them reluctant to cancel.

entries.contested_note: Some economists question whether the effect exists, arguing it reflects lack of substitutes or artificial experimental scarcity.

entries.title: Status quo bias: the pull of how things are

definition.text: A bias toward keeping things as they currently are, also called default bias.

facts.text: The current state serves as a reference point, so any change from it is felt as a loss or a gain.
It is explained by loss aversion and the endowment effect: the possible losses of switching weigh more than the possible gains.
It differs from a rational preference for the status quo, where the current state really is better, and from simple inertia.
Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed in 1988 that people stick with an option framed as the status quo, and that the pull grows as more alternatives are offered.
In a 1986 retirement study, most people never changed how they split savings between two funds, despite very different returns and no switching costs.
Automatic enrolment in retirement plans, where employees must opt out, uses this bias to raise saving.
Defaults keep their effect even when people are told why the default was chosen.

entries.title: Mental accounting: money kept in separate jars

definition.text: Richard Thaler's model of how people sort, label and judge money and economic outcomes in separate mental 'accounts'.

facts.text: People budget money into accounts such as saving for a home or spending on gas, clothing and utilities, partly to control their spending.
A person may stop eating out when that budget runs out but keep buying groceries, even though both come from the same income.
Thaler found people more willing to drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 purchase than on a $125 purchase.
It draws on prospect theory, and can make people more loss averse for some accounts than others, a systematic departure from rational consumer behaviour.
People are willing to pay more with credit cards than with cash, because the payment comes later and looks like a small addition to a large bill.
Households spend SNAP food benefits on food at a rate of 0.5 to 0.6 per dollar, much higher than the usual 0.1 from cash transfers.
Publicly setting a savings goal greatly raised savings rates in a study of savings groups in Colombia.

entries.title: The default effect: what happens when no one chooses

definition.text: The tendency for people to accept whatever option they get if they make no active choice.

facts.text: Experiments and observational studies show that making an option the default makes it more likely to be chosen.
Differences between opt-in and opt-out organ donor rules have been argued to be the main cause of large differences in donor rates between countries.
More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default.
Explanations include the mental effort of choosing, switching costs, loss aversion relative to the default, and reading the default as a recommendation.
Defaults can be mass defaults applied to everyone or personalised defaults tailored to each customer.
Setting defaults is a key example of a nudge or soft paternalist policy.

entries.title: Libertarian paternalism: steering while leaving people free

definition.text: The idea that institutions can legitimately steer people's behavior for their own good while still leaving them free to choose otherwise.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term in 2003 and defended it in their 2008 book Nudge.
It is libertarian because people can opt out of the arrangements, which is said to preserve freedom of choice.
Setting a default to exploit the default effect is a typical example.
Austria, with an opt-out organ donation system, has a consent rate of 99.98%, while Germany, with an opt-in system, has only 12%.
Firms that raised the default contribution rate of retirement plans immediately and sharply raised how much their employees saved.
Critics say it neglects the traditional libertarian concern with coercion and that other aims, such as future liberty, could be promoted instead.

entries.title: Myopic loss aversion: fixating on the short run

definition.text: The tendency, derived from prospect theory, to focus on short-term gains and losses and weigh them more heavily than long-term ones.

facts.text: It can lead people to avoid immediate losses at the expense of long-term gains.
In a 1997 betting study by Gneezy and Potters, players bet more after losing a round and less after winning one, rather than looking at total earnings.

entries.title: Loss attention: losses sharpen focus

definition.text: The tendency to pay more attention to a task when it involves losses, without giving losses more weight than gains.

facts.text: Eldad Yechiam and Guy Hochman proposed it as distinct from loss aversion.
Under loss attention, losses can reduce bias rather than cause it.
People pick options with higher expected value more often when outcomes are framed as losses.

entries.title: Escalation of commitment: doubling down on a failing course

definition.text: The tendency to keep putting resources into a failing course of action in the hope of turning losses around.

facts.text: It arises when organisations or nations must decide whether to continue an operation or withdraw from it.
It is especially likely when the decision maker can claim credit for success while others absorb the losses.

entries.text: Organizations and nations sometimes face a hard call: continue an operation or withdraw from it. It is especially likely when the decision maker can claim credit for success while others absorb the losses.

entries.title: The reversal test: a check for status quo bias

definition.text: A check for status quo bias: if changing a quantity one way is judged bad, ask whether changing it the other way is also judged bad.

facts.text: If both directions are judged bad, those judging must explain why the current value cannot be improved; if they cannot, status quo bias is suspected.
Its rationale is that of all possible values only a few can be best, so it is unlikely that the current value happens to be one of them.

entries.text: Suppose people judge that raising some quantity would be bad. The reversal test asks whether lowering it would also be bad. Of all possible values only a few can be best, so it is unlikely that the current value happens to be one of them.

entries.title: The pain of paying

definition.text: The unpleasant feeling people get when they spend money, treated as a negative response to a financial loss.

facts.text: Typical examples are watching a taxi meter or a gas pump climb.
A $30 t-shirt feels like a bigger expense paid from $50 in a wallet than from $500 in a checking account.
Consumers who feel more pain of paying for the same goods hold less debt.

The feeling has a payoff: consumers who feel more pain of paying for the same goods hold less debt.

entries.title: Strategy: a complete plan for every situation

definition.text: A player's complete plan for a game, saying what they will do in every situation that might arise.

facts.text: A move or action is any one of the options a player can choose where the best result depends on what others do as well.
A strategy is like a list of directions, and a move is a single step on that list.
A player's strategy set lists every strategy available to them, such as {rock, paper, scissors}.
In games played over time or with private information, strategies are rules for how to respond to each possible history or piece of information.
Choosing the strategy sets well is part of the art of making an applied game both solvable and meaningful.

entries.title: Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price

definition.text: A way of buying or selling something by inviting bids and then dealing with the highest (or, when buying, the lowest) bidder.

facts.text: The open ascending-price auction, where each bid must beat the one before, is probably the most common kind and has a long history.
Auctions are used to trade antiques, livestock, radio spectrum, used cars, real estate, online advertising and emission permits, among much else.
Each year the US EPA auctions about 250,000 allowances, each letting its owner emit one ton of sulfur dioxide, to the highest bidders.
Governments earn the most from spectrum auctions and quota auctions; Russia's crab quota sold for €2 billion in 2019.
The branch of economics that studies auction formats and how bidders behave is called auction theory.
Paul Milgrom and Robert B. Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Prize for introducing new auction formats.
Fishing quotas can be handed out for free or auctioned when a catch-share scheme starts.

entries.title: Zero-sum games: one side's gain is the other's loss

definition.text: A situation in which one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss, so gains and losses add up to zero.

facts.text: Cutting a cake is zero-sum if everyone values each piece equally: a bigger slice for one leaves less for others.
Poker, chess, sport and bridge are everyday examples; in finance, futures, options and swaps are zero-sum.
Such games are distributive: the pie cannot be enlarged by good negotiation, only divided.
Every two-player finite zero-sum game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies, and there Nash equilibrium, minimax and maximin all give the same answer.
The solution of a two-player zero-sum game can be found by solving a linear programming problem.
In 1944 von Neumann and Morgenstern showed any non-zero-sum game of n players equals a zero-sum game with an extra fictitious player.

They are also unusually tidy to solve. Every two-player finite zero-sum game has an equilibrium once players may randomize. There, the {{ref:nature-econ-718}} and the older minimax and maximin rules all give the same answer, which can be found with {{ref:nature-econ-456}}. In 1944 von Neumann and Morgenstern went further. They showed that any game of n players, even one whose gains and losses need not cancel, equals a zero-sum game with an extra fictitious player.

entries.title: Cooperative bargaining: splitting a surplus made together

definition.text: The problem of how two parties should split a surplus that they can only create together.

facts.text: Because the surplus can be divided many ways, the parties must negotiate; examples include firms and workers splitting profit, or trade partners setting terms of trade.
The normative approach sets out appealing rules (axioms) that a fair division should satisfy.
The positive approach studies how surpluses are actually shared, modelling bargaining as a non-cooperative game, most often sequential bargaining.
A bargaining problem consists of the set of feasible agreements and a disagreement point giving each player's payoff if no deal is reached.
Experiments found no consistent support for any bargaining model; many people settled on simple solutions good for both sides.
Kenneth Binmore used the Nash bargaining game and evolutionary game theory to explain why people see a 50–50 split as the just solution.

entries.title: The normal form: a game laid out as a table

definition.text: A description of a game as a table (payoff matrix) listing each player's possible strategies and the payoffs for every combination of them.

facts.text: Each cell gives the row player's payoff first and the column player's second.
It suits games where players move at the same time or cannot see each other's move first.
It makes dominated strategies and Nash equilibria easy to spot, but loses some information compared with the extensive form.
In the prisoner's dilemma matrix, Defect beats Cooperate whatever the other does, so (Defect, Defect) is the only Nash equilibrium.
A sequential game can be written in normal form only by listing every contingent plan, including for situations that never arise.
Every extensive-form game has an equivalent normal form, though converting can make the representation exponentially larger.

entries.title: Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone

definition.text: A situation in a game where no player could do better by changing only their own strategy while everyone else keeps theirs.

facts.text: It is used to analyse any strategic interaction, where each decision-maker's outcome depends on the others' choices as well as their own.
Nash's insight was that the choices of several decision-makers cannot be predicted by analysing each one in isolation.
It is named after John Forbes Nash Jr., but Antoine Augustin Cournot used the same idea in 1838 for firms choosing how much to produce.
A Nash equilibrium need not be Pareto optimal, so it can look irrational from outside: everyone could be better off.
In sequential games it can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfect equilibrium removes these.
It is applied to predict traffic flows, where each traveller's route time depends on the routes everyone else picks.
John Maynard Smith applied the concept to model the evolution of behaviour in 1982.

It applies to any strategic interaction, where each decision-maker's outcome depends on the others' choices as well as their own. entries.title: Strategic dominance: a choice that is always better

definition.text: One strategy dominates another if it always gives a better result, whatever the other players do.

facts.text: Strict dominance means always strictly better; weak dominance means never worse and sometimes better.
A strategy that dominates every alternative is a dominant strategy; rational players are usually assumed never to play dominated strategies.
If every player has a strictly dominant strategy, the game has a single dominant-strategy equilibrium, which need not be good for everyone.
The prisoner's dilemma is the classic case: confessing dominates for each suspect although both would do better staying silent.
Strictly dominated strategies are never part of a Nash equilibrium, but weakly dominated ones can be.

entries.title: Chicken: the game of who swerves first

definition.text: A two-player model of conflict, also called hawk–dove or snowdrift, in which each would like the other to back down but the worst outcome is that neither does.

facts.text: The name comes from two drivers heading at each other: one must swerve or both may die, and the one who swerves is called a 'chicken'.
Each driver does best by going straight while the other swerves, and a crash is the worst outcome for both.
Games of this anti-coordination type have three Nash equilibria: two where the players choose opposite actions and one mixed equilibrium where each randomizes.
The only symmetric equilibrium is the mixed one, which is often worse for both than if they could coordinate.
Where the prisoner's dilemma is about the impossibility of cooperation, Chicken is about the inevitability of conflict; repeated Chicken can lead to turn-taking.
'Schedule chicken' describes project teams each promising unrealistic dates because no one wants to be first to admit delay.

entries.title: Coordination games: the payoff of matching

definition.text: A simultaneous game in which players earn more when they choose the same course of action as one another.

facts.text: It has several pure-strategy Nash equilibria in which players choose matching strategies, and each player's best move depends on what they expect the other to do.
Choosing which side of the road to drive on is the typical example: a shared standard that saves lives if widely followed.
When it does not matter which option is picked as long as both pick the same, it is a pure coordination game.
Coordination games also have a mixed equilibrium, but it is worse for both than either pure equilibrium and is not evolutionarily stable.
They are closely tied to positive network externalities, the benefit of being in the same network as others.
The stag hunt, or assurance game, is a coordination game where the best joint outcome needs trust, while a safer option needs none.

entries.title: The stag hunt: a big prize that needs trust

definition.text: A game, also called the assurance game or trust dilemma, in which players do best by cooperating on an ambitious goal but can fall back on a safer solo option that protects them if the other does not cooperate.

facts.text: Two hunters choose separately whether to hunt a stag, which needs both of them, or a hare, which one can catch alone but is worth far less.
It has two pure equilibria: hunting stag together pays most, while hunting hare alone is the safer, risk-dominant choice.
Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is itself an equilibrium; what it needs is trust.
It is often used as an analogy for social cooperation such as international agreements on climate change.
The problem originated with Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality; David Hume gave examples such as two neighbours draining a meadow.
Orcas that cooperatively herd fish to the surface, which needs many orcas, are an animal example.
Expected punishment of defectors can turn a prisoner's dilemma into a stag hunt.

entries.title: The extensive form: a game drawn as a tree

definition.text: A way of describing a game as a tree that shows the order of moves, each player's choices at each point, what they know when they choose, and the payoffs at the end.

facts.text: It gives a fuller description than the normal form, which reduces a game to a payoff matrix.
Normal form is generally used for simultaneous games and extensive form for sequential ones; it is a many-player version of a decision tree.
Each end point (leaf) of the tree lists one payoff for every player, and a play is a path from the root to a leaf.
Chance events are modelled as moves by a fictitious player called Nature, whose branches carry probabilities.
Such games are solved by backward induction, working from the end nodes back to the root.
Harold W. Kuhn gave the general definition in 1953, extending one by von Neumann from 1928.

entries.title: Repeated games: why meeting again changes everything

definition.text: A game made of the same base game (the stage game) played over and over by the same players.

facts.text: Repetition makes players weigh how today's action affects others' future actions, an effect sometimes called reputation.
Two neighbouring petrol stations would both earn zero profit in a one-off price war, yet they make profits because they meet again every day.
Repeating the same game a finite or an infinite number of times can lead to very different equilibria and best strategies.
In the infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma the preferred strategy is to cooperate rather than play the one-shot Nash strategy.
Sustaining cooperation relies on punishing anyone who deviates; results showing which outcomes can be sustained are the folk theorems.
A game repeated an unknown number of times is treated like an infinitely repeated one, since there is no known last round.

entries.title: Bayesian games: playing with private information

definition.text: A game-theory model of strategic decisions in which players have incomplete information, such as private knowledge of their own payoffs.

facts.text: John C. Harsanyi introduced Bayesian games in three papers in 1967 and 1968 and later shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Nature assigns each player a 'type' at the start, standing for the private information that player holds.
Players hold a probability distribution over everyone's possible types; when no one has private information it is called a common prior.
Attaching probabilities to types lets games of incomplete information be solved for the first time, and far more easily than otherwise.
They avoid endless 'I think that you think' reasoning by weighting all possible outcomes by probability at once.
A buyer bidding for a used car whose quality only the owner knows, the market for lemons, is a Bayesian game linked to adverse selection.

entries.title: Tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates on the first move and then copies whatever the opponent did on the previous move.

facts.text: The phrase means 'equivalent retaliation' and was first recorded in 1558.
Anatol Rapoport entered it in Robert Axelrod's two tournaments around 1980, where it was both the simplest strategy and the most successful.
Its success may help explain how animal and human groups came to live in mostly cooperative ways.
A single misread move can trap two tit-for-tat players in an endless 'death spiral' of alternating retaliation.
It is not a subgame perfect equilibrium except under knife-edge conditions on the discount rate.
In First World War trenches it appeared as the 'live and let live' system, an unspoken truce kept by matching retaliation.
In repeated social dilemmas, cooperation may emerge when people adopt tit for tat.

entries.title: Evolutionary game theory: strategies that survive

definition.text: The use of game theory to study evolving populations of living things, modelling Darwinian competition as a contest between strategies.

facts.text: It began in 1973 with John Maynard Smith and George R. Price's formal treatment of animal contests as strategies.
Unlike classical game theory it does not need rational players, only inherited strategies whose success is tested by survival and reproduction.
It focuses on how strategies change over time, which depends on how common each competing strategy is in the population.
It has helped explain group selection, sexual selection, altruism, parental care, co-evolution and ecological dynamics.
It began from the puzzle of why animals fight in restrained, ritualized ways over resources.
Life's problems of getting food, surviving and reproducing resemble economic problems of resource management, competitive strategy and investment, which is why game theory fits biology so well.

entries.title: Cooperative game theory: coalitions and binding deals

definition.text: The branch of game theory that studies games in which groups of players can form coalitions and make binding agreements, enforced from outside, for example by contract law.

facts.text: Non-cooperative games, by contrast, allow no alliances or only agreements that enforce themselves, such as through credible threats.
Analysis focuses on which coalitions can form, what they can do jointly and the collective payoffs that result.
The main assumption is that all players form one grand coalition; the question is then how to divide its total payoff among them.
Researchers have proposed different solution concepts, such as the core and the Shapley value, based on different ideas of fairness.
Cooperative game theory has been proposed as a strategic theory of the firm, with different solutions mimicking different institutions.

entries.text: Some games allow binding deals. Non-cooperative games, by contrast, allow no alliances, or only agreements that enforce themselves, such as through threats a player would really carry out. The analysis asks which coalitions can form, what they can do jointly and what collective payoffs result. Its main assumption is that all players form one grand coalition. The question is then how to divide its total payoff. Researchers have proposed different answers, called solution concepts, such as the {{ref:nature-econ-706}} and the {{ref:nature-econ-726}}, each based on a different idea of fairness. The approach has even been proposed as a strategic theory of the firm, with different solutions mimicking different institutions.

entries.title: Mixed strategies: the value of being unpredictable

definition.text: A strategy in which the player chooses among their pure strategies at random with set probabilities, rather than committing to one plan.

facts.text: A pure strategy is a fully fixed plan; it counts as a mixed strategy that picks one option with probability 1.
Mixing helps where no pure strategy is a best response, keeping a player unpredictable; payoffs are then expected payoffs.
A soccer penalty kick has no pure-strategy equilibrium, so kicker and goalie should both randomize their direction.
Not every finite game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, as matching pennies shows, but every one has an equilibrium once mixing is allowed.

Critics in the 1980s found mixed strategies intuitively problematic; Harsanyi's purification reads them as our ignorance of players' private information, and another view treats them as shares of a population.

entries.title: Backward induction: solving a game from the end

definition.text: Solving a sequential game by starting from the last move, working out what the final mover would do, and reasoning back to the start.

facts.text: At each step it removes branches where a player would make a move that is not in their interest at that point.
Tic-tac-toe has a well-known backward-induction solution, and in theory even Go has one.
Finite repeated games can be solved this way, but games repeated forever or an unknown number of times cannot, as there is no last round.
Kaminski (2019) proved that a generalized backward induction finds all subgame perfect equilibria in a broad class of games.

entries.text: To solve a game played in turns, start at the end. Backward induction works out what the final mover would do, then reasons back step by step to the start. At each step it removes branches where a player would make a move that is not in their interest at that point. Tic-tac-toe has a well-known backward-induction solution, and in theory even Go has one. Kaminski (2019) proved that a generalized backward induction finds all of the {{ref:nature-econ-734}} outcomes in a broad class of games.
