entries.title: Subgame perfect equilibrium: ruling out empty threats

definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium for games with moves in sequence, requiring the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward.

facts.text: It rules out non-credible threats, so strategies stay rational throughout the game.
Reinhard Selten proposed it in 1965.
Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall has one.
In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite or imperfect-information games.
The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria.
In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round.
Firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium if they are patient enough.

entries.text: Reinhard Selten proposed a sharper version of the Nash equilibrium in 1965. A subgame perfect equilibrium, for games with moves in sequence, requires the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward. This rules out non-credible threats, ones a player would not actually want to carry out, so strategies stay rational throughout the game. Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall, where players remember all past actions, has one. In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite games or games with hidden moves. The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria. In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round. Yet firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium, if they are patient enough.

entries.title: The folk theorem: patience makes almost anything possible

definition.text: A family of results showing that repeated games have a great many equilibrium outcomes: almost any payoff can be sustained if players are patient enough.

facts.text: It got its name because game theorists widely knew the result in the 1950s although nobody had published it.
'Almost any' means every payoff that is feasible and individually rational, that is, better than what each player can guarantee alone.
The simplest proof uses a grim trigger strategy: cooperate until someone deviates, then punish them forever.
Friedman's 1971 version strengthened it to subgame-perfect equilibria, where punishment threats must be credible.
It explains why agreements between countries are kept without enforcement: relations are long-term, though an impatient country is hard to punish credibly.
In a close-knit community it shows how traditions and taboos can be upheld by social norms.
Franklin Fisher noted it is not a positive theory: it does not predict what firms will do, only that cost and demand alone cannot explain oligopoly.

entries.title: Evolutionarily stable strategies: holding off invaders
entries.article: Evolutionary game theory#The evolutionarily stable strategy

definition.text: A strategy that, once common in a large population, cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy.

facts.text: It is akin to the Nash equilibrium of classical game theory, but with stricter mathematical conditions.
A successful strategy must be able to spread when rare and to hold its ground once common.
In the hawk–dove game the evolutionarily stable strategy is a mixed one.
The rock-paper-scissors game played by male side-blotched lizards has no evolutionarily stable strategy, only endless cycles around a Nash equilibrium.

entries.title: Mixed-strategy equilibria: when randomizing is the answer

definition.text: A Nash equilibrium in which at least one player randomizes, choosing among strategies with set probabilities rather than always playing the same one.

facts.text: In the drive-on-the-left-or-right game, besides the two pure equilibria there is a third where each side is chosen with 50% probability.
In matching pennies, where one player wins on a match and the other on a mismatch, the only equilibrium is mixed.
An equilibrium is strict if every player would lose by switching, and weak if some player is indifferent.

entries.title: Nash's theorem: every finite game has an equilibrium

definition.text: Nash's theorem that every game with finitely many players and finitely many pure strategies has at least one Nash equilibrium once mixed strategies are allowed.

facts.text: Equilibria may fail to exist when choices are infinite and unbounded, as when two players name numbers and the larger wins.
Nash's thesis proof used Brouwer's fixed-point theorem; his 1950 paper used the simpler Kakutani fixed-point theorem.
Robert Wilson's 1971 oddness theorem says almost all finite games have a finite, odd number of Nash equilibria.

entries.title: Strong Nash equilibrium: stable against groups

definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium that is stable against deviations by any coalition of players, not just by single players.

facts.text: Ordinary Nash equilibrium counts only individual deviations, which is not convincing enough for cooperative games.

entries.text: An ordinary Nash equilibrium only checks whether a single player could gain by switching. That is not convincing enough for cooperative games, where groups can act together. A strong Nash equilibrium is a refinement that is stable against deviations by any coalition of players, not just by individuals. No group can do better by changing course together.

entries.title: Axelrod's tournaments: how nice strategies won
entries.article: Prisoner's dilemma#Axelrod's tournament and successful strategy conditions

definition.text: Computer tournaments organized by Robert Axelrod in which strategies submitted by academics competed in the repeated prisoner's dilemma.

facts.text: Greedy strategies did poorly over the long run, and the simple tit for tat won.
Axelrod concluded that successful strategies are nice, retaliating, forgiving and non-envious.
He used the results to show how altruism could evolve by natural selection from purely selfish beginnings, reported in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation.

entries.title: Four ways to run an auction

definition.text: The main ways an auction's price can be set: open rising bids, a falling price called out by the auctioneer, or one-shot sealed bids.

facts.text: In an English auction bidders openly outbid one another, each bid higher than the last.
In a Dutch auction the auctioneer starts high and lowers the price until someone accepts it or the seller's reserve is reached.
In a first-price sealed-bid auction everyone submits one secret bid at the same time and the highest bidder pays what they bid.
A Vickrey (second-price sealed-bid) auction works the same way except that the winner pays the second-highest bid; it is central to auction theory and online ad bidding.

In a first-price sealed-bid auction, everyone submits one secret bid at the same time, and the highest bidder pays what they bid. A Vickrey, or second-price sealed-bid, auction works the same way, except that the winner pays the second-highest bid. It is central to auction theory and to online ad bidding.

entries.title: Bid rigging: rings that keep prices low

definition.text: Collusion in which bidders who know each other form a ring to avoid bidding against one another and so keep auction prices low.

facts.text: Ring members may hold their own private auction afterwards and split the price difference between the two sales.
Bid rigging weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value.
Even without explicit agreement, bidders can in theory coordinate tacitly to keep bids low.

entries.text: Bidders who know one another can agree not to compete. In bid rigging, they form a ring whose members avoid bidding against each other, keeping auction prices low. Afterward, ring members may hold their own private auction and split the price difference between the two sales. The practice weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value. Even without an explicit agreement, bidders can in theory coordinate tacitly to keep bids low.

entries.title: Reserve prices: the seller's floor

definition.text: A minimum price set by the seller below which the auctioned item will not be sold.

facts.text: In a no-reserve (absolute) auction the item sells whatever the price, which can draw more bidders hoping for a bargain.
A reserve protects the seller from a low bid but may lower the final price if it dampens interest.
The reserve can be announced to bidders (public) or kept secret.

entries.title: Crossing out dominated strategies, again and again
entries.article: Strategic dominance#Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies

definition.text: A way of solving games by repeatedly crossing out dominated strategies until no more can be removed.

facts.text: Removing some strategies can make others dominated in the smaller game, so the step is repeated.
It relies on rationality being common knowledge: everyone knows that everyone knows, and so on, that all players are rational.
With weakly dominated strategies the result can depend on the order in which they are removed.

entries.text: One way to solve a game is to cross out every dominated strategy, then look again. Removing some strategies can make others dominated in the smaller game, so the step repeats until nothing more can go. This iterated elimination relies on rationality being common knowledge: everyone knows that everyone knows, and so on, that all players are rational. With weakly dominated strategies, the result can depend on the order in which they are removed.

entries.title: The hawk–dove game: when animals should fight

definition.text: The biologists' version of Chicken, in which two animals contest a shared resource and each can either fight (hawk) or back off (dove).

facts.text: John Maynard Smith and George Price first presented a form of it in their 1973 paper 'The logic of animal conflict'.
Payoffs depend on V, the value of the resource, and C, the cost of an escalated fight, and the cost is almost always assumed larger than the value.
It is the most commonly used game-theory model of aggression in biology, asking when an animal should escalate to costly combat.
If one player can be told apart as territory owner and the other as intruder, role-based pure strategies become evolutionarily stable instead of the mixed one.

entries.title: Replicator dynamics: success breeds numbers

definition.text: A simple model of how strategies spread in a population, used in evolutionary game theory.

facts.text: A strategy that does better than average grows in frequency at the expense of those doing worse than average.
One version has a single population playing against itself; another has two populations that each play only against the other.

entries.title: The volunteer's dilemma: someone else should do it

definition.text: A many-player game in which each person chooses whether to volunteer, doing best if someone else volunteers and worst if nobody does.

facts.text: It is one of the many-player games that reduce to Chicken, much as the public goods game reduces to a prisoner's dilemma with two players.
The more players there are, the more likely it is that no one volunteers.

entries.text: Each person in a group chooses whether to volunteer. Everyone does best if someone else volunteers, and worst if nobody does. This volunteer's dilemma is one of the many-player games that reduce to Chicken, much as the public goods game reduces to a prisoner's dilemma with two players. Its grim twist concerns numbers: the more players there are, the more likely it is that no one volunteers.

entries.title: The war of attrition: who gives up first

definition.text: A model of escalating conflict in which outcomes differ only by degree, as each side decides whether the prize is worth the mounting cost of carrying on.

facts.text: It differs from Chicken, where the catastrophic outcome differs in kind, such as life against death.
In biology it is a very influential model of how contests are settled when physical combat is not possible.

entries.text: Some contests end not in catastrophe but in exhaustion. In a war of attrition, conflict escalates and outcomes differ only by degree, as each side decides whether the prize is worth the mounting cost of carrying on. That sets it apart from Chicken, where the disastrous outcome differs in kind, such as life against death. In biology it is a very influential model of how contests are settled when physical combat is not possible.

entries.title: Non-zero-sum games: when both sides can win

definition.text: A situation in which one party's gain need not be another's loss, so the total of gains and losses can be more or less than zero.

facts.text: Positive-sum or win–win games are those where the parties' combined gains exceed zero.
Two countries swapping surplus bananas for surplus apples, both benefiting, is a non-zero-sum situation.
The prisoner's dilemma is a classic non-zero-sum game.
Politics and the economy need not be zero-sum because of cooperation, synergy and economic growth.

entries.title: Zero-sum thinking: 'your gain is my loss'

definition.text: The belief that a situation is zero-sum, so that one person's gain must be another's loss, summed up as 'your gain is my loss'.

facts.text: Unlike the game-theory concept, it is a psychological construct: a person's subjective reading of a situation.
Applying zero-sum logic where it does not fit can breed needless feelings of scarcity and hostility.
Economic stagnation can encourage zero-sum perceptions, which can raise support for redistribution.

entries.title: Anti-coordination games: the cost of following the crowd

definition.text: A game in which choosing the same action as others creates a cost rather than a benefit, as under negative externalities.

facts.text: Chicken (hawk–dove) is the best-known two-player example.
In a crowding game each player's payoff falls as more others choose the same strategy, as when extra cars slow a road for everyone; a congestion game is a crowding game in networks.
In a discoordination game one player wants to match and the other to mismatch, so the only equilibrium is mixed; matching pennies is the classic case.

entries.title: Coordination failure: settling for the safe option

definition.text: The common outcome in which players end up at a worse equilibrium because they pick the safer option instead of the one paying most.

facts.text: Players are more likely to fail to coordinate on the risky option when its extra reward over the safe option is small.
Laboratory results suggest coordination failure is common in stag-hunt and order-statistic games.
In one weak-link experiment groups first failed to coordinate, but about 80% coordinated successfully when the game was repeated.

entries.text: Players in a coordination game often end up at a worse equilibrium, because they pick the safer option instead of the one that pays most. Laboratory results suggest this coordination failure is common in stag-hunt and order-statistic games. It is more likely when the risky option's extra reward over the safe one is small. Experience can help. In one weak-link experiment, groups first failed to coordinate, but about 80% coordinated successfully when the game was repeated.

entries.title: Focal points: coordinating without talking

definition.text: An equilibrium that people tend to settle on when they must coordinate without talking, because it stands out for some reason.

facts.text: An equilibrium may stand out by paying more, being more salient, fairer or safer.
These reasons can clash, as in the stag hunt, where hunting stag together pays more but hunting hare is safer.

entries.text: When people must coordinate without talking, they tend to settle on an equilibrium that stands out. That is a focal point. An equilibrium may stand out by paying more, or by being more salient, fairer or safer. These reasons can clash. In the stag hunt, hunting stag together pays more, but hunting hare is safer.

entries.title: Voluntary standards: rules people adopt freely

definition.text: A de facto standard that people adopt freely, the typical social-science solution to a coordination problem.

facts.text: Such standards tend to be stable where everyone gains, but only by making mutually consistent choices.
A standard enforced by law (a de jure obligation standard) is instead a solution to a prisoner's-dilemma-type problem.

Such standards tend to be stable where everyone gains, but only by making mutually consistent choices. A standard enforced by law, called a de jure obligation standard, solves a different problem. That problem is shaped like the prisoner's dilemma.

entries.title: Finitely repeated games: how a known end unravels cooperation

definition.text: A repeated game played for a fixed, known number of rounds, with each player's total payoff the sum over all rounds.

facts.text: If the stage game has a single Nash equilibrium, players play it in every round: reasoning backward from the last round unravels any cooperation.
A known, finite end therefore undermines cooperation in every round; cooperation is possible only when the number of rounds is infinite or unknown.
If the stage game has several equilibria, the threat of switching to a worse one later can support cooperation in earlier rounds.

entries.text: In a finitely repeated game, players repeat a game a fixed, known number of times, and each player's total payoff is the sum over all rounds. A known end is corrosive. If the stage game has a single Nash equilibrium, players play it in every round. Reasoning backward from the last round unravels any cooperation, so cooperation is possible only when the number of rounds is infinite or unknown. The picture changes if the stage game has several equilibria. Then the threat of switching to a worse one later can support cooperation in earlier rounds.

entries.title: Trigger strategies: cooperate until crossed

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates until the other player deviates and then punishes them with play that lowers both players' payoffs.

facts.text: Knowing the other follows a trigger strategy, a player expects lower future payoffs if they act selfishly now.
An effective trigger makes cooperating worth more than grabbing a gain now and suffering punishment later.
The harshest form, grim trigger, punishes forever and is used to prove the folk theorem.

Knowing this, a player expects lower future payoffs if they act selfishly now. An effective trigger makes cooperating worth more than grabbing a gain now and suffering punishment later. entries.title: The disagreement point: what happens if talks fail

definition.text: The payoffs the bargaining parties can expect if negotiations break down.

facts.text: It might be a focal equilibrium both expect to play, or zero if no agreement is reached.
Since it shapes the final deal, each side gains by raising its own fallback payoff and lowering the other's, which is why it is also called the threat point.

entries.text: Every negotiation has a fallback: the payoffs the parties can expect if talks break down. Game theorists call it the disagreement point. It might be a focal equilibrium both sides expect to play, or zero if no agreement is reached. Because it shapes the final deal, each side gains by raising its own fallback payoff and lowering the other's. That is why it is also called the threat point.

entries.title: The egalitarian bargaining solution: equal gains for both

definition.text: A bargaining rule, introduced by Ehud Kalai, that gives both parties equal gains by maximizing the smaller of their payoffs.

facts.text: It drops scale invariance but keeps independence of irrelevant alternatives and resource monotonicity.
Kalai notes its closeness to the egalitarian ideas of John Rawls.

entries.text: Ehud Kalai introduced a simple rule for splitting a bargain: give both parties equal gains, by maximizing the smaller of their payoffs. Compared with the Nash bargaining solution, it drops scale invariance, the requirement that changing the units of payoffs leaves the deal unchanged. It keeps independence of irrelevant alternatives and resource monotonicity, the requirement that no one loses when there is more to share. Kalai notes its closeness to the egalitarian ideas of John Rawls.

entries.title: The Kalai–Smorodinsky solution: gains in proportion

definition.text: A bargaining rule that replaces Nash's independence axiom with resource monotonicity and keeps the players' gains in the same ratio as their maximum possible gains.

facts.text: With the disagreement point at zero, it picks the efficient point whose payoffs stand in the ratio of each player's best achievable gain.

entries.text: The Kalai–Smorodinsky bargaining solution replaces Nash's independence axiom with resource monotonicity. Its rule is proportional: keep the players' gains in the same ratio as their maximum possible gains. With the disagreement point at zero, it picks the efficient point whose payoffs stand in the ratio of each player's best achievable gain. A player who could hope for more therefore receives more.

entries.title: The Nash demand game: ask too much and lose everything

definition.text: A simple two-player game in which each player demands a share of a good and both get their demands only if the total does not exceed what is available.

facts.text: It has many Nash equilibria: any pair of demands that exactly adds up to the whole is one.
Both players demanding everything is also an equilibrium, though both get nothing.
When uncertainty about feasible payoffs vanishes, its equilibrium payoffs converge to the Nash bargaining solution.

entries.text: Two players each demand a share of a good. Both get their demands only if the total does not exceed what is available. When uncertainty about feasible payoffs vanishes, its equilibrium payoffs converge to the Nash bargaining solution.

entries.title: The Rubinstein model: bargaining over a shrinking pie

definition.text: A bargaining game in which the players take turns proposing how to split a surplus that shrinks with every round of delay.

facts.text: Its single subgame perfect equilibrium division depends on how strongly players prefer payoffs now over later.
With the surplus set to 1 and discount factor d, player 1 gets 1/(1+d) and player 2 gets d/(1+d).
As players become perfectly patient, the split converges to the Nash bargaining solution.

entries.text: In the Rubinstein bargaining model, players take turns proposing how to split a surplus, and the surplus shrinks with every round of delay. The model has a single subgame perfect equilibrium, and its division depends on how strongly players prefer payoffs now over later. That preference is captured by a discount factor d, the value today of a payoff one round away. With the surplus set to 1, player 1 gets 1/(1+d) and player 2 gets d/(1+d). As players become perfectly patient, the split converges to the Nash bargaining solution.

entries.title: Perfect and imperfect information: who saw what

definition.text: A game has perfect information when every player always knows everything that has happened so far, and imperfect information when some earlier move is hidden.

facts.text: Moves may be unobserved because they are simultaneous or hidden.
A game with any information set of more than one node has imperfect information.
An information set is drawn as a dotted line or a loop joining the nodes the player cannot tell apart.

entries.text: In some games every player always knows everything that has happened so far. Those games have perfect information. If some earlier move is hidden, because moves are simultaneous or simply unobserved, the game has imperfect information. On a game tree, the decision points a player cannot tell apart are joined by a dotted line or a loop, forming an {{ref:nature-econ-679}}. Any game in which such a set contains more than one decision point has imperfect information.

entries.title: The Harsanyi transformation: letting Nature choose the types

definition.text: The device of turning a game of incomplete information, where players do not know others' payoffs or types, into one of complete but imperfect information by letting Nature choose the types.

facts.text: For example, Nature might pick a job applicant's ability as low with probability 1/3 or high with probability 2/3, and the employer does not see the pick.
Nature has no payoffs and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.

entries.text: What if players do not know each other's payoffs or types? The Harsanyi transformation adds Nature as a player who chooses the types at the start. A game of incomplete information then becomes one of complete but imperfect information. For example, Nature might pick a job applicant's ability as low with probability 1/3 or high with probability 2/3, and the employer does not see the pick. Nature has no payoffs, and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.

entries.title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium: best play given beliefs

definition.text: The Nash equilibrium of a Bayesian game, in which each player's strategy maximizes their expected payoff given their beliefs about others' types and the others' strategies.

facts.text: Players form their beliefs about the unknown state of nature using Bayes' rule.
In dynamic games where players move in turn, it can produce implausible equilibria based on non-credible strategies or beliefs.
In mechanism design, a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which everyone reports their true preferences makes a mechanism incentive compatible.

entries.text: In a Bayesian game, players do not know each other's types. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is that game's Nash equilibrium. Each player's strategy maximizes their expected payoff, given their beliefs about others' types and the others' strategies. Players form those beliefs about the unknown state of nature using Bayes' rule, a formula for updating probabilities with new evidence. In dynamic games where players move in turn, it can produce implausible equilibria based on non-credible strategies or beliefs. It also matters in designing rules and institutions: if everyone's best play is to report their true preferences, the mechanism is called incentive compatible.

entries.title: Information sets: not knowing where you stand

definition.text: A group of a player's decision points that the player cannot tell apart, so they do not know which one they are at.

facts.text: In game trees information sets are usually drawn with dotted lines.
Chance moves are made by 'Nature', usually shown as an unfilled circle at the root of the tree.

entries.text: Sometimes a player must move without knowing exactly what has happened. An information set is the group of that player's decision points that they cannot tell apart, so they do not know which one they are at. In game trees, information sets are usually drawn with dotted lines. Chance moves are made by 'Nature', usually shown as an unfilled circle at the root of the tree.

entries.title: Behavior strategies: randomizing step by step

definition.text: A strategy that randomizes separately at each information set over the actions available there, rather than over whole plans.

facts.text: A mixed strategy randomly picks a fixed path through the game tree, while a behavior strategy takes a random path.
Kuhn's theorem shows the two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions.
The Absent-Minded Driver game shows why perfect recall is needed for this equivalence.

entries.text: A mixed strategy randomly picks a fixed path through the game tree. A behavior strategy instead takes a random path, randomizing separately at each information set over the actions available there. Kuhn's theorem shows the two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions. The Absent-Minded Driver game shows why perfect recall is needed for this equivalence.

entries.title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium: consistent beliefs, optimal moves

definition.text: An equilibrium of a sequential game with incomplete information in which beliefs are consistent with the strategies and every player chooses optimally given those beliefs.

facts.text: Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it requires play to be optimal from every information set onward, ruling out non-credible threats and beliefs.

entries.text: Games with both hidden information and moves in sequence need a sharper tool. A perfect Bayesian equilibrium requires two things. Players' beliefs must be consistent with the strategies being played, and every player must choose optimally given those beliefs. Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it demands optimal play from every information set onward. That rules out non-credible threats and beliefs.

entries.title: Generous tit for tat: forgiving now and then
entries.article: Tit for tat#Generous tit for tat

definition.text: A version of tit for tat that, after the opponent defects, usually retaliates but sometimes cooperates anyway, with a small probability.

facts.text: Occasional forgiveness breaks cycles of retaliation caused by mistakes or 'noise' and restores mutual cooperation.
Axelrod found it highly effective in noisy settings; the forgiveness probability can be around 1–5%, depending on the opponents.

entries.title: Reciprocal altruism: favors returned in nature
entries.article: Tit for tat#Explaining reciprocal altruism in animal communities

definition.text: Helping another animal in the expectation that the favour will be returned when needs reverse, explained by tit-for-tat strategies.

facts.text: It works where the cost to the helper of sharing food, mates, nests or territory is less than the gain to the one helped.
Ways of spotting and punishing 'cheaters' who fail to return favours, in effect tit for tat, keep it stable.
Tit for tat has been suggested as the mechanism behind guppies' cooperative inspection of predators.

entries.title: Tit for two tats: letting one betrayal slide

definition.text: A more forgiving version of tit for tat that retaliates only after the opponent defects twice in a row.

entries.article: Evolutionary game theory#Asymmetries that allow new strategies

definition.text: An evolutionary strategy that settles contests by using some asymmetry between the rivals, such as who already holds the resource.

facts.text: It can beat a bluffing strategy in the war of attrition when such an asymmetry exists.
In the hawk–dove game, treating one player as territory owner and the other as intruder makes role-based strategies stable.

entries.title: How can altruism evolve?

definition.text: The puzzle, noted by Darwin, of how behaviour that helps another at a cost to oneself can survive natural selection, and the game-theory routes that explain it.

facts.text: If selection acts only on individuals, altruism makes no sense, yet many social animals behave altruistically.
Kin selection explains it through shared genes; Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit.
Direct reciprocity ('I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine') and indirect reciprocity are further routes.
Without some measure of reputation, only direct reciprocity can arise in the prisoner's dilemma.

entries.contested_note: Nowak and Wilson's group-selection explanation of insect eusociality challenges the kin-selection account and is described as controversial.

entries.title: Rock, paper, scissors in nature

definition.text: Evolutionary games in which each strategy beats one rival and loses to another, so the strategies' shares cycle instead of settling down.

facts.text: Male side-blotched lizards have three throat-colour types with different mating strategies that beat one another in a circle.
Together with density effects in females, this drives a four-year population cycle.
The cyclic behaviour predicted by evolutionary game theory has also been seen in human laboratory experiments.

entries.title: The characteristic function: what each coalition can earn

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the function that gives the total payoff each possible coalition of players can secure by joining together.

facts.text: A cooperative game is specified simply by giving a value for every coalition, with the empty coalition worth zero.
Characteristic functions are often assumed superadditive: two separate coalitions together are worth at least the sum of their separate values.
In a simple game every coalition is either winning (worth 1) or losing (worth 0).

entries.title: The core: deals no group wants to walk away from

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the set of allocations from which no group of players could do better by breaking away from the whole group.

facts.text: A coalition blocks an allocation if its members could create more value on their own than they are given.
The core corresponds to situations where cooperation among all players can be kept going.
The idea appeared in Edgeworth's 1881 writing as the contract curve; the modern definition is due to Donald B. Gillies and Lloyd Shapley.
The core is always well defined but can be empty; the Bondareva–Shapley theorem says it is non-empty exactly when the game is 'balanced'.
In a game of 1000 left-shoe and 1001 right-shoe owners, the core gives the scarce left-shoe owners everything and right-shoe owners nothing.
Critics note how extremely sensitive the core is to an oversupply of one type of player.
Every Walrasian (competitive market) equilibrium lies in the core, though not every core allocation is a market equilibrium.

entries.title: The Shapley value: a fair share of joint gains

definition.text: A method of fairly dividing the total gains or costs of a group effort among its members according to each one's average contribution.

facts.text: It looks at how much the result changes when a player joins every possible combination of others, then averages those changes.
Lloyd Shapley introduced it in 1951.
It is the only division satisfying efficiency, symmetry, additivity and the null-player property, widely accepted as defining fairness.
Efficiency means all the group's gain is shared out; a player who adds nothing to any coalition gets zero.
If cooperation creates positive synergy, every member gains at least what they could get alone.
It is used to divide business profits and to measure each feature's importance in machine-learning models and sensitivity analysis.

facts.text: Convex games are totally balanced: their core, and the core of every subgame, is non-empty.
Similar results for submodular functions appear in combinatorial optimization.

definition.text: The extra surplus a coalition creates beyond what its smaller sub-coalitions already create.

facts.text: John Harsanyi used it in 1963 to generalize the Shapley value.

entries.title: The nucleolus: shrinking the loudest complaint

definition.text: The allocation of a cooperative game that makes the largest complaints of coalitions, measured by what each could gain by leaving, as small as possible.

facts.text: The nucleolus is always unique.
If the core is non-empty, the nucleolus lies inside it.

entries.title: Stable sets: the first answer for many-player coalitions

definition.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern solution: the first solution concept proposed for cooperative games with more than two players, built on which allocations a coalition would object to.

facts.text: One allocation dominates another if some coalition prefers it and could obtain at least its members' payoffs on its own.
A stable set may not exist, is usually not unique and is hard to find, which spurred the development of other solution concepts.
The core is contained in every stable set.

definition.text: A coordination game with conflicting interests: both players prefer doing the same thing over going alone but disagree on which thing to do.

facts.text: The standard story is a couple arguing over what to do at the weekend.
A round of cheap talk before play may let the players pick one of its several equilibria and earn more than without communication.

entries.title: Credible threats: would you really do it?

definition.text: A threat a player would actually want to carry out if the time came; a non-credible threat is one that would hurt the player making it.

facts.text: Plain Nash equilibrium can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfection eliminates them.
In Chicken, a player who rips out their steering wheel always wins, because the opponent's threat to crash anyway is not credible.
If punishing a deviator is costly to the punishers, the threat of punishment is not credible.

entries.title: Brinkmanship: the deliberate risk of losing control

definition.text: In game theory, a strategic move that deters an opponent from turning aggressive by credibly threatening a risk of irrational retaliation.

facts.text: The threat works only if the opponent believes there is enough risk of an irrational response, often because the threatener has given up control over it.
In everyday talk of conflict 'chicken' and 'brinkmanship' are often used as synonyms.

A protester who handcuffs themselves to an object is a real-world example: no threat can make them move.

entries.title: Optimization: the mathematics of choosing the best

definition.text: Choosing the best option, judged by some criterion, from a set of available alternatives.

facts.text: Typically it means maximizing or minimizing a function by choosing inputs from an allowed set.
It splits into discrete optimization, where the answer comes from a countable set such as whole numbers, and continuous optimization.
Optimization problems arise in every quantitative field, from engineering to operations research and economics.
An influential definition calls economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses.
Consumers are usually assumed to maximize utility and firms to maximize profit; utility maximization and its dual, expenditure minimization, are standard examples.
Since the 1970s economists have modelled decisions over time with control theory.
Fermat and Lagrange found calculus-based formulas for optima, while Newton and Gauss proposed step-by-step methods for moving towards one.
The 'programming' in linear programming comes from the US military's word for training and logistics schedules, not computer programming.

entries.text: Every economic choice is a hunt for the best option among those on offer. One influential definition calls economics the study of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Mathematical optimization is the formal version of that hunt: choosing the best option, judged by some criterion, from a set of available alternatives. In practice it usually means making a function as large or as small as possible by choosing inputs from an allowed set. A function here is simply a rule that turns inputs into an output. Some problems are discrete, with the answer drawn from a countable set such as the whole numbers. Others are continuous. Economists lean on optimization constantly. Consumers are usually assumed to maximize utility and firms to maximize profit. Utility maximization has a mirror-image twin, expenditure minimization, and both are standard examples. Since the 1970s economists have also modeled decisions that unfold over time with control theory. The tools are old. Fermat and Lagrange found calculus-based formulas for the best point, while Newton and Gauss proposed step-by-step methods for moving toward one. Optimization problems now arise in every quantitative field, from engineering to operations research. entries.title: The derivative: how fast things change right now

definition.text: A measure of how sensitive a function's output is to a small change in its input; for a single variable it is the slope of the tangent line at a point.

facts.text: It is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and finding it is called differentiation.
The tangent line it defines is the best straight-line approximation of the function near that point.
Formally, it is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero.
A function must be continuous at a point to have a derivative there; a step jump has none.
Rules for sums, products and compositions let derivatives of complex functions be built from those of simple ones.
Leibniz notation, dy/dx, was introduced by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1675.
In economics, short-run marginal cost is the slope, or first derivative, of the variable cost curve.

entries.text: How fast is something changing at this exact moment? The derivative answers that question. It measures how sensitive a function's output is to a small change in its input. For a function of one variable, it is the slope of the tangent line at a point, the straight line that just grazes the curve there. That tangent is the best straight-line approximation of the function near the point. The derivative is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and finding it is called differentiation. Formally, it is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero. A function must be continuous at a point to have a derivative there, so a sudden step jump has none. Rules for sums, products and compositions let the derivative of a complicated function be built from those of simple pieces. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz introduced the notation still used today, dy/dx, in 1675. Economists use the idea all the time. Short-run marginal cost is the slope, or first derivative, of the variable cost curve.
entries.text_plain: How fast is something changing at this exact moment? The derivative answers that question. It measures how sensitive a function's output is to a small change in its input. For a function of one variable, it is the slope of the tangent line at a point, the straight line that just grazes the curve there. That tangent is the best straight-line approximation of the function near the point. The derivative is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and finding it is called differentiation. Formally, it is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero. A function must be continuous at a point to have a derivative there, so a sudden step jump has none. Rules for sums, products and compositions let the derivative of a complicated function be built from those of simple pieces. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz introduced the notation still used today, dy/dx, in 1675. Economists use the idea all the time. Short-run marginal cost is the slope, or first derivative, of the variable cost curve.

entries.title: Differential equations: laws written as rates of change

definition.text: An equation that links one or more unknown functions to their derivatives, that is, to their rates of change.

facts.text: Such relations are common in scientific models, so differential equations are prominent in engineering, physics, economics and biology.
Only the simplest can be solved by explicit formulas, but many properties of the solutions can be found without solving them exactly.
When no formula exists, solutions can be approximated numerically on computers.
The theory of dynamical systems studies qualitative features of the solutions, such as their average long-run behaviour.
They arose with the invention of calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz; Newton listed three kinds in a 1671 work.
They are used to model almost every physical, technical or biological process, from celestial motion to bridge design to neurons.
Complex adaptive systems may have so many elements that a system of differential equations becomes impractical and stops helping understanding.

These equations arose with the invention of calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz, and Newton listed three kinds in a 1671 work. Today they model almost every physical, technical or biological process, from celestial motion to bridge design to neurons. Because such relations run through scientific models, differential equations are prominent in engineering, physics, economics and biology. The catch is that only the simplest can be solved by an explicit formula. Many properties of the solutions can still be found without solving them exactly. There are limits, though. A system of many interacting, adapting parts may have so many elements that a system of differential equations becomes impractical and stops helping anyone understand it.

entries.title: Exponential growth: the bigger it gets, the faster it grows

definition.text: Growth in which a quantity increases at a rate proportional to its current size, so the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.

facts.text: Something three times bigger is growing three times as fast; a bacterium splitting into 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32 is the usual illustration.
Exponential growth is not the same as rapid growth: it can be slow at first.
Economic growth is stated in percentages, implying exponential growth, and compound interest at a constant rate grows capital exponentially.
A bacterium that doubles every ten minutes becomes 64 bacteria after one hour.
If the constant of proportionality is negative, the quantity shrinks instead, which is exponential decay.
Over the long run, exponential growth overtakes any linear growth, which is the basis of the Malthusian catastrophe.
Malthus warned that population growing geometrically, doubling every 25 years, would outrun food production growing arithmetically.
Real exponential growth rarely lasts: external limits eventually slow it into logistic growth.

entries.title: Constrained optimization: the best choice within limits

definition.text: Finding the best value of an objective, such as a cost to minimize or a utility to maximize, when the choice variables must obey constraints.

facts.text: Hard constraints must be met; soft constraints may be broken, but each violation is penalized in the objective in proportion to how far it goes.
Consumer theory models a buyer's demand on the hypothesis of constrained optimization.
In a typical consumption model over time, discounted utility is maximized subject to a budget constraint that present-value spending cannot exceed present-value resources.
With only equality constraints, Lagrange multipliers turn the problem into an unconstrained one with one extra variable per constraint.
With inequality constraints, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions generalize Lagrange multipliers and apply under differentiability and convexity.
If the objective and all constraints are linear, the problem is linear programming; if any are nonlinear, it is nonlinear programming.

entries.text: Nobody gets to choose without limits. Constrained optimization finds the best value of an objective, such as a cost to minimize or a utility to maximize. The catch is that the choices must obey constraints, rules they cannot break. It is {{ref:nature-econ-461}} with fences. Hard constraints must be met. Soft constraints may be broken, but each violation is penalized in the objective in proportion to how far it goes. Consumer theory models a buyer's demand on exactly this hypothesis, with the {{ref:nature-econ-102}} as the fence. In a typical model of spending over time, discounted utility is maximized subject to one rule: the present value of spending cannot exceed the present value of resources. Mathematicians have a tool for each case. With only equality constraints, {{ref:nature-econ-455}} turns the problem into an unconstrained one, with one extra variable per constraint. With inequality constraints, the {{ref:nature-econ-452}} generalize that method, provided the functions are smooth and suitably bowl-shaped. If the objective and all constraints are linear, the problem is {{ref:nature-econ-456}}. If any of them are nonlinear, it is {{ref:nature-econ-425}}.

entries.title: Convex functions: why cup-shaped curves are easy to optimize

definition.text: A function whose graph lies on or below the straight line joining any two of its points, so the graph is cup-shaped; a concave function is cap-shaped.

facts.text: A twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex exactly when its second derivative is never negative.
Linear functions, quadratics like cx² with c not negative, and exponentials like ceˣ with c not negative are convex.
Convexity makes optimization easier: any local minimum of a convex function is also a global minimum, and a strictly convex function on an open set has at most one minimum.
A function f is convex exactly when its negative, −f, is concave.
Jensen's inequality: a convex function of an average is never more than the average of the convex function's values.
In consumer theory, a diminishing marginal rate of substitution along an indifference curve means preferences are convex.
Demand curves are generally considered convex, in line with diminishing marginal utility.

entries.text: A convex function is one whose graph lies on or below the straight line joining any two of its points, so the graph is cup-shaped. A concave function is cap-shaped, and a function f is convex exactly when its negative, −f, is concave. For a smooth function of one variable, convexity means the second derivative, the rate of change of the slope, is never negative ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Linear functions, quadratics like cx² with c not negative, and exponentials like ceˣ with c not negative are all convex. Any local minimum of a convex function, a low point in its own neighborhood, is also the global minimum. Jensen's inequality adds that a convex function of an average is never more than the average of the function's values. Economists meet the idea constantly. A diminishing marginal rate of substitution along an indifference curve means preferences are convex, and demand curves are generally considered convex, in line with diminishing marginal utility.

entries.title: Linear programming: planning with straight-line rules

definition.text: A method for finding the best outcome, such as maximum profit or lowest cost, in a model where the goal and all the requirements are linear relationships.

facts.text: It optimizes a linear objective subject to linear equality and inequality constraints, and is a special case of mathematical optimization.
Its feasible region is a convex polytope, the shape cut out by the linear inequalities.
Example: a farmer with limited land, fertilizer and pesticide chooses how many hectares of wheat and barley to plant to maximize revenue.
Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief independently explored its practical uses in the late 1930s; Kantorovich and T. C. Koopmans shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
George B. Dantzig developed the general formulation in 1946–1947 for US Air Force planning and invented the simplex method in 1947.
It was heavily used in the early formation of microeconomics and helped inspire key ideas in optimization such as duality and the importance of convexity.
The earliest precursor of William Nordhaus's DICE climate-economy model was a linear programming model of energy supply and demand from 1977.

entries.text: A farmer with limited land, fertilizer and pesticide must choose how many hectares of wheat and barley to plant for the most revenue. Linear programming finds the best outcome, such as maximum profit or lowest cost, when the goal and all the requirements are linear relationships, with no curves. It is a special case of {{ref:nature-econ-423}}. The inequalities cut out the set of allowed choices, a many-sided shape called a convex polytope. Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief independently explored its practical uses in the late 1930s. Kantorovich later shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with T. C. Koopmans. George B. Dantzig developed the general formulation in 1946–1947 for US Air Force planning and invented the {{ref:nature-econ-457}} in 1947. The method shaped early microeconomics and helped inspire key ideas in optimization, such as {{ref:nature-econ-438}} and the importance of convexity. The earliest precursor of the DICE climate-economy model built by {{ref:nature-hist-050}} was a linear programming model of energy supply and demand from 1977.

entries.title: Discrete and continuous time: steps or a smooth flow

definition.text: Two alternative ways of modelling variables that change over time: as values in separate periods, or as values at every instant.

facts.text: Discrete time treats a variable as fixed within each period and jumping between periods, like a digital clock jumping from 10:37 to 10:38.
Continuous time lets time range over the real numbers, so there are infinitely many moments between any two points in time.
Economic activity happens continuously but can only be measured in steps, so GDP data come as a series of quarterly values.
Discrete time suits empirical work and time series models, while continuous-time theoretical models are often easier to handle mathematically.
Discrete time uses difference equations; continuous time uses differential equations.
Total discounted utility from a stream of consumption is a sum in discrete time and an integral in continuous time.

entries.text: A digital clock jumps from 10:37 to 10:38 with nothing in between. That is discrete time: a variable is fixed within each period and jumps between periods. Continuous time instead lets time range over the real numbers, so infinitely many moments lie between any two points in time. Economists use both. Economic activity happens continuously but can only be measured in steps, which is why GDP data come as a series of quarterly values. Discrete time suits empirical work and time series models. Continuous-time theoretical models are often easier to handle mathematically. Each comes with its own tools: discrete time uses {{ref:nature-econ-436}}, while continuous time uses differential equations. The total discounted utility from a stream of consumption is a sum in discrete time and an integral, a continuous sum, in continuous time.

entries.title: Steady state: when everything flows but nothing changes

definition.text: The condition of a system whose defining variables are not changing over time.

facts.text: In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero.
Many systems pass through a transient, warm-up period before reaching steady state, and often only approach it gradually.
A reservoir in a biogeochemical box model is in steady state when its sources balance its sinks.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, the steady state is reached when gross investment in physical capital equals depreciation.
Exogenous growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero per-capita growth.
A steady-state economy has a stable population and stable consumption at or below carrying capacity.
An unstable system moves away from its steady state.

entries.text: A system is in steady state when its defining variables are not changing over time. Things may still flow through it, but nothing builds up or runs down. In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero ({{ref:nature-econ-437}}). Many systems pass through a transient, warm-up period first, and often only approach steady state gradually. In a simple model that tracks an element moving between stores in the environment, a store is in steady state when its sources balance its sinks. Economics uses the same idea. In the Solow–Swan growth model, the steady state arrives when gross investment in physical capital equals depreciation, the wearing out of existing capital. Growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero growth per person. In the sense of {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}, an economy in steady state has a stable population and stable consumption at or below {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. Not every steady state holds, though: an unstable system moves away from it.

Growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero growth per person. In the sense of The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth, an economy in steady state has a stable population and stable consumption at or below Carrying capacity: how many any place can feed. Not every steady state holds, though: an unstable system moves away from it.

entries.title: Calculus of variations: finding the best whole curve

definition.text: A branch of mathematics that finds the functions which make a quantity defined over whole functions, called a functional, as large or as small as possible.

facts.text: A functional maps a whole function to a single number, so functionals have been described as functions of functions; they are often written as definite integrals.
A simple example is finding the shortest curve joining two points; with no constraints the answer is a straight line.
Just as a function's maxima and minima lie where its derivative is zero, a functional's extrema are found where its functional derivative is zero, which leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation.
The field began with Isaac Newton's minimal resistance problem, solved in 1685, and his 1697 solution of the brachistochrone problem.
In economics, optimization over time has used the calculus of variations, following Frank P. Ramsey and Harold Hotelling.

entries.title: Computable general equilibrium: modeling a whole economy

definition.text: A class of economic models that use real economic data to estimate how a whole economy might respond to changes in policy, technology or other outside factors.

facts.text: A CGE model is a set of equations plus a detailed database consistent with them, usually assuming cost-minimizing producers and optimizing households.
They estimate how a change in one part of the economy spreads to the rest: a tax on flour might affect bread prices, the CPI, and then wages and employment.
Unlike input–output models, from which they descend, they let prices matter, so a wage rise can change how much labour is used to make bread.
They have been used widely for trade policy and, more recently, to estimate the economic effects of cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
For climate policy they can show gains and losses across groups, such as households with different incomes or in different regions.
Many are comparative static, comparing the economy with and without a policy shock at one future point, without modelling the adjustment path.
They are useful where time-series data are scarce, so developing economies are often analysed with them.
Most are now built in the GAMS or GEMPACK software systems, which lowered costs and made models more transparent and replicable.

entries.text: A tax on flour might raise bread prices, lift the consumer price index, and then ripple into wages and employment. Computable general equilibrium (CGE) models trace such chains. They use real economic data to estimate how a whole economy might respond to changes in policy, technology or other outside factors. A CGE model is a set of equations plus a detailed database consistent with them, usually assuming cost-minimizing producers and optimizing households ({{ref:nature-econ-382}}). Their ancestor is the {{ref:nature-acct-080}}, but unlike it they let prices matter, so a wage rise can change how much labor is used to make bread. They have been used widely for trade policy and, more recently, to estimate the economic effects of cutting the gases that warm the climate. For climate policy they can show gains and losses across households with different incomes or in different regions. Many are comparative static: they compare the economy with and without a policy shock at one future point, without modeling the path between. They work where time-series data are scarce, so developing economies are often analyzed with them.

entries.title: Partial derivatives: changing one thing at a time

definition.text: The derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one of them, holding the others fixed.

facts.text: It can be read as the function's rate of change in the direction of that one variable.
Partial derivatives measure change only along the coordinate axes; change in other directions is measured by directional derivatives.
The total derivative gives a complete picture by considering all directions at once.

entries.text: Many quantities depend on several inputs at once. A partial derivative isolates one of them. It is the derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one variable, holding the others fixed ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). It can be read as the function's rate of change in the direction of that one variable. Partial derivatives therefore measure change only along the coordinate axes. Change in other directions is measured by directional derivatives. The total derivative gives the complete view by considering all directions at once.

entries.title: Difference equations: change in separate steps

definition.text: An equation in which time or another variable takes only separate values, relating a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points.

facts.text: Difference equations, also called recurrence relations, are the discrete-time counterpart of differential equations.
Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation.
Economists can model a price adjusting to excess demand either as a difference equation or, in continuous time, as a differential equation.
The Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time logistic growth equation.

entries.text: Not everything changes smoothly. A difference equation relates a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points, when time or another variable takes only separate values. Also called recurrence relations, difference equations are the discrete-time counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-433}} ({{ref:nature-econ-437}}). The two can stand in for each other. Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation. An economist can model a price adjusting to excess demand, buyers wanting more than sellers offer, either way. Ecology has a matched pair too: the Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time equation for {{ref:nature-eco-580}}.

entries.title: Integer programming: when answers must be whole numbers

definition.text: Optimization in which some or all of the choice variables must be whole numbers.

facts.text: Usually it means integer linear programming, where the objective and other constraints are linear; if only some variables are integers it is mixed-integer programming.
Integers are used for quantities that cannot be fractional, since it is not possible to build 3.7 cars, and for yes-or-no decisions coded as 0 or 1.
An agricultural example is planning yields for several crops that share land, labour, capital, seeds and fertilizer, maximizing production without exceeding resources.
Integer programming is NP-complete, so many instances are intractable and heuristic methods such as tabu search are used.
Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of branch and bound.
Districting problems, including waste management districting, are solved this way, respecting natural boundaries and contiguity.

entries.text: It is not possible to build 3.7 cars. Integer programming handles choices like that: optimization in which some or all of the choice variables must be whole numbers. It usually means integer linear programming, where the objective and other constraints are linear ({{ref:nature-econ-456}}). If only some variables must be whole, it is mixed-integer programming. Integers also code yes-or-no decisions as 0 or 1. A farm can use it to plan yields for several crops that share land, labor, capital, seeds and fertilizer, maximizing production without exceeding resources. Districting problems, including waste management districting, are solved this way while respecting natural boundaries and contiguity. The difficulty is that integer programming is NP-complete, a class of problems with no known fast general method, so many instances are intractable. Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of {{ref:nature-econ-426}}. Heuristic shortcuts such as tabu search handle the rest.

The difficulty is that integer programming is NP-complete, a class of problems with no known fast general method, so many instances are intractable. Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of Branch and bound: pruning hopeless options early. Heuristic shortcuts such as tabu search handle the rest.

entries.title: Logistic growth: fast at first, then leveling off

definition.text: Growth that starts out exponential but slows as it approaches an upper limit set by external or environmental factors.

facts.text: Population growth, for instance, may level off at an upper limit because resources run short.
Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst first proposed this growth model in 1845.
It arises when negative feedbacks ignored in the exponential model become significant.
The discrete-time Beverton–Holt population model is the analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time logistic equation.
Pierre François Verhulst devised it between 1838 and 1847 as a model of population growth, adjusting the exponential growth model.
He wrote it after reading Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population, which describes unconstrained exponential growth.
In ecology the model is dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), where r is the growth rate and K the carrying capacity.
As the population grows, competition for critical resources slows growth until the population stops growing at K.

entries.text: Malthus described population growing without limit. The Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst read Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population and adjusted the picture. Logistic growth starts out exponential ({{ref:nature-econ-442}}) but slows as it approaches an upper limit set by external or environmental factors. A population, for instance, may level off because resources run short. Verhulst devised the model between 1838 and 1847 and first proposed it in 1845. It arises when self-limiting effects, the brakes ignored in the exponential model, become significant. In ecology it is a differential equation, dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), where P is the population, r the growth rate and K the {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. As the population grows, competition for critical resources slows growth until the population stops growing at K. The discrete-time Beverton–Holt population model is its step-by-step analogue.

entries.title: State and control variables: where things stand, what to choose
entries.article: Bellman equation#Analytical concepts in dynamic programming

definition.text: In a decision problem over time, the state is the information about the current situation needed to choose well, and the control variables are what the decision-maker chooses at each moment.

facts.text: Every optimization problem has an objective, such as minimizing cost or maximizing profit, described by a mathematical objective function.
For someone deciding how much to spend over time, wealth is a state variable and how much to consume now is a control variable.
Choosing the controls now may amount to choosing the next state, though other factors usually affect the next state as well.

entries.text: Someone deciding how much to spend over the years juggles two kinds of quantity. Wealth is the state: the information about the current situation needed to choose well. How much to consume now is the control variable: what the decision-maker chooses at each moment. Like every optimization problem ({{ref:nature-econ-461}}), this one has an objective, such as minimizing cost or maximizing profit, described by a mathematical objective function. The two kinds are tightly linked. Choosing the controls now may amount to choosing the next state, though other factors usually affect the next state as well.

entries.title: Optimal control: steering a system over time

definition.text: The branch of control theory that finds how to steer a system that changes over time so that an objective is optimized over a period.

facts.text: The system might be a spacecraft reaching the Moon on minimum fuel, or a national economy where fiscal and monetary policy are used to minimize unemployment.
It extends the calculus of variations and was developed mainly by Lev Pontryagin and Richard Bellman in the 1950s.
The optimal control can be found from Pontryagin's maximum principle, a necessary condition, or by solving the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, a sufficient condition.
Example: how should a driver press the accelerator on a hilly road to minimize travel time, given limits such as fuel and speed limits?
A classic resource example is a mine owner choosing how fast to extract ore over the period of ownership to maximize profit, when extraction costs rise with speed.
Most optimal control problems are nonlinear with no exact solution, so numerical methods are needed.
Finding the best strategy in a differential game is closely related to optimal control.

entries.text: How should a spacecraft reach the Moon on the least fuel? How should a government use fiscal and monetary policy to keep unemployment as low as possible? Both are optimal control problems. This branch of control theory finds how to steer a system that changes over time so that an objective is optimized over a whole period. It extends the {{ref:nature-econ-421}}, and Lev Pontryagin and Richard Bellman developed it mainly in the 1950s. Mining supplies a classic case. A mine owner chooses how fast to extract ore over the period of ownership to maximize profit, when extraction costs rise with speed. The best path can be found from {{ref:nature-econ-469}}, a necessary condition, or by solving the {{ref:nature-econ-470}}, a sufficient one. Most optimal control problems are nonlinear with no exact solution, so numerical methods are needed. Finding the best strategy in a differential game is a closely related task.

entries.title: Dynamic programming: solving big decisions in small steps

definition.text: A method of optimization, and a style of computer algorithm, that solves a complex problem by breaking it recursively into simpler subproblems.

facts.text: Richard Bellman developed it in the 1950s, and it is used in fields such as aerospace engineering and economics.
Decisions that span several points in time often break apart this way, even though some problems cannot.
The relation between the value of the whole problem and the values of its subproblems is called the Bellman equation.
Values are found by working backward from the last period, computing each earlier period's value from the next one.
In computer science it needs two features: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; without overlap the approach is called divide and conquer.
It is widely used in bioinformatics, for example in sequence alignment and protein folding.

entries.text: Some big decisions break neatly into small ones. Dynamic programming exploits that. It solves a complex problem by breaking it recursively into simpler subproblems, and it is both an optimization method and a style of computer algorithm. Richard Bellman developed it in the 1950s, and it is used in fields such as aerospace engineering and economics. Decisions that span several points in time often break apart this way, though some problems cannot. The relation between the value of the whole problem and the values of its pieces is called the {{ref:nature-econ-416}}. Values are found by working backward from the last period, computing each earlier period's value from the next one. Computer scientists say it needs two features, optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Without the overlap, the approach is called divide and conquer. It is widely used in bioinformatics too, for sequence alignment and protein folding.

entries.title: Multi-objective optimization: juggling goals that conflict

definition.text: Optimization with more than one goal, where conflicting goals force a trade-off.

facts.text: A design is Pareto optimal if no other design is better on one criterion without being worse on another; the best trade-offs trace out the Pareto frontier.
Choosing among Pareto optimal solutions is left to the decision-maker, because how to weigh the goals is missing information.
Portfolio optimization is an economic example of multi-objective optimization.

entries.text: Many choices chase more than one goal. Multi-objective optimization handles problems where conflicting goals force a {{ref:nature-econ-099}}. Mathematics can find that frontier, but choosing a point on it is left to the decision-maker, because how to weigh the goals is missing information. Portfolio optimization is an economic example.

entries.title: Antiderivatives: running differentiation in reverse

definition.text: A function whose derivative is a given function; it runs differentiation in reverse.

facts.text: Antiderivatives are not unique: adding any constant gives another, because a constant's derivative is zero.
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral of a function over an interval equals the difference of an antiderivative's values at the two ends, giving areas under curves.

entries.text: Differentiation can be run backward. An antiderivative of a function is another function whose derivative is the given one ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Antiderivatives are not unique: adding any constant gives another, because a constant's derivative is zero. Their great use comes from the fundamental theorem of calculus. The integral of a function over an interval equals the difference between an antiderivative's values at the two ends, and that gives the area under a curve.

The integral of a function over an interval equals the difference between an antiderivative's values at the two ends, and that gives the area under a curve.

entries.title: Higher-order derivatives: the rate of change of a rate

definition.text: The result of differentiating a function repeatedly: the derivative of the derivative is the second derivative, and so on.

facts.text: The nth derivative is the derivative of the (n−1)th derivative.
The sign of the second derivative tells whether a function is convex: a twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex when it is never negative.

entries.text: A derivative is itself a function, so it can be differentiated again ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Repeating the process gives higher-order derivatives. The derivative of the derivative is the second derivative, and the nth derivative is the derivative of the (n−1)th. The second derivative carries a useful message about shape. A twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex exactly when its second derivative is never negative ({{ref:nature-econ-427}}).

The derivative of the derivative is the second derivative, and the nth derivative is the derivative of the (n−1)th. The second derivative carries a useful message about shape. A twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex exactly when its second derivative is never negative (Convex functions: why cup-shaped curves are easy to optimize).

entries.title: Optimality conditions: testing whether an answer is best

definition.text: The tests a candidate solution must pass: first-order conditions set the derivative to zero, and second-order conditions tell maxima from minima.

facts.text: By one of Fermat's theorems, optima of unconstrained problems lie at stationary points, where the first derivative or gradient is zero.
More generally, optima can also lie where the derivative is undefined or on the boundary of the choice set.
The first derivative test cannot tell a minimum from a maximum; checking the second derivative, or the Hessian matrix, can.
Weierstrass's extreme value theorem says a continuous function on a compact set reaches both a maximum and a minimum.

entries.text: How can anyone tell that a candidate answer really is the best? Optimality conditions are the tests it must pass. By one of Fermat's theorems, the best points of an unconstrained problem lie at stationary points, where the first derivative, or gradient, is zero. There the curve is momentarily flat. Setting the derivative to zero is the first-order condition. More generally, the best point can also sit where the derivative is undefined, or on the boundary of the choice set. A flat spot could be a peak or a valley, and the first derivative cannot tell which. Second-order conditions can. Checking the second derivative ({{ref:nature-econ-431}}), or its many-variable version, the Hessian matrix, tells maxima from minima. Weierstrass's extreme value theorem guarantees there is something to find. A continuous function on a compact set, one that is closed and bounded, reaches both a maximum and a minimum.

entries.title: Lagrange multipliers: pricing the constraints

definition.text: A method for finding the highest or lowest value of a function when the choice variables must satisfy one or more equations exactly.

facts.text: It is named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange.
It turns a constrained problem into one where the ordinary derivative test for unconstrained problems can be used, through a new function called the Lagrangian.
At a constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is a linear combination of the constraints' gradients.
Each multiplier measures how fast the optimized quantity changes as its constraint is relaxed.
In economic models such as general equilibrium, consumers maximize utility and firms maximize profit under budget and production constraints, usually solved with Lagrange multipliers.
In optimal control, the multipliers become costate variables in Pontryagin's maximum principle.
The principle of maximum entropy used in cost–benefit analysis under uncertainty also relies on Lagrange multipliers.

entries.text: Named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange, this method finds the highest or lowest value of a function when the choices must satisfy one or more equations exactly. Its trick is a new function, the Lagrangian, that folds the constraints into the objective. The ordinary derivative test for unconstrained problems then works ({{ref:nature-econ-462}}). At the constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is a linear combination of the constraints' gradients. Each multiplier also carries economic meaning. It measures how fast the optimized quantity changes as its constraint is relaxed. That is why economists reach for the method so often. In general equilibrium models, consumers maximize utility and firms maximize profit under budget and production constraints, usually solved with Lagrange multipliers. In optimal control the multipliers turn into the time-varying values of {{ref:nature-econ-466}}.
