entries.title: The Hamiltonian: a compass for optimal control

definition.text: A function built to solve an optimal control problem, combining the objective with the equations that describe how the system's state changes.

facts.text: Lev Pontryagin developed it as part of his maximum principle; it was inspired by, but differs from, the Hamiltonian of classical mechanics.
Pontryagin proved that a necessary condition for optimal control is that the control be chosen to optimize the Hamiltonian at each moment.
It works like a Lagrangian in static optimization, except that its multipliers, called costate variables, change over time.
The state and costate equations together form a two-point boundary value problem, with conditions at the start and end times.
It can be seen as a device for generating the first-order necessary conditions of a dynamic optimization problem.
A sufficient condition for a maximum is that the Hamiltonian be concave at the solution.

entries.text: Lev Pontryagin needed one function that could guide a system steered over time. The Hamiltonian is that function. It is built to solve an {{ref:nature-econ-465}} problem, combining the objective with the equations that describe how the system's state changes. It was inspired by, but differs from, the Hamiltonian of classical mechanics. It works like a Lagrangian in static optimization ({{ref:nature-econ-455}}), except that its multipliers change over time ({{ref:nature-econ-466}}). Pontryagin proved a necessary condition for optimal control: the control must be chosen to optimize the Hamiltonian at each moment. The equations for the state and for those multipliers together form a two-point boundary value problem, with conditions at both the start and end times. In effect, the Hamiltonian is a device for generating the first-order conditions of a dynamic problem. A sufficient condition for a maximum is that the Hamiltonian be concave at the solution.

entries.title: Duality: every optimization problem has a mirror image

definition.text: The principle that any optimization problem can be viewed from two sides, the original (primal) problem or a matching dual problem.

facts.text: If the primal is a minimization problem, the dual is a maximization problem, and vice versa.
Any feasible value of the primal minimization is at least as large as any feasible value of the dual, so each bounds the other.
The usual Lagrangian dual adds the constraints to the objective using non-negative Lagrange multipliers, which become the dual variables.
Each constraint in an optimization problem has a shadow price, or dual variable.
In microeconomics, minimizing the spending needed to reach a level of happiness is the dual of maximizing utility.
John von Neumann conjectured the duality theorem of linear programming, drawing on his game theory; Albert W. Tucker's group published the first rigorous proofs in 1948.

entries.text: Every optimization problem has a twin. Duality is the principle that any such problem can be viewed from two sides: the original, or primal, problem and a matching dual problem. If the primal is a minimization, the dual is a maximization, and vice versa. The two bound each other. Any feasible value of a primal minimization is at least as large as any feasible value of its dual. The usual dual adds the constraints to the objective using non-negative Lagrange multipliers ({{ref:nature-econ-455}}), which become the dual variables. Each constraint thus has its own dual variable, which later chapters meet as a {{ref:nature-val-017}}. Microeconomics has a famous pair: minimizing the spending needed to reach a level of happiness is the dual of maximizing utility. John von Neumann conjectured the duality theorem of linear programming, drawing on his game theory. Albert W. Tucker's group published the first rigorous proofs in 1948.

entries.title: Initial conditions: where a system starts
entries.article: Differential equation#Initial conditions and boundary conditions

definition.text: Extra information, such as a system's starting values, needed to pin down which of a differential equation's many solutions applies.

facts.text: The general solution of an nth-order ordinary differential equation contains n undetermined constants.
For a moving particle, the initial conditions are usually its position and velocity at the starting time.

entries.text: A differential equation usually has many solutions, not one. The general solution of an nth-order ordinary differential equation, one with derivatives up to the nth, contains n undetermined constants. Initial conditions are the extra information, such as a system's starting values, that pin down which solution applies ({{ref:nature-econ-433}}). For a moving particle, they are usually its position and velocity at the starting time.

entries.title: Kinds of differential equations and why they matter

definition.text: The main ways differential equations are classified: ordinary or partial, linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or not, and by order.

facts.text: An ordinary differential equation has an unknown function of one variable; a partial differential equation has unknown functions of several variables and their partial derivatives.
Linear differential equations have a well-developed theory, while few nonlinear ones can be solved exactly and they can behave chaotically over long times.
The order is the highest derivative that appears; equations describing nature usually have only first and second derivatives.
The class of an equation helps guide the choice of solution method.

entries.text: Differential equations come in families, and the family helps guide the choice of solution method ({{ref:nature-econ-433}}). An ordinary differential equation has an unknown function of one variable. A partial differential equation has unknown functions of several variables and their partial derivatives ({{ref:nature-econ-430}}). The order is the highest derivative that appears; equations describing nature usually have only first and second derivatives. Equations are also linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or not. Linear ones have a well-developed theory. Few nonlinear ones can be solved exactly, and they can behave chaotically over long times.

entries.title: Strongly convex functions: a guaranteed single lowest point

definition.text: A convex function that curves upward at least as fast as a quadratic, a stronger condition than strict convexity.

facts.text: Every strongly convex function is strictly convex, but not the other way round.
A strongly convex function has a unique global minimum.
x² is strongly convex, while eˣ is strictly but not strongly convex, because its second derivative can come arbitrarily close to zero.

entries.text: Some convex functions curve upward more firmly than others. A strongly convex function curves upward at least as fast as a quadratic, a stronger condition than strict convexity ({{ref:nature-econ-427}}). Every strongly convex function is strictly convex, but not the other way round. A familiar pair shows the difference. The function x² is strongly convex. The function eˣ is strictly but not strongly convex, because its second derivative can come arbitrarily close to zero ({{ref:nature-econ-431}}). The reward for the stronger condition is certainty: a strongly convex function has a unique global minimum.

entries.title: Exponential growth bias: why doubling fools the mind

definition.text: The human tendency to underestimate how quickly compounding processes grow.

facts.text: Studies show people find exponential growth hard to grasp, and the bias can have financial consequences.
In the rice-on-a-chessboard legend, doubling the grains on each square demands over a million grains by the 21st square and more than a trillion by the 41st.
In the water lily riddle, a plant doubling daily covers half the pond on day 29, leaving only one day to save it.

entries.text: A water lily doubles its size every day and covers half the pond on day 29. That leaves only one day to save the pond. The riddle captures exponential growth bias, the human tendency to underestimate how quickly compounding processes grow ({{ref:nature-econ-442}}). The legend of rice on a chessboard makes the same point. Doubling the grains on each square demands over a million grains by the 21st square and more than a trillion by the 41st. Studies show people find exponential growth hard to grasp, and the bias can have financial consequences.

entries.title: Log-linear growth: turning curves into straight lines

definition.text: Rewriting exponential growth so that the logarithm of the growing quantity rises in a straight line over time.

facts.text: This lets an exponentially growing variable be modelled with a log-linear model.
To estimate a growth rate from data over time, one can run a linear regression of log x on time.

entries.text: A quantity growing exponentially traces an ever-steepening curve ({{ref:nature-econ-442}}). Taking its logarithm, the power to which a fixed base must be raised to reach it, straightens that curve out. A log-linear growth model rewrites exponential growth so that the logarithm of the growing quantity rises in a straight line over time. This lets an exponentially growing variable be modeled with a simple log-linear model. To estimate a growth rate from data, one can fit a straight line through the logarithm of the quantity, log x, plotted against time.

entries.title: The simplex algorithm: walking the corners to the best answer

definition.text: George Dantzig's 1947 method for linear programming, which starts at a corner of the feasible region and walks along its edges to better corners until it reaches the optimum.

facts.text: Dantzig's original example, assigning 70 people to 70 jobs, has more possible arrangements than particles in the observable universe, yet the simplex method solves it in a moment.
Khachiyan's 1979 ellipsoid method was the first worst-case polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming, though simplex remained faster in practice.
Today good simplex and interior-point implementations are thought to be similarly efficient for routine problems.

entries.text: Assigning 70 people to 70 jobs sounds simple. The possible arrangements outnumber the particles in the observable universe, yet the simplex algorithm solves the problem in a moment. George Dantzig devised the method for {{ref:nature-econ-456}} in 1947. It starts at a corner of the feasible region, the shape of allowed choices, and walks along its edges to better corners until it reaches the best one. Khachiyan's 1979 ellipsoid method was the first algorithm guaranteed to run in polynomial time, reasonably fast, even in the worst case. Simplex still stayed faster in practice. Today good simplex and interior-point implementations are thought to be similarly efficient for routine problems.
entries.text_plain: Assigning 70 people to 70 jobs sounds simple. The possible arrangements outnumber the particles in the observable universe, yet the simplex algorithm solves the problem in a moment. George Dantzig devised the method for Linear programming: planning with straight-line rules in 1947. It starts at a corner of the feasible region, the shape of allowed choices, and walks along its edges to better corners until it reaches the best one. Khachiyan's 1979 ellipsoid method was the first algorithm guaranteed to run in polynomial time, reasonably fast, even in the worst case. Simplex still stayed faster in practice. Today good simplex and interior-point implementations are thought to be similarly efficient for routine problems.

entries.title: Slack variables: counting what goes unused

definition.text: A non-negative extra variable added to a linear program to turn an inequality constraint into an equality.

facts.text: In the farm example, the slack variables stand for the unused land, unused fertilizer and unused pesticide.
Rewriting a problem with slack variables puts it in the augmented form used by the simplex algorithm.

entries.title: Branch and bound: pruning hopeless options early

definition.text: A search method for optimization that keeps the cost of the best solution found so far and abandons any partial solution that cannot beat it.

facts.text: Skipping such partial solutions saves part of the search; its efficiency depends on how well the best possible cost of extending a partial solution is estimated.

entries.text: Searching every possible answer to a large problem can take impossibly long. Branch and bound cuts the search short. It keeps the cost of the best solution found so far and abandons any partial solution that cannot beat it, which makes it a standard tool for {{ref:nature-econ-450}}. Skipping those dead ends saves part of the search. How much it saves depends on how well the method estimates the best possible cost of extending a partial solution.

entries.title: Nonlinear programming: optimization when the lines curve

definition.text: Constrained optimization in which the objective or some constraints are nonlinear and some constraints are inequalities.

facts.text: Quadratic programming, with linear constraints and a quadratic objective, is one type of nonlinear programming.
A quadratic program with a convex objective can be solved in polynomial time by the ellipsoid method; otherwise it may be NP-hard.

entries.text: Not every problem runs in straight lines. Nonlinear programming is {{ref:nature-econ-423}} in which the objective or some constraints are nonlinear and some constraints are inequalities, unlike {{ref:nature-econ-456}}. One common type is quadratic programming, which pairs linear constraints with a quadratic objective, one containing squared terms. Its difficulty hinges on shape. A quadratic program with a convex objective ({{ref:nature-econ-427}}) can be solved in polynomial time by the ellipsoid method. Otherwise it may be NP-hard, among the hardest problems to solve.

entries.title: The KKT conditions: tests for the best answer under limits

definition.text: First-derivative tests that an optimal solution of a nonlinear programming problem must pass, provided certain regularity conditions hold.

facts.text: They extend the method of Lagrange multipliers, which allows only equality constraints, to problems with inequality constraints.
Harold W. Kuhn and Albert W. Tucker published them in 1951; William Karush had stated them in an unpublished 1939 master's thesis.
With no inequality constraints, they reduce to the Lagrange conditions and the KKT multipliers become Lagrange multipliers.
Many optimization algorithms can be read as ways of numerically solving the KKT system of equations and inequalities.
They are also sufficient for an optimum when a maximization's objective is concave, its inequality constraints convex, its equality constraints affine and Slater's condition holds.
Economists use them to get qualitative results, for example that a firm maximizing sales revenue subject to a minimum profit produces where marginal revenue is below marginal cost.
Each multiplier is the rate at which the best achievable value rises as its resource constraint is loosened, an interpretation used in utility maximization.

They extend {{ref:nature-econ-455}}, which allow only equality constraints, to problems with inequality constraints. With no inequalities, they reduce to the Lagrange conditions. Under the right shapes they also guarantee an optimum. A maximization needs a concave objective, convex inequality constraints, straight-line equality constraints and Slater's condition. entries.title: The substitution method: folding the constraint in

definition.text: A way to solve a simple constrained problem by plugging the constraint into the objective, leaving an ordinary problem with fewer variables.

facts.text: Example: to maximize x times y with x + y = 10, substitute y = 10 − x to get 10x − x², whose derivative 10 − 2x is zero at x = 5, so y = 5.

entries.text: The simplest constrained problems ({{ref:nature-econ-423}}) yield to a single substitution. The method plugs the constraint into the objective, leaving an ordinary problem with fewer variables. Suppose the goal is to maximize x times y, given that x + y = 10. Substituting y = 10 − x gives 10x − x². Its derivative, 10 − 2x, is zero at x = 5 ({{ref:nature-econ-462}}), so y = 5 as well.

entries.title: Costate variables: the hidden value of a stock

definition.text: In optimal control, a variable, sometimes called the shadow price, that gives the marginal value of having a little more or less of the state variable.

facts.text: Its marginal value covers not only the next period's gain but the whole remaining duration of the program.
Solving for the costate first is a common strategy; the optimal control can then usually be found from it.
Costate variables play the role that Lagrange multipliers play in static problems, but change over time.

entries.text: In {{ref:nature-econ-465}}, a costate variable gives the marginal value of having a little more or a little less of the state variable ({{ref:nature-econ-417}}). Another name for it is the {{ref:nature-val-017}}. That value counts not only the next period's gain but the whole remaining duration of the program. Costate variables play the role that Lagrange multipliers play in static problems ({{ref:nature-econ-455}}), except that they change over time. Solving for the costate first is a common strategy, because the best control can then usually be found from it.

entries.title: Pontryagin's maximum principle: steering one moment at a time

definition.text: A rule in optimal control theory for finding the best way to steer a dynamical system from one state to another, especially when states or controls are constrained.

facts.text: It says an optimal control and its state path must solve the Hamiltonian system, a two-point boundary value problem, and maximize the control Hamiltonian.
Lev Pontryagin and his students formulated it in 1956; its first use was maximizing a rocket's final speed.
Its power is that maximizing the Hamiltonian at each moment is much easier than optimizing over whole functions.
The conditions are necessary, and become sufficient under certain convexity conditions.
Unlike the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, which must hold over the whole state space, its conditions need only hold along one path, which can make it more efficient to compute.
In differential games, open-loop strategies are found with the maximum principle and closed-loop strategies with dynamic programming.

entries.title: Linear quadratic control: the tidiest optimal control problem

definition.text: A special case of optimal control with linear dynamics and a quadratic cost, which can be solved in feedback form.

facts.text: Its cost can be read physically as minimizing control energy.
The optimal control is a feedback rule proportional to the state, with the matrix found from the Riccati equation.

entries.text: The tidiest case in {{ref:nature-econ-465}} pairs linear dynamics with a quadratic cost. Linear quadratic control can be solved as a rule that responds to the system as it goes. The best control is a rule proportional to the current state, with the matrix found from the Riccati equation. Its cost can be read physically as minimizing control energy.

entries.title: The current value Hamiltonian: removing the discount
entries.article: Hamiltonian (control theory)#Current value and present value Hamiltonian

definition.text: A version of the control Hamiltonian, common in economics, that strips out exponential discounting so that values are measured at the current date.

facts.text: In economic dynamic optimization the objective often depends on time only through exponential discounting of an instantaneous utility, or felicity, function.
Its costate variables are economically the current-valued shadow prices of the capital goods.

entries.title: Transversality conditions: how a plan should end

definition.text: An end-point condition needed for optimality in a dynamic problem whose final state is left free.

facts.text: With a free terminal value, the costate variable must equal zero at the final time.
In a lifetime consumption problem, a transversality condition says the consumer carries no debt at the end of life.
If the terminal time tends to infinity, a transversality condition on the Hamiltonian applies.

entries.title: The Euler–Lagrange equation: where the best curves hide

definition.text: The equation whose solutions are the candidate functions that maximize or minimize a functional in the calculus of variations.

facts.text: It comes from setting the functional derivative to zero, the counterpart of setting an ordinary derivative to zero to find a function's highest or lowest point.
When the variable does not appear on its own in the integrand, the equation simplifies to the Beltrami identity.

entries.text: Ordinary calculus finds a function's highest or lowest point by setting its derivative to zero ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). The {{ref:nature-econ-421}} has a counterpart. Setting the functional derivative to zero gives the Euler–Lagrange equation, whose solutions are the candidate functions that maximize or minimize a functional. When the variable does not appear on its own in the integrand, the expression being integrated, the equation simplifies to the Beltrami identity.

When the variable does not appear on its own in the integrand, the expression being integrated, the equation simplifies to the Beltrami identity.

entries.title: Model closure: deciding what a CGE model takes as given

definition.text: In a CGE model, the choice of which variables are set from outside (exogenous) rather than worked out by the model (endogenous).

facts.text: CGE models always have more variables than equations, so some must be fixed outside the model.
Technology, consumer tastes and government instruments such as tax rates are usually exogenous.
Modellers differ: some hold employment and the trade balance fixed, while others let them vary.

entries.contested_note: The choice of closure can be controversial, since modellers disagree on whether employment and the trade balance should be fixed or free.
entries.text: A CGE model ({{ref:nature-econ-475}}) always has more variables than equations, so some must be fixed from outside. Model closure is the choice of which variables are set from outside the model, called exogenous, and which it works out, called endogenous. Technology, consumer tastes and government instruments such as tax rates are usually exogenous. Beyond that, modelers differ. Some hold employment and the trade balance fixed, while others let them vary. The choice can be controversial, because modelers still disagree on whether those two should be fixed or free.

entries.title: Nested CES: layering choices inside an economic model
entries.article: Computable general equilibrium#Role of separability and nested structures

definition.text: The usual way CGE models represent production and consumption: layered constant elasticity of substitution (CES) functions in which groups of goods or inputs are treated as composites.

facts.text: A firm may first choose among capital, labour, materials and energy, then decide the mix within each; households may split spending across food, housing and transport first.
This multi-stage choice is consistent only if preferences or technologies are separable in the relevant groups.
Separability makes CGE models computationally tractable and lets them be calibrated to reproduce observed base-year data.

entries.text: A firm may first choose among capital, labor, materials and energy, then decide the mix within each. A household may first split its spending across food, housing and transport. CGE models ({{ref:nature-econ-475}}) usually represent such layered choices with a nested CES structure. It is built from the functions described in {{ref:nature-eecon-226}}, in which the ease of swapping one input for another stays fixed. In the nested version, groups of goods or inputs are treated as composites. This multi-stage choice is consistent only if preferences or technologies are separable in the relevant groups. Separability keeps the models computationally tractable and lets them be calibrated to reproduce observed base-year data.

entries.title: The duality gap: when two views disagree

definition.text: The difference between the optimal values of a primal optimization problem and its dual.

facts.text: For minimization problems the gap is never negative.
Strong duality holds when the gap is zero; otherwise it is positive and only weak duality holds.
For convex problems the gap is zero when a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition holds.

entries.text: A problem and its dual ({{ref:nature-econ-438}}) need not reach the same optimum. The duality gap is the difference between their optimal values. For minimization problems it is never negative. When the gap is zero, strong duality holds. Otherwise it is positive and only weak duality holds. For convex problems ({{ref:nature-econ-427}}), the gap closes to zero when a regularity condition such as Slater's condition holds ({{ref:nature-econ-454}}).
entries.text_plain: A problem and its dual (Duality: every optimization problem has a mirror image) need not reach the same optimum. The duality gap is the difference between their optimal values. For minimization problems it is never negative. When the gap is zero, strong duality holds. Otherwise it is positive and only weak duality holds. For convex problems (Convex functions: why cup-shaped curves are easy to optimize), the gap closes to zero when a regularity condition such as Slater's condition holds (Constraint qualifications: when the KKT tests apply).

entries.title: Stable and unstable equilibrium: the pendulum and the hilltop

definition.text: An equilibrium is stable if a small push leads only to small, local movement, and unstable if a small push can send the system far away.

facts.text: A pendulum shows stable equilibrium with small oscillations; a ball resting on top of a hill shows unstable equilibrium.
With damping, a stable equilibrium is also asymptotically stable.
For an iterated map, a fixed point is stable if the derivative there is less than 1 in absolute value and unstable if greater.

entries.text: A pendulum nudged sideways makes small oscillations around its resting point. A ball balanced on top of a hill, nudged the same way, rolls off. The first is a stable equilibrium: a small push leads only to small, local movement. The second is unstable: a small push can send the system far away. The same distinction applies to a {{ref:nature-econ-474}} and to an {{ref:nature-econ-335}}. With damping, which drains motion away, a stable equilibrium is also asymptotically stable. For a repeated map, a fixed point is stable if the derivative there is less than 1 in absolute value, and unstable if greater.
entries.text_plain: A pendulum nudged sideways makes small oscillations around its resting point. A ball balanced on top of a hill, nudged the same way, rolls off. The first is a stable equilibrium: a small push leads only to small, local movement. The second is unstable: a small push can send the system far away. The same distinction applies to a Steady state: when everything flows but nothing changes and to an Equilibrium: when the market stops moving. With damping, which drains motion away, a stable equilibrium is also asymptotically stable. For a repeated map, a fixed point is stable if the derivative there is less than 1 in absolute value, and unstable if greater.

entries.title: Stability theory: does a disturbed system come back?

definition.text: The study of whether the solutions of differential equations and the paths of dynamical systems stay close when their starting conditions are disturbed slightly.

facts.text: It asks whether a nearby path will stay close to a given one forever, and whether it will converge to it.
An equilibrium is stable if starting close keeps a system close, and asymptotically stable if the system also returns to it over time.
A key idea is to analyze behaviour near an equilibrium by linearizing the system, where eigenvalues of a matrix describe how nearby points move.
If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, the point is a stable attracting fixed point that nearby points approach at an exponential rate.
In economics, a price adjusting to excess demand converges to equilibrium only if the derivative of its rate of change with respect to price is negative.
Stability can also be applied to Nash equilibria; Cournot introduced best-response dynamics in studying the stability of equilibrium.

entries.text: If a system starts slightly off course, does it stay close or drift away? Stability theory studies whether the solutions of {{ref:nature-econ-433}} and the paths of dynamical systems stay close when their starting conditions are disturbed slightly. It asks whether a nearby path will stay close to a given one forever, and whether it will converge to it. An equilibrium is stable if starting close keeps the system close, and asymptotically stable if the system also returns to it over time ({{ref:nature-econ-472}}). The eigenvalues of a matrix, its characteristic numbers, then describe how nearby points move. If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, nearby points approach the equilibrium at an exponential rate. Economics has its own version. A price adjusting to excess demand converges to equilibrium only if the derivative of its rate of change with respect to price is negative. Cournot introduced best-response dynamics in studying the stability of equilibrium, and stability can also be applied to Nash equilibria.

entries.title: Bifurcation theory: when small changes flip a system

definition.text: The mathematical study of how the qualitative behaviour of a family of curves or equations, such as the solutions of differential equations, changes as its parameters change.

facts.text: A bifurcation happens when a small smooth change in a parameter causes a sudden qualitative change in how a dynamical system behaves.
Bifurcations occur both in continuous systems described by differential equations and in discrete systems described by maps.
Henri Poincaré introduced the name in 1885.
In ecology, regime shifts linked to a critical or bifurcation point are also called critical transitions.
Systems nearing a bifurcation point show critical slowing down: they recover more and more slowly from disturbances.
Catastrophe theory, which influenced research on regime shifts, is a branch of bifurcation theory.

entries.text: Turn a setting slowly, and at some point a whole system may suddenly behave differently. That switch is a bifurcation. A small, smooth change in a parameter, a fixed setting of the model, causes a sudden qualitative change in how the system behaves. Bifurcation theory studies how the qualitative behavior of a family of equations, such as the solutions of {{ref:nature-econ-433}}, changes as its parameters change. Henri Poincaré introduced the name in 1885. Bifurcations occur both in continuous systems described by differential equations and in discrete systems described by maps. The idea matters for nature. In ecology, abrupt shifts linked to a critical or bifurcation point are also called critical transitions. Systems nearing such a point show {{ref:nature-eco-654}}: they recover more and more slowly after being knocked off balance ({{ref:nature-econ-471}}). Catastrophe theory, which influenced research on these shifts, is a branch of bifurcation theory.

entries.title: Phase portraits: mapping where a system can go

definition.text: A picture of a dynamical system's possible paths drawn in the phase plane, with each starting point giving its own curve.

facts.text: It shows typical trajectories with arrows, stable steady states as dots and unstable ones as circles.
It reveals whether an attractor (a stable point or sink), a repeller (an unstable point or source) or a limit cycle is present.
For a system of ordinary differential equations it shows whether the system is unstable, asymptotically stable or neutrally stable.
Its shape, such as a saddle, node or spiral, can be read off the eigenvalues, or the trace and determinant, of the system.

entries.text: One drawing can show the possible paths of a simple system. A phase portrait draws a dynamical system's trajectories in the phase plane, whose axes are the system's variables, with each starting point giving its own curve. Arrows show typical trajectories. Stable steady states ({{ref:nature-econ-474}}) appear as dots and unstable ones as circles. The drawing reveals whether an attractor (a stable point, or sink), a repeller (an unstable point, or source) or a limit cycle, a repeating loop, is present. For a system of ordinary differential equations, it shows whether the system is unstable, asymptotically stable or neutrally stable ({{ref:nature-econ-471}}). Its shape, such as a saddle, node or spiral, can be read off the system's eigenvalues, or its trace and determinant.

Stable steady states (Steady state: when everything flows but nothing changes) appear as dots and unstable ones as circles. The drawing reveals whether an attractor (a stable point, or sink), a repeller (an unstable point, or source) or a limit cycle, a repeating loop, is present. For a system of ordinary differential equations, it shows whether the system is unstable, asymptotically stable or neutrally stable (Stability theory: does a disturbed system come back?). Its shape, such as a saddle, node or spiral, can be read off the system's eigenvalues, or its trace and determinant.

entries.title: Lyapunov functions: proving stability with energy
entries.article: Stability theory#Lyapunov function for general dynamical systems

definition.text: A function of a system's state whose existence demonstrates that the system is stable.

facts.text: Lyapunov functions are a general way to prove that a dynamical system is stable or asymptotically stable.
It is often useful to picture a Lyapunov function as the energy of the system.
Aleksandr Lyapunov showed in 1892 that systems of ordinary differential equations behave stably given a suitable Lyapunov function.

entries.title: Complementary slackness: loose limits carry no price
entries.article: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions#Interpretation: KKT conditions as balancing constraint-forces in state space

definition.text: The KKT condition that an inequality constraint which is not binding at the optimum gets a multiplier of zero.

facts.text: It is often written as the product of each multiplier and its constraint being zero.
Picturing the solution as a particle, a constraint can only push back when the particle touches its boundary.

entries.text: A limit that is not pressing should cost nothing. entries.title: Constraint qualifications: when the KKT tests apply

definition.text: A regularity condition that guarantees that the optimum of a constrained problem satisfies the KKT conditions.

facts.text: The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) is the most frequently used.
Slater's condition applies to convex problems: some point must satisfy the inequality constraints strictly.
Weaker qualifications are preferred in practice because they cover more problems.

Slater's condition applies to convex problems: some point must satisfy the inequality constraints strictly, with room to spare. Weaker qualifications are preferred in practice, because they cover more problems.

entries.title: Local and global bifurcations: two ways systems flip

definition.text: The two main classes of bifurcation: local ones, seen through changes in the stability of equilibria, and global ones, where larger structures of the system collide.

facts.text: A local bifurcation occurs when a parameter change alters the stability of an equilibrium.
Global bifurcations, such as a cycle colliding with an equilibrium, cannot be found just by checking the stability of equilibria.
Saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations are the only generic local bifurcations that truly need just one parameter to be varied.

entries.text: Bifurcations ({{ref:nature-econ-419}}) come in two main classes. A local bifurcation occurs when a parameter change alters the stability of an equilibrium ({{ref:nature-econ-471}}). A global bifurcation involves larger structures of the system colliding, such as a cycle running into an equilibrium. Global bifurcations cannot be found just by checking the stability of equilibria.

entries.title: Bellman's principle of optimality

definition.text: Bellman's rule that an optimal plan has the property that, whatever the starting point and first decision, the remaining decisions must also be optimal from the situation the first decision creates.

facts.text: It tells dynamic programming how to break a decision problem into smaller subproblems.
In computer science, a problem that can be broken apart this way is said to have optimal substructure.
In dynamic game theory, it is analogous to subgame perfect equilibrium.

entries.title: The Bellman equation: today's payoff plus tomorrow's value

definition.text: An equation from dynamic programming that splits a decision problem over time into a chain of simpler subproblems, following Bellman's principle of optimality.

facts.text: It writes the value of a decision problem at one moment as today's payoff plus the value of the problem left over after today's choice.
Solving it means finding an unknown function, the value function, which gives the best achievable outcome for each state; the matching best action for each state is the policy function.
The name usually refers to discrete-time problems; in continuous time the matching equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman partial differential equation.
It can be solved by backwards induction, by hand in special cases or numerically, but this may be infeasible with many state variables because of the curse of dimensionality.
Economists call dynamic programming a recursive method, because its economic applications usually give a Bellman equation in the form of a difference equation.
It has been used for optimal growth, resource extraction, public finance, asset pricing and many other economic problems.
The first known economic application is credited to Martin Beckmann and Richard Muth; Robert C. Merton's 1973 asset pricing model is a celebrated later one.

entries.title: Markov decision processes: choosing step by step under chance

definition.text: A mathematical model of making a sequence of decisions when outcomes are uncertain.

facts.text: It is defined by states, actions, the probabilities of moving between states, and rewards.
The goal is a policy, a rule giving the action for each state, that maximizes the expected discounted sum of rewards.
MDPs arose in operations research in the 1950s and are now used in ecology, economics, healthcare and reinforcement learning.
They are often solved with stochastic dynamic programming, where the Bellman equation gives the recursion for expected rewards.
The curse of dimensionality often makes exact solution infeasible because problem size grows exponentially with the number of state and action variables.
A Markov decision process is a stochastic game with only one player.
Real options can be valued by recasting them as a data-driven Markov decision process solved with deep reinforcement learning.

entries.text: Many decisions repeat under uncertainty: each result is partly luck, and each shapes the next choice. A Markov decision process (MDP) is a mathematical model of such a sequence. It is defined by states, actions, the probabilities of moving between states, and rewards ({{ref:nature-econ-417}}). The goal is a policy, a rule giving the action for each state, that maximizes the {{ref:nature-econ-756}} of the discounted sum of rewards. MDPs arose in operations research in the 1950s. They are now used in ecology, economics, healthcare and reinforcement learning, a branch of machine learning. They are often solved with stochastic, or chance-driven, dynamic programming, where the {{ref:nature-econ-416}} gives the recursion for expected rewards. Exact solutions are often infeasible, because problem size grows exponentially with the number of state and action variables. In game-theory terms, an MDP is a stochastic game with only one player.

entries.title: Ramsey's problem: how much to save for the future
entries.article: Dynamic programming#Example from economics: Ramsey's problem of optimal saving

definition.text: A classic economic planning problem of choosing how much to consume now and how much to invest in capital for future consumption.

facts.text: The planner maximizes a social welfare function linking consumption to utility, with future consumption discounted at a constant rate.
Dynamic programming lets the consumer decide one step at a time, choosing only current consumption and saving given current capital.
In the worked example, it is optimal to consume a larger share of wealth with age, using up everything in the last period of life.

entries.title: Value iteration and policy iteration

definition.text: The standard algorithms for finding the best policy in a finite Markov decision process, repeatedly updating a value for each state and a chosen action for each state.

facts.text: Value iteration, also called backward induction (Bellman 1957), starts from a guess of the value function and improves it step by step.
Policy iteration alternates computing values and improving the policy until the policy stops changing, giving a definite stopping point.
Howard invented policy iteration to optimize Sears catalogue mailing.

entries.title: LP relaxation: dropping the whole-number rule

definition.text: The linear program obtained by dropping the whole-number requirement from an integer program.

facts.text: Rounding the LP relaxation's solution is the naive approach, but the result may be neither optimal nor even feasible.
If the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, the simplex method's solution is guaranteed to be whole numbers.

entries.text: Integer programs are hard to solve ({{ref:nature-econ-450}}). The LP relaxation is the linear program obtained by dropping the whole-number requirement. Rounding its solution is the naive approach, but the result may be neither optimal nor even feasible. In one lucky case no rounding is needed. If the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, a special mathematical property, the simplex method's solution is guaranteed to be whole numbers ({{ref:nature-econ-457}}).

If the constraint matrix is totally unimodular, a special mathematical property, the simplex method's solution is guaranteed to be whole numbers (The simplex algorithm: walking the corners to the best answer).

entries.title: Bang–bang control: all on or all off

definition.text: A control rule that switches abruptly between two extreme settings, such as fully on and fully off.

facts.text: Most household thermostats are bang–bang controllers: the heater or compressor is either running or not, depending on whether the temperature is above or below the setpoint.
In optimal control, a bang–bang solution is a control that jumps from one bound to the other and never takes an in-between value.
Such solutions appear when the Hamiltonian is linear in the control, so the maximum principle pushes the control to its upper or lower limit.
Bang–bang controls are sometimes truly optimal, but they are also often used simply because they are simple or convenient.

entries.title: The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

definition.text: The partial differential equation that plays the role of the Bellman equation in continuous-time optimization problems.

facts.text: Solving it gives a sufficient condition for an optimal control, while Pontryagin's principle gives a necessary one.
It provides a necessary and sufficient condition for an optimum and extends easily to stochastic optimal control problems.
It is used to find optimal policies in continuous-time Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions.

It is used to find the best policies in continuous-time Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions.

entries.title: Hypothesis tests: could chance alone explain the data?

definition.text: A statistical hypothesis test uses sample data to decide whether a claim about a population, such as a drug lowering blood pressure, holds up.

facts.text: It builds a model of what the data would look like if chance alone produced the results, then asks how likely the actual data are under that model.
If the data are very unlikely under the null hypothesis, it is rejected; if not, the only conclusion is that the evidence against it is insufficient.
Because a sample cannot settle the truth for certain, a test's conclusion can be wrong.
Modern significance testing comes mainly from Karl Pearson, William Sealy Gosset and Ronald Fisher, while Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson developed hypothesis testing.
John Arbuthnot first used it in 1710, testing whether male and female births in London were equally likely.
A test is like a court trial: the null hypothesis, like the defendant, is presumed true until evidence shows otherwise.

entries.text: In 1710 John Arbuthnot asked whether male and female births in London were equally likely. His answer was the first statistical hypothesis test. entries.title: Correlation does not imply causation

definition.text: The principle that two things moving together, on its own, does not show that one causes the other.

facts.text: Treating a correlation as proof of cause is a logical fallacy, known in Latin as cum hoc ergo propter hoc, 'with this, therefore because of this'.
Showing a cause usually needs four things: a correlation, the cause coming first, a plausible mechanism, and ruling out common or alternative causes.
A hidden third factor can cause both observed variables, making them move together without either causing the other.
Two unrelated variables can correlate by chance, and the more things are examined the more such accidental links turn up.
Dismissing correlation entirely is the opposite mistake, since much scientific evidence rests on variables observed together.
Assumptions are always needed to draw causal conclusions, and modern causal inference focuses on testing how strong those assumptions are.
In environmental medicine many links could long only be described as correlations because studies that show causation are hard or impossible to run.
The 'credibility revolution' in economics used better methods to tell correlation from causation.

entries.title: Causal inference: finding what really causes what

definition.text: The process of working out the real, separate effect of one thing that is part of a larger system.

facts.text: Unlike finding an association, it asks how an outcome responds when one of its causes is changed.
One description: establish that cause and effect vary together, that the cause comes first, and rule out other plausible causes.
It is especially hard where experiments are difficult or impossible, which is common in most sciences.
In economics and politics it is hard because real economies are complex and many large events cannot be recreated in controlled experiments.
Because correlation does not imply causation, the work is as much about plausible causal mechanisms as about patterns in data.
Economists increasingly use natural experiments and quasi-experimental designs, and randomized field experiments help deal with confounding.
Many social scientists adopted Donald Rubin's potential outcomes framework as a standard for inferring causality.
Critics say economists and social scientists often pass off descriptive studies as causal ones.

entries.title: The Monte Carlo method: solving problems with dice

definition.text: A family of computer methods that get numerical answers by repeated random sampling.

facts.text: The idea is to use randomness to solve problems that are not random in themselves.
Its main uses are optimization, numerical integration and drawing samples from probability distributions, especially for problems with very uncertain inputs.
The simplest version estimates an average by running many simulations and averaging their results.
It is named after the Monte Carlo Casino; Stanisław Ulam, its main developer, was inspired by his uncle's gambling.
It can be very costly to compute, but the runs are independent, so they can be spread across many processors.
In cost–benefit analysis it supports formal risk analysis of uncertain costs and benefits.
The IPCC relies on it to analyse probability distributions of radiative forcing.
Unlike 'what if' scenarios built on best-guess values, it samples each uncertain variable from a probability distribution to produce hundreds or thousands of possible outcomes.

Rather than one 'what if' scenario built on best-guess values, it samples each uncertain variable from a probability distribution. The result is hundreds or thousands of possible outcomes. Its main uses are optimization, numerical integration and drawing samples, especially when inputs are very uncertain. The IPCC relies on it to analyze the probability distributions of Radiative forcing: the push on Earth's energy balance.

entries.title: Sensitivity analysis: which assumptions drive the answer?

definition.text: Sensitivity analysis studies how the uncertainty in a model's output can be traced back to, and shared among, the uncertain inputs that feed it.

facts.text: Models in fields like climate science or economics can be so complex that how their inputs drive their outputs is poorly understood.
Inputs can be uncertain because of measurement errors, missing information, poor understanding of mechanisms or the choice of underlying hypothesis.
It is almost always done by running the model many times with sampled inputs, which can be computationally expensive.
In cost-benefit analysis, a sensitivity analysis shows how the results respond when parameters change.
The European Commission, the US Office of Management and Budget, the IPCC and the US EPA include sensitivity analysis in their guidelines.
Leamer's global sensitivity analysis judges conclusions sturdy only if a credibly wide range of assumptions still gives a usefully narrow range of inferences.

entries.title: Designing experiments that can reveal causes

definition.text: Planning procedures that test how changing one part of a system leads to changes in other parts.

facts.text: It decides which parts of a system to change and which to hold fixed, based on hypotheses about what drives variation.
The changed inputs are independent variables, and the outcomes they are expected to change are dependent variables.
Main concerns are validity, reliability and replicability, along with enough statistical power.
Ronald Fisher set out a method for designing experiments in The Arrangement of Field Experiments (1926) and The Design of Experiments (1935), much of it for agriculture.
Charles S. Peirce stressed randomization-based inference in publications of 1877–1878 and 1883.
Only when participants are randomly chosen and randomly assigned can differences in outcomes be confidently put down to the different conditions.
Laws and ethics rule out some well-designed experiments on people, through review boards, informed consent and confidentiality.
Choice experiments used to value environmental goods depend on an experimental design that controls which hypothetical scenarios respondents see.

entries.text: Ronald Fisher worked out much of modern experimental method for agriculture. His books The Arrangement of Field Experiments (1926) and The Design of Experiments (1935) set out how to plan a test. Design of experiments means planning procedures that test how changing one part of a system leads to changes in other parts ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). It decides which parts to change and which to hold fixed, based on hypotheses about what drives variation. The changed inputs are independent variables; the outcomes they should change are dependent variables. Charles S. Peirce had already stressed randomization-based inference in publications of 1877–1878 and 1883. Only when participants are randomly chosen and randomly assigned can differences in outcomes be confidently put down to the different conditions. The main concerns are validity, reliability and replicability, along with enough statistical power to detect an effect. Laws and ethics rule out some well-designed experiments on people, through review boards, informed consent and confidentiality. Valuing nature uses the craft too. Choice experiments that value environmental goods depend on a design that controls which hypothetical scenarios respondents see.

entries.title: Bayesian inference: updating beliefs as evidence arrives

definition.text: A way of doing statistics that uses Bayes' theorem to work out how likely a hypothesis is from earlier evidence, and to update that probability as new information arrives.

facts.text: It starts from a prior distribution, the belief about a parameter before any data are seen, and turns it into posterior probabilities.
Updating is especially useful when data arrive in a sequence: the posterior from one stage becomes the prior for the next.
It is used in science, engineering, philosophy, medicine, sport, psychology and law.
Abraham Wald showed that every unique Bayesian procedure is admissible, which made Bayesian methods central even to frequentist estimation and hypothesis testing.
In Bayesian model comparison, the model with the highest posterior probability given the data is chosen.
Complex models often cannot be solved in closed form, so Bayesian analysis leans on Monte Carlo simulation such as Gibbs sampling and Metropolis–Hastings.
The name honours Thomas Bayes (1701–1761), but Pierre-Simon Laplace introduced what is now called Bayes' theorem.
Early Bayesian inference was called inverse probability because it reasons backwards from effects to causes.

entries.text: Thomas Bayes (1701–1761) gave the method his name, but Pierre-Simon Laplace introduced what is now called Bayes' theorem. Bayesian inference uses that theorem to work out how likely a hypothesis is from earlier evidence, and to update the probability as new information arrives. It starts from a prior distribution, the belief about a quantity before any data are seen, and turns it into posterior probabilities. Updating suits data that arrive in sequence: the posterior from one stage becomes the prior for the next. Early versions were called inverse probability, because they reason backward from effects to causes. Abraham Wald showed that every unique Bayesian procedure is admissible, which made Bayesian methods central even to rival approaches to estimation and {{ref:nature-econ-279}}. Complex models often cannot be solved by formula, so Bayesian analysis leans on {{ref:nature-econ-242}} simulation such as Gibbs sampling. The approach is used in science, engineering, medicine, sport, psychology and law.

entries.title: Maximum likelihood: the settings that best explain the data

definition.text: A way of estimating the parameters of an assumed probability distribution by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable.

facts.text: Its logic is intuitive and flexible, and it has become a dominant way of doing statistical inference.
Except in special cases the equations cannot be solved directly and must be solved step by step from an initial guess.
With enough data it is consistent, homing in on the true parameter value with arbitrary precision.
It matches the most probable Bayesian estimate when the prior over the parameters is uniform.
Predictions from it ignore the uncertainty in the estimated parameters.
Ronald Fisher created the modern method between 1912 and 1922, building on Gauss, Laplace and others.
Discrete choice, probit and logit models are typically estimated this way.

entries.text: Given some data and an assumed shape for the process behind them, which settings make the observed data most probable? Maximum likelihood estimation answers that. It estimates the parameters of an assumed probability distribution by choosing the values under which the observed data are most likely, an exercise in {{ref:nature-econ-461}}. Ronald Fisher created the modern method between 1912 and 1922, building on Gauss, Laplace and others. Its logic is intuitive and flexible, and it has become a dominant way of doing statistical inference. With enough data it is consistent, homing in on the true value with arbitrary precision. Except in special cases its equations must be solved step by step from an initial guess. It matches the most probable Bayesian estimate when the prior is uniform ({{ref:nature-econ-211}}). One weakness is that its predictions ignore the uncertainty in the estimated parameters. Probit and logit models, including those used for {{ref:nature-val-100}}, are typically estimated this way.

It estimates the parameters of an assumed probability distribution by choosing the values under which the observed data are most likely, an exercise in Optimization: the mathematics of choosing the best. It matches the most probable Bayesian estimate when the prior is uniform (Bayesian inference: updating beliefs as evidence arrives). One weakness is that its predictions ignore the uncertainty in the estimated parameters. Probit and logit models, including those used for Discrete choice: modeling either-or decisions, are typically estimated this way.

entries.title: Panel data: following the same subjects over time

definition.text: Data that follow the same subjects, such as people, firms or countries, with repeated measurements over time.

facts.text: Time series (one subject over time) and cross-sectional data (many subjects at one time) are one-dimensional special cases of panel data.
In a balanced panel every subject is observed in every period; in an unbalanced panel some are missing.
Unchanging subject traits such as a country's geography or climate cause omitted variable bias in ordinary least squares if they are correlated with explanatory variables.
Fixed effects and first-difference estimators can control for such traits; random effects is more efficient when they are uncorrelated with the regressors.
Using a lagged outcome as a regressor creates dynamic panel data, where instrumental variables or GMM methods such as the Arellano–Bond estimator are needed.
A panel of 130 countries from 1975 to 2010 found obesity rising with income in poor settings and falling in rich ones.

Using a past outcome as an explanatory variable creates dynamic panel data, which needs special methods such as the Arellano–Bond estimator.

entries.title: The null hypothesis: assuming no effect until proven otherwise
entries.article: Statistical hypothesis test#Technical description of the null hypothesis

definition.text: The null hypothesis is the default claim that a measured quantity, usually a difference or effect, is zero.

facts.text: A test weighs the null hypothesis against its negation, the alternative hypothesis.
For a heart-attack drug, a possible null hypothesis is that the drug has no effect on the risk of a heart attack.
Paul Meehl argued that when the null is simply 'no effect', a more precise experiment is a less severe test of the theory behind it.

distinct_from: Type I and type II errors
entries.text: For a heart-attack drug, a possible null hypothesis is that the drug has no effect on the risk of a heart attack. The null hypothesis is the default claim that a measured quantity, usually a difference or effect, is zero. When the null is simply 'no effect', he argued, a more precise experiment is a less severe test of the theory behind it.

entries.title: P-values: measuring how surprising a result is

definition.text: A p-value is the probability of getting a test result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true.

facts.text: If the p-value is at or below the test's significance level, written alpha, the null hypothesis is rejected.
A rejection does not mean the chance that the null hypothesis is true is below alpha.
The threshold is usually set so that results this extreme would occur less than 5% or 1% of the time under the null.
Statistical significance does not imply practical significance.

distinct_from: Type I and type II errors
entries.text: How surprising is a result, if nothing is really going on? A p-value puts a number on that. It is the probability of getting a test result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true ({{ref:nature-econ-280}}). If the p-value is at or below the test's significance level, written alpha, the null is rejected. The threshold is usually set so that results this extreme would occur less than 5% or 1% of the time under the null. Two cautions matter. A rejection does not mean the chance that the null is true is below alpha. And statistical significance does not imply practical significance: a detectable effect is not necessarily an important one.

A rejection does not mean the chance that the null is true is below alpha. entries.title: Type I and type II errors: two ways a test can fail

definition.text: A type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true (a false positive); a type II error keeps a null hypothesis when the alternative is true (a false negative).

facts.text: The probability of a type I error equals the test's significance level.
One minus the probability of a type II error is called the test's power.
A typical randomized trial accepts a 0.05, or 1 in 20, chance of wrongly finding two equally effective treatments different.
Large samples are recommended to reduce type II errors.

entries.text: Every test can go wrong in two ways. A type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive. A type II error keeps a null hypothesis when the alternative is true, a false negative ({{ref:nature-econ-280}}). The probability of a type I error equals the test's significance level. A typical randomized trial accepts a 0.05, or 1 in 20, chance of wrongly finding two equally effective treatments different. One minus the probability of a type II error is called the test's power, its ability to catch a real effect. Large samples are recommended to reduce type II errors.
entries.text_plain: Every test can go wrong in two ways. A type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive. A type II error keeps a null hypothesis when the alternative is true, a false negative (The null hypothesis: assuming no effect until proven otherwise). The probability of a type I error equals the test's significance level. A typical randomized trial accepts a 0.05, or 1 in 20, chance of wrongly finding two equally effective treatments different. One minus the probability of a type II error is called the test's power, its ability to catch a real effect. Large samples are recommended to reduce type II errors.

entries.title: Random assignment: letting chance pick the groups

definition.text: Putting people or units into the groups of an experiment by chance, so each has the same chance of ending up in any group.

facts.text: Random assignment is what separates a true experiment from an observational study or quasi-experiment.
It does not remove confounding variables, but it tends to balance known and unknown confounders between groups on average.
Comparing treatments against a control or standard treatment as a baseline is usually more valuable than isolated measurements.
Without random assignment, outcome differences between groups are likely due to some third variable.

entries.text: Chance is the experimenter's most useful ally. Random assignment puts people or units into an experiment's groups by chance, so each has the same chance of ending up in any group ({{ref:nature-econ-218}}). It is what separates a true experiment from an observational study or {{ref:nature-econ-214}}. It does not remove hidden distorting factors ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}), but it tends to balance known and unknown ones between groups on average. Without it, outcome differences between groups are likely due to some third variable. Comparing treatments against a control or standard treatment as a baseline is usually more valuable than isolated measurements.
entries.text_plain: Chance is the experimenter's most useful ally. Random assignment puts people or units into an experiment's groups by chance, so each has the same chance of ending up in any group (Designing experiments that can reveal causes). It is what separates a true experiment from an observational study or Quasi-experiments: testing causes without a lab. It does not remove hidden distorting factors (Confounding variables: the hidden third factor), but it tends to balance known and unknown ones between groups on average. Without it, outcome differences between groups are likely due to some third variable. Comparing treatments against a control or standard treatment as a baseline is usually more valuable than isolated measurements.

entries.title: Randomized controlled trials: the gold-standard experiment

definition.text: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is an experiment that tests an intervention by assigning participants to comparison groups at random, which limits bias.

facts.text: At least one group gets the intervention, while others get an alternative, a placebo or standard care.
Proper randomization removes bias in who gets treated, specifically selection bias and confounding.
RCTs are seen as the most reliable evidence in healthcare because they reduce spurious causality and bias, and their results can be pooled in systematic reviews.
If a treatment's effect is small, too few participants may make it impossible to reject the null hypothesis.
They can be costly: 28 Phase III trials funded by one US institute before 2000 cost US$335 million in total, a mean of US$12 million each.
Withholding an obviously beneficial treatment from a control group can make an RCT unethical.
Jan Baptist van Helmont first proposed an RCT, to compare two fever treatments, in a book published in 1648.

entries.text: In a book published in 1648, Jan Baptist van Helmont proposed comparing two fever treatments by assigning patients at random. It was the first proposal for a randomized controlled trial (RCT). An RCT tests an intervention by assigning participants to comparison groups at random ({{ref:nature-econ-219}}), which limits bias. At least one group gets the intervention, while others get an alternative, a placebo or standard care. Proper randomization removes bias in who gets treated, specifically {{ref:nature-econ-270}} and confounding. That is why RCTs are seen as the most reliable evidence in healthcare. They reduce spurious causality and bias, and their results can be pooled in a {{ref:nature-nbs-094}}. They have weaknesses too. If a treatment's effect is small, too few participants may make it impossible to reject the null hypothesis. They can be costly: 28 Phase III trials funded by one US institute before 2000 cost US$335 million in total, a mean of US$12 million each. And withholding an obviously beneficial treatment from a control group can make an RCT unethical.

At least one group gets the intervention, while others get an alternative, a placebo or standard care. Proper randomization removes bias in who gets treated, specifically Selection bias: when the sample tells the wrong story and confounding. That is why RCTs are seen as the most reliable evidence in healthcare. And withholding an obviously beneficial treatment from a control group can make an RCT unethical.

entries.title: Natural experiments: when the world assigns the treatment

definition.text: A study in which nature or other forces outside the researchers' control decide who is exposed to a condition and who is not.

facts.text: The exposure may resemble random assignment, but natural experiments are observational studies, not controlled ones.
They are most reliable when a clear exposure hits a well-defined group while a comparable group stays unexposed.
They are used when controlled experiments would be extremely difficult or unethical, as often in epidemiology and economics.
John Snow's study of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak, comparing water drawn above and below London's sewage outfalls, is one of the best-known early examples.
Angrist used the Vietnam War draft lottery as an instrumental variable and found veterans earned about 15 percent less than non-veterans.
When air pollution fell in the twentieth century, dark forms of the peppered moth quickly became scarce again, a large-scale natural experiment in natural selection.
Inability to control variables can stop investigators from drawing firm conclusions.

entries.text: In 1854 cholera broke out around Broad Street in London. John Snow compared water drawn above and below London's sewage outfalls, in one of the best-known early natural experiments. In such a study, nature or other forces outside the researchers' control decide who is exposed to a condition and who is not ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). The exposure may resemble random assignment, but these remain observational studies, not controlled ones. They are most reliable when a clear exposure hits a well-defined group while a comparable group stays unexposed. They are used where controlled experiments would be extremely difficult or unethical, as often in epidemiology and economics. Angrist used the Vietnam War draft lottery in this way ({{ref:nature-econ-234}}) and found veterans earned about 15 percent less than non-veterans. Nature runs its own trials too. When air pollution fell in the twentieth century, dark forms of the peppered moth quickly became scarce again. The drawback is that, without control over variables, investigators may be unable to draw firm conclusions.

entries.title: Counterfactuals: comparing reality with what might have been

definition.text: Comparing what actually happened with what would have happened without an intervention.

facts.text: The counterfactual is the outcome beneficiaries would have had without the intervention; impact is the gap between it and what was observed.
The key difficulty is that the counterfactual can never be observed directly, so it must be approximated using a comparison group.
Comparison groups can be set up in advance (prospective) or found afterwards (retrospective).
In difference in differences, the control group stands in for the counterfactual.

entries.text: What would have happened without the program? Counterfactual analysis compares what actually happened with that unseen alternative. The counterfactual is the outcome beneficiaries would have had without the intervention, and impact is the gap between it and what was observed ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). The key difficulty is that the counterfactual can never be observed directly. It must be approximated with a comparison group, set up in advance (prospective) or found afterward (retrospective). In {{ref:nature-econ-221}}, for example, the control group stands in for the counterfactual.
entries.text_plain: What would have happened without the program? Counterfactual analysis compares what actually happened with that unseen alternative. entries.title: The Rubin causal model: two possible lives for every unit

definition.text: The Rubin causal model is a way of analysing cause and effect in which a treatment's effect is the difference between the outcomes a unit would have with and without it, its potential outcomes.

facts.text: A person would have one income at age 40 if they went to college and another if they did not; the causal effect compares the two.
Jerzy Neyman first proposed potential outcomes in his 1923 master's thesis, and Donald Rubin extended the idea to observational as well as experimental studies.
Randomized experiments can estimate causal effects for a population, because random assignment makes groups equivalent on average.
The average treatment effect is the mean of all the individual causal effects.
How units are assigned to treatment matters: a 'perfect doctor' who gives each patient whatever suits them best distorts the comparison of averages.
A causal effect is only well defined if both outcomes could happen; height cannot be manipulated, so its causal effect on weight makes no sense in this framework.

entries.title: Impact evaluation: did the program cause the change?

definition.text: Assessing how far a project, programme or policy actually caused the outcomes seen, intended or not.

facts.text: Unlike monitoring whether targets were met, it asks how outcomes would have changed had the intervention not happened.
It answers evidence-based policy questions: what works, what doesn't, where, why and for how much.
Randomized field experiments are the strongest designs when feasible; otherwise evaluators use quasi-experimental methods such as matching, differencing and instrumental variables.
Whatever design is chosen, every one can yield biased estimates of a programme's effects.
The best-known early large-scale experimental evaluation was of Mexico's Progresa conditional cash transfer programme.
Theory-based evaluation maps the causal chain from inputs to outcomes rather than only reporting average differences between groups.

entries.text: Hitting a target is not the same as causing it. Impact evaluation assesses how far a project, program or policy actually caused the outcomes seen, intended or not. Unlike monitoring whether targets were met, it asks how outcomes would have changed had the intervention not happened ({{ref:nature-econ-230}}). It answers the questions of evidence-based policy: what works, what doesn't, where, why and for how much. Randomized field experiments are the strongest designs when feasible. Otherwise evaluators turn to methods such as matching, differencing and {{ref:nature-econ-234}}. Whatever design is chosen, every one can yield biased estimates. The best-known early large-scale experimental evaluation was of Mexico's Progresa, a program of cash payments tied to conditions. Theory-based evaluation goes further, mapping the causal chain from inputs to outcomes rather than only reporting average differences between groups.

It answers the questions of evidence-based policy: what works, what doesn't, where, why and for how much. Randomized field experiments are the strongest designs when feasible. Otherwise evaluators turn to methods such as matching, differencing and Instrumental variables: finding a clean lever on the cause. Whatever design is chosen, every one can yield biased estimates. entries.title: Program evaluation: does it work, and is it worth it?

definition.text: Program evaluation is a systematic way of collecting and using information to judge whether projects, policies and programs work and whether they are good value for money.

facts.text: Funders, voters and others often need or want to know whether the programs they support are producing the promised effect.
It overlaps with cost-benefit analysis, but social outcomes can be harder to assess than market outcomes and need different skills.
An evaluation can examine needs, the program's theory, its implementation, its impact and its efficiency, at different stages of the program's life.
The hardest part is often showing that the program itself, rather than outside events, caused the observed changes.
Many projects include no budget for evaluation, and an evaluation started late may have no baseline data from before the program began.
Additionality may be checked after the fact, as program evaluation often does, or beforehand as a screen for issuing environmental credits.

entries.title: The fundamental problem of causal inference
entries.article: Rubin causal model#The fundamental problem of causal inference

definition.text: The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we can never observe both potential outcomes for the same unit, so individual causal effects cannot be seen directly.

facts.text: A patient cannot both take a pill and not take it over the same period.
This does not make causal inference impossible; certain techniques and assumptions get around it.
Assumptions are needed to estimate the missing counterfactual outcomes.

definition.text: A study that tests a cause-and-effect claim without a true controlled experiment, used when a real experiment is not available.

facts.text: Experiments may be too costly, impossible for large systems such as economies, or dangerous to the people involved.
Treatments in quasi-experiments are given as if at random, for example in elections won by very slim margins.

entries.title: One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis: turning one knob

definition.text: One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis changes a single input while holding the others at baseline values, to see how the output responds.

facts.text: The input is then returned to its baseline value and the step is repeated for each other input.
Like local derivative-based methods, it examines small changes one variable at a time and does not explore the full range of inputs.

entries.title: Variance-based sensitivity analysis: sharing out the uncertainty

definition.text: Variance-based sensitivity analysis treats inputs and outputs as random variables and splits the output's variance into shares caused by each input and combination of inputs.

facts.text: The shares are calculated as Sobol indices, the proportion of output variance explained by an input or group of inputs.
The first-order index measures one input's contribution alone, averaged over variations in the others.

entries.title: P-hacking: reanalyzing until the answer looks right

definition.text: Trying many analyses, often unconsciously, until one gives the result the researcher wanted.

facts.text: It usually means adjusting the analysis until a result falls below the p<.05 level of statistical significance.

entries.title: Blinding: keeping knowledge from skewing a trial

definition.text: Blinding means keeping participants, caregivers or outcome assessors from knowing which intervention each person received.

facts.text: A placebo in the control group lets participants stay unaware of which treatment they got.
Blinding is sometimes impossible, as when a treatment such as physical therapy needs the patient's active participation.

definition.text: In economics, randomized controlled trials have become a standard way to identify causal effects, especially in development economics.

entries.title: Reverse causation: mistaking the effect for the cause
entries.article: Correlation does not imply causation#B causes A (reverse causation or reverse causality)

definition.text: The mistake of reading cause and effect the wrong way round, treating the effect as the cause.

facts.text: Seeing that windmills turn faster when there is more wind does not mean windmills make wind; wind makes them turn.
Low cholesterol goes with higher death rates partly because diseases such as cancer lower cholesterol and also raise mortality.
Two things can each partly cause the other, such as poverty and lack of education.
Where controlled experiments cannot settle the direction of causation, as often in the social sciences, the confusion can fuel long scientific arguments.
