entries.title: Confounding variables: the hidden third factor

definition.text: A variable that strongly affects a study's results but is not the thing whose effect the study is trying to measure.

facts.text: A confounder can make a factor look important in one version of a model and unimportant in another.
A third factor that causes both A and B, making A and B move together, is a confounding variable.
Assigning units to treatments at random tends to balance known and unknown confounders between groups on average.
In impact evaluation, confounding often comes from socioeconomic factors linked both to who receives a programme and to the outcome.

entries.title: Selection bias: when the sample tells the wrong story

definition.text: Selection bias arises when the people, groups or data chosen for analysis are picked in a way that makes the link between exposure and outcome differ from the link among everyone eligible.

facts.text: It typically occurs when researchers condition on a factor influenced by both the exposure and the outcome, creating a false association.
It includes loss to follow-up, volunteer bias, healthy-worker bias and nonresponse bias.
Volunteers may differ from the target population; studies find they tend to come from higher social standing.
In general it cannot be fixed by analysing existing data alone, though Heckman correction works in special cases.
Researchers' choices of where to study may bias modern estimates of biodiversity.

entries.title: Attrition bias: the problem of people who drop out

definition.text: Attrition bias is selection bias caused by losing participants, such as dropouts and non-responders, during a study.

facts.text: In a diet trial, dropping everyone who quits biases results, because most quitters are those for whom the diet was not working.
It is closely related to survivorship bias, where only subjects that survived a process are analysed.

entries.title: Sampling bias: when some people are easier to count

definition.text: Sampling bias is systematic error from a non-random sample in which some members of a population are less likely to be included than others.

facts.text: It is usually treated as a kind of selection bias, though some classify it separately.
One view holds that sampling bias threatens how far results generalize, while selection bias mainly threatens comparisons within the sample.
Examples include self-selection and pre-screening of trial participants.

entries.title: The back-door criterion: spotting confounders in a diagram

definition.text: The back-door criterion is Judea Pearl's graphical test for spotting confounding variables in a causal diagram.

facts.text: To estimate a treatment's effect, the background variables must block every back-door path in the graph.
A path can be blocked by adding the confounder as a control in a regression or by matching on it.

entries.title: SUTVA: when one person's treatment affects another
entries.article: Rubin causal model#Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)

definition.text: The stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) requires that one unit's outcome is unaffected by which treatment other units receive.

facts.text: If Mary's drug makes her cook with more salt, Joe's blood pressure depends on her treatment too, violating SUTVA.
Field experiments call it the non-interference assumption.
Violations make causal inference harder, though dependence can be handled by considering more treatments.

entries.title: Reliability and validity: can a measure be trusted?

definition.text: Reliability is how far a measure gives the same result each time it measures the same thing; validity is how far it measures what it is meant to measure.

facts.text: A poorly chosen measure can undermine an impact assessment completely by producing misleading estimates.
The more reliable a measure is, the greater its statistical power and the more credible its findings.
A measure must also be sensitive enough to detect the changes a program might cause.

facts.text: Program staff often leave the logic model unstated, so an evaluator must draw it out of them and judge whether it is plausible.

definition.text: The argument over whether randomized experiments should be the main way to evaluate development programmes.

facts.text: William Easterly called it 'The Civil War in Development economics'.
Supporters, called 'randomistas', say randomization is the only way to deal with unobservable selection bias.
Critics say random assignment rarely suits development interventions and gives results for one context with little wider relevance.

entries.title: Secular trends and maturation: change that would happen anyway

definition.text: Changes that would happen anyway during a programme, such as long-term trends, short-term events or people ageing, and that can bias estimates of its effect.

facts.text: A fertility programme may look effective simply because the community's birth rate was already falling.
A health programme for adults may look ineffective because health generally declines with age.
Keeping programme and control groups in comparable circumstances prevents this bias.

entries.text_plain: A fertility program may look effective simply because the community's birth rate was already falling. A health program for adults may look ineffective because health generally declines with age. Both traps are secular trends and maturation: changes that would happen anyway during a program and can bias estimates of its effect (Impact evaluation: did the program cause the change?). They include long-term trends, short-term events and people aging. The defense is to keep program and control groups in comparable circumstances.

entries.title: Systematic reviews: weighing all the evidence at once
entries.article: Impact evaluation#Systematic reviews of impact evidence

definition.text: A structured assessment of all existing evidence on a topic, presented in an accessible way to link research and policy.

facts.text: It follows a protocol that sets out in advance which studies to include, how to search and how to combine results.
It can also combine qualitative information, such as barriers to a programme working.
Systematic reviews, sometimes with meta-analyses, are generally ranked as the highest level of evidence in scientific and medical research.
They aim to be rigorous and transparent so that bias in the findings can be assessed and, where possible, reduced.

entries.title: Meta-analysis: combining many studies into one answer

definition.text: A method for combining the numerical results of many independent studies of the same research question.

facts.text: Its core step is computing a combined effect size from the studies' effect sizes and variances.
Pooling studies increases statistical power and can settle disagreements between individual studies.
Gene V. Glass coined the term in 1976 as 'the analysis of analyses', though Karl Pearson pooled typhoid inoculation studies in 1904.
A fixed effect model weights studies by the inverse of their variance, so large studies dominate; a random effects model allows true effects to differ between studies.
It cannot fix poor design or bias in the original studies, which argues for including only sound studies.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 180 studies found no evidence of the decoupling of growth from environmental harm needed for ecological sustainability.
A 2021 meta-analysis of 3186 estimates rejected the Cobb–Douglas production function.
Its core step is computing one combined effect size across all the studies.

entries.title: Publication bias: the missing studies that skew the record
entries.article: Meta-analysis#Publication bias: the file drawer problem

definition.text: The distortion that arises because studies with negative or insignificant results are less likely to be published, so published evidence exaggerates effects.

facts.text: Pharmaceutical companies have hidden negative studies, and unpublished dissertations or conference abstracts are easily overlooked.
It is hard to fix because no one can know how many studies went unreported.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments found that, after correcting for publication bias, financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

entries.text: A study that finds nothing is less likely to see print. Publication bias is the distortion that follows: because negative or insignificant results are published less often, the published evidence exaggerates effects ({{ref:nature-nbs-095}}). Pharmaceutical companies have hidden negative studies, and unpublished dissertations or conference abstracts are easily overlooked. The bias is hard to fix because no one can know how many studies went unreported. Correcting for it can change conclusions sharply. A 2026 meta-analysis pooled 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments. After correcting for the bias, it found that financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

entries.title: Regression analysis: the workhorse of empirical economics

definition.text: Regression analysis is a statistical method for estimating how an outcome variable relates to one or more explanatory variables.

facts.text: Its most common form is linear regression, which finds the line or plane that best fits the data by some mathematical rule.
Ordinary least squares picks the line that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the data and the line.
A regression model has unknown parameters, observed explanatory variables, an observed outcome variable and unobserved error terms.
By itself a regression is just a calculation; treating it as a model of real relationships needs assumptions such as a representative sample and error-free explanatory variables.
Including several variables in a regression isolates the effect of one of them, which mirrors the economist's idea of holding other things constant.
Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805 and Gauss in 1809, and Francis Galton coined the term regression in the 19th century.

entries.text: Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, and Gauss in 1809. Francis Galton coined the term regression in the 19th century. Regression analysis is a statistical method for estimating how an outcome variable relates to one or more explanatory variables, the factors thought to influence it. Its most common form is {{ref:nature-econ-258}}, which finds the line or plane that best fits the data by some mathematical rule. The usual rule, {{ref:nature-econ-245}}, picks the line that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the data and the line. A regression model has unknown parameters, observed explanatory variables, an observed outcome variable, and unobserved error terms that capture everything else. Its great appeal for economists is control. Including several variables in a regression isolates the effect of one of them, which mirrors the economist's idea of holding other things constant. Yet by itself a regression is just a calculation. Treating it as a model of real relationships needs assumptions, such as a representative sample and explanatory variables measured without error.

entries.title: Ordinary least squares: fitting the line that misses least

definition.text: The standard way to fit a linear regression: choose the parameters that make the sum of squared gaps between observed and predicted values as small as possible.

facts.text: Each gap between a data point and the fitted line is a residual; the sum of squared residuals measures how well the model fits.
Some sources treat it as the same thing as linear regression.
By the Gauss–Markov theorem it is the best linear unbiased estimator when errors have equal variance and are uncorrelated.
If errors are normally distributed, it gives the same answer as maximum likelihood.
Its key assumption is that the regressors are uncorrelated with the errors.
With a constant and one explanatory variable it is the 'simple regression model' taught in beginner statistics.
Cobb and Douglas used least squares to estimate a labour exponent of 0.75 for their production function.

entries.title: Endogeneity: when the cause is tangled with the effect

definition.text: In econometrics, the problem that arises when an explanatory variable is correlated with the model's error term.

facts.text: Put simply, the supposed cause is also being influenced by the outcome, as when education raises income but income also affects education.
It makes an analysis misjudge cause and effect, so the results are unreliable.
It comes from simultaneity, an omitted confounding variable, or explanatory variables measured with error.
When it is present, ordinary least squares gives biased regression coefficients.
Common fixes are instrumental variables, which are correlated with the problem variable but not with the error term, and Heckman selection correction.
It is often overlooked in non-experimental research, which weakens causal claims and policy advice.

entries.text: Education raises income, but income also affects education. When the supposed cause is itself shaped by the outcome, an analysis misjudges cause and effect. Econometricians call this endogeneity: an explanatory variable correlated with the model's error term, the part of the outcome the model leaves unexplained ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). It comes from simultaneity, an omitted confounding variable, or explanatory variables measured with error. When it is present, ordinary least squares gives biased coefficients ({{ref:nature-econ-245}}), so the results are unreliable. Common fixes are {{ref:nature-econ-234}}, which are correlated with the problem variable but not with the error term, and the Heckman selection correction. Endogeneity is often overlooked in non-experimental research, which weakens causal claims and policy advice.

entries.title: Linear regression: straight lines that can still bend

definition.text: In linear regression the outcome is modelled as a linear combination of the parameters, though not necessarily of the explanatory variables themselves.

facts.text: Simple linear regression has one explanatory variable; multiple linear regression has several.
Linear regression can model curved relationships by adding transformed predictors such as squared terms, because it only needs to be linear in the parameters.
A residual is the gap between the value the model predicts and the true value of the outcome.
Least squares estimates come from solving a set of simultaneous linear equations called the normal equations.

entries.text: Despite the name, linear regression can fit curves. The outcome is modeled as a linear combination, a weighted sum, of the parameters, though not necessarily of the explanatory variables themselves ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). Adding transformed predictors, such as squared terms, therefore lets it model curved relationships. Simple linear regression has one explanatory variable; multiple linear regression has several. A residual is the gap between the value the model predicts and the true value of the outcome. The least squares estimates come from solving a set of simultaneous linear equations called the normal equations.

entries.title: Omitted-variable bias: blaming the wrong factor

definition.text: The error that arises when a statistical model leaves out a relevant variable, so its effect is wrongly credited to the variables that were included.

facts.text: It needs two conditions: the left-out variable affects the outcome, and it is correlated with an included explanatory variable.
The estimate then mixes the direct effect of the included variable with an indirect effect running through the omitted one.
It breaks the ordinary least squares assumption that errors are uncorrelated with the regressors, making estimates biased and inconsistent.
If the omitted variable is positively related to both a regressor and the outcome, that regressor's effect is overstated.
Fixed effects models can remove it when the unobserved differences stay constant over time.

entries.text: Leave a relevant factor out of a model, and its effect gets wrongly credited to the factors left in. That is omitted-variable bias ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). It needs two conditions. The left-out variable must affect the outcome, and it must be correlated with an included explanatory variable ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}). The estimate then mixes the direct effect of the included variable with an indirect effect running through the omitted one. If the omitted variable is positively related to both the included variable and the outcome, the included variable's effect is overstated. Technically, the bias breaks the assumption of ordinary least squares that errors are uncorrelated with the explanatory variables, making estimates biased and inconsistent. When the unobserved differences stay constant over time, a {{ref:nature-econ-227}} can remove it.

entries.title: Difference in differences: comparing changes, not levels

definition.text: A quasi-experimental technique that estimates a treatment's effect by comparing how much a treated group changed over time with how much an untreated control group changed.

facts.text: It needs data on both groups from at least one period before the treatment and at least one after.
Because the groups may start at different levels, it subtracts the 'normal' gap that would exist without treatment; the rest is the treatment effect.
It is a special version of ordinary least squares, and the same estimate comes from a regression with group, period and interaction dummies.
Card and Krueger's 1994 study compared fast-food jobs in New Jersey and Pennsylvania after New Jersey raised its minimum wage, and found no fall in employment.
In environmental economics it is used to assess regulations on pollution, energy use and climate policy.
Richard Hornbeck used it in 2012 to show that heavily eroded Dust Bowl counties lost 20 to 30 percent of land values and farm revenues, with little recovery 10 years later.
It can still suffer from biases such as mean regression, reverse causality and omitted variable bias, depending on how the treated group is chosen.

It became a famous use of difference in differences, a quasi-experimental technique ({{ref:nature-econ-214}}). The method compares how much a treated group changed over time with how much an untreated control group changed. It needs data on both groups from at least one period before the treatment and one after. Because the groups may start at different levels, it subtracts the 'normal' gap that would exist without treatment. What remains is the treatment effect. It is a special version of {{ref:nature-econ-245}}. Environmental economists use it to assess regulations on pollution, energy use and climate. In 2012 Richard Hornbeck used it to show that heavily eroded Dust Bowl counties lost 20 to 30 percent of land values and farm revenues. They saw little recovery 10 years later. It can still suffer from biases such as mean regression, reverse causality and omitted variable bias, depending on how the treated group is chosen.

entries.title: Fixed effects models: controlling for what never changes

definition.text: A regression model for grouped data in which each group's average is treated as a fixed quantity rather than a random draw.

facts.text: In panel data, the fixed effects are each subject's own average, one unchanging intercept per subject.
They control for omitted variable bias from unobserved differences between subjects that stay constant over time, such as innate ability or a country's history and institutions.
These constant differences are removed by subtracting each group's average over time or by taking first differences.
Random effects models assume the subject-specific effects are uncorrelated with the explanatory variables; fixed effects models allow them to be correlated.
Random effects estimates are more efficient when their assumption holds but inconsistent when it does not; the Durbin–Wu–Hausman test is used to choose.

entries.text: Some differences between people or countries never change, such as innate ability or a nation's history and institutions. A fixed effects model controls for them. It is a regression model for grouped data in which each group's average is treated as a fixed quantity rather than a random draw ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). In {{ref:nature-econ-246}}, the fixed effects are each subject's own average, one unchanging baseline per subject. The model removes omitted variable bias from such constant differences ({{ref:nature-econ-244}}). It does so by subtracting each group's average over time or by taking first differences. Random effects models instead assume the subject-specific effects are uncorrelated with the explanatory variables, while fixed effects models allow them to be correlated. Random effects estimates are more efficient when their assumption holds but inconsistent when it does not. The Durbin–Wu–Hausman test is used to choose between them.

In Panel data: following the same subjects over time, the fixed effects are each subject's own average, one unchanging baseline per subject. The model removes omitted variable bias from such constant differences (Omitted-variable bias: blaming the wrong factor). It does so by subtracting each group's average over time or by taking first differences. entries.title: Instrumental variables: finding a clean lever on the cause

definition.text: A quasi-experimental method for estimating cause and effect when controlled experiments are not possible, using a third variable that shifts the cause but not the outcome directly.

facts.text: It is needed when an explanatory variable is correlated with the error term, which makes ordinary least squares biased.
A valid instrument changes the explanatory variable, has no effect of its own on the outcome, and is uncorrelated with the error term.
To study smoking and health, the tobacco tax rate can serve as an instrument, assuming it affects health only through smoking.
Philip G. Wright first used an instrument in a 1928 book, trying to estimate supply and demand for butter; Olav Reiersøl named the method in 1945.
Whether an instrument is truly unrelated to the error cannot be read from data and must come from understanding how the data were generated.
When effects differ between people, the standard estimate recovers a local average treatment effect rather than the population average.

entries.title: Regression discontinuity: learning from the cutoff

definition.text: A regression discontinuity design is a quasi-experimental method that estimates an intervention's effect by comparing cases just above and just below the cutoff that decides who gets it.

facts.text: If every student scoring above 80% gets a scholarship, students at 79% and 81% are likely very similar, so comparing them reveals the scholarship's local effect.
Simply comparing award winners and non-winners would overstate the effect, because strong students both win awards and keep doing well.
Donald Thistlethwaite and Donald Campbell first used it in 1960 to evaluate scholarship programs.
It requires that people cannot perfectly manipulate which side of the cutoff they land on, so assignment near the threshold is as good as random.
Done well, it can give treatment effect estimates similar to randomized studies without the ethical issues of random assignment.
Its estimates can be wrong if a curved relationship is mistaken for a jump, or if another treatment shares the same cutoff.
Other uses include age eligibility rules such as pensions or drinking ages, and elections won by a narrow majority.

entries.title: Extrapolation: predicting beyond the data

definition.text: Extrapolation is using a regression model to predict outside the range of the data it was fitted on; predicting inside that range is interpolation.

facts.text: The further a prediction goes beyond the data, the more room the model has to fail.
Extrapolation leans especially hard on the assumed form of the relationship, which can only be checked within the observed range.

entries.title: Limited dependent variables: yes-or-no outcomes

definition.text: A limited dependent variable is an outcome that is categorical or confined to a certain range, a common situation in econometrics.

facts.text: Running least-squares regression on a yes-or-no outcome gives the linear probability model.
Nonlinear models for yes-or-no outcomes include the probit and logit models, and the multinomial logit handles categories with more than two values.

entries.title: Regression assumptions: what makes a fit meaningful

definition.text: Regression assumptions are the classical conditions researchers rely on to read a regression as a meaningful model of real-world relationships.

facts.text: They include a representative sample, explanatory variables measured without error, errors averaging zero given the covariates, and constant error variance, called homoscedasticity.
If errors are not normally distributed, estimated parameters in small samples will not be normal either, which complicates inference.

They include a representative sample, explanatory variables measured without error, errors averaging zero given the explanatory variables, and constant error variance, called homoscedasticity. If errors are not normally distributed, the estimated parameters in small samples will not be normal either, which complicates inference.

entries.title: Regression diagnostics: checking the fit

definition.text: Regression diagnostics are checks of how well a fitted regression model matches the data and whether its estimated parameters are statistically significant.

facts.text: Common checks of fit include R-squared, the pattern of residuals and hypothesis tests.
Significance is checked by an F-test of overall fit followed by t-tests of individual parameters.
How these tests should be read depends heavily on the model's assumptions.

entries.title: Multicollinearity: when two causes move in lockstep

definition.text: When two explanatory variables in a model are very highly correlated with each other.

facts.text: Small changes in highly correlated data can flip a variable's estimated effect from positive to negative or back.
Spotting it in a sensitivity analysis lets researchers drop highly correlated variables and avoid such dramatic swings in results.

entries.text: Two explanatory variables can move almost in lockstep. Multicollinearity is that situation: two explanatory variables in a model are very highly correlated with each other ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). Small changes in the data can then flip a variable's estimated effect from positive to negative or back. Spotting it in a sensitivity analysis lets researchers drop highly correlated variables and avoid such dramatic swings in results.
entries.text_plain: Two explanatory variables can move almost in lockstep. Multicollinearity is that situation: two explanatory variables in a model are very highly correlated with each other (Regression analysis: the workhorse of empirical economics). Small changes in the data can then flip a variable's estimated effect from positive to negative or back. Spotting it in a sensitivity analysis lets researchers drop highly correlated variables and avoid such dramatic swings in results.

entries.title: Measurement error bias: noise that hides an effect

definition.text: Endogeneity caused when an explanatory variable cannot be measured perfectly, so the observed value carries noise.

facts.text: The noise ends up in both the regressor and the error term, so ordinary least squares underestimates the effect.
Error in measuring the outcome variable does not cause endogeneity, though it makes the error term more variable.

entries.text: Some explanatory variables can never be measured perfectly. Measurement error bias is the form of {{ref:nature-econ-223}} that results when the observed value carries noise. The noise ends up in both the explanatory variable and the error term, so ordinary least squares underestimates the effect. Error in measuring the outcome variable is different. It does not cause endogeneity, though it makes the error term more variable.

entries.title: Simultaneity bias: when two variables shape each other

definition.text: Endogeneity that arises when two variables are determined together, each affecting the other.

facts.text: The idea comes from simultaneous equations models, which separate variables set inside the model (endogenous) from those fixed in advance (exogenous).
Ignoring simultaneity gives biased and inconsistent estimates.

entries.text: Education and income each affect the other. Simultaneity bias is the form of {{ref:nature-econ-223}} that arises when two variables are determined together like this. The idea comes from simultaneous equations models, which separate variables set inside the model (endogenous) from those fixed in advance (exogenous). Ignoring simultaneity gives biased and inconsistent estimates.

entries.title: Weak exogeneity: no link with the past or present

definition.text: An assumption that a model's error term averages zero given the present and past values of the explanatory variables.

facts.text: It allows errors to be correlated with future values of the regressors, so outcomes can feed back into later causes.
Strict exogeneity, which also rules out links with future values, is often implausible in macroeconomic and financial data, so weak exogeneity is the standard there.
Jean-François Richard formalized it in 1980.

entries.text: Jean-François Richard formalized weak exogeneity in 1980. It is the assumption that a model's error term averages zero given the present and past values of the explanatory variables ({{ref:nature-econ-223}}). It allows errors to be correlated with future values of those variables, so outcomes can feed back into later causes. Strict exogeneity also rules out links with future values. That is often implausible in macroeconomic and financial data, so weak exogeneity is the standard there.
entries.text_plain: Jean-François Richard formalized weak exogeneity in 1980. That is often implausible in macroeconomic and financial data, so weak exogeneity is the standard there.

entries.title: The parallel trends assumption

definition.text: The assumption in difference in differences that, without the treatment, the treated and control groups would have changed by the same amount over time.

facts.text: It fails when something other than the treatment changes in one group but not the other at the same time.
Researchers often combine difference in differences with matching on similar pre-treatment histories to make the assumption more likely to hold.
The two groups' membership is also assumed to stay the same over time.

entries.text: Difference in differences rests on a key assumption ({{ref:nature-econ-221}}). Without the treatment, the treated and control groups would have changed by the same amount over time. This parallel trends assumption fails when something other than the treatment changes in one group but not the other at the same time. The membership of the two groups is also assumed to stay the same. Researchers often combine the method with matching on similar pre-treatment histories, to make the assumption more likely to hold.
entries.text_plain: Difference in differences rests on a key assumption (Difference in differences: comparing changes, not levels). Without the treatment, the treated and control groups would have changed by the same amount over time. This parallel trends assumption fails when something other than the treatment changes in one group but not the other at the same time. The membership of the two groups is also assumed to stay the same. Researchers often combine the method with matching on similar pre-treatment histories, to make the assumption more likely to hold.

entries.title: Poisson regression: modeling counts

definition.text: Poisson regression is a form of regression analysis built to model counts, such as how many times an event happens.

facts.text: It assumes the outcome follows a Poisson distribution and that the logarithm of its expected value is a linear combination of unknown parameters.
When an explanatory variable rises by 1, the predicted count is multiplied by the exponentiated coefficient, called the incidence ratio.
It also handles rates, such as tree species per unit area, by adding the logarithm of exposure as an offset term.
Its parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, which has no closed-form answer and must be found numerically.

entries.text: How many times does an event happen? Poisson regression is a form of {{ref:nature-econ-257}} built to model counts like that. It assumes the outcome follows a Poisson distribution, a standard pattern for counts, and that the logarithm of its expected value is a linear combination of unknown parameters. When an explanatory variable rises by 1, the predicted count is multiplied by the exponentiated coefficient, called the incidence ratio. It also handles rates, such as tree species per unit area, by adding the logarithm of exposure as an offset term. Its parameters are estimated by {{ref:nature-econ-239}}, which has no closed-form answer and must be found numerically.

entries.title: Spatial econometrics: when neighbors matter

definition.text: Spatial econometrics is the field where spatial analysis and econometrics meet, handling models in which places interact or observations are not truly independent.

facts.text: It estimates models with spatial autocorrelation or neighbourhood effects, common in regional science, real estate and housing markets.
It analyses economic effects such as externalities, interactions and spatial concentration.
Belgian economist Jean Paelinck introduced the term in May 1974.

entries.text: In May 1974 the Belgian economist Jean Paelinck introduced the term spatial econometrics. The field is where the analysis of geographic patterns ({{ref:nature-es-073}}) and econometrics meet. It handles models in which places interact, or in which observations are not truly independent ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). It estimates models in which nearby places resemble each other ({{ref:nature-es-074}}) or show neighborhood effects, common in regional science, real estate and housing markets. It analyzes economic effects such as externalities ({{ref:nature-found-031}}), interactions and spatial concentration.

The field is where the analysis of geographic patterns (Spatial analysis: asking where) and econometrics meet. It handles models in which places interact, or in which observations are not truly independent (Regression analysis: the workhorse of empirical economics). It estimates models in which nearby places resemble each other (Spatial autocorrelation: near things are related) or show neighborhood effects, common in regional science, real estate and housing markets. It analyzes economic effects such as externalities (Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else), interactions and spatial concentration.

entries.title: First differences: subtracting away what stays the same

definition.text: A way of removing unchanging individual effects from panel data by regressing each period's change in the outcome on the change in the explanatory variables.

facts.text: With two time periods it gives exactly the same result as the fixed effects estimator.
Fixed effects is more efficient when errors are well behaved; first differences is more efficient when errors follow a random walk.

entries.text: Subtract last period from this period, and anything that never changes drops out. The first difference estimator applies that idea to {{ref:nature-econ-246}}. It regresses each period's change in the outcome on the change in the explanatory variables, removing unchanging individual effects. With two time periods it gives exactly the same result as the {{ref:nature-econ-227}} estimator. Fixed effects is more efficient when errors are well behaved. First differences is more efficient when errors follow a random walk, wandering with no pull back toward an average.
entries.text_plain: Subtract last period from this period, and anything that never changes drops out. The first difference estimator applies that idea to Panel data: following the same subjects over time. It regresses each period's change in the outcome on the change in the explanatory variables, removing unchanging individual effects. With two time periods it gives exactly the same result as the Fixed effects models: controlling for what never changes estimator. Fixed effects is more efficient when errors are well behaved. First differences is more efficient when errors follow a random walk, wandering with no pull back toward an average.

entries.title: Overdispersion: when counts vary more than expected

definition.text: Overdispersion is when count data vary more than their mean, breaking the Poisson model's assumption that the mean equals the variance.

facts.text: A common cause is leaving out relevant explanatory variables, or observations that depend on each other.
Negative binomial regression loosens the equal mean and variance assumption and is a popular alternative.
Excess zeros arise when one process decides whether any events happen and another decides how many, as with non-smokers in a survey of cigarettes smoked.

entries.text: The Poisson model assumes a count's mean equals its variance ({{ref:nature-econ-247}}). Real counts often vary more than their mean, a pattern called overdispersion. A common cause is leaving out relevant explanatory variables, or observations that depend on each other. Negative binomial regression loosens the equal mean and variance assumption and is a popular alternative. A related wrinkle is excess zeros. They arise when one process decides whether any events happen and another decides how many, as with non-smokers in a survey of cigarettes smoked.
entries.text_plain: The Poisson model assumes a count's mean equals its variance (Poisson regression: modeling counts). Real counts often vary more than their mean, a pattern called overdispersion. A common cause is leaving out relevant explanatory variables, or observations that depend on each other. Negative binomial regression loosens the equal mean and variance assumption and is a popular alternative. A related wrinkle is excess zeros. They arise when one process decides whether any events happen and another decides how many, as with non-smokers in a survey of cigarettes smoked.

entries.title: Two-stage least squares: instruments in two steps
entries.article: Instrumental variables#Interpretation as two-stage least squares

definition.text: A way to calculate instrumental-variable estimates by running two regressions in turn.

facts.text: First, each problem explanatory variable is regressed on all the exogenous variables, including the instruments, to get predicted values.
Second, the main regression is run with those predicted values in place of the problem variables.

entries.text: Instrumental-variable estimates ({{ref:nature-econ-234}}) can be calculated by running two regressions in turn. That is two-stage least squares. In the first stage, each problem explanatory variable is regressed on all the exogenous variables, including the instruments, to get predicted values. In the second stage, the main regression is run with those predicted values in place of the problem variables ({{ref:nature-econ-245}}).
entries.text_plain: Instrumental-variable estimates (Instrumental variables: finding a clean lever on the cause) can be calculated by running two regressions in turn. That is two-stage least squares. In the first stage, each problem explanatory variable is regressed on all the exogenous variables, including the instruments, to get predicted values. In the second stage, the main regression is run with those predicted values in place of the problem variables (Ordinary least squares: fitting the line that misses least).

entries.title: Weak instruments: a lever that barely moves the cause

definition.text: Instruments that predict the problem explanatory variable poorly, which undermines an instrumental-variables estimate.

facts.text: If smoking hardly responds to tobacco taxes, tax variation reveals nothing about smoking's effect on health.
A common rule of thumb is that the first-stage F-statistic should be larger than 10.

entries.text: An instrument is only useful if it actually moves the cause. If smoking hardly responds to tobacco taxes, tax variation reveals nothing about smoking's effect on health. Such weak instruments predict the problem explanatory variable poorly, which undermines an instrumental-variables estimate ({{ref:nature-econ-234}}). A common rule of thumb is that the first-stage F-statistic should be larger than 10.

entries.title: Fuzzy regression discontinuity: cutoffs that bend

definition.text: A fuzzy regression discontinuity design handles cutoffs that are not strictly applied, needing only that the chance of treatment changes at the threshold.

facts.text: Real cutoffs are often bent, for instance by discretion for students just short of passing, which biases a sharp design.
Its logic is related to the instrumental variable strategy and intention to treat.

Its logic is related to the instrumental variable strategy ({{ref:nature-econ-234}}) and to intention to treat.

entries.title: Regression kink design: learning from a change in slope

definition.text: A regression kink design identifies treatment effects from a sharp change in the slope, rather than the level, of a treatment rule such as student aid that depends on family income.

facts.text: Nielsen, Sørensen and Taber named the technique in 2010.

entries.text: Some rules do not jump at a threshold; they bend. A regression kink design identifies treatment effects from a sharp change in the slope, rather than the level, of a treatment rule ({{ref:nature-econ-263}}). Student aid that depends on family income is one example. Nielsen, Sørensen and Taber named the technique in 2010.

entries.title: Testing whether a regression discontinuity holds up
entries.article: Regression discontinuity design#Testing the validity of the assumptions

definition.text: Regression discontinuity validity tests look for evidence that cases just above and just below the cutoff are not truly comparable.

facts.text: McCrary's density test checks for a bunching of observations at the threshold, such as more students just passing than just failing, a sign of gaming.
Variables fixed before treatment, such as earlier grades, should show no jump at the cutoff.
Unexpected jumps at other points of the assignment variable also make the design suspect.

entries.text: A regression discontinuity design ({{ref:nature-econ-263}}) is only as good as the comparison at its cutoff. Validity tests look for evidence that cases just above and just below it are not truly comparable. McCrary's density test checks for bunching at the threshold, such as more students just passing than just failing, a sign of gaming. Variables fixed before treatment, such as earlier grades, should show no jump at the cutoff. Unexpected jumps at other points of the assignment variable also make the design suspect.

entries.title: Truncated regression: when part of the sample is missing

definition.text: A truncated regression model handles samples from which observations above or below certain values of the outcome have been systematically left out.

facts.text: Whole observations are missing, unlike censored models where the explanatory variables are still known.
In the 1970s James Heckman linked truncated samples to other non-randomly selected samples and developed the Heckman correction.
These models are usually estimated by maximum likelihood.

entries.text: Sometimes observations with an outcome above or below certain values are systematically left out of a sample. A truncated regression model handles such samples ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). Whole observations are missing, unlike censored models, where the explanatory variables are still known. In the 1970s James Heckman linked truncated samples to other non-randomly selected samples ({{ref:nature-econ-270}}) and developed the Heckman correction. These models are usually estimated by maximum likelihood.

In the 1970s James Heckman linked truncated samples to other non-randomly selected samples (Selection bias: when the sample tells the wrong story) and developed the Heckman correction. entries.title: Logistic regression: predicting yes or no

definition.text: A statistical model for yes-or-no outcomes that treats the log-odds of the event as a weighted sum of explanatory variables.

facts.text: It uses the S-shaped logistic function to turn a combination of inputs into a probability between 0 and 1.
Its coefficients are usually estimated by maximum likelihood, using an iterative method because no closed-form answer exists.
It is used in machine learning, most medical fields and the social sciences.
Logit models of discrete choice can be estimated by logistic regression, and are used to analyse choice-based survey tasks.
Multinomial logistic regression extends it to outcomes with more than two categories.
A common alternative is the probit model.
A widely used rule of thumb asks for about 10 events per explanatory variable for stable estimates.
With its upper limit set to 1, the logistic function's output lies between 0 and 1 and can be read as a probability.

entries.text: Will an event happen or not? Logistic regression models yes-or-no outcomes by treating the {{ref:nature-econ-238}} of the event as a weighted sum of explanatory variables ({{ref:nature-econ-257}}). It uses the S-shaped logistic function, the curve behind {{ref:nature-eco-580}}, to turn a combination of inputs into a probability between 0 and 1. With its upper limit set to 1, the function's output can be read as a probability. Its coefficients are usually estimated by maximum likelihood, using an iterative method because no closed-form answer exists. An extension handles outcomes with more than two categories ({{ref:nature-val-080}}), and a common alternative is the {{ref:nature-val-081}}. A widely used rule of thumb asks for about 10 events per explanatory variable for stable estimates. It is used in machine learning, most medical fields and the social sciences. Logit models of choice can be estimated this way and are used to analyze choice-based survey tasks.

entries.title: Propensity score matching: building look-alike groups

definition.text: Propensity score matching is a way to estimate a treatment's effect from observational data by comparing treated and untreated units that were equally likely to be treated, given their observed characteristics.

facts.text: Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin introduced it in 1983, defining the propensity score as the probability of being assigned to treatment given observed covariates.
It tries to mimic randomization by building treated and untreated samples that look alike on all observed covariates.
The score is usually estimated with logistic regression, then each participant is matched to one or more similar non-participants and covariate balance is checked.
Collapsing many covariates into one score let it balance groups without needing huge samples, avoiding the dimensionality problem.
It only accounts for observed covariates, so hidden bias from unobserved factors can remain after matching.
It needs large samples with substantial overlap between treatment and control groups.

entries.contested_note: Some research finds that propensity score matching increases imbalance, inefficiency, model dependence and bias, and Judea Pearl argues matching can even raise hidden bias.
entries.text: In 1983 Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin proposed a way to make observational data behave more like an experiment. Their propensity score is the probability of being assigned to treatment given observed covariates, the measured background characteristics. Propensity score matching estimates a treatment's effect by comparing treated and untreated units that were equally likely to be treated ({{ref:nature-econ-230}}). It tries to mimic randomization by building samples that look alike on all observed covariates. The score is usually estimated with {{ref:nature-eco-582}}. Each participant is then matched to one or more similar non-participants, and balance is checked. Collapsing many covariates into one score let the method balance groups without needing huge samples. Still, it needs large samples with substantial overlap between the groups. It accounts only for observed covariates, so hidden bias can remain ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}). Its value is contested. Some research finds it increases imbalance, inefficiency, model dependence and bias, and Judea Pearl argues matching can even raise hidden bias.

Each participant is then matched to one or more similar non-participants, and balance is checked. Collapsing many covariates into one score let the method balance groups without needing huge samples. Still, it needs large samples with substantial overlap between the groups. It accounts only for observed covariates, so hidden bias can remain (Confounding variables: the hidden third factor). Its value is contested. Some research finds it increases imbalance, inefficiency, model dependence and bias, and Judea Pearl argues matching can even raise hidden bias.

entries.title: Synthetic control: building a twin from many places

definition.text: The synthetic control method builds a comparison group for a treated unit from a weighted average of untreated units, recreating the path the treated unit would have followed without the intervention.

facts.text: It is often used when only one or a few units, such as a region, are treated.
Weights are chosen from the data so the synthetic control closely matches the treated unit on key predictors, usually over a long period before the intervention.
Unlike difference in differences, it can account for confounders that change over time.
It combines elements of matching and difference in differences, and was first proposed by Alberto Abadie and coauthors.
Applications include natural catastrophes and economic growth, vaccine mandates, and drug development where randomized trials are not feasible.

entries.title: Log-odds: the logit behind logistic regression
entries.article: Logistic regression#Definition of the inverse of the logistic function

definition.text: The logit: the natural logarithm of the odds of an event, the inverse of the logistic function.

facts.text: In logistic regression the log-odds equal the linear regression expression, so the logit links probabilities to a linear model.
The odds of the outcome equal the exponential of the linear regression expression.

entries.text: Odds compare the chance that something happens with the chance that it does not. The log-odds, or logit, is the natural logarithm of those odds, and it is the inverse of the logistic function ({{ref:nature-eco-580}}). In {{ref:nature-eco-582}}, the log-odds equal the linear regression expression, so the logit links probabilities to a linear model. Put the other way round, the odds of the outcome equal the exponential of that linear expression.
entries.text_plain: Odds compare the chance that something happens with the chance that it does not. The log-odds, or logit, is the natural logarithm of those odds, and it is the inverse of the logistic function (Logistic growth: fast at first, then leveling off). In Logistic regression: predicting yes or no, the log-odds equal the linear regression expression, so the logit links probabilities to a linear model. Put the other way round, the odds of the outcome equal the exponential of that linear expression.

entries.title: Soil: the crowded living layer beneath every harvest

definition.text: A mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms that together support plant and soil life.

facts.text: Soil is a three-phase system: a solid matrix of minerals and organic matter, pores holding gases, and water carrying dissolved substances.
It serves as a habitat, a nutrient and waste recycler, a regulator of water quality and the atmosphere, and a medium for plant growth, making it a key provider of ecosystem services.
A gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, mostly microbes and largely unexplored.
A recent study suggested soil is home to 59 ± 15% of the species on Earth.
Texture, set by the proportions of sand, silt and clay, is the most important physical property for services such as crop production.
Civilizations have prospered or declined according to the availability and productivity of their soils.

entries.text: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species. Most of them are microbes, and most remain largely unexplored. One recent study suggested that soil is home to 59 ± 15% of all the species on Earth. Soil is a mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and living things that together support plant and soil life. Scientists call it a three-phase system. A solid frame of minerals and organic matter is laced with pores that hold gases, and water moves through it carrying dissolved substances. That mixture does a great deal of work. Soil is a habitat, a recycler of nutrients and wastes, a regulator of water quality and of the atmosphere, and the medium in which plants grow. Those jobs make it a key provider of ecosystem services. Its texture, set by the shares of sand, silt and clay, is the most important physical property for services such as growing crops. The stakes are ancient. Civilizations have prospered or declined according to how much good soil they had and how productive it was.
entries.text_plain: A single gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species. Most of them are microbes, and most remain largely unexplored. One recent study suggested that soil is home to 59 ± 15% of all the species on Earth. Soil is a mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and living things that together support plant and soil life. Scientists call it a three-phase system. A solid frame of minerals and organic matter is laced with pores that hold gases, and water moves through it carrying dissolved substances. That mixture does a great deal of work. Soil is a habitat, a recycler of nutrients and wastes, a regulator of water quality and of the atmosphere, and the medium in which plants grow. Those jobs make it a key provider of ecosystem services. Its texture, set by the shares of sand, silt and clay, is the most important physical property for services such as growing crops. The stakes are ancient. Civilizations have prospered or declined according to how much good soil they had and how productive it was.

entries.title: Environmentalism: from factory smoke to a global movement

definition.text: A broad philosophy and social movement that seeks to protect living things, habitats and the wider environment.

facts.text: It advocates preserving, restoring and improving the natural environment, including systems such as the climate, and is often a movement to control pollution or protect biodiversity.
At its core it tries to balance people's relations with the natural systems they depend on so that all are sustainable.
The movement began as a response to rising smoke pollution during the Industrial Revolution; Britain's Alkali Acts of 1863 were the first large-scale modern environmental laws.
The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, attended by 113 nations, led to the UN Environment Programme.
Its strands include free-market, evangelical and labour environmentalism and the conservation movement, and it gave rise to green parties.
Critics say early environmentalism reflected mostly white middle- and upper-class interests and overlooked indigenous communities and nearby low-income residents.
Every year more than 100 environmental activists are murdered worldwide.

It argues for preserving, restoring and improving nature, including systems such as the climate. In practice it often means controlling pollution or protecting biodiversity. At its core it tries to balance people's dealings with the natural systems they depend on, so that all of them can last. entries.title: Soil fertility: the power to give steady harvests

definition.text: The ability of soil to support plant growth and give steady, good-quality crop yields.

facts.text: A fertile soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and is free of toxic substances.
Helpful properties include enough depth for roots, good drainage and aeration, organic-rich topsoil, and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0.
Irrigating with salty, alkaline or acidic water can strip useful salts or build up harmful ones, cutting fertility; about 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated.
Soil organic matter and fertility are significantly correlated.

entries.text: A fertile soil does more than grow one good crop. It gives steady, good-quality yields, and that ability to support plant growth is called soil fertility. Such a soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts, and it is free of toxic substances. Several properties help: enough depth for roots, good drainage and air flow, a topsoil rich in organic matter, and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0. The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline something is. Water can undo the good work. About 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated, and watering with salty, alkaline or acidic water can strip useful salts or build up harmful ones. Studies find a clear statistical link between how much decaying organic matter a soil holds and how fertile it is.

entries.title: Autotrophs: the organisms that never need to eat

definition.text: An organism that turns non-living energy sources, such as sunlight or chemicals, into energy stored in organic compounds that others can use.

facts.text: Autotrophs build carbohydrates, fats and proteins from carbon in simple substances such as carbon dioxide.
They are the producers in a food chain, such as plants on land and algae in water, and need no living source of carbon or energy.
Heterotrophs, including all animals and almost all fungi, depend on autotrophs for raw materials and fuel.
Plants can use only about 1% of the sun's energy for photosynthesis.
The German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1892.
Researchers think the first cells were autotrophs, possibly living at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

entries.text: Every animal alive depends on organisms that never eat anything. These are autotrophs: organisms that turn non-living energy, such as sunlight or chemicals, into energy stored in organic compounds that others can use. They build carbohydrates, fats and proteins from the carbon in simple substances such as carbon dioxide. Plants on land and algae in water are the producers that every feeding chain starts from. They need no living source of carbon or energy. Organisms that must feed on others, including all animals and almost all fungi, rely on autotrophs for both raw materials and fuel. The whole system runs on a thin margin: plants can use only about 1% of the sun's energy for {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. The German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1892. Researchers think the first cells on Earth were autotrophs, possibly living at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, hot springs on the ocean floor.

entries.title: Primary production: where almost all life's food begins

definition.text: The making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water, mainly by photosynthesis.

facts.text: Almost all life on Earth relies directly or indirectly on primary production.
The organisms that do it, called primary producers or autotrophs, form the base of the food chain: mainly plants on land and algae in water.
A small share is driven by chemosynthesis, which takes energy from chemical reactions of inorganic compounds instead of light.
On land it depends mainly on water and temperature, and it is strongly limited in deserts and polar regions.
Satellite estimates put Earth's total primary production at 104.9 petagrams of carbon per year, 56.4 on land and 48.5 in the oceans.
Human societies are part of Earth's primary production cycle but influence it disproportionately.

entries.text: Almost every living thing on Earth depends, directly or indirectly, on a single process. Primary production is the making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water. It happens mainly through {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, the capture of sunlight by plants and algae. The organisms that do it are called primary producers, or autotrophs. They form the base of every feeding chain: mostly plants on land and algae in water. A small share runs on chemosynthesis instead. Chemosynthesis draws energy from chemical reactions of non-living compounds rather than from light. On land, production depends mainly on water and temperature. That is why deserts and polar regions produce so little. Satellites now let scientists add up the whole planet. Their estimate is 104.9 petagrams of carbon a year, with 56.4 made on land and 48.5 in the oceans. The sea, worked by drifting algae, nearly matches the land. Human societies are part of this cycle of production. Yet they influence it far out of proportion to their share of it.

entries.title: Biomass: weighing all the life on Earth

definition.text: The total mass of living organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time.

facts.text: It can be measured as wet weight, dry weight, or the mass of organic carbon, depending on the context.
In 2018 Earth's live biomass was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants.
Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of carbon and bacteria plus archaea 30, while animals make up less than 0.5% of the total.
By 2020 the mass of human-made materials was projected to surpass that of all living biomass on Earth.
On land biomass falls sharply at each higher trophic level, but in the oceans it can increase at higher levels.
Ocean producers account for almost half of yearly production but only about 0.2% of total biomass.
The biomass of wild land mammals is believed to be seven times lower than prehistoric values, while livestock biomass exceeds that of all wild mammals.

entries.text: By 2020, the mass of everything humans have made was projected to surpass the mass of all life on Earth. That living total is biomass: the mass of organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time. It can be weighed wet, dry, or as organic carbon, depending on the purpose. In 2018 Earth's live biomass was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants. Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of it, and bacteria plus the similar single-celled archaea hold 30. Animals make up less than 0.5% of the total. The sea breaks the pattern. Ocean producers make almost half of each year's new growth, yet they hold only about 0.2% of all biomass. On land, biomass falls sharply at each step up the ladder of who eats whom, but in the oceans it can rise. Wild land mammals are believed to weigh seven times less than in prehistoric times, and livestock now outweigh all wild mammals together.

entries.title: Phytoplankton: the invisible half of the world's plant work

definition.text: The tiny drifting organisms in oceans and lakes that make their own food by photosynthesis.

facts.text: They need sunlight, so they live in the sunlit surface layer of oceans and lakes.
They do about half of global photosynthesis and produce at least half of the oxygen, though they are only about 1% of global plant biomass.
Marine phytoplankton fix about 50 Pg of carbon a year in net primary production.
They form the base of marine and freshwater food webs and drive the biological pump that moves carbon to the deep sea.
They include cyanobacteria and protists such as diatoms; there are about 5,000 known marine species.
Their turnover takes days rather than decades, so they respond quickly to climate change; warming-driven stratification cuts nutrient supply and productivity.
Some studies indicate global phytoplankton density has decreased over the past century.

entries.text: At least half of Earth's oxygen comes from organisms too small to see. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting organisms in oceans and lakes that make their own food by capturing sunlight. Because they need light, they live in the sunlit surface layer of the water. They carry out about half of global {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, though they make up only about 1% of global plant biomass. Marine phytoplankton fix about 50 Pg, or petagrams, of carbon a year. They are the base of the feeding networks of sea and lake. They also drive the {{ref:nature-eco-204}}, which moves carbon to the deep ocean. They include cyanobacteria and single-celled protists such as diatoms, and about 5,000 marine species are known. They turn over in days rather than decades, so they respond quickly to a changing climate. Warming splits the water into layers that mix less, cutting their nutrient supply and their output. Some studies indicate that their global density has fallen over the past century.

entries.title: Abiotic components: the non-living rules of life

definition.text: The non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things and how ecosystems work.

facts.text: They include water, light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity, altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil.
Humans can create or change them: fertilizers alter habitats and greenhouse gases change the ocean's pH.
Differences in them, such as water availability between rainforests and deserts, set limits on which species can live where and shape competition.
Factors such as salinity can give one species a competitive edge over another, creating pressure that leads to new species.

entries.text: A rainforest and a desert differ above all in water, and that one difference limits which species can live in each. Water is an abiotic component of an ecosystem: one of the non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things. Others include light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity (saltiness), altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil. Such differences also shape how species compete. Humans now create and change these factors. Fertilizers alter the places species live, and heat-trapping gases ({{ref:nature-eco-162}}) change the ocean's pH, its acidity. Non-living factors can even steer evolution. Salinity, for instance, can give one species an edge over another, and that pressure can lead to new species.

entries.title: Population: one species, one place, one time

definition.text: A group of organisms of the same species living in a particular place at a particular time.

facts.text: A population is usually described by who belongs to it, its size, the area it occupies and the time period studied.
Ecologists stress individuals interacting and competing in an area; the evolutionary view stresses genes and reproduction.
Populations of different species living and interacting together make up a community.
Large populations are rarely counted in full; methods such as the Lincoln index estimate total numbers from individuals observed.
Spatially separated populations of one species can be called a metapopulation.

entries.text: Ecologists rarely count a large population in full. Methods such as the Lincoln index instead estimate the total from the individuals actually seen. In ecology, a population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular place at a particular time. A description usually names who belongs to it, its size, the area it occupies and the period studied. Ecologists stress individuals interacting and competing in one area. An evolutionary view stresses genes and reproduction instead. Populations of different species living and interacting together make up a {{ref:nature-eco-331}}. Separate populations of one species, spread out in space, can be treated as a larger unit: a {{ref:nature-eco-379}}.

entries.title: Heterotrophs: life that must feed on other life

definition.text: An organism that cannot make its own food and instead gets its carbon from other organisms or their remains.

facts.text: Heterotrophs include most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants.
In a food chain they are the consumers, while autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers.
Detritivores are heterotrophs that eat dead plant and animal matter and feces.
Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the CO2 entering the atmosphere, which plants then reuse.
By mineralization they convert organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms plants can use, which is critical to plant survival and soil fertility.

entries.text: Every mushroom is a heterotroph, and so are most animals. A heterotroph is an organism that cannot make its own food. It gets its carbon from other organisms or from their remains. The group includes most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants. In the chain of who eats whom, heterotrophs are the consumers. Autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers. Detritivores are heterotrophs that eat dead plants, dead animals and feces. Their work keeps the planet's materials moving. Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere, which plants then take up again. Through mineralization, the release of nutrients locked in dead matter, heterotrophs turn organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms that plants can use. That step is critical to plant survival and to soil fertility.

entries.title: Population ecology: births, deaths, arrivals and departures

definition.text: The study of how species populations change through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how they interact with their environment.

facts.text: Population size is the number of individuals; population density is how closely packed they are.
Change in numbers follows N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E: starting numbers plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants.
Carrying capacity is the largest population the environment's resources can sustain.
Population viability analysis, which predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a habitat patch, grew from this field and matters for conservation.
Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: recruitment, growth and mortality, including harvest mortality.
Population dynamics began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially.

entries.text: A population changes in only four ways: individuals are born, die, arrive or leave. Population ecology studies those changes, through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how populations interact with their environment. Its bookkeeping fits on one line: N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E. The new number is the starting number, plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants. Population size is the number of individuals, and population density is how closely packed they are. The largest population an environment's resources can sustain is its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. The field began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially. Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: {{ref:nature-eco-590}}, growth and mortality, including deaths from harvesting. Population viability analysis also grew from this field. It predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a patch of suitable land, and it matters for conservation.

entries.title: Ecological productivity: how fast an ecosystem grows

definition.text: The rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass, often measured in grams per square metre per day.

facts.text: Productivity of plants and other autotrophs is primary productivity; that of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity.
It depends on nutrient availability, temperature and water availability.
Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 gC/m²/yr of biomass.
Fertilizer nutrients can trigger algal blooms that raise primary production but make the ecosystem less stable.

entries.text: Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 grams of carbon in new biomass on each square meter every year. That figure measures ecological productivity: the rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass. It is often given in grams per square meter per day. The productivity of plants and other autotrophs is called primary productivity. That of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity. Three things set it: nutrient supply, temperature and water. More is not always better. Nutrients washed in from fertilizer can trigger algal blooms, sudden surges of algae. These raise primary production but leave the ecosystem less stable.

entries.title: Soil degradation: five ways soil loses its power

definition.text: The decline of soil's ability to function, through acidification, contamination, desertification, erosion or salination.

facts.text: Erosion is caused by water, wind, ice and gravity, and several kinds can occur at once.
Desertification in dry regions is often caused by poorly adapted human activities such as overgrazing or excess firewood harvesting; drought alone is a common misconception.
Salination is a build-up of salts that degrades the agricultural value of soils and vegetation.
At low levels, soil organisms can treat contamination, mainly through microbial enzymes.

entries.text: Soil can wear out. Soil degradation is the decline of soil's ability to do its jobs, and it happens in five main ways. Soil can become more acidic. It can be contaminated or eroded. It can fill with salt. And dry land can turn to desert, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. That last one is widely misunderstood. Drought alone is a common misconception as its cause. It usually comes from poorly adapted human activities, such as overgrazing or harvesting too much wood for fuel. Erosion, the wearing away of soil, is driven by water, wind, ice and gravity, and several kinds can strike at once. Salination is a build-up of salts that cuts the farming value of soils and the plants growing on them. Contamination has a partial natural remedy. At low levels, soil organisms can treat it, mainly through enzymes made by microbes.

entries.title: Gross and net primary production: what plants keep
entries.article: Primary production#Gross primary production and net primary production

definition.text: Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time; net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration.

facts.text: Net primary production is what is available for producers' growth and reproduction, and so for herbivores to eat.
Net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus the carbon producers lose through cellular respiration.
Gross production is harder to measure than net, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars produced.
Estimates scaled up from eddy covariance measurements give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon per year for 1998-2005.
NPP is calculated as gross primary production minus respiration.
Most primary production comes from photosynthesis, using sunlight, water and CO2.
Where there is no light, as in groundwater, caves and hydrothermal vents, lithoautotrophs using chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers.
Net ecosystem production subtracts the respiration of both autotrophs and heterotrophs from gross primary production.

entries.text: A plant spends part of every sugar it makes just staying alive. Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time. Net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration, the process that releases stored energy. The net share fuels the producers' growth and reproduction, and it is what plant-eaters can eat. Put simply, net equals gross minus the carbon lost to respiration. Gross production is harder to measure, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars as they are made. Scaled-up eddy covariance measurements, which track gases flowing between land and air, give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon a year for 1998-2005. Where there is no light, as in caves and hydrothermal vents, microbes that feed on chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers. A wider measure, {{ref:nature-eco-241}}, also subtracts the respiration of consumers.

Net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration, the process that releases stored energy. The net share fuels the producers' growth and reproduction, and it is what plant-eaters can eat. Put simply, net equals gross minus the carbon lost to respiration. Gross production is harder to measure, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars as they are made. Scaled-up eddy covariance measurements, which track gases flowing between land and air, give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon a year for 1998-2005. Where there is no light, as in caves and hydrothermal vents, microbes that feed on chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers. A wider measure, Net ecosystem production: the carbon an ecosystem keeps, also subtracts the respiration of consumers.

entries.title: Ecosystem ecology: the living and non-living as one system

definition.text: The study of how the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem interact as one integrated system.

facts.text: It focuses on functional processes such as primary production, decomposition and feeding relationships that keep ecosystems and their services going.
Eugene Odum and Howard T. Odum quantified flows of energy and matter through whole ecosystems.

In Guatemala's western highlands, forest loss has raised landslide and water-shortage risks, while Totonicapán, which kept its forests, is more economically stable.

entries.title: Terrestrial ecosystems: life on land

definition.text: An ecosystem found on land, such as tundra, taiga, forest, grassland or desert.

facts.text: Land ecosystems differ from aquatic ones by having soil rather than water at the surface, and plants extending above it.
Water availability varies widely on land, and temperatures swing more by day and season than in water.
Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface.
Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets their conservation, restoration and sustainable use.

entries.text: Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface. Temperatures also swing more by day and by season than they do in water. The UN goal described in {{ref:nature-gov-030}} targets the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of these ecosystems.
