entries.title: Plant defenses: tolerating and resisting herbivores

definition.text: A plant trait that improves its survival or reproduction when animals feed on it.

facts.text: Defenses fall into tolerance, withstanding damage without losing fitness, and resistance, reducing how much damage is done.
Herbivores counter defenses by choosing which plants to eat, adapting their own bodies, or modifying the plant.
Many herbivores eat a mix of plants to balance nutrients and avoid too much of any one defensive chemical.

entries.text: Many plant-eaters eat a mix of plants, balancing their nutrients and avoiding too much of any one defensive chemical. Those chemicals are one kind of plant defense against herbivory: any trait that improves a plant's survival or reproduction when animals feed on it. Defenses fall into two kinds. Tolerance means withstanding damage without losing fitness. Resistance means reducing how much damage is done. Herbivores push back. They choose which plants to eat, adapt their own bodies, or modify the plant.

entries.title: Food chain length: why chains stay short

definition.text: The number of feeding links between a consumer and the base of its food chain.

facts.text: Generally only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next; the rest is used up in metabolism.
Food chains usually have no more than five trophic levels.
Eating lower in the chain gives more energy: a salad yields more energy per pound than an animal that ate lettuce.
Ecologists have proposed that chain length grows with ecosystem volume, is capped by energy loss at each level, or reflects habitat type.

Food chains usually have no more than five trophic levels. Ecologists offer several explanations for where chains stop. Length may grow with ecosystem volume, be capped by energy loss at each level, or reflect habitat type.

entries.title: Top-down and bottom-up: what controls an ecosystem

definition.text: The two ways an ecosystem's structure is shaped: from below by how much energy plants bring in, and from above by predators.

facts.text: Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms.
Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total energy shrinks at each higher level.
Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea; the balance of the two controls is a major research question.
Herbivory can speed litter decomposition and nutrient cycling by changing litter quality and vegetation.
Top carnivores keep herbivores in check; without them herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants.
If plant populations fall sharply, herbivores decline and then carnivores decline too.
An ecosystem need not be one or the other: a marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing.

entries.text: Without top carnivores, herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants. If plant populations crash instead, herbivores decline, and then carnivores decline too. Those two chains of cause are top-down and bottom-up control, the two ways an ecosystem's structure is shaped. One works from above, through predators. Herbivores also reach down into the soil. Herbivory can speed the breakdown of fallen leaves and the cycling of nutrients by changing litter quality and vegetation.

entries.title: Apparent competition: rivals through a shared predator

definition.text: An indirect contest in which two unrelated prey species affect each other through a shared predator.

facts.text: If one prey species booms, its predator increases and then hunts both prey more heavily, so the other species declines.
Robert D. Holt coined the term in 1977.
Introduced snowshoe hares in Newfoundland may have shrunk the range of native arctic hares by boosting their shared lynx predator.
Conservation scientists see human introductions of predators or food subsidies such as garbage as an extreme, one-sided form of it.

entries.text: Introduced snowshoe hares in Newfoundland may have shrunk the range of native arctic hares, not by eating their food but by boosting their shared predator, the lynx. entries.title: Plant-pollinator networks: shared structure, shared fate

definition.text: The web of mutualistic links between plants and pollinators, which shows a similar structure across very different ecosystems and continents.

facts.text: Models suggest this structure reduces competition between pollinators and strengthens ecosystem stability.
Pollinators therefore survive harsh conditions together but collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point.
These networks have a strikingly similar structure on different continents, even with entirely different species.
Network structure may shape how pollinator communities respond to harsher conditions.

Pollinators survive harsh conditions together, but they collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point. The network's structure may shape how pollinator communities respond as conditions grow harsher.

entries.title: Are humans apex predators?

definition.text: The question of where humans sit in the food web, and whether they count as apex predators.

facts.text: A 2013 study averaged the trophic levels of foods in the human diet and found a mean of 2.21, from 2.04 in Burundi to 2.57 in Iceland.
That value is comparable to non-apex animals such as the anchovy or pig.
A 2014 critique found humans eating mainly predatory fish in two marine systems had trophic levels of 4.65 and 4.5, making them apex predators there.

entries.contested_note: Ecologists disagree whether humans are apex predators, depending on whether land-based diets or marine food webs are measured.

Humans eating mainly predatory fish in two marine systems had trophic levels of 4.65 and 4.5, making them apex predators there. The answer depends on whether land-based diets or marine food webs are measured, and ecologists still disagree.

entries.title: Mesopredator release: when the middle hunters take over

definition.text: The rise in mid-sized predators that follows when the top predators that kept them in check are removed.

facts.text: Hunting of sperm whales, with a trophic level of 4.7, has increased populations of large squid.
In North America over the past two centuries, the ranges of all apex carnivores have shrunk while those of 60% of mesopredators have grown.
Removing badgers in a bovine tuberculosis trial more than doubled hedgehog densities.

Hunting of sperm whales, with a trophic level of 4.7, has increased populations of large squid.

entries.title: Are trophic cascades weaker on land?

definition.text: The debate over whether trophic cascades on land are as strong as those in lakes, streams and seas.

facts.text: The earliest documented cascades were all aquatic, leading to speculation that cascades are mainly an aquatic phenomenon.
A 2002 meta-analysis found cascades generally weaker on land, with smaller changes in plant biomass.
A 2009 study found many tree species were heavily affected by the loss of an apex predator.
Critics note real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diet changes with growth and outside resource inputs.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether land ecosystems show cascades as strong as aquatic ones.

Critics note that real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diets that change as animals grow, and food arriving from outside. Studies still disagree.

entries.title: Foundation species: the builders of communities

definition.text: A species that plays a strong role in shaping the structure of its community.

facts.text: Foundation species can sit at any trophic level: producers, herbivores or predators.
Paul K. Dayton coined the term in 1972 for certain marine invertebrates and algae.
Corals, kelps, oysters, seagrasses, mangroves and forest trees help other organisms by creating habitat and easing physical stress such as waves and drying.
Studies removing creosote bush and eastern hemlock found species diversity rose afterwards, suggesting foundation species can sometimes limit diversity.

entries.title: The green world hypothesis: why herbivores haven't eaten everything

definition.text: The idea that the world stays green because predators keep down the herbivores that would otherwise eat the vegetation.

facts.text: It is also called the HSS hypothesis after Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin, who published it in 1960.
Sea otter studies support it: otters eat sea urchins, and without otters urchins nearly eliminate kelp forests, leaving urchin barrens.
The rival plant self-defense hypothesis says plants survive mainly through thorns, toxins and tough tissues.

entries.contested_note: The plant self-defense hypothesis offers a competing explanation that plant defenses, not predators, keep herbivores from eating all vegetation.

entries.title: The inverted biomass pyramid of the sea

definition.text: In the sea, the total mass of consumers can exceed that of the producers, turning the usual biomass pyramid upside down.

facts.text: This happens because phytoplankton grow and reproduce fast, so a small mass can sustain a high rate of primary production.
Because of this inversion, zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass.
Ocean producers are tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton, so a small mass yields high production, while land producers like mature forests need far more mass for the same output.
As a result zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass and link phytoplankton to the rest of the food web.

entries.title: The whale pump: fertilizing the ocean surface

definition.text: The process by which whales carry nutrients from the ocean depths back up to the surface.

facts.text: Whales feed deep down where krill are found but return regularly to the surface to breathe.
It reverses the usual downward flow of nutrients in the ocean's biological pump, where marine snow sinks from surface to bottom.
In the Gulf of Maine whales carry more nitrogen through their feces than all the rivers in that system combined.
Whale feces are up to 10 million times richer in iron than seawater, feeding phytoplankton in the iron-poor Southern Ocean.

entries.title: Cascade effects: one loss triggers many

definition.text: A chain of secondary extinctions set off when a key species in an ecosystem dies out.

facts.text: Species most at risk depend on a few foods, rely on the lost species, or must live alongside an invasive species.
The main cause is loss of top predators, which lets prey multiply, overuse their food and then crash.
Hunting sea otters for pelts let urchins strip the kelp, leaving barrens where urchins and kelp-dependent species died out locally.

entries.title: Why energy moves more efficiently in the sea
entries.article: Ecological efficiency#Ecological efficiency in the marine environment

definition.text: The generally higher efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels in the sea than on land.

facts.text: Transfer from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton is estimated at about 20%, compared with 10% on land.
Phytoplankton biomass can turn over 100–300 times a year, while land plants turn over only 0.5 to 2.0 times.
Coastal upwelling zones may have as few as three trophic levels and support whales, while open oceans can have six and support only small tuna and squid at the top.

entries.title: The ten percent law of energy transfer

definition.text: The rule of thumb that only about ten percent of food energy passing from one trophic level to the next is stored as new flesh.

facts.text: The rest is lost in transfer, used in respiration or lost through incomplete digestion.
It is credited to Raymond Lindeman (1942), though he did not call it a law and cited efficiencies from 0.1% to 37.5%.
In the standard example, of 10,000 J of sunlight plants take 100 J, a deer 10 J, a wolf 1 J, and a human eating the wolf 0.1 J.

entries.title: Ecological stoichiometry: the chemistry of eating

definition.text: The study of how the balance of energy and chemical elements shapes living things and their interactions in ecosystems.

facts.text: It focuses on mismatches between what organisms need and what their food contains: termites have a carbon:nitrogen ratio of about 5 yet eat wood with a ratio of 300–1000.
Plants and algae vary widely in their elemental make-up, whereas animals keep a nearly fixed composition, a trait called stoichiometric homeostasis.
Lake algae and detritus range in C:P ratio from 100 to 1000, while the zooplankton Daphnia stays near 80:1.
Nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from farming can boost stream producers and ripple up the food web.

It became a fundamental principle of marine ecology and biogeochemistry.
It is not universal: nitrogen fixation, denitrification and changing nutrient inputs can shift it.

entries.title: Decomposition: how the dead feed the living

definition.text: The breakdown of dead organic matter into simpler substances such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts.

facts.text: It is part of the nutrient cycle and essential for recycling the finite matter of the biosphere.
Abiotic decomposition happens by chemical or physical processes; biotic decomposition, or biodegradation, is done by living things, mainly microbes.
Plant matter decomposes in stages, starting with leaching of soluble compounds by water and physical fragmentation that gives decomposers more surface to attack.
Vertebrate bodies pass through five stages: fresh, bloat, active decay, advanced decay and dry remains.
Waterlogged soils slow decomposition, so carbon-rich sediments build up and act as a long-term carbon sink.
Ecosystems that lose biodiversity provide fewer services, including decomposing waste.

entries.title: Soil organic matter: the living and dead fraction of soil

definition.text: The organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes, and substances they make.

facts.text: It improves soil structure, water retention, soil biodiversity, pollutant retention, pH buffering and nutrient cycling.
It raises fertility by holding nutrients on exchange sites and slowly releasing nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur as it mineralizes.
It is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so measured soil organic carbon often stands in for it.
Microbes decompose plant litter into minerals plants can absorb (mineralization), while part becomes stable humus.
Organic matter builds up where cold or wet conditions slow decomposers, and breaks down fast in hot, rainy tropical climates.
About 70% of global soil organic carbon lies below 20 cm depth.

entries.title: Soil biology: the hidden life underfoot

definition.text: The study of the life in soil, from bacteria and fungi to earthworms and burrowing mammals, and what it does.

facts.text: Soil organisms break down organic matter, releasing nutrients for plants, which shapes fertility, soil structure and carbon storage.
Nutrients held in the bodies of soil organisms are protected from leaching, especially nitrogen and phosphorus.
A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria; a gram of garden soil can hold around 700 km of fungal hyphae.
Earthworms, ants and termites act as ecosystem engineers, mixing soil, improving water infiltration and enriching it with nutrients.
Saprotrophic fungi decompose dead matter into humus and mineral nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate.
Much about how soil populations function and interact is still unknown.

entries.title: Decomposers: the recyclers of the living world

definition.text: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and releases their nutrients into the surrounding environment.

facts.text: 'Decomposer' names a role in an ecosystem, not a particular kind of organism.
Plants cannot move to find nutrients or digest other organisms, so they rely on decomposers to free nutrients from dead matter.
Decomposers include fungi and bacteria, which digest food outside their bodies, and invertebrates such as earthworms that digest it inside and release nutrients in their faeces.
Fungi are the main decomposers in forests, because only wood-decay fungi have enzymes to break down lignin and their hyphae can penetrate large pieces of wood.
By breaking down dead matter, decomposers return carbon to the air and recycle nutrients into forms plants can use.

entries.title: The soil carbon pool: Earth's biggest living-world carbon store
entries.article: Soil organic matter#Function in carbon cycling

definition.text: The large store of carbon held in the world's soils, a key part of the global carbon cycle.

facts.text: The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the 750-gigaton atmospheric pool and 4.5 times the 560-gigaton biotic pool.
Organic carbon, mostly as soil organic matter, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons; carbonates make up the rest.
Soil can act as a carbon sink through sequestration or a source through greenhouse gas emissions, depending on outside factors.

entries.title: Detrital food webs: the economy of the dead

definition.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers and passed on to detritivores and then carnivores.

facts.text: Detritus is any non-living organic matter, such as leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung.
Detrital and grazing webs connect: mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat leaf-eating earthworms.

entries.title: Dark earths: fertile soils made by people

definition.text: Dark, carbon-rich, highly fertile soils, many of them created or enriched by human soil management.

facts.text: Amazonian Dark Earth was created deliberately by Indigenous communities and contrasts sharply with the poor weathered soils around it.
In Ghana and Liberia, combining different wastes produces African Dark Earths rich in calcium, phosphorus and carbon.
The size of pre-1492 Amazonian societies, and Dark Earth's role in them, are continually debated.

entries.title: Rate of decomposition: why some things rot faster

definition.text: How fast dead material breaks down, governed by the physical environment, the quality and amount of the material, and the microbes present.

facts.text: Decomposition is fastest in damp conditions with enough oxygen, and slow in very wet or very dry soils.
Labile compounds such as sugars break down fast, while recalcitrant ones such as lignin persist, so dead animals decay faster than leaves, and leaves faster than branches.
Tilling speeds decomposition by adding oxygen and exposing new organic matter to microbes.
Litter rich in lignin decomposes slowly, so low-lignin plant communities cycle nutrients faster.

Decomposition is fastest in damp conditions with enough oxygen, and slow in very wet or very dry soils. Labile, or easily broken, compounds such as sugars go fast. Recalcitrant, or resistant, ones such as lignin persist. Litter rich in lignin therefore decays slowly, and low-lignin plant communities cycle nutrients faster. Tilling speeds decomposition by adding oxygen and exposing new organic matter to microbes.

entries.title: Humus: the stable dark heart of soil

definition.text: Organic matter that soil organisms have broken down to the point where it resists further decay.

facts.text: Humus is usually five percent of soil or less by volume, yet it is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture.
Its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times greater than that of clay on a dry-weight basis.
Humic substances are classed as fulvic acid, humic acid and humin, in order of rising molecular weight and resistance to microbes.

facts.text: It can persist for centuries, while particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only years to decades.

entries.title: Mycorrhiza: the fungus-root partnership

definition.text: A partnership between a fungus and plant roots that benefits both.

facts.text: The fungus takes carbohydrates from the root and in return supplies the plant with nitrogen, phosphorus and moisture.
Fungi either sheath the root (ectomycorrhizae) or enter root cells as arbuscules (arbuscular mycorrhizae).
Most tree species and many crops have mycorrhizae, but the cabbage family does not.
Chemical signalling between plants through shared mycorrhizal networks remains a matter of conjecture.

entries.title: Nitrification: turning ammonia into plant food

definition.text: The step of the nitrogen cycle in which soil bacteria turn ammonium from decaying proteins into nitrates that plants can take up.

facts.text: Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas do this as autotrophic nitrifiers, making their own carbohydrate without photosynthesis.
It is an important step of the nitrogen cycle in soil, carried out with oxygen by small groups of bacteria and archaea.
Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas turn ammonia into nitrite, and others such as Nitrobacter turn nitrite into nitrate.
Converting ammonia matters because ammonia gas is toxic to plants.

entries.title: Denitrification: returning nitrogen to the air

definition.text: Processes in oxygen-poor soil that turn nitrates and nitrites back into nitrogen gas or nitrous or nitric oxide, returning nitrogen to the air.

facts.text: It is done mainly by anaerobic or facultatively anaerobic bacteria such as Pseudomonas.
Too much denitrification depletes soil nitrogen and fertility, and excess nitrogen fertilizer can cause it.
Bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus do it in low-oxygen conditions such as waterlogged soils, using nitrate in place of oxygen to respire.
Because it removes nitrate and reduces leaching to groundwater, it can be used to treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal waste.

entries.title: Nitrogen fixation: pulling plant food from the air

definition.text: The conversion of nitrogen from the air into nitrogen compounds living things can use, carried out by certain bacteria.

facts.text: It is done by free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter and cyanobacteria, or by rhizobia living in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria play a decisive role in early soil formation.
Fixation must happen before plants can take up atmospheric nitrogen.
Lightning fixes between 5 and 10 billion kg a year, but most fixation is done by bacteria called diazotrophs.

entries.title: Population dynamics: the mathematics of rising and falling numbers

definition.text: The mathematical study of how the size and age make-up of populations change over time, treating them as dynamical systems.

facts.text: It is a branch of mathematical biology that uses tools such as differential equations.
It is widely seen as beginning with Malthus, who held that with constant conditions a population grows or declines exponentially.
Simple models track four processes: births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
In a closed population, growth equals births minus deaths: dN/dt = rN.
Adding a carrying capacity gives the logistic equation, in which growth is limited as N approaches K.
Population ecologists use life-history data and projection matrices to manage wildlife stocks and set harvest quotas.

entries.title: Biological dispersal: leaving home to spread out

definition.text: The movement of living things, or their seeds and spores, from where they were born to where they breed, or from one breeding site to another.

facts.text: Technically it is any movement that could lead to gene flow.
It has three phases: departure, transfer and settlement.
Organisms disperse when the benefits, such as new resources and avoiding competition and inbreeding, outweigh the costs in energy, risk, time and opportunity.
Dispersal shapes population dynamics, population genetics and where species live.
Ecosystems depend on individuals moving between habitat patches, making dispersal critical to their stability.
Seed dispersal and the ability to disperse are counted as ecosystem services and as part of a species' capacity to adapt to climate change.

entries.title: R/K selection: many cheap offspring or a few costly ones

definition.text: An evolutionary hypothesis that species are selected either to produce many cheap offspring or few offspring with heavy parental investment.

facts.text: r-strategists have many offspring with little care each; K-strategists invest heavily in fewer offspring.
The letters come from the logistic model: r is the maximum growth rate and K the carrying capacity.
r-selection dominates in unstable environments and favours many offspring, small size, early maturity and wide dispersal; dandelions are a typical example.
K-selection dominates in stable environments, favouring strong competitors with large bodies, long lives and few well-cared-for young, such as elephants and whales.
Most organisms mix traits; the split can be recast with discounting, r-selection matching large discount rates and K-selection small ones.
MacArthur and Wilson coined the terms in 1967; the theory was popular in the 1970s and 1980s, then lost ground after empirical criticism.
Life history theory based on age-specific mortality has replaced it, and some now speak of fast versus slow life histories.
Slow-breeding, long-lived species such as orange roughy proved vulnerable to fishing models that assumed faster growth.

entries.title: The Lotka–Volterra equations: predator and prey in cycles

definition.text: A pair of differential equations, also called the predator–prey model, that describe how the numbers of a predator and its prey change together over time.

facts.text: Prey grow exponentially without predators, and are eaten at a rate proportional to how often predators and prey meet.
Predators grow by eating prey and, without prey, die off exponentially.
The model predicts endless cycles: predators thrive on plentiful prey, outstrip their food and decline, letting prey recover.
Such swings are seen in nature, as in Hudson's Bay Company lynx and snowshoe hare records and Isle Royale's moose and wolves.
Improving conditions for the prey raises the predator's equilibrium numbers, not the prey's.
Ocean iron fertilization fits this: the phytoplankton bloom is quickly eaten, so enrichment mainly boosts predators.
Lotka proposed the model in 1910 and Volterra published it independently in 1926 to explain why predatory fish rose in Adriatic catches during World War I.
In economics it models competing firms and, through Richard Goodwin's model, the link between unemployment and wage growth.

entries.title: Minimum viable population: how few is too few

definition.text: The smallest size at which a population can survive in the wild without being wiped out by disasters or by random demographic, environmental or genetic events.

facts.text: Small populations face more extinction risk because they recover less well from random events.
It is estimated with population viability analyses, computer simulations repeated thousands of times to find the starting size giving, say, a 95% or 99% chance of surviving 1,000 years.
In small populations, genetic drift erodes genetic diversity and raises inbreeding, which lowers fitness.
The '50/500 rule' is a common benchmark, but 2014 guidance says it does not apply across many taxa.
A meta-analysis found a median MVP for vertebrates of 4,169 individuals (95% CI = 3,577–5,129).
Managers can lift a population above its MVP through captive breeding or by moving in individuals from other reserves.

entries.title: The species–area relationship: bigger places hold more species

definition.text: The pattern linking the area of a habitat to the number of species found in it: larger areas tend to hold more species.

facts.text: It is often fitted with Preston's power function, which plots as a straight line on log–log axes with slope z.
Plotted on ordinary axes the curve almost always flattens as area grows.
Proposed causes include the balance of immigration and extinction, disturbance, predator–prey dynamics and clustering of individuals.
Conservation scientists use it to predict extinction rates from habitat loss and fragmentation.
Preston distinguished 'mainland' samples of continuous habitat from 'island' isolates such as islands.
Island biogeography theory was first developed to explain the species–area pattern on oceanic islands.
It is often written as the power law S = cA^z, where S is species number, A is area and z the slope.
On log–log axes it becomes a straight line: log(S) = log(c) + z log(A).

entries.title: Competitive Lotka–Volterra equations: modeling rivals

definition.text: A simple mathematical model of how the populations of species competing for a shared resource change over time.

facts.text: It builds on the logistic equation, adding for each species a term for the harm done by its competitors.
For two species, the coefficient α12 is the effect of species 2 on species 1 and α21 the reverse; in competition all these values are positive.
Each species can have its own growth rate and carrying capacity.
The model extends to any number of species, with the interaction coefficients forming a matrix.
Competitive systems cannot cycle with fewer than three species or become chaotic with fewer than four; with five or more, any behaviour is possible.
Large Lotka–Volterra systems tend to be unstable or sparsely connected, unless species' traits evolve by natural selection.

entries.title: The Allee effect: when fewer means worse off

definition.text: The link between how many individuals a population has, or how dense it is, and how well the average individual survives and reproduces; at low numbers, fewer individuals means lower fitness.

facts.text: It is usually defined as positive density dependence: individual fitness rises with population density.
The classical view held that competition makes growth fastest at low density; the Allee effect says the reverse at low density.
Warder Clyde Allee first described it in the 1930s, showing goldfish survive better in tanks with more fish.
Common causes are trouble finding mates, cooperative defence, cooperative feeding and environmental conditioning.
In fisheries science it is close to, or the same as, 'depensation'.
It can slow a population's range expansion and even prevent biological invasions.
Fishing pressure combined with Allee effects can push exploited fish populations between alternative stable states.

entries.contested_note: Sources call it contentious whether demographic stochasticity counts as an Allee effect.
entries.text: In the 1930s Warder Clyde Allee showed that goldfish survive better in tanks with more fish. His name now marks the Allee effect. It is the link between a population's size or density and how well the average individual survives and reproduces. At low numbers, fewer individuals means lower fitness. It is usually defined as positive {{ref:nature-res-044}}: individual fitness rises as density rises. That reverses the classical view, in which competition makes growth fastest at low density. Common causes are trouble finding mates, cooperative defense, cooperative feeding and environmental conditioning. In fishery research it is close to, or the same as, 'depensation'. The effect can slow a population's range expansion and even prevent biological invasions. Fishing pressure combined with Allee effects can push exploited fish populations between different steady conditions, the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-616}}. Whether random demographic chance counts as an Allee effect is contentious.

Whether random demographic chance counts as an Allee effect is contentious.

entries.title: Geometric population growth: multiplying by generation

definition.text: Growth of a population that breeds in separate seasons, multiplying by a fixed factor λ each generation.

facts.text: With constant birth and death rates, the population after t generations is λ^t times its starting size.
It grows if births exceed deaths (λ > 1), shrinks if deaths exceed births, and holds steady if they are equal.
Doubling time is the time for the population to reach twice its size, found by taking logarithms.
Real populations cannot grow forever, because lack of resources eventually raises the death rate.

entries.title: The intrinsic rate of increase: growth with no brakes

definition.text: The rate at which a population would grow, per individual, if nothing dependent on its density held it back.

facts.text: It is the r in dN/dt = rN, the maximum theoretical growth rate per individual.
It is often used in insect pest management to see how the environment affects how fast pests multiply.
It relates to the finite rate of increase λ of generation-based models by r = ln(λ).

entries.title: Recruitment: how new individuals join a population

definition.text: In population dynamics, the process by which new individuals join a population, through birth and growing up or through immigration.

facts.text: An individual often counts as recruited only once it survives to a certain size or life stage.
It is shaped by predation, birth and dispersal rates and by temperature, rainfall and disturbance, which makes it hard to measure.
High recruitment raises current and future abundance; low recruitment reduces it.
Because of their economic importance, fisheries are a common setting for recruitment studies; fishing a stock at or below MSY keeps it at maximum recruitment.

entries.title: The S-curve: how innovations spread
entries.article: Logistic function#In economics and sociology: diffusion of innovations

definition.text: Use of the logistic curve to show how an innovation spreads: slowly at first, then rapidly, then levelling off near saturation.

facts.text: Gabriel Tarde's The Laws of Imitation (1890) described three stages: a hard start, an exponential take-off, and a slowing phase.
New products such as railroads, light bulbs, electrification, cars and air travel went through rapid growth after early cost and quality gains.

entries.title: Dispersal barriers: rivers, mountains and roads

definition.text: Anything that stops organisms from moving, so that a species' dispersal range is smaller than its distribution.

facts.text: Habitat fragmentation from human land use is an artificial barrier; mountain ranges and rivers are natural ones.
The Congo River separates the ranges of the two chimpanzee species.
Barriers that cut gene flow can isolate populations and lead to allopatric speciation.

entries.title: Dispersal kernels: how far organisms travel

definition.text: A probability distribution describing how far individuals travel when they disperse.

facts.text: Dispersal is measured either as a rate, the expected share of individuals leaving an area, or as a distance.
Models use kernels such as the negative exponential, normal and inverse power distributions.
'Fat-tailed' kernels that allow rare long-distance moves are thought to fit real data best.

entries.title: Human-mediated dispersal: species on the move with people

definition.text: Movement of organisms that people cause, either by carrying them directly or by altering landscapes.

facts.text: People move organisms on purpose, as with farm animals, or by accident when they cling to people or vehicles.
Carriage by humans can move organisms much farther than natural means.
Ship ballast water and motor vehicles are new dispersal routes that can spread invasive species.

entries.title: Seed dispersal: how plants send their seeds away

definition.text: The movement of seeds away from the parent plant.

facts.text: The five main modes are gravity, wind, ballistic, water and animals.
How seeds disperse shapes the genetic structure, migration and species interactions of plant populations.
Transport by animals is especially effective because it carries seeds over long distances.
Because plants cannot move much, they rely on wind and water or on animals such as birds and mammals to carry their seeds.

entries.title: r- and K-strategists in succession: colonizers and competitors

definition.text: The pattern in which fast-breeding r-strategists colonize disturbed land first and are gradually replaced by more competitive K-strategists.

facts.text: After major disruptions such as the eruptions at Krakatoa or Mount St. Helens, the two strategies play distinct roles in regrowth.
Succession approaches a new equilibrium, sometimes called a climax community, dominated by K-strategists.
The intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds that moderate disturbance creates patches at different stages, letting colonizers and competitors coexist.

entries.title: The Leslie matrix: projecting a population by age

definition.text: A discrete-time model of population growth that tracks a population divided into age classes.

facts.text: It assumes a population closed to migration, growing without limits, and usually counts only females.
Building it requires the count in each age class, the share surviving to the next class, and fecundity for each class.
Each time step, the population vector is multiplied by the matrix to give the next step's population.
The matrix's dominant eigenvalue gives the long-run growth rate, and its eigenvector gives the stable age distribution.

At each time step, the population vector is multiplied by the matrix to give the next step's population. A key number calculated from the matrix, its dominant eigenvalue, gives the long-run growth rate. Its eigenvector gives the {{ref:nature-eco-579}}.

entries.title: The anthropogenic Allee effect: when rarity pays

definition.text: An Allee effect created by markets, when rarity makes a species so valuable that hunting the last individuals still pays.

facts.text: Classic economic theory expected exploitation to stop short of extinction, because the cost of finding the last few individuals would exceed their selling price.
When rare species fetch higher prices than common ones, rare species can be driven extinct while common ones are harvested sustainably.
It is now a standard way to think about how markets threaten endangered species.
A two-dimensional analysis shows even very large populations can be on paths to extinction.

entries.text: Classic economic theory expected hunting to stop short of extinction. Finding the last few individuals would cost more than they sold for. When rare species fetch higher prices than common ones, the rare can be driven extinct while the common are harvested sustainably. A two-dimensional analysis shows that even very large populations can be on paths to extinction. The idea is now a standard way to think about how markets threaten species at risk.

entries.title: Strong and weak Allee effects: the point of no return
entries.article: Allee effect#Strong vs. weak Allee effects

definition.text: Two kinds of Allee effect, distinguished by whether the population has a critical size below which its growth turns negative.

facts.text: Under a weak Allee effect, growth per individual slows at low numbers but stays positive.
Under a strong Allee effect, a population that falls below the threshold is headed for extinction without help.
A simple cubic growth model shows this: growth is negative between zero and a threshold A and positive between A and carrying capacity K.

entries.title: Stable age distribution: the mix a population settles into

definition.text: The steady share of individuals in each age class that an age-structured population settles into, along with a steady growth rate.

facts.text: Whatever its starting size or age mix, the population tends toward this structure, and returns to it after disturbance.
Once reached, the population grows exponentially at rate λ.
Fast-growing populations, and those with high death rates at all ages, have disproportionately young age structures.

entries.title: Photosynthesis: how sunlight becomes food and oxygen

definition.text: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria turn light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy.

facts.text: Usually it means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen.
The captured energy is stored in carbon compounds such as sugars, starch and cellulose, which cells later break down through cellular respiration.
It produces and maintains the oxygen in Earth's air and supplies most of the energy for complex life.
Global photosynthesis captures energy at about 130 terawatts, about eight times the power used by human civilization.
Photosynthetic organisms turn around 100–115 billion tons of carbon into biomass each year.
Oxygen released by cyanobacteria oxygenated the Earth, which made complex life possible.
Charles Reid Barnes proposed the term photosynthesis in 1893.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: The living world captures sunlight at a rate of about 130 terawatts, roughly eight times the power used by human civilization. The machinery doing this is photosynthesis: the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria turn light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy. These are the autotrophs met in {{ref:nature-eco-324}}, the organisms that make their own food. In its usual form, called oxygenic photosynthesis, the process splits water and releases oxygen. The captured energy is stored in carbon compounds such as sugars, starch and cellulose. Cells later break these compounds down through {{ref:nature-eco-212}} to get the energy back. The scale is immense. Each year photosynthetic organisms turn around 100–115 billion tons of carbon into biomass, the stuff of living bodies. The consequences reach far beyond any single leaf. Oxygen released by cyanobacteria long ago filled Earth's air, which made complex life possible. Photosynthesis still produces and maintains that oxygen today, and it supplies most of the energy that complex life runs on. The name is surprisingly recent: Charles Reid Barnes proposed it in 1893.

entries.title: Biogeochemical cycles: the planet's recycling loops

definition.text: A biogeochemical cycle is the movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the air and the Earth's crust.

facts.text: The major cycles include the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles.
In each cycle a substance is changed and moved by living things and through stores such as the air, the soil and the oceans.
Energy flows one way through ecosystems, arriving as sunlight and leaving as heat, but the matter that makes up living things is conserved and recycled.
Six elements common in living matter, carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, take many chemical forms as they cycle.
Geological processes such as weathering, erosion, drainage and plate subduction also help recycle materials, which is why the cycles are called biogeochemical.
Microorganisms drive much of the cycling of elements in the Earth system.
Climate change and other human impacts are changing the speed, intensity and balance of many of these cycles.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Nothing in an ecosystem is ever truly used up. A biogeochemical cycle is the movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the air and the Earth's crust. Energy and matter behave differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem: it arrives as sunlight and leaves as heat. The matter that makes up living things is instead conserved and recycled. Six elements common in living matter take many chemical forms as they move: carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. The major cycles include those of carbon, nitrogen and water. In each one, living things change and move a substance, which also passes through stores such as the air, the soil and the oceans. Microorganisms drive much of this cycling. Rocks take part too. Weathering, erosion, drainage and plate subduction, the slow sinking of one slab of Earth's crust beneath another, all help recycle materials. That mix of life, geology and chemistry is why the cycles are called biogeochemical. Today global warming and other human impacts are changing the speed, intensity and balance of many of them.

entries.title: The carbon cycle: life's main ingredient on the move

definition.text: The carbon cycle is the exchange of carbon among living things, soils, rocks, water and the air of Earth.

facts.text: Carbon is the main ingredient of living matter and a major part of many rocks, such as limestone.
The cycle covers carbon being recycled through living things and also its long-term storage in, and release from, carbon sinks.
The steps of the carbon cycle are key to making Earth able to support life.
In the air, carbon exists mainly as carbon dioxide and methane, both of which trap heat and drive part of the greenhouse effect.
Carbon dioxide leaves the air mainly through photosynthesis, entering life on land and in the ocean.
About 500 gigatons of carbon are held above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds about 1,500 gigatons.
Global average atmospheric carbon dioxide reached a record 422.7 parts per million in 2024.
Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph Priestley first described the carbon cycle, and Humphry Davy popularised it.

entries.title: The water cycle: one supply, endlessly moving

definition.text: The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water, changing between liquid, ice and vapour, on, above and below the Earth's surface.

facts.text: The total mass of water on Earth stays fairly constant, but how it is split between ice, fresh water, salt water and air varies with climate.
Water moves by evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, surface runoff and subsurface flow.
The cycle is powered by energy from the sun.
The ocean is the source of 86% of global evaporation.
Most rain falls back into the ocean or onto land, where it flows over the ground as surface runoff.
Moving water carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to waterbodies, and with groundwater it carries nitrogen too.
The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

conflicts.text: The oceans supply about 90% of the evaporated water that enters the water cycle.
conflicts.note: Another sentence on the same page gives 86% of global evaporation.

It carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to rivers, lakes and seas, and together with groundwater it carries nitrogen too. The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

entries.title: The nitrogen cycle: plenty in the air, scarce in the soil

definition.text: The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea.

facts.text: Its main steps are fixation, ammonification, nitrification and denitrification.
Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, but that gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce in many ecosystems.
Nitrogen availability can set the rate of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition.
Many of its steps are carried out by microbes harvesting energy or gathering nitrogen to grow.
Plants take up nitrate or ammonium from the soil through their root hairs.
Growing legumes, making fertilizer with the Haber–Bosch process and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into forms life can use.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, yet many ecosystems are starved of it. The gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce. The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea. Its main steps are {{ref:nature-eco-394}}, {{ref:nature-eco-178}}, {{ref:nature-eco-395}} and {{ref:nature-eco-396}}. Because usable nitrogen is so scarce, its supply can set the pace of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition. People have changed this balance sharply. entries.text_plain: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, yet many ecosystems are starved of it. The gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce. The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea. Its main steps are Nitrogen fixation: pulling plant food from the air, Ammonification: freeing nitrogen from the dead, Nitrification: turning ammonia into plant food and Denitrification: returning nitrogen to the air. Microbes carry out many of these steps, either harvesting energy or gathering nitrogen to grow. Plants take up two usable forms, nitrate and ammonium, from the soil through their root hairs. Because usable nitrogen is so scarce, its supply can set the pace of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition. People have changed this balance sharply. Growing legumes, making fertilizer with the The Haber process: fertilizer pulled from the air and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into forms life can use.

entries.title: Evapotranspiration: how land breathes water back to the sky

definition.text: Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants, through evaporation and transpiration.

facts.text: Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies, while transpiration moves water from roots through a plant and out of its stomata as vapour.
Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of rain and snow falling on land returns to the air this way.
It is measured in millimetres of water over a set time.
Its level depends mainly on how much water is available, how much energy is in the air and soil, and how much moisture the air can take up.
Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the effects of climate change on the water cycle.
Measuring it is key to water resource management and irrigation planning.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Most of the rain and snow that lands on the continents never reaches a river. Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of it returns to the air through evapotranspiration. That is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants. The word joins two processes. Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration moves water from a plant's roots, up through the plant and out of its stomata, the tiny pores in its leaves, as vapour. Evapotranspiration is measured in millimetres of water over a set time. Three things mainly set its level. One is how much water is available. Another is how much energy is in the air and soil. The third is how much moisture the air can take up. Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the ways a changing climate is altering the water cycle. The numbers matter in practice, because measuring evapotranspiration is key to managing water supplies and planning irrigation.

entries.title: Soil carbon: a store three times the size of the atmosphere's

definition.text: Soil carbon is the solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from living things and as carbonate minerals.

facts.text: It supports key soil functions such as holding water, retaining nutrients and building soil structure.
Soils store about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the atmosphere's carbon and 240 times annual fossil fuel emissions.
Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes setting how much carbon land stores.
Soil carbon acts as a carbon sink and matters for climate change mitigation and climate models.
Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil organic carbon, but people could also deliberately return carbon to soils.
Warming could change the activity of soil microbes that break down carbon, possibly adding to climate change.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Soils store about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere and 240 times a year's fossil fuel emissions. This soil carbon is the solid carbon held in soils, both as organic matter from living things and as carbonate minerals. It does daily work. It helps soil hold water, retain nutrients and build its crumbly structure. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes that set how much carbon land stores. Because soil can take up carbon from the air, it matters for slowing global warming and for the computer models scientists use to project the climate. Human activities have caused a massive loss of organic carbon from soils, but people could also deliberately return carbon to them. Warming adds a risk of its own. It could change the activity of the soil microbes that break carbon down, possibly adding to the warming.

entries.title: Infiltration: how rain soaks into the ground

definition.text: Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil.

facts.text: The infiltration capacity is the fastest rate at which water can soak in; it is usually measured in meters per day.
When rain falls faster than the soil can take it in, the extra water usually runs off over the surface.
Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand; compaction lowers infiltration further.
Wet soil soaks up water more slowly; fully saturated soil cannot take in any more.
Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks in the soil that speed infiltration; bare ground can have very low rates, causing runoff and erosion.
Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and increase runoff.
Steeper slopes shed water as runoff more readily, lowering infiltration.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Whether a storm waters a field or floods a street depends largely on one thing: how fast the ground can drink. Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil. The fastest rate at which water can soak in is called the infiltration capacity, usually measured in meters per day. When rain falls faster than that, the extra water usually runs off over the surface. Texture matters. Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand. Compaction squeezes the soil and lowers infiltration further. Wet soil soaks up water more slowly, and fully saturated soil cannot take in any more. Living things help. Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed water downward, while bare ground can have very low rates, which leads to runoff and erosion. Steeper slopes shed water more readily. Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and send more water across the ground.

entries.title: Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in

definition.text: Surface runoff, or overland flow, is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough.

facts.text: It happens when soil is already saturated or rain arrives faster than soil can absorb it, and on roofs and pavement that let no water in.
Runoff is a major part of the water cycle and the main agent of soil erosion by water.
Its main environmental harm is carrying pollutants such as petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers into surface water, groundwater and soil.
More runoff means less groundwater recharge, lowering water tables and worsening droughts for those who rely on wells.
Flooding occurs when a watercourse cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream.
Remedies include limiting paved surfaces, erosion controls on farms and building sites, green infrastructure, and controls on chemical use.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: A roof or a parking lot lets no rain soak in at all. Every drop that lands becomes surface runoff, or overland flow. This is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough. On natural ground, runoff starts when the soil is already saturated or when rain arrives faster than infiltration can take it in. Runoff is a major part of the water cycle. It is also the main way water wears soil away, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-264}}. Its main environmental harm is what it carries. Running water picks up petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers and delivers them into surface water, groundwater and soil. More runoff also means less water seeping down to refill groundwater, so water tables drop and droughts hit harder for people who rely on wells. When a stream cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream, it floods. The remedies follow from the causes. Limit paved surfaces, control erosion on farms and building sites, build the green networks described in {{ref:nature-nbs-161}}, and control how chemicals are used.

entries.title: Soil erosion: losing the ground under the crops

definition.text: Soil erosion is the wearing away of the top layer of soil by water, ice, snow, wind, plants and animals, including people.

facts.text: It can be slow and unnoticed or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil.
On farms it shrinks cropland and production potential, lowers water quality and damages drainage networks.
Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far faster than soil forms.
About 75 billion tons of soil erode from land each year, about 13–40 times the natural rate.
Water and wind erosion together cause 84% of degraded land, and about 40% of the world's agricultural land is seriously degraded.
Clay-rich and organic-rich soils resist erosion better; plant cover and roots protect soil from both water and wind.
Longer, steeper slopes erode much faster in heavy rain, especially without plant cover.
More intense rainfall expected with climate change will raise erosion unless measures are taken.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: About 75 billion tons of soil erode from the land each year, some 13–40 times the natural rate. It can be slow and unnoticed, or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil. Farming is the main accelerator. entries.title: Cellular respiration: the slow burn inside every cell

definition.text: Cellular respiration is the process by which cells break down food molecules, usually with oxygen, to make ATP, the energy carrier cells use.

facts.text: Respiration with oxygen is aerobic; respiration using another electron acceptor is anaerobic.
It is technically a combustion reaction, but one that releases energy slowly and under control.
Aerobic respiration consumes glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water and energy.
Current estimates put the yield at around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose, below the textbook figure of 38.
Aerobic metabolism is up to 15 times more efficient than anaerobic metabolism.
Although plants take in CO2 overall, plant respiration produces about half of the CO2 released each year by land ecosystems.
The energy left after respiration is what ecologists call net primary production.

conflicts.text: The total yield from fully oxidizing one glucose molecule is 30 or 32 ATP.
conflicts.note: The same page elsewhere gives current estimates of around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Cellular respiration is technically a kind of burning, but one that releases energy slowly and under control. It is the process by which cells break down food molecules, usually with oxygen, to make ATP, the energy carrier cells use. With oxygen it is called aerobic respiration. When cells pass their electrons to some other substance instead, it is anaerobic. Aerobic respiration consumes glucose, a simple sugar, and oxygen, and it produces carbon dioxide, water and energy. In effect it releases the energy that photosynthesis stored in sugar. The oxygen route pays well: aerobic metabolism is up to 15 times more efficient than anaerobic metabolism. Current estimates put the yield at around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose molecule, below the textbook figure of 38. Plants respire too. Although they take in carbon dioxide overall, plant respiration produces about half of the carbon dioxide released each year by land ecosystems. The energy left after plants' own respiration is what ecologists call net primary production.

entries.title: The Haber process: fertilizer pulled from the air

definition.text: The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, is the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen.

facts.text: It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, and most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer.
Fritz Haber showed it working in the laboratory in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF.
It met rising demand for fertilizer when mined niter and guano were thought too scarce for future needs.
The hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012.
Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas.
As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: In 1909 Fritz Haber showed in his laboratory that nitrogen from the air could be turned into ammonia. Carl Bosch then scaled the method up for the company BASF. The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, remains the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, a material that speeds the reaction. In effect it is nitrogen fixation done in a factory. Most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer. The timing mattered. Demand for fertilizer was rising, and the mined niter and guano, or bird droppings, then in use were thought too scarce for future needs. The process still leans on fossil fuel. Its hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012. Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas. As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

entries.title: The phosphorus cycle: the slow loop that skips the sky

definition.text: The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things.

facts.text: Unlike most other cycles, the air plays almost no part, because phosphorus rarely becomes a gas.
Living things need phosphorus as part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and in animals it also strengthens bones and teeth.
Phosphates move quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean, making this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles.
Its four main steps are uplift of phosphorus-bearing rock, weathering and erosion, transport by rivers to lakes and the ocean, and burial in sediments.
On land, the release of phosphorus as rocks weather limits how much is available to ecosystems.
Phosphorus can limit the growth of aquatic life, and phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can pollute lakes and streams.
Freshwater algal blooms are generally caused by excess phosphorus, while saltwater blooms tend to come from excess nitrogen.

entries.title: Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing

definition.text: Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water.

facts.text: It is a main cause of eutrophication in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where excess nutrients feed algal growth.
Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels.
Nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer that crops do not use are lost from fields and harm air and downstream water.
Excess nitrogen causes harmful algal blooms, hypoxia, acid rain, nitrogen saturation in forests and climate change.
Its economic costs include higher water treatment costs, losses to commercial and recreational fishing and shellfish, and reduced tourism income.
Health effects include excess nitrate in drinking water (blue baby syndrome) and rashes or breathing problems from swimming in algal blooms.
Remedies include vegetated buffer zones, artificial wetlands, vegetated drainage ditches, better wastewater treatment and permits under the polluter pays principle.
In Europe agriculture is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but in a lake or a bay they become pollutants. Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually these two, entering water. It is a main cause of {{ref:nature-eco-216}} in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the extra nutrients feed algal growth. Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels. Fertilizer that crops do not use is lost from fields and harms air and downstream water. Excess nitrogen brings toxic algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acidic rain, nitrogen-saturated forests and global warming. The costs are real: dearer water treatment, losses to commercial fishing, fishing for sport and shellfish, and less tourism income. Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause blue baby syndrome. Remedies include vegetated buffer strips, artificial wetlands, better wastewater treatment and permits that make the polluter pay.

entries.title: Eutrophication: when a lake is fed too well

definition.text: Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen.

facts.text: It is caused by too much of a nutrient, most often phosphates and nitrates.
It can happen naturally or be caused by sewage, industrial wastewater, fertilizer runoff and other human sources.
The resulting algal blooms and bacterial growth deplete dissolved oxygen and cause serious environmental damage.
Effects include more phytoplankton, oxygen loss, more fish kills and the loss of desirable fish species.
Surveys found 54% of lakes in Asia, 53% in Europe, 48% in North America, 41% in South America and 28% in Africa are eutrophic.
The World Resources Institute has identified 375 hypoxic coastal zones worldwide.
The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished.

entries.text: The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished, and that is exactly the trouble. Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen. Along the world's coasts, the {{ref:nature-hist-032}} has identified 375 zones where the water runs dangerously short of oxygen.

entries.title: Hypoxia: when water runs short of oxygen

definition.text: Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions, usually in the air at altitude or in natural waters.

facts.text: Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none is called anoxic.
Most fish cannot live below 30% saturation, while a healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%.
It is most often caused by nutrient pollution: algal blooms die, sink and are decomposed by bacteria that use up the oxygen.
It can also occur without pollution, as when lighter river water layers over seawater in estuaries and blocks oxygen from reaching the bottom.
Hypoxia harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Most fish cannot live once water falls below 30% of the oxygen it could hold. Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions like this, usually in natural waters or in the thin air at altitude. Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none at all is anoxic. A healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%. The usual cause is nutrient pollution. Algal blooms die and sink, and the bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen as they respire. Hypoxia can also happen without pollution. In estuaries, lighter river water can layer over seawater and block oxygen from reaching the bottom. Low oxygen is not bad for everything. It harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones, which live without oxygen.

entries.title: Dead zones: stretches of sea where life suffocates

definition.text: Dead zones are low-oxygen (hypoxic) areas in the world's oceans and large lakes where most aquatic life cannot survive.

facts.text: Hypoxia sets in when dissolved oxygen falls to 2 mg per litre or less, and mass die-offs follow below 0.5 mg per litre.
They are often caused by eutrophication: extra nitrogen and phosphorus fuel algal blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen.
A 2008 study counted 405 dead zones worldwide.
They may be permanent, temporary (lasting hours or days) or seasonal, usually in summer and autumn.
Marine dead zones were first noted in the 1970s in heavily used waters such as Chesapeake Bay, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea.
Fertilizer runoff from the Mississippi basin causes a summer dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico that reached over 22,000 square kilometres in 2017.
Because warmer water holds less oxygen, ocean oxygen is falling and dead zones are expanding with climate change.
Recovery depends on how long and how severe the low oxygen was; brief, mild events allow fast recolonisation.

entries.title: Methane: a small gas with a big warming punch

definition.text: Atmospheric methane is the methane in Earth's air, a powerful greenhouse gas whose rising level is causing climate change.

facts.text: Since about 1750, methane in the air has risen by about 160%, almost entirely because of human activities.
By 2025 its concentration had risen from 722 ppb before industry to 1936 ppb, the highest in at least 800,000 years.
Since 1750 methane has made up 3% of greenhouse gas emissions by mass but about 23% of climate forcing.
Its global warming potential is about 84 times that of CO2 over 20 years and 28 times over 100 years, because it is less persistent.
It is the second largest contributor to human-caused climate forcing.
Wetlands are the largest natural source, providing roughly 20–30% of atmospheric methane.
From 2010 to 2019, methane emissions caused 0.5 °C, about 30%, of observed global warming.
Cutting methane by the end of the century could make a substantial difference to meeting the Paris climate targets.

conflicts.text: Methane's warming potential is given as 34 times CO2's over 100 years and 86 times over 20 years.
conflicts.note: Other sentences on the page give 84 (20-year) and 28 (100-year); the figures may come from different assessment versions.

conflicts.text: NOAA measurements show methane build-up has nearly tripled since 1750.
conflicts.note: Other sentences give a rise of about 160% (a factor of 2.6).

entries.title: Cultural eutrophication: the human hand in green water

definition.text: Cultural eutrophication is eutrophication caused by human activity.

facts.text: It became more visible after chemical fertilizers spread through farming in the mid-1900s green revolution.
Phosphorus and nitrogen are its two main causes, letting algae grow fast and bloom densely.
Phosphate detergents fed it until they were phased out in the 1970s; since then sewage and agriculture are the main phosphate sources.
Nitrogen pollution comes mainly from farm runoff of fertilizer and animal waste, sewage, and nitrogen deposited from the air.

entries.title: Carbon pools: where the planet keeps its carbon

definition.text: A carbon pool, or reservoir, is a part of the Earth system, such as the air, ocean or soil, where carbon is held in some form for a period of time.

facts.text: The global carbon cycle is usually split into major carbon pools linked by pathways of exchange.
The pools include the ocean, sediments including fossil fuels, the land biosphere with its soils, the atmosphere and the rocks of the geosphere.
Most of Earth's carbon is stored inertly in the rocks of the lithosphere.
The deep ocean is the largest pool of actively cycled carbon, holding 50 times more than the atmosphere, but it exchanges carbon with the surface only over hundreds of years.
About a third of soil carbon is stored in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate.
Pool is the broader term: a carbon sink is one particular kind of carbon pool.

entries.title: Carbon sinks: the places that soak up carbon

definition.text: A carbon sink is a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases.

facts.text: Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle.
Globally, the two most important carbon sinks are vegetation and the ocean.
Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but intensive farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils.
For gases other than CO2, a sink need not store the gas; it can break it down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless N2.
Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground, but no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale.
Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change.
Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 Kyoto Protocol promoted their use as carbon offsets.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: A forest or an ocean does something no machine yet does at large scale: it pulls carbon out of the sky faster than it lets carbon go. Such a store is a carbon sink, a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally, the two most important are vegetation and the ocean. Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but heavy, industrial farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils. For gases other than carbon dioxide, a sink need not store anything. It can break the gas down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless nitrogen gas. Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground. Still, no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale. Meanwhile, deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this change in land use is one cause of global warming. Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 treaty described in {{ref:nature-clim-056}} promoted their use to offset emissions.

entries.title: Helping forests, soils and seas store more carbon
entries.article: Carbon sink#Purpose in the context of climate change

definition.text: Enhancing natural carbon sinks means managing forests, soils and other ecosystems so they remove more CO2 from the air and store it durably.

facts.text: Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks is an important climate change mitigation measure.
It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.
Restoring ecosystems and converting less land are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030.
The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, for agriculture, forestry and other land use.
Proposed ocean methods such as seaweed farming and ocean fertilisation have not yet been used at large scale.

entries.chapter: Cycles of carbon, water and nutrients
entries.text: Two of the most powerful tools for cutting emissions before 2030 are simple: restoring ecosystems and converting less land. Preserving and strengthening sinks is an important way to slow global warming. It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by replanting trees. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, short for agriculture, forestry and other land use. Ocean methods such as seaweed farming and fertilising the sea have been proposed, but none has yet been used at large scale.

entries.title: Forests as carbon sinks, and why they may falter

definition.text: Forests act as carbon sinks by taking carbon dioxide from the air and storing it as wood, roots and leaves.

facts.text: Forests take up about 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
Forests can turn from carbon sinks into carbon sources.
In 2019 forests absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of higher temperatures, droughts and deforestation.
The typical tropical forest may become a carbon source by the 2060s.
Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and later replanting, which causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage.
Forests can switch from sinks to sources of carbon; in 2019 they took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
New forests take several decades to match the carbon benefit of keeping mature forests standing, so scientists call protecting natural forests the major climate solution.
Stored carbon only stays out of the air if trees are not burned and do not rot when they die.

entries.title: Two speeds of carbon: years and millions of years

definition.text: Carbon moves in a fast cycle through living things and a slow cycle through rocks.

facts.text: The fast, biological cycle can finish within years, carrying carbon from the air into living things and back again.
The slow, geological cycle can take millions of years, moving carbon through the crust between rocks, soil, ocean and air, and may reach deep into the mantle.
How the fast carbon cycle responds to human activity will decide many of the more immediate impacts of climate change.
Though slow, the geological part is one of the most important controls on how much carbon is in the air, and so on global temperatures.

entries.title: How people knocked the carbon cycle off balance
entries.article: Carbon cycle#Human influence on fast carbon cycle

definition.text: Since the Industrial Revolution, human activity has greatly disturbed the carbon cycle by moving huge amounts of carbon out of the ground.

facts.text: Extracting and burning fossil fuels, which moves carbon straight from rock into the air, is the largest and one of the fastest growing human impacts.
As of 2020 about 450 gigatons of fossil carbon had been extracted, nearly as much as is held in all living land biomass.
Heating limestone to make clinker, the raw material of cement, also releases carbon dioxide.
Clearing forests for farms or cities releases carbon from land ecosystems into the air.
Land-use change has also cut biodiversity, weakening ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air.
Small amounts of halocarbon gases caused about 10% of the direct radiative forcing from long-lived greenhouse gases in 2019.
For now, carbon exchanges between the air and the rest of the Earth system act as negative feedbacks that dampen the climate effect of human emissions.
