entries.title: Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide

definition.text: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a set period compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: By definition CO2 has a GWP of 1.
A gas's GWP depends on how strongly it absorbs heat radiation, how fast it leaves the air, and the time frame chosen.
Methane has a GWP-20 of 81.2 but a GWP-100 of 27.9, because it leaves the atmosphere much faster than CO2.
Regulators usually use a 100-year time scale, and international agreements have adopted it as the standard.
Since 1997, Kyoto Protocol reporting has used fixed IPCC GWP values to convert gases into comparable CO2 equivalents.
Other metrics include the global temperature change potential and GWP*, which treats short-lived pollutants such as methane differently.

entries.title: Climate feedbacks: how warming amplifies or tames itself

definition.text: Processes set off by an initial warming that either amplify it (positive feedbacks) or dampen it (negative feedbacks).

facts.text: The main amplifying feedbacks are water vapour, ice–albedo and the net cloud feedback.
The main balancing mechanism is that a warmer surface gives off more heat to space.
Shrinking Arctic snow and sea ice make the surface darker, speeding Arctic warming and helping thaw permafrost, which releases methane and CO2.
Land and oceans have absorbed about half of human CO2; that share could rise to about 70% if emissions fall but drop below 40% if they rise sharply.
Feedbacks are expected to become more positive as emissions continue, raising climate sensitivity.
Uncertainty about feedbacks, especially clouds, is the main reason climate models disagree on how much warming a given amount of emissions causes.

entries.text: Climate change feedbacks are processes set off by an initial warming that either amplify it, called positive feedbacks, or dampen it, called negative feedbacks. Land and oceans have absorbed about half of human carbon dioxide. That share could rise to about 70% if emissions fall, but drop below 40% if they rise sharply. Feedbacks are expected to become more positive as emissions continue, raising the {{ref:nature-eco-158}}. entries.title: The main greenhouse gases and how long they linger
entries.article: Greenhouse gas#Contributions of specific gases to the greenhouse effect

definition.text: The gases that do most of the heat-trapping in Earth's atmosphere: water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, methane and nitrous oxide, plus clouds.

facts.text: Without the natural greenhouse effect Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of around 15 °C.
Water vapour causes about 50% of the greenhouse effect and clouds about 25%, but these change with temperature, so they are treated as feedbacks.
CO2 (about 20%), tropospheric ozone, CFCs and nitrous oxide change independently of temperature, so they count as external forcings.
Of human greenhouse gas emissions in 2019, equal to 59 billion tonnes of CO2, 75% was CO2, 18% methane, 4% nitrous oxide and 2% fluorinated gases.
Methane comes from livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills, coal mining and oil and gas; nitrous oxide mostly from microbes breaking down fertilizer.
Methane lasts about 12 years in the air on average, while CO2 lasts much longer.
By 2022 CO2 concentrations had risen about 50% and methane 164% since 1750.
In the IPCC table, nitrous oxide lasts 121 years with a 100-year GWP of 265; some fluorinated gases, such as SF6 at 23,500, are far stronger.

entries.title: Fingerprints: how scientists pin warming on people
entries.article: Climate change#Causes of recent global temperature rise

definition.text: The drivers behind today's warming, which scientists identify by comparing the 'fingerprints' of each possible cause with observed patterns.

facts.text: Natural cycles such as El Niño cause short-term spikes and dips; longer changes come from external forcings like greenhouse gases, the Sun, volcanoes and Earth's orbit.
The Sun is ruled out: its energy reaching Earth has shown no upward trend since 1880, and the upper atmosphere is cooling rather than warming.
Volcanic CO2 equals less than 1% of human emissions, and natural forcings have had negligible effect on temperature trends since the Industrial Revolution.
Human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, has raised greenhouse gas levels since the Industrial Revolution.
Aerosols from air pollution have a smaller cooling effect, and land use change so far has slightly cooled the planet by making surfaces more reflective.
Land sinks remove about 29% of yearly CO2 emissions and the ocean absorbed 20 to 30% over the last two decades.

entries.text: The sun is not to blame. Its energy reaching Earth has shown no upward trend since 1880, and the upper atmosphere is cooling rather than warming. Longer changes come from external forcings: greenhouse gases, the sun, volcanoes and Earth's orbit. Volcanic carbon dioxide equals less than 1% of human emissions, and natural forcings have had negligible effect on temperature trends since the Industrial Revolution. That leaves human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, which has raised greenhouse gas levels. Some human effects cool. Aerosols from air pollution have a smaller cooling effect, and changes in land use have so far slightly cooled the planet by making surfaces more reflective. Natural sinks absorb part of each year's emissions: land removes about 29%, and the ocean absorbed 20 to 30% over the last two decades.

entries.title: Climate models: simulating the planet

definition.text: A representation of the physical, chemical and biological processes that shape the climate system, used to project future warming.

facts.text: Models are tested by checking how well they reproduce present and past climates.
Past models underestimated how fast Arctic ice would shrink and rainfall would increase.
Some models add population, economic growth and energy use to produce emission scenarios that feed physical and carbon cycle models.
Depending on the scenario, they give CO2 concentrations ranging from 380 to 1400 ppm.

entries.text: A climate model represents the physical, chemical and biological processes that shape the climate system, and it is used to project future warming. Some models add population, economic growth and energy use to produce emission scenarios, which feed physical and carbon cycle models. Depending on the scenario, they give carbon dioxide concentrations from 380 to 1400 ppm.

entries.title: Climate sensitivity: the warming from doubled carbon dioxide

definition.text: How much Earth's surface will warm in response to a doubling of the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere.

facts.text: Warming triggers climate feedbacks, such as melting ice and more water vapour, whose strength is not known exactly.
Doubling CO2 gives a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2, which without feedbacks would cause roughly 1 °C of warming.
In 1990 the IPCC put equilibrium sensitivity between 1.5 and 4.5 °C; observations and physics now give a very likely range of 2.3 to 4.7 °C.
Because mitigation costs depend on how fast carbon neutrality is needed, sensitivity has large economic and policy consequences.
One study suggests halving the uncertainty in the transient climate response could save trillions of dollars.
If sensitivity is high, the Paris goal of well below 2 °C cannot be met, at least temporarily.

entries.text: Double the carbon dioxide in the air, and how much hotter does Earth get? Climate sensitivity is the answer. Doubling carbon dioxide gives a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2, which without feedbacks would cause roughly 1 °C of warming. But warming triggers feedbacks, such as melting ice and more water vapour, whose strength is not known exactly. In 1990 the IPCC put equilibrium sensitivity between 1.5 and 4.5 °C. Observations and physics now give a very likely range of 2.3 to 4.7 °C. The number carries a large price tag. The cost of cutting emissions depends on how fast carbon neutrality is needed, so sensitivity has large economic and policy consequences. One study suggests that halving the uncertainty in the transient climate response, a shorter-term version of the measure, could save trillions of dollars. If sensitivity is high, the Paris goal of well below 2 °C cannot be met, at least temporarily.

entries.title: Projected warming: what the coming decades may bring

definition.text: Estimates of how much hotter Earth will get, which depend mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: The IPCC expects the 20-year average to pass +1.5 °C in the early 2030s.
By 2100 warming is very likely to reach 1.0–1.8 °C with very low emissions, 2.1–3.5 °C with intermediate emissions, or 3.3–5.7 °C with very high emissions.
In the intermediate and high scenarios warming continues past 2100.
The remaining carbon budget, the CO2 that can still be emitted for a given temperature limit, comes from modelling the carbon cycle and climate sensitivity.
UNEP says a 50% chance of staying below 2.0 °C allows 900 gigatonnes of CO2 after 2023, about 16 years of current emissions.

entries.title: Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases

definition.text: The mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the Earth as much as a given mass of another greenhouse gas.

facts.text: It gives one common scale for the climate effects of different gases.
It is calculated as GWP times the mass of the gas: two tonnes of a gas with GWP 100 equal 200 tonnes CO2e.
Values depend on the time scale chosen, usually 100 or 20 years.
Carbon markets and carbon taxes price emissions per tonne of CO2 equivalent.

entries.text: Two tonnes of a gas with a global warming potential of 100 count as 200 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, or CO2e. That is the arithmetic of the unit: the mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the Earth as much as a given mass of another greenhouse gas. It gives one common scale for the climate effects of different gases. It is calculated as the gas's global warming potential times its mass. Values depend on the time scale chosen, usually 100 or 20 years. The unit matters for money, because carbon markets and {{ref:nature-pol-081}} schemes price emissions per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

entries.title: What extreme weather costs economies

definition.text: The monetary losses that extreme weather events cause to economies.

facts.text: A 2023 study put climate-change-driven extreme weather costs at about US$2.86 trillion over 2000–2019, roughly US$143 billion a year.
The IPCC estimated in 2011 that annual losses since 1980 ranged from a few billion to above US$200 billion, peaking in 2005, the year of Hurricane Katrina.
Losses of lives, cultural heritage and ecosystem services are hard to monetize, so loss estimates reflect them poorly.
In the 2023–2024 World Economic Forum risk survey, 66 percent of respondents named extreme weather a top risk.

entries.text: A 2023 study put the cost of climate-driven extreme weather at about US$2.86 trillion over 2000–2019, roughly US$143 billion a year. The risk is widely felt: in the 2023–2024 World Economic Forum risk survey, 66 percent of respondents named extreme weather a top risk.

entries.title: Water vapour feedback: warming that breeds more warming
entries.article: Greenhouse gas#Special role of water vapor

definition.text: The process in which warming lets the air hold more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which adds further warming.

facts.text: Water vapour causes 41–67% of the greenhouse effect, but people do not directly change its global level.
It stays in the air only about nine days, so local changes such as irrigation have little global effect.
Physics (the Clausius–Clapeyron relation) means warmer air holds more water vapour per unit volume.

That creates the water vapour feedback: warming lets the air hold more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which adds further warming.

entries.title: Climate change and the world's food supply

definition.text: The threat climate change poses to growing, reaching and relying on enough food.

facts.text: Causes include higher CO2, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events and shifting pests and diseases.
Disasters from extreme weather caused food production losses estimated at US$123 billion in 2025, 5% of global agricultural GDP.
It is projected to harm all four pillars of food security, affecting how much food exists, its price and quality, and how stable supply is.
Ocean biomass is expected to fall by about 5% per degree of warming, hitting tropical seas hardest.

entries.title: The economic sectors most exposed to climate
entries.article: Effects of climate change#Highly affected sectors

definition.text: The parts of the economy most exposed to climate change because they depend directly on weather: farming, fishing, forestry, tourism and energy.

facts.text: Thermal power plants need cooling water and run less efficiently when hot, while hydropower suffers when river flows fall.
Heat, lower water flow and changed rainfall could cut total energy production by 7% a year by the end of the century.
Insurance premiums, such as for flood cover, are rising, and Munich Re warned in 2019 that home insurance could become unaffordable for average-income households.
Above 1.5 °C of warming, tourism and outdoor work may reach limits to how far they can adapt.

entries.title: How climate change harms human health

definition.text: The ways climate change harms human health, from heat illness and worse air to disease spread and extreme weather.

facts.text: Longer exposure to high temperatures can cause heat illness and heat-related deaths.
Diseases spread by mosquitoes and ticks, such as dengue fever and malaria, may become more common in some regions, as may waterborne diseases.
Lower crop yields can raise food prices and cause undernutrition, and clean water supplies can shrink.
Together these can increase poverty, migration, violent conflict and mental health problems.

entries.title: Melting ice sheets and the long rise of the seas
entries.article: Effects of climate change#Ice sheets decline

definition.text: The melting of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, which will keep raising sea levels over long time-scales.

facts.text: Losing the whole West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea level by over 5 metres, and a partial collapse could be abrupt and irreversible for centuries or longer.
Sustained warming between 1 °C and 4 °C would melt the Greenland ice sheet entirely over millennia, adding 7 m to sea levels.
As the ice surface melts it gets lower and warmer, a self-reinforcing feedback that can make the loss irreversible.

entries.title: CO2 fertilization: more carbon, faster photosynthesis
entries.article: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth#CO2 fertilization effect

definition.text: The speeding-up of plant photosynthesis, with less water lost through leaves, caused by more carbon dioxide in the air.

facts.text: Its strength depends on plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available.
It has been reported to cause 44% of the increase in gross primary productivity since the 2000s, and Earth's land has greened markedly since the early 1980s.
Faster photosynthesis does not always mean more growth or carbon storage, and plants are unlikely to cut CO2 levels much over the next century.

definition.text: Research that works out how far causes such as climate change explain trends in extreme weather events.

facts.text: A single extreme event generally cannot be blamed on any one cause.
Much of the work relies on climate models, which are vital but only approximations.

entries.title: The climate sensitivity parameter: turning forcing into degrees

definition.text: A number, in kelvin per W/m2, that links a radiative forcing to the eventual change in surface temperature.

facts.text: It is the inverse of the climate feedback parameter.
A value of about 0.8 gives about 1.6 K of warming since 1750 from CO2 rising from 278 to 405 ppm, a forcing of 2.0 W/m2.
The same value predicts a further 1.4 K of warming if CO2 doubled from its pre-industrial level.

entries.title: Earth's albedo: the share of sunlight bounced back

definition.text: The fraction of incoming sunlight that Earth reflects back to space, about 0.30 (30%) on annual average.

facts.text: Clouds, aerosols, oceans, land, snow, ice and vegetation reflect sunlight; Earth absorbs the other 70%.
Deforestation typically raises reflectivity, while Arctic ice loss lowers it.

Clouds, aerosols, oceans, land, snow, ice and vegetation do the reflecting, and Earth absorbs the other 70%. Human changes push both ways. Deforestation typically raises reflectivity, while Arctic ice loss lowers it.

entries.title: Earth system sensitivity: warming over millennia

definition.text: A measure of long-term warming from doubled CO2 that also includes slow feedbacks, such as melting ice sheets and changing vegetation, which take millennia.

facts.text: These slower feedbacks make it larger than equilibrium climate sensitivity, possibly twice as large.
It is estimated from Earth's geological history, so future values are highly uncertain.

entries.title: Cattle outweigh wild mammals: measuring the human footprint

definition.text: Human impact on the environment means the changes people cause, directly or indirectly, to physical environments, ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources.

facts.text: Reshaping the environment for society is causing global warming, ocean acidification, mass extinction, biodiversity loss and ecological collapse.
Global-scale damage is linked to population growth, rapid economic growth, overconsumption, overexploitation, pollution and deforestation.
Impacts grew sharply after the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s, but people have changed their surroundings since they first spread across the Earth.
A 2018 study found 87% of the oceans and 77% of land outside Antarctica altered by people, with 23% of the land left as wilderness.
Global Footprint Network estimates put humanity's demand 70% above what all the planet's ecosystems can regenerate.
Domesticated cattle and pigs outweigh all wild mammals by 14 to 1, and the world's chickens weigh three times as much as all wild birds.
The 2019 IPBES report names overfishing as the main driver of mass species extinction in the oceans.

entries.text: Domesticated cattle and pigs now outweigh all the world's wild mammals by 14 to 1. The world's chickens weigh three times as much as all wild birds. Numbers like these measure human impact on the environment: the changes people cause, directly or indirectly, to physical surroundings, ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources. People have changed their surroundings ever since they first spread across the Earth. The impacts grew sharply after the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s. A 2018 study found 87% of the oceans altered by people, along with 77% of land outside Antarctica. Only 23% of the land was left as wilderness. Global Footprint Network estimates put humanity's demand 70% above what all the planet's ecosystems can regenerate. The damage is linked to growing populations, rapid economic growth, heavy consumption, pollution and forest clearing. It is also linked to harvesting resources faster than they renew, the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. The results include global warming, ocean acidification, the mass loss of species and the collapse of whole ecological systems, a form of {{ref:nature-found-023}}. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}} blames one driver above all. Catching fish faster than they can breed is the main cause of the mass loss of ocean species.

entries.title: Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss

definition.text: The process by which a natural habitat becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die.

facts.text: It is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and species extinction worldwide.
People cause it through resource use, agriculture, industry, urban sprawl, mining, logging and trawling.
Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse a habitat without outright destroying it.
Of about 16 million square kilometres of original tropical rainforest, less than 9 million remain.
When habitat is destroyed, the carrying capacity for native species falls and populations decline, sometimes to extinction.
Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else.
Its most profound impact on people is the loss of valuable ecosystem services such as climate regulation, pollination and water management.
Poor people suffer most, because wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

entries.text: The tropics once held about 16 million square kilometers of rainforest. Less than 9 million remain. That shrinkage is habitat destruction. A natural home for wildlife, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-294}}, becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die. It is the leading cause worldwide of lost biodiversity and of species dying out. People cause it through resource use, agriculture, industry, urban sprawl, mining, logging and fishing with trawl nets. A habitat need not be bulldozed to fail. Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse it without outright destroying it. When habitat goes, the land can support fewer native animals, and each {{ref:nature-eco-374}} declines, sometimes until it disappears. Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else. For people, the deepest cost is lost ecosystem services such as regulating climate, pollinating plants and managing water. Poor people suffer most. Wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

entries.title: Deforestation: trading forest for farms, ranches and towns

definition.text: The clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can be put to a non-forest use such as farms, ranches or towns.

facts.text: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half of that loss in the last century.
Between 2015 and 2020 deforestation ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s.
Agriculture is by far the main direct cause, with cropland expansion and pasture driving nearly 90% of global deforestation in 2025.
Logging, urbanization, mining and climate-driven wildfires are further drivers.
It destroys habitat and so causes biodiversity loss, extinctions, local climate change and displacement of forest peoples.
It reduces carbon uptake by forests, weakening their role in mitigating climate change.
Deforested regions often also suffer desertification and soil erosion.
Economic losses from deforestation in Brazil could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

entries.text: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land. That is one-third less than before agriculture spread, and half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can serve a non-forest use, such as farms, ranches or towns. It is one of the main forms of {{ref:nature-eco-041}}. Between 2015 and 2020 it ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 the spread of cropland and pasture drove nearly 90% of global deforestation. Logging, urbanization, mining and climate-driven wildfires add to it. Clearing destroys habitat, so it brings loss of biodiversity, species dying out, local climate change and the displacement of forest peoples. It also cuts the carbon forests take up, weakening their role in slowing climate change. Cleared regions often suffer soil erosion and the slide toward desert described in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. The costs can dwarf the gains. In Brazil, economic losses from deforestation could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

entries.title: Extinction: when the last of a species dies

definition.text: Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies.

facts.text: A species can be functionally extinct before its last member dies, if the few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover.
More than 99.9% of all species that ever lived are extinct, and the average species lasts 1–10 million years.
Habitat degradation is currently the main human cause of extinctions, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide.
Humans have become an extra cause of extinction, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world.
Fossil studies confirm extinction caused by climate change; a 2003 review predicted 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change.
There have been at least five mass extinctions in the history of life on Earth.
A 2014 special edition of Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.
Because the moment of extinction is hard to pin down over a large range, it is usually decided after the fact.

entries.text: More than 99.9% of all the species that have ever lived are gone. The average species lasts 1–10 million years. Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies. The exact moment is hard to pin down over a large range, so extinction is usually declared after the fact. Life on Earth has passed through at least five mass extinctions. Fossil studies confirm that climate change has caused extinctions. A 2003 review predicted that 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change. Humans have become an extra cause, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world. Today the main human cause is habitat degradation, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide. In 2014 a special edition of the journal Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.

entries.title: Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace

definition.text: The decline of living variety, either when species vanish from Earth entirely or when they decrease or disappear from a particular area.

facts.text: The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example through ecological restoration, and permanent if it cannot.
The current rate of global biodiversity loss is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background extinction rate.
All contemporary biodiversity loss has been attributed to human activities.
Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver of loss than climate change.
To measure loss at a site, scientists record its species richness and how it changes over time.
The WWF reported an average 68% population decline between 1970 and 2016 across 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 monitored populations.
Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as crop pollination, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and forest products.
Of the 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets set in 2010, only six were partially achieved by 2020.

entries.text: Between 1970 and 2016, monitored animal populations fell by an average of 68%, the WWF reported. The figure covered 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 populations. Biodiversity loss is the decline of living variety. It happens when species vanish from Earth entirely, as {{ref:nature-eco-105}} describes, or when they shrink or disappear from a particular area. To measure it at a site, scientists record the number of species present, a count explained in {{ref:nature-eco-150}}, and how it changes over time. The current global rate is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background rate at which species die out, set out in {{ref:nature-eco-078}}. All of today's loss has been attributed to human activities. Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver than climate change. The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example by repairing ecosystems as {{ref:nature-nbs-112}} describes, and permanent if it cannot. Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as pollinating crops, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and supplying goods from forests. Governments have struggled to respond. Of 20 worldwide targets for biodiversity set in 2010, covered in {{ref:nature-gov-017}}, only six were partially achieved by 2020.
entries.text_plain: Between 1970 and 2016, monitored animal populations fell by an average of 68%, the WWF reported. The figure covered 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 populations. Biodiversity loss is the decline of living variety. It happens when species vanish from Earth entirely, as Extinction: when the last of a species dies describes, or when they shrink or disappear from a particular area. To measure it at a site, scientists record the number of species present, a count explained in Species richness: counting how many kinds live here, and how it changes over time. The current global rate is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background rate at which species die out, set out in The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace. All of today's loss has been attributed to human activities. Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver than climate change. The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example by repairing ecosystems as Ecological restoration: repairing ecosystems already damaged describes, and permanent if it cannot. Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as pollinating crops, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and supplying goods from forests. Governments have struggled to respond. Of 20 worldwide targets for biodiversity set in 2010, covered in The Aichi Targets: twenty goals that were missed, only six were partially achieved by 2020.

entries.title: Invasive species: newcomers that harm their new home

definition.text: A species introduced by people to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered.

facts.text: Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity.
Invasions happen naturally, but human-assisted introductions have greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range.
Biological invasion is one of the five top drivers of global biodiversity loss and is growing with tourism and globalization.
Common traits of invaders include fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and earlier successful invasions.
An introduced species usually has to persist at low densities first, sometimes needing several introductions before it establishes.
Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative, though some can provide habitat or food for other organisms.
The term "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

entries.text: An introduced species usually starts small. It has to persist at low densities first, and sometimes it takes several introductions before it takes hold. An invasive species is one that people have carried to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered. Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity. Invasions happen naturally too, but human help has greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range. Biological invasion is now one of the five top drivers of {{ref:nature-eco-035}} worldwide, and it is growing with tourism and globalization. Successful invaders share common traits: fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and a record of earlier successful invasions. Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative. Some can still provide habitat or food for other organisms. The label itself is slippery, since "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

entries.title: Nature conservation: the movement to save what remains

definition.text: Nature conservation is the ethic and movement devoted to saving species from extinction, keeping and restoring habitats, enhancing ecosystem services and protecting biodiversity.

facts.text: Its goals include conserving habitat, preventing deforestation, keeping soil organic matter, halting extinctions, reducing overfishing and mitigating climate change.
As of 2018, 15% of land and 7.3% of the oceans were protected, and many environmentalists aim to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
Protected areas in developing countries, home to perhaps 70–80% of the world's species, still get very little effective management.
Private fundraising is not enough to pay for managing the more than 10% of the world that is legally protected.
Gifford Pinchot coined the term 'conservation' in 1907.
Early national parks often protected 'worthless lands' of little commercial interest, such as alpine and dry habitats.

entries.title: Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace

definition.text: Harvesting a renewable resource, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns.

facts.text: Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening global biodiversity.
A population is overexploited when harvested at a rate its natural mortality and reproduction cannot sustain, which can wipe out populations or whole species.
Harvesting can be sustainable if it stays within limits, as in well-managed fisheries.
An aquifer is overexploited when water is extracted faster than it recharges; it is then said to be overdrafted.
Forests are overexploited when logging outpaces reforestation.
It threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates, and has affected about 40% of the bird species extinct since 1500.
Excluding edible fish, the illegal wildlife trade is valued at $10 billion a year.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

entries.text: About 40% of the bird species lost since 1500 were affected by overexploitation. The word means harvesting a resource that renews itself, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns. A {{ref:nature-eco-374}} is overexploited when it is harvested faster than its natural births and deaths can make up. That can wipe out populations or whole species. Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening biodiversity worldwide, and it threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates. Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

entries.title: Habitat fragmentation: when one wild place becomes many islands

definition.text: The breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches, which splits populations and degrades ecosystems.

facts.text: It covers five changes: less total habitat, a lower interior-to-edge ratio, isolated fragments, one patch split into several, and smaller average patches.
People cause it by clearing native vegetation for agriculture, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs.
Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75% and impairs ecosystem functions such as biomass production and nutrient cycling.
As a rough rule, keeping 10% of a habitat as a contiguous remnant results in a 50% loss of biodiversity.
Small, isolated populations can be wiped out by minor swings in climate or resources that large populations would absorb.
Dams and water diversions fragment aquatic habitats.
Its effects keep emerging for decades; experiments show biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later.
Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation but does not restore interior habitat.

entries.text: Keep 10% of a habitat as one unbroken remnant and, as a rough rule, half its biodiversity is lost. Habitat fragmentation is the breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches. It splits populations and degrades ecosystems. Five changes come bundled together. There is less total habitat and less interior compared with edge. Fragments are cut off from each other, one patch splits into several, and patches get smaller on average. People cause it by clearing native vegetation for farms, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs. Dams and water diversions do the same to rivers and lakes. Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75%. It also impairs ecosystem functions such as biomass production and nutrient cycling. Small, isolated populations are fragile. Minor swings in climate or resources that a large population would absorb can wipe them out. The damage is slow to show, and experiments find biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later. Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation, as {{ref:nature-eco-152}} explains. It does not restore interior habitat.

entries.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to produce

definition.text: The process by which land becomes less healthy and productive through human activity or natural conditions.

facts.text: Unsustainable land management is often the main cause.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 defined it as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of drylands.
The UN estimates about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas.
Around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded every year.
Over 60% of human-induced land degradation occurs on agricultural land.
It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, raises vulnerability to floods and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases.
Degraded land is less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation.
Reversing 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year.

entries.text: Every year around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded. Land degradation is the process by which land becomes less healthy and productive, through human activity or natural conditions. Unsustainable land management is often the main cause, and over 60% of human-induced degradation occurs on farmland. The UN estimates that about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas. It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, leaves land more exposed to floods and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases. Degraded land is also less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation. The flip side is hopeful. entries.title: Desertification: how dry land turns to desert

definition.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land in dry regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities.

facts.text: Its immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation, driven by drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building.
Bare dry soil blows or washes away, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan.
Drylands cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries.
Some 10–20% of drylands are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification.
Climate change is expected to expand drylands from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100.
Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain even when they benefit society and the environment.
Shelter belts, woodlots and windbreaks are used to fix soil and cut erosion.

entries.text: Dry regions cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land in those regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities. It is the harshest form of {{ref:nature-eco-060}}. The immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building all strip it away. Bare dry soil then blows or washes off, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan. Some 10–20% of dry regions are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification. Climate change is expected to expand dry regions from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100. Remedies exist: shelter belts and woodlots, planted lines and blocks of trees, fix soil and cut erosion. Yet the economics can work against them. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.

entries.title: Genetic diversity: a species' insurance against change

definition.text: Genetic diversity is the total variety of inherited characteristics within the genetic makeup of a species.

facts.text: It lets populations adapt to changing environments, because some individuals are more likely to carry variants suited to new conditions.
Lower genetic diversity makes a population more vulnerable to changes such as climate change or new diseases; koalas' low diversity is linked to their failure to fight off chlamydia.
Small populations lose diversity by chance (genetic drift) and through inbreeding, and a bottleneck can cut diversity rapidly.
A 2007 study found that diversity within species and diversity among species depend on each other.
Loss of genetic diversity in domestic animals has been attributed to the spread of markets and economic globalization.
Mutation and gene flow, such as pollen carried by wind or migrating birds, add new genetic variants to a population.

entries.text: Koalas carry little genetic variety, and that weakness is linked to their failure to fight off chlamydia. Genetic diversity is the total variety of inherited characteristics within a species. It lets populations adapt to changing environments, because some individuals are more likely to carry variants suited to new conditions. A 2007 study found that diversity within species and diversity among species depend on each other. In farm animals, the loss of genetic diversity has been attributed to the spread of markets and economic globalization.

entries.title: Species richness: counting how many kinds live here

definition.text: Species richness is simply the number of different species in a community, landscape or region.

facts.text: It ignores how abundant each species is, so it is not the same as species diversity, which also accounts for evenness.
Larger samples tend to contain more species, so richness values are comparable only when sampling effort is standardised.
Many groups of organisms have the most species in the tropics, creating latitudinal gradients in richness.
It is often used to judge the conservation value of habitats, but it is blind to species identity: areas with many endemic or rare species usually count for more.

entries.contested_note: Studies of how productivity relates to species richness disagree, and no global consensus has emerged.
entries.text: The simplest measure of nature's variety is a headcount of kinds. Species richness is the number of different species in a community, landscape or region. It ignores how common each species is. That makes it different from a fuller measure that also weighs how evenly individuals are shared among species, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-147}}. Larger samples tend to contain more species, so richness values can be compared only when sampling effort is standardized. Many groups of organisms have the most species in the tropics, so richness changes with latitude. Conservationists often use it to judge a habitat's value, but it is blind to which species are present. Areas with many endemic or rare species usually count for more. How richness relates to an ecosystem's productivity is unsettled: studies disagree, and no global consensus has emerged.

entries.title: Wildlife corridors: reconnecting cut-off populations

definition.text: A wildlife corridor is an area that links wildlife populations cut off from each other by farms, cities, roads and other development.

facts.text: Corridors reduce the harm of habitat fragmentation, a major threat to biodiversity.
Letting animals move between populations prevents the inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity seen in isolated groups, and spreads pollen and seeds.
By linking warmer and cooler habitat, corridors help species shift their ranges as the climate changes.
They can be continuous strips of habitat or 'stepping stones' of small separate patches, and include river zones and road crossings.
In a South Carolina experiment, butterflies were two to four times more likely to move to a patch linked by a corridor than to unlinked patches.
Success needs a shared vision among stakeholders, clear rules and incentive programmes to bring in private landowners.
Corridors can overlap with settlements and bring human–wildlife conflict such as crop raiding and livestock predation.

entries.title: Abundance: how common a species is

definition.text: How well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample.

facts.text: Relative species abundance compares one species' abundance with that of others in the ecosystem; both measures feed into biodiversity calculations.
Large animals are counted with methods such as spotlight, track and roadkill counts; plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover.
In most ecosystems a few species are abundant and many are rare; abundant species tend to be generalists and rare ones specialists.
Abundant species produce more colonizing offspring, a feedback that yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

entries.text: In most ecosystems a few species are common and many are rare. Abundance measures how well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample. Relative species abundance compares one species with the others around it, and both measures feed into biodiversity calculations. Counting methods vary. Large animals are counted with spotlights, tracks and even roadkill, while plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover. Abundant species tend to be generalists that use many resources, and rare ones specialists with narrow needs. Abundant species also produce more colonizing offspring. That loop yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

entries.title: Endemism: species found in one place only

definition.text: The state of a species being found naturally in only one defined place, such as a single island, country or region.

facts.text: Conservation biology uses endemism to measure a place's biodiversity and to judge extinction risk.
Its opposite is a cosmopolitan distribution, a global or widespread range.
Endemics are not necessarily rare, and rare species are not necessarily endemic.
Isolation breeds endemism, so remote islands such as Hawaii, the Galápagos and Socotra hold many endemics.
Charles Darwin first used "endemic" for a species restricted to one place, in 1872.
Endemics are at greater risk than widespread species from habitat loss and fast climate change because their ranges are small.
Endemic species are used to find conservation priorities, an idea behind biodiversity hotspots, though some argue endemism does not track threat.

entries.contested_note: Some scientists argue endemism is a poor measure of biodiversity or threat because high-endemism areas do not consistently match them.

entries.title: Forests and climate: a feedback loop of loss

definition.text: The two-way link in which clearing forests warms the climate and a changing climate in turn damages forests.

facts.text: Land use change, mainly deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels.
Emissions come from burning forest biomass and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon.
As of 2019 deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
The relationship is an amplifying feedback: more tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms and more tree loss.
Standing tropical forests help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C.
In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and forest ecosystem collapse.

entries.text: Standing forests in the tropics help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C. Clearing them works the other way. Changing how land is used, mainly through deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels. The emissions come from burning the wood and leaves of forests and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon. As of 2019, deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. The link runs both ways, as a self-amplifying loop. More tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms, and so more tree loss. Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and the collapse of forest ecosystems.

Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. The link runs both ways, as a self-amplifying loop. More tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms, and so more tree loss. Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and the collapse of forest ecosystems.

entries.title: Poaching: illegal hunting and its ripple effects

definition.text: Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wild animals, and since the 1980s also the illegal harvesting of wild plants.

facts.text: It harms biodiversity inside and outside protected areas by depleting species and disturbing how ecosystems function.
In rural Africa the main motives are lack of jobs and limited farming potential; bushmeat sales bring cash income from cities.
International markets draw organised gangs, with crime syndicates trafficking body parts abroad.
Removing large animals defaunates forests, shifting seed dispersal so large-seeded trees dominate and small-seeded plants vanish locally.
Poachers treat the edges of protected areas as open-access resources, shrinking their effective size, and wildlife tourism loses income.
As many as 35,000 African elephants are killed each year for ivory.
Sustainable Development Goal 15 calls for action against the poaching and trafficking of protected species.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the label 'poaching' has been used to criminalise Indigenous peoples' traditional subsistence hunting.

entries.title: The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk
entries.article: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

definition.text: The Global Assessment Report is the IPBES report on the global state of biodiversity, whose summary for policymakers came out on 6 May 2019.

facts.text: It reviews 50 years of change, drawing on over 15,000 scientific publications and Indigenous knowledge; it is the first UN global biodiversity assessment since the 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
Of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species, 1 million are threatened with extinction, including 40% of amphibians and more than a third of marine mammals.
It ranks the drivers: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive alien species.
Wild mammal biomass has fallen by 82%, while humans and their farm animals now make up 96% of all mammal biomass.
Over 50 years the human population doubled and GDP per person quadrupled while biodiversity declined catastrophically.
Pollinator loss threatens food production worth $235 to $577 billion a year, and coastal losses threaten up to 300 million people's livelihoods.
It urged countries not to fixate on economic growth, to cut subsidies to industries harmful to nature and to fund beneficial programmes instead.

entries.title: Diversity indices: boiling variety down to one number

definition.text: A number that measures how many different types, usually species, a dataset or community contains, often weighted by how common each is.

facts.text: Indices summarize aspects of biodiversity such as richness, evenness and dominance, making communities or sites easy to compare.
Abundance can be measured as numbers of individuals, biomass or coverage.
Richness is a simple count of types and is popular in ecology because abundance data are often lacking.
The Shannon and Simpson indices also account for each type's proportional abundance.
The same measures are used outside ecology, for demographic groups or letters of the alphabet.

entries.text: Counting species tells only part of the story. The same measures work outside ecology, for demographic groups or even letters of the alphabet.

entries.title: Biodiversity hotspots: small areas, most of the species

definition.text: A region with exceptionally high biodiversity, especially species found nowhere else, that is threatened by human activity.

facts.text: Norman Myers developed the concept in articles in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000.
To qualify, a region must hold at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5% of the world total) and have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation.
Globally, 36 zones qualify.
Hotspots cover just 2.4% of the planet's surface yet support nearly 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species.
Most hotspots are tropical, and only a small share of their land is protected.
Critics note that the hotspot approach ignores the cost of conservation and phylogenetic diversity.

entries.title: Bushmeat: wild meat, food security and vanishing species

definition.text: Meat from wild animals hunted for people to eat, especially in Africa.

facts.text: It is a main source of animal protein and income for poor rural communities in humid tropical forests.
As of 2016, 301 terrestrial mammal species were threatened with extinction by bushmeat hunting, including all pangolin species.
The trade in West and Central Africa was estimated at 1–5 million tonnes a year around the turn of the 21st century.
Hunting for one's own use in large landscapes can be sustainable, but market hunting threatens large, slow-breeding species.
The "bushmeat crisis", coined in 2007, names the double threat of vanishing food supplies and wildlife extinctions.
Logging roads and trucks give hunters access to remote forests and carry meat to towns.
Suggested remedies include affordable alternative protein, giving communities rights over wildlife, and enforcing protected areas.

entries.title: Why forests are over-cleared: the benefits no one pays for

definition.text: The economic reason forests are over-cleared: many of their benefits are sold in no market, so owners see more profit in converting them than in keeping them.

facts.text: Many important forest functions have no markets and hence no economic value readily apparent to forest owners or dependent communities.
Short-term gains from converting forest or overharvesting wood typically lose long-term income and biological productivity.
Poverty and agricultural rent were found to be principal factors leading to deforestation.
Proposed policies would align economic activity in critical forests with their value for ecosystem services and climate mitigation, using tools such as certification, eco-tariffs and traceability.

entries.text: A forest's timber has a price, but many of its other benefits do not. Many important forest functions have no markets, and hence no economic value readily apparent to forest owners or the communities that depend on them. This gap, a case of {{ref:nature-econ-177}}, is the economic reason forests are over-cleared. Owners see more profit in converting a forest than in keeping it. Yet short-term gains from converting forest or overharvesting wood typically cost long-term income and biological productivity. Studies found poverty and agricultural rent, the income land earns from farming, to be principal factors behind deforestation. Proposed policies would align economic activity in critical forests with their value for ecosystem services and climate mitigation. Their tools include certification, traceability, which tracks where products come from, and the trade charges described in {{ref:nature-pol-112}}.

entries.title: Habitat conservation: protecting the places species live

definition.text: Habitat conservation is the management of habitats to protect and restore them and to stop species from going extinct, being fragmented or losing range.

facts.text: Natural habitats provide ecosystem services, such as timber from forests and clean water from streams.
Conserving habitat can pay through tourism and outdoor recreation, and repairing damaged ecosystems is thought to cost far more than conserving them.
Putting a value on conserving different areas is often criticised as too utilitarian.
Biodiversity hotspots and the homes of flagship, umbrella or endangered species usually get priority.
Wild relatives of crops resist disease better; the wild corn teosinte resists 4 corn diseases, so seed banks plus habitat conservation are proposed for food security.
Adaptive management handles scientific uncertainty by gathering information and adjusting conservation plans over time.
Conservation principles were first applied in practice to the forests of British India in the 18th and 19th centuries.

entries.text: Repairing a damaged ecosystem is thought to cost far more than conserving it in the first place. Habitat conservation is the management of habitats to protect and restore them, and to stop species from going extinct, being fragmented or losing range. It is a central practice of {{ref:nature-eco-140}}. Natural habitats provide ecosystem services, such as timber from forests and clean water from streams. Conserving them can also pay through tourism and time spent outdoors. Putting a value on conserving different areas is often criticized as too utilitarian, judging nature only by its usefulness. Priority usually goes to {{ref:nature-eco-081}} and to the homes of flagship, umbrella or at-risk species. Crops show what is at stake. Wild relatives of crops resist disease better, and the wild corn teosinte resists 4 corn diseases. Seed banks plus habitat conservation are therefore proposed to secure food supplies. Scientific uncertainty is handled by the approach described in {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}, which gathers information and adjusts conservation plans over time.

entries.title: Indirect drivers: the forces behind the bulldozer
entries.article: Human impact on the environment#Indirect drivers

definition.text: Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment.

facts.text: They include population, economic development, urbanization, technology and climate change.
They differ from direct drivers, such as mining, agriculture, urban infrastructure and transport, which result from them.
Overconsumption, resource use beyond what ecosystems can sustain, can be measured with the ecological footprint.
Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people.
Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how much effort it makes to preserve it.

entries.contested_note: Blaming population growth for environmental problems is controversial, and critics say it can unduly blame poor people in the Global South.

entries.title: HIPPO and the Evil Quartet: naming the drivers of loss

definition.text: The main human pressures behind today's loss of biodiversity: habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change.

facts.text: Edward O. Wilson coined the acronym HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting.
Jared Diamond describes an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, introduced species and secondary extinctions.
Habitat destruction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and species extinction worldwide.
A 2019 IPBES report found overfishing to be the main driver of mass species extinction in the oceans.
A 2021 IPBES and IPCC report found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together because they are inextricably linked.
Invasive species can drive natives extinct through competitive exclusion, niche displacement or hybridisation.

entries.text: Edward O. Wilson boiled the problem down to one acronym, HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting. Jared Diamond's version is an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, introduced species and secondary extinctions. Both lists name the main human pressures behind {{ref:nature-eco-035}}. Today's fuller list is habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change. Habitat destruction leads worldwide. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}} found catching too many fish to be the main driver of mass extinction. Invasive species can drive natives extinct by outcompeting them, pushing them out of their role in the ecosystem, or interbreeding with them. The pressures also interact. In 2021 the same panel and the UN's climate science panel issued a joint report. It found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together, because they are inextricably linked.

entries.title: Farming, the largest driver of biodiversity loss on land

definition.text: The way expanding and intensifying farmland converts and degrades natural habitat, making agriculture the largest single cause of biodiversity decline on land.

facts.text: The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment found industrial agriculture to be the primary driver of biodiversity collapse.
The UN's Global Biodiversity Outlook 2014 estimated that 70% of projected terrestrial biodiversity loss is caused by agriculture.
As of 2023 about 38% of Earth's land surface was used for agriculture, the dominant land use.
Livestock systems occupy about 77% of agricultural land but provide less than 20% of the world's calories.
More than 17,000 species risk losing habitat by 2050 as farming expands to meet food needs.
A global shift toward mostly plant-based diets would free land for restoring ecosystems and biodiversity.

entries.title: The $423 billion bill for invasive species

definition.text: The money lost to damage from invasive species and spent on controlling them.

facts.text: The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019.
This cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970.
Costs split into direct production losses in farming and forestry and the costs of management.
Counting only lost production and management understates the cost; valuing lost species and ecosystem services would raise it sharply.
Estimated damage and control costs in the United States exceed $138 billion a year.
In France, damage costs were nearly eight times higher than spending on management.
Invasive trees can bring benefits such as commercial forestry, but returns from invasive species are usually far smaller than their costs.
Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management, but it helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

entries.text: The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019. That cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970. Some invaders bring benefits, such as invasive trees used in commercial forestry, but their returns are usually far smaller than their costs. Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management. It helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

entries.title: Wildlife trade: a vast, poorly watched market

definition.text: Wildlife trade is the exchange of products from wild animals or plants, taken from nature or raised in captivity, whether alive, dead or as parts.

facts.text: Legal trade is regulated by CITES, which has 184 member countries, called Parties.
Global imports of wildlife products were worth US$187 billion in 2012, of which fisheries made up $113 billion.
Illegal wildlife trade is one of the major illegal economic activities, comparable to drug and arms trafficking; Interpol puts it at $10 billion to $20 billion a year.
Trade and other use are the second major threat to endangered mammals and among the top ten threats to birds, amphibians and cycads.
Live wildlife markets have been linked to outbreaks of zoonotic diseases including COVID-19, H5N1 bird flu, SARS and mpox.
Customs codes record most wildlife imports only under broad categories, so the trade is poorly monitored.
Legal trade with quotas, as for Florida alligators, can give an economic incentive to keep habitat.

entries.title: Island biogeography: why small, remote places hold fewer species

definition.text: Island biogeography studies what controls the number and diversification of species in isolated natural communities.

facts.text: Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson started the field in the 1960s.
Its theory holds that an island's species number is set by a balance between immigration and extinction.
Remote islands receive fewer immigrants, while larger islands have more habitat and lower chance-driven extinction.
An 'island' can be any patch of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable land, such as a mountaintop, a woodland or a national park amid development.
Simberloff and Wilson cleared arthropods from small Florida mangrove islands; within a year they were recolonized, nearer islands fastest.
Seeing reserves as habitat islands raised fears they would lose species, and led to the SLOSS debate and to wildlife corridors.

entries.contested_note: Ecologists vigorously debated its use in reserve design, notably whether one large reserve beats several small ones.

entries.title: Defaunation: the quiet emptying of animal life

definition.text: The global, local or functional loss of animal populations or species from ecological communities.

facts.text: Unlike extinction, it counts declines in animal numbers as well as disappearing species.
Population growth and better harvesting technology have stripped large vertebrates from many communities.
More than 50 percent of all wildlife is estimated to have been lost in the last 40 years.
Large mammals are especially vulnerable because they need large home ranges.
Over 50% of extinct animal species with a known cause were affected by invasive species.
Tropical regions such as the Brazilian Amazon, the Congo Basin and Indonesia are hit hardest.
Terrestrial mammal food-web links have fallen by 53% over the past 130,000 years as humans expanded.
It can weaken services such as nutrient cycling, decomposition, crop pollination, pest control and water quality.

entries.title: Conservation status: rating a species' risk of extinction

definition.text: A rating of whether a species or other group still exists and how likely it is to go extinct in the near future.

facts.text: Assessments weigh population trends, breeding success and known threats, not just how many individuals remain.
The two international systems are run by the IUCN and by CITES; others work at regional, national and local levels.
The IUCN Red List is the best-known system, sorting species into nine groups using criteria such as rate of decline, population size, range and fragmentation.
In Red List usage, "threatened" groups three categories: critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable.
Other categories run from Extinct and Extinct in the Wild to Near Threatened, Least Concern and Data Deficient.
CITES, in force since 1975, aims to ensure that international trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival.
Seafood consumer guides rate species in a similar way but also weigh fishing impacts such as bycatch and bottom trawling.

entries.title: Endangered species and the bald eagle's comeback

definition.text: A species at very high risk of going extinct in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region.

facts.text: Species become endangered mainly through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation.
On the IUCN Red List, "Endangered" sits between "Vulnerable" and "Critically Endangered".
One IUCN criterion: a population that falls 20% within five years and has fewer than 2,500 mature individuals left.
Another: a population decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer.
In 2026 the IUCN Red List named 49,500 species worldwide as threatened with extinction.
Many nations protect such species by banning hunting or harvest, restricting development or creating protected areas.
The US bald eagle recovered from 417 nesting pairs in 1963 to 71,400 by 2020 through habitat protection, legal protection and a DDT ban.

entries.title: The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace

definition.text: The normal rate at which species go extinct through Earth's history, outside mass extinction events.

facts.text: Extinction is a normal part of evolution, and the background rate measures how often it happens naturally.
It is the yardstick for showing how much faster species are vanishing today.
It is roughly one extinction per million species-years; at that rate one bird species would go extinct about every 400 years.
Under normal rates species typically last 5–10 million years; mammal species average about 1 million years.
Background rates have fallen over the Phanerozoic, which has been linked to increasing ocean oxygenation.

entries.title: Mass extinctions: when life's variety collapses

definition.text: An extinction event, or mass extinction, is a widespread and rapid fall in the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It happens when extinctions outpace both the normal background extinction rate and the rate at which new species form.
Estimates of how many major mass extinctions occurred in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty.
The largest, the end-Permian 'Great Dying', killed about 81% of marine species and an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species.
Large extinctions tend to follow when a biosphere already under long-term stress suffers a short-term shock.
Research since 1982 concludes that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is under way, with extinctions over 1,000 times the background rate since 1900.
This sixth extinction is driven by population growth, economic growth and overconsumption of natural resources.
After a mass extinction, usually only adaptable 'weedy' species survive, and new groups can take over the emptied niches.

entries.contested_note: Scientists still debate the causes of the mass extinctions.

entries.title: The Holocene extinction: the sixth great dying, caused by people

definition.text: The ongoing wave of extinctions of plants and animals, on land and at sea, caused by human activity in the current geological epoch.

facts.text: It is sometimes called the sixth extinction, and when the stress falls on human causes it is also called the Anthropocene extinction.
Species are now estimated to be disappearing 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background extinction rate.

Its drivers include climate change, destruction of wetlands, deforestation, overfishing, ocean acidification, population growth, economic growth and rising consumption, especially in affluent societies.
Scientists broadly agree that habitat destruction, resource consumption and the elimination of species are the main human drivers of the crisis.
The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment estimated that about one million species are at risk of extinction within decades because of human activities.
A 2023 study counted at least 73 animal genera lost since 1500, a rate it judged 35 times higher than the background rate without human impacts.
Population growth, economic growth and growth in consumption per person over the past two centuries are regarded as its underlying causes.
Proposed remedies include shifting economic activity toward low-impact sectors, plant-based diets, and enlarging protected areas on land and sea.

Beneath them lie two centuries of growth in population, in economic output and in consumption per person. entries.title: Extinction debt: species doomed by losses already made

definition.text: Extinction debt is the future extinction of species that has already been set in motion by past events such as habitat loss.

facts.text: It arises from time lags: long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced.
Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches.
It is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs.
The term was first used in 1994 by Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak; it is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop.
Modelling of species–area relationships suggests 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen.
In the Azores, where over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years, more than half of arthropods are thought committed to extinction.
It means protecting today's habitat may not be enough, but the long delay gives time for habitat restoration to prevent losses.

entries.title: How climate change spreads infectious disease

definition.text: Climate change is altering how widely and heavily many infectious diseases are transmitted around the world.

facts.text: Warmer, wetter conditions let vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks survive in places once too cold or dry, so dengue and Lyme disease now appear at higher latitudes and elevations.
Warmer water and more flooding spread bacteria such as Vibrio cholerae, while drought and poor water access raise the risk of diarrheal diseases.
Deforestation, habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss add to zoonotic risk, as people encroach on habitats and ecosystems favour efficient disease reservoirs.
Low-income communities with weak healthcare and sanitation are the most vulnerable, and diseases like malaria slow their path to prosperity, worsening global inequality.
The UN Environment Programme says the most fundamental protection against zoonotic diseases is to prevent the destruction of nature.
Responses increasingly follow the One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health as one.

entries.title: Soil biodiversity: the hidden life beneath a football pitch

definition.text: Soil biodiversity is the variety of life in soil and the soil properties that can be managed to support it.

facts.text: Soil is habitat mainly for microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also for protozoa, nematodes, microarthropods, earthworms, termites and millipedes.
Soil organisms' main role is recycling organic matter from the plant-based food web above ground.
Keeping soil fertile is called one of the most vital ecological services the living world performs.
Microbial secretions dominate the binding of soil particles into aggregates and protect soil carbon from breakdown.
Erosion, acidification, salinisation and chloride from potash fertilizer all threaten soil organisms.
Because soils are a dispersed asset, soil health is best secured by a broad, consistent and economically appealing approach, such as liming or no-till farming.
A football pitch is estimated to hold underground organisms equal in mass to 500 sheep.

entries.title: In-situ conservation: saving species where they live

definition.text: In-situ conservation protects species and their genetic resources on site, in the natural populations where they live.

facts.text: Its opposite is ex situ conservation, where threatened species or their material are kept elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks.
Methods include nature reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biodiversity hotspots and gene sanctuaries.
It keeps populations in the setting where they developed their traits and lets evolution and adaptation carry on.
Reserves must be large enough to hold populations with the genetic diversity needed to keep adapting.
Ex situ conservation is a last resort when in situ conservation is too difficult or impossible.

entries.title: Climate change as a threat of extinction

definition.text: Climate change can drive species extinct by shifting temperature and weather outside the conditions each species has evolved to live in.

facts.text: Species facing changing conditions can either adapt where they are or move to a new habitat with suitable conditions.
So far few recorded extinctions are blamed on climate change: the IUCN links only 20 of 864 species extinctions to it, usually on weak evidence.
A 2011 review of 74 studies found they projected an average loss of 11.2% of species by 2100.
A 2018 study estimated that at 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C of warming, 6%, 18% and about 49% of insect species would lose over half their climatic range.
Updated 2022 estimates show only 0.2% of coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves at 1.5 °C of warming, compared with 84% now.
Climate change already threatens 45% of at-risk marine species, though overfishing, the aquarium trade, urban development and pollution currently do more damage.
Loss of the species that supply food, fibre and energy hits nature-dependent communities' livelihoods, especially in Africa.
Prevention means limiting warming and protecting present and near-future habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

entries.title: Global biodiversity: how many species share the Earth

definition.text: Global biodiversity is the total variety of life forms on Earth.

facts.text: Estimates of the number of species alive today run from 2 million to 1 trillion, but most are around 11 million or fewer.
About 1.74 million species had been catalogued by 2018, and over 80% of species have not yet been described.
Biodiversity rises with the formation of new species and falls with extinction; the background rate is about one extinction per million species-years.
Insects dominate described species, with about 1,000,000 described and an estimated 5,000,000 in all.
Habitat destruction, often to expand farming, is currently a bigger driver of biodiversity loss than climate change.
Of the 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets set in 2010, only six were 'partially achieved' by 2020.

entries.contested_note: Estimates of the total number of species differ enormously, and some, such as a trillion species, are disputed.
