entries.title: Ecological stability: one word, 167 definitions

definition.text: An ecosystem's ability to return to equilibrium after a disturbance, or to avoid sudden large changes over time.

facts.text: An ecosystem can be stable in some properties and not others; a plant community in drought may keep its biomass but lose biodiversity.
In 1997 Grimm and Wissel counted 167 definitions in the literature covering 70 different stability concepts.
They proposed replacing the term with more specific ones such as constancy, resilience and persistence.
Not every ecosystem is stable, as with wolves and moose on Isle Royale.
The concept emerged in the first half of the 20th century and spread with theoretical ecology in the 1970s.

entries.title: Ecosystem health: a useful metaphor or a value judgment?

definition.text: A metaphor for the overall condition of an ecosystem.

facts.text: Fire, drought, invasive species, climate change, mining, fishing, farming and logging can all change ecosystem condition.
There is no universal benchmark; judgements depend on the metrics chosen and the goals of society.
Supporters value it as a simple communication tool, while critics call it a value-laden idea passed off as science.
Aldo Leopold spoke of land health and land sickness; the health metaphor dates back at least to the early 1800s.
The Great Lakes Basin uses a suite of 80 lake health indicators, including native fish, phosphorus and toxic chemicals.
A healthy state is hard to pin down because species in an ecosystem reshuffle over time.
Proposed neutral alternatives include ecosystem status, ecosystem prognosis and ecosystem sustainability.

definition.text: When a population grows beyond its local carrying capacity, using resources faster than they can be replaced.

facts.text: Overshoot can lead to a crash if resources are depleted faster than they regenerate; the path is called overshoot-and-collapse.
It can happen because of delayed impacts, when births keep exceeding deaths.
On St. Matthew Island, 29 reindeer introduced in 1944 grew to about 6000 by 1963, then crashed to 42 by 1965.
In the Horn of Africa, after smallpox was eradicated, a pastoralist population of about 1 million grew to 14 million, causing overgrazing and soil erosion.
Prolonged overshoot can profoundly change and simplify entire ecosystems.

entries.title: Hysteresis: when a system remembers its past

definition.text: When the state of a system depends on its history, not just on present conditions.

facts.text: Plots often form a hysteresis loop, with different values of one variable depending on which way another variable is changing.
Sir James Alfred Ewing coined the term in 1881, from a Greek word meaning 'lagging behind'.
In ecology, a system's equilibrium cannot be predicted from environmental variables alone; its past matters too, as with spruce budworm outbreaks.
A thermostat that turns heat on below 18 °C but off only above 22 °C uses hysteresis deliberately.
Agar melts at 85 °C but solidifies only at 32 to 40 °C.

entries.text: A thermostat that turns the heat on below 18 °C but off only above 22 °C uses hysteresis on purpose. Sir James Alfred Ewing coined the word in 1881, from a Greek term meaning 'lagging behind'. It describes a system whose state depends on its history, not just on present conditions. Agar melts at 85 °C but solidifies only at 32 to 40 °C. Between those temperatures, whether it is liquid or solid depends on where it started. Plotted on a graph, such systems often trace a hysteresis loop: one variable takes different values depending on which way another variable is changing. In ecology, this means environmental conditions alone cannot predict a system's equilibrium. Its past matters too, as spruce budworm outbreaks show.

entries.title: How many people can the Earth support?

definition.text: The number of people the Earth or a region can support, which depends on how people live and the technology they use.

facts.text: The agricultural and industrial revolutions raised human carrying capacity, letting population grow from 5 to 10 million in 10,000 BCE to 1.5 billion in 1900.
Without the Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people.
These successes have come at grave environmental cost, including climate change, ocean acidification and dead zones at river mouths.
Degrading the ecosystem services people depend on could lower Earth's human carrying capacity; some argue 8 billion may already be above it.
Measuring it is arbitrary: choices about what counts as food or water, and the fact that regions trade resources, change the answer.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005, involving more than 1,300 experts, warned that rapid ecosystem change threatens long-term human carrying capacity.
Crossing one planetary boundary does not prove carrying capacity is exceeded, but crossing several makes that harder to deny.
A 2004 meta-analysis of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion people, with bounds of 0.65 and 98 billion.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether today's human population already exceeds Earth's long-run carrying capacity and how far technology can raise it.

entries.title: The logistic equation: growth that levels off at K

definition.text: A population model in which growth slows as numbers approach the carrying capacity K and stops at K.

facts.text: Verhulst's equation is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where N is population size, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K the carrying capacity.
When the population is small it grows exponentially; as it nears K, growth falls and reaches zero.
Solving the equation gives the S-shaped logistic growth curve N(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(−rt)).
The letter K comes from the German Kapazitätsgrenze, meaning capacity limit.
Pierre François Verhulst published the equations in 1838 without using the term carrying capacity.

entries.text: In 1838 Pierre François Verhulst published equations for how populations level off, without ever using the term carrying capacity. Written today, his equation reads dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K). The letter K comes from the German Kapazitätsgrenze, meaning capacity limit. The logic sits in the bracket. When the population is small, the bracket is close to one and numbers grow exponentially. As N nears K, the bracket shrinks toward zero, and so does growth. Solving the equation gives the S-shaped logistic growth curve N(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(−rt)), the pattern traced in {{ref:nature-eco-376}}.

entries.title: Systems thinking: seeing wholes instead of parts

definition.text: A way of understanding complexity by looking at wholes and the relationships between parts rather than breaking things into pieces.

facts.text: It is used to find effective action in complex situations and to bring about systems change.
A system is a set of interconnected things that produce their own pattern of behaviour over time.
Ludwig von Bertalanffy and Jay Forrester were early contributors, and Peter Senge's The Fifth Discipline popularised it in the 1990s.
Donella Meadows described leverage points: places where a small change can produce a large shift in behaviour.
Its methods include system dynamics, which models stocks, flows and internal feedback loops.
Ecological economics criticises the externality concept for lacking systems thinking.

entries.title: Ecological thresholds: the small push that flips a system

definition.text: The point at which a fairly small change in outside conditions sets off a rapid change in an ecosystem.

facts.text: Once a threshold is passed, the ecosystem may not be able to return to its earlier state through its own resilience.
Thresholds show that ecosystems respond non-linearly to pressures from human activity or natural processes.
Thresholds can be sharp points or zones in which the shift from one state to another is gradual.
Many crossed thresholds have proved hard or nearly impossible to undo, which is why they are called points of no return; extinction is a definitive example.
Thresholds often show hysteresis: the way back from the altered state can be very different from the path that led there.
Detecting a threshold is not always easy; one approach scans time series for a sudden jump.
Clear lakes turning turbid is a well documented example, and a database by the Resilience Alliance and Santa Fe Institute lists over one hundred cases.
Critical load, regime shift, critical transition and tipping point are closely related terms.

entries.title: Planetary boundaries: nine limits for a livable Earth

definition.text: A framework that sets limits on how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself.

facts.text: Crossing the limits could push the Earth system out of the stable Holocene period in which human society developed.

The nine boundaries are climate change, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading.
Its authors warned that transgressing boundaries risks crossing thresholds that trigger non-linear, abrupt change at continental to planetary scale.
The framework was developed in 2009 by scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University.
In 2009 three boundaries were judged crossed; the 2015 update found four crossed.
Novel entities were judged the 5th transgressed boundary in 2022, freshwater change the 6th in 2023 and ocean acidification the 7th in 2025.
Agriculture and food contribute to the transgression of four of the nine boundaries, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows most important.
UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012, though it was later dropped from the Rio+20 text over poorer countries' worries about sidelining development.

entries.text: In 2009 scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University set out limits for the whole planet. Planetary boundaries mark how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself. Crossing them could push the Earth out of the Holocene, the stable period in which human society developed. Worse, the authors warned, transgressing a boundary risks crossing thresholds that trigger abrupt, non-linear change at continental to planetary scale, the behavior described in {{ref:nature-eco-592}}. There are nine boundaries. They cover climate change, ocean acidification, loss of stratospheric ozone, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading. The count of breaches keeps rising. Three were judged crossed in 2009 and four in the 2015 update. Novel entities, meaning new human-made substances, became the fifth in 2022, freshwater change the sixth in 2023 and ocean acidification the seventh in 2025. Agriculture and food help push four of the nine past their limits, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows the most important. Politics followed the science. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012. It was later dropped from the text of {{ref:nature-hist-008}}, because poorer countries worried it would sideline development.

entries.title: Climate tipping points: thresholds with no easy way back
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: A critical threshold in the climate system that, once crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible change.

facts.text: The IPCC defines a tipping point as a threshold beyond which a system reorganises, often abruptly or irreversibly.
A small disturbance can cause a disproportionately large change, often through self-reinforcing feedbacks.
Tipping behaviour appears in ice sheets, glaciers, ocean circulation, ecosystems and the atmosphere.
Thawing permafrost releasing methane and melting ice lowering Earth's albedo are examples that would speed warming.
Early IPCC work thought tipping likely only above 4 °C of warming; by 2021 tipping was considered significantly probable at just over 1 °C and highly probable above 2 °C.
Crossing tipping points would likely have severe impacts on human society and could accelerate global warming.

entries.title: Ecosystem collapse: when a living system loses itself

definition.text: The loss of an ecosystem's defining features and the services it provided once destabilising pressures push it past a critical threshold.

facts.text: Collapse does not mean all life disappears; the original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function.
It has been called an analogue of species extinction and is usually irreversible; any recovery is slow and needs active intervention.
Human drivers include introducing species, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and habitat destruction or fragmentation.
Collapse can occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biotic processes.
Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves, against 84% now.
Under a high-emissions scenario, tropical ocean ecosystems could face abrupt disruption before 2030, with tropical forests and polar regions following by 2050.
Little is known yet about effective ways to conserve or reverse collapsing ecosystems.

entries.text: Consider the reefs described in {{ref:nature-eco-453}}. Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's reefs could withstand marine heatwaves, against 84% now. An ecosystem loses its defining features, and the ecosystem services it provided, once destabilizing pressures push it past a critical threshold. Collapse does not mean all life disappears. The original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function. Some have called it the ecosystem version of species extinction. It is usually irreversible, and any recovery is slow and needs active intervention. Collapse can also occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biological processes. The timeline may be short. entries.title: Regime shifts: abrupt, lasting changes in how systems work

definition.text: A large, abrupt and lasting change in how an ecosystem, the climate, a financial system or another complex system is structured and works.

facts.text: A regime is a typical behaviour of a system held in place by mutually reinforcing feedbacks.
Shifts happen when stabilising feedbacks weaken or an external shock exceeds the system's capacity to absorb it.
Regime shifts matter in ecology because they can sharply change the flow of ecosystem services such as food, clean water and climate regulation.
They are hard to reverse and sometimes irreversible.
A small disturbance can produce big effects, so inputs and outputs are not proportional.
Regime shifts are expected to become more common as human influence on the planet grows.
Strong evidence emerged in the 1990s from kelp forests, coral reefs, drylands and shallow lakes.
Deforestation could shift Amazon and East Asian rainforests toward savanna, affecting food, fresh water, climate regulation and biodiversity.

entries.title: Measuring the boundaries: from 280 to 423 parts per million

definition.text: The measurable quantities and limit values the framework uses to track how far humanity has shifted the Earth away from Holocene conditions.

facts.text: The 2009 study quantified seven of the nine boundaries; by 2025 eight were quantified.
The climate boundary is 350 ppm of atmospheric CO2, against a current 423 ppm and a pre-industrial 280 ppm.
The biosphere integrity boundary is under 10 extinctions per million species-years, while the current rate is over 100.
The land system boundary keeps 75% of forests intact; the global figure is 59%.
Industrial and intentional nitrogen fixation has a boundary of 62 Tg per year against a current 165 Tg per year.
Aerosol loading and stratospheric ozone depletion are the two boundaries listed as not exceeded.
For several processes no single threshold point can be located, because the Earth system is complex and evidence is still partial.

Only two boundaries, aerosol loading and loss of stratospheric ozone, are listed as not exceeded. For several processes no single threshold point can be located, because the Earth system is complex and evidence is still partial.

entries.title: Bouncing back versus holding on: two kinds of resilience

definition.text: Two meanings of resilience: how fast a system returns to equilibrium after a shock, versus how much disturbance it can absorb while keeping the same function and structure.

facts.text: Holling called the return-time meaning 'engineering resilience' because physics and engineering use it.
Ecological resilience assumes a system can exist in multiple stable states or regimes.
Some shallow lakes can sit in a clear-water regime rich in ecosystem services or a turbid regime with fewer services and toxic algae blooms, depending on phosphorus.
Australia's Mulga woodlands can be grass-rich and good for sheep or shrub-dominated and useless for grazing, driven by fire, herbivory and rainfall.

entries.text: Some shallow lakes can exist in two quite different forms. In one, the water is clear and rich in ecosystem services. In the other, it is turbid, poorer in services and prone to toxic algae blooms. Which one a lake sits in depends on phosphorus. Holling called this engineering resilience, because physics and engineering use it. The second, ecological resilience, is how much disturbance a system can absorb while keeping the same function and structure. It assumes a system can exist in several stable states, or regimes, like those lakes. Australia's Mulga woodlands are another case. Fire, grazing animals and rainfall can leave them grass-rich and good for sheep, or shrub-dominated and useless for grazing.

entries.title: Alternative stable states: one place, two possible ecosystems

definition.text: The ecological theory that an ecosystem can settle into more than one stable state under the same conditions.

facts.text: A move between states, called a state shift, phase shift or regime shift, happens when the ecosystem is perturbed.
Feedbacks make ecosystems resist shifting, so they stay in one state unless the push is large enough.
Discrete states are separated by ecological thresholds, unlike ecosystems that change smoothly along a gradient.

entries.title: Ice sheets, currents and forests: the climate's tipping elements
entries.article: Tipping points in the climate system#Comparison of tipping points

definition.text: The parts of the climate system, such as ice sheets, ocean currents and large forests, that may have tipping points.

facts.text: As of September 2022, nine global core tipping elements and seven regional impact tipping elements had been identified.
Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheet collapse, tropical coral reef die-off and abrupt boreal permafrost thaw are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming.
Completely melting the Greenland ice sheet would raise global sea levels by 7.2 metres.
A collapse of the Atlantic overturning circulation would cool parts of Europe by over 10 °C and threaten crop yields across most world regions.
Around 500 million people depend on coral reefs, and a sustained ocean temperature rise of 1 °C above average is enough to cause bleaching.
Permafrost holds carbon from organisms that died over thousands of years.

entries.title: Positive and negative feedback: amplify or correct

definition.text: Feedback that amplifies a change (positive, or reinforcing) versus feedback that counteracts it (negative, or balancing).

facts.text: Positive feedback widens the gap between a target and the actual value; negative feedback narrows it.
Other names are self-reinforcing and self-correcting, or reinforcing and balancing.
A car's cruise control, which holds a target speed, is an example of negative feedback.
Melting snow exposes darker ground that absorbs more heat and melts more snow: the ice–albedo positive feedback.
Negative feedback is often added deliberately to make a system more stable and accurate.

entries.title: The balance of nature: an old idea ecologists abandoned

definition.text: The idea that ecosystems naturally sit in a stable equilibrium, with small changes corrected by negative feedback.

facts.text: The idea is ancient: Herodotus, Plato and Cicero all described a balance in nature.
It once governed ecological research and natural resource management, and was a central theme of Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring.
Ecologists abandoned it in the late 20th century because constant disturbance and chaotic change turned out to be the norm.
An eight-year study of isolated Baltic plankton showed species populations rising and falling chaotically even under constant conditions.
Many habitats were shaped by people, such as Aboriginal fire-stick farming in Australia.
The idea remains popular with the public, conservationists and environmental groups.

entries.contested_note: Ecologists have discredited the theory, yet some still call it a foundational metaphor and it stays popular with the public.

definition.text: The share of human demand on nature, driven by both consumption and population, that exceeds what Earth can sustainably supply.

definition.text: A view of human systems (economic, social, cultural) and natural systems (water, air, living things, rocks) as linked by two-way interactions.

facts.text: The idea is that human and environmental systems can no longer be studied as separate, isolated systems.

The phrase appears in literature from 1999, and the US National Science Foundation made it a standing research program in 2007.
It builds on social-ecological system theory but covers all aspects of human and natural life, not only social and environmental ones.

entries.title: Amazon dieback: a rainforest that waters itself

definition.text: The risk that enough forest loss pushes much of the Amazon past a threshold into drier degraded forest or savanna.

facts.text: The Amazon makes around half of its own rainfall by recycling moisture, so forest loss means less rain downwind.
A 2022 study reported the rainforest has been losing resilience since the early 2000s, measured by slower recovery from short shocks.
Modelling suggests warming of 1.5–1.9°C combined with 22–28% deforestation could trigger a transition across 62–77% of the forest.
Some 17–18% of the Amazon has already been cleared for development.

entries.title: Taking stability apart: resistance, resilience and more

definition.text: The separate kinds of stability ecologists measure, such as constancy, resistance, persistence and resilience.

facts.text: Resistance measures how little a variable changes under outside pressure; inertia or persistence is the ability to resist fluctuations.

Local stability covers small, short disturbances; global stability means strong resistance to change in species composition or food webs.

entries.title: Does diversity make ecosystems more stable?

definition.text: The long-running question of whether more diverse ecosystems are more stable.

facts.text: Charles Elton argued in 1958 that complex, diverse communities tend to be more stable; Robert May later refuted the idea that diversity begets stability.
Diversity can stabilise ecosystem functions; genetic diversity, for example, can improve resistance to disturbance.
In food-web models the effect of diversity on stability can be positive or negative, depending on network structure.

entries.title: May's limit: when more species means less stability
entries.article: Ecological stability#May stability analysis and random matrix theory

definition.text: Robert May's result that a large random ecosystem loses stability once its species number and interaction strength pass a limit.

facts.text: May linearised the species equations around equilibrium using the Jacobian, also called the community matrix.
Treating the Jacobian as a random matrix, the system loses stability when S exceeds 1/σ, where σ is the spread of interaction strengths.
The result implies diversity limits dynamical stability.

entries.text: Robert May found that a large random ecosystem loses stability once its number of species and the strength of their interactions pass a limit. He linearized the species equations around equilibrium, replacing them with simpler straight-line versions. To do so he used the Jacobian, a table of how each species affects the others, also called the community matrix. Treating it as a random matrix, the system loses stability when S, the number of species, exceeds 1/σ, where σ is the spread of interaction strengths. The result implies that diversity limits dynamical stability, a key point in {{ref:nature-eco-631}}.

entries.title: Describing nature versus grading it

definition.text: The difference between indicators used to describe trends scientifically and those used to rank conditions as good or bad for policy.

facts.text: An indicator is a measured variable used to infer trends in something unmeasured; rising chlorophyll-a in a lake may signal eutrophication.
The same chlorophyll level may be judged healthy in a natural wetland and unhealthy in a human-impacted one.
Critics say mixing the two implies values can be measured objectively, and urge keeping them separate.

The utilitarian view treats human well-being as a test of ecosystem health; the protectionist view sees humans as an invasive species.

entries.title: Will population outrun food? The neo-Malthusian debate

definition.text: The argument over whether population growth will outrun food and resources, as Malthus and later Ehrlich predicted.

facts.text: Malthus forecast in 1798 that population growth would deplete the world's food; Ehrlich revived the argument in 1968.
Economist Julian Simon countered that the Green Revolution prevented famine; grain production rose over 250% between 1950 and 1984.
Neo-Malthusians reply that the Green Revolution depends on fossil-fuel fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation.
The FAO said in 2009 that the world would need 70% more food by 2050.

entries.contested_note: Neo-Malthusians and economists such as Julian Simon disagree on whether technology can keep resources ahead of population.

entries.title: Hysteresis in economics: shocks that leave scars

definition.text: The idea that a temporary economic shock can leave lasting effects, such as permanently higher unemployment.

facts.text: Starting exports may need a big push because of fixed transport costs, but once begun little is needed to keep them going.
In recessions unemployed workers may lose skills or motivation and stay jobless during the recovery.
Olivier Blanchard and others used hysteresis to explain long-run unemployment differences between Europe and the United States.

facts.text: Methods such as principal component analysis or neural networks need long data series and only work after the threshold is crossed.
Failing to find multiple regimes in data does not rule out a future shift.
For managers, assuming a system has only one regime can be risky when the alternatives are very harmful.

entries.title: Complex adaptive systems: wholes that learn

definition.text: A system made of many interacting parts that adapt and learn, whose overall behaviour cannot be predicted from the parts alone.

facts.text: Examples include climate, cities, firms, markets, governments, ecosystems, power grids and ant colonies.
Interactions are non-linear, so small changes in inputs can cause large changes in outputs, and any interaction can feed back on itself.
Such systems often organise themselves rather than following a central hierarchy.
Their high adaptive capacity gives them resilience against disturbance.
They run far from equilibrium and need a constant flow of energy to keep their organisation.
Sociologist Walter F. Buckley coined the term in 1968.
The approach is increasingly used to study economic development and institutional change, where outcomes can be influenced but not precisely controlled.
They are often modelled with agent-based and network models.

entries.title: Adaptive governance: institutions that learn

definition.text: Governing social-ecological systems so that institutions can learn and reorganise as ecosystems change.

facts.text: Folke and colleagues contrasted the Florida Everglades and the Grand Canyon, both of which suffered degraded ecosystem services.
In the Everglades, conflict between farming and conservation interests left few feedbacks and little capacity to adapt.
At the Grand Canyon, an adaptive management workgroup used planned interventions and monitoring to learn, enabling successful reorganisation.
Introduced by Holling in 1978, it is a flexible approach to climate impacts that contrasts with mitigation-focused efforts.

entries.title: The ball-and-cup model: valleys of stability

definition.text: A picture of ecosystem states as a ball rolling on a landscape of valleys and hills.

facts.text: In the simplest version two valleys are separated by a hill; a ball in a valley sits in a stable state, or domain of attraction.
Moving the ball to another valley takes enough force to push it over the hill.
A steep-sided valley is more resilient than a shallow one.

entries.title: How people wear down ecosystem resilience

definition.text: The ways human activity makes stable ecosystem states easier to tip into worse ones.

facts.text: People reduce resilience by cutting diversity (as in overfishing), altering the physical and chemical environment, and changing disturbance regimes such as through bottom trawling.
With less resilience, minor perturbations can push ecosystems into less desirable states.
Such shifts often lose ecosystem services and have been documented on land, at sea and in fresh water.

A sending system passes a flow to a receiving system, and a spillover system is affected without being the focus.

entries.title: Critical slowing down: an early warning of tipping

definition.text: The increasingly slow recovery from small disturbances shown by a system approaching a tipping point, used as an early warning signal.

facts.text: As recovery slows, the system's autocorrelation and variance rise, giving measurable warning signs.
Since the early 2000s, more than three-quarters of the Amazon rainforest has shown slower recovery from short-term shocks, suggesting it may be nearing a critical transition.
Rising autocorrelation and variance in melt rates suggest the Greenland ice sheet is losing resilience.
Early warnings need long, good-quality data series, which are rare in ecology.
Noise-induced transitions give no such warning, and human-driven change may be too fast for signals to appear.

entries.title: Four aspects of resilience

definition.text: Brian Walker, C.S. Holling and others break resilience into latitude, resistance, precariousness and panarchy.

facts.text: Latitude is how far a system can be changed before it loses the ability to recover.
Resistance is how hard the system is to change, and precariousness is how close it currently sits to a threshold.
Panarchy is how much one level of an ecosystem's hierarchy is influenced by the other levels.
Adaptive capacity, closely linked to resilience, is people's ability to cope with environmental change by observing, learning and altering their interactions.

entries.title: Forests: where most of Earth's plant life stands

definition.text: A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees.

facts.text: There are hundreds of definitions; the FAO's is land over 0.5 hectares with trees taller than 5 metres and more than 10 percent canopy cover, not mainly farm or urban land.
The world has 4.14 billion hectares of forest, 32% of global land area or 0.50 ha per person, and 45% of it lies in the tropics.
Forests account for 75% of the biosphere's gross primary production and contain 80% of Earth's plant biomass.
Forests provide oxygen, carbon storage, climate and rainfall regulation, clean water, flood control, genetic reserves, timber, recreation, and subsistence for millions.
Forests can turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source if their plant diversity, density or area declines.
Most deforestation is now in the tropics, driven mainly by four commodities: wood, beef, soy and palm oil.
Global forest area fell by 178 million hectares between 1990 and 2020, about the size of Libya.
Some researchers note forests can also impose costs, such as reducing grazing and cropland or available water.

entries.text: Forests contain 80% of Earth's plant biomass, the total weight of living plant matter. They also account for 75% of the biosphere's gross primary production, the plant growth powered by sunlight. A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees. Pinning that down is harder than it sounds, and there are hundreds of definitions. The FAO, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, offers one. It counts land over 0.5 hectares with trees taller than 5 metres and more than 10 percent canopy cover. Land that is mainly farm or urban does not count. By that measure the world has 4.14 billion hectares of forest: 32% of global land area, or 0.50 ha per person. Some 45% of it lies in the tropics. Forests give oxygen, carbon storage, clean water, flood control, timber, genetic reserves and recreation, regulate climate and rainfall, and support millions who live from them directly. That bounty is shrinking. Global forest area fell by 178 million hectares between 1990 and 2020, about the size of Libya. Most clearing now happens in the tropics, driven mainly by four commodities: wood, beef, soy and palm oil. Loss can flip a forest's role. If its plant diversity, density or area declines, a forest can turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source. Some researchers add a caution: forests can also impose costs, such as taking land from grazing and crops or reducing available water.

entries.title: Aquatic ecosystems: life organized around water

definition.text: An ecosystem in and around a body of water, as opposed to a land-based terrestrial ecosystem.

facts.text: It holds communities of aquatic organisms that depend on each other and on their surroundings.
The two main kinds are marine and freshwater ecosystems.
Freshwater ecosystems may be lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) or wetlands.
Aquatic environments are relatively low in oxygen, so organisms must adapt, as wetland plants do by growing aerenchyma.
Algae, which build biomass from carbon dioxide using sunlight, may be the most important producers in water.
Algae and shallow-water plants together give estuaries and wetlands their extraordinary productivity, feeding fish, birds and amphibians.

entries.text: Algae may be the most important producers in water, building living matter from carbon dioxide and sunlight. They anchor the aquatic ecosystem: the community of living things in and around a body of water, as opposed to a land-based terrestrial ecosystem. Its organisms depend on each other and on their surroundings. The two main kinds are salty {{ref:nature-eco-499}} systems and {{ref:nature-eco-502}} systems. Fresh waters split further. Lentic waters are still, like ponds and lakes; lotic waters flow, like rivers; and the third type is the soaked ground covered in {{ref:nature-eco-441}}. Where algae and shallow-water plants grow together, as in estuaries and soaked shallows, productivity becomes extraordinary, feeding fish, birds and amphibians.

entries.title: Wetlands: the ground between water and land

definition.text: A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or soaked with water, either permanently or for part of the year.

facts.text: Wetlands sit between open water and dry land; their plants' roots are adapted to oxygen-poor, waterlogged soils.
They are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems, and their plants improve water quality by removing excess nitrates and phosphorus.
Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica, and their water may be fresh, brackish or salt.
Marshes are dominated by reeds, cattails and sedges, swamps by trees and shrubs; peatlands such as bogs and fens build up peat.
Hydrology, meaning how long and how often an area floods, is the most important factor that creates a wetland.
Wetlands provide services such as water purification, shoreline stabilization, storm protection and flood control.
The 2005 Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found wetlands more threatened by environmental degradation than any other ecosystem.
The largest wetlands include the Amazon basin, the West Siberian Plain, the Pantanal and the Sundarbans.

entries.title: Mangroves: trees that live in the sea's edge

definition.text: A mangrove is a tree or shrub that lives mostly in salty or brackish coastal water; the word also names the coastal vegetation these plants form.

facts.text: Mangroves grow along tropical and subtropical coasts, mostly between 30° N and 30° S, with the largest area within 5° of the equator.
Special adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and get rid of salt, so they survive where most plants die.
In 2025 the world's mangroves were estimated to cover 15.9 million hectares, with Asia holding the largest share at 6.10 million ha.
Indonesia, Brazil, Australia, Nigeria and Mexico together hold almost half (49%) of global mangrove area.
Human activity keeps destroying mangroves at an estimated 0.16% a year worldwide, and up to 0.70% a year in some countries.
A 2022 study estimated a net loss of 3,700 km2 of mangroves worldwide between 1999 and 2019.
Mangroves support coastal and marine ecosystems, shield nearby land from tsunamis and extreme weather, and store carbon well.
Although a mangrove forest has few tree species, it gives habitat to many other species, including up to 174 species of marine megafauna.

entries.title: Grasslands: the open biome that feeds herds

definition.text: A grassland is an area or ecosystem whose vegetation is dominated by grasses.

facts.text: Grasslands occur naturally on every continent except Antarctica and are among the largest biomes, covering 31–69% of Earth's land area.
They come as natural, semi-natural and agricultural grasslands.
One definition describes grasslands as kept open by fire, grazing, drought or freezing temperatures.
Grasslands support the greatest gatherings of large animals on Earth.
Their marketed and non-marketed ecosystem services are fundamental to the livelihoods of an estimated one billion people.
Grasslands hold about twenty percent of global soil carbon stocks.
They have been described as the most imperiled terrestrial biome, converted faster than forests yet given little protection.

entries.title: Peatlands: wetlands built from half-rotted plants

definition.text: A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material.

facts.text: Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen, so dead plant litter only partly decomposes.
Peatlands cover around 3 million km2 and are the largest natural carbon store on land.
Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types including forests.
Natural peatlands reduce flood risk and erosion, purify water and regulate climate.
They are threatened by peat harvesting, drainage for farming (notably palm oil in the tropics) and fires.
Destroying peatlands releases stored greenhouse gases, worsening climate change.
Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes.

entries.text: Peatlands cover around 3 million km2, yet they are the largest natural carbon store on land. A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material. Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen. Without oxygen, the microbes that break down dead plant litter work slowly, so the litter only partly decomposes and accumulates year after year. The result is staggering. Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types, forests included. Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes. Left intact, they reduce flood risk and erosion, purify water and help regulate climate. They face three main threats: peat harvesting, drainage for farming, notably for palm oil in the tropics, and fire. Destroying a peatland reverses its gift. The greenhouse gases it locked away escape into the air, worsening climate change.
entries.text_plain: Peatlands cover around 3 million km2, yet they are the largest natural carbon store on land. A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material. Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen. Without oxygen, the microbes that break down dead plant litter work slowly, so the litter only partly decomposes and accumulates year after year. The result is staggering. Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types, forests included. Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes. Left intact, they reduce flood risk and erosion, purify water and help regulate climate. They face three main threats: peat harvesting, drainage for farming, notably for palm oil in the tropics, and fire. Destroying a peatland reverses its gift. The greenhouse gases it locked away escape into the air, worsening climate change.

entries.title: What wetlands do for people, and what they are worth

definition.text: Wetlands perform functions, such as storing water and cleaning it, that give people valuable benefits known as ecosystem services.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment and the Ramsar Convention list services including flood control, groundwater recharge, storm protection, water purification, biodiversity, products, culture, recreation and climate regulation.
According to the Ramsar Convention, intact wetlands are often worth much more to society than the perceived gains from converting them to intensive land use.
Replacing wetland services would cost enormous sums for treatment plants, dams and levees, and many services cannot be replaced at all.
One analysis valued the storm protection wetlands provide against hurricanes at US$33,000/hectare/year.
Many wetlands are linked to groundwater and help refill aquifers, which supply much of the world's drinking water.
Coastal wetlands protect shores by reducing the speed and height of waves and floodwaters.
In highly developed areas, wetlands may be the only habitat left for pollinating insects, birds and mammals.

entries.title: Tropical forests: half the world's species on a fifth of its land

definition.text: Tropical forests are forested regions with tropical climates, roughly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

facts.text: The tropical domain holds the largest share of the world's forests, 45 percent, ahead of boreal, temperate and subtropical forests.
Tropical forest ecosystems cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species and about 60 percent of vascular plants.
They include evergreen rainforests but also open eucalyptus forest, tropical conifer forest, savanna woodland and mountain cloud forests.
No single scheme defines a forest, so estimates of tropical forest extent vary between sources.
Much current deforestation in biodiversity hotspots is driven by exports of beef, soy, coffee, cacao, palm oil and timber.
Valuing these forests' ecosystem services is widely held to encourage sustainable policy, but needs clear monitoring of outcomes.

entries.title: Tropical rainforests: rain every month, poor soil below

definition.text: A tropical rainforest is a dense, warm forest with high rainfall, typically within 10° north and south of the Equator.

facts.text: True rainforests have no dry season: every month averages at least 60 mm of rain, and mean monthly temperatures exceed 18 °C.
Heavy rain leaches nutrients, so soils are often poor; most nutrients sit near the surface because leaves and organisms decompose quickly.
Rainforests maintain biodiversity, store carbon, regulate the climate and support pollination; forests produce half of the Amazon's rainfall.
Tropical rainforests produce about 30% of Earth's fresh water and have among the highest primary production of land ecosystems.
Foods such as coffee, chocolate, bananas, mangoes and sugarcane originally came from tropical rainforests.
Mining, drilling and conversion to farmland drive deforestation; mineral and fossil-fuel extraction is often prioritised for economic growth.
REDD is a market incentive through which companies and governments offset emissions by financing rainforest conservation.

entries.title: Old-growth forests: centuries in the making

definition.text: An old-growth forest is a forest that has developed over a long time without disturbance.

facts.text: The FAO's related term, primary forest, means naturally regenerated native forest with no clearly visible human activity; one-third (34%) of the world's forests are primary.
Old-growth forests have large living and standing dead trees, layered canopies with gaps, and fallen woody debris on the floor.
After a severe disturbance it can take from a century to several millennia for a regrowing forest to regain old-growth character.
Their varied structure gives more diverse habitat than younger forests and shelters many rare and endangered species.
They provide services such as clean air and water, carbon storage, soil maintenance, pest control and climate regulation, which may matter more than their timber.
Carbon studies show old-growth forests store carbon more productively than younger forests.
As of January 2009 only 21% of Earth's original old-growth forests remained, and 90% of those in the contiguous United States in the 1600s have been cleared.
Primary forest was lost at 1.61 million ha a year in 2015–2025, less than half the 3.92 million ha a year of 2000–2015.

entries.title: The taiga: Earth's great northern forest

definition.text: The taiga, or boreal forest, is a biome of mostly pine, spruce and larch forest across the high northern latitudes, between the tundra and temperate forest.

facts.text: It covers 17 million km2, or 11.5% of Earth's land, with the largest areas in Russia and Canada.
Mean annual temperatures are generally −5 to 5 °C; summers last 1–3 months and freezing winters 5–7 months.
Taiga soils are young and nutrient-poor because the cold slows soil development.
The taiga stores more carbon than the world's temperate and tropical forests combined, much of it in wetlands and peat, and about twice as much per unit area as tropical forests.
Fire management costing about 12 dollars per tonne of carbon kept from release is very cheap compared with the social cost of carbon.
Its latitudes saw some of Earth's largest temperature increases in the last quarter of the twentieth century, with fewer extreme cold days helping tree-damaging insects.

entries.title: Bogs: where decay runs slower than growth

definition.text: A wetland that builds up peat, a deposit of dead plant matter, usually sphagnum moss.

facts.text: Bogs are one of the four main types of wetland; alkaline peat-forming mires are called fens instead.
They form where surface water is acidic and poor in nutrients, mostly in cooler northern climates.
Plants grow slowly, but decay is even slower in the oxygen-poor waterlogged soil, so peat piles up, sometimes many meters deep.
Most bogs get their water and nutrients from rain rather than ground or surface water, and have peat usually thicker than 30 centimetres.
The world's largest wetland is the peat bogs of the Western Siberian Lowlands, covering more than a million square kilometres.
Bogs host specialized species, such as carnivorous sundews and pitcher plants that get nutrients from insects.
Slowly accumulating plant material makes bogs a carbon sink.

entries.title: Tundra: the land too cold for trees

definition.text: Tundra is a biome where freezing temperatures and short growing seasons keep trees from growing.

facts.text: There are three types: Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic; vegetation is dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens.
The boundary between tundra and forest is the tree line.
Arctic tundra is a polar desert with about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year and winter temperatures around −28 °C.
Biodiversity is low: about 1,700 vascular plant species and 48 land mammal species, though millions of birds migrate there each summer.
Its frozen soils store biomass as carbon, making tundra soil a carbon sink.
Arctic tundra is rich in petroleum, natural gas and uranium; the Yamalo-Nenets region produces 90% of Russia's natural gas.

entries.title: The forest transition: when losing turns to gaining

definition.text: The forest transition is the shift of a region from losing forest to gaining forested land overall.

facts.text: It happens through commercial tree plantations, agroforestry by small farmers, or natural regrowth on abandoned farmland.
It can be driven by the economic value of forests, their ecosystem services, or cultural change toward valuing forests for their own sake.
Net forest loss fell from 7.8 million hectares a year in the 1990s to 4.7 million hectares a year in 2010–2020, as new forests offset part of deforestation.
Large planting programmes in China, India, the United States and Vietnam contributed, and China banned logging from 1998 because of erosion and flooding.
New forests are not equivalent to old-growth forests in species diversity, resilience or carbon capture.
In 2025 about 813 million ha, around 20% of forest area, was in legally protected areas.
Countries move from high forest cover and low deforestation, through fast deforestation and low cover, to slowing loss, stabilization and recovery.
It is not a law of nature: population density, development stage, global markets and policy shape the pattern.

entries.text: Net forest loss worldwide fell from 7.8 million hectares a year in the 1990s to 4.7 million hectares a year in 2010–2020. New forests offset part of the clearing. Behind that shift lies the forest transition: the change of a region from losing forest to gaining forested land overall. Countries tend to move through stages. They start with high forest cover and low clearing, pass through fast clearing and low cover, then see loss slow, stabilize and reverse. The gain comes three ways: commercial plantations of trees, small farmers mixing trees with crops, or natural regrowth on abandoned farmland. The drivers vary too. Forests may be valued for timber, for their ecosystem services, or simply for their own sake as culture changes. Large planting programmes in China, India, the United States and Vietnam contributed, and China banned logging from 1998 because of erosion and flooding. In 2025 about 813 million ha, around 20% of forest area, lay on legally protected land. Two cautions apply. New forests are not equal to old-growth forests in species diversity, resilience or carbon capture. And the transition is not a law of nature: population density, stage of development, global markets and policy all shape it.

entries.title: Wetland loss: two-thirds gone since 1900

definition.text: Wetlands are damaged or destroyed by drainage, pollution, dams, overfishing and other human activities as well as natural disturbances.

facts.text: Since 1900, 65–70% of the world's wetlands have been lost.
Wetlands are often drained with dykes and ditches to create farmland and increase economic output; some of the world's key farming areas were once wetlands.
Settlements built on drained wetlands become prone to land subsidence and rising flood risk.
Because wetlands hold water with little flow, they quickly concentrate toxic pollutants, harming native species.
Shrimp farming has wiped out large areas of mangrove, a damage hard to curb because of strong global demand.
In East Asia, up to 65% of coastal wetlands have been destroyed by coastal development.
Disturbances range from minor, through moderate ones a wetland recovers from alone, to severe ones needing human help.

entries.text: Since 1900, 65–70% of the world's wetlands have been lost. Wetlands are damaged or destroyed by drainage, pollution, dams, taking too many fish and other human activities, as well as by natural disturbances. Drainage is the classic story. People cut dykes and ditches to create farmland and raise economic output, and some of the world's key farming areas were once wetlands. The bill can arrive later: settlements built on drained wetlands become prone to sinking ground and rising flood risk. Because wetland water barely flows, toxic pollutants concentrate quickly and harm native species. Shrimp farming has wiped out large areas of mangrove, damage that is hard to curb because global demand is strong. In East Asia, up to 65% of coastal wetlands have been destroyed by coastal development. Damage comes in degrees. Minor and moderate disturbances let a wetland recover on its own; severe ones need human help.

entries.title: Wetland conservation: from wasteland to treasure

definition.text: Wetland conservation aims to protect wetlands and their natural functions from draining, flooding and other damaging change.

facts.text: Since the 1970s more attention has gone to preserving wetlands for their natural functions.
The Ramsar Convention, a treaty working since 1971, lists wetlands of international importance and promotes their wise use.
Ramsar methods include restricting access and teaching the public that wetlands are not wastelands.
Studies show wetlands can be conserved while improving the livelihoods of people who live in them, as with sustainably farmed dambos in Malawi and Zambia.
Wetlands cover at least six percent of Earth and became a conservation focus because of the ecosystem services they provide.
More than three billion people, around half the world's population, get their basic water needs from inland freshwater wetlands.
Coastal wetlands are estimated to save a median of US$447 billion in damages and 4,620 lives each year from storms.
Wetlands hold around 700 billion tons of carbon, mainly in peat soils, and sequester about 96 million tons a year.

entries.title: Wetland restoration: from letting go to rebuilding

definition.text: Wetland restoration helps a damaged wetland return to its natural path of development by assisting its natural processes.

facts.text: The level of restoration needed depends on how badly the wetland is disturbed; budget, time, goals and politics also shape the choice.
The cheapest, least intrusive level leaves the wetland to recover by natural succession once disturbance is stopped.
Partial reconstruction mixes natural regeneration with engineering such as ripping subsoil, mulching and mechanical seeding.
Complete reconstruction, the most expensive and intrusive, rebuilds the wetland from the ground up.
Traditional ecological knowledge offers a holistic approach that can raise wetland productivity, biodiversity and resilience.

entries.text: The cheapest way to restore a damaged wetland is often to stop harming it and step back. Wetland restoration helps a damaged wetland return to its natural path of development by assisting its natural processes. How much help it needs depends on how badly it is disturbed, though budget, time, goals and politics also shape the choice. At the light end, the wetland recovers by natural succession, the gradual return of plant and animal communities, once disturbance stops. In the middle sits partial reconstruction, which mixes natural regrowth with engineering such as ripping compacted subsoil, mulching and mechanical seeding. At the heavy end, complete reconstruction rebuilds the wetland from the ground up, the most expensive and intrusive option. Another resource is {{ref:nature-gov-176}}, the understanding built up by local peoples over generations, offers a holistic approach that can raise wetland productivity, biodiversity and resilience.

entries.title: Valuing wetlands: mapping, scoring and ranking

definition.text: Valuing wetlands means mapping them, assessing the functions and services each provides, and using that information to rank or prioritize them.

facts.text: Over the longer term it needs wetland inventories and monitoring of a sample to track changes.
Rapid assessment methods score or rank a wetland's functions, services, species and health, usually from a single visit of less than a day.
Assessments help decide which wetlands to protect and how much compensation, such as restoring wetlands elsewhere, a loss requires.
Rapid methods are needed mainly when agencies face decision deadlines or have many wetlands to assess.
Satellite and aerial imagery, increasingly combined with LiDAR, map and monitor wetlands over large areas.

entries.title: Wetlands and climate: carbon store or methane source

definition.text: Wetlands can either store carbon and slow climate change or release greenhouse gases such as methane, depending on the wetland and how it is treated.

facts.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of methane, emitting about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average 161 Tg a year.
Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils favour methane-producing microbes.
Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions, as drained peat decomposes into carbon dioxide.
Salt marshes and mangroves sequester on average 210 g CO2 m−2 y−1, compared with about 20–30 g CO2 m−2 y−1 for peatlands.
Restoring coastal blue carbon wetlands to remove CO2 has questionable cost-effectiveness if judged only as climate mitigation.
Their flood control, groundwater and storm protection services help societies adapt to the worse floods and droughts of a warming climate.

entries.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of methane, emitting about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average 161 Tg a year. A teragram (Tg) is a million tonnes. Wetlands can either store carbon and slow climate change or release greenhouse gases such as methane, depending on the wetland and how it is treated. The reason is in the mud. Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils favour methane-producing microbes. Drained peat flips the other way and decomposes into carbon dioxide. Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions. Coastal wetlands are strong absorbers. {{ref:nature-eco-428}} and mangroves take up on average 210 g CO2 m−2 y−1, compared with about 20–30 g CO2 m−2 y−1 for peatlands. Even so, restoring coastal wetlands purely to remove CO2, the idea behind {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}, has questionable cost-effectiveness. Their bigger payoff may be adaptation: flood control, underground water supplies and storm protection help societies cope with the worse floods and droughts of a warming climate.

entries.title: Drylands: where water is the limit

definition.text: Lands defined by scarce water, where rainfall is balanced by evaporation and plant transpiration.

facts.text: The UN Environment Programme defines drylands as tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65.
Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America.
They are home to more than 2 billion people, and 72% of drylands lie in developing countries.
Drylands include 45% of the world's agricultural land.
Their behaviour depends on many linked interactions among climate, soil and vegetation.
Unlike humid biomes, drylands redistribute water mainly through surface runoff.
They are highly vulnerable to climate change through shifting rainfall and land degradation.

They are highly vulnerable to climate change through shifting rainfall and land degradation.

entries.title: Agroecosystems: nature reshaped to grow food

definition.text: An agroecosystem is a natural ecosystem that people have modified and manage to produce crops or livestock.

facts.text: Like other ecosystems it combines a physical environment, living organisms such as crops and wildlife, and the interactions linking them.
It is the basic unit of study in agroecology and regenerative agriculture.
An agroecosystem extends beyond the farm to the region its activity affects, through changes to species, energy flows and nutrient balance.
Intensively managed agroecosystems have simpler species, energy and nutrient flows than natural ones, and their excess nutrients cause eutrophication downstream.
More plant diversity in sustainable agroecosystems brings both ecological and economic benefits.
Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest and most resilient agroecosystem.
A report by the International Water Management Institute and UNEP suggested assigning value to ecosystems and recognizing trade-offs among users.
Agroecology tries to blur the line with natural ecosystems, for example through polyculture, wildlife buffer strips and organic farming.

entries.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest and most resilient agroecosystem. An agroecosystem is a natural ecosystem that people have modified and manage to produce crops or livestock. Like any ecosystem, it combines a physical environment, living things such as crops and wildlife, and the interactions linking them. It is the basic unit of study in {{ref:nature-nbs-246}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}. Its reach goes beyond the farm gate, to the whole region its activity affects through changes to species, energy flows and nutrient balance. Intensively managed farms simplify those flows, and their excess nutrients cause eutrophication, an overgrowth of algae, downstream. More plant diversity brings both ecological and economic benefits. Some approaches try to blur the line with natural ecosystems, for example through polyculture, growing several crops together, wildlife buffer strips and {{ref:nature-nbs-292}}. A report by the International Water Management Institute and UNEP suggested assigning value to ecosystems and recognizing trade-offs among their users.

entries.title: Mangroves as a living sea wall

definition.text: Mangrove swamps act as a natural barrier that protects coasts from erosion, storm surges and tsunamis.

facts.text: Their huge root systems absorb wave energy, limiting erosion from high-energy waves during storm surges and tsunamis.
By slowing incoming tides, mangroves make sediment settle out, so they build up the land they grow on.
Studies show mangroves give coastal communities measurable economic protection against tropical storms.
Because of this erosion protection, mangroves are often targeted by conservation programmes, including national biodiversity action plans.
Removing mangroves disturbs the sediments beneath them, which trap heavy metals, and can release that contamination into seawater.
Wave energy may fall by 75 per cent as a wave passes through 200 meters of mangrove forest.
Shorelines covered by mangroves erode less, or much more slowly, than bare shorelines when waves are strong.
Keeping a healthy mangrove forest is cheaper than seawalls, which can increase erosion in front of the wall and on neighbouring land.

entries.text: Wave energy may fall by 75 per cent as a wave passes through 200 meters of mangroves. Mangrove swamps act as a natural barrier that protects coasts from erosion, tsunamis and the storm-driven rise in sea level called {{ref:nature-es-119}}. Their huge root systems absorb wave energy. They also slow incoming tides, so sediment settles out, and the mangroves build up the very land they grow on. When waves are strong, shorelines covered by mangroves erode less, or much more slowly, than bare ones. Studies show mangroves give coastal communities measurable economic protection against tropical storms. Keeping mangroves healthy is cheaper than building concrete walls along the shore, which can increase erosion in front of the wall and on neighbouring land. This protection is why mangroves are often targeted by conservation programmes, including national plans to protect wildlife ({{ref:nature-gov-043}}). Clearing them carries a hidden risk too. The sediments beneath trap heavy metals, and removing the trees can release that contamination into seawater.

entries.title: Forest ecology: studying the woods as a whole

definition.text: Forest ecology is the scientific study of the living things, patterns and processes found in forest ecosystems.

facts.text: A forest ecosystem is all the plants, animals and microbes of a woodland working together with its non-living physical surroundings.
Forest ecology usually studies whole populations, communities or ecosystems rather than single organisms.
Because trees vary so much in size and arrangement, forests are patchy, varied environments, and this variety supports great biodiversity.
Forests cover almost a third of all land, so forest ecology affects the whole biosphere and the human activities it supports.
Managing forests is called forestry, silviculture or forest management.
Machine learning now lets forest ecologists process larger and more complex data sets.

entries.text: Forests cover almost a third of all land, so what happens in them affects the whole biosphere and the human activities it supports. entries.title: What aquatic ecosystems do for us

definition.text: The environmental and human services aquatic ecosystems provide.

facts.text: They recycle nutrients, purify water, reduce floods, recharge groundwater and provide wildlife habitat.
Microorganisms, plankton, plants, invertebrates and fish help the water clean itself by breaking down organic matter and filtering water.
They support recreation and are very important to tourism, especially on coasts.
They also serve religious and educational uses, from pilgrimage to the Jordan River to ecological study of lakes.

entries.text: A river or lake partly cleans itself. Microorganisms, plankton, plants, invertebrates and fish break down organic matter and filter the water as they feed and grow. That is one of the functions of aquatic ecosystems: the environmental and human services they provide. They recycle nutrients, purify water, reduce floods, refill underground water and provide wildlife habitat. They also give people places to play. Water-based recreation is very important to tourism, especially on coasts. And they carry meaning beyond money, serving religious and educational uses, from pilgrimage to the Jordan River to the ecological study of lakes.

entries.title: Freshwater ecosystems: rich life in scarce water

definition.text: An aquatic ecosystem of low-salt waters such as lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, bogs and wetlands.

facts.text: Freshwater habitats can be classified by temperature, light penetration, nutrients and vegetation.
Still-water (lentic) and flowing-water (lotic) systems are the two classic freshwater types.
Many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate salt, and irrigation water can pick up harmful levels of it.
They differ from marine ecosystems, whose water is much saltier.
The three basic types are lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) and wetlands.
Freshwater ecosystems hold 41% of the world's known fish species.
Swamps, deltas and rivers make up 1% of Earth's surface, and land-based fresh waters produce about 1.5% of global net primary production.
Five broad threats are overexploitation, water pollution, changed water flows, habitat destruction and invasive species.

entries.text: Swamps, deltas and rivers make up just 1% of Earth's surface, yet freshwater ecosystems hold 41% of the world's known fish species. A freshwater ecosystem is an aquatic ecosystem of low-salt water: lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, bogs and wetlands. That sets it apart from the sea, whose water is much saltier. The three basic types are lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) and wetlands. Still and flowing water are the two classic forms. Scientists also classify freshwater habitats by temperature, light penetration, nutrients and vegetation. Land-based fresh waters produce about 1.5% of global net primary production, the plant growth left after plants meet their own energy needs. Many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate salt, and irrigation water can pick up harmful levels of it. Five broad threats stand out: overexploitation, water pollution, changed water flows, habitat destruction and invasive species.

entries.title: Marine ecosystems: the salty majority of the planet

definition.text: A salty-water aquatic ecosystem, the largest kind of aquatic ecosystem on Earth.

facts.text: Marine waters cover more than 70% of Earth's surface and hold more than 97% of its water and 90% of its habitable space.
Seawater averages a salinity of 35 parts per thousand, though it varies between ecosystems.
Marine ecosystems divide into zones by depth and shoreline, such as the open oceanic zone and the benthic zone on the seabed.
Seawater averages 35 parts per thousand salt, though salinity varies between marine ecosystems.
They range from coastal coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass meadows, kelp forests, estuaries, lagoons and salt marshes to the open ocean surface and the deep sea.
Pelagic systems regulate the global climate, feed the water cycle, maintain biodiversity, and provide food, energy, recreation and tourism.
Marine systems support billions of dollars' worth of fisheries, aquaculture, offshore oil and gas, and shipping.
Coastal capture fisheries from mangroves and coral reefs are estimated to be worth at least $34 billion per year.

entries.text: Marine waters cover more than 70% of Earth's surface and hold more than 97% of its water and 90% of its habitable space. A marine ecosystem is a salty-water aquatic ecosystem, the largest kind on Earth. Seawater averages a salinity, or saltiness, of 35 parts per thousand, though it varies between ecosystems. Scientists divide the sea into zones by depth and distance from shore, such as the open oceanic zone and the benthic zone on the seabed. The range is vast. Near the coast it includes reefs built by corals, mangroves, underwater meadows of sea plants, forests of giant seaweed, estuaries, lagoons and tidal marshes. Farther out lie the open ocean surface and the dark depths. Open-water systems regulate the global climate, feed the water cycle, maintain biodiversity, and provide food, energy, recreation and tourism. Marine systems also support billions of dollars' worth of fishing, fish farming, offshore oil and gas, and shipping. Coastal fishing from mangroves and reefs alone is estimated to be worth at least $34 billion per year.

entries.title: Estuaries: where rivers meet the sea

definition.text: A partly enclosed coastal water body where river or stream freshwater mixes with seawater to form brackish water.

facts.text: Estuaries are ecotones, transition zones where river and sea environments overlap.
Tides, waves and salt water from the sea combine with river flow and sediment to shape them.
Mixing of fresh and salt water makes them nutrient-rich and among the most productive natural habitats in the world.
Most formed in the Holocene, when rising seas flooded valleys about 10,000–12,000 years ago.
Salinity ranges from near-zero at the river's tidal limit to 3.4% at the mouth and shifts with tides and seasons, making life hard.
Of the thirty-two largest cities in the early 1990s, twenty-two stood on estuaries.

entries.text: Of the thirty-two largest cities in the early 1990s, twenty-two stood on estuaries. Most estuaries are young. They formed in the Holocene, when rising seas flooded river valleys about 10,000–12,000 years ago. The mixing of fresh and salt water makes them nutrient-rich and among the most productive natural habitats in the world. It also makes life hard. Salinity ranges from near zero at the river's tidal limit to 3.4% at the mouth, and it shifts with tides and seasons.

entries.title: The pelagic zone: life in the open ocean

definition.text: The pelagic zone is the water column of the open ocean, away from the shore and the seabed.

facts.text: Down the water column pressure rises, temperature and light fall, and salinity, oxygen and nutrients change.
The pelagic ecosystem is based on phytoplankton, which need sunlight and so live in the upper sunlit layer.
Biodiversity drops sharply below the sunlit layer as oxygen, food and light dwindle and pressure and cold increase.
Pelagic fish are often migratory forage fish such as herring and anchovies, plus the larger predators such as tuna and sharks that follow them.
About 80% of ocean carbon fixation happens in the open ocean, which covers more than 90% of the ocean area.

entries.text: About 80% of ocean carbon fixation, the capture of carbon into living matter, happens in the open ocean, which covers more than 90% of the ocean area. Its water column is the pelagic zone: the open ocean away from the shore and the seabed. Moving down it, pressure rises, temperature and light fall, and salinity, oxygen and nutrients change. The whole system rests on phytoplankton, which need sunlight and so live in the upper sunlit layer. Below that layer biodiversity drops sharply, as oxygen, food and light dwindle and pressure and cold increase. The fish of the open sea are often migratory forage fish, small schooling species such as herring and anchovies, along with the tuna and sharks that follow them.

entries.title: The deep sea: Earth's least explored biome

definition.text: The part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope.

facts.text: It is cold, dark and under high pressure, and is the least explored biome on Earth.
Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places.
Without light there is no photosynthesis, so life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents.
Its temperature is almost unchanging over long periods; no other habitat on Earth is so constant.
Salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout.
In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 10,911 m, the deepest known spot in any ocean.
Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence to hide their silhouettes.

entries.text: In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste, a deep-diving vessel, reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 10,911 m, the deepest known spot in any ocean. The deep sea is the part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope. It is cold, dark and under crushing pressure, and it is the least explored biome on Earth. Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places. No other habitat on Earth is so constant: its temperature barely changes over long periods, and salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout. Without light there is no photosynthesis. Life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents in the seafloor. Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence, light made by their own bodies, to hide their silhouettes.

The deep sea is the part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope. It is cold, dark and under crushing pressure, and it is the least explored biome on Earth. Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places. No other habitat on Earth is so constant: its temperature barely changes over long periods, and salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout. Without light there is no photosynthesis. Life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents in the seafloor. Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence, light made by their own bodies, to hide their silhouettes.

entries.title: Estuaries as nurseries, filters and buffers

definition.text: The benefits estuaries give people and nature, from fish nurseries and clean water to storm protection.

facts.text: Estuaries are nurseries for young fish and shellfish and sustain mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes that support fisheries.
Commercial fisheries depend on estuaries for approximately 68 percent of their catch by value.
Estuary wetlands filter sediment, nutrients and pollutants from upland runoff, improving water quality.
Salt marsh grasses stabilize shorelines, buffering storms and sea-level rise and protecting infrastructure.
They are migration corridors for fish and habitat for migratory birds, supporting ecotourism.

entries.title: Grassland carbon: stored out of sight

definition.text: Grasslands store carbon mostly underground, in their deep roots and the soil, rather than in above-ground plants.

facts.text: Above-ground carbon does not last long because of grazing, fire and plants dying back.
Soil carbon makes up about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems.
Carbon stocks are highest where rainfall is heaviest and fall as temperatures rise.
Soil disturbance, degradation, fire and erosion have caused large carbon losses, but good management can reverse them.
There is no agreement on how much carbon grasslands can store, partly because measurement methods differ and data are limited.

entries.text: Soil carbon makes up about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems. Grasslands store carbon mostly underground, in their deep roots and the soil, rather than in above-ground plants. There is a good reason. Carbon above ground does not last long, because grazing, fire and plants dying back keep removing it. Below ground it can stay put. Stocks are highest where rainfall is heaviest and fall as temperatures rise. Human activity has drained this store. Researchers have not agreed on how much carbon grasslands can store, partly because measurement methods differ and data are limited. Until they do, estimates of grassland carbon should be read as uncertain.

entries.title: Grassland degradation: the quiet loss of open land

definition.text: Grassland degradation is the loss or decline of grasslands, driven mainly by farming, mining and other human land use.

facts.text: Global losses from grassland degradation are estimated at over $7 billion per year.
Of 70 grassland ecoregions, 21 are less than 20% intact and only 14 keep at least 60%; 47 have declined since 2000.
Most of the world's grasslands have been converted to fields of corn, wheat and other crops.
Grasslands are vulnerable because they are misclassified, poorly protected and cultivated.
Non-native grasses are expected to outperform native ones as climate change makes many grasslands warmer and drier.

entries.title: Grassland restoration: bringing back the open range

definition.text: Grassland restoration aims to bring back degraded grasslands, though knowledge of the options is still limited.

facts.text: Only seven large, continuous grassland regions remain relatively intact on Earth.
Restoration costs vary widely and cost data are scarce.
Methods include prescribed fire, managing livestock and wild grazers, cutting trees and shrubs, controlling invasive species and reseeding native plants.
Success also needs policy recognition, standard indicators of degradation, research and data sharing.
The UN General Assembly proclaimed 2021–2030 the UN Decade on Restoration, led by UNEP and the FAO.
