entries.title: Lake layers and the autumn turnover

definition.text: In large lakes, summer warming splits the water into a warm upper layer and a cold lower layer that stay apart until autumn cooling mixes them again.

facts.text: The warm upper layer is the epilimnion, the cold bottom layer the hypolimnion, and the band of rapid temperature change between them the thermocline.
Water is densest at about 4 °C, which is why layers form as surface water warms.
Mixing to a uniform temperature is called lake turnover; in winter the layers form again in reverse beneath the ice.
Thermal stratification in larger lakes also affects how much oxygen each zone holds.

entries.text: Water is densest at about 4 °C, and that quirk splits big lakes in two each summer. As the surface warms, it forms a warm upper layer, the epilimnion, floating over a cold bottom layer, the hypolimnion. Between them lies the thermocline, a band of rapid temperature change. The layers stay apart until autumn cooling mixes the lake to a uniform temperature, a process called lake turnover. In winter the layers form again in reverse beneath the ice. This layering also affects how much oxygen each zone holds.

entries.title: What sets how much methane a wetland releases
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Controlling factors

definition.text: The factors that set how much methane a wetland releases, such as water table, temperature, soil and plants.

facts.text: Net release depends mainly on how much methane made by methanogens escapes before methanotrophs oxidize it.
Emissions are measured with eddy covariance, gradient or chamber flux methods.
Big methane releases have been seen after droughts lowered the water table, since gas moves more easily through soil than water.
Plentiful cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 give optimum conditions for methane production.

entries.text: Big bursts of methane have followed droughts that lowered a wetland's water table, because gas moves more easily through soil than through water. Many factors set how much methane a wetland releases, such as water table, temperature, soil and plants. The key balance is between two groups of microbes. Methanogens make methane; methanotrophs eat it. Net release depends mainly on how much methane escapes before it is oxidized. Plentiful cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 give optimum conditions for making methane. Scientists measure emissions with eddy covariance, gradient or chamber flux methods.

entries.title: Draining wetlands: less methane, or more
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Human development of wetlands

definition.text: How draining wetlands for development, housing and farming changes their methane emissions.

facts.text: Draining lowers the water table, which lets soil bacteria consume more methane.
But drainage ditches stay waterlogged and warm, and can emit large amounts of methane.
Lowered far enough, the water table can turn a wetland from a methane source into a methane sink.

entries.text: Draining a wetland can cut its methane, or not. Drainage for development, housing and farming lowers the water table, which lets soil bacteria consume more methane. But the drainage ditches themselves stay waterlogged and warm, and they can emit large amounts of methane. Lowered far enough, the water table can turn a wetland from a methane source into a methane sink.

entries.title: Three routes for methane to escape a wetland
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions from wetlands#Pathways of methane emission

definition.text: The three main routes by which wetland methane reaches the air: diffusion, transport through plant tissue, and bubbling (ebullition).

facts.text: Archaea produce methane by fermenting acetate, or by combining hydrogen with carbon dioxide.
When the water table is low, methane rising through soil passes a layer of methane-eating bacteria, which reduces emissions.
Plants with aerenchyma, porous air-carrying tissue, act as a shunt that lets methane skip that oxidizing layer.
In ebullition, methane pockets build in the soil until a bubble bursts, moving gas up too fast for microbes to consume it.

In ebullition, pockets of methane build in the soil until a bubble bursts, moving gas up too fast for microbes to consume it.

entries.title: What boreal ecosystems provide

definition.text: The services boreal ecosystems provide, led by timber and climate regulation through carbon cycling.

facts.text: Canada's boreal ecosystem is one of the world's largest carbon reservoirs and has high hydroelectric potential.
Boreal forests supply lumber and regulate water, soil and air quality.
Managing an ecosystem to maximize one service tends to reduce the supply of the others.

Managing an ecosystem to maximize one tends to reduce the supply of the others.

entries.title: Climate change in the boreal north

definition.text: How warming changes boreal ecosystems and how their changes feed back on the climate.

facts.text: Thawing permafrost, milder winters and hotter summers displace cold-adapted species, increase forest fires and can turn boreal areas into other ecosystem types.
Plants and animals are already shifting northward, though plant migration may lag warming by decades to a century.
Permafrost thaw, fire and insect outbreaks have led some models to suggest boreal forests are now a net carbon source rather than a sink.
Permafrost stores double the carbon now in the atmosphere, which thawing can release as greenhouse gases.

entries.title: The environmental troubles of growing cities

definition.text: Growing cities face pollution, loss of green space, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, urban heat and disease.

facts.text: Air pollution from vehicles, factories and power plants exceeds safe limits in many cities and causes respiratory and heart disease.
Forests, wetlands and grasslands are replaced by development, and losing green space lowers air and water quality, health and biodiversity.
Heavily urbanized areas have more invasive species than rural ones.
Urban heat islands make extreme heat more frequent, hitting the elderly and people without cooling hardest.

entries.title: Green and blue infrastructure: building nature into cities

definition.text: Green and blue infrastructure means building in ways that weave natural systems such as vegetation and water into human-made structures.

facts.text: Green infrastructure includes nature preserves and added vegetation such as vertical gardens.
Blue infrastructure includes stormwater management such as bioswales.
LEED-certified buildings report using 30% less energy and gaining economic and mental benefits from natural light.

entries.title: Studying city nature: a young and lopsided field

definition.text: Urban ecology, including the study of the services that urban nature provides, is a young field whose research is still limited and unevenly spread.

facts.text: A review found a strong bias toward the northern hemisphere, with case studies mostly in the United States and China.
A review of 217 papers found most urban ecosystem service studies were done in Europe, North America and China at city scale.
Assessments use biophysical models, GIS and valuation, but few findings have been turned into land use policy.
Researchers are building better tools to map services such as water regulation, air cooling and water purification.

entries.title: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: a health check for the planet

definition.text: A major United Nations-backed study of how people affect the environment, called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005.

facts.text: It popularized the term ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems.
More than 1300 authors from 95 countries contributed over four years.
It sorted ecosystem services into four groups: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, with supporting services underpinning the other three.
It found that in the past 50 years humans changed ecosystems faster and more widely than ever before, mainly to meet demand for food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel.
These changes brought gains in well-being and development, but at the cost of degrading many ecosystem services and deepening poverty for some groups.
Its bottom line was that human actions are depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations can no longer be taken for granted.
Gretchen Daily's book Nature's Services was described as a catalyst for the assessment.
The 2019 IPBES global assessment was the first UN report on the state of biodiversity since the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005.

sources.title: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: More than 1300 authors from 95 countries spent four years on one question: what are people doing to the ecosystems that keep them alive? Their answer was the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, a United Nations-backed study called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005. An earlier book, {{ref:nature-es-004}}, was described as a catalyst for it. The assessment popularized the term ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems. It sorted them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, with supporting services underpinning the other three. Its findings were sobering. In the past 50 years humans had changed ecosystems faster and more widely than ever before, mainly to meet demand for food, fresh water, timber, fiber and fuel. Those changes made many lives better and fueled development. They also degraded many ecosystem services and made some groups poorer. The bottom line was blunt. Human actions were depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations could no longer be taken for granted. The next UN report on the state of biodiversity did not come until the global assessment of {{ref:nature-gov-020}} in 2019.

Those changes made many lives better and fueled development. They also degraded many ecosystem services and made some groups poorer. The bottom line was blunt. Human actions were depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations could no longer be taken for granted. The next UN report on the state of biodiversity did not come until the global assessment of IPBES: the scientists' voice for biodiversity in 2019.

entries.title: Putting a price on nature's work

definition.text: The effort to express what ecosystem services are worth in economic terms, so that their value can be weighed in decisions.

facts.text: Many efforts translate scientific knowledge into economics, stating the results of choices in comparable units of impact on human well-being.
The idea is that, although people decide for many reasons, overall trends reveal a society's preferences, from which a service's value can be inferred.
A hard problem is that ecological information gathered at one scale of space and time may not apply at another.
The six main ways of valuing services in money are avoided cost, replacement cost, factor income, travel cost, hedonic pricing and contingent valuation.
Factor income counts how a service raises incomes, as when cleaner water increases a fishery's catch and fishers' earnings.
Salles (2011) argued that the total value of biodiversity is infinite, so debating nature's total worth is pointless because we cannot live without it.
As of 2012 many companies did not fully grasp how much they depend on ecosystems; most corporate environmental tools track impacts rather than dependence.
Tools that help businesses value services include the 2008 Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, the ARIES project from 2007 and InVEST from 2012.

entries.text: What is clean water worth to a fisher? The economics of ecosystem services tries to answer questions like that, expressing services in economic terms so their value can be weighed in decisions. It translates scientific knowledge into comparable units of impact on people's lives. People decide for many reasons, but overall trends reveal what a society prefers, and value can be inferred from them. There are six main ways to value services in money, from avoided cost and {{ref:nature-val-093}} to travel cost, hedonic pricing and {{ref:nature-val-085}}. One of them, factor income, counts how a service raises incomes, as when cleaner water increases the fish catch and fishers' earnings. Scale is a stubborn problem, because ecological data gathered at one place and time may not hold at another. Some reject the whole exercise. Salles (2011) argued that biodiversity's total value is infinite, since no one can live without it. As of 2012 many companies still did not grasp how much they depend on ecosystems.

entries.title: From Plato's springs to a scientific term

definition.text: How the idea that ecosystems provide services to people grew from ancient observations into a standard scientific term.

facts.text: Around 400 BC Plato understood that cutting down forests could cause soil erosion and dry up springs.
Modern ideas probably began in 1864, when Marsh challenged the belief that Earth's resources are unlimited by pointing to changing soil fertility around the Mediterranean.

In the late 1940s Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr, William Vogt and Aldo Leopold promoted the idea that people depend on the environment; in 1956 Paul Sears stressed ecosystems' role in processing wastes and recycling nutrients.
In 1970 Paul Ehrlich and Rosa Weigert warned that human activity could destroy the ecological systems on which the human species depends.
The term 'environmental services' appeared in a 1970 report listing insect pollination, fisheries, climate regulation and flood control; 'ecosystem services' later became the standard term.
E. F. Schumacher coined the term 'natural capital' in his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful.
In the 1990s Gretchen Daily's Nature's Services and Costanza and colleagues' first attempt to put a money value on ecosystem services became the two seminal works.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment popularised the idea in the early 2000s, and it has kept expanding to include social, economic and conservation goals.

entries.title: Protecting services when a price tag is not enough

definition.text: Efforts to protect ecosystem services through policy, institutions and management, which face large practical hurdles even where services have money values.

facts.text: Decision-makers must balance present and future human needs, often working from valid but incomplete information.
Existing laws are often seen as inadequate because they rest on human-health standards that do not match what protecting ecosystem health requires.
As of 2005, local to regional collective management was considered suitable for services such as crop pollination and for resources like water.
Since the 1990s, marketing ecosystem service protection has grown, with credits for activities such as protecting carbon sinks or restoring service providers.
Such schemes need clearly defined land rights, often missing in developing countries, and raise worries about inconsistent compensation.
Because protecting services often overlaps with protecting biodiversity, merging the two goals has been suggested.
As of 2018 the concept was not yet properly built into international and regional law, though Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets conserving, restoring and sustainably using ecosystem services.
Ecosystem services are estimated to add $125 trillion to $140 trillion to the economy each year; climate-driven biome shifts may cut them by 9% globally by 2100.

entries.text: Ecosystem services are estimated to add $125 trillion to $140 trillion to the economy each year. Even so, protecting them is hard. Decision-makers must balance present and future needs, often with valid but incomplete information. Existing laws are often seen as inadequate because they rest on human-health standards, which do not match what healthy ecosystems require. As of 2005, local to regional collective management was considered suitable for services such as pollinating crops and for resources like water. Since the 1990s, markets have grown that sell credits for protecting services, such as guarding carbon sinks or restoring service providers. These schemes need clearly defined rights to land, often missing in developing countries, and they raise worries about inconsistent compensation. Because protecting services often overlaps with protecting biodiversity, some suggest merging the two goals. Law lags behind. As of 2018 the concept was not properly built into international and regional law, though {{ref:nature-gov-030}} targets conserving, restoring and sustainably using ecosystem services. The stakes keep rising: climate-driven shifts in biomes may cut services by 9% globally by 2100.

entries.title: Tracing a product's footprint on nature's services

definition.text: Using life-cycle assessment, which tracks the environmental pressures of making products, to estimate how human activities change ecosystem services.

facts.text: Life-cycle assessment impact methods link pressures such as land-use change and eutrophication to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services.
A 2026 review found three main kinds of model: land-use impact models, extended ecosystem quality models and inventory-based models.
The models differ in which services and ecosystems they cover, their indicators, and whether they count service supply, demand or both, which limits comparison.
Freshwater and marine services remain poorly represented, so more consistent methodological guidance is needed.

entries.text: Every product leaves a trail of environmental pressures, from the land cleared to make it to the nutrients that wash into rivers. {{ref:nature-acct-050}} tracks those pressures. Its impact methods now link them, such as land-use change and eutrophication, to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services. A 2026 review found three main kinds of model: land-use impact models, extended ecosystem quality models and inventory-based models. They differ in the services, ecosystems and indicators they cover, and in whether they count supply, demand or both. That makes comparison hard. Freshwater and marine services remain poorly represented, so the field needs more consistent guidance.

entries.title: Nature's contributions to people: a broader name, or a new label?
entries.article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Nature's contributions to people

definition.text: The IPBES term for all the ways nature benefits people, adopted in place of 'nature's benefits to people'.

facts.text: The 5th IPBES Plenary in 2017 decided to use the concept in current and future assessments.
It was introduced to bring diverse worldviews, including indigenous and local knowledge, into biodiversity assessments.
Some scientists objected that the term was confusing and not significantly different from ecosystem services.

entries.contested_note: Scientists disagree whether the term adds anything beyond the ecosystem services concept.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: In 2017 the 5th plenary meeting of {{ref:nature-gov-020}} made a decision about words. Its assessments would now speak of nature's contributions to people: all the ways nature benefits people. The phrase replaced 'nature's benefits to people' from then on. The aim was to bring diverse worldviews, including indigenous and local knowledge, into biodiversity assessments. Not everyone was persuaded. Some scientists objected that the term was confusing and not significantly different from ecosystem services. Whether it adds anything beyond that older concept remains a genuine disagreement.

entries.title: Clean air, fresh water and the work behind them

definition.text: The economic benefits, in goods and services, that come from the natural workings of ecosystems.

facts.text: Ecological goods include clean air and plentiful fresh water; services include purifying air and water, breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, recharging groundwater and mitigating greenhouse gases.
They are a kind of public good.
They are being lost at an unsustainable rate, especially where land is converted from its natural state and loses its ecological functions.
A market can be created in which society demands these goods and services and public and private landowners supply them.
Paying farmers to set aside land marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.
Biodiversity underlies them, supporting services such as biological control and genetic resources.

entries.text: Clean air and plentiful fresh water are ecological goods. Purifying that air and water is a service, and so are breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, refilling underground water stores and mitigating greenhouse gases. Together they are the economic benefits of ecosystems' natural workings. Biodiversity underlies them all. {{ref:nature-hist-053}}'s original definition kept goods and services apart, but Costanza and colleagues and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment lumped both together as ecosystem services. They are a kind of public good. They are also being lost at an unsustainable rate, especially where land is converted from its natural state and loses its ecological functions. One remedy is to create a market, in which society demands these goods and services and public and private landowners supply them. Paying farmers to set land aside marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'. Regulation, land-care programs, eco-labeling, offset credits and tax rebates can secure supply too.

entries.title: When one service gains and another pays

definition.text: Cases where using or boosting one ecosystem service reduces others or harms some people, as opposed to synergies, where services rise together.

facts.text: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found many ways to conserve or enhance particular services that reduce negative trade-offs or create positive synergies with other services.
Nutrient cycling cannot simply be dialled to the best level: heavy fertilizer use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico.
In some areas there is a trade-off between farm production and restoring ecosystems.
Decisions about ecosystems create winners and losers, such as water moved from poor to rich users or a protected wetland that limits fishing rights.
Valuation can give extra weight to a service's irreplaceability or to bundled services that come together.
Tools such as InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs) and the Freshwater Health Index help managers assess trade-offs.
Landscape planning tries to exploit synergies and manage trade-offs among food production, conservation and livelihoods.

entries.text: Fertilizer spread on fields in the US Midwest grows abundant crops. Washed downriver, the same heavy fertilizer use has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico. This is an ecosystem service trade-off: using or boosting one service reduces others or harms some people. The opposite is a synergy, where services rise together. Nature's cycling of nutrients, it turns out, cannot simply be dialed to a best level. In some areas farm production competes with restoring ecosystems. Decisions also create winners and losers, as when water moves from poor to rich users or a protected wetland limits fishing rights. Yet the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment found many ways to enhance particular services while easing trade-offs or creating synergies. Valuation can give extra weight to a service that is irreplaceable, or to bundles of services that come together. Tools such as the Freshwater Health Index help managers weigh the options, and landscape planning tries to balance food production, conservation and livelihoods.

entries.title: Deciding what to do with the land

definition.text: Making land-use choices that affect ecosystem services, which means weighing ecology, technology, society and the economy together.

facts.text: These decisions are usually spatial, always have several objectives, and rest on uncertain data, models and estimates.
They must weigh all stakeholders' views, from regulators and developers to residents and NGOs; usually the best science combined with stakeholder values drives the process.
Studies have modelled stakeholders as agents, used Monte Carlo methods to capture uncertainty in landowner choices, and used Bayesian networks to combine uncertain science with stakeholder input.
Remote sensing can track the health and extent of land cover that provides services, helping planning, monitoring and communication between stakeholders.

Images of land taken from above can track the health and extent of the vegetation and ground cover that provide services.

entries.title: Who gains from nature's services

definition.text: The people who gain from a given ecosystem service, whether they live beside the ecosystem or feel its effects only indirectly.

facts.text: Some services, such as fresh water, food or beauty, directly affect nearby people's livelihoods, while others, such as climate or erosion regulation, affect people indirectly.
Ecological goods and services benefit all living things, including animals and plants, not humans alone.
In private payment deals, beneficiaries are expected to pay a price lower than the welfare gain they get from the service.
Paying landowners who supply services marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.

entries.text: Some services land right on the doorstep. Fresh water, food and beauty directly shape the livelihoods of people who live near an ecosystem. Humans are not the only ones, since ecological goods and services benefit all living things, animals and plants included. In private payment deals, beneficiaries are expected to pay less than the welfare gain the service gives them. Paying landowners who supply services marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'.

entries.title: Nature's Services: the 1997 book that framed a field

It and Costanza and colleagues' global valuation were the two seminal 1990s works on ecosystem services.
It served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

entries.title: Nutrient cycles: nature's recycling system

definition.text: A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter: nature's recycling system.

facts.text: Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is not reused, while mineral nutrients move in cycles.
The cycles include the carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen cycles, among others.
Recycling in nature is controlled largely by decomposition, and food webs full of different species do the work.
Natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human well-being.
Some ecosystems run a nutrient debt and act as sinks while others have a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology.
Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem.
In 1749 Carl Linnaeus described nature's recycling in his book Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'.

entries.text: In 1749 Carl Linnaeus wrote about nature's recycling in a book called Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'. The phrase fits. A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter. Energy and matter behave very differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is never reused, while mineral nutrients go round and round. The cycles include carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen, among others. Decomposition, the breakdown of dead matter, largely controls the recycling, and food webs full of different species do the work. Not every ecosystem balances its books. Some run a nutrient debt and act as sinks, while others carry a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology. Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same thing, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem. For people, this natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human welfare, a supporting service on which much else depends.

entries.title: Pollination: the courier service behind seeds

definition.text: Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, which lets the plant make seeds.

facts.text: Pollen can be carried by animals such as bees, beetles, butterflies, birds and bats, or by wind and water.
Between 100,000 and 200,000 animal species pollinate the world's 250,000 species of flowering plant, most of them insects.
About 80% of flowering plants rely on living pollinators.
Farms closer to natural habitat get more pollinator visits and higher crop yields.
Three quarters of the plant species that feed the world need pollinators, and insect-pollinated crops are worth over 200 billion dollars.
Animal pollination keeps plants genetically varied because it allows cross-breeding rather than self-breeding.

entries.text: Somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 animal species work as couriers for the world's 250,000 species of flowering plant, and most of them are insects. Their cargo is pollen. About 80% of flowering plants rely on living pollinators. Animal couriers bring a bonus: they allow cross-breeding rather than self-breeding, which keeps plants genetically varied. Farms closer to natural habitat get more pollinator visits and higher crop yields, a regulating service delivered free by the wild land next door.

entries.title: Food security: enough to eat, every day

definition.text: Food security means having reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food.

facts.text: The 1996 World Food Summit defined it as all people at all times having physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life.
Close to 12% of the world's people, 928 million, were severely food insecure in 2020, 148 million more than in 2019.
Hunger is often caused not by a lack of food but by people being unable to reach the food that exists, usually because of poverty.
Intensive farming can trap land in a cycle of falling soil fertility and falling yields; deforestation and overgrazing also degrade land.
Overfishing poses serious risks to food security.
Losing crop diversity threatens food security because people rely on fewer and fewer varieties of fewer crop species.
Pollinator decline could endanger food security as well as unbalance ecosystems.

entries.text: In 2020 close to 12% of the world's people, 928 million, were severely food insecure, 148 million more than a year earlier. Food security means reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food. The 1996 World Food Summit put it more fully. It usually stems not from a lack of food but from people being unable to reach the food that exists, most often because they are poor. Nature's services sit under the whole system, and they are fraying. Farming land too hard can trap land in a cycle of falling soil fertility and falling yields, while deforestation and overgrazing degrade land too. Taking too many fish poses serious risks. People rely on fewer and fewer varieties of fewer crop species, and the decline of pollinators could endanger food supplies as well as unbalance ecosystems.

entries.title: Groundwater recharge: refilling the hidden reservoirs

definition.text: Groundwater recharge is the downward movement of water from the surface into underground water stores.

facts.text: Recharge is the main way water enters an aquifer, the underground layer that holds groundwater.
It happens naturally through rain and snowmelt, and artificially when people route rainwater or reclaimed water underground.
Paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, increasing runoff and reducing recharge, while tree roots help water soak in.
Wetlands help hold up the water table; small wetlands can recharge up to 20% of their volume per season.
For groundwater use to be sustainable, the long-run rate of pumping from an aquifer should not exceed the rate it is recharged.
People move about 24,000 km3 of water a year, about double the world's yearly groundwater recharge.
Recharge rates are hard to measure because evaporation, plant transpiration and infiltration must be estimated first.
Recharge happens naturally through the water cycle and artificially when rainwater or reclaimed water is routed underground.

entries.text: People move about 24,000 km3 of water a year, roughly double the amount that seeps back into the ground worldwide. That seeping is recharge: the downward movement of water from the surface into underground stores. It is the main way water enters an {{ref:nature-res-112}}, the underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water. Recharge happens naturally through the water cycle, as rain and snowmelt soak in. It also happens artificially, when people route rainwater or reclaimed water underground. What covers the ground makes a big difference. Tree roots help water soak in, while paving, development and logging can strip topsoil, increasing runoff and reducing recharge. Wetlands help hold up the water table, and small wetlands can recharge up to 20% of their volume per season. The rule for sustainable use is simple: over the long run, pumping from such a store should not exceed its recharge. Applying it is harder, because recharge is difficult to measure. Evaporation, water given off by plants and water soaking into soil must all be estimated first.

entries.title: Storm surge: when the sea walks inland

definition.text: A storm surge is a coastal flood of rising seawater pushed ashore by a storm, usually a low-pressure system such as a tropical cyclone.

facts.text: It is measured as the rise in water above the normal tide, not counting waves, and is driven mainly by strong winds pushing water toward the coast.
Low air pressure raises sea level by about 10 mm for every millibar of pressure drop.
The deadliest surge on record, from the 1970 Bhola cyclone, killed up to 500,000 people around the Bay of Bengal.
Surges damage roads and buildings and also harm soil fertility, push saltwater inland and spread contaminants.
With stronger extreme weather and rising seas from climate change, surges are expected to pose greater risks to coastal people.
Tidal marshes protect coastal habitat from storm surge and flooding.

entries.text: In 1970 the Bhola cyclone drove a wall of seawater across the Bay of Bengal, killing up to 500,000 people, the deadliest surge on record. It is measured as the rise above the normal tide, not counting waves. Strong winds piling water toward the coast do most of the work. The damage outlasts the flood: surges wreck roads and buildings, harm soil fertility, push saltwater inland and spread contaminants. With stronger extreme weather and rising seas from climate change, surges are expected to threaten coastal people more. Nature offers a buffer. Tidal marshes protect coastal habitat from storm surge and flooding.

entries.title: Biological pest control: hiring a pest's enemies

definition.text: Biological pest control is the use of living organisms to control pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms.

facts.text: It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and can be part of integrated pest management.
The first known record comes from China around 304 AD, where citrus growers bought nests of predatory ants to protect their fruit.
Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s, when state entomologists started handing out parasitoids to fight crop pests.
Agents include predators such as lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses.
Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial control agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops.
Biological control can reduce the economic losses caused by pests, disease carriers and invasive species.
Using natural enemies instead of pesticides can also cut agricultural pollution.

entries.text: Around 304 AD, citrus growers in China bought nests of predatory ants to guard their fruit, the first known record of biological pest control. The idea is to use living organisms against pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms. It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and it can form part of {{ref:nature-nbs-283}}. Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s. State entomologists started handing out parasitoids, insects whose young develop inside or on a host and kill it. Today's agents include lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses. Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops. The payoff is economic and ecological. Biological control can cut losses from pests, disease carriers and invasive species, and natural enemies used instead of pesticides mean less farm pollution.

entries.title: Water purification: nature's filter and the engineer's

definition.text: Water purification is the removal of unwanted chemicals, germs, suspended solids and gases from water so it is fit for a given use.

facts.text: Purifying water is a regulating ecosystem service: New York City restored its polluted Catskill Watershed rather than rely only on treatment when its water fell below EPA standards.
Soil and rock layers naturally filter groundwater so well that it often needs only a disinfectant added.
In bank filtration, natural riverbank sediments give the first stage of cleaning, and slow sand filters work through biological processes rather than straining.
Engineered treatment uses physical steps such as filtration and sedimentation, chemical steps such as chlorination, and biological steps.
A diverse aquatic plant community helps purify water for human use.
A 2007 WHO report said 1.1 billion people lacked an improved drinking water supply and 1.8 million died from diarrhoeal disease each year.

entries.title: Microclimates: the weather near the ground

definition.text: A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from the surrounding area.

facts.text: A microclimate can be anything from a few meters to at most a few kilometers across.
Climate is described at nested scales: macroclimates span hundreds to thousands of kilometers, mesoclimates tens to hundreds, and microclimates far less.
Microclimates are shaped by terrain, soil, vegetation, water and human-made features, which change sunlight, wind, heat and moisture near the surface.
A wooded park stays different from a nearby industrial park because leaves absorb light and heat that roofs and parking lots radiate back into the air.
Farmers manage microclimates with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation to buffer crops from heat and drought, which matters more as climate extremes grow.
A clearing wider than twice the height of nearby trees loses the woodland's moderating effect on the microclimate.
Habitat fragmentation can change microclimates locally and regionally, affecting biodiversity.

entries.text: Step from a parking lot into a wooded park and the air changes. A microclimate is the local set of air, soil and water conditions near the ground that differs measurably from its surroundings. It spans a few meters to at most a few kilometers, far smaller than mesoclimates of tens to hundreds of kilometers or macroclimates of hundreds to thousands. Terrain, soil, vegetation, water and buildings shape it by changing sunlight, wind, heat and moisture near the surface. A wooded park stays different from a nearby industrial park because leaves absorb light and heat that roofs and pavement radiate back into the air. That moderating effect has limits: a clearing wider than twice the height of nearby trees loses it. Farmers manage microclimates with irrigation, shade, rows of trees against the wind and plants to shield crops from heat and drought, which matters more as climate extremes grow. Habitat fragmentation can alter microclimates and the biodiversity they support.

entries.title: Bioprospecting: searching living things for the next drug

definition.text: Bioprospecting is the search through living things for molecules and genetic information that could become valuable products such as drugs, cosmetics or farm inputs.

facts.text: Almost one third of small-molecule drugs approved by the US FDA between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them.
Many antibiotics in use today came from bioprospecting, such as streptomycin from a soil bacterium; the antimalarial artemisinin came from a plant.
Natural molecules are more structurally complex than synthetic ones, so they act on biological targets more precisely.
Researchers now look beyond plants and soil microbes to seas, caves, polar regions and extremophiles.
Over-harvesting desirable species for bioprospecting can push them toward extinction.
The UN and others promote bioprospecting as ethical development based on protecting biodiversity, but critics say conservation areas shut local people out of common lands.

entries.title: Medicinal plants: a pharmacy grown for defense

definition.text: Medicinal plants are plants used to keep people healthy or treat illness, in traditional medicine since prehistoric times and in modern medicine today.

facts.text: Plants make hundreds of chemicals to defend themselves against insects, fungi and grazing animals, and these are the basis of their use as drugs.
The Food and Agriculture Organization estimated in 2002 that over 50,000 medicinal plants are used worldwide.
Around a quarter of drugs prescribed in modern medicine come from medicinal plants.
By one 2023 estimate the global market was US$68 billion a year, growing 10–20% annually; China and India lead production and export.
In much of the rural developing world, traditional herbal medicine is people's only source of health care.
Wild-harvested medicinal plants are threatened by climate change, habitat loss and over-collection to meet rising demand.
As of 2015 most plant-based products had not been tested for safety and effectiveness, and being natural does not make a product safe.

conflicts.text: Kew Gardens estimated in 2016 that 17,810 plant species have a medicinal use.
conflicts.note: A more conservative count than the FAO's 2002 figure of over 50,000.

entries.title: Soil formation: the slowest factory on Earth

definition.text: Soil formation, or pedogenesis, is the slow making of soil, shaped by place, environment and history.

facts.text: It starts with the weathering of fresh parent material; microbes feed on the released nutrients and leave residues that become humus.
Over time soil develops distinct layers called horizons, differing in colour, structure, texture and chemistry.
In Sicily's Mediterranean climate, weathering makes new soil at about 1/10 mm per year.
It takes decades to several thousand years for a soil to develop a profile.
Erosion from farm fields is estimated at 11 to 20 times the soil formation rate with no-till farming, and over 100 times with conventional tillage.
Soil formation is classed as a supporting ecosystem service, and food systems depend on it.
Vasily Dokuchaev, regarded as the father of soil science, showed in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.

entries.title: Pollinator decline: how worried should anyone be?

definition.text: Pollinator decline is the drop in numbers of insect and other animal pollinators in many ecosystems around the world, recorded since the end of the 20th century.

facts.text: Evidence of falling wild pollinator numbers is strongest in Europe and North America, with similar findings from South America, China and Japan.
Managed honey bee colonies fell 25% in Europe (1985–2005) and 59% in North America (1947–2005), but global stocks rose thanks to China and Argentina.
While managed hives grew by 45%, demand for animal-pollinated crops tripled, showing the risk of relying on domesticated bees.
A 2021 century-long study found the number of bee species recorded in 2006–2015 was a quarter lower than before 1990.
About 87.5% of flowering plant species and 60% of crop species use animal pollinators, including most fruits.
Without animal pollination, US farm output is expected to fall by 3 to 8%.
In 2009 a study valued the 100 crops that need pollinators at €153 billion worldwide.
So far the theorised decline has not cut food production: yields of animal-pollinated and other crops have risen at the same rate.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on how serious the decline is: some warn of falling food supplies, while others note crop yields have not yet suffered.

entries.title: Bees for hire: the market in pollination

definition.text: Beekeepers rent their honeybee colonies to farmers for a fee, turning crop pollination into a service sold in a market.

facts.text: Honeybees do most pollination of the crops people eat, giving between $235 and $577 billion of benefits to global food production.
As of 2016, pollination rentals made up 41% of an average US beekeeper's revenue, the largest share of their income.
Pollination by beekeepers' bees is a positive externality that the market has managed to pay for.
The almond industry uses up to 82% of the pollination market, and each February around 60% of US bee colonies are moved to California's Central Valley.
Mixing hives spreads disease to wild bees too, a negative externality that reduces biodiversity.
In 2016 an almond colony earned $165 in rent, about three times other crops, yet once upkeep is counted almond pollination is barely profitable.

entries.title: Firewood: the oldest fuel

definition.text: Firewood is any wood used for fuel, usually as recognizable logs or branches rather than processed products such as pellets.

facts.text: Firewood is a renewable resource, but local demand can quickly outrun how fast trees regrow.
For most of human history firewood was the main fuel, and the right to gather it was a valued part of many medieval leases.
Along with clearing land for farming, gathering firewood is a cause of deforestation, and its smoke causes breathing problems.
Moving firewood long distances can spread tree pests, diseases and invasive species.

entries.title: The four pillars of food security

definition.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars: whether food is available, whether people can get it, how well they use it, and whether this stays stable over time.

facts.text: Availability is the supply of food through production, distribution and exchange.
Access covers whether food is affordable and how it is shared out, along with people's preferences.
Stability is the ability to get food over time; food insecurity can be passing, seasonal or chronic.
Sustainability, a further pillar, asks that food systems feed people now without undermining the bases for feeding future generations.

entries.title: Can anything be recycled forever?

definition.text: A dispute over whether matter can be recycled completely, with 100% of waste rebuilt into new material without end.

facts.text: Howard T. Odum held that living systems can gather chemical elements without limit as long as energy, such as sunlight, is available.
In 1979 Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen proposed a 'fourth law' of entropy saying complete recycling is impossible.
The fourth law has been rejected in light of observed ecological recycling, though some authors say complete recycling is impossible for technological waste.

entries.contested_note: Georgescu-Roegen said complete recycling is impossible; others reject this for ecosystems but some accept it for technological waste.

Complete recycling would rebuild 100% of waste into new material, forever. {{ref:nature-hist-063}} disagreed. Living systems, he held, can gather chemical elements without limit while energy such as sunlight lasts. The fourth law has been rejected in light of observed recycling in ecosystems. Some authors still say complete recycling is impossible for technological waste, so the dispute lives on there.

entries.title: Factories versus food webs: two kinds of recycling

definition.text: Recycling in human industry differs from recycling in ecosystems in scale, complexity and organization.

facts.text: Industrial recycling relies on people and technology rather than food webs to turn waste back into marketable goods.
Only 7% of all plastic waste is recycled by industry; the other 93% is presumably absorbed by natural recycling systems.
Many human 'technoecosystems' compete with or feed off natural ecosystems.

entries.title: Managed aquifer recharge: putting water back

definition.text: Managed aquifer recharge means deliberately putting water back into aquifers, for example through altered streambeds, bank filtration, water spreading or recharge wells.

facts.text: A facility in Orange County, California cleans and injects 100 million gallons a day, or 90 billion gallons a year.
In India, where farmers' over-pumping has depleted groundwater, the government funded dug-well recharge projects in 100 districts in 2007.

entries.title: Animals or wind: two ways to move pollen

definition.text: Biotic pollination uses living animals to carry pollen, while abiotic pollination relies on wind, water or rain.

facts.text: Some 98% of abiotic pollination is by wind.
Abiotic pollination lets a plant spend its energy on pollen rather than on flowers and nectar to attract animals.
Some plants use both kinds, such as an orchid pollinated by rain or butterflies depending on conditions.

entries.title: What farming owes to pollinators

definition.text: Many farm crops depend on pollinators, while the main staple grains such as wheat, maize and rice are pollinated by wind or by themselves.

facts.text: Among the top 15 crops in 2013, slightly over 10% of the human plant diet (211 of 1916 kcal per person per day) depended on insect pollination.
Managed US beehives fell from close to 6 million after WWII to under 2.5 million, while bee-pollinated crop area grew over 300%.
About one million hives, nearly half of US honey bees, are trucked to California almond orchards each spring.

entries.title: Holding back the sea: defenses against storm surge

definition.text: Communities can adapt to storm surges with hard infrastructure such as flood barriers, soft infrastructure such as dunes or mangroves, better building and social measures.

facts.text: Storm-surge barriers, built after the North Sea flood of 1953, stay open for shipping but close when a surge threatens.
Major barriers include the Dutch Delta Works, the Thames Barrier and the Saint Petersburg Dam.
Warnings, education and local evacuation plans reduce the toll on people.

entries.title: How seeds travel: on their own or by hitchhiking

definition.text: Seed dispersal is split into autochory, where the plant moves its own seeds, and allochory, where an outside agent carries them.

facts.text: Self-dispersal uses gravity or exploding fruit, which limits how far seeds go; the dynamite tree can throw seeds up to 100 meters.
Outside agents include wind, water and animals; seeds can ride on animals' fur or pass through their guts.
Humans move seeds on clothes (up to 250 m), shoes (up to 5 km) and cars (sometimes over 100 km).

entries.title: Three ways to deploy natural enemies

definition.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies: importation, augmentation and conservation of natural enemies.

facts.text: Importation, or classical control, brings a pest's natural enemies into a new place where they did not live before.
Augmentation releases extra natural enemies: a few at intervals to prevent outbreaks (inoculative), or many at once to knock a pest down fast (inundative).
Early importations were often unofficial, and some introduced species became serious pests themselves.
Augmentative control adds more predators, parasitoids or microbes when needed.

entries.title: Conservation biological control: feeding the farmer's allies

definition.text: Conservation biological control protects and encourages the natural enemies of pests that already live in an area.

facts.text: Nectar plants grown on rice field borders cut planthopper pests 10- to 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and gained 5% in yield.
Changing cropping systems to favour natural enemies is called habitat manipulation, for example with hedgerows, shelterbelts or beetle banks.
A meter-wide strip of tussock grass in the middle of English fields let aphid predators overwinter there and improved control.

entries.title: When the cure becomes the pest

definition.text: An introduced control agent can harm biodiversity by attacking native species as well as the pest it was meant for.

facts.text: Vertebrates tend to eat many kinds of food and seldom make good control agents; many classic failures involve them.
Cane toads released in Australia in 1935 could not reach the cane beetles, spread fast instead and harmed native frogs and predators.

entries.title: Nursery habitats: where the next generation of fish grows up

definition.text: A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population per unit area than other places they use.

facts.text: Mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass are typical nursery habitats for many marine species.
Seagrass meadows give nursery habitat to over a fifth of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species.
Losing nursery habitats can mean fewer young reaching adulthood, shrinking populations needed for both biodiversity and fishing.
Juvenile density alone is not enough evidence; the best measure is how much biomass moves from juvenile to adult populations.

entries.title: Bioprospecting contracts: who shares the profits

definition.text: Bioprospecting contracts set the rules for sharing benefits between researchers and the countries whose genetic resources they use.

facts.text: The Convention on Biological Diversity, in force from 1993, gave countries the right to control access to their genetic resources, creating this branch of law.
The contracts rest on prior informed consent and compensation and can bring royalties to poorer countries, yet not every knowledge holder is consulted or paid.
Biodiverse countries expect a share of the benefits rather than letting the discoverer keep them privately.

entries.title: CLORPT: the five factors that make a soil

definition.text: Five classic factors shape every soil: climate, organisms, relief (topography), parent material and time, remembered as CLORPT.

facts.text: Climate is the dominant factor, and soils show the traits of the climate zone where they form.
Steep slopes lose soil quickly to erosion, so soils there are shallower and less developed than on nearby level ground.
Plants hold soil against erosion and build humus, while animals break down plant matter and mix the soil.
Soil is the most species-rich ecosystem on Earth, mostly microbes, many still undescribed.

entries.title: Jenny's equation: a soil as a sum of its causes

definition.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 state equation describes a soil as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, with room for more factors.

facts.text: Unlike Dokuchaev's earlier equation, it treats time as a factor, adds relief and leaves the list open.
It is mostly solved empirically, by varying one factor while holding the others constant, giving models such as climofunctions and chronofunctions.
Soil surveyors worldwide use it as a checklist of what shapes a region's soils.

entries.title: Pollination management: bringing the bees to the field

definition.text: Pollination management is the farming practice of ensuring or improving a crop's pollination by managing pollinators, pollen-supplying plants and conditions.

facts.text: Besides honey bees, growers use blue orchard bees, bumblebees, hand pollination and even machines.
Too few pollinators can limit yield, called pollination limitation; it fell by 50% between 1950 and the 2010s, mainly because fields were supplied with managed pollinators.
Bigger monoculture fields make management more important; the blue orchard bee visits only the target tree and is 100 times more efficient per bee than a honeybee.
A 1950s grower of ten acres of watermelons had wild bees enough, but today's 200-acre grower must bring hives to the field.

entries.title: What is killing the pollinators

definition.text: Proposed causes of pollinator decline include pesticides, parasites and diseases, habitat destruction, climate change, market forces and competition with invasive species.

facts.text: Synthetic pesticides, above all neonicotinoids, are a primary driver, damaging the nerves and immune systems of bees and other pollinators.
Air pollution breaks down flower scents so they travel shorter distances, forcing pollinators to fly farther to find flowers.
Climate change can make bees emerge when no plants are flowering.
A 2021 global assessment said policy should focus on land-cover change, land management and pesticides.

entries.title: Pollinators and the vitamins on your plate

definition.text: Losing pollinators could cut the supply of vitamins and other nutrients that come mainly from animal-pollinated crops.

facts.text: An estimated 70% of dietary vitamin A and 55% of folate worldwide come from animal-pollinated crops.
If all pollinators died off, a 2015 model found 71 million more people in low-income countries would lack vitamin A.
The same model predicted 1.42 million extra deaths a year, or 700,000 if half of pollinators were lost.

entries.title: Mangroves: a coastal forest that pays many ways

definition.text: Mangrove forests are a form of natural capital that yields many goods and services to coasts, local communities and society at large.

facts.text: Some mangrove outputs, such as timber, are traded in ordinary markets, where their value shows up as a price.
Mangroves give nursery habitat to many species, including commercial fish and crustaceans, helping keep local fish and shellfish numbers up.
An estimated 75 percent of the prawns and fish caught commercially in Queensland, Australia, depend on mangroves for part of their life cycle.
Mangroves help keep water clean by cycling nutrients, and they slow water so sediment settles out.
Mangrove forests take carbon from the air and store it in their biomass and waterlogged soils, adding to coastal blue carbon stocks.
At least 35 percent of the world's mangroves were destroyed in a single decade, faster than tropical rainforests disappeared.
Economic arguments weigh most in mangrove conservation, yet the true economic value of mangroves is hard to measure and key ecological functions are undervalued.

entries.title: Climate regulation: nature's thermostat

definition.text: Climate regulation is the regulating ecosystem service by which nature dampens environmental change, for example by storing carbon and moderating local temperatures.

facts.text: A 1970 report that introduced the term 'environmental services' already listed climate regulation alongside pollination, fisheries and flood control.
Tropical rainforests are crucial for global climate regulation through carbon sequestration.
Mangroves regulate climate by sequestering carbon, and coastal seas also provide climate regulation.
Urban trees help regulate microclimate and take up carbon dioxide.
Climate regulation is among the services considered to have no viable substitute.
Regime shifts, such as forest turning into savanna or faster summer loss of Arctic ice, can weaken climate regulation.
Gross ecosystem product puts a money value on regulating services such as climate regulation.

entries.title: Mangroves as water filters
entries.article: Ecological values of mangroves#Improving coastal water quality

definition.text: Mangroves keep coastal water clean by trapping, removing and recycling nutrients, pollutants and particles from land before they reach reefs and seagrass.

facts.text: Mangrove roots slow the water so sediment settles, and toxins and nutrients bound to the sediment are removed with it.
Because building a wastewater treatment plant is costly, mangroves are often chosen to receive effluent, and purpose-built mangrove wetlands now treat sewage and aquaculture waste.
Runoff is filtered first by coastal forests, then mangroves, then seagrass beds before reaching coral reefs, which need these buffers to avoid algal overgrowth.

entries.title: Watershed services: what a healthy catchment gives

definition.text: Watershed (hydrological) services are the water-related benefits a healthy catchment gives, such as less soil erosion, lower landslide risk and milder floods and droughts.

facts.text: Watershed services are one of the three main kinds of service sold in payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes, with climate mitigation and biodiversity.
Costa Rica's payment scheme explicitly recognized hydrological services among its four environmental services.
Growing markets for hydrological services may reward forests managed with low-impact logging.

entries.title: Well-being: how well a life is going

definition.text: What is good for a person in itself: a measure of how well their life is going for them.

facts.text: It is also called welfare or quality of life.
Broadly it covers the balance of all good and bad aspects of a life; narrowly it means only the good, in contrast to ill-being.
Money and medicine can contribute to well-being as causes but are not themselves forms of it.
There is wide agreement that positive emotions, achievements, relationships and health usually contribute to it.
It can be assessed for an individual or for a whole community, whose well-being includes economic, social, environmental and cultural aspects.
Welfare economics studies how economic activity affects it, using metrics such as income distribution, GDP and consumer surplus to compare policies.
Defenders of anthropocentrism argue a healthy environment is needed for human well-being rather than for its own sake.
Its study began in antiquity as discussions of how to live a good life.

entries.title: Recreation: the human need to play

definition.text: Leisure activity done for enjoyment, amusement or pleasure.

facts.text: The need to do something for recreation is treated as a basic part of human biology and psychology.
It needs leisure: time free from work, sleep, daily chores and social duties.
Affluence, population trends and the growing commercial supply of recreation have raised its role in modern life.
Parks and beaches are key venues, and tourism has recognised that many visitors come specifically for recreation.
Recreation and tourism are among the cultural services ecosystems provide, alongside spiritual fulfilment.
When biodiversity is lost, ecosystems can no longer offer the same areas for recreation and tourism.
Leisure is a human right under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

entries.title: Outdoor recreation: a $696.7 billion slice of the economy

definition.text: Leisure activity done outdoors, usually in natural settings.

facts.text: Activities range from fishing, hunting and walking to hiking, camping, climbing, kayaking and skiing.
People pursue it for exercise, general wellbeing and spiritual renewal, with less stress on competition than organised sport.
It often takes place in thinly populated areas with mountains, lakes, rivers and scenic views.
In 2024 outdoor recreation accounted for $696.7 billion of value added, 2.4 percent of US GDP, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis.
University outdoor programs have been shown to help students' wellbeing and stress levels.
Forest managers count outdoor recreation among the objectives forests serve, alongside timber, conservation and hunting.

entries.title: Biophilia: an inborn love of living things?

definition.text: The idea that humans have an inborn urge to seek connection with nature and other living things.

facts.text: Edward O. Wilson introduced and popularised it in his 1984 book Biophilia; Erich Fromm had first used the word.
It has been developed within evolutionary psychology: ancestors with closer ties to nature may have found food, water and shelter more easily.
Research suggests modern cities are poorly suited to minds that evolved in natural settings.
It is used to explain why people keep plants, care for animals and sometimes risk their lives to save them.
Conservationists worry that losing this connection could breed disregard for wild species and speed ecosystem loss, so reconnecting people with nature has become a conservation goal.
It inspires biophilic cities with more green space, which can also serve as wildlife corridors.
Fromm treated biophilia as a biologically normal instinct, and the term has since spread to many fields of study.
Its opposite, biophobia, is an inherited fear of nature and animals, such as fear of snakes and spiders.

entries.title: Subjective well-being: asking people how happy they are

definition.text: Well-being, or happiness, as judged by the people whose lives are being assessed rather than from an outside, objective view.

facts.text: Ed Diener defined it by three signs: frequent positive feelings, infrequent negative feelings, and judgments such as life satisfaction.
Its three components are affect (emotions and moods), life satisfaction (judgments about one's life) and eudaimonia (a sense of meaning and purpose).
It is usually measured by self-report, often with questionnaires on life satisfaction, the most common measure in the field.
Its definitions usually leave out objective conditions such as material wealth or health, although these can influence ratings.
Top-down theories trace it to stable personality, while bottom-up theories see happiness built from happy experiences and fulfilled basic needs.
Quality of social connections affects it much more strongly than their number.
Nature relatedness, a person's felt connection with nature, has been found to directly affect it, raising affect and life satisfaction.
Happiness economics often uses it to appraise the wellbeing of whole populations.

entries.title: The aesthetics of nature: why landscapes move people

definition.text: The branch of philosophy that studies natural things for their beauty and other aesthetic qualities.

facts.text: It behaves like a personality trait, staying fairly stable over time and across situations, yet it can grow after time spent in nature.

entries.title: Sustainable tourism: can travel last?

definition.text: Tourism that attends to its economic, social and environmental effects while improving visitors' experiences and meeting the needs of host communities.

facts.text: It grew out of sustainable development, and the term is open to varied interpretations.
As tourism is one of the world's largest and fastest-growing industries, its growth will put heavy stress on remaining biodiverse habitats and Indigenous cultures.
Local communities can gain jobs, economic development and infrastructure from it.
Carrying capacity is a key consideration in ecologically sensitive or remote areas.
Tourism's dependence on fossil fuels ties sustainable tourism closely to sustainable transport and climate change.
The Global Sustainable Tourism Council's GSTC Criteria serve as the international standard for certifying sustainable tourism businesses.
Critics call it an oxymoron because tourism is extractive and cannot continue indefinitely.
The movement emerged after the environmental awareness of the 1960s and 1970s amid growing mass tourism.

entries.title: Ecotourism: travel that is supposed to help

definition.text: Travel to natural places that aims to do little harm and to support conservation and environmental education.

facts.text: Some definitions also require that it pays its way for the host community or makes conservation financially possible.
It is treated as one part of the wider field of sustainable tourism, and it differs from plain nature tourism by aiming to build tourists' appreciation of habitats and local culture.
Its possible benefits include visitor spending and jobs, money to run and expand protected areas, and a reason to protect or restore natural land.
In South Africa, 70% of the money national parks make comes straight from tourism.
Visitors can still damage protected areas, raise local rents and property values, and bring health risks to people and wildlife.
Most ecotourism businesses are owned by foreign investors, so most profits leave the area instead of going back into the local economy or conservation.
Like most long-distance travel, it often depends on flying, which adds to climate change, and few operators have a net-positive effect on the environment.
Weak regulation lets damaging operations such as underwater hotels and helicopter tours call themselves ecotourism, a form of greenwashing.

entries.title: Three theories of what makes a life go well

definition.text: The main philosophical accounts of what well-being consists of: hedonism, desire theories and objective list theories.

facts.text: Hedonism holds that pleasure and pain are the only factors of well-being.
Desire theories hold that people fare well when they get what they want.
Objective list theories add items such as health, friendship, achievement, knowledge and autonomy that benefit a person whether or not they care about them.
Jeremy Bentham, father of classical utilitarianism, proposed the felicific calculus to measure and add up pleasure and pain.

entries.title: Green space and the mind

definition.text: The link between spending time in natural surroundings and a person's mental health.

facts.text: Studies count almost any contact with nature as exposure, from a hike or a forest visit to a walk in a park or time by a lake.
Contact with nature is tied to lower stress, better mood, more happiness and meaning, and less mental distress.
An eighteen-year Danish study found children raised with the most green space had 55% less risk of developing several psychiatric disorders.
A 10-year UK study found that greener surroundings within 300m of home and nearby green and blue spaces both lowered the risk of anxiety and depression.
Nature exposure improves working memory, attention and cognitive flexibility, while urban settings have been linked to attention deficits.
Even short exposure helps: students who glimpsed a flowering green roof for 40 seconds made fewer errors on a dull task than those shown a concrete roof.
Modern indoor, screen-heavy lifestyles have reduced people's contact with nature.
Therapists use nature in treatments called ecotherapy.

entries.title: Attention restoration: how nature rests a tired mind

definition.text: The theory that time in nature, or even views of it, helps people recover from the mental tiredness caused by sustained deliberate focus.

facts.text: Stephen and Rachel Kaplan argued that busy modern settings tax directed attention, which can run down into attention fatigue.
Nature evokes soft fascination, effortless attention to gentle stimuli such as drifting clouds or flowing water, which lets the mind rest.
A restorative setting has four properties: being away, extent, compatibility and fascination.
It builds on William James's distinction between effortful voluntary attention and automatic involuntary attention.
Roger Ulrich's competing Stress Reduction Theory says nature's benefits come from emotional and physiological responses rather than cognitive ones.

entries.title: Nature therapy: forests as medicine

definition.text: A broad group of treatments, also called ecotherapy, that use time in nature to improve mental or physical health.

facts.text: Its forms include forest therapy, forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) and Sami Lok.
Japan's forestry ministry head Tomohide Akiyama popularised forest bathing in 1982 to get more people into forests.
Its effects are usually tied to the body's stress recovery, as contact with nature lowers cortisol and heart rate.
Qing Li's small trials from 2005 found that walking in a forest for a few hours a day raised natural killer cells by roughly 50 percent; urban walks had no such effect.
Contact with nature is associated with lower stress and fewer depressive symptoms.
It is cheap and accessible, needing only parks, community gardens or other public outdoor space.
Reviews find results vary with study design, many studies rely on self-reports, and the evidence is not yet enough for clinical guidelines or proof of cause.

entries.title: Sense of place: why some places feel like home

definition.text: The many-sided relationship between people and places, covering what makes a place special and the attachment people feel to it.

facts.text: Some treat it as a quality certain places have; others treat it as a feeling held by people rather than the place.
It need not be positive: geographer Yi-Fu Tuan pointed to senses of place such as fear.
Places with a strong sense of place have an identity deeply felt by residents and visitors, and designations such as World Heritage Sites try to protect them.
Childhood places form a primal landscape that becomes part of identity and a baseline for judging places later in life.
Climate-driven damage to valued places can bring grief and solastalgia, and many Indigenous cultures are losing their sense of place to climate change.
Contact with natural environments strengthens social ties, stewardship and sense of place.

entries.title: Cultural landscapes: where people and nature made each other

definition.text: A landscape shaped by the long interplay of human activity and the natural environment.

facts.text: The World Heritage Committee sorts them into three kinds: landscapes designed by people, organically evolved landscapes (relict or continuing), and associative landscapes valued for religious, artistic or cultural ties.
Geographer Otto Schlüter first used the term academically in the early 20th century, contrasting original landscape with landscape made by culture.
Carl O. Sauer's classic definition: culture is the agent, the natural area is the medium, and the cultural landscape is the result.
In 1992 the World Heritage Committee began revising its guidelines so properties neither purely natural nor purely cultural could be listed as cultural landscapes.
Tongariro National Park in New Zealand became the first property listed under these criteria in 1993; its mountains hold spiritual meaning for the Maori.
The concept helps conserve heritage by linking buildings, local materials and traditions into one idea of identity and place, and by shifting focus to managing future change.
The Dresden Elbe Valley was removed from the World Heritage list in 2009 after a four-lane highway was built across the Elbe.

Actions include supporting reforestation, making space for nature in urban hotels, and cutting light and water pollution.

People handle fractals with a fractal dimension between 1.3 and 1.5 especially well, and viewing them lowers physical stress and boosts thinking. Because people spend 92% of their time indoors, designers now build nature-like fractals into buildings.

entries.title: Kinship with nature in Indigenous cultures
entries.article: Biophilia hypothesis#Indigenous perspectives on the human-nature connection

definition.text: The view, common in many Indigenous cultures, that humans are part of the natural world and bound to it by kinship and reciprocity.

facts.text: Humans, animals, plants and soil are seen as depending on each other for survival and health.
It underlies traditional ecological knowledge, such as the controlled burns used by some Native American and Aboriginal Australian societies.
Indigenous and animist beliefs usually treat nature as sacred, and the Anishinaabe make offerings before harvesting wild rice.

entries.title: Sacred natural sites: groves the gods protected

definition.text: A natural feature or area of land or water that holds special spiritual meaning for a people or community.

facts.text: They include mountains, forests, groves, trees, rivers, lakes, caves, islands and springs, ranging from a single tree to whole mountain ranges.
They exist on every continent except Antarctica; India alone has at least 13,720 reported sacred groves, with an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 in total.
Many have been protected for long periods with little use, and some are notably rich in biodiversity.
Besides sheltering species, they can supply water, medicines and other ecosystem services and support pilgrimage and tourism.
Some have been governed by taboos excluding women or marginalised groups, so they should not be romanticised.
The Convention on Biological Diversity recognised an urgent need to protect them and in 2004 issued the Akwe Kon guidelines for assessing developments that may affect them.

entries.title: How many visitors is too many?

definition.text: The largest number of visitors a destination can take at once without damaging its environment, economy or community or spoiling the visitor experience.

facts.text: The idea came from range, habitat and wildlife management, where managers sought the largest population a habitat could support over a long time.
Even an imperfect estimate can guide visitor caps; Peru limits Inca Trail hikers to 500 per day because geologists warned more could cause serious erosion.
Physical capacity is how many people fit on a site, usually assumed at around 1m per person.
Social capacity is exceeded when local tolerance falls, visitor enjoyment drops and crime rises; biophysical capacity is passed when damage outruns a habitat's ability to regenerate.
Economic capacity can mark the point where tourism revenue is overtaken by the inflation tourism causes.
How much damage is acceptable is a matter of human judgment; where pristine conditions are the goal, carrying capacity may be zero.
Critics say it wrongly assumes stable social-ecological systems and is hard to calculate, and UNESCO warns it can make a site look better protected than it is.

entries.contested_note: Several authors argue the concept is flawed both in its assumptions and in practice, and it has largely been replaced by management-by-objectives frameworks.
