entries.title: Keeping ecotourism honest

definition.text: The rules and measures used to stop ecotourism operations from damaging the places they sell, from visitor limits to certification labels.

facts.text: They include setting a carrying capacity, hardening sites, sustainable design, visitor quotas, fees, access limits and visitor education.
Labels such as the European Ecotourism Labelling Standard try to certify genuine low-impact operators.
When responsible operators are not recognised, they are put at a competitive disadvantage against greenwashed ones.

entries.text: Ecotourism operators sell places they could easily damage, so managers use a toolkit to protect them. It includes setting a carrying capacity, hardening sites against wear, sustainable design, visitor quotas, fees, access limits and visitor education. Labels such as the European Ecotourism Labelling Standard try to certify genuine low-impact operators. Recognition matters: when responsible operators go unrecognized, they lose out to rivals that only claim to be green.

entries.title: The happiness set point

definition.text: The idea that each person has an inherited baseline level of subjective well-being to which they tend to return.

facts.text: Top-down theories hold that people have a genetic tendency to be happy or unhappy that fixes their well-being setpoint.
Personality studies find genetics account for 20–48% of the variance in Five-Factor traits, and the variance in subjective well-being is also heritable.

entries.title: Beautiful, sublime or picturesque

definition.text: Three classic ways of appreciating nature: the tame beauty of gardens, the awe of wild and threatening nature, and nature seen as picture-like scenes.

facts.text: Beautiful things tend to be small, smooth and fair in colour, while sublime things tend to be powerful, intense and terrifying.
The picturesque mixes the two: varied, irregular, rich and forceful.
Viewed with disinterest, the frightening side of nature, such as mountains and wilderness, can be admired rather than feared.

Viewed with disinterest, mountains and wilderness can be admired rather than feared.

entries.title: Are people losing touch with nature?

definition.text: The probable fall in people's direct contact with nature, which earlier studies link to effects on health and on care for the environment.

facts.text: One review concluded that within a generation children's lives have largely moved indoors, while childhood nature experience builds lifelong care for nature.
A global review found the evidence still too thin to judge how large or general the decline is.
Indoor lifestyles and growing screen time have cut human contact with nature.

entries.title: Nature on prescription

definition.text: Health-system programmes in which doctors or public agencies formally send people to spend time in nature.

Dose of Nature claimed a 64% recovery rate for its first 1500 patients, against 50% for talk therapy.
Finnish researchers recommend about five hours a month in nature as preventive health care.

entries.title: Measuring a bond with nature

definition.text: A 21-item questionnaire that measures how connected to nature a person feels as a lasting trait.

It shows good reliability, alpha = .87, and test-retest stability six months later, alpha = .85.

entries.title: City parks and mental health
entries.article: Nature exposure and mental health#City parks and mental health

definition.text: The benefit that parks inside cities bring to the mental health of the people living near them.

facts.text: Residents living 800m to 1.6km from a park had mental health scores 4.5 points lower than residents within 400m of one.
Urban parks help reduce stress and lower the risk of anxiety and depression.
Being cheap and open to all, urban parks can make mental health benefits accessible regardless of income or background.

entries.title: Placelessness: places that could be anywhere

definition.text: The quality of places that lack a sense of place and feel as if they could be anywhere.

facts.text: Cultural geographer Edward Relph studied placelessness, and anthropologist Marc Augé called such locations non-places.
Strip malls, petrol stations, fast food chains and chain stores are cited examples.
Historic districts heavily commercialised for tourism can lose their sense of place.

The benefits of nature therapy are usually linked to this stress recovery process.
Urban forestry has been shown to promote stress recovery and psychological healing.

entries.title: Limits of acceptable change: managing by goals, not head counts
entries.article: Tourism carrying capacity#Limits of acceptable change

definition.text: A visitor-management framework that monitors a site against set objectives instead of relying on a single maximum visitor number.

facts.text: The US Forest Service developed it in the 1980s as the first framework to follow carrying capacity.
It assumes any tourist activity has some impact, so a visitor cap is only one tool among many.
It is often summarised as a nine-step process, from selecting indicators of resource and social conditions to choosing preferred management alternatives.

entries.title: Remote sensing: watching Earth from above

definition.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it, usually by observing Earth from satellites or aircraft.

facts.text: It produces the satellite views in online maps and the cloud pictures in weather forecasts.
It reaches dangerous or remote places and can replace slower, costlier fieldwork without disturbing the site.
Brazil's space research institute has measured Amazon deforestation every year since 1988 using Landsat-class imagery.
Uses include natural resource management, mapping wildlife habitat, greenhouse gas monitoring and oil spill detection.
It can assess the health and extent of land cover that provides ecosystem services, aiding planning and monitoring.
Multispectral satellites such as Landsat have been in use since the early 1970s; satellite remote sensing began with Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Many parts of the water balance, such as soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration and snow, can be measured remotely.

entries.title: GIS: linking the world's data by location

definition.text: A GIS is a combination of computer hardware and software that stores, manages, analyses, edits and displays geographic data.

facts.text: A GIS uses location as the key that links otherwise unrelated pieces of information, much as a database links tables by a shared key.
Its core is a database holding the shape and position of geographic things along with their attributes.
Roger Tomlinson coined the phrase in the mid-1960s, though many of the methods GIS automates are much older.
Data enter a GIS by direct field measurement such as remote sensing or GPS, by digitizing paper maps, or by copying existing GIS data.
Feeding satellite data into a GIS lets researchers track changes in Earth's surface over days, months and years.
GIS is a commonly used tool for environmental management, modelling and planning, and for monitoring forest cover and deforestation.

entries.title: Landscape ecology: seeing nature as a patchwork

definition.text: The science that studies how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across whole landscapes, and how to improve those relationships.

facts.text: Its hallmark is a focus on how pattern, process and scale relate, and on broad-scale environmental problems.
Landscapes are mixed areas made of interacting patches, from forests and lakes to farms and cities.
Unlike traditional ecology, which often assumes places are uniform, landscape ecology studies spatial patterns and heterogeneity, the way parts of a landscape differ.
German geographer Carl Troll coined the term in 1939 while using aerial photographs to study how environment and vegetation interact.
Its four main principles concern how spatial heterogeneity develops, how things move across it, how it affects living and non-living processes, and how to manage it.
The field treats humans explicitly as a force that changes landscapes and proposes ways to restore degraded ones.
Its recent growth owes much to geographic information systems and large remotely sensed habitat datasets.
By 1980 it was an established discipline, having grown from European planning of human-dominated landscapes.

entries.title: System dynamics: why systems surprise their owners

definition.text: An approach to understanding how complex systems behave over time by modelling their stocks, flows, feedback loops and time delays.

facts.text: A stock is anything that builds up or runs down over time, and a flow is its rate of change.
The structure of a system, its circular, interlocking and delayed relationships, often matters as much as its individual parts.
Jay Forrester of MIT created it in the mid-1950s after showing by hand simulation that GE's employment swings came from the firm's own structure, not the business cycle.
Its best-known model is probably The Limits to Growth of 1972, which forecast economic collapse in the 21st century under many growth scenarios.
Models update all variables in small time steps, so mutual causation is handled through feedbacks and delays.
Typical applications are population, agricultural, ecological and economic systems, which interact strongly.
System dynamics and GIS are used together in spatial dynamic landscape simulation modelling in ecological economics.

entries.title: Ecosystem models: simulating centuries in minutes

definition.text: An abstract, usually mathematical, representation of an ecological system, from one population to a whole biome, studied to understand the real system.

facts.text: Relationships measured in the field, such as sunlight and water against photosynthesis, are combined into a model that predicts how the real system behaves.
Models allow experiments too costly or unethical to run on real ecosystems, and can simulate centuries in minutes.
There are two main types: simple analytic models solved by equations, and simulation models solved numerically, which are more widely used and more realistic.
Because ecosystems are so complex, models reduce them to a few state variables and group similar species into functional groups.
Spatially explicit, or landscape, models include a varied spatial environment because place can change outcomes greatly.
Models are validated against independent data sets or field observations, with an acceptable gap often set beforehand.
Gaps between a model and observations often suggest new hypotheses about unknown ecological relations.
Ecopath, a simulation system for marine ecosystems, is widely used by fisheries scientists.

entries.text: No one can ethically wreck a real ecosystem to see what happens, but a model can, and it can simulate centuries in minutes. Models are checked against independent data or field observations. The gaps often suggest new hypotheses. {{ref:nature-res-006}}, a simulation system for marine ecosystems, is widely used by fisheries scientists.
entries.text_plain: No one can ethically wreck a real ecosystem to see what happens, but a model can, and it can simulate centuries in minutes. An ecosystem model is an abstract, usually mathematical, representation of an ecological system, from one population to a whole biome. Relationships measured in the field, such as sunlight and water against photosynthesis, are combined to predict how the real system behaves. Ecosystems are so complex that models reduce them to a few state variables and group similar species into functional groups. Simple analytic models are solved by equations. Simulation models are solved numerically and are more widely used and more realistic. Spatially explicit models include a varied landscape, because place can change outcomes greatly. Models are checked against independent data or field observations. The gaps often suggest new hypotheses. Ecopath: modeling a whole sea in software, a simulation system for marine ecosystems, is widely used by fisheries scientists.

entries.title: Agent-based models: simple rules, complex worlds

definition.text: A computer model that simulates the actions and interactions of autonomous agents, such as individuals or organisations, to understand how a whole system behaves.

facts.text: In ecology it is also called an individual-based model.
Its three central ideas are agents as objects, emergence and complexity: simple rules for agents can produce complex behaviour.
Thomas Schelling's 1971 segregation model, done with coins and graph paper, was an early example of agents producing an emergent outcome.
The idea dates to the late 1940s but spread only in the 1990s because it needs heavy computing.
In economics, ABMs drop the assumption of equilibrium and replace representative agents with diverse, interdependent ones, so they can produce booms and crashes.
Combined with GIS, the ABM models the process while the GIS models the spatial pattern.
ABMs are used in water resources planning to test infrastructure and policy and to value cooperation.
Validation checks that a model relates to the real world, through calibration, sensitivity analysis and statistical tests.

entries.title: Land cover: what actually sits on the ground

definition.text: The physical material at Earth's land surface, such as plants, concrete, buildings, bare ground or water.

facts.text: Land cover differs from land use, which describes how people use the land and what economic activity happens there, though the terms are often confused.
It is captured mainly by field survey or by analysing remotely sensed images.
Surveys define similar categories differently; there are many definitions of forest, sometimes within one organisation.
FAO statistics put tree-covered areas at 4,335.00 million ha in 2015, 29.11% of land, down 99.93 million ha since 1992.
In FAO data, artificial surfaces grew from 26.04 million ha in 1992 to 55.40 million ha in 2015.
Detecting land cover change gives baseline information for judging climate change impacts on habitats, biodiversity and resources.
Human activity is the biggest cause of land cover change, with deforestation historically a primary driver.

entries.title: Scenario planning: rehearsing several futures

definition.text: A strategic planning method in which organizations imagine several plausible futures in order to make flexible long-term plans.

facts.text: Scenario analysis presents several alternative futures and the paths to them rather than one exact forecast.
Unlike a forecast, it does not just extend past trends or assume past observations will stay valid.
It draws on systems thinking: many factors can combine through feedback loops to create surprising futures.
Analysts choose scenarios that are both possible and uncomfortable, helping decision-makers anticipate change and build more robust strategies.
Most authors credit Herman Kahn, working at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s, with introducing it; Gaston Berger developed similar methods in France.
Royal Dutch Shell adopted it after energy companies lost billions in the 1970s, surprised by environmentalism and the OPEC cartel.
In business, attention has shifted from opponents' behaviour toward changes in the natural environment.

entries.title: NDVI: reading plant health from space

definition.text: NDVI is a widely used number, calculated from red and near-infrared sensor readings, that measures how dense and healthy vegetation is.

facts.text: Green plants absorb visible light for photosynthesis but strongly reflect near-infrared light, so they look dark in red and bright in near-infrared.
NDVI ranges from -1 to 1: near zero means little vegetation, negative values mean water or non-land, and high values mean dense healthy plants.
Dense canopies tend to give values of about 0.3 to 0.8, while bare soils give small positive values around 0.1 to 0.2.
Researchers studying Great Plains rangeland developed it to correct for the changing sun angle; its earliest reported use was in 1973 by Rouse and colleagues.
It remains the best-known index for detecting live green plant canopies in multispectral data.
Farmers use it to assess crop health, spot plant stress before it is visible and predict yields.
Falling NDVI can signal drought stress, deforestation or land degradation.
NDVI carries only part of the original spectral information and is affected by the atmosphere, sensor differences, soil and snow.

entries.title: Spatial analysis: asking where

definition.text: The set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics.

facts.text: In a narrower sense it is geospatial analysis, applying statistics and other analysis to data with a geographic aspect, usually with GIS software.
GIS-based spatial analysis was developed for ecology, geology and epidemiology and now reaches natural resources, disaster risk and climate change adaptation.
Basic GIS operations include map overlay and buffering, which marks areas within a set distance of features such as roads or rivers.
Spatial interaction or gravity models estimate flows of people, materials or information between places.
Its most fundamental problem is how to define where the things being studied are located.
The ecological fallacy is the error of drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.
Land surveying, an early root of spatial analysis, goes back to at least 1,400 BC in Egypt, where taxable plots were measured with ropes.

entries.text: As far back as at least 1,400 BC, Egyptian surveyors measured taxable plots with ropes, an early root of spatial analysis. Another trap is the ecological fallacy: drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.

entries.title: Species distribution models: predicting where life lives

definition.text: Using ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time.

facts.text: It can project a species' future range under climate change, its past range, or where an invasive species might spread.
A primary use is conservation: finding highly suitable habitat to prioritise sites for protection and restoration and guide protected area networks.
It helps identify climate refugia, places likely to stay suitable as the climate changes.
Correlative models fit a species' observed range to environmental conditions; mechanistic models use its physiology to work out where it could survive.
Correlative models are quicker but describe the realized niche and extrapolate poorly; mechanistic models handle shifting ranges better but need much physiological data.
MaxEnt is the most widely used method, working from presence-only records even when few are available.
Remote sensing and GIS-based environmental modelling greatly increased the data available for building these models.

entries.text: Where will a species live when the climate shifts? Species distribution modeling uses ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time. It can project a future range under climate change, a past range, or where an invasive species might spread. Its main use is conservation: finding highly suitable habitat to prioritize sites for protection and restoration. It also helps identify climate refugia, places likely to stay suitable as the climate changes. Correlative models fit a species' observed range to environmental conditions. They are quick but describe only where the species actually lives now, and they extrapolate poorly. Mechanistic models use its physiology to work out where it could survive, handling shifting ranges better but needing much data. MaxEnt, the most widely used method, works from presence-only records even when few exist. Remote sensing and GIS have greatly expanded the data available.

entries.title: Land change models: forecasting the face of the Earth

definition.text: Land change models describe, project and explain how land use and land cover change over time.

facts.text: They help explain how people have changed and will change Earth's surface, and guide resource decisions from a single plot to whole regions.
Land change modeling is an application of landscape ecology and a key part of land change science, used to assess long-term outcomes for land cover and climate.
Approaches include machine-learning models trained on past land cover, cellular models that compare neighbouring areas, economic supply-and-demand models, agent-based models and hybrids.
A 2011 study in western Mexico found two outwardly similar models gave considerably different results.
All land change models carry irreducible uncertainty, and the further into the future they project, the more uncertain they become.
The model should fit the goal: agent-based models for questions about policy and actors, machine learning and cellular models for spotting patterns and trends.
Practitioners use them to explore the future effects of policies and set guidelines, on topics from water and food to urbanization.
They predict how land may change under different circumstances, which helps risk assessment and policy, with some uncertainty.

entries.title: Active and passive sensors

definition.text: The two classes of remote sensing: passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, while active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back.

facts.text: Passive sensors most often measure reflected sunlight; cameras, radiometers and spectrometers are common examples.
Radar and lidar are active systems that time a pulse's return to find the distance to a target.

entries.text: Remote sensing instruments come in two classes. Passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, most often reflected sunlight; cameras, radiometers and spectrometers are common examples. Active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back. Radar and {{ref:nature-es-068}} are active systems that time a pulse's return to find the distance to a target.

entries.title: Lidar: measuring the world with laser light

definition.text: A way of measuring distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return.

facts.text: It is an active sensor that supplies its own light and uses the speed of light to turn return time into distance.
From an aircraft it can map terrain at 30-centimetre resolution or better.
In forestry it measures tree heights and crown widths and estimates canopy volume, biomass and carbon density.
A 2024 lidar study found England has 390,000 km of hedgerows.

entries.title: False-color images: seeing the invisible
entries.article: Remote sensing#False Color Composites (FCCs) and Pseudocolor

definition.text: An image in which wavelengths are assigned to display colours other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see.

facts.text: It is made by changing which parts of the spectrum are shown as red, green and blue.
Pseudocolor instead maps a single band onto a new colour scale; this also works for temperature or elevation.

entries.text: A false-color composite is an image in which wavelengths are shown in colors other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see. It is made by changing which parts of the spectrum are displayed as red, green and blue. Pseudocolor works differently: it maps a single band onto a new color scale, a trick that also works for temperature or elevation.

entries.title: Raster and vector: two ways to store a map

definition.text: The two traditional ways a GIS stores geographic data: as raster images made of cells, or as vector points, lines and polygons.

facts.text: Mapped things are usually treated either as discrete objects, like a house or road, or as continuous fields, like rainfall or population density.
A GIS can convert between formats, for example tracing lines around same-class cells of a satellite image to make vector shapes.
Point clouds are a newer hybrid that pair three-dimensional points with colour values.

entries.title: How sharp is a satellite's eye?

definition.text: The quality of remote sensing data, described by its spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal resolution.

facts.text: Spatial resolution is pixel size, typically squares from 1 to 1,000 metres on a side.
Radiometric resolution is how many intensity levels a sensor distinguishes, typically 8 to 14 bits, or 256 up to 16,384 shades per band.
Temporal resolution is how often a satellite or plane passes over, which matters for time series such as deforestation monitoring.
The Hyperion sensor resolves 220 bands from 0.4 to 2.5 μm, while Landsat records seven.

entries.text: Landsat records seven bands of light; the Hyperion sensor resolves 220, from 0.4 to 2.5 μm. That difference is spectral resolution, one of four ways to describe remote sensing data. Spatial resolution is pixel size, typically squares from 1 to 1,000 metres on a side. Radiometric resolution is how many intensity levels a sensor can tell apart, typically 8 to 14 bits, or 256 up to 16,384 shades per band. Temporal resolution is how often a satellite or plane passes over, which matters for tracking deforestation over time.

entries.title: Map overlay: stacking maps to find answers

definition.text: Combining several spatial datasets of the same area into a new one, like stacking maps of one region on top of each other.

facts.text: Overlays work like Venn diagrams: a union keeps everything from both inputs, an intersect keeps only where they overlap.
With rasters, overlay is done by map algebra, a function that combines each layer's cell values and can weight some inputs more than others.
Cartographic modeling, a term Dana Tomlin coined in 1983, means producing and analysing several thematic layers of the same area.

entries.title: Choosing the best site with GIS

definition.text: Using GIS to compare alternative places, such as candidate habitat for restoration, against several criteria at once.

facts.text: Decision rules combine the criteria so the alternatives can be ranked or prioritised.
It may cut the cost and time of finding potential restoration sites.

entries.text: Finding the best place to restore a habitat means juggling many criteria at once. GIS multi-criteria decision analysis compares alternative places against several criteria together. Decision rules combine the criteria so the alternatives can be ranked or prioritized. The method may cut the cost and time of finding potential restoration sites.

entries.title: Spatial interpolation: filling in the gaps between samples

definition.text: Building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between a set of measured sample points.

facts.text: Geostatistics, the branch of statistics for continuous spatial data, models spatial correlation to predict values at unmeasured places.
It is justified by spatial autocorrelation: measurements at one place closely resemble those nearby.
Methods include inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines, Thiessen polygons and trend surfaces.

entries.text: Measurements taken at one place closely resemble those taken nearby. That tendency justifies spatial interpolation: building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between measured sample points. Geostatistics, the branch of statistics for continuous spatial data, models these correlations to predict values at unmeasured places. Methods include inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines, Thiessen polygons and trend surfaces.

entries.title: Bayesian networks: reasoning backward from evidence

definition.text: A probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on one another as a diagram of arrows with no loops.

facts.text: Each node is a variable and each arrow a direct dependency; each node has a probability function based on its parent nodes.
Given an observed event, it can estimate how likely each possible cause was, as with symptoms and diseases.
It automatically applies Bayes' theorem to complex problems, updating beliefs about unobserved variables as evidence comes in.
Bayesian belief networks have been used to explore where ecological regime shifts are likely to happen.

entries.text: A doctor sees symptoms and must work back to the likely disease. A Bayesian network does this kind of reasoning. It is a probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on each other, drawn as a diagram of arrows with no loops. Each node is a variable and each arrow a direct dependency. The network applies Bayes' theorem automatically, updating beliefs about unobserved variables as evidence comes in. Ecologists have used such networks to explore where ecological regime shifts are likely.

entries.title: Causal loop diagrams: drawing the feedback

definition.text: A simple map of a system's parts and how they affect each other, drawn to reveal its feedback loops.

facts.text: Reinforcing loops amplify change, as when more adopters of a product create stronger word of mouth; counteracting loops push back.
It supports qualitative analysis; for numbers it is turned into a stock and flow diagram and simulated on a computer.
Double slashes on an arrow mark a significant delay between cause and effect.

entries.text: More buyers of a product mean stronger word of mouth, which brings more buyers. For numbers, it is turned into a stock and flow diagram and simulated on a computer.

entries.title: Edges and ecotones: life at the borders

definition.text: An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecological communities meet, such as forest giving way to grassland.

facts.text: An edge is the part of an ecosystem near its border, where neighbouring patches make conditions differ from the interior, often changing which species live there.
Ecotones can be natural, like a lakeshore, or made by people, like a field cleared from forest.
An ecotone keeps traits of both neighbouring communities and often holds species found in neither.
Fencerows, forest-to-marsh transitions and riparian zones are classic examples.

entries.title: Patches, corridors and matrix: the parts of a landscape

definition.text: A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings; patches, corridors and the background matrix together make up a landscape's mosaic.

facts.text: The matrix is the well-connected background ecological system of a landscape.
Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is; a forest with fewer open gaps has higher connectivity.
Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides.
Patches change and fluctuate over time, a process called patch dynamics.

entries.title: Fragmentation: when the landscape breaks apart

definition.text: The breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller separate pieces.

facts.text: Repeated random clearing, natural or human, can break continuous cover into isolated patches.
Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from a connected to a disconnected phase.
Metapopulation models gave conservation biologists a tool to judge how fragmentation affects whether populations survive.

entries.text: Landscape fragmentation is the breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller, separate pieces. Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from connected to disconnected. Metapopulation models, which treat scattered groups as linked populations, gave conservation biologists a tool to judge whether populations can survive this.

entries.title: Lotka and Volterra: the dance of predator and prey

definition.text: One of the earliest ecological models: a pair of equations, one for a prey species and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together.

facts.text: It was developed by Alfred Lotka in 1925 and Vito Volterra in 1926.
Volterra built it to explain swings in Adriatic fish and shark numbers after fishing was cut back in the First World War.
Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate.
Supporters of the ratio-dependent Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the data are so far from Lotka–Volterra that it can be discounted as wrong.

entries.contested_note: Proponents of the ratio-dependent Arditi–Ginzburg model argue field data reject the Lotka–Volterra form.
entries.text: After fishing in the Adriatic was cut back during the First World War, fish and shark numbers swung in puzzling ways. Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate. It is not unchallenged: supporters of the rival Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the field data reject it.

entries.title: i-Tree: putting a value on every tree

definition.text: A suite of US Forest Service software tools that measure and value the ecosystem services trees provide in cities and the countryside.

facts.text: It quantifies services such as pollution removal, carbon sequestration and avoided stormwater runoff.
Some tools work bottom-up from ground tree inventories, others top-down from remote sensing data.
Urban foresters use it to assess an urban forest's structure and turn that into ecosystem services and economic value.
It began in 2002 as a sample survey that simulated a full urban tree inventory.

entries.title: Participatory GIS: maps made by the people who live there

definition.text: A participatory approach to spatial planning that puts mapping tools in the hands of local people so their own knowledge shapes decisions.

facts.text: It combines sketch maps, 3D models, aerial photos, satellite images and GPS to turn people's spatial knowledge into maps for discussion and decisions.
Its aim is to empower marginalized groups and protect traditional knowledge by leaving control of sensitive maps with those who made them.
Uses range from neighbourhood planning to environmental and natural resource management.
Top-down and bottom-up approaches are the currently debated split, and critics ask who really gets access to the technology.

entries.contested_note: Top-down and bottom-up approaches to participatory GIS are a debated split, with questions over who actually benefits.

entries.title: InVEST: free software for mapping nature's value

definition.text: InVEST (Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs) is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services.

facts.text: It includes 20+ ecosystem service models covering land, freshwater, marine, coastal and urban settings.
It is used in more than 185 countries to map valuable ecological resources, weigh trade-offs in land and water use, and steer investments toward both conservation and development.
It is one of several tools, alongside the ARIES project and the Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, that help the private sector value ecosystem services.
Its developer works with governments, banks, companies and communities to bring nature's values into decisions through mapping, modelling and quantifying its benefits.

entries.title: The modifiable areal unit problem: same data, different answers

definition.text: A source of statistical bias that arises because results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions.

facts.text: Summary values like totals, rates and densities depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.
A population density map built on state boundaries gives radically different results from one built on county boundaries.

entries.text: Draw a population density map using state boundaries, then redraw it using county boundaries, and the results differ radically. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, a source of statistical bias. Results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions. Totals, rates and densities all depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.

entries.title: Spatial autocorrelation: near things are related

definition.text: The tendency for values at nearby locations to be related to one another, either positively or negatively.

facts.text: It breaks the independence that standard statistics assume, so regressions that ignore it can give unstable estimates and unreliable significance tests.
Spatial regression models capture it, and it can also be seen as useful information rather than a nuisance.
Classic measures include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

entries.title: Testing a land change model against reality

definition.text: Checking a land change model by comparing its processes or its predicted maps with what really happened.

facts.text: Pattern validation often uses three maps, the real maps at two dates and the simulated second map, sorting pixels into hits, misses, false alarms and similar classes.
The Figure of Merit turns hits, misses and false alarms into one percentage for the overlap between real and simulated change.
Using data from after the first time period to calibrate can make a model look far more accurate than it really is.

entries.title: Runoff curve numbers: how much rain runs off

definition.text: An empirical number used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in.

facts.text: The USDA Soil Conservation Service, now the Natural Resources Conservation Service, developed it from runoff measured on small catchments and plots.
It depends on soil group, land use and treatment, and ranges from 30 to 100, with higher numbers meaning more runoff and less permeable ground.
Soils fall into four hydrologic groups, from A, deep sands with high infiltration, to D, clays and shallow soils with very slow infiltration.
Paved parking lots and roofs have a curve number of 98, while open space in good condition on group A soil has 39.

entries.title: Use value: what a thing is good for

definition.text: The usefulness of a thing: the features that let it satisfy a human want or need, a concept from classical and Marxist economics.

facts.text: Gold, for example, can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor.
Adam Smith noted that diamonds have high exchange value but little use, while water is very useful yet cheap.
For Marx, every commodity is both a use value and an exchange value, the proportion in which it trades for other goods.
Turning a use value into a commodity needs preconditions: it must be tradable, ownership must be securely transferable, and there must be real demand.
Marginalist economics later treated use value as coming from the marginal utility consumers find in a good.
Critics of the commodification of nature draw on the Marxian idea that commodities embody both use and exchange value.

entries.text: Gold can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor. Each of those is a use, and together they make up its use value: the features that let a thing satisfy a human want or need. The idea comes from classical and Marxist economics. Adam Smith noticed that use and price can part company. Diamonds have little use but fetch a great deal in trade, while water is very useful yet cheap. For Marx, every commodity, a good made to be traded, is both a use value and an {{ref:nature-val-068}}: the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Not every useful thing can become a commodity. It must be tradable, its ownership must pass securely from one person to another, and there must be real demand. Later, marginalist economics traced use value to the {{ref:nature-econ-091}} consumers find in a good. Critics of turning nature into commodities still draw on Marx's double idea.

entries.title: Exchange value: what a thing trades for

definition.text: In political economy, especially Marxian economics, the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods.

facts.text: It is one of four attributes of a commodity, alongside use value, value and price.
For Marx, exchange value is not the same as money price; actual prices only roughly match it.
Marx held that a good's value is set by the socially necessary labour time needed to produce it.
Making something a commodity requires preconditions such as secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand.
Modern neoclassical economics no longer theorises exchange value separately; it is simply the market price.
Critics of the commodification of nature argue that expressing all kinds of worth through a single exchange value makes things commensurable.

entries.text: Marx gave every commodity four attributes: use value, exchange value, value and price. Exchange value is the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods. It is not the same as the money price, which only roughly matches it. Behind both, Marx held, lies value itself, set by the socially necessary labor time needed to produce a good: the work it typically takes. Modern neoclassical economics, the mainstream school, no longer treats exchange value as a separate idea. For it, exchange value is simply the market price, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-356}}. Before anything can be traded at all, certain conditions must hold: secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand. Critics of turning nature into commodities see a danger here. Expressing every kind of worth through a single exchange value puts very different things on one scale.

entries.title: Environmental philosophy: do rivers have rights?

definition.text: The branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it.

facts.text: It emerged as a branch of philosophy in the 1970s; early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott.
A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only instrumental value, with ecocentric and deep ecology views against human-centred ones.
Current issues include environmental activism, environmental justice, climate change and the depletion of finite resources.
Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists or is a cultural construct with colonial overtones, as William Cronon suggested.
Its questions include whether rivers have rights.

entries.title: The paradox of value: why diamonds outprice water

definition.text: The puzzle, also called the diamond–water paradox, that water is far more useful for survival than diamonds, yet diamonds cost much more.

facts.text: Adam Smith is its classic presenter, though it appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus.
Smith separated 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', noting that the most useful things often have little exchange value.
Labor theory of value supporters resolve it by saying price reflects the toil of acquiring a good.
Marginalists resolve it by distinguishing total from marginal utility: water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more.
Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons.
A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.
Adam Smith is the classic presenter of the paradox, though it appeared as early as Plato.
Smith contrasted value in use with value in exchange: nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything.

entries.title: Good as a means, or good in itself

definition.text: The philosophical distinction between what is good as a means to an end and what is good as an end in itself.

facts.text: A hammer or washing machine has instrumental value, while happiness and pleasure are usually thought valuable for their own sake.
The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms.
John Dewey thought belief in intrinsic value was a mistake and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well.
J. Fagg Foster treated sustainability as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

entries.title: Anthropocentrism: putting humans at the center

definition.text: The belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet.

facts.text: From this view humans are separate from and superior to nature, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use.
Environmental ethics often treats it as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere.
Its defenders argue that a sound long-term view keeps the environment suitable for humans, and that the real problem is shallow anthropocentrism.
William Grey called for an enriched human-centred idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views.
Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism in feminist theory.
The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify it, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation.
Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.
J. Howard Moore argued in 1906 that Darwin's theory of common descent 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism.

entries.contested_note: Environmental philosophers dispute whether human-centred thinking causes ecological harm or whether only its shallow, short-term form does.
entries.text: In 1906 J. Howard Moore argued that Darwin's theory of common descent had 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism. The idea has proved hard to kill. In this view humans stand apart from nature and above it, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use. Nature's value becomes instrumental, a means to human ends. {{ref:nature-val-037}} often treats this outlook as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere, the living envelope of the planet. Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism, the male-centered outlook, in feminist theory. Its defenders answer that the real problem is only shallow anthropocentrism. A sound long-term view, they argue, would keep the environment suitable for humans. William Grey called for an enriched idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views. Environmental philosophers still dispute who is right: whether human-centered thinking itself causes ecological harm, or only its shallow, short-term form. Religion enters the argument too. The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify the view, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation. Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks instead of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.

entries.title: Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake

definition.text: In ethics, the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else.

facts.text: It contrasts with instrumental value, which something has because of its relation to another valued thing.
Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable, such as flourishing for virtue ethics or pleasure for consequentialists.
Some conservation biologists argue nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to people.
Arne Næss's deep ecology, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings intrinsic value.
The Zoological Society of London says insect decline means a loss of species' intrinsic value as well as their instrumental value.
Whether absolute intrinsic value exists is debated; John Dewey accepted only value relative to a situation.

entries.text: The Zoological Society of London warns that insect decline means a double loss. Species lose their instrumental value, and their intrinsic value as well. Intrinsic value, in ethics, is the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else. Instrumental value, by contrast, comes from a thing's relation to some other valued thing. Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable. Virtue ethics points to flourishing; consequentialists, who judge acts by their results, point to pleasure. Arne Næss's {{ref:nature-val-062}}, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings this kind of worth. Whether absolute intrinsic value exists at all is debated. entries.title: Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness

definition.text: An environmental philosophy holding that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match.

facts.text: Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish, independent of human use.
Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss first used the phrase in a 1973 article.
Næss contrasted it with 'shallow ecology', which he criticised as utilitarian, human-centred and consumer-oriented.
It rejects the view of nature as a resource to exploit and holds that the materialist paradigm, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced.
Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring is often seen as the start of the movement.
Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores overconsumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic.
Arguments about the non-market valuation of ecosystems draw on environmental ethics and deep ecology.
Arne Næss coined 'deep ecology' in 1972, arguing that all non-human entities have intrinsic value.

entries.contested_note: Critics call it Eurocentric, misanthropic or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge.
entries.text: Rachel Carson's {{ref:nature-hist-006}}, published in 1962, is often seen as the start of the movement. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss gave it a name, coining 'deep ecology' in 1972 and first using the phrase in a 1973 article. Deep ecology holds that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match. Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish. Næss set it against 'shallow ecology', which he criticized as utilitarian, human-centered and consumer-oriented. Deep ecology rejects nature as a resource to exploit. The materialist outlook, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced. Critics push back. Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores excessive consumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic. Others call it Eurocentric or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge. Its ideas also feed arguments for valuing ecosystems outside markets.

entries.title: Ecocentrism: valuing nature as a whole

definition.text: A nature-centred rather than human-centred system of values.

facts.text: It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only or greater bearers of intrinsic value.
Aldo Leopold conceived the ethic, and his land ethic is central to it.
It values the biotic community as a whole and aims to keep ecosystem composition and processes intact, covering living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone.
Supporters argue that human-centred ethics makes protecting nature always depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives it a firmer basis.
Critics argue it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

entries.text: Where anthropocentrism puts humans at the center, ecocentrism puts nature there. It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only, or the greater, bearers of intrinsic value. It values the biotic community, all the living things of a place, as a whole. It aims to keep ecosystems' composition and processes intact. It covers living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone. {{ref:nature-hist-051}} conceived the ethic, and his {{ref:nature-val-049}} is central to it. Supporters argue that a human-centered ethic always makes protecting nature depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives protection a firmer basis. Critics reply that it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

entries.title: Biocentrism: equal worth for every living thing

definition.text: The environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things.

facts.text: It contrasts with anthropocentrism, centred on humans, and sentientism, which values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain; ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature.
Its four pillars: humans and other species share Earth's community, all species are interdependent, each organism pursues its own good, and humans are not inherently superior.
It includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism.
Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, animal rights and environmental protection.
Critics call it anti-human and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.
The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric for putting non-human species first.

Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, rights for animals and environmental protection. Critics call it anti-human, and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.

entries.title: Three ways societies value nature

definition.text: The ways societies see importance in the non-human world, grouped as extrinsic (instrumental), intrinsic and relational values.

facts.text: Extrinsic values are nature's usefulness to people, such as timber, clean water and air, carbon storage and pollination, often called ecosystem services.
Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value and so enter impact assessments, cost-benefit analyses and national accounts.
Intrinsic values hold that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans.
Relational values are the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.
IPBES, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

entries.text: Timber, clean water and air, carbon storage, pollination: these are the familiar ways nature serves people. They are only one of three kinds of value that societies see in the non-human world. The first kind is extrinsic, or instrumental, value: nature's usefulness to people, often called ecosystem services. Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value. That lets them enter impact assessments, {{ref:nature-val-001}} studies and national accounts. The second kind is intrinsic value. It holds that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans. The third kind covers meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural ties between people and nature. These are {{ref:nature-val-072}}. {{ref:nature-gov-020}}, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

It holds that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans. entries.title: Technocentrism: trusting science to fix nature

definition.text: A set of values centred on technology, holding that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science.

facts.text: Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist but do not see cutting industry as the solution.
Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature and prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

entries.text: Not everyone who worries about the environment wants to shrink industry. Technocentrism is a set of values centered on technology. It holds that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science. They prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

entries.title: Social ecology: how people treat nature and each other

definition.text: Murray Bookchin's 1982 philosophy linking how humans treat nature to how they treat each other.

facts.text: It defines nature as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom.
Bookchin argued that 'the ecological crisis is a social crisis': practices such as monocropping and overfishing mirror social tendencies to dominate people.
It calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

entries.text: 'The ecological crisis is a social crisis,' Murray Bookchin argued. His 1982 philosophy of social ecology links how humans treat nature to how they treat each other. Practices such as monocropping, growing a single crop over and over, and taking too many fish mirror social tendencies to dominate people. Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

entries.title: Rights of nature: writing nature's rights into law

definition.text: The legal recognition of nature as having rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law.

facts.text: Ecuador was the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution, in 2008.
Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution.
Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia adopted rights-of-nature laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.
It rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did.

The idea rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did. Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia have adopted such laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.

entries.title: Non-market goods: valuable but never sold

definition.text: Goods that are not bought and sold in markets, such as most environmental goods: clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests.

facts.text: Quantifying their value is inherently uncertain.
Contingent valuation surveys were first proposed by S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup in 1947 to value a non-market good.
Environmental assets are usually left out of measures of wealth, partly because non-market goods are hard to value.

entries.text: Clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests share an awkward trait for economists. They are non-market goods, things that are not bought and sold in markets. Most environmental goods fall into this group. Without prices, putting a value on them is inherently uncertain. That difficulty is one reason the environment is usually left out of measures of wealth. In 1947 S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed a way around it: surveys asking people what such a good is worth to them, the approach later called {{ref:nature-val-085}}.

Most environmental goods fall into this group. Without prices, putting a value on them is inherently uncertain. That difficulty is one reason the environment is usually left out of measures of wealth. In 1947 S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed a way around it: surveys asking people what such a good is worth to them, the approach later called Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey.

entries.title: Non-use value: caring about what you never use

definition.text: The value people place on a good, often a natural resource, even if they never have used it and never will.

facts.text: It is distinguished from use value, which comes from using the good directly.
It can include option value, bequest value, existence value and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it.
All these categories grew from the idea of option value introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964.
Because market prices and other revealed preference methods generally cannot measure it, stated preference surveys such as contingent valuation are used.
Ecosystem valuation sorts the value of ecosystem services into use and non-use categories.

entries.text: People can value a resource they have never used and never will. Economists call this non-use value. It is often attached to resources from nature, and it stands apart from use value, which comes from using a good directly. Non-use value has several strands. It can include {{ref:nature-val-055}}, {{ref:nature-val-053}}, {{ref:nature-val-054}} and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it. All these categories grew from the first of them, introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964. Measuring them is hard. Market prices and other methods that read value from what people buy generally cannot capture it, because nobody is buying anything. Economists instead ask people directly in surveys, such as {{ref:nature-val-085}}. Attempts to value ecosystems sort the value of their services into use and non-use categories.

It is often attached to resources from nature, and it stands apart from use value, which comes from using a good directly. Non-use value has several strands. It can include Option value: paying to keep choices open, Bequest value: saving nature for future generations, Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it. All these categories grew from the first of them, introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964. Measuring them is hard. Market prices and other methods that read value from what people buy generally cannot capture it, because nobody is buying anything. entries.title: Total economic value: adding up nature's worth

definition.text: The full value people get from a natural resource, heritage site or infrastructure compared with not having it, built up from several kinds of value.

facts.text: In environmental economics it adds up the values that an ecosystem provides.
It splits into use value, direct (removable products such as timber, fish and water) or indirect (non-removable things such as a sunset or waterfall), and non-use value.
Non-use value covers simply knowing a resource exists, such as knowing tigers live in the wild though you may never see one.
Option value is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when future use is unlikely.
Bequest value comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations.
Cost–benefit analysis uses a similar approach to the environmental analysis of total economic value.

entries.text: Most people will never see a tiger in the wild, yet knowing tigers live there is worth something to many of them. Total economic value tries to count that, along with everything else. It is the full value people get from a resource drawn from nature, a heritage site or piece of infrastructure, compared with not having it. In environmental economics it adds up the values an ecosystem provides. It is built in layers. Use value comes first, split into direct and indirect. Direct use covers removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use covers non-removable things such as a sunset or a waterfall. Non-use value comes next. It covers simply knowing that a resource exists, as with those tigers. Two more strands look ahead. One, {{ref:nature-val-055}}, is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when that use is unlikely. Another, {{ref:nature-val-053}}, comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Adding the layers gives a single figure. {{ref:nature-val-001}} uses a similar approach.

entries.title: Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there

definition.text: The benefit people get simply from knowing that something, such as Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species, exists.

facts.text: It is a leading example of non-use value, since no direct use of the resource is needed.
John V. Krutilla introduced the idea in his essay 'Conservation Reconsidered', arguing that undisturbed wilderness has economic value.
It is usually measured with contingent valuation surveys.
Since Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law.
Damages after the Exxon Valdez oil spill included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

entries.text: A wilderness can be worth money even if nobody ever walks into it. That was the argument of {{ref:nature-hist-041}}, in the essay that introduced the idea of existence value. It is the benefit people get simply from knowing that something exists, whether Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species. Because no direct use is needed, it is a leading example of non-use value. It is usually measured with {{ref:nature-val-085}} surveys. The idea has legal force. Since the case Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law. After the {{ref:nature-val-076}}, damages included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.
entries.text_plain: A wilderness can be worth money even if nobody ever walks into it. That was the argument of John Krutilla and the value of wilderness, in the essay that introduced the idea of existence value. It is the benefit people get simply from knowing that something exists, whether Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species. Because no direct use is needed, it is a leading example of non-use value. It is usually measured with Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey surveys. The idea has legal force. Since the case Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law. After the The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage, damages included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

entries.title: Option value: paying to keep choices open

definition.text: What people are willing to pay to keep a public asset or service available even if they are unlikely ever to use it.

facts.text: It is used in policy assessment to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services.
In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened natural resources so they might be used in future.
Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964, resting it on uncertain future need, irreversible or costly loss, and the asset not being storable.
Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility.
It differs from option value in finance, though both can be read as valuing risk.

entries.text: Why fund a rail service or a wildlife refuge that most taxpayers will rarely use? Option value is one answer. It is what people are willing to pay to keep a public facility or service available, even if they are unlikely ever to use it. Policy assessments use it to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services. In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened resources from nature so they might be used in future. Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964. He rested it on three conditions: future need is uncertain, loss would be irreversible or costly, and the thing itself cannot be stored. Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility. Option value in finance is a different idea, though both can be read as ways of valuing risk.

It is what people are willing to pay to keep a public facility or service available, even if they are unlikely ever to use it. Policy assessments use it to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services. In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened resources from nature so they might be used in future. Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964. He rested it on three conditions: future need is uncertain, loss would be irreversible or costly, and the thing itself cannot be stored. entries.title: Bequest value: saving nature for future generations

definition.text: The satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations.

facts.text: It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service.
Together with existence value it makes up non-use value.
Ecosystem valuation counts it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations.
In some optimization models it is called the 'salvage value' of the system.

entries.text: Part of what people value in nature is what they can hand on. Bequest value is the satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Together with existence value, it makes up non-use value. It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service. Attempts to value ecosystems count it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations. In some optimization models, mathematical models that search for the best plan, it goes by another name: the 'salvage value' of the system.

entries.title: Direct and indirect use: taking versus enjoying

definition.text: The split of use value into direct use, from goods taken from nature, and indirect use, from benefits nature provides without anything being removed.

facts.text: Direct use value comes from removable products such as timber, fish and water; indirect use value from things like a sunset or waterfall.
In ecosystem valuation, indirect use value comes through the positive externalities ecosystems provide.
For livestock breeds, direct use value is milk or meat, while indirect use value includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control.
Use and indirect use values can often be inferred from behaviour, such as recreational trip costs or hedonic pricing.

sources.title: Animal genetic resources for food and agriculture

entries.text: Catching a fish and watching a waterfall both use nature, but only one takes something away. Direct use value comes from removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use value comes from things like a sunset, where nothing is removed. When ecosystems are valued, indirect use value arrives through the positive externalities ecosystems provide, benefits that reach people without a price. For livestock breeds, direct use is milk or meat. Indirect use includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control. Both can often be inferred from behavior, such as trip costs.

entries.title: Relational values: ties between people and nature

definition.text: Values arising from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.

facts.text: They sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means, in one framing of nature's values.
Western regenerative agriculture has been criticised for ignoring the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice.

entries.text: Some ties to nature are neither about usefulness nor about worth in itself. Relational values arise from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. In one framing of nature's values they sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means. Ignoring them has costs. Western {{ref:nature-nbs-258}} has been criticized for overlooking the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice: a wrong done to people in their capacity as knowers.
entries.text_plain: Some ties to nature are neither about usefulness nor about worth in itself. Relational values arise from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. In one framing of nature's values they sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means. Ignoring them has costs. Western Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild, not just sustain has been criticized for overlooking the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice: a wrong done to people in their capacity as knowers.

entries.title: Revealed preference: judging people by their choices

definition.text: A way of working out what people prefer from the choices they actually make, pioneered by Paul Samuelson in 1938.

facts.text: It assumes people's preferences show in their purchasing habits.
It arose because utility, the satisfaction behind choices, could not be measured directly, so economists defined it from observed behaviour instead.
It contrasts with stated preference approaches, which ask people directly; economists usually trust revealed preferences more.
If bundle a is chosen when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b.
In ecosystem valuation, revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost link a service to a market good to estimate willingness to pay.

The logic is simple. If someone chooses bundle a when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b. entries.title: Ecosystem valuation: putting numbers on nature's services

definition.text: The process of assigning a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides.

facts.text: Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage is meant to help policy-makers compare policies through cost-benefit analysis.
In 1997 Robert Costanza and colleagues made the first estimate of the worldwide worth of ecosystem services: $33 trillion a year.
It draws on stated preference methods such as contingent valuation and revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost.
TEEB found ecosystem service values ranging from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded and may be non-rival and non-excludable.
Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and the money value society gives to services depends on how income is distributed.
Some programmes go on to pay landowners for services; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests.

entries.contested_note: Sources describe ecosystem valuation as philosophically and ethically controversial, with debate over whether nature should be priced at all.
entries.text: In 1997 {{ref:nature-hist-048}} and colleagues made the first estimate of what the world's ecosystem services are worth: $33 trillion a year. Ecosystem valuation is the process behind numbers like that. It assigns a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides. The aim is practical. Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage helps policy-makers compare policies through {{ref:nature-val-001}}. The tools come in two families. Survey methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-085}}, ask people what they would pay. Revealed preference methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-092}} and {{ref:nature-val-088}}, infer it from behavior. The results vary enormously. TEEB found values from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs. Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded. Many are also non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use leaves no less for others, and no one can be kept out. Some programs go on to pay landowners; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests. Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and that the money value of services depends on how income is distributed. Behind this lies a philosophical and ethical dispute over whether nature should be priced at all.

entries.title: Hedonic regression: reading value from house prices

definition.text: A revealed preference method that estimates the value of each characteristic of a good, such as a house, by breaking its price into contributions from its features.

facts.text: It is usually estimated with regression analysis and is used in real estate, environmental economics, marketing research and Consumer Price Index calculations.
In environmental work it measures how much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding other house features fixed.
A house is treated as a bundle of features, such as bedrooms, lot size and distance from the city centre, each given its own price.
Hedonic modelling was first published in the 1920s to value farm land, with roots also traced to Court's 1939 study of car prices.
Some critics argue its use in the US CPI can understate inflation, while studies abroad show non-hedonic methods can misstate inflation by ignoring quality change.

entries.title: Willingness to accept: the price of putting up with harm

definition.text: The smallest amount of money a person would take to sell a good or service, or to put up with a harm such as pollution.

facts.text: It is the counterpart of willingness to pay, the most a buyer would give up to get something or avoid something unwanted; both are reservation prices.
A trade's price falls between the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's willingness to accept, and the gap between them is the economic surplus.
It can be estimated with choice experiments or asked directly in contingent valuation surveys.
Formally, it is the payment that makes a person's utility after an unwanted change, with compensation, equal to their utility before it.
Which measure applies depends on property rights: if lakeside residents have a right to a clean lake, their willingness to accept compensation for pollution counts.

entries.title: Travel cost analysis: valuing a park by the trip

definition.text: A revealed preference method that values a place without a market price, such as a national park or beach, from what visitors spend in time and money to get there.

facts.text: Harold Hotelling suggested it in a 1947 letter to the US National Park Service; Trice and Wood (1958) and Clawson (1959) refined it.
People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often, while those nearby visit more and spend less.
Visitors are grouped into distance zones, each zone's visit rate is regressed on travel cost, and the result builds a demand curve for the site.
The area under that demand curve gives willingness to pay for the site, used as its value in cost-benefit analysis.

entries.text: A park may charge no market price, but reaching it costs visitors time and money. {{ref:nature-hist-062}} suggested using that fact in a 1947 letter to the US park service. People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often; those nearby visit more and spend less. Analysts group visitors into distance zones and use regression to relate each zone's visit rate to its travel cost. The result builds a {{ref:nature-econ-371}} for the site. The area under that curve gives visitors' willingness to pay, which serves as the site's value in {{ref:nature-val-001}}. Trice and Wood refined the method in 1958, and Clawson in 1959.
