entries.title: The weak axiom: a rule for consistent choice
entries.article: Revealed preference#The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)

definition.text: A consistency rule saying that if a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable.

facts.text: The strong axiom (SARP) adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other, which preserves transitivity.
The generalised axiom (GARP) extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

entries.text: Revealed preference needs a rule for what counts as consistent choice. The weak axiom of revealed preference supplies the basic one. If a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable. Stronger rules build on it. The strong axiom, SARP, adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other. That preserves transitivity. Anyone who prefers a to b and b to c then prefers c least. The generalized axiom, GARP, extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

entries.title: Afriat's theorem: from choices to a utility function

definition.text: A 1967 result by Sydney Afriat proving that a finite set of observed choices satisfying GARP can be explained by a utility function.

facts.text: Its inequalities let the utility function be built directly from the data, unlike SARP, which only proves existence for infinite datasets.
It is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and build preferences from empirical data.

entries.text: In 1967 Sydney Afriat proved a useful result for anyone studying choices. A finite set of observed choices that satisfies GARP, the generalized consistency rule, can be explained by a utility function, a rule that scores each option. His inequalities go further and let that function be built directly from the data. SARP, by contrast, only proves such a function exists for infinite datasets. The theorem is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and to build preferences from real data.

entries.title: Benefit transfer: borrowing values from earlier studies

definition.text: A valuation method that estimates a project's benefits by borrowing the data, models and results of earlier studies of similar projects or sites.

facts.text: It comes in two forms: value transfer moves a single unit value from an earlier site, while function transfer uses valuation functions drawn from many studies and can be more accurate.
Meta-analysis can be used to build a valuation transfer.
Its common errors are measurement error, from biased study selection and assumptions, and transfer error, when the original and new sites do not correspond.
It is a cheap way to value a project when time and money rule out original research.

Measurement error comes from biased study selection and assumptions. Transfer error arises when the original and new sites do not correspond.

entries.title: Replacement cost: what it takes to start over

definition.text: The amount one would have to pay at today's prices to replace an asset with an undamaged equivalent.

facts.text: It can differ from market value and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts depreciation.
Insurers use it as one way to value an insured item, such as paying the price of a similar new television today.
In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads matters because it can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

entries.text: An insurer valuing a television can pay the price of a similar new one today. That is replacement cost: the amount needed, at today's prices, to replace something with an undamaged equivalent. It can differ from market value, and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts {{ref:nature-econ-519}}. The idea matters beyond insurance. In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

entries.title: Stated preference: asking people what they value

definition.text: Valuation methods that measure what people value by asking them directly in surveys, rather than watching what they buy.

facts.text: Contingent valuation, which asks people their willingness to pay for an ecosystem or one of its services, is the best-known stated preference method.
Non-use values are usually estimated with stated preference methods such as contingent valuation or choice modelling, because people's market behaviour reveals nothing about them.
Ecosystem valuation divides its methods into stated preference and revealed preference families.
Conjoint analysis and choice modelling are also used for stated preference research, and David Hensher and Jordan Louviere are credited with the first stated preference choice models.
Many economists distrust stated preferences and prefer people's revealed preferences in binding market transactions when judging willingness to pay.
Revealed and stated preference data can be combined to get the advantages of both.

entries.contested_note: Many economists question whether survey answers can be trusted to measure willingness to pay.
entries.text: Sometimes the only way to learn what people value is to ask. Stated preference methods measure value through surveys rather than by watching what people buy. Ecosystem valuation divides its methods into this family and the revealed preference family. The best known is {{ref:nature-val-085}}, which asks people their willingness to pay for an ecosystem or one of its services. Survey-based choice experiments are also used, and David Hensher and Jordan Louviere are credited with the first stated preference choice models. Non-use values are usually measured this way, because people's market behavior reveals nothing about them. Many economists remain unconvinced. They question whether survey answers can be trusted, and prefer the evidence of binding market purchases. One middle path combines revealed and stated data to get the advantages of both.

entries.title: Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey

definition.text: A survey-based technique for putting a money value on things that are not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution.

facts.text: The survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity, or how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss.
It is called a stated preference method, as opposed to revealed preference methods that rely on prices people actually pay.
Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed the idea in theory in 1947, and Robert K. Davis first applied it in 1963 to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists.
It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s, when governments gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values.
The Exxon Valdez oil spill was the first case where its surveys were used to put numbers on damages.
Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits, and many economists prefer evidence from real market purchases.
US government departments have used it widely in cost-benefit analyses of projects that affect the environment, such as valuing river recreation below Glen Canyon dam.
Clive Spash's research found that many willingness-to-pay answers behaved like charitable donations rather than the trade prices economists assumed.

entries.contested_note: Many economists doubt that survey answers about willingness to pay reflect real values, while defenders say newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

entries.title: The NOAA panel: can surveys be trusted?

definition.text: A panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, convened by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to judge whether contingent valuation surveys could be trusted.

facts.text: It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993.
It recommended personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum format on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats.
Preferring cautious estimates, it advised measuring willingness to pay to protect a good rather than willingness to accept its loss.
It judged that well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values.

entries.text: Could surveys of willingness to pay be trusted? The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration convened a panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, to judge. It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993. Its verdict was a cautious yes. Well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values. Good design meant personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats. Preferring cautious estimates, the panel advised asking willingness to pay to protect a good, not willingness to accept its loss.

entries.title: The embedding effect: when part and whole do not add up

definition.text: A bias in contingent valuation where people struggle to put a value on one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods.

facts.text: It suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased way to measure policy effects in cost-benefit analysis.
Part-whole bias arises when willingness to pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to willingness to pay for both together.
Willingness to pay for a project is larger when it is asked about first than when it comes second in a sequence.
One fix asks first what people would pay for the whole set of items, then how much of that should go to the named item.

Part-whole bias is related: what people would pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to what they would pay for both together. The effect suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased measure of policy effects. One fix asks about the whole set first, then the named item's share.

entries.article: Willingness to accept#Standard theory versus experimental results

definition.text: The finding that people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it, even though standard theory predicts the two amounts should match.

facts.text: Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely found willingness to accept for basketball tickets was more than 10 times willingness to pay.
Explanations include income limits on what people can pay and the endowment effect, where owning something triggers loss aversion.
Plott and Zeiler argued the gaps partly reflect participants misunderstanding the experimental task.
The gap matters for contingent valuation, where endowment effects are widespread.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree whether the gap reflects real loss aversion or flaws in experimental design.

entries.title: Compensating differentials: the extra pay for a bad job

definition.text: The extra pay a worker must be offered to take an unpleasant or risky job instead of other jobs they could do.

facts.text: For an especially pleasant job the differential is negative: workers accept lower pay.
The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and wage gaps between regions.
Economists usually expect wages to be lower in places with high levels of amenity, so wage gaps can reveal how much an area's attractiveness is worth.
A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the probability of injury.

entries.text: Risky jobs have to pay extra to attract workers. A compensating differential is that extra pay, offered so someone takes an unpleasant or risky job instead of other work. For an especially pleasant job it runs the other way: workers accept lower pay. The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and regional wage gaps. A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the chance of injury. Economists expect lower wages in pleasant places, so wage gaps can reveal what an area's attractiveness is worth.

entries.title: Choice modeling: learning value from trade-offs

definition.text: A family of methods that model how a person or group decides, using either their real choices or choices they state in a set context.

facts.text: It usually infers where items sit on a hidden scale, typically utility, from repeated choices of one option over another.
It is regarded as the best method for estimating willingness to pay for quality improvements that vary in several dimensions at once.
Its roots lie in Thurstone's 1920s research on food preferences and in random utility theory, which Daniel McFadden developed in economics.
McFadden used past transport choices to predict demand for the Bay Area Rapid Transit before it was built, work that earned him the 2000 Nobel economics prize.
A survey describes a good by attributes and levels; because full combinations explode, a phone with 2 brands, 3 shapes, 3 sizes and 4 memory options has 72, only a subset is shown.
It forces respondents to weigh trade-offs between attributes and lets analysts estimate implicit prices for each attribute.
In environmental economics, non-use values are usually estimated with stated preference methods such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.

entries.title: Discrete choice: modeling either-or decisions

definition.text: Models that describe and predict choices between separate alternatives, such as which mode of transport to take, rather than how much of something to buy.

facts.text: A model gives the probability that a person chooses a given alternative as a function of features of the alternatives and of the person.
They can be derived from utility theory, and only differences in utility between alternatives affect the choice probabilities.
The first applications were in transportation planning, and in market research the approach is commonly called conjoint analysis.
Common forms include binary logit and probit, multinomial and conditional logit, nested logit and mixed logit, usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Standard logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives, a substitution pattern that is not always realistic; mixed logit relaxes it by allowing tastes to vary between people.

entries.title: Conjoint analysis: pricing a product's parts

definition.text: A survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research, that works out how much people value each attribute that makes up a product or service.

facts.text: Respondents see a controlled set of products broken down by attribute, and their choices reveal the implicit value, or part-worth, of each attribute.

It is also called discrete choice modelling or stated preference research.
Because the number of attribute combinations grows exponentially, fractional factorial designs cut the profiles respondents must judge.

entries.title: Random utility: why rational choices look random

definition.text: A random utility model describes a person's preferences when their choices are not fixed but depend on a random, unobserved state.

facts.text: Classic economics assumes a rational person picks the alternative with the highest utility, which can be inferred from observed choices.
In practice people facing the same alternatives may choose differently, so their choices look random to an observer.
The model gives each person a distribution over utility functions rather than a single one, and assumes rational behaviour given the hidden state.
Choice experiments assume how often item A is chosen over item B measures how much it is preferred.
A popular version was developed by Luce and Plackett.

entries.title: Multinomial logit: choosing among many options

definition.text: Multinomial logistic regression is a statistical method that predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables.

facts.text: It is also called the multinomial logit, softmax regression or the maximum entropy classifier, among other names.
In discrete choice theory, each outcome's score is read as the utility a person gets from choosing it, with a random part standing for unmodelled factors.
Used for choices, it assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present.
Many psychology studies show that people often violate this assumption.
In best–worst scaling studies it is often the first stage of analysis, giving average utilities for items.

entries.title: The Exxon Valdez spill: putting a price on damage

definition.text: The Exxon Valdez oil spill was a major environmental disaster in Prince William Sound, Alaska, on March 24, 1989.

facts.text: The supertanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef and spilled more than 10 million US gallons of crude oil over the next few days.
It was the first case where contingent valuation surveys were used in a quantitative assessment of damages, and use of the technique spread from there.
Existence values were part of the legal damage assessment after the spill.
An Anchorage jury awarded $287 million in actual damages and $5 billion in punitive damages, which an appeals court ordered reduced.

entries.title: The probit model: predicting yes or no

definition.text: A probit model is a regression model for a dependent variable that can take only two values, built on the normal distribution.

facts.text: It estimates the probability that an observation with given characteristics falls into one of the two categories, the same problem logistic regression handles.
It can be motivated as a latent variable model, with the outcome showing whether an unobserved variable is positive.
It is usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Chester Bliss coined the term in 1934, though the basic model goes back to Fechner in 1860.

entries.title: Mixed logit: letting tastes vary

definition.text: Mixed logit is a fully general statistical model for analysing discrete choices, in which tastes are allowed to vary randomly between people.

facts.text: It overcomes three limits of standard logit: it allows random taste variation, unrestricted substitution patterns, and correlation in unobserved factors over time.
Unlike standard logit, it does not impose the restrictive independence of irrelevant alternatives property.
With suitable specification it can approximate any random utility model of discrete choice to any accuracy.
Its choice probability has no closed form, so it must be estimated by simulation, drawing repeatedly from the taste distribution.

entries.title: Best–worst scaling: picking extremes

definition.text: Best–worst scaling is a survey choice method in which respondents pick the best and the worst item from a subset of a longer list.

facts.text: Jordan Louviere invented it in 1987 at the University of Alberta, as a form of choice modelling or discrete choice experiment.
The task is repeated with subsets varied by a statistical design, and choices are usually analysed with a random utility model.
Because respondents choose rather than rate, it avoids scale-use bias and stops every item being rated 'quite important'.
It is hard to know how to combine best and worst answers when people use different decision rules for each.

entries.title: Scope neglect: when bigger harms do not count more

definition.text: Scope neglect is a cognitive bias in which the value people place on a problem does not grow in proportion to its size.

facts.text: In one study people were willing to pay $80, $78 and $88 to save 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds.
Other willingness-to-pay studies have found a logarithmic relationship or no relationship to the size of the harm.
Daniel Kahneman explains it as judgment by prototype: people price a mental image, such as one oil-soaked bird, rather than the number affected.
It is a specific form of extension neglect, closely linked to the 'mass numbing' studied by Paul Slovic.

entries.text: In one study people would pay $80 to save 2,000 migrating birds from drowning in oil ponds. For 20,000 birds they offered $78, and for 200,000, $88. entries.title: Cheap talk: words that cost nothing

definition.text: In game theory, cheap talk is costless communication between players whose messages do not directly change the game's payoffs.

facts.text: Cheap talk is non-binding and cannot be verified by a third party, so a speaker could lie freely but may choose not to.
It differs from signalling, where sending some messages can be costly for the sender.
In a coordination game a round of cheap talk can help players reach better outcomes, but in the Prisoner's Dilemma it is ignored.

entries.title: Hypothetical bias: saying is not paying

definition.text: Hypothetical bias is the distortion in values people state in surveys about goods they do not actually have to pay for or give up.

facts.text: A public health study found hypothetical bias is greater when people have less information about a good and information is costly.
Stated willingness to pay is lower when hypothetical bias is high, widening the gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay.
John A. List studied whether explicit warnings remove hypothetical bias in elicitation procedures.

entries.title: Latent class models: finding hidden groups

definition.text: A latent class model is a statistical model that sorts multivariate discrete data into hidden groups, or classes.

facts.text: It assumes the data come from a mixture of distributions, with the variables independent within each class.
It is called latent because each data point's class is not observed.
For example, answers to a political questionnaire could reveal latent classes corresponding to political groups.

entries.title: Meta-regression: why studies disagree

definition.text: Meta-regression is a meta-analysis that uses regression to combine and compare findings from many studies while adjusting for study characteristics.

facts.text: It aims to reconcile conflicting studies or confirm consistent ones.
Fixed-effect versions assume the studies do not really differ, while mixed-effect versions allow for variation between studies and are often the most flexible choice.
It has been applied to the value of a statistical life, energy and water policy, and price elasticities for water and energy.
It is increasingly used to weigh evidence across many cost-benefit studies of a policy or programme.

entries.title: Net present value: future money in today's terms

definition.text: A way to judge an investment by turning all its future gains and costs into today's money and adding them up.

facts.text: Money now is worth more than the same amount later, because money in hand can be invested at once and start earning returns.
Each period's net cash flow is discounted back to the present at a rate equal to what a similarly risky investment could earn, and the results are summed.
A lender might pay 99 cents today for $1.00 due in a month, but much less for a dollar due in 20 years.
A positive value means expected earnings exceed costs in today's money, and the Net Present Value Rule says only such investments should be made.
The result depends heavily on the chosen discount rate and on knowing future cash flows, so sensitivity analysis is used to test it.
When large costs fall late in a project, such as mine clean-up and restoration, a high discount rate makes the project look too good.
It is purely financial and ignores non-financial considerations relevant to a decision.
As a valuation method it dates at least to the 19th century.

entries.title: Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses

definition.text: A systematic way of judging alternatives by estimating and comparing their benefits and their costs.

facts.text: It is used to decide whether a project, policy or investment is sound, and to compare options by their total expected costs and benefits.
Benefits and costs are put in money terms and adjusted for the time value of money, so flows at different dates are summed as a net present value.
A generic analysis lists alternatives and stakeholders, measures costs and benefits, converts them to one currency, discounts them, computes net present value and runs a sensitivity analysis.
Benefits are valued by listing everyone affected and adding up the money value each places on the change in their welfare.
Costs are usually measured more fully than benefits, because market data on costs are relatively plentiful.
In the 21st century environmental effects are typically valued through the ecosystem services they provide to people, such as air and water quality.
Its usefulness depends on the accuracy of the cost and benefit estimates, and comparative studies find those estimates are often flawed.
Interest groups may try to include or leave out large costs to sway the result.

entries.title: Shadow prices: money values where markets are silent

definition.text: A money value given to something that is not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects.

facts.text: Shadow prices are needed because of externalities and because taxes, subsidies, quotas and tariffs distort market prices.
They are often built from assumptions and estimates for lack of reliable data, so they are subjective and somewhat inaccurate.
They are still widely used in cost–benefit analyses to put money values on intangible costs and benefits, especially for public goods rarely bought and sold.
Tools for estimating them include contingent valuation, benefit transfer and revealed-preference methods such as hedonic pricing and the travel cost method.
Inclusive wealth measures use shadow prices as weights on produced, human and natural capital.
Their use for natural capital is controversial because little is known about how to represent the production functions of life-supporting ecosystems.

entries.text: Clean air has no price tag, yet a cost–benefit analysis needs one. A shadow price fills the gap. It is a money value given to something not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects. Shadow prices are needed for two reasons. Externalities, costs and benefits that fall on people outside a deal, go unpriced. And taxes, subsidies, quotas and tariffs distort market prices. Tools for estimating them include contingent valuation, benefit transfer, hedonic pricing and the travel cost method. Lacking reliable data, analysts often build them from assumptions, so they are subjective and somewhat inaccurate. They are still widely used to value intangible costs and benefits, especially for public goods rarely bought and sold. Measures of a nation's total wealth use them as weights on produced, human and natural capital. That use is controversial, because little is known about how life-supporting ecosystems produce their benefits.

entries.title: The value of a statistical life

definition.text: A money value for avoiding one death on average, based on what people will pay for small reductions in their risk of dying.

facts.text: It values changes in the chance of death, not what someone would pay to avoid certain death, so it is very different from the value of an actual life.
If 100,000 people would each pay $100 to cut their yearly risk of death by 1 in 100,000, together they would pay $10 million for one statistical life saved.

Economists estimate it from extra pay for risky jobs (compensating differentials), from surveys of willingness to pay, or from discounted lifetime earnings, and each method can over- or understate it.
It lets policy analysts put a money figure on lives saved so limited resources can be allocated in cost–benefit analysis.
Environmental economists use it as a health-based measure of how much people will pay to reduce their risk of dying from environmental hazards.
Values vary widely: Sweden's estimates range from 9 to 98 million SEK, and the UK put preventing a fatal casualty at £1.7m in 2013 prices.
Philosophers such as Elizabeth Anderson argue that the wage data are unreliable and that life and environmental goods cannot be put on one money scale.
Health economics more often uses the quality-adjusted life year, which scores quality of life from 0 to 1 rather than monetising willingness to pay.

entries.contested_note: Economists and philosophers dispute both the methods used to estimate it and whether lives should be valued in money at all.

entries.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis: comparing without pricing

definition.text: A form of economic analysis that compares the costs and the outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes.

facts.text: Unlike cost–benefit analysis, it does not monetise the effect, which makes it common in health care where pricing health is seen as inappropriate.
Results are usually a ratio of cost to a health gain such as years of life; the most common outcome measure is the quality-adjusted life year.
For some environmental goals with one physical outcome, such as cutting energy use, it can replace cost–benefit analysis and is less laborious.
It is preferred in climate economics when the benefits of mitigation and adaptation are hard to express in money.
Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis extends it to weigh how outcomes are spread, trading equity against efficiency.
A 1995 review of over 500 life-saving interventions found a median of $42,000 per life-year saved.

entries.title: QALYs: counting years by their quality

definition.text: A measure of health that combines how long and how well people live, where one unit equals one year in perfect health.

facts.text: Scores run from 1 for perfect health to 0 for death, so a year lived at a utility of 0.5 counts as 0.5 QALYs.
QALYs gained equal the change in health utility from a treatment times how long the effect lasts.
Health-state weights come from methods such as the time trade-off, the standard gamble and visual rating scales, or questionnaires like the EQ-5D.
Combined with costs it gives a cost per QALY, used in cost-utility analysis to compare treatments; the UK's NICE has used pounds per QALY since 1999.
Critics say it undervalues people with disabilities and the elderly and ignores how health is distributed; Oregon's 1989 Medicaid plan using it was found discriminatory.
Supporters reply that with limited health budgets it allocates resources in a roughly optimal way for society.
In 2018 HM Treasury set a 1.5% discount rate for QALYs, lower than for other costs and benefits, because a QALY measures utility directly.
The term first appeared in print in a 1976 article by Zeckhauser and Shepard.

entries.contested_note: The theoretical assumptions behind QALYs and their use to ration treatment are openly debated by health economists, disability advocates and regulators.

entries.title: Discounting: how much the future counts

definition.text: Putting costs and benefits that occur at different times on a common footing by converting them to present values with a discount rate.

facts.text: Net present value adds up each year's benefits minus costs, each divided by one plus the discount rate raised to the number of years ahead.
The choice of discount rate is subjective, and it makes a large difference for projects with long-term effects.
A small rate treats the current and future generations almost equally; a large rate such as a market return mirrors people's preference for money sooner rather than later.
If long-run stock returns are higher than risk alone explains (the equity premium puzzle), market rates would undervalue the distant future.
Critics argue discounting biases cost–benefit analysis against future generations and understates the harm from climate change.
For private firms the discount rate is often taken from asset pricing models such as the capital asset pricing model.

entries.contested_note: Scholars disagree over whether and how strongly future costs and benefits, such as climate damage, should be discounted.

entries.text: How much should harm to future generations count today? Discounting is how cost–benefit analysis answers. The choice of rate is subjective, and for long-term projects it makes a large difference. A small rate treats current and future generations almost equally. A large rate, such as a market return, mirrors people's preference for money sooner rather than later. If long-run share-market returns are higher than risk alone explains, the equity premium puzzle, market rates would undervalue the distant future. Private firms often take their rate from models such as the capital asset pricing model. Critics argue that discounting biases the analysis against future generations and understates the harm from climate change. Scholars still disagree over whether, and how strongly, such effects should be discounted.

entries.title: The case against cost–benefit analysis

definition.text: Objections that cost–benefit analysis ignores who gains and who loses, discounts the future too heavily and leaves out values that cannot be priced.

facts.text: It rests on the Kaldor–Hicks criterion, so a positive net benefit counts as decisive regardless of who wins and who loses.
As a result it can overlook equity and favour policies that help some groups while burdening others.
Discounting may undervalue distant harms such as climate change and ignore the preferences of future generations.
Because an extra dollar matters less to the rich, unweighted willingness to pay gives wealthier people's preferences more weight.
Limiting benefits to economic values leaves out things such as minority wishes, inclusiveness and respect for others' rights.
Some writers judge it unsuitable for analysing climate change mitigation as a whole.

entries.contested_note: Supporters and critics disagree on whether cost–benefit analysis can fairly judge policies with uneven or long-term effects.

entries.title: Multiple-criteria decision analysis: juggling conflicting goals

definition.text: A field of decision science that explicitly weighs several conflicting criteria, such as cost and quality, when choosing among options.

facts.text: Cost is usually one criterion and some measure of quality another, and the two often pull in opposite directions.
When stakes are high, such as deciding whether and where to build a nuclear power plant, structuring the problem and its criteria explicitly leads to better decisions.
There is usually no single best answer, so the decision-maker's preferences are needed to tell solutions apart.
Ecological economists favour multi-criteria analysis as an alternative to standard cost–benefit reasoning.
It has been applied to sustainability assessment, desertification risk and wind farm siting.

entries.title: Regulatory impact analysis: testing a rule before it takes effect

definition.text: A document prepared before a new government regulation is introduced that systematically appraises its likely impacts.

facts.text: Its central economic purpose is to make sure a regulation improves society's welfare, meaning its benefits exceed its costs.
It is usually comparative, analysing different ways of reaching the same objective.
The first ones are usually traced to the inflation impact assessments the Carter Administration required from 1978; under Reagan, benefit–cost analysis became the required method.
By 2000, 20 of 28 OECD countries required them, and virtually all OECD countries now use them; the World Bank has spread them to developing countries.
The European Commission's impact assessments, introduced in 2002, weigh economic, environmental and social effects of policy options.
The social cost of carbon is commonly used in these analyses to inform climate policy.

entries.title: DALYs: measuring the burden of disease

definition.text: A measure of disease burden in which one unit equals one year of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death.

facts.text: It adds years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability into a single number.
Each condition gets a disability weight from 0 (no disability) to 1, for example 0.666 for Alzheimer's and other dementias.
It is not a money measure, but costs can be expressed per DALY to guide health spending, such as $670 per DALY saved for a pneumococcal vaccine in Gambia.
It and the quality-adjusted life year are both health-adjusted life years.
It was developed in 1990 by Harvard for the World Bank in the Global Burden of Disease Study and adopted by the World Health Organization in 1996.
Before 2010 the WHO used age weighting and 3 percent time discounting, criticised for valuing young adults above children and the old.

entries.contested_note: Critics say DALYs measure productive capacity, while defenders reply that disability weights reflect effects on life in general, not ability to work.

entries.title: Cost–benefit review comes to US regulation

definition.text: The rise of mandatory cost–benefit review of federal rules in the United States from 1981 onward.

facts.text: Reagan's 1981 Executive Order 12291 made federal agencies produce regulatory impact analyses for rules with annual impacts above $100 million, reviewed by OIRA.
Critics in the 1980s said the method could serve political goals, was biased against regulation, and caused long delays.
Clinton's Executive Order 12866 required benefits to justify rather than exceed costs, and the practice continued under Obama.

entries.contested_note: Analysts still disagree over whether cost–benefit analysis should be used in setting regulations at all.

entries.title: Distributional weights: making a poor person's dollar count

definition.text: Weights applied to gains and losses so that a dollar to a poor person counts for more than a dollar to a rich one.

facts.text: Without weights, unweighted willingness to pay overstates costs and benefits to the wealthy and understates them for the poor.
Not weighting is itself a choice that gives richer people a bigger weight in practice.
Weights are often derived from a Bergson–Samuelson social welfare function; another option measures willingness to pay as a share of income or wealth.

entries.title: From Dupuit's bridges to government policy

definition.text: The development of cost–benefit analysis from a nineteenth-century engineering idea into a standard tool of government.

facts.text: The idea goes back to an 1848 article by Jules Dupuit and was formalised later by Alfred Marshall.
Dupuit measured the social benefit of a road or bridge by adding up what each user would be willing to pay for it.
In the US the Federal Navigation Act of 1936 required it for federal waterway projects, and the Flood Control Act of 1939 made it federal policy.
Otto Eckstein gave it a welfare-economics foundation in 1958, and in the 1960s it was applied to water quality, recreation and land conservation.

entries.title: Handling risk in cost–benefit analysis

definition.text: The ways a cost–benefit analysis handles uncertain outcomes, chiefly with probability, sensitivity analysis and simulation.

facts.text: Risk can be built into the discount rate but is usually treated separately, often allowing for people's risk aversion.
A sensitivity analysis shows how the result changes when the input values change.
A more formal risk analysis can use the Monte Carlo method, with input distributions sometimes chosen by the principle of maximum entropy.

entries.title: Payback period: how long to break even

definition.text: The time an investment takes to earn back the money spent on it, or to reach the break-even point.

facts.text: A $1000 investment that returns $500 at the end of each of its first two years has a two-year payback period.
It is often quoted for energy efficiency upgrades, such as a compact fluorescent bulb, where the return is lower operating costs.
It ignores the time value of money, risk and cash flows after payback, so economists prefer net present value or internal rate of return.
The related energy payback time is how long a project takes to save as much energy as was spent creating it.

entries.title: Shadow prices in optimization

definition.text: The change in the best achievable value of an objective when a constraint is relaxed by one small unit.

facts.text: Formally it equals the Lagrange multiplier of the constraint at the optimal solution, and every constraint has one, also called a dual variable.
In business it is the most a manager would pay for one more unit of a limited resource, such as an extra hour on a production line already at its 40-hour limit.
In optimal control theory the idea reappears as costate variables; in a Hamiltonian they are current-value shadow prices of capital goods.
Under Hotelling's rule, the resource rent equals the shadow value of the natural resource.

In optimization, the shadow price is the change in the best achievable value of an objective when a constraint is relaxed by one small unit. entries.title: Pricing the energy that is never used

definition.text: Using cost-effectiveness analysis to price the energy saved by an efficiency investment, in dollars per kilowatt-hour.

facts.text: The saved energy is never consumed, and such savings are sometimes called negawatts.
The approach avoids guessing future energy prices, removing the main source of uncertainty in appraising efficiency investments.

entries.title: Evaluation versus design problems

definition.text: The main split of multi-criteria problems, according to whether the options are listed in advance or only implicitly defined.

facts.text: Evaluation problems have a finite list of known options, each scored on several criteria.
Design problems, solved by multiple-objective mathematical programming, do not list the options explicitly.
Evaluation can mean picking the best option, sorting options into ordered classes or classifying them into unordered groups.

entries.title: Nondominated solutions: when no option beats all others

definition.text: An option that cannot be improved on one criterion without being made worse on another.

facts.text: In multi-criteria problems the idea of one optimal solution is often replaced by the set of nondominated solutions.
From any option outside this efficient set both objectives can be improved, but on the set one must be sacrificed to improve the other.
Maximising a weighted sum of the criteria finds some of these solutions, those at corner points.

entries.text: When criteria conflict, there is often no single optimal solution. entries.title: The benefit–cost ratio

definition.text: A summary indicator in cost–benefit analysis: a project's discounted benefits divided by its discounted costs, both in money.

facts.text: The higher the ratio the better the investment; as a rule of thumb, a project is worthwhile when benefits exceed costs.
Without a budget limit the projects with the highest net present value are best; under a budget limit, the ratio to constrained spending should guide choice.
Long-term ratios, such as those for climate change, are very sensitive to the discount rate, on which there is often no consensus.
It has been used most in transport appraisal.

entries.title: The risk–benefit ratio

definition.text: The ratio of the risks of an action to its potential benefits.

facts.text: People accept some risk for benefits, such as driving, but demand far lower risks, as much as a thousand times smaller, when the risk is involuntary.
Risk can be judged as real future risk, statistical risk from data, projected risk from models, or perceived risk.
Medical research is considered ethical only if its risk–benefit ratio is favourable, as the Declaration of Helsinki requires.

definition.text: A structured assessment of whether a project or proposal should go ahead, or whether it is viable.

facts.text: It often compares options using economic appraisal or another decision analysis technique.
It should weigh technical, economic, financial and social implications during the feasibility study.

entries.title: The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio

definition.text: The extra cost of one option over another divided by the extra effect it delivers.

facts.text: Cost-effectiveness is typically reported as this ratio of the change in costs to the change in effects.
In health care it is compared against a threshold, often in money per quality-adjusted life year, to allocate resources.
A 2006 review found industry-funded studies often reported ratios below $20,000 per QALY.

entries.title: Dose and response: the dose makes the poison

definition.text: How strongly an organism or biological system responds as a function of how much of a substance or stressor it is exposed to.

facts.text: Dose–response models are central to deciding safe and hazardous levels of drugs, pollutants and foods, and often underpin public policy.
The saying 'the dose makes the poison' captures how a small amount of a toxin may do nothing while a large amount kills.
Plotted with dose on one axis and response on the other, the curve is typically S-shaped; the first dose with a response above zero is the threshold dose.
Depending on the case, a threshold model or a linear no-threshold model may fit better, and some curves are U-shaped.

entries.title: Environmental ethics: arguments for protecting nature

definition.text: The branch of practical philosophy that sets out the kinds of argument that can be made for protecting nature and using natural resources sustainably.

facts.text: Its main competing views are anthropocentrism, ecocentrism (physiocentrism) and theocentrism.
It asks questions such as whether forests should be clear-cut for human consumption and which species should be valued for their own sake.
It influences environmental law, sociology, ecotheology, ecological economics, ecology and geography.
The field grew in response to Rachel Carson, Murray Bookchin and the first Earth Day in 1970.
Lynn White's 1967 paper on the roots of the ecological crisis and Garrett Hardin's 1968 'Tragedy of the Commons' had a crucial impact.
Alan Marshall sorts its approaches into libertarian extension, ecologic extension and conservation ethics.
Animal ethics and environmental ethics clash over duties to wild animals; some see them as incompatible, others as reconcilable.

entries.title: Commodification of nature: making nature tradable

definition.text: A critical field of research on how natural things and processes are made tradable in markets, and what follows from that.

facts.text: Commodification turns goods and services that were not produced for sale into something that can be exchanged.
Drawing on Marx, Polanyi, O'Connor and Harvey, it is openly normative and critical, rooted in Marxist geography and political ecology.
It is used to challenge 'market environmentalism', which sees putting nature into markets as a fix for environmental damage.
At root, commodification makes qualitatively different things equivalent and exchangeable through money, and so commensurable.
Its origins lie in the rise of capitalism and the enclosure of the commons in England.
Emissions trading is a prominent example: it turns emissions into units bought and sold within an overall cap.
Climate justice movements explicitly oppose the commodification of nature and its resources.

entries.contested_note: Market environmentalists see pricing nature as a solution to degradation, while critics argue commodification itself drives degradation and inequality.

entries.title: Animal rights: moral worth beyond human use

definition.text: The philosophy that many or all sentient animals have moral worth apart from their usefulness to people, and that their basic interests, such as avoiding suffering, deserve the same consideration as similar human interests.

facts.text: In its narrow sense, animals have rights to life, liberty and freedom from torture that cannot be overridden by appeals to total welfare.
The argument from marginal cases says that if infants and cognitively disabled people have moral status, animals lacking no relevant trait must too.
The two main philosophical approaches are utilitarian, led by Peter Singer, and rights-based, led by Tom Regan and Gary Francione.
Regan argues animals are 'subjects-of-a-life' and so bearers of rights; Francione argues they need only the right not to be owned.
Unlike animal welfare advocates, who aim to reduce suffering, animal rights supporters often seek to abolish practices such as intensive farming, animal testing and hunting.
Critics such as Carl Cohen argue rights holders must be able to understand duties, which animals cannot.

entries.contested_note: Philosophers such as Frey, Cohen, Posner and Scruton reject the claim that animals hold rights.

entries.title: Lexicographic preferences: values that refuse to trade

definition.text: Preferences in which a person prefers any amount of one good to any amount of another, looking at the second good only to break ties.

facts.text: The name comes from dictionary ordering, which attends to the first letter and only looks at the next letter in case of ties.
They are the classic example of rational preferences that cannot be represented by any utility function.
They are not continuous, which is why no real-valued utility function can capture them.
If everyone shares the same lexicographic preferences, ordinary general equilibrium cannot exist, because no one would sell.
Clive Spash used them to study ethically motivated refusals to trade species and ecosystems for money.

entries.title: The land ethic: citizens, not conquerors

definition.text: A framework for how, ethically, people should regard the land.

facts.text: Aldo Leopold coined the term in A Sand County Almanac (1949), calling for an ethic covering humans' relation to land, animals and plants.
His basic principle: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community.
It makes humans plain members and citizens of the land community rather than its conquerors.
Leopold saw two flaws in a land ethic based on economic self-interest: most members of an ecosystem have no economic worth, and conservation gets left to government.
Other land ethics rest on economics, utilitarianism, libertarianism, egalitarianism or ecology.
It is popular as a moderate view that balances human interests with a healthy, diverse natural environment.
Critics say it is vague and does not clearly explain why it should be adopted.

entries.contested_note: Scholars debate what Leopold's land ethic asserts and whether it rests on human interests or the intrinsic value of nature.

entries.title: Three objections to commodifying nature

definition.text: The objections to turning nature into commodities, which fall into practical, moral and consequential problems.

facts.text: Practically, natural things resist: fish ecology shapes how fisheries can be privatized, and water's physical properties make it hard to commodify.
Morally, a single money value denies the many cultural and social values of nature; livelihoods, territorial rights and sacredness translate poorly into prices.
Markets handle fairness and equitable distribution poorly, and critics say commodification deepens inequality.
In consequence, efficiency and profit override other concerns, and market exchange is 'reason-blind' to ecological importance.
David Harvey argues there is something 'inherently anti-ecological' about capitalist commodification.

entries.contested_note: These critiques are aimed against market environmentalism, whose proponents defend pricing nature.

entries.title: Market environmentalism: selling nature to save it

definition.text: The view, prominent in environmental policy since the late 1980s, that environmental damage comes from nature lacking prices and that markets can fix it.

facts.text: It spread with neoliberalism, which gives priority to the free market and money-based relations.
This 'selling nature to save it' approach needs economic valuation, either indirectly through cost–benefit analysis and contingent valuation or by direct commodification.
Critics say it reduces species survival to a price that rises with rarity and extinction risk.
Critics see ecotourism and bioprospecting as forcing nature to earn its right to survive in the global market.
Selling nature to save it is also called green grabbing.
It assumes private actors act rationally on the best information, and that markets pool knowledge better than regulation.
It appeals to policymakers and private interests because it seeks solutions within the capitalist system.

entries.contested_note: Its supporters treat markets as a conservation tool, while critics argue it subordinates nature to profit.

entries.title: Value pluralism: many goods, no single scale

definition.text: The idea that there are several basic values that can all be right and yet conflict with one another.

facts.text: Conflicting values are often held to be incommensurable, with no objective ranking of their importance.
It opposes value monism, which says all values can be measured on or reduced to a single scale.
Unlike relativism, it accepts limits, such as when vital human needs are violated.
Isaiah Berlin first popularised a substantial account of it.
Alan Brown objects that values are commensurable because they can be compared by their contribution to human good.
Social ecological economics builds value incommensurability and value pluralism into its approach.

entries.contested_note: Critics such as Alan Brown and Ronald Dworkin reject the claim that conflicting values cannot be compared.

entries.title: Commensurability: can values share a measure?

definition.text: Whether two values share a common measure; incommensurable values have no common standard or cannot be compared in a certain way.

facts.text: Two values such as freedom and security are incommensurable when no amount of one would make up for a loss of the other.
Two options are incomparable when neither is better and they are not exactly equally good.
Commodification makes different things commensurable by giving them a common exchange value in money.

entries.title: Fictitious commodities: land, labor and money

definition.text: Karl Polanyi's term for things treated as market commodities though not made for sale: land, labour and money.

facts.text: It comes from Polanyi's 1944 book The Great Transformation.
Before markets ordered society, land, labour and money were embedded in social relations and governed by morals, religion and community.
Treating public goods and social necessities as commodities rather than protected rights may destabilise social systems.
Because nature originates outside capitalist production, its value cannot be fully counted in money, which tends towards overexploitation.
Resistance to treating the environment as a market good is seen as Polanyi's 'double movement' of forces for and against markets.

entries.title: What is the whole Earth worth?

definition.text: The net worth of the planet, a disputed idea both in what 'value' means and in what counts as 'Earth'.

facts.text: It is usually equated with the total value of all ecosystem services.
A 1997 estimate put ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion.
Against a combined world GNP of about $18 trillion, that implied ecosystems provide 1.8 times as much value as people create.
A later estimate gave $125 trillion a year for 2011, twice world GDP, with yearly losses of 4.3–20.2 trillion.

entries.contested_note: Critics questioned the 1997 figures, especially the GNP comparison, though they accepted the basic approach.

conflicts.text: Combined world GNP closer to $28 trillion, making ecosystem services only 1.2 times as valuable.
conflicts.note: Disputes the $18 trillion GNP figure used in the 1997 comparison.

conflicts.text: World Bank total GDP in 1997 of $31 trillion, about equal to the ecosystem value.
conflicts.note: GDP rather than GNP; another benchmark for the same comparison.

entries.title: Conservation ethics: protecting nature for people's sake

definition.text: Valuing the environment only for its usefulness to people, and protecting it as a means to human welfare.

facts.text: Because it rejects deep ecology's intrinsic value, it is often called 'shallow ecology'.
It may underlie government positions at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and the 1997 Kyoto summit.

entries.title: Ecologic extension: value for whole ecosystems

definition.text: An approach to environmental ethics that stresses the interdependence and diversity of living things and gives intrinsic value to whole ecosystems.

facts.text: It is a scientific reflection on nature, where libertarian extension is a political one.
James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis, treating Earth as one whole with its own ethical value, may belong here.

entries.title: Three ethical theories applied to nature

definition.text: How the main theories of right action, consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, are used to reason about the environment.

facts.text: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, such as whether they maximise well-being, which treats nature instrumentally.
Deontology says intrinsically valuable things must be protected as ends in themselves, so damaging nature is wrong in itself, not just a net loss.
Virtue ethics asks which character traits to cultivate, which avoids defining intrinsic value but is arguably anthropocentric.

entries.title: Utilitarian and libertarian land ethics

definition.text: Land ethics that judge land use by the greatest good for people, or by individual property rights and freedom.

facts.text: Utilitarianism underpins industrial farming, which is defended for raising yields and lowering food prices.
Unlike a purely economic ethic, it can limit a farmer's profit if soil runoff damages neighbours' property.
Garrett Hardin argued in 1968 that the only solution to the tragedy of the commons was to give soil and water to private citizens.
Egalitarian land ethics arose in response, favouring equal access to land or food.

entries.title: Accumulation by dispossession: a new enclosure

definition.text: David Harvey's term for a new wave of enclosing the commons in which natural assets are released to capital at very low or no cost.

facts.text: Commodification 'stretches' across space and time and 'deepens' into more kinds of goods and services.
Bioprospecting and ecotourism are new 'commodity frontiers' alongside mining and agriculture.

In this view commodification 'stretches' across space and time, and 'deepens' into more kinds of goods and services.

entries.title: The second contradiction of capitalism
entries.article: Commodification of nature#Degradation of resources, underproduction of conditions

definition.text: James O'Connor's idea that capitalism degrades the environmental 'conditions of production' it depends on but cannot produce itself.

facts.text: Because nature's value cannot be fully counted in money, there is a tendency to overexploit and 'underproduce' it.
Capitalism is described as 'ecologically irrational', with a built-in tendency to overexploit its natural resource base.

entries.title: Deliberative monetary valuation: valuing together
entries.article: Clive Spash#Environmental Cost-Benefit Analysis, Contingent and Deliberative Valuation

definition.text: A set of approaches that combine individual willingness-to-pay valuation of environmental damage or protection with group discussion methods.

Social values are qualitatively different from the sum of individual values, a weakness of such studies.
A 'discourse based' alternative treats the valuation as a mutual agreement reached by contesting views.

entries.title: Social ecological economics: economies inside society and nature

definition.text: A proposed paradigm shift in ecological economics that integrates social, ecological and economic knowledge.

facts.text: It sees economies as emerging from and dependent on the structure and functioning of society and ecology.
It rejects reductionism and builds in value incommensurability and value pluralism.
Spash divides the field into social ecological economists, new environmental pragmatists and new resource economists.

entries.title: The small-improvement argument

definition.text: An argument that two options are incomparable: if a tiny gain to one does not make it better than the other, they cannot have been exactly equal.

facts.text: In the example, adding 5 cents a year to a banking job should not tip the choice against a professor's job if the two are too different to compare.
The three ordinary comparisons, in Ruth Chang's terms, are better, worse and equally good.

entries.title: Human development: growth as a means, not the goal

definition.text: Human development is a view of progress that widens economic development to include social, political and even ethical dimensions.

facts.text: The UN Development Programme defines it as enlarging people's choices to live a long healthy life, be educated, have a decent living standard and enjoy freedom and self-respect.
On this view economic growth is only a means of enlarging people's choices, not the goal itself.
The idea grew in the 1980s through Amartya Sen's capabilities perspective, with Mahbub ul Haq among its key early figures; the HDI stems from this work.
Aristotle already noted that wealth is merely useful for something else, not the good being sought.
Six pillars are listed: equity, sustainability, productivity, empowerment, cooperation and security.
UN Human Development Reports carry indices including the HDI, gender indices and a Human Poverty Index, later replaced by the Multidimensional Poverty Index.

entries.title: Human Development Index: ranking countries by people's lives

definition.text: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite score of life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to rank countries into four tiers of human development.

facts.text: Economist Mahbub ul-Haq created it, and the UN Development Programme's Human Development Report Office uses it to measure countries' development.
The reports, launched in 1990, aimed to move development economics away from national income accounting towards people-centred policies.
It rests on Amartya Sen's capability idea: whether people are able to 'be' and 'do' desirable things, such as being healthy or taking part in community life.
Since 2010 it combines life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per person at purchasing power parity.
Each dimension is scaled to an index between 0 and 1, and the HDI is the geometric mean of the three.
The 2010 report added an inequality-adjusted HDI, seen as the actual level of human development, while the plain HDI shows the potential with no inequality.
Critics point to its neglect of sustainability, inequality and democracy; a planetary pressures-adjusted HDI was later added to address sustainability.
One study found 11%, 21% and 34% of countries could be misclassified because of data updates, formula revisions and arbitrary thresholds respectively.

entries.text: Since 1990 the UN's Human Development Reports have tried to move development economics away from national income accounting and towards people-centred policies. Their best-known tool is the Human Development Index, or HDI. It is a single score combining life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to sort countries into four tiers of human development. It rests on Amartya Sen's capability idea: whether people are able to 'be' and 'do' desirable things, such as being healthy or taking part in community life. Since 2010 it has combined life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per person at purchasing power parity. Each dimension is scaled to an index between 0 and 1. The HDI is their geometric mean, found by multiplying the three scores and taking the cube root. Critics fault it for neglecting sustainability, inequality and democracy. In response came {{ref:nature-acct-005}} and a planetary pressures-adjusted HDI. One study found 11%, 21% and 34% of countries could be misclassified by data updates, formula revisions and arbitrary thresholds.

entries.title: Gross National Happiness: Bhutan's rival to GDP

definition.text: Gross National Happiness (GNH) is a philosophy followed by Bhutan's government, with an index measuring a population's collective happiness and well-being.

facts.text: Bhutan's 4th King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, coined it in 1972, declaring it more important than GDP.
Its four pillars are fair socio-economic development, environmental conservation, preserving culture and good governance, alongside nine domains including ecological diversity and resilience.
Each domain mixes survey-based and objective indicators, and people are classed as happy or not-yet-happy by their scores.
The GNH Index became Bhutan's official goal in its 2008 Constitution, and screening tools test new policies and projects against it.
In 2011 a UN General Assembly resolution urged members to follow Bhutan and measure happiness and well-being.
Versions of the GNH survey were used in places such as Victoria in Canada, Seattle and Vermont.
Critics call it a propaganda tool that distracted from Bhutan's expulsion of its Nepalese Hindu minority and from widespread poverty.

entries.contested_note: Critics describe GNH as a government propaganda tool, while others see it as an evolving, more democratic development philosophy.

entries.title: Beyond GDP: the search for better scorecards

definition.text: Beyond GDP is the push to develop broad measures of economic well-being that go further than GDP and other national income figures.

facts.text: Approaches include the European Union's Beyond GDP programme, the OECD's Better Lives indicators and many alternative measures of wellbeing or happiness.
Bhutan's Gross National Happiness Index was one of the earliest national attempts, and similar projects followed, such as the UK's measure of national well-being.
The European Commission sorts the alternatives into five groups: GDP itself, enlarged GDP measures, social indicators, environmental indicators and well-being measures.
Enlarged GDP measures subtract costs such as environmental degradation, resource depletion or higher income inequality.
Some proposals aim to replace GDP outright, while many others aim to supplement it with a 'dashboard' of metrics for the economy and well-being.
The World Bank suggests the HDI, Gross National Happiness and Adjusted Net Savings as alternatives to GDP.

entries.title: Green GDP: subtracting the damage from growth

definition.text: Green GDP is a measure of economic growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from a country's ordinary GDP.

facts.text: In simple form, green GDP equals GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs.
Environmental costs include depletion of resources such as oil and timber, ecological damage such as topsoil erosion, and restoration costs such as wetland restoration.
The motive is that GDP measures output alone and ignores the depletion or replenishment of the assets behind it, so it cannot tell if income is sustainable.
Benefits from forests, wetlands and farmland stay hidden in GDP because they are hard to measure and price.
Early work came from Nordhaus and Tobin (1972), Ahmad et al. (1989), Repetto et al. (1989) and Hartwick (1990).
The UN's environmental accounting system (SEEA) makes it possible to build full accounts from which green GDP can be derived and compared between countries.
In the US, early green accounts in 1994 showed GDP overstated mining's contribution to national wealth, and a 1995 amendment halted the work.
Critics say non-market assets such as ecosystem services are hard to value, and Stiglitz, Sen and Fitoussi argued green GDP does not measure sustainability itself.

entries.contested_note: Experts disagree on whether environmental adjustments should be made inside the existing national accounts or by redefining what counts as income, and whether non-market assets can be reliably valued.
entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Fell a forest for timber and GDP records the output, not the loss. GDP measures output alone and ignores the running down or replenishment of the wealth behind it, so it cannot tell whether income is sustainable. Green GDP is a measure of growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from ordinary GDP. In simple form, green GDP equals GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs. Environmental costs include the using up of resources such as oil and timber, ecological damage such as topsoil erosion, and restoration costs such as restoring wetlands. Benefits from forests, wetlands and farmland stay hidden in GDP because they are hard to measure and price. The UN's system for environmental accounts, SEEA ({{ref:nature-found-013}}), makes it possible to build full accounts from which green GDP can be derived and compared between countries. In the US, early green accounts in 1994 showed GDP overstated mining's contribution to national wealth, and a 1995 amendment halted the work. Experts still disagree on whether to adjust the existing national accounts or redefine income. They also dispute whether non-market goods such as ecosystem services can be reliably valued. Stiglitz, Sen and Fitoussi argued that green GDP does not measure sustainability itself.

entries.title: Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission: France asks what to measure
entries.article: Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress

definition.text: The Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress, known as the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission, was an inquiry set up by the French government in 2008.

facts.text: It examined how a nation's wealth and social progress could be measured without relying on the one-dimensional GDP figure.
Joseph Stiglitz chaired it, Amartya Sen was economic adviser and Jean-Paul Fitoussi coordinator; its final report came out in September 2009.
It proposed a well-being framework covering health, environment, work, physical safety, economic safety and political freedom.
Its report argued that green GDP and similar indices only charge GDP for environmental damage and do not measure sustainability as such.

entries.title: Inclusive wealth: counting every kind of capital

definition.text: Inclusive wealth is the total value of all capital assets in a place, including human, social, public and natural capital.

facts.text: Unlike GDP, the Inclusive Wealth Index lets countries check whether they are developing in a way that lets future generations meet their own needs.
UNEP developed the index with Kyushu University; it estimates stocks of human, natural and produced capital, the productive base of an economy.
The change in wealth sums the changes in each capital stock, each weighted by its shadow price, the estimated price of something with no market price.
Natural capital includes renewable resources such as farmland, forests and fisheries and non-renewables such as fossil fuels and minerals.
Inclusive Wealth Reports were published in 2012, 2014 and 2018; the first was launched at the Rio+20 conference.
The 2018 report found inclusive wealth in 140 countries rose 44% from 1990 to 2014, about 1.8% a year.
Yet 44 of the 140 countries saw inclusive wealth per person fall since 1992 while GDP per person rose in nearly all, a sign of unsustainable resource depletion.
Globally, produced capital per person has grown most, often at the expense of natural capital.

entries.contested_note: Using shadow prices for natural capital is called controversial because of gaps in knowing how life-supporting ecosystems produce value.

entries.title: Wellbeing economy: designing policy around people and nature

definition.text: A wellbeing economy is a public policy framework in which the economy is designed to serve social, health, cultural, fairness and nature outcomes.

facts.text: Its aim is to move beyond GDP as the main measure of how well a national economy is doing.
Several countries use wellbeing metrics to guide policy and budgets, focusing on education and skills, health, gender and inclusion.
Scotland, New Zealand, Iceland, Wales, Finland and Canada adopted it as national policy and formed the Wellbeing Economy Governments partnership (WEGo) in 2021.
The World Health Organization has also adopted wellbeing as a whole-of-government approach, first set out in the 2021 Geneva Charter for Wellbeing.
The Wellbeing Economy Alliance, founded in 2018, is the leading network of organisations and movements working towards a wellbeing economy.
An Ipsos survey in 17 of the G20 countries found 68% of respondents supported putting wellbeing ahead of profit.
Wellbeing economics is grouped with doughnut economics, steady-state economics and degrowth under the umbrella of post-growth thinking.

entries.title: Happiness economics: measuring what people feel

definition.text: Happiness economics is the study of happiness, well-being, life satisfaction and quality of life, linking economics with psychology, sociology and health.

facts.text: It treats happiness and quality-of-life measures, rather than wealth, income or profit, as the thing to be maximised.
Happiness is measured with self-reported surveys and with objective measures such as lifespan, income and education.
Classical and neoclassical economics saw happiness as unmeasurable; happiness economics is described as a radical break with that tradition.
Once wealth reaches subsistence level, extra wealth adds much less to well-being.
Kahneman and Deaton (2010) found day-to-day emotional well-being rose with income only up to about $75,000 a year per household, though life satisfaction kept rising.
Direct happiness surveys are increasingly used as an alternative to GDP or GNP for judging policy success.
Critics worry that happiness metrics may serve political or even authoritarian goals, and that survey scales distort results through 'rounding'.

entries.title: OECD Better Life Index: build your own measure of progress

definition.text: The OECD Better Life Index, launched in May 2011, is an OECD tool that measures several dimensions of economic and social progress beyond GDP.

facts.text: It grew out of the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission's concern that GDP failed to give a true picture of people's current and future well-being.
It covers 11 topics of well-being, including housing, income, jobs, community, education and environment, each built from 1 to 4 measures.
Users rank each topic from 0 to 5 by importance to build their own index, and the OECD reports the pooled results in its How's Life? report.
Critics say its 11 dimensions miss things such as social networks and freedom of speech, and question its use of relative rather than absolute scores.

entries.title: Social Progress Index: progress measured without money

definition.text: The Social Progress Index, created by the Social Progress Imperative, measures the real-life outcomes people experience across many social and environmental indicators.

facts.text: Unlike other Beyond GDP measures, it deliberately leaves out all indicators of economic performance.
It defines social progress as meeting basic human needs, building blocks for better quality of life, and the chance for people to reach their full potential.
It was created in 2013 because its founders found the HDI and happiness indices insufficient.
Denmark and the United States have similar GDP per person, yet Denmark scores 10 points higher in social progress.

entries.title: Adjusted net saving: is a nation getting richer or poorer?

definition.text: Adjusted net saving, or genuine savings, is ordinary net saving minus the value of resource depletion and environmental damage plus investment in human capital.

facts.text: It measures the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital stocks, valued in money.
It grew from Hartwick's rule, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital.
A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run sustainability, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero.
The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP.
Along with ecological footprint accounts, it is an example of an index focused on overconsumption.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Ordinary saving figures miss what a country uses up. Adjusted net saving, also called {{ref:nature-eecon-220}}, corrects for that. It takes ordinary net saving ({{ref:nature-econ-587}}), subtracts the value of resources used up and environmental damage, and adds investment in human capital. The result is the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital, valued in money. The idea grew from {{ref:nature-eecon-223}}, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital. A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run sustainability, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero. The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP. Along with accounts of humanity's demand on nature ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), it is an example of an index focused on consuming more than nature can sustain ({{ref:nature-eecon-185}}).
entries.text_plain: Ordinary saving figures miss what a country uses up. Adjusted net saving, also called Genuine savings: is a nation getting richer or poorer?, corrects for that. It takes ordinary net saving (Saving: income held back for later), subtracts the value of resources used up and environmental damage, and adds investment in human capital. The result is the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital, valued in money. The idea grew from Hartwick's rule: invest the resource rents, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital. A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run sustainability, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero. The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP. Along with accounts of humanity's demand on nature (Ecological footprint: how much planet a lifestyle needs), it is an example of an index focused on consuming more than nature can sustain (Overconsumption: using up faster than nature refills).

entries.title: China's green GDP experiment and its collapse
entries.article: Green gross domestic product#Green GDP in China

definition.text: China's green GDP experiment was a national attempt, announced in 2004, to replace GDP with green GDP as a performance measure for top officials.

facts.text: The first green GDP report, for 2004, put the financial loss from pollution at 511.8 billion yuan ($66.3 billion), or 3.05 percent of the economy.
The effort collapsed in 2007 when environmental adjustments cut growth to politically unacceptable levels, nearly zero in some provinces, and the 2005 report was suppressed.
Its failure is linked to a mismatch between central authorities and local governments.
