Environmental adjustments cut growth to politically unacceptable levels, nearly zero in some provinces. The 2005 report was suppressed, and in 2007 the effort collapsed. Its failure is linked to a mismatch between central authorities and local governments.

entries.title: The 2007 Beyond GDP conference and the EU's response
entries.article: Broad measures of economic progress#Beyond GDP

definition.text: The 'Beyond GDP' conference of 2007, hosted by the European Commission, European Parliament, Club of Rome, OECD and WWF, sought wider measures of progress to guide policy.

facts.text: More than 650 policy makers, experts and social activists attended.
The EU communication 'GDP and beyond' set five actions, including complementing GDP with environmental and social indicators and extending national accounts to environmental and social issues.
Results included the EU's first quality-of-life indicators and backing for UN adoption of the System of Environmental Economic Accounting as the international standard.

entries.title: Britain's programme for measuring national well-being
entries.article: Broad measures of economic progress#Measuring national well-being in the UK

definition.text: The Measuring National Well-being programme, launched in the UK in 2010 and led by the Office for National Statistics, aims to build trusted measures of the nation's well-being.

facts.text: Its well-being wheel has headline indicators for health, relationships, job satisfaction, economic security, education, environment and people's own rating of their well-being.
It has published experimental work such as household satellite accounts that value unpaid household production.

entries.title: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget puts people before growth

definition.text: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget, launched in May 2019, was the country's first budget built around people's wellbeing and the environment rather than GDP alone.

facts.text: It chose five priorities: climate and environment, productive work, Maori and Pacific opportunities, child wellbeing, and mental and physical health.
Prime Minister Ardern argued citizens' health and life satisfaction, not wealth or growth, should be the measure of a country's progress.
The next, National-led coalition government dropped the approach in 2024.

entries.title: Environmental functions: when nature's uses compete

definition.text: Environmental functions are the possible uses of our non-human-made physical surroundings, on which people depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation.

facts.text: When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete; once water pollution passes a threshold, 'dumping ground for waste' competes with 'drinking water'.
Competing functions are scarce and so are economic goods; most functions that were once free goods have become scarce.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Water can serve as drinking water or as a dumping ground for waste, but once pollution passes a threshold, the two uses compete. Each is an environmental function: a possible use of the physical surroundings people did not make, on which they depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation. When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete. Competing functions are scarce, and so they are economic goods ({{ref:nature-found-051}}). Most functions that were once free goods, so plentiful that using them cost nothing, have become scarce.
entries.text_plain: Water can serve as drinking water or as a dumping ground for waste, but once pollution passes a threshold, the two uses compete. Each is an environmental function: a possible use of the physical surroundings people did not make, on which they depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation. When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete. Competing functions are scarce, and so they are economic goods (Scarcity: why there is never enough). Most functions that were once free goods, so plentiful that using them cost nothing, have become scarce.

entries.title: Sustainable national income: what nature could support for ever

definition.text: Sustainable national income (SNI) estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever.

facts.text: Ordinary national income leaves out the loss of environmental functions, so it is always higher than the SNI.
The gap between national income and SNI shows how far production is from sustainability; a shrinking gap means progress, a growing one means drifting away.
Economist Roefie Hueting developed the framework, working with a multidisciplinary team at Statistics Netherlands for nearly forty years.
Following the precautionary principle, the SNI assumes no technological progress during the transition to sustainability.
Tinbergen and Hueting's rough 1991 world estimate put sustainable income at 50 percent of world production.
A 2001 estimate for the Netherlands also came to around 50 percent of national income, about the production level of the early 1970s.
Between 1990 and 2000 the Dutch gap between national income and SNI grew by about 10 billion euros.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: What if an economy produced only as much as nature could support for ever? Sustainable national income, or SNI, puts a number on that. It estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever. Economist Roefie Hueting developed the framework, working with a multidisciplinary team at Statistics Netherlands for nearly forty years. Ordinary national income leaves out the loss of environmental functions, so it is always higher than the SNI. The gap between the two shows how far production is from sustainability: a shrinking gap means progress, a growing one means drifting away. Following the rule of erring on the side of caution ({{ref:nature-pol-201}}), the SNI assumes no technological progress during the shift to sustainability. The estimates are stark. Tinbergen and Hueting's rough 1991 world estimate put sustainable income at 50 percent of world production. A 2001 estimate for the Netherlands also came to around 50 percent of national income, about the production level of the early 1970s. Between 1990 and 2000 the Dutch gap grew by about 10 billion euros.

entries.title: The Easterlin paradox: richer nations, no happier?

definition.text: The Easterlin paradox is the finding that richer people in a country report more happiness than poorer ones, yet average happiness does not rise as the nation's average income grows.

facts.text: Richard Easterlin formulated it from survey results comparing happiness and GDP across and within countries.
There is a significant link between GDP and happiness across nations, which some researchers in 2002 said holds only up to about $15,000 GDP per person.
Several studies in the 2000s found the opposite, and more robust research links economic development with population well-being, so the paradox is disputed.

entries.contested_note: Later studies have found a link between national income growth and happiness, so whether the paradox holds is disputed.
entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Within a country, richer people report more happiness than poorer ones. Yet as a nation's average income grows, average happiness does not seem to rise. That puzzle is the Easterlin paradox. Richard Easterlin formulated it from survey results comparing happiness and GDP across and within countries. Across nations there is a significant link between GDP and happiness, which some researchers in 2002 said holds only up to about $15,000 GDP per person. Whether the paradox holds at all is disputed. Several studies in the 2000s found the opposite, and more robust research links economic development with population well-being.

That puzzle is the Easterlin paradox. Richard Easterlin formulated it from survey results comparing happiness and GDP across and within countries. Across nations there is a significant link between GDP and happiness, which some researchers in 2002 said holds only up to about $15,000 GDP per person. Whether the paradox holds at all is disputed. Several studies in the 2000s found the opposite, and more robust research links economic development with population well-being.

entries.title: Inequality-adjusted HDI: development as people actually live it

definition.text: The inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts the HDI for inequality to show the actual level of human development.

facts.text: The plain HDI can be read as the potential, maximum human development a country could reach if there were no inequality.
The IHDI and the Gender Inequality Index were both adopted in 2010, growing out of the capability approach.

entries.title: Measure of Economic Welfare: Nordhaus and Tobin's correction

definition.text: The Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW), introduced by William Nordhaus and James Tobin in 1972, was the first model to estimate households' real yearly consumption as a welfare measure.

facts.text: Nordhaus and Tobin argued welfare must be sustainable, since nations that eat up their capital stock are less well off than national income suggests.
It belongs to a family of welfare indices, with Japan's Net National Welfare (1973) and the ISEW (1989), that add positive and negative nonmarket items to national accounts.
Clifford Cobb and John Cobb later argued the MEW failed to include the depletion of natural capital.

entries.title: Green national product: fixing GNP's backward ledger

definition.text: The green national product is a measure that folds environmental degradation and resource depletion into a country's national product.

facts.text: Critics say GNP puts the environment on the wrong side of the ledger: polluting and then cleaning up both add to GNP.
GNP lumps spending that makes people worse off, keeps them in place, or makes them better off into one figure, giving no clue about real progress.
Herman Daly argued GNP ignores a basic business accounting rule that all revenues and expenses are allocated to income.
The line of welfare adjustments runs from the MEW to the ISEW (1989) to the GPI (1995), which also adjusts for housework, volunteering, crime and leisure.

entries.title: Defensive expenditures: when fighting harm counts as growth

definition.text: In environmental accounting, defensive expenditures are spending meant to limit possible damage to oneself.

facts.text: Standard accounts do not subtract this spending to fight 'bads', so it counts as if it were a gain.
The ISEW subtracts private defensive spending and counts only non-defensive public spending.
GDP treats money spent repairing earlier harm, such as rebuilding destroyed homes, the same as money spent on new production.
Spending people make to protect themselves from pollution can also reveal how much they value avoiding it.

entries.text: Money spent rebuilding destroyed homes counts in GDP exactly like money spent on new production. In accounts for the environment, spending meant to limit possible damage to oneself is called a defensive expenditure. Standard accounts do not subtract this spending to fight 'bads'. It counts as if it were a gain. {{ref:nature-acct-001}} corrects for this: it subtracts private defensive spending and counts only non-defensive public spending. Such spending also carries information. What people pay to protect themselves from pollution can reveal how much they value avoiding it ({{ref:nature-val-087}}).

entries.title: Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare: GDP with the costs taken out

definition.text: The Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW) is an economic indicator proposed as a replacement for GDP, the main headline figure of national accounts.

facts.text: Instead of just adding up spending, the ISEW weighs consumer spending against income distribution and the costs of pollution and other unsustainable practices.

Its rough formula: personal consumption plus public non-defensive spending, minus private defensive spending, plus capital formation and household labour services, minus environmental degradation costs and natural capital depreciation.
Ecological economist Herman Daly and theologian John B. Cobb developed the ISEW in 1989 as a more valid measure of progress than GDP.
Cobb and Daly's US calculation for 1950 to 1986 found average economic welfare levelled off after the 1970s even as GDP kept growing.
They blamed the side effects of production and unequal income distribution for production gains not turning into welfare gains.
The ISEW has also been compiled for many other places, including the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Chile, Finland, Poland, Belgium, Pakistan and China.
Like GDP, the ISEW boils welfare down to one number, but it puts social and environmental issues into the sum in money terms.

entries.title: Genuine progress indicator: counting pollution as a loss

definition.text: The genuine progress indicator (GPI) is a measure proposed to replace or supplement GDP by counting environmental and social factors that GDP leaves out.

facts.text: GDP counts pollution twice as a gain, once when it is made and again when it is cleaned up; the GPI instead counts it as a loss, roughly equal to its clean-up and damage costs.
In simplified form GPI = A + B - C - D + I: income-weighted consumption plus non-market services, minus defensive costs and nature's deterioration, plus capital growth and trade balance.
The GPI rests on John Hicks's idea of sustainable income: what can be consumed in one period without reducing consumption in the next.
It is built from 26 indicators grouped into economic, environmental and social categories.
The GPI grew out of later work extending the ISEW, with extra emphasis on welfare and the ecological sustainability of the economy.
As of 2014, Vermont, Maryland, Washington and Hawaii had passed state initiatives to consider the GPI in budgeting.
Statistics Finland's series from 1945 to 2011 showed GDP and GPI rising together in the 1970s and 1980s, then diverging after the early-1990s recession.
Critics say GPI is harder to measure than GDP, depends on a contested definition of well-being, and is more open to political manipulation.

entries.contested_note: Whether money growth reflects lost well-being is called a main issue between green and neoclassical economists, and critics question whether GPI can be defined or measured objectively.

entries.title: Environmental accounting: keeping the books on nature

definition.text: A branch of accounting that measures, analyses and reports money and non-money information about environmental impacts.

facts.text: For a company it judges environmental performance and informs people inside and outside the firm; for a nation or region it records how the economy affects the environment.
It tracks resource use and environmental costs such as clean-up of contaminated sites, fines and taxes, pollution-prevention technology and waste handling.

A system combines environmentally differentiated accounting, which measures nature's effects on the firm in money, and ecological accounting, which measures the firm's effects on nature in physical units.
The field is divided into global, national and corporate environmental accounting.
At national level it is formalised internationally through SEEA, which builds on the System of National Accounts.
A 2007 United Nations assessment found environmental-economic accounting in use in 49 countries.
Explanations for why organisations do it range from manager and shareholder interests to legitimacy, stakeholder pressure and normative accountability.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts
entries.text: By 2007, a United Nations assessment found, 49 countries were using environmental-economic accounting. It tracks resource use and environmental costs, such as cleaning up contaminated sites, fines and taxes, pollution-prevention technology and waste handling. A full system has two halves. Environmentally differentiated accounting measures nature's effects on the firm, in money. Ecological accounting measures the firm's effects on nature, in physical units. The field divides into global, national and corporate environmental accounting. At national level it is formalised internationally through SEEA, which builds on the System of National Accounts ({{ref:nature-econ-596}}). Why do organisations do it? Explanations range from the interests of managers and shareholders to legitimacy, stakeholder pressure and a sense of duty to account for their impacts.

entries.title: Assets: what a business owns or controls

definition.text: In financial accounting, any resource a business or other economic entity owns or controls.

facts.text: It is anything, physical or not, that can be used to produce economic value.
A firm's balance sheet records the money value of its assets.
Tangible assets include current assets such as cash and inventory and fixed assets such as land, buildings and equipment; intangible assets include patents and goodwill.
Ownership is not needed: an asset is recognised if the entity controls it, so a leased building counts but employees do not.
The balance sheet follows the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Fixed assets except land are written off against profits over their expected life through depreciation.
In economics, an asset is any form in which wealth can be held, and social scientists study how things like ecosystems are turned into assets.

entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts
entries.text: A leased building counts as a company's asset; its employees do not. In financial accounting an asset is any resource a business or other economic entity owns or controls, and control is enough: ownership is not required. More broadly, an asset is anything, physical or not, that can be used to produce economic value. A firm's balance sheet records the money value of its assets. It follows the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities, what the firm owes, plus equity, the owners' stake. Tangible assets include current assets such as cash and inventory, and fixed assets such as land, buildings and equipment. Intangible assets include patents and goodwill. Fixed assets other than land are written off against profits over their expected life through depreciation ({{ref:nature-econ-519}}). In economics, an asset is any form in which wealth can be held. Social scientists study how things like ecosystems are turned into assets.

entries.title: Natural capital accounting: a balance sheet for nature

definition.text: The process of calculating the total stocks and flows of natural resources and services in an ecosystem or region.

facts.text: The accounts can be kept in physical units or in money, and can guide government, business and consumer choices about using resources and land.
Approaches include broad indicator dashboards, composite indices, overconsumption indices such as adjusted net savings and ecological footprints, and adjusted economic indicators such as green GDP.
Money-based indicators tend to be expressed as flows and physical indicators as stocks.
International support began with the 1987 Brundtland Report and the 1992 Rio Summit, whose Agenda 21 asked signatories to develop quantitative information on their activities.
The 2012 Rio+20 conference was described as a watershed in worldwide interest in the field.
The Netherlands, France and the Philippines were early adopters of integrated environmental-economic accounts.
A US study estimated that air-pollution damages from coal-fired power generation range from 0.8 to 5.6 times the value the industry adds.
The US Congress halted federal work on environmental accounting in 1994, after the first US integrated satellite accounts appeared.

entries.title: Triple bottom line: people, planet and profit

definition.text: An accounting framework that judges an organisation on three results: social, environmental and economic.

facts.text: In ordinary accounting the 'bottom line' is profit or loss; the triple bottom line adds social and environmental bottom lines.
Freer Spreckley first set out the framework in 1981, and John Elkington says he coined the phrase in 1994 and developed it in his 1997 book Cannibals with Forks.
Elkington's slogan 'people, planet, and profit' later titled Shell's first sustainability report in 1997.
The planet line asks firms to cut their ecological footprint, and often to use life cycle assessment to find a product's true environmental cost.
The profit line means economic value created after deducting all input costs including capital, which differs from accounting profit.
Measuring the people line is relatively new, problematic and often subjective.
Since a 2007 UN and ICLEI standard it has been the dominant approach to public-sector full cost accounting.
Critics say it treats the environment as a background externality and is hard to apply in practice.

entries.contested_note: Many people disagree that the triple bottom line is the right way to improve social and environmental conditions, citing reductive treatment of the environment and weak practical application.

entries.title: Green accounting: bringing environmental costs into the results

definition.text: Accounting that tries to bring environmental costs into the financial results of an activity.

facts.text: Its backers argue that GDP ignores the environment, so policymakers need a model that includes green accounting.
Its main aim is to help businesses manage trade-offs between ordinary economic goals and environmental goals.
It is said to secure only weak sustainability, a step toward strong sustainability.
Critics say depletion may already be counted in extraction industries and that valuing externalities can be arbitrary.
Economist Peter Wood brought the term into common use in the 1980s.
Environmental or green national accounting values environmental assets that national wealth measures usually leave out, partly because they are hard to value.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether green accounting is sound, since depletion may already be counted and externality values may be arbitrary.

entries.title: Full-cost accounting: costs counted as resources are used

definition.text: A cost-accounting method that gathers the possible environmental costs and benefits of each option under consideration, tracing direct costs and allocating indirect ones.

facts.text: It is one part of true cost accounting, alongside human and social capital.
Experts find both 'full' and 'true' troublesome labels because the words are subjective.
It counts costs as resources are used, not when cash is spent: a vehicle bought once is costed over its working life, for example ten years.
It values goods even when no cash changes hands, such as equipment paid for by a state grant.
It includes overheads, and past costs such as buying equipment and future ones such as closing a facility.
Subsidies to energy and food keep prices artificially low, hiding true costs and the externalities of fossil fuels and mechanised farming.
Florida uses it to identify and report the actual costs of solid waste management.
A major motive is anticipating market or regulatory problems that come from ignoring the whole outcome of a process.

The method is one part of True cost accounting: pricing the hidden effects, alongside human and social capital. Experts find both 'full' and 'true' troublesome labels, because the words are subjective.

entries.title: Sustainability accounting: reporting beyond the balance sheet

definition.text: Accounting, also called social and environmental accounting or non-financial reporting, that discloses information about a firm's social and environmental performance to outsiders such as investors and creditors.

facts.text: It began in the 1970s and is treated as a branch of financial accounting.
In management accounting it supports internal decisions about the firm's economic, ecological and social performance, the triple bottom line of people, planet and profit.
Corporate sustainability reporting and triple bottom line accounting are its best-known measures.
The Global Reporting Initiative was set up to give organisations guidelines so that social and environmental reports are consistent.
In the 1970s environmental matters were part of a broad social accounting movement; by 1991–1995 environmental accounting almost completely dominated social accounting.
In most countries governments do not require companies to prepare and publish sustainability reports.
The Sustainability Accounting Standards Board standardises some sustainability metrics so investors can judge corporate risk.

entries.title: True cost accounting: pricing the hidden effects

definition.text: An accounting approach that measures and puts values on the hidden effects of economic activity on the environment, society and health.

facts.text: It is also called full cost accounting or multiple capital accounting, and covers natural, human, social and produced capital.
The hidden effects are costs and benefits not reflected in market prices or in firms' profit and loss accounts.
It is closely tied to externalities and traces back to the work of Pigou and Marshall in the 1920s.
It is seen as an extension of cost-benefit analysis that adds systems thinking about many stakeholders and capitals.
A typical study uses a dozen or more indicators across environmental, health, social and economic domains.
Much of its development has been in food and farming, where hidden costs can be large.
Greenhouse gas emissions are easy to include, but effects on working conditions or cultural identity are harder to find.

entries.title: Material flow accounting: weighing what an economy takes in

definition.text: The measurement of material flows through a national or regional economy, also called economy-wide material flow analysis.

facts.text: It records materials entering an economy, changes in its stocks, and outputs as exports or as discharges to the environment.
It treats the economy as a subsystem inside the environment that, like a living thing, needs a constant throughput of materials and energy, an idea called industrial or societal metabolism.
It covers all solid, liquid and gaseous materials moved by people or livestock except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year.
Materials are grouped into biomass, fossil energy carriers, metals and non-metallic minerals.
It counts non-market flows such as grazed biomass and mining waste rock, which made up 21% of global extraction in 2010.
It is a satellite system to the national accounts and is used in SEEA.
It counts all materials humans mobilise except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year.
Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports; domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports.

entries.text: An economy, like a living thing, needs a constant flow of materials and energy through it. Domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports. The accounts are a satellite system to the national accounts and are used in SEEA.

entries.title: Integrated reporting: one report for money and nature

definition.text: Corporate reporting that produces a periodic integrated report on how a firm's strategy, governance, performance and prospects create value over time.

facts.text: It presents financial and other value-relevant information together, aimed mainly at those who allocate financial capital.
Backers argue firms must preserve value from non-financial resources such as people, intellectual property and nature, not just investors' money.
It calls for adding ecological data, such as greenhouse gas emissions, alongside financial figures.
A 2009 meeting convened by the Prince of Wales set up the International Integrated Reporting Committee, renamed a Council in November 2011, to create a global framework.
From 2010 the Johannesburg Stock Exchange required listed companies to issue an integrated report or explain why not.
In 2021 the IIRC and SASB merged into the Value Reporting Foundation, which the IFRS Foundation folded into its International Sustainability Standards Board by June 2022.

entries.title: SEEA Ecosystem Accounting: the UN standard for ecosystems
entries.article: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting#Ecosystem accounts

definition.text: SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems.

facts.text: Its accounts present the extent and condition of ecosystems and the services they provide, in physical and money terms and tied to location.
The UN Statistical Commission adopted it as a standard at its 52nd session in March 2021.
An AI-powered tool, the ARIES for SEEA Explorer, was released in April 2021 for rapid, standardised natural capital accounting.
Its forerunner, the SEEA Experimental Ecosystem Accounts, built ecosystem accounts even though many of the stocks and flows are non-market assets.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts

sources.title: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting

entries.text: In March 2021, at its 52nd session, the UN Statistical Commission adopted SEEA Ecosystem Accounting as a standard. SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems, within the wider SEEA family ({{ref:nature-found-013}}). Its accounts present three things: the extent of ecosystems, their condition, and the services they provide. These are kept in physical and money terms and tied to location. Its forerunner, the SEEA Experimental Ecosystem Accounts, built ecosystem accounts even though many of the stocks and flows are non-market assets, things never bought or sold. The next month, in April 2021, an AI-powered tool called the ARIES for SEEA Explorer was released for rapid, standardised natural capital accounting.

SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems, within the wider SEEA family (SEEA: keeping national books on nature). Its accounts present three things: the extent of ecosystems, their condition, and the services they provide. These are kept in physical and money terms and tied to location. Its forerunner, the SEEA Experimental Ecosystem Accounts, built ecosystem accounts even though many of the stocks and flows are non-market assets, things never bought or sold. The next month, in April 2021, an AI-powered tool called the ARIES for SEEA Explorer was released for rapid, standardised natural capital accounting.

entries.title: Depletion: writing off a resource as it is used up

definition.text: An accounting and tax method that records the gradual using up of natural resources such as minerals, oil and timber as an expense over time.

facts.text: Depletion means using up natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling or felling.
Like depreciation, it lets owners recover costs as a resource's reserves shrink.
For tax there are two types, percentage depletion and cost depletion; standing timber must use cost depletion.
Cost depletion spreads the resource's total cost over the estimated quantity, charging a share for each unit extracted.
Example: if a well holding 200,000 barrels cost $100,000 and 10,000 barrels are extracted in year one, the deduction is $5,000.
Percentage depletion multiplies a set percentage for each mineral by the property's gross income for the year.
It uses country data to estimate the adjustments needed for the use and depletion of a nation's natural capital.
Environmentalists use it to track resource use over time and hold governments to account; economists use it to see how reliant countries or firms are on non-renewable resources.

entries.title: Gross ecosystem product: GDP for nature's services

definition.text: A statistic giving the money value of the ecosystem services produced in an area over an accounting period, usually a year.

facts.text: It supplements GDP, which counts only market values and so misses the non-market value of ecosystem services.
It sums material services such as fish, regulating services such as pollination and cultural services such as tourism, using market and non-market valuation.
Zhiyun Ouyang and Chunquan Zhu first proposed it in 2013.
A 2020 study of Qinghai province in China found nearly 80% of the benefits in its GEP flowed to other provinces.
The UN Statistical Commission adopted it within SEEA Ecosystem Accounting in 2021.
China issued official GEP accounting guidelines in October 2022 and uses it in rural development, payments for ecosystem services and urban planning.

entries.title: Wasting assets: things that lose value for good

definition.text: An asset that loses value irreversibly over time.

facts.text: Examples include vehicles, machinery and options contracts, and mines and quarries in use.
Its decline may be handled for tax and other purposes through depreciation.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts
entries.text: A mine in use, a vehicle and an options contract share one trait: each loses value over time, and none gets it back. Accountants call such things wasting assets, assets that lose value irreversibly. Examples include vehicles, machinery, options contracts, which give a right to buy or sell at a set price before a deadline, and mines and quarries in use. Their decline may be handled for tax and other purposes through depreciation.

entries.title: Environmental management accounting: data for decisions inside the firm

definition.text: The branch of corporate environmental accounting that supports a firm's internal decisions with physical and money data on its environmental use and costs.

facts.text: It gathers physical data on energy, water, materials and waste plus money data on environment-related costs, earnings and savings.
Corporate environmental accounting splits into this internal branch and environmental financial accounting, which reports to investors, lenders and other outsiders.

entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts
entries.text: Corporate environmental accounting faces two ways. Environmental financial accounting reports outward, to investors, lenders and other outsiders. Environmental management accounting looks inward. It supports a firm's own decisions with physical and money data on its environmental use and costs. It gathers physical data on energy, water, materials and waste, plus money data on environment-related costs, earnings and savings.

definition.text: The disclosure of an organisation's environmental impacts and performance.

facts.text: It may cover environmental risks and liabilities, energy and waste costs, emissions and pollution controls.
It reaches stakeholders through annual reports, sustainability reports, integrated reports and websites.

entries.title: Environmentally adjusted net domestic product: national product minus nature

definition.text: A 'green' version of net domestic product that subtracts the using up of natural assets, also called EDP or Green NDP.

facts.text: The System of National Accounts defines net domestic product as net exports plus final consumption plus net investment.
Green accounting instead follows SEEA, which measures the depletion of scarce natural resources and the cost of environmental degradation and its prevention.
EDP adds net accumulation of produced and non-produced economic assets but deducts the net accumulation of non-produced natural assets.

entries.title: The hidden price of producing and wasting food

definition.text: The use of full or true cost accounting to price the hidden environmental and social costs of food production and waste.

facts.text: The FAO's 2014 and 2015 studies applied it to food wastage and to world food production's impact on natural capital.
The FAO put food wastage's yearly hidden cost at US$700 billion to natural capital and US$900 billion to social capital.
It estimated the environmental damage of world food production at US$2330 billion per year.

entries.title: The residence principle: whose emissions are a ship's?
entries.article: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting#Flows of materials and energy

definition.text: The SEEA rule that counts all emissions caused by a country's economy, wherever they happen, rather than those released inside its borders.

facts.text: UNFCCC climate inventories use geographic borders, so the two approaches differ mainly for transport.
Under SEEA, emissions from trucks, ships or aircraft go to their home country even when released abroad.
UNFCCC inventories treat transport as its own sector, hiding the shares of households and industries.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts

sources.title: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting

entries.text: When a ship burns fuel far from home, which country's accounts should carry the emissions? Under SEEA's residence principle, the ship's home country. The rule counts all emissions caused by a country's economy, wherever they happen, rather than those released inside its borders. So emissions from trucks, ships or aircraft go to their home country even when released abroad. The emission counts kept under the UN climate convention ({{ref:nature-clim-053}}) use geographic borders instead, so the two approaches differ mainly for transport. Those counts also treat transport as its own sector, hiding the shares of households and industries.

entries.title: The trillions hidden in the world's food bill
entries.article: True cost accounting#Hidden costs of global agrifood systems

definition.text: Estimates of the environmental, health and social costs of the world's food systems that market prices leave out.

facts.text: FOLU (2019) put them at USD 12 trillion and Hendricks et al. (2023) at USD 19 trillion, with a range of USD 7.2 to 51.8 trillion.
The FAO's 2023 State of Food and Agriculture estimated USD 12.7 trillion, assessed country by country for 154 countries.
FAO later found health costs from unhealthy diets made up 70 percent of all agrifood hidden costs in 2020.

entries.title: WAVES: helping countries put nature in their accounts
entries.article: Natural capital accounting#Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services Partnership

definition.text: WAVES is a World Bank-led global partnership that helps countries put the value of natural capital into their national accounts.

facts.text: It was launched in October 2010 at the Convention on Biological Diversity's COP-10 meeting in Japan.
Its projects in countries such as Botswana, Colombia and Madagascar built capacity to apply SEEA.
The World Bank now runs a successor, the Global Program for Sustainability.

entries.title: Environmental profit and loss: Puma's price tag on nature

definition.text: A company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its supply chain, from raw materials to the factory gate.

facts.text: It internalises externalities by counting the ecosystem services a business depends on as well as the damage it causes.
Its main purpose is to show managers and stakeholders how large the impacts are and where in the supply chain they occur.
The first one was Puma's, on 2010 data, valuing greenhouse gases, water use, other air pollution, land conversion and waste.
Its method built on input-output models and valuation work in environmental economics such as the TEEB study.
Philips's 2017 annual report put its environmental impact for that year at Euro 7.2 billion using this method.
Preparing one can be expensive, and it is seen as a first step toward prices that reflect use of environmental goods and services.

Such an account is a company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its supply chain, from raw materials to the factory gate. It internalises externalities, bringing outside costs onto the books, by counting the ecosystem services a business depends on as well as the damage it causes. Its main purpose is to show managers and stakeholders how large the impacts are and where in the supply chain they occur. The method built on models of how industries buy from one another ({{ref:nature-acct-080}}) and on valuation work in environmental economics, such as the TEEB study. Philips's 2017 annual report used it to put that year's environmental impact at Euro 7.2 billion. Preparing one can be expensive. It is seen as a first step toward prices that reflect the use of environmental goods and services.

entries.title: Material flow indicators: summing up an economy's appetite

definition.text: Standard indicators calculated from material flow accounts to summarise an economy's material use.

facts.text: Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports; domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports.
The physical trade balance is imports minus exports, the reverse of the money trade balance because goods and money flow in opposite directions.
Total material requirement adds hidden flows, materials moved but not used such as mining overburden.
Raw material consumption counts raw materials embodied in traded goods, usually via environmentally extended input-output analysis.

entries.title: SEEA-Water: putting water into the national accounts
entries.article: System of Environmental and Economic Accounting for Water

definition.text: The UN's framework for organising physical and economic information about water with the same concepts and classifications as the System of National Accounts.

facts.text: The UN Statistical Commission adopted it as an interim statistical standard in 2007.
It organises water stocks and flows into the inland water resources system, covering the natural water cycle, and the economy, covering water-using industries and households.
Its SNA compatibility lets hydrological and water-use data be combined with economic data.
More than fifty countries are implementing or planning water accounts.

entries.title: El Serafy's method for pricing resource depletion

definition.text: Salah El Serafy's method for valuing the depletion cost of natural resources, one of several alternatives for estimating resource rent in national accounts.

facts.text: Other methods compared with it are net price, sustainable price, transaction value and replacement cost.
El Serafy co-edited 'Economic Accounting for Sustainable Development', a report from UNEP-World Bank workshops held after 1983.
He disagreed with Anne Harrison: she wanted adjustments inside the existing SNA, while he proposed redefining intermediate and final demand.

entries.contested_note: Harrison and El Serafy disagreed on whether to adjust indicators within the existing national accounts or to redefine intermediate and final demand.

entries.title: Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave

definition.text: A method for adding up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

facts.text: For a manufactured product it runs from extracting raw materials (cradle) through making, distributing and using it to recycling or disposal (grave).
An LCA inventories the energy and materials needed across the supply chain and calculates the resulting emissions.
It covers more than greenhouse gases, including water pollution, air pollution and ecotoxicity.
First used mainly to compare a product with alternatives, it is now used in product design, ecolabelling, consumer education and government policy.
An LCA is only as accurate as its data, which are either unit process data or environmental input-output data.
Critics note that not every factor can be reduced to a number, and rigid system boundaries make change hard to capture.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Every manufactured product has a life story. It begins when raw materials are extracted, the cradle, and runs through making, distribution and use to recycling or disposal, the grave. Life-cycle assessment, or LCA, adds up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of that life. An LCA inventories the energy and materials needed across the supply chain and calculates the resulting emissions. It covers more than greenhouse gases, including water pollution, air pollution and ecotoxicity, harm to living things from toxic substances. At first LCA was used mainly to compare a product with alternatives. Now it informs product design, product labelling ({{ref:nature-pol-186}}), consumer education and government policy. An LCA is only as accurate as its data, which come either as unit process data or as environmental input-output data. Critics note that not every factor can be reduced to a number. Rigid system boundaries, the lines that decide what is counted, also make change hard to capture.

entries.title: Emission intensity: pollution per unit of activity

definition.text: The amount of a pollutant released per unit of an activity, such as grams of CO2 per megajoule of energy or greenhouse gases per unit of GDP; also called carbon intensity.

facts.text: Intensities let analysts estimate emissions from activity data such as fuel burned, animals kept or distances travelled.
They also let people compare the environmental impact of different fuels or activities.
Carbon intensity per kilowatt-hour is widely used to compare sources of electricity.
Coal, mostly carbon, has a high CO2 intensity; natural gas, with four hydrogen atoms per carbon, has a medium one.
In Europe from 1990 to 2007, CO2 per unit of GDP fell by 2.3% a year, faster than energy intensity at 1.4% a year.
Different calculation methods, from full LCA to combustion-only, can give different results.
It is also called carbon intensity or emissions intensity.
The carbon intensity of global energy fell 13%, from 66.3 to 58.0 kg CO2/GJ, between 1978 and 2018, mainly through more renewables and nuclear.

entries.title: Biocapacity: what nature can supply each year

definition.text: An estimate of how much an ecosystem can produce of useful biological materials and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb.

facts.text: It is the supply side that the ecological footprint is compared with to measure human impact.
In 2016 Earth had about 12.2 billion hectares of productive land and water; divided among 7.4 billion people, that is 1.6 global hectares per person.
Those 1.6 global hectares also include the space wild species need.
An area's biocapacity is its physical area multiplied by a yield factor and an equivalence factor.
It changes with technology, since what counts as a useful material can change from year to year.
Population growth can lower biocapacity per person, since Earth's resources must be shared among more people.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: In 2016 Earth had about 12.2 billion hectares of productive land and water. Divided among 7.4 billion people, that came to 1.6 hectares of average productivity each, and those 1.6 hectares also had to cover the space wild species need. That supply is biocapacity: an estimate of how much useful biological material an ecosystem can produce, and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb ({{ref:nature-found-020}}). It is the supply side against which human demand, the {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, is compared to measure human impact. An area's biocapacity is its physical area multiplied by a yield factor and an equivalence factor. It is not fixed. It changes with technology, since what counts as a useful material can change from year to year. Population growth can also lower biocapacity per person, since Earth's resources must be shared among more people.

That supply is biocapacity: an estimate of how much useful biological material an ecosystem can produce, and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb (Assimilative capacity: how much waste nature can absorb). It is the supply side against which human demand, the Ecological footprint: how much planet a lifestyle needs, is compared to measure human impact. An area's biocapacity is its physical area multiplied by a yield factor and an equivalence factor. It is not fixed. It changes with technology, since what counts as a useful material can change from year to year. Population growth can also lower biocapacity per person, since Earth's resources must be shared among more people.

entries.title: Ecological footprint: how much planet a lifestyle needs

definition.text: A measure of how much nature, counted as biologically productive land and sea, people need to support their way of life and their economies.

facts.text: Footprint accounts compare the productive area people use for their consumption with the productive area actually available, called biocapacity.
It can be calculated for an activity, a person, a city, a nation or all of humanity, and split by consumption category such as food, housing and goods.
Resource use of every kind is converted into standard land areas called global hectares.
Global Footprint Network estimated humanity's footprint for 2023 at 1.71 planet Earths: demand 1.71 times what ecosystems renewed.
Humanity's footprint grew from 7.0 billion global hectares in 1961 to 20.6 billion in 2014, driven by higher use per person and more people.
The carbon footprint is the fastest-growing part, about 60% of humanity's total ecological footprint.
Per-person footprints range from 14.3 global hectares in Qatar to 0.5 in Yemen.
Mathis Wackernagel developed the concept and method as his PhD with supervisor William Rees in Vancouver from 1990 to 1994; Rees coined the name.

entries.title: Carbon footprint: one number for climate impact

definition.text: The total amount of greenhouse gases that an activity, product, company or country adds to the atmosphere, expressed as one comparable number.

facts.text: It is usually reported in tonnes of CO2-equivalent per unit, such as per year, per kilogram of protein or per kilometre travelled.
CO2-equivalent sums all greenhouse gases, not only carbon dioxide, into one figure.
It lets people compare the climate impact of individuals, products, companies and countries and set priorities for cutting it.
The World Bank put the global average in 2014 at about 5 tonnes of CO2 per person on a production basis.
With 9–10 billion people by 2050, a footprint of about 2–2.5 tonnes CO2e per person is needed to stay within a 2 °C target.
The term was first used in a BBC vegetarian food magazine in 1999.
Focusing on carbon alone can lead people to ignore or worsen other harms such as biodiversity loss and habitat destruction.

entries.title: IUCN Red List: the world's register of threatened species

definition.text: The global inventory, founded in 1964, of the conservation status and extinction risk of the world's species.

facts.text: Its goals are to report species' status, draw attention to threatened biodiversity, and influence policy and conservation action.
As of 2023, 42,108 of 150,388 species surveyed were considered at risk of extinction from human activity such as overfishing, hunting and land development.
The IUCN aims to re-evaluate every species at least every ten years, through peer-reviewed specialist groups.
In 2012, 41% of amphibian species, 33% of reef-building corals, 25% of mammals and 13% of birds were threatened.
The first two volumes of Red Lists, for mammals and birds, were published in 1966.
A 2016 study argued its classification is inconsistent and that adding geospatial data would move many species to higher risk categories.

entries.title: Water footprint: the hidden water in what people consume

definition.text: The total volume of fresh water used to produce the goods and services that a person, community or business consumes or produces.

facts.text: Water use is counted as the volume evaporated or polluted per unit of time.
Arjen Hoekstra coined the concept in 2002 as a consumption-based indicator, analogous to the ecological footprint of the 1990s.
Unlike traditional withdrawal statistics, it shows where water is used and polluted, not only how much.
The average global water footprint of an individual is 1,385 m3 per year.
A product's footprint is the sum over all processes in its supply chain divided by the number of units.
ISO 14046:2014, issued in July 2014, gives guidance for water footprint assessments based on life-cycle assessment principles.
Critics note that a footprint means little without regional scarcity: 140 litres for a cup of coffee may be harmless in humid areas but damaging in arid ones.

entries.title: Sustainability measurement: quantifying a slippery goal

definition.text: The frameworks and indicators used to measure how sustainable a process, product, service or business is.

facts.text: Sustainability is hard to quantify, perhaps impossible, because it has no fixed definition.
Frameworks look at environmental, social and economic domains, and the tools include indicators, benchmarks and audits.
The toolbox includes life-cycle assessment for resource use, the ecological footprint for consumption, and the Environmental Performance Index for governance.
The UN Commission on Sustainable Development published a list of 140 indicators covering environmental, social, economic and institutional aspects.
A benchmark is a reference point for a measurement; once set, it allows trends and progress to be measured.
Because each country uses its own indicators, global comparisons can be misread; common indexes would allow comparison.

entries.title: Input–output models: how every industry feeds the others

definition.text: A quantitative economic model that shows how the sectors of an economy depend on one another, with each sector's output becoming other sectors' inputs.

facts.text: It is laid out as a matrix in which columns show the inputs each sector buys and rows show the outputs it sells, usually in money.
Wassily Leontief developed it and won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it; Quesnay's Tableau économique was a cruder forerunner.
Statistics offices use it in national accounts, including to calculate GDP.
It is increasingly used to quantify environmental footprints for consumption-based accounting, such as tracing embodied carbon between economies.
Being linear it is cheap to compute, but it needs huge amounts of data, so tables are often published 5–7 years late.
Because tables are in money, every dollar spent in a sector is assumed to cause the same damage, which can bias environmental estimates.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: In any economy, one sector's output becomes other sectors' inputs. An input–output model is a quantitative economic model that maps these dependencies. It is laid out as a matrix, a grid of numbers, usually in money. Columns show the inputs each sector buys; rows show the outputs it sells. Wassily Leontief developed it and won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it; a cruder forerunner was Quesnay's table of the economy ({{ref:nature-hist-018}}). Statistics offices use it in national accounts, including to calculate GDP. It is increasingly used to measure environmental footprints for consumption-based accounting, such as tracing the carbon embodied in goods traded between economies. Being linear, built from simple proportions, it is cheap to compute. But it needs huge amounts of data, so tables are often published 5–7 years late. And because tables are in money, every dollar spent in a sector is assumed to cause the same damage, which can bias environmental estimates.
entries.text_plain: In any economy, one sector's output becomes other sectors' inputs. An input–output model is a quantitative economic model that maps these dependencies. It is laid out as a matrix, a grid of numbers, usually in money. Columns show the inputs each sector buys; rows show the outputs it sells. Wassily Leontief developed it and won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it; a cruder forerunner was Quesnay's table of the economy (Quesnay's Tableau économique: the economy as a body). Statistics offices use it in national accounts, including to calculate GDP. It is increasingly used to measure environmental footprints for consumption-based accounting, such as tracing the carbon embodied in goods traded between economies. Being linear, built from simple proportions, it is cheap to compute. But it needs huge amounts of data, so tables are often published 5–7 years late. And because tables are in money, every dollar spent in a sector is assumed to cause the same damage, which can bias environmental estimates.

entries.title: Environmental indicators: simple numbers for a complex world

definition.text: A simple measure, tracked over time, that tells us what is happening in the environment.

facts.text: Indicators are a practical, cheaper way to follow a complex environment than recording every variable.
For example, the concentration of ozone-depleting substances in the air indicates the state of stratospheric ozone depletion.

Following the OECD's Pressure-State-Response model, there are state indicators, pressure indicators such as greenhouse gas emissions, and response indicators such as people served by sewage treatment.
Environmental indicators are a subset of sustainable development indicators, which also cover social and economic health.
Good indicators are judged on scientific credibility, policy relevance and practical data needs.
The public responds best to clear, simple indicators such as the UV index and air quality index.
Large indicator sets are condensed into indices, headline indicators, traffic-light visuals or dashboards.

entries.title: Embedded emissions: the carbon hidden in trade

definition.text: The greenhouse gases released in making a good, counted as belonging to whoever consumes it; also called embodied emissions or embodied carbon.

facts.text: The UNFCCC counts emissions where goods are produced, so emissions embedded in imports are attributed to the exporting country.
Choosing between production and consumption accounting is partly a question of equity: who is responsible for emissions.
Research found that in 2004, 23% of global emissions were embedded in internationally traded goods, flowing mostly from China and developing countries to the US, Europe and Japan.
Wang and Watson (2007) suggested nearly a quarter of China's CO2 emissions might come from producing exports.
In Western Europe imported emissions make up 20-50% of consumed emissions.
A carbon tariff or border carbon adjustment is a tariff on the carbon embedded in imports.
Emissions are usually counted where they are produced, as countries do when reporting to the UNFCCC.
A large share of CO2 emissions is traded internationally.

entries.title: Earth Overshoot Day: when the year's budget runs out

definition.text: The calculated date each year on which humanity's use of resources passes what Earth can regenerate in that whole year.

facts.text: It equals world biocapacity divided by world ecological footprint, multiplied by the 365 days of the year.
In economic terms it is the day the planet's yearly regenerative budget is spent and humanity starts deficit spending.
Andrew Simms of the New Economics Foundation developed the idea; Global Footprint Network calculates it.
Human consumption began to outstrip what the planet could reproduce in the early 1970s.
In 2020 coronavirus lockdowns pushed the date to 22 August, more than three weeks later than 2019; in 2024 it fell on August 1.
Critics say it mainly reflects excess carbon dioxide and measures land and water mismanagement poorly; the Breakthrough Institute called it a publicity stunt.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the date mostly reflects carbon emissions, and Global Footprint Network researchers published a response.

entries.title: Consumption-based accounting: charging emissions to the buyer
entries.article: Carbon footprint#Consumption-based emission accounting based on input-output analysis

definition.text: A way of counting a country's emissions that assigns all the emissions along a global supply chain to the place where the goods are finally consumed.

facts.text: Its opposite, production-based or territorial accounting, counts only emissions released inside the country and is what countries report to the UNFCCC.
Consumption-based accounting includes the emissions behind imported goods and services, so it is more comprehensive.
It rests on input-output analysis, extended worldwide as multi-regional input-output analysis (MRIO).
Consumption-based emissions reflect the lifestyle choices of a country's citizens.
Counting trade reverses the apparent fall in developed countries' emissions, turning a 2% decrease under production accounting into a 7% increase.
It is more complex and uncertain, since it needs an extra step and data from every trading partner; some suggest using it as a 'shadow' to production accounts.

entries.title: Scope 1, 2 and 3: sorting a company's emissions
entries.article: Carbon footprint#Types of greenhouse gas emissions

definition.text: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol's three-way split of an organization's emissions into direct ones, those from bought energy, and all other indirect ones in its value chain.

facts.text: Scope 1 covers emissions the organization causes directly, such as burning fuel on site; for a person, a car or gas stove.
Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat, cooling or steam.
Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from sources the organization does not own or control, including suppliers and product users.
In 2022 about 30% of US companies reported Scope 3 emissions.
Footprints that leave out Scope 3 can mislead customers about the real footprint of companies or products.
Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources a company owns or controls, such as its fuel and vehicles.
Scope 3 covers suppliers and product users; it made up 75% of emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project.
Oil companies claiming net-zero operations leave out customers burning their oil, 70–90% of oil-related emissions, which falls in Scope 3.

entries.title: The four phases of a life-cycle assessment
entries.article: Life-cycle assessment#Main ISO phases of LCA

definition.text: The four phases in which the ISO 14040 and 14044 standards say a life-cycle assessment is carried out: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation.

facts.text: Goal and scope set the product's function, the functional unit, the system boundaries, assumptions and allocation rules.
Life cycle inventory (LCI) quantifies raw material and energy needs and all emissions and releases over the product's life.
Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) evaluates the potential environmental and human health impacts of those flows.
Interpretation summarizes the results and ends in conclusions and recommendations.
The phases are interdependent, so no stage counts as final until the whole study is done.

entries.title: Ecological indicators: counting beetles to judge a field

definition.text: A measure that sums up the state of an ecosystem, or the human impact on it, in simple terms for the public and policy makers.

facts.text: For example, the number of beetle taxa in a field can indicate its biodiversity.
They save cost and time: instead of counting every bird and plant in a restored wetland, a few indicator species can be monitored.
Ecological indicators are a subset of environmental indicators and refer only to ecological processes.
Limits include patchy data, no international standards, missing reference levels, and neglect of hard-to-measure values such as aesthetics.

entries.title: Living Planet Index: tracking the world's wildlife

definition.text: An indicator of the state of global biodiversity built from population trends of vertebrate species around the world.

facts.text: WWF developed it in 1997 with UNEP-WCMC; since 2006 the Zoological Society of London manages it with WWF.
As of 2022 it drew on 31,821 populations of 5,230 species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
The 2024 report showed monitored wildlife populations falling by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2020.
Declines averaged 94% in Latin America and the Caribbean; land-use change and habitat loss are a key driver.
It is limited to vertebrates because long-term data for invertebrates and plants are scarcer.
Media often wrongly report it as showing that 69% of all animals or species were lost since 1970.
Studies have found it sensitive to outliers and biased by its mathematics, possibly overstating declines.
It was used to measure progress toward the Convention on Biological Diversity's 2010 target and Aichi targets.

entries.contested_note: Researchers dispute whether the index reflects true changes in abundance, with re-analyses suggesting it overstates declines and counter-critiques of those re-analyses.

entries.title: Red List categories: from Least Concern to Extinct

definition.text: The nine groups into which the IUCN Red List sorts species, from Extinct to Not Evaluated, based on criteria such as rate of decline, population size and range.

facts.text: Extinct means beyond reasonable doubt no longer alive; Extinct in the Wild means surviving only in captivity or cultivation.
"Threatened" covers three categories: Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable.
Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient and Not Evaluated complete the scheme.
All new assessments since 2001 use version 3.1 of the categories and criteria.

entries.title: Red List Index: watching extinction risk change over time

definition.text: An indicator, built from the IUCN Red List, that tracks how the extinction risk of whole groups of species changes over time.

facts.text: Repeating conservation assessments at regular intervals lets changes in species' threat status reveal trends in extinction risk.
It can be broken down by taxonomic group, biogeographic realm, habitat type or main threat.
A sampled version (SRLI) assesses a representative sample of species, since assessing every fungus, insect and plant is impractical.
The shark and ray Red List Index has fallen 19% since the 1970s because of overfishing.
Australia's national bird RLI fell from 0.927 in 1990 to 0.896 in 2020, picking up both the 2019–2020 wildfires and conservation successes.
It is the single indicator for Sustainable Development Goal target 15.5 and was used for the CBD's 2010 biodiversity target.

entries.title: Red List of Ecosystems: rating the risk of collapse

definition.text: The IUCN's global framework for assessing and recording how close ecosystems are to collapse, the ecosystem-level counterpart of the Red List of species.

facts.text: It assesses biodiversity at a level of organization above species, replacing national protocols that were often not comparable.

It aims to evaluate all the world's ecosystems by 2025 to support conservation and resource management decisions.
It helps focus limited conservation effort on the ecosystems most likely to disappear.
Some countries, such as Finland, have adopted it as their official system for assessing ecosystem risk.
Critics point to the lack of a consistent way to classify ecosystems and to debate over the concept of ecosystem collapse.

entries.title: Sustainability metrics and indices: many yardsticks, no standard

definition.text: Numerical measures that try to quantify the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainability.

facts.text: There is no universal standard, so disciplines and international organizations have proposed many different indicators.
Examples include the Ecological Footprint, the Human Development Index, the Genuine Progress Index and the Environmental Sustainability Index.

Interest in Sustainable Development Index systems has expanded since the 2010s, more in industrialized than developing countries.
Although increasingly popular, sustainability indicators often have limited effect on actual policy and practice.

entries.title: Blue, green and grey water: three shades of a footprint

definition.text: The three parts of a water footprint: blue for surface and groundwater, green for rainwater, and grey for water needed to dilute pollution.

facts.text: A blue footprint counts water taken from lakes, rivers, wetlands and aquifers that evaporates, enters a product or is returned elsewhere or later.
A green footprint counts rain stored in the soil's root zone that plants transpire or take up; it matters most for farm and forest products.
A grey footprint is the water needed to dilute pollutants until the water meets agreed quality standards.
Green water has been estimated at 94% of the water footprint of global beef cattle production.
Critics say the grey footprint treats pollution like scarcity, though the two affect people and nature differently.

entries.title: Sustainability indicators: simple questions for policy

definition.text: A measure that tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity, mainly to inform public policy.

facts.text: Indicator sets answer simple questions: what is happening (descriptive indicators), are we reaching targets (performance indicators), are we improving?

Indicators cover the environment, society or the economy, but there is no fixed definition of a sustainability indicator.

A sustainability indicator tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity. Descriptive indicators say what is happening; performance indicators say whether targets are being met. They are scientific constructs whose principal purpose is to inform public policy-making. They can cover the environment, society or the economy, but there is no fixed definition of a sustainability indicator.

entries.title: Environmentally extended input–output analysis: tracing impacts through trade

definition.text: An environmental accounting tool that attaches resource use and emissions to an economy's input-output tables, so they can be traced through production to final consumption.

facts.text: It is the main way consumption-based accounts are compiled, as trade makes global resource use more important.
Each industry's extra inputs (energy, materials, labour) and outputs (emissions) are added as an extension matrix of factors per unit of output.
Multiplying final demand by the Leontief inverse and these factor coefficients allocates resource use and emissions to domestic or export demand.
National tables are combined into multi-regional input-output (MRIO) models to reflect differing production structures.
It assumes each industry makes one homogeneous product at one price, which aggregation and by-products violate.
It also assumes constant returns to scale, an assumption shared by life-cycle assessment.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: As trade makes global resource use more important, accounts must follow emissions from producer to final buyer. Environmentally extended input–output analysis, or EEIO, is the main way such consumption-based accounts are compiled. It attaches resource use and emissions to an economy's input–output tables, so they can be traced through production to final consumption. Each industry's extra inputs, such as energy, materials and labour, and its outputs, such as emissions, are added as an extension matrix of factors per unit of output. Multiplying final demand by {{ref:nature-acct-081}} and these factors allocates resource use and emissions to domestic or export demand. National tables are combined into multi-regional input–output models, or MRIO, to reflect differing production structures. The method assumes each industry makes one uniform product at one price, which aggregation and by-products violate. It also assumes constant returns to scale, where doubling inputs doubles output, an assumption shared by life-cycle assessment.

entries.title: Happy Planet Index: long, happy lives on a small footprint

definition.text: An index, introduced by the New Economics Foundation in 2006, that measures how efficiently countries turn environmental impact into long, satisfied lives.

facts.text: Roughly, it multiplies life satisfaction by life expectancy and divides by the ecological footprint per person.
It was designed to challenge GDP and the Human Development Index, which are seen as ignoring sustainability.
Costa Rica led the 2009, 2012 and 2016 rankings and also the 2019 ranking, with a score of 62.1.
It is not a ranking of the happiest countries: the US, with high life satisfaction, ranked 108th.
Critics say it weights the footprint so heavily that the US would have needed a life expectancy of 439 years to match Vanuatu in 2006.
Data gaps forced estimates of footprint and life satisfaction for several countries.

entries.title: Environmental Performance Index: ranking countries' green policies

definition.text: A score that ranks countries on the environmental performance of their policies.

facts.text: It was started in 2002 by the World Economic Forum with Yale and Columbia University centres, and the report appears every two years.
The 2024 report uses 58 indicators to rank 180 countries on climate change mitigation, ecosystem vitality and environmental health.
In 2024 Estonia, Luxembourg, Germany, Finland and the United Kingdom ranked top, and India, Myanmar, Laos, Pakistan and Vietnam last.
Scores rise with national wealth, but with diminishing returns; rule of law and regulatory quality predict performance better than wealth.
Wealth funds clean water and waste management but also raises consumption, waste and emissions.
Critics fault its arbitrary choice of metrics and its bias against data-poor countries; India rejected its 176th place in 2024.

entries.contested_note: Critics, including India's environment ministry, argue its indicators are arbitrary or biased; the index has since added and reweighted indicators.

conflicts.text: The 2024 index groups its 58 indicators into 11 issue categories.
conflicts.note: S:fa56d028d239 on the same page says the 58 indicators are grouped into 30 issue categories.

entries.title: DPSIR: from drivers to responses

definition.text: A cause-and-effect framework that sorts information about a society–environment problem into drivers, pressures, state, impacts and responses.

facts.text: Drivers are social, demographic and economic developments, such as population growth, that lead to human activities affecting the environment.
Pressures, such as emissions or waste, change the state of the environment, which in turn has impacts on human well-being.
Responses are actions, mostly policy, that adjust drivers, reduce pressures, restore the state or soften impacts.
The European Environment Agency developed it in 1999, building on the OECD's 1993 Pressure-State-Response framework.
Critics say its categories are ill-defined: a wastewater plant is a response to pollution but a pressure when its effluent causes eutrophication.
It is also criticized for oversimplifying and for sidelining local and indigenous knowledge.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Population grows, people do more, emissions and waste rise, the environment changes, well-being suffers, and governments act. The DPSIR framework sorts that chain into five links: drivers, pressures, state, impacts and responses. Drivers are social, demographic and economic developments, such as population growth, that lead to human activities affecting the environment. Pressures, such as emissions or waste, change the state of the environment, which in turn has impacts on human well-being. Responses are actions, mostly policy, that adjust drivers, reduce pressures, restore the state or soften impacts. The European Environment Agency developed it in 1999, building on the OECD's 1993 Pressure-State-Response framework. Critics say its categories are ill-defined. A wastewater plant is a response to pollution, but a pressure when its outflow causes eutrophication ({{ref:nature-eco-216}}). It is also criticized for oversimplifying and for sidelining local and indigenous knowledge.

entries.title: Ecological footprints by country: an unequal planet

definition.text: Comparisons of national footprints that show how unequally countries use the planet's resources.

facts.text: A nation's total footprint is its footprint per person multiplied by its population.
In 2022 China had the largest total footprint, 5.54 billion global hectares, followed by the United States with 2.66 billion.
Plotting footprints against the Human Development Index shows that higher living standards generally tend to be less sustainable.
Footprints also vary widely within a country, with individual lifestyles and wealth.

entries.title: Is the ecological footprint fair? The critics' case

definition.text: The scholarly argument over whether the ecological footprint is a reliable and fair measure of human demand on nature.

facts.text: Critics and Global Footprint Network researchers wrote a joint paper setting out the terms of the controversy.
Government agencies that repeated the calculations largely confirmed the results, getting near-identical numbers.
Replacing old forests with high-yield plantations can raise measured biocapacity and so lower the footprint, a perverse result.
Some argue the measure has an anti-urban bias, making dense cities look "parasitic".

entries.contested_note: Researchers have published critiques, replies and rejoinders on the method's reliability since 1999.

entries.title: Peas versus beef: the carbon footprint of food

definition.text: The greenhouse gas emissions caused by producing a food, which differ greatly between plant-based foods and meat or dairy.

facts.text: 100 grams of protein from peas emits 0.4 kg CO2eq; the same protein from beef emits nearly 90 times more, 35 kgCO2eq.
Most of a food's footprint comes from the farm or land use change, little from transport and packaging, so what you eat matters more than food miles.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

Most of a food's footprint comes from the farm or from land clearing ({{ref:nature-res-108}}), and little from transport and packaging. So what people eat matters more than how far it travelled.
