entries.title: Whose carbon? The personal footprint debate
entries.article: Carbon footprint#Shifting responsibility from corporations to individuals

definition.text: The dispute over whether promoting personal carbon footprints shifts responsibility for climate change from fossil fuel companies to individuals.

facts.text: BP ran a large advertising campaign that helped popularize the personal carbon footprint.
Critics say many fossil fuel companies used this strategy to blame individual choices for their industries' harms.
The IPCC notes that individual behaviour changes alone cannot deliver deep emission cuts.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue the concept was promoted to move blame onto consumers, while it remains widely used for personal choices.

conflicts.text: BP's campaign was run in 2004.
conflicts.note: Other sentences on the same page date the BP/Ogilvy campaign to 2005 (S:43510061ec64, S:f3a35f7ce3d6).

entries.title: Economic input–output LCA: life cycles at industry scale
entries.article: Life-cycle assessment#Economic input–output life cycle assessment

definition.text: A form of life-cycle assessment that uses sector-level data on each industry's environmental impact and its purchases from other industries.

facts.text: It captures long supply chains, such as cars needing energy and energy needing vehicles, easing the scoping problem of process LCA.
But it relies on sector averages that may not fit a specific product, and its translation of money into impacts is not validated.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Cars need energy, and making energy needs vehicles. Chains like that run on and on, and an assessment built process by process must cut them off somewhere. Economic input–output life-cycle assessment eases that problem by using sector-level data on each industry's environmental impact and its purchases from other industries. That way it captures long supply chains. But it relies on sector averages that may not fit a specific product, and its translation of money into impacts is not validated.

entries.title: Cradle to grave, cradle to gate: LCA boundaries

definition.text: The variants of life-cycle assessment that differ in which stretch of a product's life they cover, such as cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-gate and gate-to-gate.

facts.text: Cradle-to-grave covers the full life from resource extraction to disposal; cradle-to-gate stops at the factory gate and leaves out use and disposal.
Cradle-to-cradle is a cradle-to-grave assessment whose final step is recycling into new products.
Well-to-wheel is the variant used for transport fuels and vehicles.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Not every life-cycle assessment covers a product's whole life. Cradle-to-grave covers the full life, from resource extraction to disposal. Cradle-to-gate stops at the factory gate and leaves out use and disposal. Gate-to-gate is a narrower variant still. Cradle-to-cradle is a cradle-to-grave assessment whose final step is recycling into new products. For transport fuels and vehicles, the variant used is well-to-wheel.

entries.title: Life cycle energy analysis: counting every joule

definition.text: An approach that counts all the energy a product needs, including the energy used to make its components, materials and services.

facts.text: Net energy content is a product's energy minus the energy used to extract and convert it.
A controversial early result claimed that making solar cells needed more energy than they recover.
Energy alone ignores whether flows are renewable and whether wastes are toxic.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Does a solar cell recover the energy it took to make? One controversial early result claimed it did not. Questions like that belong to life cycle energy analysis, which counts all the energy a product needs, including the energy used to make its components, materials and services. A key figure is net energy content: a product's energy minus the energy used to extract and convert it. Energy is not the whole story. Counting it alone ignores whether flows are renewable and whether wastes are toxic.

entries.title: Daly's three rules for living within nature's means
entries.article: Sustainability metrics and indices#"Daly Rules" approach

definition.text: Herman Daly's three operating rules for ecological sustainability, covering renewable resources, nonrenewable resources and pollution.

facts.text: Renewable resources such as fish, soil and groundwater must be used no faster than they regenerate.
Nonrenewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels must be used no faster than renewable substitutes can be put in place.
Pollution and wastes must be released no faster than natural systems can absorb, recycle or neutralize them.
Daly built on theory from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book The Entropy Law and the Economic Process.
Some see the rules as the physical counterpart of the Brundtland definition, which supplies the ethical goal of not depleting natural capital.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: {{ref:nature-hist-040}} set out three operating rules for ecological sustainability. First, renewable resources such as fish, soil and groundwater must be used no faster than they regenerate. Second, nonrenewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels must be used no faster than renewable substitutes can be put in place. Third, pollution and wastes must be released no faster than natural systems can absorb, recycle or neutralize them ({{ref:nature-found-020}}). Daly built on theory from a 1971 book by {{ref:nature-hist-044}} on the economic process. Some see the rules as the physical counterpart of the definition from {{ref:nature-eecon-222}}, which supplies the ethical goal of not depleting natural capital.

Daly built on theory from a 1971 book by Georgescu-Roegen: entropy and the economic process on the economic process. entries.title: Circles of Sustainability: choosing the right indicators

definition.text: A framework for choosing sustainability indicators, organized around four domains: economics, ecology, politics and culture.

facts.text: Rather than prescribing indicators, it guides decisions about which indicators are most useful.
Each domain has seven sub-domains, each linked to indicators.
Agencies including the UN Global Compact Cities Programme have used it since 2010.

entries.title: Emission factors: activity times a rate

definition.text: A fixed rate linking an activity to the emissions it causes, so that emissions equal activity multiplied by the emission factor.

facts.text: CO2 and SO2 from burning fuel can be estimated very precisely, because they depend almost entirely on the fuel's known carbon and sulphur content.
Other pollutants depend on combustion technology, so their factors are less certain.
A major use is in national greenhouse gas inventories reported to the UNFCCC, with IPCC Guidelines as the main source of default factors.

entries.title: Emission inventories: tallying a year of pollution

definition.text: An account of how much of one or more pollutants or greenhouse gases all sources in an area release over a set period, usually a year.

facts.text: Emissions are the starting point of every pollution problem, so inventories are needed to understand problems and track progress on them.
Each pollutant's emissions are usually estimated by multiplying each activity's level by an emission factor.
Countries report annual national inventories to the UNFCCC for greenhouse gases and to the LRTAP convention for air pollutants.
Facility-level reporting schemes such as Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers support public participation in decisions.
Scientists use inventories as inputs to air quality models, often needing finer spatial and time detail than national totals.
Greenhouse gas inventories also count removals by carbon sinks, unlike some other air emission inventories.

Unlike some other air emission inventories, greenhouse gas inventories also count removals by carbon sinks, which take carbon out of the air.

entries.title: Lifecycle emissions of electricity: coal against the rest

definition.text: The total greenhouse gases released per unit of electricity over the whole life of each kind of power plant, as compiled by the IPCC in 2011.

facts.text: Median values in g CO2-eq per kWh: hydroelectric reservoir 4, nuclear 16, solar PV 46.
Natural gas combined cycle without scrubbing emits 469 g per kWh and coal 1001.

Solar PV emits 46, nuclear 16 and a hydroelectric reservoir 4. These are IPCC medians compiled in 2011. They count the total greenhouse gases released per unit of electricity over a plant's whole life.

entries.title: National water footprints: relying on foreign water

definition.text: The water used to produce the goods and services consumed by a nation's inhabitants, wherever that water is used.

facts.text: The internal footprint uses domestic water; the external footprint is water used abroad to make imported goods.
It is calculated from domestic water use by subtracting virtual water exported and adding virtual water imported.
It shows that several countries rely heavily on foreign water, and such dependencies are likely to grow with trade liberalisation.

distinct_from: Blue, green and grey water footprints
entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Much of the water a nation consumes may be used far away. A national water footprint counts the water used to produce the goods and services a nation's inhabitants consume, wherever that water is used. The internal footprint uses domestic water; the external footprint is water used abroad to make imported goods. It is calculated from domestic water use by subtracting the water embodied in exports and adding the water embodied in imports ({{ref:nature-res-111}}). It shows that several countries rely heavily on foreign water, and such dependencies are likely to grow as trade is liberalised.

The internal footprint uses domestic water; the external footprint is water used abroad to make imported goods. It is calculated from domestic water use by subtracting the water embodied in exports and adding the water embodied in imports (Virtual water: the water hidden in what we trade). It shows that several countries rely heavily on foreign water, and such dependencies are likely to grow as trade is liberalised.

entries.title: Hubbert's peak as a measure of depletion

definition.text: The use of the Hubbert production curve, which rises to a peak and then declines, as a measure of how far a non-renewable resource has been depleted.

facts.text: A modified Hubbert curve applies to any resource harvested faster than it is replaced, such as an over-pumped aquifer.
Fisheries such as whaling and North Sea cod show that human pressure is pushing many resources through a Hubbert-like depletion cycle.
Phosphorus, essential to farming, is estimated to run out in 60 to 130 years.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

A modified curve applies to any resource harvested faster than it is replaced, such as over-pumped groundwater. Fisheries such as whaling and North Sea cod show human pressure pushing many resources through a Hubbert-like cycle of depletion. Phosphorus, essential to farming, is estimated to run out in 60 to 130 years.

entries.title: Leontief inverse: the coal behind the steel

definition.text: The matrix (I−A)^−1 that turns final demand into the total output every sector must produce, counting all direct and indirect inputs.

facts.text: A technical coefficient is the amount of one good needed to make one unit of another.
In a two-sector coal and steel example, the economy must produce 19.19 units of coal to deliver only 7 to consumers.
The gap is indirect demand: coal to make steel and more coal, round after round, which the Leontief inverse sums.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

The gap is indirect demand: coal to make steel and more coal, round after round. The Leontief inverse is the matrix, written (I−A)^−1, that sums all those rounds, turning final demand into the total output every sector must produce. It is built from technical coefficients: the amount of one good needed to make one unit of another.

entries.title: Physical input–output tables: counting materials, not dollars

definition.text: An input-output table measured in physical units instead of money, built to estimate environmental impacts more faithfully.

facts.text: Monetary tables must assume one price per good for the whole year and constant returns to scale.
Price does not track damage well: a $200 bottle of wine is unlikely to cause twenty times the impact of a $10 one.

entries.title: Embodied carbon: why the greenest building already exists

definition.text: The emissions from extracting, making, transporting and installing a building's materials, and from its repair and end-of-life treatment, as opposed to the emissions from running it.

facts.text: Studies estimate embodied carbon at 30% to 40% of global carbon emissions in the construction sector.
As buildings run more efficiently, embodied carbon's share of a building's life-cycle emissions has risen from about 20% to 50%.
Hence the saying "The greenest building is the building that is already built": re-use avoids large construction emissions.
It can be cut by using less material and substituting lower-carbon materials such as timber, bamboo or cement alternatives.

entries.text: "The greenest building is the building that is already built." The saying rests on embodied carbon in buildings. Studies put it at 30% to 40% of global carbon emissions in the construction sector. As buildings run more efficiently, its share of a building's life-cycle emissions has risen from about 20% to 50%. Re-use avoids large construction emissions. Otherwise it can be cut by using less material and lower-carbon materials such as timber, bamboo or cement alternatives.

entries.title: Top-down, bottom-up and hybrid carbon accounting
entries.article: Embedded emissions#Top-down, bottom-up and hybrid approaches

definition.text: The three main ways to quantify embodied carbon: bottom-up process-based LCA, top-down environmentally extended input-output models, and hybrids of the two.

facts.text: Bottom-up LCA can assess specific products but suffers truncation, because no study can follow the whole supply chain.
Top-down EEIO multiplies greenhouse gas intensity, such as tCO2e per dollar, by the final demand for each product.
EEIO's sector aggregation makes specific products hard to assess; hybrid methods combine both to reduce each one's weakness.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: There are three main ways to quantify embodied carbon. Top-down environmentally extended input–output models multiply greenhouse gas intensity, such as tonnes of CO2-equivalent per dollar, by the final demand for each product. Their grouping by sector makes specific products hard to assess. Hybrid methods combine both to reduce each one's weakness.

entries.title: MIPS: material used per unit of service
entries.article: Material input per unit of service

definition.text: A measure of eco-efficiency, developed at the Wuppertal Institute in the 1990s, that divides the total material input of a product over its life by the units of service it provides.

facts.text: For a car, the service units are passenger kilometres over its life; less material per kilometre means a more eco-efficient car.
MIPS falls if less material is used or more service is delivered, for example by sharing a newspaper or a car, or making products last longer.
It counts five resource categories: abiotic, biotic, earth movements, water and air.
Its main weakness is that it ignores the toxicity of materials, so it should be used alongside other methods.

entries.title: Biocapacity deficit: living beyond local means

definition.text: The gap that opens when a population's ecological footprint is larger than the biocapacity of the area it lives in.

facts.text: A deficit comes from overusing one's own ecosystems, net imports, or use of the global commons.
A region whose biocapacity exceeds its footprint has a biocapacity reserve.
Using 1.7 Earths means a year's resource use takes one year and eight months to regenerate.
Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the dominant cause of global overshoot.

entries.title: Red List of Ecosystems categories and criteria
entries.article: IUCN Red List of Ecosystems#Categories and Criteria

definition.text: The eight risk categories and five criteria (A to E) the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems uses to rate an ecosystem's risk of collapse.

facts.text: Collapsed means the ecosystem's defining features and native biota are virtually certainly lost; only the Aral Sea and the Central Ayeyarwady palm savanna are so listed.
Unlike species extinction, ecosystem collapse is in theory reversible.
Formally, Critically Endangered means a 50% chance of collapse within 50 years, Endangered 20% within 50 years, and Vulnerable 10% within 100 years.
Criteria A and B measure spatial symptoms (declining or restricted distribution), C and D functional ones, and E models overall collapse risk.

entries.title: Five tests of a good emission inventory

definition.text: The standards the UNFCCC and LRTAP conventions require of a national emission inventory: transparent, consistent, comparable, complete and accurate.

facts.text: Transparent means assumptions and methods are explained clearly enough for others to replicate the inventory.
Consistent means the same methods and data sets are used for the base year and all later years.
Accurate means estimates are systematically neither above nor below true emissions, with uncertainties reduced as far as practicable.

entries.title: Emergy sustainability index: yield against environmental load
entries.article: Sustainability metrics and indices#Energy, Emergy and Sustainability Index

definition.text: An index proposed by M.T. Brown and S. Ulgiati in 1997 that divides the emergy yield ratio by the environmental loading ratio.

facts.text: Emergy means embodied energy; Howard T. Odum coined the term and its accounting system in 1956.
The index accounts for yield, renewability and environmental load.
Leone notes that it calculates supply constraints that reporting schemes like the GRI do not.

entries.title: Natural Step framework: conditions for a sustainable society
entries.article: Sustainability metrics and indices#Natural Step approach

definition.text: A science-based definition of sustainability, built by consensus after the Brundtland report, that sets out system conditions a sustainable society must meet.

facts.text: Swedish cancer scientist Karl-Henrik Robèrt coordinated the consensus process behind it.
A sustainable society does not keep raising concentrations of substances taken from the Earth's crust or made by society, does not degrade the environment, and lets people meet their needs.

entries.title: Consumer or producer: who answers for embodied impacts?
entries.article: Environmentally extended input–output analysis#Distributing environmental responsibility

definition.text: The choice of whether environmental impacts in input-output accounts are assigned to final consumers, to producers, or shared between them.

facts.text: Allocating all impacts to final consumers is consumer-based responsibility; allocating direct impacts to producers is production-based responsibility.
Hybrid schemes, including income-based ones and sharedness, have been proposed.
The importer gets the product, but the exporter gets the income, so how to share responsibility is unsettled.

entries.contested_note: It has yet to be determined how responsibility for impacts embodied in exports should be shared between importing and exporting economies.
entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: The importer gets the product; the exporter gets the income. So who should answer for the pollution released in making it? Input–output accounts can assign environmental impacts to final consumers, to producers, or share them. Allocating all impacts to final consumers is consumer-based responsibility. Allocating direct impacts to producers is production-based responsibility. Hybrid schemes have been proposed, including income-based ones and an approach called sharedness. How to share responsibility for impacts embodied in exports between importing and exporting economies has yet to be settled.

entries.title: Material footprint: the ore behind the phone

definition.text: A consumption-based indicator of material use: all the raw materials needed along the supply chain to make the goods a country consumes, also called raw material equivalents.

facts.text: It counts direct and indirect flows, such as the ore mined for a phone's metal and the coal burned to power the refining.
It is comparable to carbon and water footprints, and is calculated with environmentally extended input-output analysis.
The total material footprint sums biomass, fossil fuels, metal ores and non-metal ores; it is an indicator for Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 12.
Material footprint per person rose 39 per cent from 2000 to 2017, reaching 12.18 tonnes.

facts.text: A simple waste footprint ignores that waste is usually treated into a less harmful form before recycling or disposal.
The model follows waste as treatment turns it into secondary waste and residues, through to recycling and final disposal.

entries.title: Global hectares: a common currency for land

definition.text: The adjusted unit of footprint accounting: a hectare with the world's average biological productivity in a given year.

facts.text: It is needed because not all hectares produce the same amount of ecosystem services.
Footprint studies turn the use of energy, food, fibre, building materials and water into global hectares.
Wackernagel and Rees's early estimate of about 1.3 hectares per person was lower partly because those studies did not yet use global hectares.

entries.title: HANPP: humanity's share of the planet's plant growth

definition.text: An indicator, abbreviated HANPP, of how much of the plant growth that ecosystems produce each year is taken or prevented by human use, used as a proxy for human impact on nature.

facts.text: Josep Garí coined HANPP in 1996 and introduced it at the first conference of the European Society for Ecological Economics.
Land-use change has cut net primary production by 9.6% across the global land mass, and end consumption raises total HANPP to 23.8% of potential vegetation.
This share reduces the energy left for other species, affecting biodiversity, carbon and water flows, and ecosystem services.
The planetary boundaries framework uses HANPP to measure biosphere integrity.

entries.part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
entries.text: Land clearing and conversion have cut plant growth across the world's land by 9.6%. Add what people harvest and consume, and humans take or prevent 23.8% of what natural vegetation would produce. That share is human appropriation of net primary production, or HANPP ({{ref:nature-eco-302}}). It measures the plant growth taken or prevented by human use each year. It serves as a proxy for human impact on nature. The share it measures reduces the energy left for other species, affecting biodiversity, carbon and water flows, and ecosystem services. Josep Garí coined HANPP in 1996. The planetary boundaries framework uses HANPP to measure biosphere integrity.

entries.title: Particulate matter: the most dangerous thing in the air

definition.text: Particulate matter is microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air.

facts.text: Particles mixed with air are called an aerosol; they come from both natural and human sources.
Major components include wind-blown mineral dust, sea salt, organic matter and particles formed from gases such as SO2 and ammonia.
It is considered the most dangerous air pollution because particles reach deep into the lungs and travel in the blood to organs such as the brain.
There is no safe level of exposure, and airborne particulate matter is a Group 1 carcinogen.
Fine particles (PM2.5) are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide.
Because many sources are human, it is a risk that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it.
After the US Clean Air Act of 1970, combined emissions of criteria and precursor pollutants fell 79% from 1970 to 2024.

entries.text: No level of exposure is safe. Others are organic matter, or form in the air from gases such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ammonia. The danger lies in how far they travel inside the body. Particles reach deep into the lungs and then ride the blood to organs such as the brain. Airborne particulate matter is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen, a substance known to cause cancer. Because so many sources are human, the risk is one that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it. After the United States passed its {{ref:nature-pol-153}} of 1970, combined emissions of the main regulated pollutants and the gases that form them fell 79% between 1970 and 2024.

Others are organic matter, or form in the air from gases such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ammonia. The danger lies in how far they travel inside the body. Fine particles, called PM2.5 (PM10 and PM2.5: sizing up deadly dust), are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide. Yet this is also a hopeful story. Because so many sources are human, the risk is one that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it. After the United States passed its The US Clean Air Act of 1970, combined emissions of the main regulated pollutants and the gases that form them fell 79% between 1970 and 2024.

entries.title: Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky

definition.text: Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, with a low pH.

facts.text: Most water has a pH between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition sets the line at a pH below 5.
Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid.
Today's acid rain comes mainly from human sources such as coal-fired power stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles.
Power plants produce a quarter of the nitrogen oxides and two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air.
Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg of sulfur a year as SO2, against 2.8 Tg from wildfires and 7–8 Tg from volcanoes.
In 1852 Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution, in Manchester.
Heavily affected regions include eastern Europe into Scandinavia, the eastern third of the United States and southeastern Canada.

entries.title: Municipal solid waste: what a city throws away

definition.text: Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish, the trash or garbage of items thrown away by the public.

facts.text: Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time; where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and non-recyclable packaging.
Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste and sewage sludge.
Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper.
The industry has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and waste-to-energy incineration.
Waste hierarchies rank methods from most to least preferred: reduce and reuse, recycle or compost, recover energy, then treat and dispose.
It produces large amounts of methane, nearly 90% of which could be avoided with existing technologies.

entries.text: What a city throws away says a lot about it. Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish: the trash or garbage of items thrown out by the public. Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste, and sewage sludge. Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time. Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper. Where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and packaging that cannot be recycled. The industry that handles it has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and burning waste to make energy. Waste hierarchies rank these methods from most to least preferred. Reducing and reusing come first, then recycling or composting, then recovering energy, and only last treatment and disposal. The ranking matters for the climate too. Municipal waste produces large amounts of methane, and nearly 90% of it could be avoided with existing technologies.

entries.title: Landfill: burying the rubbish, and the costs

definition.text: A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish.

facts.text: It is the oldest and most common way of disposing of waste, though systematic burial with daily and final covers only began in the 1940s.
The modern sanitary landfill is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps.
Landfills take up much land and pose environmental risks such as groundwater and soil contamination.
Nuisances include dust, odour, noise, disease-carrying rats and flies, and lower local property values.
Permitting a US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars.
Closed landfills are often reused as parks, bike courses or solar farms.

entries.text: Burying rubbish is the oldest and most common way to get rid of it. A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish ({{ref:nature-pol-064}}). It is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, and it was widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps. Landfills still carry costs. They take up much land and can contaminate groundwater and soil. Neighbors put up with dust, odor, noise, and disease-carrying rats and flies, and local property values fall. Permitting a new US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars. When a site closes, it often gets a second life as a park, a bike course or a solar farm.

entries.title: Hazardous waste: rubbish that stays dangerous

definition.text: Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment.

facts.text: Waste can be hazardous because it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable.
As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of hazardous waste a year.
Common sources include solvents, batteries and by-products of metal refining.
Many ordinary businesses, such as dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs, generate it.
Mismanaged hazardous waste can pollute the air, raising illness and death, and contaminate groundwater and soil.
It is regulated at local, national and international levels.

entries.text: Some rubbish stays dangerous long after it is thrown away. Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment. It earns that label in one of four ways: it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable. As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of it a year. The sources are surprisingly ordinary. Solvents, batteries and the by-products of metal refining are common ones. So are dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs. Handled badly, this waste becomes {{ref:nature-found-079}} of the worst kind. It fouls the air, raising illness and death, and contaminates groundwater and soil. That is why it is regulated at local, national and international levels.

entries.title: Nonpoint source pollution: contamination with no address

definition.text: Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from a single identifiable source.

facts.text: It is often the combined effect of small amounts of pollutants gathered from a large area.
It contrasts with point source pollution, which comes from a single source.
It arises from land runoff, rain, deposition from the air, drainage and seepage, which makes tracing it to one source difficult.
Paved urban surfaces and farms that apply fertilizer and manure are major sources.
A smokestack is a point source, but its pollution, carried far and mixed with others, acts as nonpoint where it lands.
It is the leading cause of water pollution in the United States, mainly from farm runoff and altered waterways.

entries.text: A single factory pipe is easy to find. A thousand fertilized fields are not. entries.title: Brownfield land: the polluted leftovers of industry

definition.text: Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use.

facts.text: Definitions vary by country, mainly over whether contamination must be present.
Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations.
Typical contaminants are spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead.
The US is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below Superfund level.
The term was first used at a US congressional field hearing on June 28, 1992.
Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems supporting rare plants, animals and invertebrates.
Redeveloping brownfields has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

entries.title: How breathing particles shortens lives

definition.text: Breathing particulate matter is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths.

facts.text: It contributes to stroke, heart disease, respiratory disease, many cancers and preterm birth, and to cognitive impairment.
Worldwide, PM2.5 exposure contributed to 7.9 million deaths in 2023: 4.9 million linked to outdoor and 2.8 million to household air pollution.
The link between particle pollution and premature deaths was first shown in the early 1970s; the 1993 Harvard Six Cities study established it firmly for cities.
Both short-term and long-term exposure cause harm.
In the EU, PM2.5 deaths fell 57% between 2005 and 2023, attributed to policies that cut primary PM2.5 emissions by 38%.
China's 2013 air pollution action plan cut annual average PM2.5 by a third by 2017, with fewer deaths.

entries.title: What acid rain does to lakes, forests and stone

definition.text: Acid rain harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health.

facts.text: Lower pH and more aluminium in surface water harm fish, other aquatic animals, microbes and plants.
Below pH 5 most fish eggs will not hatch, and below pH 4 adult fish die.
Acid kills sensitive soil microbes and disables their enzymes, causing soil functions such as decomposition to collapse.
High-altitude forests are especially vulnerable because the clouds and fog around them are more acidic than rain.
Acids react with limestone and marble in buildings and statues to form gypsum, which flakes off.
Breathing pollutants linked to acid rain, such as nitrogen dioxide, can damage the respiratory tract.

entries.title: Damage functions: pricing each degree of warming
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Damage functions

definition.text: A relationship used in cost-benefit analysis that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming.

facts.text: Damage functions have been built for sea level rise, farm productivity and the effect of heat on labour productivity.
A common base form makes damages grow with the square of warming: 2 °C causes 4 times and 3 °C 9 times the damage of 1 °C.
Some versions add tipping points so damages speed up, or jump, once warming passes 2-3 °C.
Estimates of the social cost of carbon are highly sensitive to the damage function chosen, along with the discount rate.
A 2020 paper using an updated damage function found that around 2 °C of warming would be "optimal" in the DICE model.
Nicholas Stern argued that damage functions miss many of society's most important risks.
Damage functions are central to estimating the costs of climate-related hazards.
They have been built for sea level rise, farm productivity and the effect of heat on labour productivity.

entries.contested_note: Critics such as Nicholas Stern argue standard damage functions leave out major risks, and updated functions change the 'optimal' warming results.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change
entries.text: How much does one more degree of warming cost? A damage function is the economist's answer: a relationship, used in {{ref:nature-val-001}}, that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming. Researchers have built them for rising seas, farm productivity and the effect of heat on how much work people get done. A common base form makes damages grow with the square of warming. So 2 °C causes 4 times the damage of 1 °C, and 3 °C causes 9 times. Some versions add tipping points, so damages speed up, or jump, once warming passes 2-3 °C. Estimates of the {{ref:nature-clim-241}}, the money value of harm from each extra unit of emissions, are highly sensitive to the damage function chosen, along with the discount rate. A 2020 paper using an updated function found that around 2 °C of warming would be 'optimal' in one leading climate-economy model, DICE. Critics such as {{ref:nature-hist-045}} argue that standard damage functions miss many of society's most important risks. The argument is far from settled.

entries.title: How airborne particles cool and cloud the planet

definition.text: Aerosols change Earth's climate by altering how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat the planet keeps.

facts.text: They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles.
The direct effect produces a net negative radiative forcing, that is, cooling.
Aerosol effects are the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.
Soot is a strong absorber of radiation, while sea-salt particles only scatter it.

entries.text: Particles in the air do not only harm lungs; they also change the climate. Aerosols alter how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat Earth keeps. They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles. Not all particles behave alike. Soot absorbs radiation strongly, while sea-salt particles only scatter it. Overall, the direct effect is a negative {{ref:nature-eco-004}}, which means cooling. Aerosol effects remain the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.

entries.title: Coarse, fine and ultrafine: sorting particles by size

definition.text: Particles are grouped by diameter: coarse PM10 (10 micrometres or less), fine PM2.5 (2.5 micrometres or less) and ultrafine particles.

facts.text: Size is a key factor in how much harm a particle can do.
Coarse PM10 particles lodge in the nose, throat and upper airways.
Fine PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the smallest airways and air sacs.
Across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

That is why, across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

entries.title: Filters, scrubbers and charged plates that catch dust

definition.text: Industries control particle emissions with dust collection systems such as cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.

facts.text: Particle emissions are highly regulated in most industrialised countries.
Fabric filters, or baghouses, are the most common in general industry.
Electrostatic precipitators charge particles and collect them on large charged plates.

entries.title: The WHO's limits for safe air

definition.text: The World Health Organization sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise.

facts.text: For PM2.5 the annual mean should not exceed 5 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 15 μg/m3.
For PM10 the annual mean should not exceed 15 μg/m3 and the 24-hour mean 45 μg/m3.
Under the 2021 guideline, 97% of the world's population is exposed to unsafe PM2.5 levels.

entries.title: Acid deposition: wet and dry routes to the ground

definition.text: Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, either washed down by precipitation (wet) or settling without it (dry).

facts.text: Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface.
Dry deposition, when particles and gases stick to ground, plants or other surfaces, can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition.

entries.text: Acid does not need rain to fall. Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, by two routes. Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface. Dry deposition happens when particles and gases simply stick to the ground, plants or other surfaces. That quieter route matters. Dry deposition can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition, so {{ref:nature-pol-046}} tells only part of the story.

entries.title: How scrubbers, treaties and trading tamed acid rain

definition.text: Acid rain has been reduced by scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, international treaties and emissions trading.

facts.text: Flue-gas desulfurization removes 95% or more of the SO2 from a typical coal-fired station's exhaust.
Under the 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, sulfur and particle emissions fell 30-80% in Europe and 30-40% in North America since 1990.
In emissions trading, each polluter holds allowances for its emissions and can sell those it no longer needs after installing controls, giving an economic incentive to cut pollution.
The first emissions trading market was created by the US Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 to cut SO2 at the lowest cost to society.

entries.title: Alternatives to burying waste

definition.text: Alternatives to landfill include waste reduction and recycling, waste-to-energy incineration, anaerobic digestion, composting and other treatments.

facts.text: Depending on local economics and incentives, these can be made cheaper than landfilling.
Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland have banned landfilling untreated waste.
The UK taxes biodegradable waste sent to landfill, and England set up a scheme for councils to trade landfill quotas.
The zero waste concept aims to minimise landfill volume.

entries.text: Burying waste is not the only option, and not always the cheapest. entries.title: Landfill gas: methane from buried rubbish

definition.text: Landfill gas is the mix of mainly methane and carbon dioxide produced when microbes digest organic waste without oxygen.

facts.text: On average it is about half methane and slightly less than half CO2.
Landfills are the 3rd largest emitter of methane worldwide.
Well-managed landfills collect the gas, either flaring it or using it to generate electricity; more than 850 US landfills recover it.
Capturing landfill methane is a common type of carbon offset project.

entries.title: Leachate: the poisoned liquid under a landfill

definition.text: Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through landfill waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants.

facts.text: If not contained, it can contaminate groundwater.
Modern landfills use impermeable liners several metres thick, stable sites and collection systems to capture it.
Full landfills are sealed to stop rain entering and forming new leachate.

entries.title: Landfill aftercare: a cost that may never end

definition.text: Aftercare is the long period after a landfill is full and capped, when liners, gas capture and leachate treatment continue to limit harm.

facts.text: Aftercare may last from several decades up to forever, costing more than 20 million euros per landfill in the Netherlands.
Because sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, replacing liners and treating leachate is an indefinite requirement.

entries.title: Inside a landfill: the slow life of buried waste

definition.text: A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor in which microbes break organic waste down into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases.

facts.text: First, oxygen trapped in the waste supports aerobic breakdown until microbes use it up.
In the acid phase, fatty acids build up and leachate pH falls from about 7.5 to 5.6.
In the longest phase, methane-making microbes turn the acids into methane and CO2.
Finally methane production almost stops as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

Finally methane production almost stops, as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

entries.title: Reuse: keeping things in service

definition.text: Reuse means using items again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away.

facts.text: Reuse lengthens product life and reduces the need for fresh raw materials.
Online networks such as Freecycle list unwanted items for others to reuse, reducing landfill pollution.
Unlike recycling, it does not break items down into raw materials, which saves time, money, energy and resources.
Extending an item's use is preferable to recycling or disposal because it is the least energy-intensive option.

entries.title: Source separation: sorting waste where it starts
entries.article: Municipal solid waste#Waste handling and separation, storage and processing at the source

definition.text: Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced.

facts.text: It improves recycling, prevents contamination, allows composting and ensures hazardous waste is properly treated.
Separated and mixed wastes are processed at materials recovery facilities using hand sorting, screens, magnets and optical sorting.
Segregation, composting and recycling can cut methane emissions from municipal waste.

entries.title: Waste-to-energy: power from rubbish

definition.text: Waste-to-energy is the generation of power from municipal waste, by burning it or by capturing landfill gas, pyrolysis or gasification.

facts.text: Older incinerators emitted many pollutants, but new rules and technology have greatly reduced this.
US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels and mercury by over 90%.
Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as bioenergy.

entries.title: Disposing of hazardous waste: bury, burn or recycle

definition.text: Hazardous waste is disposed of by treating and stabilising it for secure landfills, burning it, or recycling it.

facts.text: Incinerators burn it at 870–1400 °C, greatly shrinking it, but the leftover ash and gases can also be hazardous.
Some hazardous materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products.
Landfills for such waste need barriers along their foundations to stop groundwater contamination.
Plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert rock-like slag; it is very expensive but suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

entries.text: Dangerous waste has three main exits: secure landfills, fire and recycling. For landfilling, it is first treated and stabilized, and the landfill needs barriers along its foundations to stop groundwater contamination. Some materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products. At the extreme, plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert, rock-like slag. It is very expensive, but it suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

entries.title: Exporting poison: the trade in hazardous waste

definition.text: Hazardous waste has been shipped from rich countries to poorer ones with weaker rules, prompting the Basel Convention to curb the trade.

facts.text: As laws such as RCRA raised disposal costs in developed nations in the 1970s, the waste trade to poorer countries grew fast.
In 1990 OECD countries exported around 1.8 million tons of hazardous waste.
199 countries signed the 1992 Basel Convention to stop this flow.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 includes sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

entries.title: Who lives next to hazardous waste

definition.text: Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to hazardous waste and its pollution.

facts.text: An Austrian study found people living near industrial sites are more often unemployed, less educated and twice as likely to be immigrants.
Groups who rely on local land and streams for food and water, including Native Americans, face multiplied risk.

entries.title: Slowing the runoff: controlling diffuse pollution

definition.text: Nonpoint pollution is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water.

facts.text: Grass buffer strips between paved areas and water let soil absorb pollutants first.
Retention ponds let contaminants in stormwater settle out and stay trapped.
Farmers use contour ploughing, mulching, crop rotation, perennial crops, riparian buffers and conservation tillage.
Agroforestry can also improve air quality by absorbing pollutants such as particulate matter.

entries.text: Stopping diffuse pollution mostly means slowing water down. {{ref:nature-pol-075}} is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water. Grass buffer strips between paved areas and streams let soil absorb pollutants first. Retention ponds hold storm runoff so contaminants settle out and stay trapped. Farmers use contour plowing, mulching, rotating crops, perennial crops and plowing less. They also leave strips of vegetation along waterways ({{ref:nature-nbs-260}}). Mixing trees with farming ({{ref:nature-nbs-247}}) can also clean the air by absorbing pollutants such as particulate matter.

entries.title: Why diffuse pollution escapes the regulators
entries.article: Nonpoint source pollution#Regulation of Nonpoint Source Pollution in the United States

definition.text: Nonpoint pollution is hard to regulate because it has no single discharge point; US federal law leaves it largely to states and voluntary programs.

facts.text: Diffuse sources were excluded from the US Clean Water Act's permit programme for that reason.
State programmes rely on best management practices, seeking the least costly way to cut the most pollution.
A 2015 article found the Clean Water Act effective for point sources but not for nonpoint sources.
Since 1987 federal grants under section 319 have funded state nonpoint management programmes.

entries.title: Sediment, nutrients, toxins and germs in runoff
entries.article: Nonpoint source pollution#Principal types (for water pollution)

definition.text: The main nonpoint water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens.

facts.text: Sediment clouds water, cutting light for underwater plants and the fish and shellfish that depend on them.
Phosphorus and nitrogen are the two nutrients of most concern.
Heavy metals and compounds such as PCBs and DDT resist breakdown and persist in the environment.
Coliform bacteria in runoff are used as an indicator of water pollution rather than being a cause of disease.

entries.title: Why polluted land sits empty for decades

definition.text: Many contaminated brownfields sit unused for decades because cleaning them costs more than the land would then be worth.

facts.text: Brownfields carry an environmental stigma that can delay redevelopment.
The US Superfund law has been criticised for pushing investment to greenfields through severe no-fault liability.
Redevelopment grew in the 2000s as developable land became scarcer in crowded areas.
Governments offer help: the EPA awarded nearly 1,000 cleanup grants worth almost $190 million from 2002 through 2013, and cleanup costs are fully tax-deductible.

entries.title: Cleaning up brownfields

definition.text: Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused.

facts.text: Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, in situ oxidation and soil vapour extraction, often combined.
Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching.
Phytoremediation uses deep-rooted plants to draw heavy metals out of the soil.

entries.title: What is a polluted plot worth?

definition.text: Valuing a brownfield needs specialised appraisal, because contamination changes a site's best use and value before and after cleanup.

facts.text: The value should allow for lingering stigma and possible liability to third parties.
Normal appraisal often fails, so appraisers use contingent valuation, case studies or statistical analysis.
A 2014 study of EPA cleanup grants from 2002 through 2008 found an average benefit of almost $4 million per site, with a median of $2.1 million.
Some environmental firms team up with insurers to guarantee cleanup costs.

entries.title: Environmental law: the rules that protect nature

definition.text: The body of treaties, statutes, regulations and policies meant to protect the natural environment and manage how human activity affects ecosystems and natural resources.

facts.text: It covers pollution control, resource conservation, biodiversity protection, climate change mitigation and sustainable development.
Under the old common law the main protection was the law of nuisance, which allowed only private lawsuits when land was harmed and proved inadequate for threats to shared resources.
London's Great Smog of 1952 led to the Clean Air Act 1956, which set emission limits for households and businesses enforced by an inspectorate.
Pollution-control laws cover air quality, water quality, waste management, contaminant cleanup and chemical safety; resource laws cover water, minerals, forests, wildlife and fish and game.
Debates continue over the necessity, fairness and cost of environmental regulation, and over whether regulations or market solutions better achieve agreed goals.
Regulated industries commonly argue against regulation on grounds of cost, while many environmental groups argue current rules are too weak.
Smaller firms can bear disproportionately large costs from environmental regulation, which can become a barrier to entry for new firms.

entries.contested_note: The necessity, fairness and cost of environmental regulation, and regulation versus market solutions, remain debated.

It also manages how human activity affects ecosystems and the resources nature provides. Before such laws, the main protection was the old common-law idea of nuisance. Modern environmental law covers {{ref:nature-found-079}} control, resource conservation, biodiversity protection, cutting climate change and {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Pollution laws deal with air and water quality, waste, contaminant cleanup and chemical safety. Resource laws govern water, minerals, forests, wildlife, and fish and game. None of it is settled. Regulated industries commonly argue against rules on grounds of cost, while many environmental groups say current rules are too weak. Smaller firms can bear disproportionately large costs, which can keep new firms out. Debates continue over whether regulation is necessary, fair and worth its cost, and whether rules or market solutions better reach agreed goals.
entries.text_plain: London's Great Smog of 1952 changed British law. It led to a 1956 clean-air statute that set emission limits for households and businesses, enforced by an inspectorate. That is environmental law at work. It is the body of treaties, statutes, regulations and policies meant to protect the natural environment. It also manages how human activity affects ecosystems and the resources nature provides. Before such laws, the main protection was the old common-law idea of nuisance. It allowed only private lawsuits when someone's land was harmed, and it proved inadequate for threats to shared resources. Modern environmental law covers Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill control, resource conservation, biodiversity protection, cutting climate change and Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later. Pollution laws deal with air and water quality, waste, contaminant cleanup and chemical safety. Resource laws govern water, minerals, forests, wildlife, and fish and game. None of it is settled. Regulated industries commonly argue against rules on grounds of cost, while many environmental groups say current rules are too weak. Smaller firms can bear disproportionately large costs, which can keep new firms out. Debates continue over whether regulation is necessary, fair and worth its cost, and whether rules or market solutions better reach agreed goals.

entries.title: Environmental impact assessment: look before you build

definition.text: A study of the likely environmental effects of a project, plan or policy, done before anyone decides whether to go ahead with it.

facts.text: Its aim is to make sure that the people deciding on a project take its environmental effects into account.
An EIA does not demand a set environmental outcome; it requires decision-makers to weigh environmental values and justify their choice using studies and public comments.
EIAs began in the 1960s amid growing environmental awareness, and in the United States gained formal status with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
More than 180 countries use environmental impact assessments, making them a widely used tool of international environmental governance.
At the end of a project an audit can compare actual impacts with predicted ones, to check the predictions and how well mitigation worked.
Few national EIA laws explicitly require assessing a project's contribution to climate change.
Biodiversity offsetting is often applied through EIA processes, guided by the mitigation hierarchy.

entries.title: The Endangered Species Act of 1973

definition.text: The main United States law for protecting imperilled species, signed in 1973 to stop extinctions caused by economic growth that ignored conservation.

facts.text: Its two aims are to prevent extinction and to recover species until the law's protection is no longer needed.
Agencies list species as 'endangered' or the lesser 'threatened'; Section 9 bans 'take', meaning to harass, harm or hunt them.
Since 1982, listing decisions must be made solely on biological and trade information, without weighing economic effects.
Habitat loss is the main threat to most imperilled species, so the Act lets agencies designate 'critical habitat' zones.
By August 2023, 1,780 species had been listed; 99% were still alive but only 64 had recovered enough to be removed from the list.
The American alligator, listed in 1967, was delisted as fully recovered twenty years later.
It underpins US conservation banking, which offsets harm to species protected under the Act.

entries.contested_note: It is described as one of the most powerful and controversial US environmental laws, chiefly over its economic costs.

entries.title: NEPA: the law that made agencies look first

definition.text: The 1969 United States law, in force from 1970, that requires federal agencies to weigh environmental effects before acting and created the Council on Environmental Quality.

facts.text: It grew out of 1960s environmental concern, fed by Silent Spring, the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill and protests against highway building.
Agencies follow three levels of review: a categorical exclusion, an environmental assessment ending in a finding of no significant impact, or a full environmental impact statement.
The history of EIA in other countries, such as Australia, is linked to NEPA's requirement for environmental impact statements.
A federal study of 2013-2018 found a full NEPA review took an average of 4.5 years.
With no enforcement power at the Council, violations go through the courts; the usual remedy is ordering the review to be redone.
Evidence on its costs and benefits is limited: reviews have grown longer, while case studies suggest it curbed some of the worst abuses.
NEPA is the law most used in US climate change litigation, with 322 cases filed.

entries.contested_note: Defenders see it as a key safeguard, while critics blame it for long delays; changes under successive administrations reflect this dispute.

entries.title: Zoning: deciding what goes where

definition.text: A way for a local government to divide land into zones, each with its own rules on what may be built and how the land may be used.

facts.text: Zones may allow a single use such as housing or industry, mix compatible uses, or, in form-based zoning, govern building size and shape whatever the use.
Single-use zoning separates uses thought incompatible; in practice it also protects existing uses and a community's character.
Overlay zones add rules for a particular concern such as wetlands or a natural hazard without rewriting the whole code.
Environmental activists argue that separating everyday uses forces car ownership and increases traffic.
Some economists say zoning reduces efficiency and raises housing costs; one 2017 study estimated large GDP gains from partial deregulation.
Zoning regulations and land-use measures are key institutional tools for climate change adaptation and flood management in cities.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue zoning raises housing costs, inequality and car dependence, while supporters see it as essential to separate harmful uses.

entries.title: Natura 2000: Europe's web of protected places

definition.text: The European Union's network of protected nature areas on land and at sea, designated under the Birds and Habitats Directives.

facts.text: It joins Special Protection Areas for birds under the 1979 Birds Directive with Special Areas of Conservation under the 1992 Habitats Directive.
In 2022 it covered more than 18% of the EU's land area and more than 7% of its marine area.
Sites are not strictly closed to people: many are farmed, forested or even urban.
Designation is nearly complete, but management and enforcement lag and many sites lack management plans.
Its benefits are estimated at €200-300 billion a year.
Developers, farmers and politicians criticise it as a brake on development, and its habitats assessment triggered the Dutch nitrogen crisis.

entries.contested_note: Developers and farmers see it as blocking development; legal scholars question whether its habitats test fits climate and ecosystem-service goals.

entries.title: Point source pollution: pollution with an address

definition.text: Pollution of air, water, heat, noise or light that comes from a single identifiable source, such as a factory outlet or smokestack.

facts.text: It is called a point source because in models it can be treated as a single mathematical point.
Examples include factories, power plants, sewage treatment plants and some farms such as concentrated animal feeding operations.
It contrasts with nonpoint sources, diffuse pollution from wide areas such as urban and farm runoff.
Direct regulation works relatively well for point sources but struggles with diffuse, nonpoint pollution.
Carbon capture and storage captures carbon dioxide from large point sources such as cement factories.

entries.text: A factory outlet, a smokestack, a sewage plant: each is a place where pollution can be pinned down. Point source pollution is pollution of air, water, heat, noise or light that comes from a single identifiable source. The name comes from modeling, where such a source can be treated as a single mathematical point. Examples include factories, power plants, sewage treatment plants and some farms, such as large livestock feedlots ({{ref:nature-res-141}}). It contrasts with {{ref:nature-pol-075}}, which comes from wide areas such as city and farm runoff. That difference shapes policy. Direct regulation works relatively well for point sources but struggles with diffuse pollution. Large point sources such as cement factories are also where {{ref:nature-clim-185}} can capture carbon dioxide.

entries.title: Regulatory economics: when governments set the rules

definition.text: The study and use of government rules to achieve economic aims, such as correcting market failures and protecting the environment.

facts.text: Regulation is law imposed by government on people and private firms to change economic behaviour; some industries instead regulate themselves.
Government agencies are always at risk of regulatory capture by the industries they regulate.
Principal-agent theory treats the government as principal and the regulated operator as agent, to deal with the operator knowing more than the regulator.
Supporters argue regulation guards against monopoly, instability and environmental harm, drawing on thinkers such as Karl Polanyi.
Economists such as Milton Friedman, George Stigler and Friedrich Hayek argue for limiting government's role in markets.
Regulatory intervention can counter a market failure, so some economists think some regulation beats an unregulated market.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree sharply on whether regulation generally improves or worsens market outcomes.

entries.title: International environmental law: rules across borders

definition.text: The part of international law dealing with global and regional environmental problems, made up of treaties, customary rules and the decisions of international courts.

facts.text: Most international environmental agreements are multilateral treaties, often filled out later by protocols that can add new scientific knowledge.
Protocols let countries agree on a framework that would be too contentious if every detail had to be settled first; the Kyoto Protocol is the best-known example.
Customary rules include the duty to warn other states promptly of environmental dangers they face.
A major challenge in international decisions is setting adequate compensation for environmental damage.

entries.text: Pollution ignores borders ({{ref:nature-econ-298}}), so law has had to follow it. International environmental law is the part of international law that deals with global and regional environmental problems. It is made up of treaties, customary rules and the decisions of international courts. Most agreements are multilateral treaties, signed by many countries, and often filled out later by protocols that can add new scientific knowledge. That two-step design lets countries agree on a framework that would be too contentious if every detail had to be settled first. The {{ref:nature-clim-056}} is the best-known example. Customary rules include the duty to warn other states promptly of environmental dangers they face. One major challenge remains: setting adequate compensation for environmental damage.

entries.title: The guiding principles of environmental law

definition.text: A set of guiding ideas, not universally accepted, that run through environmental law, such as sustainable development, equity, prevention, precaution and polluter pays.

facts.text: Equity includes intergenerational equity, the right of future generations to a fair share of the common inheritance, and intragenerational equity among people alive today.
Transboundary responsibility is an obligation to protect one's own environment and prevent damage to neighbouring ones, which can limit a sovereign state's rights.
Prevention is an overarching aim served by prior assessment of harm, licensing, emission limits and best available techniques.
The Rio Declaration's precautionary principle says lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective measures against serious or irreversible damage.
The polluter pays principle holds that environmental costs of economic activity, including preventing harm, should be borne by those causing them rather than by society at large.
Public participation and transparency appear in environmental impact assessment, laws on access to environmental data, and administrative procedure.

entries.title: Shoot, shovel and shut up: when protection backfires
entries.article: Endangered Species Act of 1973#Economic consequences and perverse incentives

definition.text: The problem that strict species-protection rules can make an endangered species a financial burden for landowners, tempting them to destroy habitat before the species arrives.

facts.text: Because species could be listed without considering economic costs, the Act soon became controversial; landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays.
A 1995 study of about 1,000 private forest plots found owners more likely to harvest pines as they matured enough to attract endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers.
The western saying 'shoot, shovel, and shut up' sums up the extreme form of this response.
Economists suggest compensating property owners for protecting species, so a listed species is not seen as a potential financial loss.
Agreements between landowners and the agency helped the woodpecker be downlisted from endangered to threatened by 2024.

entries.contested_note: Many hold that protections curtail economic activity and create perverse incentives, while others defend the Act's species-first approach.
entries.text: In the American West, a grim saying sums up the worst case: 'shoot, shovel, and shut up'. The problem behind it is a perverse incentive. Strict species-protection rules can turn an endangered species into a financial burden for the landowner who hosts it. That tempts owners to destroy habitat before the species arrives. Because species could be listed under the {{ref:nature-pol-159}} without considering economic costs, the law soon became controversial. Landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays. The evidence is more than anecdote. A 1995 study of about 1,000 private forest plots found owners more likely to harvest pines as the trees matured enough to attract endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers. Economists suggest a fix: compensate property owners for protecting species, so a listed species is no longer a potential financial loss. Cooperation can work. Agreements between landowners and the agency helped the woodpecker move from endangered to threatened by 2024. The wider argument goes on. Many hold that the protections curtail economic activity and create perverse incentives, while others defend the law's species-first approach.

entries.title: Strategic environmental assessment: judging plans, not just projects

definition.text: A systematic process for making sure environmental, and sometimes wider sustainability, effects are considered when policies, plans and programmes are made.

facts.text: It grew from a weakness of project-level EIA: many damaging choices are made earlier at a strategic level, for example new infrastructure that generates more travel.
An SEA usually comes before the related project EIAs, so its findings cascade down the tiers of decision-making and reduce later work.
Under the EU directive its phases are screening, scoping, a baseline of the environment, estimating likely impacts, influencing the decision and monitoring afterwards.
The EU SEA Directive 2001/42/EC made SEA legally required for many regional, local, development, waste and transport plans.
The UNECE Protocol on Strategic Environmental Assessment came into force in July 2010 and, unlike the EU directive, can be applied to policies and legislation.
Donors use SEA in development co-operation to make sure aid delivered through strategic-level interventions considers the environment.

entries.title: Environmental standards: the rules for treating nature

definition.text: A rule, regulation or practice, usually set by government, that says how the environment must be treated and kept, such as a pollution limit or a permit requirement.

facts.text: Standards can ban specific activities, fix how often and how monitoring is done, or require permits to use land or water.
They rest on scientific opinion from several fields, public views and social context, so setting them is complex.
Their development has been shaped by two competing views: ecocentrism, which gives nature intrinsic value, and anthropocentrism, which values it only for human survival.
European legislation sets precise pollutant concentrations as well as target concentrations to be reached by given dates.
US EPA technology standards set minimum performance levels rather than requiring specific technologies, often based on the industry's top performers.
The ISO 14001 environmental management standard is held by about 363,000 companies and organisations worldwide.

entries.text: A pollution limit and a permit requirement have something in common. Both are environmental standards: rules, regulations or practices, usually set by government, that say how the environment must be treated and kept. Standards can ban specific activities, fix how often and how monitoring is done, or require permits to use land or water. Setting them is complex, because they rest on scientific opinion from several fields, public views and social context. Two competing views have shaped them: {{ref:nature-val-063}}, which gives nature value in itself, and {{ref:nature-val-059}}, which values it only for human survival. Practice varies. European law sets precise pollutant concentrations, plus targets to be reached by given dates. US EPA technology standards set minimum performance levels, often based on the industry's top performers, without requiring specific technologies. Some standards are voluntary: about 363,000 companies and organizations worldwide hold the ISO 14001 environmental management standard.

entries.title: The Clean Water Act: permits for every pipe

definition.text: The main United States federal law controlling pollution of surface waters, adopted as the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972.

facts.text: It created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System: point sources such as factories and sewage plants may not discharge into surface waters without a permit.
Farm stormwater and irrigation return flows were exempted as nonpoint sources; Congress instead funded research and assistance to improve farm runoff practices.
The 1972 Act paid for municipal sewage treatment plants through grants, with federal funds covering 75% of project costs.
Any citizen may sue someone who violates a discharge permit, after giving 60 days' notice.
Its 1983 'fishable and swimmable' goal has not been met: more than half of stream and river miles and about 70 percent of lakes still violate water quality standards.
Analysts credit it with controlling point sources but say it has not worked for nonpoint sources.
Section 404 of the Act is the legal basis for wetland mitigation banking in the United States.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether its benefits justify its costs and how much it reduced water pollution.

entries.title: Command and control: regulating by rule and penalty

definition.text: Direct regulation by law that states what an industry or activity may and may not do, backed by penalties for breaking the rules.

facts.text: The 'command' is a standard or target set by a government authority; the 'control' is the sanction, such as prosecution, for not complying.
It differs from using economic incentives such as taxes and subsidies to encourage compliance.
In environmental policy it relies on three main kinds of standards: ambient standards, emission standards and technology standards, usually used in combination.
It dominated environmental policy in industrial nations in the 1970s, when the focus was on remedying problems rather than broad prevention.
It works fairly well for point sources but struggles with diffuse sources: ten big power stations are easy to regulate, millions of motorists are not.
Uniform sanctions can make small businesses feel the burden of regulation more than large companies.
Some commentators prefer the term 'direct regulatory instrument' because 'command and control' carries negative connotations.

entries.title: Emission standards: legal limits on what comes out

definition.text: A legal limit on how much of a given air pollutant a particular source may release over a set period.

facts.text: Emission standards are usually designed to achieve air quality standards and protect human life.
Many target cars and other vehicles; others cover industry, power plants and small equipment such as lawn mowers and diesel generators.
The first car emission standards were enacted in the United States in 1963, mainly in response to smog in Los Angeles; Japan followed three years later.
Different regions and countries set different vehicle standards.
Higher emission standards are one way to make sure efficiency gains actually cut fuel use, alongside green taxes and cap and trade.

entries.title: Renewable portfolio standards: a quota for clean power

definition.text: A rule requiring electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources such as wind, solar, biomass and geothermal.

facts.text: Certified renewable generators earn certificates for each unit of electricity, sell them to suppliers, who hand them to the regulator to prove compliance.
Supporters say relying on the market brings competition and innovation that deliver renewable energy at the lowest cost.
RPS-type schemes exist in the UK, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Chile and in 29 of 50 US states.
A US national laboratory credits state standards with 60% of the rise in US renewable electricity since 2000, though their share of new builds is falling.
Like subsidies, renewable portfolio standards create protected markets for renewable energy, an alternative to feed-in tariffs.

entries.title: Rules or prices? The command-and-control debate

definition.text: The long-running argument over whether direct rules or price-based tools such as taxes and tradable permits protect the environment at lower cost.

facts.text: Critics call command and control inefficient; a summary of 10 studies found significant cost differences between it and least-cost alternatives.
A carbon tax, unlike classic command and control, lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution instead of limiting each polluter.
Defenders note that incentive schemes need monitoring and administration too, so their total costs can sometimes be higher.
Incentive schemes often need complex rules, inspection and enforcement that make them resemble command and control.
Supporters of direct rules say fixed legal standards let regulators respond quickly to violations and give clarity to those regulated.
Enthusiasm for economic incentives has grown since the 1970s, partly from disenchantment with command and control.

entries.contested_note: Economists often favour incentives as cheaper, while others argue direct regulation can be less costly once monitoring and administration are counted.

entries.text: Two policies can reach the same pollution target at very different costs. Instead of limiting each polluter, it lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution. Fixed legal standards, defenders add, let regulators respond quickly to violations and give clarity to those regulated. The debate is open: economists often favor incentives as cheaper, while others argue direct rules can cost less once monitoring and administration are counted.
