entries.title: Best available technology: a standard that keeps moving

definition.text: The technology or techniques that regulators approve as the standard for meeting a process's output limits, such as for pollution control.

facts.text: It is a moving target, since changing values and advancing techniques shift what counts as 'best available'.
Read literally it would demand the best technology regardless of cost, but in practice costs are also taken into account.
The older UK idea of 'best practicable means' appeared in the Salmon Fishery Act 1861; the EEC introduced 'best available techniques not entailing excessive costs' in 1984.
Under the EU Industrial Emissions Directive, BAT conclusions are the reference for permit conditions of large industrial installations, without prescribing any particular technology.
Under the US Clean Water Act, EPA picks a model technology, sets a numeric discharge limit based on it, and lets each facility meet that limit with any technology.
BAT standards are a classic example of command-and-control regulation, in contrast to emissions trading.

entries.title: CAFE: averaging the fuel economy of a fleet

definition.text: United States rules, first enacted in 1975 after the 1973-74 oil embargo, requiring the cars and light trucks each maker sells to meet an average fuel economy.

facts.text: CAFE does not reward buyers or change fuel prices; it works indirectly by penalising automakers that build inefficient vehicles.
A 2002 National Academy of Sciences report found fuel use would have been about 14 percent higher without CAFE, but lighter vehicles may have caused 1,300 to 2,600 extra deaths in 1993.
Since 2008 targets depend on a vehicle's 'footprint' (wheelbase times track width), so makers of larger vehicles face lower targets.
Certifying minivans and later SUVs as trucks let makers meet the less strict truck standard, contributing to their rise.
Better fuel efficiency leads people to drive more: a 10% efficiency gain raises travel distance by an average of 1-2%.
Since 2007 makers can trade fuel-economy credits between vehicle categories and sell them to others.
Critics argue the fines were too small to matter; in 2025 they were eliminated, effectively mooting the standards.

entries.contested_note: The safety effects, costs and real fuel savings of CAFE are actively debated.

entries.title: The Porter hypothesis: can tough rules make firms stronger?

definition.text: The idea that strict environmental regulation can push firms to become more efficient and innovative, improving their competitiveness.

facts.text: Economist Michael Porter proposed it in 1991, and with Claas van der Linde set it out in detail in a 1995 article.
Regulation is said to trigger cleaner technologies (the innovation effect) whose cost savings more than cover compliance and innovation costs.
Firms in early-regulating countries may gain a first-mover advantage through learning effects or patents.
Studies support the 'weak' version, that stricter regulation stimulates innovation, but evidence is mixed for the 'strong' version, that it boosts business performance.
A study of OECD countries found no permanent effect of tighter environmental policy on productivity, whatever the type of regulation.
The idea is often cited in support of green growth.

entries.contested_note: Evidence is mixed on whether stricter regulation actually improves business performance.
entries.text: Can a strict rule make a company stronger? In 1991 the economist Michael Porter argued that it can, and with Claas van der Linde he set out the case in a 1995 article. The Porter hypothesis holds that strict environmental regulation can push firms to become more efficient and innovative, improving their competitiveness ({{ref:nature-econ-363}}). The mechanism is the innovation effect. Regulation triggers cleaner technologies ({{ref:nature-econ-318}}) whose cost savings more than cover the costs of complying and innovating. Firms in countries that regulate early may also gain a first-mover advantage, through learning or patents. The idea is often cited in support of {{ref:nature-eecon-152}}. The evidence splits in two. Studies support a 'weak' version, that stricter regulation stimulates innovation. Evidence is mixed for the 'strong' version, that it boosts business performance. One study of OECD countries found no permanent effect of tighter environmental rules on productivity, whatever the type of regulation.

entries.title: The environmental impact statement

definition.text: In United States law, a document required under the National Environmental Policy Act for federal actions that significantly affect the quality of the human environment.

facts.text: An EIS describes the good and bad environmental effects of a proposed action and usually lists alternative actions that could be chosen instead.
A shorter environmental assessment is prepared first to decide whether a full EIS is needed; it ends in either a Finding of No Significant Impact or an EIS.
The adequacy of an EIS can be challenged in federal court, and major projects have been blocked because an agency failed to prepare an acceptable one.

entries.title: Cleanup law: dealing with pollution after the fact

definition.text: Laws governing the removal of pollution from soil, sediment, surface water or groundwater after contamination has happened.

facts.text: Unlike pollution-control laws, cleanup laws respond after the fact, so they must define both the needed response and who must carry it out or pay for it.
Their rules may cover emergency response, liability allocation, site assessment, remedial action, monitoring after cleanup and site reuse.

entries.text: Most environmental law tries to stop pollution. Cleanup law deals with pollution that has already happened. These laws govern removing contamination from soil, sediment, surface water or groundwater. Because they respond after the fact, they must define both the needed response and who must carry it out or pay for it. Their rules may cover emergency response, sharing out liability, site assessment, remedial action, monitoring after cleanup and reuse of the site.

entries.title: Air quality law: limits on what we breathe

definition.text: Laws that govern the release of air pollutants into the atmosphere, mostly to protect human health.

facts.text: Regulators identify and classify pollutants, set limits on acceptable emissions and prescribe control technologies.
The US Clean Air Act names six 'criteria' pollutants for nationwide regulation: ozone, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and lead.
Some air laws address wider ecological problems, such as ozone-depleting chemicals or emissions trading for acid rain and climate change.

entries.title: The US Clean Air Act

definition.text: The main United States federal law for preventing and reducing air pollution, first passed in 1963 and greatly expanded by later amendments.

facts.text: The 1970 amendments created national ambient air quality standards, performance standards for new sources and standards for hazardous air pollutants, and strengthened federal enforcement.
States write implementation plans to meet the Act's requirements and EPA reviews and approves them, a cooperative model reflecting the need for local knowledge.
The 1990 amendments created the Acid Rain Program, the first US cap-and-trade programme, to cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from power plants.
EPA's removal of lead from US gasoline from 1971 has been called one of the great public health achievements of the 20th century.
A 2022 review found overwhelming causal evidence that the Act improved air quality.
A 2011 EPA study projected that by 2020 the 1990 amendments would cost about $60 billion a year while yielding about $2 trillion a year in health benefits.
EPA began regulating greenhouse gases after the 2007 Supreme Court ruling in Massachusetts v. EPA and its later endangerment finding.
Ethnic-minority people in the US are 1.5 times more likely than majority people to live in areas burdened by air pollution.

entries.title: Section 404: permits to fill wetlands
entries.article: Clean Water Act#Dredge and fill permits

definition.text: Permits required under the US Clean Water Act before dredged or fill material may be placed in streams, wetlands and other regulated waters.

facts.text: They are issued by the US Army Corps of Engineers and are key to protecting wetlands that developers would otherwise fill.
Biodiversity banking grew out of US wetland mitigation banking and the 'no net loss' policies tied to the Act in the 1970s.
Its application to farming caused controversy, and the 1977 amendments added six exemptions for activities such as normal farming.

entries.text: Before a developer can fill in a US wetland, it usually needs a permit. Section 404 of the {{ref:nature-pol-155}} requires one before dredged or fill material is placed in streams, wetlands and other regulated waters. The US Army Corps of Engineers issues them, and they are key to protecting wetlands that would otherwise be filled. Applying the rule to farming caused controversy, and the 1977 amendments added six exemptions, for activities such as normal farming. The permits also spawned a market. Wetland banking, and the 1970s policies under the Act of allowing no overall loss of wetlands, grew into {{ref:nature-mkt-120}}.

entries.title: The case against environmental impact assessment

definition.text: Objections that environmental impact assessments are too narrow in scope, handle uncertainty poorly, have little influence on decisions and can delay projects.

facts.text: In practice almost all EIAs address only direct, immediate on-site effects, although indirect effects of development can be much larger.
Because EIA aids decisions rather than making them, some argue its influence on decisions is limited.
Researchers argue that uncertainties get too little systematic attention in environmental studies.
EIAs can delay environmentally friendly projects and raise their costs.

entries.title: Assessing harm that crosses borders

definition.text: Assessing the environmental effects of a project that cross national borders, such as pollution reaching another country.

facts.text: The Espoo Convention of the UN Economic Commission for Europe provides an international legal framework for transboundary EIA.
With no world legislature, international treaties develop in parallel and are hard to enforce, which has led to duplications and failures.
International advisory opinions in 2024 and 2025 confirmed that EIAs must consider harm beyond national borders, including to the global climate system.

entries.title: Zoning that bargains: performance and incentive zoning

definition.text: Flexible zoning approaches that judge projects by their effects or let developers build more in return for public benefits such as open space.

facts.text: Performance zoning, first advocated by Lane Kendig in 1973, may let developers earn points for limiting environmental impacts or adding public amenities.
US cities most often use incentive zoning to win mixed use, open space conservation, walkability, affordable housing and parks.
Cluster zoning lets homes sit closer together so more land is kept as open space.

entries.title: Can rules and penalties work for the whole planet?

definition.text: The question of how well direct regulation, built for national governments, can work for problems that cross borders, such as ozone depletion and climate change.

facts.text: The 1987 Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting chlorofluorocarbons is often cited as an international command-and-control success, though some see it as a special case.
Climate change is often used to show its failings: the problem is complex, uncertain and needs more proactive action than traditional models deliver.
Because it relies on prohibitions enforced by sanctions, scaling it up to the international level is problematic.
A blend of approaches and actors, including environmental NGOs, may be the best answer.

entries.title: The kinds of standard direct regulation uses

definition.text: The kinds of standards direct regulation uses: general environmental standards, target standards about the receiving environment, and performance standards on releases.

facts.text: Target standards split into ambient standards, which set goals for regulators, and receptor standards, maximum levels the regulated must not exceed.
Performance standards determine what releases of a pollutant are acceptable.
Which standard is used depends on the nature of the problem and the administrative capacity of the government.

entries.title: National Ambient Air Quality Standards

definition.text: United States limits on the concentration in outdoor air of six pollutants that cause smog, acid rain and other health hazards.

facts.text: The six 'criteria' pollutants are ozone, particulate matter, lead, carbon monoxide, sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides.
Primary standards protect health; secondary standards protect other public welfare, such as agricultural values.
Areas that miss the standards are 'nonattainment areas' and must plan for 'reasonable further progress'.
A 2025 study found the standards produced more than a trillion dollars in welfare gains since 1997.

entries.title: Why regulate, and how? Two kinds of theory

definition.text: Two families of theory: positive theories explain why regulation happens, normative theories say how regulators should act.

facts.text: Positive theories say regulation arises to overcome information gaps, protect customers from market power, protect operators from rivals or from government opportunism.
Normative theories say regulators should reduce information costs, set efficient prices and run independent, transparent and predictable processes.

entries.text: Economists ask two questions about regulation: why does it exist, and how should it work? Positive theories answer the first, in the sense of {{ref:nature-econ-140}}. They say regulation arises to overcome information gaps ({{ref:nature-econ-330}}), to protect customers from market power, or to protect firms from rivals or from government opportunism. Normative theories answer the second. They say regulators should reduce information costs, set efficient prices, and run independent, transparent and predictable processes.

entries.title: Performance standards and technology standards

definition.text: The two main forms of direct pollution rules: a performance standard sets a numerical emission limit for each polluter, while a technology standard dictates the equipment it must use.

facts.text: A performance standard is typically a numeric limit measured at the discharge point, and the facility may meet it with any technology it chooses.
Regulators often base a performance standard on a model technology, as US EPA does for industrial wastewater.
Letting firms choose how to meet the limit makes performance standards slightly more efficient than technology standards.
Both are less cost-effective than cap and trade, because the burden of cutting emissions cannot shift to firms that can cut more cheaply.
Examples include the US New Source Performance Standards for new industrial facilities and EU CO2 performance standards for new cars.

entries.text: A regulator can tell a factory what to achieve, or how to achieve it. Those are the two main forms of direct pollution rules. A technology standard dictates the equipment it must use. The line blurs in practice, because regulators often base a performance standard on a model technology, as US EPA does for industrial wastewater. entries.title: Two layers of discharge limits for US waters

definition.text: Two layers of discharge limits under the Clean Water Act: a national floor based on what control technology can achieve, topped up by stricter limits where a water body stays polluted.

facts.text: Technology-based standards are set for whole categories of dischargers from the performance of control technologies, regardless of the receiving water.
Congress meant them to create a 'level playing field' with a basic national standard for every facility in a category.
Water quality standards have four parts: designated uses, water quality criteria, an antidegradation policy and general policies.

entries.text: The Clean Water Act sets discharge limits in two layers. The first is a national floor. Where a water body stays polluted, stricter water-quality-based limits are added on top. These rest on water quality standards, which have four parts: designated uses, water quality criteria, an antidegradation policy and general policies.

entries.title: Emission performance standards for power plants

definition.text: A limit on emissions above which a different type of emission-control technology may be needed.

facts.text: Such standards have limited conventional pollutants such as nitrogen and sulphur oxides and may also be used for carbon dioxide.
In the US the limit is given in pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt-hour; elsewhere in kilograms per megawatt-hour.

entries.title: Euro 4, 5, 6: Europe's vehicle emission limits

definition.text: The European Union's set of emission limits that all new road vehicles must meet, graded in stages such as Euro 4, Euro 5 and Euro 6.

facts.text: They cover all road vehicles, trains, barges and non-road machinery such as tractors, but not seagoing ships or aircraft.
EU Regulation No 443/2009 set an average CO2 target for new cars of 130 grams per kilometre, tightened to 95 grams per kilometre from 2021.
Many other countries adopt the Euro stages, for example all new vehicles in ECOWAS must meet Euro 4 since 2021.

entries.text: Every new road vehicle in the European Union must meet a set of emission limits, graded in stages such as Euro 4, Euro 5 and Euro 6. entries.title: Low-emission zones: charging dirty vehicles to enter

definition.text: An area, usually in a city, where polluting vehicles are barred or charged for entering, to improve air quality.

facts.text: Many zones do not physically block entry but fine non-compliant vehicles unless a daily charge has been paid, often checked by number-plate cameras.
They work: diesel particulates fall in most zones and health improves, often because people replace polluting vehicles with cleaner ones.
People who need a car but cannot afford a cleaner one are hit hardest, so some cities enforce zones only where public transport exists or subsidise alternatives.
As of 2019 there were about 250 low-emission zones helping meet EU health-based air quality limits; London's, from 2008, was the world's largest.

entries.title: Minimum energy performance standards for appliances

definition.text: A mandatory specification that caps how much energy an appliance or other device may use to do a given task.

facts.text: It usually requires a set test procedure, and may include non-energy requirements so that performance and user satisfaction do not suffer.
A refrigerator, for example, must hold set temperatures while using at most a specified amount of electricity, depending on its size and features.
California began appliance efficiency rules in 1978, and they became US national standards in 1988.
Standards are often paired with energy rating labels that help consumers choose products using less energy.

entries.title: Voluntary standards companies set for themselves

definition.text: Environmental standards that companies adopt for themselves, beyond what the law requires, usually to satisfy customers, governments and industry partners.

facts.text: Government is the strongest influence on companies' standards, followed by customers and then industry networks with codes of conduct.
Companies are often said to focus on how their commitments look in advertising rather than on real implementation.
Whether self-imposed environmental standards are effective is controversial.

entries.title: Enforcement: making environmental rules stick

definition.text: The work of checking whether polluters and other regulated parties follow environmental rules, and of penalising those who do not.

facts.text: Under the US Clean Air Act, EPA monitors compliance, seeks penalties and compels violators to comply, but cases usually settle with penalties well below the legal maximum.
The Acid Rain Program required continuous emissions monitoring to ensure compliance and give credibility to allowance trading.
In China strict central rules are monitored and enforced mostly by local governments more interested in economic growth.
International environmental agreements are criticised for lacking monitoring and enforcement.

entries.text: A rule is only as strong as its enforcement. Environmental enforcement and compliance is the work of checking whether polluters follow environmental rules and penalizing those who do not. entries.title: Becker's rational rule-breaker

definition.text: Gary Becker's approach of treating rule-breaking as a rational choice: a profit-maximising firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying.

facts.text: Becker applied economic reasoning to crime and other non-market behaviour, assuming people act rationally.
His model assumes random inspection, whereas real regulators target firms more likely to be violating.
The same logic predicts illicit markets wherever the expected net return from evasion exceeds what is available legally.

entries.text: Why would a firm obey a rule? Gary Becker gave an economist's answer: because breaking it does not pay. Becker applied economic reasoning to crime and other non-market behavior, assuming people act rationally. In his model, a profit-maximizing firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying. The expected fine is an {{ref:nature-econ-756}}: the fine weighted by the chance of being caught. The model assumes random inspection, whereas real regulators target firms more likely to be violating. The same logic predicts illicit markets wherever the expected net return from evasion beats what is available legally.

In his model, a profit-maximizing firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying. The expected fine is an Expected value: the average of what might happen: the fine weighted by the chance of being caught. The model assumes random inspection, whereas real regulators target firms more likely to be violating. The same logic predicts illicit markets wherever the expected net return from evasion beats what is available legally.

entries.title: The Harrington paradox: why firms obey cheap-to-break rules

definition.text: The puzzle that firms mostly obey environmental rules even though inspections are rare, violators are seldom punished and expected fines are small next to compliance costs.

facts.text: Winston Harrington first described it in a 1988 paper based on US enforcement data from the late 1970s and early 1980s.
It contradicts Gary Becker's rational-crime theory, under which a profit-maximising firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds the cost of complying.
Harrington's own explanation is targeted enforcement: regulators inspect more often the firms more likely to be violating, instead of at random.
Other explanations include leniency for firms that self-report violations, and firms' altruism or concern for their self-image.
Empirical evidence is rare: in Norway most firms had minor deviations, while major violations faced strict punishment, consistent with Becker's theory.

entries.contested_note: Researchers question whether the paradox really exists, since evidence is scarce and major violations do face heavy penalties.
entries.text: By the textbook logic, firms should break environmental rules often. Inspections are rare, violators are seldom punished, and expected fines are small next to the cost of complying. Yet most firms comply. Winston Harrington first described this puzzle in a 1988 paper based on US enforcement data from the late 1970s and early 1980s. It contradicts {{ref:nature-pol-181}}, under which a profit-maximizing firm complies only if the expected fine exceeds its compliance cost. Harrington's own explanation is targeted enforcement: regulators inspect likely violators more often, instead of choosing at random. Others point to leniency for firms that report their own violations, and to firms' altruism or concern for their self-image. Evidence is rare, and some researchers doubt the paradox exists. In Norway, most firms had minor deviations, while major violations faced strict punishment, just as Becker's theory predicts.

entries.title: Environmental liability: making polluters owe

definition.text: The legal responsibility of a polluter to pay for preventing and repairing the environmental damage it causes.

facts.text: The EU's 2004 Environmental Liability Directive, on preventing and remedying environmental damage, is based on the polluter pays principle.
Under US Superfund, liability is generally joint and several among responsible parties, and sellers of land cannot pass liability for past contamination to unknowing buyers.
Environmental liability insurance covers injury, property damage and cleanup costs from the release of pollutants.
Before modern statutes, the common law of nuisance allowed only private suits when land was harmed.

entries.text: Making polluters pay requires a law that says they owe. Environmental liability is the legal responsibility of a polluter to pay for preventing and repairing the environmental damage it causes. The EU's 2004 Environmental Liability Directive, on preventing and remedying environmental damage, rests on the {{ref:nature-pol-095}}. Under US {{ref:nature-pol-176}}, liability is generally joint and several among responsible parties, so any one can be made to pay the whole bill. Sellers of land cannot pass liability for past contamination to unknowing buyers. Environmental liability insurance covers injury, property damage and cleanup costs from pollutant releases.

entries.title: Superfund: the law that bills polluters for cleanup

definition.text: The common name for the 1980 US law (CERCLA) and its trust fund that pay for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites and make polluters liable for the costs.

facts.text: Congress passed it in 1980 in response to hazardous waste disasters such as Love Canal in New York.
Because responsible parties were hard to find, it set up a fund financed by taxes on certain industries plus a broad liability framework.
Liability is generally joint and several: each potentially responsible party can be held liable for the whole cleanup cost, then seek contributions from others.
Historically about 70 percent of Superfund cleanups have been paid for by potentially responsible parties.
Until the mid-1990s an excise tax on the petroleum and chemical industries funded it, reflecting polluter pays; after it lapsed, taxpayers bore most costs until a chemical tax returned in 2021.
Sites are scored from 0 to 100 by a Hazard Ranking System; a score of 28.5 puts a site on the National Priorities List for long-term cleanup.
Its strict, no-fault liability has been blamed for creating brownfields, as investors avoid contaminated land for greenfield sites.
Minority and low-income communities have had less chance of getting nearby sites listed and cleaned up than richer areas.

entries.title: Natural resource damage assessment: billing for injured nature

definition.text: A legal process in which public trustees measure the harm done to natural resources by pollution, so the polluter can be made to pay for restoring them.

facts.text: Superfund authorises federal, state or tribal natural resource trustees to carry out such assessments.
After the Deepwater Horizon spill, federal agencies and five Gulf states formed a trustee council; its assessment found extensive ecological injuries across the Gulf of Mexico.
A 2016 settlement included up to $8.8 billion for natural resource damage assessment and restoration.

entries.title: Low-carbon fuel standards: counting from well to wheels

definition.text: A tradable-credit rule that requires the average carbon intensity of a region's transport fuels to fall below that of petrol and diesel.

facts.text: It counts emissions over the fuel's whole life cycle, 'well to wheels', not just from the tailpipe.
California enacted the first one in 2007, aiming for at least a 10 percent cut in transport fuel carbon intensity by 2020.
Whether to count emissions from indirect land-use change caused by biofuels was fiercely debated by scientists and the biofuel industry.
Canada requires liquid fossil fuel suppliers to cut carbon intensity to 15% below 2016 levels by 2030.

entries.contested_note: Scientists disagreed on whether indirect land-use emissions from biofuels could be estimated well enough to include.

entries.title: Pollution prevention: not making it in the first place
entries.article: Regulation and monitoring of pollution#Pollution prevention

definition.text: A strategy of cutting the amount of waste created in the first place, rather than treating it after release, especially by industry, farms and consumers.

facts.text: Many large corporations see it as a way to make production more efficient and profitable through less waste and better technology.
In the US it was written into law through the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990 and the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments.

entries.title: Regulating and monitoring pollution

definition.text: The laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measurement of pollution levels.

facts.text: Locally, regulation is usually overseen by environmental agencies or the public health system.
The modern regulatory system began with US rules on industrial and mining air and water pollution in the 1960s and 1970s.
Because many pollutants cross borders, UN treaties regulate them, such as the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting chemicals in 1987.
Polluters have historically lobbied governments of poorer countries to keep regulation lax.

entries.title: Pigouvian taxes: charging for harm done to others

definition.text: A Pigouvian tax is a tax on a market activity that imposes costs on third parties, known as negative externalities.

facts.text: Ideally the tax equals the external marginal cost of the harm, correcting a market failure.
When outsiders bear part of the cost, the private cost understates the total and the market produces too much of the activity.
It is named after the English economist Arthur Cecil Pigou, who argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) for taxing producers whose private and social costs diverge.
The tax shifts the producer's marginal private cost up by the size of the externality, so output falls toward the socially best level.
Taxing emissions themselves can reach the long-run social optimum, while taxing proxies such as output may fail to.
For positive externalities the mirror policy is a Pigouvian subsidy, such as subsidies for flu vaccines or research.
Governments often use it because it has relatively low transaction costs compared with regulation or subsidies.
Environmental taxes, including carbon and fuel taxes, are a classic example of Pigouvian taxes.

When outsiders bear part of the cost, the private cost understates the total, and the market produces too much of the activity. Ideally the tax equals the external {{ref:nature-econ-347}} of the harm. It shifts the producer's marginal private cost up by the size of the externality, so output falls toward the socially best level and a {{ref:nature-found-045}} is corrected. What gets taxed matters. Taxing emissions themselves can reach the long-run social optimum, while taxing stand-ins such as output may fail to. For benefits that spill over to others, the mirror policy is a Pigouvian payment that rewards the activity, such as payments that support flu vaccines or research ({{ref:nature-pol-205}}). Governments like the tool partly because its transaction costs are relatively low compared with regulation or such payments. Taxes on environmental harm, including {{ref:nature-pol-081}}es and taxes on fuel, are the classic example.

entries.title: Environmental taxes: making harm cost more

definition.text: An environmental tax, also called an ecotax or green tax, is a tax on activities that harm the environment, meant to steer people toward cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Ecotaxes are a kind of Pigouvian tax, a tax on goods whose making or use imposes costs on others.
They can address the failure of free markets to limit environmental harm, and can complement or replace command-and-control regulation.
Ireland's €0.22 plastic bag tax cut plastic bags' share of litter from 5% to 0.13% in 14 years and raised over €200 million.
Because the poor spend more of their income on consumption, taxes on consumption can be regressive.
Germany enacted an ecotax through laws in 1998, 1999 and 2002, cutting income taxes so the total tax burden stayed constant.
In 2018 China replaced its 1979 Pollutant Discharge Fee with an environmental protection tax.
Economists critical of degrowth argue that price incentives through environmental taxes or tradable permits are much more effective.

entries.contested_note: Some green tax shift proposals have been criticized as regressive, falling harder on poorer households.

entries.title: The carbon tax: a price on emissions

definition.text: A carbon tax is a tax charged on the carbon released when goods and services are produced.

facts.text: It aims to make the hidden social costs of carbon emissions visible by raising the price of fossil fuels.
Higher prices cut demand for high-emission goods and push producers to make them less carbon-intensive.
Unlike command-and-control rules that cap each polluter, a carbon tax lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution.
Its design turns on two choices: how high to set the tax, usually based on the social cost of carbon, and what to do with the revenue.
In its simplest form it covers only CO2, but it can also tax methane or nitrous oxide by their CO2-equivalent warming potential.
Research shows carbon taxes do often reduce emissions; a 2015 British Columbia study found cuts of 5–15% with negligible overall economic effects.
As of 2019 carbon taxes had been implemented or scheduled in 25 countries, and 46 countries priced carbon in some form.
David Gordon Wilson first proposed this type of tax in 1973.

entries.contested_note: Studies find it can hit poor households harder than rich ones, but Gilbert Metcalf disputed that it would be regressive in the US.

entries.title: The polluter pays principle

definition.text: The polluter pays principle says that whoever causes pollution should pay for the damage it does to the environment.

facts.text: It has also been used to make polluters bear the cost of preventing pollution.
Economics supports it: assigning all costs of a decision, including pollution harm, to the decision-maker removes externalities and is a condition for Pareto efficiency.
It underpins policies such as ecotaxes, and cap-and-trade schemes apply it by making polluters buy allowances to cover their emissions.
It is principle 16 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, though not binding in all areas of international environmental law.
It is used in all the major US pollution laws, including the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act and Superfund.
Historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz notes that paying compensation for pollution was already the rule favored by 19th-century industrialists.
It has been doubted where nobody knew a pollutant was dangerous when it was emitted, as with early industrial carbon dioxide.

entries.title: Excise: the tax on particular goods

definition.text: An excise is a tax on a particular category of goods, usually charged when they are made for sale at home.

facts.text: Unlike a sales tax or VAT charged as a share of the price, an excise is usually a fixed amount per unit, falls on few products and is heavier.
It is an indirect tax: the producer pays it but is expected to pass it on to buyers through higher prices.
Tobacco, alcohol and fuel are its three main targets in most countries.
Excises can correct externalities by charging for costs that buyers or sellers impose on society but that prices leave out.
Excises are increasingly placed on polluting transport and on products that create hard-to-recycle waste.

entries.title: Congestion pricing: charging for crowded roads

definition.text: Congestion pricing charges users of crowded public goods, such as busy roads, higher prices at peak times to reduce overuse.

facts.text: It manages crowding by regulating demand rather than adding supply.
The theory is that drivers in a jam impose costs on one another that they do not pay; a price makes them cover this social cost.
It encourages people to shift trips to other times, places or substitutes such as public transport.
Singapore was first to price congestion on urban roads, in 1975, building on William Vickrey's 1963 call to price traffic on Pigou's welfare principle.
Road schemes take four forms: a cordon around a city centre, area-wide pricing, a city-centre toll ring, or pricing of a single corridor or facility.
A 2019 study found that without congestion pricing, Stockholm's air would have been 5 to 15 percent more polluted between 2006 and 2010.
It remains highly controversial with the public, mainly over fairness, effects on businesses and fears it is just another tax.
New York City became the first US city to adopt it, in 2025.

entries.contested_note: Even advocates acknowledge practical limits, and public acceptance remains contested before and after schemes start.

entries.title: Eco-tariffs: taxing trade to cut pollution

definition.text: An eco-tariff, or environmental tariff, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution.

facts.text: It targets goods with a large carbon footprint or goods from countries with lax environmental rules; a carbon tariff is one type.
Supporters say it could stop foreign countries gaining advantage from weak rules and bring trading partners' standards into line.
Critics argue it reduces trade without reaching the main sources of pollution, much of which arises within a country's own borders.
Developing countries fear it as green protectionism: using environmental goals as cover for shielding domestic industry.
Tariffs on imports alone can weaken export competitiveness and contribute to deindustrialisation.

entries.contested_note: There is debate over whether freer international trade increases pollution or, by raising incomes, ends up reducing it.

entries.title: Regressive taxes: when the poor pay a bigger share

definition.text: A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the amount being taxed rises, so poorer people pay a larger share of what they have.

facts.text: A tax can also count as regressive when the taxed activity is done more by the poor than by the rich.
Its opposite, a progressive tax, takes a higher percentage from those with higher incomes.
Taxes on everyday essentials such as food, fuel, energy and housing, including carbon taxes, are often regressive.
Because spending on necessities like food barely rises with income, such taxes weigh most heavily on lower-income households.
Some governments give rebates to lower-income households to soften the effect.
A number of studies find a carbon tax without extra benefits or tax credits hits poor households harder than rich ones.

entries.title: Fuel taxes: the most common price on carbon

definition.text: A fuel tax, also called a gas tax or fuel duty, is an excise tax charged on the sale of fuel, usually transport fuel.

facts.text: Its revenue is often earmarked for transport projects, making it a kind of user fee; elsewhere it goes to general revenue.
It is sometimes used as an ecotax, and fuel taxes can act as an implicit price on carbon.
The IPCC, International Energy Agency, IMF and World Bank have urged governments to raise gasoline taxes to cover the social and environmental costs of its use.
Agencies such as the US Internal Revenue Service often regard fuel taxes as regressive.
Between 2003 and 2015 more countries raised gasoline taxes than cut them, yet the global mean gasoline tax fell because low-tax countries consumed more.
Indirect carbon prices such as fuel taxes are far more common than carbon taxes; in 2021 the OECD found 67 of 71 assessed countries had some fuel tax.
Jet fuel for commercial flights within the EU cannot be taxed under the 2003 Energy Taxation Directive.

entries.text_plain: In 2021 the OECD found that 67 of 71 countries it assessed had some kind of fuel tax. A fuel tax, also called a gas tax or fuel duty, is an Excise: the tax on particular goods charged on the sale of fuel, usually transport fuel. Its revenue is often earmarked for transport projects, making it a kind of User fees: paying for what you use; elsewhere it goes into general revenue. It can also work as an ecotax and as an indirect price on carbon, and such indirect prices are far more common than carbon taxes. The IPCC, the International Energy Agency, the IMF and the World Bank have all urged higher gasoline taxes. The aim is to cover the social and environmental costs of its use. Agencies such as the US Internal Revenue Service often regard fuel taxes as regressive. A quirk: between 2003 and 2015 more countries raised gasoline taxes than cut them, yet the global average fell, because low-tax countries consumed more. And under the EU's 2003 Energy Taxation Directive, jet fuel for commercial flights within the EU cannot be taxed.

entries.title: Carbon tariffs: pricing the carbon in imports

definition.text: A carbon tariff, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them.

facts.text: Its usual aim is to prevent carbon leakage from states that have no carbon price.
High-carbon imports that might face one include coal-fired electricity, blast-furnace iron and steel, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
Only California applies one for electricity, while the European Union and the United Kingdom will apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Carbon credits, carbon taxes and Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms are all forms of carbon pricing.
Likely targets include electricity from coal-fired power stations, iron and steel from blast furnaces, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
California has applied one to imported electricity since 2011, and the EU and UK apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Border adjustment is considered an economically efficient fix for leakage, but it might disguise trade protectionism.
Current WTO rules may prohibit some types, and the WTO has not reached a conclusion.

entries.title: Four kinds of environmental tax

definition.text: Environmental taxes are usually sorted into four categories: energy, transport, pollution and resource taxes.

facts.text: Energy taxes, levied on producing, distributing or using fuels such as coal, oil and gas, are the most common environmental taxes worldwide.
Transport taxes, the second most notable kind, fall on vehicle ownership and use, such as registration taxes based on weight, fuel efficiency or emissions.
Pollution taxes cover measured emissions to air and water and the management of waste and noise.
Resource taxes on extracting water, forests or wildlife are the least common; depletion is usually handled by government fees instead.

entries.text: Environmental taxes come in four broad kinds: energy, transport, pollution and resource taxes. Taxes on energy ({{ref:nature-pol-106}}) are the most common worldwide. They are levied on producing, distributing or using fuels such as coal, oil and gas. Transport taxes are the second most notable kind. They fall on owning and using vehicles, for example registration taxes based on weight, fuel efficiency or emissions. Pollution taxes cover measured emissions to air and water, and the management of waste and noise. Resource taxes, on extracting water, forests or wildlife, are the least common. Governments usually handle the depletion of these resources with fees instead. The sorting shows where the money mostly comes from: the fuels that power the economy, rather than the resources it draws down.

entries.title: Energy taxes: raising the price of fuel and power

definition.text: An energy tax is a tax that raises the price of energy, usually charged on the fuels themselves.

facts.text: Energy taxes are the most commonly used environmental taxes in the world.
They can be levied on producing, distributing or using energy, mainly fossil fuels and sometimes electricity.
Arguments for them include cutting fiscal deficits as well as reducing pollution.
A weakness is that they impose costs in reduced economic output and jobs.
Energy taxes and the removal of fossil fuel subsidies can be seen as pricing carbon implicitly, because they change fossil fuel prices.
A US BTU tax proposed in 1993 to tax fuels by heat content passed the House but was rejected by the Senate after heavy lobbying.

A weakness is the cost in lost economic output and jobs. Because energy taxes change fossil fuel prices, they can be seen as pricing carbon indirectly ({{ref:nature-pol-025}}), as can removing support payments that cheapen fossil fuels. Politics can stop them. In 1993 the US proposed a BTU tax on fuels by their heat content. It passed the House but was rejected by the Senate after heavy pressure from interest groups.

entries.title: Optimal taxation: raising money with the least damage

definition.text: Optimal tax theory studies how to design taxes that do the most for overall social welfare within economic limits.

facts.text: Taxes are needed to fund public goods and redistribution, but most taxes distort behaviour by making the taxed activity less attractive.
The task is to raise the needed revenue and redistribution while causing as little distortion as possible.
Lump-sum taxes and Pigouvian taxes are thought to distort less; a Pigouvian tax moves consumption toward the efficient level.
Frank Ramsey (1927) proposed that each good's tax should depend on how sensitive its supply and demand are to price.
Optimal taxes should also be fair: equal tax for equal ability to pay, and more tax for those with more ability.

entries.title: Effluent: the wastewater that reaches rivers

definition.text: Effluent is wastewater from sewers or industrial outlets that flows into rivers, lakes or the sea, either treated or untreated.

facts.text: It can carry fats and oils, solvents, detergents, heavy metals and food waste from many industries.
Warm cooling-water effluent from power stations causes thermal pollution.
In the US the Clean Water Act requires a permit for every direct discharge of effluent into surface waters.

In the United States, the Clean Water Act requires a permit for every direct discharge of effluent into surface waters.

entries.title: Emissions taxes versus taxes on fuel

definition.text: An emissions tax makes each emitter pay a charge for every tonne of greenhouse gas it releases, while an energy tax is charged on the fuels themselves.

facts.text: Emissions taxes and energy taxes are two taxes closely related to the carbon tax.
A carbon tax encourages using less fuel but does not reward cutting emissions by other means such as carbon capture and storage, so it is not a perfect substitute for an emissions tax.

entries.title: Environmental pricing reform: getting prices right

definition.text: Environmental pricing reform, or ecological fiscal reform, adjusts market prices through taxes or subsidies so they reflect environmental costs and benefits.

facts.text: It responds to externalities: when prices leave out environmental costs, self-interested choices can harm the environment and distort the economy.
Each market-based instrument, such as ecotaxes, tradeable pollution permits or paying for ecological services, is one instance of it.
It can cover the whole economy or focus on one sector or one problem such as climate change.
Environmental tax reform began in the Nordic countries in the early 1990s and spread to the Netherlands, Germany and the United Kingdom.
IMF economists found that a tax 50% above or below marginal damage still captures about three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more than precision.
The World Bank reported carbon pricing revenue rose from under $30 billion in 2016 to more than $107 billion in 2025.

entries.title: Tax shifts: swapping one tax for another

definition.text: A tax shift, or tax swap, cuts some taxes and raises others while keeping total revenue the same.

facts.text: It can mean a desired move toward socially efficient taxes such as ecotaxes and sin taxes.
A green tax shift raises taxes on pollution while lowering taxes such as income, payroll or property taxes.
Its aim is often 'full cost accounting', using fiscal policy to fold externalities into prices.
Tax shifts usually aim to stay revenue-neutral and keep the system progressive, protecting the most vulnerable.
British Columbia's carbon tax shift gave it one of Canada's lowest income tax rates as of 2012.

entries.title: The double dividend: two benefits from one tax swap?

definition.text: The double dividend hypothesis holds that swapping environmental taxes for other taxes, without changing total revenue, could deliver two benefits at once.

facts.text: The first dividend is a cleaner environment; the second is a more efficient tax system from cutting distorting taxes such as income tax.
Tullock first advanced the idea in 1967, and David Pearce popularized the term in 1991.
Fullerton and Metcalf note that every $1 raised in taxes puts a $1.35 burden on the economy; the second dividend aims to remove part of that excess.
Bovenberg and de Mooij proposed a 'tax interaction effect' that could make the second dividend negative.

Goulder (1994) split it into a weak form, that cutting distorting taxes beats lump-sum refunds, and a strong form, that the reform lowers overall economic cost; the strong form needs special conditions.
Fullerton and Metcalf concluded it cannot be established as a whole; each case depends on existing taxes and where the revenue goes.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree on whether the second, tax-efficiency dividend is positive or negative.

The double dividend hypothesis holds that swapping environmental taxes for other taxes, without changing total revenue, could deliver two benefits. The first dividend is a cleaner environment. The weak form says cutting distorting taxes beats handing the money back as lump sums. The strong form says the whole reform lowers the economy's overall cost, and it needs special conditions. Fullerton and Metcalf concluded that the hypothesis cannot be established as a whole: each case depends on existing taxes and where the revenue goes. Economists still disagree on whether the second dividend is positive or negative.

entries.title: Sin taxes: pricing vice

definition.text: A sin tax is an excise on goods and services seen as harmful, such as alcohol, tobacco, sugar, gambling or polluting vehicles.

facts.text: Unlike a Pigouvian tax, which charges for the damage done to others, a sin tax raises the price mainly to cut use.
Raising a sin tax is often more popular than raising other taxes.
Critics call sin taxes regressive and say they encourage smuggling and black markets.
A government may come to depend on the revenue and so need the 'sinful' behaviour to continue.

entries.title: Can anyone measure the right Pigouvian tax?

definition.text: The measurement problem is the criticism that governments cannot know the true social cost of an externality, so they cannot set the right Pigouvian tax.

facts.text: Pigou and Friedrich Hayek both saw the assumption that government can price the harm as a weakness of the tax.
William Baumol argued that social costs are extraordinarily hard to measure, partly because many are psychological and individual.
Lobbying by polluters or by opponents can push the tax level below or above the best level.

entries.contested_note: Critics from Pigou to Baumol doubt that the optimal tax level can ever be measured.

entries.title: Noise taxes: charging for the din

definition.text: A noise tax is a charge meant to limit noise pollution that disturbs nearby communities or wildlife.

facts.text: Most noise taxes concern aviation and urban infrastructure such as highway building.
France taxes commercial and non-commercial aircraft landing at its 10 busiest airports.

entries.title: Plastic taxes
entries.article: Pigouvian tax#Plastic taxes (e.g. on plastic bags)

definition.text: A plastic tax charges for plastic use or plastic waste to cut waste and encourage recycling.

facts.text: Since 2021 the EU budget has collected a contribution from member states based on their non-recycled plastic packaging waste.
Ireland's €0.22 point-of-sale tax on plastic bags shifted shoppers toward other bags and cut plastic bags' share of litter.

entries.title: Second-best taxes: taxing gasoline instead of exhaust
entries.article: Pigouvian tax#Second-best optimal Pigouvian taxation (indirect taxation)

definition.text: Second-best Pigouvian taxation taxes a product linked to a harm when the harm itself cannot be taxed directly.

facts.text: For example, policymakers may tax gasoline instead of vehicle emissions.
Because people buy different amounts and drive vehicles in different states, the tax falls unevenly relative to the harm each causes.
Knittel and Sandler found such taxes an inefficient way to reduce vehicle emissions.

entries.text: Sometimes the harm itself cannot be taxed, so governments tax something linked to it. That is second-best Pigouvian taxation. Policymakers may tax gasoline, for example, instead of vehicle emissions. The fit is loose. People buy different amounts and drive vehicles in different states of repair, so the tax falls unevenly relative to the harm each causes. Knittel and Sandler found such taxes an inefficient way to reduce vehicle emissions.

entries.title: The tax interaction effect

definition.text: The tax interaction effect is the idea that an environmental tax, by raising prices, worsens the distortions already caused by income taxes.

facts.text: Bovenberg and Mooij argue that where an income tax already distorts labor supply, the best environmental tax is below the full Pigouvian level.
As consumers switch from the taxed dirty good to a clean one, the tax base and its revenue shrink, so income taxes cannot stay low.
Goulder, Parry and Burtraw agree that the net welfare effect of an environmental tax depends on the existing tax rate.

entries.text: A green tax does not land on a blank slate. The tax interaction effect is the idea that an environmental tax, by raising prices, worsens the distortions already caused by income taxes ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). Bovenberg and Mooij argue that where an income tax already distorts how much people work, the best environmental tax is below the full Pigouvian level. As consumers switch from the taxed dirty good to a clean one, the tax base and its revenue shrink, so income taxes cannot stay low. Goulder, Parry and Burtraw agree that the net welfare effect of an environmental tax depends on the existing tax rate.

entries.title: Deposit-refund: pay now, get it back on return

definition.text: A deposit-refund system adds a surcharge when a product is bought and pays it back when the product or its packaging is returned.

facts.text: It works like a Pigouvian tax that is refunded once the product is returned, rewarding proper disposal.
Beverage containers are the usual case, but it is also used for batteries, tyres, motor oil, electronics and shipping pallets.
It discourages illegal dumping, eases monitoring and is hard to evade.
It can end up favoring single-use packaging over refillable systems, as in Germany.
It is said to rest on the principles of extended producer responsibility.

entries.title: Meat taxes: pricing livestock's footprint

definition.text: A tax on meat or other animal products meant to cover the health and environmental costs of using animals for food.

facts.text: Livestock contributes significantly to global warming and harms global nitrogen cycles and biodiversity.
Researchers and groups such as Chatham House have called for taxes on red meat or high-emission foods, citing climate and health benefits.
Opponents call it regressive and authoritarian or doubt its health and economic claims.
In June 2024 Denmark announced a tax on livestock carbon dioxide emissions from 2030, the first country to do so.

entries.title: Prices or quantities: fix the cost or fix the amount?

definition.text: Price-based instruments such as taxes fix the price of pollution and let the amount vary, while quantity-based instruments such as cap-and-trade fix the amount and let the price vary.

facts.text: In theory the two give the same result when pollution and costs match expectations, but they diverge when they do not.
Emissions trading sets a limit and lets permits be traded among emitters, while a carbon tax sets a price.

entries.title: Revenue recycling: what to do with green tax money

definition.text: Revenue recycling means using the money raised by an environmental tax to cut other taxes or return it to people, rather than adding it to general spending.

facts.text: How the revenue is used greatly affects the economic cost of an environmental tax reform.
If revenue is not used to cut distorting taxes or is badly spent, the overall benefits fall quickly.
Recycling revenue makes a carbon tax revenue-neutral, for example by lowering income tax or paying citizens a dividend.
Using a tax's revenue to reduce other distorting taxes is what opens the possibility of a double dividend.
IMF authors warn that dedicated funds can lead governments to set rates by the fund's needs instead of by actual damage.
The UK Climate Change Levy dropped revenue recycling in 2010, sending the money to the Exchequer.

entries.text: How a government spends the money from a green tax can matter as much as the tax itself. Revenue recycling means using that money to cut other taxes or return it to people, rather than adding it to general spending. It makes a carbon tax revenue-neutral, for example by lowering income tax or paying citizens a dividend. Using the money to reduce other distorting taxes is what opens the possibility of a {{ref:nature-pol-089}}. If revenue is not used that way, or is badly spent, the overall benefits fall quickly. IMF authors warn that dedicated funds can lead governments to set rates by the fund's needs instead of by actual damage. Policies change: the UK Climate Change Levy dropped revenue recycling in 2010, sending the money to the treasury.

entries.title: Carbon fee and dividend: tax carbon, pay everyone back

definition.text: Carbon fee and dividend taxes fossil fuels for their carbon and pays the money back to everyone in equal per-person payments.

facts.text: The fee is charged where fuels enter the economy, such as the well, mine or port, and rises over time to give a predictable price signal.
A border adjustment charges imports from countries without an equivalent carbon fee.
Returning all net fees makes the scheme revenue-neutral, which appeals to those who do not want government to grow.
Paying out the revenue as a universal climate income largely offsets the higher prices a carbon tax causes.
As of July 2022 eight jurisdictions used a form of it, including Switzerland, Austria and several Canadian provinces.
Switzerland returns about two-thirds of its carbon tax revenue through health insurance bills, but a 2019 survey found only 11.8% of residents knew most funds were redistributed.
A 2021 study of Canada and Switzerland found that returning the money did little to make carbon taxes more popular.

entries.title: British Columbia's carbon tax

definition.text: The British Columbia carbon tax, in force from 2008 until its repeal on 1 April 2025, taxed fossil fuels while cutting income and corporate taxes by about the same amount.

facts.text: It began at $10 per tonne of CO2e on 1 July 2008, the first such tax in North America, and was designed to be revenue-neutral.
It was collected at the point of retail sale, such as the gas pump, with a tax credit to protect low-income families.
The rate reached $40 per tonne in 2019 and $80 per tonne in 2024.
A 2013 review reported per-capita fossil fuel use down 17.4% while GDP growth kept pace with the rest of Canada.
A 2017 paper found a small but significant 0.74 percent annual employment increase over 2007–2013.
A 2021 counterfactual study found no significant negative impact on GDP and complete pass-through of the tax into energy prices.

entries.contested_note: Critics argued that falling fuel use reflected cross-border shopping and a Vancouver gas levy rather than the tax.

entries.title: Earmarked taxes: money with a destination

definition.text: A hypothecated, or earmarked, tax is one whose revenue is set aside for a particular kind of spending.

facts.text: It departs from the usual practice of paying all government spending out of one consolidated fund.
In strong hypothecation the tax funds only that service and the service is funded only by that tax; otherwise it is weak.
Supporters cite transparency, trust and public acceptance of higher taxes when people see where the money goes.
Critics say spending should follow policy rather than revenue, and earmarking reduces fiscal flexibility.

entries.text: Most government money goes into one big pot. A hypothecated, or earmarked, tax is different: its revenue is set aside for a particular kind of spending. In strong hypothecation the tax funds only that service, and the service is funded only by that tax; anything looser is weak hypothecation. Supporters cite transparency and trust, and say people accept higher taxes when they see where the money goes. Critics say spending should follow policy rather than revenue, and that earmarking reduces a government's flexibility.

entries.title: Landfill taxes: making dumping dearer

definition.text: A landfill tax is a charge per tonne or per unit of volume that raises the cost of dumping waste in landfill.

facts.text: It can raise revenue, fund environmental mitigation, or deter landfilling by making better alternatives cheaper by comparison.
Landfilling is discouraged because of landfill gas from biodegradable waste, scarce sites, lost recyclable materials and local opposition.
The UK's landfill tax, introduced in 1996, was its first environmental tax.
By making landfill dearer it creates an incentive to recycle plastics.

entries.title: Per unit taxes: a fixed charge on each item

definition.text: A per unit, or specific, tax is a fixed amount charged on each unit of a good sold, such as cents per kilogram, whatever its price.

facts.text: Excise taxes fall into this category; by contrast an ad valorem tax is a fixed percentage of the product's value.
On a supply-and-demand graph it shifts the supply curve up by exactly the amount of the tax, parallel to the original curve.
For tobacco, specific taxes cut consumption well, while ad valorem taxes can push smokers to cheaper brands.

entries.title: Steering taxes: taxes meant to change behavior

definition.text: A steering tax, or ecological incentive tax, is meant to change taxpayers' behaviour rather than to raise revenue.

facts.text: A Pigouvian tax is a special case of a steering tax aimed at a negative externality.
If the tax succeeds in changing behaviour, its revenue falls, so the steering aim and the revenue aim pull against each other.
Some, like the Swiss tax on volatile organic compounds, are fully paid back to the population, rewarding people who pollute less.
A Swiss study found a per-person refund is the most progressive way to return environmental tax revenue.

entries.text: Some taxes succeed by raising less money. A steering tax, or ecological incentive tax, is meant to change behavior rather than to raise revenue. A Pigouvian tax is a special case, aimed at a harm done to others. If it works, its revenue falls, so the steering aim and the revenue aim pull against each other. Some steering taxes, such as the Swiss tax on volatile organic compounds, are fully paid back to the population, rewarding people who pollute less. A Swiss study found that an equal refund per person is the most progressive way to return such revenue.

entries.title: Stormwater fees: paying for paved-over ground

definition.text: A stormwater fee charges property owners for polluted rainwater runoff from their hard, waterproof surfaces.

facts.text: The charge grows with the area of roofs, driveways and paving that stop rain soaking into the ground.
In Germany builders install rain storage tanks and soakaways to lower the fee, raising rainwater recycling and cutting tap water use.
A 2023 study counted at least 2,100 stormwater utilities in 42 US states and the District of Columbia.
Maryland's 2012 fee, dubbed a 'rain tax', funded runoff controls to clean up the Chesapeake Bay but was made optional in 2015.

entries.title: Cost pass-through: who ends up paying

definition.text: Cost pass-through is the extent to which a business changes its prices when its own costs change.

facts.text: It is measured as a pass-through rate; firms may absorb part of a cost change (rate below 1.0) or amplify it (above 1.0).
When buyers must have a good whatever the price, the whole cost increase reaches consumers; when buyers would leave at any price rise, producers absorb it all.
Pass-through is higher when demand is less sensitive to price and supply more sensitive.
A 2021 study found British Columbia's carbon tax was passed fully into energy prices.

When buyers must have a good whatever the price, the whole increase reaches consumers; when buyers would leave at any price rise, producers absorb it all. Pass-through is higher when demand is less sensitive to price ({{ref:nature-econ-358}}) and supply more sensitive. A 2021 study found British Columbia's carbon tax was passed fully into energy prices.

entries.title: Road pricing: paying for the roads you use

definition.text: Road pricing means charging drivers directly for road use, through tolls, distance or time fees, congestion charges or charges on more polluting vehicles.

facts.text: The charges may mainly raise money for roads or manage demand to cut congestion, pollution, noise and crashes.
William Vickrey built on Pigou's ideas to make the theoretical case for road pricing in the 1950s, proposing electronic charging for busy roads.
Distance-based lorry charges in Austria (2004) and Germany (2005) vary by emissions level and axles.
A Stockholm study found that without congestion pricing the city's air would have been five to ten percent more polluted in 2006–2010, with 45 percent more asthma attacks in young children.

conflicts.text: The Congestion pricing article reports the same Stockholm finding as 5 to 15 percent more polluted air.
conflicts.note: Two articles quote the same Stockholm 2006–2010 study with different upper bounds.

entries.title: Feebates: fees on the dirty, rebates on the clean

definition.text: A feebate charges a fee on products with harmful side effects and uses the money to give rebates on cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Feebates are usually revenue-neutral, with the fees paying for the rebates.
Arthur H. Rosenfeld coined the idea in the 1970s; it has mostly been used in transport and energy.
Car buyers discount future fuel costs heavily, so a feebate puts the cost into the purchase price where it is noticed.

entries.title: User fees: paying for what you use

definition.text: A user fee is a payment charged to people for using a facility or service, such as a park, toll road or parking space.

facts.text: Fuel taxes that fund highways act as user fees: those who drive more pay more for roads.
Unlike broad taxes, user fees fall only on those who use the service.
Critics argue that fees for basic services in developing countries hurt the poorest most.

entries.title: Pricing pollution you can measure

definition.text: Pollution pricing reform adjusts market prices to include directly measurable pollution, such as dust and exhaust from road vehicles.

facts.text: It differs from general ecotaxes, which are not tied to a short-term measurement of the impact.
Options include extra taxes on dirtier fuels, annual taxes on more polluting engine types, and daily traffic limits set by measured pollution.

entries.title: Plastic bag charges and bans

definition.text: A plastic bag ban or charge is a law that restricts or puts a price on the lightweight plastic bags handed out by shops.

facts.text: Charges and bans are the two most popular ways to phase bags out; as of 2018, 30 countries charged consumers and 27 had banned the bags.
A 2018 study found a five-cent tax on disposable bags cut their use by 40 percentage points.
Ireland's €0.15 levy in 2002 cut bag use by 90% within weeks.
Bans can raise use of unregulated paper or thicker plastic bags and feed black markets.

entries.title: Reforming fossil fuel subsidies
entries.article: Environmental pricing reform#Fossil Fuel subsidy reform

definition.text: Fossil fuel subsidy reform removes subsidies that keep fossil fuel prices below their supply cost or below their full environmental cost.

facts.text: The IMF separates explicit subsidies, where consumer prices are below supply cost, from implicit ones, where prices omit environmental damage.
Explicit subsidies reached 1.3% of global GDP in 2022 and fell to 0.6% in 2024, the IMF estimated.
Removing fossil fuel subsidies counts as an implicit carbon price.
Phase-out is politically difficult.

entries.text: Fossil fuel subsidy reform removes subsidies that keep fossil fuel prices below their supply cost or below their full environmental cost. The IMF separates explicit subsidies, where consumer prices are below supply cost, from implicit ones, where prices leave out environmental damage. Explicit subsidies reached 1.3% of global GDP in 2022 and fell to 0.6% in 2024, the IMF estimated. Removing them counts as pricing carbon indirectly ({{ref:nature-pol-025}}). Phasing them out is politically difficult.

entries.title: Putting a carbon price on shipping

definition.text: Carbon pricing on shipping charges ships for the greenhouse gases they emit.

facts.text: Maritime transport makes up 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
A carbon price is meant to close the cost gap between heavy fuel oil and low-carbon fuels, breaking a stand-off where fuel suppliers and shipowners each wait for the other to move first.
In 2023 the EU Emissions Trading System was extended to shipping, and the International Maritime Organization set a goal of net-zero shipping emissions by around 2050.
An IMO pricing scheme would be the first global carbon pricing system; countries including China, Brazil and South Africa oppose it as unfair to developing countries.

entries.contested_note: Stakeholders disagree over whether shipping carbon revenue should be spent within shipping or as general climate finance.
entries.text: Ships carry 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Carbon pricing on shipping charges ships for the gases they emit. The price is meant to close the cost gap between heavy fuel oil and low-carbon fuels. That could break a stand-off in which fuel suppliers and shipowners each wait for the other. In 2023 the EU extended its carbon market ({{ref:nature-pol-253}}) to shipping, and the International Maritime Organization set a goal of net-zero shipping emissions by around 2050. An IMO scheme would be the first global system of its kind, but China, Brazil, South Africa and others oppose it as unfair to developing countries. Stakeholders also disagree over whether the revenue should stay in shipping or fund climate action generally.

An IMO scheme would be the first global system of its kind, but China, Brazil, South Africa and others oppose it as unfair to developing countries. Stakeholders also disagree over whether the revenue should stay in shipping or fund climate action generally.

entries.title: Global warming taxes

definition.text: Taxes proposed or imposed to raise money for dealing with global warming, or to discourage the activities that cause it.

facts.text: The British economist Arthur Pigou advocated corrective taxes for pollution in the early 20th century, which is why they are called Pigovian taxes.
Using a Pigovian tax against global warming was proposed as far back as 1992 by economist Martin Feldstein.
A San Francisco Bay Area fee on carbon dioxide emissions was meant to pay for monitoring greenhouse gases rather than to deter emissions.

entries.text: Taxes against global warming have two possible jobs: to discourage the activities that cause it, or to raise money for dealing with it. Their roots go back to the British economist Arthur Pigou, who advocated corrective taxes for pollution in the early 20th century. As far back as 1992, the economist Martin Feldstein proposed using such a tax against global warming. Not every climate charge aims to deter. A San Francisco Bay Area fee on carbon dioxide emissions was meant to pay for monitoring greenhouse gases instead.
entries.text_plain: Taxes against global warming have two possible jobs: to discourage the activities that cause it, or to raise money for dealing with it. Their roots go back to the British economist Arthur Pigou, who advocated corrective taxes for pollution in the early 20th century. As far back as 1992, the economist Martin Feldstein proposed using such a tax against global warming. Not every climate charge aims to deter. A San Francisco Bay Area fee on carbon dioxide emissions was meant to pay for monitoring greenhouse gases instead.

entries.title: Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits

definition.text: A market-based way of controlling pollution in which a government caps total emissions and issues permits that polluters can buy and sell.

facts.text: Also called cap and trade, it is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases as well as sulfur dioxide and other pollutants.
Polluters must hold permits equal to their emissions; one that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell.
In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions.
Its goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost, letting firms decide how to meet it, unlike command-and-control rules.
Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, which lets them cut emissions when it is most efficient.
Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target.
A 2024 meta-analysis of 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems found average emission cuts of about 5–21% (around 4–15% after correcting for publication bias).

entries.text: What if the right to pollute were something a firm had to buy? Emissions trading, also called cap and trade, rests on that idea. A government caps the total amount of a pollutant that may be released and issues permits up to that cap. Each polluter must hold permits equal to its emissions. One that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell. In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions. A {{ref:nature-found-031}}, a cost dumped on others, so acquires a price. The goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost. Unlike {{ref:nature-pol-147}}, which tells each firm what to do, trading lets firms decide how to meet the target. Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, so they can cut emissions when it is most efficient. Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target. The approach is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, and for sulfur dioxide and other pollutants. Does it work? A 2024 meta-analysis pooled 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems. It found average emission cuts of about 5–21%, or around 4–15% after correcting for {{ref:nature-econ-241}}.

entries.title: Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases

definition.text: A government policy that puts a money cost on greenhouse gas emissions so that polluters burn less fossil fuel.

facts.text: A carbon price usually takes the form of a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme in which firms must buy allowances to emit.
It tackles the problem that greenhouse gas emissions are a negative externality: a harm that no market charges for.
Many economists consider it the most economically efficient way to cut emissions, because it fixes the unpriced external cost at its source.
Carbon pricing covered 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, and in 2020 it raised $53B in revenue.
Of 21 carbon pricing schemes evaluated, at least 17 reduced emissions, by between 5% and 21%.
About one third of schemes price carbon below $10/tCO2 and most below $40; only Sweden and Switzerland exceed $100/tCO2.
The IPCC says prices of $135–$5500 per tonne in 2030 and $245–$13,000 in 2050 would be needed to stay below the 1.5°C limit.
A 2020 study found that carbon prices have not harmed economic growth in wealthy industrialized democracies.

entries.text: Burning coal, oil or gas releases greenhouse gases, and no market charges for the harm they do. That makes the emissions a negative {{ref:nature-found-031}}, and carbon pricing is the standard remedy. It is a government policy that puts a money cost on {{ref:nature-eco-163}}, so that polluters burn less fossil fuel. The price usually takes one of two forms: a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, or an emissions trading scheme in which firms must buy allowances to emit. Many economists consider it the most economically efficient way to cut emissions, because it fixes the unpriced external cost at its source, in the spirit of a {{ref:nature-pol-088}}. In 2025 carbon pricing covered 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2020 it raised $53B in revenue. Of 21 schemes evaluated, at least 17 reduced emissions, by between 5% and 21%. A 2020 study found that carbon prices have not harmed economic growth in wealthy industrialized democracies. The weak point is the level of the price. About one third of schemes charge less than $10 per tonne of carbon dioxide ($10/tCO2), and most less than $40. Only Sweden and Switzerland exceed $100/tCO2. The IPCC says prices of $135–$5500 per tonne in 2030 and $245–$13,000 in 2050 would be needed to stay below the 1.5°C limit.
