entries.title: Carbon markets: trading the right to emit greenhouse gases

definition.text: Emissions trading applied to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases: a market with a limited number of allowances to emit, created to limit climate change.

facts.text: A total limit on all participants' emissions sets the price; a polluter emitting more than its quota must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions.
It works by creating property rights to the atmosphere, a global public good, to deal with an international externality.
Compliance is checked by comparing each emitter's actual emissions with the permits it surrenders.
Countries use it to meet their Paris Agreement pledges, with schemes running in China, the European Union and elsewhere.
In September 2021 allowance prices ranged from €7 per tonne in China's national scheme to €63 per tonne in the EU ETS.
In 2023 the global carbon market was worth a record 881 billion euros, about 87% of it in the EU ETS.
Schemes are usually not matched to the carbon budgets needed for 1.5 °C or 2 °C, and oversupply can push allowance prices too low to matter.

A polluter emitting more than its quota must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions. In economic terms, the scheme creates property rights to the atmosphere, a global {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, to deal with an externality that crosses borders. Compliance is checked by comparing each emitter's actual emissions with the permits it surrenders. Countries use these markets to meet their pledges under the {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, with schemes running in China, the European Union and elsewhere. Prices vary widely. In September 2021 allowances cost €7 per tonne in China's national scheme and €63 per tonne in the EU's. The markets share two weaknesses. Their caps are usually not matched to the total emissions allowed if warming is to stay within 1.5 °C or 2 °C. And oversupply can push allowance prices too low to matter.

entries.title: Carbon leakage: cuts at home, emissions abroad

definition.text: A rise in greenhouse gas emissions in one country caused by another country cutting its own emissions under stricter climate policies.

facts.text: The leakage rate is the rise in emissions outside the acting countries divided by the cut inside them, as a percentage that can exceed 100%.
A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions.
Leakage happens when climate policy raises local costs, so production moves to countries with laxer rules while demand stays the same.
It can also happen through fuel markets: lower demand cuts fuel prices, and countries without a carbon price use more.
Estimates for action under the Kyoto Protocol ranged from 5 to 20%, but were seen as very uncertain; there is no consensus on long-term leakage.
The EU gives free ETS allowances to sectors at high risk of leakage, such as aluminium, using a Carbon Leakage Indicator of trade intensity times emission intensity.
Firm-level evidence found the EU ETS cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed carbon leakage.
It happens when regulating emissions in one place pushes them to places with less regulation.

entries.contested_note: Sources say there is no consensus on how large long-term carbon leakage is.

The leakage rate divides the rise in emissions outside the acting countries by the cut inside them. A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions. The EU gives free allowances to sectors at high risk, such as aluminum, ranked by trade intensity times emission intensity. Yet firm-level evidence found its trading scheme cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed leakage.

entries.title: China's national carbon market: the largest of its kind

definition.text: China's national emissions trading system for carbon dioxide, which caps emissions per unit of output rather than in total, and began operating in 2021.

facts.text: China proposed a carbon tax in 2010 but never passed it, setting up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021 instead.
It began with power plants and covers 40% of China's emissions, which is 15% of world emissions; it is the largest scheme of its kind.
In July 2021 permits were handed out free and traded at around RMB 50 per tonne, roughly half the EU ETS price.
Seven pilot markets, starting in Shenzhen on June 18, 2013, preceded it, with compliance rates over 96%.
Studies find it cut carbon emissions by up to 18.2%, cut power sector emissions by 13% in 2013-2020, and delivered about a third of China's air pollution health benefits.
Some researchers found it can reduce GDP or hold back innovation.
By 2027 it is expected to cover all major industrial emitters and move to an absolute cap on emissions for stable sectors.

entries.title: Why permit trading puts the cheapest cuts first

definition.text: The idea that trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost.

facts.text: Each polluter chooses between buying or selling permits, installing cleaner technology or cutting output, depending on its marginal abatement cost and the permit price.
In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules.
In a Lagrange optimization of the least-cost target, the Lagrange multiplier plays the role of the market permit price.
This is a version of the equi-marginal principle used in economics to find the most efficient decision.
Coase (1960) argued social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power.

entries.text: Trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. The logic runs through each firm's books. A polluter compares the permit price with its {{ref:nature-clim-245}}: the extra cost of cutting one more unit of pollution, a kind of {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. Then it chooses to buy or sell permits, install cleaner technology or cut output. In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules. Coase (1960) argued that social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power ({{ref:nature-econ-629}}).

entries.title: Free or auctioned: how permits are handed out

definition.text: How a trading scheme hands out its permits: either free to existing emitters or sold at auction.

facts.text: Under free allocation the government earns no carbon revenue; under auctioning it receives the full value of the permits on average.
Either way the permits are equally scarce, so they sell at the same market price.
Emitters generally profit from permits given to them free, while paying for them reduces their profits.
Advance notice or a gradual introduction keeps the one-time cost of a new carbon price small.

entries.text: Once a government decides how many permits to issue, it must decide who gets them. There are two routes. Under free allocation, existing emitters receive permits and the government earns no carbon revenue. Under auctioning, it sells them and receives their full value on average. Either way the permits are equally scarce, so they sell at the same market price. The difference lies in who keeps the money. Emitters generally profit from permits given to them free, while paying for permits reduces their profits. Advance notice or a gradual introduction keeps the one-time cost of a new carbon price small.

entries.title: The EU Emissions Trading System: Europe's carbon market

definition.text: The European Union's cap-and-trade scheme for greenhouse gases, begun in 2005, in which each allowance permits its holder to emit 1 ton of CO2.

facts.text: It was the first large greenhouse gas trading scheme in the world and operates in 30 countries: the 27 EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
As of 2026 it covers around 40% of the EU's emissions; its cap should reach zero by 2039.
Between 2005 and 2023, emissions from covered power plants and factories fell by 47%.
A 2023 study found it cut emissions by 10% between 2005 and 2012 with no significant effect on profits or employment.
Phase I over-allocation drove the carbon price to zero in 2007.
It has been criticised for over-allocation, windfall profits, price volatility and failure to meet its goals.
Auction revenue in 2013 - 2025 exceeded €245 billion, most of it going directly to member states.
It has suffered fraud: hackers stole 28 to 30 million euros of allowances in 2011, and VAT fraud cost Germany about €850 million.

entries.contested_note: Critics say it has failed its goals through over-allocation and windfall profits, while proponents call Phase I a learning phase and point to measured cuts.

entries.title: The case against carbon trading

definition.text: The arguments that carbon emissions trading is ineffective, unfair or open to abuse.

facts.text: Critics argue climate change needs more radical, systemic cuts in fossil fuel use than pollution trading can deliver.
Carbon trading has been called a form of colonialism that lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad.
The market picks the easiest short-term carbon savings, which may differ from the steps needed to reduce climate change.
Some companies in China and India produced greenhouse gases artificially in order to earn credits for destroying them.
Schemes have been criticised for creating speculative markets through financial derivatives, and for changes linked to money laundering.

entries.contested_note: Supporters see carbon trading as an efficient climate tool, while critics call it ineffective, unjust and open to manipulation.
entries.text: Supporters see carbon trading as an efficient climate tool. Critics call it ineffective, unjust and open to manipulation, and the argument is far from settled. The first objection is scale. Climate change, critics argue, needs more radical, systemic cuts in fossil fuel use than pollution trading can deliver. The second is direction. The market picks the easiest short-term carbon savings, which may differ from the steps needed to reduce climate change. The third is fairness. Carbon trading has been called a form of colonialism that lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad. Then there is abuse. Some companies in China and India produced greenhouse gases artificially in order to earn credits for destroying them. Schemes have also been criticized for creating speculative markets through financial derivatives ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}), and for changes linked to money laundering.

entries.title: Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon
entries.article: Carbon price#Carbon tax versus emissions trade

definition.text: The policy choice between a carbon tax, which fixes the price of each tonne emitted, and emissions trading, which fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price adjust.

facts.text: A carbon tax is generally favoured for its simplicity and price stability, while cap-and-trade can in principle hold emissions to a remaining carbon budget.
A tax is easier to enforce broadly; British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months.
Industries may lobby their way out of a carbon tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behaviour.
Most cap-and-trade programmes lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline; permits suit cases where emissions certainty is needed.
Both instruments are efficient and have the same social cost and effect on profits if permits are auctioned.
Prices under a cap are more volatile, which makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits.
Some economists say a cap stops other policies such as renewable subsidies from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree over whether a tax or a cap is the better way to price carbon.

It is also easier to enforce broadly: British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months. A cap can in principle hold emissions to a fixed remaining total. Most cap-and-trade programs lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline. Permits therefore suit cases where certainty about emissions is needed. Prices under a cap are more volatile, though. That makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits. Both tools can be bent by politics. Industries may lobby their way out of a tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behavior. On paper the two are close cousins. Both are efficient, and if permits are auctioned they have the same social cost and effect on profits. A last dispute concerns other climate policies. Some economists say a cap stops measures such as renewable energy support from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts ({{ref:nature-pol-242}}).

entries.title: Internal carbon pricing: companies that charge themselves

definition.text: A carbon price that a company sets on its own greenhouse gas emissions, voluntarily and on top of any price a government imposes.

facts.text: As of 2024, 1,753 companies in 56 countries reported using an internal carbon price through the Carbon Disclosure Project.
Tools include internal emissions trading, proxy prices, carbon fees, implicit prices and hybrids of these.
Proxy pricing, used by about two-thirds of reporting companies, puts a set carbon price into investment decisions without any actual payment.
Companies often base their price on the social cost of carbon or on the marginal abatement cost of reaching a target.
An analysis of 500 firms reporting from 2011 to 2018 linked adoption to a significant fall in emissions per unit of revenue and per employee.
Some researchers worry it can serve as greenwashing that deters governments from stricter carbon rules.
It works like a Pigouvian tax inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive.
As of 2024, 1,753 companies across 56 countries reported using it through the Carbon Disclosure Project.

Some researchers worry it can serve as Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action, deterring governments from stricter carbon rules.

entries.title: Kyoto's flexible mechanisms: cutting emissions where it costs least

definition.text: The three Kyoto Protocol tools, emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, that let countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries.

facts.text: They rest on the idea that cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens.
International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets.
Kyoto caps required Annex I countries to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
The main argument for them is cost-effectiveness, separating fairness from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply.
Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries.
Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement are their successor.

entries.contested_note: Negotiators disagreed over whether flexibility was efficient or let developed countries avoid domestic cuts at developing countries' expense.

entries.title: The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade

definition.text: A US Environmental Protection Agency emissions trading programme that cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause acid rain, from power plants.

facts.text: Title IV of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments set a falling cap on SO2, aiming to bring emissions to 50% of 1980 levels.
It was the first cap-and-trade emissions programme in the United States and became a model for later greenhouse gas schemes.
Plants need an allowance for each ton of SO2 and pay a fine of $2,000 for each ton emitted beyond the allowances they hold.
In 2007 total SO2 emissions were 8.9 million tons, reaching the long-term goal ahead of the 2010 deadline.
The EPA expected compliance costs of $1 billion to $2 billion a year by 2010, only one fourth of what was first predicted.
A 2021 study found it caused lasting air quality gains, cutting mortality risk by 5% over 10 years.
Early over-allocation in Phase I let sources bank allowances, which they drew down in Phase II.
Critics note it cut SO2 by 40%, less than the more than 70% achieved by conventional regulation in the European Union.

entries.contested_note: The EPA, industry and economists call it a success, while sceptical environmentalists argue the cuts came from broader trends and other regulation.

entries.title: Europe's carbon charge at the border

definition.text: A European Union carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports such as steel, cement and some electricity.

facts.text: Its main aim is to stop carbon leakage by charging covered imports the same carbon price as EU producers pay under the EU ETS.
Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with EU ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods.
It covers aluminium, cement, electricity, fertilisers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023 and payment from 2026.
Free EU ETS allowances in the covered sectors will be phased out by 2034.
It may push other countries to adopt carbon pricing; Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it.
Some see it as the start of a climate club of the kind William Nordhaus proposed.
An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU.
Questions remain over its compatibility with WTO rules and its effect on least developed countries.

entries.contested_note: Supporters call it a key fix for carbon leakage, while critics say it does little for emissions, burdens EU firms and may clash with trade rules.
entries.text: Since 2026, firms bringing steel or cement into the European Union have had to pay for the carbon released in making it. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, is a {{ref:nature-pol-265}} on carbon-intensive imports. Its main aim is to stop {{ref:nature-pol-252}} by charging imports the same carbon price that EU producers pay under the EU ETS. Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods. It may push other countries to price carbon: Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it. entries.title: Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol mechanism letting one developed (Annex I) country invest in an emission-cutting project in another and count the cuts towards its own target.

facts.text: Projects earn Emission Reduction Units, each equal to one tonne of CO2 equivalent, taken from the host country's pool of assigned amount units.
Because credits come from the host's pool, the total of credits among Annex I parties does not change.
It raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the CDM, since hosts also have emission commitments.
Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, which were expected to total around 300 million ERUs by 2012.

entries.text: Joint Implementation is a mechanism of the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Under it, one developed (Annex I) country invests in an emission-cutting project in another and counts the cuts towards its own target. Projects earn credits ({{ref:nature-pol-271}}), each equal to one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These come out of the host country's own pool of units, so the total among Annex I parties does not change. Because hosts also have emission commitments, it raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}. Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, expected to total around 300 million units by 2012.
entries.text_plain: Joint Implementation is a mechanism of the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries. Under it, one developed (Annex I) country invests in an emission-cutting project in another and counts the cuts towards its own target. Projects earn credits (Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation), each equal to one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These come out of the host country's own pool of units, so the total among Annex I parties does not change. Because hosts also have emission commitments, it raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market. Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, expected to total around 300 million units by 2012.

entries.title: Baseline and credit: rewards for beating your own past

definition.text: A trading scheme in which polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their historical emissions.

facts.text: The credits can be bought by polluters that face a regulatory limit.
Credit programmes usually require additionality: cutting more than existing rules already demand.
Additionality is hard to define and monitor; some companies deliberately raised emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

entries.text: Not every trading scheme starts with a cap. In a baseline-and-credit scheme, polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their own historical emissions. Polluters that face a regulatory limit can then buy those credits. Programs usually require {{ref:nature-mkt-144}}: the cuts must go beyond what existing rules already demand. That test is hard to define and monitor. Some companies deliberately raised their emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

In a baseline-and-credit scheme, polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their own historical emissions. Polluters that face a regulatory limit can then buy those credits. Programs usually require Additionality: would it have happened anyway?: the cuts must go beyond what existing rules already demand. That test is hard to define and monitor. Some companies deliberately raised their emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

entries.title: From computer models to carbon markets

definition.text: The development of cap and trade from computer studies of air pollution costs in the late 1960s to national and global carbon markets.

facts.text: Simulation studies between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional abatement strategies.
The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant.
The first cap-and-trade system was the US Acid Rain Program under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in environmental policy.
The approach then spread from US clean air policy to global climate policy and the European Union.

entries.text: Emissions trading began as a computer result. Simulation studies of air pollution costs between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional ways of cutting pollution. The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant. The first cap-and-trade system was the US {{ref:nature-pol-262}} under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in {{ref:nature-pol-018}}. From US clean air policy, the approach then spread to the European Union and to global climate policy.

entries.title: Linking carbon markets across borders

definition.text: Separate cap-and-trade systems joined together by recognising each other's allowances for compliance.

facts.text: Linking makes a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity and stabilise prices.
Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy.
California and Québec linked their systems in 2014; the EU ETS has linked with Switzerland's system.

entries.text: California and Québec linked their cap-and-trade systems in 2014, and the EU's scheme has linked with Switzerland's. Linking means each system recognizes the other's allowances for compliance. The result is a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity, the ease of finding a buyer or seller, and stabilize prices. Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy, built from existing national and regional schemes.

entries.title: Measure, report, verify: keeping a carbon market honest
entries.article: Emissions trading#Measuring, reporting, verification and enforcement

definition.text: The checks that make an emissions market credible: measuring or calculating emissions, reporting them, and having them verified by government or third-party auditors.

facts.text: Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead.
Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions; concerns include the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying.
Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily.
Robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the Core Carbon Principles for voluntary credits.

sources.title: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

entries.text: A permit market is only as good as its numbers. Monitoring, reporting and verification are the checks that make it credible: emissions are measured or calculated, reported, then verified by government or third-party auditors. Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead. Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily. Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions. The worries are the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying. For voluntary credits, robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the {{ref:nature-hist-034}}.

entries.title: The safety valve: a cap with a price limit
entries.article: Emissions trading#Prices versus quantities, and the safety valve

definition.text: A hybrid of a cap and a tax: a cap-and-trade system in which the permit price is held below a maximum, or above a minimum.

facts.text: Emitters can buy permits on the market or from the government at a set trigger price.
Setting the trigger price high enough, or the permits few enough, lets it mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument.
A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit.
A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

entries.text: A safety valve is a hybrid of a cap and a tax. Emitters can buy permits on the market, or from the government at a set trigger price, which holds the permit price below a maximum. Some designs instead hold it above a minimum. A trigger price set high enough, or a permit supply small enough, lets the system mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument ({{ref:nature-pol-256}}). Each limit has a cost. A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit. A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.
entries.text_plain: A safety valve is a hybrid of a cap and a tax. Emitters can buy permits on the market, or from the government at a set trigger price, which holds the permit price below a maximum. Some designs instead hold it above a minimum. A trigger price set high enough, or a permit supply small enough, lets the system mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument (Prices or quantities: fix the cost or fix the amount?). Each limit has a cost. A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit. A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

entries.title: Auctioning permits: making polluters pay up front

definition.text: Selling emission permits to firms at auction, so that the government receives their value.

facts.text: Businesses tend to oppose auctioning, while economists almost uniformly recommend it.
Auction revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes.
Auctioning can be more efficient and equitable than free allocation and removes grandfathering's perverse incentive.

entries.text: Businesses tend to oppose auctioning emission permits. Economists almost uniformly recommend it. Under auctioning, firms buy their permits at auction and the government receives their value. That revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes, the kind that discourage useful work and investment. Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the perverse incentive created by {{ref:nature-pol-246}}.

Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the perverse incentive created by Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters.

entries.title: Carbon trading and the neighbors of polluters
entries.article: Carbon emission trading#Relevance to climate justice

definition.text: The question of whether carbon trading helps poorer countries and communities or leaves them bearing more of the pollution.

facts.text: Trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action.
Because schemes cap only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits instead of cutting local air pollution.
Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap.

entries.contested_note: Sources say carbon trading can advance climate justice but has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.
entries.text: Carbon trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action. That is its promise as a tool of {{ref:nature-gov-162}}. The problem starts at the factory gate. Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so a factory can buy permits instead of cutting its local air pollution. Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap. The sources record both sides: trading can advance that cause, yet it has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

That is its promise as a tool of Climate justice: those who suffer most did least. The problem starts at the factory gate. Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so a factory can buy permits instead of cutting its local air pollution. Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap. The sources record both sides: trading can advance that cause, yet it has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

entries.title: Toward a single global carbon market
entries.article: Carbon emission trading#Potential global carbon market

definition.text: A proposed worldwide market in emission allowances, for which the Paris Agreement provides a legal basis.

facts.text: In 2023 the global value of carbon markets was $948.75 billion, expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028.
The Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets, formed at COP 30, plans a global cap near current emissions that falls to net zero by 2050.
Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programmes.

entries.text: In 2023 carbon markets worldwide were worth $948.75 billion, a figure expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028. A truly worldwide market in emission allowances is still a proposal, though the {{ref:nature-clim-074}} provides a legal basis for one. At COP 30, the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets formed with a plan for a global cap near current emissions, falling to net zero by 2050. Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries, while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programs.

A truly worldwide market in emission allowances is still a proposal, though the The Paris Agreement: every country pledges provides a legal basis for one. At COP 30, the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets formed with a plan for a global cap near current emissions, falling to net zero by 2050. Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries, while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programs.

entries.title: Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters

definition.text: Giving out emission permits for free according to how much each firm emitted in the past.

facts.text: It can create perverse incentives, such as a firm that cuts emissions sharply receiving fewer permits later.
Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits.
The EU ETS gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition.
Free allocation is complex and encourages rent-seeking and lobbying of governments.

entries.text: Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages {{ref:nature-pol-042}}, the pursuit of favors from government, and pressure on officials ({{ref:nature-pol-034}}).
entries.text_plain: Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth, the pursuit of favors from government, and pressure on officials (Lobbying: influencing the people who make the rules).

entries.title: Too many permits: how a carbon price collapses

definition.text: The risk that a regulator issues too many emission permits, pushing their price so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions.

facts.text: Issuing too few permits has the opposite risk: an excessively high permit price.
The EU ETS price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession.
Under the Kyoto Protocol, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse; buying them would not have reduced emissions.

entries.text: A permit market lives or dies by the number of permits. Issue too many and the price sinks so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions. Issue too few and the risk flips to an excessively high price. Europe's trading scheme showed the first danger. Its price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession. Under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse. Buying them would not have reduced emissions.

Issue too few and the risk flips to an excessively high price. Europe's trading scheme showed the first danger. Its price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession. Under the The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse. Buying them would not have reduced emissions.

entries.title: Certified emission reductions: credits from developing countries

definition.text: A carbon credit issued by the Clean Development Mechanism for verified emission cuts made by its projects under the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of CO2e, measured against a baseline.
Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their targets.
Between 2001 and 7 September 2012 the CDM issued 1 billion CERs; by 2013, 57% came from destroying HFC-23 or N2O.
Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012 amid recession and EU ETS over-allocation.

entries.text: Between 2001 and 7 September 2012, the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} issued 1 billion certified emission reductions, or CERs. Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of {{ref:nature-eco-160}} (CO2e), measured against a baseline. Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their Kyoto targets. By 2013, 57% came from destroying just two gases, HFC-23 or N2O. Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012, amid recession and over-allocation in Europe's trading scheme.
entries.text_plain: Between 2001 and 7 September 2012, the The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market issued 1 billion certified emission reductions, or CERs. Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases (CO2e), measured against a baseline. Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their Kyoto targets. By 2013, 57% came from destroying just two gases, HFC-23 or N2O. Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012, amid recession and over-allocation in Europe's trading scheme.

entries.title: Carbon revenue: what to do with the money

definition.text: The choices governments make about how to spend the money raised by a carbon tax or by selling emission permits.

facts.text: One standard proposal returns the money to the public per person; richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, and poorer people can come out ahead.
Other proposals fund renewable energy subsidies, research, public transport and car sharing.
Revenue could also subsidise negative emissions, which cost about $150–165 per ton of CO2 depending on the technology.
Per-person refunds would not cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses.

entries.text: A carbon tax or a permit auction raises money, and governments must decide how to spend it. One standard proposal returns it to the public per person. Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund renewable energy support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund renewable energy support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

entries.title: Why renewable energy support adds nothing under a binding cap
entries.article: Carbon price#Interactions with renewable energy policies

definition.text: The way a carbon tax or an emissions cap changes what other climate policies, such as renewable energy subsidies, can achieve.

facts.text: Under a carbon tax, subsidies for renewable energy add to the emission cuts.
Under a binding cap, renewable subsidies bring no further emission cuts while the cap applies.

entries.text: Under a carbon tax, public support for renewable energy adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap ({{ref:nature-pol-240}}) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.
entries.text_plain: Under a carbon tax, public support for renewable energy adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap (Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.

entries.title: Assigned amount units: Kyoto's national allowances

definition.text: A tradable Kyoto Protocol unit allowing a country to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

facts.text: Units were issued up to each Annex 1 country's Kyoto emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period.
Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs.
Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action.

entries.text: Under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, each Annex 1 country received assigned amount units up to its emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period. Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action: a top-up to cuts at home, not a replacement.

entries.title: Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project.

facts.text: Landfill gas capture is an example: methane has a 100-year global warming potential of 25 compared with carbon dioxide.
Burning one tonne of captured methane yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 ERUs.
ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

entries.title: EU ETS2: a carbon market for buildings and road transport

definition.text: A second EU emissions trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original ETS.

facts.text: It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them.
Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005, with revenue partly funding a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups.
Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2025 its start was delayed to 2028 under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability.

entries.title: The Market Stability Reserve: soaking up surplus permits
entries.article: European Union Emissions Trading System#Reform of the EU-ETS and introduction of the Market Stability Reserve (MSR)

definition.text: An EU ETS mechanism that changes how many permits are auctioned each year according to how many surplus permits are in circulation.

facts.text: It runs on predefined rules with no discretion for the Commission or member states.
Back-loading and the MSR law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2.
Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated; about 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated. About 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

entries.title: Water trading: markets for the right to use water

definition.text: Buying and selling water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers.

facts.text: A seller holds water rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more.
Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more economically productive uses; urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers.
First-in-time prior appropriation rights led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology.
Water is a common-pool resource that behaves like a private good once rights make its use rival and excludable.
Trades can harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller.
Water is not a standard commodity: supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin.
Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.
Chile's 1981 Water Code made water rights freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial.

entries.title: CORSIA: offsetting the growth of international flights
entries.article: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation

definition.text: The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, which makes airlines buy carbon credits to offset growth in emissions from international flights.

facts.text: The International Civil Aviation Organization adopted it in October 2016, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020.
It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory; least developed and small island states are not required to join.
Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions.
Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organisations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

entries.contested_note: Supporters call it a compromise step forward, while environmental groups argue it will not cut aviation emissions enough.

sources.title: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation

entries.title: Personal carbon trading: an allowance for every adult

definition.text: Proposed schemes that would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national carbon budget, to be surrendered when buying fuel or electricity.

facts.text: People who emit more than their allowance would buy credits from those who use less, who would profit.
Research finds it would be progressive, moving money from rich to poor, unlike a carbon tax before revenue is redistributed.
Critics point to complexity, high implementation costs and possible political unacceptability; a 2008 UK study found it ahead of its time.
Norfolk Island trialled the world's first personal carbon trading programme starting in 2011.

entries.contested_note: Proponents call it equitable and effective, while critics and a UK government study call it costly, complex and premature.

entries.title: Market design: engineering the rules of exchange

definition.text: The branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes.

facts.text: It is closely related to mechanism design and auction theory.
Applications pioneered by Alvin Roth include labour-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice.
Under the revenue equivalence theorem, expected revenue is the same in sealed first-price and second-price auctions with independent private values.
Roth and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design.

entries.title: Voluntary emission reductions: offsets bought by choice

definition.text: A carbon offset, also called a Verified Emission Reduction, traded in the voluntary market and usually certified outside the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: One VER equals 1 tonne of CO2 emissions.
Companies and individuals buy them to compensate voluntarily for their emissions.
Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

entries.text: Not every carbon offset is bought to meet a legal target. A Voluntary Emission Reduction, also called a Verified Emission Reduction or VER, is traded in the voluntary market. Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

entries.title: Windfall gains: income that drops from the sky

definition.text: A sudden, usually unexpected addition to income well above the norm, arising from luck or circumstance rather than planning.

facts.text: A windfall profit is the business version, caused for example by unexpected demand or government regulation.
Under the EU ETS, fossil generators priced freely allocated permits into electricity, reaping a massive windfall gain.
Some legislators favour a windfall profits tax, since taxing unforeseen profits should not hurt the company.

entries.title: Cap and dividend: sell the permits, pay the citizens

definition.text: A cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices.

facts.text: A cap is placed on greenhouse gases, often on upstream sources such as fossil fuel suppliers, and they must buy permits for their emissions.
Unlike cap and trade, no permits are given away free; the pollution rents are captured publicly rather than becoming private assets.
Households that emit least receive a bigger dividend than they pay in higher prices, rewarding those who conserve.
The idea was first proposed by Peter Barnes as "Skytrust" in his 2001 book Who Owns the Sky?.
A 2009 US bill would have auctioned 100 percent of permits and returned all proceeds as a monthly dividend, but it did not pass.

entries.contested_note: The policy was vigorously debated, called 'fatally incomplete' by one critic and hailed by Time magazine.

entries.title: Green certificates: trading proof of renewable power

definition.text: A tradable certificate proving that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, was generated from renewable sources.

facts.text: The certificates represent the environmental value of renewable energy and can be traded separately from the electricity itself.
Countries such as Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use them as a more market-like alternative to feed-in tariffs.
Buying one only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

entries.title: Pollution hot spots: when location matters

definition.text: The problem that a regional pollutant traded under a cap can pile up in some places, since the same amount does far more harm in some locations than others.

facts.text: CO2 has a similar effect wherever it is released, so location does not matter, unlike regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury.
Because carbon trading limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed.
Markets in location-based pollution licences, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point, are one answer to the problem.

entries.text: Carbon dioxide has a similar effect wherever it is released, so for trading its location does not matter. Regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury are different. The same amount does far more harm in some places than in others, so under a cap it can pile up in hot spots. Carbon trading has a related blind spot. Because it limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed. One answer is markets in location-based pollution licenses, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point ({{ref:nature-pol-260}}).

entries.title: Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution

definition.text: Markets in licences that give the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount, rather than the right to emit a set amount.

facts.text: Pollution at each location is modelled as a linear combination of emissions through a diffusion matrix H, with q=H⋅e.
A polluter that affects several monitoring points must hold a portfolio of licences covering all of them.
Montgomery showed both markets allocate licences efficiently, but pollution-licence markets apply more widely.

entries.text: An ordinary permit grants the right to emit a set amount. An ambient permit grants the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount. Pollution at each monitoring point is modeled as a weighted sum of all emissions, written q=H⋅e, where the diffusion matrix H records how each source's output spreads. A polluter that affects several points must hold a portfolio of licenses covering all of them. Montgomery showed that both kinds of market allocate licenses efficiently, but pollution-license markets apply more widely.

entries.title: Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost

definition.text: A market-based approach, run at watershed scale, in which sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly.

facts.text: It rests on the fact that different sources in a watershed face very different costs to control the same pollutant.
Most programmes trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programmes must meet the Clean Water Act.
Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

Sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly. Most programs trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen ({{ref:nature-eco-245}}). The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programs must meet the {{ref:nature-pol-155}}. Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

entries.title: White certificates: trading proof of saved energy

definition.text: Tradable certificates proving that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved, usually tied to an obligation on energy suppliers to save energy.

facts.text: Suppliers of electricity, gas and oil must deliver efficiency measures equal to a set percentage of their annual sales or pay a penalty.
As with emissions trading, tradability in theory meets the overall saving target at least cost.
Great Britain started a scheme in 2002, Italy in 2005, and France and Denmark a year later.

entries.title: Carbon retirement: taking permits off the market for good

definition.text: Permanently removing emission allowances or carbon credits from circulation so they can never be sold or used again.

facts.text: Retiring allowances shrinks supply under a cap, which raises their scarcity and price.
The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026.
In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate; a record 164 million were retired in 2023.
Citizen groups have bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions to cut the supply available to polluters.

entries.title: Transferable development rights: paying land to stay open

definition.text: A land-use tool that lets developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area and use them to build more densely in a receiving area.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that land carries a bundle of property rights, including the right to develop.
Sending areas are farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development; receiving areas are urban areas suited to higher density.
Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development.
TDR programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.

entries.text: Land carries a bundle of {{ref:nature-econ-621}}, including the right to develop it. Transferable development rights let that one right be sold on its own. Developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area: farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development. They use those rights to build more densely in a receiving area, an urban place suited to higher density. Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development. Such programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.

entries.title: Subsidies: paying people to do more of something

definition.text: A form of government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses to support them or encourage some activity.

facts.text: Subsidies take forms such as direct spending, tax incentives, cheap loans, price support and government-provided goods and services.
The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations, not only governments.
Governments may hand out direct payments in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity.
Spending on subsidies stays high in many countries, often several percentage points of GDP.
Some governments subsidise rail and bus transport, which cut congestion and pollution compared with cars.
Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences.

entries.text: Many governments spend several percentage points of their GDP on subsidies, year after year. A subsidy is government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses, to support them or to encourage some activity. The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations. Subsidies come in many shapes. Some are direct spending, such as the payments governments may hand out in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity. Others are {{ref:nature-pol-237}}, cheap loans, price support, or goods and services the government provides. Some do clear environmental good. Governments that subsidize rail and bus transport cut congestion and pollution compared with cars. But the tool cuts both ways. Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences, a theme that runs through this chapter.

Some are direct spending, such as the payments governments may hand out in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity. Others are Tax incentives: encouraging activity through the tax code, cheap loans, price support, or goods and services the government provides. Some do clear environmental good. Governments that subsidize rail and bus transport cut congestion and pollution compared with cars. But the tool cuts both ways. Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences, a theme that runs through this chapter.

entries.title: The precautionary principle: caution before proof

definition.text: An approach to new activities or technologies that might cause harm when scientific knowledge about them is still incomplete, favouring caution and review first.

facts.text: Policy makers often use it when a decision might cause harm and conclusive evidence is not yet available.
The English term is generally thought to come from the German Vorsorgeprinzip, adopted in the 1970s in response to forest decline and sea pollution.
It shifts the burden of proof: whoever proposes an activity must show it will not, or is very unlikely to, cause significant harm.
Its second core idea is that the response should be proportionate to the risk and to the cost and feasibility of acting.
One study found 14 different formulations of the principle in treaties and declarations.
EU environmental policy must be based on the precautionary principle along with prevention, fixing damage at source and polluter pays.
It is typically applied to climate change, new organisms such as GMOs, public health threats and long-term effects of new technologies.
Critics argue it is vague, self-cancelling, unscientific and an obstacle to progress.

entries.contested_note: Supporters see it as needed caution under uncertainty, while critics call it vague, incoherent and a barrier to innovation.

entries.title: Ecolabels: the environment on the package

definition.text: A labelling system on food and consumer products that tells shoppers about the product's environmental impact.

facts.text: Ecolabels are voluntary, whereas green stickers are required by law.
There are 456 ecolabels in 199 countries across 25 industry sectors, according to the Ecolabel Index.
Some labels measure pollution or energy use with scores or units, while others certify that a set of minimum practices was followed.
Through certification, a farm, forest, fishery or mine can show it meets a standard and sell its products as certified.
Some manufacturers have set up 'rubber stamp' labels to greenwash products, so trust in labels is an issue for consumers.
The German Blue Angel, from 1978, was the world's first ecolabel.
Labels apply market pressure on industries to cut their environmental impact by linking products to informed consumer wishes.

entries.title: Sustainability standards: voluntary rules for good practice

definition.text: Voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show they use good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices.

facts.text: More than 400 such standards exist around the world.
A standard is usually written by stakeholders and experts in a sector and lists practices, such as how a crop should be grown sustainably.
Certification checks that a business meets the standard, and traceability follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers.
The standards grew up where national and global laws were weak but consumers and campaign groups demanded action.
Some standards set a high bar and work with top performers, while others aim to remove the worst practices across most of an industry.
Standards also differ in whether checking is done by a first, second or third party and whether certified and uncertified material may be mixed.
Agriculture has the most widely adopted standards: 40% of global coffee production is certified, and about 15–20% of cocoa and tea production meets major standards.
Researchers continue to debate how effective these schemes are and how they are governed.

entries.title: Fair trade: a better deal for producers in poorer countries

definition.text: A trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards.

facts.text: It focuses on commodities exported from poorer to richer countries, notably handicrafts, coffee, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold.
The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s, and sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived.
Fairtrade labelling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and the guarantee of a minimum price is its most distinctive feature.
In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system.
Coffee is the most established fair trade commodity.
Direct trade, which skips certification overhead, is proposed as an alternative.

entries.title: Energy subsidies: who pays for cheap power

definition.text: A government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs.

facts.text: Energy subsidies can be direct cash payments or indirect support such as tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access.
The International Renewable Energy Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies in 2020, around 70% of them for fossil fuels.
Of that 2020 total, about 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear.
Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution.
Choosing to subsidize one energy source more than another can affect the environment.
Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring renewable energy to market and cut emissions worldwide.
Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the World Trade Organization is often seen as necessary.

entries.title: Fossil fuel subsidies: public money for coal, oil and gas

definition.text: Energy subsidies for coal, oil and gas: any government action that lowers the cost of producing fossil fuel energy, raises producers' prices or lowers consumers' prices.

facts.text: Under a narrow definition they totalled around $725 billion (0.6% of global GDP) to $900 billion in 2024; under a broader one, $6.7 trillion (5.8% of GDP).
Most of the money supports oil and natural gas.
They are mainly consumption subsidies, such as lower sales tax on home-heating gas, or production subsidies, such as tax breaks for oil exploration.
Letting fuel users pollute the air and warm the climate without paying is also counted as a subsidy under broad definitions.
They act as a negative carbon price and use government money that could be spent on other things.
Economists agree the rich get most of the absolute benefit, since the poorest people usually do not own cars.
Subsidies are estimated to cause hundreds of thousands of deaths from air pollution each year.
Removing them would cut air-pollution health risks and greatly reduce global carbon emissions.

entries.title: Sustainable procurement: buying for the whole life cycle

definition.text: Buying goods, services and works in a way that gives value for money over the whole life cycle while also benefiting society and staying within the environment's limits.

facts.text: Procurement has traditionally weighed only price and quality; sustainable procurement adds the third-party effects of buying decisions.
It favours renewable or recycled materials and less waste, and checks suppliers for pollution or harm to habitats.
Public spending averages 12% of GDP in OECD countries and up to 30% in developing countries, giving governments enormous purchasing power.
Purchases can exceed 50% of a company's expenses, and over 80% in retail, electronics and cars, so firms can also shift markets.
Sustainable options often cost about the same, and even pricier ones can save money through lower energy, water and waste costs over their life.

entries.title: Extended producer responsibility: makers pay for the waste

definition.text: A policy that makes manufacturers responsible for the environmental costs of their products across the whole life cycle, mainly the costs of dealing with them as waste.

facts.text: The concept was first formally put forward in Sweden by Thomas Lindhqvist in a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry.
It uses money incentives: producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products.
It rests on the idea that brand owners control product design and so are best placed to cut toxicity and waste.
It can take the form of reuse, buyback or recycling programs, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products.
Unlike product stewardship, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of recycling into the product price and relieves local governments.
In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%.
A drawback is the administrative burden from rules that differ between countries and waste streams.
The deposit-refund system is described as based on the principles of extended producer responsibility.

entries.title: Nudges: steering choices without forcing them

definition.text: The idea from behavioural science that changing how choices are presented (choice architecture) can steer people's behaviour without forcing them.

facts.text: Nudging differs from other ways of getting compliance, such as education, legislation or enforcement.
The 2008 book Nudge by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein made the idea popular.
A nudge alters the setting so that fast, automatic thinking favours the desired choice.
Nudges are small, cheap changes; techniques include defaults, social proof and making an option more noticeable.
More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default option.
In tourism, nudges led people to reuse towels, choose more sustainable hotels and offset their carbon voluntarily.
Governments use them through 'nudge units', such as the British Behavioural Insights Team set up in 2010.
A 2021 meta-analysis found nudging effective with moderate publication bias, but a later correction for that bias found no evidence of an effect.

entries.title: The Common Agricultural Policy: Europe's farm support

definition.text: The European Union's farm policy, which runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programmes.

facts.text: It was introduced in 1962 and has been changed to cut its share of the budget, from 73% in 1985 to 37% in 2017, and to add rural development.
The 'Agenda 2000' reforms split it into two pillars: production support and rural development.
Critics say it creates artificially high food prices, helped by import tariffs estimated at 18–28%.
Guaranteed prices led the EU to buy and store huge surpluses, nicknamed 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes'.
Because it has rewarded higher output, larger farms have gained far more from subsidies than smaller ones.
A 2024 study reported that 80% of its subsidies in 2013 supported emissions-intensive animal products.

entries.title: What a subsidy does to a market

definition.text: How a subsidy changes a market: it shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy.

facts.text: In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, creating deadweight loss.
Deadweight loss from a subsidy is the amount by which its cost exceeds its gains, and it grows with the subsidy's size.
A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them.
Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions.
In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

entries.text: A subsidy shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy ({{ref:nature-econ-360}}). Which curve moves matters. A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them. In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, the point where supply meets demand. The result is {{ref:nature-econ-345}}: the amount by which the subsidy's cost exceeds its gains, which grows with the subsidy's size. The effects cross borders. Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions. In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and to phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

entries.title: Perverse subsidies: support that harms twice over

definition.text: Subsidies whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment.

facts.text: A subsidy rarely starts out perverse but can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal.
They drain government budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health.
They cause environmental damage such as resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor.
They become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia, so they are hard to remove.
In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion and EU farmers $47 billion in agricultural subsidies.
Government subsidies in agriculture often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and overfishing.

entries.title: Tax incentives: encouraging activity through the tax code

definition.text: Part of a government's tax policy that encourages a particular economic activity by lowering the tax owed.

facts.text: For individuals they include deductions, exemptions and credits, such as the hybrid vehicle tax credit.
Tax incentives aimed at single companies are generally seen as inefficient, costly, distorting and regressive.
A 2020 study found some job gains from US state and local business incentives but no evidence of wider economic growth.
Badly designed incentives can harm a government's finances.

entries.title: Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power

definition.text: A policy that speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply.

facts.text: Feed-in tariffs usually guarantee grid access, offer long-term contracts and pay prices based on generating costs.
Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts.
Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power.
A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in tariffs the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity.
When funded by a surcharge on bills they raise power prices, adding 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017.
Renewables can also lower spot market prices through the merit order effect, which happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.
As of 2019 more than 50 countries had feed-in tariff policies.

entries.title: Pollution registers: the public's right to know

definition.text: A system that collects and publishes information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities.

facts.text: Several countries set them up after the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to know about toxic chemicals.
They aim to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions.
A protocol to the Aarhus Convention requires its parties to set up such registers; the 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them.
Data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

entries.title: Environmental certification: choosing to be checked

definition.text: A voluntary form of environmental regulation in which a company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service.

facts.text: Most certification services have a logo, commonly called an ecolabel, that certified products can carry.
It is seen as a form of corporate social responsibility, letting firms reduce environmental harm by following external, measured objectives.
Companies take it up to sell ethical products, improve their image, get on better with stakeholders and earn more profit.
It only works if there are consumers willing to buy the resulting green products.
Consumers may be willing to pay extra for ethically produced goods.
Firms may seek certification to avoid accusations of greenwashing by having their green claims checked independently.

entries.title: ISO 14000: international standards for environmental management

definition.text: A set of international standards for environmental management systems, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in 1996.

facts.text: The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws, and keep improving.
Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself.
ISO 14001 is the core standard; it sets out a framework for an environmental management system but no required level of environmental performance.
The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself.
As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries.
Firms adopting it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs and may gain a competitive advantage.
Its predecessor was BS 7750, the world's first environmental management system standard, published in 1992.

entries.title: Forest certification: a label for responsibly managed wood

definition.text: A voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard.

facts.text: An independent body writes the forest management standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it.
Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting.
Third-party forest certification was pioneered in the early 1990s by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests.
With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners offer forest certification worldwide.
The two largest international programs are the FSC and the PEFC, and PEFC covers about two-thirds of certified forest area.
About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program.
Some commentators, including Jared Diamond, say logging companies set up rival standards to confuse consumers.
Demand is driven by publishers' paper commitments, green public procurement, green building standards and laws against illegal logging.

entries.title: Direct or indirect, production or consumption: sorting subsidies

definition.text: Subsidies are sorted as direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow.

facts.text: Direct subsidies are cash outlays to a specific person or household, such as cash grants; indirect ones include tax breaks and low-interest loans.
Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs; consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay.
Consumption subsidies are most common in developing countries, for basics such as food, water, electricity and education.
Broad subsidies are hard to identify and include non-monetary support; environmental externalities are the most common type.

entries.title: Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries

definition.text: Government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting market failures and moving toward a low-carbon economy.

facts.text: Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable.
Subsidies for a targeted sector are its most common form; tools also include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green public procurement.
New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones because of path dependency, so governments nurture technological niches.
German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004.
Without government intervention the market is unlikely to move to a low-carbon economy on its own.

entries.title: The Inflation Reduction Act: America's biggest climate law

Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels after the act.

entries.title: Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ
