entries.title: Strong and weak precaution

definition.text: Two versions of the precautionary principle: the strong one requires regulation whenever harm is possible, the weak one only permits action without full proof.

facts.text: Strong precaution demands regulation even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high, a 'no-regrets' stance that ignores cost.

Weak formulations allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay.

definition.text: The common objection that weak versions of the precautionary principle are trivial and strong versions are incoherent.

facts.text: Cass Sunstein argued that the weak version only states a truism.

facts.text: Ecolabelling encourages new green products and improves firms' environmental management strategy.
In the cycle, consumers' expectations are met, firms gain value, and governments foster cleaner production and consumption.

entries.title: Can ecolabels become trade barriers?

definition.text: The concern that the spread of ecolabels creates obstacles to international trade other than tariffs.

facts.text: To qualify for a foreign ecolabel, exporters must adjust to each market's production standards, which can cost money, information and expertise.
Labelling programs often reflect the importing country's priorities and technologies and may not fit the exporting country's environment.
Since 1995 the World Trade Organization agreements have covered the possible effects of voluntary product standards and labels.

facts.text: The yellow US EnergyGuide label estimates an appliance's energy use, compares it with similar products and lists rough yearly running costs.
Canadian law requires the EnerGuide label on every new electrical appliance made in or imported into Canada.
These labels show energy used in operation, while energy input labelling shows the energy used to make the product.

entries.title: Three types of environmental label

definition.text: The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types by what they cover and how strictly they are checked.

facts.text: Type I (ISO 14024) is a voluntary multi-criteria label checked by an independent third party that looks at a product's life cycle impacts.
Type II (ISO 14021) is a claim a manufacturer or retailer makes about itself without third-party auditing.
Type III (ISO/TR 14025) is a declaration of measured life cycle data that does not rate the product but helps buyers compare.
'Type I-like' labels cover a single issue, such as a pass/fail energy limit for appliances.

entries.title: Does fair trade help the farmers?

definition.text: The debate over whether fair trade actually benefits poor producers, given studies that find both gains and little effect.

facts.text: A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero because of an oversupply of certification.
Little of the extra retail price may reach farmers: one estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee.
Because coffee demand is highly inelastic, economists argue higher fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers.
A study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found it meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries.

Groups often spend it on public goods that government fails to provide, such as environmental projects, schools and water projects.

entries.title: Energy subsidies: the case for and against
entries.article: Energy subsidy#Overview of all sources of energy

definition.text: The debate over whether governments should support energy prices or producers, weighing supply security and social aims against waste and environmental harm.

facts.text: Supporters say subsidies secure domestic supply, cut air pollution, help meet climate pledges, widen access to energy for the poor and protect jobs.
Critics say fossil fuel subsidies raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies.
In developing countries most benefits of fossil fuel subsidies go to the richest 20% of households.
The World Bank found subsidies to large energy companies unjustified but saw a case for helping the poorest households get modern energy.

entries.contested_note: Sources set out explicit arguments for and against energy subsidies, and reform is opposed by many who see it as governments taking something away.

facts.text: It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve resource efficiency and grow the market for greener products.
It relies heavily on life cycle costing, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.
Rules steer public bodies to buy items such as efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and renewable energy, which can drive green innovation.

entries.title: Making electronics makers pay for e-waste

definition.text: The use of producer responsibility rules to deal with e-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash.

facts.text: E-waste contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium, which are dangerous to health and the environment.
Making producers pay for recycling may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against planned obsolescence.
Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them.

entries.contested_note: Supporters say it drives greener design while critics argue it raises costs, slows innovation and is not clearly speeding greener design.

entries.title: Take-back programs: returning products to their makers

definition.text: Waste policies that require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and recycling.

facts.text: They were adopted where collection of hazardous products was lacking or too costly for local governments.
They aim to encourage designs for reuse and recycling, put waste costs into product prices and promote recycling innovation.
The earliest take-back schemes began in Europe, driven by scarce landfill space and hazardous parts.

Projects can include protecting water quality, sustainable land management and planting trees against erosion and floods.
It works through seven-year rural development programmes, of which there are 118 in the EU.

facts.text: Farmers who fail the strict environmental requirements of cross compliance face cuts in their subsidies.
The aim was to free more money for environmental quality and animal welfare programmes.
In England the Single Payment Scheme paid a flat rate of around £230 per hectare for keeping land fit for cultivation.

definition.text: The criticism that EU farm subsidies drove a large expansion of production using fertilisers and pesticides, with serious environmental harm.

In 2024 the European Court of Auditors warned the policy was not aligned with the EU's Green Deal climate goals.

entries.title: Voluntary agreements: environmental action by deal, not decree

definition.text: Policy tools in which firms or other actors agree, without being forced, to take environmental action, often in a deal with government.

facts.text: They differ from market-based instruments and from command-and-control rules, where authorities dictate the performance or technology required.
Since the 1980s many governments have turned from regulation toward 'new' instruments, notably market instruments and voluntary agreements.
In industrial countries they let companies gain recognition for going beyond minimum regulatory standards.
In developing countries such as in Latin America, they are more often used to fix widespread non-compliance with mandatory rules.
The EU first tackled car CO2 emissions through a voluntary agreement and later replaced it with mandatory limits for new cars.

entries.title: Picking winners: the risks of green industrial policy

definition.text: The concerns that governments may back the wrong firms or industries and that support invites rent-seeking and regulatory capture.

facts.text: Subsidies are especially prone to rent-seeking, because special interests lobby to keep them even when they are no longer needed.
Policy may end up driven by political rather than economic concerns.
Some failures are inevitable, and governments can reduce risk by testing policies in parts of the country first.

entries.title: Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems

definition.text: A commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems.

facts.text: It typically covers air and water pollution, waste, ecosystem management, biodiversity, natural resources and endangered species.
It aims to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people.
In 1863 the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate after harmful chemical releases caused health problems.
Government involvement is often justified by market failures such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons.
Its effectiveness is judged by how far it reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.
Pollution of air and water tends to spur action more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems.

entries.title: Market-based instruments: using prices to cut pollution

definition.text: Policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution.

facts.text: They tackle the market failure of externalities by charging for external costs through taxes, or by creating property rights and a market for using environmental services.
They are also called economic instruments, price-based instruments or new environmental policy instruments.
Examples include environmental taxes, charges and subsidies, emissions trading, deposit-refund systems, eco-labelling laws and property rights; the EU Emission Trading Scheme is one.
They differ from voluntary agreements and from command-and-control rules that dictate performance or technology, though they usually still need some regulation.
David Lloyd George's fuel tax of 1909-1910 may have been the first UK market-based environmental instrument.
Environmental advocates first opposed them, but after successful credit trading in the US lead phasedown they came to support trading, starting with the acid rain allowance market.

entries.title: Public choice: politics without romance

definition.text: The use of economic tools such as rational choice and game theory to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact.

facts.text: It stresses that political agents are self-interested and that collective decisions combine many individual choices.
It doubts that government simply maximizes social welfare, modelling officials who may also act for their own benefit, as in the budget-maximizing model of bureaucracy.
James Buchanan described it as 'politics without romance'.
Duncan Black, sometimes called its founding father, laid groundwork for median voter theory in papers from 1948 to 1958.
Its Nobel laureates include Kenneth Arrow, James Buchanan, George Stigler, Gary Becker, Amartya Sen, Vernon Smith and Elinor Ostrom.
Steven Pressman argues it fails to explain key political behaviour, such as why politicians vote against their constituents' interests.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue public choice cannot explain why people vote or many choices politicians make.

entries.title: Rules, prices and persuasion: the three families of policy tools

definition.text: The main families of tools governments use to carry out environmental policy: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion.

facts.text: Regulation sets rules, often backed by law, that ban, require or limit behaviour, such as pollution limits or bans on hazardous substances.
Critics call regulation a top-down 'command and control' approach because it leaves little choice in how goals are met.
Economic instruments use incentives: taxes, fees, subsidies, and markets for trading rights in pollutants or resources such as SO2, CO2, water and fishing quotas.
Economic instruments assume people act mainly from rational self-interest, a premise that decision-making studies cast doubt on.
Normative or 'hortatory' instruments rely on persuasion and information, such as awareness campaigns and voluntary agreements with businesses.

entries.text: Governments carry out environmental policy with three main families of tools: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion. Regulation sets rules, often backed by law, that ban, require or limit behavior. Pollution limits and bans on hazardous substances are examples. Critics call it a top-down 'command and control' approach, because it leaves little choice in how goals are met. Economic instruments work through incentives instead: taxes, fees, subsidies, and markets for trading rights in pollutants or resources such as SO2, CO2, water and fishing quotas. They assume people act mainly from rational self-interest, a premise that studies of decision-making cast doubt on. The third family, normative or 'hortatory' instruments, relies on persuasion and information. Awareness campaigns and voluntary agreements with businesses belong here.

entries.title: Which tool works best? The instrument debate

definition.text: The debate over whether regulation, taxes, tradable permits or other tools work best for a given environmental problem.

facts.text: Market instruments are often promoted as a more efficient, cost-effective alternative to regulation.
Many analysts argue regulation, incentives, market instruments, taxes and subsidies can achieve the same results.
Kemp and Pontoglio found no evidence that market-based approaches are better for eco-innovation, and some evidence that regulation spurs more radical innovation.
Hahn called the performance of economic instruments 'not very impressive', and Tietenberg concluded they are 'no panacea'.
Instruments differ in how costs and benefits are shared, so distributional, ethical and political aspects matter as well as efficiency.
Tradeable permits handed to resource users are generally preferred by affected industries, which helps explain their popularity since the rise of neoliberalism.

entries.contested_note: Analysts disagree whether market instruments are more efficient and innovation-friendly than regulation, or simply distribute costs differently.

Analysts still disagree whether market instruments are truly more efficient and innovation-friendly, or simply spread costs differently.

entries.title: Taxes or tradable permits: price certainty versus quantity certainty

definition.text: The trade-off between a pollution tax, which fixes the cost of cutting pollution, and a tradable permit system, which fixes the total amount allowed.

facts.text: A transferable permit system sets a cap on pollution and is likely to reach it more cheaply than other means, possibly undershooting it as technology improves.
A tax has no cap: the pollution cut depends on the rate chosen, which can be adjusted until the incentive works best.
Taxes have lower compliance costs than permits but are less reliable at hitting a target quantity.
Tax revenue can be used to cut other distorting taxes, a possible 'double dividend', though less pollution also means less revenue.
Permits can be auctioned or handed out free by grandfathering, and critics say formal emission rights amount to a licence to pollute.

entries.title: Induced innovation: expensive inputs spur new inventions

definition.text: The idea that when one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it.

facts.text: John Hicks first proposed it in 1932 in The Theory of Wages.
It is often illustrated by higher wages encouraging labour-saving inventions, and has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency.
Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption.
After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s.
In farming, when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that substitute more abundant inputs.
The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it does not include induced technological change.

entries.text: John Hicks proposed an idea in The Theory of Wages in 1932. When one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it. This is induced innovation. The classic illustration is higher wages encouraging labor-saving inventions. The idea has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency. Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption. After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s. Farming shows the same pattern: when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that use more abundant inputs instead. Not every model captures it. The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it leaves out induced technological change.

entries.title: Environmental policy analysis: three ways to study policy

definition.text: The academic study of how environmental policies are made, how well they work and how they could be improved.

facts.text: The analycentric or rational approach uses mainly quantitative methods to find the most cost-effective solution, favouring tools such as cost-benefit analysis, taxes and tradable permits.
The policy process approach stresses politics and power, tracing steps from agenda setting through implementation to evaluation.
The meta-policy approach studies how institutions, culture, economic systems and discourses shape policymaking.

entries.title: Environmental policy integration: the environment in every policy

definition.text: The idea that policies in every area should take account of their effects on the environment and on other areas.

facts.text: It has been discussed since the 1980s as policy mainstreaming, policy coordination and holistic governance.

entries.text: Transport, farming and trade policies all affect the environment. The idea has been discussed since the 1980s, under names such as policy mainstreaming, policy coordination and holistic governance.

entries.title: Implicit carbon prices: charging for carbon without saying so

definition.text: A cost placed on greenhouse gas emissions indirectly, by measures that change the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself.

facts.text: Examples are fuel taxes aimed at local pollution and removing fossil fuel subsidies.
Explicit carbon prices, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading, target emissions directly; implicit and explicit together make the effective carbon price.
Fuel taxes are positive implicit prices, while fossil fuel subsidies are negative ones because they make emitting cheaper.
Implicit prices are more common worldwide: almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing.
They spread more easily because they tackle local problems, need less administrative capacity and face less political opposition.
The EU's border carbon adjustment counts only explicit prices, while a proposed US version would include implicit ones.

entries.text: Almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing. A fuel tax is an implicit carbon price. It puts a cost on greenhouse gas emissions indirectly, through a measure that changes the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself. Explicit carbon prices, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading, target emissions directly. Implicit and explicit prices together make the effective carbon price. Implicit prices can also be negative. Fuel taxes raise the cost of emitting, but fossil fuel subsidies make emitting cheaper. Implicit prices spread more easily, because they tackle local problems, need less administrative capacity and face less political opposition. The difference matters at borders. The EU's border carbon adjustment counts only explicit prices, while a proposed US version would include implicit ones.

entries.title: Constitutional economics: agreeing on the rules of the game

definition.text: A research programme that applies public choice and political economy to the design of constitutional rules.

facts.text: Buchanan and Tullock argued that for government to benefit everyone, people must agree on the rules, not on every government action.
They split decisions into constitutional ones, which set lasting rules, and political ones made within those rules.

entries.title: Rational ignorance: why many voters stay uninformed

definition.text: The theory that a self-interested voter may sensibly choose not to vote or get informed, because one vote almost never decides an election.

facts.text: Anthony Downs argued in An Economic Theory of Democracy that for many citizens rational behaviour means investing nothing in political information.
Even in a close election the chance that one vote decides the result is effectively zero, so expected gains from voting are near zero.

entries.title: Markets or mandates: flexible tools versus fixed rules
entries.article: Market-based environmental policy instruments#Market-based vs command and control

definition.text: The comparison between flexible market-based tools and prescriptive rules such as emission standards and equipment requirements.

facts.text: Market instruments do not dictate technology or equal cuts for every firm, giving firms more flexibility.
Command and control is criticised for blocking innovation, though empirical studies show external price changes can induce it.
Command and control may suit cases where regulators lack information, where trading markets are too thin, or where emissions have purely local impacts.
Command-and-control rules often set the same emission limit for every firm, even though some can cut pollution cheaply and others only at high cost.

entries.contested_note: Critics say command and control stifles innovation, while empirical studies and some analysts see roles where it works better than markets.

entries.title: Policy mix: combining tools that do not clash

definition.text: A combination of several policy instruments used together; in macroeconomics, the combination of a country's monetary and fiscal policy.

facts.text: Environmental problems have many aspects, so several instruments may be needed together.
Measures should be designed not to undermine each other, since overlapping policies add unnecessary administrative costs.
In the macroeconomic sense, monetary policy is set by the central bank and fiscal policy by the government.

entries.title: Gossen's second law: getting the most from a budget

definition.text: The principle that a person gets the most from a budget by spending so that the extra satisfaction per unit of money is equal across all goods.

facts.text: It is named after Hermann Heinrich Gossen (1810–1858).
If the last unit of money spent on one good bought less extra satisfaction than it could have on another, the person would do better to switch.
Formally it follows from maximizing utility under a budget constraint with Lagrange multipliers.

entries.title: Lobbying: influencing the people who make the rules

definition.text: Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges.

facts.text: Its main form is meeting lawmakers directly, armed with research, data and draft proposals.
Lobbyists can be individuals, corporations, nonprofits, interest groups and political action committees.
Inside lobbying deals with decision-makers directly; outside lobbying pressures them by mobilising public opinion.
Research documents three effects: trading money for access, persuading officials with information, and mobilising citizens or coalitions.
Lobbying can pull politicians away from the median voter, especially when special-interest money is high and public attention low.
It can encourage lax enforcement of laws and is seen as one cause of a democratic deficit.
Many governments require lobbyists to register and disclose spending, clients and issues.
A 2011 study found that firms spending most on lobbying relative to assets earned 'blistering' returns.

entries.contested_note: The ethics of lobbying are disputed: it is defended as legitimate advocacy and attacked as corrupting the law for private interests.

Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges. Its main form is meeting lawmakers directly, armed with research, data and draft proposals. Lobbyists can be individuals, corporations, nonprofits, interest groups and political action committees. Inside lobbying deals with decision-makers directly; outside lobbying pressures them by mobilizing public opinion. Research documents three effects: trading money for access, persuading officials with information, and mobilizing citizens or coalitions. Lobbying can pull politicians away from the median voter, especially when special-interest money is high and public attention low. It can also encourage lax enforcement of laws. Many governments require lobbyists to register and disclose spending, clients and issues. Its ethics remain disputed: defenders call it legitimate advocacy, critics say it corrupts the law for private interests.

entries.title: Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth

definition.text: Rent-seeking is increasing one's wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth.

facts.text: It wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk.
Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain, adding no value.
Unlike profit-seeking, which creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade, rent-seeking redistributes existing wealth.
Here 'rent' means economic rent: income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use.
Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, quotas or rules that hobble competitors.
Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows economic growth.
Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organised interest groups lose vitality and decline.
Critics say it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

entries.title: Path dependence: why history matters

definition.text: Path dependence is when past events or decisions constrain later ones, so that 'history matters' for where a system ends up.

facts.text: Economists developed it to explain how technologies are adopted and industries evolve.
A path-dependent process may settle into one of several equilibria depending on its starting point and chance events, unlike simple neoclassical models with one outcome.
Paul David argued in 1985 that a first-to-market standard such as the QWERTY keyboard can become entrenched even if inferior.
More than half the world's railways use the 143.5 cm standard gauge, inherited from early coal tramways.
Drivers include lock-in, positive feedback, increasing returns and self-reinforcement.
Commercial fisheries' harvest rates have been found to be path dependent, because institutions adapt slowly while ecosystems change fast.
Liebowitz and Margolis argue that inefficient lock-in is rare and that no real-world private cases exist.

entries.contested_note: Economists still argue whether cases like QWERTY show real inefficient lock-in.

entries.title: Regulatory capture: when the watchdog serves the watched

definition.text: Regulatory capture is when a regulator or policymaker is co-opted to serve the interests of a small group, such as an industry, instead of the public.

facts.text: A special interest is then put ahead of the general public, causing a net loss for society.
Groups with high stakes focus resources on regulation, while the dispersed public, each with little at stake, does not.
George Stigler, a Nobel laureate economist, was a major developer of the theory.
A captured regulator can be worse than no regulation because it wields government authority; transparency may reduce the damage.
Smaller government units are easier for concentrated industries to capture, as with timber states blocking national policy.
The US Minerals Management Service was widely cited as captured after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.
Water management in Australia's Murray–Darling Basin has been analysed as a case of rent-seeking and regulatory capture.

entries.title: The median voter theorem: why the middle wins

definition.text: The median voter theorem says that when voters and candidates line up along one left-right spectrum, majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle (median) voter prefers.

facts.text: Voters are assumed to rank candidates by closeness; the candidate nearest the median voter then beats every rival by a majority.
Duncan Black first derived it in 1948, and Kenneth Arrow independently.
With two candidates a simple majority vote satisfies it; with more, any Condorcet method does.
In more than one dimension there may be no majority winner, as the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem shows.
It is popular in political economy because it yields testable links between voter characteristics and policy outcomes.
Levitt (1996) found senators from the same state but different parties voted only slightly more alike than random pairs, contradicting the theorem.

entries.contested_note: Empirical studies from the US Senate and India find voting outcomes that contradict the theorem's predictions.

entries.title: The fossil fuels lobby: big money against climate rules

definition.text: The fossil fuels lobby is the paid representatives of oil, gas and coal companies and related industries such as chemicals, plastics and aviation.

facts.text: Their wealth and economic importance give them the means to seek outsized influence on government policy.
The lobby promotes climate change denial and obstructs environmental and climate policy.
Lobbyists work to keep fossil fuel subsidies.
Fossil fuel interests spent $2 billion on climate-change lobbying in the US from 2000 to 2016, many times what citizens and environmentalists spent.
The five biggest oil and gas companies spent at least 251 million euros lobbying the EU on climate policy since 2010.
According to the UNFCCC, 636 fossil fuel lobbyists attended COP27.
In Canada, fossil fuel lobbyists contacted officials five times more than environmental groups between 2011 and 2018.
The lobby has used crises such as COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine to try to roll back regulations.

entries.title: The logic of collective action: why small groups win

definition.text: Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action argues that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests, because large groups suffer worse free-riding.

facts.text: Members of any group providing a public good are tempted to free ride on others' efforts.
Without selective incentives, collective action is unlikely even among large groups with shared interests.
Large groups face higher organising costs and each member gains less, so they are less able to act than small groups.
A minority bound by concentrated incentives can therefore dominate the majority.
Susanne Lohmann notes the US sugar import quota created 2,261 jobs while reducing overall welfare, and blames information asymmetry rather than free riding.
Gunnar Trumbull counters that diffuse interests such as consumers can win through a 'legitimacy premium' and coalitions.

entries.contested_note: Lohmann, Trumbull, Marwell and Oliver, and Wilson each dispute parts of Olson's argument.

entries.title: The Tullock paradox: why political favors come so cheap

definition.text: The Tullock paradox is the puzzle that rent-seekers can buy political favours for far less than the favours are worth to them.

facts.text: A rent-seeker hoping to gain a billion dollars may need to spend merely ten million, about 1% of the gain.
Proposed explanations include voters punishing lavish politicians, competition among politicians to offer favours, and lack of trust in illicit deals.

entries.title: Critical junctures: moments that set a lasting course

definition.text: A critical juncture is a moment when contingent choices set an institution on a path of development that is hard to reverse.

facts.text: Ruth and David Collier made the framework prominent in political science.
It has been used to explain the rise and persistence of welfare states and differences in economic development between countries.
Kathleen Thelen warns such frameworks are too deterministic, since institutions keep evolving.

entries.title: Money or mindset: two types of regulatory capture

definition.text: Regulatory capture comes in two basic types: materialist (financial) capture driven by the regulator's self-interest, and non-materialist (cognitive) capture driven by biased views.

facts.text: Materialist capture can result from bribery, revolving doors, political donations or a regulator's wish to keep its funding.
Specialised technical industries risk cultural capture because regulators must hire experts who mostly come from the industry.
The top 5 financial companies account for around 80% of revolving-door movements, showing that big firms do most capturing.

entries.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: strange allies behind a rule

definition.text: Bootleggers and Baptists is Bruce Yandle's idea that regulations win support both from groups that want their stated purpose and from groups that profit from undermining it.

facts.text: The name comes from Sunday alcohol bans backed by Baptist activists and by bootleggers, who sold more when legal sales were restricted.
The 'Baptists' take the moral high ground and give politicians cover, while the 'bootleggers' lobby quietly behind closed doors.
It predicts that coalitions of opposing interests agreeing on one rule succeed more often than one-sided groups.
Such coalitions tend to produce suboptimal laws; a surtax on Sunday sales, for instance, could cut drinking as much as a ban.
Yandle and Buck applied it to the Kyoto Protocol: environmental groups gave moral support while corporations and nations sought advantage over rivals.
Smith and Yandle later distinguished covert, noncooperative, cooperative and coordinated patterns of interaction.
It has not been systematically validated empirically and is a useful catch-phrase rather than an accepted principle.

entries.title: The Hotelling–Downs model: parties drifting to the middle

definition.text: The Hotelling–Downs model predicts that politicians who care only about winning will move to the median voter's position.

facts.text: It adapts Hotelling's 1929 principle of minimum differentiation in business competition, applied to politics by Anthony Downs in 1957.
In a two-party system it predicts both parties drift toward the median voter.
Primaries and most voting rules in national use break the conditions, so candidates may not converge.

entries.title: International trade: goods, money and pollution across borders

definition.text: The exchange of capital, goods and services across national borders to meet a need or demand.

facts.text: A product sold from one country to another is an export for the seller's country and an import for the buyer's.
It is usually more costly than domestic trade because of tariffs and non-tariff barriers such as border delays, language and legal differences.
Because capital and labour move less easily between countries, a country can instead import goods that embody those inputs.
In 2025 world trade totalled 80,733 billion US dollars, of which merchandise made up 52,865 billion.
Mineral fuels and oils were the top traded commodity by export value in 2022.
Organisations such as the World Trade Organization work to ease and expand trade between countries.
A 2020 study of 189 countries found most are more exposed to over-exploited water, energy and land resources through trade, mainly from distant sources.

entries.title: The World Trade Organization: referee of world trade

definition.text: The intergovernmental organization, formed in 1995, that regulates and eases trade between countries.

facts.text: Its forerunner, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), was set up by 23 countries in 1947; its early negotiating rounds concentrated on cutting tariffs.
The Marrakesh Agreement, signed on 15 April 1994 at the end of the Uruguay Round, officially established the WTO.
It has 166 members and 23 observer governments.
It provides a forum for negotiations and settling disputes, reviews national trade policies and helps poorer countries adjust to its rules.
It sets the rules of trade policy rather than outcomes, and members agree to settle disputes through it rather than act alone.
Studies find it boosted trade; without it, the average country would face tariffs on its exports 32 percentage points higher.
The Doha Round, launched in 2001 to make globalization help the world's poor, stalled over farm subsidies, industrial tariffs and non-tariff barriers.
Its director-general has called for reform of subsidy and competition rules, decision-making and global public goods such as climate protection.

entries.title: The global waste trade: shipping rubbish across borders

definition.text: The international trade in waste, shipped between countries for treatment, disposal or recycling.

facts.text: Toxic or hazardous wastes are often imported by developing countries from developed ones.
Richer, more urbanised countries produce more solid waste, and waste mostly flows from the Global North to be disposed of in the Global South.
Scholars link its sharp growth to the free-market policies of the 1980s, which pushed developing countries to import waste as a route to economic expansion.
Supporters argue that importing waste can stimulate the economies of countries with little else to offer the global economy.
Critics note that most hazardous waste is produced in the United States and Europe, yet the health harms fall on poorer countries that did not produce it.
Poorer countries often lack safe recycling facilities, so people handle toxic waste by hand and poor disposal poisons the surroundings, causing illness and death.
Areas around dump sites carry very high levels of heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants that kill birds, fish and other wildlife.
It is hard to regulate: volumes are huge, laws are hard to enforce, and vague definitions let hazardous waste be exported as commodities or raw materials.

Dump sites carry heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants that kill birds, fish and other wildlife. The trade is hard to regulate, since vague definitions let hazardous waste be exported as commodities or raw materials.

entries.title: Local or imported: which is greener?
entries.article: International trade#International trade vs local production

definition.text: The debate over whether goods, especially food, should be produced locally or imported, weighing environmental, economic and security effects.

facts.text: Studies find food miles are a relatively minor source of carbon emissions, though localising food may allow recycling of energy, water and nutrients.
Different harvest seasons can make importing from far away greener than local storage or greenhouse growing.
A 2020 study found local crops within 100 km could not meet demand for most food crops for 72-89% of the world's population.
Studies disagree on jobs: one found trade can raise local employment, another that import exposure cut local employment and labour income.
Regional differences can make some places better suited to a product, favouring trade; local production may need policies such as eco-tariffs to compete.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree on the environmental and employment trade-offs between local and distant production.

entries.title: Non-tariff barriers: trade limits beyond taxes

definition.text: Restrictions on imports or exports other than tariffs, such as quotas, licences, subsidies, customs delays and technical standards.

facts.text: They are controversial because they may comply with trade rules yet serve protectionist purposes.
A 2019 UNCTAD report found trade costs from non-tariff measures were more than double those of traditional tariffs.
As tariffs fell through GATT and WTO negotiation rounds, protectionism turned to new measures such as technical barriers to trade.
They are grouped as protectionist, assistance (such as domestic subsidies) or non-protectionist, the last aimed at health, safety and the environment.
Most can be called protectionist unless they address market problems such as externalities or information asymmetries, as safety standards and labels do.
Rising consumer demand for safe and environmentally friendly products has made technical barriers to trade more popular.

entries.title: Green exceptions in trade rules
entries.article: World Trade Organization#Principles of the trading system

definition.text: Provisions in WTO agreements that let countries restrict trade to protect the environment and health, as long as the measures are not disguised protectionism.

facts.text: In specific circumstances governments may restrict trade: WTO agreements allow measures to protect the environment as well as public, animal and plant health.
Members must not use environmental protection measures as a way of disguising protectionist policies.
The WTO's Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures governs quarantine rules for pests and diseases.
In 2006 the WTO ruled that the European Union broke trade law between 1999 and 2003 with its moratorium on approving imports of genetically modified organisms.
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety states that trade and environment agreements should be mutually supportive.
In 2024 US Democrats argued that a carbon border adjustment is a fee permissible under WTO rules, not a carbon tax.

entries.title: Has the WTO delivered? The critics' case

definition.text: Arguments that WTO-led trade liberalisation has not delivered the promised growth, poverty reduction and fair sharing of gains.

facts.text: Ha-Joon Chang notes that developing countries grew faster in 1960–1980 than in 1980–2000, even though their trade policies are now far more liberal.
Critics say the benefits of WTO-backed free trade are not shared equally, pointing to widening gaps between rich and poor.
Liberalising too early is feared to trap developing economies in the primary sector, which often needs little skilled labour.
Vietnam cut poverty and grew fast while liberalising slowly with safeguards, whereas El Salvador's growth stayed weak after it removed import barriers and cut tariffs.

entries.contested_note: Studies credit the WTO with boosting trade, while critics dispute that liberalisation reliably brings growth and less poverty.

entries.title: Equal terms for all: the WTO's non-discrimination rule
entries.article: World Trade Organization#Principles of the trading system

definition.text: The WTO's non-discrimination rule: a member must offer all other members equal terms and treat imports no worse than its own goods.

facts.text: Most-favoured-nation treatment means the best terms a member gives any WTO member for a product must be given to all members.
Exceptions include free trade agreements and preferential treatment for developing countries.
National treatment means imports must be treated no less favourably than domestic goods once inside the market; it targets non-tariff barriers such as discriminatory technical standards.
The WTO's other key principles are reciprocity, binding and enforceable commitments, transparency and safety valves.

entries.title: The pollution haven hypothesis: do dirty industries flee strict rules?

definition.text: The idea that firms investing abroad move to countries with cheap resources and weak environmental rules, making those countries havens for pollution.

facts.text: Countries with stricter environmental rules become more expensive for firms because of compliance costs.
Regulations raise input costs for pollution-intensive goods and reduce a place's comparative advantage, pushing firms to lower-standard countries.
Evidence supports the weaker claims that pollution control costs affect trade and investment, but their importance relative to other factors is still controversial.
After the US tightened lead air standards in 2009, exports of used lead-acid batteries to Mexico rose four-fold, followed by more low-birth-weight babies near Mexican recycling plants.
It may partly explain the environmental Kuznets curve, as polluting industry shifts from richer to poorer economies.
It has three strengths: pollution costs matter at the margin; they measurably shift trade and investment; or countries deliberately set standards too low to attract investment.
The first two versions have empirical support, but how much the effect matters next to other trade and investment factors is disputed.
Economists model economic activity as falling with regulatory stringency, because regulation raises input costs and erodes comparative advantage in pollution-intensive goods.

entries.title: When green standards keep out foreign goods

definition.text: Product standards on labelling, testing and composition that protect health and the environment but can also keep out foreign goods.

facts.text: Standards enacted for health and safety can be used for protectionist and political ends.
Tariffs raise marginal costs and grow with volume, while testing or labelling rules impose fixed costs.
Fixed compliance costs can push small exporters out while leaving large multinationals untouched, shifting profits toward them.
This logic explains why large chemical producers supported the EU's REACH regulation.
Non-protectionist barriers include import bans based on objectionable harvesting or fishing methods.

entries.title: The Bamako Convention: Africa bans imported hazardous waste

definition.text: A 1991 treaty in which African nations, unhappy with the Basel Convention, banned imports of hazardous waste.

facts.text: Unlike the Basel Convention, it bans imports of all hazardous waste generated outside the Organization of African Unity and treats imports from non-parties as illegal.
Limited resources and weak enforcement meant members could not stop toxic dumping, so its application was very limited.
Similarly, the Lomé IV Convention banned exports of hazardous wastes from the European Community to African, Caribbean and Pacific states.

entries.title: The economic case for exporting waste

definition.text: The argument that sending hazardous waste to low-wage, less polluted countries makes economic sense, famously made in a 1991 memo by Lawrence Summers.

facts.text: Summers, then World Bank chief economist, wrote that the economic logic of dumping toxic waste in the lowest-wage country was 'impeccable'.
The memo called countries in Africa 'vastly under polluted' and asked whether the World Bank should encourage dirty industries to move to the least developed countries.
A Cato Institute article argued that people in developing countries would rationally accept more exposure to pollutants in exchange for higher productivity and income.
The case rests mainly on the view that developing countries need to further their economic development.

entries.title: The e-waste trade: rich countries' old electronics

definition.text: The shipment of discarded electrical and electronic devices, mostly from rich countries, to developing countries for processing and recycling.

facts.text: An estimated 50 million tons of e-waste are produced each year, mostly in the United States and Europe, and most is shipped to Asia and Africa.
Its growth comes from fast technological change, falling prices and planned obsolescence.
Heavy metals and toxins leak into waterways and groundwater, exposing dump workers, children searching for items to sell and nearby residents.
Guiyu, China, possibly the world's largest e-waste dump, has workers dismantling over 1.5 million pounds of junked electronics a year.

definition.text: The international trade in waste plastics, identified as the main cause of marine litter.

facts.text: Countries importing waste plastics often lack the capacity to process all of it.
The United Nations therefore restricts trade in plastic waste unless it meets certain criteria.
In 2018 Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte threatened war unless Canada took back 64 tonnes of garbage, shipped by a plastic-recycling firm and mislabelled as recyclable.

Old ships were built under weaker environmental rules and contain asbestos, lead oxide, mercury, arsenic and tributyltin.
Workers traditionally lack proper equipment or protective gear when handling these substances.

entries.title: Toxic colonialism: poorer countries as dumping grounds

definition.text: The use of poorer countries as cheap places to export or dump the hazardous waste of developed countries.

facts.text: It is the core critique of the global waste trade.

T.V. Reed links it to colonial views of indigenous land as empty 'waste', which make Global South land seem expendable for Western wastes.
Laura Pratt argues international agreements have not stopped it, because waste moves under false permits, bribes, improper labels or the pretext of recycling.

entries.title: Import quotas: capping what crosses the border

definition.text: A limit, by value or quantity, on how much of a good may be imported or exported over a period.

facts.text: Quotas usually raise costs, narrow consumers' choice and raise import prices for companies.
'Voluntary' export restraints are limits an exporter accepts under threat of sanctions.
Embargoes are the extreme case: an outright ban on trade in certain goods.

entries.title: Paying landowners for the services their land provides

definition.text: Payments offered to farmers or landowners in return for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.

facts.text: One definition calls PES a transparent system for the additional provision of environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers.
The 'big three' services drawing most money are climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation.
The provider usually holds property rights over the land, and receives compensation from those who benefit from its services.
Beneficiaries should pay less than their welfare gain, and providers should accept more than their cost of supplying the service.
Most PES programmes are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, rather than direct buyer-seller contracts.
PES is promoted as a rural development tool, though programmes are usually not designed mainly to reduce poverty.
National set-aside style PES programmes exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland as well as the US and China.

entries.text: Slowing climate change, watershed services and biodiversity conservation draw most of the money. They are the 'big three' of payment for ecosystem services, or PES. The idea is simple: farmers or landowners are paid to manage their land so that it keeps providing an ecosystem service. One definition calls PES a transparent system for securing additional environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers. The provider usually holds the property rights over the land and is compensated by those who benefit from its services. For a deal to make sense to both sides, beneficiaries should pay less than the service is worth to them. Providers, in turn, should accept more than it costs them to supply it. In practice, few deals are direct contracts between a buyer and a seller. Most programs are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, groups that sit outside government. PES is often promoted as a tool for rural development, though most programs are not designed mainly to reduce poverty. National programs that pay farmers to set land aside exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland, as well as the US and China.

entries.title: Additionality: would it have happened anyway?

definition.text: Whether an intervention, such as a payment or credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a baseline.

facts.text: A baseline is a prediction of what the actors would do without the policy, holding everything else constant.
It can be checked after the fact, as in programme evaluation, or beforehand, as an eligibility screen for issuing environmental credits.
Additionality is the impact of the intervention minus the impact of a reference case, net of deadweight, leakage, displacement and substitution.
A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead anyway, for example because it is profitable without carbon credits; that scenario is called business as usual.
Biodiversity offsets must show additionality to compensate for losses, and large offset markets have shown serious shortcomings on it.
The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market cited additionality concerns in excluding several renewable energy crediting methods.
Problems with additionality and double counting can undermine the credibility of carbon offsets.
A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway.

entries.text: Paying someone to do what they were going to do anyway buys nothing. Additionality is the test for that trap. It asks whether an intervention, such as a payment or a credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened otherwise. The answer depends on a baseline, a prediction of what people would do without the policy, with everything else held constant. Strictly, additionality is the intervention's impact minus the impact of that reference case. It must also be counted net of side effects such as deadweight, paying for what would happen anyway, and leakage, harm pushed somewhere else. Displacement and substitution can shrink the gain in similar ways. A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway. That scenario is called business as usual. Additionality can be checked after the fact, as in program evaluation, or beforehand, as a screen for which projects may issue environmental credits. The stakes are high. Large markets for {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} have shown serious shortcomings on it. Problems with additionality and double counting can also undermine trust in the offsets described in {{ref:nature-mkt-081}}. One industry watchdog, the {{ref:nature-hist-033}}, cited additionality concerns when it excluded several renewable energy crediting methods. Every payment scheme in this chapter rises or falls on this question.

entries.title: Watershed management: sharing the water a landscape gathers

definition.text: The planning and running of programmes that sustain a watershed's functions and share its resources sustainably among its plant, animal and human communities.

facts.text: It covers water supply, water quality, drainage, stormwater runoff and water rights.
On farms it uses buffer strips, grassed waterways, restored wetlands and practices such as conservation tillage and crop rotation.
In towns, retention ponds, filters and wetlands let stormwater soak in so soil and plants filter it before it reaches streams.
Donors backed by the World Bank argue freshwater should be governed as an economic good through pricing, while NGOs see it as a social good.
Groups sharing a watershed often have unequal, divergent interests, so one group's actions can harm others downstream.
Network governance, in which stakeholders form voluntary partnerships, has been adopted by states sharing the Rhine, Nile and Lake Chad basins.

entries.text: One group's actions upstream can harm everyone downstream, and that is why watersheds need managing. A watershed is the land that drains into one river, lake or stream. Watershed management plans and runs programs that keep a watershed working and share its resources sustainably among its plants, animals and people. It covers water supply, water quality, drainage, runoff from storms and the legal rights to use water. On farms the tools include buffer strips, grassed waterways, restored wetlands, plowing less and rotating crops. States sharing the Rhine, Nile and Lake Chad basins have tried network governance, in which stakeholders form voluntary partnerships.

entries.title: The Conservation Reserve Program: paying US farmers not to plow

definition.text: A US Department of Agriculture programme that pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips.

facts.text: Its aims are to reduce erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife.
It grew out of the 1950s Soil Bank and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill with 10 to 15 year contracts.
Payments are rental payments, cost-share of up to 50% of establishing cover, and extra incentives.
Money limits enrolment, so only the most qualified land receives payments.
By December 1, 2015, it had prevented more than 9 billion tons of soil from eroding.
In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving fields.
Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

entries.title: Three ways of seeing payments for nature

definition.text: The three main ways of viewing PES: environmental economics, ecological economics, and the rejection of ecosystem services altogether.

facts.text: Environmental economics sees PES as a voluntary, conditional deal between a service buyer and seller, rooted in the Coase theorem.
In reality transaction costs are almost always present, future payment promises are not time consistent, and financing often runs short.
Ecological economics treats natural and manufactured capital as complements, and judges PES by the weight of the incentive, how direct the transfer is, and how far the service is commodified.
Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard.
Critics argue nature should be valued for its own sake and that market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people.
Pragmatists accept the problems of valuing nature but argue that in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'.

entries.contested_note: Environmental and ecological economists disagree on how to frame PES, and some reject valuing ecosystem services at all.
entries.text: Is paying a farmer to keep a forest a sensible trade, an imperfect tool, or a moral mistake? Thinkers give three broad answers, and they still disagree. Environmental economics sees a payment for ecosystem services as a voluntary, conditional deal between a buyer and a seller of a service, rooted in the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. Reality is messier than the theory. Transaction costs, the costs of making and policing a deal, are almost always present. Promises of future payments are not time consistent, meaning a payer may later prefer to break them. Financing often runs short. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} treats natural and manufactured capital as complements: one cannot simply stand in for the other. It judges a scheme by the weight of its incentive, how directly the money reaches providers, and how far the service is turned into a commodity. Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard. The third view rejects the idea of ecosystem services altogether. These critics argue that nature should be valued for its own sake, and that a market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people. Pragmatists accept the problems of putting a value on nature. Still, they argue, in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'. The split between the first two schools is traced in {{ref:nature-found-039}}.

entries.title: Reverse auctions: letting sellers bid the price down

definition.text: An auction with one buyer and many sellers, in which sellers compete by underbidding each other.

facts.text: In an ordinary, or forward, auction buyers bid prices up; in a reverse auction prices typically fall.
Government procurement through public tenders is a common example.
Reverse auctions can reveal sellers' private opportunity costs, which helps design incentive programmes for public goods, common-pool resources and ecosystem services.
In a scoring auction, the buyer announces in advance how price and other attributes of each offer will be scored.
A supplier should first work out the lowest price it will accept, which requires knowing its true marginal cost.

entries.text: In an ordinary, or forward, auction, buyers bid prices up. A reverse auction flips the roles. One buyer faces many sellers, and the sellers compete by underbidding each other, so prices typically fall. Government procurement through public tenders is a common example. For conservation the format has a special use. A landowner knows the {{ref:nature-econ-095}} of setting land aside, while the program paying for it does not. Bids in a reverse auction reveal those private costs, which helps design incentive programs for public goods, shared resources and ecosystem services. Each seller should first work out the lowest price it will accept, which requires knowing its true marginal cost, the cost of supplying one more unit. In a scoring auction, the buyer announces in advance how it will score the price and other features of each offer.

entries.title: Grain for Green: China trades fields for forest

definition.text: A Chinese programme launched in 1999 that pays farmers to convert erosion-prone farmland back to vegetation to curb flooding and soil erosion.

facts.text: It is an example of payment for ecosystem services, offering farmers grain for not farming forested slopes.
It cost $43 billion by one account, with some sources citing $95 billion for the whole programme.
It has involved 124 million people in 1,897 counties in 25 provinces.
By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation.
It has generally been economically positive and has reduced erosion and flooding.
Many plantings were cheap monocultures that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.

entries.text: Some 124 million people in 1,897 counties across 25 provinces have taken part in Grain for Green. China launched the program in 1999 to pay farmers for turning erosion-prone farmland back into vegetation, curbing flooding and soil erosion. It is a payment for ecosystem services in a very literal form: farmers receive grain for not farming forested slopes. By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation. The bill is large and uncertain. One account puts the cost at $43 billion, while some sources cite $95 billion for the whole program. On the whole it has paid off economically and reduced erosion and flooding. Its weak spot is wildlife. Many plantings were cheap single-species stands that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.

entries.title: Costa Rica's pioneering national payment scheme

definition.text: Costa Rica's Pagos por servicios ambientales, set up in 1997 as the first PES programme run on a national scale.

facts.text: It pays for four services: greenhouse gas mitigation, water services, biodiversity protection and scenic beauty.
It was funded at first partly by a fuel tax, with a water tariff added in 2006.
By the end of 2005 its contracts covered 10% of the country, and it is estimated to have prevented 11 million tons of carbon emissions from 1999 to 2005.
Its flat-rate payment leaves many high-value areas unenrolled because their opportunity costs are higher than the payment.

entries.title: Uganda's forest payment experiment
entries.article: Payment for ecosystem services#Hoima and Kibaale, Uganda

definition.text: A 2010 to 2013 PES scheme in Uganda that was the first set up as a randomized controlled trial to measure its effect on deforestation.

facts.text: Forest owners were paid $28 per hectare per year for two years for keeping forest intact, about 5% of typical annual income.
Deforestation was 2 to 5% in participating villages against 7 to 10% in control villages.
The scheme ended after the evaluation, and old forest practices are assumed to resume once payments stop.

entries.title: Vittel pays farmers to protect its spring water

definition.text: A negotiated deal in which the Vittel mineral-water brand paid nearby farmers to adopt practices that protect its groundwater.

facts.text: Intensifying farming from the 1970s raised nitrate levels in the aquifer, threatening the brand.
The pollution came from many diffuse sources, so no single farmer's share could be measured.
The company bought some land and gave technical support and time-limited payments, making it perhaps the world's best-known PES built on direct negotiation.
It is seen as a case of Coasean bargaining, though community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

The deal is perhaps the world's best-known payment for ecosystem services built on direct negotiation. It is often cited as a case of the private bargaining described by the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. Community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

entries.title: Baselines: measuring against a world that never happened

definition.text: The predicted outcome without a payment or project, against which its real effect is measured.

facts.text: Establishing baselines and counterfactuals is a key challenge for claims that PES is effective.
Under the Clean Development Mechanism, credits are issued for the monitored difference between baseline and actual emissions.
The baseline cannot be observed, so it is built from hypothetical scenarios, similar activities elsewhere, or emissions before the project.
Project partners may gain from a high baseline, risking spurious credits, and offsets can even reward emitting more to inflate the baseline.
How much leakage is counted depends partly on how the baseline is defined.

entries.text: Knowing what a payment achieved means knowing what would have happened without it, and that world can never be observed. The baseline, or counterfactual, is that predicted outcome without the payment or project, against which its real effect is measured. Establishing it is a key challenge for any claim that payments for ecosystem services work. Carbon markets show why. Under the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}, credits are issued for the monitored gap between baseline and actual emissions. Because the baseline cannot be seen, it is built from hypothetical scenarios, similar activities elsewhere, or emissions before the project. That invites gaming. Project partners may gain from a high baseline, risking spurious credits, and offsets can even reward emitting more to inflate it. How much leakage gets counted also depends partly on how the baseline is drawn. It is the hidden half of every judgment about additionality.

entries.title: No service, no payment: the rule of conditionality

definition.text: The rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up.

facts.text: PES has been defined as additional environmental services secured through conditional payments to voluntary providers.
Design debates focus on how conditionality is set and enforced through monitoring and verification.
Conditional cash transfers for schooling and health use the same idea; in Mexico conditions raised secondary-school attendance most.
Proponents of a rights-based approach to development argue strongly against attaching conditions to social cash transfers.

entries.text: No service, no money. Conditionality is the rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up. It sits inside one well-known definition of PES: additional environmental services secured through conditional payments to voluntary providers. Most design debates turn on how conditions are set and enforced through monitoring and verification. The idea also runs through social policy. The programs described in {{ref:nature-mkt-146}} pay families for schooling and health care, and in Mexico the conditions raised secondary-school attendance most. Conditions are not welcome everywhere. Supporters of a rights-based approach to development argue strongly against attaching them to social cash transfers.

entries.title: Paying for results, not promises

definition.text: Payments made only for measured, verified environmental results, such as emission reductions, rather than for planned actions.

facts.text: Most PES programmes pay for management practices and only less commonly for measured outcomes.
REDD+ uses results-based payments to put a financial value on carbon stored in forests, as the last of four stages after readiness, a finance agreement and verification.
The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility's Carbon Fund pays only after independent verification of reported emission reductions.
Countries seeking REDD+ results-based payments must report how the Cancún safeguards are respected and have an assessed forest reference level.
The Green Climate Fund ran a REDD+ results-based payments pilot from 2017 to 2022 and made it a permanent window in 2024.
In farming, the European Commission defines results-based schemes as paying for outcomes such as breeding birds, leaving the methods to the farmer.
REDD+ aims to give financial value to forest carbon through results-based payments.
Payments need a national forest monitoring system, documented methods and data, and reporting under the Warsaw Framework on REDD-plus.

entries.text: Most payment programs pay for management practices, and only less commonly for measured outcomes. Results-based payments reverse that. It also needs an assessed benchmark of its past forest emissions and a report on how agreed social and environmental safeguards are respected. The European Commission defines results-based schemes as paying for outcomes such as breeding birds, leaving the methods to the farmer.

entries.title: How New York City keeps its water clean by guarding its watersheds
entries.article: New York City water supply system

definition.text: The network of reservoirs, aqueducts and tunnels that supplies New York City with fresh water, kept clean largely by protecting its upstate watersheds.

facts.text: Its three systems, Croton, Catskill and Delaware, reach up to 125 miles (201 km) north of the city.
Since 1997 the city has bought or protected through conservation easements over 130,000 acres (53,000 ha) of watershed land.
Because its watersheds are protected, the system is partly exempt from filtration rules, avoiding more than $10 billion for a filtration plant and at least $100 million a year to run it.
Only 10% of its water is filtered, though all of it is disinfected.
The Department of Environmental Protection runs a $1.5 billion Watershed Protection Program.
It delivers over 1.2 billion US gallons a day to more than eight million city residents.
In 2018 the city announced a US$1 billion investment to keep its unfiltered supply pure, partly against climate-driven turbidity.

sources.title: New York City water supply system

entries.text: Only 10% of New York City's water is filtered, though all of it is disinfected. The rest stays clean because the city protects the upstate watersheds that supply it. Its three systems, Croton, Catskill and Delaware, reach up to 125 miles (201 km) north of the city. Together they deliver over 1.2 billion US gallons a day to more than eight million residents. Since 1997 the city has bought, or protected through legal limits on development, over 130,000 acres (53,000 ha) of watershed land. The Department of Environmental Protection runs a $1.5 billion Watershed Protection Program. The payoff is a partial exemption from filtration rules. That spares the city more than $10 billion for a filtration plant and at least $100 million a year to run it. In 2018 the city announced a further US$1 billion investment to keep its unfiltered supply pure, partly against cloudier water driven by climate change. Here a protected landscape does the work of a machine.

entries.title: Conditional cash transfers: paying families to choose school

definition.text: Programmes that fight poverty by paying cash only to people who meet conditions, such as sending children to school or getting vaccinations.

facts.text: Few development programmes have been evaluated as rigorously.
By 2011 they had spread to 18 Latin American countries, covering up to 129 million people.
Brazil's Bolsa Família pays poor households if school-age children are enrolled and younger children vaccinated.
Evidence from Mexico and Malawi found conditions raised school enrolment compared with unconditional payments.

entries.text: Few development programs have been evaluated as rigorously as conditional cash transfers. Brazil's Bolsa Família, for example, pays poor households if school-age children are enrolled and younger children vaccinated. The conditions seem to matter. Evidence from Mexico and Malawi found they raised school enrollment compared with unconditional payments.

definition.text: Directing conservation payments to the places where they buy the most environmental benefit for the money.

facts.text: Costa Rica's flat-rate payments leave many high-value areas unenrolled because landowners there face higher opportunity costs.
Its watershed-bound water tariff was criticised for concentrating money in areas of relatively low ecological importance.
Reverse auctions can reveal landowners' private opportunity costs, helping design payment programmes.
With limited money, the Conservation Reserve Program admits only the most qualified land.

entries.title: Farm stewardship schemes in England and Switzerland

definition.text: A mechanism that gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment.

facts.text: England runs such schemes under Environmental Stewardship, administered by Natural England.
After leaving the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, the British government started its Environmental Land Management scheme in 2024.
Since 1998 Switzerland has tied farm subsidies to good environmental practice, such as keeping at least 7% of farmland as ecological compensation areas.

entries.title: Environmental mitigation: avoid, reduce, then make up for harm

definition.text: The process of applying measures to avoid, minimise or compensate for harm to the environment.

facts.text: In planning such as Environmental Impact Assessments it is usually guided by the mitigation hierarchy: avoid, reduce, restore, and offset.
In practice it means creating new habitat, restoring degraded habitat, or protecting existing habitat to offset harm that cannot be avoided or reduced.
It is broader than climate change mitigation, which focuses only on cutting net greenhouse gas emissions.
191 UN member states have Environmental Impact Assessment laws and more than 108 countries have biodiversity offsetting policies.
In the US, the Fish and Wildlife Coordination Act of 1934 first expressed a legal duty to minimise and compensate for environmental harm.
Its usual goals are no net loss or a net positive impact on biodiversity.

entries.contested_note: Whether aims like no net loss and tools like offsetting advance or undermine conservation goals is disputed.

entries.title: No net loss: balancing damage with equal gains

definition.text: An environmental policy approach that aims to balance out a development's harm to the environment through mitigation measures.

facts.text: It began in the US in the 1980s as a goal for wetland conservation; George H. W. Bush promised "no net loss of wetlands" in his 1988 campaign.
It is now an objective for biodiversity offsetting in many countries, and by 2018 was in place in at least 69.
It is applied through Environmental Impact Assessments using the mitigation hierarchy.
Lenders such as the International Finance Corporation require it on projects they co-finance.
A study of US mitigation banking found it was producing a net loss of wetland area nationally.
A study of a Victorian (Australia) scheme found up to 86% of offsets did not make up for losses of native vegetation.
There is no agreed metric for measuring losses and gains, and baselines are often undefined.

entries.contested_note: Some reject no net loss as impossible or unacceptable for ecological, social or cultural reasons, while others see it as a way to reconcile development with conservation.
entries.text: In his 1988 campaign, George H. W. Bush promised 'no net loss of wetlands'. The phrase named an approach that had begun in the US earlier in the 1980s as a goal for wetland conservation. No net loss aims to balance a development's harm to the environment with mitigation measures, so that the total stays level. It has spread far beyond wetlands. It is now an objective of {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} in many countries, at least 69 by 2018. It is applied through Environmental Impact Assessments using the {{ref:nature-mkt-130}}. Lenders such as the International Finance Corporation require it on projects they co-finance. The record is sobering. A study of US {{ref:nature-mkt-124}} found it was producing a net loss of wetland area nationally. In one scheme in Victoria, Australia, up to 86% of offsets did not make up for lost native vegetation. Part of the problem is measurement: there is no agreed metric for losses and gains, and baselines are often undefined. Views divide sharply. Some reject no net loss as impossible or unacceptable for ecological, social or cultural reasons. Others see it as a way to reconcile development with conservation.
