entries.title: The mitigation hierarchy: offsetting comes last

definition.text: A sequence of steps (avoid, minimise, restore, then offset) applied in order to reduce a project's harm to the environment until none remains.

facts.text: Avoiding harm is the first step and widely seen as the most important.
Minimising reduces harm that cannot be avoided; restoring helps damaged ecosystems recover; offsetting compensates for whatever harm remains.
Offsetting is the "final resort" in the hierarchy.
It is commonly built into Environmental Impact Assessment and licensing rules, and some jurisdictions require it by law.
France writes it into law as the ERC sequence: avoid, reduce, compensate.
Versions have been proposed for waste, food waste, energy and carbon, and extensions such as the Mitigation and Conservation Hierarchy.

entries.text: Offsetting is the 'final resort'. The mitigation hierarchy sets out the steps a project takes, in order, to shrink its harm to the environment until none remains: avoid, minimize, restore, then offset. Avoiding harm comes first and is widely seen as the most important. Minimizing reduces the harm that cannot be avoided. Restoring helps damaged ecosystems recover. Offsetting compensates for whatever harm is left. The sequence is commonly built into Environmental Impact Assessment and licensing rules, and some jurisdictions require it by law. France writes it into law as the ERC sequence: avoid, reduce, compensate. Versions have been proposed for waste, food waste, energy and carbon, along with extensions such as the Mitigation and Conservation Hierarchy.

entries.title: Biodiversity offsetting: repaying nature somewhere else

definition.text: A system, used mainly by planning authorities and developers, for fully compensating the harm a development does to biodiversity.

facts.text: Offsets are measurable conservation gains designed to make up for significant harm left over after prevention and mitigation; the aim is no net loss of biodiversity, ideally a net gain.
Offsetting is the last step of the mitigation hierarchy: harm must first be avoided, minimised and reversed before what remains is offset.
Practitioners measure the amount, type and quality of habitat a project will damage, then find receptor sites where the same can be re-created.
Offsets must show additionality: a gain in biodiversity that would not have happened anyway.
As of 2019, over 100 countries had or were developing offset policies and more than 37 required offsets by law.
England's Biodiversity Net Gain rule, in force from February 2024, requires developers to show a 10% net gain in biodiversity to get planning permission.
Evidence is mixed: offsets work better in simpler, fast-recovering habitats such as wetlands, and a review found about one-third of policies and offsets reported achieving no net loss.
Critics call offsetting a "licence to trash" that legitimises habitat destruction, and question whether biodiversity in one place can be swapped for biodiversity elsewhere.

entries.contested_note: Supporters and opponents disagree on whether offsets are feasible or ethical, given the difficulty of measuring biodiversity and swapping it between places.

entries.title: Biodiversity banking: turning offsets into tradable credits

definition.text: A market-based form of biodiversity offsetting in which conservation gains are turned into credits that developers can buy to offset their damage.

facts.text: It is also called habitat banking, conservation banking, mitigation banking or biodiversity trading, depending on what is being conserved and where.
At a bank site, work such as reintroducing native plants, removing invasive species or filling ditches to restore a swamp generates credits for gains that would not otherwise happen.
It turns offsets into tradeable assets by creating credits in advance of a development and away from its site.
It grew out of US wetland mitigation banking in the 1980s, which arose from the no net loss policies of the 1970s Clean Water Act.
A bank's land is usually locked in by a conservation easement or covenant that binds future owners, often with a trust fund for long-term management.
More than 100 countries require biodiversity offsetting, but banking frameworks are less widespread.
A 2006 analysis of Canadian habitat banking found 25% of projects achieved no net loss of habitat productivity and 12% a net gain.

entries.text: Filling in ditches to bring back a swamp can earn money, if it happens at a biodiversity bank. Biodiversity banking is a market-based form of offsetting. Gains made at a bank site, such as reintroducing native plants or removing invasive species, become credits that developers can buy to offset their damage. Credits count only for gains that would not otherwise happen. Because they are created in advance and away from the development, offsets become tradable assets. The practice goes by several names, such as habitat banking or biodiversity trading, depending on what is conserved and where. entries.title: Wetland mitigation banks: restore first, sell credits later

definition.text: A market-based system of debits and credits, used mainly in the United States, in which wetlands are restored, created or enhanced to make up for unavoidable damage to wetlands elsewhere.

facts.text: Mitigation banks are sites where wetland projects are carried out before the damage they compensate for; their results become credits that developers can buy.
It grew from compensatory mitigation under section 404 of the US Clean Water Act, aiming at "no net loss of wetlands".
The first wetland mitigation banks were set up in the early 1980s following 1983 guidance from the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
Regulators often require more habitat than is damaged, a mitigation ratio, which serves the public interest.
Credits are released in stages as a bank meets performance milestones over an establishment period of about 10 to 12 years.
By 2024 more than 1200 mitigation banks were operating in the US, with 750,000 credits approved.
Studies suggest a significant share of compensation sites fail to meet administrative and ecological performance standards.

entries.title: Conservation banks: credits for endangered species

definition.text: A market-based method of offsetting harm to threatened or endangered species protected under the US Endangered Species Act by creating conservation banks.

facts.text: Conservation banks are permanently protected parcels of land managed to keep endangered species and their habitat alive.
Developers who must harm protected species can buy credits from a bank instead of protecting small patches themselves.
Pooling mitigation into larger reserves gives better habitat and connectivity than small isolated patches, and is cheaper to maintain.
California created the first conservation bank in 1995 and leads with over 30; the nation's 130 banks protect over 160,000 acres.
Credit prices are set largely by supply and demand and range from $1500 for a Gopher Tortoise to $325,000 for vernal pool preservation.
Unlike wetland mitigation banking, conservation banking does not require no net loss.

entries.title: Safe harbor agreements: rewarding landowners who help rare species
entries.article: Endangered Species Act of 1973#Safe Harbor Agreements

definition.text: A voluntary US agreement in which a landowner improves land for a listed species and in return is allowed some future harm to that species.

facts.text: It covers species already listed as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act.
The policy was developed under the Clinton administration; the Environmental Defense Fund designed the plan in 1995 to give landowners incentives to help endangered species.
In 2024 it was merged with another programme into Conservation Benefits Agreements.
Unlike a habitat conservation plan, the activities a Safe Harbor Agreement covers are designed to protect species.

distinct_from: Perverse incentives of endangered species protection
entries.text: In 1995 the Environmental Defense Fund designed a plan to give landowners incentives to help endangered species. Developed into policy under the Clinton administration, it became the Safe Harbor Agreement. In this voluntary US deal, a landowner improves land for a species listed as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act. In return, the landowner is allowed some future harm to that species. Unlike a habitat conservation plan, the activities it covers are designed to protect species. In 2024 it was merged with another program into Conservation Benefits Agreements.

entries.title: Biodiversity Impact Credits: pricing a lower risk of extinction

definition.text: A transferable biodiversity credit designed to reduce the global risk of species extinction.

facts.text: Its metric, developed by academics at Queen Mary University of London and Bar-Ilan University, measures how interventions change the average long-term survival chances of species.
For each species it adds up the change in global population divided by the current population, so restoring one threatened species from near zero gives about one credit.
It targets Target 4 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework on cutting extinction risk, and the TNFD recommends its use.
Critics of biodiversity credits say monetising nature oversimplifies it and that credits can be used for greenwashing or merely to offset damage.

entries.contested_note: Critics say pricing nature through credits oversimplifies it and invites greenwashing, while proponents point to growing private investment.
entries.text: Restoring one threatened species from near zero earns about one credit under a scheme built to cut the global risk of extinction. Academics at Queen Mary University of London and Bar-Ilan University developed its metric. It measures how interventions change the average long-term survival chances of species. For each species it adds up the change in global population divided by the current population. It targets the global biodiversity goal on extinction risk, Target 4. Critics say credits oversimplify nature and invite false green claims, while supporters point to growing private investment.

entries.title: Averted loss: offsetting by preventing damage

definition.text: A biodiversity offset that prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened, rather than restoring or creating habitat.

facts.text: Examples include creating protected areas, removing invasive species, or offering alternative livelihoods to stop deforestation.
Activities without a measurable gain for biodiversity, such as funding general research, do not count as offsets.
Poorly designed offset policies can create perverse incentives that encourage further biodiversity decline.

entries.text: Not every offset builds new habitat. An averted loss offset instead prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened. Examples include setting aside land for protection, removing invasive species, or offering people other livelihoods so they stop clearing forest. The gain must be measurable: funding general research, for instance, does not count. Because the damage it prevents never happens, everything rests on {{ref:nature-mkt-144}}. Poorly designed policies can backfire, creating perverse incentives that encourage further decline.

entries.title: Conservation credits: habitat sold by the unit

definition.text: A unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers can buy to offset their impact on biodiversity.

facts.text: Receptor-site land is also valued in credits, covering both the cost of restoring habitat and its long-term management.
This lets developers buy and landowners sell credits, creating a market for keeping and restoring habitat.

entries.text: Developers can offset damage to nature one unit at a time. A conservation credit is a unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers buy to offset their impact on biodiversity. With a common unit, developers can buy and landowners can sell, creating a market for keeping and restoring habitat.

entries.title: Receptor sites: where offset habitat is made

definition.text: Land offered by a company or individual for payment in return for creating or restoring wildlife habitat to offset damage elsewhere.

facts.text: The habitat work is paid for by developers seeking to offset their impact.
The biodiversity gained at the receptor site should equal or exceed the loss at the original impact site.

entries.text: Every offset needs somewhere to happen. A receptor site is land that a company or individual offers, for payment, to create or restore wildlife habitat that offsets damage elsewhere. The developers seeking to offset their impact pay for the habitat work. The rule is balance or better: the biodiversity gained at the receptor site should equal or exceed the loss at the original site.

entries.title: Compensatory mitigation: the American name for offsetting

definition.text: Measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided; the US term for biodiversity offsetting.

facts.text: It applies only after the mitigation sequence of avoid, minimise, then compensate has been followed.
It can be on-site, on or next to the damaged area, or off-site.
Besides banks, it can be done through in-lieu fee programmes, where permittees pay into an approved fund, or permittee-responsible projects, where they do and answer for the work themselves.
Revised US rules in 2008 made mitigation banks the preferred method of compensatory mitigation.

entries.text: In the United States, biodiversity offsetting goes by another name: compensatory mitigation. It means measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided. It applies only after the sequence of avoid, minimize, then compensate has been followed. It can happen on or next to the damaged area, or off-site. Besides banks, permit holders can pay into an approved fund, called an in-lieu fee program, or do and answer for the work themselves. Revised US rules in 2008 made mitigation banks the preferred method.

entries.title: Conservation easements: protection that runs with the land

definition.text: A voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a government agency or conservation group that restricts future development on a site, setting it aside permanently for conservation.

facts.text: In the US, land used for mitigation banking must be protected by a conservation easement.
The commitment binds future owners of the land, and a trust fund may pay for long-term management.
Landowners may see the permanent restriction as a drawback because it limits future uses and can lower land value.
It 'runs with the land', binding present and future owners, and is usually permanent.

entries.contested_note: Critics say easement tax deductions are abused as a tax avoidance scheme, and US courts have penalised overstated easement values.

entries.title: Debits and credits for nature

definition.text: A system set up by a governing body that allocates debits for planned environmental damage and credits for conservation gains, so damage can be offset by buying credits.

facts.text: Credits come from banks where a resource has been improved; debits arise where significant harm is planned at a permitted site.
Biodiversity banking and its forms, such as mitigation, habitat, species and conservation banking, are examples.
Key difficulties are choosing the unit of exchange, making debits and credits ecologically equivalent, and proving additionality.

entries.contested_note: Some consider measuring biodiversity in credit and debit units impossible or reject it on ethical grounds.
entries.text: An environmental crediting system works like a ledger for nature. A governing body allocates debits for planned environmental damage and credits for conservation gains, so damage can be offset by buying credits. Credits come from banks where a resource has been improved; debits arise where significant harm is planned at a permitted site. Biodiversity banking in all its forms is an example. Three problems recur: choosing the unit of exchange, making debits and credits ecologically equivalent, and proving additionality. Some consider measuring biodiversity in such units impossible, or reject it on ethical grounds.

entries.title: Net positive impact: leaving nature better off

definition.text: A goal under which a project's environmental gains from mitigation outweigh its harms, leaving more biodiversity than before.

facts.text: Net gain or net positive impact is used instead of no net loss when the aim is to leave biodiversity better than before.
England's Biodiversity Net Gain policy requires a 10% net gain compared with the previous state.
Net positive impact usually applies to a single development project, while no net loss is applied at many geographic scales.

entries.title: Offset ratios: paying back more than was taken

definition.text: Rules that set how much habitat must be credited for each unit of damage (mitigation ratios) and require offsets to match or exceed the biodiversity lost (like-for-like).

facts.text: Credit ratios have been proposed as a way to deal with uncertainty in offsetting.
A coverage ratio of 3:1 requires 3 compensatory mitigation credits for each unit of ecological damage.
Uganda's law requires offsets to follow the "like-for-like or better" principle; China's eco-compensation does not require like-for-like offsets.
Friends of the Earth argues that like-for-like compensation of lost biodiversity may not be possible.

entries.text: Under a coverage ratio of 3:1, a developer must supply 3 compensatory mitigation credits for each unit of ecological damage. entries.title: Carbon credits: buying a tonne of avoided emissions

definition.text: A tradable certificate claiming that greenhouse gas emissions were avoided or that greenhouse gases were removed from the air.

facts.text: One credit stands for one metric ton of carbon dioxide, or the equivalent amount of another greenhouse gas, avoided or removed.
Carbon offsetting means using credits to counter an organisation's own reported greenhouse gas emissions.
Crediting programs let project developers earn credits for emission-cutting projects and sell them to buyers who want to claim an offset.
Carbon credits are one form of carbon pricing, alongside carbon taxes and carbon border adjustments.
Projects include forest protection and tree planting, wind farms, biogas digesters, energy efficiency, carbon capture and capturing methane from landfills.
The underlying economic idea is that cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, so trading credits can lower the total cost of meeting targets.
Compliance markets make up most of the credit market: about 12 GtCO2e traded, against 300 MtCO2e on voluntary markets in 2021.
Wetland offsetting under the US Clean Water Act in the 1990s set the precedent for carbon offsetting; the Kyoto Protocol created the first international offset markets in 1997.

entries.text: One carbon credit stands for one metric ton of carbon dioxide kept out of the air or removed from it. Other greenhouse gases count by their equivalent warming effect. entries.title: The Clean Development Mechanism: Kyoto's offset market

definition.text: A UN-run offset scheme under the Kyoto Protocol that let rich countries fund emission-cutting projects in developing countries and count the savings toward their own targets.

facts.text: Projects earned Certified Emission Reduction units (CERs), bought by industrialised countries because cuts were cheapest in developing ones.
It aimed both to aid sustainable development in poorer countries and to help rich countries meet their commitments.
From 2001 to 7 September 2012 it issued 1 billion CERs; by June 2013, 57% came from destroying HFC-23 or N2O.
The IPCC projected that using CDM and Joint Implementation would cut OECD Europe's GDP losses to 0.13–0.81%, versus 0.31–1.50% with domestic action only.
Its revenues were the largest source of mitigation finance to developing countries, and a 2% levy funded the Adaptation Fund.
Weak demand after the 2008 financial crisis drove CER prices from 20 USD in 2008 to 5 USD in 2012 and below 1 USD the next year.
Avoided deforestation and forest conservation were excluded in the Kyoto Protocol's first commitment period.

entries.text: From 2001 to 7 September 2012, a UN scheme issued 1 billion offset credits. entries.title: Forest degradation: decline without disappearance

definition.text: A lasting decline in the biological richness of a forest, where the forest remains but is in worse condition.

facts.text: A degraded forest has fewer trees, fewer species or more disease, without losing area.
Degradation lowers a forest's value and can lead on to deforestation.
Unlike visible deforestation, it can proceed without clear signs, making it hard to measure; in 2009 more than 50 definitions were counted.
Causes include over-harvesting of timber and charcoal, roads, mining, urban sprawl, grazing and fragmentation.
One Bolivian mapping study treated 30–70% remaining forest cover as degraded, under 30% as deforested and over 70% as intact.
Measuring degradation remains a weak point of REDD+ monitoring.
A degraded forest has fewer trees, fewer species, or species hit by pests, which lowers its value and may lead to deforestation.
It is one kind of the wider problem of land degradation.

entries.contested_note: The term itself is disputed, with many and often subjective definitions.
entries.text: A forest can lose much of its value while still looking like a forest on the map. Forest degradation is a lasting decline in a forest's biological richness: the forest remains but is in worse condition. It has fewer trees, fewer species, or species hit by pests and disease, without losing area. That lowers its value and can lead on to outright deforestation. It is one kind of the wider problem of {{ref:nature-eco-060}}. entries.title: REDD+: paying countries to keep their forests

definition.text: A voluntary UN climate framework that pays and supports developing countries to cut emissions from deforestation and forest degradation and to conserve and build up forest carbon.

facts.text: The name stands for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries; the plus adds conservation and enhancement of forests.
The underlying idea is to reward reduced deforestation by giving forest carbon a value.
Cutting deforestation and degradation is estimated to be one of the cheapest ways to mitigate climate change.
In 2019 the IPCC put net land-sector emissions at about 13 GtCO2-eq, about 22% of global net human emissions, roughly half from land use change, mainly deforestation.
Countries need a national strategy, a forest reference level, a national forest monitoring system and a system reporting on safeguards.
Because most deforestation drivers lie outside forestry, such as farming, roads and mining, strategies combine forest measures with land-use and agricultural reforms.
Alongside the UN track, many voluntary-market forest projects calling themselves REDD+ issue credits under private standards, mostly the Verified Carbon Standard.
REDD was first proposed in 2005 by Papua New Guinea and Costa Rica for the Coalition for Rainforest Nations.

entries.text: In 2019 the IPCC put net emissions from land at about 13 GtCO2-eq a year, about 22% of global net human emissions. Roughly half came from changes in land use, mainly deforestation. This voluntary framework pays and supports developing countries to cut those emissions and build up forest carbon. The idea is to reward reduced deforestation by giving forest carbon a value. entries.title: Carbon credit quality: is this tonne real?

definition.text: How confident one can be that using a carbon credit leaves the world at least as well off as if the buyer had cut its own emissions.

facts.text: A credit is meant to substitute for reductions the buyer could have made itself.
High-quality credits come from reductions that are additional, robustly measured, not claimed by anyone else and free of serious social or environmental harm.
Quality checks usually cover the baseline, additionality, permanence, double counting and co-benefits.
Reviews have found overestimated sequestration, double-counted credits and projects that added nothing beyond what would have happened anyway.
From around 2020, credit-rating initiatives and labels such as the Core Carbon Principles appeared to help buyers tell good credits from bad.

entries.text: A carbon credit is meant to substitute for cuts the buyer could have made itself. Credit quality is how confident one can be that using it leaves the world at least as well off as that cut would have. High-quality credits come from reductions that are additional, robustly measured, not claimed by anyone else, and free of serious social or environmental harm. Checks usually cover the baseline, additionality, permanence, double counting and side benefits. Reviews have found the opposite too often: overestimated carbon storage, double-counted credits and projects that added nothing beyond what would have happened anyway. From around 2020, credit-rating initiatives and labels such as the {{ref:nature-hist-034}} appeared to help buyers tell good credits from bad.

entries.title: The case against carbon offsets
entries.article: Carbon offsets and credits#Limitations and drawbacks

definition.text: The case that offsets let polluters carry on with business as usual instead of cutting emissions at source.

facts.text: Research from the Australia Institute suggested at least 25% of offsets may lack integrity.
A 2016 Öko-Institut study found 85% of the CDM projects it analysed were unlikely to be truly additional or likely overestimated reductions.
Offsets can create perverse incentives to emit more so that cuts are measured from an inflated baseline.
Several standards measure baselines and additionality differently, and no single standard governs the industry.
Companies that buy offsets tend, on evidence, to make more ambitious emission cuts than those that do not.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether offsets delay real emission cuts or accompany more ambitious ones.
entries.text: A 2016 study by the Öko-Institut found that 85% of the Clean Development Mechanism projects it analyzed were unlikely to be truly additional or likely overstated their reductions. That finding sits at the center of a broader charge. Critics argue that offsets let polluters carry on with business as usual instead of cutting emissions at the source. Research from the Australia Institute suggested at least 25% of offsets may lack integrity. The design itself can backfire. Offsets can create perverse incentives to emit more, so that cuts are measured from an inflated baseline. Standards also measure baselines and additionality differently, and no single standard governs the industry. The evidence does not all point one way, though. Companies that buy offsets tend to make more ambitious emission cuts than those that do not. Whether offsets delay real cuts or accompany bolder ones remains in dispute.

entries.title: The voluntary carbon market: offsets nobody is required to buy
entries.article: Carbon offsets and credits#Voluntary carbon markets and certification programs

definition.text: A largely unregulated market where companies, people and organisations with no legal duty to cut emissions buy offsets to meet goals they set themselves.

facts.text: Credits are issued under independent standards such as Verra's Verified Carbon Standard, the Gold Standard, the Climate Action Reserve, the American Carbon Registry and Plan Vivo.
Certification programs set accounting rules, project eligibility and monitoring, reporting and verification procedures.
In 2022 prices for common project types ranged from $8 to $30 per tonne of CO2e.
Credits from projects that store carbon, with extra social and environmental benefits, or with recent vintages tend to fetch higher prices.
Oversupply keeps prices low; without the surplus prices could be at least $10/tCO2e higher.
The voluntary market covers less than 1% of the reductions pledged in national climate plans for 2030.
Issuance and retirement of voluntary offsets more than tripled between 2017 and 2021.

entries.text: The voluntary carbon market covers less than 1% of the reductions countries have pledged for 2030. Oversupply keeps prices low; without the surplus, prices could be at least $10/tCO2e higher. Even so, issuing and retiring of voluntary offsets more than tripled between 2017 and 2021.

entries.title: The case against REDD+

definition.text: Objections from researchers, Indigenous organisations and civil-society groups to the effectiveness, governance and fairness of REDD+.

facts.text: Unclear land tenure and carbon rights make consent and benefit-sharing harder and open the door to elite capture.
Indigenous groups warn that forest-carbon schemes can restrict customary land use; in 2007 an Indigenous forum opposed REDD outright.
Broad definitions of forest can include plantations, which may reward tree cover regardless of biodiversity.
Outcomes depend on domestic politics, tenure arrangements and administrative capacity.

entries.contested_note: Supporters and critics, including Indigenous organisations, disagree over REDD+'s fairness and effects.
entries.text: In 2007 an Indigenous forum opposed REDD outright. Its objection is one of several that researchers, Indigenous organizations and civil-society groups raise about the effectiveness, governance and fairness of REDD+. Land ownership is the first problem. Unclear land tenure and carbon rights make consent and benefit-sharing harder, and they open the door to elite capture, where powerful insiders take the gains. Indigenous groups warn that forest-carbon schemes can restrict traditional uses of their land. Definitions matter too. Broad definitions of forest can include plantations, which may reward tree cover regardless of biodiversity. Outcomes also depend on domestic politics, tenure arrangements and the capacity of government offices. Supporters and critics, including Indigenous organizations, still disagree over whether REDD+ is fair and whether it works.

entries.title: Leakage: when saving one forest dooms another

definition.text: The displacement of forest loss: protecting one area can push deforestation or degradation somewhere else, cancelling the gain.

facts.text: The Cancún safeguards call for action to reduce such displacement, and many standards include leakage accounting.
Quantified outcomes and issued credits are sensitive to how leakage is handled.

entries.text: Protecting one patch of forest can simply push the chainsaws elsewhere. That displacement of forest loss is called leakage: deforestation or degradation moves to another area and cancels the gain. It is the forest version of {{ref:nature-pol-252}}. The {{ref:nature-mkt-108}} for REDD+ call for action to reduce such displacement, and many crediting standards include leakage accounting. The choice matters, because the outcomes reported and the credits issued are sensitive to how leakage is handled.

entries.title: Has REDD+ actually saved forests?

definition.text: The question of how much REDD+ and other forest-carbon schemes have actually reduced forest loss.

facts.text: A 2024 multi-country evaluation found modest average forest gains, limited welfare effects and impacts not always lasting.
A study of 40 Verified Carbon Standard REDD+ projects in nine countries found less deforestation than in matched comparison areas over the first five years.
An analysis in the Brazilian Amazon concluded that many project baselines assumed more deforestation than comparison methods suggested.
Results depend heavily on the counterfactual baseline chosen, on proving additionality and on measuring degradation and below-ground carbon.
UN-reported results and voluntary-market credits are not directly comparable, since one uses national reference levels and the other project baselines.
Brazil submitted the first quantified REDD+ results to the UNFCCC on 31 December 2014, for the Amazon.

entries.contested_note: Evaluations report mixed, context-dependent results, and some argue project baselines are inflated.
entries.text: Brazil submitted the first quantified REDD+ results to the UN climate convention on 31 December 2014, for the Amazon. Since then, the central question has been how much REDD+ and other forest-carbon schemes actually reduced forest loss. The answers are mixed and depend on context. A 2024 multi-country evaluation found modest average gains in forest, limited effects on welfare, and impacts that did not always last. A study of 40 REDD+ projects in nine countries, all certified under Verra's standard, found less deforestation than in matched comparison areas over the first five years. Yet an analysis in the Brazilian Amazon concluded that many project baselines assumed more deforestation than comparison methods suggested. Results hinge on the baseline chosen, on proving additionality, and on measuring degradation and carbon below ground. UN-reported results and voluntary-market credits are not directly comparable either. One uses national reference levels; the other uses project baselines. Some argue that project baselines are inflated, and the debate is not settled.

entries.title: The Cancún safeguards: rules to protect people and forests

definition.text: Seven social, environmental and governance safeguards for REDD+ adopted at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún.

facts.text: They cover forest governance, the rights and participation of Indigenous peoples and local communities, conservation of natural forests and biodiversity, and risks of reversal and displacement of emissions.
They bar REDD+ actions from being used to convert natural forests and call for protecting forests and their ecosystem services.
They arose from concerns that forest mitigation could harm people through insecure tenure or harm nature by converting natural forest.
Countries must report how safeguards are respected before receiving results-based REDD+ payments.
Because they are broad principles, countries apply them very differently, and how reported information should be checked is debated.

entries.text: Paying to save forest carbon could, in the wrong hands, harm the people who live in forests or the forests themselves. The Cancún safeguards, seven principles adopted at the 2010 UN climate conference, arose from exactly those concerns about insecure land tenure and the conversion of natural forest. They cover forest governance and the rights and participation of Indigenous and local communities. They also cover conservation of natural forests and biodiversity, and the risks of emissions being reversed or displaced. They bar REDD+ actions from being used to convert natural forests. Countries must report how the safeguards are respected before receiving results-based payments. Because they are broad principles, countries apply them very differently, and how reported information should be checked is still debated.

entries.title: The Verified Carbon Standard: Verra's forest credit rulebook

definition.text: A standard, run by the nonprofit Verra, for certifying carbon credits used to offset emissions.

facts.text: By 2024 more than 2,300 projects were registered, issuing over 1.3 billion credits, of which more than 776 million had been retired.
It is the main program for forest credits in the voluntary market and covers almost all REDD+ projects.
It began in 2005 as a quality standard for carbon credits outside the Kyoto Protocol, such as projects in rich countries that the CDM could not credit.
The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market lists it as CCP-Eligible.

Industrial gases such as HFCs and PFCs warm far more than carbon dioxide and are easy to destroy at source.
Renewable energy projects may not qualify as offsets.

entries.title: Phantom credits: doubts over forest offsets
entries.article: Carbon offsets and credits#Concerns with forestry projects

definition.text: The criticism that forest-based carbon credits often fail to deliver the climate benefits they claim.

facts.text: News stories from 2021 to 2023 criticised nature-based offsets, REDD+ and certifiers.
One estimate held that around 90% of Verified Carbon Standard rainforest credits are likely "phantom credits".
Trees take decades to mature, and no one can guarantee a forest will escape clearing, burning or mismanagement.
Planting fast-growing invasive species can damage native forest and biodiversity.
Tree planting in high latitudes may warm the climate, because dark tree cover absorbs sunlight.
Projects can clash with local and Indigenous communities whose forest use they curtail.

entries.contested_note: Critics and investigative reports dispute whether many forest credits represent real reductions.

entries.title: Emissions baselines: the yardstick for every claimed cut

definition.text: An estimate of the emissions that would have occurred without a project, against which its reductions are measured.

facts.text: Emission reductions equal the emissions without the project minus the project's actual emissions.
Baselines often rest on hypothetical scenarios, emissions from similar activities, or emissions before the project began.
Offsets can create a perverse incentive to inflate the baseline so that larger cuts can be claimed.
In REDD+, choices about reference periods and data can strongly change credited results.
The baseline sets the potential for emission cuts and the cost of policies to achieve them.
A business-as-usual baseline assumes past trends continue with no new policy and often implies high emissions.
An efficient baseline assumes all resources are used efficiently, so cost per unit cut can be high but total cost low.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change
entries.text: Every claimed emission cut is a subtraction. Reductions equal the emissions there would have been without the project minus the project's actual emissions. The first number, the emissions baseline, can never be measured directly. It often rests on hypothetical scenarios, emissions from similar activities, or emissions before the project began. That creates a temptation. Offsets can reward inflating the baseline so that larger cuts can be claimed, and in REDD+ choices of reference period and data can strongly change credited results. In policy, the baseline sets the potential for cuts and their cost. A business-as-usual baseline assumes past trends continue with no new policy and often implies high emissions. An efficient baseline assumes all resources are used efficiently, so the cost per unit cut can be high while the total cost stays low.

entries.title: Forest reference levels: the benchmark for REDD+ results

definition.text: A benchmark of a country's forest emissions or removals, in tonnes of CO2e per year, against which REDD+ results are judged.

facts.text: Results-period emissions and removals are compared with the reference period to measure performance.
Reference levels usually draw on historical data on forest-area change combined with emission estimates.
Each submission for results-based payments undergoes a UN technical assessment, and countries may improve them step by step.
Choices of reference period, data, activities and carbon pools change how many results are counted.
Simple extrapolation of past forest loss could tempt countries to deforest more during the reference period to earn more credits later.
Nesting links project baselines with jurisdiction-wide reference levels to avoid double counting.

entries.text: A country claiming REDD+ results must first say what its forests would have emitted anyway. Its forest reference emission level is that benchmark, measured in tonnes of CO2e per year. Emissions and removals in the results period are compared with the reference period to measure performance. Reference levels usually combine historical data on changes in forest area with emission estimates. Each one submitted for results-based payments gets a UN technical assessment, and countries may improve them step by step. Choices of reference period, data, activities and carbon pools change how many results are counted. A simple projection of past forest loss has a perverse edge: it could tempt countries to clear more during the reference period to earn more credits later. Nesting links project baselines with these national levels to avoid counting the same cut twice.

Projects must prove additionality, avoid double certification and contribute to at least three Sustainable Development Goals.
Eligible types are renewable energy, energy efficiency, afforestation and reforestation, and agriculture.

entries.title: Markets or funds: the early fight over paying for REDD+

definition.text: The early dispute over whether REDD+ should be paid for by selling forest credits as offsets or through public funds.

facts.text: Critics argued that floods of forest credits could depress carbon prices and weaken incentives to cut emissions at home.
Since COP 17, UN decisions allow REDD+ to be financed by both market and non-market sources.

Since the COP 17 climate conference, its decisions allow REDD+ to be financed by both market and non-market sources.

entries.title: The five activities REDD+ counts

definition.text: The five kinds of action REDD+ counts: reducing deforestation, reducing forest degradation, conserving forest carbon, managing forests sustainably and enhancing forest carbon stocks.

facts.text: Together they cover avoiding forest loss, avoiding decline in forest condition, keeping existing stocks and managing forests to sustain them.
Enhancement means activities that raise the carbon stored in forests over time, such as replanting or natural regrowth.
Reduced-impact logging can fall under sustainable management of forests.

entries.title: REDD+ in phases: getting ready before getting paid

definition.text: The UN plan for REDD+ to move in stages: readiness, then national policies and measures, then fully measured results-based actions.

facts.text: The first stage, called readiness, covers national strategies, monitoring capacity, reference levels, safeguards and stakeholder participation.
Readiness has been funded through bodies such as the UN-REDD Programme, set up in 2007 by UNDP, UNEP and FAO, and the World Bank's Forest Carbon Partnership Facility.
Norway's International Climate and Forest Initiative, announced in 2007, has funded forest programmes including Brazil's Amazon Fund.

entries.title: Forest inventories: counting the trees

definition.text: The systematic collection of data about a forest, such as its trees, timber and wildlife, for assessment or analysis.

facts.text: Measurements include species, diameter at breast height, height, site quality, age and defects.
From these one can calculate trees per acre, basal area, timber volume and value.
It began in late 18th-century Europe from fear that wood, the main fuel, would run out.
Ground inventories are combined with satellite remote sensing in national forest monitoring for REDD+.

entries.title: National forest monitoring: watching forests from space and ground

definition.text: A country's institutions and techniques for monitoring its forests and producing information for decisions and reporting.

Between 2005 and 2020 countries with good remote-sensing forest monitoring rose from 55 to 99, and with good national inventories from 48 to 102.

entries.title: HFC-23: the offset that paid to make pollution

definition.text: CDM credits paid for destroying HFC-23, a super-potent by-product of refrigerant making, which became the classic case of a perverse offset incentive.

facts.text: With a warming potential 11,000 times that of CO2, destroying one tonne earned 11,000 credits.
Destruction cost only 0.2–0.5 €/tCO2, while buyers paid around 20 €/tCO2.
By June 2013, 23 HFC-23 projects had received 38% of all CERs.
The EU banned HFC-23 credits from its trading system from 1 May 2013, citing perverse incentives and lack of additionality.

entries.contested_note: Critics condemned the windfall profits, while the Carbon Trust argued that criticising the CDM for finding cheap reductions was perverse.

facts.text: It also pledges to restore hundreds of millions of acres of degraded land.

entries.title: The time value of carbon: why sooner cuts count more

definition.text: The idea that cutting a tonne of greenhouse gas now is worth more than cutting the same tonne later, so emissions are discounted over time like money.

facts.text: It is a discount rate on the physical carbon itself, not the money discount rate used to appraise carbon projects.
Pathways that reach zero emissions on the same date emit different totals: early deep cuts emit least, delayed cuts most.
A high carbon discount rate rewards cutting emissions early; a low one weakens the push for immediate action.
If the time value is positive, even temporary storage of carbon in trees or soil has real value because it delays warming.

entries.title: Corresponding adjustments: stopping two countries claiming one cut

definition.text: An accounting step under the Paris Agreement that subtracts a transferred emission cut from the seller country's tally so that only the buyer counts it.

facts.text: They prevent double claiming, where both the transferring and acquiring country count the same reduction toward their national targets.
Transferred outcomes must be recorded as a gain for one party and a reduction for the other.
Rules adopted at COP26 set out how corresponding adjustments and reporting work in practice.
When a host government authorises voluntary-market credits for Article 6 use, a corresponding adjustment may be required.

entries.title: Over-crediting: more credits than cuts

definition.text: Issuing more carbon credits than the real emission cuts or removals a project achieved, sometimes producing so-called phantom credits.

facts.text: Perverse incentives can reward over-crediting when buyers focus on headline tonnes rather than real impact.
One estimate held that about 90% of Verified Carbon Standard rainforest credits were likely phantom credits.
Critics note that over-crediting persisted even where programs already applied additionality, conservative measurement and permanence rules, often through inflated baselines.
The risk of over-crediting is a central worry in debates over trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

entries.contested_note: Commentators dispute how far over-crediting undermines Article 6 trading and voluntary markets.

entries.title: Bonds: lending money in a form that can be sold

definition.text: A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable security: the issuer borrows money and promises to pay the holder interest and repay the principal.

facts.text: Interest is usually paid at fixed intervals, often every six months or every year.
Bonds fund borrowers' long-term investments, or for governments, current spending.
Bondholders are lenders while stockholders are owners; bondholders are repaid first if the company goes bankrupt.
Bonds usually have a fixed term, or maturity, unlike stocks; most last less than 30 years.
They are issued by governments, banks, companies and international institutions, and are mostly bought by institutions such as pension funds and insurers.
The coupon is the interest rate the issuer pays; it can be fixed or float with a reference rate.

entries.title: Return on investment: what you get back for what you put in

definition.text: Return on investment is the ratio of the profit an investment earns to what it cost.

facts.text: A high return on investment means the gains compare well with the cost.
It is used to judge how efficient one investment is or to compare several, and the one with the highest return is usually chosen first.
A simple form is the gain from the investment minus its cost, divided by its cost.
Example: $10,000 invested plus $200 in fees, worth $12,500 after a year with $300 in dividends, gives an annual return.
It is not adjusted for time, so long-term investments need a discounted version using net present value.
Traditional ROI ignores the value and risks of natural and social capital because it leaves out environmental, social and governance performance.

entries.title: Stock: owning a slice of a company

definition.text: Stock is all the shares into which ownership of a company is divided; one share is a fraction of ownership.

facts.text: A share usually entitles its holder to part of the company's earnings, part of what is left after debts in liquidation, and votes.
Common stock usually carries votes; preferred stock usually does not but gets dividends first.
Selling shares to the public on a stock exchange for the first time is an initial public offering, or IPO.
Raising money by selling stock is equity financing, while issuing bonds is debt financing that avoids giving up ownership.
A share's price at any moment is set by supply and demand for it.
Shareholders' claims on company assets rank below those of creditors.

entries.text: Buy one share and you own a fraction of a company. Stock is all the shares into which a company's ownership is divided. entries.title: Environmental finance: making investment less harmful to nature

definition.text: Environmental finance is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature.

facts.text: It seeks to move business resources toward sustainable investments while keeping profits.
Richard Sandor proposed a course on emission markets in 1992 at the University of Chicago, later called Environmental Finance.
Inspired by the idea of social cost, Sandor focused on cap-and-trade along with taxes and subsidies.
Under cap-and-trade, a total emissions cap is set and firms receive permits they can buy or sell, rewarding cuts and penalising excess.
The Dow Jones Sustainability Index, launched in 1999, rates the ecological and social impact of stocks for investors.
Climate finance, a part of it, splits into mitigation finance, which cuts emissions, and adaptation finance; mitigation takes over 90% of climate spending.

entries.title: Official development assistance: the measure of foreign aid

definition.text: Official development assistance is the OECD's measure of foreign aid: money that rich countries' governments give to promote poorer countries' development and welfare.

facts.text: The OECD Development Assistance Committee adopted the concept in 1969.
Most is grants, but soft loans count if their grant element is at least 25%.
ODA was US$168 billion in 2019, of which US$152 billion came from DAC donors.
In 2019, 28% of all ODA was multilateral, pooled through bodies such as the EU, the World Bank's IDA and UN agencies.
In 2025 aid from DAC donors fell 23% after inflation, the biggest yearly drop on record.
Critics call it an untidy, somewhat arbitrary category that counts spending mainly benefiting donors, such as refugee costs at home.
It is a channel for international public conservation finance, through grants, concessional loans and technical help.

entries.title: The economics of biodiversity: how life props up the economy

definition.text: The economics of biodiversity studies how the variety of life supports the economy and how economic activity in turn harms it.

facts.text: Biodiversity underpins ecosystem services, the benefits people get from ecosystems, and affects how productive ecosystems are.
It supplies food, medicines and industrial materials such as wood, cotton, wool and silk, and supports recreation and tourism.
The WWF Living Planet Report of 2018 argued that the whole global economy, worth US$125 trillion, ultimately relies on nature.
Most species have never been assessed for their present or future economic importance.
Valuing biodiversity mainly for its benefits to people is debated by economists, as is its value in itself.
Nature also inspires industrial design: the field of biomimetics copies natural models, as when humpback whale fin ridges inspired wind turbine blades.
Biodiversity is a source of food, medicines and industrial materials, and recreation and tourism also rely on it.
The WWF's 2018 Living Planet Report argued that the whole global economy of US$125 trillion ultimately relies on nature.

entries.contested_note: Economists debate whether biodiversity should be valued only for its benefits to people and whether money values for it are reliable.

entries.title: Conservation finance: raising money to protect nature

definition.text: Conservation finance is raising and managing money to protect land, water and natural resources.

facts.text: It draws on public, private and nonprofit money, using tools from loans and grants to tax breaks and market-based mechanisms, at local to national scales.
Conservation has traditionally been paid for by donations, foundation grants and government money such as tax incentives, ballot measures, bonds and agency budgets.

It is sometimes set apart from fundraising: fundraising gathers money that is never paid back, while conservation finance uses a wider set of financial tools to mobilise and manage capital for conservation results.
Its supporters argue that public and charitable funding falls far short of global needs; one widely cited estimate put yearly needs in the hundreds of billions of dollars, far above actual flows.
To close that gap it tries to add money from financial markets, through debt financing, tax benefits, private equity and project finance.
Early tools were debt-for-nature swaps in the 1980s, followed by incentive-based approaches such as payments for ecosystem services.
By the mid-2000s it was described as a distinct field, and recent analyses stress drawing in private capital through labelled bonds and blended finance.
Deals are usually built around an identifiable source of cash flow or budget authority that can pay for conservation over time.

entries.title: Debt-for-nature swaps: trading debt for conservation

definition.text: A debt-for-nature swap forgives part of a developing country's foreign debt in exchange for that country investing locally in conservation.

facts.text: Thomas Lovejoy of WWF proposed the idea in 1987, after the Latin American debt crisis cut indebted countries' ability to fund conservation.
The first swap, in 1987, let Conservation International buy US$650,000 of Bolivian debt for US$100,000 in return for conservation commitments.
Swaps work where default risk is high, so funders can buy debt well below face value; the government then pays in local currency for conservation.
Most swaps occur in tropical, species-rich countries with rapid deforestation and fairly stable political systems.
Since 1987 they have generated over US$1 billion for conservation in developing countries.
Swaps fell from about five a year in the late 1980s and early 1990s to about two a year after 2000, partly because commercial debt became pricier.
Swap experience shaped later tools such as conservation trust funds.

entries.title: Blended finance: using public money to draw in private investors

definition.text: Blended finance uses public development money and charitable funds strategically to draw private investment into developing countries.

facts.text: It mixes public and private funds in one deal, each party using its expertise in a complementary way.
It aims at the Sustainable Development Goals, which in 2017 estimates needed an extra $2.5 trillion a year in financing.
Philanthropic or concessional money takes the first losses, reassuring private investors that their principal is protected.
Each concessional dollar can attract several private dollars, often 3x to 10x; a $2 million first-loss layer drawing $10 million is a 5x multiplier.
The OECD's Development Assistance Committee adopted blended finance principles in 2018.
The OECD identified 180 blended finance funds and facilities with $60.2 billion invested across 111 developing countries.
Critics say it shifts profits to private, mostly Northern, investors while leaving risks with Southern governments, and that its complexity weakens transparency.
In nature conservation it is used to overcome risk, small deal sizes and transaction costs that deter private investors.

entries.contested_note: Scholars and NGOs criticise blended finance for shifting profits to private investors and risks to poorer countries' governments.

entries.title: Diversification: not putting all your eggs in one basket

definition.text: Diversification is spreading money across different investments so that no single asset or risk can do too much harm.

facts.text: The proverb 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' sums it up: more risk of losing one egg, less of losing them all.
If prices do not move in perfect step, a diversified portfolio varies less than the average of its parts.
It narrows the range of outcomes: returns never beat the best single asset nor fall below the worst.
Holding just one stock is risky; a single stock can fall 50% in a year.
A 1977 study found 30 stocks gave almost the same risk reduction as 1,000, and even four gave most of it.
Market correlations tend to rise in crises, weakening diversification just when investors need it.

entries.title: Trophy hunting: can killing animals save them?

definition.text: Trophy hunting is hunting for sport in which parts of the killed animal, such as the head, horns or hide, are kept and displayed.

facts.text: Supporters argue it gives economic reasons to conserve wildlife areas: 'if it pays it stays'.
The IUCN recognises that well-managed trophy hunting can create strong incentives to conserve species and habitats outside protected areas.
After South Africa legalised white rhino hunting, landowners reintroduced the species and numbers rose from under one hundred to more than 11,000.
Poorly managed, it can distort age and sex structures, disrupt social groups and cause population declines.
A 2017 Economists at Large report found trophy hunting was under one percent of tourism revenue in eight African countries, and critics say little reaches local communities.

entries.contested_note: Supporters say trophy hunting funds conservation, while opponents say it is immoral and brings little money to conservation or local people.

entries.title: Fiduciaries: managing money in someone else's interest

definition.text: A fiduciary is a person trusted to look after money or other assets for someone else and to act only in that person's interest.

Under Delaware law, which governs most large US firms, directors owe duties of care, loyalty and good faith.

entries.title: Why the economy keeps eating into biodiversity
entries.article: Economics of biodiversity#Impact of economic activity on biodiversity

definition.text: Economic activities often harm biodiversity, and their profits mean they are usually favoured over conservation and restoration.

facts.text: Main causes include habitat loss, land-use change, pollution and overexploitation.
BCG estimates that over 90% of human drivers of biodiversity loss come from agriculture, infrastructure, fashion and energy.
The IUCN estimates that 79% of threatened species are affected by agriculture, infrastructure, energy and mining.
Failing to halt land biodiversity loss between 2000 and 2010 was estimated to cost the global economy $500 billion.
Continued loss raises long-term risks such as pandemics, floods and droughts.

entries.title: Bond yield: the return a bond pays

definition.text: A bond's yield is the rate of return an investor earns from it.

facts.text: Current yield is the yearly interest divided by the bond's market price.
Yield to maturity estimates the total return from buying at today's price and holding to the end, counting the present value of all payments.
Yield and price move in opposite directions: when market interest rates rise, bond prices fall.

entries.title: Additionality, leakage and permanence: three tests of paid conservation

definition.text: Three tests of whether paid-for conservation really works: whether the result would not have happened anyway, whether harm simply moves elsewhere, and whether gains last.

facts.text: Additionality asks whether a financed action achieves conservation that would not have happened without the payment.
Leakage, or spillover, is when protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another, cutting the net benefit.

Permanence worries arise where results depend on people keeping to agreements over long periods; durability depends on contract length, enforcement, land pressures and whether behaviour persists after payments stop.
Setting baselines and counterfactuals is hard in practice, which weakens claims of additionality and impact.

entries.text: Paying for conservation raises three awkward questions. Would the result have happened anyway? Did the harm simply move? Will the gain last? The first is additionality: whether a financed action achieves conservation that would not have happened without the payment. The second is leakage, or spillover, when protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another and cuts the net benefit. The third is permanence. Worries arise wherever results depend on people keeping agreements over long periods. Durability then depends on contract length, enforcement, pressure on the land, and whether behavior persists after payments stop. All three rest on baselines and counterfactuals, which are hard to set in practice, and that weakens claims of impact.

entries.title: Return on integration: counting nature in the bottom line

definition.text: Return on integration widens return on investment to count the long-term environmental and social returns of an investment alongside financial ones.

facts.text: The social cost of carbon can be built in to capture the damage an investment's emissions do to society.
It supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, combining financial, environmental and social results in one balance sheet.
A related method, social return on investment, measures environmental and social value not shown in ordinary accounts.

entries.title: Tax breaks for giving up development rights

definition.text: In the United States, donating a qualifying conservation easement can earn the landowner federal income tax deductions and other tax breaks.

facts.text: The donation's value is the drop in the property's market value caused by the easement, set by a qualified appraiser.
To qualify the easement must be perpetual, held by a qualified public or nonprofit body, and serve a real conservation purpose.
Easements can also cut estate taxes, since heirs pay on farmland value rather than development value.
Some states give tax credits, and Colorado and Virginia let landowners sell them to others.

States commonly fund conservation through real estate transfer taxes, bonds and lottery proceeds.
Many states and counties run programmes to buy agricultural easements that keep farmland from development.

entries.title: The 0.7% aid target that few countries meet

definition.text: The best-known aid target says rich countries should give 0.7% of their national income as official development assistance.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly formalised it on 24 October 1970; Sweden and the Netherlands first met it in 1974, and few others have since.
DAC donors as a group have given around 0.3-0.35% of their income since the 1970s.
In 2019 six countries met the target, and the UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of income in 2021.

A review found that in 2009, 51% of contract value was spent in donor countries though donors reported only 14% of aid as tied.

entries.title: The case against debt-for-nature swaps

definition.text: Critics argue that debt-for-nature swaps bring little real debt relief, send money to the wrong places and can harm local people.

facts.text: Debt relieved by swaps is under 1% of total external debt even in countries that use them often.
Early on, nearly three-quarters of swap funds went to Costa Rica, while Brazil, despite rapid deforestation, took little part.
Early swaps often overlooked people living on the land set aside, and some were labelled eco-colonialism.
Supporters, by contrast, describe swaps as deals in which every party benefits.

entries.title: Three kinds of debt-for-nature swap

definition.text: Debt-for-nature swaps come in three kinds: commercial three-party swaps run by NGOs, bilateral swaps between two governments, and multilateral swaps among several.

facts.text: In a three-party swap an NGO buys debt from commercial banks on the secondary market and passes it to the debtor in return for conservation commitments.
In a bilateral swap a creditor country forgives part of another government's debt in exchange for environmental commitments.
Recorded three-party swaps raised nearly US$140 million and bilateral and multilateral swaps nearly US$900 million for conservation from 1987-2010.

definition.text: Agricultural biodiversity is all the parts of biodiversity that matter for food and farming, the origin of every crop and farm animal.

facts.text: It earns income through food and raw materials and through services farms need, such as pollination, pest control, nutrient cycling and climate regulation.
Around 25% of the world's people are estimated to work in agriculture.
Putting a money value on biodiversity in farming and wild food is both hard and controversial.
By 2006 over 3 billion people depended on marine and coastal biodiversity for their livelihoods.

Introducing control species without enough research can backfire: cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles became an invasive species.

entries.title: How blended finance lowers investors' risk

definition.text: Development funders support private investors in blended deals through technical assistance, risk underwriting and market incentives.

facts.text: Technical assistance uses grants to build investees' capacity and lower transaction costs.
Guarantees, insurance and concessional tranches reduce risks such as currency swings, political instability and default.
Because concessional capital is catalytic rather than continuous, it can be recycled into new projects once investors gain confidence.

entries.title: The math of diversification

definition.text: Mixing assets can bring a portfolio's variance, a measure of risk, below that of even its least risky asset.

facts.text: With fraction q in asset X and 1-q in uncorrelated asset Y, portfolio variance is q²σx² + (1-q)²σy².
Variance is lowest at q = σy²/(σx²+σy²), giving σx²σy²/(σx²+σy²), below either asset held alone.
Markowitz's 1952 mean-variance framework showed portfolio risk depends on the covariance among returns, not just each asset's variance.

Land trusts date back at least to Roman times, but their clearest history begins in Henry VIII's England.
In Australia, Aboriginal land trusts hold freehold title to land on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

entries.title: Conservation land trusts: private groups that protect land

definition.text: A conservation land trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation.

facts.text: It may own land outright or buy an easement or development, mining or logging rights while the land stays private.
Land trusts rely on donations, grants and public programmes; landowners often donate easements or land itself.
Many depend on volunteers: in the 2005 US census, 54% of land trusts were all-volunteer.
The first, the Trustees of Reservations in Massachusetts, was founded in 1891; by 2021 the US had over 1,300.

definition.text: A Natural Asset Company is a corporation set up to hold and manage natural assets so that private investors can fund conservation and regenerative land use.

facts.text: Each company holds rights to land or sea areas such as forests, ranches, grasslands or marine areas, and is run to maximise their ecological value.
It reports yearly both ordinary financial statements and Ecological Performance Reports valuing ecosystem services such as carbon retention and freshwater.
The NYSE proposed listing them publicly in 2021 but withdrew the proposal in January 2024 amid political backlash.
Critics on the right fear locked-up public land and speculation; critics on the left doubt markets are a responsible way to steward nature.

entries.contested_note: Critics on both left and right dispute whether natural asset companies are a sound way to manage nature.

entries.title: Conservation trust funds: money that lasts

definition.text: A conservation trust fund is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work, often set up as an endowment or a fund spent down over time.

facts.text: They help pay for managing protected areas, including the running costs that short-term grants struggle to cover.
Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape later tools such as conservation trust funds.

entries.text: Short-term grants struggle to pay the running costs of a nature reserve year after year. A conservation trust fund is built for that job. It is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work. Many are endowments that live off their returns; others are spent down over time. Such funds help pay for managing land set aside for nature. Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape them.

entries.title: Measuring what conservation money achieves

definition.text: Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved.

facts.text: Reports may separate outputs, such as area under management, from outcomes, such as changes in ecological condition.
The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures recommends reporting nature-related dependencies and impacts, though data gaps limit consistency.
Payment schemes also raise equity questions: who can be paid, how schemes affect land tenure and livelihoods, and whether wealthier landholders benefit most.

entries.title: Where conservation money comes from
entries.article: Conservation finance#Sources of capital and actors

definition.text: Money for nature comes from domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment.

facts.text: Market-rate capital can come from private investors and from public or charitable investors working through development finance institutions and multilateral development banks.
Conservation NGOs and foundations often act as go-betweens that implement projects.
Because NGOs receive much of their income from governments and foundations, adding up total conservation finance risks counting the same money twice.
Public and charitable money is sometimes described as catalytic: covering early costs or sharing risk so that private investment follows.

entries.title: Transaction costs: the hidden price of conservation deals

definition.text: The costs of finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring conservation projects, often cited as a barrier to scaling up.

facts.text: These costs bite hardest where projects are small, varied or need intensive monitoring and verification.
They can make projects less investable and raise the cost of capital.
Debt-for-nature swaps, for example, need coordination among debtor governments, creditors and NGOs.

entries.title: Catastrophe bonds: investors who bet against disaster

definition.text: A catastrophe bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors.

facts.text: If the named disaster happens, the principal goes to the sponsor to fund recovery; otherwise investors get it back at maturity plus interest.
They were first used in the mid-1990s after Hurricane Andrew and the Northridge earthquake.
Rising climate-related disaster risk has led governments and insurers to use them when reinsurance is unavailable or too costly.
Investors like them because returns are largely uncorrelated with stocks and ordinary bonds, aiding diversification.
Swiss Re estimated the market at $43.1 billion at the end of 2023, with a record $15.4 billion issued that year.
Most are rated below investment grade, B or BB, based on the probability a qualifying disaster triggers a loss.

entries.title: What sets off a catastrophe bond

definition.text: Catastrophe bonds pay out under different triggers: the insurer's actual losses, modelled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured event parameters.

facts.text: Triggers closer to the insurer's own losses protect it better; index and parametric triggers spare investors from the insurer's claims handling.
A trigger can apply per single event or to the sum of losses over a period, usually a year.
Example: with a $90 billion aggregate attachment, three $20 billion hurricanes and a $40 billion earthquake total $100 billion and trigger payout.

entries.title: Parametric insurance: paying out when the wind passes a line

definition.text: Parametric, or index-based, insurance pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached.

facts.text: Ordinary indemnity insurance pays the assessed loss after an event; parametric insurance only checks that the trigger was passed, using weather services, sensors or satellites.
Its main benefit is fast payout, giving cash for recovery soon after a disaster, and lower transaction costs.
Its main drawback is basis risk: payouts follow parameters, so they may not cover the full damage.
Mexico's Quintana Roo insures a coral reef with a wind-triggered policy paying up to $3.8 million a year; Hurricane Delta in 2020 triggered an $850,000 payout.
Pooled schemes such as the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, set up in 2007, let countries buy cover more cheaply than alone.

entries.title: Sustainable finance: seeking returns while weighing the planet

definition.text: Sustainable finance covers the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns.

facts.text: It is often used as a synonym for ESG investing, but the wider field also includes impact investing, social finance and ethical investing.
The Paris Agreement asks parties to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development.
It is described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets.
Green, social and sustainability bonds and sustainability-linked bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025.
Public finance stays important, but much of the money for climate goals is expected to come from the private sector.
Over two decades it grew from a niche topic into a recognised field of research and university teaching.

entries.title: ESG: judging companies by more than their profits

definition.text: ESG is an investing approach that weighs a company's environmental, social and corporate governance record alongside its finances.

facts.text: The term came to prominence in the 2004 UN-backed report 'Who Cares Wins'.
By 2023 ESG represented more than US$30 trillion in assets under management.
Environmental issues it weighs, such as emissions, biodiversity and waste, often reflect externalities not handled by markets.
The social pillar covers effects on workers and communities, and the governance pillar covers how firms are directed and controlled, including ethics, corruption and tax.
ESG saw outflows for the first time in 2023, and many US funds have dropped ESG terms from their names amid greenwashing claims.
Critics cite poor data and standards, greenwashing and claims that big asset managers impose rules without democratic oversight.
A 2005 legal report for UNEP's finance initiative concluded that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably part of investors' fiduciary duty.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute ESG's data quality, its standards and its political legitimacy.
entries.text: By 2023, investments managed under the ESG label topped US$30 trillion. ESG, short for environmental, social and governance, is an investing approach that weighs a company's record on those three fronts alongside its finances. The term came to prominence in a 2004 UN-backed report, 'Who Cares Wins'. The environmental pillar covers issues such as emissions, biodiversity and waste, which often reflect externalities that markets do not handle. The social pillar covers effects on workers and communities. The governance pillar covers how firms are directed and controlled, including ethics, corruption and tax. A 2005 legal report for UNEP's finance initiative concluded that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably part of an investor's duty to clients. The backlash has been real. ESG funds saw outflows for the first time in 2023, and many US funds have dropped ESG terms from their names amid claims of misleading green marketing. Critics point to poor data and standards, and argue that big asset managers impose rules without democratic oversight. Its data, standards and political legitimacy all remain disputed.

entries.title: Green bonds: borrowing only for green projects

definition.text: A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits.

facts.text: Like ordinary bonds, they can be issued by governments, development banks or companies, which repay the bond plus interest.
Eligible projects include renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution control, sustainable land use, biodiversity, clean transport and climate adaptation.
The European Investment Bank issued a Climate Awareness Bond in 2007, and the World Bank issued the first labelled green bond in 2008.
Green bonds mobilised over $93 billion in 2016, still only around 1% of global bond issuance.
By 2024 cumulative green bond issuance had reached about $700 billion.
Legally they barely differ from ordinary bonds: green promises are often not written into the contract in a binding way.
The EU Green Bonds Regulation came into force on 21 December 2024, creating the 'European Green Bond'.
Critics question the green credentials of some bonds and issuers, as when the Climate Bonds Initiative refused to list a Repsol bond in 2017.

conflicts.text: Green bond issuance rose 92% to $92 billion from 2015 to 2016.
