entries.title: Impact investing: profit with a measurable purpose

definition.text: Impact investing puts money into companies, organisations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return.

facts.text: It aligns an investor's values with where capital goes, in fields such as renewable energy, education and microfinance.
It spans asset classes such as private equity, venture capital and debt, and can target returns from below-market to above-market.
The term was coined in 2005, and modern impact funds grew prominent soon after the Great Recession.
In 2024 about 3,907 organisations managed an estimated $1.571 trillion in impact assets, far smaller than the $78 trillion global equity market.
Research finds many impact investors accept expected returns 2-4 percentage points lower in exchange for measurable social impact.
The SDGs need an estimated $5-7 trillion of investment a year, mostly expected from private capital, and impact investors linked their funds to them.

entries.title: Climate, green and sustainable finance: three nested terms

definition.text: UNEP separates three nested terms often used as synonyms: climate finance, green finance and sustainable finance.

facts.text: Climate finance mainly funds adaptation, resilience, mitigation and a just transition.
Green finance covers climate finance plus other environmental issues such as protecting biodiversity.
Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports sustainable development.
One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

entries.text: Money for climate, green finance and sustainable finance are often treated as the same thing. The UN Environment Programme separates them as three nested circles. {{ref:nature-clim-042}}, the smallest, mainly funds adaptation, resilience, cutting emissions, and a fair shift away from fossil fuels. Green finance covers that plus other environmental issues, such as protecting biodiversity. Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports development able to last. The field has a short history. One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

entries.title: Green taxonomies: official lists of what counts as green

definition.text: A taxonomy is an official classification that says which economic activities count as green or sustainable for investors.

facts.text: The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define such a classification, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020.
Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make greener choices.
Investments are judged against six objectives: climate mitigation, climate adaptation, the circular economy, pollution, water and biodiversity.
Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, with some expert advisers threatening to resign over gas.
Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

entries.contested_note: Whether fossil gas and nuclear power belong in the EU taxonomy is disputed.
entries.text: Which investments deserve the green label? A sustainable finance taxonomy answers with an official classification of the economic activities that count as green or sustainable. Its aim is to stop misleading green claims and help investors make greener choices. The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define one, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020. Investments are judged against six objectives: cutting emissions, adapting to climate change, reusing materials, pollution, water and biodiversity. The hardest calls were political. Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, and some expert advisers threatened to resign over gas. Whether either belongs in the taxonomy is still disputed. The EU was not alone: Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

entries.title: Does ESG pay? The evidence on returns
entries.article: Environmental, social, and governance#Relationship between ESG and Corporate Valuation

definition.text: Economists disagree about whether attention to ESG raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns.

facts.text: Milton Friedman argued that social responsibility harms a firm's financial performance.
A 2011 study found the '100 Best Companies to Work For' beat their peers' stock returns by 2-3% a year.
Some studies link ESG indicators to higher value, while others say overinvesting in ESG can hurt it.
Some research suggests an inverted-U shape, with an optimal level of ESG spending beyond which returns fall.

entries.contested_note: Studies of ESG and company value give mixed results, from positive to negative to inverted-U.
entries.text: Milton Friedman argued that social responsibility harms a firm's financial performance. Economists still disagree about whether attention to environmental, social and governance issues raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns. Some evidence points the other way from Friedman. A 2011 study found the '100 Best Companies to Work For' beat their peers' stock returns by 2-3% a year. Other studies link ESG indicators to higher company value. Still others warn that overinvesting in ESG can hurt it. Some research suggests an inverted U: value rises with ESG spending up to an optimal level, then falls. The results so far are mixed, from positive to negative to that middle ground, and no single answer has won out.

entries.title: Five ways investors put their values to work

definition.text: Responsible investors steer money using several methods: positive selection, exclusion, engagement, activism and integration of ESG factors.

facts.text: Positive selection picks companies meeting ESG criteria or the best performers in each sector.
Exclusion removes sectors or firms from consideration on ESG grounds; integration adds ESG risks and opportunities to ordinary financial analysis.
Engagement and activism use shareholder dialogue and voting to push companies to change.
The best-known early case was the 1970s and 1980s disinvestment from South Africa over apartheid.
Screening brings its own risks, such as concentration in a few sectors.

entries.text: The best-known early case of responsible investing was the disinvestment from South Africa in the 1970s and 1980s, in protest against apartheid. Today responsible investors steer money using five main methods. Positive selection picks companies that meet ESG criteria, or the best performers in each sector. Exclusion removes sectors or firms from consideration on ESG grounds. Integration adds ESG risks and opportunities to ordinary financial analysis. Engagement and activism use dialogue with companies and shareholder voting to push them to change. Each method has trade-offs. Screening, for example, brings its own risks, such as concentrating money in a few sectors.

entries.title: Eco-investing: betting on clean technology

definition.text: Eco-investing, or green investing, is socially responsible investing focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices.

facts.text: Unlike broader socially responsible investing, it narrows to environmental issues, especially renewable energy and clean technology.
One tracker estimated over $1.248 trillion invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007.
New green technologies carry high up-front costs that are harder to justify to investors.

entries.title: Aggregate confusion: why ESG scores disagree

definition.text: Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare.

facts.text: Many bodies write reporting standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors.
One paper found ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time, against 99% for credit ratings from the largest agencies.
This spread is called the ESG ratings gap or 'aggregate confusion'.
Because standards vary and change, some funds labelled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.

entries.title: Green central banking: should central banks fight climate change?

definition.text: Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use monetary policy and capital rules to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment.

facts.text: In 2018 eight central banks created the Network for Greening the Financial System, which has grown to nearly 116 central banks and supervisors.
Banks have proposed a lighter 'green-supporting factor' on capital rules, while central bankers and nonprofits prefer heavier capital charges on fossil-fuel assets.
Many researchers argue that pursuing such goals strains the legitimacy of independent central banks, whose mandates rarely include climate aims.

entries.title: Disclosure rules: making companies report climate risk

definition.text: Rules and standards that ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them.

facts.text: The Financial Stability Board launched the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures in 2015 to push firms to report climate risks and how they govern them.
Research shows disclosure policies have limited effect when they stay voluntary.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, adopted in October 2022, widens coverage to about 50,000 companies from about 11,700.

entries.title: The greenium: paying extra to be green

definition.text: The greenium is the lower yield, or pricing premium, that green bonds often carry because investors want them.

facts.text: Empirical studies find high demand gives green bonds lower yields than ordinary equivalents.
The primary-market greenium ranges from -85 to +213 basis points, while the secondary market averages -1 to -9 basis points.
Voluntary green labels with weak oversight leave room for greenwashing, which may lead investors to accept lower returns than for brown investments.

Voluntary labels with weak oversight leave room for false green claims, which may lead investors to accept lower returns than on ordinary, or brown, investments.

entries.title: Fiduciary duty and ESG: may investors weigh the planet?

definition.text: A debate over whether investors' legal duty to beneficiaries allows, or even requires, them to weigh environmental, social and governance issues.

facts.text: A 2015 report, 'Fiduciary Duty in the 21st Century', concluded that ignoring long-term value drivers including ESG is itself a failure of fiduciary duty.
In the United States, some question whether pension funds that weigh such factors break their duty to maximise returns.
A 2005 legal report for UNEP similarly found that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably required.
One US state pension board blocked fossil fuel divestment on fiduciary grounds, though a 2019 analysis found the divested fund would have earned more.

entries.title: Social finance: private money for public needs

definition.text: Social finance is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return.

facts.text: Unlike philanthropy, it sustains itself by being profitable for investors rather than relying on donors.
It has no agreed definition but includes impact investing, socially responsible investing and lending to social enterprises.
It grew quickly after the 2008 financial crisis as investors sought ethical alternatives.
Critics argue it pulls capital from productive uses, while backers say it adds direct investment where charity is declining.
It struggles with low returns, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect by mainstream banks and poor access to retail investors.

entries.contested_note: Scholars dispute whether social finance adds value beyond corporate social responsibility or simply diverts capital.

entries.title: Social impact bonds: investors paid only for success

definition.text: A social impact bond is an outcomes-based contract in which private investors fund a public programme and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary bonds, they have no fixed return; payment depends on social outcomes.
The first, launched in the UK in 2010, funded prisoner rehabilitation at Peterborough Prison.
By 2022 there were 276 projects with $745m raised, used in 23 countries as of May 2023.
Backers say taxpayers pay only for success; critics say they displace other funding and are an expensive way to run programmes.

entries.title: Sustainability-linked bonds: interest tied to targets

facts.text: Performance is tracked with key performance indicators measured against sustainability performance targets.

Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020; over 85% were tied to environmental indicators, most often emissions cuts.

entries.title: CITES: a treaty to police the wildlife trade

definition.text: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a treaty that protects endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade.

facts.text: Its text was agreed by 80 countries in Washington, D.C. on 3 March 1973, and it entered into force on 1 July 1975.
It is legally binding on its Parties, but each must pass its own laws to apply it nationally.
It works by controlling trade in listed species as they cross borders, including products made from them such as traditional medicines.
Over 40,900 species, subspecies and populations are protected.
It works as a negative list: trade in any species is unregulated unless it is listed, so many species are traded with no review.
Critics say it ignores habitat loss and poverty and does not address market demand; listings can even increase speculation in high-value species.
As of 2002, 50% of Parties lacked one or more of its four major implementation requirements.

entries.title: Integrated conservation and development: making protection pay locally

definition.text: A biodiversity conservation project that also invests in rural development, so that local people gain from protecting nature.

facts.text: WWF introduced them in the mid-1980s to fix problems with the non-participatory "fines and fences" approach.
They are usually tied to a protected area and funded from outside by conservation and development agencies.
They assume that more varied livelihoods will ease human pressure on biodiversity.
Critics say projects were designed with little local input and rarely share costs and benefits with women and minority groups.
They can overlook outside pressures such as market demand and illegal logging, and may collapse when external funding ends.

entries.contested_note: WWF says its projects work with local organisations, while critics say they exclude local voices and can harm communities.
entries.text: In the mid-1980s WWF set out to fix the problems of 'fines and fences', a style of conservation that gave local people no say. Its answer was the integrated conservation and development project: a biodiversity project that also invests in rural development, so local people gain from protecting nature. Such projects are usually tied to a park or reserve and funded from outside by conservation and development agencies. They assume that more varied livelihoods will ease human pressure on biodiversity. Critics say many were designed with little local input and rarely shared costs and benefits with women and minority groups. They can also overlook outside pressures such as market demand and unlawful tree felling, and may collapse when outside funding ends. WWF says its projects work with local organizations, so the record remains disputed.

entries.title: The ivory trade and the fight over elephants

definition.text: The commercial, often illegal trade in the tusks of elephants and of other animals such as hippopotamus, walrus and narwhal.

facts.text: Elephant ivory has been exported from Africa and Asia for millennia; at its colonial-era peak 800 to 1,000 tonnes a year went to Europe alone.
African elephants fell from about 1.3 million in 1979 to 600,000 in 1989, with around 75,000 killed each year for ivory worth about 1 billion dollars.
The main threat turned out to be the international ivory trade rather than habitat loss.
Southern African states opposed the 1990 ban, saying their elephant herds were well managed and ivory revenue funded conservation.
Zimbabwe and others argued wildlife needs economic value to survive and local communities must be involved.
In 1997 CITES let Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe sell 49 tonnes of registered stockpiles to Japan as an "experiment".
The piano industry abandoned ivory keys in the 1980s for plastic, and synthetic ivory now exists.

entries.contested_note: States disagree on whether a total ban or regulated sales that fund conservation best protect elephants.

The ivory trade, the commercial and often illegal trade in tusks of elephants and animals such as hippos, walruses and narwhals, is ancient. At its colonial-era peak, 800 to 1,000 tonnes a year went to Europe alone. The crash showed that the international ivory trade, more than habitat loss, was the main threat, and a ban followed in 1990. Southern African states opposed it. They said their herds were well managed and ivory revenue funded conservation, and Zimbabwe argued that wildlife needs economic value to survive. In 1997 {{ref:nature-mkt-001}} let Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe sell 49 tonnes of stockpiled ivory to Japan as an 'experiment'. Whether a total ban or regulated sales best protect elephants is still disputed. Demand can shift: the piano industry dropped ivory keys for plastic in the 1980s.

entries.title: Reserve design: where to put a park and how big

definition.text: Planning a nature reserve's size, shape, location and links so that it actually achieves its goal of protecting biodiversity.

facts.text: Planners must weigh habitat preferences, migration, climate change and public support.
A reserve set up where people depend on the land for their livelihood often fails, as when Bolivia's expanded Amboró park later had to be shrunk.
Too-small reserves bring carnivores into contact with people, raising their mortality.
Reserve networks linked by wildlife corridors protect species that migrate, and can raise movement between patches by up to 50%.
To be cost-effective, reserves should be placed in species-rich places such as biodiversity hotspots.
Designs must allow for future ranges, since 80% of observed range shifts have moved polewards or upward at an average of 6.1 km per decade.

entries.text: Bolivia expanded Amboró park into land people depended on for their living, and later had to shrink it again. Networks linked by wildlife corridors protect species that migrate and can raise movement between patches by up to 50%. For value for money, reserves should sit in species-rich places such as biodiversity hotspots. They must also allow for future ranges, since 80% of observed range shifts have moved toward the poles or uphill, at an average of 6.1 km per decade.
entries.text_plain: Bolivia expanded Amboró park into land people depended on for their living, and later had to shrink it again. Reserve design is the planning of a reserve's size, shape, location and links so that it actually protects biodiversity. Planners must weigh habitat needs, migration, climate change and public support. Size matters: reserves that are too small bring carnivores into contact with people, raising their death rate. Networks linked by wildlife corridors protect species that migrate and can raise movement between patches by up to 50%. For value for money, reserves should sit in species-rich places such as biodiversity hotspots. They must also allow for future ranges, since 80% of observed range shifts have moved toward the poles or uphill, at an average of 6.1 km per decade.

entries.title: Human–wildlife conflict: when people and animals collide

definition.text: Harmful encounters between people and wild animals, with bad results both for people and their property and for wildlife and its habitat.

facts.text: It comes from competition between people and wildlife for natural resources, and has grown with population growth and changing land use.
Consequences include destroyed crops, livestock killed by predators, human injury and death, damaged infrastructure and disease spread.
Crop damage by elephants can lead locals to kill elephants in retaliation; in Sri Lanka up to 80 people and over 230 elephants die each year.
Hidden costs include health impacts, opportunity costs and transaction costs.
Fear of predators can worsen conflict more than the actual damage done.

entries.text: In Sri Lanka, up to 80 people and over 230 elephants die each year in clashes between the two. Elephants raid crops, and farmers kill them in revenge. Human–wildlife conflict covers such harmful encounters, which hurt both people and their property and wildlife and its habitat. It comes from competition for land, water and food and has grown with population and changing land use. The damage includes destroyed crops, livestock killed by predators, injury and death, damaged infrastructure and the spread of disease. There are hidden costs too, in health, opportunity costs and transaction costs. Fear itself matters: fear of predators can worsen conflict more than the damage they actually do.

entries.title: The three CITES lists

definition.text: The three CITES lists that rank protected species by how much international trade threatens them, and set the trade controls that apply.

facts.text: Appendix I species face extinction: commercial trade in wild specimens is banned and other trade needs both import and export permits.
Appendix II species are not necessarily threatened but need controlled trade; most listed taxa are here and need an export permit.
Appendix III species are protected in at least one country that has asked other Parties to help control trade.
Captive-bred specimens of Appendix I species may be traded as if they were Appendix II.

entries.text: CITES sorts protected species into three lists, or appendices, by how much international trade threatens them. Appendix I species face extinction: commercial trade in wild specimens is banned, and other trade needs both import and export permits. Appendix II holds most listed species; they are not necessarily threatened but need controlled trade and an export permit. Appendix III species are protected in at least one country that has asked other members to help control trade. Captive-bred specimens of Appendix I species may be traded as if they were Appendix II.

entries.title: Fences, dogs and compensation: easing conflict with wildlife

definition.text: The methods used to reduce harmful encounters between people and wildlife, from fences and guard dogs to paying people for their losses.

facts.text: The most successful solutions involve local communities in planning, implementation and maintenance.
Some governments pay compensation for wildlife losses to discourage retaliatory killing; results vary because of under-payment and late payment.
Livestock-guarding dogs cut animal losses to on average 60 times lower than the norm.
Moving problem animals elsewhere is largely ineffective and can harm the species.

entries.text: Livestock-guarding dogs cut animal losses to, on average, 60 times lower than the norm. Some governments pay compensation to discourage revenge killing, with mixed results because payments come late or fall short. Moving problem animals elsewhere is largely ineffective and can harm the species.

entries.title: Conservation triage: choosing which species to save

definition.text: The idea that not every species can be saved, so conservationists must choose which ones to spend their limited efforts on.

facts.text: The pressure comes from extinction threats estimated at 15 to 37 percent of all species by 2050.
Critics say "endangered species triage" decides which species to let go instead of re-examining the economics driving the decline.

entries.contested_note: Supporters see triage as realistic priority-setting, while rights-of-nature critics say it accepts losses instead of changing the economics behind them.

entries.title: Marxan: software that designs reserves

definition.text: A family of software for systematic reserve design that finds networks of sites meeting biodiversity targets at low cost.

facts.text: It uses simulated annealing to minimise the total cost of a reserve system while representing a set share of each feature.
Computationally it solves a conservation version of the 0-1 knapsack problem.
It is the most widely used conservation planning software, used for systems covering about 5% of Earth's surface, including the Great Barrier Reef reserve network.
Exact integer programming tools such as prioritizr guarantee optimal solutions and can find cheaper ones faster.

entries.text: Marxan is the most widely used conservation planning software, behind systems covering about 5% of Earth's surface, including the Great Barrier Reef reserve network. It finds networks of sites that meet biodiversity targets at low cost. It uses simulated annealing, a trial-and-error search, to minimize a reserve system's total cost while covering a set share of each feature. In computing terms it solves a conservation version of the 0-1 knapsack problem: picking items of the most value within a budget. Exact tools such as prioritizr guarantee the best solution and can find cheaper ones faster.

entries.title: Paper parks: protected in name only

definition.text: A protected area that exists on paper but has little real management or protection on the ground.

facts.text: It can result from weak governance, weak regulations or lack of enforcement.
A 2020 study of 3,449 European marine protected areas found 70% faced at least one significant threat and 86% of the network was hit by damaging fishing gear.

entries.title: Natural resources: where every product begins

definition.text: Something drawn from nature and used with few changes, such as sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife.

facts.text: Every man-made product is made, at bottom, from natural resources.
Some resources are renewable and are restored by natural processes, while many extractive industries rely on non-renewable resources that can be extracted only once.
Who gets natural resources is at the centre of many economic and political confrontations, especially when scarcity is increasing.
Resource extraction is a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage.
In 1982 the UN's World Charter for Nature recognised the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity.
Natural resource management focuses on how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life for present and future generations.

entries.text: Trace any man-made product back far enough and it ends in nature. A natural resource is something drawn from nature and used with few changes: sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife. Economists count these among the basic inputs to production, the {{ref:nature-econ-086}}. Some resources are restored by natural processes. Many extractive industries, though, rely on materials that can be dug or pumped out only once. That difference shapes much of what follows. Who gets these resources sits at the center of many economic and political confrontations, and the fights sharpen as scarcity increases. Extraction is also a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage. In 1982 the United Nations' {{ref:nature-gov-056}} recognized the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity. A whole field now asks how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life, for people alive today and for generations to come.

entries.title: Resource depletion: using nature faster than it returns

definition.text: The using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced.

facts.text: A resource's value depends on how much of it exists in nature and how costly it is to extract; under supply and demand, scarcer resources become more valuable.
Types of depletion include wetland and ecosystem degradation, soil erosion, aquifer depletion and overfishing.
Extraction of both renewable and non-renewable resources rose sharply with the Industrial Revolution, as new technology and economic growth raised demand.
Although rooted in colonialism and industrialisation, depletion has been a major concern only since the 1970s.
Wealthy nations have been described as outsourcing resource depletion to poorer nations, which suffer the greatest ecosystem losses.
The tragedy of the commons is used to explain many forms of resource depletion.

entries.text: The problem is centuries old, but it became a major concern only in the 1970s. Resource depletion is the using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced. It takes many shapes: degraded wetlands and other ecosystems, eroded soil, drained underground water stores, and fish caught faster than they can breed. Its roots lie in colonialism and industrialization. With the Industrial Revolution, new technology and economic growth raised demand, and extraction of every kind of resource rose sharply. entries.title: Non-renewable resources: the stock that does not come back

definition.text: A natural resource, also called a finite resource, that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with how fast people use it.

facts.text: Minerals and metal ores, fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) and groundwater in some aquifers are all non-renewable.
Ore deposits form only where geological processes concentrate metals, which takes tens of thousands to millions of years, so near-surface deposits are non-renewable on human time-frames.
Coal, oil and gas take thousands of years to form and cannot be replaced as fast as they are used; fossil fuels are the main energy source humans use today.
Some argue carbon fuel is practically inexhaustible if methane hydrates on the sea floor are counted, though whether they can be extracted at viable cost is unknown.
In economics, a non-renewable resource is a good where using more today means less is available tomorrow.
David Ricardo argued that a mineral's price should rise over time, with the costliest mine setting the price and cheaper mines earning a differential rent.
Without regulation, people and firms tend to keep using non-renewable resources because the easier, cheaper option often differs from the environmentally friendly one.

entries.title: Renewable resources: the stock that regrows, if allowed

definition.text: A natural resource, also called a flow resource, that replaces what is used up through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale.

facts.text: Resources whose recovery is unlikely ever to exceed a human time scale are called perpetual resources.
Water, forests, plants and animals are renewable only as long as they are adequately monitored, protected and conserved.
Water stays renewable only when its use is carefully controlled; groundwater pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable.
Sun, wind, water movement and geothermal heat are practically infinite and cannot be depleted.
Unregulated industrial growth endangers renewable resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them.
Overuse of renewables such as deforestation, overgrazing and overfishing was already a large problem in early modern times.
An unregulated industry practice can lead to complete depletion of a renewable resource, as overfishing shows.
Building renewable energy devices still uses non-renewable resources such as mined metals and land.

entries.text: A forest can regrow and a fish population can breed back, but only if people let them. A renewable resource, also called a flow resource, replaces what is used through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale. Some sources, such as sun, wind, moving water and geothermal heat, are practically infinite and cannot be depleted. Resources whose recovery will probably never outlast a human time scale get a name of their own, {{ref:nature-res-215}}. Water, forests, plants and animals stay renewable only as long as they are monitored, protected and conserved. Water shows the catch. It is renewable only when its use is carefully controlled, and underground water pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable. Overuse is not new: deforestation, overgrazing and fishing too hard were already large problems in early modern times. Unregulated industrial growth endangers these resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them. Fisheries show how far it can go, since an unregulated industry can wipe a renewable resource out completely. Even clean energy has a hidden draw: building renewable energy devices uses mined metals and land.

entries.title: Natural resource economics: running an economy within nature's limits

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources.

facts.text: A main aim is to understand nature's role in the economy so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available for future generations.
Its focus is how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's natural resources.
The traditional curriculum centred on fisheries, forestry and mineral extraction models: fish, trees and ore.
More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond optimal commercial exploitation alone.
Its traditional topics include welfare theory, land use, pollution control, resource extraction, non-market valuation, exhaustibility and sustainability.
The subfield began when researchers were mainly concerned with optimal commercial exploitation of natural resource stocks; environmental economics was once distinct from it.
Ecological economics criticises resource economics for focusing mainly on efficient allocation and less on fair distribution and the scale of the economy.

entries.text: Fish, trees and ore: for decades, those three made up the core of the subject. Natural resource economics is the branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources. It began when researchers mainly wanted to know how to exploit stocks of resources commercially in the best way. Its traditional curriculum centered on models of fisheries, forests and mineral extraction. Its classic topics include welfare theory, how land is used, pollution control, resource extraction, valuing what markets do not price, exhaustibility and sustainability. Environmental economics was once a separate subject. More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond commercial exploitation alone. The field's main aim now is to understand nature's role in the economy, so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available to future generations. Put simply, it asks how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's resources. Not everyone is satisfied. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} criticizes the field for focusing mainly on efficient allocation, and less on fair distribution and on the scale of the economy.

entries.title: Exploiting natural resources to fuel growth

definition.text: Using natural resources, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development.

facts.text: It is often accompanied by environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict.
It reached an industrial scale in the 19th century as mining, steam power and machinery expanded extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels.
Drivers include better technology, which speeds extraction, and overconsumption and consumerism, which raise demand.
Raw materials are often taken from developing countries by foreign industries, with local communities receiving little of the profit.
About 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and more than 90% could be degraded by 2050, according to the FAO.
To be sustainable, the rate at which a resource is consumed must stay equal to or below the rate at which it is supplied.
Economist Julian Simon rejected the idea that resources are finite, arguing that substitution, recycling and new technology make scarcity increasingly tenuous.

entries.contested_note: Julian Simon and others reject the view that natural resources are fundamentally finite.
entries.text: In the 19th century, mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels. The exploitation of natural resources means using them, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development. Two forces speed it up: better technology, which makes extraction faster, and rising consumption and consumerism, which raise demand. The costs often land on others. Exploitation tends to bring environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict. Foreign industries often take raw materials from developing countries, and local communities see little of the profit. Soil shows the scale. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) finds that about 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and that more than 90% could be by 2050. The rule for sustainable use is simple to state: consume a resource no faster than it is supplied. Not everyone accepts that resources are finite at all. The economist Julian Simon argued that substitution, {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} and new technology make scarcity ever more doubtful, a view others strongly dispute.

entries.title: Malthusianism: when population outruns food

definition.text: The theory that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily, so living standards eventually fall until population declines.

facts.text: It stems from Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 An Essay on the Principle of Population.
Malthus argued that technology could raise resources and living standards, but the extra abundance would fuel population growth until resources per person fell back to their old level.
A Malthusian catastrophe, or Malthusian trap, is predicted if population outpaces farm output, causing famine or war.

Evidence fits the pre-industrial era: from 1 to 1500 AD better technology raised population density but not living standards, and a labourer's daily wage bought about 15 pounds of wheat in ancient Babylonia and 13 in England in 1800.
After World War II, mechanised farming and the Green Revolution greatly raised crop yields, and most developed countries' populations grew slower than productivity.
Many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in character, predicting that consumption will outstrip new supply and cause a crisis.
Critics such as William Hazlitt argued Malthus confused natural limits on output with the artificial way society distributes it.

entries.contested_note: Critics from Ricardo onward have disputed Malthus's theory, and 20th-century growth did not produce the predicted catastrophe.

Critics from Ricardo onward disputed the theory, and the 20th century's growth did not bring the predicted catastrophe. Still, many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in shape, predicting that consumption will outrun new supply.

entries.title: Economic rent: income that rewards no effort

definition.text: Any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use.

facts.text: Classical economists saw rent as payment for non-produced inputs such as land and location, or for privileges such as patents.
Rent is seen as unearned income, unlike economic profit, and competition cannot eliminate it.
In farming and extraction, economic rent arises from the scarcity and uneven spread of natural resources such as land, oil and minerals.
Scarcity rent is what is paid for identical land when supply is short of demand; differential rent is the surplus from better land over the poorest land in use.
Governments can collect part of resource rent as royalties or extraction fees on minerals, oil and gas.
Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity and proposed it as the main source of public revenue.
Since the late 1800s the term has had several conflicting definitions, often used interchangeably, causing considerable confusion.
Public choice theorists later used rent for wealth transferred through state-granted rights, the source of the term rent seeking.

entries.text: Some income rewards no effort at all. Economic rent is any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use. Unlike economic profit, rent counts as unearned income, and competition cannot wipe it out. In farming and extraction, rent arises because land, oil and minerals are scarce and unevenly spread. Scarcity rent is paid for identical land when supply falls short of demand. Differential rent is the surplus that better land earns over the poorest land in use. Governments can collect part of it as royalties on minerals, oil and gas. Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity, and proposed it as the main source of public revenue. Later, public choice theorists used the word for wealth transferred through rights the state grants, the origin of the term rent seeking.
entries.text_plain: Some income rewards no effort at all. Economic rent is any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use. Unlike economic profit, rent counts as unearned income, and competition cannot wipe it out. In farming and extraction, rent arises because land, oil and minerals are scarce and unevenly spread. Scarcity rent is paid for identical land when supply falls short of demand. Differential rent is the surplus that better land earns over the poorest land in use. Governments can collect part of it as royalties on minerals, oil and gas. Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity, and proposed it as the main source of public revenue. Later, public choice theorists used the word for wealth transferred through rights the state grants, the origin of the term rent seeking.

entries.title: The resource curse: riches that hold countries back

definition.text: The idea that countries rich in natural resources such as oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources.

facts.text: Richard Auty first used the term 'resource curse' in 1993 for mineral-rich countries that grew more slowly than countries without plentiful resources.
The idea is older: in 1711 The Spectator observed that the most plentiful countries often had the poorest living.
A 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong link between resource abundance and poor economic growth.
The IMF counts 51 countries as resource-rich, meaning at least 20% of exports or 20% of government revenue comes from nonrenewable resources; 29 of them are low or lower-middle income.
Oil and mineral prices swing widely, so governments that depend on them face volatile revenues that disrupt planning and debt payments.
Extraction tends to form an enclave with few links to the rest of the economy, and its high profits draw the best workers and investment away from other industries.
Countries whose economies are dominated by extraction tend to be less democratic and more corrupt; petroleum is the resource most consistently tied to weaker institutions.
Most experts think the curse is not universal or inevitable, but strikes certain kinds of countries under certain conditions.

entries.contested_note: There is no academic consensus on whether resource abundance harms development; studies with empirical support reach contradictory findings.

entries.title: Ecological yield: the harvest an ecosystem can spare

definition.text: The amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover.

facts.text: It is most often measured in forestry, where sustainable forestry harvests no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch.
If more is consumed than is renewed, the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time.
It is a theoretical quantity that can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's.
Firms that borrow to buy land rights may face debt that demands more yield than the land can renew, and the winner's curse leads winning bidders to overestimate it.
Only about 10% of biomass passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of herbivores and 1 kg of carnivores.
In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic biomass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis.
Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating land productivity, that is, ecological yield.

entries.text: A forest can give up some wood each year and still stand. Ecological yield is the amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover. It is most often measured in forests, where sustainable harvesting takes no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch. Take more than is renewed and the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time. The figure can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's. Firms that borrow to buy rights to land may owe debts that demand more yield than the land can renew. Food chains shrink yield fast. Only about 10% of biomass passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of plant-eaters and 1 kg of meat-eaters. In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated that humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic biomass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis. Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating this yield.

entries.title: Sustainable yield: harvesting without shrinking the stock

definition.text: The amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it.

facts.text: Formally, it is the ecological yield that can be taken without shrinking the natural capital itself, keeping ecosystem services at the same level or higher.
It applies only to renewable resources, since extracting non-renewable resources always reduces natural capital.
It is often calculated as half the carrying capacity, the population level at which a stock can be harvested and still regrow.
It changes over time: a forest hit by a natural disaster needs more of its own yield to recover, so its sustainable yield falls.
It is used mostly in forestry, fisheries and groundwater, where a 'safe yield' marks the extraction rate beyond which an aquifer is overdrawn.
Overfishing in the mid-1850s led to maximum sustainable yield becoming a reference point for fishery management.
Sustainable yield forestry is criticised for focusing only on wood, changing landscapes and reducing biodiversity; the term has also been called anthropocentric.
In fisheries, fishing shrinks the original population while breeding and growth add to it; sustainable yield is the balance between the two.

conflicts.text: Under the logistic model, maximum sustainable yield is at exactly half the carrying capacity.
conflicts.note: Different model assumptions (logistic vs modern age-structured models), noted for the verifier; not strictly the same definition.

entries.text: A stock of fish or trees can be harvested forever, as long as the harvest stays within one limit. Sustainable yield is the amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it. Formally, it is the ecological yield that can be taken without shrinking the natural capital itself. It applies only to renewable resources, because extracting non-renewable ones always reduces natural capital. It is often calculated at half the carrying capacity, a level at which a stock can be harvested and still regrow. A forest hit by a natural disaster needs more of its own growth to recover, so its sustainable yield falls. The idea is used mostly for forests, fisheries and underground water, where a 'safe yield' marks the pumping rate beyond which the store is overdrawn. After fish were overharvested in the mid-1850s, {{ref:nature-res-013}} became a reference point for managing fisheries. Critics say forest harvesting planned this way values only wood, changes landscapes and reduces biodiversity, and some call the whole idea anthropocentric, centered on human needs.

entries.title: The Hubbert curve: how a resource rises, peaks and falls

definition.text: A bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time.

facts.text: Geologist M. King Hubbert first presented it in 1956 to the American Petroleum Institute.
Using the 1948 peak in oil well discoveries, Hubbert predicted that oil production in the contiguous United States would peak around 1970.
It is a symmetric logistic distribution curve, often confused with the normal (Gaussian) curve, which it resembles.
Real production curves are often lopsided because of new extraction techniques, competing resources and government regulation.
US output followed the curve for 35 years after the early-1970s peak, but new extraction methods pushed it to a record 10.07 million barrels a day in November 2017.
It has been applied to natural gas, coal, uranium, copper, helium and water, and a modified version fits any resource harvested faster than it is replaced.

entries.text: In 1956 the geologist M. King Hubbert presented the American Petroleum Institute with a curve and a forecast. The Hubbert curve is a bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time. Using the 1948 peak in oil well discoveries, Hubbert predicted that oil production in the contiguous United States would peak around 1970. After an early-1970s peak, US output followed his curve for 35 years. Then new extraction methods pushed it to a record 10.07 million barrels a day in November 2017. Real production curves are often lopsided like this, bent by new techniques, competing resources and government rules. Strictly, the curve is a symmetric logistic distribution, often confused with the normal, or Gaussian, curve it resembles. It has been applied to natural gas, coal, uranium, copper, helium and water. A modified version fits any resource harvested faster than it is replaced.

entries.title: Peak oil: the top of the world's production curve

definition.text: The point when world petroleum production reaches its highest rate, after which it declines for good.

facts.text: Predictions of the peak range from 2025 to after 2050.
Reserves are finite, but the key issue is whether extraction is economically viable at current prices.
Conventional oil production is recognised to have peaked around 2005–2006; rapid growth in US tight oil since 2008 has kept total output rising.
Every oilfield eventually declines: output typically rises, plateaus and then falls, the assumption behind Hubbert peak theory.
Past predictions often failed: forecasts in 2007 and 2009 of an imminent peak were followed by record production in 2018 and 101.73 million barrels per day in 2023.
A sharp fall in oil supply could raise the costs of transport, food, heating and electricity worldwide, since modern farming depends on oil-derived fuel and chemicals.
Critics argue that as prices rise, unconventional sources become economically viable, so the world is only running out of cheap oil.

entries.contested_note: Peak oil theory is controversial; critics argue new reserves and unconventional oil have postponed any peak.
entries.text: Every oilfield eventually runs down: output rises, levels off, then falls. Still, a sharp fall in supply could raise the cost of transport, food, heating and electricity everywhere, because modern farming depends on fuel and chemicals made from oil.

entries.title: Resource rent: what nature pays after the bills

definition.text: The economic rent earned from using natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind.

facts.text: It is the surplus left after selling a resource's output and paying all extraction and production costs, including a normal return.
Differential (Ricardian) rent comes from better sites: a coal firm with $20/t costs earns more rent than one with $30/t costs at the same price.
Scarcity (Hotelling) rent arises because extracting a finite resource today leaves less for later; if oil's price rises from $50 to $70 while costs stay $30, rent per barrel rises from $20 to $40.
Entrepreneurial rent, or quasi-rent, comes from management skill or investment that cuts costs or raises price.
Resource rents have been called a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources.
In fisheries, maximum economic yield is the catch at which resource rent is greatest; catching more counts as economic overfishing.

entries.text: Sell a resource's output, pay every cost of getting it out, including a normal return, and what is left is resource rent. It is the economic rent earned from natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind. It comes in several kinds. Differential, or Ricardian, rent comes from better sites: at the same price, a coal firm with costs of $20/t earns more rent than one with $30/t. Scarcity rent arises because extracting a finite resource today leaves less for later. If oil's price rises from $50 to $70 while costs stay at $30, rent per barrel rises from $20 to $40. Entrepreneurial rent, a form of {{ref:nature-res-219}}, comes from skill or investment that cuts costs or raises the price. Some call resource rents a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources. In fisheries, the catch that makes this rent largest is {{ref:nature-res-084}}, and catching more only shrinks the rent.

Entrepreneurial rent, a form of Quasi-rent: a machine's temporary windfall, comes from skill or investment that cuts costs or raises the price. Some call resource rents a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources. In fisheries, the catch that makes this rent largest is Maximum economic yield: the catch that pays best, and catching more only shrinks the rent.

entries.title: Hotelling's rule: why oil in the ground should gain value

definition.text: A rule describing how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it so as to earn the most rent.

facts.text: With efficient extraction, the net price rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, maximising the present value of the resource.

The rule implies that efficient use of a non-renewable, non-augmentable resource under stable conditions leads to its depletion, with a net price rising at the rate of interest to reflect growing scarcity.
The maximum rent obtainable while emptying the stock is called Hotelling rent or scarcity rent.
This resource rent equals the resource's net price, its selling price minus costs, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital.
Harold Hotelling published the analysis in the Journal of Political Economy in 1931; L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.
It is one of the best known early attempts at the economics of exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels.

conflicts.text: Hotelling's rule is dated to 1938.
conflicts.note: Natural resource economics gives 1938; Hotelling's rule and Non-renewable resource pages give 1931.

entries.text: An owner of oil faces a choice each year: extract now, or leave it in the ground and sell later. In 1931 {{ref:nature-hist-062}} published the classic answer in the Journal of Political Economy. Hotelling's rule describes how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it to earn the most rent. The net price is the selling price minus costs. With efficient extraction it rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, which maximizes the present value of the resource. The rule also implies that efficient use of a resource that cannot be added to, under stable conditions, ends in its depletion. The largest rent obtainable while emptying the stock is the subject of {{ref:nature-res-252}}. That rent equals the net price, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital still in the ground. L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.

entries.title: Sorting natural resources four ways

definition.text: Ways of sorting natural resources by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership.

facts.text: By origin, resources are biotic, from living things (including fossil fuels formed from decayed organic matter), or abiotic, from non-living material such as land, water and ores.
By stage of development, potential resources are known but unused, such as unextracted petroleum, while actual resources are surveyed and in use.
By ownership, resources can be individual, community, national or international, such as international waters.

entries.text: Coal and oil count as living resources, at least by origin. Natural resources can be sorted by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership. By origin, biotic resources come from living things, including fossil fuels formed from decayed organic matter. Abiotic ones come from non-living material such as land, water and ores. By stage, potential resources are known but unused, like unextracted petroleum, while actual resources are surveyed and in use. By ownership, they can be individual, community, national or international, as with international waters.

entries.title: Dutch disease: when a boom hollows out the rest

definition.text: The apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in other sectors such as manufacturing or agriculture.

facts.text: The Economist coined the term in 1977 for the decline of Dutch manufacturing after the Groningen gas field was discovered in 1959.
Boom revenues strengthen the country's currency, making its other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose competitiveness.
It can follow any large inflow of foreign currency, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment, not just resource discoveries.
Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialise in extraction, but this can backfire when resources deplete, since manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left.
Remedies include saving boom revenues abroad in a sovereign wealth fund, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for lagging sectors.
It is hard to diagnose, but evidence suggests very large unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average raise the real exchange rate and shrink lagging sectors.

entries.text: In 1959 the Netherlands discovered the Groningen gas field, and Dutch manufacturing then declined. In 1977 The Economist coined a name for the pattern: Dutch disease. It describes the apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in others such as manufacturing or agriculture. The mechanism runs through the currency. Boom revenues strengthen it, making the country's other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose ground. Any large inflow of foreign currency can do this, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment. Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialize in extraction, but this backfires when the resource runs down, because manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left. Diagnosis is hard. Still, very large, unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average seem to raise the real exchange rate and shrink lagging sectors. Remedies include saving boom revenue abroad in a {{ref:nature-res-243}}, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for the lagging sectors.

entries.title: Ricardo's law of rent

definition.text: The principle that the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labour and capital.

facts.text: David Ricardo formulated it around 1809 and set it out fully in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation; it is the origin of the term Ricardian rent.
In Ricardo's example, plots yield 100, 90 and 80 units of corn; once the 90-unit plot must be farmed, the best plot earns a rent of 10 units.
Ricardo argued that 'corn is not high because a rent is paid, but rent is paid because corn is high'.
The output of the best rent-free land is called the margin of production; rent is the difference between a site's productive capacity and this margin.
It applies to urban and rural land alike, and to any natural factor of production that is privately owned.
Ricardian rent differs from contract rent, the actual payments tenants make for using others' property.

entries.title: Marine resources: what the oceans offer

definition.text: Physical and biological things found in the oceans that are useful to people.

facts.text: They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine renewable energy.
The term was popularised by Sustainable Development Goal 14, which aims to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.
Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

entries.text: The oceans hold far more than fish. Marine resources are the physical and biological things in the oceans that are useful to people. They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine renewable energy. The term spread through the UN goal set in 2015 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources, {{ref:nature-gov-027}}. Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

entries.title: The blue economy: making a living from water

definition.text: Economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably.

facts.text: There is no agreed definition; the World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving ocean ecosystem health.
It spans fisheries, aquaculture, shipping and tourism as well as emerging activities such as offshore renewable energy, blue carbon and seabed mining.
It also covers unpriced ocean ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration, coastal protection and biodiversity.
The term was popularised by the Rio+20 UN Conference on Sustainable Development in 2012.
Mangrove forests support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s.
In 2023 the EU's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added.
Misleading claims about effects on aquatic environments have been called bluewashing, by analogy with greenwashing.

entries.text: In 2023 the European Union's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added. The blue economy is the economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably. There is no agreed definition. The World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving the health of ocean ecosystems. It spans fisheries, fish farming, shipping and tourism, plus newer activities such as offshore renewable energy, {{ref:nature-nbs-034}} and seabed mining. It also covers unpriced ocean services such as storing carbon, coastal protection and biodiversity. Mangrove forests show what is at stake. They support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s. The term spread after a UN conference on sustainable growth in 2012, {{ref:nature-hist-008}}. Misleading claims about effects on waters have their own label, {{ref:nature-nbs-080}}.
entries.text_plain: In 2023 the European Union's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added. The blue economy is the economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably. There is no agreed definition. The World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving the health of ocean ecosystems. It spans fisheries, fish farming, shipping and tourism, plus newer activities such as offshore renewable energy, Blue carbon: the climate value of coastal mud and seabed mining. It also covers unpriced ocean services such as storing carbon, coastal protection and biodiversity. Mangrove forests show what is at stake. They support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s. The term spread after a UN conference on sustainable growth in 2012, Rio+20: the summit that called for new global goals. Misleading claims about effects on waters have their own label, Bluewashing: greenwashing for the oceans.

entries.title: Fixed stock or opportunity cost: two ways to count what is left

definition.text: A debate over whether to treat a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock, or to measure its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost.

facts.text: How best to describe resource depletion analytically is still debated.
Tilton and Lagos (2007) argued the opportunity cost view is better because price and opportunity cost represent the usable quantity.
Because total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists do not see physical scarcity as a good guide to a resource's availability.

entries.contested_note: Sources describe the question of how to model depletion analytically as an ongoing debate.
entries.text: How much of a mineral is left? The answer depends on what is counted. One view treats a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock that use steadily draws down. The other measures its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost. Tilton and Lagos (2007) argued the second view is better, because price and opportunity cost represent the quantity people can actually use. Since total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists doubt that physical scarcity is a good guide to availability. How best to model depletion remains an open debate.

entries.title: Underground water that will not refill in time
entries.article: Resource depletion#Groundwater as a non-renewable resource

definition.text: The view that much groundwater is effectively non-renewable because it refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes.

facts.text: Less than six percent of the world's water is replenished on a human timescale of 50 years.
Of the groundwater used for farming, 16–33% is non-renewable.
Overusing groundwater can lower water levels and dry up streams, harming surface ecosystems.

Pumping too much lowers water levels and can dry up streams, harming the ecosystems on the surface. {{ref:nature-res-133}} looks at this hidden store in more depth.

entries.title: Cornucopianism: the case for endless plenty

definition.text: The view that advancing technology can keep supplying humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited.

facts.text: The name comes from the cornucopia, the horn of plenty of Greek mythology; cornucopians or boomsters are contrasted with Malthusian doomsters.
Julian Simon's 1981 book The Ultimate Resource argued that humans have always found ways to develop resources past nearly any roadblock.
Simon held that free markets are needed: when a resource's price rises because supply is short, research into cheaper alternatives follows.
The label is rarely self-applied and is mostly used critically by those who see the view as over-optimistic.
Naomi Oreskes argued that many key innovations came from government action and that technological progress has not stopped the climate crisis.

entries.contested_note: Critics such as Lindsey Grant and Naomi Oreskes reject cornucopian arguments as flawed or over-optimistic.
entries.text: In Greek mythology the cornucopia, the horn of plenty, never runs dry. Cornucopianism borrows the name for the view that advancing technology can keep meeting humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited. Its believers, the 'boomsters', are set against Malthusian 'doomsters'. The economist Julian Simon made the classic case in his 1981 book The Ultimate Resource. Humans, he argued, have always found ways to develop resources past nearly any roadblock. Free markets were essential to his story: when shortage raises a resource's price, research into cheaper alternatives follows. Few people call themselves cornucopians. The label is mostly used by critics who find the view over-optimistic. Lindsey Grant and Naomi Oreskes reject its arguments as flawed. Oreskes points out that many key innovations came from government action, and that technological progress has not stopped the climate crisis.

entries.title: The Simon–Ehrlich wager: betting on scarcity

definition.text: A 1980 bet between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich on whether natural resources would become scarcer, measured by metal prices up to 1990.

facts.text: Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb (1968), expected resources to be outstripped by population growth; Simon bet that raw material prices would not rise in the long run.
Ehrlich chose copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, buying $200 of each on paper on 29 September 1980, with payoff on 29 September 1990.
All five fell in inflation-adjusted price even though world population grew by more than 800 million, and Ehrlich paid Simon $576.07.
Over 1980–2011 Simon would have lost on four of the five metals, and one study found he would have won in only 38.4% of periods from 1900 to 2008.
Some analysts conclude the bet shows luck mattered more than expertise, and does not prove there are no environmental limits to growth.
Simon declined Ehrlich and Schneider's later offer to bet on 15 environmental trends; he would have lost on 11 of them.

entries.contested_note: Observers disagree on what the wager proves, since the result depends heavily on the time period chosen.

entries.title: Land: the resource no one can make more of

definition.text: The idea that land can be reused but not created on demand, so economists treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price.

facts.text: Land surface can count as either renewable or non-renewable depending on what it is compared with.
In economic terms land has perfectly inelastic supply.
Unlike capital goods, land and non-renewable resources cannot be produced or increased.

entries.text: Land can be reused endlessly, but no one can create more of it on demand. Economists therefore treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price: in their terms, its supply is perfectly inelastic. Unlike machines and other capital goods, land and non-renewable resources cannot be produced or increased. Whether land surface counts as renewable or non-renewable depends on what it is compared with.

entries.title: Is nuclear fuel renewable?

definition.text: The question of whether nuclear fuels should count as renewable, since mined uranium is finite but breeder reactors make more fuel than they use.

facts.text: In 1987 the World Commission on Environment and Development classed breeder reactors, which produce more fissile fuel than they consume, as renewable energy sources.
Uranium, the most common fission fuel, occurs at low concentrations and is mined in 19 countries.
Nuclear power provides about 6% of the world's energy and 13–14% of its electricity.
Nuclear plants produce about 10,000 metric tons of high level waste each year worldwide, which is hazardous if not properly contained.

entries.title: Resource wars: fighting over what lies in the ground

definition.text: A war caused by conflict over resources, typically between whoever controls a resource and an aggressor who wants it.

facts.text: Industrialisation raised the raw materials nations need, and such power struggles have underlain conflicts since the late 19th century.
A classic example is the 19th-century conflict over guano, a nutrient-rich fertiliser, on Peru's Chincha Islands.
The geopolitical view sees resource conflict as strategic; the environmental security view sees it as a response to scarcity.
Conflicts can occur over control of resources and their revenues, one of the arguments linking resources with war.

entries.title: Grading mineral deposits by confidence and profit

definition.text: Systems for grading mineral deposits by how well they are known and whether they can be mined at a profit.

facts.text: A mineral resource is material in or on the Earth's crust with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction.
Resources are split, in increasing geological confidence, into inferred, indicated and measured.
A mineral reserve is the economically mineable part of a measured or indicated resource, divided into probable and, with highest confidence, proved reserves.
Most schemes follow the CRIRSCO International Reporting Template, such as Australia's JORC Code; the UN Framework Classification for Resources dates from 1997.
Ores are concentrated unevenly, so extraction eventually meets diminishing returns as it moves to less accessible sites and lower grades.

Because ores are concentrated unevenly, extraction eventually meets diminishing returns as it moves to poorer, less accessible sites.

entries.title: Malthus's two brakes on population

definition.text: Malthus's two kinds of brake on population: preventive checks that lower birth rates and positive checks that shorten lives.

facts.text: Preventive checks include celibacy and chastity; positive checks are chiefly war, plague and famine, but also poor health and economic conditions.
When positive checks cause high rates of premature death, the result is called a Malthusian catastrophe.

entries.text: Malthus saw two kinds of brake on population. Preventive checks lower birth rates, through celibacy and chastity. Positive checks shorten lives: chiefly war, plague and famine, but also poor health and economic conditions. When positive checks cause high rates of premature death, the result is called a Malthusian catastrophe.

entries.title: Neo-Malthusianism: the old fear in modern form

definition.text: The concern that overpopulation and overconsumption will deplete resources and degrade the environment until ecosystems collapse.

facts.text: Post-war crop gains were followed by rapid population growth, prompting Paul R. Ehrlich and others to predict an imminent Malthusian catastrophe.
A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that sustainability concerns had shifted from population growth to the balance between consumption and saving.
Herman Daly and Jeremy Rifkin raised neo-Malthusian concerns about modern mechanised agriculture.

sources.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population

entries.text: After the Second World War, crop gains were followed by rapid growth in human numbers. Paul R. Ehrlich and others then predicted an imminent Malthusian catastrophe. Neo-Malthusianism is the concern that too many people consuming too much will exhaust resources. The fear is that the environment then degrades until ecosystems collapse. {{ref:nature-hist-040}} and Jeremy Rifkin raised such concerns about modern mechanized farming. The emphasis has shifted, though. A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that sustainability worries had moved from the number of people to the balance between consumption and saving.

entries.title: Quasi-rent: a machine's temporary windfall

definition.text: A short-run, rent-like return earned by a factor of production, such as a machine or building, whose supply is fixed for the time being.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall developed the idea to extend rent reasoning from land to durable man-made factors fixed in supply in the short period.
Unlike pure rent, quasi-rent rewards the action needed to earn it, and in the long run it is competed away as new capital enters.

entries.text: Rent is not only for land. Alfred Marshall extended the idea to machines, buildings and other durable man-made factors whose supply is fixed for the time being. Quasi-rent is the short-run, rent-like return such a factor earns. Unlike pure rent, it rewards the action needed to earn it. And it does not last: in the long run it is competed away as new capital enters.

entries.title: Proven, probable, possible: counting oil reserves

definition.text: The grouping of oil reserves by how likely they are to be produced: proven, probable and possible.

facts.text: 1P (proven) reserves have at least a 90% probability of production, 2P (proven and probable) at least 50%, and 3P (proven, probable and possible) at least 10%.
Conventional and unconventional reserves are counted separately.
Critics say stated world reserves are inflated, with many so-called reserves actually being resources not available for production.

entries.text: Oil companies sort reserves by how likely they are to be produced. Proven, or 1P, reserves have at least a 90% probability of production. entries.title: Peak oil demand: when people stop wanting more

definition.text: The idea that world oil use will peak because people deliberately reduce demand, before supply runs short.

facts.text: The International Energy Agency argues demand will be cut first to address climate change and greenhouse gas emissions.
It relies on technologies such as electric vehicles and possibly biofuels replacing gasoline and diesel vehicles.
About 50% of oil use in OECD countries is for road transport.

The idea relies on electric vehicles and possibly biofuels replacing gasoline and diesel vehicles. Road transport is the obvious target: it takes about 50% of oil use in OECD countries.

entries.title: Unconventional oil: the hard-to-get barrels

definition.text: Oil that is difficult to extract, such as oil sands, as opposed to conventional oil from easy onshore and shallow offshore fields.

facts.text: The many processing steps make its production costs extremely high.
As conventional oil becomes scarcer, liquids from tight oil, oil sands, oil shale, gas-to-liquids, coal-to-liquids and biofuels can replace it.
