entries.title: The food system: from field to fork to bin

definition.text: All the connected people, institutions, policies and infrastructure involved in feeding a population.

facts.text: It covers production, processing, packaging, distribution, marketing, consumption and disposal of food waste.
Conventional food systems run on economies of scale, specialization, long supply chains and global trade to cut unit costs.
They have raised productivity and food availability but are linked to soil degradation, biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and unequal access to food.
Since 1961, food supply per person has risen by more than 30%.
The food system causes more than a third (34%) of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Conventional systems depend heavily on cheap fossil fuels for machinery, fertilizer and processing.

entries.text: Since 1961, food supply per person has risen by more than 30%. Conventional food systems cut unit costs through economies of scale, the savings of producing in bulk, along with specialization, long supply chains and global trade. They depend heavily on cheap fossil fuels for machinery, fertilizer and processing. The results cut both ways. These systems raised productivity and food availability, supporting {{ref:nature-es-108}}. They are also linked to soil degradation, biodiversity loss and unequal access to food. And the food system causes more than a third (34%) of global greenhouse gas emissions.

entries.title: Silviculture: growing trees as a crop

definition.text: The practice of controlling how forests grow, what they are made of and their quality, mainly to produce timber.

facts.text: It works at the level of the individual stand of trees, whereas forestry is the broader field.
It is essentially the commercial business of growing forest crops, based on knowledge of how trees and stands live.
Regeneration can come from self-sown seed, artificially sown seed or planted seedlings.
Tending treats a crop after planting, by spacing, pruning and thinning trees or by weeding out competing vegetation.
Pruning lower branches lets clear, knot-free wood grow, which is worth more.
In 16th-century Germany landowners developed silviculture to deal with deforestation.
On old, poor soils or where dry-season fires threaten the crop, trees may grow too slowly for silviculture to pay.

entries.text: In 16th-century Germany, landowners facing deforestation developed a new discipline: silviculture. It is the practice of controlling how forests grow, what they are made of and their quality, mainly to produce timber. Forestry is the broad field; silviculture works at the level of the stand, a single group of trees. At heart it is the commercial business of growing forest crops, built on knowledge of how trees and stands live. A new crop can come from self-sown seed, sown seed or planted seedlings. Tending follows: spacing, pruning and thinning trees, or weeding out competing plants. Pruning has a clear payoff. Removing lower branches lets clear, knot-free wood grow, which is worth more. It does not always pay, though. On old, poor soils, or where dry-season fires threaten the crop, trees may grow too slowly.

entries.title: LULUCF: counting the carbon from land and forests
entries.article: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: A greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals from direct human land use, land-use change and forestry.

facts.text: These activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or remove it, which influences climate.
UNFCCC guidelines require human-caused emissions to be reported in six sectors, LULUCF among them.
The Kyoto Protocol made accounting for afforestation, reforestation and deforestation mandatory, and for forest, cropland and grazing management voluntary.
Land-use, land-use change and forestry emissions averaged 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt C per year (4.1 ± 2.6 Gt CO2) over 2014–2023.
Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration, both of which affect climate.
A 2021 study found land-use change affected 17% of land in 1960–2019, with global trade affecting agriculture as a main driver.

conflicts.text: IPCC estimates land-use change contributes a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt carbon per year.
conflicts.note: Older IPCC estimate versus updated 2014–2023 average; different periods.

sources.title: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

entries.text: Over 2014–2023, land use, land-use change and forestry released an average of 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt of carbon a year, or 4.1 ± 2.6 Gt of carbon dioxide. A Gt, or gigatonne, is a billion tonnes. These emissions get their own line in greenhouse gas accounts, a sector known as LULUCF. It covers emissions and removals from direct human land use, changes in land use, and forestry. Such activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or take it out. UN climate guidelines require countries to report human-caused emissions in six sectors, and LULUCF is one. The {{ref:nature-clim-056}} made accounting for planting and clearing forests mandatory, but accounting for forest, cropland and grazing management voluntary. Changing land also alters how much sunlight the ground reflects and evapotranspiration, the water soil and plants release into the air. Both affect climate. A 2021 study found that changes in use touched 17% of land in 1960–2019, with global trade a main driver.

entries.title: Food loss and waste: a third of the harvest, thrown away

definition.text: Food that is thrown away or otherwise lost without being eaten.

facts.text: It happens at every stage of the food system, but most food waste arises after consumers buy food.
About one-third of the world's food is thrown away, wasting the resources used to produce it.
Global food waste is 931 million tonnes a year (about 121 kg per person): 61 percent from households, 26 percent from food service and 13 percent from retail.
Wasted food accounts for 3.3 billion tons of CO2-equivalent emissions a year, and landfilled food is a major methane source.
The FAO defines it as a decrease in the quantity or quality of food along the supply chain; definitions of loss versus waste vary.
Reducing it brings social gains, such as productivity, food security and lower environmental impact, that individual actors may not take into account.
The SDGs aim to halve per capita retail and consumer food waste by 2030.

entries.title: Clearcutting: felling a whole forest at once

definition.text: A logging practice in which most or all of the trees in an area are cut down at once.

facts.text: It is the most economically efficient way to log, and is also used to clear land for farming.
It mimics the start of forest regrowth after a fire or windthrow and favors fast-growing, sun-loving tree species.
Variants include standard, patch and strip clearcuts and clearcutting with reserves.
It differs from selective logging, where only a few trees per hectare are harvested.
Removing trees reduces water retention, which can worsen flooding and wash nutrients out of the soil.
One study found clear-cut zones had nearly three times the erosion from slides, about five times once logging roads were counted.
Its long-run effects depend on how well the forest is managed and whether the land is converted to other uses.

entries.contested_note: Loggers and forest-worker unions defend it on scientific, safety and economic grounds, while critics call it deforestation that destroys habitat; the costs of side effects like topsoil loss are intensely debated.

entries.title: Pastoralism: herding where crops cannot grow

definition.text: A way of raising livestock by letting the animals graze on large open pastures, historically by nomadic people who moved with their herds.

facts.text: It is practised where dryness, poor soils, extreme temperatures or lack of water make growing crops difficult or impossible.
As of 2019 between 200 million and 500 million people practised pastoralism, and 75% of all countries had pastoral communities.
Pastoralists manage rangelands covering about a third of Earth's land surface, producing food where crops cannot grow.
Mobile forms range from short daily moves, to transhumance between seasonal pastures, to fully nomadic herding.
Enclosure of common land, harder borders, fences and expanding crop farming have made settled pastoralism more common.
One review of many studies found pastoralism 2 to 10 times more productive per unit of land than capital-intensive alternatives, yet policies often try to replace it.
Grazing on savannas and woodlands can help keep their biodiversity and stop them turning into dense shrubland or forest.
Because they work marginal land in extreme environments, pastoral communities are very vulnerable to global warming.

entries.title: Shifting cultivation: farm a plot, then let it rest

definition.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while, then left to regrow wild vegetation while the farmer moves on to another plot.

facts.text: Cropping usually stops when the soil tires or, more often, weeds take over, and the fallow period is usually longer than the cropping period.
Land is often cleared by slash-and-burn, and after two or three years of crops the plot is left for another.
Fallows are not idle: they supply timber, firewood, medicines and game, and tree fallows protect soil from erosion and lift nutrients from deep layers.
It was one of the first forms of farming, and it is still widespread in the tropical developing world.
Stable cycles are vulnerable to fast population growth and outside economic change; chain saws and cash crops have shortened fallows and lengthened cropping.

Shifting cultivators are often blamed for forest loss, but sources argue tropical deforestation is driven by the same forces that cleared Europe's forests: urbanization, industrialization, affluence and population growth.
FAO's naming of shifting cultivation, but not logging, as a cause of deforestation led to a clash with environmental groups.

entries.text: Shifting cultivation was one of the first forms of farming, and it is still widespread in the tropical developing world. The fallow, the resting period, usually lasts longer than the cropping. Fallows are not idle. They supply timber, firewood, medicines and game, and tree fallows protect soil from erosion and lift nutrients from deep layers. Shifting cultivators are often accused, but some sources argue it comes from the forces that cleared Europe's forests: urbanization, industrialization, affluence and population growth. When the FAO named shifting cultivation, but not logging, as a cause of deforestation, it clashed with environmental groups.

entries.title: Slash-and-burn: fertilizing a field with fire

definition.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to make a field, called a swidden.

facts.text: The cut vegetation dries and is burned, leaving nutrient-rich ash that fertilizes the soil and briefly clears weeds and pests.
After about three to five years nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade, so farmers move on; recovery takes from five to more than twenty years.
A rough estimate is that 200–300 million people worldwide use it.
It has been used to clear land for crops and livestock since Neolithic times.
On the very poor, leached soils of places like the Amazon it is one of the few kinds of farming possible, and it has been sustainable for thousands of years.
It is sustainable only with a huge amount of land or few people, and is poorly suited to cash crops.
It is a common method of agricultural deforestation that has become less sustainable.
Replacing it with slash-and-char could offset up to 12% of human carbon emissions from land-use change each year (0.21 gigatonnes).

entries.text: Roughly 200–300 million people worldwide farm by slash-and-burn, a method in use since Neolithic times. The nutrient-rich ash fertilizes the soil and briefly clears weeds and pests. After about three to five years the nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade, so farmers move on. There it has been sustainable for thousands of years. But it works only with a huge amount of land or few people, and it suits cash crops poorly. It has become a common, and less sustainable, method of agricultural deforestation. Replacing it with {{ref:nature-clim-179}} could offset up to 12% of human carbon emissions from changing land use each year, some 0.21 gigatonnes.

entries.title: Groundwater depletion: pumping faster than it refills

definition.text: Pumping groundwater out faster than an aquifer's equilibrium yield, also called overdrafting.

facts.text: Excessive pumping is the main cause, and insufficient recharge makes the aquifer less useful.
Safe yield is what can be withdrawn without exceeding long-term recharge; sustainable yield also accounts for impacts on surface water.
Pumping creates a cone of depression around a well that widens as extraction continues.
Overdrafting lowers the water table, shrinks streams, wetlands and lakes, and can cause subsidence and saltwater intrusion.
Roughly 40% of global irrigation relies on groundwater, and irrigation is the main cause of storage loss in the US.
About 800 km3 of US groundwater was depleted during the 20th century.
Remedies include artificial recharge, better governance, conservation incentives and more efficient farming.

entries.text: During the 20th century, the United States drew down about 800 cubic kilometers of its groundwater. That is groundwater depletion, also called overdrafting: pumping water from an aquifer faster than its equilibrium yield, the rate at which it stays in balance. Excessive pumping is the main cause, and too little recharge makes the aquifer less useful. Two limits guide managers. Safe yield is what can be withdrawn without exceeding long-term recharge. Sustainable yield also accounts for the effects on surface water. The damage starts at each well. Pumping creates a cone of depression, a funnel-shaped dip in the water table around the well, that widens as extraction goes on. Across a region the water table falls. Streams, wetlands and lakes shrink, the ground can subside, and salt water can push in. Farms are the main driver. Roughly 40% of global irrigation relies on groundwater, and irrigation is the main cause of storage loss in the US. It is a form of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. Remedies include artificial recharge, better governance, incentives to conserve and more efficient farming.

entries.title: Land value tax: taxing the ground, not the building

definition.text: A tax on the value of land alone, ignoring buildings and other improvements on it.

facts.text: Many economists favor it, arguing that it does not cause economic inefficiency and helps reduce inequality.
Most taxes discourage useful activity; property taxes, for example, discourage building and repair because the tax rises with improvements.
Because the amount of land is fixed, the tax cannot be passed on to tenants, consumers or workers, so it falls on landowners, who tend to be rich.
It removes the reward for holding unused land just to wait for its price to rise, freeing more land for productive use.
It is hard to evade, since land cannot be hidden or moved abroad and titles are publicly registered.
Supporters argue that land value comes from its surroundings rather than from anything the owner does.
Adam Smith first analyzed it rigorously in 1776, and Henry George later campaigned for a single tax on land to replace all other taxes.
Levying it requires a land valuation and a title register, and it is impractical where land titles and tenure are uncertain.

entries.text: Most taxes discourage something useful. A property tax rises when an owner builds or repairs, so it discourages both. A land value tax avoids that trap by taxing the value of land alone, ignoring buildings and other improvements. Many economists favor it, arguing that it causes no economic inefficiency and helps reduce inequality. Because the amount of land is fixed, the tax cannot be passed on to tenants, consumers or workers. Its {{ref:nature-pol-128}} falls on landowners, who tend to be rich. It also removes the reward for holding unused land just to wait for its price to rise, freeing land for productive use. Evasion is hard, since land cannot be hidden or moved abroad and titles are publicly registered. Supporters add that land value comes from its surroundings, not from anything the owner does. Adam Smith first analyzed the tax rigorously in 1776, and Henry George later campaigned for a single tax on land to replace all others. It needs a land valuation and a title register, and it is impractical where titles and tenure are uncertain.

entries.title: Forest products: wood, paper and a global trade

definition.text: Any material taken from forestry for direct use or sale, such as lumber, paper or livestock fodder.

facts.text: Wood is by far the main product, used as fuel, building material and pulp for paper.
All other products from forests are grouped as non-timber forest products, seen as less harmful to forest ecosystems while giving local income.
In 2023, global exports of wood and paper products were worth US$482 billion.
Industrial roundwood removals were 1.92 billion cubic meters and sawnwood production 445 million cubic meters.
Wood products store carbon, and timber can replace concrete as a recyclable building material.
Burning bioenergy initially emits more greenhouse gas per unit of energy than fossil fuels; regrowing trees takes decades or centuries to reabsorb it.
Access restrictions, harvesting fees and harvest limits are policies that shape forest product economics.

entries.title: Non-timber forest products: nuts, mushrooms and medicine

definition.text: Useful foods, materials and other goods taken from forests other than timber.

facts.text: They include game, nuts, berries, mushrooms, oils, sap, medicinal plants, fuelwood, fish, insects, spices and forage, harvested from the wild or farmed.
Non-wood forest products are a subset that excludes woodfuel and charcoal; FAO estimated they generated US$88 billion in 2011.
Around 1 billion people depend to some extent on wild foods, and several million households rely on these products for income.
More than 28,000 plant species are recorded as medicinal, many of them from forests.
Their total economic value is hard to estimate because no broad system tracks the hundreds of products involved.
Research treats them as commodities that can make keeping forests pay, and in some places as a route out of poverty.
Community forestry often manages forests for income from both timber and non-timber products.

entries.title: Illegal logging: timber taken outside the law

definition.text: Harvesting, transporting, buying or selling timber in breach of the law.

facts.text: It includes logging without permission, in protected areas, of protected species, or beyond agreed limits, often through corruption.
Fraudulent customs declarations, tax avoidance and fake certification during trade are called wood laundering.
Demand for raw materials, land grabbing and demand for cattle pasture drive it.
Illegal logging on public land alone causes losses of over US$10 billion a year, and more than half of global logging may be illegal.
Governments tend to underestimate it while NGOs publish alarming figures, so estimates need caution.
It drives deforestation and biodiversity loss, fosters corruption and tax evasion, and cuts producer countries' revenue.
The EU's 2003 FLEGT Action Plan works mainly through Voluntary Partnership Agreements with timber-producing countries.

entries.title: Water rights: who may take water from a river

definition.text: A user's legal right to take and use water from a source such as a river, stream, pond or groundwater.

facts.text: Where water is plentiful and users few, such rights are simple, but in dry irrigated areas they often cause legal and physical conflict.
Often they rest on owning the land the water touches, known as riparian rights, and are judged by a test of reasonable use.
Where water is scarcer, as in the western United States, rights follow prior appropriation: first in time, first in right.
Each appropriative right has an annual yield and a date, and it keeps that date when sold.
In ancient Rome people could gain temporary rights to running water that did not depend on owning land and lasted while use continued.
Over time rights broadened from land-based to use-based, letting non-landowners hold enforceable rights to clean water.
Some systems treat surface water and groundwater alike, while others apply different rules to each.

entries.title: Land use change: when forest becomes farm or city

definition.text: The change of a piece of land from one land-use category to another.

facts.text: Together with fossil fuel use, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide.
Human activity is the biggest cause of land cover change, and people also feel its environmental consequences.
Deforestation has historically been a main driver; global forest cover has shrunk by 35% since farming began.
Urban areas cover just 3% of Earth's surface but drive land change elsewhere through rising consumption.
A Soviet irrigation diversion cost the Aral Sea 85% of its area and 90% of its volume, wrecking its fishery.

entries.text: Since farming began, global forest cover has shrunk by 35%. Most of that loss is land use change: a piece of land switching from one land-use category to another, such as forest to cropland. Deforestation has historically been its main driver. Together with burning fossil fuels, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide. Human activity is the biggest cause of changes to what covers the land, and people also feel the consequences. Cities show how far the effects reach. Urban areas cover just 3% of Earth's surface, but their rising consumption drives land change far away. The starkest example is the Aral Sea. A Soviet irrigation diversion cost it 85% of its area and 90% of its volume, and its fishery collapsed. Every switch in land use, in other words, changes what the land can give back.

entries.title: Sustainable forest management: three pillars in balance

definition.text: Managing forests according to the principles of sustainable development.

facts.text: It must balance three pillars: ecological, economic and sociocultural.
Its benefits range from protecting local livelihoods and biodiversity to reducing rural poverty and easing some effects of climate change.
The Forest Principles adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit captured the international understanding of it at that time.
Forest under management plans grew by 365 million ha since 1990 to 2.13 billion ha, 55% of all forest in 2025.
Biodiversity conservation is the main aim in around 13% of the world's forests, and protecting soil and water in more than 30%.

entries.title: Economic water scarcity: plenty of water, no pipes

definition.text: Water scarcity caused by too little investment in the infrastructure or technology needed to draw water from rivers, aquifers and other sources.

facts.text: It also reflects weak human capacity to meet water demand.
The UN Development Programme says it is the most common cause of water scarcity, because most regions have enough water but lack the means to deliver it.
A quarter of the world's population is affected, much of Sub-Saharan Africa among them.
People without reliable access may travel long distances to fetch water, which is often unclean.

Central Asia, West Asia, North Africa and most of Australia are examples of arid areas.
Around a fifth of the world's population lives in regions affected by physical water scarcity.
The two-type distinction was first defined in a 2007 study led by the International Water Management Institute on 50 years of farm water use.

entries.title: Land grabbing: the global rush for farmland

definition.text: The large-scale buying or leasing of land by domestic or foreign companies, governments and individuals.

facts.text: In the 21st century the term mainly refers to large land acquisitions that followed the 2007–08 world food price crisis.
The crisis set off a sharp rise in mostly foreign agricultural investment in the Global South to grow industrial food and biofuels.
Securing water is usually central to these deals, which has produced a related trend called water grabbing.
Investors fall into three broad types: agribusinesses, governments and speculative investors.
Food-driven deals make up roughly 37% of land investments worldwide, and biofuel production about 21%.
Estimates of the area involved vary: the World Bank reported 46 million ha announced by 2010, while a 2011 estimate put it above 80 million ha; one 2013 review warned the scale may be exaggerated.
Critics point to weak land tenure, poor consultation, displacement of local people without adequate compensation, and the turn to large-scale industrial farming.
A World Bank study estimated that only 2 to 10 percent of land in Africa is formally tenured, which leaves many users exposed.

entries.title: Prior appropriation: first in time, first in right

definition.text: A rule for sharing water under which the first person to take water for a beneficial use keeps the right to go on taking that amount for that use.

facts.text: It is often summed up as "first in time, first in right"; later users may take only what is left without harming earlier users.
It gives a right to withdraw water, not full ownership, and the right can be lost if left unused for a long time.
Rights are first allotted by date of use and can then be traded on the open market like other property.
Each year the holder with the earliest date takes their full allocation first, then the next, and in a shortage senior users need not cut back.
It arose in Gold-Rush-era California and spread to the arid western United States, where water is scarce.
Because users who leave part of their allotment unused risk losing it, the rule discourages conservation, and most western water still goes to agriculture.
Streams can become over-appropriated, holding more rights than there is water, so the newest users almost never receive any.
The doctrine has historically excluded ecological uses such as keeping water in a river for wildlife, though some jurisdictions now accept them.

entries.text: In Gold-Rush-era California, miners needed water and settled who got it with a simple rule: first come, first served. Prior appropriation is that rule for sharing water. The first person to take water for a beneficial use keeps the right to go on taking that amount for that use. The right is to withdraw water, not to own it, and it can be lost if left unused for a long time. In a shortage, senior users need not cut back. The rule spread across the arid western United States and has flaws. Users who leave part of their allotment unused risk losing it, so it discourages conservation, and most western water still goes to farming. Streams can become over-appropriated, holding more rights than water, so the newest users almost never get any. The doctrine has also historically excluded ecological uses, such as keeping water in a river for wildlife, though some places now accept them.

entries.title: Riparian rights: water shared by the riverbank

definition.text: A system that shares water among the owners of land along a river, lake or other water body.

facts.text: It comes from English common law and is used in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the eastern United States.
All owners whose land touches the water may make reasonable use of it; in a shortage, shares usually follow the length of each owner's frontage.
The rights cannot be sold apart from the land, and water cannot be moved out of the watershed without regard for downstream owners.
Downstream owners have a right to receive water undiminished in flow and quality.
In the United States the arid western states mainly follow prior appropriation, while the eastern states follow riparian law.

entries.title: Peak water: the limits of a watery planet

definition.text: The idea that the availability, quality and use of fresh water face growing limits.

facts.text: Peter Gleick and Meena Palaniappan defined it in 2010, separating peak renewable, peak non-renewable and peak ecological water.
Their point is that although the planet holds a vast amount of water, sustainably managed water is becoming scarce.
Of an estimated 1.34 billion cubic kilometres of water on Earth, 96.5% is salty and less than 1% is accessible to people.
Agriculture accounts for 70% of freshwater use worldwide.
Fossil water behaves like oil: pumping it faster than natural recharge can in theory give a Hubbert-type production peak.
The Ogallala Aquifer is mined far faster than it refills, a classic case of peak non-renewable water.
Saudi Arabia reached peak water in the early 1990s at more than 30 billion cubic metres a year and now produces about half that peak rate.
Typically only 35% to 50% of water withdrawn for irrigation reaches the crops, and higher water prices have been shown to improve efficiency of use.

entries.title: The hidden costs of food

definition.text: The environmental, social and health costs of producing and eating food that are not reflected in food prices, also called external costs.

facts.text: Examples include food's contribution to climate change, farmworker poverty and diet-related illness, all paid for by society.
Estimates of the total hidden costs of global agrifood systems range from USD 12 trillion to USD 19 trillion per year.
Hidden health costs amount to USD 8.1 trillion.
Greenhouse gas costs are fairly easy to measure; effects on working conditions and communities are harder.

entries.text: The price on a supermarket shelf leaves out a lot. entries.title: Environmental flows: water left for the river

definition.text: The amount, timing and quality of river flow needed to sustain freshwater and estuarine ecosystems and the people who depend on them.

facts.text: Managers aim for a flow pattern that serves human uses while keeping river ecosystems healthy, not necessarily restoring pristine flows.
More than half of the world's large rivers are dammed, and dams change downstream water quality, temperature, sediment, fish and livelihoods.
The idea grew from 1970s 'minimum flows' for single species such as trout, then 'instream flows'.
By the 1990s scientists saw that one minimum flow could not capture river systems.
The 2007 Brisbane Declaration was endorsed by more than 750 practitioners from more than 50 countries.
More than 200 methods exist; holistic ones include DRIFT, the Building Block Methodology and ELOHA.
Dam reoperation combined with floodplain restoration has sometimes increased hydropower water while reducing flood risk.

entries.title: Water stress indicators: measuring scarcity with a number

definition.text: Simple measures of how scarce water is, such as the ratio of water use to water available or the water available per person each year.

facts.text: The Falkenmark Water Stress Indicator counts water stress below 1,700 cubic meters per person per year and water scarcity below 1,000 cubic meters.
The FAO defines water stress as total freshwater withdrawn divided by total renewable freshwater minus environmental flow requirements.
Under that definition, below 10% is low stress and above 80% is very high stress.
Country averages hide uneven rainfall and access, so they can misstate scarcity.

entries.text: Below 1,700 cubic meters of water per person per year, a country is under water stress; below 1,000, it faces scarcity. That is the Falkenmark Water Stress Indicator, one of several simple measures of how scarce water is. Others compare water use with the water available. The FAO divides total freshwater withdrawn by total renewable freshwater, minus what rivers need to stay healthy. Below 10% counts as low stress, and above 80% as very high. Such numbers have limits. Country averages hide uneven rainfall and access, so they can misstate scarcity.

entries.title: The Dublin Principles: water as an economic good

definition.text: Four principles for water management set out in the 1992 Dublin Statement.

facts.text: They hold that fresh water is finite and vulnerable, that management should be participatory, and that women play a central role.
The fourth principle says water has economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognized as an economic good.
They have guided reform of national water law around the world since 1992.

entries.text: In 1992 a statement agreed in Dublin set out four principles for managing water. Fresh water is finite and vulnerable. Its management should be participatory. Women play a central role. The fourth principle broke new ground: water has economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognized as an economic good. Since 1992 the principles have guided reform of national water law around the world.

entries.contested_note: Studies disagree on whether reduced-impact logging is financially worse or better for loggers than conventional logging.
entries.title: Reduced-impact logging: cutting with care

definition.text: A set of carefully planned and controlled timber-harvesting practices, carried out by trained workers, that make selective logging of tropical forests less damaging.

facts.text: Selective logging removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing, unlike clearcutting.
Selective logging is estimated to affect 1 billion hectares of forest worldwide, including 680 million hectares of tropical forest.
Done by untrained, poorly supervised crews too often or too heavily, selective logging badly damages the stand, water functions and biodiversity.
The term arose in the late 1990s after mechanized logging was seen to threaten long-term sustainability.
FAO's model code calls for a minimum 20-year cutting cycle, removing no more than one-third of stand basal area, and directional felling.
It damages fewer trees and less soil, but in Southeast Asia logging more than 8 trees per hectare cancels its benefits.
Whether it costs loggers money is contested: studies show both losses and gains from less wasted timber.
It can earn rewards through carbon retention and payments for environmental services, and is an eligible REDD+ activity.

entries.text: Selective logging touches an estimated 1 billion hectares of forest worldwide, including 680 million hectares of tropical forest. It removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing, unlike {{ref:nature-res-115}}. Done badly, by untrained crews cutting too often or too heavily, it ruins the stand, its water functions and its biodiversity. Reduced-impact logging is the answer: carefully planned and controlled harvesting by trained workers. The term arose in the late 1990s, after mechanized logging was seen to threaten long-term sustainability. The FAO's model code calls for a cutting cycle of at least 20 years, removing no more than one-third of the stand's trunk area, and directional felling. It damages fewer trees and less soil, but in Southeast Asia logging more than 8 trees per hectare cancels its benefits. It can earn rewards for keeping carbon in the forest and is an eligible REDD+ activity. Whether it costs loggers money is disputed. Some studies find losses, while others find gains from wasting less timber.

entries.title: Faustmann's formula: when to cut a forest

definition.text: A formula giving the present value of the income from repeatedly growing and harvesting a forest, used to find the best age to cut it.

facts.text: German forester Martin Faustmann derived it in 1849.
Because timber is renewable, waiting longer for a bigger harvest has a cost: it delays replanting and the next rotation.
It values the forest as pf(T) times the sum of discounted future harvests, PV = pf(T)/(exp(rT) − 1), where r is the discount rate.
The best time to cut is when the forest's value grows at the rate of interest on the forest plus interest on the land.
Bertil Ohlin solved the maximization in 1921, giving the Faustmann–Ohlin theorem.
Because it accounts for the time value of money, the financially optimal rotation is usually shorter than the biologically optimal one.
It remains widely used in natural resource valuation and policy analysis.

entries.text: Waiting longer gives a bigger tree, but it also delays the next crop. In 1849 German forester {{ref:nature-hist-080}} worked out how to weigh the two. His formula gives the {{ref:nature-econ-762}} of the income from growing and harvesting a forest again and again. It values the forest as pf(T) divided by (exp(rT) − 1): the harvest value at age T over an endless series of rotations, with r the discount rate. Because timber is renewable, delay has a cost. The best time to cut is when the forest's value grows at the rate of interest on the forest plus interest on the land. Bertil Ohlin solved the maximization in 1921, giving the Faustmann–Ohlin theorem. Because it counts the time value of money through {{ref:nature-econ-745}}, the financially best rotation is usually shorter than the biologically best one. The formula remains widely used in natural resource valuation and policy analysis.
entries.text_plain: Waiting longer gives a bigger tree, but it also delays the next crop. In 1849 German forester Martin Faustmann, father of forest economics worked out how to weigh the two. His formula gives the Present value: what future money is worth today of the income from growing and harvesting a forest again and again. It values the forest as pf(T) divided by (exp(rT) − 1): the harvest value at age T over an endless series of rotations, with r the discount rate. Because timber is renewable, delay has a cost. The best time to cut is when the forest's value grows at the rate of interest on the forest plus interest on the land. Bertil Ohlin solved the maximization in 1921, giving the Faustmann–Ohlin theorem. Because it counts the time value of money through Discounting: paying to put off a payment, the financially best rotation is usually shorter than the biologically best one. The formula remains widely used in natural resource valuation and policy analysis.

entries.title: Precision agriculture: farming field by field, row by row

definition.text: A farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to tailor decisions to local variation and use resources more efficiently.

facts.text: It applies precise amounts of water, fertilizer and pesticides at the right time, and can cut inputs while raising yields.
Farmers earn back their investment by saving on water, pesticide and fertilizer; targeting inputs also benefits soils and groundwater.
It relies on GPS, geographic information systems, variable-rate technology, grid sampling and remote sensing.
The idea first emerged in the United States in the early 1980s.

entries.text: Precision agriculture treats a field as many small patches rather than one. It is a farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to fit decisions to local variation. It applies precise amounts of water, fertilizer and pesticides at the right time, cutting inputs while raising yields. It relies on GPS, mapping software, variable-rate machinery, grid sampling and {{ref:nature-es-057}}. entries.title: Alternative food systems: shorter chains, closer links

definition.text: Initiatives that organize food production, distribution and eating differently from conventional industrial systems.

facts.text: They include farmers' markets, community-supported agriculture, food cooperatives and buying groups.
They are marked by locality, short supply chains and direct links between producers and consumers.
Fair trade aims to give developing-country producers more control and a bigger share of the sale price.

entries.text: Farmers' markets, community-supported agriculture, food cooperatives and buying groups share one thing: they bypass the industrial food chain. They are alternative food systems, initiatives that organize growing, distributing and eating food differently. They are marked by locality, short supply chains and direct links between producers and consumers. Fair trade aims to give producers in developing countries more control and a bigger share of the sale price.

entries.title: Sustainable food systems: feeding people without the damage

definition.text: A food system that provides healthy food while sustaining the environmental, economic and social systems around food.

facts.text: It starts from sustainable farming and distribution, sustainable diets and less food waste.
Around 69 million hectares a year grow food that is lost or wasted before reaching consumers.
Sustainable food systems are argued to be central to many or all 17 SDGs.

entries.title: Coppicing: a forest that regrows from its stumps

definition.text: A way of regrowing a forest that relies on cut trees sending up new shoots from their stumps.

facts.text: Most hardwoods, the coast redwood and certain pines sprout from stumps and can be coppiced.
It is generally used to produce fuelwood, pulpwood and other small-tree products.
The three recognized systems are simple coppice, coppice with standards, where some fine trees are kept for several rotations, and the coppice selection system.

entries.text: Cut down many trees and they do not die; they sprout again. Coppicing is a way of regrowing a forest that relies on that habit. Most hardwoods, the coast redwood and certain pines can be coppiced. It is generally used for fuelwood, pulpwood and other small-tree products. There are three recognized systems: simple coppice, coppice with standards, where some fine trees are kept for several rotations, and the coppice selection system.

entries.title: Even-aged and uneven-aged forest management

definition.text: The two broad families of methods that combine harvesting timber with re-establishing the forest, differing in how much of the stand is cut at once.

facts.text: Uneven-aged methods harvest single trees or small groups now and then, keeping mixed sizes and ages; even-aged methods remove most or all of the overstory, leaving a stand of one age.
The shelterwood system removes a stand through several partial cuts over years, ending in a new even-aged stand.
Selection systems suit places where keeping continuous forest cover for scenic or environmental reasons matters most.
Variable retention, a newer system, leaves stumps, logs, snags and live trees for at least one rotation to keep environmental values.

entries.text: Foresters can cut a stand all at once or a little at a time. Those choices define two broad families of methods for harvesting timber and re-establishing the forest. Even-aged methods remove most or all of the tallest trees, leaving a stand of one age. Uneven-aged methods harvest single trees or small groups now and then, keeping mixed sizes and ages. The shelterwood system removes a stand through several partial cuts over years. Selection systems suit places where continuous forest cover matters most, for scenic or environmental reasons. Variable retention, a newer system, leaves stumps, logs and live trees for at least one rotation.

entries.title: Forest thinning: fewer trees, faster growth

definition.text: Cutting out some of the trees in a stand so that the remaining ones grow faster.

facts.text: Its aim is to control how much growing space each tree gets, shaping the growth, quality and health of those left.
Precommercial thinning of dense young stands can greatly raise the yield of saleable wood and shorten the rotation.
Repeated thinnings over a rotation have been shown to store more carbon than clear-cutting on short rotations.

entries.text: Sometimes the way to grow more wood is to cut trees down. Forest thinning removes some trees from a stand so the rest grow faster. It controls how much growing space each tree gets, shaping the growth, quality and health of those left. Thinning dense young stands early can greatly raise the yield of saleable wood and shorten the rotation. Repeated thinnings have been shown to store more carbon than clear-cutting on short rotations.

entries.title: Net animal losses: the calories lost in feeding livestock
entries.article: Food loss and waste#Net animal losses

definition.text: A measure of food waste: the calories in human-edible crops fed to animals minus the calories returned as meat, dairy and fish.

facts.text: These losses are higher than all conventional food losses combined.
Measuring loss in tonnes ignores economic value and can overweight heavy, low-value products.

entries.text: Feeding crops to animals loses more food than all conventional food losses combined. Net animal losses measure that: the calories in human-edible crops fed to animals, minus the calories returned as meat, dairy and fish. The measure also shows why counting loss in tonnes misleads. Tonnes ignore economic value and can overweight heavy, low-value products.

entries.contested_note: Hardin's view that pastoral commons inevitably degrade is disputed by Ostrom and many other scholars.
entries.title: Hardin, Ostrom and the fate of shared pastures

definition.text: The dispute over whether shared grazing lands are bound to be overused, as Garrett Hardin argued in 1968, or can be governed well by communities, as Elinor Ostrom showed.

facts.text: Hardin treated pastoralist land use as unstable and a cause of environmental degradation, and his paper gave a basis for privatizing land.
Many scholars call his assumption that herders cannot communicate or make agreements implausible, yet it shaped development projects that broke up working pastoral governance, often disastrously.
Ostrom argued grazing commons can be managed more sustainably by community groups and cooperatives than by privatization or full state control.

entries.text: In 1968 {{ref:nature-hist-052}} argued that shared grazing land is bound to be overgrazed, a claim at the heart of the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. He treated pastoralist land use as unstable and a cause of environmental damage, and his paper gave a basis for privatizing land. Many scholars call his assumption that herders cannot talk or make agreements implausible. Yet it shaped development projects that broke up working pastoral governance, often disastrously. {{ref:nature-hist-039}} disputed Hardin's view. She argued that community groups and cooperatives can manage shared pastures more sustainably than privatization or full state control.

entries.title: Multiple use and sustained yield

definition.text: A forest management principle, written into a 1960 United States law, of using a forest's timber, range, water, recreation and wildlife together while keeping their output going indefinitely.

facts.text: Multiple use means managing all a forest's renewable surface resources in the combination that best meets people's needs.
Sustained yield means keeping a high regular output of renewable resources forever without harming the land's productivity.
The 1960 act was the first law to treat the five major uses of national forests equally, with timber sales no longer always the limiting factor.

entries.text: On June 12, 1960, a United States law gave national forests five equal jobs: timber, range, water, recreation and wildlife. It was the first law to treat these major uses equally, so timber sales were no longer always the limiting factor. The principle it set is multiple use and sustained yield. Multiple use means managing all of a forest's renewable surface resources in the combination that best meets people's needs. Sustained yield means keeping a high, regular output of those resources forever without harming the land's productivity.

It was the first law to treat these major uses equally, so timber sales were no longer always the limiting factor. The principle it set is multiple use and sustained yield. Sustained yield means keeping a high, regular output of those resources forever without harming the land's productivity.

entries.title: Who pays when the water table falls

definition.text: The unequal economic burden created as falling water tables force users to dig deeper wells.

facts.text: In Punjab, the cost of deeper wells hurt small landholders more than large ones, who could afford the technology.
Prior appropriation rights let established, richer users keep their water while newcomers and small farmers get less.

entries.text: As water tables drop, every well must go deeper, and deeper wells cost money. That burden falls unevenly. In Punjab, the cost of deeper wells hurt small landholders more than large ones, who could afford the technology. Water law can deepen the gap. Under {{ref:nature-res-151}}, established, richer users keep their water while newcomers and small farmers get less.

entries.title: Agricultural economics: economics for the farm

definition.text: A branch of applied economics that uses economic theory to improve how food and fibre are produced and distributed.

facts.text: It began as a branch dealing with land use, aiming to maximize crop yields while keeping soils healthy.
It grew to prominence around the turn of the 20th century and made early contributions to econometric methods.

In environmental economics, agricultural economists design incentives to control externalities like farm water pollution and estimate the value of non-market benefits such as attractive rural landscapes.
The farm sector is often cited as a prime example of perfect competition.

entries.text: Economists often cite the farm sector as a prime example of perfect competition, many sellers with no power over price. It rose to prominence around the turn of the 20th century and made early contributions to statistical methods in economics. Today agricultural economists design incentives to control farm water pollution and other externalities. They also estimate the value of non-market benefits such as attractive rural landscapes.

entries.title: Saving tropical rainforests, and making it pay

definition.text: Efforts to protect and restore tropical rainforests, ranging from strict preservation to sustainable management by people living in them.

facts.text: Its building blocks include ecotourism, rehabilitation, reforestation and restoration.
Approaches differ: Asian governments such as Vietnam and China fund planting directly, while Peru and Brazil give farmers incentives like tax credits to reduce deforestation.
Countries can earn carbon credits by conserving or replanting rainforest, making conservation pay economically.
The Bonn Challenge, signed in 2011 by 58 countries, pledged to restore 150 million hectares of forest by 2020, later raised to 350 Mha by 2030.

entries.text: In 2011, 58 countries signed the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}}, pledging to restore 150 million hectares of forest by 2020, later raised to 350 Mha by 2030. Tropical rainforest conservation covers efforts to protect and restore these forests, from strict preservation to sustainable management by the people who live in them. Its building blocks include ecotourism, rehabilitation, replanting and restoration. Approaches differ. Vietnam and China fund planting directly, while Peru and Brazil give farmers incentives such as tax credits to reduce deforestation. Countries can also earn carbon credits by conserving or replanting rainforest, so conservation pays.

entries.title: Should water be bought and sold?

definition.text: The process of turning water, especially fresh water, from a public good into a commodity that can be bought and sold.

facts.text: It is usually done in the hope that the resource will be managed more efficiently.
It grew sharply during the 20th century alongside concern about water scarcity and environmental damage.
Its theoretical case draws on Garrett Hardin's Tragedy of the Commons: water as a common good has been overused and poorly managed.
Putting a price on water aims to bring the costs of using it into economic decisions, on the logic that a correctly valued resource can be protected.
For most of the 20th century water was publicly provided by the state, with the emphasis on social equity.
Critics argue that the poor lose out as equality and universal access are traded for efficiency and profit.
Karen Bakker argues full commodification is nearly impossible because water's physical traits resist standardization.

entries.contested_note: Proponents say markets allocate and protect water better than regulation; critics say commodification deepens inequality and harms ecosystems.
entries.text: For most of the 20th century, states supplied water as a public service, with the emphasis on fairness. Then the idea of water as a commodity grew sharply, alongside worries about scarcity and environmental damage. Commodification of water is the process of turning water, especially fresh water, from a {{ref:nature-econ-633}} into a commodity that can be bought and sold. It is usually done in the hope that the resource will be managed more efficiently. Its theoretical case draws on the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}, an argument made by {{ref:nature-hist-052}}: water held in common has been overused and poorly managed. A price aims to bring the costs of using water into economic decisions, on the logic that a correctly valued resource can be protected. Critics reply that the poor lose out, as equality and universal access are traded for efficiency and profit. Karen Bakker argues full commodification is nearly impossible, because water's physical traits resist standardization. The argument is unsettled. Supporters say markets allocate and protect water better than regulation. Critics say commodification deepens inequality and harms ecosystems.

It is usually done in the hope that the resource will be managed more efficiently. Its theoretical case draws on the The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused, an argument made by Garrett Hardin and the tragedy of the commons: water held in common has been overused and poorly managed. A price aims to bring the costs of using water into economic decisions, on the logic that a correctly valued resource can be protected. Critics reply that the poor lose out, as equality and universal access are traded for efficiency and profit. Karen Bakker argues full commodification is nearly impossible, because water's physical traits resist standardization. The argument is unsettled. Supporters say markets allocate and protect water better than regulation. Critics say commodification deepens inequality and harms ecosystems.

entries.title: Water privatization: private firms at the tap

definition.text: The involvement of private companies in providing water supply and sanitation services.

facts.text: There are two broad forms: full privatization, where assets are sold permanently, and public–private partnerships, where the public keeps ownership and hands some functions to a firm for a set period.
Full privatization is now rare, limited to England, Chile and some US cities.
Supporters say it raises efficiency and service quality and can bring fiscal benefits; critics say it raises tariffs and conflicts with the human right to water.
Private utilities were common in the 19th century, faded as public utilities grew, and returned in the early 1990s, pushed partly by World Bank and IMF lending conditions.
Like all water utilities, private operators are monopolies and need regulation of tariffs, service quality and environmental compliance.
The evidence on its impact is mixed, and both sides tend to cite the studies that suit them.
A World Bank review found no statistically significant difference in efficiency between public and private operators.
A study of Latin American concessions found modest returns, averaging 7 percent a year on capital employed.

entries.title: First in time, first in right, beyond water

definition.text: The use of the first in time, first in right principle for resources other than water, such as mineral deposits, farmland and pollution rights.

facts.text: Gold Rush miners applied it to mineral deposits: the first to find and mine a deposit gained the legal right to mine it.
Granting pollution rights to existing polluters, from which a cap-and-trade market could develop, would apply the same theory to air pollution.
Carbon markets that let firms offset new emissions against cuts at existing sources in effect recognize a prior right of existing emitters.

Carbon markets that let firms offset new emissions against cuts at old sources in effect recognize a prior right of existing emitters, as in {{ref:nature-pol-253}}.

entries.title: Backstop water sources: the expensive last resort

definition.text: Water sources, such as desalinated seawater, that can replace unsustainable or non-renewable water use, usually at a higher cost.

facts.text: A backstop resource is one abundant and sustainable enough to replace a non-renewable one, as renewable energy is for fossil fuels.
Desalination is the classic backstop; transfers between river basins and trucked water are others, and all are last-resort, expensive options.
Desalination is limited by its energy needs, brine disposal, high capital and water costs, and the cost of moving water.
Desalination cost US$0.53 per cubic metre in Israel in 2005 and US$0.49 in Singapore in 2006.

entries.title: Criteria and indicators: scoring forest sustainability
entries.article: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management

definition.text: Policy tools for evaluating and reporting how sustainably forests are managed in a country or region.

facts.text: Criteria set the objectives; indicators are the variables that show whether they are being met.
The idea dates to the 1992 Forest Principles and Agenda 21 adopted at the UN Conference on Environment and Development.
The Pan-European set has 6 criteria, such as forest health and biodiversity; the Montréal Process set has 7 criteria and 54 indicators.
They also help develop forest certification standards.

entries.title: Water bankruptcy: past the point of recovery

definition.text: A state in which long overuse of a water system has caused damage so lasting that it can no longer return to its former supply and ecosystem services.

facts.text: It has two parts: withdrawals exceed renewable inflows and safe depletion limits, and the damage cannot be undone without disproportionate cost.
It differs from water scarcity, water stress and a water crisis, which may still be reversible, by stressing insolvency and lost recoverability.
Kaveh Madani formally defined it, and a United Nations University report of 20 January 2026 declared the world had entered a global water bankruptcy era.

entries.title: Water abstraction charges: paying to take water

definition.text: Fees some countries levy for taking water directly from rivers, lakes and aquifers, which in most countries is free.

facts.text: They are typically charged to industries, utilities and farmers.
Few countries outside the OECD charge them, and where they exist fees are often nominal or poorly enforced.
Agriculture, the largest water user worldwide, is exempt in almost all countries that charge them.

entries.title: Restoration hotspots: where regrowing rainforest pays most
entries.article: Tropical rainforest conservation#Keys to successful restoration

definition.text: Areas where restoring rainforest gives the highest social and economic benefits and is most feasible.

facts.text: They matter because, for an individual landowner, clearing forest often pays more than keeping it.

Benefits are scored on biodiversity, climate mitigation, climate adaptation and water security; feasibility on the opportunity cost of taking land out of farming, the forest's ability to recover, and the chance it lasts.
By these criteria over 863 Mha of rainforest qualifies, nearly a third of it in Brazil.

entries.title: Von Thünen's rings: distance shapes the farm

definition.text: Johann Heinrich von Thünen's model of farmland use, set out in The Isolated State (1826), in which the cost of transporting goods eats into the rent land can earn.

facts.text: It is considered the first example of marginal analysis and an early explicit, abstract model to which mathematics could be applied.
Von Thünen developed the spatial analysis of rents, stressing the importance of centrality and transport.
Its publication is said to mark the real start of location theory, and von Thünen has been called the father of location theorists.
Critics say it oversimplified the problem by assuming an isolated state or a single city.

entries.title: The human right to water and sanitation
entries.article: Water resource policy#Human right to water and sanitation

definition.text: The principle that clean drinking water and sanitation are a universal human right because every life depends on them.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly recognized it as a human right on 28 July 2010.
Its clearest definition came in General Comment 15 of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, drafted in 2002.
Only a few countries have written it into enforceable law.

Only a few countries have written the right into enforceable law.

entries.title: Water resource policy: blue, green and grey water

definition.text: The policy-making and laws that govern how water is collected, treated, used, disposed of and protected.

facts.text: It varies by region with water availability, the state of aquatic systems and local needs.
For policy, water is often sorted into blue water (surface and groundwater), green water (rain held in soil for plants), grey water (contaminated by use) and virtual water.
Drought frequency and intensity are rising with climate change, but water policy tends to react rather than plan ahead.

entries.title: Transboundary water agreements: sharing rivers across borders

definition.text: Treaties and other agreements between countries on how to share and manage water that crosses their borders.

facts.text: About 60% of the world's freshwater flows across political boundaries, because basins do not follow national borders.
An estimated 3600 water treaties have existed, more than 150 of them new since 1950.
Rivers that form a border and can be shared equally tend to cause less conflict than upstream–downstream arrangements.
Growing scarcity, climate change and poorer water quality have increased international conflict over water.

entries.title: The water-energy nexus: two resources tied together

definition.text: The two-way link between the water used to produce energy and the energy used to extract, treat, move, heat and dispose of water.

facts.text: Every form of energy production needs some water, and every stage of the water cycle needs energy, so the two cannot be separated.
Water is used when it is returned to its source, as in power-plant cooling, and consumed when it is removed by evaporation or by crops or people.
Thermoelectric power plants, which use water for cooling, are by far the largest users of water.
Some low-carbon options, such as biofuels, concentrating solar power, carbon capture and nuclear power, are quite water-intensive.
Gulf states spend 10–25% of their electricity on desalinating water.

entries.title: Natural resource management: caring for land, water and life

definition.text: Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future.

facts.text: It deals with how people and natural landscapes interact, recognizing that livelihoods depend on healthy, productive land.
It brings together heritage protection, land-use planning, water management, biodiversity conservation and the future of farming, mining, tourism, fishing and forestry.
In the 20th century people saw that strict preservation had not stopped resources declining, so a more integrated approach took in social, economic and political sides.
Its issues are complex and contested: natural cycles are linked, and a change in one can have long-lasting, even irreversible, effects.
Managers must also weigh many stakeholders, policies, politics, borders and economic effects.
Tools such as GIS help by overlaying data sets, for example rainfall, cleared land and erosion, to plan bush regeneration.

Geographic information systems, or GIS, overlay data sets such as rainfall, cleared land and erosion to plan where native bush should regrow.

entries.title: Who owns nature: four property regimes

definition.text: Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix.

facts.text: Under state property the state owns and controls the resource, and others use it only with permission, as in US national forests and parks.
Under private property a defined person or company owns the resource and bears both its benefits and its duties.
Common property is in effect the private property of a group, such as a community forest.
Open-access resources have no owner, anyone may use them, and they are the most exploited; a lake fishery is an example.
Many real cases are hybrids, such as native vegetation in New South Wales, protected in the public interest but mostly on private land.

entries.title: The commons: resources that belong to everyone

definition.text: The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth.

facts.text: Commons can also mean resources that a group of users governs for themselves, through rules they create, rather than through the state or the market.
The word comes from the old English legal term for common land, and Garrett Hardin's 1968 article 'The Tragedy of the Commons' made it a general term for shared resources.
Before Hardin's article, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' or 'common property' were very rare.
In Mongolia, where herders moved collectively between pastures, grassland degradation was about 9%, against about 75% in Russia and 33% in China under state or household pastures.
Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake that encourages them to prevent overuse.
Globalization brings new pressures: resources like fish and timber are sold on world markets, making impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

entries.title: Enclosure: fencing off England's common land

definition.text: Enclosure was the English practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, which stripped commoners of their traditional rights to use it.

facts.text: It merged scattered strips of land into large fields bounded by hedges, walls or fences, kept for the sole use of individual owners or their tenants.
Enclosure happened by owners making 'closes', by groups of proprietors enclosing whole parishes, and by acts of Parliament, the first in 1604.
Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable.
In Tudor England high wool profits led lords to turn common arable land into sheep pasture, evicting villagers.
Historians see enclosure riots as the leading form of social protest from the 1530s to the 1640s.
The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural labour moved to towns to become industrial workers.
The Hammonds said enclosure ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters, while Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs.
Many Marxists see enclosure as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

entries.contested_note: Historians disagree on whether enclosure mainly impoverished rural people or raised food output and rural employment.

entries.title: Community-based natural resource management
entries.article: Natural resource management#Community-based natural resource management

definition.text: Community-based natural resource management combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities.

facts.text: It assumes locals are best placed to conserve resources, that people conserve only when benefits exceed costs, and that they protect what is tied to their quality of life.
It rests on subsidiarity, the principle of handling decisions at the most local level that can manage them.
Critics such as Tania Murray found that in upland Southeast Asia it could force communities to meet discriminatory conditions before gaining legal rights to resources.
Social capital and gender shape how it works in practice.

entries.title: Community forestry: forests run by the people who live there

definition.text: Community forestry is a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities take an active part in managing forests and deciding land use.

facts.text: The FAO defines it as any situation that closely involves local people in forestry.
It manages forests both for income from timber and non-timber products and for ecosystem services such as watershed protection and carbon storage.
It is seen as one of the most promising ways to combine forest conservation with rural development and poverty reduction.
Nepal's democratically run Forest User Groups have regenerated forests, with some regions seeing a 37% rise in forest cover.
Secure land tenure decides whether communities can invest in sustainable practices; unclear boundaries, elite capture and weak enforcement threaten projects.
Certification and carbon credits open global markets, but high certification costs remain a barrier for smallholders.
There is no single blueprint, because regional social, economic and environmental conditions differ.

entries.title: The global commons: oceans, air and space

definition.text: The global commons are shared resource areas, such as the high seas, the atmosphere, outer space and Antarctica, that lie beyond the political reach of any single nation.

facts.text: They hold common-pool resources: goods it is costly but not impossible to keep users out of, and which are used up by use, so they suffer congestion, overuse and degradation.
Their governance must avoid a worldwide tragedy of the commons, where shared resources are overexploited.
Global users are more varied than local ones, resources are less stable and harder to understand, and many are non-renewable on human time scales.
Carbon dioxide that drives climate change keeps doing so for at least a millennium after it enters the atmosphere.
International environmental agreements multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm conference, but they are often slow, settle for the lowest common denominator and lack enforcement.
The Montreal Protocol, in force from 1 January 1989, is widely seen as a highly successful model for managing the global commons.
The 1961 Antarctic Treaty sets Antarctica aside as a scientific preserve and bans military activity there.

entries.title: Ostrom's design principles for a lasting commons

definition.text: A set of rules Elinor Ostrom found in commons that are governed successfully, such as clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions.

facts.text: Early tragedy-of-the-commons work suggested all commons were doomed, but later economists found many successful ones, and Ostrom won the Nobel Prize for analysing them.
Ostrom found that farmers have run grazing commons in the Swiss Alps successfully for hundreds of years.
Her principles are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognised rights to organize and nested enterprises.
The principles work best when more than nine are used together.
The related 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. Rose in 1986, describes users policing their own use to keep or improve a commons.

entries.text: Farmers in the Swiss Alps have run shared grazing land successfully for hundreds of years. From them she drew a set of design principles found in well-governed commons. They are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognized rights to organize and nested enterprises. Graduated sanctions mean penalties that grow with repeated offenses. The principles work best when more than nine are used together. A related idea, the 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. entries.title: Common ownership: assets held as one

definition.text: Common ownership means holding an organization's or community's assets as one undivided whole, not in the names of individual members.

facts.text: Forms of common ownership exist in every economic system.
Advocates separate collective ownership, shared by agreement among a set of members such as a producer cooperative, from common property open to all, such as a public park.
In capitalist economies it is practised by voluntary associations, non-profits and, implicitly, all public bodies.
Common ownership of the means of production is a central goal of socialist movements.

entries.title: Customary land: held by custom, not by title

definition.text: Customary land is land held and used under unwritten local custom rather than written, codified law.

facts.text: It is the tenure usually tied to indigenous communities, as opposed to statutory tenure mostly brought in during colonial times.
In many countries most land is customary, including 90% in Africa and 97% in Papua New Guinea.
The gap between formally recognized and customarily managed land is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental degradation.
The World Bank and others promote formal land titles, but opinion is divided on whether this always helps the poor.
Where several groups claim the same land, as often in Sub-Saharan Africa, formal titling can favour some and create tension.

entries.title: Integrated natural resource management
entries.article: Natural resource management#Integrated natural resource management

definition.text: Integrated natural resource management manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic aspects to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals.

facts.text: It focuses on sustainability and brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict.
It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and adaptive management.

entries.title: Stakeholder analysis: who has a stake in a forest

definition.text: Stakeholder analysis identifies the different interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved.

facts.text: Borrowed from business management, it is hard to apply because it is difficult to say who has a stake in a resource.
Its stages include identifying decision-makers and stakeholders, investigating their interests, and mapping conflicts, trade-offs and synergies.
A proposal to represent nature itself as a stakeholder has been rejected by many scholars as hard to put into practice.

entries.title: Joint Forest Management in India

definition.text: Joint Forest Management is India's term for partnerships in which state forest departments and local communities share forest protection and development.

facts.text: It is set out in India's National Forest Policy of 1988 and guidelines of 1990, and began in Odisha in 1988.
With Nepal's Forest User Groups, it was an early response to failing centralized forest policy.

entries.title: Commoning: the commons as something people do

definition.text: Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources, rather than as a thing.

facts.text: Some authors separate the shared resources, the community that governs them, and commoning, the act of managing them together.
In farming, commoning is the joint stewardship of shared land, and it matters to food systems in many communities worldwide.

entries.title: Urban commons: city spaces run by citizens

definition.text: Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price.

facts.text: David Harvey argued that public spaces are not automatically commons; they become commons when citizens take political action there.
Urban commons work alongside the state and the market rather than replacing them.

entries.title: The open-field system before enclosure

definition.text: Before enclosure, English common land lay under the manorial lord, with a manor made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own demesne farm.

facts.text: Tenants held rights such as pasture, pannage and estovers, and landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used.
Its end came with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

entries.title: Ostrom's IAD framework for studying the commons

definition.text: The IAD framework is Elinor Ostrom's theoretical tool for studying how people, called actors, interact with common-pool resources.

facts.text: Common-pool resources are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces others', and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical; forests and pastures are examples.
Built on rational choice assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, actors' positions and formal and informal rules.
It breaks complex collective action problems into smaller 'action arenas'.
Institutions are studied through seven rule types: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

entries.text: Forests and pastures share a tricky pair of traits. They are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces what others get, and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical. To study how people manage such resources, {{ref:nature-hist-039}} built the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, or IAD. Built on {{ref:nature-econ-098}} assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, the positions of the people involved, called actors, and their formal and informal rules. It breaks complex problems of collective action into smaller 'action arenas'. Institutions are studied through seven types of rule: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

entries.title: Joint ownership and who controls an asset

definition.text: In the incomplete-contracts approach of Oliver Hart and colleagues, ownership matters because the owner holds residual control rights: the say over an asset in any situation a contract does not cover.

facts.text: Owners have stronger incentives than non-owners to make investments tied to a relationship, so ownership can ease the hold-up problem.
A central result of this approach is that joint ownership, where each party can veto use of the asset, is suboptimal.
Later work shows joint ownership can be optimal when parties are unequally informed, in long-term relationships, or able to disclose know-how.

entries.title: Governing the Commons: Ostrom's answer to Hardin

definition.text: Governing the Commons (1990) is Elinor Ostrom's best-known book, showing that communities worldwide have managed shared resources successfully through local rules.

facts.text: It drew on irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, and fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia.
In it Ostrom set out eight design principles found in long-lasting common-pool resource institutions.
It argues that self-interest need not always cause degradation and can lead people to care for common property resources.
