entries.title: Nature-based solutions: hiring ecosystems to do the work

definition.text: Nature-based solutions (NBS) are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while benefiting both people and biodiversity.

facts.text: They address challenges such as climate change mitigation and adaptation, water and food security, and disaster risk reduction.
The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and provide environmental, social and economic benefits at once.
Mangrove restoration is an example meeting several goals: it buffers waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and controls erosion.
Green roofs, blue roofs and green walls in cities can cool urban heat islands, capture stormwater, reduce pollution and store carbon.
The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s and was taken up by the IUCN and the World Bank for working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering.
Around 130 Nationally Determined Contributions, 65% of signatories, commit to nature-based solutions, though pledges rarely become measurable action.
A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as or more effective than conventional flood management, with 66% reporting positive ecological outcomes.
The IUCN treats NBS as an umbrella concept covering ecological restoration, ecological engineering, ecosystem-based adaptation and Eco-DRR.

entries.text: A strip of mangrove forest along a tropical coast does four jobs at once. It breaks the force of waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and holds the shoreline against erosion. That bundle of benefits is the idea behind nature-based solutions, or NBS. They are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. The challenges are big ones: slowing climate change and adapting to it, securing water and food, and reducing disaster risk. Cities have their own versions. Roofs covered in plants or built to hold rain, and walls draped in greenery, can cool overheated city centers, capture rainwater, cut pollution and store carbon. The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s. The IUCN and the World Bank took it up to describe working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering. The IUCN now treats NBS as an umbrella over {{ref:nature-nbs-112}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-216}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-218}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-224}}. The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and deliver environmental, social and economic benefits at once. The flood evidence is encouraging. A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as conventional ways of handling floods, or more so, and 66% reported positive ecological outcomes. Politics has followed. Around 130 national climate pledges, known as {{ref:nature-clim-071}} documents, commit to NBS: 65% of signatories. Yet those pledges rarely become measurable action.

entries.title: Ecosystem-based adaptation: living defenses against a changing climate

definition.text: Ecosystem-based adaptation (EbA) is the use of biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change.

facts.text: It conserves, sustainably manages and restores ecosystems such as forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs to reduce harm from storms, changing rainfall and temperature extremes.
EbA can stand alone or be combined with engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and early warning systems.
Examples: restoring reefs, mangroves and marshes against storm surges; agroforestry against drought; forest management to stabilise slopes and prevent flash floods.
Claimed co-benefits include better health, food and water security, disaster risk reduction, carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation.
The term was coined by the IUCN in 2008 and officially defined at the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2009; it sits within nature-based solutions.
Many countries cite EbA in their Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement.
It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle climate change and poverty together in developing countries where people depend on natural resources.

entries.text: When a storm surge rolls toward a coast, a healthy reef, mangrove stand or marsh can take much of the blow. Using such living defenses on purpose is called ecosystem-based adaptation, or EbA. It uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change. In practice, EbA conserves, sustainably manages and restores forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs. The goal is less harm from storms, shifting rainfall and temperature extremes. The examples are concrete. Restored reefs, mangroves and marshes soften storm surges. Trees grown among crops, a practice called {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, help farms ride out drought. Well-managed forests hold slopes in place and prevent flash floods. EbA can work alone or alongside engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and systems that warn people early. Supporters claim a long list of side benefits: better health, food and water security, fewer disasters, stored carbon and conserved biodiversity. The IUCN coined the term in 2008, and the {{ref:nature-gov-015}} defined it officially in 2009. It sits inside the wider family of nature-based solutions. Many countries cite EbA in their climate pledges under the {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle hardship and the climate crisis together in developing countries, where people depend on natural resources.

entries.title: Ecological engineering: a small push that steers big natural forces

definition.text: Ecological engineering uses ecology and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that benefit both human society and nature.

facts.text: Howard Odum coined the term in 1962, describing cases where a small human energy input steers large natural processes.
Mitsch and Jorgensen's five basic concepts: it relies on ecosystems' self-design, tests ecological theory, uses systems approaches, conserves non-renewable energy, and supports conservation.
Projects range from restored wetlands to greenhouse systems that turn wastewater into fertiliser, flowers and drinking water.
Applications work at three scales: mesocosms (about 0.1 to hundreds of metres), ecosystems (about one to tens of km) and regional systems.
Design choices should use ecological economics to evaluate alternatives, guided by values that favour conservation.
Unlike civil engineering, which focuses on built infrastructure, it focuses on natural infrastructure and the relationship between people and planet.

entries.title: The case against nature-based solutions

definition.text: Critics argue nature-based solutions can serve as greenwashing and distract from cutting emissions, and that their evidence base is uneven.

facts.text: The Indigenous Environmental Network calls NBS a greenwashing tool; converting non-forest land to plantations can take land from smallholders and pastoralists.
The IPCC warns NBS cannot be an alternative to, or a reason to delay, deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.
Of 257,266 papers on natural climate solutions, fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.
Most case studies come from the Global North, leaving gaps for low- and middle-income countries, including cost analyses.

entries.contested_note: Indigenous groups and the IPCC question whether NBS are framed as a substitute for emission cuts and whether they harm land rights.

entries.title: Green plus grey: why hybrids beat either alone

definition.text: Hybrid green–grey infrastructure combines nature-based solutions with conventional built ('grey') infrastructure, which studies find works better than either alone.

facts.text: Studies find NBS improve flood resilience but cannot act alone and must be coordinated with grey infrastructure.
Used together, the benefits go beyond flood management to better social conditions, more carbon sequestration and resilience planning.
Researchers urge looking for synergies rather than framing NBS as an alternative to engineered approaches.

entries.title: Three types of nature-based solution, from hands-off to built

definition.text: A scientific typology sorts nature-based solutions by how much they engineer ecosystems and how many services and stakeholder groups they target.

facts.text: Type 1 involves minimal intervention, such as protecting mangroves against storms or creating marine protected areas that export fish to fishing grounds.
Type 2 manages landscapes to be sustainable and multifunctional, as in agroforestry or diversifying tree species for forest resilience.
Type 3 manages ecosystems intensively or creates new ones, such as green roofs and walls or constructed wetlands.
The typology assumes that the more services and stakeholders a solution targets, the less it can maximise any single one.

entries.text: Nature-based solutions come in three broad types, sorted by how much people engineer the ecosystem. Type 1 barely intervenes: protecting mangroves against storms, or creating marine reserves that export fish to nearby fishing grounds. Type 2 manages landscapes to be sustainable and do several jobs, as in growing trees among crops ({{ref:nature-nbs-247}}) or mixing tree species so forests resist shocks. Type 3 manages ecosystems intensively or creates new ones, such as planted roofs and walls or wetlands built from scratch. The typology carries a trade-off. The more services and stakeholder groups a solution targets, the less it can maximize any single one.

entries.title: Why ecosystem-based adaptation is slow to spread

definition.text: Although case studies show EbA can be effective and cost-effective, several recognised challenges slow its adoption.

facts.text: It is unclear beyond what limits ecosystems can keep providing adaptation services as the climate changes.
Inconsistent methods and no comparable measures of success make it hard to argue the economic case for EbA.
Governance is hard because EbA spans sectors that manage ecosystems and sectors that benefit from them.
Poverty, development needs, limited access to finance and cultural preferences about landscapes also constrain uptake.

entries.text: Case studies show ecosystem-based adaptation can work and can save money. So why is it not everywhere? First, nobody knows beyond what limits ecosystems can keep providing protection as the climate changes. Second, methods vary and nobody measures success the same way, so the economic case is hard to argue. Third, governance is awkward, because EbA spans the sectors that manage ecosystems and the different sectors that benefit from them. Finally, low incomes, pressing development needs, limited finance and cultural preferences about landscapes all slow its uptake.

entries.title: Five ways to put an ecosystem to work
entries.article: Ecological engineering#Design guidelines, functional classes, and design principles

definition.text: Mitsch and Jorgensen sort ecological engineering designs into five functional classes by how the ecosystem is used.

facts.text: An ecosystem can be used to solve pollution, as in wastewater wetlands and stormwater bioretention.
An ecosystem can be imitated to address a resource problem (replacement wetlands, rain gardens) or recovered after disturbance (mine-land or lake restoration).
An ecosystem can be modified in an ecologically sound way, or used for benefit without destroying its balance, as in agroforestry and multispecies aquaculture.

entries.text: Mitsch and Jorgensen sorted ecological engineering designs into five classes by how the ecosystem is used. An ecosystem can solve a pollution problem, as wetlands that treat wastewater and planted beds that filter runoff do. It can be imitated to fix a resource problem, as with replacement wetlands and small planted hollows that soak up rain. It can be recovered after disturbance, as when old mine land or a lake is restored. It can be modified in an ecologically sound way. Or it can be used for benefit without upsetting its balance, as in growing trees among crops or raising several species together in fish farms.

entries.title: Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction: buffers that also feed people

definition.text: Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction (Eco-DRR) uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters.

facts.text: It maintains ecosystems as buffers against dangerous natural events while still supplying communities with food and water.
Its measures are often closely linked or similar to those of ecosystem-based adaptation.
The Sendai Framework calls for cross-border cooperation on ecosystem-based approaches in shared river basins and coastlines to reduce disaster risk.
Research has focused on cities in the Global North; more is needed in coastal, dryland and watershed areas of the Global South.

entries.text: Some of the best disaster defenses also put food on the table. This approach, a form of {{ref:nature-clim-226}} known as Eco-DRR, uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters. Its measures are often closely linked to those of ecosystem-based adaptation, or much the same. entries.title: Stormwater: where city rain goes

definition.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow.

facts.text: It can soak into soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land.
In forests and other natural landscapes, soil and plants absorb much of it.
In cities, unmanaged stormwater causes two main problems: flooding and water pollution.
Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush runoff into waterways, causing erosion and floods and leaving little to recharge groundwater.
Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without treatment.
Phosphorus carried in runoff feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes.
Stormwater is a major cause of urban flooding.

entries.text: In a forest, a heavy shower mostly disappears, because soil and plants absorb much of it. Stormwater is the water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow. It has four possible fates. It can soak into the soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land as {{ref:nature-eco-275}}. Cities tilt the odds toward running off. Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush the rest into waterways. The results are erosion and floods, with little water left to recharge groundwater. Unmanaged stormwater causes two main urban problems: flooding and water pollution. It is a major cause of flooding in cities. Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without any treatment. Phosphorus is one culprit it carries. Washed into lakes, it feeds blooms of algae and toxic cyanobacteria. Much of this chapter is about ways to make city rain behave more like forest rain.

entries.title: Flood management: living with water that rises

definition.text: The methods, also called flood control, used to reduce or prevent the harm done by flood waters.

facts.text: Floods come from a mix of natural causes, such as extreme weather upstream, and human changes to water bodies and runoff.
Methods are structural, which physically hold back water, or non-structural, which do not.
More hard surfaces, or wildfires that remove vegetation, make flooding worse.
Natural seasonal floods also do good: they renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.
The cost of protection rises with the number of people and amount of property protected.
The US FEMA estimates that every $1.00 spent on mitigation saves $4.00.
Wetlands help manage floods, especially on coasts, by holding excess water and shielding inland communities from storm surges.

entries.text: The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) estimates that every $1.00 spent on flood mitigation saves $4.00. Flood management, also called flood control, covers the methods used to reduce or prevent the harm floodwaters do. Floods come from a mix of causes. Some are natural, such as extreme weather upstream. Others are human, such as changes to water bodies and to how rain runs off the land. More hard surfaces make flooding worse, and so do wildfires that strip away vegetation. The methods fall into two families. Structural methods physically hold water back; non-structural methods do not. Wetlands are one of nature's own tools. They hold excess water and, especially on coasts, shield inland communities from storm surges. Protection is not cheap, and its cost rises with the number of people and the amount of property it covers. Yet floods are not simply enemies. Natural seasonal floods renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.

entries.title: Green infrastructure: building with nature

definition.text: A network of natural or nature-like features, also called blue-green infrastructure, used to solve urban and climate problems by building with nature.

facts.text: When people harness nature and use it as an infrastructure system, it is called green infrastructure.
Nature can protect communities from flooding or extreme heat and improve air, soil and water quality.
Its main parts include stormwater management, climate adaptation, reducing heat stress, biodiversity, food production, cleaner air and water, and recreation and shade.
The term has no widely agreed definition and is often expanded to 'multifunctional' green infrastructure, meaning several functions share the same land.
Its stormwater ideas began in mid-1980s proposals for practices to reduce runoff volume and erosion and recharge aquifers.
The term itself first appeared in the early 1990s, in a 1994 report on the Florida Greenways Project.
Examples include urban forests, constructed wetlands, green roofs, rain gardens, stormwater basins and bioswales.

entries.title: Urban flooding: when the drains give up

definition.text: Flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage systems such as storm sewers.

facts.text: It can happen whether or not a community lies on a floodplain or near water.
Anything that enlarges impermeable surfaces, such as soil sealing, raises flood risk.
Climate change is expected to make storm surges, heavy rain and river overflow more frequent and severe.
In 2020, floods caused an estimated 6,000 deaths and US$51.3B in damages worldwide.
Where homes have basements, it is the main cause of basement and sewer backups, and chronically wet houses are linked to respiratory illness.
Responses include grey infrastructure, green infrastructure, better drainage and changing land use toward more vegetated open space.

entries.title: Constructed wetlands: marshes built to clean water

definition.text: An artificial wetland built to clean sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

facts.text: It is an engineered system that uses the natural work of plants, soil and microorganisms to give wastewater a secondary treatment.
Plant roots, stems and leaves give microorganisms a surface to grow on while they break down organic material.
Physical, chemical and biological processes act together in the wetland to remove contaminants such as nitrogen, phosphorus and dissolved metals.
Constructed wetlands copy natural wetlands to capture stormwater, cut nutrient loads and create varied wildlife habitat.
Because they largely run themselves, their lifetime costs are much lower than those of conventional treatment plants, and their building costs are often lower too.
They need a lot of space, so they are not favoured where land is expensive.
Cattails and common reed are the main plants used, even though both can become invasive outside their native range.
Stormwater wetlands can act as 'ecological traps' for amphibians, whose larvae suffer from the pollutants that collect there.

entries.text: A marsh can be built to clean dirty water. A constructed wetland is an artificial wetland made to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater. It is engineered, but it relies on the natural work of plants, soil and microorganisms to give wastewater a secondary treatment. Roots, stems and leaves give microbes a surface to grow on while they break down organic matter. Physical, chemical and biological processes together strip out nitrogen, phosphorus and dissolved metals. Stormwater versions copy natural wetlands to capture runoff, cut nutrient loads and create varied wildlife habitat. Because they largely run themselves, their lifetime costs are far lower than conventional treatment plants, and building them is often cheaper too. The catch is space, so they lose out where land is expensive. Cattails and common reed are the main plants, though both can turn invasive outside their native range. Stormwater wetlands can also become 'ecological traps' for amphibians, whose larvae suffer from the pollutants collected there.

entries.title: Bioswales: planted ditches that clean the street

definition.text: A channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution.

facts.text: It is a drainage course with gently sloped sides of less than 6%.
It is designed to keep water in the swale as long as safely possible, since longer stays remove more pollutants.
Plants catch pollutants, which then enter the soil and are broken down by bacteria.
Bioswales can also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion and give pollinators habitat.
They suit streets and parking lots, where car pollution is washed off by the first rain.
There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet bioswales.
Poor maintenance can lead to high repair costs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.
In 1996, 2330 lineal feet of bioswale were installed at Willamette River Park in Portland, and check dams cut suspended solids entering the river by 50%.

entries.text: In 1996, Portland installed 2330 lineal feet of bioswale at Willamette River Park. Small barriers called check dams cut the suspended solids entering the river by 50%. A bioswale is a channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution. Its sides slope gently, at less than 6%. The trick is patience. A bioswale keeps water as long as safely possible, because longer stays remove more pollutants. Plants catch the pollutants, which then enter the soil, where bacteria break them down. Bioswales suit streets and parking lots, where the first rain washes off car pollution. They also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion, and give pollinators habitat. There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet. Neglect leads to costly repairs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.

entries.title: Sustainable drainage: making pipes behave like soil

definition.text: A set of water management practices, also called SuDS, that make modern drainage work with natural water processes as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy.

facts.text: SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the natural water cycle, especially surface runoff and water pollution.
When vegetation is replaced by concrete, asphalt and roofs, land loses its ability to absorb rain, which then overloads drains and causes floods.
SuDS often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible.
Typical components include bioswales, permeable paving, artificial wetlands, retention basins, green roofs, rain gardens and downspout disconnection.
Plants and soil remove stormwater pollutants by adsorption, filtration and plant uptake.
In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff.
Planting a rain garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.
Drainage systems have been found in ancient cities more than 5,000 years old, but modern systems appeared only in 19th-century Western Europe, mainly to deal with sewage.

entries.title: Water-sensitive urban design: rain as a resource

definition.text: A planning and engineering approach, called WSUD, that builds the whole urban water cycle (stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply) into city design to limit environmental harm and improve amenity.

facts.text: WSUD is the term used in Australia and the Middle East; it resembles low-impact development in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom.
It treats urban stormwater as a resource rather than a nuisance, a shift from conventional drainage that sent runoff quickly to streams.
Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, improving the quality of water leaving cities and maximizing reuse of stormwater, recycled water and greywater.
Common practices include bioretention systems, infiltration trenches, porous paving, sedimentation basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks.
The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s.
In Victoria, new residential developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces.
Regulatory barriers and fragmented institutions across state and local government are major obstacles to its adoption.

entries.text: Conventional drainage treated city rain as a nuisance and sent it quickly to streams. Water-sensitive urban design, or WSUD, treats it as a resource. This planning and engineering approach builds the whole urban water cycle into city design: stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply. Its aims are to limit environmental harm and make cities more pleasant. The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s, and the term is used there and in the Middle East. It resembles {{ref:nature-nbs-197}} in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom. Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, sending cleaner water out of cities and reusing as much stormwater, recycled water and greywater as possible. Common tools include planted filter beds, gravel trenches, porous paving, settling basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks. In Victoria, new housing developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces. Regulatory barriers and institutions split across state and local government are its main obstacles.

entries.title: Bioretention: how a planted bed scrubs out metals

definition.text: The removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area.

facts.text: A bioretention cell aims to reduce peak runoff and remove pollutants.
A typical cell has a sand bed, layers of filter media and plants on top; stored water seeps into the soil below over several days.
The name refers to plants and bacteria in the media that hold, absorb, break down and cycle contaminants.
Filtration, adsorption, chemical change and biological breakdown are its main ways of treating pollutants.
Untreated nitrogen and phosphorus in runoff cause eutrophication downstream; well-designed media can sharply reduce both.
In laboratory tests, cells removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and more than 95% of cadmium at typical stormwater levels.
Its capacity for heavy metals is limited, so the media must eventually be replaced where metal loads are high.
Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule it out.

Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule bioretention out.

entries.title: Rain gardens: small hollows that swallow storms

definition.text: A shallow planted hollow, also called a bioretention facility, that helps rain runoff soak back into the soil.

facts.text: Rain gardens cut the speed, amount and pollution of runoff from roofs, driveways, parking lots and compacted lawns.
Plants and soil hold stormwater and filter pollutants carried by urban runoff.
Central urban areas can be 90 to 100 percent hard surfaces, against 5 to 10 percent in suburbs.
A typical soil mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil.
Native plants are usually chosen because they tolerate local conditions, root deeply and add habitat.
Residential rain gardens began in 1990 in Prince George's County, Maryland, replacing a conventional stormwater pond, and proved highly cost-effective.
Water ponding for more than 48 hours may signal clogging, one of the most common problems.
A study rain garden in Xi'an held most of 28 large storms over four years; only 5 made it overflow.

entries.title: Low-impact development: handling rain where it falls

definition.text: A North American land planning and engineering approach, called LID, that manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure.

facts.text: It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime by infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source.
Similar terms include SuDS in the UK and water-sensitive urban design in Australia.
It began in Prince George's County, Maryland in 1990, because conventional detention ponds were not cost-effective and missed water quality goals.
Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize hydrological impact, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution.
Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and rainwater harvesting.
Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks.
It can remove the need for stormwater ponds on expensive land, letting developers build more homes on the same plot.
In some municipalities it is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows.

entries.text: Conventional detention ponds in Prince George's County, Maryland, were not cost-effective and missed their water quality goals. So in 1990 the county tried low-impact development, or LID. This North American approach to land planning and engineering manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure. It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime, infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source. Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize the impact on water flows, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution. Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and collecting rainwater. Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of the water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks. Developers gain too, since dropping ponds on expensive land lets them build more homes on the same plot. In some municipalities LID is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows, when pipes carrying both rain and sewage spill into rivers.

entries.title: Permeable paving: a parking lot that drinks

definition.text: Paving made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below.

facts.text: Materials include pervious concrete, porous asphalt, paving stones and interlocking pavers.
It reduces runoff and traps suspended solids, filtering pollutants from stormwater.
It can reduce downstream flooding and bank erosion and keep base flows in rivers.
Where soil cannot absorb water, the pavement stores it and releases it slowly between storms.
Some estimates put it at about one third more expensive than conventional paving, though it can reduce the need for other stormwater facilities.
Without regular cleaning its pores clog and it starts to behave like an impervious surface.
It should not be used at pollution 'hot spots' such as fuelling stations, where it could contaminate groundwater.

entries.title: Stormwater management: from street sweeping to sewer fees

definition.text: Managing the quantity and quality of stormwater, using both engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices.

facts.text: Best management practices include structures such as retention ponds and procedures such as street sweeping.
Technical measures include source control of hazardous materials, retention basins and filters, protecting natural waterways, and nature-based solutions working alongside pipes.
Institutional measures include stormwater user fees or utilities, asset management, updated regulations and community education.
Conventional facilities let particles larger than 40 micron settle out and hold water back to reduce flooding downstream.
Stormwater infrastructure is a costly long-term investment that performs worse as climate, urbanization and rules change.
In the US, the EPA regulates stormwater under the Clean Water Act, but farm runoff counts as nonpoint source pollution and needs no permit.

entries.title: Structural flood control: walls, banks and reservoirs

definition.text: Reducing flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels.

facts.text: Some methods are ancient: planting vegetation to hold water, terracing hillsides and digging floodways to divert water.
Many dams keep reservoir levels low before the rainy or melt season to leave room for floodwater.
Levees, bunds, reservoirs and weirs keep rivers from bursting their banks.
Coastal flooding is met with sea walls, beach nourishment and barrier islands.
Excess floodwater can be diverted onto land that absorbs it, recharging groundwater and easing later droughts.

entries.text: Some flood defenses are ancient: planting vegetation to hold water, terracing hillsides and digging floodways to divert it. Structural flood control reduces flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels. Levees and bunds, which are raised banks, along with reservoirs and weirs, keep rivers from bursting their banks. Many dams keep reservoir levels low before the rainy or melt season, leaving room for floodwater. On coasts, sea walls, added beach sand and barrier islands hold back the water. Floodwater can even become a resource. Diverted onto land that absorbs it, the excess recharges groundwater and eases later droughts.

entries.title: Non-structural flood management: maps, rules and stilts

definition.text: Ways of reducing flood risk that do not physically hold back water, such as zoning, mapping, modelling and planning.

facts.text: Land zoning rules can limit how much is built on floodplains and other flood-prone areas.
Stakeholder engagement helps the public and officials agree on flood policy, including emergency and land-use planning.
Property owners can flood-proof homes by blocking doors and vents, waterproofing and sandbagging; such private measures are increasingly important.
Buildings can be designed for resilience, for example by raising homes on stilts, so a city recovers quickly after a flood.

entries.title: Green versus grey: what the ledgers show

definition.text: The comparison of costs and benefits between green infrastructure and conventional 'grey' infrastructure such as concrete pipes and tunnels.

facts.text: A 2012 study of 479 US green infrastructure projects found 44% reduced costs while 31% increased them.
The largest savings came from less stormwater runoff and lower heating and cooling bills.
Philadelphia found a green plan would cost $1.2 billion over 25 years, against $6 billion for a grey plan.
Philadelphia's plan was also expected to raise property values by $390 million over 45 years, increasing the city's property tax income.
New York City's green plan was expected to cost $1.5 billion less than a comparable grey approach.
A 2016 UK study found residents were willing to pay more for green infrastructure that was visibly greener, accessible and multifunctional.
In fragile states, upfront building costs for green infrastructure were up to 8% higher than for other projects.

entries.title: Green gentrification: when a new park prices people out

definition.text: The displacement of lower-income residents when new green spaces raise property values and attract wealthier people.

facts.text: Projects meant to make cities greener and more liveable, as in Chicago, often raise social justice concerns such as gentrification.
Their benefits are often unevenly shared, usually serving wealthier, whiter neighbourhoods.
A study of Los Angeles housing prices linked green infrastructure to 'green climate gentrification'.
Greening can push out homeless people and others with poor access to housing, undoing some of its benefits.
Planners are urged to combine environmental goals with social equity and to work with community residents.
Green amenities include green spaces, parks, green roofs, gardens and green, energy-efficient building materials.
New green amenities can push out low-income households through rising housing costs and can also displace long-time residents culturally and politically.
The term was first coined by Sieg and colleagues in 2004 and blends older ideas of gentrification and environmental justice.

entries.title: Sponge cities: China's bet on soaking up floods

definition.text: A nature-based urban planning model from China that uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods.

facts.text: The name reflects how green landscapes store, slow and soak up surface water like a sponge.
Its philosophy is to retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects, the reverse of grey infrastructure's pipes, reservoirs and walls.
Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero.
Proposed by landscape architect Kongjian Yu, it became national Chinese policy in 2014 after the 2012 Beijing flood killed 79 people.
Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015, growing to 87 cities by 2017.
Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030.
Studies show it reduces runoff and improves water quality, but monitoring data are scarce and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

entries.text: In 2012 a flood in Beijing killed 79 people. In 2014 China made the sponge city national policy. The name says it: green landscapes store, slow and soak up water like a sponge. Its philosophy reverses the pipes, reservoirs and walls of conventional engineering. Retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects. Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero. Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015 and grew to 87 cities by 2017. Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030. Studies show less runoff and cleaner water. But monitoring data are scarce, and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

entries.title: Beaver dams: flood control built by rodents

definition.text: A dam built by beavers, creating a pond that protects them from predators and stores food for winter.

facts.text: By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a keystone species and ecosystem engineers.
In their native range, beaver dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks.
The dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and sustaining flow in dry spells.
Bacteria in the debris behind dams turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some pesticides.
Beaver ponds trapped 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams in an Alberta study.
Dams typically run from a few metres to about 100 metres long; the largest known is 775 metres.
They can flood farmland, roads and railways, and introduced beavers in Tierra del Fuego are considered a plague.
Abandoned dams leave wetlands that become meadows and then forest, slowly building up valley bottomland.

When dams are abandoned, their wetlands become meadows and then forest, slowly building up the valley floor.

entries.title: Flood peak attenuation: flattening the spike
entries.article: Flood management#Flood levels: blunting the peak

definition.text: Slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered.

facts.text: Flood water levels tend to rise and fall very abruptly.
Marshes, river meanders, vegetation, porous materials and a river spreading over its floodplain all slow parts of the flow and blunt the spike.

entries.text: Flood water tends to rise and fall very abruptly. Flood peak attenuation means slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered. Many natural features do this. Marshes, river meanders, vegetation and porous materials each slow part of the flow. So does a river spreading out over its floodplain. Together they blunt the spike, so less water arrives at any one moment.

entries.title: Flood risk mapping: knowing where the water will go

definition.text: Drawing maps of where floods may reach, so policy makers can make informed decisions about flood hazards.

facts.text: Producing flood risk maps is described as the most effective way to reduce risk to people and property, and most countries have them.
Flood modelling simulates flood hazards and how their drivers interact, and their effects on people and the environment.
In Bangladesh, where nearly 80% of people live on low floodplains, hazard maps pick out areas prone to repeated or severe floods.

entries.title: Managed retreat from floodplains: giving land back to the river

definition.text: Removing buildings from flood-prone areas and leaving the land as parks or wilderness.

facts.text: Floodplain buyout programs have run in New Jersey, Charlotte in North Carolina, and Missouri.

entries.text: Sometimes the best flood defense is to leave. Planned withdrawal from floodplains, a case of what {{ref:nature-nbs-040}} describes, means removing buildings from flood-prone areas and turning the land into parks or wilderness. Nothing is left to damage, and the floodplain is free to flood. Programs in which governments buy out floodplain homeowners ({{ref:nature-nbs-042}}) have run in New Jersey, in Charlotte in North Carolina, and in Missouri.

entries.title: Storm surge barriers: gates against the sea

definition.text: A floodgate built to stop a storm surge or spring tide from flooding the area behind it.

facts.text: It is almost always part of a larger system of floodwalls, levees and natural features.
London's Thames Barrier has operated since 1982 to guard against surges like the North Sea flood of 1953.
Such barriers were introduced after the North Sea Flood of 1953.
Storm surge warnings help decide when to close the floodgates.

facts.text: Because green projects produce many benefits, they can compete for many different funding sources.
Some government tax incentive programs can be used to attract finance to green infrastructure projects.
In fragile states, weak governance and limited institutional capacity can stop countries benefiting from green infrastructure investment.

definition.text: City infrastructure that involves water, such as rivers, ponds, lakes and harbours.

facts.text: When combined with green infrastructure it is called blue-green infrastructure.
It can support aquatic insects, amphibians and water birds in cities.
Accessible blue infrastructure is also called blue space, and access to it may benefit people's health and wellbeing.

entries.title: Floating wetlands: gardens that clean the water beneath

definition.text: A planted structure that floats on a lake, river, estuary or coastal water and supports wetland vegetation.

facts.text: Its plants can remove heavy metals and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and may store carbon.
It gives habitat to insects and wildlife and makes hardened urban shorelines look better.

entries.title: Downspout disconnection: unplugging the roof from the sewer

definition.text: Cutting a roof's downspout off from the sewer and sending the roof water onto ground that can soak it up.

facts.text: In heavy rain a building's downspouts can send 12 gallons of water a minute into the sewer, raising the risk of basement backups and overflows.
It is especially useful in cities with combined sewer systems.

US programs run by the EPA aim to improve water quality by managing stormwater runoff more widely and easing the load on sewers.

entries.title: Stormwater basins: hollows that catch the rain

definition.text: A planted hollow in the ground that collects rainwater to cut runoff to sewers, reduce erosion, filter water and prevent flooding.

facts.text: Newer designs with sturdier plants instead of mowed grass, often called bioretention basins, are good at removing pollutants and trapping sediment.
Stormwater basins are an important part of the sponge city idea for managing floods.

entries.title: Floodplain restoration: reconnecting rivers to their land

definition.text: Returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its condition before levees were built and wetlands drained.

facts.text: Its goals include fewer floods, habitat for aquatic species, better water quality and more groundwater recharge.
Methods focus on reconnecting rivers to floodplains: setting back levees, removing dams or weirs, and restoring drained wetlands.
It is a nature-based solution that lowers flood risk by boosting the ecosystem's ability to slow and hold water.
Vegetation can cut wave energy during floods by about 70% in salt marshes and 65% in mangroves.
It works best for frequent, low to moderate floods and has limited benefit for extreme floods on its own.
Whether restoration increases coastal wetlands' carbon sequestration is debated, though their role in reducing flood risk is well supported.
Projects can stall when immediate flood defence and current land uses are valued above ecological benefits.
At Nijmegen, moving a dike 350 metres inland and digging a side channel lowered peak water levels by about 35 cm.

entries.title: Stream restoration: healing rivers for fish, floods and people

definition.text: Work to improve the environmental health of a river or stream, for biodiversity, recreation, flood management or landscape.

facts.text: Approaches split into form-based restoration, which physically alters the stream, and process-based restoration, which restores natural water and sediment processes.
It differs from river engineering, which alters water bodies for navigation, flood control or water supply without an ecological aim.
Activities range from fixing a culvert or removing a weir that blocks fish, to stabilizing banks, restoring riparian zones or adding constructed wetlands.
Projects usually begin by assessing climate, geology, hydrology, sediment transport, channel shape and flood records.
A US database built in the 2000s held over 35,000 stream restoration projects.
Its effectiveness remains poorly measured because of thin data, too little monitoring and differing yardsticks.
It is entering law, for example through the European water framework's commitment to restore surface waters.

entries.title: Dam removal: letting rivers run free again

definition.text: Demolishing a dam to return natural water flow to a river.

facts.text: The case for removal weighs dams' benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against their harms.
Dams can reduce primary productivity, biodiversity and native species, and ageing brings weakness, sediment build-up and high maintenance costs.
About 900 US dams were removed between 1990 and 2015, and by 2015 the rate was 50 to 60 a year.
Many removals aim to restore river habitat and native fish, as in the Elwha Ecosystem Restoration.
Releasing trapped sediment can rebuild habitat downstream, but toxic sediment can do harm, as when PCBs were released after a Hudson River dam was removed.
Removal is always costly, and the cost is usually shared between the owner and government.
The European Commission counts at least 150 000 barriers in European rivers that no longer serve a purpose.
The EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to restore free flow to 25,000 kilometres of river by 2030.

entries.title: What urban floods cost

FEMA says almost 40% of small businesses never reopen after a flooding disaster.
Urban flooding is estimated to cost £270 million a year in England and Wales.
In the UK, expected annual surface water damages may rise by £60–200 million under 2–4°C warming.

entries.title: Grey infrastructure: fighting water with concrete

definition.text: Conventional infrastructure such as dams, seawalls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water.

facts.text: It can prevent flood damage and be economically valuable, but models suggest it may grow less effective as climate change intensifies floods.
Grey approaches centralize water in big reservoirs, speed it through pipes and fight it with higher walls, the opposite of sponge city design.
Overuse of grey infrastructure can cause water shortages, pollution and loss of water ecosystem services.

Managing the urban water cycle as a whole aims to use resources more efficiently, with economic, social and environmental gains.
Integrated stormwater management can improve runoff quality, cut flood risk and add to drinking water supply.

entries.title: Three kinds of urban flood

definition.text: The three kinds of urban flood planners distinguish: pluvial (from heavy rain), fluvial (from a river overflowing) and coastal (often from storm surges).

facts.text: Each type has different impacts and needs different mitigation.
Erratic rainfall is expected to make both pluvial and fluvial flooding more frequent and severe.
Coastal cities may be hit hardest by sea level rise and heavier rain.

entries.title: Subsurface flow wetlands: cleaning water out of sight

definition.text: A constructed wetland in which the wastewater flows among plant roots below a gravel surface, so no water shows at the top.

facts.text: Keeping water below the surface makes the system more efficient, less smelly, less attractive to mosquitoes and less affected by winter.
It needs less land to treat water than a surface flow wetland.
Its cost depends mainly on the sand used to fill the bed.
It is a secondary treatment, so solids must first be removed by a primary treatment step.

entries.title: Surface flow wetlands: open water that kills germs

definition.text: A constructed wetland with open water flowing horizontally across plant roots, also called a free water surface wetland.

facts.text: It is used to polish effluent from wastewater treatment plants and to treat stormwater drainage.
Sunlight, predators, settling and natural decay destroy pathogens in the open water.
It needs more land than a subsurface system and may smell more and work less well in winter.
Open water can breed mosquitoes, which makes it harder to fit into city neighbourhoods.

entries.title: Infiltration trenches: gravel that lets rain sink in
entries.article: Water-sensitive urban design#Infiltration trenches and systems

definition.text: A shallow trench filled with gravel or rock that holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater.

facts.text: It is not mainly a treatment measure, but it can hold back some pollutants and sediment.
Sand filters work on the same principle and suit runoff from car parks and dense built-up areas.

entries.title: Sedimentation basins: the first stop for dirty runoff

definition.text: A basin that holds stormwater briefly and slows it so coarse and medium sediments settle out.

facts.text: It is often the first element of a treatment train, protecting later elements from being smothered by sediment.
Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

It is often the first element in a treatment train, a series of steps that clean water in turn. By catching sediment early, it keeps later elements from being smothered. Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

entries.title: Retention basins: ponds that never dry

definition.text: An artificial pond, also called a wet pond, with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water, used to manage stormwater.

facts.text: It is used to control runoff, protect against floods and erosion, and improve the quality of nearby water.
It differs from a detention basin or 'dry pond', which holds water only after a storm and then drains at a controlled rate.
It also differs from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

entries.title: Four families of permeable pavement

definition.text: The families of porous paving materials, each with its own advantages for particular uses.

facts.text: Pervious concrete is widely available and carries frequent traffic.
Porous asphalt is laid like normal asphalt but leaves out fine aggregate, so open voids let water through.
Plastic grids holding gravel or turf make a fully porous surface popular with homeowners.
Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have open spaces between units and carry light and heavy traffic.

entries.title: Room for the River: the Dutch stop raising dikes

definition.text: A Dutch government plan, run from 2006 to 2015, that protects against floods by giving the country's rivers more space while improving landscape and environment.

facts.text: It followed the 1993 and 1995 floods, when over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta were evacuated.
Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains, lowering groynes, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass.
A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion.
Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with natural river dynamics.

entries.text: In 1993 and 1995, floods forced the evacuation of over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta. The Dutch response was Room for the River, a government plan run from 2006 to 2015. It protects against floods by giving rivers more space while improving landscape and environment. Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains and the low cross-walls that trap sand, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass. A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion. Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with the river's natural dynamics.

entries.title: The flood pulse concept: why floods feed rivers

definition.text: The idea that a river's regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between the channel and its floodplain.

facts.text: It treats the annual flood pulse as the most biologically productive feature of a river ecosystem, unlike older theories that saw floods as catastrophes.
The flood pulse maintains species and genetic diversity on the floodplain and brings in oxygen.
Dams, channelization, levees and other human changes disrupt the pulse and can devastate riparian ecosystems.
It was developed by W. J. Junk in 1989 and is one of three main models of large rivers, with the river continuum and serial discontinuity concepts.

entries.contested_note: Many theorists criticize its assumptions and prefer the river continuum concept, while its authors argue that concept does not fit large rivers.

entries.title: Beaver dam analogs: building dams for beavers

definition.text: A human-built structure that imitates a beaver dam, to gain its benefits or to attract beavers to settle.

facts.text: Builders may drive wooden posts into the stream bed to hold branches that would otherwise wash away.
Even if beavers never take over, analogs provide many of the benefits of natural dams, such as water retention and wetland ponds.

entries.title: Taming a dam without tearing it down

definition.text: Ways of reducing a dam's harm without removing it, such as better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders.

facts.text: Fewer than 1% of US dams are being considered for removal.
Varying the water released by season mimics natural flow changes.
The effectiveness of fish ladders is debated, though some fish pass rather than none.
Plans for decommissioning and river restoration should be drawn up well before a dam reaches its design life.

entries.title: Four ways to take down a dam

definition.text: The four common ways of removing a dam, chosen mainly by how the sediment behind it is handled.

facts.text: Notch and release drains the reservoir slowly through cut notches so the ecosystem can adjust; it can take over a year.
Rapid release is quickest and cheapest but can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream.
Dig and dewater, usually the most expensive, removes dried sediment for safe disposal, needed when it contains toxins.
Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

entries.title: Replanting riverbanks: plant them or let them return

definition.text: Bringing back riparian plants either by planting them (active) or by removing the disturbance and letting them return (passive).

facts.text: Active planting may be fastest but can be too costly in resources.
Fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities.
Passive recovery can be undermined when exotic species colonize first.

entries.text: Riverside plants can come back in two ways. Active revegetation plants them. Passive revegetation removes the disturbance and lets them return on their own. Active planting may be fastest but can cost too much. Passive methods can work well: fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities. The risk is that exotic species colonize first and undermine the recovery.

entries.title: Engineered log jams: putting wood back in rivers

definition.text: Placing large wood in a stream to recreate the natural log jams that channelization and beaver removal took away.

facts.text: Log jams add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow.

entries.text: Straightened channels and the loss of beavers stripped many streams of their natural log jams. An engineered log jam places large wood back in a stream to recreate them. The logs change how water moves. They add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow, giving the stream more varied places for life.

entries.title: Form-based restoration: reshaping the channel

definition.text: Restoration that changes a stream channel's physical shape to improve its condition.

facts.text: Tools include deflectors, cross-vanes, weirs and step-pools, engineered log jams, bank stabilization and channel reconfiguration.
It gives immediate change but can fail when degradation comes from a wider area.
Critics say it works at too small a scale and aims for what people think a stream should look like, not its geomorphic setting.

entries.contested_note: Scientists criticize form-based restoration as working at too small a scale and imposing a socially preferred stream shape.

entries.title: Natural Channel Design: a cookbook for streams

definition.text: A US method from the 1990s that classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed and then redesigns the channel to a target form.

facts.text: Its design phase has 8 phases and 40 steps.
Fluvial geomorphologists call it a 'cookbook' approach that untrained practitioners misuse, leading to failures.
Its focus on channel stability can limit a stream's ability to adapt.

entries.contested_note: Fluvial geomorphologists criticize the method as a cookbook approach that can cause project failures.

entries.title: Process-based restoration: let the river do the work

definition.text: Restoration that rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form.

facts.text: It has grown in popularity since the mid-1990s as a more ecosystem-centred approach.
It restores connections between stream and floodplain and along the stream, often by removing levees, dams or grade controls.
It aims to make the system as resilient as possible and need little maintenance, though benefits can take time to appear.

entries.title: Freedom space: a corridor for a wandering river
entries.article: Stream restoration#Implementing a minimum stream corridor width

definition.text: A band of land, set by a stream's hydrology and geomorphology, within which the stream is left free to move with minimal intervention.

facts.text: The idea goes by many names: river corridor in the US, room for the river in the Netherlands, freedom space in France, making space for water in the UK.
A cost-benefit analysis found it could pay off long term through lower maintenance costs, less erosion and flood damage, and ecological services.

entries.title: Streambank bioengineering: roots instead of rock

definition.text: Stabilizing stream banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap and gabions.

facts.text: Roots from sprouting live branches anchor the soil and prevent erosion.
This makes bioengineered structures more natural and adaptable than hard engineering.
Some bank erosion is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riparian habitats.

entries.text: Stream banks can be held in place by living plants. Streambank bioengineering stabilizes banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap, loose rock armor, and gabions, wire cages of stone. Live branches sprout roots that anchor the soil and prevent erosion. That makes these structures more natural and adaptable than concrete and rock. Some bank erosion is welcome anyway, since it is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riverside habitats.

entries.title: The first flush: a storm's dirtiest minutes

definition.text: The first runoff of a rainstorm, which washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces.

facts.text: Urban and suburban first-flush runoff is described as highly toxic.
Bioswales are built to handle the first flush, so they suit roads, parking lots and roofs.
Rainwater tanks may use a first-flush diverter to keep contaminants out of stored water.

entries.title: Source water protection: guarding drinking water at the start

definition.text: Planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination.

facts.text: It involves identifying sources, assessing contamination threats, informing the public and acting to remove contamination.
It applies to lakes, rivers and groundwater.
Canada adopted it as part of a multi-barrier approach after drinking water in Walkerton, Ontario was contaminated with E. coli.
Researchers have begun bringing ecosystem service assessments into source water protection.

entries.title: Blue carbon: the climate value of coastal mud

definition.text: Carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways that people can manage.

facts.text: Most often the term means the carbon captured by tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows.
These vegetated coastal ecosystems bury carbon fast because they pile it up in their soils and sediments.
Coastal sediments lack oxygen, so organic carbon in them can be preserved for decades to millennia, far longer than most land carbon stocks.
When blue carbon ecosystems are damaged or lost, they release their carbon back to the air and add to greenhouse gas emissions.
Managing them counts as an ocean-based biological form of carbon dioxide removal, and can serve both climate mitigation and ecosystem-based adaptation.
The term was coined in 2009 to stress that coastal vegetated ecosystems contribute far more than their share to global carbon sequestration.
Seagrass, salt marshes and mangroves are sometimes called 'blue forests', in contrast to green forests on land.

entries.contested_note: Sources say the long-term effectiveness of blue carbon as a carbon dioxide removal method is still under debate.

entries.title: Coastal erosion: the sea takes back the land

definition.text: The loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline by waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice or storms.

facts.text: It works through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and chemical dissolving of rock by seawater.
Softer rock erodes faster than harder rock, carving tunnels, arches and pillars, and over time the coast evens out.
Storms can erode coasts hundreds of times faster than normal weather.
Rising seas let waves reach further inland, speeding shoreline retreat.
It destroys dunes, wetlands, beaches and barrier islands that buffer storms, and it reduces biodiversity.
It damages infrastructure and property, raises protection costs, and harms tourism and fisheries.
Human action can speed it up: Hallsands in Devon was washed away in 1917 after shingle was dredged from its bay.

entries.text: In 1917 the village of Hallsands in Devon was washed into the sea. Shingle had been dredged from its bay, leaving it unprotected. Coastal erosion is the loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline. Waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice and storms all do the work. They act through the hydraulic force of water, abrasion by hurled stones, attrition as stones grind each other down, and seawater chemically dissolving rock. Softer rock erodes faster than harder rock, carving tunnels, arches and pillars, until over time the coast evens out. Storms can erode coasts hundreds of times faster than normal weather. Rising seas let waves reach further inland, speeding the retreat. The losses compound. Erosion destroys the dunes, wetlands, beaches and barrier islands that buffer storms, and it reduces biodiversity. It damages infrastructure and property, raises protection costs, and harms tourism and fisheries.

entries.title: Coastal management: defending where people crowd

definition.text: Defending coasts against flooding and erosion, including techniques that stop erosion to claim land.

facts.text: Coastal zones cover less than 15% of Earth's land yet host more than 40% of the world's people.
Nearly 1.2 billion people live within 100 km of a coastline and 100 m of sea level.
Protection matters more as climate change speeds up sea level rise in the 21st century.
Before the 1950s the norm was hard structures such as seawalls, revetments and groynes.
From the late 1940s, cost and ugliness pushed engineers toward artificial beaches and stabilized dunes that copy natural protection.
Measures often worked locally but made problems worse elsewhere, sometimes tens of kilometres away.

entries.title: Managed retreat: moving out of harm's way

definition.text: The planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk.

facts.text: It can respond to many hazards, including floods, wildfire and drought.
Sea level rise from climate change is drawing attention from politicians, insurers and residents to retreat from low-lying coasts.
Its form depends on the location, the type of hazard and local policies.
Some low-lying countries facing flooding, such as Kiribati, are planning to relocate their populations.
Managed retreat can be very controversial, yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise.
One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue rather than a technical one.
Retreating from high-risk areas such as floodplains reduces exposure.
Whether migration counts as adaptation is debated; the IPCC says it may or may not.

entries.title: Seawalls: holding the line in concrete

definition.text: A hard coastal defence built where the sea acts directly on the land, to protect people, property and activities from tides, waves or tsunamis.

facts.text: It works by reflecting wave energy back out to sea, leaving less energy to cause erosion.
Reflected waves can scour and lower the beach in front, and the wall can speed erosion of neighbouring unprotected coasts.
Being static, a seawall clashes with the moving coast and blocks the exchange of sediment between land and sea.
High costs and environmental side effects have led to more use of soft options such as beach replenishment.
Rising seas raise both normal water levels and storm wave heights, which existing walls may not withstand.
At least 43 percent of Japan's coastline is lined with seawalls or similar structures, yet in 2011 the tsunami overwhelmed seawalls in most areas.
A cost-benefit approach helps decide whether a seawall is worth its expense.

entries.title: Oyster reefs: living breakwaters that filter the sea

definition.text: A dense colony of oysters that builds up into a large reef, also called an oyster bed, bank or bar.

facts.text: New reefs form on stone or hard debris because oyster larvae must settle on hard surfaces; they then grow as young oysters settle on older shells.
Over the last few centuries, overharvesting, lime production and coastal degradation have caused large declines worldwide; 85% of oyster reefs have been removed in two centuries.
Oysters filter phytoplankton and organic matter from the water, buffering estuaries against eutrophication.
Reefs stabilize shorelines by trapping sediment and damping waves, and are recognized as green infrastructure for shoreline protection.
Their nooks shelter prey and young animals, increasing prey biomass.
Restored intertidal eastern oyster reefs can match natural oyster densities and regain stability in about 6 years.

entries.title: Beach nourishment: buying time with sand

definition.text: Replacing sand lost from a beach through erosion or longshore drift with sediment brought from elsewhere.

facts.text: A wider beach soaks up wave energy across the surf zone, shielding buildings behind it from storm surges and unusually high tides.
It counts as soft engineering: it keeps the beach and avoids the harms of hard structures.
It must be repeated, because it eases the effects of erosion without removing its causes.
The first US project was at Coney Island, New York, in 1922–1923, and the US has spent $9 billion rebuilding beaches since 1923.
The added sand's grain size must closely match the native sand.
New sand can bury bottom-dwelling organisms, disturb seafloor habitat and cut light to nearby reefs and seagrass.
Benefits include higher nearby property values and more tourism, but high erosion rates can make it financially impractical.

entries.title: Five ways to answer a moving coast

definition.text: The broad choices for responding to coastal change: abandon, retreat, armour, build seaward, or raise land and buildings.

facts.text: The five generic strategies are abandonment, managed retreat or realignment, armouring with hard structures, building defences seaward, and elevating land and buildings.
The choice depends on local sea-level change, landforms, sediment supply and erosion, plus social, economic and political factors.
Integrated coastal zone management can instead keep development out of erosion- or flood-prone areas.
Moving seaward can create valuable new land but leaves developed coasts open to coastal squeeze.
Limited intervention, used where land has little economic value, lets salt marshes and dunes develop and absorb wave energy.

entries.text: Faced with a changing coast, people have five broad choices. They can abandon the land. They can retreat or realign, moving back in a planned way. They can armor the shore with hard structures. They can build defenses out to sea. Or they can raise land and buildings. The right choice depends on local sea-level change, landforms, sediment supply and erosion. Social, economic and political factors weigh just as much. Building seaward can create valuable new land, but it leaves developed coasts exposed to {{ref:nature-nbs-066}}, which traps habitats against fixed defenses. Where land has little economic value, limited intervention is an option. It lets salt marshes and dunes develop and absorb wave energy. {{ref:nature-gov-123}} offers another route, keeping development out of erosion- or flood-prone areas in the first place.

entries.title: Soft engineering: shores held by plants and logs

definition.text: A shoreline management practice that uses ecological principles and natural materials to stabilize shorelines and protect waterside habitats.

facts.text: It places vegetation, stones, sand, logs and similar materials to reduce erosion, soften the land-water edge and lower restoration costs.
Its guiding principles are to imitate nature, use gentle slopes that spread wave energy, use living 'soft armour', and mix materials for biodiversity.
The most basic technique is planting native vegetation whose roots bind the soil.
Other tools include coir logs, live stakes and fascines, brush mattresses, live cribwalls and vegetated riprap.
Coastal engineering shifted gradually toward including the natural environment late in the 20th century.
Soft and hard engineering can be blended, especially on fast-flowing waters.
Around the Detroit River, 38 soft engineering projects cost $17.3 million and showed strong economic and social benefits.

entries.title: Managed realignment: letting the sea back in

definition.text: Deliberately removing or breaching coastal flood defences so the sea can reclaim land and form natural soft landforms such as salt marsh.

facts.text: In the UK its main aim is coastal stability, replacing hard defences with natural soft landforms.
Its big drawback is that land must be given up to the sea, but the new natural areas buffer land further inland by absorbing water and damping waves.
It is also used to make up for lost intertidal habitat such as salt marsh lost to erosion and coastal squeeze.
At Abbott's Hall Farm in Essex, five breaches in an old sea wall let the sea create nearly 280 hectares of salt marsh.
Few sites are monitored consistently, so results have been very unpredictable.

entries.title: Sand dune stabilization: holding the coast's sand bank

definition.text: A coastal management practice that keeps sand dunes from eroding.

facts.text: Dunes protect inland areas from storms, waves and seawater, and can resupply eroded beaches with sand.
They also give habitat to specialized plants and animals, including rare and endangered species.
Stabilizing them combines planting vegetation against wind and water, wooden sand fences that hold sand, and footpaths that keep walkers off.
Vegetation binds the sand; without it, wind moves sand inland in a process called sand encroachment.
In about 30 years, nearly 75% of the Mediterranean's coastal dunes were damaged or destroyed, mainly by tourism.
Dune management counts as a soft technique, unlike hard defences whose end effects cause erosion on neighbouring coasts.
Without public understanding and support, coastal dune management is virtually impossible.

entries.title: Oyster reef restoration: rebuilding a lost reef

definition.text: Repairing and rebuilding degraded oyster reefs.

facts.text: By 2011 an estimated 85% of the world's oyster reefs had been lost to over-harvesting, destructive fishing, pollution and disease.
Projects aim for a working three-dimensional reef that supports biodiversity, protects shorelines, traps sediment and cleans water.
Sites are chosen by surveys of salinity, water quality, past reefs, substrate, disease, predators and other factors.
Restored reefs can recover oyster densities to match healthy natural reefs.
Cleaner water from healthy oysters benefits commercial and recreational fishing, boating and ecotourism, and projects create and safeguard jobs.
Introducing non-native oyster species to a new habitat can do more harm than good.

entries.title: Deep blue carbon: the ocean's largest, least manageable store

definition.text: Carbon stored in deep ocean waters and the sea floor of the high seas, beyond national jurisdictions.

facts.text: It covers carbon in continental shelf waters, deep-sea waters and the sea floor beneath them, and makes up 90% of all ocean carbon.
It is seen as less amenable to management because data on how permanent these stores are is lacking.
Below about 3 km, CO2 becomes liquid and sinks to the seafloor because it is denser than the seawater around it.
Techniques being explored include seaweed farming, ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and basalt storage.

definition.text: Seagrass meadows bury a large share of ocean carbon in their sediments despite covering a tiny part of the sea floor.

Global seagrass meadows may store as much as 19.9 Pg of organic carbon.
Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 138 g C m−2 yr−1.

entries.title: Does seaweed count as blue carbon?

definition.text: The open question of whether seaweed (macroalgae) forests should count as blue carbon ecosystems.

facts.text: Seaweed forests are strong candidates because they are highly productive and cover coasts worldwide.
A 2016 report estimated they could sequester 173 TgC per year (range 61–268), but the estimate is very uncertain.
Their carbon can be stored by burial in nearby sediments, export to the deep ocean, or as dissolved organic carbon that resists breakdown.
Tracking where seaweed carbon ends up is very hard, so precise estimates of their sequestration capacity are lacking.

entries.title: Tidal marshes: carbon stored in roots and mud

definition.text: Tidal marshes are intertidal ecosystems of non-woody plants that act as important carbon sinks.

facts.text: Marshes lock carbon in their roots and buried plant matter because sediment builds up fast and decomposition happens largely without oxygen.
Much of their production is belowground, and these deposits can be up to 8 m deep.
Salt marshes cover roughly 22,000 to 400,000 km2 worldwide and bury an estimated 210 g C m−2 yr−1.
They also shelter birds and young fish, protect coasts from storm surge and flooding, and cut nutrient loads reaching coastal waters.

They also shelter birds and young fish, protect coasts from storm surge and flooding, and cut the nutrients reaching coastal waters.

entries.title: Coral reef restoration: replanting the reef

definition.text: Natural and human-led processes for restoring damaged coral reefs.

facts.text: Reefs host over 25% of marine life, buffer coasts from storms and erosion, and support food, jobs and tourism for coastal communities.
Half the world's coral has disappeared since 1970.
The usual method is to break mature corals into fragments, grow them on lines or supports, and transplant them to the reef once large enough.
Restoration has grown in prominence because of unprecedented reef die-offs around the planet.
Coral gardening may not save every species; instead it can help natural recovery and widen a species' genetic pool.
Propagated corals raise the worry that some may spread like invasive species and harm biodiversity.

entries.title: Shoreline mapping: tracking a line that never stays put

definition.text: Recording where the shoreline is and how it moves over time, a basic need for coastal scientists, engineers and managers.

facts.text: Defining the shoreline is hard because coasts are dynamic and tides shift its position at any moment.
Data come from historical maps, aerial photographs used since the 1920s, beach profiling surveys, remote sensing and video.
Monitoring campaigns show past shoreline movement and support predictions of future change.
