definition.text: Programs in which government buys at-risk properties and relocates or demolishes them, a form of managed retreat.

facts.text: Relocation has been used inland and on coasts after severe flooding and hurricanes.
Sometimes single homes are bought after disasters; sometimes whole communities move, as at Valmeyer, Illinois, or Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana.

entries.title: Natural coastal barriers: living seawalls

definition.text: Coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs and coastal vegetation that blunt tsunamis and storm surges like a living seawall.

facts.text: A UNEP report found the 26 December 2004 tsunami did less damage where mangroves, coral reefs or coastal vegetation were present.
Weeks after that disaster, India began planting Casuarina and coconut saplings along its coast as a natural barrier.
Reefs can damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters.

entries.title: Mangroves are vanishing faster than rainforests

definition.text: The rapid worldwide decline of mangrove forests, driven by clearing for development, aquaculture and farming and by climate change.

facts.text: Mangroves are being lost faster than inland tropical rainforests.
At least 35% of global mangrove area has been lost, and the decline continues at 1-2% per year.
Mangroves make up only 0.7% of tropical forest area but their clearing contributes 10% of global CO2 emissions from deforestation.
Whether a mangrove forest survives sea level rise depends on whether its sediment builds up as fast as the sea rises.

entries.title: Mangrove restoration: why planting is not enough

definition.text: Rehabilitating degraded or destroyed mangrove forests so they return to a state like their condition before disturbance.

facts.text: Mangroves provide water filtration, fish nurseries, medicines, food and timber, and protect coasts from erosion and storm surges.
Mangroves store three to four times more carbon than other tropical forests.
Simply planting single-species stands in places thought suitable usually fails, because the soil and water needs of mangroves are not met.
Better methods let damaged areas regrow naturally by secondary succession, provided tidal and freshwater flows work and seedlings are available.
Mangroves are seen as one of the easiest coastal systems to restore because seedlings can survive where no adult trees remain.
Successful restoration would need an estimated US$0.3–1.6 billion per year until 2050; debt-for-nature swaps have been proposed to help pay.
Long-term success depends on support and participation of local communities.

entries.title: Hard engineering: concrete, steel and rock

definition.text: Protecting shorelines with non-living reinforcing materials such as concrete, steel and rock to stop erosion and flooding.

facts.text: The four main hard structures in coastal engineering are the seawall, revetment, groyne and breakwater.
Hard shoreline engineering mainly serves navigation, industry and commerce.
It destroyed biological communities, cut off waterside habitats and disrupted natural sediment movement; the Detroit River lost as much as 97% of its coastal wetlands.
Each hard structure gives only temporary protection and creates an end effect that erodes neighbouring coasts.

entries.title: Soft, hard or leave: three answers to erosion

definition.text: The three common ways to deal with coastal erosion: soft controls, hard controls, and relocation.

facts.text: Hard controls such as seawalls and groynes are more permanent; a seawall lasts about 50–100 years and a groyne 30–40 years.
Soft controls such as sandbags and beach nourishment slow erosion temporarily and are not meant as permanent fixes.
Vegetated 'living shorelines' such as marshes resist storms well; fifteen feet of marsh can absorb fifty percent of incoming wave energy.
Public support for retreat has typically been low.

entries.title: Groynes: walls that catch sand

definition.text: A wall or barrier built at right angles to the coast to trap sand carried along the shore and so build up a beach.

facts.text: Sand piles up on one side, widening the beach, but beach material is lost on the other side.
Groynes are cheap, need little maintenance and are among the most common defences, though many communities oppose their look.
The last groyne in a series stops sand from reaching beaches further along, a problem called terminal groyne syndrome.

entries.title: Hold the line: keeping the shore where it is

definition.text: A coastal strategy that keeps the shoreline where it is, usually by hardening it with permanent concrete and rock structures.

facts.text: Seawalls, groynes, detached breakwaters and revetments make up more than 70% of protected shorelines in Europe.
Soft options such as beach nourishment and dune stabilization can also hold the line by working with natural processes.
Armouring often just moves the problem to another stretch of coast, and maintenance costs can eventually force a change of strategy.

entries.title: Living shorelines: marsh in place of walls

definition.text: A way of protecting shorelines and marshes from erosion that uses as many natural elements as possible instead of walls.

facts.text: Unlike bulkheads and seawalls, which worsen erosion, living shorelines buffer wave energy more effectively.
Building one is a form of soft engineering, applying ecological principles to shoreline stabilization.
Common materials include sand, wetland plants, oyster reefs, submerged aquatic vegetation, stones and coir fibre logs.
Benefits include filtering runoff, creating habitat, absorbing wave energy and supporting fisheries, possibly at lower cost than seawalls.
Projects move through site analysis, permitting, site preparation, installation, then maintenance and monitoring.
Low rock sills or breakwaters seeded with oyster spat calm the water so marsh grasses can be planted behind them.

entries.title: Shrimp among the mangroves

definition.text: A farming system, also called silvofishery, that grows shrimp in ponds alongside planted mangrove trees as a way to rehabilitate mangroves.

facts.text: Expanding shrimp farms are a main cause of mangrove loss, even though shrimp ponds depend on the services mangroves provide.
Like extensive farming, it relies on natural feed and wild shrimp brought in by the tides rather than chemicals and formulated feed, so running costs are low.
Studies in Vietnam found net profit peaks with 30%-50% mangrove cover, while rules requiring 60-80% cover have discouraged farmers.
Benefits include biodiversity, blue carbon storage, coastal protection and steady income, but unequal timber benefit-sharing and conflicting policies hold it back.

entries.title: Dune plant zones: from salt spray to forest

definition.text: The bands of plants across a beach dune, from the sea-facing foredune through the backdune to a later shrub stage.

facts.text: Foredune plants must tolerate salt spray, strong winds and burial by blowing sand.
On the dune plain and backdune, plants grow into dense 'dune mats' that hold the dune together.
Once these herbaceous plants are established, deeper-rooted shrubs can follow, and the shrub stage may eventually give way to forest or chaparral.
In New Zealand, introduced marram grass built steep, storm-vulnerable dunes and crowded out native plants; it is now classed as a pest.

entries.title: Cultching: giving baby oysters somewhere to land

definition.text: Laying down cultch, such as old shell or similar hard material, to give young oysters surfaces to settle on and rebuild a reef.

facts.text: Oyster larvae swim freely for about three weeks, then must attach to a hard surface to become spat.
Used oyster and clam shells from farmers and restaurants are cleaned and returned to the water as settling surfaces.
Cultching, pioneered for oyster farming in the early 19th century, has been the most successful way to reform oyster beds.

entries.title: Climate-driven relocation: towns that move away

definition.text: Whole or partial abandonment of places, or plans to move their people, because of human-caused climate change.

facts.text: Causes include rising seas, more flooding, land turning into wetland, coastal erosion, cyclones, droughts, water shortages and wildfires, which often overlap.
Isle de Jean Charles in Louisiana, about 100 people, became the first total community migration in that state, because of saltwater intrusion and sea level rise.
Vunidogoloa became the first town in Fiji to be depopulated and relocated, after persistent flooding, saltwater intrusion and coastal erosion.
In the Lake Chad Basin, 30,000,000 people are affected by droughts, floods and the lake's shrinking.

entries.title: Coral gardening: growing reefs in nurseries

definition.text: Cultivating coral by growing small fragments in nurseries until mature, then moving them to damaged reefs.

facts.text: A wild colony is cut into smaller pieces, which grow asexually into new colonies genetically identical to the parent.
Ocean-based nurseries hang fragments on lines or fix them to structures; land-based nurseries grow them in tanks.
Fragmentation gives about an 8x increase in colony growth compared with the donor coral.
Most colonies grow only about an inch a year, and land tanks shield them from storms, predators and disease.

entries.title: Microfragmentation: corals in months, not years

definition.text: A coral-growing technique that cuts live coral into very small pieces which, fixed to plugs in tanks, grow much faster.

facts.text: It was developed by David Vaughan in 2006 and relies on coral's ability to clone itself.
It speeds up the growth of reef-building corals from years to, often, months.

entries.title: Coastal squeeze: habitats trapped against the wall

definition.text: The loss of coastal habitat when rising seas push zones such as salt marsh landward and they run up against seawalls or other solid structures.

facts.text: Where sea walls block landward migration and sediment supply is limited, salt marsh cannot keep up with sea level rise.
Wetlands, salt marshes, mangroves and neighbouring freshwater wetlands are especially vulnerable.

When colonial and post-colonial states took control of mangroves, local people were alienated and the forests were logged and farmed heavily.
Community-managed mangroves show remarkable recovery, and local people have proved effective stewards.
Success depends on communities' willingness to pay and on balancing ecological, economic and social sustainability.

Sea rewilding projects are less common than rewilding on land.

entries.title: The urban heat island: why cities run hot

definition.text: The urban heat island effect is the way cities become noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.

facts.text: The main cause is how cities change land surfaces; waste heat from energy use is a secondary cause.
Dark materials like asphalt and concrete absorb much more sunlight and store heat, so city surfaces warm faster than rural ones.
The city–countryside difference is usually greater at night than by day and is clearest when winds are weak.
Urban areas cover about 0.5% of Earth's land but hold more than half the world's people.
Heat islands can lengthen and intensify heat waves, raise demand for air conditioning, and warm streams fed by hot stormwater.
Climate change does not cause the effect but amplifies it.
Remedies include planting trees, white or reflective cool roofs, light-coloured concrete, green infrastructure such as green roofs, and passive radiative cooling.
Luke Howard first described it in the 1810s, reporting that central London was 2.1 °C warmer at night than the surrounding countryside.

entries.title: Urban green space: country in the city

definition.text: In town planning, urban green spaces are open areas set aside for parks and other greenery.

facts.text: The World Health Organization defines urban green space as all city land covered by vegetation of any kind.
Green spaces include plant life and water features, called blue spaces, and range from playing fields to wilder-looking land.
Their benefits fall into four groups: recreation, ecology, beauty and health.
Green spaces can clean city air, shelter wildlife and lower flood risk by draining rainwater.
Homes near urban open spaces tend to be worth more.
Visitors gain more from green spaces with more biodiversity, so quality and variety matter, not just greenness.
The Romans used the phrase 'rus in urbe', country in the city, around the first century C.E.

entries.title: Green roofs: gardens on top of buildings

definition.text: A building roof partly or fully covered with plants and a growing medium, laid over a waterproof membrane.

facts.text: Besides plants and soil, a green roof may have a root barrier, drainage layers and irrigation.
Green roofs cut energy use: they add mass and insulation against heating needs and ease the urban heat island effect by raising evapotranspiration.
A study cited by the US EPA found green roofs reduced rainwater runoff by over 75% during rainstorms.
Green roofs create habitat; even 19 stories up they can attract beneficial insects, birds, bees and butterflies.
Plants on the roof absorb carbon and store it in plant tissue and in the soil through litter and root exudates.
An extensive system can cost $108–$248/m2, an intensive one $355–$2,368/m2, and the up-front cost can be double that of a normal roof.
Covering the waterproof membrane with soil and plants shields it from sunlight and damage, which can extend a roof's life by over 200%.
Toronto approved a by-law in May 2009 requiring green roofs on residential and industrial buildings.

entries.title: Urban agriculture: farms inside the city

definition.text: Urban agriculture covers the growing, processing and distribution of food in towns and cities.

facts.text: It also includes raising animals, fish farming, beekeeping and horticulture in cities, and differs from peri-urban farming at the rural edge of suburbs.
Gardens and farms are its two main types; the USDA counts as a farm any place that produces and sells $1,000 or more of farm products.
Urban and peri-urban farming supplies fresh produce, jobs and income, and can improve city dwellers' food security and nutrition.
Growing food locally cuts transport energy; one study found non-local food distribution used 4 to 17 times more fuel than local and regional transport.
Urban farms can act as carbon sinks, offsetting some of the carbon build-up in places where pavement and buildings outnumber plants.
Expanding city farming often means dealing with old soil contamination, especially lead and other heavy metals.
City land is scarce and expensive, and irrigating with untreated wastewater can spread waterborne disease.

entries.title: Urban parks: shade, play and a cooler summer

definition.text: An urban or city park is a park or garden in a town or suburb that gives residents and visitors green space and places to relax and play.

facts.text: Urban parks are usually designed landscapes rather than land left natural, and are mostly run by local government.
Trees are picked for beauty and shade, with growing focus on reducing the urban heat island.
A 2025 satellite study of 2,083 parks found well-treed parks were on average 3.4°C cooler in summer daytime than surrounding urban areas.
Early purpose-built public parks included Princes Park in Liverpool, opened in 1843, and Birkenhead Park, which Olmsted visited in 1850.
As city land prices rose, most new US urban parks since the 1960s have been small pocket parks.
The UK has about 27,000 public parks with around 2.6 billion visits a year, but councils have no legal duty to fund them.

entries.title: Urban forestry: trees as city infrastructure

definition.text: The care and management of individual trees and groups of trees in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

facts.text: Urban forestry treats trees as a vital part of a city's infrastructure, and covers planting, care, protection and managing trees as a shared resource.
City trees filter air pollution, regulate local climate and store carbon dioxide.
Trees cool the urban heat island by shading pavement, helping air move and through evapotranspiration.
The United States has around 3.8 billion urban trees, with an estimated structural value of $2.4 trillion.
Heat waves kill 1,300 people a year in the United States, more than any other weather event, which gives urban shade health value.
City trees face cramped roots and canopy, poor soil, too much or too little water and light, heat, pollution and physical damage.
Urban forests bring both ecosystem services and disservices, which planners weigh beforehand.

entries.title: Green walls: gardens that grow sideways

definition.text: A green wall, living wall or vertical garden is an upright built structure deliberately covered with plants.

facts.text: Unlike a green facade, where climbing plants grow from soil at the base, a green wall holds its growing medium on the wall face itself.
French botanist Patrick Blanc is often credited with popularizing green walls, starting with a large indoor wall in Paris in 1986.
Plant surfaces cooled by transpiration stay no more than 4–5 °C above air temperature, so green walls lower building temperatures in cities.
They make good use of vertical surfaces in cities, and in dry areas their circulating water evaporates less than in flat gardens.
Living walls are credited with cleaning indoor and outdoor air; one computer model showed a wall absorbing nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter.
Green walls are often said to provide ecosystem services, and deeper substrates tend to support the most species.
They are classed by growth medium: freestanding, media-free, loose, mat and structural media.

entries.title: Green belts: a ring of countryside around the city

definition.text: A green belt is a planning policy and zone that keeps mostly undeveloped, wild or farmed land around or beside towns and cities.

facts.text: It works like an invisible border that blocks building and lets wildlife return; greenways and green wedges are similar but run through a city as strips.
Stated aims include protecting natural areas, improving city air, giving townspeople access to the countryside and keeping rural communities from being swallowed by suburbs.
Octavia Hill first used the term about London's growth in 1875, and the UK pioneered green belt policy.
England's fourteen green belt areas cover 16,716 km2, or 12.4% of England.
Critics such as the Institute of Economic Affairs say green belts stop new housing meeting demand and so push up house prices.
Because a green belt has an outer edge, building can leap over it, which may increase urban sprawl and lengthen commutes.
Defenders point to peri-urban farming in green belts, which stores carbon, reduces urban heat and provides habitat.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue green belts raise house prices and spread sprawl, while supporters stress their environmental and farming benefits.

entries.title: Urban forests: woods inside the city limits

definition.text: An urban forest is a forest or grove of trees growing inside a city, town or suburb.

facts.text: Unlike a forest park, an urban forest often lacks amenities such as toilets, paved paths or clear borders; its care is called urban forestry.
Urban forests moderate local climate, slow wind and stormwater, filter air, and help cool the urban heat island.
Models suggest 100 million trees in US cities could cut annual energy use by 30 billion kWh, saving $2 billion and 9 million tons of power plant CO2 a year.
A 40-year study in Tucson calculated $600,000 saved in stormwater treatment costs thanks to urban trees.
A Finnish study found property values rose 4.9% for each kilometre closer to a forest; a front-yard tree may add $7,130 to a home's price.
In Philadelphia, residents below the poverty line near 'greened' vacant lots reported a 68% fall in feelings of depression.
Johannesburg, on naturally treeless grassland, reportedly has 10 million planted trees and is often called the largest man-made urban forest.

conflicts.text: Another source claims the property value increase near forests can be as high as 20%.
conflicts.note: Different studies of the same premium; the 4.9% figure is per kilometre closer in Finland.

entries.title: Green space and health: why parks are medicine

definition.text: The World Health Organization treats urban green space as important to people's mental and physical health.

facts.text: Green space encourages exercise and reduces air pollution, heat, traffic noise and emissions, all of which raise the risk of chronic and mental illness.
People living within 1 km of green space show lower cardiovascular disease risk.
The closer people live to parks, and the more land is parks, the fewer local treatments for anxiety and mood disorders.
Areas with many trees have markedly lower levels of pollutants such as ozone, PM10, NO2, SO2 and CO.
Plant choice matters: large tree canopies can add to asthma and allergies.
Children with more access to parks are more active, and green space is linked to better focus and working memory at school.

entries.title: Urban ecology: studying nature among the buildings

definition.text: Urban ecology is the scientific study of how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings in cities.

facts.text: Urban environments are dominated by dense buildings and paved surfaces, which create a distinctive landscape.
Its goal is a balance between human culture and the natural environment; ecologists turned to cities largely from the 1970s.
Researchers use chemical tests, temperature records and heat maps, remote sensing and long-term ecological research sites.
Urban demand for chemicals disturbs biogeochemical cycles, causing acid rain, eutrophication and global warming, while paving stops nutrients returning to soil.
Green infrastructure can make urban areas better homes for wildlife.
Many effects of urbanization are still poorly understood because the field is young.

Dense buildings and paved surfaces create a distinctive landscape. Its goal is a balance between human culture and the natural environment. Researchers use chemical tests, temperature records and heat maps, remote sensing and long-term research sites. Cities disturb nature's chemical cycles. Their demand for chemicals contributes to acid rain, eutrophication and global warming, while paving stops nutrients returning to the soil. Green infrastructure can make cities better homes for wildlife. Because the field is young, many effects of urban growth remain poorly understood.

entries.title: Urban heat inequity: who swelters
entries.article: Urban heat island#Aspects of social inequality

definition.text: Urban heat inequity, or thermal inequity, is the uneven spread of heat across a city that hits some communities harder than others.

facts.text: Unequal heat stress often tracks race, ethnicity, income, education and age.
In most US cities, people of color are more likely than white residents to live in the hottest areas.
Past redlining shaped land use and still leaves vegetation, and so heat, unevenly shared.
Top-floor homes, dark roofs, poor insulation and lack of affordable air conditioning make the heat worse for low-income households.

entries.title: Biophilic design: building nature back into daily life

definition.text: Biophilic design tries to connect people more closely with nature, and with nature-like design, to improve their health and well-being.

facts.text: By adding natural features such as sunlight, it offers health, environmental and economic benefits with few drawbacks.
Stephen Kellert, a pioneer of the field, built a framework of direct experience of nature, indirect experience such as images and natural materials, and experience of space and place.
In experiments, people recovered from stress faster and more fully when exposed to natural rather than urban surroundings.
Plants, trees, rain gardens and green roofs reduce hard surfaces, helping buildings and cities manage stormwater runoff.
Peter Newman estimated that biophilic design could save New York City nearly $470 million through higher worker productivity and $1.7 billion through lower crime costs.
Natural elements can cost a little more to install and maintain, but their health and environmental benefits are believed to outweigh this.
The WELL Building Standard and the Living Building Challenge are its most prominent backers in building rating systems.

entries.title: Urban resilience: cities that bend without breaking

definition.text: Urban resilience is a city's or urban community's ability to withstand, recover from or adapt to human-made and natural disasters.

facts.text: It covers physical infrastructure as well as social, health and economic systems.
Research has focused on three main threats: climate change, natural disasters and terrorism.
A study of 616 cities, home to 1.7 billion people, found floods endanger more city residents than any other natural hazard, followed by earthquakes and storms.
Greening is among the most often cited heat strategies: covering surfaces with plants reduces heat-absorbing material and shades concrete and asphalt.
Replacing hard surfaces with greenery lets soil and plants soak up excess rain, and deeper green roof soils absorb more.
Older people make up most heat-related deaths in cities, and social isolation adds to their risk.
Building resilience means investing in options that work across uncertain futures, since risk can never be fully removed.

entries.title: Blue roofs: storing the storm on top

definition.text: A blue roof is designed to store rainwater for a while and then release it slowly.

facts.text: They are built on flat roofs in cities where too few permeable surfaces let rain soak into the ground, raising flood risk.
By easing the load on storm sewers, they help stop combined sewers overflowing untreated wastewater into rivers and coasts.
Active blue roofs control drainage with valves, while passive ones slow water by lengthening its path to the drain.
In dry climates they serve as a water-saving tool by harvesting roof rainfall.

entries.title: Urban biodiversity: wildlife in the concrete

definition.text: The variety of plant and animal life found in cities, which planners can sustain by enlarging green areas and linking them with green corridors.

facts.text: Increasing green areas and building a network of green corridors is a successful way to keep urban biodiversity high.
In temperate countries, urbanization often adds non-native species while cutting native ones, lowering overall species richness.
Cities reduce diversity by removing and fragmenting habitat and by making once-distinct communities more alike.
Green roofs, tree inventories, planting of hardy species and protecting parks and woodlots can all support urban biodiversity.
Safe movement paths for wildlife, better habitat and fewer human threats help sustain it.

facts.text: Street trees soak up stormwater, remove air pollutants and give shade that eases the urban heat island.
Because they grow among large paved areas, street trees make up an important share of a district's tree cover.

entries.title: Urban rewilding: letting wild nature into town

definition.text: Urban rewilding is a form of rewilding that tries to bring working ecosystems, from plants to animals, into cities.

facts.text: There are four types: urban greening, corridors, small-scale projects under 50 hectares and large-scale projects over 50 hectares.
Corridors such as restored waterways or green paths link habitats so city animals can move freely.
Benefits include cleaner air, stored carbon, more pollination, fertile soil, clean water and lower stress.
Projects are costly and carry an opportunity cost, since owners could use the land for more profitable purposes.

He argues biophilic design helps cities adapt to the stresses of a changing climate.
Singapore, nicknamed a 'city in a garden', built a network of nature reserves, parks, connectors and tree-lined streets to bring back wildlife and reduce urban heat.

entries.title: Pocket forests: dense, fast and disputed

definition.text: A small forest made by planting many different native trees and shrubs close together, usually to restore native plants quickly in damaged places.

facts.text: Instead of passing through early growth stages, a pocket forest is planted densely with mature-stage species that race each other for sunlight.
Interest grew largely from Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki, whose 'Miyawaki forests' inspired many methods suited to different climates.
Forestry scholars say claims that Miyawaki forests grow ten times faster are unsubstantiated, and the method is called costly and unworkable for large areas.
Dense, layered pocket forests can catch embers and act as a fuel ladder, raising wildfire risk in cities.

definition.text: Green urbanism is the practice of building communities that are good for both people and the environment.

facts.text: Timothy Beatley describes it as shaping more sustainable places and lifestyles that use less of the world's resources.
Its principles start from the view that urbanization is a key driver of carbon emissions, resource depletion and environmental damage, and aim for zero fossil fuels, zero waste and zero emissions.
In 1989 ecologist H.T. Odum called cities 'parasites' that make no food and clean no air but only consume.
It is interdisciplinary, drawing on planners, ecologists, engineers, economists, psychologists and others.

entries.title: Reforestation: growing back the forests that were lost

definition.text: Reforestation is restoring forests and woodlands that once stood on a site but were destroyed or damaged.

facts.text: The earlier loss may have come from deforestation, clearcutting or wildfire.
Programs have three main purposes: growing wood to harvest, slowing climate change, and restoring ecosystems and habitat.
It differs from afforestation, which makes new forest on land that was not forest before.
Reforestation and cutting deforestation store more carbon by enlarging forests, making them denser in carbon, replacing fossil fuels with forest products, and avoiding emissions from forest loss.
Because new trees take decades to match mature tropical forests, reducing deforestation usually helps the climate more than reforestation.
Up to 90% of newly planted seedlings often fail.
Some reforestation trees, such as Eucalyptus globulus, draw so much water from the soil that other plants cannot grow.
Large programs, such as China's Three-North 'Great Green Wall' begun in 1978, blur the line between reforestation and afforestation.

And large programs, such as China's Three-North program begun in 1978, blur the line between restoring old forest and creating new.

entries.title: Afforestation: planting forests where none recently stood

definition.text: Afforestation is creating a forest or stand of trees on land that has had no recent tree cover.

facts.text: It differs from reforestation, which turns back into forest land that once held forest but was converted to another use.
There are three types: natural regeneration, agroforestry and tree plantations.
It can help slow climate change by storing carbon in trees.
New trees can raise local rainfall, block strong winds, and reduce soil erosion, floods and landslides.
Projects create jobs, especially in rural areas, and supply wood products.
The process starts by choosing a site and studying its climate, soil, vegetation and human use, which decide the tree species and planting method.
Researchers debate whether it is always beneficial, since tree planting is not the only way to capture carbon.
Australia, Canada, China, India, Israel, the United States and Europe run afforestation programs, some also to reduce desertification.

It differs from reforestation, which turns land that once held forest back into forest. There are three types: natural regeneration, growing trees among crops as in {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, and plantations. The case for it is strong. Afforestation is creating a forest or stand of trees on land that has had no recent tree cover. It differs from reforestation, which turns land that once held forest back into forest. There are three types: natural regeneration, growing trees among crops as in Agroforestry: trees and crops on the same ground, and plantations. The case for it is strong. Trees store carbon, so new ones can help slow climate change, the link traced in Forests as carbon sinks, and why they may falter. New trees can also raise local rainfall, block strong winds, and reduce soil erosion, floods and landslides. Projects create jobs, especially in rural areas, and supply wood products. The work starts with the site. Planners study its climate, soil, vegetation and human use, and these decide which species to plant and how. Australia, Canada, China, India, Israel, the United States and Europe all run programs, some also to reduce desertification. Still, researchers debate whether afforestation always helps, especially where land was never forest. Planting trees is not the only way to capture carbon.

entries.title: Ecological restoration: repairing ecosystems already damaged

definition.text: Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed.

facts.text: It differs from conservation by repairing ecosystems already damaged rather than preventing damage.
It can help reverse biodiversity loss, fight climate change, keep ecosystem services flowing and support local economies.
Methods include erosion control, reforestation, weed and non-native species removal, reintroducing native species and building wildlife corridors.
Restoration ecology is the scientific study of restoration; ecological restoration is the practical work.
Projects have grown exponentially, with hundreds of thousands worldwide.
Reasons include restoring natural capital such as clean water, helping endangered species, adapting to climate change and storing carbon.
Restorations often miss their goals, and high costs can be seen as a drawback; public support fades if costs seem to outweigh benefits.
The United Nations named 2021–2030 the Decade on Ecosystem Restoration.

entries.text: Hundreds of thousands of restoration projects now run worldwide, and their number has grown exponentially. Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed. That sets it apart from conservation, which tries to prevent damage in the first place. Restoration repairs what is already harmed. The methods are hands-on: controlling erosion, replanting forests, removing weeds and non-native species, reintroducing native species and building wildlife corridors. The reasons vary just as much. Projects aim to restore natural capital such as clean water, help endangered species, adapt to climate change and store carbon. Done well, restoration can help reverse biodiversity loss, keep ecosystem services flowing and support local economies. The field has two halves. Restoration ecology is the scientific study; ecological restoration is the practical work. The record is mixed. Restorations often miss their goals, and their high costs can be seen as a drawback. Public support fades if the costs seem to outweigh the benefits. Even so, the United Nations named 2021–2030 a decade devoted to this work, the {{ref:nature-nbs-137}}.

entries.title: Rewilding: stepping back so nature can run itself

definition.text: Rewilding is a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence.

facts.text: Its key feature is replacing human management with natural processes.
Unlike other restoration, it accepts novel ecosystems with new species and interactions.
It often brings back large mammals to rebuild food webs and make ecosystems self-regulating.
The term was coined by Earth First! in 1990 and given a scientific basis by Michael Soulé and Reed Noss in 1998.
Soulé and Noss built it on 'cores, corridors and carnivores': large protected areas, links between them, and large predators.
It is promoted as a natural climate solution through carbon storage, flood management and lower wildfire risk.
In a Guyana forest, going from 5 to 35 mammal species raised tree and soil carbon four to five times.
The UN lists rewilding as one method needed for large-scale restoration by 2030 under the 30x30 campaign.

entries.contested_note: Rewilding is described as controversial, with critics questioning its evidence and effect on farming and livelihoods.

entries.title: Paying people to plant forests or leave them standing

definition.text: Payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down.

facts.text: A proposed 'compensated reduction' scheme would pay developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period.
Under that proposal the scheme is voluntary, but a country that signs up must cut emissions, and a missed target rolls into its next period.
Selling carbon sequestration credits to companies and people offsetting their footprint is an emerging way to fund reforestation.
Carbon credits let farmers and private landowners earn money from replanting while gaining healthier soil.
Governments also offer tax breaks to encourage companies to support reforestation.

entries.text: A standing forest earns nothing for the person who could have cut it down. Financial incentives try to change that sum. They are payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down. One proposal, 'compensated reduction', would pay developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period. Joining would be voluntary. But a country that signs up must cut emissions, and a missed target rolls into its next period. An emerging source of money is the sale of credits for carbon locked away in trees to companies and people offsetting their footprint. Such credits let farmers and private landowners earn money from replanting while gaining healthier soil. Governments also offer tax breaks to encourage companies to support reforestation.

entries.title: Plantation forests: trees in rows, grown for wood

definition.text: Plantation forests are intensively managed stands of one or two tree species of the same age, planted in regular rows mainly to produce wood.

facts.text: They cover about 131 million ha: 3% of the world's forest area and 45% of all planted forest.
Planted forests grew from 4.1% to 7.0% of total forest area between 1990 and 2015.
Other planted forests, 55 percent of the total, are not intensively managed and may come to resemble natural forests; they can serve restoration and soil and water protection.
Over 90% of the world's forests regrow naturally rather than by planting.
Of planted forests worldwide, 18% of the area holds exotic species and the rest native ones.
Plantations are often monocultures, which brings drawbacks such as biodiversity loss.

conflicts.text: Plantation forests made up 280 million ha in 2015.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 280 million ha for plantation forests in 2015, while the methods section gives about 131 million ha; the 280 million ha figure may refer to all planted forests.

entries.title: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, 2021 to 2030

definition.text: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration is a United Nations campaign running from 2021 to 2030 to promote the repair of degraded ecosystems worldwide.

facts.text: It aims to fight climate change, protect biodiversity, and improve food security and water supply through restoration.
It began on World Environment Day, 5 June 2021, after the UN General Assembly adopted it on 1 March 2019, following a proposal by El Salvador.
The UN asked nations to deliver existing restoration pledges of over 1 billion hectares, an area bigger than China.
About half the world's GDP depends directly on nature, yet people use up natural resources about 1.6 times faster than nature restores them.
The UN defines ecosystem restoration as halting and reversing degradation so that ecosystem services improve and biodiversity recovers.
It is co-led by UNEP and the Food and Agriculture Organization.
Recommended approaches include regenerative agriculture, ecological restoration and rewilding.

entries.title: Can restoring nature replace cutting emissions?
entries.article: Ecological restoration#Restoration as a substitute for steep emission reductions

definition.text: The debate over relying on nature restoration to fight climate change instead of quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions.

facts.text: Climate benefits of restoration are described as dwarfed by ongoing fossil fuel emissions.
One study concluded land restoration matters but cannot make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions, as it is too slow to lower peak temperatures in coming decades.
Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and replanting, which causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage.
Forestry-based carbon offsetting is controversial and is sometimes criticised as carbon colonialism.

entries.contested_note: Sources dispute how much weight restoration should carry against cutting fossil fuel use.
entries.text: Planting trees and healing land feels like progress, but its climate benefits are described as dwarfed by ongoing fossil fuel emissions. That gap sits at the center of a debate over relying on nature restoration to fight climate change instead of quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions. One study concluded that restoring land matters but cannot make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions. It is too slow to lower peak temperatures in the coming decades. The kind of action matters too. Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and replanting, because clearing causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage. The money side is contested as well. Offsetting carbon through forestry, where polluters pay for trees to balance their emissions, is controversial. Critics sometimes call it carbon colonialism. Sources still dispute how much weight restoration should carry against cutting fossil fuel use. On one point they agree: restoration cannot simply replace the cuts.

entries.title: Africa's Great Green Wall: a belt of trees across the Sahel

definition.text: The Great Green Wall is an African Union project, adopted in 2007, first meant to stop desertification in the Sahel by planting a belt of trees from Djibouti to Senegal.

facts.text: The wall was planned to be 15 km wide and 7,775 km long.
It grew from tree planting into a mosaic of green, productive landscapes using water harvesting and local land-use methods.
It aims by 2030 to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs.
A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered, with 4 million hectares planted.
In January 2021 partners pledged USD 14.3 billion for the Great Green Wall Accelerator; by March 2023, $2.5 billion had been paid out.
As of 2024, about 30 million hectares had been restored, 30% of the target.
In 2023 it was said to face collapse from terrorism, weak political leadership and too little funding.
Critics point to colonial roots of the term 'desertification' and mostly European funding, seen as neocolonialism.

entries.contested_note: Critics question its progress, funding and colonial framing, and some call for scrapping it.

conflicts.text: The $8-billion project would create 350,000 rural jobs by 2030.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 10 million jobs by 2030 as the goal (S:4032cccb380e).

conflicts.text: The estimated $33 billion to fund the project.
conflicts.note: Another sentence calls it an $8-billion project (S:eec8f102e8b5).

entries.title: Species reintroduction: returning animals and plants to the wild

definition.text: Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive.

facts.text: The aim is a healthy, genetically varied, self-sustaining population where the species had died out, or a boost to an existing one.
Candidates are usually threatened or endangered, but reintroduction can also control pests, such as wolves curbing too many deer.
Individuals come either from wild populations (in situ) or from captivity such as zoos or botanic gardens (ex situ); wild sourcing is preferred where possible.
Source populations should resemble the release site genetically and ecologically so the animals or plants are well adapted.
Captive-bred animals can adapt to captivity, becoming tamer, less stress-tolerant and losing local adaptations.
Small reintroduced populations risk inbreeding, which can erode crucial genetic diversity.
There is no agreed definition of success, but it should produce viable, self-sustaining populations long term.

entries.text: Bringing wolves back can curb too many deer. Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive. Candidates are usually threatened or endangered, but pest control is another reason. Individuals come from wild populations, called in situ, or from zoos and botanic gardens, called ex situ. Wild sourcing is preferred where possible, and the source should resemble the release site. Captive-bred animals can become tamer and less stress-tolerant, and lose local adaptations. Small released populations risk inbreeding, which erodes genetic diversity. There is no agreed definition of success, but it should mean viable populations that sustain themselves long term.

entries.title: Novel ecosystems: nature in mixes never seen before

definition.text: A novel ecosystem is one that human activity, land use and climate change have pushed into a mix of species and conditions never seen before.

facts.text: They are human-altered places where a self-sustaining ecosystem forms without ongoing human management.
The term was first used in 2006.
Defining features: change past a threshold, caused by people, and self-sustaining afterwards.
Without rapid climate action they could cover more than 50% of Earth's land by 2100 and 80% by 2300.
Examples include a quarry colonised by weedy species and coral reefs taken over by algae.
Some scientists argue that even if an ecosystem cannot return to its original state, a novel ecosystem's functions are still valuable.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree on how to define novelty, and some argue against any sharp definition.

entries.title: Land restoration: returning land to a chosen state

definition.text: Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose.

facts.text: Purposes include making land safe, stabilising ecological communities, cleaning up pollution, creating novel ecosystems or returning to a historical condition.
It is an antidote to damage caused mostly by people, such as pollution, deforestation, salination and species endangerment.
It differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems to make way for farming or building.
It can increase the supply of valuable ecosystem services.
Projects choose a reference ecosystem to measure success against and survey existing conditions first.
Traditional ecological knowledge used alongside Western science is becoming the mainstream approach.

entries.text: Restoring land starts with a choice: restore it to what? Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose. The purposes vary. A project might make land safe, stabilize its ecological communities, clean up pollution, create a {{ref:nature-nbs-150}} or return land to a historical condition. Restoration answers damage caused mostly by people, such as pollution, deforestation, salination and species endangerment. It differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems to make way for farming or building. The payoff can be economic, because restored land can supply more valuable ecosystem services. Projects begin by surveying existing conditions. They then choose a reference ecosystem, a real or described system to measure success against. Increasingly, the mainstream approach uses Indigenous knowledge of the land, the subject of {{ref:nature-nbs-120}}, alongside Western science.

entries.title: Land rehabilitation: making damaged ground useful again

definition.text: Land rehabilitation is returning damaged land, for example after industry or natural disasters, to some degree of its former state.

facts.text: Mining, farming and forestry are among the activities that degrade land.
In parts of the United States, 'reclamation' means returning disturbed land to an improved state.
Mine rehabilitation reshapes waste dumps against erosion, covers them with topsoil and plants vegetation to hold the material.
Sulfide-bearing ore is covered with clay so rain and air cannot turn it into sulfuric acid.
Closed mines can be reused for heat, water or methane recovery, keeping the methane out of the air.

entries.text: Mining, farming and forestry are among the activities that degrade land. Rehabilitation reshapes waste dumps so they resist erosion, covers them with topsoil and plants vegetation to hold the material in place. Ore that contains sulfide minerals poses a special risk. Rain and air can turn it into sulfuric acid, so it is covered with clay to keep them out. Even closed mines can be put back to work. They can be reused for heat, water or methane recovery, which also keeps the methane out of the air.

entries.title: When new forests compete with farms and homes
entries.article: Reforestation#Competition with other land uses and displacement risk

definition.text: The problem that reforestation can take land and water needed for food, grazing and housing, and may push out people who use that land.

facts.text: Government reforestation pledges add up to 1.2bn hectares by 2060, a tenth of the world's land area, which is seen as unrealistic.
Almost 300 million people live on land in the Global South identified as tropical forest restoration opportunity.
Agroforestry, such as growing coffee under trees, can blend forests with other land uses.
Programs focused on carbon storage rather than nearby communities' needs have been criticised.

entries.contested_note: A WRI and IUCN map of 2 billion hectares for forest restoration is criticised for including 900 million hectares of grassland.

entries.title: Will the carbon stored in new forests stay put?

definition.text: The risk that carbon stored by reforestation returns to the air, for example through fire, insect outbreaks or harvesting.

facts.text: Harvesting and using wood from reforested land limits how long its carbon stays stored.
Nearly half of the Bonn Challenge pledges were found to be areas set aside for commercial wood use.
Emissions from damage to tropical rainforests may be underestimated by a factor of six.
Many standards hold buffer reserves of credits and keep monitoring to manage such reversals.

Emissions from damage to tropical rainforests may also be underestimated by a factor of six. To manage such reversals, many carbon standards hold buffer reserves of credits and keep monitoring.
entries.text_plain: A forest that burns gives its carbon back. Permanence is the risk that carbon stored by reforestation returns to the air, through fire, insect outbreaks or harvesting. Harvesting and using wood from reforested land limits how long its carbon stays stored. Nearly half of the pledges under the The Bonn Challenge: a global pledge to restore land were found to be areas set aside for commercial wood use. Emissions from damage to tropical rainforests may also be underestimated by a factor of six. To manage such reversals, many carbon standards hold buffer reserves of credits and keep monitoring.

entries.title: Why dark new forests can warm the planet

definition.text: New forest canopy can darken Earth's surface, lowering its albedo so it absorbs more heat and may warm the planet.

facts.text: The effect matters most in snowy regions, where white snow reflects far more sunlight than dark forest.
The extra heat absorbed by trees could cancel part of the carbon benefit of afforestation.
A 2023 study using 176 flux stations found a trade-off: more carbon uptake from afforestation comes with lower albedo.
Tropical reforestation instead helps form clouds that reflect sunlight and lower temperatures.

entries.title: Should trees be planted on grasslands and savannas?

definition.text: A criticism of tree-planting campaigns that put forests where they would not grow naturally, such as grasslands and savannas.

facts.text: Critics say treeless ecosystems are not necessarily degraded and can store carbon already; savannas and tundra store it underground.
Grasslands and savannas need their own management, since they are not meant to be forests.
Carbon forecasts for such programs often leave out soil carbon losses and the slowing of tree growth over time.

entries.title: Single-species plantations: tree cover without the wildlife

definition.text: A criticism of planting forests of a single tree species, often conifers: tree cover rises but the varied habitat wildlife needs is missing.

facts.text: Single-species plantations are often planted for commerce or easy management and lack the biodiversity of natural forests.
They offer limited food, shelter and nesting sites, and dense conifers let little light reach the forest floor.
A meta-analysis found mixed-species plantations would store more carbon alongside other benefits.

entries.title: Succession: how restoration borrows nature's own recovery

definition.text: Ecological succession is the way a community of living things changes over time, especially after a disturbance.

facts.text: Ecosystems often move from a few pioneer species to a complex community of many interdependent species.
Restoration often means starting, helping or speeding up succession, depending on how severe the disturbance was.
After severe damage, such as in cities, restorers may first have to recreate conditions that let succession happen.

entries.title: Secondary forest: the woods that grow back on their own

definition.text: A secondary forest is woodland that has grown back largely by natural processes after logging, clearing for farming or a similar natural disturbance.

facts.text: It differs from old-growth (primary) forest, which has not recently been disturbed.
Cleared land is first taken over by pioneer species, then shrubs, and finally trees of the original forest.
It typically takes 40 to 100 years to start to resemble the original old-growth forest.
Most forests of the United States and Europe are secondary forest.
Species numbers can recover quickly, but which species and how common they are take much longer.
Secondary forests store more soil carbon than tree plantations, though less than primary forests.
They protect watersheds, provide habitat, link forest fragments and supply wood to rural communities.
By some estimates, more than 50 acres of new secondary forest grow for every acre of old-growth forest cut.

verification.title: Biodiversity recovery of Neotropical secondary forests
verification.evidence: Secondary forests take a median time of five decades to recover the species richness of old-growth forest (80% recovery after 20 years) based on rarefaction analysis.

verification.title: Soil Carbon Stocks Decrease following Conversion of Secondary Forests to Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) Plantations
verification.evidence: We found that forest-to-rubber plantation conversion resulted in losses of soil carbon stocks by an average of 37.4±4.7 (SE) Mg C ha(-1) in the entire 1.2-m depth over a time period of 46 years, which was equal to 19.3±2.7% of the initial soil carbon stocks in the secondary forests.

entries.title: Forest restoration: speeding a forest back toward maturity

definition.text: Forest restoration is action that speeds the return of a forest's structure, ecological workings and biodiversity toward those of a climax forest, the end stage of natural succession.

facts.text: Climax forests are fairly stable ecosystems with the most biomass, structure and species that climate and soil allow without human disturbance.
It is a special kind of reforestation whose main goals are biodiversity recovery and environmental protection, unlike timber plantations.
It can range from protecting leftover vegetation, by preventing fire or keeping out cattle, to planting trees or sowing seeds directly.
Success is measured by more biodiversity, biomass, productivity, soil organic matter and water-holding capacity, plus the return of rare and keystone species.
Economic measures of success include the value of forest products and services such as watershed protection and carbon storage.
Payments for ecological services and forest products can give local people strong reasons to restore forests.
Active restoration can speed carbon recovery in human-modified tropical forests by as much as 50%.
Because climate shapes climax forests, climate change may shift restoration goals.

entries.title: Forest landscape restoration: planning for people and wildlife

definition.text: Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process to regain ecological integrity and improve human well-being across deforested or degraded landscapes.

facts.text: It links restoration at single sites to goals for a whole landscape, agreed through participation among stakeholders.
The concept grew out of work by the IUCN, WWF, the World Resources Institute and the International Tropical Timber Organization.
It seeks compromises between the needs of people and wildlife, with local communities central to planning.
Desired outcomes include tackling root causes of degradation, settling land-use conflicts, agreeing benefit-sharing and providing watershed services.
An FLR program can mix protecting secondary forest, assisted natural regeneration, framework tree planting, timber plantations and agroforestry.
FAO set up the Forest and Landscape Restoration Mechanism in 2014 to help countries meet the Bonn Challenge.

entries.title: The Bonn Challenge: a global pledge to restore land

definition.text: The Bonn Challenge is a global goal to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030.

facts.text: Germany and the IUCN launched it in Bonn on 2 September 2011.
The IUCN estimates meeting it would bring about $84 billion a year in net benefits, helping rural incomes.
Meeting it is estimated to shrink the carbon dioxide emissions gap by 11-17%.
Reaching 350 million hectares by 2030 could bring up to $9 trillion in net benefits.
Nearly half of the pledges were found to be land set aside for commercial wood use.
Pakistan's Billion Tree Tsunami restored 350,000 hectares, beating its Bonn Challenge pledge.

entries.title: Assisted natural regeneration: helping forests regrow themselves

definition.text: Assisted natural regeneration (ANR), or managed regrowth, is protecting and caring for tree seedlings that sprout naturally so a forest regrows.

facts.text: It removes barriers to regrowth, such as weeds, poor soil, fire-prone grasses like Imperata, and other disturbance.
New trees are planted only where needed, which is called enrichment planting.
It is cheaper than replanting because it skips nurseries, site preparation and raising seedlings.
Forests grow faster than they would on their own, adding to carbon storage.
It needs enough natural seedlings (200 to 800 per hectare suggested), nearby seed sources and control of grazing, fire and logging.
Labour such as weeding and firebreaks can create local jobs.
Regrowing trees from roots that survive in cleared land is also called farmer-managed natural regeneration, and seedlings survive better because roots already reach groundwater.
A practical approach is to plant tough, fast-growing native species that start rebuilding degraded land.

entries.title: Passive rewilding: letting abandoned land go wild

definition.text: Passive rewilding is letting land, usually after it has been abandoned, return to nature with little or no human management.

facts.text: It is also called natural or spontaneous regeneration, and differs from other rewilding because people do not intervene directly.
Its three parts are letting wildlife return, reconnecting landscapes so plants and animals can move, and allowing disturbances such as fires, pests and floods.
Land is left to rewild either on purpose or because of socio-economic change.
Forests have been regrowing on abandoned pastures and scrub across Europe and North America.
In Spain, regrowth on abandoned farmland has raised fire risk, and effects on biodiversity depend on the site.
The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone has seen boars, lynxes, wolves and brown bears return.
Bruce Sterling coined 'involuntary park' in 1998 for once-inhabited places left to go wild.

entries.title: Restoration ecology and conservation biology: sister sciences
entries.article: Ecological restoration#Contrasting restoration ecology and conservation biology

definition.text: Two related sciences that both value protecting and restoring habitat, but conservation biology studies species populations while restoration ecology works at the community level.

facts.text: Conservation biology often centres on animals; restoration ecology centres on plants, because projects usually start by establishing plant communities.
Restoration ecology puts more weight on soils, fungi and microbes, the base of land ecosystems.
Restoration ecology became a separate field in the late twentieth century.

entries.title: Mine reclamation: turning a pit back into land

definition.text: Mine reclamation is reshaping mined land so it again works as an ecosystem or can be used economically.

facts.text: It happens after mining ends, but may be planned before a mine is permitted.
The practice began at the start of the 20th century, and many abandoned mines were never reclaimed.
Full return to the original landscape is often impossible; usually the limit is making mine waste physically and chemically stable.
In open-cut mines, rock backfills the pit, stored soil and topsoil go on top, and vegetation is restored.
Reforestation is the main way of restoring post-mining sites.
Under the US 1977 SMCRA law, operators post a performance bond equal to the reclamation plan's cost, released only after reclamation succeeds.
A coal tax of $0.12 per ton underground and $0.28 per ton surface-mined funds reclamation of abandoned US mines.

entries.title: The case against rewilding

definition.text: Objections to rewilding from governments, farmers, conservationists and others, about livelihoods, evidence and conflicts with people.

facts.text: Some officials say strict no-extraction areas limit people's ability to earn a living; others reply that ecotourism creates jobs.
Some farmers say it abandons productive farmland while world population grows.
Some scientists say its benefits lack evidence and it may pull funding from better-supported conservation.
Reintroduced predators can cause conflict, such as brown bears in Trentino, Italy.

definition.text: Ecosystem engineers are living things that clearly reshape the structure of their habitats.

facts.text: Rewilding uses beaver, elephants, bison, elk, and cattle and pigs as stand-ins for extinct aurochs and wild boar.
Large mammals shape the structure and makeup of habitats.

entries.title: Pleistocene rewilding: bringing back Ice Age giants

definition.text: Pleistocene rewilding is bringing back surviving Ice Age megafauna, or close stand-ins for extinct ones, to restore how ecosystems work.

facts.text: Advocates say ecosystems that evolved alongside such animals now lack large mammals and may collapse.
Critics say today's communities cannot be assumed to work like those of 10,000 years ago.

entries.title: Trophic rewilding: putting predators back at the top

definition.text: Trophic rewilding restores food-web interactions, especially top predators controlling plant-eaters, by (re)introducing species so ecosystems regulate themselves.

facts.text: Apex predators may be needed to stop grazers from over-breeding and stripping vegetation, as in the mass starvation at Oostvaardersplassen in the Netherlands.

entries.title: The Trillion Tree Campaign

definition.text: The Trillion Tree Campaign is a project to plant one trillion trees worldwide to fight climate change.

facts.text: It grew out of the Billion Tree Campaign, inspired by Wangari Maathai and launched by UNEP in 2006.
In December 2011 UNEP handed the program to the youth-led Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation.
In 2015 Tom Crowther found about 3 trillion trees exist; planting 1.2 trillion more was later estimated to offset 10 years of human CO2 emissions.
By 30 May 2021, 13.96 billion trees had been planted, 1.396% of the goal.

entries.title: Bringing forests back after fire

definition.text: Restoring forest after fire, a heavy cause of forest loss in many parts of the world.

facts.text: Fires may be set to clear land for crops, or occur naturally or on purpose in dry areas.
Burnt land can lose much ecosystem value and degrade further through erosion and desertification.
Sometimes fire raises a site's biodiversity, and restoration plans then look for a different land use.

entries.title: Fencing out deer to save young forests
entries.article: Forest restoration#Protecting regeneration areas from browsing animals

definition.text: Shielding young, regrowing forest from deer and other browsing animals that can over-graze seedlings.

facts.text: Over-grazed saplings may be damaged beyond recovery, reducing biodiversity.
Deer fencing is used, or where it is too costly, trees that recover structurally are planted instead.

entries.title: Does restoring nature pay for itself?

definition.text: The comparison of what restoring ecosystems costs with the benefits it returns, and with the cost of doing nothing.

facts.text: On average, benefits of ecosystem restoration exceed the initial investment tenfold, while the cost of inaction is at least three times the cost of restoring.
Restoring 350 million hectares by 2030 could generate US$9 trillion in ecosystem services and remove 13 to 26 gigatons of greenhouse gases.
Degradation of land and marine ecosystems costs about 10% of annual global GDP (c. $6.3 trillion).
UK peatland restoration by 2027 was estimated to yield £191 million a year net of restoration costs.
Assisted natural regeneration cuts costs by skipping site preparation and seedling raising, appealing for large projects.
In Oregon, each dollar invested in restoration generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars of economic activity.
When clean-up and restoration costs fall late in a project, a high discount rate makes the project look better than it is.

entries.title: The restoration economy: jobs from repairing nature

definition.text: The restoration economy is the economic activity that comes from repairing land and nature, such as ecological restoration work.

facts.text: It is set against economic activity built on sprawl or on extracting and using up natural resources.
The idea is that repairing past damage to nature and communities often pays off economically at local, regional and national scales.
The phrase became popular after Storm Cunningham's 2002 book The Restoration Economy, which sorted restorative development into eight sectors.
Four of the sectors focus on nature: ecological restoration, watershed restoration, fishery restoration and regenerative agriculture.
Restoration projects need workers, materials and services, so spending on them can create jobs and business activity in local economies.
A study across Oregon found 15-24 jobs per million invested, and each dollar generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars of economic activity.
The same Oregon study found restoration spending has similar economic and job effects to public infrastructure such as road building.
Hand work such as tree planting and thinning tends to pay less than logging, is less reliable, and is mostly done by immigrant workers.

Groups include intensive land-use biomes such as croplands, pastures, plantations and cities, and artificial wetlands such as reservoirs and rice paddies.

entries.title: Three ways to handle a novel ecosystem

definition.text: The choices for handling novel ecosystems: tolerating them, managing against them back toward history, or managing for them as new systems.

facts.text: Too little funding and information has made tolerance and inaction the default.
Managing against them means traditional restoration: removing non-native species and bringing back natives toward historical benchmarks.
Fast climate change often makes historical baselines unreachable, so scientists increasingly aim for resilient, adaptive ecosystems.

facts.text: First, grasses, shelterbelts, windbreaks and woodlots fix the soil so dunes stop moving.
Shelterbelts are rows of trees set across the prevailing wind.
Next, nitrogen-fixing plants enrich the soil, crops are grown at once, and crops are rotated yearly to avoid draining trace elements.

entries.title: Mine rehabilitation bonds: paying for repair up front

definition.text: A rehabilitation security bond is money a mining company must put up before mining begins to guarantee it will repair the land afterwards.

facts.text: In Australia, rehabilitation is a legal duty backed by bonds, and could create regional jobs and investment if laws were enforced.

NSW's Auditor General questioned whether bonds are big enough to cover full rehabilitation costs.
Reclaiming abandoned mines in the US is estimated to cost $9.6bn, paid from operating mines and public sources.

definition.text: The Forestry Reclamation Approach (FRA) is a set of guidelines for regrowing forest on land mined for coal.

facts.text: It calls for at least four feet of good rooting material, such as topsoil or weathered sandstone, loosely graded to avoid compaction.
It plants early successional trees for wildlife and soil, then commercially valuable crop trees.

entries.title: Rewetting peatlands to stop them leaking carbon

definition.text: Rewetting returns a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming plants can recover.

facts.text: It keeps soil moist and slows drainage by blocking and filling canals; dams of peat or plastic block channels and gullies.
A higher water table slows plant decay and so cuts greenhouse gas emissions.
Wet conditions produce some methane, but because methane stays in the air for a shorter time, the long-run effect is likely cooling.

entries.title: Sustainable agriculture: farming that can last

definition.text: Farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively.

facts.text: Agriculture has a huge environmental footprint; food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions.
It aims to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm.
Its elements can include permaculture, agroforestry, mixed farming, multiple cropping and crop rotation.
In 1977 the USDA defined it as practices that, over the long term, meet food needs, improve the environment, use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' quality of life.
Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are called externalities.
Investment in it is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid, yet gets only three percent of humanitarian funds.
Many certification systems exist, including organic certification, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade.
People disagree on its definition: an ecocentric view favours low growth and organic methods, a technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

entries.title: Soil health: judging soil as a living system

definition.text: The state of a soil that performs the full range of ecosystem functions suited to its environment.

facts.text: It arises from good interactions among a soil's living and non-living parts, such as microbes, plants and animals.
It covers sustaining productivity, biodiversity, water and air quality, and human health.
The term has largely replaced soil quality, which judged soil only for one purpose such as growing maize.
It depends on soil biodiversity and improves when soil is kept covered and given carbon-rich amendments.
Some microbiologists believe 80% of soil nutrient functions are controlled by microbes.
US soils have lost up to 75% of their carbon over 40 years, though how much is debated.
A soil can be healthy for ecosystems without directly serving crop production, so terms and measures are debated.

It arises from good interactions among a soil's living and non-living parts, such as microbes, plants and animals. It covers sustaining productivity, biodiversity, water and air quality, and human health. The term has largely replaced soil quality, which judged soil for one purpose only, such as growing maize. Soil health depends on soil biodiversity. It improves when soil is kept covered and given carbon-rich amendments. The stakes are real. US soils have lost up to 75% of their carbon over 40 years, though how much is debated. Definitions are contested too. A soil can be healthy for ecosystems without directly serving crops, so scientists still debate how to define and measure it.

entries.title: Carbon farming: pulling carbon from the air into soil

definition.text: A set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plant material.

facts.text: Its overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked into soil and plants.
Converting forests, grasslands or savannas into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%.
Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding biochar, and changing which crops are grown.
Mixing biochar into soil locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original biomass.
Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year; by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares.
The stored carbon is not permanent: disturbing the soil or tilling intensively turns it back into a net source of greenhouse gases.
If incentives reward only stored carbon, it could encourage land clearing, monocultures and biodiversity loss.
Farmers who store carbon can sell carbon credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia.

entries.contested_note: Sources say the effect of more soil carbon on crop yield is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

entries.title: Crop rotation: changing what grows, season by season

definition.text: Growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons.

facts.text: It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance.
Growing the same crop year after year, monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialised pests.
Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to later crops.
Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon.
Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat.
Different crops spread the farmer's risk from bad weather.
In the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers.
US organic certification requires a crop rotation.

entries.text: Plant the same crop year after year and the soil tires of it. Growing one crop repeatedly, called monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialized pests. Crop rotation is the fix: growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons. It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance. Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat. Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to the crops that follow. Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon. Different crops also spread the farmer's risk from bad weather. During the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers. Today US rules for certified organic farms require it.

entries.title: Agricultural pollution: farming's spillover

definition.text: Contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming.

facts.text: It comes from single discharge points and, more often, from diffuse non-point sources across the landscape, as well as air pollution.
Farm pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts, reaching lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater.
Runoff concentrated in large water bodies causes dead zones downstream.
Poor management, such as overgrazing, ploughing and badly timed pesticide use, drives much of it.
Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on pollutants entering the environment.
Agricultural economists design incentives to control such externalities, for example water pollution from farming.

entries.text: Runoff from farms, gathered in large water bodies, creates dead zones downstream. Agricultural pollution is contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming. Some comes from single discharge points. More often it comes from diffuse non-point sources spread across the landscape, and from air pollution. The list of pollutants is long: sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts. They reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater. Poor management drives much of it, such as overgrazing, plowing and badly timed pesticide use. Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on the pollutants entering the environment. Economists see the problem as an externality, a cost the farmer does not pay. So agricultural economists design incentives to control it, for example to curb water pollution from farms.

entries.title: Soil conservation: keeping topsoil and fertility

definition.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination.

facts.text: Deforestation typically causes large-scale erosion, nutrient loss and sometimes desertification.
Techniques include crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage and windbreaks.
Farmers have practised it for millennia.
The EU's Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover crops, plant residues and grass margins.
Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, including changing how land is valued.
Each one percent increase in soil organic matter lets soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
Taxing pesticides at different rates is one option studied for cutting their use.
