entries.title: Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild, not just sustain

definition.text: An approach to farming that aims to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

facts.text: It is not one practice but a combination of sustainable agriculture techniques, such as recycling farm waste and adding compost.
The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s.
A 2020 review of 229 articles and 25 websites found no legal or broadly accepted definition; some definitions name practices, others outcomes.
Its four most consistent principles are improving soil health, optimising resource use, easing climate change and improving water quality and availability.
An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began.

A 2023 review found reduced tillage, cover crops, crop–livestock integration and agroforestry can improve soil carbon or yields in some conditions, but evidence on benefits and profitability is limited.
Some scientists call proponents' climate claims exaggerated and unsupported.

entries.contested_note: Scientists dispute claims that regenerative practices, especially grazing, can store enough carbon to counter climate change.

entries.title: No-till farming: growing crops without plowing

definition.text: Growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

facts.text: It reduces erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils, and can improve water infiltration, organic matter and nutrient cycling.
Worldwide area grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 111 million ha in 2009.
In Argentina it cut erosion losses by 80% and costs by more than 50%; in Paraguay net farm incomes rose 77%.
Fewer machinery passes lower fuel and labour costs.
Without tillage to remove weeds, farmers commonly use herbicides such as glyphosate, increasing herbicide use.
Nitrogen tied up in residue can mean higher fertilizer rates, and cold, wet spring soil can delay planting.
Whether it increases soil carbon is debated; some studies suspect flawed testing or losses deeper in the soil.
England's DEFRA pays farmers £73 per hectare to convert.

entries.contested_note: Sources debate whether the extra soil carbon reported under no-till is real or an artefact of testing methods.

entries.title: Permaculture: designing farms like ecosystems

definition.text: An approach to designing land use and settlements that copies the arrangements found in thriving natural ecosystems.

facts.text: It rests on design principles drawn from whole-systems thinking, applied to farming, town planning, rewilding and community resilience.
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978, in opposition to industrial farming methods.
Earlier ideas of permanent agriculture, such as F. H. King's 1911 book and J. Russell Smith's Tree Crops of 1929, inspired it.
Holmgren set out twelve design principles, such as observe and interact, catch and store energy, and obtain a yield.
It favours perennial crops that need no yearly tilling and planting.
Critics say it is loosely defined and largely isolated from scientific literature.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue permaculture lacks a clear definition and a scientific basis.

entries.title: Cover crops: plants grown to protect the soil

definition.text: A plant grown to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

facts.text: Cover crops help manage erosion, soil fertility, water, weeds, pests, diseases and wildlife on a farm.
They are often grown only to prevent erosion: roots anchor soil and the canopy slows raindrops and runoff.
A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found they raised topsoil organic carbon by about 10% and nitrogen by about 20%.
They reduce water pollution and take carbon dioxide out of the air.
Thick stands smother weeds, and some suppress weeds chemically through allelopathy.
In one study songbird densities were 7–20 times higher in cotton fields with a clover cover crop.
Effects on the next crop's water and yield vary, especially in semi-arid regions, and long-term profitability is uncertain.

entries.title: Intercropping: two crops, one field, same time

definition.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

facts.text: Its main goal is a larger total yield by using resources a single crop would leave unused.
Crops are paired to avoid competing, such as deep-rooted with shallow-rooted, or tall with shade-tolerant.
In low-input systems it can give higher yields for the same input, or steadier yields with less.
A companion crop can support plants prone to falling over, or supply nutrients.
Results vary: a 2008 review found predators rose in only 53% of studies and yields in only 32%.
Crop rotation differs because its crops grow in separate seasons.

entries.text: A single crop leaves some light, water and nutrients unused. Intercropping is growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture. entries.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to the farm

definition.text: The study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming systems, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment.

facts.text: The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement.
It is multidisciplinary, drawing on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history.
It studies agroecosystem properties such as productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability, at scales from a gene to the globe.
Unlike natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces governing agroecosystems.
Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are its three certified varieties; organics is practised in 188 countries.
Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue food sovereignty.
Researchers heatedly debate which model of agriculture or agroecology policy should support.

entries.title: Agroforestry: trees and crops on the same ground

definition.text: A way of managing land that grows trees together with crops or pasture on the same ground.

facts.text: It can yield timber, fruit, nuts, mushrooms, medicinal plants, animals and other products.
It is managed to make the most of helpful interactions between plants and animals, using the forest as a model, and is described as applied agroecology.
Benefits include higher farm productivity and profits, less soil erosion, wildlife habitat, more biodiversity and carbon sequestration, provided the farm is well managed.
Growing varied products such as fuelwood and medicinal plants makes farm income more secure.
Trees store carbon in soil and wood and can recapture some carbon lost when forests were cut.
It is most common on tropical smallholdings, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, and has spread to the US and Europe.
A survey of over 700 East African households found at least 50% had begun planting trees to adapt to climate change.
The term was coined in 1973 by forester John Bene, but the practice is millennia old.

entries.title: Landscape-scale conservation: managing the whole picture

definition.text: An approach that manages a whole landscape to balance nature conservation against farming, forestry and other economic uses of the same land.

facts.text: It is an alternative to protecting single sites.
Its backers argue that poverty, food security, climate change, water scarcity and biodiversity loss are linked, so they need coordinated action across a landscape.
A river basin, for example, supplies water, timber, crops and habitat, and each use affects the others.
Rather than serving a single land use, it tries to meet the interests of many different stakeholders.
The IUCN applied it in 27 landscapes in 23 countries.
Often called the landscape approach, it was described by UNEP in 2015 as embodying ecosystem management.
Landscape approaches try to meet several Sustainable Development Goals at once, for example raising farm output, flood defence, biodiversity and carbon storage within one river catchment.
A review found five barriers, including confusing terminology, long delays before action, and sectors working in silos.

entries.title: Riparian buffers: green strips that guard streams

definition.text: A strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from the effects of nearby land use.

facts.text: Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and pesticides in runoff before they reach the water.
They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilise banks against erosion.
They provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farming areas.
A nine-year University of Georgia study found buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer runoff.
Buffers can raise land value and allow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut.
Programmes such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers to make up for taking buffer land out of production.
A 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

entries.title: Land sharing: making room for wildlife on the farm

definition.text: A strategy, also called wildlife-friendly agriculture, that makes room for biodiversity inside farmed areas by farming less intensively.

facts.text: Agroforestry and mixed crop-livestock systems are examples.
Reviews more often find it better for food security and livelihoods, in 58% of studies.

entries.title: Land sparing: farm hard here so nature can stay wild there

definition.text: A strategy that keeps farmland and nature strictly apart, farming some land intensively for high yields so that other land can stay wild.

facts.text: It has been the dominant strategy in developed countries for over 150 years.
Reviews find it generally favoured for conserving tropical forest biodiversity, in 67% of relevant studies.

facts.text: The debate has run for over a decade without a clear consensus.
Sparing tends to win for tropical forest biodiversity, sharing for food security and livelihoods.
A third option, land blending, has been proposed because each strategy's success depends on the landscape.

entries.title: Sustainable intensification: more food without more land

definition.text: Farming methods that raise production while also improving environmental outcomes, without clearing more land.

facts.text: It differs from earlier intensification by putting weight on broader environmental results.
By 2018 an estimated 163 million farms in 100 nations used it, on 453 million ha, equal to 29% of farms worldwide.
Whether ecosystem services can replace non-renewable inputs while keeping yields high has been much debated.
In east Asian rice fields, nectar plants that support pest predators cut insecticide need by 70% with a 5% yield gain.

entries.title: Hedges: living boundaries that shelter wildlife

definition.text: A line of shrubs, sometimes with trees, planted and trained as a barrier or boundary; old field-boundary hedges are called hedgerows.

facts.text: Hedges often act as windbreaks that improve conditions for crops.
The first hedges enclosed cereal fields in the Neolithic, 4000–6000 years ago.
They help prevent soil loss, reduce pollution, regulate water and reduce flooding.
One study found 100% of northwest European farms have hedges, providing 43% of the wildlife habitat there.
Removing hedges makes bigger, cheaper-to-farm fields with more yield and profit, but weakens soil and causes erosion.
UK hedge removal was subsidised after World War II, and over half of UK hedgerows have vanished since the 1950s.
The UK government now increasingly compensates farmers for maintaining them.

entries.title: Rotational grazing: moving herds so pasture can rest

definition.text: Moving livestock between sections of pasture, called paddocks, so that the rest of the pasture can recover.

facts.text: It usually yields less than intensive livestock operations but needs fewer inputs, so net income per animal can be higher.
Each cow produces less, but more cows can graze each acre, giving more output per acre at less cost.
Pastures under some rotational systems erode less, and it may reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Manure returns most nutrients to the pasture, and swards with over 40% legumes need no commercial nitrogen.
Grazing animals on young legume-rich pasture risks bloat, which can be fatal.
In 87% of experiments, plant production was equal or greater under continuous grazing.
Virtual fencing with GPS collars can automate rotations.

entries.title: Silvopasture: trees, grass and livestock together

definition.text: Combining trees, forage plants and grazing livestock on the same land so each benefits the others.

facts.text: It is a form of agroforestry that uses managed grazing.
Selling tree crops, forage and livestock together can raise productivity and long-term income.
Partial tree cover moderates temperature: one study found near-ground air up to 7% cooler than in open pasture.
Carbon uptake is lowest in open pastures, intermediate in silvopastures and highest in forests.
It needs heavy upfront investment and typically takes 3–6 years to give returns.
Barriers include policy hurdles, land tenure, lack of knowledge, economic constraints and cultural change.
If done correctly it can count as a nature-based solution to climate change.

entries.title: Conservation agriculture: three rules for protecting farmland

definition.text: A farming system, defined by the FAO, that protects farmland from loss and restores degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and a variety of crops.

facts.text: Its first principle, minimal soil disturbance such as no-till, keeps minerals in the soil and prevents erosion and water loss.
Its second principle, a permanent organic cover of mulch, shields the soil from rain and wind and builds organic matter.
Its third principle is diverse crop rotation, which breaks pest and weed cycles and improves water infiltration.
Farmers can save 30% to 40% of time and labour by not tilling.
Benefits come slowly: building organic matter takes years, and early years can bring financial losses.
Barriers include the high cost of special planting equipment and competition with livestock for crop residues.

entries.title: Farming's greenhouse gases: cows, fertilizer and cleared land

definition.text: The heat-trapping gases released by farming, both directly from crops and livestock and indirectly from clearing land for farms.

facts.text: Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Nitrous oxide and methane make up over half of agriculture's direct emissions.
Making and using nitrogen fertilizer contributes around 5% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
Livestock production alone accounts for almost 60% of food-system greenhouse gas emissions.
Ruminants such as cows and sheep give off methane made by microbes in their guts.

entries.title: Climate-smart agriculture: three goals at once

definition.text: A set of farming methods that try at once to adapt farming to climate change, raise yields for food security, and cut farm greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: The World Bank calls it practices and technologies that together boost productivity, build resilience and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
The FAO says it is not a new set of practices but an approach fitted to local contexts.
Examples include heat-tolerant crop varieties, mulching, boundary trees and suitable housing and spacing for cattle.
Carbon farming is one of its components.
Agriculture, forestry and land use produce 13%–21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Rainfed farming makes up 80% of global agriculture, so shifting rainfall threatens many poor farmers in Asia and Africa.
No accepted standard defines it, and critics call the label greenwashing for big businesses.

entries.title: Biodiversity on farmland

definition.text: The variety of living things found on farmland.

facts.text: Biodiversity on farms falls as varied landscapes are lost and native plants are replaced by crops.
The FAO estimates more than 40% of Earth's land surface is used for agriculture, making habitat loss the main driver of biodiversity loss.
Fallow land, grass margins and scrub strips between fields add habitat variety and so raise farm biodiversity.
Smaller fields have been linked to greater species richness.
In Asian rice, flowering strips beside fields cut insecticide spraying by 70% and raised yields by 5%, an economic advantage of 7.5%.
Low crop diversity can increase pests and pesticide resistance, causing ecological and economic losses.

entries.title: Fertilizer runoff: when nutrients escape the field

definition.text: The loss of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized fields into water and air, where they cause pollution.

facts.text: Fertilizers vastly raised yields: at 1900 yield levels, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land.
Nitrate dissolves easily, so it runs off into surface water and leaches into groundwater.
Nitrate above 10 mg/L in groundwater can cause blue baby syndrome in infants.
Phosphorus is the largest contributor to eutrophication, especially in fresh water.
Fertilization also releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that harms stratospheric ozone.

entries.title: Ecological farming: rebuilding what the land provides

definition.text: Farming focused on the environmental side of sustainable agriculture, using methods that rebuild ecosystem services.

facts.text: It aims to prevent erosion, improve water infiltration, store carbon as humus and raise biodiversity.
Techniques include no-till farming, multispecies cover crops, strip cropping, terraces and shelter belts.
Crop genetic diversity lowers the risks of monocultures, which can be vulnerable to a changing climate.

entries.title: The rotation effect: why rotated crops yield more

definition.text: The yield gain that rotated crops show compared with crops grown alone year after year.

facts.text: It arises mainly from relieving the problems of monoculture: better nutrition, less pest and weed stress and better soil structure.

facts.text: Farmers in Europe moved to it from the two-field system between the 9th and 11th centuries, and it lasted until the 20th century.
Two thirds of the land was planted instead of half, and the legume crops improved people's nutrition.

definition.text: Rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around crops.

facts.text: They raise yields by reducing crop drying and stopping plants from being blown over.
The USDA lists windbreaks as one of five temperate agroforestry practices.

entries.text: Wind dries crops and knocks them flat. Windbreaks are rows of trees or shrubs planted to slow the wind over and around fields. They raise yields by reducing crop drying and stopping plants from being blown over. The USDA lists them as one of five temperate agroforestry practices.

entries.title: Testing soil health

definition.text: Measuring a soil's physical, chemical and biological condition against benchmarks of healthy function.

facts.text: Benchmarks include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Many labs resist new biological tests because fertility testing rests on crop-response models with no equivalent for soil health.

entries.title: Contour plowing: furrows that follow the hill

definition.text: Ploughing furrows along a slope's contour lines so they stay level, which slows runoff.

facts.text: It can raise crop yields by 10 to 50 percent, partly by keeping soil in place.
The ancient Phoenicians used it on slopes of two to ten percent.

entries.text: Contour plowing can raise crop yields by 10 to 50 percent, partly by keeping soil in place. Farmers plow furrows along a slope's contour lines so the furrows stay level and slow runoff. The idea is old: the ancient Phoenicians used it on slopes of two to ten percent.

entries.title: Keyline design: shaping a whole watershed

definition.text: An extension of contour farming that shapes contour lines around the whole watershed.

facts.text: It is used in regenerative farms alongside diverse livestock and crop production.

entries.text: Keyline design extends contour plowing from one field to a whole watershed. It shapes contour lines around the entire drainage basin so water spreads and soaks in. It is used on regenerative farms alongside diverse livestock and crop production.

entries.title: Managing salt in farm soils

definition.text: Preventing and reducing the build-up of salt in soil, which mainly comes from irrigating with salty water.

facts.text: Salt breaks down soil structure and causes infertility; salinity affects about one third of the earth's arable land.
After the 1970 Aswan Dam, a raised water table salinised soils in Egypt.
Salt-tolerant plants such as saltbush can lower water tables and slow surface salt build-up.

entries.title: Terrace farming: steps cut into hillsides

definition.text: Cutting a hillside into a series of nearly level steps for growing crops.

facts.text: Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water and are more common on small farms.

entries.text: A steep hill can be farmed if it is cut into steps. Terrace farming carves a hillside into a series of nearly level platforms for crops. Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water, which keeps soil from washing away. They are more common on small farms.
entries.text_plain: A steep hill can be farmed if it is cut into steps. Terrace farming carves a hillside into a series of nearly level platforms for crops. Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water, which keeps soil from washing away. They are more common on small farms.

entries.title: Holistic planned grazing: imitating wild herds

definition.text: Moving livestock herds constantly between fields to imitate how wild herds graze.

facts.text: Supporters say trampling restores soil, stimulates regrowth and raises soil carbon and water infiltration.
A meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it did no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass.
Allan Savory claimed in a TED talk that it could bring carbon dioxide back to pre-industrial levels in 40 years; critics reject this.

entries.contested_note: Evidence on its carbon benefits is mixed, and critics reject the claim that it can reverse climate change.

entries.title: Bamboo as a carbon crop

definition.text: Growing bamboo plantations as a way to store carbon on farmland.

facts.text: A bamboo forest holds less total carbon than most mature forests but can match rubber plantations and orchards and exceed agroforests, palm oil plantations and grasslands.
Bamboo plantations take up carbon faster than mature forests, but only when new or actively managed.

It can match rubber plantations and orchards, though, and beats agroforests, palm oil plantations and grasslands. Bamboo takes up carbon faster than mature forests, but only when new or actively managed.

entries.title: Scoring how well farms can weather climate change

definition.text: A scoring tool that measures how resilient farming systems are to climate change.

facts.text: The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and resource efficiency, environmental sustainability and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience.
It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience.
A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare the country's agro-climatic zones.

It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience. A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare its agro-climatic zones.

entries.title: Climate-smart farming that works for women

definition.text: Designing climate-smart farming programmes to address the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

facts.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more climate risk because they have less access to land resources, money and advice.
They are often left out of decisions, which can limit their adoption of practices that help them adapt.

entries.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more danger from climate change than men. They have less access to land, money and advice. They are also often left out of decisions, which can limit their use of practices that help them adapt. Gender-responsive climate-smart agriculture designs programs around the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

entries.title: Conservation tillage: disturbing the soil less

definition.text: A group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled.

facts.text: No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, but no-till is not the same thing.
Tillage, mechanically stirring the soil, has been used since at least 3000 B.C.
By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.

entries.text: People have stirred the soil mechanically, called tillage, since at least 3000 B.C. Conservation tillage is a group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled. No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, though no-till is not the same thing as the whole group. By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.

entries.title: Hügelkultur: buried wood that holds water

definition.text: Burying wood in mounds or beds so that it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist.

facts.text: Enough buried wood can hold rainy-season water to carry crops through the dry season.

entries.text: Rotting logs can water a garden. Hügelkultur is burying wood in mounds or beds so it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist. With enough buried wood, the mound can hold rainy-season water and carry crops through the dry season.

entries.title: The three ethics of permaculture

definition.text: The three core ethics of permaculture: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption and sharing the surplus.

facts.text: Mollison formulated them in 1988; Holmgren restated the third in 2002 as setting limits to consumption and reproduction and redistributing surplus.

entries.text: Permaculture rests on three core ethics: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption while sharing the surplus. Mollison formulated them in 1988. In 2002 Holmgren restated the third as setting limits to consumption and reproduction and redistributing surplus.

entries.title: Permaculture zones: placing things by how often they are used

definition.text: A layout that places parts of a design by how often people use them, numbered 0 to 5 outward from the house.

facts.text: Elements tended or harvested often go close to the house in zones 1 and 2; those used less are farther out.

entries.text: A permaculture design is laid out in zones numbered 0 to 5, moving outward from the house. Each part is placed by how often people use it. Things tended or harvested often go close to the house, in zones 1 and 2. Things used less go farther out, saving daily walking and effort.

entries.title: Plant guilds: species that help each other

definition.text: A mutually beneficial group of species that each provide different services within a larger ecosystem.

facts.text: Guild plants may supply food, draw up deep nutrients, fix nitrogen, attract helpful insects or repel pests.

entries.text: A plant guild is a mutually beneficial group of species, each providing a different service within a larger ecosystem. One may supply food. Another may draw up deep nutrients or fix nitrogen. Others attract helpful insects or repel pests.

entries.title: Rainwater harvesting: catching rain before it runs off

definition.text: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground.

facts.text: It supplies drinking water, livestock water and irrigation, and roof collection can significantly add to drinking water supply.

entries.text: Rain that runs off a roof is water lost. Rainwater harvesting collects and stores rain for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground. It supplies drinking water, livestock water and irrigation. Collecting from roofs can significantly add to drinking water supply.

entries.title: Sheet mulching: copying the forest floor

definition.text: Layering materials such as leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil to imitate a forest floor.

facts.text: Mulch absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion.
It is also used in regenerative agriculture to smother weeds and feed the soil.

entries.text: A forest floor is a thick blanket of leaves and wood. Sheet mulching copies it by layering leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil. The mulch absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion. Regenerative farmers also use it to smother weeds and feed the soil.

entries.title: Green manure: a crop grown to feed the soil

definition.text: A cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually ploughed in before it matures.

facts.text: Green manures are commonly legumes, which are high in nitrogen and can supply what a crop needs.
This replaces nitrogen that conventional farms apply as chemical fertilizer.

entries.text: Some crops are grown only to be plowed back in. Green manure is a cover crop grown to raise soil fertility, usually turned into the soil before it matures. Green manures are commonly legumes, which are high in nitrogen and can supply what the next crop needs. They replace nitrogen that conventional farms apply as chemical fertilizer.

entries.title: Organic farming: natural inputs, fewer synthetics

definition.text: A farming system that relies on natural inputs such as compost, manure and green manure and on methods like crop rotation, and largely bans synthetic pesticides and fertilizers.

facts.text: Genetically modified organisms, sewage sludge, growth hormones and routine antibiotics in livestock are prohibited.
It began early in the 20th century as a reaction to fast-changing farming.
By 2022 it was practised in 188 countries on about 96,000,000 hectares by 4.5 million farmers.
The organic market reached $150 billion worldwide in 2022.
On average 30% more species live on organic farms, though this ignores extra land needed for lower yields.
A 2012 meta-analysis found organic farming needs 84% more land for the same harvest.
Emissions per area of land are lower, but per unit of food nitrogen leaching and related pollution are higher.
There is not enough evidence that organic food is safer or healthier than conventional food.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on its environmental record: lower impact per hectare but often higher impact per unit of food because yields are lower.

verification.title: The effects of organic agriculture on biodiversity and abundance: a meta‐analysis
verification.evidence: Organic farming usually increases species richness, having on average 30% higher species richness than conventional farming systems.

entries.title: Syntropic agroforestry: food forests that follow succession

definition.text: An organic agroforestry system, developed by Ernst Götsch in Brazil, that copies natural forest succession to build productive food forests.

facts.text: It relies on dense mixed planting of perennial and annual crops and on cutting fast-growing pioneer plants to build up nutrients.
Documented benefits include better water penetration, higher productivity on poor land and moderated soil temperature.

entries.text: In Brazil, Ernst Götsch developed a way of farming that imitates a forest regrowing. entries.title: Organic certification: who gets to say organic

definition.text: Rules, voluntary or set by law, that define how organic food must be produced and allow it to be labelled organic.

facts.text: Private groups certified organic producers in the 1970s; legislated standards spread from the 1991 EU regulation.
By 2007 over 60 countries regulated organic farming.
Agencies usually accredit certification groups rather than individual farms.

entries.title: The organic price premium

definition.text: The higher price organic food fetches over conventional food, which is key to whether organic farming pays.

facts.text: With premiums, US organic farming was 2.7 to 3.8 times more profitable; globally 22–35% more profitable.
In 2013 premiums were 100% for organic vegetables and 57% for organic fruit.
Globally, premiums of only 5-7% were needed to break even with conventional farming.
Premiums have narrowed, weakening the incentive to convert; without them profitability is mixed.

entries.title: The organic yield gap: can organic feed the world?

definition.text: The difference between organic and conventional crop yields and whether organic farming could feed the world.

facts.text: A 2012 meta-analysis found organic productivity on average 25% lower.
The gap depends on crop and site: about 5% for rain-fed legumes and perennials, about 13% under best organic practice.
In 2007 the FAO said organic farming could not feed the current population.

entries.contested_note: Estimates of the yield gap vary widely with crop, site and study.

conflicts.text: A 2011 meta-analysis of 362 datasets found organic yields were on average 80% of conventional yields.

entries.title: Trap crops: luring pests away

definition.text: A crop grown to lure pests away from the valuable crop.

facts.text: Once pests gather, the small trap area can be treated or the pests physically removed.
Mustard and radish trap nematodes, cutting their populations by 70–99%.

entries.title: Plastic on the farm

definition.text: Plastic from greenhouse sheeting, storage bags, silage wrap and mulch film that ends up in farmed land.

facts.text: A 2021 FAO study estimated farming produces 10 million tons of plastic waste a year.
Very little agricultural plastic is collected worldwide.

entries.title: The risks of using living things against pests

definition.text: The debate over releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to control farm pests in place of pesticides.

facts.text: Biocontrol can cut pollution from pesticide use.
Once released, an agent may be impossible to recall and may spread into the wild or switch to native hosts.

entries.contested_note: The merits of introducing non-native biocontrol agents are widely debated.
entries.text: Releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to fight farm pests can cut pollution from pesticides. But the method carries its own risk. entries.title: How much warming comes from livestock?
entries.article: Agricultural pollution#Greenhouse gases from fecal waste

definition.text: The dispute over how large a share of human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock.

facts.text: The FAO estimated 18% of human greenhouse gases come directly or indirectly from livestock, more than transport.
Critics say the comparison is unfair because the FAO used a full life-cycle assessment for livestock but not for transport.
Others claim livestock could cause up to 51% of emissions.

entries.contested_note: Estimates of livestock's share of emissions range from 18% to up to 51%, and the FAO method has been called a misrepresentation.

Treatment reduces the manure to transport, nutrients to spread and pathogens.
Anaerobic digestion breaks down liquid manure without air, producing fertilizer liquid and methane that can be burned for heat and power.

entries.title: Inga alley cropping: an alternative to slash-and-burn

definition.text: Growing crops between rows of nitrogen-fixing Inga trees, whose pruned leaves form a thick mulch.

facts.text: It lets land be farmed repeatedly, offering an alternative to destructive slash-and-burn cultivation.
Mike Hands developed and trialled it in Costa Rica in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

entries.text: Slash-and-burn farming destroys forest to get a few harvests. Inga alley cropping offers another way. entries.text_plain: Slash-and-burn farming destroys forest to get a few harvests. Inga alley cropping offers another way. Mike Hands developed and trialed it in Costa Rica in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

entries.title: Relay cropping: sowing the next crop early

definition.text: Sowing a second crop while the first is still growing, so the first is harvested to make room for the second.

facts.text: Related temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing crop with a slow one, harvesting the fast crop first, and can out-yield either alone.

entries.title: Wood pasture: Europe's ancient grazing woods

definition.text: A traditional European system in which open woodland gave grazing animals shelter and forage while also yielding timber and fuel.

facts.text: It is one of the oldest land-use practices in human history.
Since Roman times, pigs have been turned into beech and oak woods to eat acorns and beech mast.

entries.title: Integrated landscape management: planning beyond the farm

definition.text: A way of managing a landscape sustainably by bringing together stakeholders who want different things from the land.

facts.text: Sara Scherr coined the term in 2012 for planning whole regions rather than single farms or plots.
By 2016 it had five steps: stakeholders meet, share information, plan together, carry out the plan, and monitor and adapt.
It seeks synergies among conservation, farm production and rural livelihoods.

entries.title: Buffers shaped by groundwater, not a ruler

definition.text: A riparian buffer whose width follows local groundwater flow instead of a fixed distance.

facts.text: Groundwater enters streams at hotspots that matter disproportionately for temperature, acidity and nutrient retention.
Soil wetness maps from elevation models show where buffers should be wider.
Designing by hydrology rather than fixed width can save money in forestry.

entries.title: The three zones of a riparian buffer

definition.text: The usual three-zone layout of a riparian buffer, from stream-side trees to outer grass strips.

facts.text: The zone next to the water holds fast-growing native trees that shade the stream and stabilise the bank.
The middle zone of native shrubs gives wildlife habitat and absorbs what the outer zone misses.
The outer grass zone is the first defence, slowing runoff and absorbing contaminants.
A typical recommended width is 50 feet (15 m) on each side of the stream.

entries.title: Agri-environment schemes: paying farmers to farm greener

definition.text: Programmes, compulsory for EU member states, that pay farmers to adopt environmentally friendlier methods to make up for the cost of changing.

facts.text: Farmers join voluntarily and commit for at least five years.
In 2009 they covered 38.5 million hectares, 20.9% of farmland in the then 27 EU states.
In 2012 the European Commission spent €3.23 billion on them, far more than the €39.6 million spent managing Natura 2000 sites.
Their aim shifted from protecting threatened habitats, to keeping wildlife on farmland, to improving services such as pollination.
A 2015 review found schemes that take land out of production did better at boosting species than in-production schemes.

definition.text: Restoring a hedge by cutting most of the way through each stem near the base, bending it over and weaving it between stakes.

facts.text: It encourages new growth from the base and was originally done to keep hedges stock-proof.

entries.title: Hooper's rule: dating a hedge by its species

definition.text: A rule of thumb that estimates a hedge's age as the number of woody species in a thirty-yard stretch times 110 years.

facts.text: Max Hooper published it in 1974; it can be off by a couple of centuries and fails for hedges over a thousand years old.

facts.text: Butterfly abundance has been found to increase with heterogeneity.
The Green Revolution, since 1966, spread a few crops such as wheat, rice and maize, reducing heterogeneity and local crop diversity.

entries.title: Regenerative economics: renewing Earth's capital

definition.text: An economic approach that aims to renew capital assets, treating the Earth as the original capital asset, instead of using them up.

facts.text: In standard theory an asset can be regenerated or consumed until it no longer yields goods or services.
Supporters say ignoring nature's value has caused uneconomic growth, Herman Daly's term, which they see as its opposite.
It has four components: circulation, organisational structure, relationships and values, and collective learning.
Unlike ecological economics, which sets limits on the economy, it focuses on the reproduction of life in nature.

entries.title: Integrated pest management: control, not eradication

definition.text: A pest control approach that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides.

facts.text: The FAO describes it as combining biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use.
It aims at control, not eradication, since wiping out a pest is often impossible, costly and unsafe.
Prevention comes first: resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping.
It reduces risks such as pest resurgence, pesticide resistance and residues on food.
Alternating between classes of control helps stop pests becoming resistant.
It runs as six repeated steps: sample, identify, learn the pest's biology, set an action threshold, choose tactics, evaluate.
In 1986 Indonesia banned 57 pesticides and stopped subsidising them.

entries.title: The economic injury level: when a pest is worth fighting

definition.text: The pest population at which the crop damage would cost more than treating the pest.

facts.text: The economic threshold is the lower population at which action must be taken to stop pests reaching the economic injury level.
IPM sets these action thresholds from estimated economic damage and treats only when they are exceeded.
Thresholds depend on the pest and the site.
Letting a pest survive at a tolerable level reduces selection pressure for resistance.

definition.text: Pest control that pairs an attractive trap crop pulling pests in with a repellent crop pushing them away from the main crop.

facts.text: In a 2006 review of 100 trap crops, only 10 succeeded commercially, all with added measures to stop insects returning to the main crop.

entries.title: Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action

definition.text: Advertising or public relations meant to mislead people into believing an organization's products, goals or policies are good for the environment.

facts.text: The word blends 'green' with 'whitewashing'.
Firms greenwash to win legitimacy with environmentally minded people, to look responsible to the wider public, and to distance themselves from their own or their suppliers' environmental failings.
A common rule of thumb: an organization is greenwashing if it spends far more on advertising a green image than on actually acting in environmentally sound ways.
With no agreed definition, consumers and regulators can find it hard to decide whether a given case is greenwashing.
New York environmentalist Jay Westerveld coined the term in a 1986 essay on hotels urging guests to reuse towels to 'save the environment', which mainly cut laundry costs.
A 2020 European Union study found over 50% of examined environmental claims were vague, misleading or unfounded, and 40% were unsubstantiated.
Many companies pledged net-zero emissions after the 2015 Paris Agreement, but critics say they make unfeasible plans instead of actually cutting emissions.
Critics argue that widespread greenwashing, with weak regulation and enforcement, makes consumers doubt all green claims and weakens their power to push firms toward greener practices.

entries.title: Monoculture: one crop, one field, short-term gains

definition.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at a time.

facts.text: Uniform planting, care and harvest make monocultures easy and efficient in the short term, often giving higher yields and lower costs.
Over the long term they are more prone to disease and pest outbreaks because of reduced local biodiversity and nutrient depletion.
Diversity can be added over time through crop rotation or in space through polyculture or intercropping.
Monoculture and synthetic fertilizers have reduced the extra land needed to grow food, which is called land sparing.
Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soils and encourage soil-borne disease.
Declining soil health leads to more synthetic fertilizer, whose excess nitrogen can contaminate drinking water and feed algal blooms.
Over 600 million liters of pesticides are sprayed each year after pest outbreaks, harming nearby small farms and community health.
Agroecology, silvopastoral systems and mixed-species plantations are common alternatives that keep productivity while preserving biodiversity.

entries.title: Albedo: how much sunlight a surface throws back

definition.text: The share of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects.

facts.text: It runs from 0, a black body absorbing everything, to 1, a surface reflecting everything.
Fresh snow reflects about 0.9 to 0.95 of visible light, while charcoal reflects about 0.04.
Oceans and most forests have low albedo, while deserts are among the most reflective landforms.
Albedo shapes climate by setting how much radiation a planet absorbs.
Deciduous trees have an albedo of about 0.15 to 0.18 and conifers about 0.09 to 0.15.
Land-use changes such as deforestation, farming and urbanization alter albedo and can perturb Earth's energy balance.

entries.title: Tree planting: putting seedlings in the ground

definition.text: Transplanting young tree seedlings into the ground, usually for forestry, land reclamation or landscaping.

facts.text: In forestry it is called reforestation where land was recently forested and afforestation where it was not.
Done properly it can regenerate a deforested area, but a planted forest rarely matches the biodiversity and complexity of a natural one.

Outside interests often profit more from fast-growing species such as eucalyptus or pine, whose plantations bring far smaller biodiversity benefits than native forest and are often controversial as offsets.
Many environmentalists argue that only native trees should be planted, to help native ecosystems regrow.
Planted forests covered an estimated 312 million ha in 2025, 8% of all forest area, and grew by 120 million ha since 1990.
Almost all plantation forests (95%) in South America are of introduced species.
Tree-planting initiatives can harm biodiversity, especially in tropical savannas.

entries.title: Tree plantations: forests built to produce wood

definition.text: A forest planted to produce large volumes of wood, usually as a single-species monoculture.

facts.text: Managed timber forests commonly yield 1 to 3 cubic meters of wood per hectare per year, while fast-growing plantations commonly yield 20 to 30 or more.
In 2000 plantations made up 5% of global forest but supplied an estimated 35% of the world's roundwood.
Industrial plantations are large, even-aged blocks of one or two species, often bred for fast growth and pest resistance.
Trees are usually harvested after 10 to 60 years, so plantations lack the growth, soil, wildlife and decaying dead wood of old-growth forest.
Fast-wood plantations or fiber farms, started in Brazil in the 1970s, run on rotations as short as 5 to 15 years.
Eucalyptus is the most widely planted plantation tree worldwide.
Long-term carbon storage depends on what happens to the harvested wood.
Fiber plantations offer local people a much narrower range of services than the natural forest they replace, sometimes ignoring local rights.

entries.title: Policing green claims: rules against greenwashing

definition.text: Laws, codes and guidelines that govern what businesses may say about the environmental benefits of their products, aimed at curbing greenwashing.

facts.text: Rules on misleading environmental claims differ worldwide, ranging from criminal liability to fines to voluntary guidelines.
The US Federal Trade Commission's voluntary 'green guides' say any qualifications must be clear, prominent and understandable enough to prevent deception.
The UK Competition and Markets Authority published a Green Claims Code in September 2021 to protect consumers from misleading environmental claims.
A January 2021 European Commission review found that green claims on 42 percent of consumer websites examined were likely false and misleading.
In June 2024 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled that firms advertising as 'climate neutral' must define the term, because it is otherwise too vague.
EU rules require companies with over 250 staff and €40 million turnover to disclose ESG information, which is expected to help combat greenwashing.
Firms may also seek environmental certification so that independent checks verify their green claims.

entries.title: Forest monocultures: carbon gains, local losses

definition.text: Plantations made up of a single tree species, often grown for timber.

facts.text: After deforestation, single-species afforestation has become popular for ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration to fight climate change.
Eucalyptus, pines and acacias are common choices in the tropics and Global South, often imported species that replace native forest.
Such schemes may bring global climate benefit yet cause local harm, including soil depletion and altered water cycles.
Single-species forests reduce biodiversity, lowering forest productivity and native plant and animal populations, and weakening resistance to pests and disease.
Plantations often offer few local jobs, and profits tend to follow a boom-and-bust pattern rarely reinvested in the land.
In China, a shift to low-cost monoculture of mostly red pine meant trees that died never delivered their expected carbon offset.

entries.title: The forest albedo trade-off: carbon versus darkness

definition.text: The way dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling gained when new trees store carbon.

facts.text: Forests have low albedo because they absorb most ultraviolet and visible light for photosynthesis.
In snowy regions, treeless winter albedo is 10% to 50% higher than nearby forest, because snow does not cover trees as readily.
Hadley Centre studies found new tropical and midlatitude forests tended to cool, while high-latitude forests such as in Siberia were neutral or perhaps warming.
For snowy evergreen forests, the albedo effect can be large enough that clearing them causes net cooling.
A 2023 study of 176 flux stations found afforestation may cause moderate warming for about 20 years before turning to significant cooling.
Tropical reforestation helps form clouds that reflect sunlight, while boreal reforestation swaps bright snow for dark canopy and helps the climate less.
Evapotranspiration from trees is usually treated as net cooling, so the overall effect of deforestation depends heavily on local climate.

entries.text: Forests look dark from above because they absorb most ultraviolet and visible light for photosynthesis. That darkness creates a trade-off. Tropical reforestation helps form clouds that reflect sunlight. Boreal reforestation swaps bright snow for dark canopy and helps less. Trees also release water vapor, which is usually treated as net cooling. So the overall effect depends heavily on local climate.

entries.title: Planting trees to fight climate change: promise and limits
entries.article: Tree planting#Role in climate change mitigation

definition.text: Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it, as a way to limit climate change.

facts.text: Forests act as carbon sinks and take up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
Forests can switch from sinks to sources: in 2019 they absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Avoiding deforestation beats clearing and replanting, which causes irreversible biodiversity loss and soil damage; new forests also take several decades to deliver comparable carbon benefits.
Scientists call protecting and restoring carbon-rich, long-lived ecosystems, especially natural forests, 'the major climate solution'.
An estimate of room for 0.9 billion ha more tree canopy has been criticized; counting albedo and other feedbacks, the area that truly cools is 20-80% lower.
Such planting would store 205 billion tons of carbon only if the trees survive future climate stress to maturity.
Stored carbon must not return to the air through burning or rotting when trees die.
A meta-analysis found mixed-species plantations would store more carbon than single-species ones.

entries.contested_note: The global estimate of land available for climate-cooling tree planting has been criticized as far too high.

entries.title: Greenscamming: green names for anti-green groups

definition.text: Giving an organization or product a name that falsely suggests it is environmentally friendly.

facts.text: Industrial firms and associations use such front groups to dispute scientific findings that threaten their business, for example denial of human-caused global warming by fossil energy companies.
Deceptive names are used because openly arguing for environmentally damaging activities is hard when environmental protection enjoys broad public support.
ExxonMobil supported more than 100 climate denial organizations and spent about 20 million U.S. dollars on greenscamming groups.

entries.title: The seven sins of greenwashing

definition.text: A list of seven kinds of misleading environmental claims, set out by the consultancy TerraChoice in 2007 to help shoppers spot them.

facts.text: The sins are hidden trade-off, no proof, vagueness, worshipping false labels, irrelevance, lesser of two evils, and fibbing (a plainly false claim).
A 'hidden trade-off' calls a product green on the basis of a narrow set of attributes while ignoring other important environmental issues.
TerraChoice reported that by 2010 about 95% of U.S. consumer products claiming to be green committed at least one of the sins.
The United Nations lists similar tactics, such as announcing future environmental milestones without real plans to reach them, or highlighting one good practice while doing nothing else.

entries.title: Types of greenwashing: where the deception starts

definition.text: Ways of sorting greenwashing by where the misleading claim or misconduct arises: in a firm itself, in its suppliers, in a product, or across the whole organization.

facts.text: Direct greenwashing is when a firm's own processes contradict its environmental claims; indirect greenwashing is when a supplier's false claims harm the firm it supplies.
Vicarious greenwashing is when a firm that calls itself green partners with a polluting supplier and is blamed for that supplier's misconduct.
At product level, 'claim' greenwashing uses misleading statements or unverified labels such as 'eco-friendly', while 'executional' greenwashing relies on green colours and nature imagery.
Firm-level greenwashing promotes sustainability in campaigns while the company's operations keep damaging the environment.

entries.title: Agro-extractivism: farming for export, controlled from abroad

definition.text: Foreign control over farming driven by large-scale production of agricultural commodities for export, often grown as monocultures.

facts.text: Large tropical monocultures have reduced local and indigenous food sovereignty, food security and access to land and water.
More than 46 million hectares of soy have been planted in South America, while over half a million hectares are deforested each year for cultivation.
Repeated single-crop cultivation exhausts soil nutrients and microbial diversity, increasing reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

These have reduced local and indigenous food sovereignty, food security and access to land and water. Repeated single cropping exhausts soil nutrients and microbes, increasing reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

entries.title: Genetic monoculture: when every plant is the same

definition.text: Planting crops, or raising animals, with little or no genetic variation across a whole region.

facts.text: When all plants in a region are genetically alike, one disease they cannot resist can wipe out entire crops.
Ireland's reliance on a single potato variety, the 'lumper', led to the Great Famine of 1845–1849 once Phytophthora infestans arrived.
Gros Michel bananas, all clones, fell to Fusarium wilt, and growers switched to the Cavendish by the early 1960s; it faces similar risk.
Genetic monoculture in the global food supply is a significant threat to food security.

entries.title: Mixed-species plantations: more species, more value

definition.text: A tree plantation that grows several species together instead of one.

facts.text: Several studies show well-managed mixed-species plantations earn more from timber than monocultures.
Mixed-species forests store more carbon and hold more biodiversity.
They remain less common because of a mistaken belief that they cost more and are harder to manage.

entries.title: How cities and farms change Earth's brightness
entries.article: Albedo#Changes to albedo due to human activities

definition.text: Changes in how much sunlight the land reflects caused by human land use such as cities, farms and deforestation.

facts.text: Urban areas are commonly 0.01–0.02 lower in albedo than nearby cropland, which adds to warming.
Raising urban albedo on purpose can ease the urban heat island effect.
A 2022 estimate found that raising albedo by 0.1 across the world's urban areas would cool as much as absorbing ~44 Gt of CO2.

entries.title: The ice-albedo feedback: melting that feeds itself

definition.text: A self-reinforcing loop in which melting snow or ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more heat and cause more melting.

facts.text: Snow albedo ranges from about 0.9 when fresh to about 0.4 when melting and 0.2 when dirty.
It is one of the main reinforcing climate feedbacks, along with water vapour and the net effect of clouds.
Melting Arctic ice leaves darker water and ground, so less heat is reflected back to space.

It is one of the main reinforcing climate feedbacks, with water vapor and the net effect of clouds.

entries.title: When systematic reviews mislead
entries.article: Systematic review#Out-dated or risk of bias

definition.text: The ways systematic reviews can mislead, through biased inputs, outdated searches or poor reporting, despite being treated as the strongest evidence.

facts.text: A 2003 review of 300 studies found systematic reviews were not all equally reliable.
Of 100 reviews monitored, 7% needed updating on publication, another 4% within a year and another 11% within 2 years.
Around half of clinical trials never report results, and 'positive' trials were twice as likely to be published as 'negative' ones, skewing what reviews can find.
Many reviews comply poorly with reporting guidelines and have weak, hard-to-reproduce search strategies.

definition.text: A review that maps the concepts, language and data around a topic, refining its search as it goes, to gauge how much evidence an area holds.

facts.text: It often comes before a systematic review, to judge whether a full review is possible or worthwhile.
Its methods may change during the work, sometimes departing from the original protocol.
A related mapping review or systematic map sorts existing literature by quantity, quality and study design to show where more research is needed.

entries.title: Introduced species in plantations

definition.text: Planting tree species far outside their natural range because they grow fast and suit industrial use.

facts.text: Globally, 44 percent of plantation forests are made up mainly of introduced species.
Introduced species dominate planted forests in South America (88%), Oceania (75%) and East and Southern Africa (65%), but are only 1%, 3% and 8% in North America, West and Central Asia, and Europe.
Pine, spruce and eucalyptus are the classic examples, valued for fast growth and tolerance of degraded farmland.

entries.title: Do plantations spare natural forests or replace them?

definition.text: The argument over whether high-yield plantations spare natural forests from logging or instead replace them.

facts.text: In principle plantations need less land for the same wood; in New Zealand 19% of the forest area supplies 99% of industrial roundwood.
According to the FAO, about 7% of natural closed forest lost in the tropics is converted to plantations, and 93% to agriculture and other uses.
An estimated 15% of plantations in tropical countries are set up on closed-canopy natural forest.
Using plantations to cut carbon dioxide is challenged because the stored CO2 is eventually released after harvest.

Still, the FAO finds only about 7% of tropical natural forest lost goes to plantations, and 93% to agriculture and other uses. Their carbon benefit is also challenged, since the CO2 is eventually released after harvest.

definition.text: False or misleading claims about how an action affects water and ocean environments, by analogy with greenwashing.

It is used in discussions of the blue economy, the sustainable development of coastal and ocean resources.

entries.title: Putting a price on a warming world

definition.text: The use of economic tools and models to estimate how large climate change damages are and who bears them.

facts.text: It studies the costs of climate impacts, the costs and benefits of preventing climate change, and the cost of adapting.
It can also suggest the best mitigation and adaptation policies from an economic point of view.
Its main tools are process-based integrated assessment models, structural models such as CGE and cost-benefit models, and statistical (econometric) methods.
Econometric models estimate how weather and climate affect economic variables, globally or in one sector.
The economics of mitigation is a contentious part of climate policy.
Ordinary economic signals such as the stock market underestimate or cannot value the social benefits of mitigation.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change
entries.text: How much will climate change cost, and who will pay? Economic analysis of climate change uses the tools and models of economics to estimate how large climate damages are and who bears them. It studies three bills at once: the cost of climate impacts, the costs and benefits of preventing climate change, and the cost of adapting to it. From those sums it can suggest which policies make the most economic sense. Mitigation means cutting the emissions that cause warming, and adaptation means adjusting to the warming that comes anyway. The toolkit has three main parts. Process-based models, described in {{ref:nature-clim-248}}, trace the links between the economy and the climate. Structural models, such as computable general equilibrium (CGE) models and cost-benefit models, represent how the whole economy fits together. Statistical, or econometric, methods estimate from data how weather and climate affect economic variables, either globally or in one sector. The economics of mitigation is one of the most contentious parts of climate policy. One reason is that ordinary economic signals miss much of the picture. The stock market, for example, underestimates or cannot value the social benefits of cutting emissions. The approach extends {{ref:nature-val-001}} to the harms described in {{ref:nature-eco-017}}.

Structural models, such as computable general equilibrium (CGE) models and cost-benefit models, represent how the whole economy fits together. Statistical, or econometric, methods estimate from data how weather and climate affect economic variables, either globally or in one sector. The economics of mitigation is one of the most contentious parts of climate policy. One reason is that ordinary economic signals miss much of the picture. entries.title: Climate risk: when the old extremes no longer hold

definition.text: The chance that the impacts of climate change will cause harm to societies or ecosystems.

facts.text: It covers physical risks, such as extreme weather, and transition risks, the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.
Risk can also come from the measures people take in response to climate change, not only from the changes themselves.
Climate risk is harder to assess than ordinary hazard risk because the climate no longer stays within a stable range of extremes.
Scientists use climate change scenarios when they analyse climate risk.
Risks are grouped by sector, such as agriculture, water, cities, ecosystems, health and livelihoods.
In 2020 the World Economic Forum ranked climate change as the biggest risk to economy and society.
Adaptation and mitigation can both reduce climate-related risks, and they can work together.

entries.text: In 2020 the World Economic Forum ranked climate change as the biggest risk to the economy and society. Climate risk is the chance that the impacts of climate change will harm societies or ecosystems. It comes in two broad kinds. Physical risks are direct blows, such as extreme weather. Transition risks are the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society. Risk can also come from the measures people take in response, not only from the changes themselves. Climate risk is harder to assess than ordinary hazard risk. The climate no longer stays within a stable range of extremes, so the past is a weaker guide. Scientists therefore lean on pictures of possible futures, described in {{ref:nature-clim-252}}, when they analyze it. They also group risks by sector: agriculture, water, cities, ecosystems, health and livelihoods. Two kinds of response can lower these risks. Adaptation adjusts to the changes and mitigation slows them, and the two can work together. Like every question of {{ref:nature-econ-772}}, climate risk deals in chances rather than certainties.

entries.title: The social cost of carbon: pricing one more ton

definition.text: An estimate, usually in dollars, of the economic damage caused by emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: By putting climate effects into money terms, it lets policymakers weigh actions that raise or cut greenhouse gas emissions.
It is widely used in regulatory impact analyses, cost-benefit assessments and climate policy.
Its roots lie in Arthur Pigou's 1912 proposal to tax activities that cause negative externalities such as pollution.
Estimates are very sensitive to a few assumptions, above all the discount rate, the damage function and climate sensitivity.
US values have swung from $6 per ton under Trump (7% discount rate) to over $51 per ton under Biden (3% rate).
The SCC is distinct from carbon pricing tools such as taxes or cap-and-trade, though it can inform them.
Some scholars argue its one-extra-ton logic is mismatched to the climate crisis, and that carbon budgets or caps may fit better.

entries.contested_note: Economists, scientists and ethicists criticize the SCC for its sensitivity to assumptions, its ethics and its political volatility.
distinct_from: Calculating the social cost of carbon
Tipping points in the social cost of carbon
entries.text: What is the damage from one more ton of carbon dioxide worth? The social cost of carbon (SCC) answers in money, usually dollars. Putting climate effects into money terms lets policymakers weigh actions that raise or cut greenhouse gas emissions. The idea has old roots. Arthur Pigou proposed in 1912 to tax activities that cause negative externalities, harms that fall on people outside a deal, such as pollution. Today the SCC is widely used in regulatory impact analyses, cost-benefit assessments and climate policy. It is not itself a carbon price. Taxes and cap-and-trade schemes are separate tools, though the SCC can inform them. Its weakness is sensitivity. A few assumptions drive the answer, above all the discount rate, the damage function and climate sensitivity. The discount rate, explained in {{ref:nature-econ-745}}, sets how much future harm counts today. In the United States, values have swung from $6 per ton under Trump, using a 7% rate, to over $51 under Biden, using 3%. Economists, scientists and ethicists criticize the SCC for that volatility, for its ethics and for its dependence on assumptions. Some scholars argue that its one-extra-ton logic fits the climate crisis poorly, and that limits on total emissions may serve better.

entries.title: Carbon accounting: keeping the books on emissions

definition.text: A set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits.

facts.text: Organizations use it to set an emissions baseline, set reduction targets and track progress.
It works at scales from companies and cities to national greenhouse gas inventories.
Carbon credit markets depend on accurate measurement of emissions and reductions.
Standards such as the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and ISO 14064 group emissions into Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased energy) and Scope 3 (value chain).
Scope 3 is often the largest source of corporate emissions and the hardest to report accurately.
There is some evidence that programs requiring GHG accounting help to lower emissions.
It helps investors understand the climate risks of companies they invest in.

entries.text: No one can cut what they cannot count. Carbon accounting is a set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits. Organizations use it to set a baseline, choose reduction targets and track progress. It works at every scale, from companies and cities up to national greenhouse gas inventories. Standards such as {{ref:nature-gov-109}} and ISO 14064 sort emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 covers direct emissions, Scope 2 purchased energy, and Scope 3 the wider value chain. Scope 3 is often the largest share of a company's emissions and the hardest to report accurately. Accurate counts matter beyond the firm. Carbon credit markets depend on them, and investors use them to judge a company's climate risks. There is some evidence that programs requiring this accounting help lower emissions.

entries.title: The Stern Review: the greatest market failure

definition.text: A 700-page review of the economics of climate change released for the UK government in October 2006 by economist Nicholas Stern.

facts.text: It called climate change the greatest and widest-ranging market failure ever seen.
Its main conclusion is that the benefits of strong, early action far outweigh the costs of not acting.
Without action, it estimated losses equal to at least 5% of global GDP each year, possibly 20% or more counting wider risks.
It proposed investing 1% of global GDP a year; in 2008 Stern raised this to 2% because climate change was faster than expected.
Its near-zero pure rate of time preference, which Stern held to be the only ethical choice, was the most debated point.
Economists were split: some called it deeply flawed while others, including Kenneth Arrow, judged its main conclusion justified.
In 2008 Stern said the Review had underestimated the risks and damages of warming.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree sharply over the Review's discount rate, damage estimates and mitigation costs.
entries.text: On 30 October 2006, the economist Stern, profiled in {{ref:nature-hist-045}}, released a 700-page review of the economics of climate change for the UK government. It called climate change the greatest and widest-ranging market failure ever seen. Its main conclusion was that the benefits of strong, early action far outweigh the costs of not acting. Without action, it estimated losses of at least 5% of global GDP each year, possibly 20% or more counting wider risks. It proposed investing 1% of global GDP a year. In 2008 Stern raised that to 2%, saying the Review had underestimated the risks and that warming was faster than expected. The most debated point was its near-zero pure rate of time preference, which counts future welfare almost as much as today's. Stern held it to be the only ethical choice. Some economists called the Review deeply flawed, while others, including Kenneth Arrow, judged its main conclusion justified. The disputes over its discount rate, damages and costs continue.

entries.title: Climate scenarios: plausible stories about the future

definition.text: A plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on a set of assumptions about the main forces driving climate change.

facts.text: Scenarios are used to explore how well mitigation and adaptation will work over the long term.
Pathways are related but more concrete: a roadmap of actions needed to make a scenario come true.
Three key inputs are population, economic activity and new technology.
A baseline scenario is the reference against which an alternative, such as a mitigation scenario, is compared.
Economic growth has been found compatible with both rising and falling emissions, depending on efficiency, energy sources and the shift to services.
Countries use scenarios when drawing up adaptation plans and nationally determined contributions.

entries.text: Nobody can forecast the far future, but analysts can sketch the possibilities. A climate change scenario is a plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on assumptions about the main forces driving climate change. Three key inputs are population, economic activity and new technology. Scenarios help test how well mitigation and adaptation will work over the long term. A baseline scenario is the reference case, against which an alternative such as a mitigation scenario is compared. Pathways are related but more concrete: a roadmap of the actions needed to make a scenario come true. One finding cuts against intuition. Economic growth has proved compatible with both rising and falling emissions, depending on efficiency, energy sources and the shift toward services. Countries use scenarios when drawing up adaptation plans and the climate pledges each country makes.

entries.title: Integrated assessment models: the economy and the sky in one framework

definition.text: A kind of scientific modelling that links the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in one framework.

facts.text: Its goal is to inform policy-making, usually on climate change.
All climate IAMs include economic processes and the processes that produce greenhouse gases.
They do not predict the future; they estimate what possible scenarios look like.
One split is between process-based models, which map detailed pathways, and aggregate models, which total the costs of climate change and mitigation.
Cost-benefit IAMs such as DICE, PAGE and FUND are the main tools for calculating the social cost of carbon.
Critics say they create an illusory sense of precision and handle justice poorly.
They have been criticized for undervaluing wind and solar power while overvaluing bioenergy and carbon capture.

entries.contested_note: IAMs have been severely criticized for their assumptions, false precision and treatment of uncertainty and justice.
entries.text: Climate policy needs a tool that links factories to the atmosphere. Integrated assessment modelling tries to provide one, joining the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in a single framework. Its goal is to inform policy-making, usually on climate change. Every climate integrated assessment model (IAM) includes economic processes and the processes that produce greenhouse gases. These models do not predict the future. Instead they estimate what possible scenarios look like. They come in two broad families. Process-based models map detailed pathways. Aggregate models add up the total costs of climate change and of mitigation. Cost-benefit IAMs such as DICE, PAGE and FUND are the main tools for estimating the social cost of carbon. The models have been severely criticized. Critics say they create an illusory sense of precision and handle justice poorly. They have also been accused of undervaluing wind and solar power while overvaluing bioenergy and carbon capture. Because the models exist to inform policy, such biases matter. Their treatment of uncertainty remains disputed as well.

entries.title: Five possible worlds: the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways

definition.text: Scenarios of how global society and economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.

facts.text: They pair storylines of alternative socio-economic development with data on population, urbanization and GDP per person.
They are used with integrated assessment models to derive emissions scenarios under different climate policies.
The five are SSP1 Sustainability, SSP2 Middle of the road, SSP3 Regional rivalry, SSP4 Inequality and SSP5 Fossil-fueled development.
IPCC scenario names combine the SSP with forcing in 2100, such as SSP2-4.5.
Projected warming for 2081–2100 ranges from 1.4 °C under SSP1-1.9 to 4.4 °C under SSP5-8.5.
A 2025 assessment put median warming under current policies at about 2.7 °C by 2100, closest to SSP2-4.5.

entries.text: Will the world of 2100 be cooperative or divided, green or fossil-fueled? The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) offer five answers. They are scenarios of how global society and the economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. Each pairs a storyline of socio-economic development with data on population, urbanization and GDP per person. The five are SSP1 Sustainability, SSP2 Middle of the road, SSP3 Regional rivalry, SSP4 Inequality and SSP5 Fossil-fueled development. On their own they describe societies, not emissions. Run through integrated assessment models, they yield emissions scenarios under different climate policies. IPCC scenario names combine the pathway with the forcing, the extra warming push on the planet, in 2100. SSP2-4.5 is one example. The spread of outcomes is wide. Projected warming for 2081–2100 runs from 1.4 °C under SSP1-1.9 to 4.4 °C under SSP5-8.5. A 2025 assessment put median warming under current policies at about 2.7 °C by 2100. That is closest to SSP2-4.5, the middle of the road.
