entries.title: Marginal abatement cost: the price of the next cut

definition.text: The cost of reducing pollution by one more unit.

facts.text: Marginal cost is the cost of one additional unit, so this measures the cost of the next unit of pollution cut.
It can be negative when the low-carbon option is cheaper than business as usual, but it often rises steeply as more pollution is cut.
A marginal abatement cost curve ranks reductions by their marginal cost.
Policymakers use the curves to see how much abatement is possible at what cost; carbon traders use them to model carbon prices.
Studies worldwide find that making buildings more energy efficient and replacing fossil power with renewables are usually the cheapest cuts.
The curves are criticized for poor transparency and weak treatment of uncertainty, timing, sector interactions and side benefits.

entries.contested_note: The way marginal abatement cost curves are built and used to choose measures has been criticized.
entries.text: Cutting the first ton of pollution can be cheap, and cutting the last far more expensive. The marginal abatement cost is the cost of reducing pollution by one more unit. It applies the idea of marginal cost, the cost of one additional unit, to the next unit of pollution removed. Sometimes it is negative, when the low-carbon option is cheaper than business as usual. But it often rises steeply as more pollution is cut. A marginal abatement cost curve ranks the possible reductions by their cost. Policymakers use these curves to see how much abatement is possible at what cost, and carbon traders use them to model carbon prices. Studies worldwide find that more efficient buildings and renewables replacing fossil power are usually the cheapest cuts. The curves are contested. Critics fault their poor transparency and weak handling of uncertainty, timing, links between sectors and side benefits.

entries.title: Cumulative emissions: the long memory of carbon
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions#Cumulative and historical emissions

definition.text: Emissions added up over long periods, which indicate who is responsible for the build-up of greenhouse gases in the air.

facts.text: CO2 stays in the atmosphere for at least 150 and up to 1000 years, while methane disappears within about a decade.
Between 1890 and 2007 the US caused 28% of energy-related CO2 emissions, the EU 23% and China 9%.
Over that period developed countries caused 67.8% of total CO2 emissions.
The countries with the highest historical emissions are not always today's largest emitters.

entries.text: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for at least 150 and up to 1000 years, while methane disappears within about a decade. So responsibility for warming builds up over time. Cumulative emissions add up emissions over long periods to show who caused the build-up. Between 1890 and 2007 the United States caused 28% of energy-related CO2 emissions, the EU 23% and China 9%. Developed countries together caused 67.8%. Today's largest emitters are not always those with the highest historical emissions.

entries.title: Where emissions come from, sector by sector

definition.text: The division of global greenhouse gas emissions among the sectors of the economy that cause them.

facts.text: About two-thirds of emissions come from burning fuels for energy; the rest come from other processes.
Counted where they are produced, electricity generators make about 25% of global emissions.
Of non-energy emissions, 12% of the total comes from agriculture, 7% from land use change and forestry, 6% from industrial processes and 3% from waste.
Just 5% of the world's power plants produce almost three-quarters of electricity-sector carbon emissions.

entries.text: About two-thirds of the world's greenhouse gas emissions come from burning fuels for energy. Dividing emissions among the economic sectors that cause them shows the rest of the picture. Counted where they are produced, electricity generators make about 25% of global emissions. Among non-energy sources, agriculture adds 12% of the total, land use change and forestry 7%, industrial processes 6% and waste 3%. Power is strikingly concentrated: just 5% of the world's power plants produce almost three-quarters of the sector's carbon emissions.

entries.title: Emissions inequality: the rich pollute more
entries.article: Greenhouse gas emissions#By socio-economic class and age

definition.text: The large gap in greenhouse gas emissions between rich and poor people, driven by a strong link between income and per capita emissions.

facts.text: The richest 1% caused twice as much carbon emissions as the poorest 50% over 1990–2015.
The wealthiest 5% were responsible for 37% of the absolute rise in global emissions.
Annual per capita emissions in industrialized countries are typically up to ten times those in developing countries.

entries.text: Between 1990 and 2015, the richest 1% of people caused twice as much carbon emissions as the poorest 50%. That gap is emissions inequality, driven by a strong link between income and emissions per person. The wealthiest 5% were responsible for 37% of the absolute rise in global emissions. Between countries the pattern repeats. Yearly emissions per person in industrialized countries are typically up to ten times those in developing countries.

entries.title: What adapting to climate change will cost
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Costs of adaptation

definition.text: The costs of planning, preparing for, enabling and carrying out adaptation to climate change.

facts.text: Adaptation benefits can be measured as the damages it avoids.
Every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion.
More resilient infrastructure in developing countries would yield an average of $4 of benefit for each $1 invested.
A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion a year up to 2030.
Another 2023 study, based on national plans from 85 countries, put developing countries' annual adaptation needs at US$387 billion up to 2030.
Both cost and needs estimates are highly uncertain.

entries.title: The bill for cutting emissions
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Costs of mitigation

definition.text: The economic cost of actions that cut greenhouse gas emissions or enlarge the carbon sinks that absorb them.

facts.text: Economists estimate the cost of mitigation at between 1% and 2% of GDP.
A 2024 study found keeping warming below 2 °C may cost about 1% of world GDP a year but could prevent losses of 10–20% of GDP by mid-century.
Estimates depend on the baseline scenario, the way costs are modelled and assumptions about future policy.
Early, well-planned action keeps costs down, while delayed global cooperation raises them.
Costs are higher in carbon-intensive, fossil-fuel-exporting and poorer regions when all regions face one carbon value.
Policymakers can compare the marginal abatement costs of different measures, which vary by country, sector and time.
Models assuming perfect markets and policy give low costs; relaxing those assumptions raises estimates, while faster technological learning lowers them.
Economists estimate mitigation costs at between 1% and 2% of GDP, far less than the IMF's estimate of over $5 trillion a year in fossil fuel subsidies.

entries.title: Weighing climate costs and benefits in dollars
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Cost–benefit analysis

definition.text: Applying standard cost-benefit analysis to climate change by turning the good and bad effects of an action into money values.

facts.text: Most climate cost-benefit analyses are done with aggregate integrated assessment models designed for the purpose.
Costs and benefits are valued by willingness to pay or willingness to accept, then discounted to present values.
The usual test for accepting a policy is the Kaldor–Hicks compensation principle: winners could compensate losers and still gain.
Future generations who gain from mitigation cannot compensate the present generation that pays for it.
Valuing impacts on ecosystems and human health is hard, which makes climate cost-benefit analysis controversial.
It may be unsuitable for judging mitigation as a whole, but is still useful for comparing a 1.5 °C target with 2 °C.

entries.contested_note: Sources call the valuation of climate impacts in cost-benefit analysis controversial.
distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change
entries.text: Can the welfare of people a century from now be weighed against today's bills? Cost-benefit analysis of climate change tries, turning an action's good and bad effects into money values. Most such analyses run on aggregate integrated assessment models built for the purpose. Costs and benefits are valued by willingness to pay or willingness to accept, then discounted to present values. A policy usually passes the Kaldor–Hicks test: the winners could compensate the losers and still come out ahead. Climate strains this logic. Future generations who gain from mitigation cannot compensate the present generation that pays for it. Valuing impacts on ecosystems and human health is also hard, which makes the method controversial. It may be unsuitable for judging mitigation as a whole. It is still useful for comparing a 1.5 °C target with 2 °C.
entries.text_plain: Can the welfare of people a century from now be weighed against today's bills? Cost-benefit analysis of climate change tries, turning an action's good and bad effects into money values. Most such analyses run on aggregate integrated assessment models built for the purpose. Costs and benefits are valued by willingness to pay or willingness to accept, then discounted to present values. A policy usually passes the Kaldor–Hicks test: the winners could compensate the losers and still come out ahead. Climate strains this logic. Future generations who gain from mitigation cannot compensate the present generation that pays for it. Valuing impacts on ecosystems and human health is also hard, which makes the method controversial. It may be unsuitable for judging mitigation as a whole. It is still useful for comparing a 1.5 °C target with 2 °C.

entries.title: How much a warmer world costs the global economy
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#At the global level

definition.text: The total predicted impacts of climate change across all market sectors, plus non-market impacts on ecosystems and health.

facts.text: Estimates rise non-linearly as global average temperature rises.
The 2022 IPCC report found that with about 4 °C of warming and little adaptation, annual global GDP might be 10–23% lower by 2100.
With low warming and more adaptation, the same assessment found GDP reductions of 1–8%.
Total damages are estimated to be 90% less if warming is held to 1.5 °C rather than 3.66 °C.
Losses from extreme weather, climate and water events rose sevenfold from the 1970s to the 2010s.
One study put losses attributable to climate change at an average US$143 billion a year over 2000–2019.
Global estimates handle tipping points poorly and leave out well-being and distributional effects.
Climate impacts add to inflation through higher insurance premiums, energy costs and food prices.

entries.title: How much carbon stays in the air, and for how long

definition.text: Measures of how much of an emitted greenhouse gas stays in the air and for how long, set by the balance between its sources and sinks.

facts.text: The annual airborne fraction of CO2 has been stable at 0.45 for six decades, so 0.55 is taken up by sinks within the first year.
In high-emission scenarios, carbon sinks become less effective, raising the airborne fraction.
A gas's atmospheric lifetime is the time needed to restore equilibrium after a sudden change in its concentration.

entries.text: For six decades, the share of each year's carbon dioxide emissions that stays in the air has held steady at 0.45. That airborne fraction means 0.55 is taken up by carbon sinks within the first year. A gas's atmospheric lifetime is the time needed to restore equilibrium after a sudden change in its concentration. Both measures are set by the balance between a gas's sources and sinks. The balance can shift. In high-emission scenarios, sinks become less effective, so the airborne fraction rises.

entries.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three roots of climate risk

definition.text: The IPCC framework in which climate risk arises from the interaction of three factors: hazards, vulnerability and exposure.

facts.text: Vulnerability measures how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change, formally their propensity to be adversely affected.
Each of the three factors may be uncertain in size and likelihood.
Adaptation can lower climate risk by acting on all three interacting factors.
Global disaster losses have grown mainly because more people and wealth are exposed, though human-caused climate change also plays a part.

entries.text: Global disaster losses have grown mainly because more people and wealth are exposed, though human-caused climate change also plays a part. The IPCC captures this in a framework where climate risk arises from three interacting factors. A hazard is the climate event itself. Exposure is who and what lies in its path. The third factor, described in {{ref:nature-clim-025}}, measures how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed, formally their propensity to be adversely affected. Each factor may be uncertain in both size and likelihood. Because risk comes from their interaction, adaptation can lower it by acting on all three.

entries.title: DICE: Nordhaus's model of climate and the economy

definition.text: William Nordhaus's integrated assessment model that combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change.

facts.text: Nordhaus first proposed it in a 1992 Cowles Foundation discussion paper; a regional variant, RICE, followed in 1996.
It is one of three main models the US Environmental Protection Agency uses to estimate the social cost of carbon.
Its central assumption is that externalities create costs missing from prices, which government must add.
It uses the market return on capital, around 4% on average, as its discount rate.
In 2020, a rerun with updated science and discount rates found the optimal goal was below 2.0 °C of warming, not the 3.5 °C Nordhaus first found.
A 2020 paper with an updated damage function found warming of around 2 °C would be optimal, depending on climate sensitivity.
It treats innovation as external; a variant with induced technical change favours strong early investment in mitigation.
Critics have attacked its sensitivity to assumptions and its choice of discount rate.

entries.contested_note: The model's damage function and discount rate are disputed by critics, and a 2020 rerun changed its optimal warming goal.

verification.title: Climate economics support for the UN climate targets
verification.evidence: This analysis shows that the 2 °C target is economically optimal in a version of the DICE model that includes updated climate science, climate damage estimates and evidence on social discount rates.

entries.title: The Kaya identity: four levers behind every ton of CO2

definition.text: An equation that breaks total CO2 emissions into four factors multiplied together: population, GDP per person, energy per unit of GDP, and emissions per unit of energy.

facts.text: It was developed by the Japanese energy economist Yoichi Kaya.
It is a form of the I = PAT equation of Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren for environmental impact.
The factors would cancel out in theory, but it lets emissions be estimated from readily available data.
It shows the levers for cutting emissions, notably energy intensity of GDP and emissions per unit of energy.
It plays a core role in building future emissions scenarios in the IPCC Special Report on Emissions Scenarios.
Energy intensity of GDP has generally declined worldwide, through efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.

entries.text: Total carbon dioxide emissions can be written as four numbers multiplied together. entries.title: Carbon lock-in: why fossil systems are hard to leave

definition.text: The self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems that holds back efforts to bring in alternative energy technologies.

facts.text: Gregory Unruh coined the term in a 1999 doctoral thesis.
It arises as technology networks and the institutions and habits that benefit from them grow together, fed by increasing returns to scale.
It explains why cost-effective low-carbon technologies spread slowly, a puzzle called the climate policy paradox.
Car-based transport and fossil-fuel power systems are examples.
A 2007 report sorted lock-in barriers into cost-effectiveness, financial/legal and intellectual property barriers.
Building new natural gas infrastructure risks lock-in and stranded assets.

entries.text: Low-carbon technologies that are already cost-effective often spread slowly, a puzzle called the climate policy paradox. Carbon lock-in helps explain it. Gregory Unruh coined the term in a 1999 doctoral thesis for the self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems. Technology networks grow together with the institutions and habits that benefit from them, fed by increasing returns to scale. The result is a form of the pattern described in {{ref:nature-pol-038}}. Car-based transport and fossil-fuel power systems are examples. A 2007 report sorted the barriers into three kinds: cost-effectiveness, financial and legal, and intellectual property. The risk is current. Building new natural gas infrastructure threatens fresh lock-in and investments that lose their value early, the subject of {{ref:nature-clim-175}}.

entries.title: The side effects of cutting emissions
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Ancillary impacts

definition.text: The side effects of mitigation policies, beyond their effect on the climate, which can raise or lower estimated costs.

facts.text: Fewer deaths and less illness are potentially a major side benefit of mitigation.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change
entries.text: Cutting emissions can also save lives. Fewer deaths and less illness are potentially a major side benefit of mitigation. Economists call such effects, beyond any effect on the climate, ancillary benefits. Some side effects help and some hurt, so they can either lower or raise the estimated costs of mitigation.

entries.title: Cost-effectiveness: the cheapest route to a set goal
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Cost-effectiveness analysis

definition.text: A method that ranks policy options by their cost per unit of a set goal, used when benefits are hard to put in money terms.

facts.text: For mitigation the goal is usually tonnes of greenhouse gas cut, giving a cost such as dollars per tonne of CO2.
Adaptation has no common goal, so the measure might be, for example, hectares of land at risk from sea level rise.
It can find the cheapest way to meet a fixed target, such as a sector's emissions cut.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

Adaptation has no common goal, so the measure might be hectares of land at risk from rising seas. The method can find the cheapest way to meet a fixed target, such as a sector's emissions cut.

entries.title: Who should pay for climate change?
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Efficiency and equity

definition.text: The debate over who should bear the costs of adaptation and mitigation, on which there is no consensus.

facts.text: One approach charges those who benefit most from the public good of a stable climate.
On a utilitarian basis, an argument can be made for richer countries carrying most of the mitigation burden.
Industrialized countries contributed over two-thirds of the human-made greenhouse gas stock, a stock called an environmental debt.
A 2019 study found climate change had already widened global economic inequality, with poor hot countries growing less.

entries.contested_note: Sources say no consensus exists on who should bear the burden of climate costs, and equity issues cannot be resolved by economics alone.

entries.title: Deciding now, revising later
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Iterative risk management

definition.text: Handling climate uncertainty by making a series of decisions that are revised as better information arrives.

facts.text: It is closely related to iterative risk management.
Stringent near-term cuts keep open the option of a low stabilization target, such as 450 ppm CO2, which weaker cuts may close.
It weighs the irreversibility of climate damages against the irreversibility of investments to cut emissions.

entries.title: Dividing up the work of cutting emissions
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Sharing of mitigation costs

definition.text: The competing proposals for deciding which countries should bear how much of the job of cutting emissions.

facts.text: Equal per capita entitlements, derived from egalitarianism, are the most widely cited way to share abatement costs.
The historical responsibility view bases emission rights on past emissions; two-thirds of today's atmospheric greenhouse gas stock comes from developed countries.
Other proposals rest on basic needs, ability to pay, willingness to pay, or the status quo of current emissions.
Allocating permits by current emissions leaves developing countries worse off, while per capita convergence leaves them better off.

entries.contested_note: No consensus exists on who should bear the costs of mitigation and adaptation.

Allocating permits by current emissions leaves developing countries worse off, while per-person convergence leaves them better off. No consensus exists.

entries.title: Are climate damage estimates far too low?
entries.article: Economic analysis of climate change#Underestimation of economic impacts

definition.text: The argument that economic estimates of climate damages are too low because models leave out tipping points, tail risks and knock-on effects.

facts.text: Tipping points are thresholds beyond which large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system follow.
A 2018 study found global economic impact is underestimated by a factor of two to eight when tipping points are left out.
Many models leave out some climate risks and do not fully trace how damage in one industry or region spreads to others.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree over whether standard estimates such as the Stern Review's capture the full damages.

entries.title: How climate change threatens ecosystems

definition.text: The ways climate change threatens ecosystems and the services they provide.

facts.text: The main risks are biodiversity loss, changes in ecosystem structure, more tree deaths, more wildfire and losses of ecosystem carbon.
Wildfires and pest outbreaks driven by climate change caused much of the recent tree mortality in North America.
Losing species can raise the risks to ecosystem health.

The main threats are biodiversity loss, changes in ecosystem structure, more tree deaths, more wildfire and losses of ecosystem carbon. The risks compound, because losing species can raise the risks to ecosystem health.

entries.title: The moral questions climate change forces

definition.text: The study of the moral questions that climate change raises.

facts.text: Developed countries have gained most from burning fossil fuels, while most climate impacts will fall on the developing world.
Climate change plays out over many generations, setting today's economic and political interests against those of future people.
Economics can predict how policies affect the economy but cannot say which path to choose; that depends on society's values.
Half the world's carbon is emitted by its richest 500 million people, so emissions rise with income wherever one lives.
Poorer people are more exposed to climate effects because they have fewer means to adapt.
Prioritarianism can justify a high discount rate, while utilitarianism favours a low or zero rate.
A rights-based view holds that climate change threatens rights to life, health, food, water, security and shelter.

Disagreement runs deep, over whether and how far society should act, and over the ethical basis for discounting the future.

entries.title: The carbon bubble: fossil fuel wealth that cannot be burned

definition.text: A suspected overvaluation of fossil fuel companies, because reserves that cannot be burned within carbon budgets are still counted as valuable.

facts.text: A carbon budget is the upper limit on CO2 emissions that keeps warming below a given level.
In 2011 the Carbon Tracker Initiative found the world could burn only 20% of its fossil fuel reserves to stay below 2 °C.
The rest would become stranded assets, though investors treated them as low-risk.
A 2021 analysis found 90% of coal and 60% of oil and gas reserves could not be extracted for even a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C.
The term was coined by the Carbon Tracker Initiative in reports from 2011 and 2013.
Quarterly results and accounting standards push investors to ignore these long-term risks.
An orderly transition away from fossil fuels could prevent a disruptive bursting of the bubble.

entries.title: Five steps to a social cost of carbon

definition.text: The chain of steps used to estimate the social cost of carbon, from projecting emissions to discounting future damages.

facts.text: The steps are: project future emissions, model the climate response, assess impacts, put a money value on damages, and discount them.
A low discount rate of 1–2% values future welfare nearly equal to today's; a high rate of 4–5% discounts future damages heavily.
Recent literature supports declining discount rates that start higher and fall over time.
Some versions add a catastrophic risk premium to account for possible disasters and society's dislike of risk.

entries.title: DICE, FUND and PAGE: three models, three answers
entries.article: Social cost of carbon#Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs)

definition.text: The three main integrated assessment models that have historically underpinned social cost of carbon estimates.

facts.text: DICE finds a single global optimal path and assumes damages grow with the square of temperature, without tipping points.
FUND models impacts by region and sector and allows some regions to gain from warming.
PAGE is probabilistic, using Monte Carlo simulations of thousands of futures and modelling catastrophic risks.
Their different methods can give dramatically different values; the Obama-era SCC averaged runs of all three.

PAGE is probabilistic, using Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials, of thousands of futures, catastrophes included. Their methods can give dramatically different values, so the Obama-era estimate averaged runs of all three.

entries.title: Adding tipping points to the social cost of carbon

definition.text: Extensions to climate-economy models that add abrupt, irreversible damages when warming crosses critical thresholds.

facts.text: Standard models assume smooth, continuous damages, which may underestimate risk.
Modelling studies suggest that including tipping points can double the social cost of carbon.
One method adds a probability of a tipping event times its expected catastrophic damages.

entries.title: Mitigation scenarios: futures where warming is curbed

definition.text: A possible future in which global warming is reduced by deliberate actions, such as a broad switch away from fossil fuels.

facts.text: A typical one picks a long-range target, such as a CO2 concentration, then fits actions to it, for example a cap on emissions.
They let analysts test the effect of different carbon prices on an economy.
A 550 ppm target, roughly a doubling of pre-industrial CO2, implies about three degrees of warming by conventional estimates.
Reaching a 450 ppm target depends heavily on bioenergy with carbon capture, according to the IEA and OECD.

entries.title: Representative Concentration Pathways: futures named by forcing

definition.text: IPCC scenarios that project future greenhouse gas concentrations, not emissions.

facts.text: The original four, RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP6 and RCP8.5, are named for their radiative forcing in 2100 in W/m2.

entries.title: Process-based models: mapping the road sector by sector

entries.title: Fat tails: when disaster is likelier than it looks

definition.text: A probability distribution in which extreme outcomes are much more likely than in a normal or exponential distribution.

facts.text: The most extreme case is a distribution whose tail decays like a power law.
Fitting a normal distribution to fat-tailed data understates the true risk.
Market crashes such as those of 1929, 1987 and 2008 are examples of events that are not mathematically well-behaved.
Martin Weitzman argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails, which standard climate economics handles poorly.

Fitting a normal distribution to fat-tailed data understates the true risk. Weitzman, profiled in {{ref:nature-hist-081}}, argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails, which standard climate economics handles poorly.

entries.title: Fast and slow: two measures of climate sensitivity

definition.text: The two main measures of climate sensitivity: the short-term transient climate response and the long-term equilibrium climate sensitivity.

facts.text: The transient climate response is the warming around the time CO2 doubles, in a simulation where CO2 rises 1% a year.
Equilibrium sensitivity is the long-term rise once feedbacks have played out, which can take centuries or millennia.
Equilibrium sensitivity is higher because the oceans buffer warming in the short term.

Because of the ocean buffer, the equilibrium figure is the higher of the two.

entries.title: Duties to people not yet born

definition.text: The duty of people alive now to use resources sustainably and protect the interests of future generations from climate change.

facts.text: Emissions today affect future generations more than the people who cause them.
Pushing impacts onto future people weakens the felt link between cause and effect and can sap the will to act.
Democracies work on election cycles of a few years, while climate change unfolds over hundreds to thousands of years.

entries.title: Deep uncertainty: when even the odds are unknown

definition.text: Uncertainty so great that decision-makers do not know or agree on how actions lead to outcomes or on the probabilities of key inputs.

facts.text: Robust decision-making describes it with ranges or sets of plausible probability distributions rather than one best estimate.
Decision-making under deep uncertainty may use many climate scenarios to test actions across different possible futures.
The DICE model has been criticized for ignoring deep uncertainty, which tends to lower its social cost of carbon.

entries.text: Ordinary risk comes with known odds. Deep uncertainty does not: decision-makers do not know, or cannot agree on, how actions lead to outcomes or the probabilities of key inputs. One response, {{ref:nature-clim-266}}, describes it with ranges or sets of plausible probability distributions rather than one best estimate. Decision-making under deep uncertainty may also test actions across many climate scenarios. The DICE model has been criticized for ignoring deep uncertainty, which tends to lower its social cost of carbon.

entries.title: Robust decision-making: plans that survive being wrong

definition.text: An iterative framework for finding strategies that hold up across many possible futures, exposing their weak points and the trade-offs among them.

facts.text: It is meant for deep uncertainty, where people do not know or agree on how actions lead to outcomes or on the probabilities involved.
It judges policies by robustness rather than optimality, often accepting slightly worse best-case performance for less sensitivity to wrong assumptions.
Instead of predict-then-act, it asks which uncertainties would make a strategy fail, using scenario discovery on large sets of simulations.
It was developed mainly by researchers at the RAND Corporation; an early 1996 study applied it to adaptive strategies for cutting emissions.

entries.text: Most planning predicts the future, then acts. Robust decision-making reverses the order. The process repeats, exposing weak points and trade-offs. Researchers at the RAND Corporation developed most of it, and an early 1996 study applied it to adaptive strategies for cutting emissions.

entries.title: FUND: Richard Tol's region-by-region model

definition.text: An integrated assessment model that estimates climate damages region by region and sector by sector, used for the social cost of carbon.

facts.text: It models impacts such as agriculture, health and sea level rise by region and includes some adaptation over time.
It allows negative damages, meaning some regions or sectors gain from warming.
Its assumptions about adaptation and warming benefits can understate damages.
It is Richard Tol's model; a reviewer of the Copenhagen Consensus said relying on it alone was not reasonable.

entries.title: The green paradox: when climate policy speeds extraction

definition.text: Hans-Werner Sinn's argument that climate policy expected to tighten over time pushes fossil fuel owners to extract faster, speeding up global warming.

facts.text: Policies that will get greener lower future fuel prices more than current ones, so owners extract more now and invest the proceeds in capital markets.
Countries that do not cut demand burn both the carbon freed by green countries (leakage) and the extra carbon extracted early.
Sinn argues climate policy must target the supply side, for example by taxing resource owners' capital gains or a global emissions trading cap.
Critics note that Sinn overlooks large government support to fossil fuels, put at US$160–200 billion a year in OECD and key emerging economies.

entries.contested_note: The source calls the book controversial, and its claims about renewable support are disputed.
entries.text: Could tougher climate policy make warming worse? Hans-Werner Sinn argues it can. Policies that will get greener lower future fuel prices more than current ones. So fossil fuel owners extract more now and invest the proceeds in capital markets. Countries that do not cut demand then burn both the carbon freed by greener countries and the extra carbon extracted early. Sinn wants policy aimed at supply, such as taxing owners' capital gains or a global emissions trading cap. His book is controversial. Critics note that he overlooks fossil fuel support of US$160–200 billion a year in OECD and key emerging economies.

entries.title: Efficiency: the first fuel

definition.text: Reducing the amount of energy needed to provide the same products and services.

facts.text: Insulating a building, for example, lets it stay comfortable while using less energy for heating and cooling.
Its two main motives are saving operating costs and cutting greenhouse gas emissions; it can also reduce dependence on imported energy.
Efficient technology usually carries an upfront capital cost, and the costs can be compared using life-cycle assessment.
Energy policy increasingly treats it as the 'first fuel': the IEA found efficiency measures over 1974–2010 avoided more energy use in member states than any single fuel supplied.
Better efficiency in buildings, industry and transport could cut the world's energy needs in 2050 by one third, and the IEA estimates it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris goals need.
Its extra benefits, such as cleaner air, better health and energy security, have sometimes been valued above the energy savings themselves.
California's efficiency standards from the mid-1970s kept its per-capita energy use about flat while US consumption doubled.
Policies to promote it include carbon taxes, efficiency standards for appliances, buildings and vehicles, and subsidies for efficient equipment.

entries.title: Energy economics: how societies supply and use power

definition.text: The study of how societies supply and use energy, and of the costs and value of energy services.

facts.text: Energy services are the end uses energy provides, such as lighting, heating and fuel, and the aim is to deliver them with the least energy input.
It is an applied branch of economics drawing on engineering, geology, political science and ecology, not a self-contained discipline.
Its topics include the elasticity of supply and demand in energy markets and the liberalisation and regulation of electricity markets.
Energy issues have been prominent in economics since the 1973 oil crisis, but W.S. Jevons worried about coal depletion as early as 1865.
Harold Hotelling's rule gave an early price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels.
Its theory has grown around three themes: the rebound effect, the energy efficiency gap and, more recently, green nudges.
Vaclav Smil argues every economic activity is at root a conversion of energy, with money only a rough proxy for valuing energy flows.

entries.text: In 1865 W.S. Jevons worried that Britain would run short of coal. Energy has been prominent in economics since the 1973 oil crisis, but the worry is old. Energy economics studies how societies supply and use energy, and the costs and value of energy services. Those services are the end uses energy provides, such as lighting, heating and fuel, and the aim is to deliver them with the least energy input. It is an applied branch of economics, drawing on engineering, geology, political science and ecology rather than standing alone. Its topics include how strongly supply and demand respond to price in energy markets, and the liberalization and regulation of electricity markets. Hotelling's rule gave an early price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels. Its theory has grown around three themes: the way efficiency saves less than expected, the energy efficiency gap and, more recently, gentle pushes toward greener choices. Vaclav Smil goes further. He argues that every economic activity is at root a conversion of energy, with money only a rough proxy for valuing energy flows.

entries.title: Energy security: when supply becomes a matter of state

definition.text: The link between a nation's security and the reliable availability of energy resources.

facts.text: Modern economies depend on affordable energy, and the uneven spread of supplies among countries creates serious vulnerabilities.
Threats include instability in producing countries, supply manipulation, and attacks on pipelines and grids.
The 1973 oil crisis and the rise of the OPEC cartel pushed countries such as Japan to diversify into gas, nuclear power, mass transit and conservation.
Imported natural gas creates sharper short-term risks than oil, as the Russia–Ukraine gas disputes of 2006 and 2009 showed.
Wind, solar and efficiency are spread across many countries, unlike fossil fuels, so deploying them and diversifying sources raises energy security.
Carefully phasing out fossil fuel subsidies would increase energy security, according to the International Institute for Sustainable Development.
Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine made energy security a stronger driver of the energy transition in Europe.

entries.title: The price of oil: one number the world watches

definition.text: The spot price of a barrel of benchmark crude oil, such as Brent or West Texas Intermediate, used as a reference by buyers and sellers.

facts.text: It is set by global supply and demand rather than any one country's output, though the OPEC cartel pushes prices up.
Prices were fairly steady from 1861 until the 1970s, when the 1973 and 1979 oil crises drove a significant rise.
Its main drivers have been supply, demand and storage shocks and shocks to global economic growth.
Oil peaked at US$147 in July 2008 and fell to US$34 by December 2008 as the financial crisis took hold.
The 2014–2016 drop of 70% after a supply glut was one of the three biggest declines since World War II.
High oil prices generally hurt global growth and raise the cost of many products, including food.
Production costs differ widely: in 2019 Middle Eastern oil broke even at about US$42 a barrel and oil sands at US$83.

entries.title: Energy intensity: how much energy each dollar takes

definition.text: The amount of energy an economy uses per unit of GDP or other economic output.

facts.text: It differs from energy efficiency: climate, economic structure such as services versus manufacturing, and trade all affect it.
Cold or hot climates raise it through heating and cooling needs, and higher living standards bring more energy-using goods.
Using 2003–2004 figures, the US used 8,553 BTU per dollar of GDP, Bangladesh about a quarter of that, and Russia more than double.
Its inverse, economic energy efficiency, counts GDP produced per unit of energy; the change in energy use needed to raise a country's GDP over time is its energy elasticity.
It is one of the four factors in the Kaya identity, alongside population, GDP per capita and carbon intensity of energy.
Global energy intensity has generally fallen over recent decades with better efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.
Official statistics count only commercially marketed energy, so firewood, charcoal and similar small sources are left out.

It is one of the four factors in the Kaya identity, and it has generally fallen worldwide with better efficiency, technology and structural shifts. Official statistics count only marketed energy, so firewood, charcoal and similar sources are left out.

entries.title: Rebound: why efficiency saves less than expected

definition.text: The tendency for efficiency gains to save less energy than expected because they make energy services cheaper, so people use more of them.

facts.text: Fuel-efficient cars make travel cheaper, so drivers may go farther and offset part of the savings.
Estimates range from roughly 5% to 40%, likely under 30% for households and nearer 10% for transport.
A 30% rebound means an efficiency gain delivers 70% of the energy savings engineering models predict.
Historical analysis shows efficiency gains were almost always outpaced by economic growth, so total resource use and pollution still rose.

entries.title: Demand response: bending use to fit supply

definition.text: Changes in how much electricity customers use, made to better match demand to the available supply.

facts.text: Instead of adjusting power plant output, it adjusts demand in real time, and can be seen as a technology-enabled rationing system for electricity.
Utilities signal customers through cheaper off-peak rates or smart meters that send price changes, and customers respond by delaying power-hungry tasks or paying more.
Most consumers pay a fixed average price, so their short-run use does not respond to the real cost of production.
It can be cheaper than building extra generating capacity to meet peaks and occasional demand spikes.
A study found a 1% shift in peak demand would save 3.9%, and a 5% cut in demand might have halved peak prices in California's 2000–2001 electricity crisis.
Controlling flexible loads helps smooth the swings in output from wind and solar, and heat pumps can serve as such a flexible resource.
There is an economic limit, because consumers lose the productive or convenience value of electricity they do not use.

entries.title: Energy poverty: life without modern energy

definition.text: Lack of access to modern energy services, such as electricity and clean cooking fuel, in the home.

facts.text: In 2024 an estimated 655 million people had no electricity and about two billion cooked with polluting fuels and technologies.
Its causes include missing infrastructure such as power plants, lines and pipelines, and prices that poorer households cannot afford.
It harms health, education and women's opportunities; household air pollution caused about 2.9 million deaths in 2021, by the WHO's estimate.
Women and children in homes using wood, charcoal or dung do most of the cooking and fuel collection, so they bear most of the health burden.
Ninety percent of children in Sub-Saharan Africa attend primary schools without electricity.
In the Global North it is usually called fuel poverty: households that cannot afford to heat, cool and power their homes because of high prices, low incomes and inefficient appliances.
There is no agreed standard for basic energy services and no single indicator accepted internationally, so measures range from yes-or-no access to composite indices.
Clean, efficient cook stoves running on LPG or electricity are a recommended low-cost way to cut its health harms.

entries.title: The experience curve: cheaper with every doubling

definition.text: The pattern in which the cost of making something falls by a steady share each time the total amount ever produced doubles.

facts.text: In 1936 engineer Theodore Paul Wright found that each doubling of total aircraft production cut the labour needed for a new aircraft by 20%, now called Wright's law.
Other industries show reductions from a couple of percent up to 30% per doubling, usually constant within each industry.
Bruce Henderson of the Boston Consulting Group coined the term 'experience curve' from cost studies in the 1960s.
Causes include workers' growing skill, standardisation and specialisation, new technology, fuller use of equipment and product redesign.
It implies firms gain by expanding early: more output brings learning, lower costs and prices, and larger market share.
Storage costs follow such curves: lithium-ion battery prices fall 19% with each doubling of capacity, while pumped hydro has barely fallen.
Critics note that experience effects are tangled with economies of scale and may be hard to separate.

Firms therefore gain by expanding early, winning lower costs and larger market share. entries.title: Capacity factor: how hard a power plant really works

definition.text: The ratio of the electricity a power plant actually produces over a period to what it would produce running at full rated power the whole time.

facts.text: It can be computed for any power plant or class of plants, and is used to compare different kinds of electricity generation.
It is usually calculated over a year to average out fluctuations, though monthly values show seasonal swings.
A plant needed only from 8 am to 8 pm, even at full power every day, would have a 50% capacity factor.
Nuclear plants sit at the high end, about 88.7% on average for US plants over 2006–2012; typical wind farms run between 25 and 45%.
For wind, solar and hydro, the main limit is whether the 'fuel' of wind, sunlight or water is available.
Photovoltaic plants are at the low end, from 29.1% at an Arizona plant to 12.0% at one in Bavaria, because output depends on daylight and latitude.
Peaking plants have low capacity factors, so their electricity is relatively expensive: few hours of output must cover their fixed costs.

entries.text: A plant that runs at full power from 8 am to 8 pm every day, and sits idle otherwise, has a 50% capacity factor. The measure compares the electricity a plant actually produces with what it would make running at full rated power the whole time. It is usually calculated over a year, to average out fluctuations, and it lets different kinds of generation be compared. Nuclear plants sit near the top, about 88.7% on average for US plants over 2006–2012. Typical wind farms run between 25 and 45%. Peaking plants run rarely, so their few hours of output must cover fixed costs, making their power expensive.

entries.title: Variable renewables: power that follows the weather

definition.text: Renewable power sources such as wind and solar whose output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be adjusted on demand.

facts.text: Their traits are unpredictability, variability and low operating costs, which make matching supply and demand harder for grid operators.
Small amounts barely affect the grid, but large amounts may require upgrading or redesigning grid infrastructure.
Wind and solar supplied 15% of world electricity in 2024 and together overtook hydropower for the first time.
Integration options include storage, demand response, overcapacity, interconnecting grids and linking power with heat, transport and industry.
Spreading wind farms over wide areas lowers overall variability, because distant turbines' outputs are imperfectly correlated.
Combined wind and solar could reach 70% to 90% of supply without aggregation, demand management or storage, and up to 94% with 12 hours of storage.
The size of the extra costs of variability is debated, but they are small at low shares and expected to rise with higher shares.

entries.contested_note: Sources call the magnitude of the economic costs of wind and solar variability debated, varying by location.

The extra costs are small at low shares and expected to rise as shares grow.

entries.title: Grid storage: saving electricity for later

definition.text: Technologies connected to the power grid that store electricity for later use.

facts.text: It balances supply and demand by storing surplus power from variable renewables such as solar and inflexible sources such as nuclear, then releasing it when needed.
Storage is one of the three main ways to replace the flexibility fossil fuels have given the grid.
As of 2023 pumped hydro was the largest form, at 181 GW, ahead of about 88 GW of batteries combined.
Lithium-ion batteries suit storage of under 8 hours; flow batteries and compressed air suit medium durations; hydrogen and heat suit seasonal storage.
Battery costs fell by 90% from 2010 to 2023.
Below 40% variable renewables only short storage under 4 hours is needed; at 80% medium-duration storage is needed, and above 90% long-duration storage.
It can also help restart the grid after a blackout.

entries.title: Levelized cost of electricity: comparing power plants fairly

definition.text: The average cost of electricity from a generator over its lifetime, expressed in today's money per unit of energy produced.

facts.text: It is the constant price per unit of energy that would give the project a net present value of zero.
It divides the discounted sum of investment, maintenance and fuel costs by the discounted sum of electricity produced over the plant's life.
It is used to compare generating technologies on a consistent basis for investment planning and energy policy.
It estimates the cost of production, not the price of electricity, which also reflects markups and price controls.
The discount rate is one of its most contested inputs: public comparisons tend to use about 3%, private banks 7–15%, and low rates favour nuclear and renewables with high upfront costs.
Since 2013 the LCOE of wind has been below that of all fossil fuels, and solar followed in 2015.
It ignores when power is produced, so wind and solar without storage may generate when electricity is worth little or even negative.
It often leaves out indirect costs such as the social cost of greenhouse gases and air pollution, as well as co-benefits.

entries.text: Since 2013, power from new wind has been cheaper over its lifetime than power from any fossil fuel, and solar followed in 2015. The yardstick is the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE): the average lifetime cost of a generator's electricity, in today's money per unit of energy. It divides the discounted sum of investment, maintenance and fuel costs by the discounted sum of electricity produced. Equivalently, it is the constant price that would give the project a net present value of zero. It measures production cost, not the price, which also reflects markups and price controls. The discount rate is hotly contested. Public comparisons tend to use about 3%, private banks 7–15%, and low rates favor nuclear and renewables with high upfront costs. LCOE ignores when power is produced, so wind and solar may generate when electricity is worth little. It often leaves out the social cost of greenhouse gases and air pollution, and co-benefits.

entries.title: The merit order: cheapest power first

definition.text: The ranking of power sources from cheapest to most expensive to run, which sets the order in which they are switched on to meet demand.

facts.text: Plants with the lowest short-run marginal costs are brought online first and the costliest last, which minimises the cost of producing electricity.
The marginal cost of the last generator needed to meet demand sets the system price for one more MWh.
In most power systems the wholesale price equals the marginal cost of the most expensive generator running, so prices often vary two- to fivefold over a day.
Plants sometimes run out of merit order because of transmission congestion or reliability needs.
Environmental dispatch adds the goal of minimising pollutant emissions to that of minimising fuel costs.
Policy-makers use marginal abatement cost curves in the same way, as merit order curves of emission-cutting options.

entries.text: Every moment, a grid must decide which plants to run. The merit order ranks power sources from cheapest to most expensive to run, and plants switch on in that order. Those with the lowest short-run marginal costs come online first, which minimizes the cost of producing electricity. The last generator needed to meet demand sets the system price for one more megawatt-hour (MWh). Because the wholesale price usually equals the costliest running plant's marginal cost, prices often vary two- to fivefold over a day. Plants sometimes run out of order because of transmission congestion or reliability needs. Environmental dispatch adds the goal of minimizing pollutant emissions to that of minimizing fuel costs. Marginal abatement cost curves work the same way, as merit order curves of emission-cutting options.

entries.title: Energy conservation: simply using less

definition.text: Actively using less energy, through changes in behaviour as well as through more efficient technology.

facts.text: Examples without any efficiency gain include heating a room less, driving less, air-drying clothes and using a computer's power-saving mode.
The line between conservation and efficiency can be fuzzy, but both matter environmentally and economically.
Energy conservation sits at the top of the sustainable energy hierarchy.
Burning fossil fuels for transport and electricity is less than 50% efficient, with much heat wasted.

entries.text: Heating a room less, driving less and air-drying clothes save energy without any gain in efficiency. entries.title: Energy resilience: bending without breaking

definition.text: The ability of an energy system to adjust to and withstand interruptions in supply.

facts.text: Some argue energy independence is unrealistic, and resilience is a more practical goal.
The 1982 book Brittle Power argued the real weakness is centralised, interdependent infrastructure, and recommended decentralised efficiency and renewables.
A diverse supply is less affected when any one source is disrupted.

entries.title: Strategic petroleum reserves: oil in the bank

definition.text: A government stockpile of oil held as a buffer against the economic and political shocks of an energy crisis.

facts.text: All 31 members of the International Energy Agency hold at least 90 days of their oil imports.
These countries also committed to emergency response plans for oil supply shocks.

entries.title: Operating reserve: the grid's spare capacity

definition.text: Spare generating capacity a grid keeps ready to follow changes in demand or replace generation that is suddenly lost.

facts.text: Capacity that can replace lost generation within about 30 seconds to 30 minutes is called spinning reserve.
Wind does not need 100% back-up, because reserves are calculated for the whole system rather than for each plant.
Thermal plants running as reserve or peakers are less efficient than when run as base load.

entries.text: A grid must cope when a plant suddenly fails. An operating reserve is spare generating capacity kept ready to follow changes in demand or replace lost generation. Capacity that can step in within about 30 seconds to 30 minutes is called spinning reserve. Wind does not need 100% back-up, because reserves are calculated for the whole system rather than each plant. Reserve has a cost: thermal plants running as reserve or peakers are less efficient than when run as base load.

entries.title: Sector coupling: linking power, heat and transport

definition.text: Linking the power system with transport, heating and gas so that demand and generation can be better matched.

facts.text: Electric vehicles are expected to become the largest source of storage capacity, charging when production is high and sometimes feeding power back to the grid.
The International Energy Agency says it is needed to handle the mismatch between seasonal demand and supply.
It may cost more than other flexibility options and suits grids with high shares of variable renewables.

entries.title: The 1970s oil crises
entries.article: Price of oil#Global oil prices: a chronology

definition.text: The 1973 and 1979 oil supply shocks that sharply raised world oil prices and reshaped energy policy.

facts.text: In the 1973 crisis Arab oil producers embargoed shipments to Western Europe and the United States over their support for Israel.
In 1979 the Iranian Revolution constrained supply and the oil price more than doubled.
Countries such as the US, Germany, Japan and Canada responded with national energy programmes focused on secure oil supply.
The crises gave rise to speculative trading and crude oil futures markets.

entries.text: In 1973 Arab oil producers embargoed shipments to Western Europe and the United States over their support for Israel. In 1979 the Iranian Revolution constrained supply and the oil price more than doubled. These two shocks sharply raised world oil prices and reshaped energy policy. The US, Germany, Japan and Canada responded with national energy programs focused on secure oil supply. The crises also gave rise to speculative trading and crude oil futures markets.

entries.title: Oil futures: betting on tomorrow's price
entries.article: Price of oil#Speculative trading and crude oil futures

definition.text: Contracts to buy or sell oil at a set future date, through which investors bet on oil prices and firms hedge against price swings.

facts.text: NYMEX launched crude oil futures in 1983 and the IPE in 1988, and world crude prices came to be published through these markets.
Futures helped reduce the economic hazards of swings in the spot price.
A 2008 US task force found the 2003–2008 price rise was due mainly to supply and demand, not speculation, given low price elasticity.
In the contango trade, companies buy cheap oil for storage and hold it until prices rise.

entries.text: NYMEX launched crude oil futures in 1983 and the IPE followed in 1988. Futures are contracts to buy or sell oil at a set future date. Investors use them to bet on prices and firms to hedge against swings, and world crude prices came to be published through these markets. Futures reduced the hazards of spot-price swings. Did speculators drive the 2003–2008 price rise? A 2008 US task force said no, blaming mainly supply and demand. In the contango trade, companies buy cheap oil, store it and wait for prices to rise.

entries.title: Green nudges: steering energy choices gently

definition.text: Government interventions, such as feedback on energy bills, that steer energy users toward greener choices without forcing them.

facts.text: The term was coined by Thaler and Sunstein in 2008.
They respond to the finding that energy consumers do not behave fully rationally, something the energy efficiency gap idea leaves out.
They arose because the energy efficiency gap idea ignored consumers' behavioural quirks.
Energy economics research now focuses on influencing decisions to close the energy efficiency gap.

entries.title: Peak demand: building for the busiest hours
entries.article: Demand response#Electricity grids and peak demand response

definition.text: The highest level of electricity use on a grid, which sets how much generating capacity must be built.

facts.text: Because supply and demand must balance at every moment, total capacity is sized to the peak plus a safety margin.
Peaks occur only a few times a year, so the plants and lines built for them sit mostly idle, and customers pay for that idle capacity.
One coalition estimated that 10%–20% of US electricity costs come from peak demand in only 100 hours of the year.

entries.title: Load shedding: switching some users off

definition.text: Deliberately cutting power to some users when generating capacity falls below demand.

facts.text: Utilities may use targeted or rolling blackouts, or agreements with big industrial users to switch off at system-wide peaks.
Users may be rewarded for firm commitments to cut use at peak times; such saved power is called negawatts, a term coined by Amory Lovins in 1985.
Industrial plants are well suited because their loads are large and they already have control systems.

entries.title: Measuring energy poverty in seven dimensions

definition.text: A composite index that classes people as energy poor according to how many kinds of energy deprivation they face.

facts.text: Its seven indicators are access to light, modern cooking fuel, fresh air, refrigeration, recreation, communication and space cooling.
It multiplies the share of people who are energy poor by the average intensity of their deprivation, capturing both breadth and depth.
Other indices include the IEA's Energy Development Index, which tracks a country's shift to modern fuels, and the household-level Energy Poverty Index.

entries.title: How energy storage makes money
entries.article: Grid energy storage#Market and system value

definition.text: How storage earns money and what it costs, measured over its lifetime and against the services it provides to the grid.

facts.text: The levelized cost of storage is lifetime cost per MWh discharged, including investment, operating and charging costs.
Storage earns value from power quality, reliability, better use of grid assets, and arbitrage between low and high prices, which has the largest potential.
More storage on the market shrinks price gaps, so storage 'cannibalises' its own income even more than renewables do.
Because storage loses some energy, small price differences may not justify charging and discharging; demand response or grid expansion may be cheaper options.

entries.title: Pumped hydro: storing power as water uphill

definition.text: Storing electricity by pumping water uphill to a reservoir when demand is low and releasing it through turbines when demand peaks.

facts.text: It was the largest form of grid storage in 2023, with 181 GW installed worldwide.
It is 75% to 85% efficient and responds within seconds to minutes, which suits daily swings in demand.
It expanded fast during the 1960s–1980s nuclear boom because nuclear plants cannot quickly follow demand.

entries.title: Wright's law: the math of learning
entries.article: Experience curve effect#Wright's law unit cost curve

definition.text: A power-law formula in which unit cost falls by a fixed proportion, the learning rate, with each doubling of cumulative production.

facts.text: The progress ratio b gives the remaining share of cost after each doubling, and one minus b is the learning rate.
Across many industries b ranges from 0.75 to 0.9, so costs fall 10% to 25% per doubling.
A curve with a 15% cut per doubling is called an '85% experience curve'.
The exponent is a statistical estimate, so it cannot exactly predict any future unit's cost.

entries.title: Levelized avoided cost: what a new plant is worth

definition.text: The discounted costs a new generator would avoid, divided by its discounted lifetime output, used as a measure of its value to the grid.

facts.text: In 2014 the US Energy Information Administration recommended comparing wind and solar costs with this measure rather than with fossil plants' LCOE.
Its ratio to the LCOE is the value-cost ratio; above 1, a project counts as economically feasible.
System LCOE and similar metrics instead add the cost of storage or backup plants needed when wind and solar are unavailable.

System LCOE takes another route, adding the cost of storage or backup for when wind and solar are unavailable.

entries.title: Base load and peaking plants
entries.article: Capacity factor#Determinants of a plant capacity factor

definition.text: The split between power plants run continuously at high output and plants switched on only when demand is high.

facts.text: Base load plants are designed for maximum efficiency and run continuously, so their cost per unit of electricity is usually low.
Geothermal, nuclear, coal and solid-fuel bioenergy plants are almost always run as base load because their output is hard to adjust.
Peaking plants may run only a few hours a year, or several hours a day, when electricity is needed and prices are high enough.

entries.text: Some power plants run nearly all the time; others wait for the busiest hours. Peaking plants switch on only when demand is high and prices justify it. Some run only a few hours a year, others several hours a day.

entries.title: Economic dispatch: running the grid at least cost

definition.text: The short-term choice of how much each power plant should produce to meet load at the lowest possible cost within grid and operating limits.

facts.text: It can be framed as maximising the economic welfare of a power network subject to power balance and line capacity constraints, solved with Lagrange multipliers.
Transmission limits make the cost of one more MWh differ by location; these are called locational marginal prices.
The equations are nonlinear and hard to solve, so a simplified linear 'DC power flow' model is often used.

entries.text: Economic dispatch decides, moment to moment, how much each plant should produce to meet load at the lowest cost within grid and operating limits. It can be framed as maximizing a network's economic welfare subject to power balance and line capacity, solved with Lagrange multipliers. Transmission limits make the cost of one more MWh differ by place, giving locational marginal prices. The full equations are nonlinear and hard, so a simplified linear 'DC power flow' model is often used.

entries.title: The merit order effect: how wind and sun cut prices
entries.article: Merit order#The effect of renewable energy on merit order

definition.text: The lowering of wholesale electricity prices when wind and solar, which have near-zero fuel costs, push expensive plants out of the merit order.

facts.text: Wind and solar have very low marginal costs because they pay nothing for fuel, so they are bought first and displace costly peak power.
A Fraunhofer ISI study found solar cut prices on the German exchange by 10% on average and up to 40% in the early afternoon.
In Germany 2008–2012, each extra GWh of renewables cut day-ahead prices by 0.11–0.13 ¢/kWh.
Solar peaks at noon while demand in warm climates peaks in late afternoon, producing the so-called duck curve.

entries.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the cause

definition.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change; also called decarbonisation.

facts.text: The IPCC defines it as a human intervention to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases.
Main actions are saving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy; changing land use and removing CO2 are secondary strategies.
There are four types of measures: sustainable energy and transport, energy conservation, sustainable agriculture and green industry, and enhancing sinks and carbon removal.
2022 assessments said emissions must peak before 2025 and fall about 43% by 2030 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.
Adopted policies would still lead to about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100, well above the Paris Agreement goal.
Solar and wind can replace fossil fuels at the lowest cost of the renewable options.
Air travel and cement production are among the processes hardest to decarbonise.
Mitigation is often seen as a burden to share, but it can also be an opportunity for industrial development and exports.

entries.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away

definition.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, a place in the Earth system where carbon stays for a period of time.

facts.text: By lowering the carbon dioxide in the air it helps manage the carbon cycle and limit climate change.
The two main types are biologic sequestration, also called biosequestration, and geologic sequestration.
Plants take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow and bind it into biomass; people can speed this up through land use and farming.
Biological stores such as forests may be temporary, since fires, disease, economic pressure and politics can release the carbon.
Injecting CO2 underground or turning it into carbonate salts locks carbon away for thousands to millions of years.
Within carbon capture and storage, sequestration is the storage step.
A 2025 study found that using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C.

entries.text: Using all of Earth's geologic storage would limit warming by only 0.7 °C, a 2025 study found. Storage is no cure-all, yet it is a real tool. entries.title: The carbon budget: how much CO2 is left to burn

definition.text: The largest total amount of carbon dioxide humanity can still emit, added up over time, while keeping global warming below a chosen limit.

facts.text: Counted from the pre-industrial year 1750 it is the total carbon budget; counted from a recent date it is the remaining carbon budget.
It is also called an emissions budget, quota or allowable emissions.
Global warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative carbon dioxide emissions, which is what makes a budget meaningful.
The warming that results does not depend on where the emissions come from and depends little on when they happen.
From 1750 to 2019 about 2390 gigatonnes of CO2 had already been emitted worldwide.
Estimates depend on the temperature target, the chosen probability of staying below it, and how far other greenhouse gases are cut too.
A 2023 update found 250 GtCO2 left from January 2023 for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C, about 6 years of current emissions.
For a 50% chance of staying below 2 degrees, the same update gave 1220 GtCO2, about 30 years of current emissions.

entries.title: The low-carbon economy

definition.text: An economy that absorbs as much greenhouse gas as it emits, or more broadly one whose activities produce far lower emissions.

facts.text: Similar terms include green economy, carbon-neutral economy and decarbonised economy; 'carbon' stands for all greenhouse gases.
Getting there means cutting emissions in every sector, through renewables, efficiency, electric vehicles, heat pumps and climate-smart agriculture.
It needs energy policies and financial incentives such as emissions trading and carbon taxes.
Besides mitigation it brings benefits for ecosystems, trade, jobs, health, energy security and competitiveness.
Workers in carbon-intensive industries are more likely to lose jobs, while new jobs come from renewables and building renovation.
Switching to lower-emission technologies often pays back within 0.5–5 years.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: each country gains from others' mitigation but loses by going low-carbon alone.

entries.title: Carbon capture and storage: catching CO2 at the chimney

definition.text: Separating carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moving it to long-term storage, usually deep underground; known as CCS.

facts.text: Around 80% of captured CO2 is used for enhanced oil recovery, so CCS is also called carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS).
Capture usually passes exhaust through an amine solvent that binds CO2.
As of 2023 CCS captured around 0.1% of global emissions, about 45 million tonnes of CO2.
Capture costs US$15–25 per tonne for concentrated streams such as gas processing but US$40–120 for dilute streams from power, cement and steel plants.
Compared with other ways to cut emissions it is very expensive; many options cost under US$20 per tonne.
Site-specific designs limit cost cuts through learning-by-doing.
The literature gives CCS a small but critical role, while fossil fuel companies promote it to extend the fossil era, making it politically divisive.

entries.contested_note: CCS remains politically divisive, with disagreement over its cost-effectiveness and whether it prolongs fossil fuel use.

entries.title: Biochar: charcoal that feeds the soil

definition.text: A charcoal made by heating biomass with little oxygen, intended for use in soil and other organic uses.

facts.text: It is made by pyrolysis, heating biomass without oxygen, which yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas.
In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions from the soil.
Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity.
Because it is so stable, it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies biochar carbon removal.
Pre-Columbian Amazonians made it by smouldering farm waste, creating soils settlers called terra preta.
It benefits degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones.
A 1–2% share of biochar works best in concrete, cutting emissions from cement.

Biochar is that kind of charcoal: made by heating biomass with little oxygen, and meant for soil and other organic uses. The process, pyrolysis, yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas. In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions. It helps degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones. Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity. Biochar is so stable that it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies its use for carbon removal, described in Biochar carbon removal: the leader in delivered removals. A 1–2% share in concrete also cuts emissions from cement.

entries.title: Co-benefits: what cutting emissions also buys

definition.text: Side benefits of cutting emissions beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security; also called ancillary benefits.

facts.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution is estimated to kill over 5 million people a year as of 2019.
Replacing coal plants with renewables can more than double the jobs per megawatt of capacity in some cases.
Countries that import energy can gain independence and supply security by building renewables.
The IPCC noted in 2007 that co-benefits are often neglected and not quantified or monetised by decision-makers.
Counting co-benefits properly can change decisions about when and how much to mitigate.

entries.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution is estimated to kill over 5 million people a year as of 2019. Cutting emissions would also cut that toll. Co-benefits are the side benefits of mitigation beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security. They are also called ancillary benefits. Replacing coal plants with renewables can, in some cases, more than double the jobs per megawatt of capacity. Countries that import energy can gain independence and supply security by building renewables. Yet the IPCC noted in 2007 that decision-makers often neglect co-benefits and do not quantify or monetize them. Counting them properly can change decisions about when and how much to mitigate.

entries.title: Demand-side mitigation: wanting less carbon

definition.text: Cutting emissions by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them, through behaviour, infrastructure and end-use technology.

facts.text: Examples include eating less meat, building good public transport and insulating houses.
Demand-side solutions could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 40% to 70% by 2050 while improving well-being.
The richest 10% of people cause about half of all lifestyle emissions.
High-impact personal actions include flying less, avoiding petrol cars, eating mainly plants and electrifying homes.

entries.title: Mitigation sector by sector

definition.text: The grouping of emission cuts by the part of the economy where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use.

facts.text: Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions; about half their energy goes to heating space and water.
Transport causes 15% of emissions; public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them.
Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter; electrification, green hydrogen and circular economy measures can cut them.
Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle produce 21% of global methane.
A modern heat pump moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses.

entries.text: Emissions come from every corner of the economy, so cuts are grouped by where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use. Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions. About half their energy goes to heating space and water. Heat pumps are a strong tool there, because a modern one moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses. Transport causes 15% of emissions. Public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them. Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter. Switching to electricity, green hydrogen and measures that keep materials in use can reduce its share. Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle alone produce 21% of global methane. Each sector therefore needs its own mix of measures.

entries.title: Protecting the sinks that soak up carbon
entries.article: Climate change mitigation#Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks

definition.text: Managing Earth's natural carbon sinks so they keep or increase their ability to take CO2 from the air and store it durably.

facts.text: Globally the two most important carbon sinks are vegetation and the ocean.
Examples are preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.
Ecosystem restoration and less land conversion are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030.
The economic potential of forest and ecosystem measures is 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.
The Stern Review said in 2007 that curbing deforestation was a highly cost-effective way to cut emissions.
