entries.title: Adaptive capacity: the stock of ways to adjust

definition.text: The ability of people, institutions, ecosystems and other organisms to adjust to potential harm, seize opportunities or cope with consequences.

facts.text: In climate risk, adaptive capacity sits alongside hazard, exposure and vulnerability as a key component of risk.
It works as a stock of resources and assets from which adaptations can be drawn as future conditions require.
In social systems it rests on institutions that learn, flexible decision-making and power structures responsive to all stakeholders.
The ODI's local adaptive capacity framework names five features: assets, institutions and entitlements, knowledge, innovation, and flexible forward-looking governance.
A stable, prosperous economy helps, and wealthier nations are generally better prepared for climate impacts.
Barriers to adaptation can be overcome, whereas limits cannot; lack of land to relocate to is a common external barrier.
For species, it depends on phenotypic plasticity, dispersal ability and genetic diversity.

entries.title: The adaptation gap: a bill far bigger than the budget

definition.text: The cost of adapting to climate change, and the shortfall between that cost and the money available, known as the adaptation gap.

facts.text: Costs rise sharply with more warming; globally they likely run to tens or hundreds of billions of dollars a year for decades.
The IPCC puts adaptation costs at $15 to 411 billion per year to 2030, with most estimates above $100 billion.
The gap is widening because most tracked climate finance goes to mitigation.
UNEP's 2023 report put the adaptation finance gap at $194 billion to $366 billion a year.
Developing countries' needs, $215 to $387 billion a year, are 10–18 times current international public adaptation finance.
In many specific settings, adaptation investment costs less than the damage it avoids, though global estimates are very uncertain.

entries.title: Why private money avoids adaptation
entries.article: Climate change adaptation#Incentivizing private investment in adaptation

definition.text: The reasons private investors find adaptation harder to fund than mitigation, chiefly the lack of a clear income stream.

facts.text: Adaptation often serves non-market sectors or public goods that benefit many, so few projects attract private money.
Costs come now while benefits come later, and investors prefer short-term returns.
Uncertainty about future impacts and benefits leaves investors short of information.
Innovation is increasing the potential for private finance to help close the adaptation gap.

entries.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three parts of climate risk
entries.article: Climate change adaptation#Reduce risk factors: vulnerability and exposure

definition.text: The three interacting ingredients of climate risk: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability.

facts.text: Exposure is the presence of people, livelihoods, ecosystems and assets in places that could be harmed.
Exposure falls with retreat from floodplains and better early warning and evacuation.
Vulnerability, the IPCC's propensity to be adversely affected, includes sensitivity and lack of capacity to cope.
Insurance, livelihood diversification, social protection and sturdier infrastructure reduce vulnerability.
Protecting mangroves, which dampen storm energy, is ecosystem-based adaptation that cuts vulnerability.

entries.text: A storm is only part of the story. Climate risk needs three ingredients together: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability. Better early warning and evacuation also reduce it. {{ref:nature-clim-025}}, in the IPCC's words a propensity to be adversely affected, includes sensitivity and a lack of capacity to cope. Insurance, more varied livelihoods, social protection and sturdier infrastructure all reduce it. So does nature. Protecting mangroves, which dampen storm energy, is ecosystem-based adaptation that cuts vulnerability.

entries.title: Climate change vulnerability: who stands to be hurt most

definition.text: How strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change; formally, their propensity to be adversely affected.

facts.text: It includes capacity to cope and adapt, and is one component of climate risk.
Earlier IPCC reports made vulnerability a function of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity; the Fifth report moved exposure to be a separate element of risk.
About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people were estimated in 2021 to live in highly vulnerable contexts.
People with low incomes, Indigenous peoples, women, children and the elderly tend to be more vulnerable.
Developing countries were judged more vulnerable, partly because adaptation costs are high relative to their GDP.
It can be reduced by adaptation, by tackling poverty, inequality and conflict, and by mitigation that makes impacts less severe.

entries.title: Disaster risk reduction: acting before the disaster

definition.text: Actions that make disasters less likely and less damaging, by preventing new risk, reducing existing risk and managing what remains.

facts.text: Disaster risk is the potential loss of life, injury or damaged assets, arising from hazard, vulnerability and exposure together.
It aims to make communities more resilient and less vulnerable.
Its scope is much broader than conventional emergency management; disaster risk management is its practical implementation.
Experts often see climate change adaptation as one of many processes within DRR.
Since the mid-1970s the field has shifted from response and recovery toward understanding causes and reducing risk beforehand.
Women and girls are disproportionately harmed: after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, 77% of deaths in North Aceh were female.
It aims to make communities stronger and better prepared, that is, more resilient and less vulnerable.
It is also called DRR or disaster risk management.

entries.title: International adaptation finance: helping poorer countries adapt

definition.text: Money from richer countries and international funds that helps developing countries adapt to climate change.

facts.text: UNFCCC funds include the Special Climate Change Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and the Adaptation Fund.
In 2009 rich nations pledged $100 billion a year by 2020 for mitigation and adaptation; by December 2020 it had not been fully delivered.
The Green Climate Fund was created in 2010 as one channel for this finance.
Adaptation received only 21% of public climate finance provided in 2020.
Multilateral development banks gave over €19 billion for adaptation in 2021.
In 2022 nations agreed to set up a loss and damage fund for harms beyond what adaptation can handle.

entries.title: Limits to adaptation: where adjusting stops working

definition.text: The points beyond which adaptation can no longer protect people or ecosystems from climate risks.

facts.text: The IPCC's 2022 report distinguishes soft limits, where options exist but are not yet usable, from hard limits.
Some systems in Australia, small islands, the Americas, Africa and Europe have already hit soft limits.
At 1.5 °C, glacier-dependent regions and small islands reach hard limits; at 2 °C many staple crops hit soft limits.
As risks grow, incremental adjustments become insufficient and larger, costlier transformational adaptation is needed.

entries.title: Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented

definition.text: The harms from climate change that mitigation and adaptation fail to prevent, and the question of how to deal with them.

facts.text: Loss means irreversible harm, such as extinction or islands lost to sea; damage means harm that can be repaired or compensated.
Economic losses affect traded goods and services; non-economic losses, like lost family members or cultures, involve things not traded in markets.
It covers both sudden disasters such as cyclones and slow-onset change such as sea level rise.
Small island and least developed countries have long sought liability and compensation, which developed countries resist.
In 1991 small island states proposed an insurance pool funded by countries' shares of emissions and income; it was rejected.
A 2026 study estimated US CO2 emissions from 1990 to 2020 caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020.
The IPCC found residual risks beyond adaptation will rise with further warming.

entries.title: Maladaptation: when adapting makes things worse

definition.text: An adaptation action that ends up increasing vulnerability to climate change or reducing the ability to adapt sustainably later.

facts.text: The IPCC introduced the term in 2001 and notes it is usually an unintended consequence.
Adjusting to short-term variability can be maladaptive for long-term trends, as with irrigation expansion in Egypt's Western Sinai.
Air conditioning powered by carbon-intensive electricity adds to the emissions causing the problem.
Seawalls can waterlog fields and reduce soil fertility.
Community-driven bottom-up approaches generally carry lower risk of maladaptation than top-down technical fixes.
The IPCC first introduced the term in 2001.

The IPCC describes it as actions that may raise climate-related risk, including through higher greenhouse gas emissions, shifted vulnerability, more inequitable outcomes or reduced welfare; it is usually unintended.
Adapting to short-term climate swings can cause maladaptation to longer-term trends, as with irrigation expanded into Egypt's Western Sinai desert despite projected drying.

entries.title: Retreat, accommodate or protect: adapting to rising seas

definition.text: The ways societies respond to rising seas: retreating, accommodating coastal change, or protecting coasts with hard or soft defences.

facts.text: Cutting emissions can slow sea level rise after 2050 but cannot stop it, so adaptation is inevitable.
Hard adaptation relies on capital-intensive infrastructure such as seawalls; soft adaptation strengthens natural defences like dunes with local, modular means.
Adaptation in 136 large coastal cities could cut annual flood costs from $1 trillion by 2050 to a little over $60 billion, at a cost of $50 billion per year.
Higher-value areas are more likely to be protected, leaving lower-value areas to retreat.
Retreat often costs livelihoods, and displaced people can strain their new communities.
In a 2023 survey of planners, 98% knew the projections but 26% had not yet put them into policy.

entries.text: Cutting emissions can slow {{ref:nature-clim-037}} after 2050 but cannot stop it, so adaptation is inevitable. Societies have three broad choices: retreat, accommodate coastal change, or protect coasts with defences. Hard adaptation relies on capital-intensive infrastructure such as seawalls. Soft adaptation strengthens natural defences like dunes, using local, modular means. The economics can be striking. Without adaptation, annual flood costs in 136 large coastal cities could reach $1 trillion by 2050. Adaptation costing $50 billion per year could cut that to a little over $60 billion. But protection is not shared evenly. Higher-value areas are more likely to be defended, leaving lower-value areas to retreat. Retreat often costs people their livelihoods, and displaced people can strain their new communities. Planning lags too: in a 2023 survey, 98% of planners knew the projections, but 26% had not yet put them into policy.

entries.title: Climate risk insurance: fast money after the storm

definition.text: Insurance designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially extreme weather.

facts.text: It gives quick money after disasters for relief and rebuilding, and is seen as an important adaptation measure.
Because weather disasters hit whole regions at once and trigger many claims together, it must be sold at a large, diversified scale.
High premiums in risky areas could discourage people from settling there.
Critics say it puts the cost on communities that emitted least, and start-up and data costs are high for low-income countries.
The InsuResilience Global Partnership, launched at COP23, supports such schemes.
It is often seen as a way to improve the climate resilience of poor and developing communities.
It provides money after a disaster for relief and rebuilding, and helps prepare to reduce future vulnerability.
Insurance pools risks, but because climate risks are partly correlated, pooling works less well for them.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue it shifts costs onto low-emitting communities, while supporters see it as a safety net.
entries.text: Climate risk insurance is designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially {{ref:nature-eco-001}}. Its appeal is speed. It provides money quickly after a disaster for relief and rebuilding, and helps prepare to reduce future vulnerability. It is often seen as a way to make poor and developing communities more resilient, and as an important adaptation measure. Its scale is a challenge. Insurance works by pooling many separate risks, but weather disasters hit whole regions at once and trigger many claims together. Because climate risks are partly correlated in this way, pooling works less well, so cover must be sold at a large, diversified scale. High premiums in risky areas could discourage people from settling there. The InsuResilience Global Partnership, launched at COP23, supports such schemes. Opinion is split. Supporters see a safety net, while critics say it puts the cost on communities that emitted least, and start-up and data costs are high for low-income countries.

entries.title: Early warning systems: buying time before a hazard hits

definition.text: A chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm.

facts.text: A complete system covers risk analysis, monitoring and warning, dissemination and communication, and response capability.
To work, it must involve at-risk communities, raise awareness, spread alerts effectively and keep people prepared.
The UN recommends early warning systems as key to climate adaptation, and runs the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems partnership for high-risk countries.
Interest surged after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004.

entries.text: Interest in early warning surged after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004. An early warning system is a chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm. A complete system has four parts: risk analysis, monitoring and warning, spreading the message, and the capability to respond. Technology alone is not enough. To work, a system must involve at-risk communities, raise awareness, deliver alerts effectively and keep people prepared. The UN recommends early warning systems as key to climate adaptation. It runs the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems partnership for high-risk countries.

entries.title: The Adaptation Fund: paying for adaptation through carbon credits

definition.text: An international fund under the Kyoto Protocol that pays for projects helping developing countries adapt to climate change.

facts.text: It was established in 2001 at COP7 in Marrakech and officially launched in 2007.
Its original funding was a 2% share of credits issued for CDM projects; as carbon prices fell, donations from rich countries became more important.
Its direct access mechanism lets accredited national and regional bodies in developing countries receive funds directly.
By 2024 it had committed over 1 billion US dollars since 2010 and reports over 43 million beneficiaries.

conflicts.text: The Adaptation Fund resulted from negotiations at COP15 and COP16 in 2009 and 2010.
conflicts.note: The Adaptation Fund page says it was established in 2001 and launched in 2007 (de7d48d120da); the CDM page says it was established in 2007 (e13102edd0f0).

entries.title: When adapting and cutting emissions help or hinder each other

definition.text: The ways actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce or work against each other.

facts.text: Public transport is a synergy: lower emissions per kilometre and easier evacuation in disasters.
Compact cities cut transport and building emissions but can worsen the urban heat island.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap
entries.text: Actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce each other or work against each other. Public transport is a synergy. It produces lower emissions per kilometre and makes evacuation easier in disasters. Compact cities show the trade-off. They cut transport and building emissions, but packing buildings close together can worsen the urban heat island, the extra warmth that builds up in cities.

entries.title: Additionality: new money or relabelled aid

definition.text: The principle that adaptation money should be extra to existing development aid rather than redirected from it.

facts.text: Four main definitions exist, from finance additional to the Millennium Development Goals to climate finance unconnected to aid budgets.
Critics say it encourages business as usual because it ignores future climate risks.
Denmark raised adaptation aid from 0.09% to 0.12% of GDP between 2010 and 2020 by taking it from other aid.

entries.title: Climate services: climate information people can use

definition.text: Systems that deliver usable climate information to people and organisations to support adaptation, mitigation and risk decisions.

facts.text: They help users foresee and manage hazards of a changing climate.
They are demand-driven, designed with users through co-design, rather than supply-driven research products.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

Instead of handing over research products, providers design them together with users, a process called co-design.

entries.title: Four kinds of adaptation: built, institutional, behavioral and natural
entries.article: Climate change adaptation#Options by type of action

definition.text: The four kinds of adaptation action: infrastructural, institutional, behavioural and nature-based.

facts.text: Built-environment options protect against flooding, sea level rise and extreme heat.
Institutional responses include zoning rules, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination.
Behavioural options include farmers changing planting times or switching crops and livestock.
Nature-based solutions work with ecosystems to benefit both people and biodiversity.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap
entries.text: Adaptation comes in four kinds. Infrastructural options use the built environment to protect against flooding, sea level rise and extreme heat. Institutional responses change the rules, through zoning, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination. Behavioural options change what people do, such as farmers shifting planting times or switching crops and livestock. Nature-based solutions work with ecosystems, aiming to benefit both people and biodiversity.

entries.title: The economics of prevention: five to ten dollars saved per dollar
entries.article: Disaster risk reduction#Financing needs and finance flows

definition.text: The costs of disasters and the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery.

facts.text: Climate-related disasters have cost over US$330 billion a year on average over 2015–2021, likely an underestimate.
Every dollar spent on risk reduction saves between $5 and $10 in disaster losses.
Yet around 90% of international DRR funding goes to response and recovery, and only about 0.5% of development aid goes to pre-disaster risk reduction.
For many countries less than 1% of the national budget is available for DRR.
New instruments include risk disclosure rules, resilience bonds and green bonds.

distinct_from: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
entries.text: Every dollar spent on reducing disaster risk saves between $5 and $10 in disaster losses. The economics of {{ref:nature-clim-226}} looks at what disasters cost and makes the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery. The costs are large. For many countries, less than 1% of the national budget is available for DRR. New instruments are emerging, including rules requiring firms to disclose risk, resilience bonds and green bonds.

entries.title: Climate resilient development: three goals pursued together

definition.text: Development that pursues adaptation, mitigation and sustainable development together, using their synergies and reducing trade-offs.

facts.text: It has become a new, if contested, paradigm for sustainable development, especially in the water sector.
Governments on every continent are adopting policies for climate-resilient economies, pushed by the Paris Agreement and the SDGs.

entries.contested_note: Sources describe the paradigm itself as contested.

Governments on every continent are adopting policies for climate-resilient economies, pushed by {{ref:nature-clim-074}} and {{ref:nature-gov-010}}.

entries.title: Measuring resilience with proxies

definition.text: Tools and indicators for tracking the climate resilience of households, communities or nations to guide spending on resilience.

facts.text: It helps locate vulnerability hotspots and judge whether interventions work.
Resilience has no single observable metric and includes intangibles like social capital, so toolkits rely on long lists of proxy indicators.
Common objective measures include FAO's RIMA and the Livelihoods Change Over Time index.

entries.text: Money spent on resilience should go where it helps most. Resilience measurement provides tools and indicators for tracking the {{ref:nature-clim-014}} of households, communities or nations. It helps locate vulnerability hotspots and judge whether interventions work. The difficulty is that resilience has no single observable metric. It includes intangibles like social capital, the trust and networks people can draw on. So toolkits rely on long lists of proxy indicators, stand-ins that track it indirectly. Common objective measures include FAO's RIMA and the Livelihoods Change Over Time index.

entries.title: Climate risk management: reducing harm and seizing gains

definition.text: Strategies for reducing climate risk that draw on adaptation, disaster management and sustainable development.

facts.text: It is a general approach to climate-sensitive decisions that aims to reduce vulnerability.
Tools include early response systems, diversification, flexible resource-allocation rules, insurance, infrastructure design and capacity building.
It also seeks gains, such as farmers using favourable seasonal forecasts to raise yields.

entries.text: Climate risk management is a general approach to climate-sensitive decisions. It draws on adaptation, disaster management and development that can last to reduce vulnerability. Its tools include early response systems, diversification, flexible rules for allocating resources, insurance, infrastructure design and capacity building. It is not only defensive. It also seeks gains, such as farmers using a favourable seasonal forecast to raise their yields.

entries.title: Ecological anthropology: how cultures fit their environments

definition.text: The branch of anthropology that studies how human cultures adapt to and shape their environments.

facts.text: It emerged in the 1960s from Julian Steward's cultural ecology.
Roy Rappaport's work with the Maring of Papua New Guinea examined ritual in the relationship between culture and nature.
Long-term traditional ecological knowledge can inform adaptation strategies and community monitoring.
Critics said it assumed static equilibrium and oversimplified systems, prompting a shift toward political ecology.

entries.title: The Sendai Framework: seven targets for safer societies
entries.article: Disaster risk reduction#Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

definition.text: The international framework adopted on March 18, 2015, setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030.

facts.text: It aims to cut disaster deaths, people affected, economic loss and damage to infrastructure.
Other targets increase access to warning systems, aid to developing countries and national DRR strategies.
Countries with national DRR strategies rose from 55 to 123 by 2022.

entries.text: On March 18, 2015, countries adopted the Sendai Framework, an international plan setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030. Its targets aim to cut disaster deaths, the number of people affected, economic loss and damage to infrastructure. Others aim to widen access to warning systems, increase aid to developing countries and spread national DRR strategies. That last goal has made progress. Countries with national strategies rose from 55 to 123 by 2022.

entries.title: The Loss and Damage Fund: a breakthrough after three decades
entries.article: Loss and damage (climate change)#Loss and Damage Fund

definition.text: A climate finance fund agreed at COP27 in Egypt in 2022 to support communities where adaptation is inadequate or comes too late.

facts.text: It was agreed after years of negotiation.
Before the June 2023 Paris finance summit, over 100 economists proposed an extreme wealth tax to fund loss and damage; it was not adopted.
It was agreed after three decades of negotiation on loss and damage and was seen by many as a major breakthrough.
It operates as a financial mechanism of the Paris Agreement.

entries.title: The Warsaw International Mechanism: talking about loss without liability
entries.article: Loss and damage (climate change)#Warsaw International Mechanism for Loss and Damage

definition.text: The UN body created in 2013 to address loss and damage in highly vulnerable countries through research and dialogue.

facts.text: It recognises that loss and damage can go beyond what adaptation can reduce.
It makes no provision for liability or compensation, and the Paris Agreement says it gives no basis for either.
Developed countries, particularly the United States, insisted on the no-liability clause.

entries.title: Social vulnerability: harm shaped by society

definition.text: The inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses such as social exclusion and natural hazards.

facts.text: It arises partly from social interactions, institutions and cultural values.
Marital status, employment and income affect individual vulnerability.
Understanding catastrophe requires looking at people's assets and entitlements, not just the severity of shocks.

entries.text: Social vulnerability is the inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses, such as social exclusion and natural hazards. It arises partly from social interactions, institutions and cultural values. At the individual level, marital status, employment and income all affect it. The lesson is that a catastrophe cannot be understood from the size of the shock alone. It also requires looking at people's assets and entitlements, what they own and what they can claim.

entries.title: Biophysical and social vulnerability

definition.text: The main split between biophysical vulnerability, the effects of physical hazards, and social vulnerability, shaped by political, economic and social structures.

facts.text: Early studies focused on biophysical vulnerability, drawing on natural hazards research.
Social vulnerability is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more, driven by poverty, poor governance and conflict.
Place-based vulnerability is highest where sea level rise and changes in ecosystem services such as food access strike.

entries.text: Climate vulnerability splits into two main kinds. Biophysical vulnerability concerns the effects of physical hazards. Early studies focused on it, drawing on natural hazards research. Social vulnerability, described in {{ref:nature-clim-026}}, is shaped by political, economic and social structures. It is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more, driven by poverty, poor governance and conflict. Where the two meet, in a particular place, vulnerability peaks where sea level rise and changes in ecosystem services such as food access strike.

entries.title: Climate vulnerability assessment: scoring who is at risk

definition.text: Tools that measure climate vulnerability, from global indices to local models and participatory methods, to guide responses.

facts.text: Global indices include the ND-GAIN Country Index, the INFORM Risk Index and the WorldRiskIndex.
Composite indices usually average a set of standardised indicators into a score.
Vulnerability curves link levels of a hazard, such as extreme heat or sea level rise, to the damage caused.

entries.text: To act on {{ref:nature-clim-027}}, decision-makers first need to measure it. Assessment tools range from global indices to local models and participatory methods. entries.title: Crop insurance: governments step in for farmers

definition.text: Government-subsidised insurance bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue.

facts.text: Governments stepped in because markets failed to give farmers tools to manage production risk.
Hail insurance is offered privately because hail is a narrow, local peril; multi-peril cover is vulnerable to large-scale events.
In the United States the federal government subsidises on average 62 percent of the premium, and about 90% of crop acreage is insured.
India's National Agriculture Insurance Scheme insures whole areas rather than individual farms, paying for yield shortfalls against the past five years.

entries.text: Crop insurance is government-subsidised cover bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue. Governments stepped in because markets failed to give farmers tools to manage production risk. Hail is the exception. It is a narrow, local peril, so private firms insure it, while multi-peril cover is exposed to large-scale events. In the United States the federal government pays on average 62 percent of the premium, and about 90% of crop acreage is insured. India's National Agriculture Insurance Scheme insures whole areas instead of single farms, paying for yield shortfalls against the past five years.

entries.title: Index-based insurance: paying out by rainfall, not by claim

definition.text: Insurance, mainly for farming, that pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger.

facts.text: Assessing actual losses is too costly for smallholders in developing countries, so traditional indemnity insurance is usually not viable.
Paying by index avoids the cost of checking individual claims.
It sidesteps moral hazard because no one can manipulate the weather that triggers payment.
Weather disasters hit many people at once, unlike thefts, which makes them hard to insure conventionally.
Many indices now use satellite imagery.
In developing countries it has so far needed subsidies to be viable, and uptake among smallholders remains low.

entries.text: Sending an assessor to every small farm after a drought costs more than the farms' policies are worth. For smallholders in developing countries, traditional indemnity insurance, which pays for each person's verified loss, is usually not viable. Index-based insurance offers a workaround. It pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger. Paying by index avoids the cost of checking individual claims. It also sidesteps {{ref:nature-econ-004}}, because no one can manipulate the weather that triggers payment. Weather disasters hit many people at once, unlike thefts, which makes them hard to insure conventionally. Many indices now use satellite imagery. The results so far are modest. In developing countries it has needed subsidies to be viable, and uptake among smallholders remains low.

entries.title: Flood insurance: protection that can encourage risk

definition.text: Insurance against losses from flooding, one of the most widely used forms of climate risk insurance.

facts.text: Rising sea levels, floods and windstorms threaten the affordability of flood-exposed areas.
Critics say the subsidised US programme encouraged building and rebuilding in floodplains and coasts.
Its rules make flood-prone homes more likely to be rented cheaply to low-income, older or infirm people, an example of adverse selection.

entries.title: Basis risk: when the index and the farm disagree

definition.text: The mismatch in index insurance between what the index pays and the losses a particular farmer actually suffers.

facts.text: An index covers an area where farmers' experience of rainfall can differ, so some lose crops but get no payout, or vice versa.
Because of basis risk, farmers are reluctant to pay the same premiums as for standard insurance.
Researchers aim to reduce it with new data sources.

Because of this, farmers are reluctant to pay the same premiums as for standard insurance. Researchers aim to reduce basis risk with new data sources.

entries.title: The UN climate convention: where the world negotiates
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

definition.text: The international treaty, and the UN process built on it, through which countries negotiate how to limit dangerous climate change.

facts.text: It was signed by 154 states at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro and entered into force in 1994.
Its ultimate aim, in Article 2, is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system.
It set the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, with developed countries expected to lead because of their larger historical emissions.
By 2022 it had 198 parties, and its supreme body, the Conference of the Parties, meets every year.
Its work now centres on carrying out the Paris Agreement, which entered into force in 2016.
Decisions are taken by consensus, giving any party a veto, and it has been criticised as unsuccessful at cutting emissions.

entries.title: Climate finance: following the money

definition.text: Money, such as loans, grants or government budget spending, used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience.

facts.text: The money can come from private or public sources and can pass through intermediaries such as multilateral development banks and development agencies.
Under the UN Climate Convention, climate finance means transfers of public money from high-income to low- and middle-income countries, in line with their duty to provide new and additional resources.
It has two main subcategories: mitigation finance, which aims to reduce emissions, and adaptation finance, which responds to the consequences of climate change.
Global climate finance was estimated at around $1.3 trillion per year in 2021/2022, up from more than US$600 billion in 2019 by one estimate.
Most of it, 84% in 2021/2022, is raised and spent within the same country.
A 2024 report estimated that flows must rise at least sixfold on 2021/2022 levels, to $8.5 trillion per year by 2030.
Public budgets are widely seen as too small to meet the need, so private finance is expected to be important for closing the gap.
Its main challenges are measuring and tracking flows, fair support for developing countries, and giving private investors suitable incentives.

entries.title: The Montreal Protocol: the treaty that worked

definition.text: An international treaty that protects the ozone layer by phasing out the production of substances that deplete it.

facts.text: It was agreed on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989.
With 198 parties it was the first universally ratified treaty in UN history and is often called the most successful international environmental agreement.
Developing countries get extra time to comply under Article 5, and a financial mechanism under Article 10 helps them.
Concentrations of the main CFCs have levelled off or fallen, and the Antarctic ozone hole is slowly recovering.
It has also benefited climate change mitigation; HCFCs, which it phases out, are very potent greenhouse gases.
It is cited as a precedent that the UN consensus approach to global problems can work.

entries.title: Fossil fuel divestment: pulling money out of oil and coal

definition.text: Pressuring institutions to sell off stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change.

facts.text: It began on US university campuses in 2011, and by 2015 was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history.
As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of divestment.
Divesters act to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk.
One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off.
Its aim is to speed the renewable energy transition by stigmatising fossil fuel companies.
Fossil fuel companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for their rising cost of capital.

entries.title: The COPs: the yearly climate summits

definition.text: The yearly conferences, known as COPs, at which the parties to the UN climate convention meet to assess and negotiate climate action.

facts.text: The first, COP 1, was held in Berlin in 1995.
Since 2005 they also serve as the meeting of the Kyoto Protocol's parties, and from 2011 to 2015 they were used to negotiate the Paris Agreement.
Any final text of a COP must be agreed by consensus.
Hosting rotates among the five UN regional groups.
More than 5,350 fossil fuel industry lobbyists attended the four conferences from 2021 to 2024.

entries.title: Annex I, Annex II and the rest: sorting countries by duty
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Classification of Parties and their commitments

definition.text: The UNFCCC's grouping of countries into industrialised and transition economies (Annex I), richer donor countries (Annex II) and mostly developing countries (non-Annex I), each with different duties.

facts.text: There are 43 Annex I parties, including the EU; 14 of them are economies in transition, the former Soviet-bloc economies.
Annex I countries should adopt national policies to limit their emissions and report on returning to their 1990 levels.
The 24 Annex II parties are OECD members who must give financial and technical support to transition economies and developing countries.
49 parties are least-developed countries with special status, and developing countries may volunteer to join Annex I once sufficiently developed.

sources.title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

entries.text: The climate convention does not treat all countries alike. Since 1992 it has sorted them into groups with different duties. Annex I holds industrialised countries and economies in transition. There are 43 Annex I parties, including the EU. Fourteen of them are economies in transition, the former Soviet-bloc economies. Annex I countries should adopt national policies to limit their emissions and report on returning to their 1990 levels. Annex II is a smaller, richer group. Its 24 parties are OECD members, the club of wealthy market economies, and they must give financial and technical support to transition economies and developing countries. Everyone else, mostly developing countries, is non-Annex I. Among all parties, 49 are least-developed countries with special status. The lines can move. Developing countries may volunteer to join Annex I once sufficiently developed.

entries.title: The Kyoto Protocol: binding cuts for rich countries

definition.text: An international treaty extending the UNFCCC that committed its parties to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: It was adopted in Kyoto on 11 December 1997 and entered into force on 16 February 2005.
Its main feature was legally binding emission-cut commitments for Annex I (industrialised) parties, based on common but differentiated responsibilities.
It covered seven gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide; the first commitment period ran from 2008 to 2012.

The 36 fully participating countries pledged a 4% aggregate cut from 1990 and achieved emissions 24.2% below 1990 in 2008–2012, largely thanks to the Soviet Union's collapse and the 2008 financial crisis.
Even so, global emissions rose by 32% from 1990 to 2010, since the committed countries made up only 24% of global emissions in 2010.
The United States never ratified it and Canada withdrew effective December 2012.
It was followed in 2015 by the Paris Agreement, a separate instrument under the UNFCCC rather than an amendment.

entries.title: The Paris Agreement: every country pledges

definition.text: An international climate treaty, negotiated in 2015 and signed in 2016, covering mitigation, adaptation and finance.

facts.text: It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and preferably to 1.5 °C, with emissions reaching net zero by mid-century.
It was negotiated by 196 parties at the 2015 UN climate conference near Paris and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
Each country sets its own contributions, and each new target should go beyond the last, though nothing forces a country to set a specific target.
Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, it blurs the line between developed and developing countries, so developing countries must also submit emission-cut plans.
The EU and 194 states, covering over 98% of greenhouse gas emissions, have ratified or joined it; the United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again in 2026.
It recognises loss and damage as a separate pillar, but states it cannot be used as a basis for liability.
Global emissions kept rising after it was signed, and most experts say it is insufficient for its 1.5 °C goal.

entries.title: Nationally determined contributions: each country's own pledge

definition.text: A country's own pledge, under the Paris Agreement, of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change.

facts.text: NDCs are described as being at the heart of the Paris Agreement; each country decides for itself what to contribute.
They must be renewed every five years, and each should be more ambitious than the last, a rule called the principle of progression.
The pledges themselves are not binding, but preparing, communicating and updating them is; there is no way to force a country to meet its target.
Some pledges are unconditional, while others depend on outside finance, technical support or other countries' ambition.
They are the first UNFCCC emission targets that apply equally to developed and developing countries.
Emission cuts must rise 80% beyond current NDCs to likely meet 2 °C; on current trends the chance of staying below 2 °C is only 5%.

entries.title: Article 6: how countries can cooperate on their pledges
entries.article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: The part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their nationally determined contributions.

facts.text: It aims to allow higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation while promoting sustainable development, on condition of environmental integrity, transparency and robust accounting.
It has three pathways: cooperative approaches that trade ITMOs (6.2), a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4) and non-market approaches (6.8).
The core 'Article 6 rulebook' was adopted at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, and later decisions have focused on putting it into practice.
It succeeds the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, with the transition expected to be completed by 2025.
Its impact is debated, especially over environmental integrity, governance capacity and the risk of over-crediting.

entries.contested_note: Analysts debate whether Article 6 transfers mainly lower costs and mobilise finance or undermine integrity through over-crediting, weak baselines and 'hot air'.

entries.title: The convention's ultimate goal: avoiding dangerous interference
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Interpreting ultimate objective in Article 2

definition.text: The UNFCCC's Article 2 goal of stabilising greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate.

facts.text: Article 2 says this should happen fast enough to let ecosystems adapt naturally, keep food production safe and let economic development continue sustainably.
Stabilising concentrations requires global emissions to peak and then decline, and earlier for lower stabilisation levels.
Science can describe climate risks, but deciding which risks count as dangerous needs value judgements.
Following the precautionary principle, acknowledged in Article 3, uncertainty about climate effects is no reason for inaction.

sources.title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

entries.text: Article 2 of {{ref:nature-clim-053}} sets its ultimate objective: stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate. It adds a speed limit. This should happen fast enough to let ecosystems adapt naturally, keep food production safe and let economic development continue sustainably. Stabilising concentrations requires global emissions to peak and then decline, and earlier for lower stabilisation levels. One word is hard. Science can describe climate risks, but deciding which risks count as dangerous needs value judgements. Article 3 acknowledges the precautionary principle, so uncertainty about climate effects is no reason for inaction.

entries.title: Climate targets: goals set by politics and science

definition.text: A measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy, also called a climate goal or pledge, aimed at limiting climate change.

facts.text: Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming, and these underpin carbon budgets and emission targets.
At least 164 countries have climate targets in their national legislation.
Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
An emissions target may differ from a scientific carbon budget, since it can reflect political palatability rather than a specific temperature limit.
Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions, and many rely on negative-emission technologies not yet developed.

entries.text: At least 164 countries have climate targets written into their national law. A climate target, also called a climate goal or pledge, is a measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy aimed at limiting climate change. Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming. These targets underpin carbon budgets and emission targets. Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. An emissions target may differ from what science allows, because it can reflect what is politically palatable. Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions. Many also rely on negative-emission technologies, ways of pulling carbon out of the air, that are not yet developed.

entries.title: Common but differentiated responsibilities: a shared duty, unequally held

definition.text: The principle, set in the 1992 UN climate convention, that all countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage but not to the same degree.

facts.text: Because developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation.
It can be seen as based on the polluter pays principle, with historical contribution and ability to act as the measures of responsibility.
Article 3 of the UNFCCC says developed countries should take the lead in combating climate change.
Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits; under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change.
Critics argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage; developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

entries.contested_note: Some, including US negotiators, argue the rich–poor split is outdated or unfair, while developing countries defend it.
entries.text: All countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage, but not to the same degree. That principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, was set in the 1992 UN climate convention. Developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, so they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation. Article 3 says they should take the lead. The principle can be read as a form of polluter pays, measuring responsibility by historical contribution and ability to act. Its meaning changed over time. Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits. Under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change. It remains disputed. Critics, including US negotiators, argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage. Developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival, while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

entries.title: Adaptation finance: the public money that keeps people safe

definition.text: Climate finance that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: It comes from governments, development finance institutions and multilateral climate funds, and from private sources such as banks, investors, companies and households.
Around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources, partly because adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return.
Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation.
Benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion.
A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030.
Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.

entries.text: Adaptation finance is the part of {{ref:nature-clim-042}} that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change. It can come from governments, development finance institutions and {{ref:nature-clim-047}}, and from banks, investors, companies and households. In practice, around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources. Adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return. Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation. The benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion. A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030. Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.
entries.text_plain: Adaptation finance is the part of Climate finance: following the money that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change. entries.title: Mitigation finance: the bulk of climate money

definition.text: Investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: Mitigation accounts for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance.
Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to renewable energy; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors.
Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation.
The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.
The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year.

entries.text: Mitigation finance is investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. It dominates, accounting for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance. entries.title: The global stocktake: checking the world's progress

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly review of how far the world as a whole has got toward the agreement's goals.

facts.text: It links countries' NDCs to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next NDCs to raise ambition.
It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out.
After debate, it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance.
It runs in three phases: collecting information, technical assessment, and political messages for policy.
The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

entries.text: Every five years, the Paris Agreement asks a collective question: how far has the world as a whole got toward its goals? The global stocktake is that review. It links countries' {{ref:nature-clim-071}} to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next pledges and raise ambition. It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out. Its scope was debated. In the end it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance. It runs in three phases. First comes collecting information, then technical assessment, and finally political messages for policy. The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

entries.title: The enhanced transparency framework: checking what countries do

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's common system, under Article 13, for monitoring, reporting and verifying what countries do on climate and the support they give or receive.

facts.text: Parties are legally bound to have their progress toward their NDCs checked by technical expert review.
Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review.
It has built-in flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

entries.text: Pledges mean little if no one can check them. The enhanced transparency framework, set by Article 13 of {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, is a common system for checking countries' climate action. Developed and developing countries alike report every two years and face technical and peer review. It has flexibility in scope, detail and frequency of reporting for countries with less capacity.

entries.title: Climate debt: who owes whom for a warming planet

definition.text: The debt said to be owed by developed countries to developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions.

facts.text: It is part of the broader idea of ecological debt and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s.
Its two main parts are adaptation debt, help owed for adapting to climate change, and emissions debt, owed for excessive past emissions.
It gained attention at the 2009 Copenhagen conference, where developing countries led by Bolivia sought its repayment.
Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs; criticism comes mostly from developed nations.
Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts.
Some say that, even if ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

entries.contested_note: Developing countries and NGOs press for climate debt to be repaid, while developed nations and some analysts reject the idea that a debt is owed.
entries.text: At the 2009 Copenhagen conference, developing countries led by Bolivia demanded repayment of a debt. Not a loan, but climate debt: what developed countries are said to owe developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions. The idea is part of the broader concept of {{ref:nature-gov-199}} and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s. It has two main parts. {{ref:nature-clim-081}} is the help owed for adapting to climate change. {{ref:nature-clim-080}} is owed for excessive past emissions. Views split along familiar lines. Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs, and criticism mostly from developed nations. Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts. Others say that even if the idea is ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

entries.title: Action for Climate Empowerment: education and participation
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Six priority areas (Action for Climate Empowerment)

definition.text: The UNFCCC's name, adopted in 2015, for its work on climate education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information and cooperation on these.

facts.text: It refers to Article 6 of the 1992 convention text.
It calls on governments to run education and awareness programmes, train experts, open up information and promote public participation.

entries.title: Why critics say the UN climate process has failed
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#Criticism of processes

definition.text: The argument that the UNFCCC and Kyoto Protocol have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended.

facts.text: With over 190 countries deciding by consensus, small groups of countries can often block progress.
Japan refused a second Kyoto term in 2010 because it would face limits its competitors China, India and Indonesia did not.
The UNFCCC also failed, mainly under Kyoto, to transfer environmentally sound technologies to developing countries.

entries.contested_note: Critics call the consensus process ineffective, while historical responsibility for emissions remains a contentious issue in the talks.

sources.title: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

entries.text: Critics argue that the UN climate convention and {{ref:nature-clim-056}} have failed to cut greenhouse gas emissions as intended. With over 190 countries deciding by consensus, small groups of countries can often block progress. Competition gets in the way. In 2010 Japan refused a second Kyoto term because it would face limits that its competitors China, India and Indonesia did not. The convention also failed, mainly under Kyoto, to transfer environmentally sound technologies to developing countries. Historical responsibility for emissions remains contentious in the talks.

entries.title: National communications: each country's climate report
entries.article: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change#National communication

definition.text: A report that each country party to the UNFCCC submits on its climate measures and vulnerabilities.

facts.text: Developed countries must submit one every four years; developing countries should do so.
They are often several hundred pages long, while the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement are shorter and less detailed.
Some least developed countries have not submitted one in 5–15 years, mostly for lack of capacity.

entries.title: The Doha Amendment: Kyoto's shrinking second act

definition.text: The 2012 extension of the Kyoto Protocol that set a second commitment period running to 2020.

facts.text: It was agreed on 8 December 2012 in Doha, with 37 countries holding binding targets, and set 2015 as the date for a successor agreement.
Japan, New Zealand and Russia took on no new targets, and the second period covered only about 11% of global annual emissions.
It entered into force on 31 December 2020, after 144 states accepted it, on the very day the second period ended.

entries.text: On 8 December 2012 in Doha, countries extended {{ref:nature-clim-056}} with a second commitment period running to 2020. Thirty-seven countries held binding targets, and 2015 was set as the date for a successor agreement. Japan, New Zealand and Russia took on no new targets, and the second period covered only about 11% of global annual emissions. The ending was awkward. The amendment entered into force on 31 December 2020, after 144 states accepted it, on the very day the second period ended.

entries.title: Hot air: surplus allowances that cut nothing

definition.text: The large surplus of Kyoto emission allowances held by former Soviet-bloc economies, whose sale would not actually cut emissions.

facts.text: Russia, Ukraine and the new EU-12 states had surplus allowances because their emissions targets were set above their actual emissions.
These transition economies saw the surplus as 'headroom' to grow their economies.
Countries short of allowances could buy them from those with a surplus, but without further commitments this trade would not reduce emissions.

entries.text: Under Kyoto, Russia, Ukraine and the new EU-12 states got emission targets set above their actual emissions. That left them with a large surplus of allowances, permits to emit, which became known as hot air. These transition economies saw the surplus as 'headroom' to grow their economies. Countries short of allowances could buy them from those with a surplus. But without further commitments that trade would not reduce emissions at all.

entries.title: Kyoto's compliance mechanism: penalties with little bite

definition.text: The Kyoto Protocol's system for monitoring whether parties meet their commitments and penalising those that do not.

facts.text: A party that misses its emissions limit must make up the difference in the second commitment period plus an additional 30%.
It is also suspended from making transfers under emissions trading.
Grubb judged the treaty's consequences for non-compliance weak compared with domestic law, and the compliance section was hotly contested in the Marrakesh Accords.

Grubb judged the consequences for non-compliance weak compared with domestic law, and the compliance section was hotly contested in the Marrakesh Accords.

entries.title: The 2 degree target: the line the world drew

definition.text: The international policy goal of keeping global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels.

facts.text: It is a political decision based on science about the likely consequences of warming, dating from the 2009 Copenhagen conference, and is central to the Paris Agreement.
It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature.
The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss.
The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100, exceeding the target.
An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down by late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

entries.text: Keep global warming below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels. That is the 2 degree target, an international policy goal. It is often criticised as too high, since two degrees of warming would have serious effects on people and nature. The IPCC's 2018 special report warned that 2 °C rather than 1.5 °C would worsen extreme weather, sea-ice loss, sea-level rise, coral bleaching and ecosystem loss. The world is not on course to meet it. The UNFCCC predicts a likely 2.1 to 2.9 °C of warming by 2100. An 'overshoot pathway' would pass 2 °C and then bring warming back down late in the century, requiring management over many decades.

entries.title: Is the Paris Agreement working

definition.text: The debate over whether the Paris Agreement can achieve its temperature goals.

facts.text: Most experts say it is insufficient for the 1.5 °C goal, though some argue it is too early to judge.
UNEP said in 2020 that current commitments would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100.
Studies in Nature found that as of 2017 none of the major industrialised nations was implementing its pledged policies.
The stocktake report credits it with a large effect: the expected 2100 warming fell from 3.7–4.8 °C in 2010 to 2.4–2.6 °C at COP 27.

entries.contested_note: Most experts judge the agreement insufficient for 1.5 °C, while others point to the drop in projected warming since it was adopted.

entries.title: Intended nationally determined contributions: the first drafts

definition.text: The initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges countries made before the 2015 Paris Agreement, which became their first NDCs.

facts.text: UNFCCC parties were asked to publish them at the 2013 Warsaw climate conference.
The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones.
Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015; 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

entries.text: Before the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries made initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges called intended nationally determined contributions. These became their first {{ref:nature-clim-071}}. Parties were asked to publish them at the November 2013 Warsaw climate conference. The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones. Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015. The timing was tight: 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

entries.title: The ratchet mechanism: tightening pledges every five years

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges, designed to raise countries' climate ambition over time.

facts.text: Countries publish biennial progress reports that undergo technical review.
These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all NDCs together are enough.
The stocktake's findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

entries.text: A ratchet turns only one way. The Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism is a five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges designed to raise climate ambition over time. Countries publish progress reports every two years, which undergo technical review. These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all pledges together are enough. Its findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

entries.title: Pledge and review: from rejected idea to central approach

definition.text: A way of organising international climate action in which each country makes its own pledge, others review its progress, and stronger pledges follow.

facts.text: It is a 'bottom-up' approach, unlike legally binding targets imposed 'top-down' by a central body.
Japan first proposed it in 1991; it was rejected at the first COP in 1995 in favour of binding targets, which led to the Kyoto Protocol.
Revived at Copenhagen in 2009, it drew pledges from countries producing about 80% of global emissions, versus 25% covered by Kyoto's first targets.
By 2015 it was the central approach, though at Paris the pledges were renamed Nationally Determined Contributions.
It became dominant because binding greenhouse-gas targets proved hard to agree and impossible to enforce on powerful nations.
Critics called it 'hedge and retreat' or 'second best', while others called it an essential pillar of mitigation.

entries.contested_note: Environmental groups and some academics have called pledge-and-review inadequate, while other academics see it as essential.

entries.title: The Glasgow Climate Pact: phasing down coal

definition.text: The agreement reached at the 2021 UN climate conference (COP26) in Glasgow.

facts.text: It was the first climate agreement explicitly planning to reduce unabated coal use.
A pledge to 'phase out' coal was changed late in the talks to 'phase down', at the urging of coal-reliant countries such as India and China.
Countries agreed to revisit their emission plans in 2022 to keep the 1.5 °C target within reach, and committed to climate finance for developing countries.
Around it, more than 140 countries had pledged net-zero emissions and more than 100 pledged to reverse deforestation by 2030.

entries.title: The adaptation finance gap: needs ten times the money
entries.article: Climate finance#Current levels of financing and the finance gap

definition.text: The difference between the estimated cost of adapting to climate change and the money available for adaptation.

facts.text: International public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year between 2017 and 2021.
On 2017–2021 data, estimated needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments.
A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans estimated developing countries' adaptation needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030.
More public and private finance, remittances and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed could help close it.

entries.text: Between 2017 and 2021, international public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year. The adaptation finance gap is the difference between the estimated cost of adapting and the money available for it. A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans put developing countries' needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030. On 2017–2021 data, needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments. Several things could help close it: more public and private finance, remittances, the money migrants send home, and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed.

entries.title: The climate finance gap: hard to measure, easy to inflate

definition.text: The shortfall between the climate investment that is needed and what is actually provided.

facts.text: Estimates of the gap vary with the places, sectors, timescale, target and assumptions used.
Research finds bilateral climate finance well below official figures, partly because there is no agreed definition of international climate finance and no oversight.
This has let non-climate projects be counted and raised doubts about official reporting.

entries.title: Debt-for-climate swaps: turning repayments into projects

definition.text: A deal in which a country's debt is repaid on new discounted terms and the repayments, in local currency, are redirected to domestic climate projects.

facts.text: Projects funded this way can include carbon sequestration, renewable energy and conservation of biodiversity and oceans.
In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work.
Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism in a similar debt-for-nature swap.

entries.title: Multilateral climate funds: pooled money from many governments

definition.text: Funds governed by several national governments together that pay out money for climate action.

facts.text: As of 2022, the UNFCCC coordinated five: the Green Climate Fund, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund, the Special Climate Change Fund and the Global Environment Facility.
The World Bank coordinates the Climate Investment Funds, active since 2008, made up of the Clean Technology Fund and the Strategic Climate Fund.
Some give only grants; others also use concessional loans, equity and risk tools meant to crowd in other finance.
In 2016 the four main multilateral climate funds approved $2.78 billion of project support.

entries.title: The Green Climate Fund: the largest pot, and its quarrels

definition.text: A climate finance fund set up under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation.

facts.text: It is considered the world's largest fund of its kind and is the largest of the five multilateral climate funds coordinated by the UNFCCC.
It was named in the 2009 Copenhagen Accord, formally established at the 2010 Cancun conference, and its governing instrument was adopted in Durban in 2011.
It is based in Songdo, South Korea, and governed by a 24-member board with a secretariat.
As of November 2026 its portfolio was over $22.3 billion USD, or over $87.1 billion USD including co-financing.

One of its most controversial features is the Private Sector Facility: many rich countries want it to attract institutional investors, while developing countries and NGOs want pro-poor finance for small firms.
In March 2015 its board refused an explicit ban on fossil fuel projects, effectively allowing coal plants to be funded.

entries.contested_note: Rich and developing countries disagree over whether its private-sector arm should court large investors or support small firms, and over relying on private rather than pledged public money.

entries.title: Private climate finance: why public money is not enough

definition.text: Climate investment from private sources such as banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households.

facts.text: Public budgets are often too small for large infrastructure projects, especially in lower-income countries, so private money is seen as needed to cover the shortfall.
Climate-friendly projects can cost more up front and carry more risk than fossil-fuel ones, so they must be bankable to attract private investors.
Over 90% of private climate flows are estimated to stay within national borders.
The IMF and OECD warn that private capital alone cannot close the gap, since many adaptation and innovation projects bring high social benefits but low private returns.

entries.title: The Kigali Amendment: tackling the ozone fix that warms

definition.text: A 2016 amendment to the Montreal Protocol under which countries promised to cut their use of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by more than 80% over 30 years.

facts.text: It came into force on 1 January 2019.
HFCs replaced CFCs and do not harm the ozone layer, but they are greenhouse gases with a high global warming potential.
A 2009 study calculated that a fast HFC phasedown could avoid up to 8.8 Gt CO2-eq per year of emissions by 2050.

entries.title: The Montreal Protocol's Multilateral Fund

definition.text: The fund that helps developing countries with low use of ozone-depleting substances comply with the Montreal Protocol.

facts.text: It serves countries using less than 0.3 kg of ozone-depleting substances per person a year; 147 of the 196 parties qualify.
It embodies the principle of common but differentiated responsibility to protect the global commons.
It is run by an executive committee with equal numbers of industrialised and developing countries, the first such democratically managed treaty fund.

entries.title: Climate clubs: fixing free-riding by excluding outsiders

definition.text: A voluntary coalition of countries that agree on a common climate standard, such as a carbon price, and penalise non-members.

facts.text: Membership is voluntary and excludable, avoiding the need for every country to agree.
Countries join for the shared benefit of lower global emissions and to escape sanctions, such as tariffs, imposed on outsiders.
William Nordhaus pioneered the idea in 2015: members price carbon and charge a fee on imports from countries without similar pricing.
A 2025 Econometrica paper found such a club, with border taxes to deter free-riding, could achieve 33–68% of the globally optimal carbon reduction.
The G7 Climate Club, launched in December 2022, favours partnerships over penalties and had 46 member states as of May 2025.
Exporting countries fearing fees and researchers sceptical of carbon pricing have criticised it; the EU's CBAM has been called a possible first climate club.

entries.contested_note: Critics fear export fees and doubt carbon pricing, while others argue supposed losers such as China and India would gain.

entries.title: Additionality of climate finance: is the money really new

definition.text: The rule that climate finance given to developing countries should be new money, additional to existing development aid.

facts.text: The Cancun agreements require such finance, including through the Green Climate Fund, to be new and additional.
New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years.
There is no strict definition of additionality, which has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging CDM emission reductions.

entries.text: Climate finance given to developing countries is supposed to be new money, additional to existing development aid. The Cancun agreements require this, including for money through {{ref:nature-clim-051}}. New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years. But there is no strict definition of additionality. The same vagueness has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging emission reductions under {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}.

entries.title: Climate reparations: compensation as a moral debt

definition.text: Requested loss-and-damage payments for harm caused by climate change, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions and possibly including debt cancellation.

facts.text: Unlike plain 'loss and damage', the term treats compensation as an ethical and moral obligation that holds countries accountable for past emissions.
A 2023 study estimated that the top 21 fossil fuel companies will owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative reparations over 2025–2050.
Proposed channels include an international compensation commission, lawsuits, the polluter pays principle, debt forgiveness and direct grants.
The wealthiest nations have consistently opposed it at the UNFCCC, and before COP27 talks were steered to 'cooperation and facilitation' rather than liability.

entries.contested_note: Developing nations and campaigners press for reparations, while rich nations oppose them and some argue current generations are not responsible for past emissions.

entries.title: Green banks: public money that draws in private investors

definition.text: A usually public or quasi-public financial institution that works with private investors to speed up the spread of clean energy technologies.

facts.text: It uses public funds to leverage private investment in clean technologies that are commercially viable but slow to spread.
It lowers risk for private investors through tools such as concessional finance, guarantees, credit enhancement, co-investment and securitisation.
Its public capital can be reinvested again and again across many clean energy projects.
The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allotted $27 billion to green banks through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund.
