entries.title: The Bali Action Plan: a road map toward Copenhagen
entries.article: United Nations Climate Change Conference#2007: COP 13/CMP 3, Bali, Indonesia

definition.text: The 2007 decision at COP 13 in Bali that set a timeline and structure for negotiating a climate framework for after 2012.

facts.text: Developed countries agreed to comparable quantified emission targets, while developing countries agreed to nationally appropriate mitigation actions supported by technology, finance and capacity building.
It set up a new body, the Ad Hoc Working Group on Long-term Cooperative Action, for these negotiations, which ran through 2008 and 2009 toward Copenhagen.
The Bali conference also drew attention to the 20% of global emissions caused by deforestation.

entries.title: ITMOs: emission cuts that cross borders
entries.article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.2: Cooperative approaches

definition.text: Measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement and that count toward the buyer's NDC.

facts.text: Article 6.2 lets countries trade them through bilateral or multilateral deals without using the central crediting mechanism.
They can be expressed in tonnes of CO2-equivalent or other metrics, and can come from crediting projects or from linked emissions trading systems.
By 2024 over 80 bilateral agreements were in place; the first completed trade, between Thailand and Switzerland, was reported in January 2024.

entries.contested_note: Commentators disagree on whether these transfers mainly cut costs or risk over-crediting and 'hot air'.

entries.title: Corresponding adjustments: counting each cut once
entries.article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Accounting, reporting and transparency architecture

definition.text: The accounting step that makes sure an emission reduction transferred between countries is counted in only one country's NDC.

facts.text: It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit.
Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this shows up in their NDC accounting.
Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

entries.text: If one country sells an emission cut to another, both cannot claim it. A corresponding adjustment is the accounting step that makes sure a transferred reduction counts in only one country's pledge. It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit. Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this appears in their accounts. Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.
entries.text_plain: If one country sells an emission cut to another, both cannot claim it. A corresponding adjustment is the accounting step that makes sure a transferred reduction counts in only one country's pledge. It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit. Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this appears in their accounts. Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

entries.title: Non-market approaches: cooperation without trading
entries.article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.8: Non-market approaches

definition.text: Voluntary cooperation between countries under Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement that involves no international transfer of emission reductions.

facts.text: They can combine mitigation and adaptation and involve finance, technology transfer and capacity building.
A work programme and the Glasgow Committee on Non-market Approaches were set up at COP26 in 2021; the committee began work in 2022.

entries.title: The Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism: UN-supervised credits
entries.article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (Article 6.4)

definition.text: A UN-supervised scheme set up under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals.

facts.text: Its credits are called Article 6.4 emission reductions (A6.4ERs) and are tracked in a registry with unique identifiers.
A share of proceeds goes to the Adaptation Fund, and a portion of units is cancelled to deliver an overall mitigation in global emissions.
Activities are validated, registered, monitored and independently verified before units are issued, under the oversight of the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body.

entries.title: The global climate regime: the rules of the game

definition.text: The worldwide framework of rules for regulating how human activity affects the climate system, in order to limit climate change.

facts.text: Its framework was set by the UNFCCC, and its first legally binding result was the Kyoto Protocol.
Between 2013 and 2015 there was no legally binding global climate regime, and the voluntary Copenhagen Accord pledges served in practice.
The 2015 Paris Agreement became the regime, with all countries signed on to balancing greenhouse gas sources and sinks in the second half of the century.

Governments usually give soft loans to projects they consider worthwhile, and the World Bank and other development institutions give them to developing countries.
Some official development assistance is counted as the concessional value of soft loans.

entries.title: Contraction and Convergence: equal shares per person

definition.text: A proposed global framework that shrinks total greenhouse gas emissions to a safe level while bringing every country's emissions per person to the same level.

facts.text: It was conceived by the Global Commons Institute in the early 1990s and is expressed as a simple mathematical formula.
Emission entitlements start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated rate of convergence.
Earlier convergence gives more entitlements to low-emitting, typically poorer, countries; the rate is described as a key equity lever.
Critics say a per-person basis could reward population growth, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

Critics say a per-person basis could reward countries whose populations grow, so the model lets negotiators fix a population base year.

entries.title: The ICJ climate opinion: a court weighs in
entries.article: Obligations of States in respect of climate change

definition.text: A 2025 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice on what international law requires states to do to protect the climate, requested by the UN General Assembly in 2023.

facts.text: The request, led by Vanuatu and driven by Pacific island students, was adopted by the General Assembly by consensus on 29 March 2023.
The Court unanimously held that the UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement create binding obligations, including submitting NDCs and acting on common but differentiated responsibilities.
Failing to meet these obligations is an internationally wrongful act that can require cessation, guarantees of non-repetition and full reparation, given a clear causal link.
Because the climate is a global common good, any state may invoke another's responsibility for breaches; the opinion is not binding but is expected to be used in courts.

entries.title: The New Collective Quantified Goal: from $100 billion to $300 billion

definition.text: The new climate finance target, negotiated at COP29 in 2024, for supporting developing countries after 2025, building on the earlier $100 billion a year goal.

facts.text: The earlier goal, set in 2009 and agreed at Cancún in 2010, was for developed countries to mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
That target was missed in 2020 and reached only in 2022; an OECD report gave $132.8 billion in 2023 and $136.7 billion in 2024.
At COP29 in Baku, delegations agreed that developed nations would pledge $300 billion a year by 2035, from public and private sources.
Poorer nations called this insufficient and many pushed for at least $500 billion; some critics, including UN officials, called it a betrayal.
A key tension was the donor base: the US and EU wanted countries such as China and the Gulf states to contribute, but the text only encouraged voluntary contributions.
Talks at COP30 were expected to address scaling finance from the $300 billion agreed in Baku to $1.3 trillion.

entries.title: A short history of climate policy
entries.article: History of climate change policy and politics

definition.text: The history of political actions, policies, controversies and activism concerning climate change.

facts.text: Formal global environmental politics began with the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm.
The first World Climate Conference in 1979 framed climate change as a global political issue, and the IPCC was set up in 1988.
Efforts have mostly sought consensus at the UN under the UNFCCC, with the 1987 Montreal Protocol cited as a precedent that this can work.
Critics of this top-down approach propose bottom-up governance instead.
Adaptation was long seen as a distraction from mitigation and gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder.
Climate policy became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s, with the US partisan gap the widest in history in 2020.

It gained attention only around 2009 and 2010, after the Copenhagen summit made progress on emissions look harder. Climate policy also became increasingly polarised in the late 2000s. By 2020 the US partisan gap was the widest in history.

entries.title: The first global stocktake: a verdict delivered in Dubai

definition.text: The first Paris Agreement stocktake, concluded at COP 28 in Dubai in December 2023 as part of the UAE Consensus.

facts.text: It found pledges insufficient: a 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected.
It set 2030 targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double global energy efficiency.
For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050.
It set up the loss and damage fund with $700 million in start-up capital, to be administered by the World Bank.

entries.title: Adaptation debt: paying for harm others caused

definition.text: The compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that poorer nations suffer the worst consequences of a problem they did little to cause.
Lacking infrastructure and capital, poor countries often borrow at higher interest to recover from disasters, worsening their prospects.
The UNFCCC notes it can be met through financial aid and help coping with natural disasters.

entries.title: Emissions debt: overusing the atmosphere

definition.text: The part of climate debt said to be owed by developed countries for having used more than their fair share of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions.

facts.text: The atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions is called the total carbon space; the claim is that rich countries overused their fair allocation of it.
Since around 1750 the United States alone has produced 25% of all carbon emissions, and developed countries together 70%.
Repayment would mean helping poorer countries industrialise cleanly and sharing out the remaining carbon space by population.

entries.title: Too weak or too strong: the case against Kyoto

definition.text: The debate over whether the Kyoto Protocol's commitments were too weak, too costly, or wrongly designed.

facts.text: Some environmentalists and scientists found its commitments too weak, while several economists thought them stronger than justified.
Stavins called it 'too little, too fast', and Stern said its lack of a long-term goal kept it from sending a credible signal.
Critics objected that it set cuts only for rich countries and none for fast-growing economies such as China and India.
Nordhaus argued its quantity-type instruments were less efficient than price-type ones and that it might be better redesigned as a global carbon tax.

entries.title: The Cancún agreements: pledges and a new fund

definition.text: Decisions taken at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún, including national mitigation pledges and the creation of the Green Climate Fund.

facts.text: They included voluntary pledges from 76 developed and developing countries, which together produced 85% of global annual emissions in 2010.
Parties agreed that future warming should stay below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.
Developed countries committed to jointly mobilise US$100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
They require climate finance to developing countries to be 'new' and 'additional' to existing aid.

entries.title: The Copenhagen Accord: a deal the conference only noted

definition.text: A 2009 agreement produced by a group of countries at the Copenhagen climate conference, which the conference only 'took note of'.

facts.text: It said global warming should be limited to below 2.0 °C, which the UNFCCC reads as relative to pre-industrial temperatures.

entries.title: Ecological economics: the economy inside the ecosystem

definition.text: A field of research, drawing on many disciplines, that studies how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together over time and space.

facts.text: It treats the economy as a subsystem of Earth's larger ecosystem and stresses keeping natural capital intact, which sets it apart from mainstream environmental economics.
Ecological economists favour strong sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
A main aim is to ground economic thinking in physical reality, especially the laws of thermodynamics and knowledge of living systems.
Besides efficient allocation, it puts weight on two further problems: fair distribution, and the size of the economy relative to the ecosystems it relies on.
Where mainstream economists tend to be technological optimists, ecological economists lean towards scepticism and favour precaution, since destroying key environmental resources may be irreversible.
Its topics include weak versus strong sustainability, energy economics and energy accounting, environmental services, cost shifting, modelling and monetary policy.
Economist Malte Faber describes the field as defined by its focus on nature, justice and time.
It was founded as a modern discipline in the 1980s through the work of European and American academics.

entries.title: Heterodox economics: the schools outside the mainstream

definition.text: A broad term for schools of economic thought that are not generally seen as part of mainstream economics.

facts.text: It is defined by contrast with whichever schools are most influential at a given time and place, so it has no fixed definition.
Schools usually counted as heterodox include the Austrian, ecological, Marxist-historical, post-Keynesian and modern monetary approaches.
Four frames of analysis are central to heterodox thought: history, natural systems, uncertainty and power.
It is an umbrella term rather than a single school, but its schools often see neoclassical economics as flawed.
Economist Marcos Lisboa argues that the assumptions critics attack are often not essential to neoclassical economics.
Frederic S. Lee estimated in 2007 that 5 to 10 percent of American economists were heterodox.
Student movements such as Rethinking Economics campaign for more pluralism, including heterodox approaches, in economics degrees.

entries.title: Systems ecology: ecosystems as complex systems

definition.text: A holistic, interdisciplinary branch of ecology that studies ecosystems as complex systems, applying general systems theory to ecology.

facts.text: Its central idea is that an ecosystem is a complex system with emergent properties.
It is especially concerned with how human interventions affect ecosystem functioning, and so includes economics in studying ecological-economic systems.
A central feature is applying the principles of energetics to all systems at every scale; Howard T. Odum was its most notable proponent.
Ecological work deals almost entirely with open systems, which exchange with their surroundings across their boundaries.
Ecological engineering combines systems ecology with engineering design.

entries.text: An ecosystem, in systems ecology, is more than the sum of its species. This holistic branch of ecology studies ecosystems as complex systems with emergent properties, features that appear only in the whole. It applies general systems theory to ecology, and its central tool is energetics, the principles of energy applied to systems at every scale. {{ref:nature-hist-063}} was its most notable proponent. Ecological work deals almost entirely with open systems, which exchange with their surroundings across their boundaries. Because the field cares about how human interventions affect ecosystems, it brings economics into the study of ecological-economic systems. Combined with engineering design, it becomes ecological engineering.

Because the field cares about how human interventions affect ecosystems, it brings economics into the study of ecological-economic systems. Combined with engineering design, it becomes ecological engineering.

entries.title: Cost shifting: when harm is the business model

definition.text: The ecological-economics view that environmental and social harms are not occasional side effects ('externalities') but costs that businesses routinely shift onto others.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp's work explains why calling these harms 'externalities' is a misnomer: modern business makes profit by shifting costs onto others as normal practice.
Clive Spash notes that externality theory wrongly treats environmental and social problems as small exceptions in an otherwise efficient system.
On this view, internalising an odd externality does nothing about the structural problem.
Joan Martinez Alier points out that most affected consumers are future generations, who cannot influence today's prices.
By contrast, Paul Hawken argues that unsustainable goods are cheaper only because of a hidden subsidy paid by the environment, communities or future generations.

entries.contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that harms can be corrected by internalising externalities.

entries.title: The case against putting a price on nature

definition.text: The argument, made by Douglas McCauley among others, that putting money values on nature and its services can harm conservation.

facts.text: Not all ecosystem services are financially beneficial: mangroves protect coasts, but wolves hunt cattle.

Money values tie conservation to fluctuating markets: bee pollination near a Costa Rican farm was valued at over US$60,000 a year until coffee prices fell and the fields were replanted with pineapple, which needs no bees.
Human ingenuity can replace ecosystem services by artificial means, which also lowers their value.
Conserving an ecosystem is not always more profitable than altering it, as local fish trade after the Nile perch was introduced to Lake Victoria shows.
McCauley concludes that campaigns should appeal to morality rather than money.

entries.contested_note: Monetary valuation of nature is widely accepted among ecologists and conservationists, but some argue it is inherently false.

entries.title: Growth versus development: more is not the same as better

definition.text: The distinction ecological economics draws between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life.

facts.text: Ecological economists argue that neoclassical economics confuses growth with development.
Beyond modest levels, higher consumption per person may not raise well-being and may harm the environment and society.
Growth of this harmful kind is sometimes called uneconomic growth.
Well-being in ecological economics is distinguished from the welfare concept used in mainstream and environmental economics.

entries.text: An economy can get bigger without people's lives getting better. Ecological economics draws a line between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life. entries.title: From Malthus to a journal: how ecological economics began

definition.text: How ecological economics grew from 19th-century and early 20th-century ideas into a discipline with its own society and journal by 1989.

facts.text: Its roots go back to the 19th-century Romantics, Malthus's worries about population and Mill's hope for a stationary state.
Frederick Soddy's 1926 book criticised the idea of the economy as a perpetual motion machine able to create infinite wealth.
Georgescu-Roegen's The Entropy Law and the Economic Process (1971) gave the field a framework based on material and energy flows.
The first organised meetings began in 1982 in Sweden; the field was formally founded in 1988 after a series of conferences.
In 1989 the International Society for Ecological Economics was founded and began publishing the journal Ecological Economics, with Robert Costanza as first president and editor.
The main founders were Herman Daly and Robert Costanza from the US, AnnMari Jansson from Sweden and Juan Martínez-Alier from Spain.

entries.title: The laws of thermodynamics: why no machine runs forever

definition.text: The basic physical laws governing energy, heat, work, temperature and entropy, which rule out things such as perpetual motion machines.

facts.text: Thermodynamics traditionally recognises three laws, with a more basic 'zeroth law' defining thermal equilibrium and temperature added later.
The first law says energy cannot be created or destroyed; the second says the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases.
The first two laws rule out machines that make work without energy input, and machines that turn heat spontaneously into work.
The first and second laws were established by 1860 through Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson.
Ecological economics uses the first and second laws to build economic models that respect physical limits; by these laws a perpetual motion economy is impossible.

Ecological economics uses them to build models that respect physical limits. By these laws, a perpetual motion economy is impossible.

entries.title: Entropy: the measure of energy spreading out

definition.text: A physical quantity often described as a measure of how spread out, or dispersed, energy is in a system; loosely, its degree of disorder.

facts.text: By the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy of an isolated system tends not to decrease.
Lower entropy marks more useful energy: energy supplied at a high temperature tends to be more useful than the same amount at a lower temperature.
Rudolf Clausius named the concept in 1865, from the Greek word for 'transformation'.
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen brought entropy into ecological economics, coining 'entropy pessimism', a position Herman Daly continued to promote.
Because of rising entropy, recovering materials dispersed as pollution and waste needs energy and resources that rise steeply as the recycled share grows.
Entropy is the only physical quantity that seems to give time a direction, sometimes called the arrow of time.

entries.title: Uneconomic growth: when getting bigger makes life worse

definition.text: Economic growth that reflects or causes a fall in quality of life.

facts.text: Herman Daly says it occurs when extra production costs more in resources and well-being than the goods made are worth.
The costs arise from the social and environmental sacrifices of a growing economy encroaching on the ecosystem.
David Suzuki argued in the 1990s that ecosystems can sustain only about 1.5–3% new growth per year, so demanding more from farms or forests eats into natural capital.
It is described as a pervasive ecological market failure: in a 'full-world economy' the ecological costs of growth may exceed its benefits.
The idea is usually credited to Daly, though some credit Marilyn Waring, who developed it in her study of the UN System of National Accounts.

entries.title: Spaceship Earth: one ship, limited supplies, one crew

definition.text: A worldview that sees Earth as a spaceship with limited supplies, whose passengers must act as one crew for the common good.

facts.text: The earliest known use is in Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879).
Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay contrasted the past 'cowboy economy' of seemingly endless resources with a future 'spaceman economy' with no unlimited reservoirs for extraction or pollution.
Boulding argued the economic system must fit itself to an ecological system with limited pools of resources.
Buckminster Fuller popularised the phrase in his 1968 Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth.
UN Secretary-General U Thant used it on Earth Day 1971, referring to the services Earth provides and our duty to protect it.
Sociologist Steffen Roth argues a realised Spaceship Earth would be the most total institution in human history.

entries.title: The first law of thermodynamics: energy is never made or lost

definition.text: The law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

facts.text: In an isolated system, the total of all forms of energy stays constant.
It distinguishes two main ways energy moves into or out of a system: as heat and as work.
It has been precisely supported, and never violated, in many careful experiments.
Kenneth Boulding used the conservation of matter and energy to argue that the flow of resources through the economy roughly measures GNP, so GNP should be treated as a cost to minimise.

entries.text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. That is the first law of thermodynamics, the conservation of energy applied to heat and work. The law has been precisely supported, and never violated, in many careful experiments. Kenneth Boulding drew an economic lesson from it. Because matter and energy are conserved, the flow of resources through the economy roughly measures GNP, the yearly value of a nation's output. GNP, he argued, should therefore be treated as a cost to minimize.

entries.title: Embodied energy: the energy hidden inside things

definition.text: The total energy needed to produce a good or service, counted as if it were stored inside the product.

facts.text: It aims to add up the energy of a product's whole life cycle, from raw material extraction and transport to manufacture, installation and disposal.
Because energy use usually brings greenhouse gas emissions, it helps judge whether a product adds to or reduces global warming.
A key use is comparing the energy a product produces or saves with the energy used to make it.
Common units are MJ/kg and tonnes of CO2; converting between them depends on the energy source used.
Values vary widely because there is no international agreement on data and methods, though products can still be ranked against each other.
Today's main methods grew out of Wassily Leontief's input-output model, adapted by Hannon to ecosystem energy flows.

entries.title: Exergy: the part of energy that can do work

definition.text: The maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it comes into balance with its surroundings; often called 'available energy'.

facts.text: It depends on both the system and its environment, arising from the difference between them.
Energy in and out always balance by the first law, but in real processes part of the exergy input is always destroyed, as the second law requires.
Solar radiation provides most of the exergy for processes on Earth, including those that sustain life.
Exergy use has spread from engineering to industrial ecology, ecological economics and systems ecology.
Some systems ecologists see exergy as the natural world's analogue of economic currency.
Zoran Rant proposed the concept in 1956, extending work by Gibbs and Helmholtz.

entries.title: Energy return on investment: it takes energy to get energy

definition.text: The ratio of usable energy delivered by an energy source to the energy spent to obtain it.

facts.text: If EROI is one or less, the source becomes a net energy sink and can no longer serve as an energy source.
A fuel or energy source needs an EROI of at least 3:1 to be viable as a major source.
Charles A. S. Hall popularised energy analysis; his 1984 paper on the cover of Science gave EROI its greatest exposure.
Only human-applied energy counts as invested: sunlight driving biofuel crops is left out.
When EROI of an economy's main energy sources falls, energy gets harder to obtain and its relative price may rise.
For US fossil fuel discovery the ratio fell from about 1000:1 in 1919 to only 5:1 in the 2010s.
Researchers disagree on how far back into the supply chain to count energy inputs, so they reach different numbers for the same source.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree on how to measure energy inputs, and an IEA-endorsed method gives more favourable values for solar panels.

entries.title: The stationary state: the classical end of growth
entries.article: Steady-state economy#Concept of the stationary state in classical economics

definition.text: The classical economists' idea that an economy would eventually stop growing and settle with a constant population and stock of capital.

facts.text: Classical economists contrasted scarce farmland with growing population and capital.
Capital accumulation would end once the rate of profit fell to a minimum or zero.
Adam Smith believed every national economy would sooner or later reach stationarity.
Unlike Smith and Ricardo, John Stuart Mill was optimistic about the stationary state, making what has been called a quality-of-life argument for it.

entries.text: The classical economists expected growth to stop. Farmland was scarce, while population and {{ref:nature-econ-083}} kept growing. Once the rate of profit fell to a minimum or zero, capital accumulation would end. The economy would then settle into a stationary state, with constant population and capital. Adam Smith believed every national economy would sooner or later get there, and he and Ricardo saw it gloomily. John Stuart Mill did not. He welcomed the stationary state, making what has been called a quality-of-life argument for it.

entries.title: Buddhist economics: the most well-being from the least stuff

definition.text: A spiritual and philosophical approach to economics that aims for the most well-being with the least use of resources.

facts.text: Its most basic feature is seeing people as interdependent with one another and with nature.
E. F. Schumacher coined the term in 1955 while advising Burma's government, and his essay was republished in Small Is Beautiful (1973).
Drawing on 'Right Livelihood', Schumacher held that work should develop a person's abilities, connect them with others and produce what is needed for a decent life.
Where traditional economics seeks profit and individual gain, Buddhist economics seeks to minimise suffering and to simplify desires.
It holds that non-renewable resources should be used only when most needed, and that relying on them means living on capital rather than income.
Traditional economics ignores 'primordial stakeholders' such as future generations and the natural world, who have no purchasing power.
Bhutan has promoted gross national happiness since 1972, based on Buddhist values, as an alternative to judging development by GDP.

entries.text: In 1955, advising Burma's government, {{ref:nature-hist-060}} coined the term "Buddhist economics". It is a spiritual and philosophical approach that aims for the most well-being with the least use of resources. Its starting point is that people are interdependent with one another and with nature. Where traditional economics seeks profit and individual gain, it seeks to reduce suffering and simplify desires. Drawing on "Right Livelihood", Schumacher held that work should develop a person's abilities, connect them with others and produce what a decent life needs. Using non-renewable resources, in this view, means living on capital rather than income. It also counts "primordial stakeholders", such as future generations and the natural world, who have no purchasing power. Since 1972 Bhutan has promoted gross national happiness, built on Buddhist values, instead of judging development by GDP.

It also counts "primordial stakeholders", such as future generations and the natural world, who have no purchasing power. Since 1972 Bhutan has promoted gross national happiness, built on Buddhist values, instead of judging development by GDP.

entries.title: Thermoeconomics: an economy run on physics

definition.text: A school of heterodox economics, also called biophysical economics, that applies the laws of thermodynamics to economic theory.

facts.text: It studies how societies obtain and use energy and other resources to produce, distribute and consume goods while generating waste and environmental impacts.
Thermoeconomists hold that economies can be modelled as thermodynamic systems always involving matter, energy, entropy and information.
The global economy is treated as an open system, and economic activity as a dissipative system that thrives by consuming free energy.
It develops economic analogues of the first and second laws of thermodynamics.
A 2020 analysis concluded that GDP in advanced economies is likely to fall once credit can no longer prop up consumption and energy becomes lower in quality and more costly.

entries.text: Thermoeconomics, also called biophysical economics, is a {{ref:nature-eecon-115}} school that applies the {{ref:nature-eecon-118}} to economic theory. It studies how societies get and use energy and resources to produce, distribute and consume goods, while generating waste and environmental impacts. Its practitioners model economies as thermodynamic systems involving matter, energy, {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} and information. The global economy is an open system, and economic activity a dissipative system, one that thrives by consuming free energy. The school develops economic versions of the first and second laws. A 2020 analysis drew a sobering conclusion: GDP in advanced economies is likely to fall. That happens once credit can no longer prop up consumption, and energy becomes lower in quality and more costly.

entries.title: Social metabolism: the material flows that keep a society alive

definition.text: The flows of materials and energy between nature and society, between societies, and within them.

facts.text: These flows exist in every society, but their size and variety depend on culture, or the 'sociometabolic regime'.
They begin with humans taking materials and energy from nature, which are transformed, circulated, consumed and finally returned to nature as waste.
In-use stocks such as buildings, vehicles and infrastructure are built and maintained by these flows and provide shelter, transport and communication.
The concept extends the idea of metabolism from living bodies to the physical basis of society.
Each process's environmental impact depends on how it is done, the amounts involved, where it happens and nature's capacity to regenerate.
John Bellamy Foster built on Marx's ideas about social metabolism to develop the concept of metabolic rift.

entries.text: A body takes in food and air and gives off waste. Social metabolism extends that idea to society: the flows of materials and energy between nature and society, between societies, and within them. People take materials and energy from nature, transform, circulate and consume them, and finally return them as waste. These flows also build and maintain in-use stocks, such as buildings, vehicles and infrastructure, that provide shelter, transport and communication (see {{ref:nature-econ-594}}). Every society has such flows, but their size and variety depend on its culture, or "sociometabolic regime". Each process's impact depends on how it is done, how much, where, and nature's capacity to regenerate. John Bellamy Foster built on Marx's ideas here to develop {{ref:nature-eecon-120}}.

entries.title: Costanza's $33 trillion price tag for nature

definition.text: A 1997 study led by Robert Costanza that tried to put a total money value on the services the world's ecosystems provide.

facts.text: Published in Nature, it arrived at $33 trillion, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when total global GDP in 1997 was $27 trillion.
Half of the value came from nutrient cycling; estuaries, swamps and floodplains, and seagrass and algae beds had the highest values per hectare.
It averaged values from studies done in very specific settings and transferred them without regard to that setting.
Critics in the journal Ecological Economics still granted that valuing the global ecosystem had positive potential.

distinct_from: Source and sink functions of the environment
entries.text: In 1997 a team led by {{ref:nature-hist-048}} published in Nature a total money value for the world's ecosystem services. It came to $33 trillion a year, within a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion. Global GDP that year was $27 trillion. Half the value came from nutrient cycling. Estuaries, swamps, floodplains, seagrass and algae beds had the highest values per hectare. The study averaged values from very specific local studies and transferred them without regard to setting. Even critics in Ecological Economics granted that valuing the global ecosystem had positive potential.

entries.title: Ecological-economic modeling: equations for economy and nature

definition.text: The use of mathematical models to analyse how economies and ecosystems interact.

facts.text: Approaches include evolutionary, input-output, entropy and thermodynamic, multi-criteria and agent-based models, the environmental Kuznets curve and stock-flow consistent frameworks.
System dynamics and GIS are used for spatial simulation of changing landscapes.

entries.text: Ecological-economic modeling uses mathematical models to analyze how economies and ecosystems interact. The toolbox is wide: evolutionary, input-output, entropy and thermodynamic, multi-criteria and agent-based models, the {{ref:nature-eecon-165}}, and stock-flow consistent frameworks. For changing landscapes, system dynamics and GIS, digital mapping, are used to simulate change across space.

entries.title: Energy accounting: following every joule

definition.text: Tracking energy into and out of a system, the useful work done and the energy lost, to judge resource use and environmental impact.

facts.text: An energy balance uses the first and second laws of thermodynamics to show how much energy each point in a system needs and in what form.
A key idea is net energy gain: every energy source needs an initial energy investment, so its energy return must exceed one to be useful.
The net energy gain from coal, oil and gas has fallen over time as the easiest sources were depleted first.

entries.title: The green economy: low-carbon, efficient and fair

definition.text: An economy that is low-carbon, efficient in its use of resources and socially inclusive; green economics is a more politically applied relative of ecological economics.

facts.text: The idea grew in policy circles first as a response to financial crisis and then as a vehicle for growth and development.
UNEP's definition was developed further in 2011 to stress a fair shift to a low-carbon, resource-efficient, socially inclusive economy.
It looks to cleaner, resource-saving technologies that cut emissions while addressing resource exhaustion.
It is closely related to ecological economics but has a more politically applied focus.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute whether market-based green economy policies can address the real causes of environmental crisis.

entries.title: Money and ecological economics

definition.text: Ecological economics' work on money and monetary policy, aimed at sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation.

facts.text: This work can be traced to Frederick Soddy's writing on money.
It asks whether interest-bearing debt forces growth, what money is, and whether alternatives such as alternative currencies and public banking would help.

entries.text: Ecological economists also study money itself, aiming for monetary policy that serves sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation. The work traces back to Frederick Soddy's writing on money. It asks what money is, whether interest-bearing debt forces an economy to grow, and whether alternatives such as alternative currencies and public banking would help.

entries.title: Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj: non-western roots
entries.article: Ecological economics#Non-traditional approaches to ecological economics

definition.text: Cultural and traditional economic outlooks, such as Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj, that stress harmony with nature and are now counted as ecological economic practice.

facts.text: Buen Vivir ('Good Life') is a South American movement that rejects the western development model and does not value material accumulation.
Ecological Swaraj, from India, respects physical limits and non-human species and pursues equity through direct democracy.
Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful brought non-western ideas such as Buddhist economics into mainstream thought.

entries.text: Some ecological economic thinking comes from outside the West. Buen Vivir, "Good Life", is a South American movement that rejects the western development model and does not value piling up material wealth. Schumacher's {{ref:nature-hist-019}} brought such ideas, including {{ref:nature-eecon-093}}, into mainstream thought.

entries.title: Schools of ecological economics: from pragmatists to radicals

definition.text: The competing camps within ecological economics, from those close to mainstream resource economics to far more heterodox ones.

facts.text: Clive Spash sorts environmental work into three groups: new resource economists, new environmental pragmatists and radical social ecological economists.
Degrowth is a growing radical strand that addresses biophysical limits and global inequality.
Critics of degrowth among new resource economists point instead to the momentum of sustainable development and the green economy.

entries.title: The second law of thermodynamics: why heat never flows uphill

definition.text: The law that natural processes are irreversible: the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases, so heat never flows by itself from cold to hot.

facts.text: Its simplest form, the Clausius statement, is that heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder to a hotter body.
All natural processes are irreversible; reversible processes are only a theoretical limit.
It was first formulated by Sadi Carnot in 1824 in his study of the motive power of fire.
Georgescu-Roegen called it the 'entropy law' and made it central to his economics.

entries.text: A cup of hot coffee always cools in a cold room; a cold room never heats the coffee. That is the second law of thermodynamics in its simplest form, the Clausius statement: heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder body to a hotter one. More generally, the total {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} of interacting systems never decreases, so all natural processes are irreversible. Reversible processes are only a theoretical limit. Sadi Carnot first formulated the law in 1824, studying the motive power of fire. Georgescu-Roegen called it the "entropy law" and put it at the center of his economics.

entries.title: Conservation of mass: matter is only rearranged

definition.text: The physical law that in a system closed to matter flowing in or out, total mass stays constant: matter is neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged.

facts.text: In a chemical reaction, the mass of the starting materials equals the mass of the products.
Antoine Lavoisier confirmed it in the late 18th century, building on Jean Rey's 1630 demonstration.
Tracking how mass is distributed in a system over time is the engineering method called mass balance.
It holds only in the classical limit; Einstein's E=mc2 unified it with conservation of energy as mass–energy equivalence.
Hydrologists use it as a water balance to estimate how long water stays in a reservoir.

entries.text: Burn a log and its matter does not vanish; it is rearranged. In a system closed to matter flowing in or out, total mass stays constant. In a chemical reaction, the starting materials weigh the same as the products. Antoine Lavoisier confirmed this in the late 18th century, building on Jean Rey's 1630 demonstration. Tracking how mass moves through a system over time is the engineering method of mass balance. Hydrologists use it as a water balance to estimate how long water stays in a reservoir. The law holds only in the classical limit: Einstein's E=mc2 merged it with conservation of energy.

entries.title: Metabolic rift: the broken loop between city and soil

definition.text: A theory, credited by sociologist John Bellamy Foster to Karl Marx, that capitalism breaks the natural exchange of materials between society and nature, producing ecological crisis.

facts.text: Foster, not Marx, coined the term, starting with his book Marx's Ecology.
Marx wrote during England's 'second' agricultural revolution (1815–1880), when soil exhaustion pushed Britain to import bone and guano for fertiliser.
It drew on Justus von Liebig's 1840 explanation of how soil nutrients feed plant growth.
Nutrients sent to cities as food were not returned to the land as waste, a one-way 'robbing of the soil' that linked urban pollution with soil depletion.
Originally a critique of capitalist agriculture, it has been extended to marine ecology and to a 'carbon rift' from rising carbon dioxide emissions.
Foster sees in it evidence that Marx held an ecological outlook, against claims that Marx ignored nature.

entries.contested_note: Historical materialists such as Jason W. Moore read the rift's origins and nature very differently from Foster.

entries.title: Entropy pessimism: can technology beat physics?

definition.text: The view that technology cannot escape the laws of physics, since every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises entropy.

facts.text: Neoclassical production functions treat technology as a factor of production with no mention of natural resource inputs.
In ecological economics, technology is the way natural resources are transformed in production.
Robert Solow replied in 1997 that 'elementary physics' had not by itself prevented growth in industrialised countries.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagree on whether technology can overcome natural resource limits.

entries.title: Resource decoupling: growing on less
entries.article: Steady-state economy#Resource decoupling and the rebound effect

definition.text: Economic activity becoming less demanding on nature, so fewer natural resources are needed per unit of output.

facts.text: It is measured by the ratio of total natural resource consumption to GDP.
Relative decoupling is a decline in resource use with all else equal; absolute decoupling is a decline in resource use while GDP keeps growing.
A 2019 review found that attempts to grow without environmental destruction had not succeeded.

entries.text: Can an economy grow while using less of nature? Resource decoupling means needing fewer natural resources per unit of output, measured by the ratio of resource consumption to GDP. Relative decoupling is a fall in resource use per unit, all else equal; absolute decoupling is a fall in total resource use while GDP keeps growing. The record is poor. A 2019 review found that attempts to grow without environmental destruction had not succeeded.

entries.title: Four books, six years: the founding works

definition.text: Four works published between 1966 and 1972 on the importance of natural resources and the environment that led to ecological economics.

facts.text: Boulding's 1966 essay on Spaceship Earth argued that the economy must fit a closed, cyclical system.
Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used.
Howard T. Odum's 1971 Environment, Power and Society proposed the maximum power principle.
The Limits to Growth (1972) projected that output, food per person and population would peak and then decline.

entries.title: Escaping to space: a way out of limits to growth?
entries.article: Steady-state economy#Pushing some of the terrestrial limits into outer space

definition.text: The proposal that settling outer space could ease overpopulation and resource limits on Earth.

facts.text: In the 1970s Gerard K. O'Neill planned space settlements to solve overpopulation and limits to growth without political repression.

entries.text: If Earth is full, why not build new worlds? Some proposed that settling outer space could ease {{ref:nature-eecon-187}} and resource limits. In the 1970s Gerard K. O'Neill planned space settlements to solve the problems of too many people and finite resources without political repression. The idea answers worries about {{ref:nature-eco-596}} by moving the boundary rather than living within it.

entries.title: Sustainability science: a field built around problems

definition.text: An applied academic discipline, emerging in the 1980s, that studies sustainability and sustainable development and links knowledge to action.

facts.text: William C. Clark describes it as a field defined by the problems it addresses rather than the disciplines it uses.
It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report Our Common Future (1987).
It was officially launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam.
Recognising the epochal human impacts of the Anthropocene is at the core of much of the field.

entries.text: Most fields are defined by their methods. Sustainability science, says William C. Clark, is defined by the problems it tackles. This applied discipline, emerging in the 1980s, studies sustainability and {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} and links knowledge to action. It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report of 1987, {{ref:nature-hist-004}}. It was launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam. At its core is the recognition of humanity's epochal impact in the Anthropocene.

entries.title: Ecologically unequal exchange: trade that drains the South

definition.text: The idea that world trade hides an unfair flow of materials, energy and environmental damage, not just labour, from poorer to richer countries.

facts.text: It describes an asymmetric flow of embodied materials and energy from peripheral countries, mostly in the Global South, to the developed core.
Southern countries serve as sources of raw materials, sinks for waste and sites of 'sacrifice zones', which deepens global inequality.
It builds on world-systems theory, which splits the world economy into a rich core and a poorer periphery with surplus flowing to the core.
Dorninger and colleagues found that half of all materials consumed by high-income countries are extracted from poorer countries, while rich countries gain trade surpluses.
A study of EU consumption from 1995 to 2019 found large parts of its environmental impacts outsourced abroad, while more than 80% of the economic benefits stayed in the EU.
Its logical result is that the Global North owes the South an ecological debt; unequal exchange is the mechanism and the debt its historical accumulation.
Jason Hickel proposes degrowth in the Global North to end these relations.
Peter Somerville criticised the theory as confused and internally inconsistent.

entries.contested_note: Most cited studies support the theory, but critics such as Peter Somerville call it confused and inconsistent.

entries.title: Unequal exchange: the hidden transfer from poor to rich

definition.text: The hidden transfer of labour and ecological value from poor countries, mainly in the Global South, to rich countries and corporations, mainly in the North, through structurally unequal trade.

facts.text: Because of biased terms of trade, poor countries must export much more labour and resources than they import to keep trade in monetary balance.
It rejects the Ricardian and neoclassical claim that free trade based on comparative advantage benefits all parties.
Arghiri Emmanuel and Samir Amin traced it mainly to wage differences between core and periphery.
Hickel and colleagues calculated the drain from the Global South from 1990 to 2015 as equivalent to 242 trillion in 2010 US dollars.
Northern power is maintained partly through patents: 97% of all patents are held by corporations in high-income countries.
A common critique is that wage gaps reflect higher productivity in the North; supporters reply that productivity is measured by prices.

entries.title: Stock-flow consistent models: macroeconomics that adds up

definition.text: A family of non-equilibrium macroeconomic models built on strict accounting so that every flow and stock in an economy is included and adds up.

facts.text: They are popular in the post-Keynesian school and contrast with the DSGE models of mainstream macroeconomics.
Their accounting rule is that one party's asset is another's liability and no money comes from or vanishes into nowhere.
Wynne Godley used them to warn from 2000 that the US housing market would weaken and cause a recession.
They are now widely used in ecological macroeconomics, adding resource, energy and ecosystem stocks and flows, drawing on Georgescu-Roegen's flow-fund models.

facts.text: Rational, maximising behaviour underpins rational choice theory and is for many economists synonymous with economic behaviour.
Critics note that social constraints or coercion, or poor judgement of choices, may stop people from maximising pleasure.

Heat and radiation cannot be fully converted to work; the upper limit for heat is the Carnot efficiency, found by Sadi Carnot in 1824.
High-exergy energy carriers can do more kinds of work and so can be held to have more economic value.

entries.title: Emergy: pricing everything in sunlight

definition.text: The total energy of one kind, usually sunlight, used directly and indirectly to make a product or service; a way of expressing differences in energy quality.

facts.text: It puts sunlight, fuel, electricity and human services on a common basis by expressing each in the solar energy needed to produce them, measured in solar emjoules (seJ).
Howard T. Odum, studying energy flow in ecosystems from the 1950s, argued that different energy sources cannot be added without converting them to a common measure of quality.
Odum's first formal statement came in 1973; David Scienceman proposed the name 'emergy' in 1986.
Emergy accounting draws a system diagram, builds a table of resource, labour and energy flows, converts each to emergy and sums them.
Its stated goal is an 'ecocentric' valuation that adds information rather than replacing economic values.

entries.title: Throughput: the river of matter running through the economy

definition.text: The flow of matter and energy that enters the economy from nature as resources and leaves it again as waste and pollution.

entries.title: The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth

definition.text: An economy with a constant stock of physical wealth (capital) and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time.

facts.text: Herman Daly's version keeps both stocks constant by a flow of natural resources through the system; that flow is the new ecological element added to the classical stationary state.
Both stocks should be as durable as possible: longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow, and a durable population has long lives with low birth and death rates.
It rests on the view that the economy is an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem, and must therefore itself stop growing at some point.
This contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households with no physical contact with nature.
Since the 1970s the idea has been linked mainly with Herman Daly.
It can apply to a city, region, country or the whole world.
Daly concedes that a steady state only postpones, not prevents, eventual exhaustion of minerals.
Sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

entries.text: Can an economy be healthy without growing? The steady-state economy says yes. It keeps a constant stock of physical wealth, or capital, and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time. It can apply to a city, a region, a country or the whole world. The idea updates the classical {{ref:nature-eecon-073}}. Its main champion since the 1970s, {{ref:nature-hist-040}}, added the ecological piece: both stocks are kept constant by a flow of natural resources, the {{ref:nature-eecon-136}}. Both stocks should be as durable as possible. Longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow. A durable population means long lives with low birth and death rates. The reasoning starts from a view of the economy as an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem. A part cannot grow forever inside a whole that does not grow. That contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households, with no physical contact with nature. Daly admits the limits of his own idea. A steady state only postpones, and does not prevent, the eventual exhaustion of minerals. Even sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

The reasoning starts from a view of the economy as an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem. A part cannot grow forever inside a whole that does not grow. That contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households, with no physical contact with nature. Daly admits the limits of his own idea. A steady state only postpones, and does not prevent, the eventual exhaustion of minerals. Even sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

entries.title: The declining-state economy: should the economy shrink?

definition.text: The argument, from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen and degrowth thinkers, that a shrinking economy is better than a steady one for stretching finite minerals.

facts.text: Georgescu-Roegen argued Earth's carrying capacity will fall as finite minerals are extracted, so the world economy heads for collapse.
He proposed a 'minimal bioeconomic program' with restrictions stricter than Daly's.
Daly accepts a declining path but sees the steady state as the necessary first step: an economy must stop before it can reverse.
Rifkin, Latouche and Kerschner argue for declining-state strategies.

entries.contested_note: Steady-state and degrowth advocates disagree whether the economy should stabilise or shrink.

As finite minerals are extracted, he argued, Earth's carrying capacity will fall, so the world economy is heading for collapse. A shrinking economy, not a steady one, would stretch those minerals furthest. He proposed a "minimal bioeconomic program" with restrictions stricter than Daly's. Steady-state advocates want the economy to stabilize; their more radical allies want it to shrink. Both accept that {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} and finite {{ref:nature-res-209}} stocks set the terms of the argument.

entries.title: Can capitalism stop growing?

definition.text: The question, raised by radical critics, of whether a steady or shrinking economy can be imposed on top of capitalism.

facts.text: Critics point to growth drives built into capitalism: the profit motive, jobs that depend on sales, credit creation by banks and labour-saving technology.
Governments need tax revenue from economic activity, and globalisation forces countries to compete.
Daly holds that the growth versus steady-state debate cuts across the left-right divide.

The second issues transferable reproduction licences at the replacement fertility level.
The third sells depletion quotas that cap the flow of resources; unlike taxes, quotas directly minimise throughput.

entries.title: The solar-income budget: living on sunlight
entries.article: Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy

definition.text: Daly's term for the limit humans lived within before industrialisation, relying on the steady flow of sunlight rather than the stock of minerals.

facts.text: Daly sees two sources of wealth: a stock of minerals, which we can extract as fast as we choose, and a flow of solar energy beyond our control.
Because the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the mineral stock is the crucial scarcity.
The Industrial Revolution broke the budget by extracting minerals at a rapidly increasing rate.

entries.title: Post-normal science: when facts are uncertain and stakes are high

definition.text: A problem-solving approach for science used in policy when 'facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent', developed by Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz in the 1990s.

facts.text: In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, judged by internal and extended peer communities.
Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science.
It complements risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis rather than replacing them.
It is meant to guide knowledge for decisions on pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and sustainability transitions; ecosystem services are a topical subject for it.
In modelling it favours 'models to map our ignorance about the future' over models to predict and control it.
Critics say it adds no new epistemology, turns climate scientists into 'stealth advocates', and undermines empiricism.

entries.contested_note: Critics argue it retraces older debates and weakens scientific neutrality and empiricism.

MuSIASEM, built around Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi, studies subsectors of present economies with tailor-made accounts within a set 'grammar'.

entries.title: MuSIASEM: accounting across scales

It tracks who uses which resources and why, the resulting environmental pressures, and how far needs and pressures are shifted abroad through trade.
Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi created it around 1997 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
It suits analysis of the nexus between food, energy, water and land use, and has been tested with the FAO.

entries.title: Hunters, farmers, industry: three sociometabolic regimes
entries.article: Social metabolism#Social metabolism as a proxy for human development

definition.text: Rolf Sieferle's classification of human history into hunter-gatherer, agrarian and industrial regimes according to their main energy source and conversion technology.

facts.text: Hunter-gatherers relied on 'passive solar energy' from recent photosynthesis, giving nomadic societies with low population density.
The Neolithic Revolution brought an agrarian regime of 'active solar energy use', with deforestation for farming, settled life and faster population growth.
The industrial regime relies on fossil fuels as its main energy source.
Indicators used to reconstruct this history include Total Primary Energy Supply and Human Appropriation of Net Primary Production (HANPP).

definition.text: An approach in ecological economics that studies change as mutual feedback and selection between social, environmental and economic systems.

facts.text: Ecological economics itself is defined as studying the interdependence and coevolution of economies and ecosystems.
The idea began in biology for two species evolving together and later grew into gene-culture coevolution.
Richard Norgaard brought it into ecological economics, showing how pests coevolved with pesticides and the institutions regulating them.
Norgaard and Giorgos Kallis applied it to water development, urbanisation and rural communities with their ecosystems.

definition.text: The application of conservation of mass to the economy: tracking the mass of materials through a system so that everything that goes in is accounted for as product, stock or waste.

facts.text: Material flow analysis rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance.
Mass balance ensures waste and by-product flows are not overlooked, whereas economic input-output tables often leave them out because they lack economic value.
Allen Kneese, Robert Ayres and Ralph d'Arge set out a 'materials balance approach' to economics and the environment in 1970.
The principle came from Lavoisier's chemistry into chemical engineering and finally environmental science.

entries.title: The extended peer community: more voices checking the science

definition.text: In post-normal science, the wider group of stakeholders, beyond scientists, who share in checking the quality of scientific inputs to a decision.

facts.text: Participants are not treated as passive learners convinced by experts but resolve issues through debate and dialogue.
These spaces express differing values and power in a setting of inequality and conflict, so agreement is not guaranteed.
Some argue conservation science, with its many layers of policy-makers and stakeholders, has always been an extended peer community.

entries.title: Green logistics: moving goods with less harm

definition.text: Efforts to measure and reduce the environmental impact of moving and storing goods, information and services.

facts.text: It began in the mid-1980s and aims to balance economic and environmental efficiency.
Packaging decisions set how many items fit per container and so strongly shape CO2 emissions per product transported.
Costs can be high: ammonia is 3-7 times more expensive than traditional marine fuels.

entries.title: Weak and strong sustainability: can machines replace nature?

definition.text: Weak and strong sustainability are two opposing approaches from environmental economics that differ on whether natural capital can be replaced by human-made capital.

facts.text: Weak sustainability treats natural and human capital as interchangeable, so losing natural capital is acceptable if human capital rises by at least as much.
Strong sustainability holds that some natural assets have critical ecological functions no human-made alternative can replace, so they must be kept regardless of gains elsewhere.
Example: under weak sustainability, replacing a natural forest with a park or farmland can count as sustainable if its value equals the biodiversity lost; under strong sustainability it may not.
Pearce, Markandya and Barbier's Blueprint for a Green Economy (1989) was among the first works to discuss the ideas.
Since the 1990s there has been a heated debate over how far natural and human-made capital can substitute for each other.
Wilfred Beckerman rejects both: weak sustainability is 'redundant and illogical', and strong sustainability a 'morally repugnant and totally impracticable objective'.

entries.title: Environment, society, economy: the three dimensions of sustainability

definition.text: The three dimensions of sustainability are the environmental, social and economic areas that scholars usually distinguish within the concept.

facts.text: Writers also call them pillars, components, aspects or goals; all mean the same here.
The familiar three-circle Venn diagram first appeared in a 1987 article by the economist Edward Barbier.
The paradigm has few theoretical foundations, though it dominates the literature.
Agenda 21 (1992) and Agenda 2030 (2015) both frame sustainability through economic, social and environmental dimensions.

entries.title: Elasticity of substitution: how easily one input replaces another

definition.text: The elasticity of substitution measures how easily one input or good can be swapped for another: the percentage change in their ratio of use for a percentage change in their relative marginal values or prices.

facts.text: Its most common use is the ratio of capital to labour relative to the ratio of their marginal products or prices.
John Hicks introduced it in 1932, and Joan Robinson independently discovered it in 1933.
It measures the curvature of an isoquant; the larger it is, the more readily one input is substituted for another.
Below one, goods are gross complements and relative spending on a good rises with its relative price; above one they are gross substitutes and it falls.
At exactly one, the Cobb–Douglas case, relative spending does not depend on relative prices.

entries.text: If capital gets cheaper relative to labor, how much more capital will firms use? The elasticity of substitution answers that. It measures the percentage change in the ratio of two inputs used for a percentage change in their relative prices or marginal values. Its most common use is capital against labor. Geometrically, it measures the curvature of an {{ref:nature-econ-308}}: the larger it is, the more readily one input stands in for another. Below one, goods are gross complements, and relative spending on a good rises with its relative price. Above one, they are gross substitutes, and it falls. At exactly one, the Cobb–Douglas case, relative spending ignores relative prices. John Hicks introduced it in 1932, and Joan Robinson independently discovered it in 1933.

entries.title: The Cobb–Douglas production function

definition.text: The Cobb–Douglas production function is a widely used mathematical form linking the amounts of inputs, especially labour and capital, to the output they can produce.

facts.text: Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas developed and tested it against statistical evidence between 1927 and 1947.
In its common form the exponents α and β, each between 0 and 1, are the labour and capital elasticities of output; with α = 0.45, 1% more labour gives about 0.45% more output.
It obeys diminishing returns: each extra unit of a factor raises output, but by less and less.
Its elasticity of substitution between inputs is constant and equal to 1.
If the exponents sum to 1 returns to scale are constant; below 1 decreasing; above 1 increasing.
It is the limiting case of the CES production function as its substitution parameter goes to zero.
Critics fault its lack of foundation and its assumption of a constant labour share of output, which is now widely seen to be declining.

entries.title: Constant elasticity of substitution: one formula, many shapes

definition.text: Constant elasticity of substitution (CES) is a common form for production and utility functions in which the ease of substituting one input or good for another stays the same at all levels of output or utility.

facts.text: The two-factor capital-labour CES production function was introduced by Solow and popularised by Arrow, Chenery, Minhas and Solow.
Linear (perfect substitutes), Cobb–Douglas and Leontief (perfect complements) functions are special cases of it.
With more than two factors it generally cannot keep a constant elasticity between every pair, as Uzawa showed.
Nested CES functions are common in partial and general equilibrium models, letting each nest carry its own elasticity.
As a utility function, goods are perfect substitutes as the elasticity approaches infinity and perfect complements as it approaches zero.

entries.text: Constant elasticity of substitution (CES) functions keep the ease of swapping one input or good for another the same at all levels of output or utility. Solow introduced the two-factor capital-labor version, popularized by Arrow, Chenery, Minhas and Solow. Linear functions (perfect substitutes), Cobb–Douglas and Leontief functions (perfect complements) are all special cases. With more than two factors, Uzawa showed, it generally cannot keep the elasticity constant between every pair. Modelers therefore nest CES functions, giving each nest its own elasticity. As a utility function, goods become perfect substitutes as the elasticity approaches infinity and perfect complements as it approaches zero.

entries.title: The economic dimension of sustainability

definition.text: The economic dimension of sustainability concerns how economic development fits with protecting the environment and meeting basic needs, and it is controversial.

facts.text: The controversy arises because 'development' can be read as just economic growth, which can promote a system bad for the environment.
Economic development can reduce hunger and energy poverty, which is why SDG 8 calls for growth, measured partly by real GDP per capita.
The challenge is to expand economic activity while cutting its environmental impact.
The Brundtland Report holds that poverty both causes and results from environmental problems.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree whether economic growth belongs in sustainability or undermines it.

entries.title: The nested model: economy inside society, society inside nature

definition.text: The nested model ranks the three dimensions of sustainability, drawing the economy inside society and society inside the environment.

facts.text: Many publications treat the environmental dimension, ecological or planetary integrity, as the most important, so it sets limits on economic and social development.
The SDG 'wedding cake' model likewise shows the economy as a subset of society, and society as a subset of the biosphere.
A 2022 assessment argued the SDGs fail to make protecting planetary integrity an end in itself.

entries.title: Sustainability barriers: why it is so hard

definition.text: Sustainability barriers are the reasons sustainability is so hard to achieve.

facts.text: Intrinsic barriers come from nature's complexity and the human condition, such as the value-action gap, where people do not act on their convictions.
Extrinsic barriers can be overcome, for example by putting a price on the consumption of public goods.
Competitive market economies carry a structural imperative to grow, which inhibits needed change.
Political pressure favours the short term over the long term.

Competitive market economies carry a structural imperative to grow, which blocks change. And political pressure favors the short term over the long.

entries.title: Sustainability transition: changing the whole system

definition.text: A sustainability transition (or transformation) is a deep, system-wide change in technology, economy, society, values and goals towards sustainability.

facts.text: It must happen at every scale, from local communities to global governance institutions.
It is politically debated, since stakeholders may disagree on goals and methods and it can challenge existing power and resource distribution.
It may only work if far-reaching lifestyle changes accompany technological advances.

entries.title: Can human-made capital replace nature?

definition.text: Substitutability of natural capital is the question of how far human-made capital (buildings, machinery, technology) can replace natural capital (forests, water, clean air).

facts.text: It is the dividing line of the weak versus strong sustainability debate, argued over ardently since the 1990s.
Solow showed that, given some substitutability, accumulating produced capital fast enough can offset a shrinking exhaustible resource stock.
Solow and Stiglitz both held that across-the-board substitution of man-made for natural capital is a real possibility.
Georgescu-Roegen countered that, since the economic process steadily increases entropy, such across-the-board substitutability is untenable.
William Rees criticises mainstream economics for assuming perfect substitutability between manufactured or financial capital and natural capital.

entries.title: Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later

definition.text: Sustainable development is an approach to growth and human development that aims to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

facts.text: The widely used definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, which stresses the essential needs of the world's poor and the limits technology and social organisation place on the environment.
It tries to balance economic development, environmental protection and social well-being.
Its roots lie in 17th- and 18th-century European ideas of sustainable forest management, such as von Carlowitz's sustained-yield forestry.
The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio began the Rio Process that put sustainable development on the international agenda.
It is the foundational concept of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals adopted by all UN members in 2015.
Critics ask what exactly is to be sustained, and argue that no use of a non-renewable resource can be sustainable since any extraction eventually exhausts a finite stock.
The debate assumes societies manage economic, social and natural capital, which may not substitute for one another and whose use may be irreversible.

entries.contested_note: Scholars understand the concept in many ways and criticise it from several angles, including what is to be sustained.

entries.title: The Brundtland Commission

definition.text: The Brundtland Commission, formally the World Commission on Environment and Development, was a UN body set up to unite countries in pursuit of sustainable development.

facts.text: It was founded in 1983 with former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland as chair, and dissolved in 1987 after releasing Our Common Future.
Its report popularised 'sustainable development' and gave the most widely used definition: development meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
It responded to the conflict between globalised economic growth and accelerating ecological degradation by redefining economic development as sustainable development.
Its definition centres on the needs of the global poor and on limits technology and social organisation place on the environment, ideas close to intergenerational equity.
Its call for an international meeting led to the 1992 Rio summit and Agenda 21.
The definition's openness won wide support but was also criticised as 'self-defeating and compromised rhetoric'.
