entries.title: Recycling: giving waste a second life

definition.text: Turning waste materials into new materials and objects.

facts.text: It is the third step in the 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' hierarchy.
It saves materials and energy and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution from incineration and water pollution from landfills.
Ideally a material becomes a fresh supply of the same material, as metal cans can; for many materials that is hard or costly, so they become different, lesser products.
Recycling aluminium uses only 5% of the energy of virgin production.
Two-thirds of all new steel is estimated to come from recycled steel.
Much of the difficulty comes from products not being designed for recycling; in the USA only about 6 to 7 percent of plastic is recycled.
Large investment in recycling came in the 1970s because of rising energy costs.

entries.title: Circular economy: closing the loop on take-make-waste

definition.text: An economic system that tries to keep products, parts and materials in use at their highest value for as long as possible.

facts.text: It is set against the linear 'take-make-waste' economy, in which resources are extracted, used and thrown away, putting heavy pressure on the environment.
Extracting and processing material resources accounts for over 55 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Circularity can be raised in four ways: narrowing the loop (using fewer resources), slowing it (reuse and repair), closing it (recycling), and substituting renewable or less harmful inputs.
The European Parliament describes it as sharing, leasing, reusing, repairing, refurbishing and recycling existing materials and products for as long as possible.
Global implementation could cut emissions by 22.8 billion tons, equal to 39% of global emissions in 2019.
Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay 'The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth' contrasted an open 'cowboy economy' with a closed one and is often cited as the idea's first expression.
Pearce and Turner's 1990 book described a system where waste from extraction, production and consumption is turned back into inputs.
The concept draws on industrial ecology, biomimicry and cradle-to-cradle design; the Ellen MacArthur Foundation spread it in Europe and the Americas.

entries.title: Plastic pollution: cheap to make, slow to vanish

definition.text: The build-up in the environment of plastic objects and particles, such as bottles, bags and microbeads, that harms people, wildlife and habitats.

facts.text: Plastics are cheap and durable, so manufacturers favour them, but most resist natural breakdown and degrade slowly.
Pollutant plastics are sorted by size into micro-, meso- and macro-debris; macrodebris is larger than 20 mm.
Around 275 million tonnes of plastic waste is generated each year, of which between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes is dumped into the sea.
Packaging is the largest use of plastic, at 219 Mt as of 2024.
More than 900 marine species are affected by plastic pollution.
Governments most often target plastic bags, by bans or fees, followed by plastic cutlery and microbeads.
Industry leaders knew in the early 1970s that most plastic would never be recycled, yet later ran a $50 million a year campaign saying it was.
Many academics and NGOs call for a legally binding international treaty that would cap plastic production.

entries.title: Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems

definition.text: The study of how materials and energy flow through industrial systems.

facts.text: It aims to move industry from open-loop systems, where resources end as waste, to closed loops where wastes become inputs for new processes.
Its name reflects the idea of using natural ecosystems, which have no waste, as a model for designing sustainable industry.
Main research areas include industrial metabolism, life-cycle assessment, eco-design, extended producer responsibility and eco-industrial parks.
It was popularised in a 1989 Scientific American article by Robert Frosch and Nicholas Gallopoulos, who asked why one industry's outputs could not be another's inputs.
It combines engineering, economics, sociology, toxicology and the natural sciences.
Its principles are now appearing in policy areas such as the circular economy, for example by using waste heat from one process to run a cooler one.

entries.title: Resource recovery: treating waste as raw material

definition.text: Using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products.

facts.text: It aims to cut waste and landfill needs while getting the most value from waste, and it delays the need for raw materials.
It is part of a circular economy that minimises resource extraction and waste.
Metals such as lithium, cobalt and vanadium can be recovered from industrial landfills and old mine wastes for electric vehicles and wind turbines.
Its potential shrinks because materials are irreversibly mixed and diluted (their entropy rises) through manufacture, use and landfilling.
Capturing landfill gas for energy counts as recovery but is a last resort, since the point is to avoid landfill altogether.

entries.text: Lithium, cobalt and vanadium for electric vehicles and wind turbines can be pulled from industrial landfills and old mine wastes. That is resource recovery: using wastes as raw material to make valuable new products. It aims to cut waste and the need for landfill while getting the most value out of what is thrown away. It also delays the need to dig up fresh raw materials. Recovery is one piece of a {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}, which minimizes both resource extraction and waste. It goes beyond {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} to include any way of winning value back from {{ref:nature-pol-064}} and industrial waste. Its potential shrinks with time. Through manufacture, use and landfilling, materials are irreversibly mixed and diluted; physicists would say their entropy, their disorder, rises. The more scattered a material becomes, the harder it is to win back. Some recovery is a sign of failure. Capturing landfill gas for energy counts as recovery, but it is a last resort, because the whole point is to avoid landfill altogether.

entries.title: The waste hierarchy: a pyramid of better and worse

definition.text: A ranking of ways to deal with waste, from the most to the least environmentally preferable, usually drawn as a pyramid.

facts.text: Its aim is to get the most practical benefit from products while generating the least waste.
The EU's 2008 Waste Framework Directive sets five steps in order: prevention, reuse, recycling, other recovery including energy recovery, and safe disposal as a last resort.
The idea traces to 'Lansink's Ladder', proposed by Dutch MP Ad Lansink in 1979.
Applied well, it can cut greenhouse gas emissions and pollutants, save energy and resources, create jobs and spur green technology.
Life-cycle thinking can justify departing from it: replacing an old, inefficient washing machine is often better than keeping it, because most of its impact comes during use.
An early EU proposal that put recycling level with incineration was heavily criticised and replaced by the five-step version.

entries.title: Zero waste: designing waste out from the start

definition.text: A set of principles focused on preventing waste by redesigning how resources flow so that all products are reused or repurposed.

facts.text: Its goal is to send nothing to landfills, incinerators, oceans or anywhere else in the environment.
It aims to prevent waste rather than manage it at the end of the pipe, as a 'whole systems' change in how materials flow through society.
Currently 9% of global plastic is recycled.
Reaching it requires products that are easy to take apart for recycling, plus durability, repairability and minimal packaging.
Bea Johnson's '5 Rs' (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot) extend the 3 Rs for households.
Many organisations and cities adopt the zero waste slogan without pressing for its key changes.

entries.text: Only 9% of global plastic is currently recycled. Zero waste aims at a far bolder target: sending nothing to landfills, incinerators, oceans or anywhere else in the environment. entries.title: Dematerialization: doing more with less stuff

definition.text: Making more goods, or serving the same economic needs, with less material.

facts.text: It can be absolute or relative: a cut in total material use, or in material per unit of economic output.
Products are dematerialised in three ways: optimising (less mass), digitising (paper to e-book) and servitising (renting instead of selling).
Between 1977 and 2001 the material needed to meet Americans' needs fell from 1.18 to 1.08 trillion pounds while population grew by 55 million.
Cars weigh 30% less than in the early 1960s, and aluminium soda cans are six times lighter.
Critics note extraction of six minerals and cement production grew faster than GDP from 1960 to 2019.
Part of rich countries' dematerialisation comes from outsourcing material-intensive production to developing countries.

entries.contested_note: Critics say there is little evidence of global dematerialization, only regional shifts caused by outsourcing.

entries.title: Does recycling pay? The economics of recycling

definition.text: The dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs.

facts.text: Critics argue collection and transport costs and energy can outweigh the savings in production.
It is often cheaper for cities to landfill household waste than to recycle it, and virgin plastic resin costs 40 percent less than recycled resin.
Comparing only market prices ignores externalities, such as the extra pollution from making new plastic.
Life cycle assessment can measure these externalities, and tools such as a carbon tax can bring them into market prices.
Communities save money when recycling replaces, rather than adds to, their usual waste system.

entries.contested_note: Critics and proponents disagree over whether recycling's costs and energy use exceed its savings.
entries.text: Virgin plastic resin costs 40 percent less than recycled resin. For many cities it is also cheaper to landfill household waste than to recycle it. Numbers like these fuel the economics of recycling, a dispute over whether recycling's economic and environmental benefits outweigh its costs. Critics argue that collecting and trucking materials costs money and burns energy, enough to outweigh the savings in production. Supporters answer that comparing market prices alone leaves things out. Making new plastic causes extra pollution that nobody pays for, an {{ref:nature-found-031}}. Life cycle assessment can measure such hidden costs, and tools such as a carbon tax can build them into market prices. How a program is set up matters too. Communities save money when recycling replaces their usual waste system rather than adding to it. The two sides still disagree over whether recycling's {{ref:nature-econ-114}} and energy use exceed its savings, and the answer may differ from place to place.

entries.title: The sharing economy: using what sits idle

definition.text: An economic system in which people share in making, distributing, trading and using goods and services, often through online platforms.

facts.text: It puts the spare capacity of goods and services to use; the classic example is that the average car sits unused 95% of the time.
It can be run by non-profits, like a lending library, or by companies for profit, such as Uber and Airbnb.
It can reduce environmental harm by cutting the number of goods that must be produced.
There is no consensus on its definition.
Critics say platforms avoid taxes, regulation and insurance costs and can cause a 'race to the bottom' in wages.
Whether its workers should be treated as independent contractors or employees is debated.

entries.contested_note: Its labour effects and whether its gains come from real efficiency or from avoiding regulation are disputed.

entries.title: Circular business models: profit from keeping things in use

definition.text: Ways of running a firm, such as product-as-a-service, sharing platforms and life-extension services, that make money while keeping resources in use.

facts.text: They aim to use resources better, cut waste and create value for firms and customers.
A key idea is to create loops that recapture value that would otherwise be lost.
Firms adopting secondary raw materials do not necessarily cut short-term costs and may face higher perceived production costs.
Digital tools such as the internet of things, big data and AI are seen as key enablers for scaling them up.
Early talk of circularity centred on 're-X' steps such as recycling, remanufacturing, reuse and recovery.
Four strategies: narrowing loops (using fewer materials), slowing loops (repair, reuse, resale, rental), closing loops (recycling into new production) and regenerating natural systems.
They can cut costs and create new offers, but face hurdles in technology, consumer habits and profitability.

entries.text: A firm can make money by selling a product as a service, running a sharing platform or extending product life. These are circular business models: ways of earning a {{ref:nature-econ-409}} while keeping resources in use. They aim to use resources better, cut waste and create value for firms and customers. The key idea is to build loops that recapture value that would otherwise be lost. Early talk centered on 're-X' steps such as recycling, {{ref:nature-eecon-043}}, reuse and recovery. Today four strategies are named. Narrowing loops uses fewer materials. Slowing loops relies on repair, reuse, resale and rental. Closing loops recycles into new production, and the fourth regenerates natural systems. Digital tools such as the internet of things, big data and AI are seen as key to scaling up. Hurdles remain in technology, consumer habits and profitability. Firms switching to secondhand raw materials do not necessarily cut short-term costs.

entries.title: Critiques of the circular economy: can loops really close?
entries.article: Circular economy#Critiques of circular economy models

definition.text: Objections that the circular economy keeps growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice.

facts.text: Zink and Geyer argued proponents treat the world as an engineering system and questioned whether closing loops really prevents new primary production.
Because of the second law of thermodynamics, recovering dispersed materials takes energy that rises nonlinearly as recycled shares rise, so recovery can never be 100%.
Product-level efficiency gains can be offset by growth in total consumption, so some argue for a post-growth circular economy.
Most circular economy plans do not ask who controls the technologies or how costs and benefits are shared, prompting calls for a 'circular society'.

entries.contested_note: Scholars dispute whether closing material loops actually displaces primary production and whether circularity is compatible with growth.
entries.text: Physics sets a ceiling on circularity. Under the second law of thermodynamics, scattered materials take energy to gather back up, and that energy rises steeply as the recycled share rises. Recovery can therefore never reach 100%. This is one of several critiques of the {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}: objections that it leaves growth unquestioned, ignores economics and thermodynamics, and neglects social justice. The economic objection came from Zink and Geyer. They argued that supporters treat the world as an engineering system. They also questioned whether closing loops really prevents new primary production, or simply adds recycled material on top of it. Growth is a third worry. Efficiency gains for each product can be swamped by growth in total consumption. Some scholars therefore call for a post-growth circular economy. The fourth critique concerns fairness. Most circular economy plans do not ask who controls the technologies or how the costs and benefits are shared. That gap has prompted calls for a 'circular society'. These questions are open. Scholars still dispute whether closing material loops actually displaces primary production, and whether circularity is compatible with growth at all.

entries.title: R-hierarchies: ranking refuse, reuse, recycle and the rest
entries.article: Circular economy#"Re-" models to rank circularity priority

definition.text: Ranked lists of 're-' actions (refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle and so on) that order circular strategies by how much value they keep or waste they avoid.

facts.text: They are probably inspired by the 1970s motto 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle'.
In 2018 Reike and colleagues compared 69 different R hierarchies and found 38 distinct 're' words, which they unified into a 10R framework.
Refusing and reducing raw material use rank highest; reuse, repair, refurbishing, remanufacturing and repurposing come next; recycling and then energy recovery by incineration rank lowest.

entries.text: In 2018 Reike and colleagues compared 69 different R hierarchies and found 38 distinct 're' words. R-hierarchies are ranked lists of 're-' actions, such as refuse, reduce, reuse, repair and recycle. They order circular strategies by how much value they keep or how much waste they avoid. They are probably inspired by the 1970s motto 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle', and they extend the logic of the {{ref:nature-eecon-022}} to the {{ref:nature-eecon-001}}. Reike's team unified the jumble into a 10R framework. At the top sit refusing and reducing raw material use, because the best waste is the one never created. Next come reuse, repair, refurbishing, rebuilding to factory standard, and finding new uses, which keep a product or its parts working. Recycling ranks near the bottom, since it breaks products down to their materials. Lowest of all is energy recovery by incineration, which keeps only the heat.

entries.title: Cradle to cradle: materials as nutrients that circulate

definition.text: A nature-inspired way of designing products and systems in which materials are treated as nutrients that circulate safely and endlessly.

facts.text: The name plays on the phrase 'cradle to grave', the usual one-way path of a product from making to disposal.
It aims for systems that are not only efficient but essentially waste-free.
It builds on John T. Lyle's regenerative design and can be applied to cities, buildings, economies and social systems as well as products.
At Ford's River Rouge plant, a planted roof formed part of an $18 million rainwater system that saved Ford $30 million in mechanical treatment facilities.
Recycling sites usually crush whole products rather than taking them apart, which makes recovering rare-earth elements and sorting alloys uneconomical.
'Cradle to Cradle' is a trademark of the consultancy MBDC, which in 2012 handed its certification to an independent non-profit institute after criticism.

The goal is systems that are not just efficient but essentially waste-free. It builds on John T. Lyle's regenerative design and can apply to cities, buildings, economies and social systems. entries.title: Waste valorization: turning residues into value

definition.text: Giving economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials.

facts.text: It usually means using the residue of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another.
Industrial wastes suit it best because they are more consistent and predictable than household waste.
Interest grew with tighter regulation of residues and the spread of sustainable development and circular economy ideas in the 1990s and 2000s.
Mine tailings, red mud from alumina production, and even spent nuclear fuel can be valorised.

entries.text: Red mud from alumina production, mine tailings and even spent nuclear fuel can be turned into something useful. Waste valorization gives economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials. It usually means using the leftovers of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another, the core idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}. Industrial wastes suit it best. They are more consistent and predictable than household waste, so a factory can plan around them. Household rubbish varies from bin to bin. Interest grew in the 1990s and 2000s for two reasons. Regulators tightened the rules on residues, making them costlier to dump. At the same time, ideas of sustainable development and the circular economy spread. Valorization is a close cousin of {{ref:nature-eecon-044}}, with the stress on the value created.

entries.title: Remanufacturing: rebuilt as good as new

definition.text: Rebuilding a used product to the original maker's specifications from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts.

facts.text: Unlike other recovery processes, it is complete: a remanufactured machine should meet the same customer expectations as a new one.
A discarded product is fully taken apart, usable parts are cleaned and refurbished, and it is reassembled into a unit equal or sometimes better than new.
In 2020 it made up 2% of all US manufacturing and 1.9% in the EU.
It can be done with or without loss of the original product's identity, as with photocopiers and toner cartridges.

entries.text: A remanufactured machine should meet the same customer expectations as a new one. That promise sets remanufacturing apart from other recovery processes, which stop short of it. Remanufacturing rebuilds a used product to the original maker's specifications, from a mix of reused, repaired and new parts. The process is thorough. A discarded product is taken fully apart. entries.title: Upcycling: making trash worth more than before

definition.text: Turning waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value.

facts.text: It is a subset of recycling that adds value, unlike downcycling, which turns waste into lower-quality products.
Before the Industrial Revolution, upcycling to repair goods was common; mass production and a linear model of throwing things away reduced it.
The terms upcycling and downcycling first appeared in print in a 1994 SalvoNEWS article.
It is a circular economy strategy that cuts resource use by raising product value and extending product lifespans through repair and repurposing.
In poorer countries it reflects a lack of access to new goods; in rich countries, more concern for the environment.

entries.title: Material flow analysis: following matter through a system

definition.text: A method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system.

facts.text: It is a core method of industrial ecology and of the study of social and industrial metabolism.
It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter.
Every MFA system has a boundary, processes, flows between processes and stocks within them.
Unlike economic accounting, it also covers waste flows, emissions and natural resources that have no market.
It can be applied to a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life cycle, or a whole national economy.
The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.

entries.text: Matter is never created or destroyed, so every tonne entering a system must leave it or pile up inside. Material flow analysis builds on that fact. It is a method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system, and a core method of {{ref:nature-eecon-008}}. It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter. Every analysis has a boundary, processes, flows between them and stocks within them. Unlike economic accounting, it also tracks waste, emissions and natural resources that have no market. It can cover a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life or a whole national economy. The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.
entries.text_plain: Matter is never created or destroyed, so every tonne entering a system must leave it or pile up inside. Material flow analysis builds on that fact. It is a method for measuring the flows and stocks of materials or substances within a clearly defined system, and a core method of Industrial ecology: factories modeled on ecosystems. It rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance, the conservation of matter. Every analysis has a boundary, processes, flows between them and stocks within them. Unlike economic accounting, it also tracks waste, emissions and natural resources that have no market. It can cover a single plant, a supply chain, a product's life or a whole national economy. The method was developed during the 1980s and 1990s.

entries.title: The bioeconomy: growing the economy from living resources

definition.text: The part of the economy that uses renewable biological resources and biotechnology to produce food, materials, products and energy.

facts.text: Its resources come from land and sea: crops, forests, fish, animals and micro-organisms.
It aims to secure food, use natural resources more sustainably and reduce dependence on fossil resources and minerals.
The term became popular from the mid-2000s when the EU and OECD adopted it as a policy framework; the OECD (2006) and EU (2012) created bioeconomy strategies.
Its products include food, feed, bio-based products, bioenergy and services based on biological resources.
Critics fear its 'green growth' framing keeps an unsustainable model in place and may lead to an economisation of living things.

entries.title: Collecting recyclables: curbside, drop-off and buy-back

definition.text: The ways recyclables are gathered from the waste stream: drop-off centres, buy-back centres and curbside collection.

facts.text: Systems trade off public convenience against government ease and expense.
Buy-back centres pay for cleaned, sorted recyclables, giving a clear incentive; drop-off centres are easiest to set up but have low, unpredictable throughput.
Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection, gives the purest recyclates.

entries.title: Recycling policy: securing supply and creating demand

definition.text: Laws that secure a steady supply of recyclable material and a market for recycled products.

facts.text: Supply is created by mandatory collection, container deposit laws and refuse bans.
Demand is raised by minimum recycled content mandates, utilization rates, procurement policies and recycled-product labelling.

entries.title: Types of recycling: mechanical, chemical, closed and open loop

definition.text: The main ways of recycling, grouped by process and by what the material becomes.

facts.text: Mechanical recycling shreds, melts and reforms materials, while chemical recycling breaks them into chemical components.
Closed-loop recycling makes the same product without significant quality loss; open-loop recycling makes different, often lower-quality products.
Closed-loop recycling is generally seen as more sustainable because it loses fewer resources.

One study found a circular bioeconomy may be necessary for a carbon-neutral future in line with the Paris Agreement.

entries.title: Pay as you throw: a bill for every bag

definition.text: Charging households for rubbish collection according to how much waste they put out, instead of a flat fee.

facts.text: Under a flat rate or tax, everyone pays the same and there is no incentive to reduce waste.
It rests on the polluter pays principle and shared responsibility.
Waste can be measured by weight, size, or counts of special bags, tags or containers; recycling and composting are often collected free.
In North America it cut residential waste by 9-38% and raised recycling by 6-40%.
In Ferrara, Italy, it led to a 30% overall drop in waste and a 40% rise in recycling.
Charging for waste can lead to illegal dumping ('fly-tipping').

entries.title: Product-service systems: selling light, not light bulbs

definition.text: A business model in which a firm sells a combined package of products and services that together meet a customer's need.

facts.text: The idea is that customers want the function a product provides, not necessarily to own it, so firms may be paid per unit of service delivered.

Research identifies three classes: product-oriented (ownership passes with added services), use-oriented (the provider keeps ownership and sells use through sharing, pooling or leasing) and result-oriented (services replace products).
Examples include Xerox's pay-per-copy model and Philips' pay-per-lux lighting, where customers pay for a promised level of light.
Not every PSS reduces material use, but they are increasingly seen as part of firms' environmental strategy.
The concept was first developed at the Politecnico di Milano between 1993 and 1996.
Some authors claim PSS can improve eco-efficiency by a factor of 4 or more.

entries.title: Biorefineries: an oil refinery for plants

definition.text: A facility that converts biomass into energy and other useful products such as chemicals.

facts.text: The IEA defines biorefining as sustainable processing of biomass into food, feed, chemicals, materials and bioenergy.
Like an oil refinery, it splits biomass into intermediates such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats; each refining step is called a cascading phase.
Its goals include supplying fuels and chemicals, creating rural jobs, valorising waste and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Systems are classified by platform, product, feedstock and conversion process (mechanical, biochemical, chemical or thermochemical).
Biobased products can still cause land-use change, eutrophication and pesticide pollution, so life cycle assessment is used to compare them with conventional options.
The pulp and paper industry is considered the first industrialised biorefinery system.

entries.title: Right to repair: who gets to fix your phone

definition.text: The legal right of owners to maintain, repair or modify their own devices and equipment, such as cars, electronics and farm machinery.

facts.text: Obstacles such as manufacturer-only servicing, restricted parts and tools, and software locks create a 'repair monopoly'.
Repair monopolies have been found to raise prices, cause delays and reduce consumer choice.
Its goals are to favour repair over replacement and make repairs cheaper, supporting a more sustainable economy and less electronic waste.
Broken and used electronics became the fastest-growing waste stream as smartphones and computers spread.

definition.text: Tiny insoluble plastic particles, from 1 micrometre to 5 mm across, that pollute water, soil and air.

facts.text: Primary microplastics, such as microbeads, clothing microfibres and pellets, are already small when released; secondary ones come from larger items breaking down.
By 2050 the weight of microplastics in the sea is estimated to exceed that of fish.
Because some plastics take hundreds to thousands of years to degrade, microplastics are likely to be eaten and accumulate in organisms.

Nutrients in wastewater and excreta are widely reused in farming, often unsafely; WHO guidelines from 2006 set a framework for doing it safely.

Biological nutrients are organic materials that decompose into soil and feed small life forms without harming the environment.
In a hypothetical cradle-to-cradle shoe, the sole is a biological nutrient and the upper a technical one, separated when the shoe is returned.

entries.title: Life cycle thinking: from raw material to rubbish

definition.text: An approach that looks at and reduces a product's environmental impacts at every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

facts.text: A core aim is to avoid burden shifting, where an improvement at one stage causes harm at another.

Life-cycle assessment follows impacts from raw material extraction through manufacture, distribution, use, repair, disposal and recycling. The EU Waste Framework Directive brought this thinking into waste policy.

entries.title: Eco-efficiency: more value, less damage

definition.text: Providing goods and services that meet human needs while steadily cutting their environmental impact and resource use over their whole life cycle.

facts.text: It means creating more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution.
It is measured as the ratio of value produced, such as GDP, to environmental impact, such as CO2 emissions.
The World Business Council for Sustainable Development coined the term in its 1992 publication 'Changing Course', and the 1992 Earth Summit endorsed it.
With consistency and eco-sufficiency, it is one of the three basic sustainability strategies.
It relies on technological innovation, business, markets, and an acceptance of growth.
Huesemann and Huesemann showed with historical evidence that efficiency gains have not reduced overall resource use and pollution.

entries.title: Product stewardship: everyone shares the responsibility

definition.text: An approach in which everyone who makes, sells, buys, uses or disposes of a product shares responsibility for reducing its environmental and health impacts over its life.

facts.text: For manufacturers it includes planning, and if necessary paying, for recycling or disposal at end of life.
Products can be redesigned to use fewer harmful substances and be more durable, reusable and recyclable.
It differs from extended producer responsibility, which places the burden on manufacturers, by spreading it to retailers, consumers and recyclers too.
Australia's Product Stewardship Act 2011 created voluntary, co-regulatory and mandatory schemes; its TV and computer scheme has recycled about 230,000 tonnes of e-waste.

entries.title: Container deposits: a refund for every bottle

definition.text: A system in which buyers pay a refundable fee on a bottle or container, which they get back when they return it.

facts.text: Unclaimed fees can pay for landfill or litter control.
Anyone who finds and returns a bottle can claim the fee, so collecting them is a means of survival for some homeless people in US cities.
The same principle is applied to paint and tyres, where buyers pay up front for disposing of the toxic waste they become.

entries.title: Industrial symbiosis: one firm's waste, another's input

definition.text: A part of industrial ecology in which separate firms exchange materials, energy, water and by-products so that one firm's waste becomes another's input.

facts.text: Such networks optimise material and energy use beyond what any single process could achieve alone.
Collaboration and geographic proximity are seen as its keys, though proximity is neither necessary nor sufficient.
At Kalundborg in Denmark, a power station's gypsum by-product becomes raw material for a plasterboard maker.
The Kalundborg web of exchanges evolved spontaneously over a long time; designing such systems from above in a short time is hard.
By-products are usually treated as waste and not listed on any exchange, so information about them is hard to get.
Keeping resources in use longer reduces demands on Earth's resources and is a stepping-stone toward a circular economy.

facts.text: Firms in such parks physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, a form of industrial symbiosis.
They may share waste treatment, move by-products between plants, and reuse one plant's processed water in another.

definition.text: Turning food waste into food or feed products, or extracting food or feed ingredients from it.

facts.text: Landfilled food waste releases methane and other harmful compounds.
Food wastes can yield biofertilisers, bioplastics, biofuels, chemicals and nutraceuticals, and can be converted into insect protein.
About 30% of the food livestock eat comes from food waste or crops grown and processed in the supply chain.

Biodegradable plastic has been made from chicken feathers, which are 90% keratin and over 6 million tons of waste a year in the EU and US.

entries.title: Cascading use of biomass: highest value first
entries.article: Bioeconomy#Getting the most out of the biomass

definition.text: Processing biomass in an ordered pattern so that it yields the highest-value products before lower-value ones.

facts.text: The order runs from fine chemicals and medicines, through chemicals and bioplastics and transport fuels, to electricity and heat, which need the most biomass for the least value.
Finding the best pattern for a given biomass is called biorefining.

entries.title: Source reduction: stopping waste before it starts

definition.text: Cutting hazardous and other waste before it arises, by changing how things are produced.

facts.text: It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product formulation, and is sometimes called pollution prevention.
Toxics use reduction, a more controversial form, targets upstream use of toxic chemicals and has been opposed by chemical manufacturers.

entries.title: Servitization: selling the service, not the thing

definition.text: Meeting customer needs by selling a product's function or output, or a product-service package, rather than the product itself.

facts.text: It turns a one-time sale into a long-term service relationship, such as a maintenance-free service contract.
It can give access to people who cannot afford to buy outright, as with car-pooling, car-sharing or rent-to-own.
Servitizing, alongside optimizing and digitizing, is one of three main ways to dematerialize a product.

entries.title: Sustainable materials management: the whole life of stuff

definition.text: A systemic approach to using and reusing materials more productively across their whole life cycle.

facts.text: Global raw material use rose during the 20th century at about twice the rate of population growth.
Each 1 percent rise in GDP has raised raw material use by 0.4 percent.
Unlike waste management, which deals only with end-of-life waste, it covers the whole life cycle and holds every industry and consumer in it responsible.
The OECD and the US EPA have adopted it; the OECD issued a policy brief on it in 2012.

entries.title: The linear economy: take, make, waste

definition.text: The conventional 'take-make-waste' economy in which resources are extracted, made into products, used and thrown away.

facts.text: Its processes use up finite reserves to make short-lived products that end in landfills or incinerators.
It puts great pressure on the environment through extraction, energy-intensive production and large amounts of waste.
The circular economy and circular fashion are defined in contrast to it.

entries.title: Integrated product policy: acting where it counts

definition.text: A policy approach that reduces product-related environmental damage by acting at whichever life-cycle stage is most effective.

facts.text: It combines economic instruments, substance bans, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines rather than one measure.
The European Commission issued a green paper on it on 7 February 2001.

entries.title: Life cycle costing: the full price of owning something

definition.text: Adding up all the costs a product or system incurs over its whole life to find the cheapest way of providing it.

facts.text: Product-service systems use it by lowering the maintenance and storage costs a consumer would otherwise bear.
Life cycle thinking shows how the environmental cost of owning a product depends on its running costs for energy and consumables.

entries.title: Circular fashion: clothes that come back around

definition.text: Applying the circular economy to clothing so that fashion products last longer and are reused, recycled or repurposed instead of discarded.

facts.text: It replaces the take-make-use-dispose model with reduce, reuse, recycle and regenerate.
Practices include designing clothes for longevity, sustainable materials, recycling programmes and second-hand markets.
A 2017 Ellen MacArthur Foundation report, 'A New Textiles Economy', brought the term into the mainstream.

entries.title: Circular procurement: buying for the loop

definition.text: Buying goods and services that follow circular economy principles, favouring reuse, durability and recycling to extend product lives and cut waste.

facts.text: It may mean buying durable or reusable goods, shared-use models, refurbished assets or products with recycled content.
It is often seen as part of sustainable procurement and supports SDG 12's target on sustainable public procurement.
Risks include greenwashing, and barriers include high infrastructure costs and no standard definitions.

entries.title: Urban mining: digging gold out of old gadgets

definition.text: Recovering rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment.

facts.text: A 2010 Japanese government study estimated 6,800 tonnes of gold could be recovered from used electronics in Japan.
Its main aim is recovering materials, whereas landfill mining aims to fix problems at the disposal site.
In developing countries e-waste is often recycled informally, even inside homes, without proper equipment.
Shifting from primary production to urban mining needs detailed accounts of materials in use and in obsolete stocks.

entries.title: Managing people, not nature

definition.text: The management of how human societies interact with and affect the environment, rather than management of the environment itself.

facts.text: It aims to protect ecosystem services for future generations and keep ecosystems intact, weighing ethical, economic and ecological factors.
It links to natural resource, fisheries, forest and wildlife management and to environmental management systems.
The economy works within and depends on goods and services from natural ecosystems.
Its strategies rest on views of the human-nature relationship, from anthropocentrism, which values nature only for people, to ecocentrism, which grants nature intrinsic value.
ISO 14001 is the most widely used environmental management standard and is closely aligned with the EU's Eco-Management and Audit Scheme.
Resilience thinking calls for a shift from maximum sustainable yield toward environmental resource and ecosystem management.

entries.text: A forester cannot negotiate with a forest. What foresters, fishery officers and planners actually manage is people: how societies use, change and harm the environment around them. That is environmental resource management. Its goal is to keep ecosystems intact and protect the services nature provides for future generations, weighing ethical, economic and ecological concerns together. The reason is simple. The economy works inside nature and depends on the goods and services that natural ecosystems supply. The field links several older trades, including fisheries, forest and wildlife management. It also takes in the formal systems firms use to track their environmental impact. ISO 14001 is the most widely used standard of this kind. It lines up closely with the EU's Eco-Management and Audit Scheme. Underneath every strategy lies a view of how humans relate to nature. At one end sits anthropocentrism, which values nature only for what it does for people. At the other sits ecocentrism, which grants nature value in itself. Thinking has shifted too. Resilience thinking, which asks how systems absorb shocks, urges managers to stop chasing maximum sustainable yield, the largest harvest that can be taken year after year. It asks them to manage whole ecosystems instead.

entries.title: Adaptive management: learning while you decide

definition.text: A structured, repeated process for making decisions under uncertainty that uses monitoring to learn and reduce that uncertainty over time.

facts.text: Each decision serves management goals while also gathering information that improves future management.
Its main features are iterative decisions, feedback between monitoring and decisions, and treating uncertainty as a way to build understanding.
Passive adaptive management values learning only for better outcomes, while active adaptive management builds learning into the objective itself.
The hard part is balancing learning for the future against the best short-term result from current knowledge.
C. S. Holling and C. J. Walters at the University of British Columbia developed the approach and distinguished its passive and active forms.
In conservation it has three parts: testing assumptions, adapting interventions to monitoring results, and documenting lessons for learning.
Its effectiveness is hard to test, because one cannot see how another approach would have done in exactly the same situation.
Each decision both pursues management goals and gathers information to improve future management.

entries.text: Every management decision is also an experiment, whether anyone admits it or not. Adaptive management makes that explicit. It is a structured, repeated way of deciding under uncertainty, described in {{ref:nature-econ-772}}: act, monitor what happens, learn, and adjust. Each decision chases management goals while also gathering information that will improve the next one. The approach was developed by C. J. Walters and his colleague Holling at the University of British Columbia. They split it into two forms. Passive adaptive management values learning only because it leads to better outcomes. Active adaptive management writes learning into the objective itself. Its main features are decisions made in rounds, feedback between monitoring and those decisions, and treating uncertainty as a chance to understand more. In conservation it has three parts: testing assumptions, changing interventions in light of monitoring, and recording lessons. The hard part is balance. Managers must weigh learning for the future against getting the best result now from what they already know. Proving that the method works is also hard. Nobody can watch another approach play out in exactly the same situation.

entries.title: Environmental governance: who decides about nature

definition.text: The ways decisions are made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources, involving government, business and civil society.

facts.text: Key principles include building the environment into every level of decision-making and treating cities, economic and political life as part of the environment.
It also promotes a shift from open-loop, cradle-to-grave systems toward closed-loop, cradle-to-cradle systems such as zero-waste strategies.
Challenges include weak global agreements, poor coordination among the UN, governments, business and civil society, and an imbalance with trade and finance bodies such as the WTO.
The time lag between human action and environmental effect can be as long as a generation.
Since the 1970s many new international institutions have appeared, causing overlap and fragmentation but also chances for cooperation.
A 2018 study of 461 waterbird species at more than 25,000 sites found strong environmental governance was one of the most reliable predictors of conservation success.
Local governance stresses community participation and decentralisation, a bottom-up departure from earlier state-driven, top-down approaches.

Strong environmental governance was among the most reliable predictors of whether conservation succeeded. Environmental governance is the way decisions get made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources. Governments take part, but so do businesses and civil society. Its key principles include building the environment into every level of decision-making. Cities, economic life and politics are treated as part of the environment, not separate from it. It also pushes a shift from cradle-to-grave systems, where products end as waste, toward cradle-to-cradle systems that loop materials back, such as zero-waste strategies. The obstacles are large. Global agreements are weak, and the UN, governments, business and civil society coordinate poorly. Trade and finance bodies such as the WTO carry more weight than environmental ones. The gap between a human action and its environmental effect can last a generation. Since the 1970s many new international institutions have appeared, which brings overlap and fragmentation but also chances to cooperate. Locally, the emphasis has moved toward community participation and decentralization, a bottom-up break from earlier top-down, state-driven approaches.

entries.title: Treaties for the planet: international environmental agreements

definition.text: A treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources.

facts.text: An agreement between two nations is bilateral; one among three or more is a multilateral environmental agreement (MEA).
The first MEA, in 1857, regulated water flowing from Lake Constance to Austria and Switzerland; 747 MEAs were concluded between 1857 and 2012.
They multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm Conference, whose declaration was the first universal document of importance on an environmental issue.
Tools for effectiveness include trade sanctions against non-signatories and funds to share costs, such as the Montreal Protocol's $240 million fund.
Differential obligations, as in the Kyoto Protocol, give countries different targets based mainly on their development and can widen participation.
Because sovereignty means no country can be forced to join, a country facing economic costs may shirk while others comply, a classic free-rider problem.
They are criticised as slow, tending to the lowest common denominator, and lacking monitoring and enforcement.

entries.text: The first one, in 1857, dealt with water flowing from Lake Constance to Austria and Switzerland. By 2012, countries had concluded 747 more like it. An international environmental agreement is a treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources. A deal between two nations is bilateral. One among three or more is a multilateral environmental agreement, or MEA. Their numbers grew after the 1972 Stockholm Conference, whose declaration was the first universal document of importance on an environmental issue. They face a basic weakness. No country can be forced to join, so a nation facing costs may shirk while others comply and still enjoy the benefits. That is the classic free-rider problem, explained in {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Treaty makers have tools against it. Trade sanctions can target non-signatories. Shared funds can spread costs, like the Montreal Protocol's $240 million fund. Differential obligations, as in the Kyoto Protocol, set different targets based mainly on each country's level of development, which can widen participation. Even so, critics call these agreements slow. They say the deals drift toward the lowest common denominator and lack monitoring and enforcement.

entries.title: National parks: protected land and its critics

definition.text: A government-owned and protected area of natural, semi-natural or developed land set aside for conservation because of its outstanding national natural, historic or cultural value.

facts.text: Yellowstone, established by the United States in 1872, is widely held to be the world's first national park.
The IUCN classes national parks as Category II protected areas; in 1971 its criteria included a minimum size of 1,000 hectares and a ban on exploiting natural resources.
Many countries use the term loosely; in the UK a national park is a scenic, lightly developed area with planning limits and may contain sizeable settlements.
Parks Canada, set up in 1911, is the world's oldest national park service, and Canada has 450,000 km2 of national park space.
Parks support nature-based tourism; in Costa Rica park tourism rose by 400% from 1985 to 1999.
Critics say parks in former colonies removed native communities and reinforce the idea that nature is protected only where people are absent.

entries.contested_note: Critics see national parks in former colonies as a form of eco-land grabbing that displaced native communities.

entries.title: The European Green Deal and its discontents

definition.text: A set of European Commission policies, approved in 2020, whose overarching aim is to make the European Union climate neutral by 2050.

facts.text: It reviews every existing law on its climate merits and adds new laws on the circular economy, building renovation, biodiversity, farming and innovation.
It includes carbon tariffs on countries that cut emissions more slowly, through the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
Its parts include a Farm to Fork food strategy, a Zero Pollution Action Plan, the EU Biodiversity Strategy and the binding Nature Restoration Law.
A Just Transition Mechanism gives more financial aid to countries with more coal and oil shale workers or higher emissions.
In 2017 more than 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions came from producing and using energy.
Critics say it falls short of ending fossil fuels, while others blame it for higher energy prices, lost competitiveness and farmer protests.

entries.contested_note: Environmental groups call the deal too weak, while some governments, industries and farmers oppose its costs and timeline.
entries.text: In 2017, more than 75% of the European Union's greenhouse gas emissions came from producing and using energy. entries.title: The Rio Declaration: 27 principles for a fair future
entries.article: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development

definition.text: A short document of 27 principles, produced at the 1992 Earth Summit, to guide countries in future sustainable development.

facts.text: Its first principle says sustainable development is chiefly about people, who are entitled to healthy, productive lives in harmony with nature.
Principle 15 states the precautionary principle, to be applied by states according to their capabilities.
Principle 16 encourages the polluter pays principle where it serves the public interest and does not distort trade and investment.
Principle 10 stresses citizens' participation and access to environmental information, later elaborated by the Aarhus Convention.
It built on the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, aiming to set out principles states can write into their own laws.
It raised environmental awareness, but evidence from 2007 suggested little of its environmental goals had been achieved.

sources.title: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
Declaration of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

entries.text: The Rio Declaration fits on a few pages. Produced at the 1992 summit in Rio, described in {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, it sets out 27 principles to guide countries toward sustainable development. Its first principle puts people at the center: they are entitled to healthy, productive lives in balance with nature. Principle 15 states the precautionary principle, to be applied by each state according to its capabilities. Principle 16 encourages the polluter pays principle where it serves the public interest and does not distort trade and investment. Principle 10 stresses citizens' right to take part and to see environmental information, ideas later spelled out in a treaty signed in Aarhus, Denmark. The declaration built on the declaration of the 1972 Stockholm Conference, aiming for principles states could write into their own laws. It raised environmental awareness. Yet evidence from 2007 suggested that little of its environmental goals had been achieved.

entries.title: Agenda 21: a global plan with local roots

definition.text: A non-binding United Nations action plan for sustainable development, produced by the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

facts.text: 178 governments voted to adopt it at the Earth Summit in June 1992.
Its four sections cover social and economic dimensions, conservation and management of resources, the role of major groups, and means of implementation.
It is meant to be carried out at local, national and global levels, and every local government is expected to draw up its own local Agenda 21.
Implementation by member states is voluntary and has varied.
The 2015 Sustainable Development Goals took its goals and reaffirmed them as the basis of sustainable development, in 17 goals.
In the United States it became the target of conspiracy theories claiming a UN plot against property rights and sovereignty.

entries.text: In June 1992, 178 governments at the summit in Rio de Janeiro voted to adopt Agenda 21. It is a United Nations action plan for sustainable development, and it binds no one. It has four sections. They cover social and economic issues, managing resources, the role of major groups in society, and the means of putting it into practice. It is meant to work at local, national and global levels. Every local government is expected to write its own local version. Because carrying it out is voluntary, results have varied from country to country. Its ideas lasted. The 2015 global development goals took up its goals and reaffirmed them, in 17 goals. In the United States, the plan also became a target of conspiracy theories that called it a UN plot against property rights and sovereignty.

entries.title: Ecosystem management: keeping the whole system working

definition.text: An approach to natural resource management that aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs.

facts.text: Indigenous communities practised it implicitly for millennia, but it became a formal concept in the 1990s; the US Forest Service chief F. Dale Robertson formalised the term in 1992.
Unlike command-and-control management, which often weakens ecological resilience, it is holistic and adaptive.
Industrial societies had managed ecosystems mainly to maximise yields of one resource, as when US fire suppression led to fuel buildup and more intense fires.
A core principle is that long-term production of goods and services is a precondition for management, not an afterthought.
It is carried out through adaptive management, strategic management and landscape-scale conservation, with broad stakeholder participation.
It remains ambiguous and controversial, partly because some formulations rest on contested policy and scientific claims.

entries.contested_note: Ecosystem management is described as ambiguous and controversial because some formulations rest on contested claims.
entries.text: American fire suppression shows what goes wrong when one goal rules. Putting out every fire let fuel build up, and later fires burned hotter. Industrial societies often managed nature this way, maximizing the yield of a single resource. Ecosystem management takes the opposite view. It aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs. Indigenous communities practiced it implicitly for millennia. It became a formal concept in the 1990s, and US Forest Service chief F. Dale Robertson formalized the term in 1992. Unlike command-and-control management, which often weakens an ecosystem's resilience, its ability to recover from shocks, it is holistic and adaptive. It treats long-term production of goods and services as a precondition, not an afterthought. It works through adaptive and strategic management, conservation across whole landscapes and broad involvement of the public. The idea is still ambiguous and controversial. Some versions rest on contested claims about policy and science.

entries.title: Global governance: rules without a world government

definition.text: The institutions that coordinate the behaviour of actors across borders, help them cooperate, settle disputes and ease collective-action problems.

facts.text: It means making, monitoring and enforcing rules among interdependent actors when there is no overarching political authority.
Many kinds of actors, not only states, exercise power within it, including intergovernmental bodies, NGOs, businesses and civil society.
The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was one of the first organisations to promote it.
Its arrangements may be formal laws and institutions, or informal practices, guidelines and coalitions.
Treaty secretariats, such as that of the UN climate convention, have significant influence but cannot enforce laws.
Governance for sustainability is highly fragmented: a 2022 study counted 335 international organisations in the field, often weakly connected and competing for resources.

entries.text: No world government exists, yet countries still make, monitor and enforce rules together. Global governance is the set of institutions that coordinates behavior across borders. It helps actors cooperate, settles disputes and eases collective action problems, where everyone gains from cooperation but each is tempted to hold back. Power in it is spread out. Intergovernmental bodies, NGOs, businesses and civil society all exercise influence alongside states. Its arrangements can be formal laws and institutions, or informal guidelines, practices and coalitions. The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was one of the first organizations to promote it. Treaty secretariats, like that of the UN climate convention, carry real influence but cannot enforce laws. For sustainability, the system is badly fragmented. A 2022 study counted 335 international organizations in the field, often weakly connected and competing for resources.

entries.title: Ecosystem-based management: no park is an island

definition.text: An environmental management approach that considers all the interactions within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of single issues, species or ecosystem services in isolation.

facts.text: Its roots lie in the Great Lakes ecosystem policy of the late 1970s and the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, built on the claim that 'no park is an island'.
In 1932 an Ecological Society of America committee argued that US national parks had to protect all the ecosystems they contained, ideas that became its foundation.
The Craigheads found in 1979 that Yellowstone's grizzly bears could not survive within park boundaries alone, supporting broader ecosystem definitions.
Goals must cover social, cultural and economic values, not only scientific ones, and communities and stakeholders must be involved throughout.
In the oceans it moves away from single-species or single-sector management toward weighing all the human activities that affect marine environments.
Because linked social-ecological systems cannot be fully predicted or controlled, an adaptive management approach is recommended.
Scientific consensus now favours ecosystem-based fisheries management as the most viable way to balance human needs and keep ecosystem services.

entries.contested_note: A debate continues over whether ecosystem-based management has been fully put into practice.
entries.text: In 1979 the Craigheads found that Yellowstone's grizzly bears could not survive inside the park's boundaries alone. Their finding backed an older insight. Back in 1932, an Ecological Society of America committee had argued that US national parks must protect all the ecosystems they contain. Ecosystem-based management grew from such ideas. It weighs every interaction within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of tackling single issues, species or services one at a time. Its roots also run through Great Lakes policy of the late 1970s. The 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement rested on the claim that "no park is an island." Its goals must cover social, cultural and economic values as well as scientific ones, and communities take part throughout. At sea, it means weighing all the human activities that affect marine life together. Since linked human and natural systems cannot be fully predicted, adaptive management is recommended. Scientists now favor this approach for fisheries, though a debate continues over whether it has been fully put into practice.

entries.title: The ecosystem approach of the biodiversity convention

definition.text: A framework under the Convention on Biological Diversity for the integrated management of land, water and living resources that promotes conservation and fair, sustainable use.

facts.text: It brings people, the economy and ecology together into the solution of a given problem.
It became a central topic for the Convention on Biological Diversity at its second Conference of the Parties in November 1995.
At the fifth Conference of the Parties, the parties asked their scientific advisory body for a description of the approach with 12 principles.
Ecosystem management and ecosystem-based management are close relatives; all three aim to conserve and protect ecosystems but differ in framework and methods.
Applied to fisheries, it becomes the ecosystem approach to fisheries, which builds local strategies for each fishery ecosystem.

entries.text: Under the UN's biodiversity treaty, one idea became central in November 1995: the ecosystem approach. It is a framework for managing land, water and living resources together, promoting conservation and fair, sustainable use. It brings people, the economy and ecology into the solution of a given problem. At their fifth meeting, the parties asked their scientific advisory body to describe the approach, and that description came with 12 principles. It has two close relatives, ecosystem management and ecosystem-based management. All three aim to conserve ecosystems but differ in framework and methods. Applied to fishing, it becomes the ecosystem approach to fisheries, which builds a local strategy for each fishery's ecosystem.

entries.title: Public participation: a say for those affected

definition.text: Involving the public, especially those affected by or interested in a decision, in the activities and decisions of an organisation or project.

facts.text: Its core principle is that people affected by a decision have a right to take part in making it.
It is more inclusive than stakeholder engagement and implies that public input can change outcomes.
It is recognised as an environmental principle and enshrined in the Rio Declaration.
Because government alone cannot solve environmental problems, involving the public can improve transparency, accountability and compliance with environmental law.
Low-income citizens often struggle to take part because of childcare costs, time off work and limited access to education on public matters.
The hoped-for gains in public trust from participation have yet to be confirmed.

entries.text: People affected by a decision have a right to help make it. That is the core of public participation: involving the public, especially those affected or interested, in the decisions of an organization or project. It goes further than stakeholder engagement, because it implies that what the public says can change the outcome. It is a recognized environmental principle, enshrined in the Rio Declaration. Governments cannot solve environmental problems alone, and involving the public can improve transparency, accountability and compliance with environmental law. Taking part is not equally easy for everyone. Low-income citizens often struggle with childcare costs, time off work and limited access to education about public matters. And the hoped-for gain in public trust has yet to be confirmed.

entries.title: The Basel Convention and the waste trade

definition.text: An international treaty that limits the movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from developed to less developed countries.

facts.text: It was opened for signature on 21 March 1989, entered into force on 5 May 1992, and had 191 parties as of June 2024.
It arose because tighter laws in rich countries in the 1970s made waste disposal costly, so hazardous waste trade to poorer countries grew rapidly.
A trigger was the Khian Sea incident, in which a ship carrying Philadelphia incinerator ash dumped half its load on a beach in Haiti.
It requires notice, consent and tracking for cross-border waste shipments and aims to manage waste as close to its source as possible, giving an incentive to cut waste.
In May 2019 it was amended to include plastic waste as a regulated material, though the United States, a non-party, opposed this.
It calls illegal hazardous waste traffic criminal but contains no enforcement provisions.

entries.text: A ship loaded with incinerator ash from Philadelphia dumped half its cargo on a beach in Haiti. The Khian Sea incident helped trigger the Basel Convention, a treaty limiting movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from rich to poorer ones. The trade had grown because tighter laws in rich countries in the 1970s made disposal costly. Opened for signature on 21 March 1989, the convention entered into force on 5 May 1992 and had 191 parties as of June 2024. It requires notice, consent and tracking for every cross-border shipment. It also aims to deal with waste as close to its source as possible, which rewards producing less. In May 2019 it was amended to cover plastic waste, over the objection of the United States, a non-party. It calls illegal waste traffic criminal, yet contains no enforcement provisions.

entries.title: Climate governance: steering the world on climate

definition.text: The diplomacy, mechanisms and responses aimed at steering societies to prevent, mitigate or adapt to the risks of climate change.

facts.text: Modern international climate governance rests on three pillars: mitigation, adaptation and means of implementation.
A defining milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which sought to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement each country submits its own nationally determined contribution, which is not legally binding.
The North–South divide between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
It works across supranational, national, regional and local scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts as actors alongside states.
It increasingly relies on market mechanisms, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, clean development mechanism and joint implementation, alongside command-and-control rules.
A country that stays out of an agreement can still benefit from others' emission cuts without acting itself.

entries.text: A country that stays out of a climate agreement still gains when others cut their emissions. That free benefit haunts climate governance, the diplomacy and mechanisms meant to steer societies to prevent, slow or adapt to climate change. It rests on three pillars: mitigation, which cuts emissions; adaptation, which copes with change; and the means to carry them out. A milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which hoped to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, each country submits its own pledge, a nationally determined contribution that is not legally binding. A divide runs between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones. It underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Governance works at many scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts acting beside states. It leans increasingly on markets, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, alongside command-and-control rules.

That free benefit haunts climate governance, the diplomacy and mechanisms meant to steer societies to prevent, slow or adapt to climate change. It rests on three pillars: mitigation, which cuts emissions; adaptation, which copes with change; and the means to carry them out. A milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which hoped to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, each country submits its own pledge, a nationally determined contribution that is not legally binding. A divide runs between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones. It underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Governance works at many scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts acting beside states. It leans increasingly on markets, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, alongside command-and-control rules.

entries.title: Taking climate change to court

definition.text: The use of lawsuits to set legal precedents that push governments and companies to act on climate change.

facts.text: It grew as activists and lawyers turned to courts because climate politics was slow to deliver mitigation.
Cases usually rest on one of five kinds of claim: constitutional, administrative, private law, fraud or consumer protection, or human rights.
Cases rose from 884 in 24 countries in 2017 to at least 1,550 in 38 countries by July 2020, most of them in the United States.
In the Urgenda case, Dutch courts ordered the government to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by the end of 2020.
In 2021 a Hague court ordered Royal Dutch Shell to cut its global carbon emissions by 45% by 2030 compared with 2019 levels, including scope 3 emissions.
In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights became the first international court to rule that state inaction on climate change violates human rights.
Results are mixed, and companies may answer successful cases with 'backlash' suits, such as RWE's claim against the Netherlands under the Energy Charter Treaty.

entries.title: The Aarhus Convention: rights to know, speak and sue

definition.text: A 1998 UNECE treaty, signed in Aarhus, Denmark, that gives the public rights to environmental information, participation in decisions and access to justice.

facts.text: It rests on three pillars: access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice when environmental law is broken.
It entered into force in 2001, and in April 2023 had 49 parties, 48 states and the European Union, almost all in Europe and Central Asia.
It binds public authorities but excludes the private sector, whose disclosure stays voluntary.
Its compliance mechanism is unique in international environmental law because members of the public can complain directly to a committee of legal experts.
Its Kyiv Protocol is the first legally binding international instrument on pollutant release and transfer registers, inventories of pollution from industry and other sources.
Kofi Annan called it the most impressive elaboration of Principle 10 of the Rio Declaration on citizen participation.
Critics say its focus on procedures over outcomes makes it vague, and that ordinary citizens often lack the means to take part.

entries.contested_note: Critics question whether NGOs faithfully represent citizens under the convention and whether its procedural focus leaves it too vague.
entries.text: Signed in Aarhus, Denmark, on 25 June 1998, this UNECE treaty gives the public three environmental rights. People may get environmental information, take part in decisions, and go to court when environmental law is broken. It entered into force on 30 October 2001. They say its focus on procedure makes it vague, that ordinary citizens lack the means to take part, and that NGOs may not faithfully represent them.

entries.title: Multi-level governance: power up, down and sideways

definition.text: The way power is spread vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state organisations.

facts.text: Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks developed the concept in the early 1990s from studying the structures the EU created under the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.
It describes authority shifting both up from central states to bodies like the EU and down to subnational authorities.
The vertical dimension links higher and lower levels of government; the horizontal dimension covers cooperation between regions or municipalities.
Cities may contribute up to 75% of global carbon dioxide emissions, so national climate targets depend on local and subnational action.
Critics say the idea of 'levels' implies a hierarchy, when real levels interact in complex, non-hierarchical ways.

entries.text: Cities may produce up to 75% of global carbon dioxide emissions. National climate targets therefore depend on what towns and regions do. Multi-level governance describes this spread of power. It runs vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state bodies. They saw authority shifting both up, from central states to bodies like the EU, and down, to regions and cities. The vertical side links higher and lower governments. entries.title: Spatial planning: deciding what goes where

definition.text: Managing space and resources by making and carrying out plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed.

facts.text: It is usually done by national, regional or local governments and balances competing demands on land from the state, the market and local communities.
It is needed because the economy, housing and environmental protection all compete for space.
Its disciplines include land-use, urban, regional, transport and environmental planning, as well as maritime spatial planning.

entries.text: Housing, industry and nature all want the same land. Spatial planning manages that contest. It makes and enforces plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed. National, regional or local governments usually do it, balancing demands from the state, the market and local communities. It spans several disciplines: land-use, urban, regional, transport and environmental planning, and maritime spatial planning at sea.
