entries.title: The law of the sea and the constitution of the oceans

definition.text: The body of international law setting out the rights and duties of states at sea, from navigation to seabed minerals and coastal waters.

facts.text: It derives mainly from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, in force since 1994 and sometimes called the 'constitution of the oceans'.
In 1945 US President Truman extended American jurisdiction to the natural resources of its continental shelf, and Chile, Peru and Ecuador soon claimed 200 nautical miles.
UNCLOS gives each state an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles with exclusive rights to fisheries, minerals and seabed deposits.
As of June 2019 UNCLOS had been ratified by 168 states, and non-parties such as the US still treat its provisions as customary law.
It is enforced through bodies such as the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg.
About 64% of the world's oceans are international waters subject to the Law of the Sea.

entries.text: About 64% of the world's oceans are international waters governed by the law of the sea. This body of international law sets out what states may and must do at sea, from shipping to coastal waters and seabed minerals. The modern rules began with a land grab offshore. In 1945 US President Truman claimed the natural resources of the American continental shelf. Chile, Peru and Ecuador soon claimed 200 nautical miles. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS, in force since 1994, is sometimes called the "constitution of the oceans." It gives each coastal state an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles, with sole rights to fish, minerals and seabed deposits. By June 2019, 168 states had ratified it. Non-parties such as the US still treat its rules as customary law. Bodies such as the International Seabed Authority and a tribunal in Hamburg enforce it.

entries.title: Global environmental governance: a crowded, tangled system

definition.text: The worldwide system of institutions and agreements that tackles transboundary environmental problems such as climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation.

facts.text: A 2020 publication called it one of the most institutionally dynamic areas of world politics over the previous thirty years.
As of 2020 the International Environmental Agreement Database counted almost 1300 multilateral and over 2200 bilateral agreements.
Policy made separately by theme, sector or territory has produced treaties that overlap or clash.
UNEP coordinates environmental responses within the UN but is widely considered a weak organisation.
Some Global South countries see environmental governance as a 'luxury' priority of the Global North that conflicts with economic development.

entries.text: As of 2020 the world had almost 1300 multilateral environmental agreements and over 2200 bilateral ones. And some countries of the Global South see the whole effort as a "luxury" priority of the Global North that conflicts with economic development.

entries.title: The race to the bottom

definition.text: A situation in which governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards or regulations to cut costs and attract economic activity.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary competition, which tends to improve goods and services, it erodes labour laws, tax rates and environmental rules.
Places with stricter labour or environmental rules or higher taxes can lose business to less regulated places, pushing them to lower their own standards.
The term traces to US Justice Louis Brandeis, describing states competing to attract corporations in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
Firms may move to countries that do not require them to treat chemical waste before dumping it, avoiding costly treatment.
Globalisation lets a producer unconcerned with biodiversity undercut one who cares, driving a race to the bottom in conservation rules.
Whether it really happens is debated: Daniel Drezner calls it a myth, and a 2022 study found no evidence of it in labour standards, though Nita Rudra found it in developing countries.
Some US states pursue the opposite, a 'race to the top', with innovative environmental policies other states may copy.

entries.contested_note: Scholars disagree on whether a race to the bottom actually occurs, with empirical evidence on both sides.
entries.text: If one country lets factories dump untreated chemical waste, firms may move there to avoid paying for treatment. Rival countries may then loosen their own rules to keep the business. That spiral is a race to the bottom. Governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards to cut costs and attract economic activity. Ordinary competition tends to improve goods and services. This kind erodes labor laws, tax rates and environmental rules. The phrase traces to US Justice Louis Brandeis, describing states competing for corporations in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Globalization adds pressure: a producer who ignores biodiversity can undercut one who protects it. Whether the race really happens is debated. Daniel Drezner calls it a myth, and a 2022 study found no evidence of it in labor standards. Nita Rudra did find it in developing countries. Some US states even run a "race to the top," with bold environmental policies that others copy.

entries.title: Stewardship: caring for what you hold

definition.text: An ethical practice of responsibly planning and managing resources, which can be applied to the environment, economics, property and more.

facts.text: The word comes from the duties of a household steward, a keeper of the hall.
Natural resource management focuses on how management affects quality of life for present and future generations, which is called stewardship.
Stewardship councils certify products, such as the Forest Stewardship Council since 1993 and the Marine Stewardship Council since 1996.

entries.text: The word comes from the household steward, the keeper of the hall who looked after an owner's property. Stewardship is the ethical practice of planning and managing resources responsibly. Applied to nature, it means managing resources with an eye on quality of life for people now and in the future. Stewardship councils certify products made this way, such as the Forest Stewardship Council since 1993 and the Marine Stewardship Council since 1996.

entries.title: The Vienna Convention: a framework to save the ozone layer
entries.article: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

definition.text: A 1985 multilateral agreement that set the framework for international cuts in chlorofluorocarbons, which destroy the ozone layer.

facts.text: Research in the 1970s showed that man-made CFCs, used in products such as refrigerators, break down atmospheric ozone.
It entered into force in 1988 and provided the framework for the binding Montreal Protocol, though it set no binding CFC cuts itself.
Ratified by 198 states and the European Union, it is one of the most universally accepted treaties ever.
A Multilateral Fund has aided projects in nearly 150 countries, preventing the use of roughly 250,000 tons of ozone-depleting chemicals.

sources.title: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

entries.title: Local Agenda 21: sustainability at town hall

definition.text: Local programmes in which towns and cities carry out Agenda 21's sustainable development plan, as its Chapter 28 recommends.

facts.text: The Rio+10 report found over 6400 local governments in 113 countries engaged in Local Agenda 21, and 5120 of them were in Europe.
Sweden reported that 100% of its municipalities had adopted it by 2002.
ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990, is widely seen as a model of Agenda 21 implementation.

entries.title: The Bloomington school and the governed commons

definition.text: A research tradition in political economy, built around Elinor and Vincent Ostrom at Indiana University Bloomington, that studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems.

facts.text: It focuses on governance, collective action and institutional diversity, especially for common-pool resources, decentralisation and self-governance.
The Ostroms founded its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, in 1973.
Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990) challenged the 'tragedy of the commons' by showing communities worldwide managing common-pool resources successfully.
Her research named eight design principles for successful commons, among them clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution.
Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it.
Critics say its findings are hard to scale up to national or global levels and that it underplays power and inequality.

entries.contested_note: Some economists doubt Ostrom's commons findings scale up, and critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.
entries.text: One researcher at Indiana University, Ostrom, looked at pastures, fisheries and irrigation systems around the world and found something the theory said should not exist. Communities were managing shared resources well, without either the state or private owners in charge. Her 1990 book Governing the Commons challenged the tragedy of the commons, the idea that shared resources are always overused. She and Vincent Ostrom built a research tradition around such questions at the Bloomington campus. Its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, opened in 1973. The Bloomington school studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems, especially common-pool resources, decentralization and self-governance. Her work named eight design principles for lasting commons, including clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and ways to resolve conflict. In 2009 she won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it. Critics raise two doubts. Some economists question whether her findings scale up to national or global problems. Critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.

entries.title: Fisheries co-management: sharing the helm

definition.text: A flexible, cooperative way of managing aquatic resources in which fishing communities and government share responsibility.

facts.text: Five types are recognised by how power is shared: instructive, consultative, cooperative, advisory and informative management, running from government-led to user-led.
It arose because top-down fisheries management often failed and communities ignored rules, such as cuts in total allowable catch, that they did not understand.
Unlike community management, the government takes part in decisions, and rules are made and enforced jointly.
It combines scientific and traditional knowledge, and users who agree to rules are more likely to obey and help enforce them.
It is slow and costly, and some argue it empowers the already wealthy and powerful.

entries.contested_note: Some argue co-management entrenches existing inequalities, while others see it as a means of empowering communities.
entries.text: Fishers tend to ignore rules they do not understand, such as a sudden cut in the total allowable catch. Top-down fisheries management often failed for that reason. Fisheries co-management is the response: fishing communities and government share responsibility for managing aquatic resources. Five types are recognized, from government-led to user-led: instructive, consultative, cooperative, advisory and informative. Unlike pure community management, government takes part, and rules are made and enforced jointly. It blends scientific and traditional knowledge. Fishers who agree to rules are more likely to obey them and help enforce them. It is slow and costly, though. Some argue it entrenches the power of the already wealthy, while others see it as a way to empower communities.

entries.title: A treaty against air pollution that crosses borders
entries.article: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution

definition.text: A UNECE treaty that commits its parties to limit, gradually reduce and prevent air pollution, including pollution that travels long distances across borders.

facts.text: It opened for signature on 13 November 1979 and entered into force on 16 March 1983; it now has 51 parties.
Eight protocols set specific emission cuts, including the 1985 Helsinki Protocol on sulphur and the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol on acidification, eutrophication and ground-level ozone.
It was an early international effort to protect the atmosphere as a global commons, and is listed among the treaties used against acid rain.

sources.title: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution

It opened for signature on 13 November 1979 and entered into force on 16 March 1983. It now has 51 parties. Eight protocols set specific cuts, such as the 1985 Helsinki Protocol on sulphur and the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol on acidification and ground-level ozone. It was an early effort to treat the atmosphere as a shared global resource.

entries.title: The London Convention: no more dumping at sea
entries.article: London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter

definition.text: A 1972 treaty to control pollution of the sea from the deliberate dumping of wastes from ships, aircraft and platforms.

facts.text: It entered into force on 30 August 1975 and uses a 'black list' of banned materials and a 'grey list' needing special care.
Its 1996 Protocol codified the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle, and switched to a 'reverse list' banning any dumping not explicitly allowed.
In 2013 parties to the London Protocol adopted a legally binding framework for regulating marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilisation.
It does not cover land-based sources such as pipes and outfalls.

sources.title: London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter

entries.text: Ships, aircraft and platforms once dumped waste into the sea with few limits. A treaty signed on 29 December 1972 set out to control that pollution. Its Protocol of 17 November 1996 flipped the logic to a "reverse list": any dumping not explicitly allowed is banned. The protocol also wrote in the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle. In 2013 its parties adopted binding rules for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization. It does not cover pipes and outfalls on land.

entries.title: The Forest Principles: a compromise on the world's forests

definition.text: A non-binding 1992 Earth Summit document setting out recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing all types of forests.

facts.text: Negotiations were complicated by developing nations in the Group of 77 seeking more aid to pay for forest reserves, and the final text was a compromise.
They linked deforestation to third world debt and poor technology transfer, and said the extra cost of forest conservation should be shared equitably.
They led to the Montréal Process on criteria and indicators for temperate and boreal forests in 1994.

entries.text: At the 1992 summit in Rio, forests split rich and poor nations. Developing countries in the Group of 77 wanted more aid to pay for forest reserves, and the final text was a compromise. The Forest Principles are non-binding recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing every kind of forest. They tied deforestation to third world debt and weak technology transfer. They said the extra cost of saving forests should be shared fairly. They led in 1994 to the Montréal Process, which set criteria and indicators for temperate and boreal forests.

entries.title: Earth system governance: steering a planet in the Anthropocene

definition.text: A field of research that places environmental policy and conservation in the wider context of human-caused change to the whole Earth system.

facts.text: In simple terms, it is the mix of rules and efforts by actors at every level, from local to global, that aim to prevent, reduce and adapt to environmental change.
It draws on political science, sociology, economics, ecology, policy studies, geography, sustainability science and law.
Its research is organised around five linked problems: architecture, agency, adaptiveness, accountability and legitimacy, and allocation and access.
Four cross-cutting themes run through these problems: power, knowledge, norms and scale; all levels of governance matter, not only the global one.
The idea was developed by Frank Biermann in a lecture published in 2007, and the global Earth System Governance Project began in 2009.
Critics say it is too top-down; Mike Hulme argues it is hubristic to try to control the global climate through universal governance regimes.

entries.contested_note: Some critics call earth system governance too top-down and hubristic, while others say that reading of the concept is too narrow.
entries.text: Humans now change the whole Earth system, so who steers that change? Earth system governance is the research field built around the question. In simple terms, it studies the rules and efforts of actors at every level, local to global, that aim to prevent, reduce and adapt to environmental change. Frank Biermann developed the idea in a lecture published in 2007, and the global Earth System Governance Project began in 2009. It draws on political science, sociology, economics, ecology, policy studies, geography, sustainability science and law. Its research centers on five linked problems: architecture, agency, adaptiveness, accountability and legitimacy, and allocation and access. Four themes cut across them: power, knowledge, norms and scale. Every level matters, not just the global one. Critics call the field too top-down. Mike Hulme argues it is hubristic to try to control the global climate through universal regimes. Defenders reply that this reading of the concept is too narrow.

entries.title: Managing the coast as one system

definition.text: A process for managing coasts sustainably that works across geographic and political boundaries and weighs natural, social and economic systems together.

facts.text: The concept was developed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio and set out in Chapter 17 of Agenda 21.
Coastal margins cover 8% of the world's surface but provide 25% of global resources, and about 70% of people live within a day's walk of the coast.
It runs in five steps: situation assessment, plan, institutionalisation of the plan, implementation and ongoing evaluation, with no end state.
Its main constraints are institutional rather than technological, and treating the coast as common property hampers top-down control.

Its main obstacles are institutional, not technical. Because the coast is treated as common property, top-down control is hard.

entries.title: The three Rio Conventions

definition.text: The three conventions agreed at the June 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro: on climate change (UNFCCC), biological diversity (CBD) and desertification (UNCCD).

facts.text: The summit also produced Agenda 21, the Forest Principles and the Rio Declaration.
The CBD's three objectives are conserving biodiversity, using its components sustainably and sharing fairly the benefits of genetic resources.
The UNFCCC aims to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system.
The UNCCD links sustainable land management to land degradation and aims at land degradation neutrality, with a focus on restoring drylands.

entries.text: The June 1992 summit in Rio de Janeiro, described in {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, produced three conventions, on climate, biodiversity and desertification. The UNFCCC aims to hold greenhouse gas levels where they prevent dangerous human interference with the climate. The CBD has three goals: conserve biodiversity, use it sustainably, and share fairly the benefits drawn from the genes of living things. The UNCCD ties sustainable land management to land degradation and aims for no net loss of healthy land, with a focus on restoring drylands. The summit also produced Agenda 21, the Forest Principles and the Rio Declaration.

entries.title: Polycentric governance: many centers, no single boss

definition.text: Governance by many overlapping, independent decision-making centres operating at different scales, rather than by one central authority.

facts.text: Vincent Ostrom argued such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving.
It challenged the usual choice between central government control and privatisation, suggesting self-organising systems often beat top-down solutions.
Elinor Ostrom proposed that key management decisions be taken as close as possible to the events and actors involved.
Some question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.
In a polycentric network, a resource that cannot be monitored as a whole is less likely to be well managed, as with space debris.

entries.contested_note: Critics question whether polycentric governance applies where institutional capacity is weak or corruption is high.
entries.text: Must every shared resource be run either by a central government or by private owners? Vincent Ostrom said no. Polycentric governance means rule by many overlapping, independent decision-making centers at different scales, instead of one central authority. Ostrom argued that such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving. The idea suggested that self-organizing systems often beat top-down solutions. His fellow Bloomington scholar, Elinor, added that key management decisions should be made as close as possible to the events and people involved. The approach has limits. A resource that cannot be monitored as a whole, such as space debris, is less likely to be well managed in a polycentric network. Critics also question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.

entries.title: Governing through goals

definition.text: A way of governing globally through goals that are not legally binding, leave each country flexibility and come without strong institutions.

facts.text: The Sustainable Development Goals for 2015 to 2030 are an example, following the Millennium Development Goals of 2000 to 2015.

entries.text: Some global governance works without binding law. In global goal-setting, countries sign up to goals that are not legally binding, keep flexibility in how they meet them, and lack strong institutions to enforce them. The UN's goals for sustainable development from 2015 to 2030 are an example. They followed the Millennium Development Goals, which ran from 2000 to 2015.

entries.title: Orchestration: steering the world indirectly

definition.text: A soft, indirect form of global steering in which an actor such as an international organisation recruits voluntary intermediaries to influence a target group.

facts.text: It fills gaps by complementing existing regimes; its three activities are agenda setting, coordination and support.
The UN's five regional economic commissions act as orchestrators for the Sustainable Development Goals.

entries.text: An international organization often lacks the power to order anyone around. Orchestration is its workaround. It is a soft, indirect form of global steering: the organization recruits willing intermediaries, who then influence a target group. It complements existing regimes and fills their gaps through three activities: agenda setting, coordination and support. The UN's five regional economic commissions, for example, act as orchestrators for the UN's goals for sustainable development.

entries.title: Institutional fit: matching rules to the problem's size

definition.text: The match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it.

facts.text: Such mismatches reduce how well interventions work.
Elinor Ostrom and others argued that mismatch often causes unsustainable management and that no simple fixes have been found.
Collaborative environmental governance aims to deal with scale mismatches in social-ecological systems.

entries.text: A river basin may span three countries while each country manages only its own stretch. Institutional fit is the match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it. Mismatches make interventions work less well. The political economist Ostrom and others argued that mismatch often causes unsustainable management, and no simple fixes have been found. Getting agencies and communities to cooperate across scales is one attempt to close the gap.

entries.title: Marine spatial planning: zoning the sea

definition.text: A public process of mapping and allocating where and when human activities take place at sea to meet ecological, economic and social goals set through politics.

facts.text: It is similar to land-use planning, but for marine waters, and generally uses maps of how an area is used and what resources and habitats it holds.
Planning lets managers weigh the combined effects of maritime industries and reduce conflicts between users of the same sea area.
Its aim is to use marine resources within clear environmental limits so ecosystems stay healthy and biodiversity is conserved.
The EU's Maritime Spatial Planning Directive required coastal member states to set up their own plans by 2021, covering fishing, aquaculture, conservation, shipping and renewable energy.
It can speed offshore renewable energy by streamlining licensing and reducing conflict among sea users.

entries.text: A single stretch of sea may host fishing boats, shipping lanes, wind farms and protected habitat at once. Marine spatial planning is a public process that maps and allocates where and when human activities happen at sea, to meet goals set through politics. It works like land-use planning for marine waters, using maps of how an area is used and what habitats it holds. Planners can weigh the combined effects of maritime industries and reduce conflicts among users. The aim is to use marine resources within clear environmental limits, so ecosystems stay healthy. The EU required its coastal member states to set up plans by 2021, covering fishing, aquaculture, conservation, shipping and renewable energy. Planning can also speed offshore wind and other renewables by streamlining licensing.

entries.title: The Basel Ban: closing the recycling loophole

definition.text: A 1995 amendment to the Basel Convention that bans exports of hazardous waste from mostly OECD developed countries to developing countries, for any reason including recycling.

facts.text: It came because the original convention only required prior informed consent and traders were justifying exports as recycling.
Croatia became the 97th country to ratify it on 6 September 2019, so it entered into force on 5 December 2019.
Industry groups and countries including Australia and Canada strongly opposed it.

entries.contested_note: Parties disagreed over how many ratifications were needed for the amendment to enter into force.
entries.text: Waste traders had found a loophole: call a shipment "recycling" and send it abroad. The original Basel Convention only required prior informed consent. The Basel Ban Amendment of 1995 bans hazardous waste exports from mostly OECD developed countries to developing countries, for any reason, recycling included. Industry groups, Australia and Canada strongly opposed it. Parties even disagreed over how many ratifications it needed. Croatia became the 97th country to ratify on 6 September 2019, and the ban entered into force on 5 December 2019.

entries.title: The Lisbon Principles for shared resources

definition.text: Six principles set out in 1997 by ecological economist Robert Costanza for the sustainable governance of the oceans and other shared resources.

facts.text: Access to environmental resources brings a duty to use them in ways that are ecologically sustainable, economically efficient and socially fair.
Under uncertainty about irreversible harm, decisions should err on the side of caution, and the burden of proof should fall on those whose activities may cause damage.
All internal and external costs and benefits should be identified and allocated, and markets adjusted to reflect full costs where appropriate.
Governance should sit at scales that have the best information and can act quickly, and all stakeholders should take part.

entries.text: In 1997, the ecological economist Costanza set out six principles for governing the oceans and other shared resources sustainably. Access to a resource brings a duty to use it in ways that are ecologically sustainable, economically efficient and socially fair. When irreversible harm is possible but uncertain, decisions should err toward caution. The burden of proof falls on those whose activities may cause damage. All costs and benefits, including those borne by outsiders, should be counted, and markets adjusted to reflect full costs where appropriate. Governance should sit at the scale with the best information and quickest response, and every stakeholder should take part.

entries.title: Earth system law: law for a whole planet

definition.text: A young legal field, part of earth system governance, that imagines law rooted in the planetary scale of the Anthropocene and its socio-ecological crisis.

facts.text: As of 2021 the concept was still in its infancy, and its precise content, purpose and scope remain a work in progress.

entries.text: Law has usually been built around nations and property. Earth system law, a young branch of earth system governance, imagines law rooted instead in the planetary scale of the Anthropocene and its social and ecological crisis. As of 2021 the idea was still in its infancy. Its precise content, purpose and scope remain a work in progress.

entries.title: Planetary justice: fairness for people and nature

definition.text: A view of justice that extends environmental justice to the whole human and non-human world, covering fairness among people and between people and nature.

facts.text: Scholars called for planetary justice as early as 1972.
Five main approaches to planetary stewardship are market liberal, bioenvironmentalist, ecomodernist, institutionalist and social green, and none yet delivers a pro-poor vision of justice.

entries.text: One kind of justice asks whether people share environmental harms fairly. Planetary justice widens the circle. It covers fairness among people and also between people and the rest of the living world. Scholars called for it as early as 1972. Five main approaches to caring for the planet exist: market liberal, bioenvironmentalist, ecomodernist, institutionalist and social green. None yet offers a vision of justice that puts the poor first.

entries.title: Freedom of the seas: can anyone own the ocean?

definition.text: The principle that the open sea is international territory that every nation may use but none may own.

facts.text: Hugo Grotius set it out in Mare Liberum in 1609, arguing the sea, like air, cannot be occupied and is meant for everyone's use.
John Selden replied in Mare Clausum that the sea could be appropriated by states just like land.
National waters were long limited to a belt of usually three nautical miles under the 'cannon shot' rule.
The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea replaced the older freedom-of-the-seas concept.

entries.contested_note: Grotius argued the sea is common to all, while Selden argued it could be owned like land.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

entries.text: In 1609 Hugo Grotius argued in Mare Liberum that the sea, like the air, cannot be occupied and belongs to everyone's use. John Selden answered in Mare Clausum that states could claim the sea just like land. Grotius's view became the principle of freedom of the seas: the open sea is international territory that every nation may use and none may own. National waters long stopped at a narrow belt, usually three nautical miles, under the "cannon shot" rule. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea later replaced the old concept.

entries.title: Sharing rivers across borders

definition.text: The rules and agreements that govern how states share transboundary waters, meaning rivers, lakes, seas or groundwater bordered by two or more states.

facts.text: Countries negotiate transboundary water agreements to reduce the risk of conflict, but many shared international rivers still lack treaties.
Such agreements often focus on water infrastructure and water quality.
The UNECE Water Convention on transboundary watercourses and international lakes, signed in Helsinki in 1992, entered into force on 6 October 1996.
Its principles of 'prior appropriation' and 'riparianism' can worsen conflict by legally fixing who has water abundance and who has scarcity.

entries.text: Many rivers flow through several countries, and many of them still lack any treaty. International water law is the set of rules and agreements governing how states share transboundary waters: rivers, lakes, seas or groundwater bordered by two or more states. Countries negotiate such agreements to lower the risk of conflict, often focusing on infrastructure and water quality. The UNECE Water Convention, signed in Helsinki in 1992, entered into force on 6 October 1996. Some legal principles can backfire. "Prior appropriation" and "riparianism" can deepen conflict by fixing in law who has plenty of water and who has too little.

entries.title: Where science meets policy

definition.text: The meeting ground where scientists and policy-makers work together so that research can inform, and be guided by, decisions.

facts.text: IPBES was established by governments in 2012 to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services.
The IPCC was the first of three global science-policy panels, followed by IPBES in 2012 and a panel on chemicals, waste and pollution in 2025.
Translating research into governance is hard because science and politics treat uncertainty very differently.
A review of pollution found a lack of a globally supported formal science–policy interface to inform action, research and funding.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: Scientists and politicians treat uncertainty very differently, which makes it hard to turn research into rules. The science-policy interface is the meeting ground where the two work together, so research can inform decisions and be guided by them. The IPCC was the first of three global panels built for this. A biodiversity panel followed in 2012, for biodiversity and ecosystem services, and a panel on chemicals, waste and pollution came in 2025. A review of pollution still found no globally backed formal interface to guide action, research and funding.

entries.title: Collaborative environmental governance

definition.text: An approach to environmental governance that builds cooperation among actors across scales and jurisdictions to deal with mismatches of scale in linked human and natural systems.

facts.text: Collaboration can create new knowledge through social learning, in which what individuals learn by interacting changes a whole community's understanding.
It can bring Indigenous and traditional knowledge into decisions, which may raise trust and the sense that the process is fair.
Collaboration costs time and resources and can be too slow for urgent problems.
Where large state actors dominate, collaboration can become co-optation that reinforces uneven power.

entries.text: Rivers, forests and fisheries rarely respect the lines between agencies and jurisdictions. Collaborative environmental governance builds cooperation among actors across those scales to manage linked human and natural systems. It can create new knowledge through social learning, where what individuals learn together changes a whole community's understanding. It can also bring Indigenous and traditional knowledge into decisions, which may raise trust and a sense of fairness. The costs are real. Collaboration takes time and resources and can be too slow for urgent problems. Where large state actors dominate, it can become co-optation that deepens uneven power.

entries.title: Environmental policy beyond the nation

definition.text: Environmental policy that tackles global problems such as climate change, ozone depletion or marine pollution and involves actors from at least two sovereign states.

facts.text: As of 2018 more than 1,800 multilateral environmental agreements were in effect, more than 190 of them on climate change.
The 1972 Stockholm conference is seen as the beginning of international environmental law and policy.
Transnational environmental NGOs drive change through market-based certification, of which the Forest Stewardship Council is among the most successful.

entries.title: Transition management: steering toward sustainability

definition.text: A governance approach that tries to speed up sustainability transitions through a participatory process of shared visions, learning and experiments.

facts.text: Participants meet in a 'transition arena' to define shared problems and visions, which are then tested through experiments and reflection.
It takes a long view of one to three generations and favours 'learn by doing, doing by learning' at the niche level.
Rather than control change by command and control, it steers and indirectly redirects actors' choices toward sustainability.
The Dutch government used it in the early 2000s to manage a radical transformation of its energy system.
With few case studies, its methodology is still debated.

entries.text: In the early 2000s the Dutch government tried to steer a radical transformation of its energy system. It used transition management, a way of speeding sustainability transitions through shared visions, learning and experiments. Participants meet in a "transition arena" to define common problems and goals. These ideas are then tested in small experiments and reflected on. The approach takes a long view of one to three generations and favors "learn by doing, doing by learning" at the level of small, innovative niches. It does not command change. It nudges and redirects actors' choices toward sustainability. With few case studies, its method is still debated.

entries.title: Landscapes, regimes and niches: how systems change

definition.text: A framework that sees change in socio-technical systems as playing out across three levels: the broad landscape, the dominant regime and innovative niches.

facts.text: The landscape is the wider setting of values, beliefs, institutions and market conditions, and it changes slowly.
The regime is the set of dominant practices, rules and technologies that keep the current system stable.
Rising environmental awareness, a landscape change, pressures regimes such as aviation and agriculture and opens room for new technologies.

entries.text: Why do new technologies sometimes break through and sometimes stall? The multi-level perspective sees change in systems that combine technology and society as unfolding on three levels. The landscape is the wide setting of values, beliefs, institutions and market conditions, and it shifts slowly. The regime is the set of dominant practices, rules and technologies that keeps the current system stable. Niches are where innovations start. When the landscape shifts, as with rising environmental awareness, it pressures regimes such as aviation and agriculture. That opens room for new technologies from the niches.

entries.title: The Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals for 2030

definition.text: Seventeen global goals that all UN members adopted in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

facts.text: The 17 goals come with 169 measurable targets and link the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development.
The SDGs are universal, time-bound and legally non-binding policy objectives agreed by governments.
Each goal typically has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, averaging 1.5 indicators per target.
Three goals focus on the environment: SDG 13 (climate), SDG 14 (oceans) and SDG 15 (land), but there is no overarching planetary goal.
On 25 September 2015 the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted the agenda titled 'Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'.
The SDGs succeeded the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015; critics note there are many more goals than the eight MDGs.
A 2024 UN report found only 17% of SDG targets on track; the 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress and 18% were in reverse.
Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten progress, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed it.

entries.text: On 25 September 2015, the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted a plan with a bold title: "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." At its heart sit the Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs. There are 17 goals with 169 measurable targets, and they tie together the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development. Each goal usually has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, about 1.5 on average. The goals are universal and time-bound, but they bind no one legally. Three focus on the environment: SDG 13 on climate, SDG 14 on oceans and SDG 15 on land. There is no single goal for the planet as a whole. The SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015. Critics note the new list is much longer than the eight goals it replaced. Progress is slow. A 2024 UN report found only 17% of targets on track. The 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress, while 18% were going backward. Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten the rest, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed things further.
entries.text_plain: On 25 September 2015, the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted a plan with a bold title: "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." At its heart sit the Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs. There are 17 goals with 169 measurable targets, and they tie together the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development. Each goal usually has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, about 1.5 on average. The goals are universal and time-bound, but they bind no one legally. Three focus on the environment: SDG 13 on climate, SDG 14 on oceans and SDG 15 on land. There is no single goal for the planet as a whole. The SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015. Critics note the new list is much longer than the eight goals it replaced. Progress is slow. A 2024 UN report found only 17% of targets on track. The 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress, while 18% were going backward. Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten the rest, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed things further.

entries.title: The Convention on Biological Diversity

definition.text: A multilateral treaty, known informally as the Biodiversity Convention, for conserving the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It has three main goals: conserving biodiversity, using its components sustainably, and sharing fairly the benefits from genetic resources.
It opened for signature at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.
As of 2016 it had 196 Parties; the United States is the only UN member state that has not ratified it, citing sovereignty and economic interests.
It has two supplementary agreements, the Cartagena Protocol on biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on benefit-sharing.
Its regulated issues include access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge, with prior informed consent of the providing party.
The idea was conceived at a UNEP expert working group in November 1988; its Secretariat in Montreal operates under UNEP.
Its Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020 contained the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, later followed by the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework.

entries.title: Protected areas: fencing off nature's value

definition.text: A place that is protected because of its recognised natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited.

facts.text: The IUCN defines it as a clearly defined space managed, by legal or other effective means, for the long-term conservation of nature and its ecosystem services.
As of 2016 over 161,000 protected areas covered about 17 percent of the world's land surface, excluding Antarctica.
14,688 marine protected areas cover about 10.2% of coastal and marine areas and 4.12% of the global ocean.
Protecting biodiversity in them also protects ecosystem services such as water, fuel, carbon sequestration and climate regulation.
Under Article 8 of the Biodiversity Convention, parties agreed to establish a system of protected areas.
Protecting places is not new: over 2000 years ago royal decrees in India protected certain areas.
New restrictions can displace local people, souring relations with conservationists and sometimes driving poaching.

entries.text: Over 2000 years ago, royal decrees in India set certain areas apart. Protecting places is old. A protected area is a place guarded for its natural or cultural value, where human use of resources is limited. The IUCN, the world conservation body, defines it more precisely. It is a clearly bounded space managed, by law or other means, to conserve nature and its services long term. Those services are a big part of the point. Protecting biodiversity also protects water, fuel, carbon storage and climate regulation. Under Article 8 of the Biodiversity Convention, parties agreed to build systems of protected areas. As of 2016, over 161,000 of them covered about 17 percent of the world's land, not counting Antarctica. At sea, 14,688 marine protected areas cover about 10.2% of coastal and marine areas and 4.12% of the global ocean. Protection has a cost for some people. New restrictions can displace local communities. That sours relations with conservationists and sometimes drives poaching.

entries.title: Genetic resources: who owns life's code?

definition.text: Genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources that has actual or potential value.

facts.text: They are one of the three levels of biodiversity defined by the Biodiversity Convention in 1992.
Germplasm, for example, is genetic material kept for breeding, preservation and research.
Earlier agreements treated genetic resources as common heritage; the CBD instead gave each state sovereign rights over those in its territory.
Developing countries criticised the common heritage approach for letting their resources be exploited without compensation and commercialised in industrialised nations.

entries.text: A seed bank is a library of genes. Germplasm, genetic material kept for breeding, preservation and research, is one example. Genetic resources are genetic material from plants, animals, microbes or other sources with actual or potential value. The Biodiversity Convention in 1992 named them one of the three levels of biodiversity. Earlier agreements treated them as the common heritage of humankind, open to all. Developing countries objected. Their resources were taken without payment and turned into products in industrialized nations. The convention changed the rule, giving each state sovereign rights over the genetic resources on its territory.

entries.title: UNCLOS: the treaty that governs the oceans
entries.article: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

definition.text: An international treaty, known as UNCLOS, that sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities.

facts.text: It came out of the third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea, 1973 to 1982, and entered into force on 16 November 1994.
It replaced the 17th-century 'freedom of the seas' idea, under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation.
It set zones measured from a baseline, including exclusive economic zones extending 200 nautical miles.
Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to license seabed mining and distribute royalties.
Part XII obliges all states to cooperate in protecting the marine environment.
It has 172 parties; the United States signed but has not ratified it.
The 2023 High Seas Treaty was added because UNCLOS gave no framework for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

entries.text: Negotiations ran from 1973 to 1982 at the third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea. The result, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities. It entered into force on 16 November 1994. It replaced the 17th-century idea of freedom of the seas, under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation. It sets zones measured from a coastal baseline, including exclusive economic zones reaching 200 nautical miles. Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to license seabed mining and share royalties. Part XII obliges all states to cooperate in protecting the marine environment. It has 172 parties, and the United States has signed but not ratified it. It had a gap: no framework for biodiversity beyond national waters. A 2023 treaty, described in {{ref:nature-gov-049}}, was added to fill it.

entries.title: SDG 14: life below water

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life below water': to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.

facts.text: It has ten targets, covering marine pollution, ecosystem protection, ocean acidification, sustainable fishing and conserving coastal and marine areas.
Target 14.5 aimed to conserve at least 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020, measured by protected-area coverage.
Target 14.4 is measured by the share of fish stocks within biologically sustainable levels.
Ocean pH now averages 8.1, about 30% more acidic than in pre-industrial times.
Sustainable fisheries made up roughly 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017.
Oceans cover over 70% of Earth's surface, yet from 2013 to 2021 only 1.1% of national research budgets went to ocean science.
The World Economic Forum estimates US$175 billion a year of blue finance is needed to achieve SDG 14.

entries.title: SDG 13: climate action

definition.text: The UN goal 'Climate action': to take urgent action to limit climate change and adapt to its impacts.

facts.text: It has five targets for 2030, including strengthening resilience to climate disasters and building climate measures into national policy.
Target 13.a refers to developed countries' commitment to mobilise $100 billion a year by 2020 for developing countries.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C, but pledges would still lead to about 2.7 °C by 2100.
Indicator 13.2.1 counts countries with nationally determined contributions and adaptation plans.
COVID-19 cut 2020 emissions about 6% below projections, but the fall was only temporary.
Critics say it overlooks climate migration as an adaptive response.

entries.title: IPBES: the scientists' voice for biodiversity
entries.article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

definition.text: An independent intergovernmental body, set up by governments in 2012, that links biodiversity science to policy-making.

facts.text: It plays a role similar to the IPCC, but besides assessments it also builds knowledge, capacity and policy support tools.
A 2010 UN General Assembly resolution asked UNEP to convene a meeting to establish it; its members meet in Plenaries every one to two years.
Its 2019 Global Assessment, adopted by representatives of 132 members in Paris, was the largest study to date of biodiversity and ecosystem services.
A 2020 IPBES report said preventing pandemics through conservation is more cost-effective than responding after outbreaks.
IPBES and the IPCC shared the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity in October 2022.
In January 2026 the United States announced its withdrawal from IPBES.

entries.title: The UN treaty against desertification
entries.article: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

definition.text: A UN treaty to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through long-term national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

facts.text: It defines desertification as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions caused by climate variations and human activities.
Adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and in force since December 1996, it is the only convention arising directly from the Rio Agenda 21.
It is the only legally binding international framework on desertification and has 197 parties.
National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities, are its key instruments.
Its 2018–2030 Strategic Framework includes supporting land degradation neutrality and strengthening drought resilience.
At COP16 in Riyadh in December 2024, more than US$12 billion was pledged for desertification, land degradation and drought.

sources.title: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

entries.text: Desertification, in the treaty's words, is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions, caused by climate swings and human activity. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification tackles it, and eases drought, through long-term national programs backed by international cooperation. It was adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and has been in force since December 1996. It is the only convention to grow directly out of Agenda 21, and the only binding international framework on desertification. It has 197 parties. Its key tools are National Action Programmes, drawn up with local communities. Its 2018–2030 framework aims for land degradation neutrality, no net loss of healthy land, and stronger drought resilience. At its COP16 meeting in Riyadh in December 2024, countries pledged more than US$12 billion.

entries.title: Biodiversity action plans: a country's to-do list for nature

definition.text: A national or local program for protecting and restoring threatened species and habitats, prepared under the Biodiversity Convention.

facts.text: The concept emerged from the 1992 Biodiversity Convention, which asked nations to develop strategies for conserving biodiversity.
A typical plan inventories species or habitats, assesses their conservation status, sets targets, and lays out budgets, timelines and partners.
Plans can focus on species, habitats or agricultural production.
As of 2009, 191 countries had ratified the CBD, but only some had produced comprehensive plans.
A country plan may cost up to 100 million pounds sterling, with yearly upkeep about ten percent of that, which strains poorer countries.
Critics note many plans are pro-forma and almost all overlook fungi, invertebrates and micro-organisms.
Some developing countries object that the plans put wildlife protection above food and industrial production.

entries.title: SDG 15: life on land

definition.text: The UN goal 'Life on land': to protect, restore and sustainably use land ecosystems, manage forests, combat desertification and halt biodiversity loss.

facts.text: It has 12 targets to be achieved by 2030, measured by 14 indicators.
Outcome targets include ending deforestation, restoring degraded land, protecting habitats and sharing benefits from genetic resources fairly.
Forests cover roughly 4 billion hectares, or 30.7 per cent of the world's land; 93 percent are natural and 7 percent planted.
Target 15.5 on threatened species is measured by the Red List Index.
Target 15.9 asks countries to build ecosystem and biodiversity values into national planning and accounts.
As of 2023 there was about a $700 billion gap in financial support for low-income countries to protect biodiversity.
Deforestation is estimated to have risen by 12% from 2019 to 2020.

entries.title: World Heritage Sites: places that belong to everyone

definition.text: A landmark or area protected under a UNESCO-run treaty because of its outstanding cultural, historical or natural value to humanity.

facts.text: The World Heritage Convention was adopted by UNESCO on 16 November 1972, took effect on 17 December 1975, and had 196 states as of November 2024.
Sites must have 'outstanding universal value' and meet at least one of ten criteria, including containing key natural habitats for conserving biodiversity.
Listing brings international recognition, legal protection, possible World Heritage Fund money, and often more tourism revenue.
Nearly three-quarters of bird species and two-thirds of mammals have been recorded at World Heritage Sites, which cover less than 1% of the planet.
Threatened sites can go on the List of World Heritage in Danger; only three have ever been delisted.
Critics point to a lobbying industry driven by tourism returns and costly bids that disadvantage poorer countries.

entries.title: The Ramsar Convention: saving the world's wetlands

definition.text: An international treaty, signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance.

facts.text: It took effect on 21 December 1975 and is also called the Convention on Wetlands.
In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres.
To join, a country had to designate at least one wetland site and guarantee its protection.
World Wetlands Day, 2 February, marks its adoption in 1971.
Domestic implementation is often half-hearted and inadequate.

entries.text: Every 2 February is World Wetlands Day. It marks the signing of a treaty at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance. At home, though, countries often put the treaty into practice half-heartedly and inadequately.

entries.title: The Aichi Targets: twenty goals that were missed
entries.article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020

definition.text: Twenty international targets for 2011–2020, set under the Biodiversity Convention, to protect biodiversity, species and sustainable use of resources.

facts.text: They were part of the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020, agreed at COP 10 in Nagoya in October 2010, and addressed five strategic goals.
Goal A sought to tackle the underlying causes of biodiversity loss by mainstreaming biodiversity across government and society.
Other goals aimed to cut direct pressures, safeguard ecosystems, species and genetic diversity, and enhance benefits from ecosystem services.
Countries failed to meet them because they lacked clarity, were hard to measure, went unreported and had limited funding.
The CBD mapped synergies between the 17 SDGs and the 20 Aichi targets.

entries.text: In October 2010, at a meeting in Nagoya, Japan, the parties to the Biodiversity Convention agreed 20 targets for the decade to 2020. These were the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, part of a strategic plan with five broad goals. Goal A went after the root causes of biodiversity loss by building nature into every part of government and society. Others aimed to cut direct pressures on nature, safeguard ecosystems, species and genetic diversity, and increase the benefits of ecosystem services. The convention later mapped how they overlapped with the 17 SDGs. Countries failed to meet them. The targets lacked clarity, were hard to measure, went unreported and had too little funding.

entries.title: The Nagoya Protocol: paying for the genes you take

definition.text: A 2010 supplementary agreement to the Biodiversity Convention on access to genetic resources and fair sharing of the benefits from their use.

facts.text: It implements the CBD's third objective, the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
Adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, it entered into force on 12 October 2014; by August 2025 it had 142 parties.
It gives each country sovereign rights over its biological resources, making biopiracy illegal.
Access requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms; benefits may be monetary or non-monetary, such as royalties or shared research results.
It also covers traditional knowledge linked to genetic resources, which cannot be accessed without permission from the communities holding it.
Users must monitor genetic resources after they leave a country through checkpoints along the value chain, from research to commercialisation.
Marine genetic resources from the high seas fall outside its benefit-sharing regime, because it covers only national jurisdiction.

entries.text: Taking a plant's genes from another country without permission is now illegal under the Nagoya Protocol. This 2010 add-on to the Biodiversity Convention carries out the treaty's third goal: fair sharing of the benefits from genetic resources. It was adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, and entered into force on 12 October 2014. By August 2025 it had 142 parties. Access needs prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms. Benefits may be money, such as royalties, or something else, such as shared research results. Traditional knowledge about genetic resources is covered too, and cannot be used without the holding communities' permission. Users must track resources after they leave a country, through checkpoints from research to sale. One gap remains. Genes from the high seas fall outside it, because it covers only national territory.

entries.title: The High Seas Treaty: governing ocean no one owns

definition.text: A legally binding agreement under the Law of the Sea convention to conserve and sustainably use marine life in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

facts.text: Areas beyond national jurisdiction, the high seas and the international seabed, make up about two-thirds of the ocean and were largely unregulated.
The text was adopted on 19 June 2023; Morocco's ratification on 19 September 2025 made 60, and it took effect on 17 January 2026.
It covers four elements: marine genetic resources, area-based tools including marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, and capacity building.
Benefits from marine genetic resources, used in cosmetics and medicines, are to be shared, both monetary and non-monetary; fish and fishing are excluded.
Marine protected areas on the high seas can be adopted by consensus or a three-quarter majority and then bind all parties.
Parties must carry out environmental impact assessments for activities that may affect the marine environment.
Negotiations turned on the tension between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

entries.title: Conservation outside the fence: OECMs

definition.text: Sites outside formal protected areas that are governed and managed in ways that conserve biodiversity in place over the long term.

facts.text: Unlike protected areas, OECMs need not be dedicated to conservation, but must deliver effective long-term conservation of biodiversity.
The term first appeared in Aichi Target 11 in 2010, which sought to conserve 17% of land and inland waters and 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020.
The CBD formalised the definition in 2018 through Decision 14/8 at COP 14, building on Canadian guidelines and IUCN advice.
OECMs count towards Target 3 of the Global Biodiversity Framework.
As of June 2026, 7,488 OECM sites cover 1.31% of Earth's surface, about 1.1% on land and 0.21% at sea.
They allow small-scale uses such as fisheries and low-impact agroforestry and aim to be more equitable than protected areas, which have caused displacement.
Locally managed marine areas are one form of OECM.

entries.text: Some of the best-kept nature on Earth sits outside any official reserve. Other effective area-based conservation measures, or OECMs, are such sites: governed and managed so that they conserve biodiversity in place over the long term. Unlike protected areas, they need not be set aside for conservation, but they must deliver it. The term first appeared in Aichi Target 11 in 2010. That target sought to conserve 17% of land and inland waters and 10% of coastal and marine areas by 2020. Locally managed marine areas are one form. They aim to be fairer than protected areas, which have displaced people.

entries.title: What the SDGs would cost

definition.text: Estimates of how much money reaching the SDGs would take, and where it might come from.

facts.text: In 2014 UNCTAD estimated the cost of reaching the goals at US$2.5 trillion per year.
A 2020 estimate put the financing gap in developing countries at US$2.5 trillion per year before COVID-19, projected to rise to US$4.2 trillion in 2020.
The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda is one UN process for financing the SDGs, and private investment is seen as essential.
Blended finance is designed to support progress towards the SDGs.

entries.text: In 2014, UNCTAD estimated that reaching the Sustainable Development Goals would cost US$2.5 trillion a year. A 2020 estimate put developing countries' financing gap at the same US$2.5 trillion a year before COVID-19, rising to US$4.2 trillion in 2020. The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda is one UN process for raising the money. Private investment is seen as essential, and blended finance, which mixes public and private money, is designed to help.

entries.title: Measuring the goals: targets and indicators

definition.text: Indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track progress towards each SDG target.

facts.text: Targets are either outcome targets, numbered (6.1), or means-of-implementation targets, lettered (6.a).
For each indicator an expert group tried to name a custodian agency responsible for methods, data collection and reporting.
Critics worry about the large number of indicators and the cost of monitoring them, estimated in the billions of dollars.
The UN High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development monitors the SDGs, and countries can file voluntary national reviews of their progress.

entries.text: A goal means little unless someone can tell whether it is being met. For the SDGs, indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track each target. Outcome targets carry numbers, like 6.1. Targets about the means of getting there carry letters, like 6.a. For each indicator, an expert group tried to name a custodian agency to handle methods, data and reporting. A UN forum monitors the whole effort, and countries may file voluntary reviews of their progress. Critics worry about the sheer number of indicators and the cost of tracking them, estimated in the billions of dollars.

entries.title: Are the SDGs too soft on the planet?
entries.article: Sustainable Development Goals#Weak on environmental sustainability

definition.text: The criticism that the SDGs treat economic growth as foundational and do not make protecting the Earth system an end in itself.

facts.text: Environmental constraints and planetary boundaries are underrepresented, and the SDGs do not pursue planetary integrity as such.
Even within the environment-focused goals, most indicators measure social or economic outcomes.
Some studies argue that planetary integrity and justice would require limits to economic growth.
A 2022 meta-analysis of over 3,000 articles found the SDGs have had only limited transformative political impact.

entries.contested_note: Environmentalists call for redefining sustainable development in the SDGs, against their growth-centred design.
entries.text: The SDGs treat economic growth as a foundation. Critics say that is the problem. In their view the goals never make protecting the Earth system an end in itself, and environmental limits, including the planet's safe boundaries, are underrepresented. Even within the environmental goals, most indicators measure social or economic results. Some studies argue that real planetary integrity and justice would require limits to growth. A 2022 review of over 3,000 articles found the SDGs had only limited power to transform politics. Many environmentalists want sustainable development redefined, against the goals' growth-centered design.

entries.title: When the goals pull against each other

definition.text: The concern that pursuing some SDGs can work against others, so that not all 17 can be reached together.

facts.text: Cited examples: reconciling ending hunger, economic growth and income equality with environmental sustainability.
Critics say the SDGs rely on dubious claims about decoupling and resource efficiency instead of addressing the tension between growth and sustainability.
Synergies also exist: the IPCC sees robust synergies between climate action and the goals on health, clean energy, cities, consumption and oceans.
Countries tend to prioritize socioeconomic goals over environmental ones, and SDGs 1 and 8 were found to be most widely prioritized.

entries.contested_note: Scholars disagree whether the goals are internally coherent or contain inherently conflicting targets.
entries.text: Can the world end hunger, grow economies and narrow income gaps while also protecting the environment? Critics doubt that all 17 SDGs can be reached together, because some work against others. They say the goals lean on doubtful claims that growth can be decoupled from resource use, instead of facing the tension head-on. Synergies exist too. The IPCC sees strong links between climate action and the goals on health, clean energy, cities, consumption and oceans. In practice, countries favor social and economic goals, with SDGs 1 and 8 the most widely prioritized. Scholars still disagree on whether the goals are coherent or built on conflicting targets.

entries.title: The COP: the Biodiversity Convention's parliament
entries.article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Conference of the Parties (COP)

definition.text: The governing body of the Biodiversity Convention, made up of all governments that have ratified it.

facts.text: It reviews progress, sets priorities and work plans, and can amend the Convention and create expert advisory bodies.
COP met yearly for three years after 1994 and then every two years; COP 1 was in Nassau, Bahamas.
A scientific expert committee, the SBSTTA, advises the COP on scientific and technical issues.
COP 15, planned for Kunming in 2020, was postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic and split into two sessions.

entries.text: Every government that has ratified the Biodiversity Convention sits on its governing body, the Conference of the Parties, or COP. The COP reviews progress, sets priorities and work plans, and can amend the convention and create expert advisory bodies. One of these, the SBSTTA, advises it on science and technical matters. The first COP met in Nassau, Bahamas. Meetings ran yearly for three years after 1994, then every two years. COP 15, planned for Kunming in 2020, was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and split into two sessions.

entries.title: The Kunming-Montreal framework: a Paris Agreement for nature

definition.text: The global plan for nature adopted at the 2022 UN Biodiversity Conference (COP15) under the Biodiversity Convention.

facts.text: It was adopted on 19 December 2022 and promoted as a 'Paris Agreement for Nature'; it is the most significant CBD agreement to date.
It contains four global goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030, and succeeds the Strategic Plan 2011–2020 with its Aichi targets.
Goal A aims to cut the extinction rate and risk of all species tenfold by 2050 and halt human-induced extinction of threatened species.
Target 3, the '30 by 30' target, asks governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and water area by 2030.
Countries are also to stop subsidising activities that destroy wilderness, such as mining and industrial fishing.
Target 13 commits parties to share fairly the benefits from genetic resources and digital sequence information.
It is not legally binding, and its targets are criticised as vague, lacking measurable indicators; by COP16 only 44 of 196 parties had new biodiversity plans.
It is named after Kunming, the original host city, and Montreal, which hosted COP15 after Kunming withdrew because of China's COVID policy.

entries.contested_note: Critics, including the IPBES chair, warn it may yield business as usual because its targets are vague and non-binding.
distinct_from: GBF implications for business and finance
entries.text: On 19 December 2022, nearly every country on Earth agreed a new plan for nature. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted at the UN Biodiversity Conference, COP15, and promoted as a "Paris Agreement for Nature." It is the most significant agreement under the Biodiversity Convention so far. It replaced the plan that held the missed Aichi targets. It sets four global goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030. Goal A aims to cut the extinction rate and risk of all species tenfold by 2050 and halt human-caused extinctions of threatened species. Target 3, described in {{ref:nature-gov-033}}, asks governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and water by 2030. Countries are also to stop subsidizing activities that destroy wild places, such as mining and industrial fishing. Target 13 commits them to share fairly the benefits from genetic resources and their digital sequence data. The name tells a story. Kunming was the original host, but Montreal took over after China's COVID policy forced Kunming to withdraw. The framework is not legally binding. Critics, including the chair of IPBES, warn its vague targets may yield business as usual. By COP16, only 44 of 196 parties had new biodiversity plans.

entries.title: 30 by 30: protecting a third of the planet

definition.text: A global initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean area by 2030.

facts.text: It was proposed in a 2019 Science Advances article, 'A Global Deal for Nature', partly to help mitigate climate change.
Launched by the High Ambition Coalition in 2020, it had more than 100 supporting countries by October 2022.
In December 2022 it became Target 3 of the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
As of May 2026, 17.3% of land and inland waters and 9.8% of marine areas were protected; counting OECMs, 18.4% and 10.0%.
Some conservationists say the 30% figure lacks clear scientific justification, while others argue it is too low and point to the Half-Earth idea of conserving about 50%.
Critics warn that broad definitions counting OECMs with intensive industrial activity could inflate reported progress.
NGOs and Indigenous groups warn it could lead to forced evictions, 'green grabbing' and green colonialism without human-rights safeguards.

entries.contested_note: Researchers dispute whether 30% is scientifically justified, too low, or a risk to Indigenous land rights.
entries.text: Protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030. The goal fits on a bumper sticker, and that is part of its power. It was proposed in a 2019 Science Advances article, "A Global Deal for Nature," partly to help slow climate change. The High Ambition Coalition launched it in 2020, and more than 100 countries backed it by October 2022. In December 2022 it became Target 3 of the global biodiversity framework. As of May 2026, 17.3% of land and inland waters and 9.8% of marine areas were protected. Counting conservation sites outside formal reserves, the shares were 18.4% and 10.0%. The number itself is disputed. Some conservationists say 30% lacks clear scientific backing, while others say it is too low and point to the Half-Earth idea of conserving about 50%. Critics warn loose definitions could count industrial areas and inflate progress. NGOs and Indigenous groups warn that without human-rights safeguards it could bring forced evictions and green colonialism, land seized in the name of nature.

entries.title: A hard treaty gone soft: criticism of the Biodiversity Convention

definition.text: Arguments that the Biodiversity Convention has been weakly enforced and unfair to biodiversity-rich poorer countries.

facts.text: Brazil argued that wealthier countries benefit from access to resources but give too little financial and technological support for conservation.
The CBD is described as a hard treaty gone soft, and countries face no penalties for ignoring it.
National strategies in practice neglect groups such as fungi, bacteria and protists.
Some scientists fear the Nagoya Protocol hampers disease prevention and conservation research.

entries.contested_note: Developing countries and critics dispute whether richer nations have met their obligations under the Convention.
entries.text: Countries face no penalty for ignoring the Biodiversity Convention, which is why critics call it a hard treaty gone soft. Brazil argued that wealthy countries benefit from access to nature's resources but give too little money and technology for conservation. Developing countries and their allies dispute whether richer nations have met their obligations at all. National strategies in practice neglect groups such as fungi, bacteria and protists. Some scientists also fear its Nagoya Protocol hampers disease prevention and conservation research.

entries.title: Mapping the ocean's most important places
entries.article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Marine and coastal biodiversity

definition.text: Ocean areas identified under the Biodiversity Convention, using scientific criteria, as especially important for marine life.

facts.text: Expert workshops from 2018 to 2022 explored options for revising EBSA descriptions and describing new areas.
The aim is an international legally binding instrument under UNCLOS for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, the High Seas Treaty.

entries.text: Some patches of ocean matter far more to marine life than others. Under the Biodiversity Convention, scientists identify these Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas, or EBSAs, using scientific criteria. Expert workshops from 2018 to 2022 explored how to revise the descriptions and add new areas. The work feeds a binding instrument under the Law of the Sea for biodiversity beyond national waters: the High Seas Treaty.
