entries.title: The World Charter for Nature, 1982

definition.text: A UN declaration adopted on 28 October 1982 setting out five principles of conservation to guide all human conduct affecting nature.

facts.text: Its principles include respecting nature, safeguarding genetic viability and habitats, and managing resources for sustainable productivity without endangering other species.
The vote was 111 for, one against (the United States) and 18 abstentions; the IUCN prepared it.
It gave the first international recognition to a strong form of the precautionary principle.

sources.title: International Union for Conservation of Nature

entries.text: On 28 October 1982 the UN adopted a declaration meant to guide all human conduct that affects nature. The vote was 111 for and 18 abstentions. The single vote against came from the United States. Prepared by the IUCN, the World Charter for Nature sets out five principles of conservation. They include respecting nature, protecting genetic viability and habitats, and managing resources for lasting productivity without endangering other species. It gave the first international recognition to a strong form of the precautionary principle.

entries.title: Six kinds of protected area
entries.article: Protected area#IUCN Protected Area Management Categories

definition.text: Six categories, set by the IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas, that classify protected areas by their management objectives.

facts.text: They provide international standards for defining protected areas and are recognised by many governments and the UN.
They range from Category Ia, strict nature reserve, and Category II, national park, to Category VI, protected areas with sustainable use of natural resources.

entries.text: "Protected area" covers everything from untouched wilderness to working landscapes. The IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas sorts them into six categories by management goal. They run from Category Ia, the strict nature reserve, through Category II, the national park, to Category VI, where natural resources are used sustainably. Many governments and the UN recognize these categories as the international standard.

entries.title: Do protected areas work?

definition.text: How well protected areas actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for example by comparing populations inside and outside them.

facts.text: Vertebrate populations declined about five times more slowly inside protected areas (−0.4% per year) than at similar unprotected sites (−1.8% per year).
Effectiveness is limited by small size, isolation, high costs and growing conflict with human demands for resources.
Only 18% of the area covered by protected areas has been assessed, so most of them have unclear effectiveness.

entries.text: Inside protected areas, vertebrate populations declined about 0.4% a year. At similar unprotected sites, they fell about 1.8% a year, roughly five times faster. Protected area effectiveness asks exactly this: how well reserves actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for instance by comparing populations inside and outside. Small size, isolation, high costs and rising conflict over resources all limit what reserves achieve. And only 18% of the area under protection has been assessed, so most reserves' effectiveness is unclear.

Small size, isolation, high costs and rising conflict over resources all limit what reserves achieve. entries.title: Digital sequence information: genes as data

definition.text: A placeholder policy term, used especially in the Biodiversity Convention, for data such as DNA sequences derived from genetic resources.

facts.text: It is crucial to research in public health, medicine, biodiversity, breeding and evolution.
Researchers share it freely online, which conflicts with benefit-sharing duties because users can access it without agreements.
At COP 15 in 2022 parties agreed a multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism that decouples access from benefit-sharing.
At COP 16 in 2024 they set up the Cali Fund, to which industries using DSI, such as pharma and cosmetics, are expected to contribute part of their profits.
Half of the Cali Fund is to go to local and Indigenous groups.

entries.contested_note: The term itself remains disputed, and parties disagree over how open data should be reconciled with benefit-sharing.
entries.text: Digital sequence information, or DSI, is the placeholder policy term for such data, like DNA sequences drawn from genetic resources. It is crucial to medical, biological and breeding research. Researchers share it freely online. That clashes with benefit-sharing rules, because anyone can use it without an agreement. At COP 15 in 2022, parties agreed a shared mechanism that separates access from benefit-sharing. At COP 16 in 2024 they created the Cali Fund. Industries using DSI, like cosmetics, should pay in part of their profits, half going to local and Indigenous groups.

entries.title: Paying fleets to empty the sea
entries.article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Target 14.6: End subsidies contributing to overfishing

definition.text: Government payments to fishing fleets that encourage overcapacity, overfishing or illegal fishing, which SDG Target 14.6 aims to end.

facts.text: Capacity-enhancing subsidies help developing countries compete with large fishing nations, but bring no long-term benefit if they cause overfishing.
The WWF estimates illegal fishing costs up to $36.4 billion a year globally.
The Global Biodiversity Framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidising destructive activities such as industrial fishing.

entries.text: Some government money pushes fishing fleets to grow too big, catch too much or fish illegally. These harmful fisheries subsidies are what SDG Target 14.6 aims to end. Subsidies that add capacity can help developing countries compete with large fishing nations. But they bring no lasting benefit if they cause overfishing. Illegal fishing alone costs up to $36.4 billion a year, by the WWF's estimate. The global biodiversity framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidizing destructive activities such as industrial fishing.
entries.text_plain: Some government money pushes fishing fleets to grow too big, catch too much or fish illegally. These harmful fisheries subsidies are what SDG Target 14.6 aims to end. Subsidies that add capacity can help developing countries compete with large fishing nations. But they bring no lasting benefit if they cause overfishing. Illegal fishing alone costs up to $36.4 billion a year, by the WWF's estimate. The global biodiversity framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidizing destructive activities such as industrial fishing.

entries.title: Giant marine reserves
entries.article: Sustainable Development Goal 14#Large-Scale Marine Protected Areas (LSMPAs)

definition.text: Marine protected areas of at least 100,000 square km, set up to cut overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems.

facts.text: Concerns about them span resource management, conflicts between rival countries, and trade-offs between people's needs and the environment.
The management challenge is inadequate monitoring and enforcement of protection measures.

entries.text: Some marine protected areas are vast, at least 100,000 square km each. These large-scale reserves are set up to curb overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems. They raise hard questions about managing resources, rivalry between countries, and trade-offs between people's needs and nature. The biggest practical problem is policing them. Monitoring and enforcement of their protections are often inadequate.

entries.title: The Cartagena Protocol: rules for moving modified organisms

definition.text: A supplement to the Biodiversity Convention that governs the movement of genetically modified organisms between countries to protect biodiversity.

facts.text: Adopted on 29 January 2000, it entered into force on 11 September 2003; by July 2020 it had 173 parties.
It rests on the precautionary principle of the 1992 Rio Declaration: lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to delay cost-effective protection.
Countries may ban imports of GMOs lacking evidence of safety, and exporters must label shipments of altered commodities such as corn or cotton.
Its Advance Informed Agreement procedure lets importing countries assess risks before the first import of an organism meant for release.
Importing countries may also weigh socio-economic considerations when deciding on imports.

entries.text: Exporters shipping genetically modified corn or cotton must now label it. That rule comes from the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, an add-on to the Biodiversity Convention that governs the movement of genetically modified organisms between countries. It was adopted on 29 January 2000 and entered into force on 11 September 2003. It rests on the precautionary principle from the 1992 Rio Declaration: lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to delay cost-effective protection. Countries may ban imports that lack evidence of safety. Importers can assess risks before the first shipment and weigh social and economic concerns.

entries.title: The Bonn Convention: protecting animals that cross borders
entries.article: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals

definition.text: An international agreement, also called the Bonn Convention, to conserve migratory animals throughout their ranges.

facts.text: It was signed on 23 June 1979 in Bonn and took effect on 1 November 1983; its secretariat is run by UNEP.
Appendix I lists migratory species threatened with extinction, which range states must strictly protect.
Appendix II lists species that would benefit from international cooperation, the basis for regional or global agreements.
As a framework convention it has spawned seven agreements, such as one covering 254 wetland-dependent bird species, plus several memoranda of understanding.

sources.title: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals

entries.text: A bird that breeds in one country and winters in another needs protection in both. The Convention on Migratory Species, also called the Bonn Convention, aims to conserve migratory animals across their whole range. Appendix I lists migratory species threatened with extinction, which range countries must strictly protect. Appendix II lists species that would gain from cooperation, the basis for regional deals. It has spawned seven agreements, including one covering 254 wetland bird species.

entries.title: Climate and biodiversity: one crisis, two faces
entries.article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Cooperation with IPCC

definition.text: The idea, set out in a joint IPBES–IPCC report, that climate change and biodiversity loss are linked and must be tackled together.

facts.text: In June 2021 IPBES and the IPCC released a co-sponsored workshop report on biodiversity and climate change.
Efforts to address one problem can worsen the other if their links are overlooked.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: Climate change and biodiversity loss feed each other, and fixing one can worsen the other if their links are ignored. In June 2021, IPBES and the IPCC released a joint workshop report making exactly that case. The two problems, it argued, must be tackled together.

entries.title: The IPBES Nexus Assessment
entries.article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Nexus Assessment

definition.text: An IPBES report, approved on 17 December 2024, on how biodiversity, water, food and health are connected.

facts.text: It looks for ways to maximise benefits across five nexus elements: biodiversity, water, food, health and climate change.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: Biodiversity, water, food, health and climate change are tangled together, so a fix for one can help or hurt the others. An IPBES report approved on 17 December 2024 studied those links. It looks for ways to get the greatest benefit across all five at once.

entries.title: The IPBES Transformative Change Assessment
entries.article: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services#Transformative Change Assessment

definition.text: An IPBES report, approved on 18 December 2024, on the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and how to bring about transformative change.

facts.text: It builds on the 2019 Global Assessment, which found that only transformative change can achieve global development goals.
The 2019 assessment also warned that society should not focus solely on economic growth given the loss of biodiversity.

sources.title: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

entries.text: The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment reached a blunt conclusion. Only transformative change, a deep shift in how societies work, can achieve global development goals. It also warned against focusing solely on economic growth while biodiversity disappears. A follow-up report, approved on 18 December 2024, examined the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and how such change can be brought about.

entries.title: Ending the illegal wildlife trade
entries.article: Sustainable Development Goal 15#Target 15.c: Combat global poaching and trafficking

definition.text: SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and tackle both demand and supply of illegal wildlife products.

facts.text: Illegal wildlife trade has become one of the world's largest black markets, valued at tens of billions of dollars.
Trade policies that reward sustainable use typically help wildlife populations faster than outright trade bans.
Trafficking is usually driven by organised crime and eased by corruption and weak governance.

entries.text: Illegal wildlife trade has become one of the world's largest black markets, worth tens of billions of dollars. SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c aim to end poaching and trafficking of protected species by tackling both demand and supply. Trafficking is usually run by organized crime and helped by corruption and weak governance. Outright bans are not always the fastest remedy. Trade policies that reward sustainable use typically help wildlife populations recover faster.

entries.title: What the biodiversity framework means for business

definition.text: Expected effects of the global biodiversity framework on companies, banks and central banks, according to the UNEP Finance Initiative.

facts.text: Companies are expected to face mandatory disclosure of their impacts on biodiversity.
Banks are expected to shift money into nature-restoring projects, and central banks to treat nature-loss risk as part of their mandates.
Nature-positive, the goal of halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, has helped mainstream the framework in business and governance.
In May 2024 UNEP and China launched the Kunming Biodiversity Fund, with China committing $230 million USD.

entries.text: The global biodiversity framework is aimed at governments, but money will feel it too. Banks are expected to move money into projects that restore nature, and central banks to treat nature loss as a risk within their mandate. entries.title: The EU's biodiversity plan for 2030

definition.text: The European Commission's 2020 plan for biodiversity, offered as the EU's contribution to the post-2020 global framework.

facts.text: It plans to make 30% of EU territory protected by 2030, with 10% strictly protected.
It proposed binding nature restoration targets and is a core part of the European Green Deal.
As of 2023 the EU was not on track to meet its targets.

entries.text: On 20 May 2020 the European Commission set out its plan for nature, offered as Europe's contribution to the coming global framework. The EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 aims to protect 30% of EU territory by 2030, with 10% strictly protected. It proposed binding targets for restoring nature and is a core part of the European Green Deal. As of 2023, the EU was not on track to meet its targets.

entries.title: Paper parks: protected only on the map

definition.text: Protected areas that exist in law but lack the funding, staff or enforcement to stop poaching, logging or development inside them.

facts.text: Modelling suggests that for exploited species, better enforcement in existing reserves often helps more than expanding area without more resources.
Where threats such as over-harvesting are intense, spending on compliance and management can beat creating new, weakly managed reserves.
Where pressures cluster near reserve edges, enlarging protected areas can create secure core refuges even without more staff.
Meeting percentage targets without governance capacity risks spreading scarce conservation money too thin.

entries.text: A reserve can exist in law and still be logged, poached and built on. Such paper parks lack the money, staff or enforcement to stop damage inside them. Modeling suggests that for exploited species, better enforcement in existing reserves often helps more than adding area without more resources. Where over-harvesting is intense, spending on management can beat creating new, weak reserves. Where threats cluster at reserve edges, though, enlarging an area can create a safe core even without more staff. Chasing percentage targets without the capacity to govern risks spreading scarce money too thin.

entries.title: Red tape or fair play? Criticism of the Nagoya Protocol

definition.text: Concerns that the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy harms biodiversity research, conservation and disease response.

facts.text: Some developing countries have refused permits for basic biodiversity research and even prosecuted scientists.
Its bilateral transfer system has low throughput, whereas the plant genetic resources treaty's multilateral system allows 8500 transfers every week.
Lack of national implementation is often blamed for the protocol's failure.

entries.contested_note: Scientists and museums see the protocol as red tape, while providers of genetic resources defend it as protection against biopiracy.
entries.text: Some developing countries have refused permits for basic biodiversity research, and some have even prosecuted scientists. Critics blame the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy for harming research, conservation and disease response. Its country-by-country permit system moves slowly. By contrast, the multilateral system of the treaty on plant genetic resources allows 8500 transfers every week. Weak national implementation is often blamed for the failure. Scientists and museums see red tape. Countries that supply genetic resources see protection against the theft of their genetic wealth.

entries.title: The EU Nature Restoration Law

definition.text: A 2024 European Union regulation that makes binding targets for restoring damaged nature across the EU.

facts.text: Member states must restore at least 30% of habitats in poor condition by 2030, 60% by 2040 and 90% by 2050.
It responds to more than 80% of Europe's habitats being in poor condition.
Its aims include protecting ecosystem services, mitigating climate change and reducing risks to food security.
Farm groups and the European People's Party opposed it as a threat to livelihoods; the Parliament passed it 329 to 275 and it took effect on 18 August 2024.

entries.contested_note: Farming groups and centre-right parties opposed it as harmful to farmers, while scientists and the IUCN backed it.

entries.title: National biodiversity strategies: the convention at home

definition.text: A country's main plan for carrying out the Biodiversity Convention at home, known as an NBSAP.

facts.text: The Convention requires each country to prepare a national biodiversity strategy and build it into planning in every sector that affects biodiversity.
As of early 2012, 173 Parties had developed NBSAPs.
Countries were expected to present updated NBSAPs to meet the Kunming-Montreal targets before COP16, but only 25 of 195 had done so.
Only five of the 17 megadiverse countries and four G7 nations submitted theirs by the deadline.
Japan's 2023 NBSAP includes the aim of a nature-positive economy.

entries.text: Before COP16, countries were meant to present updated plans for meeting the Kunming-Montreal targets. Only 25 of 195 did. Only five of the 17 megadiverse countries, the richest in species, and four G7 nations met the deadline. Japan's 2023 plan includes the aim of an economy that restores more nature than it destroys.

entries.title: The common heritage of humankind

definition.text: The principle that certain resources, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation.

facts.text: Plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage before the CBD and could be freely exchanged for breeding and research.
Developing countries criticised this approach because their resources could be exploited without compensation; the CBD replaced it with national sovereignty.
High Seas Treaty talks turned on the contrast between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

entries.contested_note: Developing countries and industrialised nations disagree over whether genetic resources should be common heritage or sovereign property.
entries.text: Some resources, such as the deep seabed, are said to belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation. That is the common heritage principle. Before 1992, plant genetic resources were treated this way, freely exchanged for breeding and research. Developing countries objected that their resources were being exploited without payment. The Biodiversity Convention replaced the principle with national sovereignty. The tension returned in the High Seas Treaty talks, which turned on common heritage versus freedom of the seas. Rich and poor nations still disagree over which rule should apply.

entries.title: The 2010 Biodiversity Target: a promise unkept

definition.text: A global conservation target to halt, or significantly slow, the decline of biodiversity by the end of 2010.

facts.text: EU leaders first adopted it at Gothenburg in June 2001; in 2002 the CBD's COP 6 committed to a significant reduction in the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.
The 2002 Johannesburg World Summit on Sustainable Development confirmed the target.
Measuring the rate of biodiversity loss to check the target proved a challenge.
The world largely failed to meet it; 2010's 110 national reports showed little progress.

The world largely failed. In 2010, 110 national reports showed little progress.

entries.title: Indigenous peoples: who they are, and who decides

definition.text: Peoples marked by self-identification, cultural difference from others in their state, a special bond with their traditional territory, and a history of domination and discrimination; no single definition is generally accepted.

facts.text: There are some 5,000 distinct Indigenous peoples on every inhabited continent and in every inhabited climate zone.
Most are minorities in the state or territory where they live and have been dominated by other groups.
The UN has adopted no definition; its Permanent Forum holds that any single definition would be over- or under-inclusive.
Many states avoid the term and use labels such as 'scheduled tribes' in India or 'national minorities' in China.
Europeans justified colonising Indigenous lands partly by calling them terra nullius, 'no one's land'.
Since 2002 Indigenous environmental rights have gained international recognition, but few countries respect them in practice.

entries.contested_note: There is no agreed definition, and whether particular African or Asian groups count as Indigenous is disputed.

conflicts.text: 21st-century estimates of the Indigenous population range from 250 million to 750 million.
conflicts.note: The lead (d157ee4d2687) gives 250 million to 600 million; a 2007 estimate (f206b4ad3db2) gave 750 million to a billion.

entries.text: There are some 5,000 distinct Indigenous peoples, living on every inhabited continent and in every climate zone people live in. Yet no one agrees on exactly who counts. The UN has adopted no definition. Its Permanent Forum holds that any single definition would include too many or too few. Most accounts point to four marks. People identify themselves as Indigenous and differ culturally from others in their state. They have a special bond with their traditional territory and share a history of domination. Most are minorities where they live. Many states avoid the term altogether, using labels such as "scheduled tribes" in India or "national minorities" in China. Whether particular groups in Africa or Asia count as Indigenous is disputed. History explains much of their position. Europeans justified colonizing Indigenous lands partly by calling them terra nullius, "no one's land." Since 2002, Indigenous environmental rights have gained international recognition. Few countries respect them in practice.

entries.title: Environmental justice: who lives next to the dump?

definition.text: A social movement against the harm done to poor or marginalized communities by hazardous waste, resource extraction and other land uses they do not benefit from.

facts.text: Hundreds of studies from the movement argue that exposure to environmental harm is unequally distributed.

The US Environmental Protection Agency defines it as fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people, regardless of race, colour, national origin or income, in environmental laws and policies.
The movement began in the United States in the 1980s, shaped by the civil rights movement and focused on environmental racism.
In 1982 residents of Warren County, North Carolina, protested a landfill for PCB chemicals; the six weeks of protest led to over 500 arrests.
A United Church of Christ study found race was the most important factor predicting where US hazardous waste facilities were placed.
Tighter waste rules in rich countries led to a surge of hazardous waste exports to the Global South in the 1980s and 1990s, which helped make the movement global.
It has added ideas such as ecological debt, environmental racism, climate justice, ecocide and sacrifice zones to political ecology.
It overlaps with movements for Indigenous land rights and for the human right to a healthy environment.

distinct_from: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South
entries.text: In 1982, residents of Warren County, North Carolina, protested a landfill for toxic PCB chemicals. Six weeks of protest led to over 500 arrests. That fight helped launch the environmental justice movement in the United States. Shaped by the civil rights movement, it opposes harm done to poor or marginalized communities by waste, mining and other land uses that bring them no benefit. Its early focus was race, covered in {{ref:nature-gov-173}}. A United Church of Christ study found that race was the most important factor predicting where US hazardous waste facilities were placed. Hundreds of studies from the movement argue that exposure to environmental harm is unequally distributed. The US Environmental Protection Agency now defines environmental justice as fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people in environmental laws and policies. That covers every race, color, national origin and income. The movement went global in the 1980s and 1990s. Tighter waste rules in rich countries sent a surge of hazardous waste to the Global South. It has since spawned new ideas, among them the debt rich nations may owe poor ones and the unequal burden of climate change. It overlaps with campaigns for Indigenous rights to land and for a human right to a clean environment.

entries.title: Political ecology: power and the environment

definition.text: The study of how political, economic and social factors relate to environmental issues and climate change.

facts.text: Unlike conventional ecology, it puts power relations at the centre of environmental issues.
It joins ecological social science with political economy, covering degradation and marginalisation, environmental conflict, conservation and control, and social movements.
A core assumption is that environmental change does not affect society evenly: political, social and economic differences shape who bears costs and who gains benefits.
Frank Thone first coined the English term in 1935; anthropologist Eric R. Wolf revived it in 1972.
Piers Blaikie's work on the social and political roots of soil erosion showed that problems blamed on local resource misuse often stem from the wider political and economic context.
It links today's uneven environmental burdens to policies and power relations rooted in colonialism.
Critics such as Vayda and Walters argue it presupposes the importance of political factors, and propose 'event ecology' instead.

entries.text: Farmers eroding their soil looks like a local failure. Piers Blaikie dug deeper. His work on the social and political roots of soil erosion showed that problems blamed on local misuse often stem from the wider political and economic context. That insight is the heart of political ecology, the study of how political, economic and social forces shape environmental problems and climate change. Critics such as Vayda and Walters argue it assumes politics matters before showing it, and propose "event ecology" instead.

entries.title: Traditional ecological knowledge

definition.text: Knowledge, practices and beliefs about how living things, including people, relate to each other and their surroundings, built up over generations and passed on through culture.

facts.text: It rests on long-term observation and experience rather than the standardized experiments of Western science, which has fuelled debate over how to use it in ecological management.
It is not a universal set of principles but a family of practices tied to particular places and worldviews.
It is usually kept as oral tradition, so it may lack the written records that legal claims require.
Its knowledge guides everyday needs such as weather reading, medicine, water management, farming, hunting, fishing and the classification of living things.
The 1987 UN report Our Common Future said Indigenous and tribal lifestyles could teach modern societies how to manage forest, mountain and dryland ecosystems.
Ecosystem management can combine science and TEK to gain long-term records that would otherwise be missing.
Climate change can make TEK less accurate, since Indigenous peoples rely on signs in nature to plan activities and forecast weather.
Whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over their traditional knowledge is still debated in international law.

entries.contested_note: Scholars debate how TEK should be combined with Western science and whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over it; some critics call the term itself an appropriation.
entries.text: Long before weather forecasts, people read the wind, the blooming of plants and the arrival of birds. Traditional ecological knowledge, or TEK, is that kind of understanding. It is knowledge, practice and belief about how living things, people included, relate to each other and their surroundings. It builds up over generations and passes on through culture. It guides everyday needs such as weather reading, medicine, water management, farming, hunting, fishing and naming living things. It is not one universal system. It is a family of practices tied to particular places and worldviews. It rests on long observation and experience rather than standardized experiments, and that has fueled debate over its use in management. Combined with science, though, it can supply long-term records that would otherwise be missing. A 1987 UN report, described in {{ref:nature-hist-004}}, said Indigenous and tribal ways of life could teach modern societies how to manage forest, mountain and dryland ecosystems. TEK is usually oral, so it may lack the written records that legal claims require. Whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over it is still debated in international law. Some critics call the term itself an appropriation. Climate change adds a threat, making the signs in nature that TEK relies on less dependable.

entries.title: Extractivism: digging up and shipping out

definition.text: The removal of large amounts of natural resources, mainly for export, with little or no processing.

facts.text: The term was coined in Portuguese as "extractivismo" in 1996 to describe for-profit exploitation of Brazil's forest resources.
It is common across the Global South and the Arctic, but also occurs in sacrifice zones of the Global North.
Extraction has gone on for over 500 years; under colonialism, colonies in Africa, Asia and the Americas shipped resources to metropolitan centres.
Transnational corporations are the main actors, helped by weak governance in resource-dependent economies.
Resources such as gold, oil, lumber, water and food are taken by mining, drilling and deforestation, then processed elsewhere for world markets.
Extraction at this scale can turn renewable resources into non-renewable ones, because they are taken faster than nature can replace them.
Local and especially Indigenous communities often oppose it because it uproots them or degrades their quality of life.

entries.text: Gold, oil, lumber, water and food leave a region raw and get processed somewhere else. Extractivism is the removal of large amounts of natural resources, mainly for export, with little or no processing. The term was coined in Portuguese, "extractivismo," in 1996 to describe profit-driven exploitation of Brazil's forests. The practice is far older. For over 500 years, colonies in Africa, Asia and the Americas shipped resources to imperial centers. Today transnational corporations are the main actors, helped by weak governance in economies that depend on resources. It is common across the Global South and the Arctic, and in neglected, heavily polluted pockets of the Global North. Taken fast enough, even renewable resources become non-renewable, because nature cannot replace them in time. Local and especially Indigenous communities often resist, because it uproots them or degrades their lives.

entries.title: Land law: who may use, sell or fence the ground

definition.text: The branch of law that deals with the rights to use land, transfer it, or keep others off it.

facts.text: In many places land is called real estate or real property, as distinct from personal property.
One person's encumbrance on land, such as an easement, may be another person's land right.
Land rights are so basic that they arise even without a state; the claim clubs of the American West enforced mining rules on their own.
Squatting, occupying land without owning it, happens all over the world.
Land reform means government policies that take or redistribute land, such as a land grant.
In customary-law places, customary land is the main form of ownership; in common-law places, Indigenous land rights are called aboriginal title.

entries.text: Rights to land are so basic that they arise even without a government. In the American West, miners' claim clubs enforced their own rules. Land law is the branch of law covering the rights to use land, transfer it, or keep others off it. Land is often called real estate or real property, as distinct from personal belongings. One person's burden on land, such as a neighbor's right of way, may be another person's right. Squatting, living on land without owning it, happens all over the world. Land reform means government policies that take or redistribute land. Where customary law rules, customary land is the main form of ownership. In common-law countries, Indigenous peoples' claims to land have their own legal name, described in {{ref:nature-gov-216}}.

entries.title: Ecological debt: what the North owes the South

definition.text: The debt some campaigners say the Global North owes the Global South for historical environmental injustice, such as resource exploitation, habitat damage and pollution.

facts.text: It has two main parts: ecological damage a country causes to others or to shared ecosystems, and its use of ecosystems at the expense of other countries' fair rights to them.
The term first appeared in 1985 in a booklet by German ecofeminist Eva Quistorp; Global South NGOs took it up in the 1990s.
Early reports took opposite approaches: a Chilean report treated it in moral and political terms, while a Swedish one tried to put a money value on it.
At the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, NGOs drafted a Debt Treaty demanding compensation for 500 years of damage; it was never recognised by international institutions.
At the 2009 Copenhagen talks, vulnerable countries demanded reparations for decades of excess pollution; the US envoy flatly rejected owing such a debt.
Climate debt, the best-developed attempt to quantify it, has two parts: adaptation debt and emissions debt.
Proposed ways to settle it include cancelling poor countries' financial debts or paying a basic income.

entries.contested_note: How to define it, which past emissions count, and how it should be repaid are all debated, and some argue it risks commodifying nature.
entries.text: At the 1992 summit in Rio, campaign groups drafted a Debt Treaty demanding compensation for 500 years of damage. No international institution ever recognized it. Their claim was ecological debt: the idea that the Global North owes the Global South for past environmental injustice, such as resource plunder, habitat damage and pollution. It has two parts. One is damage a country does to others or to shared ecosystems. The other is its use of ecosystems at the expense of other countries' fair share. The German ecofeminist Eva Quistorp first used the term in a 1985 booklet. Early reports split on approach: a Chilean one treated it in moral terms, a Swedish one tried to price it. At the 2009 Copenhagen talks, vulnerable countries demanded reparations for decades of excess pollution, and the US envoy flatly rejected the idea. Climate debt, the best-developed attempt to measure it, splits into adaptation debt and emissions debt. Proposals to settle it include canceling poor countries' financial debts. Almost everything about it is disputed, and some warn it risks putting a price on nature.

entries.title: Biopiracy: patenting other people's knowledge

definition.text: Taking the genetic resources and knowledge of farming and Indigenous communities without permission, to gain monopoly control through patents.

facts.text: Pat Mooney, founder of ETC Group, coined the term in the early 1990s.
A company patent can bar anyone, including the Indigenous group itself, from using or selling the resource.
Nearly one third of small-molecule drugs approved by the US FDA between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them.
Critics say the TRIPS agreement treats knowledge as private property and recognises inventions only if they can make industrial profit.
The 1992 CBD required host-country consent for bioprospecting and fair sharing of benefits; the 2010 Nagoya Protocol made this concrete.
The Nagoya rules had the unintended effect of blocking biodiversity research, as developing countries hesitated to approve even basic studies.
Critics label bioprospecting and biopiracy modern forms of extractivism.
The term was coined by Pat Mooney for profiting from indigenous knowledge of nature without permission or payment.

entries.text: Nearly one third of the small-molecule drugs the US FDA approved between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them. The 1992 Biodiversity Convention required host-country consent and fair sharing of benefits, and the 2010 Nagoya Protocol made this concrete. The unintended result was blocked research. Critics call both biopiracy and the search for useful compounds modern extractivism.

entries.title: Indigenous land stewardship
entries.article: Indigenous peoples#Environmental and economic benefits of the Indigenous stewardship of land

definition.text: The care of land by Indigenous peoples with secure tenure, which yields environmental and economic benefits for everyone.

facts.text: A WRI report says tenure-secure Indigenous lands generate billions, sometimes trillions, of dollars in benefits such as carbon storage, reduced pollution and clean water.
Such lands have low deforestation, cut greenhouse gas emissions, and limit erosion and flooding by anchoring soil.
At least 37% of remaining natural lands lie within Indigenous territories.
The often-cited claim that Indigenous peoples steward 80% of the world's biodiversity was found baseless by a 2024 study in Nature.

entries.contested_note: The popular figure that Indigenous lands hold 80% of biodiversity is disputed; a 2024 study found it has no sound basis.
entries.text: At least 37% of the world's remaining natural lands lie within Indigenous territories. Where Indigenous peoples hold secure title, their care of the land benefits everyone. A report by the research group WRI says such lands generate billions, sometimes trillions, of dollars in benefits, such as carbon storage, cleaner air and clean water. Deforestation on them is low. They cut greenhouse gas emissions, and their rooted soils limit erosion and flooding. One popular claim does not hold up. The often-repeated figure that Indigenous peoples steward 80% of the world's biodiversity was found baseless by a 2024 study in Nature.

entries.title: Climate change and Indigenous peoples

definition.text: The disproportionate impact of climate change on Indigenous peoples worldwide compared with non-Indigenous peoples.

facts.text: There are over 370 million Indigenous people in more than 90 countries, and about 22% of the planet's land is Indigenous territory.
Some Indigenous scholars link these impacts to ongoing colonialism, seeing climate change as an intensification of settler colonialism's effects.
Indigenous farmers have long timed crops by wind direction, blooming, bird migration and other signs, which climate change disrupts.
Indigenous knowledge helps detect local climate impacts where scientific models often fail, and programmes shaped with Indigenous input have higher participation.
Indigenous people in the Ecuadorian Amazon were left out of the 2005 REDD+ project despite suffering deforestation's effects.
The Arctic is warming at twice the global rate, posing unprecedented challenges for its Indigenous nations.
Pacific islands have been lost to sea-level rise, displacing and killing Indigenous people.

entries.text: The Arctic is warming at twice the global rate, and its Indigenous nations face challenges with no precedent. Indigenous farmers have long timed crops by wind direction, flowering and bird migration, signs that a changing climate scrambles. Some Indigenous scholars see climate change as an intensification of settler colonialism's effects. Their knowledge is also an asset. It detects local impacts where scientific models often fail, and programs shaped with Indigenous input draw more participation. Yet Indigenous people in the Ecuadorian Amazon were left out of a 2005 forest-carbon project despite suffering deforestation's effects.

entries.title: Ecocide: killing the home

definition.text: The destruction of the environment by humans; the word joins Greek oikos, 'home', and Latin caedere, 'to kill'.

facts.text: An expert panel in 2021 defined it as unlawful or wanton acts committed knowing they are substantially likely to cause severe and widespread or long-term environmental damage.
Common causes include war, pollution, wanton overexploitation of resources and industrial disasters.
Olof Palme popularised the term at the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment, accusing the US of ecocide for using Agent Orange in Vietnam.
The US Air Force sprayed 20 million gallons of herbicides such as Agent Orange on 6 million acres of forests and crops.
The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court covers environmental damage only in wartime, not peacetime.
Ten countries have made ecocide a crime in peacetime, and campaigners seek to add it to the crimes tried by the International Criminal Court.
Destroying the environment can amount to cultural genocide by stopping people, especially Indigenous peoples, from following their way of life.

entries.contested_note: Criminalising ecocide is proposed as a deterrent to corporations driving climate change, but others argue it would not address the crisis's root causes.

entries.title: Environmental conflict: fighting over nature's spoils

definition.text: A social conflict caused by environmental damage or by unequal sharing of environmental resources; also called an ecological distribution conflict.

facts.text: The Environmental Justice Atlas documented 3,100 such conflicts worldwide as of April 2020, with many more undocumented.
They are rooted in the industrial economy: with less than 10% of materials and energy recycled, extraction keeps expanding at commodity frontiers.
A study of over 2743 conflicts found mining (21%), fossil energy (17%), biomass and land use (15%) and water management (14%) were the most challenged sectors; defenders were killed in 13% of cases.
Low-income countries see more conflicts over conservation, water and land; in high-income countries almost half concern waste, tourism, nuclear power and infrastructure.
Around 17% of conflicts in the EJAtlas record environmental justice 'successes', such as stopping an unsustainable project.
In environmental conflict resolution, the best predictor of success is adequate consultation with all parties.

entries.text: As of April 2020, the Environmental Justice Atlas had documented 3,100 environmental conflicts worldwide, and many more go unrecorded. Fossil energy followed at 17%, biomass and land use at 15%, and water at 14%. Defenders were killed in 13% of cases. Poor countries see more fights over conservation, water and land. In rich countries almost half concern waste, tourism, nuclear power and infrastructure. Around 17% end in a justice "success," such as stopping a project. The best predictor of resolving one is proper consultation with every party.

entries.title: Procedural justice: fair process, not just fair results

definition.text: The idea of fairness in the processes used to settle disputes and share out resources.

facts.text: It concerns fair and transparent decision processes, in contrast with distributive justice (fair outcomes) and retributive justice (fair punishment).
Hearing all parties before deciding is one step that helps make a process procedurally fair.
Research by Tom R. Tyler found that simply giving people a voice, even one that does not change the decision, can be enough for a process to seem fair.
In 1976 Gerald Leventhal proposed six rules for judging procedures: consistency, bias suppression, accuracy, correctability, representativeness and ethicality.
Under the participation model, a fair procedure gives those affected a chance to take part in the decision.
In energy justice, procedural justice means access to information and meaningful participation in decisions.
In law it appears as due process in the US and natural justice in other common-law countries.

entries.text: People often accept a decision they dislike if they feel they were heard. Research by Tom R. Tyler found that simply giving people a voice, even one that changes nothing, can make a process feel fair. Procedural justice is fairness in how disputes are settled and resources shared. It differs from distributive justice, which asks whether outcomes are fair, and retributive justice, which asks whether punishment is fair. In 1976 Gerald Leventhal proposed six tests for a fair procedure: consistency, lack of bias, accuracy, the chance to correct errors, representativeness and ethics. Hearing all parties before deciding is a basic step. In energy and environmental matters, it means access to information and real participation. In law it appears as due process in the US and natural justice elsewhere.

entries.title: Climate justice: those who suffer most did least

definition.text: A form of environmental justice concerned with how unequally climate change harms marginalized and vulnerable people.

facts.text: It aims to share fairly both the burdens of climate change and the work of cutting emissions, through advocacy and policy change.
Those who gained most from industrialization, such as coal, oil and gas businesses, are seen as carrying most responsibility for the carbon dioxide built up in the atmosphere.
Many of the people and countries hit hardest by climate change did least to cause it.
When the people least responsible are also harmed by the responses to climate change, this is called the 'triple injustice' of climate change.
Views of climate justice fall into two groups: procedural justice, about fair and inclusive decision-making, and distributive justice, about who bears the costs.
Pakistan produces less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet its 2022 floods affected over 33 million people.
The richest 1% of people are responsible for twice as many emissions as the poorest 50%.
Lawsuits are one tool: a 2017 UN Environment Programme report counted 894 ongoing climate legal actions worldwide.

entries.contested_note: The term is used in many ways, and its different meanings are sometimes disputed; whether capitalism itself is a root cause is also debated.

entries.title: Climate change and poverty

definition.text: The close link between climate change and poverty, since climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest.

facts.text: Poor people face more exposure and vulnerability, meaning they are less able to cope with climate extremes.
The UN Development Programme says developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change.
A 2020 World Bank paper estimated climate change will push 32 million to 132 million more people into extreme poverty by 2030.
For poor households, a disaster, a bad harvest or an illness can be a crippling economic shock.
Climate-driven extremes could raise food prices by 3–84% by 2050.
Pro-poor adaptation links adaptation to poverty reduction; adaptation that ignores how poverty differs between people will be ineffective and unfair.
Poorer countries are hit harder yet have fewer assets and capacities to adapt.

entries.text: For a poor household, one disaster, bad harvest or illness can be crippling. That fragility is why climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest. The UN Development Programme says developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change. Poor people are more exposed and less able to cope with extremes, and poorer countries have fewer assets to adapt. A 2020 World Bank paper estimated climate change will push 32 million to 132 million more people into extreme poverty by 2030. Climate extremes could raise food prices by 3–84% by 2050. Adaptation that ignores how poverty differs from person to person will be ineffective and unfair. Pro-poor adaptation ties coping with climate change to reducing poverty.

entries.title: Environmental racism

definition.text: The disproportionate burden of environmental hazards, pollution and ecological damage on marginalized communities and people of colour.

facts.text: It is built into policy-making at home and abroad and is a form of structural racism that creates health hierarchies.
Benjamin Chavis coined the term in 1982 while opposing a PCB waste landfill in Warren County, North Carolina.
Its causes include competition for cheap land, dismissive attitudes to harmful projects, and affected communities' lack of political power, mobility and money.
Some critics argue cost–benefit analysis can feed it by valuing environmental resources by their usefulness to society, through willingness to pay.
Communities of colour and low-income communities bear more of the air and water pollution from fossil fuel processing; such places are called sacrifice zones.
Between 1989 and 1994 an estimated 2,611 metric tons of hazardous waste went from OECD countries to non-OECD countries.
A US Government Accountability Office study after the 1982 Warren County protests was among the first to link the race and income of communities to hazardous waste sites.

entries.text: In 1982, protesting a PCB waste landfill in Warren County, North Carolina, Benjamin Chavis gave the problem a name: environmental racism. It means the heavier burden of pollution, hazards and ecological damage borne by marginalized communities and people of color. A US Government Accountability Office study after the protests was among the first to link the race and income of communities to hazardous waste sites. Causes include the hunt for cheap land, dismissive attitudes to harmful projects, and affected communities' lack of political power, mobility and money. It is built into policy at home and abroad, a form of structural racism that creates hierarchies of health. Some places, described in {{ref:nature-gov-224}}, absorb an outsized share of fossil fuel pollution. Some critics argue cost-benefit analysis feeds the problem, because it values resources by what people are willing to pay. The pattern crosses borders: between 1989 and 1994, an estimated 2,611 metric tons of hazardous waste went from OECD countries to poorer ones.

entries.title: Climate change as a human rights issue

definition.text: A conceptual and legal framework for studying and addressing how global warming affects international human rights.

facts.text: Governments, UN bodies, advocates and academics use it to guide climate policy under the UNFCCC and the core human rights treaties.
Most statements stress threats to the rights to life, food, water, health, housing, development and self-determination.
Human rights treaties rarely mention the environment; protection is derived from rights such as life, food, water and health.
In 2005 Inuit activist Sheila Watt-Cloutier petitioned the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights over US contributions to global warming; the petition was rejected but testimony was later heard.
The UN Human Rights Council unanimously adopted Resolution 7/23 recognising climate change as a threat to the full enjoyment of human rights.
On 8 October 2021 the Human Rights Council recognised a human right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment in resolution 48/13.
The UN Development Programme estimates an additional 600 million people will face malnutrition because of climate change.
Research suggests climate change may create some 50 to 200 million new displaced persons and refugees by 2100.

entries.title: The right to a healthy environment

definition.text: The human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, seen as necessary for enjoying rights such as life, health, food and water.

facts.text: The UN Human Rights Council recognised it on 18 October 2021 (HRC/RES/48/13), and the UN General Assembly did so on 28 July 2022.
The Human Rights Council vote was 43 in favour, none against and 4 abstentions; it was the first time the Council had recognised a human right in a resolution.
The General Assembly resolution passed with 161 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions, though such resolutions are not legally binding.
165 countries recognise the right through their constitutions, laws or treaties they have ratified.
It protects the environment through its effects on individual people, unlike traditional regulation focused on other states or on nature itself.
It obliges states to regulate and enforce environmental law and control pollution, and has helped build legal precedent for climate change litigation.
The 1972 Stockholm Declaration recognised it in its first principle but was not legally binding.

entries.title: Access and benefit-sharing agreements

definition.text: An agreement that sets out how the benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly and equitably.

facts.text: They usually arise from bioprospecting, where Indigenous knowledge guides the search for commercially valuable genetic and biochemical resources, and recognise that knowledge holders deserve a share.
Before the Convention on Biological Diversity, plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage of mankind and could be freely exchanged.
The CBD, in force from 1992, gave each state sovereign rights over genetic resources in its territory.
The Nagoya Protocol, adopted in 2010 and in force from 2014, requires access to take place with prior informed consent and on mutually agreed terms.
Monetary benefits include lump sums, milestone payments and royalties; non-monetary ones include shared research, joint intellectual property, technology transfer and training.

Digital sequence information can be used without physical samples, which escapes the access-based model; COP16 in Cali created a fund that gives half its resources to Indigenous peoples and local communities.
Biodiversity-rich developing countries push for stronger benefit-sharing duties, while developed countries with big users of genetic resources prefer narrower ones.
Under the CBD, parties should ease access to genetic resources for environmentally sound uses and share research results and commercial benefits fairly.

entries.contested_note: The CBD's access and benefit-sharing principle provoked heated debate that left most stakeholders unsatisfied, and whether benefit-sharing should apply to freely available sequence data is disputed.
entries.text: When a healer's knowledge leads a company to a valuable plant, who should be paid? An access and benefit-sharing agreement answers that, setting out how the benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly. Such deals usually come from bioprospecting, the search for valuable compounds that Indigenous knowledge often guides. Biodiversity-rich developing countries want stronger duties, while rich countries with big users of genetic resources prefer narrower ones.

entries.title: Fortress conservation: protecting nature by removing people

definition.text: A conservation approach that tries to protect nature by creating protected areas cut off from people.

facts.text: The United States pioneered it; after the 1872 national park law, army cavalry guarded new parks, often expelling Native Americans.
Evicting residents to protect nature has been called the Yosemite model.
A UN special rapporteur says up to 250,000 people have been forcibly evicted for conservation projects since 1990; another estimate puts displacement between 10.8 million and 173 million.
Conservation charities have increasingly militarized anti-poaching work, sometimes arming paramilitary groups.
Ecotourism income and carbon credits from preserved forests are economic motives behind it.
Many Indigenous groups lack formal title deeds despite living in forests for centuries, which leaves them exposed to eviction.
Giving land title to communities has led to less forest clearing than state-run parks in the Brazilian Amazon, and community concessions in the Congo show less deforestation.
Evicted residents may end up working for extractive companies, so exclusion often leads to more exploitation of the land.

entries.contested_note: Some conservation leaders argued for removing people from protected areas, while Indigenous rights advocates argue that handing land rights to inhabitants protects forests better.

entries.title: Indigenous land rights

definition.text: The rights of Indigenous peoples, individually or collectively, to land and the natural resources on it, mostly in colonised countries.

facts.text: Land matters to Indigenous peoples for religious meaning, self-determination, identity and economic reasons.
In some Indigenous societies, earth and sea resources form the basis of the household economy, so ownership secures access to them.
Claims may rest on international law, treaties, common law, or national constitutions and laws.
Key international texts include ILO Convention 169 of 1989 and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples of 2007.
The gap between formally recognised land and land held and managed by custom is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental degradation.
In Brazil, only 14% of Indigenous lands ended up demarcated under 1983 laws, and much land was lost to mining companies.

entries.title: Green grabbing: land seized in nature's name

definition.text: Taking land and resources, often by foreign actors, in the name of environmental goals, in a way that produces unjust development; also called green colonialism.

facts.text: Land may be taken for ecotourism, protecting biodiversity or ecosystem services, carbon trading, or growing biofuels.
It is a narrower kind of land grabbing in which the motive is environmental, and it counts as a subtype of green imperialism.
Journalist John Vidal coined the term in 2008 in a Guardian article, 'The great green land grab'.
Carbon-trading firms may take land to plant trees and sell the resulting offsets.
The International Land Coalition says 59% of land grabs between 2000 and 2010 were for biofuels.
Green grabs cover thousands or millions of hectares and can drive Indigenous or peasant communities off their land.
Governments in debt are especially exposed, since they may sell public assets to avoid bankruptcy.
Critics worry the 30 by 30 protected-area target could bring new green grabbing.

entries.title: Environmental gentrification: when greening pushes people out

definition.text: A process in which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises local property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected neighbourhood.

facts.text: Green amenities include parks, green roofs, gardens and green, energy-efficient building materials.
Greening can displace low-income households physically through rising housing costs, and can also displace long-time residents culturally, socially and politically.
The term was first coined by Sieg and colleagues in 2004 and combines the older topics of gentrification and environmental justice.
Green spaces tend to raise housing prices when housing supply is too small to meet local or regional demand.
Property prices near New York's High Line rose by 35%, and near Chicago's Bloomingdale Trail by 13.8% to 48.2%.
After Superfund cleanups, wealthier and more educated newcomers tend to move in while earlier residents are slowly priced out.
Cooling measures against the urban heat island, such as green walls and green roofs, can also trigger higher prices and displacement.

entries.text: Property prices near New York's High Line, an old rail line turned into a park, rose by 35%. Near Chicago's Bloomingdale Trail, the rise was 13.8% to 48.2%. Cleaner, greener neighborhoods become more desirable, and that can be a problem for the people who already live there. Environmental gentrification is the process by which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected area. The amenities include parks, green roofs, gardens and energy-efficient buildings. The mechanism is supply and demand. Green spaces tend to raise housing prices when there is too little housing to meet demand. Rising rents can push low-income households out physically. Long-time residents can also be displaced culturally, socially and politically, even if they stay. The same pattern follows cleanup of toxic Superfund sites. Wealthier, better-educated newcomers tend to move in while earlier residents are slowly priced out. Even measures against urban heat, such as green walls and roofs, can trigger it. Sieg and colleagues first named the process in 2004, joining two older topics: gentrification and environmental justice.

entries.title: Environmental defenders: risking life for land

definition.text: A person or group that protects the environment from harms such as resource extraction, hazardous waste dumping, infrastructure projects or land seizure.

facts.text: In 2019 the UN Human Rights Council unanimously recognised their importance for environmental protection.
Global Witness counted 1,922 murders of environmental defenders in 57 countries between 2002 and 2019, about a third of them Indigenous people.
On average three defenders are killed every week, and up to one hundred are intimidated, arrested or harassed for every one killed.
The Environmental Justice Atlas documents over 3500 ecological distribution conflicts worldwide; Indigenous people are involved in 41% of cases.
Campaigns that succeed usually use many non-violent tactics; 26.7% of reported campaigns ended in the project being cancelled.
Many conflicts arise from renewable energy or conservation projects; hydroelectric dams are the most frequent cause in the renewable energy sector.
The 1998 Aarhus Convention gives individuals rights to environmental information, participation in decisions and access to justice.

entries.contested_note: The term is disputed because it lumps together very different groups, many of whom do not call themselves environmental defenders or aim chiefly at protecting the environment.

entries.title: Free, prior and informed consent

definition.text: The principle that an Indigenous people must be consulted, bottom-up, before development starts on its ancestral land or uses resources in its territory.

facts.text: Free means no coercion or bribery; prior means consent is sought well before activities begin; informed means people get adequate information on the project's nature, size, pace and duration.
Critics note many treaties require only consultation, not consent, so Indigenous peoples cannot veto projects that affect them.
UNDRIP states that no relocation of Indigenous peoples may take place without their free, prior and informed consent.
The Philippines' Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 was the first national law to include it.
It has been applied widely in REDD+ forest projects; UN-REDD issued mandatory guidelines in 2013.
Industry representatives argue it lets Indigenous peoples block projects that could benefit the public; others reply that extraction for profit repeats neocolonial patterns.

entries.contested_note: Definitions differ, and states and industry often treat it as consultation rather than a right to say no.

Others reply that extraction for profit repeats neocolonial patterns.

entries.title: Critical environmental justice

definition.text: An approach created by David Pellow that questions the assumptions and gaps of earlier environmental justice studies.

facts.text: Its scholars hold that several forms of inequality together drive environmental injustice.
It rests on four pillars: intersectionality, spatial and temporal scale, seeking justice outside the state, and treating all beings as indispensable.

entries.text: David Pellow created critical environmental justice to question the assumptions and blind spots of earlier studies. Its scholars hold that several forms of inequality work together to drive environmental injustice. It rests on four pillars. The first is intersectionality, the way inequalities of race, class and gender combine. The others are attention to scale in space and time, seeking justice outside the state, and treating all beings as indispensable.

entries.title: The three dimensions of environmental justice

definition.text: The main kinds of fairness environmental justice asks for: fair sharing of environmental benefits and burdens, a real say in decisions, and recognition of marginalized groups.

facts.text: Distributive justice means sharing benefits like clean water and green space, and burdens like pollution, equitably across communities.
Procedural justice means affected communities get information, take part in policymaking and have access to justice.
Recognition justice means respecting the distinct cultures and histories of marginalized groups, including Indigenous peoples.
Robert Bullard instead groups equity into procedural, geographic and social kinds; geographic equity concerns how close communities live to hazards such as landfills and incinerators.

entries.title: Shipping toxic waste to the Global South

definition.text: The shifting of toxic waste from rich countries to the Global South, where weaker rules make disposal cheaper.

facts.text: Exports of toxic waste from the US escalated through the 1980s and 1990s.
Many receiving countries lack proper disposal systems, and local communities are not told about the hazards.
The Khian Sea incident, in which Philadelphia incinerator ash was dumped on a Haitian beach, contributed to the creation of the Basel Convention on international toxic waste movement.

entries.title: Indigenous environmental justice

definition.text: Environmental justice as understood by Indigenous peoples, framed by their colonial situation and possibly aiming at decolonization.

facts.text: In the US, Native Americans fall under a separate legal regime as citizens of Indigenous nations, based on sovereignty recognised by treaty, not as ethnic minorities.
Scholars such as Dina Gilio-Whitaker argue that distributive justice assumes land is a commodity, which clashes with many Indigenous worldviews.

entries.title: Green imperialism: environmentalism as interference?

definition.text: A critical label for what is seen as a Western strategy of influencing the internal affairs of developing nations in the name of environmentalism.

facts.text: Helge Ole Bergesen used it in 1988 to sum up how Third World elites viewed the Brundtland report.
The label eco-colonialism first appeared around debt-for-nature swaps from 1989.
Malaysia's leaders opposed European timber boycotts and palm-oil restrictions as imposing rich countries' priorities.
In 1994 Brazil, India and Singapore opposed linking trade to pollution controls, calling it hidden protectionism.

entries.contested_note: The term is a derogatory epithet; a 1990s survey found 66% of respondents did not see debt-for-nature swaps as eco-colonialism.

entries.title: Who should pay for climate change?
entries.article: Climate justice#Common principles of justice in burden-sharing

definition.text: Three rules for deciding who should carry the larger costs of climate change: those who caused most of it, those most able to pay, and those who benefited most.

facts.text: A 2023 study estimated the top 21 fossil fuel companies would owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative climate reparations over 2025–2050.
Some cities apply these ideas through intersectional adaptation policy; Barcelona requires 30% of new housing developments to be social housing.

Some cities apply these ideas in adaptation policy. Barcelona, for example, requires 30% of new housing developments to be social housing.

entries.title: Climate fairness across generations

definition.text: The fairness question raised because the generations mainly responsible for climate change are not the ones who will bear most of its damage.

facts.text: Under current pledges, children born in 2020 will face 2–7 times as many heat waves over their lives as people born in 1960.
Emissions from one generation can lock in damage for one or more future generations.
In April 2021 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court said one generation must not use up much of the CO2 budget and leave later generations a drastic reduction burden.

entries.text: Under current pledges, children born in 2020 will face 2–7 times as many heat waves in their lives as people born in 1960. In April 2021, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled on this point. One generation, it said, must not use up much of the carbon budget and leave later ones a drastic burden of cuts.

entries.title: Community-based conservation

definition.text: A conservation movement from the 1980s that involves local communities in protecting nature, in reaction to top-down conservation that ignored them.

facts.text: It grew out of opposition to fortress conservation, under which more than 20 million people are estimated to have been displaced.
In 1975 the IUCN first accepted that traditional ways of life could support biodiversity conservation.
The 2003 World Parks Congress and a 2004 CBD meeting recognised Indigenous peoples and local communities as governors of protected areas.
Co-management shares responsibility for protected areas between the state and local communities, blending traditional knowledge with science.
Livelihood strategies include ecotourism, rotational grazing, non-timber forest products, sustainable fisheries and carbon projects.
Community-managed lands in parts of Kenya have shown higher nutrient levels and plant productivity.
Benefits are often captured by local elites, while costs such as lost access to land fall on poorer households, as in Madagascar.
Legal recognition of communal land rights is essential for long-term success.

entries.text: More than 20 million people are estimated to have been displaced by fortress conservation. Community-based conservation grew in the 1980s as a reaction, involving local communities in protecting nature instead of pushing them out. In 1975 the IUCN first accepted that traditional ways of life could support conservation. The 2003 World Parks Congress and a 2004 Biodiversity Convention meeting recognized Indigenous peoples and local communities as governors of protected areas. Co-management splits responsibility between the state and communities, blending traditional knowledge with science. Livelihoods include ecotourism, rotational grazing, forest products other than timber, sustainable fisheries and carbon projects. Community-managed lands in parts of Kenya have shown richer soils and more plant growth. The benefits are not always shared fairly. In Madagascar, local elites captured the gains while poorer households lost access to land. Legal recognition of communal ownership of land is essential for lasting success.

entries.title: Territories of life: Indigenous and community conserved areas

definition.text: Territories and areas governed, managed and conserved in practice by Indigenous peoples or local communities, with clear benefits for biological and cultural diversity.

facts.text: Since about 2020 they are also called 'territories of life'.
An ICCA is marked by a strong bond between a community and a site, the community's leading role in managing it, and conservation outcomes even when conservation is not the aim.

The IUCN World Parks Congress of 2003 defined them as ecosystems with significant biodiversity voluntarily conserved by Indigenous and local communities through customary law or other effective means.
They may or may not meet the IUCN definition of a protected area, but when they do they can fit any IUCN category.
ICCAs are said to cover as much land as government protected areas, yet tens of thousands of sites lack government recognition.
Threats include mining, logging and other imposed development, and the takeover of community land to create state-run protected areas.
At CBD COP 10 in Nagoya in 2010, decision X/31 invited countries to recognise these areas and the communities behind them.

entries.title: Harmony with Nature

definition.text: A principle of friendly, holistic coexistence between humanity and nature.

facts.text: It is used mainly in debates on sustainable development and the rights of nature.
The United Nations created a Harmony with Nature programme in 2009, and Bolivian support led to further General Assembly resolutions.
Bolivia's proposal for the 2012 Rio+20 conference argued that nature, like humans, has rights, including the right to exist and to regenerate its vital cycles.
The same proposal argued that GDP is an inadequate measure of well-being and called for indicators of environmental destruction.

entries.text: Ahead of a 2012 UN conference in Rio, Bolivia made a bold claim. Nature, it argued, has rights just as humans do, including the right to exist and renew itself. Harmony with Nature is the principle behind that claim: a friendly, holistic coexistence between people and the natural world. It appears mainly in debates on sustainable development and the rights of nature. The United Nations created a Harmony with Nature program in 2009, and Bolivian support led to further resolutions. Bolivia's proposal also called GDP an inadequate measure of well-being and asked for indicators of environmental destruction.

entries.title: A patent treaty for genes and traditional knowledge
entries.article: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge

definition.text: A 2024 international treaty, known as GRATK, that requires patent applicants to disclose when inventions are based on genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge.

facts.text: It aims indirectly to fight biopiracy and support access and benefit-sharing rules through its disclosure requirement.
It was concluded in Geneva on 24 May 2024 after more than two decades of work by WIPO's intergovernmental committee.
It is the first WIPO treaty with provisions specifically for Indigenous peoples and local communities.
It enters into force three months after 15 countries ratify or accede; 44 countries had signed by May 2025.

sources.title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge

entries.title: Six facets of traditional ecological knowledge
entries.article: Traditional ecological knowledge#Aspects of traditional ecological knowledge

definition.text: Nicholas Houde's six-part breakdown of TEK: factual observations, management systems, past and current uses, ethics and values, culture and identity, and cosmology.

facts.text: Factual observations are long-term generalised observations, checked against accounts of other knowledge holders.
Management systems cover practices such as pest control, multiple cropping and ways of estimating the state of resources.
The ethics facet refers to environmental values that keep exploitation in check.

entries.text: Nicholas Houde broke traditional ecological knowledge into six parts. Factual observations are long-term general observations, checked against other knowledge holders' accounts. Management systems cover practices such as pest control, growing several crops together, and judging the state of resources. Then come past and current uses, and ethics and values, which keep exploitation in check. The last two are culture and identity, and cosmology, a people's view of how the world is ordered.
