entries.title: Cultural burning: fire as a tool and a practice
entries.article: Traditional ecological knowledge#Karuk and Yurok Burning

definition.text: Traditional controlled burning used by Indigenous peoples as a land management tool and spiritual practice.

facts.text: The Karuk and Yurok Tribes of California organised controlled burns in their ancestral lands to reduce wildfire risk and restore resources depleted by decades of fire exclusion.
An Indigenous nation in Australia that regained land reinstated its traditional controlled burning.
Colonists in California prohibited cultural burning in the late 1700s to early 1800s.

entries.text: Colonists in California banned Indigenous burning in the late 1700s to early 1800s. Decades of fire exclusion followed. Cultural burning is traditional controlled burning that Indigenous peoples use to manage land and as a spiritual practice. The Karuk and Yurok Tribes of California have revived it on their ancestral lands, to cut wildfire risk and restore depleted resources. In Australia, an Indigenous nation that regained land brought back its traditional burning too.

entries.title: Neo-extractivism: mining for social programs

definition.text: A development model in which governments take greater control of resource extraction and its revenue in order to fund social programmes.

facts.text: It was adopted mainly by Latin American 'Pink Tide' governments during the commodity boom of the early 2000s.
States revise contracts, raise export taxes and push state ownership, while the economy remains export-driven.
Under Ecuador's Correa government, which expanded oil and mining, poverty fell by 37% and extreme poverty by 49%.
Critics say tying social programmes to commodity exports leaves them exposed to price drops and concentrates executive power.

entries.text: Under Ecuador's Correa government, which expanded oil and mining, poverty fell by 37% and extreme poverty by 49%. It spread mainly among Latin America's left-leaning "Pink Tide" governments during the commodity boom of the early 2000s. States rewrite contracts, raise export taxes and push state ownership, while the economy still runs on exports. Critics say tying welfare to commodity sales leaves it exposed to price drops and concentrates power in presidents' hands.

entries.title: Land rights: security, not just access

definition.text: The ability to freely obtain, use and possess land, as long as doing so does not infringe on others' rights.

facts.text: Land rights differ from mere access to land: someone with only access can be expelled at the owner's choice, which limits financial stability.
Land law sets the legal rules on ownership, while land rights describe how far society accepts that ownership in practice.
UN research finds that rural landlessness strongly predicts poverty and hunger.
Customs often bar women from inheriting or buying land, leaving them dependent on male relatives even when they farm it.

entries.text: Being allowed onto land is not the same as having rights to it. Someone with only access can be expelled whenever the owner chooses, which makes life financially insecure. Land rights are the ability to obtain, use and hold land freely, so long as others' rights are respected. Land law sets the rules on ownership. Land rights describe how far society accepts that ownership in practice. UN research finds that rural landlessness strongly predicts poverty and hunger. Customs often bar women from inheriting or buying land, leaving them dependent on male relatives even when they farm it.

entries.title: Putting a number on ecological debt

definition.text: Attempts to put numbers on ecological debt, mostly by comparing each country's emissions with its fair per-person share.

facts.text: In 2000 Neumayer calculated a 'historical emissions debt': the gap between actual past emissions and equal per-capita emissions.
In principle a money value could be set by adding the external costs of past resource extraction to the share of global pollution poor countries bear from rich countries' consumption.
Matthews's 2015 method compares the warming caused by each country's emissions since 1960 with its population share of global warming.
A 'modified equal shares' approach weights each country's share of emissions by its basic needs.

entries.text: How much might rich countries owe? Most attempts compare each country's emissions with its fair share per person. In 2000, Neumayer calculated a "historical emissions debt": the gap between a country's actual past emissions and an equal per-person share. Matthews's 2015 method compares the warming each country has caused since 1960 with its share of world population. A "modified equal shares" approach weights shares by each country's basic needs. In principle, a money value could add up the outside costs of past extraction and the pollution poor countries bear from rich countries' consumption.

entries.title: The Hoodia case: the San people get a share

definition.text: A dispute over a patented weight-loss compound from the Hoodia plant, long used by the San people, that ended in a benefit-sharing deal.

facts.text: South Africa's CSIR isolated the P57 molecule from Hoodia in 1996, and the patent rights were sold to Pfizer and Phytopharm.
After the San demanded restitution, a confidential agreement gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

A confidential benefit-sharing deal gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

entries.title: The neem tree fights back

definition.text: A challenge to US and European patents on pesticide and antifungal products from the neem tree, used by Indian farmers for around 2,000 years.

facts.text: W.R. Grace patented a neem oil antifungal spray in 1994, although rural Indian farmers had used neem extracts for around 2,000 years.
The patent was overturned by the European Patent Office in 2000, and the neem tree became a symbol of resistance to corporate control of Indigenous knowledge.

entries.text: Indian farmers have used extracts of the neem tree for around 2,000 years, against pests and fungi. In 1994, the company W.R. Grace patented a neem oil antifungal spray anyway. The neem tree became a symbol of resistance to corporate control of Indigenous knowledge.

entries.title: Conservation refugees

definition.text: A person, usually Indigenous, displaced from their homeland when a park or other protected area is created.

facts.text: Many were already marginalised, end up living on the edges of towns with few opportunities, and rarely have legal recourse against powerful conservation interests.
John Muir's view that wilderness should be cleared of inhabitants became US policy with the 1964 Wilderness Act.
In Guinea, 663,000 people have been displaced from protected areas; Liberia claims over 120,000 conservation refugees and Senegal has 65,000 displaced.
Anthropologist Darrell Posey argued that landscapes that look natural may be shaped by Indigenous peoples, who should be seen as models for conservation.

The anthropologist Darrell Posey disagreed, arguing that landscapes that look natural may have been shaped by Indigenous peoples.

entries.title: Locally unwanted land uses

definition.text: A facility or project, such as a landfill, power plant or prison, that a local community opposes because of the harms it expects from it.

facts.text: The expected costs include health hazards, ugliness, lower home values and sometimes higher utility costs.
Such facilities tend to end up in poor, minority or politically under-represented places that cannot fight them off.
Their harms keep high-earning buyers away, trapping low-income residents in a cycle of cheap housing near landfills and highways.
Of more than 1,000 US Superfund sites, 25% lie on or near Native American reservations.

entries.text: Nobody wants a landfill, power plant or prison next door. Planners call such a project a locally unwanted land use: a facility a community opposes because of the harms it expects. Those harms include health hazards, ugliness, lower home values and sometimes higher utility bills. Such facilities tend to land in poor, minority or politically weak places that cannot fight them off. They then keep wealthier buyers away, trapping low-income residents in cheap housing near dumps and highways. Of more than 1,000 US Superfund toxic sites, 25% lie on or near Native American reservations.

entries.title: Sacrifice zones

definition.text: A geographic area permanently damaged by heavy environmental change or economic neglect, often through locally unwanted land uses.

facts.text: A 2022 UN report found that millions of people live in pollution sacrifice zones, mostly around heavy industry and mining, and that marginalised groups are hit hardest.
Sacrifice zones go with 'abundance zones': damage in some places sustains privileges and lifestyles elsewhere.
A 1973 US National Academy of Sciences report on strip-mined coal lands in the American West introduced the term 'national sacrifice area'.
Louisiana's "Cancer Alley" is an 85-mile stretch along the Mississippi with over 200 petrochemical plants and a disproportionately black, low-income population.
Naomi Klein argued in 2014 that an economy run on fuels that release poisons when extracted and refined has always required sacrifice zones.

entries.title: Thinking seven generations ahead

definition.text: The principle that people today should live and work for the benefit of the seventh generation to come.

facts.text: It is believed to come from the Great Law of the Haudenosaunee, which holds that decisions should be judged by their effect seven generations ahead.
The often-quoted line about considering the seventh generation does not appear in written transcriptions of the Haudenosaunee constitution, which instead urges leaders to consider future generations.
Some green economists advise measuring a project's impacts from the viewpoint of the seventh generation.

entries.title: Ethnoecology: how cultures read their environment

definition.text: The scientific study of how different groups of people understand the ecosystems around them and their relationships with their environments.

facts.text: Harold Conklin coined the term in his 1954 dissertation on how the Hanunoo culture relates to the plant world.
To learn how cultures classify their environment, ethnoecology borrows methods from linguistics and cultural anthropology.
It treats humans as part of ecosystems: people can act as a keystone species, shaping soil formation, seed dispersal and biodiversity.
According to the WHO, almost 80% of the world's population relies on ethnobotanical methods as a main source of treatment for illness.

entries.title: Atmospheric colonization

definition.text: The idea that rich Global North countries have taken over most of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb greenhouse gases, leaving the Global South to bear the consequences.

facts.text: Global North countries, with 19% of world population, account for 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions; the Global South accounts for 8%.
Countries such as Ecuador emit relatively little carbon dioxide but have far fewer resources to cope with local climate impacts.

entries.title: Climate apartheid: when only the rich escape
entries.article: Climate change and poverty#Human rights and democracy

definition.text: A situation in which only the rich can escape the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: UN Special Rapporteur Philip Alston warned of it in June 2019, saying it could undermine human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
He cited Superstorm Sandy in 2012, when most of New York lost power while Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags.

entries.title: Ecological distribution conflicts

definition.text: A concept coined in 1995 by Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor for conflicts over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens.

facts.text: It extends the political-economy idea of economic distribution conflicts to unequal distribution of environmental resources.
Damage such as a factory polluting a river is often not valued by the market, so those harmed go uncompensated.
Neoclassical economics treats such impacts as externalities to price; ecological economists and political ecologists reject this monetary commensuration.
Movements may demand money compensation when weak (weak sustainability) but argue from values money cannot measure when strong (strong sustainability).

entries.contested_note: Whether environmental harms can be priced and compensated, as neoclassical economics holds, is rejected by ecological economists and political ecologists.
entries.text: When a factory pollutes a river, the market usually puts no price on the harm, so the people downstream go uncompensated. In 1995, Joan Martínez-Alier and Martin O'Connor coined a term for such fights: ecological distribution conflicts. These are clashes over unfair access to natural resources and unequal pollution burdens. Mainstream economics treats such harms as externalities, costs to outsiders that could be priced. Ecological economists and political ecologists reject the idea that money can measure them. Movements may ask for money when weak, but argue from values money cannot measure when strong.

entries.title: The environmentalism of the poor

definition.text: Social movements that arise when poor people fight powerful state or private interests threatening their livelihood, health, sovereignty and culture.

facts.text: Unlike mainstream environmentalism, which centres on conservation and eco-efficiency, it puts social justice first.
Joan Martinez Alier describes it as the struggles poor people wage when they face ecological distribution conflicts, where an activity's environmental harms fall unevenly and unjustly.
Peruvian historian Alberto Flores Galindo suggested the term in 1988; in 1997 Martinez-Alier and Ramachandra Guha contrasted it with the 'full-belly environmentalism' of the global North.
Examples include the Chipko movement, Indigenous struggles against Brazilian agribusiness, and the Green Belt Movement led by Wangari Maathai.
Women often lead these movements because their daily roles, such as fetching water and growing crops, bring them into direct contact with nature.
Several leaders, such as Berta Cáceres and Chico Mendes, were assassinated for their activism.
Transnational environmental justice networks let local defenders seek international support against large corporations.

entries.title: Who pays for green policy?

definition.text: How the costs and benefits of an environmental policy fall on different groups, and whether it widens or narrows environmental and social injustice.

facts.text: Distributional effects are one of the criteria, besides efficiency and cost-effectiveness, used to judge environmental policies.
A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the taxed amount rises; a carbon tax that does not return its revenue is naturally regressive and hits the lowest incomes hardest.
A study found carbon pricing is on average progressive in countries with per capita incomes below USD 15,000 a year but tends to be regressive in richer countries.
Because carbon pricing is somewhat regressive, economists say poor people should be compensated.
A 2019 study found energy efficiency standards are more regressive than energy taxes.
Global estimates of climate damage costs usually leave out distributional effects.

entries.contested_note: Whether carbon taxes are regressive is disputed; Gilbert Metcalf, for one, disputed that they would be in the US.
entries.text: A carbon tax that keeps its revenue hits the poorest households hardest. That is because it is regressive: its burden falls, as a share of income, the richer people are. Not all agree on the premise: Gilbert Metcalf disputed that a US carbon tax would be regressive. Global estimates of climate damage usually leave these effects out.

entries.title: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples

definition.text: A declaration adopted by the UN in 2007 that sets out the collective rights of Indigenous peoples, including self-determination.

facts.text: It covers rights to self-determination and to protect cultures, identities, languages, ceremonies and access to resources.
It does not define Indigenous peoples but affirms their right to decide their own identity.
It is the clearest statement of free, prior and informed consent in international development.
It offers benchmark standards on Indigenous land rights.

Those rights include self-determination and the protection of cultures, identities, languages, ceremonies and access to resources. The declaration does not define Indigenous peoples. It affirms instead their right to decide their own identity. It is the clearest statement of free, prior and informed consent in international development. It also offers benchmark standards on Indigenous land rights.

entries.title: Environmental personhood: when a river becomes a person

definition.text: A legal idea that gives certain natural entities, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person.

facts.text: Legal personhood gives the entity rights, protections, responsibilities and legal liability; because a river cannot go to court, a guardian acts on its behalf.
A legal person cannot be owned, so no one can own an entity that has been given legal personality.
Christopher D. Stone first proposed legal personality for natural objects in the 1970s in his article "Should trees have standing?"
New Zealand declared Te Urewera a legal entity in 2014 and the Whanganui River a legal person in 2017, represented by one guardian from the iwi and one from the Crown.
An Indian state High Court gave the Ganges and Yamuna legal-entity status in March 2017, but sceptics noted that the declaration alone would not stop their pollution.
In 2022 Spain recognised the Mar Menor lagoon and its basin as a legal person, the first ecosystem in Europe with its own rights.
Supporters say it lets people sue to protect nature without showing harm to humans, and honours Indigenous relationships with the land.
Critics note that a legal person can also be sued, raising questions about who is liable for harms such as natural disasters.

entries.contested_note: The idea is controversial even among environmentalists, some of whom back rights of nature but not personhood as the way to secure them.
entries.text: In 2017, New Zealand declared the Whanganui River a legal person. It is represented by two guardians, one from the Māori iwi and one from the Crown. entries.title: Rawls's three kinds of procedural justice

definition.text: John Rawls's division of procedural justice into perfect, imperfect and pure forms, set out in A Theory of Justice.

facts.text: Perfect procedural justice has an independent standard of a fair outcome and a procedure that guarantees reaching it.
Imperfect procedural justice has the independent standard but no procedure that guarantees the fair outcome.
Pure procedural justice has no standard of a just outcome other than the procedure itself.

entries.text: In A Theory of Justice, John Rawls split procedural justice into three forms. Perfect procedural justice has an independent standard of a fair result and a procedure that guarantees reaching it. Imperfect procedural justice has the standard but no procedure that guarantees the fair result. Pure procedural justice has no standard of a just result apart from the procedure itself.

entries.title: Environmental reparations

definition.text: Payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by the presence of industry.

facts.text: Possible recipients include people living near industry, disaster victims and climate refugees.
They can range from direct payouts to funds for cleaning waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighbourhoods, or public transport.

Recipients might be people living near industry, disaster victims or climate refugees. The forms vary widely: direct payouts, funds to clean waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighborhoods, or public transport.

entries.title: Climate refugees and the gap in the law

definition.text: People forced to move by climate change who fall into a legal gap because such migration is not yet covered by international law.

facts.text: Climate-induced migration is one of the most disputed effects of climate change.
Asian and African mega-deltas and small islands face high flood and storm risk and large-scale displacement.
The International Organization for Migration defines environmental migrants as people obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives.

entries.contested_note: How much migration climate change will cause, and who counts as a climate refugee, are disputed and undefined in law.

entries.title: Aboriginal title: land rights that outlive conquest

definition.text: A common-law doctrine holding that Indigenous peoples' customary land rights survive after a settler state takes sovereignty.

facts.text: It is called native title in Australia, customary title in New Zealand and original Indian title in the US.
Indigenous land rights were long undermined by the doctrine of terra nullius, Latin for "land belonging to no one".
In Australia's Mabo case, begun by Meriam people in 1971, the High Court recognised native ownership and rejected terra nullius.
In the US case Johnson v. McIntosh (1823), the doctrine of discovery was used to rule that Native Americans had only occupancy rights to their land.

entries.text: In 1971, Meriam people in Australia began a case that would overturn a legal fiction. In the Mabo case, the High Court recognized native ownership and rejected terra nullius, the doctrine that the land had belonged to no one. McIntosh (1823), the doctrine of discovery was used to rule that Native Americans had only rights of occupancy.

entries.title: Three kinds of environmentalism
entries.article: Environmentalism of the poor#Varieties of environmentalism

definition.text: Martinez-Alier's division of environmentalism into three currents: the cult of the wilderness, the gospel of eco-efficiency, and environmental justice or the environmentalism of the poor.

facts.text: The cult of the wilderness, tied to the conservation movement, tries to separate economic activity from nature, mainly through reserves and protected areas.
The gospel of eco-efficiency accepts economic growth but seeks growth that uses fewer resources and makes less waste, the so-called dematerialization of the economy.
Critics of dematerialization say the entropy law limits efficiency gains, and that rich economies decouple only by outsourcing material-heavy production to poorer countries.
Wilderness thinking has at times expelled poor and Indigenous people from their lands to create reserves.

entries.text: Joan Martinez-Alier divides environmentalism into three currents. The cult of the wilderness, tied to older conservation campaigns, tries to keep economic activity away from nature, mainly through reserves. It has at times expelled poor and Indigenous people to create them. The gospel of eco-efficiency accepts growth but wants growth that uses fewer resources and makes less waste. Critics say physical laws limit efficiency gains, and that rich economies cut material use only by outsourcing heavy production to poorer countries. The third current is environmental justice, the environmentalism of the poor.

entries.title: Ancestral domain: more than a land title

definition.text: The lands, territories and resources of Indigenous peoples, a term used especially in the Asia-Pacific region.

facts.text: Unlike land title, 'domain' covers spiritual and cultural ties to land, not just ownership that can be traded.
Indigenous peoples may prefer to be called custodians of their lands rather than owners; tradable private land was often introduced by colonialism.
The Philippines' Indigenous People's Rights Act of 1997 defines it to include lands, inland waters, coasts and natural resources held by Indigenous peoples or their ancestors.
The ILO's 1957 Convention No. 107 assumed Indigenous peoples would be integrated into wider society; it was replaced in 1989 by Convention No. 169.

entries.title: Feminist political ecology

definition.text: A feminist approach within political ecology that studies how gender shapes people's access to, control over and knowledge of natural resources.

facts.text: It argues that mainstream environmental policies rest on gender-neutral assumptions that can overlook women's knowledge of resource management.
It combines three areas it treats as gendered: knowledge, environmental rights, and grassroots activism.
It explains differences in environmental experience by social constructs of gender, not biology.
A key founding text is the 1996 book Feminist Political Ecology by Dianne Rocheleau and colleagues.

entries.title: Writing the rights of nature into law

definition.text: The writing of the rights-of-nature theory into constitutions, statutes, treaties, local laws and court rulings.

facts.text: It treats ecosystems and species as having inherent rights, much like fundamental human rights.
As of 2022, nature's rights laws existed in 39 countries; initiatives numbered 409 in June 2021 and 495 in May 2024.
Ecuador's 2008 constitution gives nature, or Pachamama, the right to exist and regenerate its vital cycles, and lets any person demand those rights be respected.
In 2019 Bangladesh's High Court recognised the Turag River, and by extension all the country's rivers, as living entities with legal rights.

entries.title: Gender and the environment

definition.text: The study of how relations between women, men and the environment shape resource use, the sharing of responsibilities and people's well-being.

facts.text: Interest grew from Ester Boserup's 1960s book Woman's Role in Economic Development; from the 1980s policymakers paid more attention to gender in resource management.
Women do 80% of food production in sub-Saharan Africa, 60% in Asia and 50% in Latin America, yet men generally own the land.
Improving women's access to farm resources could raise yields by 20–30% and total output in poor countries by 2.5–4%.
Feminist economists argue the growth paradigm keeps gender and environmental injustices in place and propose degrowth work-sharing.

entries.title: ILO Convention 169
entries.article: Free, prior and informed consent#International Labour Organization

definition.text: An international treaty on Indigenous and tribal peoples adopted by the International Labour Organization in 1989.

facts.text: It aims to end discrimination against Indigenous peoples and give them a role in decision-making, built on participation and consultation.
The duty to consult falls on the state, not on companies, and aims at agreement or consent to the proposed development.

entries.title: Consent protocols written by Indigenous peoples
entries.article: Free, prior and informed consent#Indigenous Peoples' FPIC protocols

definition.text: Rules written by Indigenous peoples themselves, since the early 2000s, for how consent processes must be carried out.

facts.text: The first protocols were sector-specific, the second were bio-cultural protocols tied to CBD access and benefit-sharing, and the third are autonomous protocols, mostly from Latin America.

The second were bio-cultural protocols linked to the Biodiversity Convention's rules on access to genes. The third, mostly from Latin America, are autonomous protocols.

entries.title: Poverty: lacking the basics

definition.text: A condition in which a person lacks the money and essentials needed for a basic standard of living.

facts.text: Absolute poverty compares income with what is needed for basic needs such as food, clothing and shelter; relative poverty compares living standards with others in the same time and place.
The 'dollar a day' poverty line, introduced in 1990, became US$1.90 a day in 2015, measured at purchasing power parity rather than exchange rates.
As of 2019, in PPP dollars, 85% of people lived on less than $30 a day, two-thirds on less than $10, and 10% on less than $1.90.
Poor people are more vulnerable to the environmental effects of industry, climate change, natural disasters and extreme weather.
Economic pressures on poor communities often play a part in deforestation and biodiversity loss.
Even when countries develop, the poorest citizens of middle-income countries often fail to gain enough of the new wealth to leave poverty.
Sustainable Development Goal 1, 'No Poverty', adopted by the United Nations in 2015, sums up the international framework for poverty alleviation.

entries.title: Does poverty damage nature, or protect it?

definition.text: The two-way link between poverty and damage to nature: the poor suffer most from degradation, and some argue poverty itself drives it.

facts.text: The poor tend to suffer most from environmental degradation caused by exploiting natural resources.
About 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to Global North countries, yet developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change.
This unfair split of environmental burdens and benefits gave rise to the global environmental justice and climate justice movements.

The Brundtland Report concluded that poverty causes environmental degradation, while the environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds that the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability.
A 2016 UN report claimed that by 2030 climate change could drive an additional 122 million people into extreme poverty.
Conservation can also burden the poor: fortress conservation has evicted indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.

entries.contested_note: The Brundtland Report says poverty causes environmental degradation, while the environmentalism-of-the-poor view sees the poor as a leading force for sustainability.

That lopsided split of burdens and benefits gave rise to the global movements for environmental justice and climate justice. The link between poverty and environmental damage runs both ways. The poor tend to suffer most when natural resources are exploited and ecosystems degrade. The Brundtland Report concluded that it does. The environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds the opposite: the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability. Conservation itself can burden the poor too. Fortress conservation has evicted Indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.
entries.text_plain: Developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change. Yet about 92% of accumulated greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to the Global North. That lopsided split of burdens and benefits gave rise to the global movements for environmental justice and climate justice. The link between poverty and environmental damage runs both ways. The poor tend to suffer most when natural resources are exploited and ecosystems degrade. A 2016 UN report claimed that by 2030 climate change could push an additional 122 million people into extreme poverty. Does poverty also cause degradation? Here the experts split. The Brundtland Report concluded that it does. The environmentalism-of-the-poor view holds the opposite: the global poor may be the most important force for sustainability. Conservation itself can burden the poor too. Fortress conservation has evicted Indigenous people, and green colonialism grabs land in the name of environmentalism.

entries.title: Degraded land and deprivation: a vicious circle

definition.text: The way degraded land and human deprivation reinforce each other, as falling land productivity cuts food, income and security.

facts.text: Land degradation brings lower crop yields, less food, more vulnerability to floods and droughts, people losing their homes, and economic problems.
It can reduce land's natural capacity to store and filter water, leading to water scarcity.

Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are where degraded lands coincide with high poverty and childhood stunting; in 2025, 47 million stunted under-fives lived where stunting overlaps big degradation-driven yield losses.
Most of sub-Saharan Africa shows fairly low yield losses from degradation, not because soils are healthier but because poor access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets limits yields more.
Of the world's 570 million farms, 85% are under 2 hectares and work just 9% of farmland; farm size shapes farmers' ability to tackle degradation.
Soil degradation increases competition for farmland, and all but 3 conflicts inside African states since the 1990s are linked to such competition.
It can also drive environmental migration.

entries.title: The cycle of poverty

definition.text: A situation, also called a poverty trap, in which poverty seems to be passed down, so that later generations cannot escape it.

facts.text: Self-reinforcing mechanisms keep poverty going once it exists, unless someone from outside steps in.
Applied to developing countries, the same idea is called a development trap.
Lack of money, education and social connections all help keep poor families in the cycle.
Children are the most vulnerable, since they depend on guardians and are too young to work their own way out.
The cycle of poverty makes the harms of climate change worse.
People living in degraded ecosystems and a poverty trap may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let ecosystems and resources regenerate.
Conditional cash transfers aim to help poor families now and to break the cycle for the next generation by building their skills and health.

entries.text: Children born into poverty depend on their guardians and are too young to work their own way out. That makes them the most vulnerable part of the cycle of poverty, also called a poverty trap. In this situation, poverty seems to pass down, and later generations cannot escape it. Self-reinforcing forces keep it going unless someone from outside steps in. Lack of money, education and social connections all hold families in place. Applied to whole developing countries, the idea is called a development trap. The cycle has an environmental edge. People living in degraded ecosystems may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let land and resources regenerate. The cycle also makes climate harms worse. Conditional cash transfers, payments tied to steps such as schooling or health checks, aim to help families now and break the cycle for the next generation.

entries.title: Sustainable livelihoods

definition.text: An idea from development and environmental studies about how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can recover from shocks.

facts.text: It widens poverty studies beyond material want to include vulnerability and social exclusion.
The idea was introduced by the Brundtland Commission, and the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty.
The approach seeks human-centered, participatory development that links concern for environmental and economic resources.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals for 2030, are an example; the COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

entries.text: Poverty is not only a lack of money. The sustainable livelihoods idea widens the view to include vulnerability and social exclusion. It asks how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can bounce back from shocks. The Brundtland Commission introduced the idea. The 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty. The approach favors development centered on people and shaped by their participation, linking environmental and economic concerns. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 for 2030, are one example. The COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

entries.title: Cheap water that misses the poor

definition.text: The pattern in which subsidies that make piped water cheap mostly help richer connected households, while many poor people go unserved.

facts.text: Water consumption subsidies go mostly to those connected to the supply grid, typically the richer, urban population outside informal housing.
With heavy subsidies, water prices in developing countries cover on average only 30% of supply costs.
Utilities then lack incentives to maintain or expand networks: leaks lose enough water for 200 million people a year, and many poor stay unconnected.
The poor instead buy from water vendors at about 5 to 16 times the metered price; subsidising new connections has shown more promise.

entries.text: Poor families without a piped connection often buy water from vendors at about 5 to 16 times the metered price. Meanwhile, subsidies that make piped water cheap flow mainly to households already connected, typically richer urban ones outside informal settlements. With heavy subsidies, water prices in developing countries cover on average only 30% of supply costs. Utilities then have little reason to maintain or extend their networks. Leaks lose enough water for 200 million people a year, and many poor homes stay unconnected. Subsidizing new connections has shown more promise.

entries.title: Energy poverty and development

definition.text: The link between lack of modern energy and lack of development, since businesses, public services and households all depend on energy.

facts.text: Poor energy access is associated with infant mortality, illiteracy and lower life expectancy, and can push people to move to cities.
Energy use and economic growth have historically risen together, though it is unclear which causes the other.
By the early 2000s rich countries were growing without a matching rise in energy use, but in developing countries the two stayed closely linked.
Energy-poor households often burn traditional biomass such as wood and dung, whose incomplete combustion releases black carbon, a health hazard.

entries.title: Why whole countries stay poor

definition.text: The ways whole poor countries stay stuck in poverty, through causes such as lack of credit, environmental degradation, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure.

facts.text: Extreme environmental degradation is one cause, because it reduces how much farmland can produce.
Jeffrey Sachs argues the extreme poor lack six kinds of capital, including natural capital, and capital per person can fall each generation when population grows faster than savings.
Sachs argues that large, lasting foreign aid can raise the capital stock enough to lift households above subsistence.
He wants public money to go to health, education, infrastructure and natural capital such as conserving biodiversity and ecosystems, leaving business investment to private firms.

entries.title: Five kinds of capital for a livelihood

definition.text: The United Nations Development Programme's way of assessing livelihoods by the five kinds of capital people can draw on: human, social, natural, physical and financial.

facts.text: How much access people have to these assets shapes how the UNDP designs its development projects.
The approach also looks at how people use their assets to cope with shocks and stresses.
The UK's Department for International Development and CARE also use sustainable livelihood frameworks in place of sector-by-sector approaches.

entries.text: The United Nations Development Programme sizes up how people make a living by the five kinds of capital they can draw on. Human capital is skills and health. Social capital is relationships. Natural capital is land, water and other resources. Physical capital is tools and infrastructure, and financial capital is money. How much people can reach of each shapes how the UNDP designs its projects. The framework also asks how people use these assets to cope with shocks. The UK's Department for International Development and the charity CARE use similar frameworks instead of sector-by-sector approaches.

entries.title: Making money without wrecking the world around you

definition.text: Running a business so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible.

facts.text: Such firms aim at the triple bottom line of profit, people and planet, weighing environmental, economic and social factors in their decisions.
A green business offers products that cut demand for harmful ones, keeps its finances sound, respects human rights and supports inclusion of local and global communities.
The idea grew out of late-20th-century debates on sustainable development; the 1987 report Our Common Future shaped how private firms thought about managing the environment.
A central aim is to cut the environmental harm from making and using goods, for example by measuring carbon footprints, cutting waste and redesigning products to last longer.
The business historian Geoffrey Jones traces green business back to start-ups in organic food and wind and solar energy before World War 1.
If a firm's whole model is unsustainable, becoming sustainable can mean rebuilding it, for example moving from selling cars to offering car sharing.
Firms often meet only the lowest standards; real sustainability is said to need a purpose that goes beyond legal compliance.

entries.title: Nature-positive: halt the loss by 2030, recover by 2050

definition.text: A goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050.

facts.text: Progress is measured against a baseline of biodiversity in 2020.
It matches the 2030 mission and 2050 vision of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, though the framework does not name it.
It was proposed as a single global goal for nature to sit beside climate and development goals, aiming at an 'Equitable, Nature-Positive, Carbon Neutral world'.
Unlike earlier approaches, it covers a company's whole value chain, not just direct impacts, and aims for absolute rather than relative gains.
Over 90 world leaders signed the Leaders' Pledge for Nature, and the G7 committed to it at its 2021 summit.
Critics call it vague and open to greenwashing, and warn of the 'financialization of nature'.
To avoid greenwashing, Milner-Gulland proposed it needs a measured baseline, timeframe, target, clear actions, regular monitoring and disclosure.
Its 'net' approach is criticised for implying continued loss and assuming like-for-like compensation is possible.

entries.contested_note: Critics call nature-positive vague, open to greenwashing and a route to financializing nature, while its proponents say business must be part of the solution.

entries.title: The environmental management system: a firm's green rulebook

definition.text: A system of policies, procedures and processes that a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance to people inside and outside the firm.

facts.text: The most widely used standard for an EMS is ISO 14001, part of the ISO 14000 family first developed in March 1996.
Its goals are to increase compliance with legal standards and to reduce waste, going beyond compliance to cut environmental impact.
An EMS meeting ISO 14001 helps an organization identify and control its environmental impacts, improve its performance continually, and set and track objectives.
It follows a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, a process of continual improvement in which the system is constantly reviewed and revised.
The model can be used by organizations ranging from factories to service industries to government agencies.
Organizations usually seek certification from independent bodies, which confirm the EMS conforms to ISO 14001.
An EMS also encourages contractors and suppliers to set up their own systems.

entries.text: In March 1996 the ISO 14000 family of standards was first developed. Its member ISO 14001 is now the most widely used standard for an environmental management system, or EMS. An EMS is a set of policies, procedures and processes a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance. Its goals are to obey legal standards more fully and to reduce waste, then to go beyond compliance. It helps an organization identify and control its impacts and set and track objectives. The system runs on a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, constantly reviewed and revised. Factories, service industries and government agencies can all use it. Independent bodies usually certify that a system conforms to ISO 14001. A good EMS also nudges contractors and suppliers to set up their own.

entries.title: The environmental audit: checking a firm against the rules

definition.text: An evaluation that finds gaps in an organization's compliance with environmental rules and in its environmental management system, and sets out corrective actions.

facts.text: Environmental audits do for environmental performance what financial audits do for accounts.
There are two main types: compliance audits and management system audits.
Compliance audits check a site against the laws, regulations, permits and local codes that apply to it.
A multimedia audit covers all environmental media such as air, water and waste; a programmatic audit covers only chosen areas, such as air.
ISO 14001 certification does not by itself prove legal compliance, though the standard requires firms to evaluate their compliance.
Auditors work from a checklist called a protocol, and there is no standard protocol in form or content.
Professionals have long debated detailed, prescriptive protocols against flexible ones that rely on auditor expertise.
Satellite imagery and geographic information systems are an emerging audit technology.

entries.contested_note: Audit professionals disagree on whether detailed prescriptive protocols or flexible expert-led ones work better.

entries.title: The EU taxonomy: an official list of green activities

definition.text: A European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable, created under the European Green Deal.

facts.text: Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make informed sustainable investment decisions.
It covers six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, circular economy, pollution prevention, water and marine resources, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
The Taxonomy came into force in July 2020 as part of the European Green Deal, which aims for a carbon neutral economy by 2050.
A Technical Expert Group set up in 2018 developed the technical screening criteria used to judge whether an activity is sustainable.
The Environmental Delegated Act, published on 21 November 2023, set criteria for the remaining objectives, including protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
Banks must disclose a 'green asset ratio'; early estimates put the EU banks' average at 2.23%.
An EU green bond standard under development would require issuers to fund activities aligned with the taxonomy.

entries.title: Design for the environment: cutting harm at the drawing board

definition.text: A design approach that cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life cycle.

facts.text: Its four parts are cleaner processing and manufacturing, greener packaging, design for disposal or reuse, and energy efficiency.
Life-cycle assessment is used to compare design options and pick the least harmful.
Claimed benefits are cost savings, lower risk, new market openings and meeting regulations.
Sustainable business leaders treat it as part of their work, along with counting life-cycle costs.

entries.title: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: counting a firm's emissions

definition.text: A set of standards that organizations use to measure and track their greenhouse gas emissions, the most common in greenhouse gas accounting.

facts.text: The World Resources Institute worked with companies to develop it, and its first version was published in September 2001.
It sorts an organization's emissions into Scope 1, 2 and 3; Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from its activities.
For most businesses the great majority of emissions are Scope 3, coming from the wider supply chain rather than the site or purchased energy.

entries.title: Stakeholder theory: who a company answers to

definition.text: The view that a firm is answerable not only to its shareholders but to every group with a relationship to it, such as workers, customers, suppliers and communities.

entries.title: Corporate social responsibility: business beyond profit

definition.text: Companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably so that their overall effect on society is positive.

facts.text: It is a form of private business self-regulation that aims to help social and environmental goals by reducing harm, such as cutting a firm's carbon footprint.
Since the 1960s it has gone by many names, including corporate sustainability, sustainable business, corporate citizenship and responsible business, and there is little agreement on a definition.
A business person may see it as strategy, an NGO activist as greenwash and a government official as voluntary regulation.
Howard Bowen's 1953 book Social Responsibilities of the Businessman is widely seen as the founding work; he argued business leaders' duties go beyond making profit.
Firms take it up for strategic, ethical or instrumental reasons; for listed companies it often takes the form of ESG practices and reports.
It has been shifting from voluntary choices by single firms toward mandatory schemes at regional, national and international levels.
Its scope widened from a firm's own conduct to its suppliers, how its products are used and how they are thrown away.
Supporters say it raises long-term profits; critics say it distracts from a firm's economic role or is mere window-dressing.

entries.title: Sustainability reporting: telling outsiders how a firm behaves

definition.text: The disclosure, voluntary or required, of a company's non-financial performance information to people outside the organization.

facts.text: It covers environmental, social, economic and governance issues, the criteria grouped under the acronym ESG.
It goes by many names, including ESG reporting, non-financial reporting, CSR reporting and social reporting.
It grew from environmental reporting, which became popular in the 1970s, and has expanded greatly over the last twenty years.
It rests on the stakeholder model: following Freeman, employees, customers, suppliers, communities and governments matter as well as shareholders.
Its growth was driven by awareness of the ecological crisis and by corporate scandals such as Enron and the 2008 financial crisis.
The Global Reporting Initiative standards are the most widely used benchmark for sustainability reports worldwide.
Critics say the many competing frameworks make reports hard to compare, undermining transparency.
Some firms manipulate reports by hiding negative or over-stating positive environmental data, a practice linked to greenwashing.

entries.title: Ethical consumerism: voting with your wallet

definition.text: Choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, according to how products affect people, animals and the environment.

facts.text: It is a form of consumer activism based on 'dollar voting'.
Its rise over the last two decades is linked to the rise of CSR.
Criteria-based ethical and environmental ratings of companies, first used for shoppers, are now common in business sustainability ratings, and ESG ratings reach stock traders' screens.
More consumers demand sustainable goods, especially when they think firms neglect the environment.
Its growth is held back by routine buying that leaves no room for reflection and by competing moral demands in daily life.

entries.title: Profit for owners, or duties to society?

definition.text: The argument over whether a company exists only to earn returns for its owners within the law, or also owes duties to society and the environment.

facts.text: Milton Friedman argued a firm's purpose is to maximize returns to shareholders, and that obeying the law is socially responsible enough.
Friedman said people may spend their own money on causes, but owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers.
In the 1930s Berle and Dodd debated whether directors should be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders.
Some argue better government regulation is the alternative to voluntary CSR; others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated.
Some studies find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost, a kind of agency problem.

entries.contested_note: Friedman and others hold that a firm's only duty is profit within the law, while CSR supporters argue firms owe wider duties to society.
entries.text: Milton Friedman gave the blunt answer. A firm's purpose, he argued, is to maximize returns to its shareholders, and obeying the law is socially responsible enough. People may spend their own money on causes, he said. But owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers. This is one side of a long argument. Does a company exist only to earn returns for its owners, or does it also owe duties to society and the environment? The argument is older than Friedman. In the 1930s the legal scholars Berle and Dodd debated it. Should directors be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders? The other side is {{ref:nature-gov-067}}, backed by {{ref:nature-gov-068}}, which holds that firms owe wider duties. The debate remains unsettled. Some argue better government regulation is the real alternative to voluntary CSR. Others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated. Some studies even find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost. Economists call that an agency problem: hired managers acting for themselves rather than for the owners they work for.

entries.title: The social license to operate: permission no law grants
entries.article: Corporate social responsibility#Social license to operate

definition.text: The ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give to a company's activities.

facts.text: The term was introduced in 1997 and has been used mostly in resource extraction industries to describe company-community relations.
Without it, local people may block projects, staff may leave and firms may face ongoing legal challenges.
It is granted by communities, not governments, and can take a long time to win but be lost very quickly.
It rests on relationships and trust; local firms tend to gain it more easily than outside ones.
Showing commitment to CSR is one way to earn it, by improving a firm's reputation.

entries.title: Corporate sustainability: the long game in strategy

definition.text: A business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into company strategy.

facts.text: It is often confused with corporate social responsibility, but scholars say the key difference is time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations.
The idea grew out of sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission, and John Elkington's 1997 'triple bottom line'.
In the research literature it is usually treated as a three-part idea combining social, environmental and economic factors.
Its most widely accepted test is whether a firm uses natural capital efficiently, including keeping vital ecosystem services such as climate regulation and water purification.
Firms often state their commitment through Corporate Sustainability Standards, policies meant to meet or go beyond minimum legal requirements.
Whether it can be measured is disputed, because there is no generally accepted set of indicators separating sustainable from unsustainable operation.
Short-term thinking is described as the main enemy of corporate sustainability.

entries.title: The TCFD: telling investors about climate risk
entries.article: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

definition.text: An international task force whose recommendations tell investors how companies are managing the risks of climate change and how they are governed.

facts.text: It was set up in December 2015 by the G20 and the Financial Stability Board, and was chaired by Michael Bloomberg.
Its recommendations cover four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets.
It was formed partly in response to the 2015 Paris Agreement, whose national pledges were criticized for lacking transparent disclosure standards.
Its aim is to give investors, lenders and insurers the information they need to assess and price climate-related risks and opportunities.
It is described as the main framework used globally for climate disclosure in ESG.
Ahead of COP26 in 2021, the UK became the first G20 country to require 1,300 of its largest companies to disclose in line with it.
At COP26 the IFRS announced the International Sustainability Standards Board, into which the TCFD will converge.

entries.title: Creating shared value: profit from solving social problems

definition.text: A business strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations, improving its competitiveness and the conditions of its communities at once.

facts.text: Michael Porter and Mark Kramer introduced the idea in a 2006 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in a January 2011 follow-up.
Companies can create shared value in three ways: reconceiving products and markets, redefining productivity in the value chain, and enabling local cluster development.
Kramer says the main difference from corporate social responsibility is that CSR is about responsibility, while shared value is about creating value.
Accounting for ecological costs is hard: up to 90% of the ecological footprint in food processing comes from land management outside corporations' control.
Counting ecosystem services at the farm level lets shared value include positive environmental externalities in the economic system.
Reviewers found little rigorous analysis of its impact; most evidence comes from standalone case studies of mixed quality.
The Economist called the concept 'undercooked', and a common criticism is that it plays down the trade-offs businesses must make.
Critics have noted its 'striking resemblance' to Jed Emerson's earlier idea of blended value.

entries.title: Supply chain sustainability: greening every link

definition.text: Managing the environmental, social and economic effects of goods and services, and encouraging good governance, across their whole life cycle from suppliers to customers.

facts.text: Traditional supply chain goals were lower costs, just-in-time delivery and faster transport; rising environmental and social costs and consumer pressure added sustainability as a new measure.
Many firms can measure only their own operations, not their suppliers' and customers', which makes their true environmental and social costs hard to know.
Depending on industry and position, suppliers can account for most of a company's total emissions.
Buyers use their purchasing power to set standards for suppliers, treating sustainability like cost, quality and timeliness.
Tools include supplier scorecards, life-cycle assessments, surveys and rewards for suppliers that improve.
A 2017 study found suppliers farther upstream, away from the end user, had the most to gain financially from sustainable supply chain management.
After the COVID-19 disruptions, sustainable supply chains proved more resilient, with lower supplier risk.
A 2020 Boston Consulting Group survey found 70% of consumers willing to pay a 5% premium for more sustainably made products.

entries.title: CSR as misdirection: good deeds as a smokescreen

definition.text: The criticism that companies use social responsibility programs to draw attention away from harmful parts of their business.

facts.text: Unproven social claims and outright greenwashing have made consumers more cynical and distrustful.
The tobacco industry funded research in genetics, viruses and air pollution, which drew attention from the link between smoking and cancer.
US firms convicted of bribery got more lenient fines if they were seen to engage in CSR: a 20% rise in corporate giving went with a 40% lower fine.
A review of 700 sources found firms engage in CSR mainly for expected financial gain rather than a wish to serve society.

entries.title: The CSR-consumer paradox: saying green, buying cheap

definition.text: The gap between consumers saying they will buy only from responsible companies and what they actually buy.

facts.text: Many consumers want to buy from responsible firms, yet ethical purchases are a small share of household spending.
One explanation is the bystander effect: people act less when others seem not to care.
Another is that ethical products cost more but give the buyer little extra in return.
A Lisbon study found price, limited access and lack of education held back less engaged shoppers of sustainable fashion.

entries.title: Carroll's pyramid: four layers of corporate duty

definition.text: Archie Carroll's four-part framework of what society expects of business: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.

facts.text: Carroll began developing it after his 1979 Academy of Management Review article on corporate social performance.
It is often drawn as a pyramid of responsibilities: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic.

entries.title: The resource-based view: CSR as hard-to-copy advantage

definition.text: A way of judging the costs and benefits of CSR by asking whether it gives a firm a competitive advantage that rivals cannot copy.

facts.text: Barney (1990) held that lasting advantage needs resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable.
Reinhardt (1998) found a CSR-based strategy earns above-normal returns only if competitors cannot imitate it.
McWilliams and Siegel argued managers can set CSR spending through cost-benefit analysis like any other investment.
Waddock and Graves (1997) linked social and financial performance; McWilliams and Siegel (2000) said innovation, not CSR, drove the gains.

entries.contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether CSR itself or innovation explains the link between social and financial performance.

facts.text: They are corporate philanthropy, community volunteering, socially responsible business practices, cause promotion, cause-related marketing and corporate social marketing.

entries.title: Corporate environmental responsibility: a firm's duty to nature

definition.text: A company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment.

facts.text: The term comes from corporate social responsibility (CSR); CER deals strictly with environmental effects inside company strategy, while CSR leans toward social matters.
Protecting the environment used to be seen as the government's job, done through rules and penalties; the private sector has since taken on a shared responsibility.
Its main elements are using resources efficiently and limiting activities that would spoil resources for future generations.
Its main drivers are government policies and rules, backed by subsidies, tariffs and taxes, plus pressure from media, the public, shareholders and NGOs.
Obstacles include the cost of regulation, uncertain economic gains, expensive new technology and rules that differ from country to country.
It is unclear which emissions a firm answers for when they are spread across suppliers and outsourcing, or whether it should answer for past emissions made before the harm was known.
Stakeholders' growing awareness of how much harm business does to the environment has made it more institutionalized.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether firms must go beyond the law or should first make profits for shareholders, and on which emissions a firm is responsible for.

entries.title: How business responds to climate change

definition.text: What businesses do about climate change, from cutting their own emissions to trying to influence climate regulation such as the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: Business helps mitigation by investing in new energy technologies and energy efficiency.
Firms act to improve their image, align with owners, staff, suppliers and customers, cut costs and reduce exposure to costs they cannot control.
Energy efficiency often pays off only in the medium to long term while shareholders want short-term results, so regulation is often needed.
Many firms that once denied climate change, including major oil and car companies, changed position as scientific and political consensus grew.
By 2007 the Carbon Disclosure Project published emissions data for 2400 of the largest corporations, backed by investors with $41 trillion in assets.
Small and medium enterprises account for around 13% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Physical risks of climate change top the list of business concerns for US and EU firms.
A 2025 PwC report found 84% of companies keeping or speeding up their climate targets.

entries.title: Sustainable sourcing: buying responsibly from the start

definition.text: Obtaining the materials, products and services a company needs from suppliers in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound.

facts.text: Global supply chains and pressure to cut costs have harmed environments and communities, especially in developing nations, and awareness has grown since the 1990s.
A company is understood to be only as sustainable as the start of its supply chain.
Supply chains harm nature mainly through resource depletion and pollution, leading to biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and soil degradation.
Firms put it into practice through supplier codes of conduct, supplier selection and assessment, and supplier development.
It grew out of corporate social responsibility, which took on environmental duties in the 1990s with Elkington's triple bottom line.
Responsible sourcing means complying with ethical rules such as no child labour; sustainable sourcing goes further and acts to improve conditions.
The growing number of standards has raised costs for producers and caused confusion over their meaning and legitimacy.
It relates directly to Sustainable Development Goal 12, responsible consumption and production.

entries.title: Scope 3: the emissions a company does not make itself

definition.text: The indirect greenhouse gas emissions in a company's value chain, such as those of its suppliers and from the use of its products.

facts.text: Scope 1 covers a firm's direct emissions from its own facilities, and Scope 2 the emissions from energy it buys.
Scope 3 emissions are especially hard to estimate.
In 2020, 81% of S&P 500 companies reported Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requires large and listed firms to disclose material Scope 3 emissions, starting with 2025 reports on 2024 data.
The US SEC's 2024 rule requires Scope 3 reporting if emissions are material or part of corporate targets, though the regulator has signalled it may change this.
In 2021, 61% of Chevron shareholders backed a resolution asking it to cut emissions including Scope 3.

entries.title: Science-based targets: emission cuts that match the climate goal

definition.text: Company targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions that are set in line with climate science and the Paris Agreement goals.

facts.text: The Science Based Targets initiative, set up in 2015, helps companies set such targets and validates them.
As of 2025, over 10,000 companies had set or committed to setting targets validated by the SBTi.
In October 2021 the SBTi launched the first net zero standard, for targets consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 °C.
Best practice includes transition plans covering scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, short-term milestones, board oversight and executive pay linked to milestones.
The SBTi says residual emissions in most sectors should fall below 10% of an organization's baseline by 2050.
A 2024 plan to let companies use environmental attribute certificates against Scope 3 targets drew protest from SBTi staff, who argued offsets are incompatible with the Paris Agreement.

entries.contested_note: Whether companies may count carbon offsets or certificates toward science-based targets is disputed, including within the SBTi.

entries.title: Does going green pay? The evidence is split

definition.text: The debate over whether a company's environmental and social efforts raise or lower its profits.

facts.text: A positive link between environmental performance and economic performance has been reported.
A 2026 study of Indian firms found that steady improvement in environmental performance went with better financial results.
A 2023 study of European listed firms found the opposite of a 'win-win': stronger sustainability practices went with lower profitability, at least for a time.
Studies link sustainability practices to financial success and customer satisfaction, but mostly at larger firms with more money to spend on them.
Gains can include attracting staff, tax breaks and new markets.

entries.contested_note: Some studies find sustainability raises financial performance while a 2023 study of European firms found it lowered profitability.
entries.text: Do a company's environmental and social efforts raise its profits or lower them? The evidence points both ways. A positive link between environmental performance and economic performance has been reported. A 2026 study of Indian firms found that steady improvement in environmental performance went with better financial results. Other studies link sustainability practices to financial success and customer satisfaction. Gains can include attracting staff, tax breaks and new markets. There is a catch. Those positive links show up mostly at larger firms, which have more money to spend on such efforts. And not every study finds a win-win. A 2023 study of European listed firms found the opposite: stronger sustainability practices went with lower profitability, at least for a time. So the question remains open. The answer may depend on the firm, its size and how long one waits for results. For {{ref:nature-gov-059}}, that uncertainty matters, because the case for change often rests on the promise that it will pay.

entries.title: Insetting: meeting targets without cutting your own emissions
entries.article: Science Based Targets initiative#Carbon offsets controversy

definition.text: A business-coined way for a company to claim it has met emission targets by means other than cutting its own emissions.

facts.text: The SBTi's forestry, land and agriculture guidance of September 2022 allows insetting, breaking with its long-held view that targets be met only by emission cuts.
The term was created by the private sector and is not defined in international standards such as ISO 14050 or the IWA 42 Net Zero Guidelines.

entries.title: Eco-efficiency and socio-efficiency: value per unit of impact

definition.text: Eco-efficiency compares the economic value a firm adds with its total ecological impact; socio-efficiency compares that value with the firm's social impact.

facts.text: Most corporate effects on the environment are assumed to be negative, while social effects can be positive, such as job creation, or negative, such as work accidents.
Both measures mainly aim at economic sustainability, treating natural and social capital as tools for win-win gains.
Some authors argue sustainable development instead needs eco-effectiveness, socio-effectiveness, sufficiency and eco-equity.

entries.title: Do no significant harm: green in one way, harmful in none

definition.text: The rule that an activity counts as sustainable under the EU taxonomy only if it contributes substantially to one environmental objective without seriously harming any of the other five.

facts.text: An activity must meet four requirements: a substantial contribution to one objective, no significant harm to the others, minimum social safeguards, and the technical screening criteria.
The Technical Expert Group held back from including nuclear energy because it could not settle whether nuclear met this principle.

entries.title: Gas and nuclear: the EU taxonomy's hardest fight

definition.text: The dispute over whether fossil gas and nuclear power should be labelled as environmentally sustainable investments under the EU taxonomy.

facts.text: The Complementary Climate Delegated Act, the most controversial one, listed certain gas and nuclear activities as transitional activities that help mitigate climate change.
Expert advice split: the Technical Expert Group did not recommend including nuclear, while the Joint Research Centre found its impact would stay below harmful levels.
Some countries see gas as a bridge from coal to renewables, while the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Denmark opposed including it.
On 6 July 2022 a resolution to reject the act failed in the European Parliament: 278 MEPs backed it when 353 votes were needed.

facts.text: Its aim is to improve both environmental and economic performance through better use of materials and energy.
Developed in Germany in the 1980s, it became very successful in Japan, where up to 300 companies had used it by 2010.
In 2011 the International Organization for Standardization published a standard for it, ISO 14051.

definition.text: Visits to supplier sites to check that they meet social and environmental standards.

facts.text: Audits can certify a supplier against an outside standard such as SA8000 or ISO 14001, or against a buyer's own supplier code of conduct.

entries.title: Stockholm 1972: the world's first environment summit
entries.article: United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, was the first global conference on environmental issues.

facts.text: Sweden proposed the idea to the UN Economic and Social Council in 1968, and preparations took four years, involved 114 governments and cost over $30,000,000.
The conference created the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi.
It agreed a Declaration of 26 principles on environment and development, an Action Plan of 109 recommendations, and a Resolution.
Divisions between rich and poor countries surfaced; developing countries made up 70 of the 122 countries attending, while the Soviet bloc boycotted it.
Indira Gandhi's speech linked ecological management with relieving poverty, which became one of the conference's central themes.
It spurred countries to monitor their environments and set up environment ministries and agencies.
The 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the 2002 Johannesburg summit and Rio+20 in 2012 all took the Stockholm declaration as their starting point.

entries.title: Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties

definition.text: The Earth Summit was the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992.

facts.text: It was attended by 108 heads of state and government and helped establish and spread the idea of sustainable development.
A key achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the summit.
It produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, which 178 governments voted to adopt, and set up the Commission on Sustainable Development to oversee them.
It helped spread key treaty principles: the precautionary principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, and the polluter pays principle.
Critics note that many Rio agreements, on fighting poverty and cleaning up the environment, were never realized, and some leaders called it green imperialism by the global North.

entries.text: In June 1992, 108 heads of state and government gathered in Rio de Janeiro. The Earth Summit, formally the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, ran from 3 to 14 June. It built directly on {{ref:nature-hist-002}} twenty years earlier, and it did more than any meeting before it to spread the idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Its biggest achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature there too. The summit also produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, a plan of action. In all, 178 governments voted to adopt them, and a Commission on Sustainable Development was set up to oversee them. Rio helped spread three principles that run through later treaties. The precautionary principle says to act against serious threats even before the science is complete. Common but differentiated responsibilities means all countries share the duty but not equally. The polluter pays principle puts the cost of pollution on whoever causes it. Not everyone was impressed. Critics note that many Rio promises on poverty and cleanup were never kept, and some leaders called the whole effort green imperialism by the global North.
