entries.title: Classical economics: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus and Mill

definition.text: Classical economics is the school of economic thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, led by Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill.

facts.text: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations of 1776 is usually taken to mark its beginning.
The classical economists saw markets as largely self-regulating systems, a view captured by Smith's metaphor of the invisible hand.
Smith held that a nation's wealth is its yearly income, produced by labour, land and capital and shared out as wages, rent and profits.
They favoured free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists, and Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage.
John Stuart Mill believed a future 'stationary state' with constant population and capital was inevitable and desirable, an idea now called a steady-state economy.
From the 1870s it gave way to neoclassical economics, though many of its ideas remain fundamental.
Thomas Carlyle nicknamed it 'the dismal science', a jibe often linked to Malthus's gloomy analysis.

entries.text: In 1776 Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations, and a new way of thinking about the economy began. Classical economics is the school of thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century. Its leaders were Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill. These thinkers founded {{ref:nature-found-044}} as we know it. They saw markets as largely self-regulating, a view summed up in Smith's image of the {{ref:nature-econ-387}}. For Smith, a nation's wealth was its yearly income. Labor, land and capital produced it, and it was shared out as wages, rent and profits. Land, in other words, sat at the heart of the system. The classical economists favored free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists. Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage: each country does best by specializing in what it gives up least to produce. Mill went further than the others in a direction that sounds modern. entries.title: Our Common Future: defining sustainable development

definition.text: Our Common Future, or the Brundtland Report, is the 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development that set out the best-known definition of sustainable development.

facts.text: It defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It treated environment and development as one single issue and stressed the interlocking economic, environmental and social sides of human development.
It held that poverty worsens environmental pressure, and recognized that environmental limits to economic growth exist.
The report came out of a 900-day worldwide exercise of public hearings and expert testimony, chaired by former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.
It laid the groundwork for the 1992 Earth Summit, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration.
In 1988 Helge Ole Bergesen wrote that Third World elites saw the report as green imperialism.

entries.title: The conservation movement: saving resources for later

definition.text: The conservation movement is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect natural resources, wild species and their habitats for the future.

facts.text: It grew from the practical need to keep up fisheries, wildlife, water, soil and forests.
It is often traced to John Evelyn's Sylva of 1662, which urged England to manage the rate of tree felling and replant cut trees.
Its 19th-century ethic held that human activity harms the environment, that there is a civic duty to keep it for future generations, and that science should guide that duty.
The first practical use of scientific conservation was in the forests of India in the mid-19th century.
It has broadened from sustainable yields of resources and wilderness preservation to the preservation of biodiversity.
Scholars note that early conservation often protected game for elite white hunters while policing hunting by Indigenous and poor people.

entries.title: Silent Spring: the book that turned the US against DDT

definition.text: Silent Spring is Rachel Carson's 1962 environmental science book documenting the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT.

facts.text: Carson argued that pesticides harm the wider environment and should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests.
She accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question.

Despite fierce opposition from chemical companies, it shifted public opinion, reversed US pesticide policy, led to a national ban on DDT for farm use, and fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency.
It became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the beginning of the contemporary deep ecology movement.
One scholar said that after it, no one could sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress so easily.
Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT restrictions; scientists and journalists have dismissed this claim as a myth.

In Silent Spring, her 1962 book, she argued that these chemicals should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests. The book documented the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT and its spread through the wider environment as Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill. Carson accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question. Chemical companies fought back hard. They lost the argument with the public. Silent Spring shifted opinion, reversed US pesticide policy and led to a national ban on DDT for farm use. It also fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency. The book became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the start of the deep ecology movement. As one scholar put it, after Carson no one could so easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress. A dispute still clings to it. Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT was restricted. Scientists and journalists have dismissed that claim as a myth, but it has not gone away.

entries.title: Rio+20: the summit that called for new global goals
entries.article: United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development

definition.text: Rio+20, the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, was a 2012 summit in Rio de Janeiro that sought to reconcile the world's economic and environmental goals.

facts.text: Held from 13 to 22 June 2012, it marked 20 years since the 1992 Earth Summit in the same city.
Its two main themes were building a green economy that lifts people out of poverty, and an institutional framework for sustainable development.
Its 49-page nonbinding outcome document, 'The Future We Want', called for the Sustainable Development Goals, a set of measurable targets.
Nations agreed to explore alternatives to GDP that count environmental and social factors, such as nature's carbon storage and habitat protection.
All nations reaffirmed commitments to phase out fossil fuel subsidies.
It popularised the term blue economy and saw the launch of the Inclusive Wealth Report.
Leaders such as Obama, Merkel and Cameron stayed away, which was read as a sign that sustainability was not their priority.

entries.title: The Club of Rome and The Limits to Growth

definition.text: An informal non-profit group of intellectuals and business leaders, founded in Rome in 1968, that critically discusses pressing global problems.

facts.text: Italian industrialist Aurelio Peccei and British scientist Alexander King founded it, sharing doubts that development and technological progress could solve the world's problems.

Its first report, The Limits to Growth (1972), used computer simulations suggesting that growth in production and consumption could not continue indefinitely because of resource depletion or pollution.
The report sold 30 million copies in more than 30 languages, making it the best-selling environmental book in history.
Its questioning of growth provoked hostile reactions at the OECD, which set its course on unfettered growth.
Economist Robert Solow called The Limits to Growth scenarios 'simplistic'; a 1973 Sussex University study, Models of Doom, found its forecasts hinged on a few unduly pessimistic assumptions.
In 2009 Solow allowed that rapid growth in India and China might make real demands on natural resources dramatically different.
As of 2025 there had been 55 reports to the club; its Earth4All initiative published 'Earth for All' in 2022, naming five pathways: energy, food, poverty, inequality and population.

entries.contested_note: Critics such as Robert Solow and the Sussex Models of Doom team judged the club's world modelling simplistic and too pessimistic.

entries.title: Earth Day: a teach-in that became a global event

definition.text: Earth Day is an annual event held on April 22 to show support for environmental protection, first held in 1970.

facts.text: US Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in for April 22, 1970, and hired the young activist Denis Hayes to coordinate it.
Nelson was moved to act after the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, which released over 3 million US gallons of oil and killed more than 10,000 seabirds and sea mammals.
The 1970s that followed brought major US environmental laws such as the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act, the creation of the EPA, and bans on DDT and leaded gasoline.
In 1990 it went global, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries and helping pave the way for the 1992 Earth Summit.
The Paris Agreement was signed on Earth Day 2016 by leaders of 175 nations.
Nelson summed up the movement's view: 'The economy is a wholly owned subsidiary of the environment, not the other way around.'

entries.title: Physiocracy: when wealth came only from the land

definition.text: Physiocracy, from the Greek for 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French economic theory holding that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land and farming.

facts.text: It was one of the first well-developed theories of economics, led by François Quesnay, the Marquis de Mirabeau and Turgot, just before Adam Smith's classical economics.
The physiocrats saw productive work as the source of national wealth, unlike the mercantilists who focused on the ruler's gold or the balance of trade.
Only farm labour created value in their view; industry and other work were 'unproductive appendages' to agriculture.
They believed in a 'natural order' and in laissez-faire, the idea that self-interest and free trade, not state restriction, make the economy work.
Turgot was among the first to see diminishing returns: adding more of an input raises output at a falling rate, so wealth cannot grow without limit.
Their ideas influenced Smith, Ricardo and Mill, and Henry George's proposal to fund government by taxing land values.

entries.title: TEEB: putting a price on the loss of nature
entries.article: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity

definition.text: TEEB was an international study, led by Pavan Sukhdev from 2007 to 2011, that set out to show the global economic benefits of biodiversity and the rising cost of losing it.

facts.text: Germany and the European Commission launched TEEB in 2007, answering a proposal by G8+5 environment ministers meeting in Potsdam for a global study of the economics of biodiversity loss.
Its 2008 interim report focused largely on forests and put the loss of natural capital from deforestation and degradation at US$2–4.5 trillion per year.
It estimated that investing US$45 billion a year in protected areas alone could secure ecosystem services worth some US$5 trillion a year.
Phase II was presented in October 2010 at the 10th Conference of the Parties of the Convention on Biological Diversity in Nagoya, Japan.
A central aim was an economic yardstick better than GDP, and national accounts broad enough to measure the welfare benefits ecosystems provide.
TEEB reported that ecosystem service values run from about $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to over $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Critics argue that basing nature's value on human preferences cannot tell us what is ecologically essential to keep life-support systems working.

entries.contested_note: Critics dispute whether valuing ecosystems by human preferences, as TEEB does, can guide what nature must be protected.

entries.title: Johannesburg 2002: Rio+10 and its partnerships

definition.text: The World Summit on Sustainable Development, nicknamed Rio+10, was held in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002.

facts.text: There, sustainable development was recognized as an overarching goal for national, regional and international institutions.
Instead of new treaties it produced almost 300 'partnership initiatives' meant to help reach the Millennium Development Goals, plus the Johannesburg Declaration.
US President George W. Bush boycotted the summit, which left it partly impotent.

entries.title: Small Is Beautiful: economics as if people mattered

definition.text: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered is a 1973 essay collection by the economist E. F. Schumacher that criticizes mainstream economics for ignoring nature's limits.

facts.text: Schumacher argued that the modern economy is unsustainable because it treats natural resources such as fossil fuels as spendable income rather than as capital that will run out.
He added that nature's ability to absorb pollution is also limited.
His philosophy of 'enoughness' grew from his study of village economies, which he called Buddhist economics.
The title came from his teacher Leopold Kohr's case for small, appropriate technologies over 'bigger is better'; the book inspired the appropriate technology movement.
The 1973 energy crisis helped it reach a wide audience, and in 1995 it was ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II.

entries.title: A Sand County Almanac and the land ethic

definition.text: A Sand County Almanac is a 1949 book of essays by the American ecologist and forester Aldo Leopold that argues for a 'land ethic', a responsible relationship between people and the land.

facts.text: Leopold's land ethic holds that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community, and wrong when it does not.
Leopold argued that land is not a commodity to be owned, and objected that policy makers always need an economic motive before they will conserve.
The essay 'Thinking Like a Mountain' describes, in plain words, how killing top predators such as wolves ripples through the rest of the ecosystem.
Little noticed at first, it became a surprise bestseller in the 1970s; over two million copies have been printed.
A 1990 poll of the American Nature Study Society ranked it with Silent Spring as the two most significant environmental books of the 20th century.

entries.title: Malthus and the race between people and food
entries.article: An Essay on the Principle of Population

definition.text: An Essay on the Principle of Population is Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 book arguing that population tends to grow until it outruns the supply of food and other basic resources.

facts.text: Malthus argued that population expands in times of plenty until it becomes too large for the more modest supply of primary resources, causing distress.
He named two checks that hold population within resource limits: preventive checks that lower births, such as delayed marriage, and positive checks that raise deaths, such as hunger, disease and war.
He linked population to wages: when workers multiply faster than food output, food costs rise and real wages fall, which in turn slows population growth.
Darwin and Wallace both credited Malthus with helping them develop the theory of natural selection.
Critics such as Julian Simon note that huge 20th-century population growth did not bring a Malthusian catastrophe, thanks to better farming, machinery, high-yield crops and pesticides.
Later works such as The Population Bomb and The Limits to Growth have been called Malthusian.

entries.contested_note: Whether Malthus's limits on population hold is disputed: critics point out that food output kept pace with 20th-century population growth.

Positive checks raise deaths, through hunger, disease and war. Malthus also tied population to wages: as workers multiply faster than food, food costs rise, real wages fall, and growth slows. Darwin and Wallace both credited him with helping them see natural selection. Whether his limits hold is disputed. Critics such as Julian Simon point out that huge 20th-century population growth brought no catastrophe, thanks to better farming.

entries.title: The Population Bomb: a famine forecast that missed

definition.text: The Population Bomb is a 1968 book by Paul and Anne Ehrlich that predicted worldwide famines from overpopulation and called for immediate limits on population growth.

facts.text: Its opening claimed that in the 1970s hundreds of millions would starve to death whatever was done.
Critics call it a restatement of Malthus's argument that population will outgrow farm output unless controlled.
Instead, the global death rate kept falling, from 13 per 1000 in 1965–74 to 10 per 1000 in 1985–90, while calories per person rose 24%.
Julian Simon and Hans Rosling argued its forecasts wrongly assumed exponential growth would continue with no technological or social progress.
Barry Commoner argued that helping poor people grow richer would lower birth rates on its own, making coercive population policies unnecessary.
The Ehrlichs stand by its core claim that population growth is a major problem and say it brought human numbers into environmental debate.

entries.contested_note: Critics say its famine predictions failed and its thesis was wrong, while the authors and some supporters hold its core warning was prescient.

entries.title: The Stockholm Declaration's 26 principles
entries.article: Declaration of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The Stockholm Declaration of 1972 was the first United Nations declaration on the global environment, a set of 26 principles agreed at the Stockholm Conference.

facts.text: Its first principle says people have a right to an environment of a quality that allows a life of dignity and well-being, and a duty to protect it for present and future generations.
It says Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be maintained and, where practicable, restored.
Principle 21, its legal core, gives states sovereign rights over their own territory along with a responsibility not to harm others across borders.
Developing countries argued that rich nations used most resources and caused most pollution, so the Global North should bear most of the responsibility.
Indira Gandhi's line that 'poverty is the worst form of pollution' framed a North–South divide that lasted for decades.
It is not legally binding; it counts as soft law, and critics called much of it too vague for legal use.
It shaped later treaties, and the 1992 Rio Declaration adopted a modified Principle 21.

entries.title: Mercantilism: the race to hoard gold

definition.text: Mercantilism is a nationalist economic policy that aims to maximize a country's exports and minimize its imports.

facts.text: Mercantilists held that money and precious metals were the only true riches, so tariffs should encourage exports and discourage imports.
They believed international trade could not benefit all countries at once.
It dominated modernizing Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries; Adam Smith vigorously opposed it and argued for free trade.

Its followers believed trade could not benefit all countries at once: one nation's gain was another's loss. It dominated modernizing Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries. Adam Smith vigorously opposed it and argued for free trade.

entries.title: From philosophy to economics: a short history

definition.text: The history of economic thought is the study of the thinkers and theories behind political economy and economics, from the ancient world to today.

facts.text: In the West, economics was part of philosophy rather than a separate discipline until the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Mercantilism dominated Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, until the physiocrats and then Adam Smith's classical economics challenged it.
Neoclassical economics developed in the 1870s in three independent schools: the Cambridge, Austrian and Lausanne schools.
In 1920 Arthur Cecil Pigou argued that markets fail when there are externalities, so the state must step in.
In the 1930s economists began modelling how to manage non-renewable resources and whether welfare can be sustained in an economy that uses them up.
Malthus on overpopulation and Mill on the stationary state anticipated the concerns of ecological economics, founded in the work of Boulding, Georgescu-Roegen and Daly.

entries.text: Until the Industrial Revolution, economics in the West was a branch of philosophy rather than a subject of its own. The history of economic thought studies its thinkers and theories. {{ref:nature-hist-022}} dominated Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, until the physiocrats and then Adam Smith challenged it. In 1920 {{ref:nature-hist-038}} argued that markets fail when there are side effects on others, so the state must step in. In the 1930s economists began modeling how to manage resources that run out. entries.title: Natural price: the classical theory of value

definition.text: The classical theory of value explained prices by a 'natural price' set by lasting forces, toward which day-to-day market prices tend to move.

facts.text: William Petty first separated the market price, pushed about by passing influences, from the natural price.
Smith said market prices are drawn toward natural prices, somewhat like gravity.
For Smith the natural price was the sum of the natural rates of wages, profits and rent.
Petty held a land-and-labour theory of value, while the labour theory of value later clashed with Ricardo's comparative advantage.

entries.contested_note: The theory of value, and how classical economics relates to neoclassical economics, are still debated.

entries.title: Quesnay's Tableau économique: the economy as a body

definition.text: The Tableau économique is an economic model François Quesnay described in 1759 that traced how production and money flow between social classes.

facts.text: It had three classes: landowners, farm workers as the 'productive' class, and artisans and merchants as the 'sterile' class.
Quesnay, a physician, likened the circulation of wealth to the circulation of blood in the body.
It holds the origins of modern ideas about the circulation of wealth and how the parts of an economy depend on one another.

entries.title: The Dasgupta Review: we are living on 1.6 Earths

definition.text: A 2021 report on the economics of biodiversity, led by economist Partha Dasgupta and commissioned by the UK government.

facts.text: Commissioned by the British Treasury and published in February 2021, it found that biodiversity is declining faster than at any time in human history.
It argued that human demands far exceed nature's capacity to supply the goods and services we rely on, and that current living standards would need 1.6 Earths.
It called for changes akin to or greater than the Marshall Plan, including abandoning GDP as the measure of economic success and social progress.
In June 2021 the UK government committed to a nature-positive future in response to its findings.
The review advocated natural capital thinking; ecological economist Clive Spash published critical deconstructions of it.

entries.title: The Economics of Welfare: Pigou's tax on harm

definition.text: The Economics of Welfare is Arthur Cecil Pigou's 1920 book that introduced the idea of the externality and proposed correcting it with a tax.

facts.text: Pigou built on Alfred Marshall's idea of an externality: a cost or benefit falling on others that the person causing it does not account for.
It first planted the idea that governments should tax activities that put uncompensated costs on others, now called a Pigouvian tax.
Pigou applied the reasoning to traffic congestion, an early case of what became congestion pricing.
It argued that markets are inefficient when externalities exist, so the state must intervene.

entries.title: Conservation Reconsidered: valuing what we never use

definition.text: Conservation Reconsidered is John V. Krutilla's 1967 paper describing the economic value of undisturbed natural places such as rivers and forests.

facts.text: In it Krutilla introduced existence value, the value people get from the mere existence of something such as unspoiled wilderness or a species, even if they never use it.
This idea of 'nonuse value' made Krutilla a pioneer of environmental economics.

entries.title: Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing

definition.text: Herman Daly (1938–2022) was an American ecological economist, best known as a senior economist at the World Bank and for the idea of a steady-state economy.

facts.text: As Senior Economist in the World Bank's Environment Department he helped draft policy guidelines on sustainable development.
He co-founded the journal Ecological Economics and served as an associate editor.
His 1973 anthology Toward a Steady-State Economy gathered writers such as Georgescu-Roegen, Boulding and Hardin, and was revised in 1980 and 1993.
In 1989 he and John B. Cobb proposed the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare as a better measure of progress than GDP.
He is widely credited with originating the idea of uneconomic growth, though some credit Marilyn Waring.
He drew on his professor Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen's view linking the economy to the entropy law.
In 1996 he received the Right Livelihood Award for defining a path of ecological economics joining ethics, quality of life, environment and community.

entries.title: Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons

definition.text: Elinor Ostrom (1933–2012) was an American political scientist and political economist who showed how communities can manage shared resources themselves.

facts.text: Against the predictions of the tragedy of the commons, her field studies showed users of pastures, fisheries and forests making their own rules to manage them sustainably.
In Governing the Commons (1990) she summarized eight design principles shared by long-lasting common-pool resource institutions.
She favoured a polycentric approach, with key management decisions made as close as possible to the places and people involved, rather than a single global authority.
With co-researchers she built the Social-Ecological Systems (SES) framework for studying common-pool resources and self-governance.
In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Oliver E. Williamson.
The Nobel citation said her work showed common resources can be managed successfully without government regulation or privatization.
"Ostrom's law" sums up her challenge to theory: a resource arrangement that works in practice can work in theory.

entries.title: Ronald Coase and the problem of social cost

definition.text: Ronald Coase (1910–2013) was a British economist whose work on transaction costs and property rights reshaped how economists think about externalities.

facts.text: His 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost" argued that it is unclear where the blame for an externality lies.
His example was a rancher whose cattle stray onto a neighbour's crops: restraining the cattle harms the rancher just as unrestrained cattle harm the farmer.
He argued that without transaction costs, the initial assignment of property rights does not affect whether the efficient outcome is reached.
The Coase theorem says that with tradeable externalities and low enough transaction costs, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome whatever the starting allocation of property.
In practice, obstacles to bargaining or poorly defined property rights can block Coasean bargaining.
His analysis challenged Pigou's: he argued taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain.
His 1937 essay "The Nature of the Firm" explained firms as a way of avoiding the transaction costs of using the market.

entries.title: Garrett Hardin and the tragedy of the commons

definition.text: Garrett Hardin (1915–2003) was an American ecologist and microbiologist, best known for his 1968 paper "The Tragedy of the Commons".

facts.text: His 1968 Science paper drew attention to the damage that innocent individual actions can do to the environment.
The essay drew on an 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd about herders overgrazing a shared parcel of land.
He applied the model to population growth, natural resource use and the welfare state, writing that freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
Critics said he ignored the demographic transition and confused common property with open-access resources, and Elinor Ostrom's work contradicted his pessimism.
His First Law of Human Ecology holds that we can never do just one thing, since any intrusion into nature has many unpredictable effects.
His hardline positions on immigration, race and eugenics have led several sources to label him a white nationalist.

entries.contested_note: His tragedy-of-the-commons argument is disputed by critics and contradicted by Ostrom's field studies of successful commons.

entries.title: William Stanley Jevons and the coal question

definition.text: William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882) was an English economist and logician, a leader of the marginal revolution and author of The Coal Question.

facts.text: In The Coal Question (1865) he drew attention to the gradual exhaustion of Britain's coal supplies.
He argued that improving energy efficiency lowers energy costs and so increases rather than decreases energy use, now called the Jevons paradox.
His Theory of Political Economy (1871) set out a theory of value based on marginal utility, developed independently of Menger and Walras.
Joan Martinez Alier traces the 'gospel of eco-efficiency' to the 19th-century writings of Malthus and Jevons.
His energy-depletion arguments have been revisited by writers on peak oil.

Writers on peak oil have revisited his arguments about energy running out.

entries.title: Robert Costanza and the $33 trillion valuation

definition.text: Robert Costanza (born 1950) is an American/Australian ecological economist at University College London's Institute for Global Prosperity.

facts.text: He co-founded the International Society for Ecological Economics, was its first president, and was founding chief editor of its journal Ecological Economics from 1989 to 2002.
In 1997 he led an attempted valuation of the global ecosystem, published in Nature.
The study put the value of ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, within a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when global GDP was $27 trillion.
Half of that value came from nutrient cycling.
His work lumped ecosystem goods and services together as ecosystem services, unlike Gretchen Daily's original definition.
He studied under H.T. Odum and directed the Gund Institute for Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont.

entries.title: Arthur Cecil Pigou, father of the pollution tax

definition.text: Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959) was an English economist, best known for the idea of taxing activities that cause negative externalities.

facts.text: In The Economics of Welfare (1920) he introduced the externality concept and the idea that a tax could correct externality problems, now called a Pigouvian tax.
He argued that harmful side effects should be offset by a tax and beneficial ones by a subsidy.
He studied under Alfred Marshall and succeeded him as Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge in 1908.
In the early 1960s Ronald Coase criticised his analysis, arguing that taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain.
The externality concept remains central to welfare economics and especially to environmental economics.
The Pigou Club, named after him, groups modern economists who back a carbon tax against climate change.

entries.title: Georgescu-Roegen: entropy and the economic process

definition.text: Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (1906–1994) was a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist whose work on entropy and natural resources helped found ecological economics.

facts.text: His 1971 book The Entropy Law and the Economic Process argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used in economic activity.
He described the economy as turning valuable low-entropy resources into worthless high-entropy waste and pollution, which is why resources are scarce.
He argued Earth's carrying capacity will shrink as its finite mineral stock is used up, leading the world economy towards eventual collapse.
By bringing resource flows into economic models, his work was decisive in establishing ecological economics as a separate sub-discipline in the 1980s.
He taught Herman Daly, but later criticised his student's steady-state economy in several articles.
The degrowth movement of the early 2000s treats him as its main intellectual influence.
Mistakes from his incomplete grasp of thermodynamics have caused controversy among physicists and ecological economists.

entries.contested_note: His application of thermodynamics to economics contains mistakes that physicists and ecological economists have argued over.

entries.title: William Nordhaus and the economics of climate

definition.text: William Nordhaus (1941–2026) was an American economist at Yale, best known for economic modelling of climate change.

facts.text: He shared the 2018 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Paul Romer, for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis.
He developed the DICE and RICE integrated assessment models linking economics, energy use and climate change.
His model is used to examine the effects of climate policies such as carbon taxes.
He was an early advocate of carbon taxes or other ways of pricing carbon dioxide emissions.
In 1972, with James Tobin, he introduced the Measure of Economic Welfare as a first attempt at environmental accounting.
In 2007 he criticised the Stern Review for using a low discount rate.
Critics fault DICE's discounting, its damage function and its handling of low-probability, high-consequence 'fat tail' outcomes, and some objected to his low carbon tax levels.

entries.contested_note: Economists and climate scientists dispute his model's discounting, damage function and low recommended carbon taxes.

entries.title: Harold Hotelling and the price of running out

definition.text: Harold Hotelling (1895–1973) was an American mathematical statistician and economic theorist, known for Hotelling's law, Hotelling's lemma and Hotelling's rule.

facts.text: His 1931 analysis of non-renewable resource management in the Journal of Political Economy produced Hotelling's rule.
Hotelling's rule, a price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels, is one of the best-known early works on the economics of exhaustible resources.
He pioneered the study of non-convexities, which are linked to market failures and arise with environmental goods and other externalities.
He became an early advocate of congestion pricing, a toll meant to change behaviour rather than recoup investment costs.
His 1929 article founded spatial economics, treating space as a field where competitors jostle to be nearest their customers.
He argued in 1938 that selling at marginal cost is a condition of maximum general welfare.

entries.title: Howard T. Odum: ecosystems as electric circuits

definition.text: Howard T. Odum (1924–2002) was an American ecologist known for pioneering ecosystem ecology and for linking ecological energy flows to economics.

facts.text: He modelled the energy flow pathways of ecosystems with analogue electrical circuits, one of the earliest instances of systems ecology.
While directing the University of Texas Marine Institute (1956–1963) he funded research using conventional economics to put dollar values on ecological resources.
He coined the term ecological engineering in 1962.
In the 1990s he and David Scienceman developed emergy, a measure of energy used in the past; the idea remains controversial and little recognised.
He took part in the 1982 meeting in Sweden that helped launch ecological economics, alongside Robert Costanza and Herman Daly.

entries.title: C. S. Holling and the idea of resilience

definition.text: C. S. 'Buzz' Holling (1930–2019) was a Canadian ecologist and one of the conceptual founders of ecological economics.

facts.text: He introduced ideas including resilience, adaptive management, the adaptive cycle and panarchy.
His 1973 paper on the resilience of ecological systems had a large impact across natural and social sciences.
In his usage, resilience is an ecosystem's resistance to shifting into another state.
He was among the first ecologists to recognise the importance of nonlinear dynamics.
He founded the Resilience Alliance and the journal Conservation Ecology, now Ecology and Society.

entries.title: William Rees and the ecological footprint

definition.text: William E. Rees is a Canadian human ecologist and ecological economist, best known for co-developing the ecological footprint with his graduate students.

facts.text: The ecological footprint estimates humanity's demand on nature through measurable flows of energy and materials to and from ecosystems.
He coined the term in 1990, replacing 'regional capsule' in a manuscript after a colleague's remark about his computer's small desk footprint.
He describes ecological overshoot as human demand on ecosystems exceeding Earth's capacity to regenerate and absorb wastes, beyond long-term global carrying capacity.
He criticises mainstream economics for treating nature as an externality and assuming perfect substitutability between manufactured and natural capital.
He argues growing economies remain dependent subsystems of the ecosphere, so growth is ultimately limited by its finite capacity.
Neoclassical economists and ecomodernists have pushed back against his theories.

entries.title: E. F. Schumacher, who named natural capital

definition.text: E. F. Schumacher (1911–1977) was a German-born British economist best known for proposing human-scale, decentralised and appropriate technologies.

facts.text: He first coined the term 'natural capital', in his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful.
Small Is Beautiful argues that production cannot be called solved if it recklessly erodes finite natural capital and robs future generations of its benefits.
He coined 'Buddhist economics' in 1955 while working as an economic consultant in Burma, holding that people need good work to develop properly.
He pioneered appropriate technology, meaning user-friendly, ecologically suitable technology scaled to the community, and founded the Intermediate Technology Development Group in 1966.
As chief economic adviser to the National Coal Board from 1950 to 1970 he saw oil as a finite resource and feared its depletion.
Key ideas of ecological economics appear in his writings and in Kenneth Boulding's.

entries.title: Joan Martinez Alier and the environmentalism of the poor

definition.text: Joan Martinez Alier (born 1939) is a Spanish economist whose work in ecological economics and political ecology is summed up in the idea of the environmentalism of the poor.

facts.text: He argues, against neoclassical economists, that the economy is not circular but entropic: energy is not recycled and materials only partly so.
With Martin O'Connor he introduced ecological distribution conflicts in 1995 as a concept for documenting and analysing environmental conflicts.
He describes the environmentalism of the poor as the struggles poor people wage when ecological distribution conflicts threaten them.
He is a founding member and past president of the International Society for Ecological Economics.
He won the 2023 Holberg Prize for research in ecological economics, political ecology and environmental justice.

entries.title: Nicholas Stern and the greatest market failure
entries.article: Nicholas Stern, Baron Stern of Brentford

definition.text: Nicholas Stern (born 1946) is a British economist, banker and academic who led the Stern Review on the economics of climate change.

facts.text: The Stern Review, produced by his team at HM Treasury, was released in October 2006.
The Review described climate change as an externality, and Stern later called it the greatest market failure the world has seen.
It recommended regulation, carbon taxes, carbon trading, pollution permits and property rights, and urged immediate emission cuts at a significant but manageable cost.
Economists reacted in mixed ways; some called the Review deeply flawed, while others found its conclusions reasonable even if its method was wrong.
He chairs the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics.

entries.contested_note: Economists disagreed over the Stern Review, some calling it deeply flawed and others defending its conclusions.

entries.title: Donella Meadows and thinking in systems

definition.text: Donella Meadows (1941–2001) was an American environmental scientist and writer, best known as lead author of The Limits to Growth and Thinking in Systems.

facts.text: In 1972 she was on the MIT team that built the World3 global computer model for the Club of Rome, the basis of The Limits to Growth.
The book studied long-term global trends in population, economics and the environment and began a still-running debate about the limits of Earth's capacity to support economic expansion.
Her 1999 essay Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System describes the most and least effective kinds of intervention in any system.
With Dennis Meadows she created the Balaton Group in 1982, a network of researchers on resource use, conservation, systems modelling and sustainability.
She trained under Jay Forrester's system dynamics group at MIT and later taught at Dartmouth College for 29 years.

entries.title: Mathis Wackernagel and the Global Footprint Network

definition.text: Mathis Wackernagel is a Swiss-born sustainability advocate who co-created the ecological footprint and heads the Global Footprint Network.

facts.text: The ecological footprint concept and calculation method was his PhD work with supervisor William Rees at the University of British Columbia, from 1990 to 1994.
Footprint and biocapacity accounts compare human demand on nature with what nature can supply, and Global Footprint Network has developed them further since 2003.
He holds that climate change, biodiversity loss and food shortage are symptoms of one theme: humanity's use of resources has grown large compared with what Earth can renew.
With Rees he proposed that cost savings from efficiency gains be taxed away so they cannot cause a rebound in use.

entries.title: William Forster Lloyd, who first told the commons story

definition.text: William Forster Lloyd (1794–1852) was an English writer on economics, best known for an 1833 lecture that first set out the tragedy of the commons.

facts.text: In Two Lectures on the Checks to Population (1833) he introduced the idea of a common being overused by those with rights to use it.
His example: herders each entitled to graze cows on shared land overuse it, to the detriment of all its users.
He reasoned that an extra animal on a common takes food shared among everyone's cattle, so only a small part of the cost falls on its owner.
H. Scott Gordon and later Garrett Hardin developed his idea; Hardin later said he should have called it the tragedy of the unmanaged commons.
He also gave an early statement of diminishing marginal utility, placing him among the proto-marginalists.

entries.title: Partha Dasgupta: the economy embedded in nature

definition.text: Sir Partha Dasgupta (born 1942) is an Indian-British economist at the University of Cambridge whose long-standing interest is ecological economics.

facts.text: With Karl-Göran Mäler he developed 'inclusive wealth' as a measure of human well-being.
His 1982 monograph The Control of Resources set a research agenda linking population, consumption and the natural environment.
He led The Economics of Biodiversity: The Dasgupta Review, commissioned by the UK government and published in February 2021.
The Review aimed at a measure of natural capital usable in judging investment projects and the sustainability of economic programmes.
The Review rebuilds growth, development and poverty economics on the view that the human economy is embedded in Nature, not external to it.
He helped set up the journal Environment and Development Economics in 1996.

entries.title: Aldo Leopold, forester of the land ethic

definition.text: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948) was an American forester, ecologist, writer and conservationist, known for his land ethic.

facts.text: His land ethic widens the idea of community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, together called the land.
He described conservation as a state of harmony between people and land, in his posthumous 1949 book A Sand County Almanac.
His 1933 book Game Management helped found wildlife management as a science and was its leading textbook for over 40 years.
In 1921 he argued for preserving roadless wilderness in national forests, proposing the Gila headwaters as a prime case.

entries.title: Robert Ayres and the metabolism of industry

definition.text: Robert Ayres (1932–2023) was an American-born physicist and economist who applied the laws of thermodynamics to economics and originated the idea of industrial metabolism.

facts.text: He pioneered the field sometimes called industrial metabolism or industrial ecology, the study of material flows and transformations.
He argued that the first law of thermodynamics makes 'consumption' misleading, because transforming materials unavoidably creates large amounts of waste, some of it toxic.
He criticised growth models whose production functions leave out energy, as if output came from labour and capital alone.
With Benjamin Warr he found growth accounting improves when the efficiency of energy conversion is included.
He is named among the figures of ecological economics.

entries.title: Ecological Economics, the field's flagship journal

definition.text: Ecological Economics is a peer-reviewed journal published by Elsevier for the International Society for Ecological Economics, covering research on ecological economics.

facts.text: Robert Costanza founded it in 1989 as its first editor-in-chief.
It aims to integrate understanding of the interplay between 'nature's household' (ecosystems) and 'humanity's household' (the economy).
It publishes both neoclassical and heterodox work, which has sparked lively debate among the membership.

entries.title: Kenneth Boulding and Spaceship Earth

definition.text: Kenneth Boulding (1910–1993) was an English-born American economist, educator, peace activist and interdisciplinary thinker.

facts.text: His 1966 essay "The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth" argued that the economy must fit itself to an ecological system with limited resources.
He suggested treating Earth's ecosystem as a stock of assets.
He stressed that economic behaviour is embedded in a larger interconnected system and promoted an evolutionary rather than equilibrium approach to economics.

entries.title: Gifford Pinchot and the wise use of forests

definition.text: Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946) was an American forester and politician, a key figure in the history of conservation and natural resource management in the United States.

facts.text: He promoted scientific forestry and the controlled, profitable use of forests and other natural resources for the greatest benefit to people.
In 1905 he and Theodore Roosevelt persuaded Congress to create the United States Forest Service, and he became its first chief.
He advocated the wise use of natural resources, framing conservation as a way to secure long-term benefits for society.
Joan Martinez Alier names him one of the leading proponents of the 'gospel of eco-efficiency'.

entries.title: Gretchen Daily and Nature's Services

definition.text: Gretchen Daily (born 1964) is an American environmental scientist and tropical ecologist who advanced the science of ecosystem services and ways to value nature in decisions.

facts.text: She edited Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems (1997), a foundational framework for understanding nature's benefits to people.
Nature's Services served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the UN's Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
Her original definition kept ecosystem goods and ecosystem services apart, a distinction later work lumped together.
In 2005 she co-founded the Natural Capital Project with The Nature Conservancy and World Wildlife Fund to bring nature's values into decision-making.
The Project's open-source software InVEST is used in 185 countries to show nature's values in specific decisions.
Her 2002 book with Katherine Ellison, The New Economy of Nature, gives cases where companies or governments profited from conservation.

entries.title: William Baumol on why harm is hard to price

definition.text: William Baumol (1922–2017) was an American economist, among the world's most influential, whose work included environmental economics.

facts.text: He was instrumental in framing Pigou's work for modern economics in 1972.
His environmental economics research recognised the fundamental role of non-convexities in causing market failures.
He argued that the social cost of an externality is extraordinarily difficult, almost impossible, to measure, a key criticism of Pigouvian taxes.

entries.title: Dennis Meadows and the limits of growth

definition.text: Dennis Meadows (born 1942) is an American systems scientist best known as a co-author of The Limits to Growth.

facts.text: From 1970 to 1972 at MIT he directed the Club of Rome project that built the world computer model behind The Limits to Growth.
The 1972 book used the World3 model to explore how exponential growth interacts with finite resources, rather than to make specific predictions.
By the 2004 30-Year Update the message had shifted from slowing growth to managing an orderly reduction of activity back below the Earth's limits.
He received the Japan Prize in 2009 for work towards a sustainable society in harmony with nature.

entries.title: David Pearce, who priced the environment

facts.text: He set out techniques for valuing nature, arguing that the environment is under-priced and that the benefits of environmental services can be calculated.
His early work on cost-benefit analysis, pollution and resource depletion came before these ideas reached mainstream economics and policy.
He advised UK ministers and was a convening lead author for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
He criticised the assumptions behind discounting future goods.

entries.title: Kate Raworth and doughnut economics

definition.text: Kate Raworth (born 1970) is an English economist known for doughnut economics, a model balancing essential human needs against planetary boundaries.

facts.text: She first set out the doughnut idea in a 2012 paper and expanded it in her 2017 book Doughnut Economics.
She criticises the principle of unlimited growth as destroying planetary resources while serving human needs poorly.
Her model aims to give everyone basic needs such as food and education without limiting future generations' opportunities.
She worked on the UN Human Development Report and spent over a decade as a senior researcher at Oxfam.

He argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails that standard models handle poorly.
He showed when price controls beat quantity controls under uncertainty.
He co-wrote Climate Shock (2015) with Gernot Wagner.

entries.title: Serge Latouche, voice of degrowth

definition.text: Serge Latouche (born 1940) is a French emeritus professor of economics and one of the best-known advocates of degrowth.

facts.text: He denounces economism, consumer society and the notion of sustainable development, and criticises economic efficiency and economic rationalism.
In Farewell to Growth he credited Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as the main theoretical source of degrowth.
The same manifesto proposes 'ecomunicipalism' to start a virtuous cycle of quiet contraction of economic activity.

entries.title: Milner Schaefer and the economics of fishing

definition.text: Milner Baily Schaefer (1912–1970) was an American fisheries scientist notable for his work on the population dynamics of fisheries.

facts.text: At the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission he published a fishery equilibrium model based on the Verhulst growth model, with a catch equation known as the Schaefer short-term catch equation.
He extended the model to an unregulated fishery where effort rises until no profit is left, the equilibrium H. Scott Gordon called bionomic equilibrium.
Together, Schaefer's and Gordon's work, now the Gordon–Schaefer model, laid the basis for quantitative fisheries economics.

Together their work, the {{ref:nature-res-017}}, laid the basis of quantitative fisheries economics.

He was the first president of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and a founding editor of the Journal of Environmental Economics and Management.
He worked at Resources for the Future from 1961, and shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with John V. Krutilla in 1990.

entries.title: Richard Norgaard and coevolving societies

facts.text: His research treats development as a process of coevolution between social and environmental systems.
A 1975 paper showed farmers who hired independent pest-control experts earned more and used half as much pesticide as those advised by agribusiness.
He was president of the International Society for Ecological Economics from 1998 to 2001.
In Development Betrayed he argues traditional economics has hijacked the language of development.

He argued that 'externality' is a misnomer, and his theory offers the heterodox alternative to the neoclassical definition of social cost.
His 1950 work is counted among the European predecessors of ecological economics.

entries.title: Serhiy Podolynsky: energy and labor in 1880

definition.text: Serhiy Podolynsky (1850–1891) was a Ukrainian socialist, physician and sociologist, an early pioneer of ecological economics.

facts.text: He tried to reconcile socialist thought with the second law of thermodynamics, drawing on Marx, Darwin and Sadi Carnot.
In 1880 he proposed a labour theory of value based on embodied energy; Marx and Engels read and critiqued it.
He held that human labour only changes natural objects, and that the resources available to people grow only through photosynthesis capturing the Sun's energy.

entries.title: John Krutilla and the value of wilderness

definition.text: John V. Krutilla (1922–2003) was an American environmental economist who invented the concept of existence value, the economic value of undisturbed wilderness.

facts.text: He introduced existence value, the value of an amenity such as wilderness or a species simply existing, in his essay "Conservation Reconsidered".
He has been described as creating or stimulating most of the agenda of modern environmental economics.
He worked at Resources for the Future until retiring in 1988, and shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with Allen V. Kneese in 1990.

entries.title: Pavan Sukhdev, the banker who priced nature

definition.text: Pavan Sukhdev (born 1960) is an Indian environmental economist working on the green economy, biodiversity, natural capital and sustainable finance.

TEEB's 2008 Interim Report showed the economic significance of losing nature's services and linked it to ethics, equity and poverty reduction.
He headed UNEP's Green Economy Initiative, which argued that greening economies drives wealth, jobs and poverty reduction rather than burdening growth.
A banker by background, he spent 14 years at Deutsche Bank and was president of WWF International from 2017 to 2021.

entries.title: UNEP: the UN's voice on the environment

definition.text: The body that coordinates responses to environmental issues within the United Nations system.

facts.text: It was created in 1972 after the Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment and is based in Nairobi, Kenya.
Its mandate covers climate change, managing marine and land ecosystems, and green economic development.
Maurice Strong was its first head; under Mostafa Tolba it negotiated the 1987 Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer.
Its governing body, the UN Environment Assembly, was created in 2012 and has 193 members.
Its expert working group on biological diversity, begun in 1988, led to the draft Convention on Biological Diversity.
It administers the CITES secretariat and runs the Regional Seas Programme, set up in 1974.
Its achievements include the 2017 Minamata Convention limiting toxic mercury.
A 2020 UNEP report found that most global biodiversity efforts had failed to meet their goals.

entries.title: IUCN and the Red List of Threatened Species
entries.article: International Union for Conservation of Nature

definition.text: An international organization of governments and conservation groups working on nature conservation and the sustainable use of natural resources.

facts.text: It was founded on 5 October 1948 in Fontainebleau, France, on the initiative of UNESCO and its first director general, Julian Huxley.
It produces the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, first published as the Red Data Book in 1964, and the Red List of Ecosystems.
Its 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report to include a chapter on sustainable development.
Drafting that strategy led IUCN to accept that conservation by banning human presence no longer worked.
Its members agreed a definition of nature-based solutions at the 2016 World Conservation Congress.
It advises conventions such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, CITES and the UN climate convention.
Critics say it long favoured removing people from protected areas and took a mainly Northern view of conservation.
Its 2012 income was 114 million CHF, mostly from official development assistance budgets.

Its 1980 World Conservation Strategy was the first report with a chapter on sustainable development. Drafting it led IUCN to accept that conservation by banning people no longer worked. It advises the major biodiversity and climate conventions. Critics say it long favored removing people from protected areas and took a mainly Northern view.

entries.title: The International Society for Ecological Economics

definition.text: The main international scholarly society for ecological economics, founded in 1989 largely on Herman Daly's work.

facts.text: It recognizes that the human economy is part of a finite biosphere and should be subject to ecological limits.
Through education, research, policy and social action it works toward an equitable and ecologically sustainable society.
Robert Costanza was its first president and the first editor of its journal.
It publishes the monthly journal Ecological Economics, launched with Elsevier in 1989, and holds regular conferences.
Herman Daly, a key founding figure, received the Right Livelihood Award in 1996 for defining a path of ecological economics.
Regional societies such as the Mesoamerican society are affiliated with it.

entries.title: World Resources Institute: measuring the planet

definition.text: A global non-profit research organization, founded in 1982, that studies sustainable practices for business, economics, finance and governance.

facts.text: Its work centres on food, forests, water, energy, cities and climate.
With IUCN and WWF it is seen as a driving force behind environmental organizations' rising influence at the UN.
It worked with companies to develop the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a common standard for measuring and managing emissions.
With Google Earth Engine it built Global Forest Watch, which maps forest change from Landsat satellite images.
In 1997 and 2000 it published the first comparative study of material flow accounting.
Anil Agarwal criticized a 1990 WRI emissions study as environmental colonialism, sparking debate over how national responsibility should be measured.

entries.title: The Integrity Council and the quality of carbon credits
entries.article: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

definition.text: An independent governance body that publishes the Core Carbon Principles, criteria meant to define high-integrity carbon credits in the voluntary carbon market.

facts.text: It was set up in 2021 following the recommendations of the private-sector Taskforce on Scaling Voluntary Carbon Markets.
It assesses carbon crediting programs, judging them CCP-Eligible, and approves categories of credits that may then carry a CCP-Approved label.
In 2024 it ruled several renewable energy crediting methods ineligible for the label because of additionality concerns.
In an August 2024 test, around a third of credits did not meet its benchmark.
Critics such as Barbara Haya noted that existing programs already used ideas like additionality and permanence, yet over-crediting still happened.

entries.contested_note: Critics doubt principle-based benchmarks can screen out over-credited projects, while supporters say they make programs more comparable.

entries.title: How climate change affects the mind

definition.text: The effects climate change can have on people's mental and emotional well-being.

facts.text: Three pathways have been suggested: direct exposure to extreme weather, indirect effects such as lost income, and awareness of climate risk.
Climate change cuts farm output and deters tourism, and the resulting financial stress can lead to depression.
Using US and Mexican data, suicide rates rose by 0.7% and 3.1% respectively for a 1 °C rise in monthly average temperature.
Eco-anxiety is very rarely severe enough to need clinical treatment.

entries.text: Climate change can harm people's mental and emotional well-being, not only their bodies. Three pathways have been suggested: direct exposure to extreme weather, indirect effects such as lost income, and simple awareness of climate risk. Falling farm output and lost tourism bring financial stress, which can lead to depression. In US and Mexican data, suicide rates rose by 0.7% and 3.1% for a 1 °C rise in monthly temperature. Eco-anxiety, though, is very rarely severe enough to need clinical treatment.

entries.title: National adaptation plans for the poorest countries

definition.text: A plan in which a least developed country tells the UN climate convention its most urgent and immediate needs for adapting to climate change.

facts.text: Government ministries, usually helped by development agencies, assess the country's vulnerability to climate change and extreme weather and draw up a prioritized list of adaptation projects.
NAPAs use existing information rather than original research.
Submitting a NAPA makes a country eligible for project funding from the Least Developed Countries Fund.
The fund had at least US$415 million, with US$177 million approved for 47 projects, attracting over US$550 million in co-financing.

entries.title: Core Carbon Principles: ten tests for a credit
entries.article: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market#Core Carbon Principles

definition.text: The ten principles the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market uses as a threshold benchmark for carbon credit quality.

facts.text: They include effective governance, tracking, transparency, third-party validation and verification, additionality, permanence, robust quantification, no double counting, sustainable development safeguards and contribution to net zero.
They are grouped under governance, emissions impact and sustainable development, and applied through assessment criteria.
The full document set was published in January 2024.
They respond to concerns that credit quality is hard to judge because claimed impacts depend on counterfactual baselines and on handling leakage, non-permanence and double counting.

The full set was published in January 2024. They answer a real difficulty: a credit's claimed impact depends on guessing what would have happened without it.

ecosystem.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of energy and nutrients.

biodiversity.text: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

ecosystem service.text: Ecosystem services are the many benefits people get from ecosystems.

natural capital.text: Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, including rocks, soils, air, water and all living things.

sustainability.text: Sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time; today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future.

environmental degradation.text: Environmental degradation is the worsening of the environment through loss of resources such as clean air, water and soil, destruction of ecosystems and habitats, extinction of wildlife, and pollution.

biosphere.text: The biosphere is the sum of all the world's ecosystems: the zone of life on Earth.

anthropocene.text: The Anthropocene is a name for the period in which humanity has become a force that changes the whole planet.

ecosystem service categories.text: The ways ecosystem services are sorted into groups, most famously the four groups of the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

biodiversity and ecosystem services.text: The link between how varied life is in a place and the benefits that place gives people.

latitudinal diversity gradient.text: The pattern in which the number of species rises from the poles toward the tropics.

cultural services.text: The non-material benefits of nature, such as recreation, beauty, learning and spiritual meaning.

provisioning services.text: The products people obtain from ecosystems, also called ecosystem goods.

ecosystem goods.text: The tangible, material products of ecosystems, such as water, food, fuel, building material and medicinal plants.

regulating services.text: The benefits people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests.

supporting services.text: The background services, such as nutrient cycling and soil formation, that make all other ecosystem services possible.

freshwater depletion.text: The using up and spoiling of Earth's limited fresh water, a major part of environmental degradation.

natural capital protocol.text: A standard framework, released in 2016, that helps organisations identify, measure and value their impacts and dependencies on natural capital.

natural capital declaration.text: A 2012 pledge by finance-sector leaders to build natural capital into their products and reporting.

natural capital valuation debate.text: The argument over whether nature and its free services should be given a money value.

system of environmental-economic account.text: The international statistical standard (SEEA) for measuring the environment and how it relates to the economy.

assimilative capacity.text: Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it.

eco-capitalism.text: Eco-capitalism, or green capitalism, is the view that nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends, so markets should be used to solve environmental problems.

anthropocene start-date debate.text: The disagreement over when the human-shaped era of Earth's history began.

homogenocene.text: A name for the present age in which ecosystems worldwide grow more alike, mainly because people move species around the globe.

short-termism.text: Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action.

economics.text: The social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used.

externality.text: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it.

triple planetary crisis.text: A UN term for three linked global environmental crises: pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss.

sustainability and environmental managem.text: Managing the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale according to sustainability principles.

accommodative capacity.text: The rate at which waste can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

market failure.text: A situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost.

environmental economics.text: The branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them.

scarcity.text: The basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit.

negative externality.text: A harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party and is not counted in the market price.

social cost.text: The full cost of an activity to society: the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated.

externality supply and demand diagram.text: A standard supply and demand graph with an extra curve added to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society.

positive externality.text: A beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it.

environmental valuation.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

environmental versus ecological economic.text: The contrast between environmental economics, which applies standard economics to the environment, and ecological economics, which treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem.

ecological market failure.text: A market failure in which economic activity exhausts vital non-renewable resources, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste.

government failure.text: Economic waste caused by government action, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative.

objections to market failure theory.text: Arguments from several schools of thought that the idea of market failure is misleading, too narrow or does not justify government action.

absolute scarcity.text: A condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available, linked to the ideas of Thomas Malthus.

relative scarcity.text: A condition in which many different wants exceed the available means, which can be put to alternative uses, so people must choose.

causes of externalities.text: The view that externalities come mainly from poorly defined property rights and from the costs of making trades.

ecological critique of externalities.text: The argument from ecological and heterodox economists that treating environmental harm as an occasional 'externality' misreads how the economy works.

marginal social cost.text: The total cost to society of producing one more unit of a good: marginal private cost plus marginal external cost.

inframarginal externality.text: An externality that does not affect the marginal consumer, so it causes no market inefficiency.

positional externality.text: A side effect in which one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own.

environmentally harmful subsidies.text: Government payments that reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them.

unpriced natural capital costs.text: The value of nature that industries use up without paying for it, which would change their profits if it were priced.

failure of competition.text: A market failure in which a firm or small group gains enough market power to block trades that would benefit both sides.

macroeconomic market failures.text: Unemployment, inflation and disequilibrium seen as market failures at the level of the whole economy.

unequal bargaining power.text: A market failure in which one side of a deal, such as an employer, can hold out longer than the other and so sets the terms.

types of scarcity.text: The division of scarcity into demand-induced, supply-induced and structural kinds.

kapp's theory of social costs.text: K. William Kapp's heterodox view that social costs are the share of production costs businesses shift onto society to raise profits.

measuring social costs.text: The difficulty of putting numbers on social costs, especially future, environmental and long-range harms.

pecuniary externality.text: A side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others.

tyranny of small decisions.text: The way many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted.

pollution.text: The release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm.

causes of government failure.text: The main reasons government interventions go wrong, such as missing information, political pressure and short-term thinking.

market distortion by government.text: The way taxes, subsidies and price controls can change prices artificially and disturb how markets share out scarce resources.

review of environmental economics and po.term: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy
review of environmental economics and po.text: A peer-reviewed environmental economics journal, published twice a year, written to be readable by non-specialists.

pollutant.text: A substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful.

air pollution.text: The presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment.

noise pollution.text: Sound that can harm the health of people and animals.

economic costs of air pollution.text: The losses air pollution causes to economies through ill health, lost work, lower crop yields and other damage.

health effects of air pollution.text: The diseases and early deaths caused by breathing polluted air.

particulate pollution.text: Pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space.

stock and fund pollutants.text: The division of pollutants by how well the environment can absorb them: stock pollutants build up, fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough.

history of pollution.text: How pollution grew from prehistoric fires to the industrial age and how societies began to respond.

pollution control.text: The management of emissions and effluents released into air, water or soil.

socially optimal level of pollution.text: The amount of pollution at which society's welfare is greatest, where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it.

pollution abatement cost.text: What it costs a firm to cut the pollution it produces, called marginal abatement cost when measured per extra unit cut.

air pollution laws and standards.text: Laws that set limits on pollutant concentrations in the air or on emissions from sources such as vehicles.

history of air pollution control.text: The story of how societies came to regulate air pollution, from early anti-smoke groups to international treaties.

primary and secondary air pollutants.text: The division of air pollutants into those released directly by a source and those that form in the air from other pollutants.

ground-level ozone.text: Ozone near the ground, formed mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

air pollution damage to agriculture.text: The losses in crop output and farm productivity caused by polluted air, especially ozone.

unequal exposure to air pollution.text: The pattern in which poorer groups and some racial groups breathe more polluted air than others.

pollutant risk thresholds.text: Concentration levels, such as the no-observed-adverse-effect level, used in risk assessment to decide how much of a chemical is safe.

zones of influence of pollutants.text: A way of grouping pollutants by where they do damage, horizontally (local or regional) and vertically (surface or atmosphere).

health effects of noise.text: The harm that unwanted sound does to people's physical and mental health.

measuring noise.text: Quantifying noise exposure as sound pressure levels in decibels, a logarithmic scale linked to how people hear.

noise control.text: The rules and methods governments and communities use to limit harmful noise exposure.

utility.text: In economics, utility is a measure of how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world.

microeconomics.text: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how they interact.

goods.text: In economics, goods are things that give someone welfare or satisfaction.

noise impacts on wildlife.text: The ways human-made noise disrupts animals that rely on sound to communicate, find mates, navigate and avoid predators.

pm10 and pm2.5.text: The two main size classes of particulate matter: coarse particles of 10 micrometres and smaller, and fine particles of 2.5 micrometres and smaller.

economic value.text: Economic value is a measure of the benefit a good or service gives to a person, firm or other economic agent.

incentive.text: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organisation to change their behaviour toward a desired outcome.

ceteris paribus.text: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'other things being equal', used to study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same.

economic model.text: An economic model is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them.

preference.text: In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted.

indifference curve.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining all the combinations of two goods that a consumer likes equally well.

complementary goods.text: Complementary goods are goods used together, so that one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular.

ordinal utility.text: Ordinal utility ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much.

positive and normative economics.text: Positive economics describes and explains how the economy works, while normative economics says what people or societies ought to do.
