nature-econ-091.a: The extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs.

nature-econ-155.q: What did Veblen mock about the mainstream view of a person?
nature-econ-155.a: That it treats a person as 'a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains'.

nature-econ-411.q: What does a perfect substitute let you do?
nature-econ-411.a: Use it in exactly the same way as the good it replaces.

nature-econ-101.q: What can ordinal utility tell us, and what can it not?
nature-econ-101.a: It can rank options, such as two ice creams beating one, but not say by how much.

nature-econ-096.q: Give some examples of explicit costs.

nature-econ-123.a: The substitution effect, by adjusting income so the person stays equally satisfied.

nature-econ-083.q: How does capital differ from raw materials or energy?
nature-econ-083.a: It is not used up in one round of production but keeps giving services over many rounds.

nature-econ-143.q: What does a point inside the production possibility frontier mean?
nature-econ-143.a: Resources are wasted or sitting idle.

nature-econ-146.q: Name a few things that can change a good's value after it is made.
nature-econ-146.a: Age, personal attachment, cultural meaning or scarcity, as with collectable cars and comic books.

nature-econ-084.a: Government-owned infrastructure such as highways, water treatment, power grids, hospitals and schools.

nature-econ-144.q: What else is the marginal rate of transformation called?
nature-econ-144.a: The marginal opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other.

nature-econ-135.q: Give typical examples of fixed and variable costs.
nature-econ-135.a: Rent, salaries and utility bills are fixed; raw materials, delivery and production supplies are variable.

nature-econ-111.q: What is the difference between a normal good and an inferior good?
nature-econ-111.a: People buy more of a normal good as income rises, and less of an inferior good.

nature-econ-344.q: Why might someone pay more for a soft drink at a luxury resort than at a local shop?
nature-econ-344.a: Because willingness to pay depends on context.

nature-econ-335.q: What happens at a market equilibrium?
nature-econ-335.a: Rivalry among sellers sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce.

nature-econ-371.q: What is the difference between moving along a demand curve and shifting it?
nature-econ-371.a: A price change moves buyers along the curve; a change in anything else, such as income or expectations, shifts the whole curve.

nature-econ-385.q: What does Engel's law say about food?
nature-econ-385.a: Spending on food grows more slowly than income.

nature-econ-402.q: What is the difference between a price ceiling and a price floor?
nature-econ-402.a: A ceiling sets the most that may be charged, like rent control; a floor sets the least, like the minimum wage.

nature-econ-409.q: Why is economic profit smaller than accounting profit?
nature-econ-409.a: Because it subtracts hidden (implicit) costs as well as the costs recorded on the books.

nature-econ-364.q: Why are firms in an oligopoly called interdependent?
nature-econ-364.a: Each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions.

nature-econ-367.q: What do profit-seeking firms use cost curves for?
nature-econ-367.a: To decide how much to produce.

nature-econ-386.q: What does the inverse demand function tell you?
nature-econ-386.a: The highest price that could be charged while still selling a given quantity.

nature-econ-351.q: Name some indirect ways a state can grant a monopoly.

nature-econ-382.q: What does the first welfare theorem say about market equilibria?
nature-econ-382.a: They are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.

nature-econ-373.q: On which side of a market does most of a tax's burden fall?
nature-econ-373.a: The side less able to change how much it buys or sells.

nature-econ-384.q: What does a higher value of this index mean?
nature-econ-384.a: The market is more concentrated in a few firms.

nature-econ-377.q: How does a monopsonist differ from an ordinary buyer?
nature-econ-377.a: It sets the price it pays for an input instead of taking the market price.

nature-econ-406.q: Why might a minimum wage set above the market wage cut jobs?
nature-econ-406.a: Employers hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines.

nature-econ-345.q: What makes deadweight loss different from most losses?
nature-econ-345.a: Most losses are someone else's gain, but deadweight loss is regained by no one.

nature-econ-340.q: Producer surplus is roughly equal to what?
nature-econ-340.a: Profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss.

nature-econ-410.q: When does a shortage last instead of disappearing?
nature-econ-410.a: Only when something stops the price from rising until demand matches supply.

nature-econ-307.q: For a bakery, which costs are fixed and which are variable?
nature-econ-307.a: Rent and the phone line are fixed; wages are variable, since more output needs more workers.

nature-econ-310.q: As you add more of one input to a fixed amount of another, how does marginal product change?
nature-econ-310.a: It first rises, then falls, and can finally turn negative.

nature-econ-299.q: Why is the short-run average cost curve usually U-shaped?
nature-econ-299.a: Fixed costs are spread over more units at first, then rising marginal costs push it back up.

nature-econ-308.q: What is an isoquant the producer's version of?
nature-econ-308.a: An indifference curve, but its output can be measured exactly in physical units.

nature-econ-306.q: Do economies of scale always lead to monopoly, according to Morroni?
nature-econ-306.a: No, not once knowledge and the organisation of deals are taken into account.

nature-econ-314.q: Why does a price-taking firm always produce beyond stage 1?
nature-econ-314.a: In stage 1 output per unit of the variable input is still rising toward its peak.

nature-econ-326.q: How did Edith Penrose describe a firm?
nature-econ-326.a: As a collection of productive resources whose growth depends on managers finding new uses for idle ones.

nature-econ-158.q: Are allocative and productive efficiency the same thing?
nature-econ-158.a: No: a market can have one without the other.

nature-econ-160.q: What do economists use social welfare functions for?
nature-econ-160.a: To decide which of two outcomes, such as two income distributions, is better for society as a whole.

nature-econ-178.q: With no externalities, where is net social benefit largest?
nature-econ-178.a: At the market equilibrium, where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.

nature-econ-200.q: When is an economy productively inefficient?
nature-econ-200.a: When capital or labour sit idle or are put into the wrong industries.

nature-econ-165.q: Why is there a trade-off between efficiency and equity?

nature-econ-169.q: How does a strong Pareto improvement differ from an ordinary one?
nature-econ-169.a: A strong one makes everyone strictly better off; an ordinary one needs only one person better off and nobody worse off.

nature-econ-167.q: How does this approach judge efficiency and distribution?
nature-econ-167.a: Separately: efficiency by the Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks tests, distribution by the choice of social welfare function.

nature-econ-184.q: How long do the two people keep trading?
nature-econ-184.a: As long as their marginal rates of substitution differ.

nature-econ-204.q: How has diminishing marginal utility been used to justify transfers from rich to poor?
nature-econ-204.a: The poor gain more from an extra unit of income than the rich do.

nature-econ-192.q: With unequal information, can a government with no better information still improve on the market?
nature-econ-192.a: Yes: it can find policies that make someone better off and no one worse off.

nature-econ-180.q: For elections, what does this condition amount to?

nature-econ-195.q: Who is generally credited with first stating this problem?

nature-econ-290.q: What did Coase argue would happen if making deals cost nothing?
nature-econ-290.a: People would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources, whatever the starting legal rights.

nature-econ-294.q: What tax did Pigou propose to correct an externality?
nature-econ-294.a: A tax equal to the marginal damage per unit.

nature-econ-641.q: What are the three groups of transaction costs?
nature-econ-641.a: Search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs.

nature-econ-610.q: Why do fish stocks run down without management?
nature-econ-610.a: Each fisher has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does.

nature-econ-661.q: Which market failures does public economics focus on?
nature-econ-661.a: Public goods, externalities and imperfect competition, along with taxes and government spending.

nature-econ-652.q: What can land tenure rest on?
nature-econ-652.a: Official laws and policies, or informal local customs.

nature-econ-609.q: Why might turning a common resource into private property help?
nature-econ-609.a: It gives the new owner a reason to keep the resource productive.

nature-econ-629.q: What problem was Coase thinking about when he developed his theorem?
nature-econ-629.a: Radio stations interfering with each other; the station that gained more would pay the other not to interfere.

nature-econ-636.q: Why do people worry about digital public goods like open projects?
nature-econ-636.a: A small group of maintainers often keeps them going for many users, risking burnout and underfunding.

nature-econ-634.q: How did Coase argue lighthouses could be paid for?
nature-econ-634.a: By bundling their costs into port fees.

nature-econ-611.q: What happens if you take more than a renewable resource's flow?
nature-econ-611.a: The stock shrinks, which shrinks future flows, and sometimes the loss cannot be undone.

nature-econ-620.q: Why do groups often reward members who punish free riders?

nature-econ-608.q: According to Carol Rose, what is the bigger risk for 'comedic' public resources?
nature-econ-608.a: Too little investment, rather than overuse.

nature-econ-662.q: What did this analysis add to Ramsey's study of taxation?
nature-econ-662.a: It considered how income is shared out together with raising revenue.

nature-econ-607.q: How does being watched change how much people take from a common pool?
nature-econ-607.a: They take less when others can see them than when they act anonymously.

nature-econ-669.q: What did Jefferson mean by 'Earth belongs in usufruct to the living'?
nature-econ-669.a: Each generation may use the earth but must not impoverish it for those to come.

nature-econ-648.q: What happened to the talks on trading environmental goods?

nature-econ-005.a: The losses from an agent straying from the interest of the person they act for.

nature-econ-016.a: When it costs low-quality senders more to produce or copy than high-quality ones.

nature-econ-013.q: What would a complete contract do?
nature-econ-013.a: Set the legal consequences of every possible situation.

nature-econ-002.q: Who is credited with the idea of incentive compatibility?

nature-econ-015.q: How can pay get an agent to act in the principal's interest?
nature-econ-015.a: By tying pay to output the principal can observe.

nature-econ-772.a: A state of limited knowledge where the possible futures, their chances or their values cannot all be fully described.

nature-econ-757.q: How are interest rates normally quoted?

nature-econ-762.q: Why is a dollar today worth more than a dollar tomorrow?
nature-econ-762.a: Today's dollar can be invested and earn interest.

nature-econ-844.q: What four rules about preferences did von Neumann and Morgenstern say lead a person to act as if maximising expected utility?

nature-econ-805.q: What is a deductible in insurance?
nature-econ-805.a: The amount the insured person must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim.

nature-econ-792.q: When valuing future cash flows, what two parts make up the discount rate?
nature-econ-792.a: The time value of money (the risk-free rate) plus a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive.

nature-econ-779.q: What does a person get from an annuity sold by a life insurer?
nature-econ-779.a: Regular income, often for retirement, in return for a lump sum or premiums.

nature-econ-752.q: How does a higher social discount rate affect a social project's chance of being funded?
nature-econ-752.a: It makes the project less likely to be funded.

nature-econ-755.q: Did the Stern Review use a zero discount rate?
nature-econ-755.a: No. That is a common misconception: its projections used many positive rates, while taking time preference near zero.

nature-econ-804.q: What did Milton Friedman's monetarism hold about inflation?
nature-econ-804.a: That inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

nature-econ-748.q: How does hyperbolic discounting differ from exponential discounting?
nature-econ-748.a: Under hyperbolic discounting, value falls quickly over short early delays and more slowly over longer ones; exponential discounting lowers value by a constant factor per unit of delay.

nature-econ-761.q: Why do longer-lasting assets usually have to offer higher yields?
nature-econ-761.a: Because of the effect that shows up as a yield gap between assets of different maturities and conversion costs.

nature-econ-788.a: Applying the normative approach in practice: building tools and software to help people decide better.

nature-econ-810.q: How does index-based crop insurance decide when to pay farmers?
nature-econ-810.a: It pays when a modelled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur.

nature-econ-822.q: Under constant relative risk aversion, how does wealth affect the share put in a risky asset?
nature-econ-822.a: It does not: the share does not depend on how rich one is.

nature-econ-798.q: In the St. Petersburg game, how does the prize grow and when does the game end?
nature-econ-798.a: The prize doubles each time the coin lands heads, and the game ends at the first tails.

nature-econ-815.q: Why did Aristotle and the Scholastics think charging interest was unjust?
nature-econ-815.a: They held that money is by nature sterile, so it was unjust to charge for being parted from it.

nature-econ-843.q: How might feeling connected to one's future self affect choices over time?
nature-econ-843.a: It may make it easier to delay gratification.

nature-econ-829.q: How does the Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model treat saving differently from the Solow–Swan model?
nature-econ-829.a: Solow–Swan fixes the saving rate; this model derives saving from a household's optimisation over time.

nature-econ-830.q: How is the elasticity of intertemporal substitution related to relative risk aversion?
nature-econ-830.a: It is formally the inverse: high relative risk aversion means a low elasticity and a stronger wish to smooth consumption.

nature-econ-750.q: In quasi-hyperbolic discounting, how are rewards taken now treated?
nature-econ-750.a: They are not discounted at all.

nature-econ-785.q: What is a firm's cost of capital?
nature-econ-785.a: The minimum return it must earn on its assets to satisfy its lenders, owners and other capital providers, or they will invest elsewhere.

nature-econ-826.q: Why did John Harsanyi use the original position to argue for utilitarianism?
nature-econ-826.a: Because rational agents weigh expected outcomes rather than worst cases.

nature-econ-828.q: What does Kimball's measure of absolute prudence capture?
nature-econ-828.a: The precautionary motive for saving, just as risk aversion measures the desire for insurance.

nature-econ-531.q: Which writer may have first used the term human capital?
nature-econ-531.a: Irving Fisher, though Adam Smith earlier counted people's acquired and useful abilities as capital.

nature-econ-604.q: Where does a firm's financial capital come from?
nature-econ-604.a: From its retained earnings or from lenders and investors; it is used to buy real capital equipment.

nature-econ-595.q: Why is climate change mitigation called a stock-and-flow problem?
nature-econ-595.a: Because it means cutting the stock of greenhouse gases in the air by reducing emissions and increasing carbon dioxide removal.

nature-econ-592.q: What can happen to bonding groups without bridging ties?
nature-econ-592.a: They can become isolated from the rest of society.

nature-econ-601.q: What did Reiner Kümmel conclude about the Solow residual?
nature-econ-601.a: That it can be explained very well by an economy's energy input.

nature-econ-576.q: Why does the Paasche index understate inflation?
nature-econ-576.a: It assumes consumers adjust their purchases instantly to new prices.

nature-econ-566.a: Output, spending and income of households, corporations and government, their links with other countries, and their net worth.

nature-econ-486.q: What is the factor used to convert GDP from current to constant values called?

nature-econ-586.q: Why can nominal GDP rise even when physical output stays the same?

nature-econ-526.q: How does the GDP deflator's basket differ from the CPI's?
nature-econ-526.a: The CPI has a fixed basket; the deflator's changes each year with spending and investment patterns.

nature-econ-554.q: When is stabilisation policy expansive and when contractive?
nature-econ-554.a: Expansive in a recession, contractive when the economy overheats.

nature-econ-564.a: Because conventional policy can fail in a liquidity trap.

nature-econ-524.q: What happens to interest-rate cuts in a liquidity trap?
nature-econ-524.a: They fail to boost demand because banks will not lend and consumers will not spend.

nature-econ-491.q: For a firm, how can gross income be defined?
nature-econ-491.a: As all revenue minus the cost of goods sold.

nature-econ-510.a: The minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing.

nature-econ-517.q: How are net measures such as net domestic product found?
nature-econ-517.a: By deducting consumption of fixed capital from GDP and GNI.

nature-econ-489.q: How can a traffic jam raise GDP while making life worse?
nature-econ-489.a: Extra fuel use adds to GDP, while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted.

nature-econ-548.q: What did economists use before rational expectations?
nature-econ-548.a: Adaptive expectations, where people look only at the recent past.

nature-econ-513.q: In Friedman's theory, into what two parts is income split?
nature-econ-513.a: Transitory and permanent parts, whose changes affect consumption differently.

nature-econ-482.q: What was the classical view, from Adam Smith, of how inequality affects growth?
nature-econ-482.a: Inequality boosts saving by the wealthy, speeding capital accumulation and growth.

nature-econ-571.q: Whose income does national income cover?

nature-econ-546.q: What did Keynes explain about a small fall in consumption or investment?
nature-econ-546.a: It could be magnified into declines across the economy.

nature-econ-498.q: Why does a parent's unpaid childcare not show up in GDP while a nanny's does?
nature-econ-498.a: GDP counts only the paid nanny's income, not unpaid work at home.

nature-econ-503.q: What does the five-sector circular flow model add?
nature-econ-503.a: Banks and other intermediaries that borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

nature-econ-536.q: Why does the definition of intermediate consumption strongly affect GDP?
nature-econ-536.a: Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP.

nature-econ-567.q: What do national balance sheets record?
nature-econ-567.a: The stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time.

nature-econ-034.q: What makes a game cooperative rather than non-cooperative?
nature-econ-034.a: Players can make binding, externally enforced commitments; in a non-cooperative game agreements must enforce themselves.

nature-econ-039.q: What is the dilemma in the prisoner's dilemma?
nature-econ-039.a: Betraying is rational for each player, yet both would get a higher payoff by cooperating.

nature-econ-071.q: How does a satisficer choose among options?
nature-econ-071.a: They set an aspiration level, take the first option that meets it, and lower the level if nothing meets it in time.

nature-econ-024.q: How can a nudge make a complex decision easier?
nature-econ-024.a: By presenting information clearly, reducing mental effort.

nature-econ-036.q: In the trust game, what would a purely self-interested trustee return, and what do people actually do?
nature-econ-036.a: Nothing; but in experiments people do place trust, expecting reciprocity.

nature-econ-029.q: How did behavioural economists respond to studies failing to reproduce?
nature-econ-029.a: They turned from lab experiments to field studies.

nature-econ-040.q: In a repeated prisoner's dilemma with a known, fixed number of rounds, what is the equilibrium?

nature-econ-076.q: Name some social preferences that pull people away from pure self-interest.
nature-econ-076.a: Altruism, fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion.

nature-econ-055.q: What error does the representativeness heuristic lead to by ignoring how common each category is?

nature-econ-072.q: How does survey satisficing show up in answers?
nature-econ-072.a: As 'don't know' answers, the same rating for every item, agreeing with any statement, or picking the first reasonable option.

nature-econ-077.q: Give an example of reciprocal altruism in the prisoner's dilemma.

nature-econ-069.q: How do people's choices change when the same options are worded as gains or as losses?
nature-econ-069.a: As gains, most prefer a sure gain to a chance of gain; as losses, people tend to pick a gamble over a sure loss.

nature-econ-078.a: Loss aversion and the endowment effect: the possible losses of switching weigh more than the possible gains.

nature-econ-068.q: What can myopic loss aversion lead people to do?
nature-econ-068.a: Avoid immediate losses at the expense of long-term gains.

nature-econ-731.q: How does a strategy differ from a move?
nature-econ-731.a: A strategy is like a list of directions; a move is a single step on that list.

nature-econ-718.q: What was Nash's key insight about decisions made by several people?
nature-econ-718.a: Their choices cannot be predicted by analysing each one in isolation.

nature-econ-728.q: How does the stag hunt differ from the prisoner's dilemma?
nature-econ-728.a: In the stag hunt mutual cooperation is itself an equilibrium; what it needs is trust.

nature-econ-737.q: Who entered tit-for-tat in Axelrod's tournaments, and how did it do?
nature-econ-737.a: Anatol Rapoport; it was both the simplest strategy and the most successful.

nature-econ-734.q: What does subgame perfect equilibrium rule out?
nature-econ-734.a: Non-credible threats, so strategies stay rational throughout the game.

nature-econ-721.q: When may a Nash equilibrium fail to exist?
nature-econ-721.a: When choices are infinite and unbounded, as when two players name numbers and the larger wins.

nature-econ-673.q: What is the trade-off of setting a reserve price at an auction?
nature-econ-673.a: It protects the seller from a low bid but may lower the final price if it dampens interest.

nature-econ-685.q: What does the war of attrition model in biology?
nature-econ-685.a: How contests are settled when physical combat is not possible.

nature-econ-703.q: What can make one equilibrium stand out over others?
nature-econ-703.a: Paying more, or being more salient, fairer or safer.

nature-econ-693.q: Which thinker's ideas does Kalai say his bargaining solution is close to?
nature-econ-693.a: The egalitarian ideas of John Rawls.

nature-econ-716.q: In a game, does Nature have payoffs?
nature-econ-716.a: No; Nature has no payoffs, and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.

nature-econ-678.q: What does occasional forgiveness achieve in a repeated game with mistakes?
nature-econ-678.a: It breaks cycles of retaliation caused by mistakes or noise and restores mutual cooperation.

nature-econ-712.q: Give examples of evolutionary games found in nature.
nature-econ-712.a: Predator–prey competition, host–parasite co-evolution and mutualism.

nature-econ-706.q: When does a coalition block an allocation?
nature-econ-706.a: When its members could create more value on their own than they are given.

nature-econ-697.q: Where does the nucleolus lie when the core is non-empty?

nature-econ-684.q: When does a brinkmanship threat work?
nature-econ-684.a: Only if the opponent believes there is enough risk of an irrational response, often because the threatener has given up control over it.

nature-econ-433.q: What can be done when a differential equation has no explicit formula for its solution?
nature-econ-433.a: Its solutions can be approximated numerically on computers.

nature-econ-456.q: What does linear programming optimise, and under what constraints?
nature-econ-456.a: A linear objective, subject to linear equality and inequality constraints.

nature-econ-430.q: What does a partial derivative measure?
nature-econ-430.a: The function's rate of change in the direction of one variable.

nature-econ-465.q: Who mainly developed optimal control theory?
nature-econ-465.a: Lev Pontryagin and Richard Bellman in the 1950s.

nature-econ-431.q: Where do the optima of unconstrained problems lie?
nature-econ-431.a: At stationary points, where the first derivative or gradient is zero.

nature-econ-438.q: If the primal problem is a minimisation, what is the dual?
nature-econ-438.a: A maximisation problem, and vice versa.

nature-econ-444.q: What does the water lily riddle show about exponential growth?
nature-econ-444.a: A plant doubling daily covers half the pond on day 29, leaving only one day to save it.

nature-econ-426.a: A type of nonlinear programming with linear constraints and a quadratic objective.

nature-econ-469.q: What is the power of Pontryagin's maximum principle?
nature-econ-469.a: Maximising the Hamiltonian at each moment is much easier than optimising over whole functions.

nature-econ-476.q: Why must some variables in a CGE model be fixed outside the model?
nature-econ-476.a: Because CGE models always have more variables than equations.

nature-econ-419.a: A sudden qualitative change in a dynamical system's behaviour caused by a small smooth change in a parameter.

nature-econ-454.a: For convex problems, some point must satisfy the inequality constraints strictly.

nature-econ-441.q: How does dynamic programming simplify the consumer's saving problem?
nature-econ-441.a: It lets the consumer decide one step at a time, choosing only current consumption and saving given current capital.

nature-econ-279.q: If data are not very unlikely under the null hypothesis, what can be concluded?
nature-econ-279.a: Only that the evidence against it is insufficient.

nature-econ-218.q: What are independent and dependent variables in an experiment?
nature-econ-218.a: The changed inputs are independent variables; the outcomes expected to change are dependent variables.

nature-econ-281.q: When is the null hypothesis rejected using a p-value?
nature-econ-281.a: When the p-value is at or below the test's significance level, alpha.

nature-econ-243.a: No; the exposure may resemble random assignment, but they are observational studies.

nature-econ-249.q: Why do funders and voters want programs evaluated?
nature-econ-249.a: To know whether the programs they support are producing the promised effect.

nature-econ-275.q: In one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis, what happens after an input is changed?
nature-econ-275.a: It is returned to its baseline value and the step is repeated for each other input.

nature-econ-256.q: Why give the control group a placebo?
nature-econ-256.a: So participants stay unaware of which treatment they got.

nature-econ-272.q: Why does dropping everyone who quits a diet trial bias the results?
nature-econ-272.a: Most quitters are those for whom the diet was not working.

nature-econ-251.q: How does a measure's reliability affect an evaluation?
nature-econ-251.a: The more reliable it is, the greater its statistical power and the more credible its findings.

nature-nbs-095.q: Why do researchers pool many studies together in a meta-analysis?
nature-nbs-095.a: Pooling studies increases statistical power and can settle disagreements between individual studies.

nature-econ-223.q: What goes wrong when the supposed cause is also shaped by the outcome?
nature-econ-223.a: The analysis misjudges cause and effect, so its results are unreliable; for example, education raises income but income also affects education.

nature-econ-227.q: In data that follow the same subjects over time, what kind of hidden differences do fixed effects control for?
nature-econ-227.a: Unobserved differences between subjects that stay constant over time, such as innate ability or a country's history and institutions.

nature-econ-261.q: Which models are used for outcomes that are simply yes or no?
nature-econ-261.a: The linear probability model, and nonlinear models such as probit and logit; the multinomial logit handles more than two categories.

nature-econ-225.q: What happens to an estimated effect when the explanatory variable is measured with noise?
nature-econ-225.a: The noise ends up in both the explanatory variable and the error term, so ordinary least squares underestimates the effect.

nature-econ-278.a: It estimates models where nearby places affect each other, as in housing markets, and analyses effects such as externalities and spatial concentration.

nature-econ-265.q: Why can bent cutoffs cause trouble for a regression discontinuity design?
nature-econ-265.a: Real cutoffs are often bent, for instance by leniency for students just short of passing, which biases a sharp design.

nature-econ-252.q: What is a propensity score, and what is matching on it trying to imitate?
nature-econ-252.a: It is the probability of being assigned to treatment given observed traits; matching tries to mimic randomization by building treated and untreated groups that look alike.

nature-eco-314.q: What does environmentalism try to balance at its core?
nature-eco-314.a: People's relations with the natural systems they depend on, so that all are sustainable.

nature-eco-326.q: In what ways can biomass be measured?
nature-eco-326.a: As wet weight, dry weight, or the mass of organic carbon, depending on the context.

nature-eco-362.q: What role do heterotrophs play in a food chain?
nature-eco-362.a: They are the consumers, while autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers.

nature-eco-303.q: How does net primary productivity differ from gross primary productivity?
nature-eco-303.a: Net equals gross minus the carbon producers lose through their own respiration, and it is what is left for growth and for herbivores to eat.

nature-eco-388.q: What is a typical soil made of?
nature-eco-388.a: About 45% mineral and 5% organic matter, with the pores split equally between water and gas.

nature-eco-316.q: What idea did trade unions develop to promote green jobs?
nature-eco-316.a: The idea of a just transition, in response to the dilemma between economic growth and the ecological crisis.

nature-eco-286.a: Living and non-living features such as water and soil, across land and water ecosystems; it is the largest scale of biodiversity.

nature-eco-310.q: Why are amphibians useful as indicator species?
nature-eco-310.a: Their permeable skin and ties to wetlands make them very sensitive to environmental harm, so they can act as a 'miner's canary'.

nature-eco-327.q: What shapes the community of living things in a biome?
nature-eco-327.a: Its physical environment and regional climate.

nature-es-086.q: Why are beavers the classic example of an ecosystem engineer?
nature-es-086.a: By felling trees and building dams they change the distribution and abundance of many organisms.

nature-eco-369.q: How do parasites differ from decomposers?
nature-eco-369.a: Parasites feed on living hosts, while decomposers feed on dead matter.

nature-eco-311.q: Why does protecting an umbrella species like the monarch butterfly help other wildlife?
nature-eco-311.a: It migrates through many ecosystems across North America, so protecting it protects much else.

nature-eco-328.q: What two factors does Whittaker's biome scheme use?
nature-eco-328.a: Precipitation and temperature; it simplified Holdridge's scheme and is easier to use but less specific.

nature-eco-370.q: Why are parasitoids considered close to predators?
nature-eco-370.a: They are insects that eventually kill their hosts.

nature-eco-339.q: Why do individuals that resemble a competing species leave fewer offspring?
nature-eco-339.a: They face stronger competition; Darwin's finches on the Galapagos are an example.

nature-eco-290.q: How are woodpeckers an example of an allogenic engineer?
nature-eco-290.a: The holes they carve in trees later house other birds and mammals.

nature-eco-293.q: What goes wrong if you count too many or too few traits when measuring functional diversity?
nature-eco-293.a: Too many can overestimate it, while too few can wrongly class vital species as redundant.

nature-eco-353.q: How does a food web differ from a food chain?
nature-eco-353.a: A food chain shows who eats whom by level; a food web is the network formed when many food chains interconnect.

nature-eco-321.q: Why do apex predators matter to ecosystems?
nature-eco-321.a: They are central to how ecosystems function, to regulating disease and to maintaining biodiversity.

nature-eco-300.q: Why is it imprecise to assign each organism to one trophic level?

nature-eco-307.q: What is 'fishing down the food web'?
nature-eco-307.a: Steep declines in the average trophic level of catches, as fishing shifted from fish like cod and haddock to shrimp and herring.

nature-eco-361.q: What are the two kinds of plant defense against herbivores?
nature-eco-361.a: Tolerance, withstanding damage without losing fitness, and resistance, reducing how much damage is done.

nature-eco-367.q: What happens to pollinators in this kind of network once conditions pass a critical point?
nature-eco-367.a: They survive harsh conditions together but collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point.

nature-eco-355.q: Who coined the term foundation species, and at what trophic levels can they sit?
nature-eco-355.a: Paul K. Dayton coined it in 1972; foundation species can be producers, herbivores or predators.

nature-eco-345.q: How does energy transfer from phytoplankton to grazers compare with transfer on land?
nature-eco-345.a: It is about 20% in the sea, compared with 10% on land.

nature-eco-402.q: How does soil organic matter raise soil fertility?
nature-eco-402.a: It holds nutrients on exchange sites and slowly releases nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur as it breaks down.

nature-eco-298.a: Any non-living organic matter, such as leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung.

nature-eco-405.q: How long does mineral-bound soil organic matter last compared with plant remains in soil?
nature-eco-405.a: It can persist for centuries, while little-decomposed plant remains last only years to decades.

nature-eco-585.q: Who is seen as the founder of population dynamics, and what did he hold?
nature-eco-585.a: Malthus, who held that with constant conditions a population grows or declines exponentially.

nature-eco-584.q: Why are small populations at greater risk of extinction?
nature-eco-584.a: They recover less well from random events.

nature-eco-587.q: When does a population grow, shrink or hold steady under geometric growth?
nature-eco-587.a: It grows if births exceed deaths, shrinks if deaths exceed births, and holds steady if they are equal.

nature-eco-575.q: In what two ways is dispersal measured?
nature-eco-575.a: As a rate, the expected share of individuals leaving an area, or as a distance.

nature-eco-571.q: How can rarity drive a hunted species to extinction?
nature-eco-571.a: When rare species fetch higher prices than common ones, they can be hunted out while common ones are harvested sustainably.

nature-eco-164.q: What does the carbon cycle cover?
nature-eco-164.a: Carbon being recycled through living things and its long-term storage in, and release from, carbon sinks.

nature-eco-259.q: How much carbon do soils store compared with the atmosphere?
nature-eco-259.a: About 2,700 Gt, roughly three times the atmosphere's carbon.

nature-eco-230.q: What does the Haber-Bosch process make, and where does most of it go?
nature-eco-230.a: It combines nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron catalyst into ammonia, most of which goes into nitrogen fertilizer.

nature-eco-214.q: What usually causes dead zones in the water?
nature-eco-214.a: Eutrophication: extra nitrogen and phosphorus fuel algal blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen.

nature-eco-171.q: What changes does protecting carbon sinks require?
nature-eco-171.a: Changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.

nature-eco-198.q: How do compacted soils and paved surfaces change the water cycle?
nature-eco-198.a: They reduce how much water soaks in and increase surface runoff.

nature-eco-204.q: Where does the ocean's biological pump start?
nature-eco-204.a: With phytoplankton in the sunlit surface layer building carbon compounds.

nature-eco-246.q: Why does water quality trading work?
nature-eco-246.a: Polluters face very different costs to control the same pollutant, so cheap cutters sell reduction credits to those for whom control is expensive.

nature-eco-192.q: What does the Calvin cycle make, and with what?
nature-eco-192.a: It uses ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions to form carbohydrates such as glucose.

nature-eco-276.q: What is the difference between infiltration-excess and saturation-excess runoff?
nature-eco-276.a: Infiltration excess happens when rain is too intense or soils are sealed, as in drylands and paved areas; saturation excess happens when rain keeps falling on soil already full of water.

nature-eco-219.q: How can harmful algal blooms threaten people?
nature-eco-219.a: Dying or eaten algae release nerve and liver toxins, which can reach people through shellfish poisoning.

nature-eco-225.q: Why can recovery from eutrophication take a long time?
nature-eco-225.a: Nutrients stored in sediments keep being released, and a water body can have several stable but very different states.

nature-eco-267.q: What causes eroded hilltops in farm fields?
nature-eco-267.a: Tillage, since water erosion removes soil mainly from mid and lower slopes.

nature-eco-229.q: How can evapotranspiration be worked out from a catchment water balance?
nature-eco-229.a: The balance relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and groundwater recharge, so evapotranspiration can be solved for.

nature-eco-208.q: Where does the dissolved organic carbon in the microbial loop come from?
nature-eco-208.a: From bursting bacteria, leakage from phytoplankton, sloppy feeding by zooplankton and animal wastes.

nature-eco-247.q: How do load-oriented and source-oriented approaches to pollution apportionment differ?
nature-eco-247.a: Load-oriented ones work back from stream monitoring data; source-oriented ones model emissions using figures from similar catchments.

nature-eco-197.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
nature-eco-197.a: In ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow, which hold 68.7% of all fresh water.

nature-eco-236.q: Why can lakes run short of oxygen in winter?
nature-eco-236.a: Ice and snow cut light for photosynthesis and block oxygen exchange with the air while respiration continues.

nature-eco-211.a: It frees the energy stored in organic molecules and recycles matter as nutrients for other organisms.

nature-eco-187.q: How has the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus changed, and with what effect?
nature-eco-187.a: It has risen over the last 40 years, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems.

nature-eco-231.q: Why has synthetic fertilizer been called the detonator of the population explosion?
nature-eco-231.a: It helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018.

nature-clim-206.q: Why is it hard to tell whether ocean iron fertilization stores more carbon?
nature-clim-206.a: The ocean is vast and consumers respond quickly to extra growth.

nature-eco-254.q: What does a rising Revelle factor mean for the ocean's uptake of carbon dioxide?
nature-eco-254.a: The lower the factor, the more CO2 water can take in; it rises as CO2 rises, so the ocean will take a smaller share of human emissions.

nature-eco-233.q: What harm can extra nitrogen deposition do?
nature-eco-233.a: It can acidify soils, streams and lakes and change forest and grassland productivity.

nature-eco-162.q: Which gases in air absorb heat radiation, and which barely do?
nature-eco-162.a: Nitrogen and oxygen barely absorb it, while CO2, methane and nitrous oxide do, producing the greenhouse effect.

nature-eco-017.q: Why do climate tipping points matter?
nature-eco-017.a: Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed.

nature-eco-009.q: How cold would Earth's surface be without the natural greenhouse effect?
nature-eco-009.a: About −18 °C on average instead of around 15 °C.

nature-eco-012.q: When does the IPCC expect average warming to pass +1.5 °C?
nature-eco-012.a: In the early 2030s, measured as a 20-year average.

nature-eco-019.q: How does climate change harm food production?
nature-eco-019.a: Through higher CO2, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events and shifting pests and diseases.

nature-eco-008.q: What does the strength of the CO2 fertilization effect depend on?
nature-eco-008.a: Plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available.

nature-eco-129.q: What drives humanity's global-scale damage to the environment?
nature-eco-129.a: Population growth, rapid economic growth, overconsumption, overexploitation, pollution and deforestation.

nature-eco-026.q: Which non-native species count as invasive?
nature-eco-026.a: Established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity.

nature-eco-091.q: What is the immediate cause of desertification?
nature-eco-091.a: The loss of most vegetation, driven by drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees.

nature-eco-069.q: What does relative species abundance compare?
nature-eco-069.a: One species' abundance with that of others in the ecosystem.

nature-eco-123.q: How many species did the IPBES global assessment find threatened with extinction?
nature-eco-123.a: 1 million of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species.

nature-eco-056.q: Why do forest owners often overlook many forest functions?
nature-eco-056.a: Many important functions have no markets and so no readily apparent economic value.

nature-eco-027.q: How has the economic cost of invasive species changed over time?
nature-eco-027.a: It has quadrupled every decade since 1970, exceeding $423 billion a year as of 2019.

nature-eco-099.q: How do species mainly become endangered?
nature-eco-099.a: Through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation.

nature-eco-022.q: How fast are species now disappearing compared with the natural rate?
nature-eco-022.a: An estimated 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background extinction rate.

nature-eco-131.q: How does in situ conservation differ from ex situ conservation?
nature-eco-131.a: In situ protects species where they live, in places like reserves and parks; ex situ keeps them or their material elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks.

nature-eco-054.a: The conversion of forest to other land uses, whether or not people caused it.

nature-eco-040.q: Why are freshwater ecosystems so important for biodiversity?
nature-eco-040.a: They cover 1% of Earth's surface but are home to about one third of vertebrate species.

nature-eco-029.q: Which body oversees the Ballast Water Management Convention?

nature-eco-074.q: Why are seed banks considered a fairly reliable way to keep genetic diversity?
nature-eco-074.a: Stored material changes little over the long term.

nature-eco-101.q: Why has private rhino farming helped rhino numbers?
nature-eco-101.a: Ecotourism and sales give owners strong incentives to look after rhinos rather than poach them.

nature-eco-108.q: What does the rediscovery of the coelacanth show about extinction?
nature-eco-108.a: How hard it is to establish exactly when a species has gone extinct; it was found alive in 1938 after being known only from fossils.

nature-eco-024.q: What has been the main cause of mammal extinctions since the Late Pleistocene?
nature-eco-024.a: Human activity; megafaunal extinctions correlate with the arrival of humans.

nature-eco-092.q: What is now thought to mainly cause drought in the Sahel?
nature-eco-092.a: Rainfall variability driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases, rather than overgrazing as early studies claimed.

nature-mkt-009.q: What did a review of fragmentation effects suggest about one large versus several small reserves?
nature-mkt-009.a: Most significant effects of fragmentation itself were positive, implying several small patches can sometimes beat one large one.

nature-eco-071.q: What are the limits of DAFOR and ACFOR ratings?
nature-eco-071.a: They give rough estimates but are not exact or objective, so better methods should be used where available.

nature-eco-076.q: In Whittaker's scheme, what does total landscape diversity depend on?
nature-eco-076.a: On local diversity (alpha) and on how much sites differ (beta).

nature-eco-067.q: How does deforestation affect local climate?
nature-eco-067.a: Reduced rainfall brings a hotter, drier climate, longer dry seasons, more fires and disrupted pollination.

nature-eco-148.q: What happens to Hill-number diversity as q is raised?
nature-eco-148.a: More weight goes to the most abundant species, so larger q gives lower diversity for the same data; at q = 0 it equals species richness.

nature-eco-085.q: How did falling fish stocks in Ghana affect wildlife?
nature-eco-085.a: People turned to hunting animals in nature reserves, and wildlife declines were tied to a falling fish supply.

nature-eco-155.q: What is the case for a regulated legal wildlife trade, and what is its main obstacle?
nature-eco-155.a: It could push down illegal prices, cutting the incentive to poach, or raise conservation money; laundering and corruption are major obstacles.

nature-eco-111.q: Why is extinction debt hard to measure?
nature-eco-111.a: The processes are slow and noisy and tiny remnant populations are hard to count, so estimates are very uncertain.

nature-acct-088.q: What does this index show about local land biodiversity?
nature-acct-088.a: How it responds to pressures such as land-use change and intensification.

nature-eco-031.q: What role are introduced Aldabra giant tortoises playing on islets off Mauritius?
nature-eco-031.a: They are replacing extinct native tortoises as seed dispersers and grazers of invasive plants.

nature-eco-117.q: In Whittaker's view, what sets gamma diversity?
nature-eco-117.a: The average diversity of local sites (alpha) and how much those sites differ (beta).

nature-eco-624.q: Name some kinds of natural disturbance an ecosystem can face.
nature-eco-624.a: Fires, floods, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions; they range from one falling tree to a mass extinction.

nature-eco-640.q: What does the word hysteresis mean, and who coined it?
nature-eco-640.a: Sir James Alfred Ewing coined it in 1881, from a Greek word meaning 'lagging behind'.

nature-eco-597.q: What could happen if humanity crosses the planetary boundaries?
nature-eco-597.a: The Earth system could be pushed out of the stable Holocene period in which human society developed.

nature-eco-598.q: What is the climate boundary for carbon dioxide in the air, and where are we now?
nature-eco-598.a: The boundary is 350 ppm; the current level is 423 ppm, against 280 ppm before industry.

nature-eco-608.q: Which tipping elements are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming?
nature-eco-608.a: Collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, die-off of tropical coral reefs and sudden thaw of northern permafrost.

nature-eco-643.q: What did William R. Catton Jr.'s 1980 book Overshoot blame?

nature-eco-602.q: What does William Schlesinger warn about managing an ecosystem up to a threshold?
nature-eco-602.a: It lets slow, spread-out damage carry on almost indefinitely.

nature-eco-626.q: How does a mountain pine beetle outbreak change a western North American forest?
nature-eco-626.a: It kills old pines, opening gaps where other trees do well until the pines grow back.

nature-eco-612.q: Around what level of warming might this threshold lie?
nature-eco-612.a: Researchers proposed about 2 °C above pre-industrial levels.

nature-eco-631.q: Who argued that diverse communities are more stable, and who refuted it?
nature-eco-631.a: Charles Elton argued it in 1958; Robert May later refuted the idea that diversity begets stability.

nature-eco-641.q: How can a recession leave lasting unemployment?
nature-eco-641.a: Jobless workers may lose skills or motivation and stay out of work even during the recovery.

nature-eco-650.q: What are the four phases of the adaptive cycle?
nature-eco-650.a: A slow move from exploitation (r) to conservation (K), then a fast release (Omega) and reorganisation (alpha) before exploitation again.

nature-eco-618.q: How do state variables differ from parameters?
nature-eco-618.a: State variables, like population densities, respond quickly to feedbacks; parameters respond slowly or not at all.

nature-eco-655.q: What is panarchy in resilience theory?
nature-eco-655.a: How much one level of an ecosystem's hierarchy is influenced by other levels; C.S. Holling developed the idea.

nature-eco-410.q: Why can mangroves live where most plants die?
nature-eco-410.a: Special adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and get rid of salt.

nature-eco-563.q: Why are rainforest soils often poor?
nature-eco-563.a: Heavy rain washes out nutrients, and most nutrients sit near the surface because leaves and organisms rot quickly.

nature-eco-565.q: What are the three types of tundra?

nature-eco-449.q: What is the cheapest, least intrusive way to restore a wetland?
nature-eco-449.a: Stop the disturbance and leave the wetland to recover by natural succession.

nature-es-082.q: How do mangroves build up the land they grow on?
nature-es-082.a: By slowing incoming tides, they make sediment settle out.

nature-eco-530.a: They are transition zones where river and sea environments overlap.

nature-eco-470.q: Where is most grassland carbon stored?
nature-eco-470.a: In the soil, which holds about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems.

nature-eco-478.q: Why does draining a peatland release greenhouse gases?
nature-eco-478.a: Drainage lets oxygen into the peat, so it decomposes and gives off carbon dioxide and methane.

nature-eco-513.q: Why do caribou move into boreal areas in winter?

nature-eco-561.q: How does this forest biome's share of world forest compare with the boreal forest's?
nature-eco-561.a: It is second largest with 25%, behind the boreal forest's roughly 33%.

nature-eco-417.q: What share of land-dwelling organisms do forests host?

nature-eco-535.q: How do algal blooms eventually affect fish?
nature-eco-535.a: They can briefly boost fish numbers, but continued loss of oxygen then makes fish populations fall.

nature-eco-453.q: How much of the ocean do coral reefs cover, and how many marine species live there?
nature-eco-453.a: Less than 0.1% of the ocean, yet at least 25% of all marine species.

nature-eco-422.q: How do kelp forests and coral reefs compare in area and productivity?
nature-eco-422.a: They cover only 0.1% of Earth's surface but account for 0.9% of global primary productivity.

nature-eco-460.q: Do marine protected areas always work?
nature-eco-460.a: Their effectiveness is debated: some sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict.

nature-eco-427.q: How can overfishing destroy a kelp forest?
nature-eco-427.a: Removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren.

nature-eco-459.a: Rising sea temperatures from greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-eco-462.q: Why are floodplain soils often very fertile?

nature-eco-472.q: Why was a map of land for forest restoration criticised?
nature-eco-472.a: It included 900 million hectares of grasslands among its 2 billion hectares.

nature-eco-484.q: What does a strip of undisturbed land along a stream do during logging?
nature-eco-484.a: It gives shade, leaf litter and wood, and holds back soil eroded from the logged area.

nature-eco-466.q: Where does much of the phosphorus in fresh water come from?
nature-eco-466.a: Wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff.

nature-eco-435.q: How has the view of salt marshes changed?
nature-eco-435.a: Once seen as wasteland, they are now known as among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivalling tropical rainforests.

nature-eco-560.a: The average time for fires to burn an area equal to the whole ecosystem.

nature-eco-426.q: How much carbon dioxide do seaweeds such as kelp take up each year?

nature-eco-489.q: How do seagrass leaves shape the seafloor?
nature-eco-489.a: They slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the bottom; without them, currents carry it away.

nature-eco-542.q: What keeps mangroves in warm climates?

nature-eco-543.q: After about how long does a mangrove forest stop adding biomass?
nature-eco-543.a: About 20–30 years; carbon fixed after that must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air.

nature-eco-527.a: In Western Asia and South America.

nature-eco-529.q: What makes dryland restoration more successful, according to case studies?
nature-eco-529.a: Involving indigenous knowledge and local communities.

nature-eco-557.q: What feeds the food web in small, shaded headwater streams?

nature-eco-519.q: What makes these ecosystems unusual in their energy source?
nature-eco-519.a: They are among the few that do not depend on sunlight.

nature-eco-496.q: What mainly decides how much methane a wetland releases?
nature-eco-496.a: How much methane made by methanogens escapes before methanotrophs break it down.

nature-eco-439.q: What happens when cities replace forests, wetlands and grasslands?
nature-eco-439.a: Losing green space lowers air and water quality, health and biodiversity.

nature-es-005.q: What did Plato understand about forests around 400 BC?
nature-es-005.a: That cutting them down could cause soil erosion and dry up springs.

nature-es-002.q: Give examples of services that nature provides.
nature-es-002.a: Purifying air and water, breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, recharging groundwater and reducing greenhouse gases.

nature-es-084.q: How do energy and nutrients move differently through an ecosystem?
nature-es-084.a: Energy flows one way and is not reused, while mineral nutrients move in cycles.

nature-es-119.q: What mainly drives a storm surge?
nature-es-119.a: Strong winds pushing water toward the coast.

nature-es-104.q: Where did streptomycin and artemisinin come from?
nature-es-104.a: Streptomycin came from a soil bacterium; the antimalarial artemisinin came from a plant.

nature-es-107.q: Firewood is renewable, so how can it run out?
nature-es-107.a: Local demand can quickly outrun how fast trees grow back.

nature-es-095.q: What is the main agent of non-animal pollination?
nature-es-095.a: Wind, which accounts for some 98% of it.

nature-es-090.q: What is habitat manipulation in pest control?
nature-es-090.a: Changing cropping systems to favour pests' natural enemies, for example with hedgerows, shelterbelts or beetle banks.

nature-es-118.q: How is this soil-formation equation mostly solved?
nature-es-118.a: Empirically, by varying one factor while holding the others constant.

nature-es-081.q: How do mangroves help keep local fish numbers up?
nature-es-081.a: They give nursery habitat to many species, including commercial fish and crustaceans.

nature-es-043.q: What other names is well-being known by?

nature-es-036.q: What are the three components of subjective well-being?
nature-es-036.a: Affect (emotions and moods), life satisfaction (judgments about one's life) and eudaimonia (a sense of meaning and purpose).

nature-es-012.q: How does ecotourism differ from plain nature tourism?
nature-es-012.a: It aims to build tourists' appreciation of habitats and local culture.

nature-es-020.q: Who popularised forest bathing, and why?
nature-es-020.a: Tomohide Akiyama, head of Japan's forestry ministry, in 1982, to get more people into forests.

nature-es-039.q: What does responsible tourism aim for?
nature-es-039.a: To maximise benefits to local communities and minimise harmful social or environmental impacts.

nature-es-013.q: Name some ways to manage visitor impacts.
nature-es-013.a: Setting a carrying capacity, hardening sites, sustainable design, visitor quotas, fees, access limits and visitor education.

nature-es-018.q: What do the three subscales of nature relatedness measure?
nature-es-018.a: Identifying with nature, concern about human effects on the environment, and comfort and wish to be in nature.

nature-es-057.q: Why is remote sensing useful for fieldwork?
nature-es-057.a: It reaches dangerous or remote places and can replace slower, costlier fieldwork without disturbing the site.

nature-es-061.q: What are the three central ideas of agent-based models?
nature-es-061.a: Agents as objects, emergence and complexity: simple rules for agents can produce complex behaviour.

nature-es-073.q: Where has GIS-based spatial analysis spread beyond its origins?
nature-es-073.a: From ecology, geology and epidemiology to natural resources, disaster risk and climate change adaptation.

nature-es-068.a: It sends out its own light and uses the speed of light to turn the return time into distance.

nature-es-053.q: How does a union overlay differ from an intersect?
nature-es-053.a: A union keeps everything from both inputs; an intersect keeps only where they overlap.

nature-es-078.q: What does a reinforcing loop do?
nature-es-078.a: It amplifies change, as when more adopters of a product create stronger word of mouth; counteracting loops push back.

nature-es-065.q: Which tree services do these tools put numbers on?
nature-es-065.a: Pollution removal, carbon storage and avoided stormwater runoff.

nature-es-067.q: What does the Figure of Merit measure?
nature-es-067.a: As one percentage, the overlap between real and simulated land change, built from hits, misses and false alarms.

nature-val-070.q: How did Adam Smith frame the paradox of value?
nature-val-070.a: He separated 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', noting the most useful things often have little exchange value.

nature-val-062.q: What is the core principle of deep ecology?
nature-val-062.a: The living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish, apart from human use.

nature-val-064.q: How do ecocentrics see themselves differently from technocentrics?
nature-val-064.a: Ecocentrics see themselves as subject to nature and prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance; technocentrics do not see cutting industry as the solution.

nature-val-052.q: What does total economic value add up?
nature-val-052.a: The values an ecosystem provides: direct and indirect use value, plus non-use value.

nature-val-071.q: How does direct use value differ from indirect use value?
nature-val-071.a: Direct use value comes from removable products such as timber, fish and water; indirect from things like a sunset or waterfall.

nature-val-092.q: What does hedonic pricing measure in environmental work?
nature-val-092.a: How much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding other house features fixed.

nature-val-096.q: What is this rationality test widely used for?
nature-val-096.a: In econometrics, to test whether choices are rational and to build preferences from real data.

nature-val-086.q: What did the panel recommend for contingent valuation surveys?
nature-val-086.a: Personal interviews, a yes-or-no vote on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats.

nature-val-100.q: What does a discrete choice model give?
nature-val-100.a: The probability that a person picks a given option, based on features of the options and of the person.

nature-val-081.q: What problem does a probit model solve?
nature-val-081.a: It estimates the probability that an observation falls into one of two categories, as logistic regression also does.

nature-val-084.a: When people have less information about a good and information is costly.

nature-val-017.a: Because of externalities and because taxes, subsidies, quotas and tariffs distort market prices.

nature-val-006.q: Why can cost-benefit analysis overlook fairness?
nature-val-006.a: It treats a positive net benefit as decisive regardless of who wins and who loses.

nature-val-005.q: What did critics in the 1980s say about cost-benefit analysis of rules?
nature-val-005.a: It could serve political goals, was biased against regulation, and caused long delays.

nature-val-024.q: What is the payback period of a $1000 investment returning $500 a year?

nature-val-020.q: As a rule of thumb, when is a project worthwhile by its benefit-cost ratio?
nature-val-020.a: When benefits exceed costs; the higher the ratio, the better.

nature-val-037.q: What are the main competing views in environmental ethics besides anthropocentrism?

nature-val-049.q: What is Aldo Leopold's basic principle of the land ethic?
nature-val-049.a: A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the living community.

nature-val-046.a: When no amount of one would make up for a loss of the other, as with freedom and security.

nature-val-039.q: Which famous hypothesis may belong to ecologic extension?
nature-val-039.a: James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis, treating Earth as one whole with its own ethical value.

nature-val-032.q: Why does nature tend to be overexploited, on this view?
nature-val-032.a: Because its value cannot be fully counted in money, it is overexploited and 'underproduced'.

nature-acct-021.q: How does the UN Development Programme define human development?
nature-acct-021.a: Enlarging people's choices to live a long healthy life, be educated, have a decent living standard and enjoy freedom and self-respect.

nature-acct-010.q: What is green GDP in simple form?
nature-acct-010.a: GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs.

nature-acct-019.q: What does this approach aim to maximise instead of wealth?

nature-acct-011.q: Why did China's green GDP effort collapse in 2007?
nature-acct-011.a: Environmental adjustments cut growth to politically unacceptable levels, nearly zero in some provinces.

nature-acct-024.q: Why is ordinary national income always higher than sustainable national income?
nature-acct-024.a: It leaves out the loss of environmental functions.

nature-acct-017.q: Why do critics say GNP puts the environment on the wrong side of the ledger?
nature-acct-017.a: Polluting and then cleaning up both add to GNP.

nature-acct-089.q: What costs does environmental accounting track?
nature-acct-089.a: Resource use and costs such as cleaning up contaminated sites, fines and taxes, pollution-prevention technology and waste handling.

nature-acct-094.q: Why do backers of green accounting say policymakers need it?
nature-acct-094.a: Because they argue GDP ignores the environment, so a model that includes green accounting is needed.

nature-acct-111.q: How does material flow accounting picture the economy?
nature-acct-111.a: As a subsystem inside the environment that, like a living thing, needs a constant throughput of materials and energy, called industrial or societal metabolism.

nature-acct-109.q: What does GDP miss that this measure adds?
nature-acct-109.a: GDP counts only market values, so it misses the non-market value of ecosystem services.

nature-acct-095.q: What does green accounting measure, following SEEA?
nature-acct-095.a: The depletion of scarce natural resources and the cost of environmental damage and of preventing it.

nature-acct-097.q: When and where was this partnership launched?
nature-acct-097.a: In October 2010, at the Convention on Biological Diversity's COP-10 meeting in Japan.

nature-acct-050.q: What do cradle and grave mean in a product's life cycle?
nature-acct-050.a: Cradle is the extraction of raw materials; grave is recycling or disposal, with making, distributing and using in between.

nature-acct-031.a: All greenhouse gases, not only carbon dioxide, combined into one figure.

nature-acct-070.q: Why use indicators to follow the environment?
nature-acct-070.a: They are a practical, cheaper way to follow a complex environment than recording every variable.

nature-clim-164.q: What is the difference between Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions?
nature-clim-164.a: Scope 1 is emissions caused directly, such as burning fuel on site; Scope 2 is indirect emissions from bought electricity, heat, cooling or steam.

nature-acct-086.q: How can repeated assessments reveal trends in extinction risk?
nature-acct-086.a: Repeating them at regular intervals shows changes in species' threat status over time.

nature-acct-057.q: What is the main purpose of indicator sets?
nature-acct-057.a: To inform public policy-making; they are scientific constructs that answer simple questions such as what is happening.

nature-acct-029.q: How is a nation's total footprint worked out?
nature-acct-029.a: Its footprint per person is multiplied by its population.

nature-acct-052.q: How does cradle-to-gate differ from cradle-to-grave?
nature-acct-052.a: Cradle-to-grave runs from extraction to disposal; cradle-to-gate stops at the factory gate, leaving out use and disposal.

nature-acct-067.q: How are a pollutant's emissions usually estimated?
nature-acct-067.a: By multiplying each activity's level by an emission factor.

nature-acct-081.a: The amount of one good needed to make one unit of another.

nature-acct-083.q: What makes a car more eco-efficient under this measure?
nature-acct-083.a: Using less material per passenger kilometre over its life.

nature-acct-041.q: What does emergy mean, and who coined it?
nature-acct-041.a: Embodied energy; Howard T. Odum coined the term.

nature-acct-074.q: What does a simple waste footprint ignore?
nature-acct-074.a: That waste is usually treated into a less harmful form before recycling or disposal.

nature-pol-068.a: Particles mixed with air, coming from both natural and human sources.

nature-pol-054.a: Being toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable.

nature-pol-048.q: At what acidity do fish eggs fail and adult fish die?
nature-pol-048.a: Below pH 5 most fish eggs will not hatch; below pH 4 adult fish die.

nature-pol-074.q: Which particle control device is most common in general industry?

nature-pol-049.q: How much SO2 does flue-gas desulfurization remove?
nature-pol-049.a: 95% or more of the SO2 in a typical coal-fired station's exhaust.

nature-pol-062.q: Why must landfill aftercare go on indefinitely?
nature-pol-062.a: Sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, so liners must be replaced and leachate treated without end.

nature-pol-055.q: What is a drawback of burning hazardous waste?
nature-pol-055.a: Though burning shrinks it greatly, the leftover ash and gases can also be hazardous.

nature-pol-076.q: How does sediment harm life in water?
nature-pol-076.a: It clouds the water, cutting light for underwater plants and the fish and shellfish that depend on them.

nature-pol-132.q: Does an environmental impact assessment demand a set outcome?
nature-pol-132.a: No; it requires decision-makers to weigh environmental values and justify their choice using studies and public comments.

nature-pol-169.q: Which two kinds of protected site does this network join?
nature-pol-169.a: Special Protection Areas for birds and Special Areas of Conservation under the Habitats Directive.

nature-pol-141.a: The right of future generations to a fair share of the common inheritance.

nature-pol-155.q: What does the permit system require of point sources such as factories?
nature-pol-155.a: They may not discharge into surface waters without a permit.

nature-pol-148.q: How does a carbon tax differ from classic command and control?
nature-pol-148.a: It lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution instead of limiting each polluter.

nature-pol-133.q: What does an environmental impact statement describe?
nature-pol-133.a: The good and bad environmental effects of a proposed action, usually with alternative actions.

nature-pol-134.q: Which effects do almost all impact assessments cover in practice?
nature-pol-134.a: Only direct, immediate on-site effects, though indirect effects can be much larger.

nature-pol-154.q: What do primary and secondary air standards protect?
nature-pol-154.a: Primary standards protect health; secondary ones protect other public welfare, such as farm values.

nature-pol-139.q: Which vehicles do these standards leave out?

nature-pol-181.q: What did Becker apply economic reasoning to?
nature-pol-181.a: Crime and other non-market behaviour, assuming people act rationally.

nature-pol-183.q: Who carries out these assessments under Superfund?
nature-pol-183.a: Federal, state or tribal natural resource trustees.

nature-pol-088.q: Ideally, how large should this tax be?
nature-pol-088.a: Equal to the external marginal cost of the harm, which corrects a market failure.

nature-pol-114.q: Who pays an excise and who is expected to bear it?
nature-pol-114.a: The producer pays it but is expected to pass it on to buyers through higher prices.

nature-pol-087.q: Where does fuel tax money often go?
nature-pol-087.a: Often to transport projects, making it a kind of user fee; elsewhere to general revenue.

nature-pol-113.q: What causes thermal pollution from industry?
nature-pol-113.a: Warm cooling water released by power stations.

nature-pol-126.q: How does a sin tax differ from a Pigouvian tax?
nature-pol-126.a: A Pigouvian tax charges for damage done to others; a sin tax raises the price mainly to cut use.

nature-pol-090.q: Why should an environmental tax sit below the full Pigouvian level, say Bovenberg and Mooij?
nature-pol-090.a: Because an income tax already distorts how much people choose to work.

nature-pol-097.q: Where is this carbon fee charged?
nature-pol-097.a: Where fuels enter the economy, such as the well, mine or port.

nature-pol-121.q: How does a per-unit tax shift the supply curve?
nature-pol-121.a: Up by exactly the amount of the tax, parallel to the original curve.

nature-pol-125.q: Who made the theoretical case for road pricing in the 1950s?
nature-pol-125.a: William Vickrey, building on Pigou's ideas, proposing electronic charging for busy roads.

nature-pol-199.q: How does the IMF tell explicit from implicit subsidies?
nature-pol-199.a: Explicit: consumer prices below supply cost. Implicit: prices that leave out environmental damage.

nature-pol-244.q: What happens to a polluter emitting more than its quota?
nature-pol-244.a: It must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions.

nature-pol-272.q: What was first about the EU's emissions trading scheme?
nature-pol-272.a: It was the world's first large greenhouse gas trading scheme.

nature-pol-262.q: Why is the US sulfur dioxide programme historically important?
nature-pol-262.a: It was the first US cap-and-trade programme and a model for later greenhouse gas schemes.

nature-pol-255.q: How did the 1977 offset mechanism work?
nature-pol-255.a: A firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant.

nature-pol-250.q: Why can carbon trading leave local air pollution in place?
nature-pol-250.a: Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so factories can buy permits instead of cutting local pollution.

nature-pol-241.q: Who gains when carbon money is returned per person?
nature-pol-241.a: Richer people with bigger footprints pay more, and poorer people can come out ahead.

nature-pol-273.q: How much discretion does this reserve mechanism allow?
nature-pol-273.a: None: it runs on predefined rules with no discretion for the Commission or member states.

nature-pol-283.q: Why do companies and individuals buy these credits?
nature-pol-283.a: To compensate voluntarily for their emissions; each one equals 1 tonne of CO2.

nature-pol-260.q: What must a polluter affecting several monitoring points hold?
nature-pol-260.a: A portfolio of licences covering all of them.

nature-pol-205.q: What forms can a subsidy take?
nature-pol-205.a: Direct spending, tax incentives, cheap loans, price support and government-provided goods and services.

nature-pol-221.q: What kinds of goods does fair trade focus on?
nature-pol-221.a: Goods exported from poorer to richer countries, such as coffee, cocoa, handicrafts, fruit and gold.

nature-pol-194.q: How does making producers responsible push greener design?
nature-pol-194.a: Producers who pay end-of-life costs have a money incentive to design greener products.

nature-pol-208.q: How can a subsidy become perverse?
nature-pol-208.a: By not being withdrawn after it has reached its goal.

nature-pol-229.q: Do these standards concern the product itself?
nature-pol-229.a: No; like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made.

nature-pol-220.q: Who can join this EU scheme?
nature-pol-220.a: Any type of organisation worldwide; it is voluntary.

nature-pol-198.q: Why are IMF subsidy estimates much larger than others?
nature-pol-198.a: Because they count unpriced externalities, unlike the OECD and IEA definitions.

nature-pol-185.q: How does ISO develop sustainability standards?

nature-pol-217.q: What changed in 2011 for qualifying products?
nature-pol-217.a: Instead of manufacturers' own data, which was open to fraud, independent labs and certifiers must test them.

nature-pol-193.q: What do critics say fossil fuel subsidies do?
nature-pol-193.a: Raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies.

nature-pol-214.q: What happens to farmers who fail cross compliance?

nature-pol-236.q: What does the Marine Stewardship Council do?
nature-pol-236.a: It runs a certification program for consumer seafood products.

nature-pol-018.q: What does environmental policy aim to do?
nature-pol-018.a: Steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people.

nature-pol-020.q: Why are market instruments often promoted?
nature-pol-020.a: As a more efficient, cost-effective alternative to regulation.

nature-pol-023.q: Give an example of integrating environment into other policy.
nature-pol-023.a: Fuel taxes aimed at local pollution, or removing fossil fuel subsidies.

nature-pol-029.q: Why do market instruments give firms more flexibility?
nature-pol-029.a: They do not dictate technology or equal cuts for every firm.

nature-pol-042.q: What is Robert Shiller's classic example of rent-seeking?
nature-pol-042.a: A landowner who chains a river and charges boats to lower the chain, adding no value.

nature-pol-035.q: How has the fossil fuel lobby affected policy?
nature-pol-035.a: It promotes climate change denial and obstructs environmental and climate policy.

nature-pol-041.q: Why do technical industries risk cultural capture?
nature-pol-041.a: Regulators must hire experts who mostly come from the industry itself.

nature-pol-007.q: Which agreement officially set up the WTO?
nature-pol-007.a: The Marrakesh Agreement, signed on 15 April 1994 at the end of the Uruguay Round.

nature-pol-008.q: When may WTO members restrict trade?
nature-pol-008.a: To protect the environment or public, animal and plant health, but not as disguised protectionism.

nature-pol-004.q: How do tariffs differ in cost from testing or labelling rules?
nature-pol-004.a: Tariffs raise costs that grow with volume; testing or labelling rules impose fixed costs.

nature-pol-016.q: Why does the UN restrict trade in plastic waste?
nature-pol-016.a: Importing countries often lack the capacity to process all of it.

nature-mkt-136.q: Which three services draw most PES money?
nature-mkt-136.a: Climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation.

nature-mkt-137.q: Which idea is PES rooted in, according to environmental economics?
nature-mkt-137.a: The Coase theorem: a voluntary, conditional deal between a service buyer and seller.

nature-mkt-140.q: Did paying forest owners reduce deforestation?
nature-mkt-140.a: Yes: 2 to 5% in participating villages against 7 to 10% in control villages.

nature-mkt-152.q: What do most PES programmes pay for?
nature-mkt-152.a: Management practices; only less commonly measured outcomes.

nature-mkt-129.q: What are the steps of the mitigation hierarchy?

nature-mkt-124.a: A site where wetland projects are done before the damage they compensate for, producing credits developers can buy.

nature-mkt-121.q: Does funding general research count as a biodiversity offset?
nature-mkt-121.a: No; activities without a measurable gain for biodiversity do not count.

nature-mkt-126.q: How is US mitigation-bank land protected?
nature-mkt-126.a: By a conservation easement that also binds future owners of the land.

nature-mkt-104.q: Why did industrialised countries buy CDM credits?
nature-mkt-104.a: Because cutting emissions was cheapest in developing countries.

nature-mkt-090.q: What did the 2016 Öko-Institut study find about CDM projects?
nature-mkt-090.a: 85% were unlikely to be truly additional or likely overestimated reductions.

nature-mkt-108.q: What do the safeguards bar REDD+ actions from being used for?

nature-mkt-088.q: What do soil carbon projects try to do?
nature-mkt-088.a: Keep or raise the carbon stored in soil.

nature-mkt-091.q: Who created the Gold Standard, and why?
nature-mkt-091.a: WWF and partners in 2003, to make sure credits are real, verifiable and help sustainable development.

nature-mkt-114.q: What monitoring systems are REDD+ countries encouraged to build?
nature-mkt-114.a: Transparent systems combining satellite remote sensing with ground forest inventories.

nature-mkt-103.q: What did the January 2023 investigation find about Verra rainforest credits?
nature-mkt-103.a: About 94% did not represent a real tonne of CO2e.

nature-mkt-065.a: Borrowers' long-term investments, or for governments, current spending.

nature-mkt-056.q: Can loans count as official development assistance?
nature-mkt-056.a: Yes, soft loans count if their grant element is at least 25%; most aid is grants.

nature-mkt-049.a: Public and private funds in one deal, each party using its expertise.

nature-mkt-029.q: What are the main causes of biodiversity loss?
nature-mkt-029.a: Habitat loss, land-use change, pollution and overexploitation.

nature-mkt-015.a: When protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another, cutting the net benefit.

nature-mkt-057.q: Which countries first met the aid target, and when?

nature-mkt-026.q: What share of cancer drugs are natural or inspired by nature?
nature-mkt-026.a: 70% of all cancer drugs are natural or bioinspired products, and over 40% of medicines come from nature.

nature-mkt-028.q: Why do criminal and terrorist groups take part in wildlife trafficking?
