nature-mkt-028.a: They use trafficking to raise money; other demand comes from culture, such as bushmeat and traditional medicine.

nature-mkt-054.q: How can a land trust protect land without owning it outright?
nature-mkt-054.a: It can buy an easement or development, mining or logging rights while the land stays private.

nature-mkt-016.q: Where do these extra costs bite hardest?
nature-mkt-016.a: Where projects are small, varied or need a lot of monitoring and checking; the costs can make projects less attractive to investors.

nature-mkt-040.q: Which report brought the term ESG to prominence?

nature-mkt-042.q: What did Milton Friedman argue about social responsibility?
nature-mkt-042.a: That it harms a firm's financial performance.

nature-mkt-021.q: How well do disclosure rules work when they stay voluntary?
nature-mkt-021.a: Research shows they have limited effect.

nature-mkt-048.q: Why do green bonds tend to pay lower yields than ordinary bonds?
nature-mkt-048.a: Because high demand for them pushes their yields down, as studies find.

nature-mkt-061.q: How do these bonds differ from ordinary bonds?
nature-mkt-061.a: They have no fixed return; what they pay depends on social outcomes.

nature-mkt-010.q: What problem were these projects introduced to fix?
nature-mkt-010.a: WWF brought them in during the mid-1980s to fix the problems of the 'fines and fences' approach, which left local people out.

nature-mkt-004.q: Which solutions to human-wildlife conflict tend to work best?
nature-mkt-004.a: Those that involve local communities in planning, carrying out and maintaining them.

nature-res-204.q: Why do scarcer resources become more valuable?
nature-res-204.a: Value depends on how much exists in nature and how costly it is to extract; under supply and demand, scarcity raises value.

nature-res-220.q: When did resource extraction reach an industrial scale?
nature-res-220.a: In the 19th century, as mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond earlier levels.

nature-res-244.q: Why does sustainable yield apply only to renewable resources?
nature-res-244.a: Because taking non-renewable resources always shrinks natural capital.

nature-res-221.q: Under efficient extraction, how fast does a resource's net price rise?
nature-res-221.a: Each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate.

nature-res-245.q: How does the World Bank describe the blue economy?
nature-res-245.a: As sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while keeping ocean ecosystems healthy.

nature-res-242.q: In the famous bet, what did Simon expect raw material prices to do?
nature-res-242.a: Not rise in the long run, while Ehrlich expected population growth to outstrip resources.

nature-res-238.q: What makes material in the Earth's crust a mineral resource?
nature-res-238.a: It has reasonable prospects of eventually being extracted at a profit.

nature-res-224.q: How likely to be produced are proven (1P) reserves?

nature-res-202.q: Which book popularised the idea of petro-aggression?
nature-res-202.a: Jeff Colgan's 2013 book, which found petrostates far more likely to start international conflicts.

nature-res-216.q: What is the classic example of a resource nobody needs any more?
nature-res-216.a: Arrowhead-grade flint, since sharpened scrap steel is simpler.

nature-res-230.q: In the resource movement effect, what does a boom do to workers?
nature-res-230.a: It pulls them into the booming sector, called direct deindustrialisation.

nature-res-228.q: Is there an agreed definition of a critical raw material?
nature-res-228.a: No; criticality varies with time, country and context.

nature-res-033.q: How does the FAO define a fishery?
nature-res-033.a: As an activity leading to harvesting fish, whether caught wild or farmed.

nature-res-001.q: When do wild fish stocks count as renewable?
nature-res-001.a: When they produce a yearly surplus that careful management can harvest without lowering future productivity.

nature-res-080.q: Which fields does marine conservation draw on?
nature-res-080.a: Marine biology, ecology, oceanography and fisheries science, plus economics, maritime law and policy.

nature-res-057.q: What mainly causes illegal and unreported fishing?
nature-res-057.a: Failure to enforce existing laws, often rooted in poor national governance.

nature-res-028.a: Depleting the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock.

nature-res-066.q: What is the most common form of recreational fishing?
nature-res-066.a: Angling with rod, reel, line, hooks and bait.

nature-res-082.q: What does the treaty's Multilateral System provide?
nature-res-082.a: Free access to 64 of the world's most important crops for research, breeding and training.

nature-res-015.q: Why do many conservation biologists distrust maximum sustainable yield?
nature-res-015.a: They see it as dangerous and misused, and blame it for the collapse of many fisheries.

nature-res-006.q: How did NOAA honour this tool in 2007?
nature-res-006.a: It named it one of the ten biggest scientific breakthroughs in its 200-year history.

nature-res-012.q: Why was the United States Fish Commission set up?
nature-res-012.a: To find out why New England fisheries were declining.

nature-res-065.q: In the simplest growth model, what is a fish's growth in length proportional to?
nature-res-065.a: The gap between its current length and its ultimate length.

nature-res-042.q: How does a turtle excluder device work?
nature-res-042.a: A grid deflects turtles out of the trawl net through an opening.

nature-res-011.q: Which parts of the sea floor have been trawled repeatedly?
nature-res-011.a: Nearly all continental shelves and large areas of slopes, ridges and seamounts.

nature-res-029.q: What does economic overfishing add to the judgement?
nature-res-029.a: The cost of fishing, making the fishery less profitable than it could be.

nature-res-076.q: Who launched the first seafood certification program?

nature-res-070.q: Where do fisheries data come from?
nature-res-070.a: From the fishery itself, such as recorded landings, and from independent surveys using nets or acoustic and video methods.

nature-res-063.q: Why is virtual population analysis called 'virtual'?
nature-res-063.a: Population size is never measured directly but worked backwards from catches and an assumed natural death rate.

nature-res-020.q: How do catch shares change fishers' lives?
nature-res-020.a: They can schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust cycles fade, and fishing in dangerous weather becomes unnecessary.

nature-res-085.q: How do you get the equilibrium catch for a level of fishing effort?
nature-res-085.a: Set the catch equal to the stock's natural growth.

nature-res-107.q: Into which categories does the IPCC group land?
nature-res-107.a: Forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands.

nature-res-088.q: If the world has enough fresh water, where does scarcity come from?
nature-res-088.a: A mismatch between when and where people need water and when and where it is available.

nature-res-169.q: What do people with high water security have?
nature-res-169.a: Always enough water of acceptable quality for health, livelihoods and production.

nature-res-123.q: At which stage does most food waste arise?

nature-res-160.q: In slash-and-burn farming, why do farmers eventually move on?
nature-res-160.a: After a few years nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade.

nature-res-174.q: Which products do non-wood forest products leave out?

nature-res-093.q: Which three pillars must sustainable forest management balance?

nature-res-151.q: How is prior appropriation often summed up?
nature-res-151.a: 'First in time, first in right': later users take only what is left without harming earlier ones.

nature-res-136.q: Why does using deep, confined aquifers help?
nature-res-136.a: It gives more protection from contamination at the surface.

nature-res-144.q: What tool does land-use planning nearly always rely on?
nature-res-144.a: Land-use regulation, typically zoning, which controls what may happen on a piece of land.

nature-res-120.q: Why is water in endorheic basins often saltier than the ocean?
nature-res-120.a: Where evaporation is the main way water leaves, salt is left behind; the Dead Sea is an extreme case.

nature-res-141.q: What do intensive animal operations aim for?
nature-res-141.a: Maximum output at the lowest cost.

nature-res-104.q: What three principles does integrated water resources management rest on?
nature-res-104.a: Social equity, economic efficiency and ecological sustainability.

nature-res-153.q: How does selective logging differ from clearcutting?
nature-res-153.a: It removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing.

nature-res-158.q: What is coppicing generally used to produce?
nature-res-158.a: Fuelwood, pulpwood and other small-tree products.

nature-res-145.q: What does 'multiple use' mean in forest management?
nature-res-145.a: Managing all a forest's renewable surface resources in the mix that best meets people's needs.

nature-res-164.q: What are the two broad forms of water privatization?
nature-res-164.a: Full privatization, selling assets for good, and public-private partnerships, where the public keeps ownership.

nature-res-100.q: Which big water user is exempt from abstraction charges almost everywhere?
nature-res-100.a: Agriculture, the largest water user worldwide.

nature-res-166.q: Why does so much fresh water cross political boundaries?
nature-res-166.a: Because river basins do not follow national borders.

nature-res-191.q: What did enclosure do to scattered strips of land?
nature-res-191.a: It merged them into large fenced or hedged fields for the sole use of individual owners or their tenants.

nature-res-184.q: Where did Ostrom find farmers running grazing commons successfully?
nature-res-184.a: In the Swiss Alps, for hundreds of years.

nature-res-179.q: Why is stakeholder analysis hard to apply to natural resources?
nature-res-179.a: It is difficult to say who has a stake in a resource.

nature-res-194.q: What two features define common-pool resources?
nature-res-194.a: One person's use reduces what others get, and keeping people out is impractical.

nature-nbs-218.q: What can ecosystem-based adaptation be combined with?
nature-nbs-218.a: Engineered works like dykes, hybrid measures like artificial reefs, and early warning systems.

nature-nbs-221.q: What does a Type 1 nature-based solution involve?
nature-nbs-221.a: Minimal intervention, such as protecting mangroves against storms.

nature-nbs-209.q: What two main problems does unmanaged stormwater cause in cities?

nature-nbs-158.q: What do plants do for microorganisms in a constructed wetland?
nature-nbs-158.a: Roots, stems and leaves give them a surface to grow on while they break down organic material.

nature-nbs-183.q: How do plants and soil in a rain garden help?
nature-nbs-183.a: They hold stormwater and filter out pollutants carried by city runoff.

nature-nbs-178.q: How can zoning rules reduce flood risk?
nature-nbs-178.a: By limiting how much is built on floodplains and other flood-prone areas.

nature-nbs-195.q: What do beaver dams do in their native range?
nature-nbs-195.a: Reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks.

nature-nbs-181.q: What helps decide when to close a storm surge barrier?

nature-nbs-163.q: How much of the rain falling on a green roof can it hold back?
nature-nbs-163.a: Forty to eighty percent, releasing the rest slowly.

nature-nbs-199.q: What does the case for removing a dam weigh?
nature-nbs-199.a: Its benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against its harms.

nature-nbs-159.q: Why keep water below the surface in a treatment wetland?
nature-nbs-159.a: It is more efficient, less smelly, less attractive to mosquitoes and less affected by winter.

nature-nbs-204.q: How does porous asphalt let water through?
nature-nbs-204.a: It leaves out fine aggregate, leaving open voids.

nature-nbs-200.q: What is the downside of rapid release in dam removal?
nature-nbs-200.a: It can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream, though it is quickest and cheapest.

nature-nbs-190.q: What does this river restoration approach reconnect?
nature-nbs-190.a: The stream with its floodplain and along its length, often by removing levees or dams.

nature-nbs-034.q: Which ecosystems does 'blue carbon' most often refer to?
nature-nbs-034.a: Tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows.

nature-nbs-071.q: How does a seawall protect the coast?
nature-nbs-071.a: It reflects wave energy back out to sea, leaving less to cause erosion.

nature-nbs-041.q: What is the big drawback of managed realignment?
nature-nbs-041.a: Land must be given up to the sea, though the new natural areas buffer land further inland.

nature-nbs-037.q: How much of the ocean floor does seagrass cover?
nature-nbs-037.a: Only 0.1%, yet it accounts for roughly 10-18% of ocean carbon burial.

nature-nbs-058.q: Why is it hard to define the shoreline?
nature-nbs-058.a: Coasts keep changing and tides shift its position at any moment.

nature-eco-415.q: How much carbon do mangroves store compared with other tropical forests?

nature-nbs-065.q: Are soft controls like sandbags meant to be permanent?
nature-nbs-065.a: No; they slow erosion only temporarily.

nature-nbs-068.q: What is a main cause of mangrove loss?
nature-nbs-068.a: Expanding shrimp farms, even though shrimp ponds depend on what mangroves provide.

nature-nbs-050.q: What coral ability does micro-fragmentation rely on?
nature-nbs-050.a: Coral's ability to clone itself; it was developed by David Vaughan in 2006.

nature-nbs-019.q: What is the main cause of the urban heat island?
nature-nbs-019.a: How cities change land surfaces; waste heat from energy use is secondary.

nature-nbs-030.q: What do urban forests do for a city?
nature-nbs-030.a: They moderate local climate, slow wind and stormwater, filter air and help cool the heat island.

nature-nbs-021.q: What does a city's albedo measure?
nature-nbs-021.a: Its reflectiveness; dark surfaces absorb heat and lower it.

nature-nbs-013.q: What did experiments show about stress and natural surroundings?
nature-nbs-013.a: People recovered from stress faster and more fully in natural rather than urban surroundings.

nature-nbs-017.q: What social benefit do community gardens often bring?
nature-nbs-017.a: They strengthen local social networks and give neighbourhoods a focus that builds pride.

nature-nbs-008.a: Soak up stormwater, remove air pollutants and give shade that eases the heat island.

nature-nbs-107.q: How does reforestation differ from afforestation?
nature-nbs-107.a: Afforestation makes new forest on land that was not forest before; reforestation replants lost forest.

nature-nbs-109.q: Under the compensated reduction proposal, who would be paid?
nature-nbs-109.a: Developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period.

nature-nbs-111.q: What limits how long reforested land keeps its carbon stored?

nature-nbs-155.q: Besides saving threatened species, what else can reintroduction do?
nature-nbs-155.a: Control pests, such as wolves curbing too many deer.

nature-nbs-154.q: In what order does cleared land regrow into secondary forest?
nature-nbs-154.a: Pioneer species first, then shrubs, then trees of the original forest.

nature-nbs-138.q: What does assisted natural regeneration do to help a forest regrow?
nature-nbs-138.a: It removes barriers to regrowth such as weeds, poor soil and fire-prone grasses, and plants new trees only where needed.

nature-nbs-118.q: Why do land managers often find restoration research unhelpful?
nature-nbs-118.a: They often find the research questions not useful, and studies are often small and controlled, unlike real projects.

nature-nbs-136.q: What objection do some officials raise against strict no-extraction areas, and what is the reply?
nature-nbs-136.a: They say such areas limit people's ability to earn a living; others reply that ecotourism creates jobs.

nature-nbs-141.q: Which campaign did this tree-planting program grow out of?
nature-nbs-141.a: The Billion Tree Campaign, inspired by Wangari Maathai and launched by UNEP in 2006.

nature-nbs-157.q: How do the benefits of restoring ecosystems compare with what it costs?
nature-nbs-157.a: On average the benefits are ten times the initial investment, and doing nothing costs at least three times as much as restoring.

nature-nbs-144.q: In Australia, what backs the legal duty to rehabilitate mines?
nature-nbs-144.a: Bonds: rehabilitation is a legal duty backed by bonds, and enforcing it could create regional jobs and investment.

nature-nbs-130.q: What yearly benefit was estimated for restoring 20% of Scotland's peatland?

nature-nbs-226.q: What is the overall goal of carbon farming?
nature-nbs-226.a: A net removal of carbon from the air, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked into soil and plants.

nature-nbs-290.q: What does no-till farming do for the soil?
nature-nbs-290.a: It reduces erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils, and can improve water soaking in, organic matter and nutrient cycling.

nature-nbs-247.q: What kinds of products can a forest garden yield?
nature-nbs-247.a: Timber, fruit, nuts, mushrooms, medicinal plants, animals and other products.

nature-nbs-239.q: In the land sparing versus sharing debate, which side tends to win for what?
nature-nbs-239.a: Sparing tends to win for tropical forest wildlife, sharing for food security and livelihoods.

nature-nbs-263.a: A form of agroforestry that uses managed grazing.

nature-nbs-268.q: Why does nitrate from fertilizer end up in water?
nature-nbs-268.a: It dissolves easily, so it runs off into surface water and leaches into groundwater.

nature-nbs-277.q: What did the three-field system gain over the two-field system?
nature-nbs-277.a: Two thirds of the land was planted instead of half, and the legume crops improved people's nutrition.

nature-nbs-249.q: Why is shade-grown coffee a good example of agroforestry?
nature-nbs-249.a: Shading cuts weeding costs and improves coffee quality.

nature-nbs-308.q: Why is salt in soil a problem?
nature-nbs-308.a: Salt breaks down soil structure and makes it infertile.

nature-nbs-227.q: When do bamboo plantations take up carbon faster than mature forests?
nature-nbs-227.a: Only when they are new or actively managed.

nature-nbs-301.q: How can buried wood help crops in a dry season?
nature-nbs-301.a: Enough buried wood can hold rainy-season water to carry crops through the dry season.

nature-nbs-303.a: It absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion.

nature-nbs-250.q: What does syntropic farming rely on?
nature-nbs-250.a: Dense mixed planting of long-lived and yearly crops, and cutting fast-growing pioneer plants to build up nutrients.

nature-nbs-257.q: What happens once pests gather on a trap crop?
nature-nbs-257.a: The small trap area can be treated or the pests removed by hand or machine.

nature-nbs-273.a: The amount of manure to transport, the nutrients to spread and the germs.

nature-nbs-264.q: Since Roman times, why have pigs been turned into beech and oak woods?
nature-nbs-264.a: To eat acorns and beech nuts.

nature-nbs-244.q: How do farmers take part in agri-environment schemes?
nature-nbs-244.a: They join voluntarily and commit for at least five years.

nature-nbs-266.q: How does the FAO describe integrated pest management?
nature-nbs-266.a: As combining biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use.

nature-nbs-075.q: Where does the word 'greenwashing' come from?

nature-nbs-098.q: How did plantations' share of global forest compare with their share of wood supply in 2000?
nature-nbs-098.a: They were 5% of global forest but supplied about 35% of the world's roundwood.

nature-nbs-088.q: Why did forests absorb less carbon in 2019 than in the 1990s?
nature-nbs-088.a: Heat, drought and deforestation; forests can switch from soaking up carbon to releasing it.

nature-nbs-083.q: What is the danger of all crops in a region being genetically alike?
nature-nbs-083.a: One disease they cannot resist can wipe out entire crops.

nature-nbs-096.q: When is a scoping review often done?
nature-nbs-096.a: Before a systematic review, to judge whether a full review is possible or worthwhile.

nature-clim-222.q: What two kinds of climate risk does it cover?
nature-clim-222.a: Physical risks, such as extreme weather, and transition risks, the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.

nature-clim-248.q: What is the goal of an integrated assessment model?
nature-clim-248.a: To inform policy-making, usually on climate change.

nature-clim-260.q: How much of greenhouse gas emissions comes from burning fuels for energy?
nature-clim-260.a: About two-thirds; the rest comes from other processes.

nature-clim-228.q: How do estimates of climate damage change as the world warms?
nature-clim-228.a: They rise faster and faster, not in a straight line, as global average temperature rises.

nature-clim-251.a: Technology networks and the institutions and habits that benefit from them grow together, fed by returns that increase with size.

nature-clim-231.q: What is the most widely cited way to share the costs of cutting emissions?
nature-clim-231.a: Equal entitlements per person, drawn from egalitarianism.

nature-clim-242.q: What does a low discount rate mean for future welfare?
nature-clim-242.a: A low rate of 1–2% values future welfare nearly equal to today's, while a high rate of 4–5% heavily discounts future damages.

nature-clim-249.q: What have integrated assessment models been used to explore?
nature-clim-249.a: Pathways for meeting targets such as the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C goal.

nature-clim-266.q: How does robust decision-making judge policies?
nature-clim-266.a: By robustness rather than being the best, often accepting a slightly worse best case for less sensitivity to wrong assumptions.

nature-clim-108.q: What are the two main motives for energy efficiency?
nature-clim-108.a: Saving running costs and cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-clim-109.q: How can fuel-efficient cars cancel some of their own savings?
nature-clim-109.a: Travel gets cheaper, so drivers may go farther.

nature-clim-130.q: What traits of wind and solar power make grids harder to run?
nature-clim-130.a: Unpredictability, variability and low operating costs, which make matching supply and demand harder.

nature-clim-151.q: Name ways to conserve energy without any efficiency gain.
nature-clim-151.a: Heating a room less, driving less, air-drying clothes and using a computer's power-saving mode.

nature-clim-132.q: What is expected to become the largest source of energy storage?
nature-clim-132.a: Electric vehicles, which charge when production is high and sometimes feed power back to the grid.

nature-clim-107.a: Power saved by users who commit to cut use at peak times; Amory Lovins coined the term in 1985.

nature-clim-118.q: In learning curves, what is the progress ratio b?
nature-clim-118.a: The share of cost left after each doubling of output; one minus b is the learning rate.

nature-clim-149.q: How does the IPCC define climate change mitigation?
nature-clim-149.a: A human action to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases.

nature-clim-185.q: What is most captured CO2 used for?
nature-clim-185.a: Around 80% goes to enhanced oil recovery, which is why CCS is also called CCUS.

nature-clim-159.q: What are the world's two most important carbon sinks?

nature-clim-209.q: Which sources count as low-carbon electricity?
nature-clim-209.a: Wind, solar, nuclear and most hydropower; fossil plants count only with carbon capture.

nature-clim-154.q: Why can focusing on risks produce deadlock?
nature-clim-154.a: Because people weigh possible losses more than benefits.

nature-clim-146.q: How can mineral carbonation be sped up, and at what cost?
nature-clim-146.a: With heat, pressure, catalysts or grinding minerals, but this needs extra energy.

nature-clim-187.q: What harms come from burning more fuel to run carbon capture?
nature-clim-187.a: More upstream harm such as mining and methane leaks, and possibly more local air pollution.

nature-clim-205.q: Why is responsibility for emissions shared between consumer and producer?
nature-clim-205.a: The consumer starts production, but the producing country also gains GDP from it.

nature-clim-192.q: How does direct air capture differ from CCS?
nature-clim-192.a: CCS captures CO2 at a source like a factory; direct air capture lowers the CO2 level of the whole atmosphere.

nature-clim-166.q: What is a main reason many net zero claims lack credibility?

nature-clim-165.q: Why can net zero for CO2 be reached sooner than for all greenhouse gases?
nature-clim-165.a: Partly because farm methane is harder to phase out.

nature-clim-163.q: Why must removals that balance CO2 last much longer than those for methane?
nature-clim-163.a: Methane lasts around 12 years in the air, but CO2 lasts 300 to 1,000 years.

nature-clim-212.q: Why are sulfates the usual proposal for stratospheric aerosol injection?
nature-clim-212.a: Because volcanic eruptions release them naturally.

nature-clim-215.q: What share of world energy use comes from fossil fuels?
nature-clim-215.a: 85%, and the energy system causes 76% of greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-clim-172.q: What are the three dimensions of energy justice?

nature-clim-176.q: Who is affected by stranded asset risk?
nature-clim-176.a: Oil, gas and coal companies, industries like steel, aluminium and cement, and fossil-exporting countries and workers.

nature-clim-171.q: How is the energy transition expected to change trade?
nature-clim-171.a: It should reduce reliance on long-distance fossil fuel trade and raise the role of regional markets.

nature-clim-188.q: What did the 2023 UN climate conference agree about coal, and what was the criticism?
nature-clim-188.a: To phase down unabated coal, but it left 'abated' undefined, which critics say invites abuse.

nature-clim-002.q: Give examples of climate change adaptation.
nature-clim-002.a: Seawalls, new insurance schemes, changing crop planting times and installing green roofs.

nature-clim-001.a: As a stock of resources and assets from which adaptations can be drawn as future conditions require.

nature-clim-027.q: How did the IPCC's Fifth report change the treatment of exposure?
nature-clim-027.a: Earlier reports made vulnerability depend on exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity; the Fifth moved exposure to be a separate part of risk.

nature-clim-018.q: What is the difference between 'loss' and 'damage'?
nature-clim-018.a: Loss is harm that cannot be undone, like extinction; damage is harm that can be repaired or compensated.

nature-clim-034.q: What does a complete early warning system cover?
nature-clim-034.a: Risk analysis, monitoring and warning, spreading and communicating alerts, and ability to respond.

nature-clim-003.q: Name institutional responses to climate change.
nature-clim-003.a: Zoning rules, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination.

nature-clim-030.q: What did Roy Rappaport study among the Maring of Papua New Guinea?
nature-clim-030.a: The role of ritual in the relationship between culture and nature.

nature-clim-028.a: Poverty, poor governance and conflict; it is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more.

nature-clim-040.q: Why may flood maps based on older data understate hazards?

nature-clim-086.q: Where and when did the fossil fuel divestment movement begin?

nature-clim-071.q: What is the principle of progression for NDCs?
nature-clim-071.a: NDCs must be renewed every five years, each more ambitious than the last.

nature-clim-084.q: Why did developed countries agree to take greater responsibility for cutting emissions?
nature-clim-084.a: They industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change.

nature-clim-076.q: How is countries' progress toward their NDCs checked?
nature-clim-076.a: By technical expert review, which they are legally bound to undergo.

nature-clim-065.q: How often must developed countries submit a national communication?
nature-clim-065.a: Every four years; developing countries should do so.

nature-clim-075.q: What did UNEP say in 2020 about current commitments?
nature-clim-075.a: They would likely lead to more than 3 °C of warming by 2100.

nature-clim-087.q: What change was made late in the Glasgow talks about coal?
nature-clim-087.a: 'Phase out' was changed to 'phase down', urged by coal-reliant countries such as India and China.

nature-clim-051.q: Where was the Green Climate Fund formally established?
nature-clim-051.a: At the 2010 Cancun conference, after being named in the 2009 Copenhagen Accord.

nature-clim-052.q: What does 'new' mean for climate finance pledges?
nature-clim-052.a: Pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years.

nature-clim-070.q: What kinds of double counting does it guard against?
nature-clim-070.a: Double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit.

nature-clim-085.q: How does Contraction and Convergence set emission entitlements?
nature-clim-085.a: They start from current emissions and move toward equal shares per person at a negotiated pace.

nature-clim-081.q: What idea does climate debt rest on?
nature-clim-081.a: That poorer nations suffer the worst effects of a problem they did little to cause.

nature-eecon-059.q: How does ecological economics see the economy?
nature-eecon-059.a: As a subsystem of Earth's larger ecosystem, stressing keeping natural capital intact.

nature-eecon-064.q: What happened to the value of bee pollination near a Costa Rican farm?
nature-eecon-064.a: When coffee prices fell the fields were replanted with pineapple, which needs no bees, so the value vanished.

nature-eecon-109.q: Why is energy at a high temperature more useful?
nature-eecon-109.a: It has lower entropy, which marks more useful energy.

nature-eecon-095.q: What does embodied energy aim to add up?
nature-eecon-095.a: The energy of a product's whole life, from extracting raw materials and transport to manufacture, installation and disposal.

nature-eecon-093.q: What is the most basic feature of Buddhist economics?
nature-eecon-093.a: Seeing people as interdependent with one another and with nature.

nature-eecon-069.q: What are system dynamics and GIS used for in ecological economics?

nature-eecon-067.a: A South American 'Good Life' movement that rejects the western development model and does not value piling up material goods.

nature-eecon-076.q: How does ecological economics view technology?
nature-eecon-076.a: As the way natural resources are transformed in production.

nature-eecon-085.q: What roles do Southern countries play in ecologically unequal exchange?
nature-eecon-085.a: Sources of raw materials, sinks for waste and sites of 'sacrifice zones', deepening global inequality.

nature-eecon-132.q: What does energetics in ecology look for?
nature-eecon-132.a: The principles governing energy flow through the feeding levels of ecological networks.

nature-eecon-099.q: How does emergy put different energy sources on a common basis?
nature-eecon-099.a: By expressing each in the solar energy needed to produce it, measured in solar emjoules.

nature-eecon-108.q: What can overcome some problems of energy payback limits?
nature-eecon-108.a: A solar breeder, a panel factory powered by its own panels.

nature-eecon-163.q: Why might growth driven by knowledge still not solve the problem of scale?
nature-eecon-163.a: Faster computers lead to more computers being bought.

nature-eecon-078.q: Why did Georgescu-Roegen think the world economy heads for collapse?
nature-eecon-078.a: Earth's carrying capacity will fall as finite minerals are extracted.

nature-eecon-084.q: How does the economy behave in long stagnation?
nature-eecon-084.a: It works more and more like a zero-sum system.

nature-eecon-101.q: What does the emergy sustainability index combine, and what do its two parts measure?
nature-eecon-101.a: It is the emergy yield ratio divided by the environmental loading ratio. The yield ratio shows how much an investment lets a process tap local resources; the loading ratio compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy and signals stress on ecosystems.

nature-eecon-087.q: What main energy source marks each of the three broad energy regimes in human history?
nature-eecon-087.a: Hunter-gatherers lived on 'passive solar energy' from recent plant growth; farming societies after the Neolithic Revolution used 'active solar energy' by clearing land for crops; the industrial regime relies mainly on fossil fuels.

nature-eecon-139.q: How did Richard Norgaard use the idea of coevolution in ecological economics?
nature-eecon-139.a: He showed how pests coevolved with pesticides and with the institutions that regulate them, carrying an idea from biology, where two species evolve together, into the study of economies and ecosystems.

nature-eecon-092.q: When did this approach begin, and what does it try to balance?
nature-eecon-092.a: It began in the mid-1980s and aims to balance economic efficiency with environmental efficiency.

nature-eecon-225.q: In the Cobb-Douglas production function, what happens to output when the exponents add up to exactly 1, less than 1, or more than 1?
nature-eecon-225.a: If they sum to 1, returns to scale are constant; below 1 they are decreasing; above 1 they are increasing.

nature-eecon-213.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic barriers to sustainable development?
nature-eecon-213.a: Intrinsic barriers come from nature's complexity and the human condition, such as the value-action gap where people do not act on their beliefs. Extrinsic barriers can be overcome, for example by putting a price on using public goods.

nature-eecon-222.q: What definition of sustainable development did the Brundtland Commission's report make popular?
nature-eecon-222.a: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

nature-eecon-218.q: Why does strong sustainability refuse to trade natural assets for human-made ones?
nature-eecon-218.a: It holds that the environment performs some functions that people and human-made capital cannot duplicate, such as the ozone layer's protection, so nature must be passed on intact to the next generation.

nature-eecon-220.q: What does weak sustainability say governments should aim for with genuine savings?
nature-eecon-220.a: They should keep genuine savings, a measure of net investment in capital, at or above zero; a positive value is linked to possible long-run sustainability.

nature-eecon-203.q: What shape do most non-human populations follow as they grow, and when does it level off?
nature-eecon-203.a: They follow a logistic, S-shaped path rather than exponential growth, levelling off at carrying capacity, usually when the population has used up most of its natural resources.

nature-eecon-205.q: What does total factor productivity include besides technological progress, and how do economists separate it out?
nature-eecon-205.a: It also includes lasting gains in how efficiently inputs are combined. Economists use Solow's growth accounting to separate the effects of technology, capital and labour on growth.

nature-eecon-154.q: What computer model did The Limits to Growth use, and what did it conclude about continued growth?
nature-eecon-154.a: It used the World3 model, built on Jay Forrester's work at MIT. It concluded that if growth trends continued unchanged, limits would be reached within a hundred years, probably with a sudden fall in population and industry, but that a stable, sustainable balance was still possible.

nature-eecon-143.q: Why does degrowth reject GDP growth as a goal?
nature-eecon-143.a: It argues that capitalism's focus on growth causes wide ecological damage and is not needed to raise living standards, so GDP growth is a poor measure of human development.

nature-eecon-146.q: In the doughnut model, what do the inner hole and the outer crust stand for?
nature-eecon-146.a: The hole stands for people lacking life's essentials such as healthcare and education; the outer crust stands for ecological ceilings that must not be overshot.

nature-eecon-173.q: What is global ecological overshoot, and what day marks it each year?
nature-eecon-173.a: It is when humanity demands more than Earth's biosphere can renew. Earth Overshoot Day marks the date each year when humanity's resource use passes what Earth can regenerate that year.

nature-eecon-194.q: What are the three sustainability strategies in Joseph Huber's triad?
nature-eecon-194.a: Sufficiency, which cuts consumption and production without threatening needs; efficiency, which cuts resource use per unit of output; and consistency, which shifts to ways of producing more in tune with nature, such as renewable energy and circular design.

nature-eecon-151.q: What did a 2020 study find about decoupling economic growth from environmental harm?
nature-eecon-151.a: It found no evidence of economy-wide decoupling at national or international level, and studies found absolute decoupling to be rare.

nature-eecon-193.q: How can resource productivity be expressed, using irrigation water as an example?
nature-eecon-193.a: As money earned per unit of resource, such as 'crop per drop' of irrigation water.

nature-eecon-157.q: What did Graham Turner find in 2008 when he compared real data with The Limits to Growth?
nature-eecon-157.a: Thirty years of data on industrial production, food production and pollution matched the book's 'business as usual' scenario, which leads to collapse in the 21st century.

nature-eecon-166.q: What pattern does steel production follow as economies grow, and in which countries?
nature-eecon-166.a: It follows a Kuznets-type curve, rising and then falling, in economies including the United States, Japan, South Korea and China.

nature-eecon-145.q: How does agrowth differ from green growth?
nature-eecon-145.a: Green growth holds that growth and sustainability are compatible; agrowth is agnostic about growth and focuses on cutting environmental harm with effective tools whether the economy grows or shrinks.

nature-eecon-175.q: Why has the environmental space concept been largely replaced by the ecological footprint?
nature-eecon-175.a: Environmental space needs the maximum sustainable use of every resource, which is hard to estimate, and each resource has its own units, so the spaces cannot be added up. The ecological footprint converts all resource use into land area.

nature-eecon-038.q: Where does recycling sit in the 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' hierarchy, and what does it save?
nature-eecon-038.a: It is the third step. It saves materials and energy and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution from burning waste and water pollution from landfills.

nature-eecon-044.q: Why does the potential for resource recovery shrink over a product's life?
nature-eecon-044.a: Because materials become irreversibly mixed and diluted, their entropy rising, as they go through manufacture, use and landfilling.

nature-eecon-050.q: What spare capacity does the sharing economy put to use, and what is the classic example?
nature-eecon-050.a: It puts unused capacity in goods and services to work; the classic example is that the average car sits unused most of the time.

nature-eecon-055.q: What does waste valorisation usually mean, and why do industrial wastes suit it best?
nature-eecon-055.a: It usually means using the residue of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another. Industrial wastes suit it best because they are more consistent and predictable than household waste.

nature-eecon-041.q: Which recycling collection method gives the purest recycled materials?
nature-eecon-041.a: Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection.

nature-eecon-005.q: What was the first circular economy standard, and who launched it?
nature-eecon-005.a: BS 8001:2017, launched by the British Standards Institution in 2017.

nature-eecon-048.q: What are some examples of reusing waste items for a new purpose?
nature-eecon-048.a: Tyres used as boat fenders, drums used as feeding troughs or compost bins, and Earthship houses that use tyres as insulating walls and bottles as glass walls.

nature-eecon-058.q: What does the zero waste hierarchy add to the 3Rs, and who is it meant for?
nature-eecon-058.a: It adds depth to the 3Rs and encourages policy and investment at the top of the hierarchy. It is meant for everyone from policymakers to industry and individuals, and helps evaluate proposed solutions.

nature-eecon-027.q: What does eco-efficiency mean, and how is it measured?
nature-eecon-027.a: It means creating more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution. It is measured as the value produced, such as GDP, divided by environmental impact, such as CO2 emissions.

nature-eecon-018.q: What do firms in an eco-industrial park exchange with one another?
nature-eecon-018.a: They physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, for example sharing waste treatment and reusing one plant's processed water in another.

nature-eecon-023.q: How does source reduction cut waste, and what is it sometimes called?
nature-eecon-023.a: It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product formulation, and is sometimes called pollution prevention.

nature-eecon-030.q: Does integrated product policy rely on a single measure?
nature-eecon-030.a: No. It combines economic instruments, substance bans, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines.

nature-gov-159.q: What does environmental resource management aim to protect, and what does it weigh?
nature-gov-159.a: It aims to protect ecosystem services for future generations and keep ecosystems intact, weighing ethical, economic and ecological factors.

nature-gov-135.q: How does the European Green Deal deal with countries that cut emissions more slowly?
nature-gov-135.a: It puts carbon tariffs on them through the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.

nature-gov-116.q: What did the Craigheads find about Yellowstone's grizzly bears, and why did it matter?
nature-gov-116.a: They found the bears could not survive within park boundaries alone, which supported defining ecosystems more broadly than park lines.

nature-gov-131.q: Why did climate change litigation grow?
nature-gov-131.a: Activists and lawyers turned to the courts because climate politics was slow to deliver cuts in emissions.

nature-gov-142.q: What does UNCLOS give each coastal state in its exclusive economic zone?
nature-gov-142.a: Exclusive rights to fisheries, minerals and seabed deposits out to 200 nautical miles.

nature-gov-128.q: Which organisation is widely seen as a model of carrying out Agenda 21 at the local level?
nature-gov-128.a: ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990.

nature-gov-136.q: Why were the negotiations over the Forest Principles complicated?
nature-gov-136.a: Developing nations in the Group of 77 sought more aid to pay for forest reserves, so the final text was a compromise.

nature-gov-138.q: What is an example of governance through goals?
nature-gov-138.a: The Sustainable Development Goals for 2015 to 2030, which followed the Millennium Development Goals of 2000 to 2015.

nature-gov-144.q: Under uncertainty about irreversible harm, how should decisions be made and who should bear the burden of proof?
nature-gov-144.a: Decisions should err on the side of caution, and the burden of proof should fall on those whose activities may cause damage.

nature-gov-160.q: Why was IPBES established, and when?
nature-gov-160.a: Governments set it up in 2012 to strengthen the link between science and policy for biodiversity and ecosystem services.

nature-gov-010.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there, and what do they link?
nature-gov-010.a: There are 17 goals with 169 measurable targets, linking the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development.

nature-gov-052.q: What older idea did the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea replace?
nature-gov-052.a: The 17th-century 'freedom of the seas', under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation.

nature-gov-055.q: How does the UN Convention to Combat Desertification define desertification?
nature-gov-055.a: As land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions caused by climate variations and human activities.

nature-gov-051.q: What did a country have to do to join the Ramsar Convention?
nature-gov-051.a: It had to designate at least one wetland site and guarantee its protection.

nature-gov-014.q: Which UN process is one route for financing the SDGs, and what kind of money is seen as essential?
nature-gov-014.a: The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda; private investment is seen as essential.

nature-gov-024.q: What does Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the '30 by 30' target, ask of governments?
nature-gov-024.a: It asks them to protect 30% of Earth's land and water area by 2030.

nature-gov-056.q: What did the World Charter for Nature first give international recognition to?
nature-gov-056.a: A strong form of the precautionary principle.

nature-gov-029.q: What is the main management challenge for protected marine areas and shared waters?
nature-gov-029.a: Inadequate monitoring and enforcement of protection measures.

nature-gov-022.q: What did the 2019 IPBES Global Assessment find was needed to reach global development goals?
nature-gov-022.a: Only transformative change can achieve them, and it warned that society should not focus solely on economic growth given the loss of biodiversity.

nature-gov-037.q: What is often blamed for the Nagoya Protocol's failure?

nature-gov-184.q: Why has the UN adopted no definition of Indigenous peoples?
nature-gov-184.a: Its Permanent Forum holds that any single definition would include too many or too few groups.

nature-gov-209.q: How can extraction on a large scale turn renewable resources into non-renewable ones?
nature-gov-209.a: By taking them faster than nature can replace them.

nature-gov-186.q: How does climate change disrupt Indigenous farming?
nature-gov-186.a: Indigenous farmers have long timed crops by signs such as wind direction, blooming and bird migration, and climate change disrupts these signs.

nature-gov-193.q: Why are poor people hit harder by climate change?
nature-gov-193.a: They face more exposure and vulnerability, so they are less able to cope with climate extremes; for a poor household a disaster, bad harvest or illness can be a crippling economic shock.

nature-gov-179.q: What does the Nagoya Protocol require before someone accesses genetic resources?
nature-gov-179.a: Access must take place with prior informed consent and on mutually agreed terms.

nature-gov-167.q: How did the UN Human Rights Council treat environmental defenders in 2019?
nature-gov-167.a: It unanimously recognised their importance for environmental protection.

nature-gov-171.q: Why do some scholars say distributive justice fits poorly with many Indigenous worldviews?
nature-gov-171.a: Scholars such as Dina Gilio-Whitaker argue it assumes land is a commodity, which clashes with many Indigenous worldviews.

nature-gov-214.q: What marks an Indigenous and community conserved area (ICCA)?
nature-gov-214.a: A strong bond between a community and a site, the community's leading role in managing it, and conservation results even when conservation is not the aim.

nature-gov-178.q: Why did the Karuk and Yurok Tribes of California organise controlled burns?
nature-gov-178.a: To reduce wildfire risk and restore resources depleted by decades of keeping fire out of their ancestral lands.

nature-gov-192.q: What did the San people receive after demanding restitution over the Hoodia patent?
nature-gov-192.a: A confidential agreement gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

nature-gov-224.q: How are sacrifice zones linked to 'abundance zones'?
nature-gov-224.a: Damage in some places sustains privileges and lifestyles elsewhere.

nature-gov-195.q: What example did Philip Alston give of climate apartheid?
nature-gov-195.a: During Superstorm Sandy in 2012, most of New York lost power while Goldman Sachs's headquarters had its own generator and sandbags.

nature-gov-183.q: How does the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples handle the question of who is Indigenous?
nature-gov-183.a: It does not define Indigenous peoples but affirms their right to decide their own identity.

nature-gov-188.q: How does the International Organization for Migration define environmental migrants?
nature-gov-188.a: As people obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives.

nature-gov-223.q: What does Ecuador's 2008 constitution grant to nature?
nature-gov-223.a: It gives nature, or Pachamama, the right to exist and regenerate its vital cycles, and lets any person demand that those rights be respected.

nature-gov-006.q: What gave rise to the global environmental justice and climate justice movements?
nature-gov-006.a: The unfair split of environmental burdens and benefits, with the poor tending to suffer most from environmental damage caused by exploiting natural resources.

nature-gov-009.q: Who mostly benefits from water consumption subsidies?
nature-gov-009.a: Those connected to the supply grid, typically the richer, urban population outside informal housing.

nature-gov-059.q: What is the triple bottom line that green businesses aim for?
nature-gov-059.a: Profit, people and planet, weighing economic, social and environmental factors in their decisions.

nature-gov-066.q: What tool is used in green product design to compare design options?
nature-gov-066.a: Life-cycle assessment, used to compare options and pick the least harmful.

nature-gov-102.q: What issues does sustainability reporting cover, and what acronym groups them?
nature-gov-102.a: Environmental, social, economic and governance issues; the criteria are grouped under ESG.

nature-gov-092.q: What do scholars see as the key difference between corporate sustainability and corporate social responsibility?
nature-gov-092.a: Time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations.

nature-gov-075.q: Why do firms mainly engage in corporate social responsibility, according to a large review?
nature-gov-075.a: Mainly for expected financial gain rather than a wish to serve society.

nature-gov-073.q: Is there a single fixed standard for social and environmental accounting?
nature-gov-073.a: No. Frameworks include AA1000, the Global Reporting Initiative guidelines and ISO 14000.

nature-gov-089.q: Why is regulation often needed to get businesses to invest in energy efficiency?
nature-gov-089.a: Energy efficiency often pays off only in the medium to long term, while shareholders want short-term results.

nature-gov-087.q: What does the Science Based Targets initiative do?
nature-gov-087.a: Set up in 2015, it helps companies set emission-cutting targets and checks, or validates, them.

nature-gov-098.q: What made the EU taxonomy's Complementary Climate Delegated Act controversial?
nature-gov-098.a: It listed certain gas and nuclear activities as transitional activities that help mitigate climate change.

nature-gov-091.q: What do researchers argue should be done about 'carbon bombs'?
nature-gov-091.a: Defusing them, the large coal, oil and gas projects, should be a priority for climate policy.

nature-gov-103.q: Which companies must report under the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive?
nature-gov-103.a: Those exceeding two of three thresholds: 250 employees, a €25 million balance sheet, or €50 million net turnover.

nature-hist-002.q: What UN agency did the 1972 Stockholm conference create, and where is it based?
nature-hist-002.a: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi.

nature-hist-006.q: Why did Rachel Carson say pesticides should be called 'biocides'?
nature-hist-006.a: Because their effects rarely stop at the target pests; they harm the wider environment.

nature-hist-001.q: Who launched TEEB, and in response to what?
nature-hist-001.a: Germany and the European Commission launched it in 2007, answering a proposal by G8+5 environment ministers for a global study of the economics of biodiversity loss.

nature-hist-020.q: Why do critics say The Population Bomb's forecasts went wrong?
nature-hist-020.a: Julian Simon and Hans Rosling argued they wrongly assumed exponential growth would continue with no technological or social progress; instead the global death rate kept falling and calories per person rose.

nature-hist-013.q: How did Adam Smith see the relationship between market prices and natural prices?
nature-hist-013.a: Market prices are drawn toward natural prices, somewhat like gravity; the natural price is the sum of the natural rates of wages, profits and rent.

nature-hist-040.q: What measure did Herman Daly and John B. Cobb propose as a better gauge of progress than GDP?
nature-hist-040.a: The Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, in 1989.

nature-hist-077.a: Jevons argued that improving energy efficiency lowers energy costs and so increases rather than decreases energy use.

nature-hist-050.q: What did William Nordhaus win the Nobel prize for, and what models did he build?
nature-hist-050.a: He shared the 2018 prize for building climate change into long-run economic analysis, and developed the DICE and RICE models linking economics, energy use and climate change.

nature-hist-060.q: Which term did E. F. Schumacher first coin in Small Is Beautiful?

nature-hist-076.q: Why, in William Forster Lloyd's example, do herders overuse a shared pasture?
nature-hist-076.a: An extra animal on the common takes food shared among everyone's cattle, so only a small part of the cost falls on its owner.

nature-hist-043.q: What did Kenneth Boulding's essay on 'Spaceship Earth' argue?
nature-hist-043.a: That the economy must fit itself to an ecological system with limited resources.

nature-hist-057.q: What did David Pearce argue about the price of the environment?
nature-hist-057.a: That the environment is under-priced and that the benefits of environmental services can be calculated.

nature-hist-054.q: What did Allen Kneese's research add to economic models?
nature-hist-054.a: It built pollution into economic models and studied economic incentives for environmental improvement.

nature-hist-073.q: Where did Sergei Podolinsky say the resources available to people ultimately come from?
nature-hist-073.a: He held that human labour only changes natural objects, and that available resources grow only through photosynthesis capturing the Sun's energy.

nature-hist-031.q: When and why was UNEP created, and where is it based?
nature-hist-031.a: It was created in 1972 after the Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment and is based in Nairobi, Kenya.

nature-hist-033.q: What does the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market do with carbon credits?
nature-hist-033.a: It assesses carbon crediting programs and approves categories of credits, which may then carry a CCP-Approved label.

eed7e11d5f5e.title: Ecosystem
eed7e11d5f5e.sentence: An ecosystem (or ecological system) is a system formed by organisms in interaction with their environment, where the biotic and abiotic components are linked together through nutrient cycles and energy flows.

7e650a7eb1f1.title: Ecosystem
7e650a7eb1f1.sentence: Biotic factors are living things, such as plants, while abiotic factors are non-living components, such as soil.

e7d75998df20.title: Ecosystem
e7d75998df20.sentence: Plants allow energy to enter the system through photosynthesis, building up plant tissue.

dcc1d5eb9ca5.title: Ecosystem
dcc1d5eb9ca5.sentence: Animals play an important role in the movement of matter and energy through the system, by feeding on plants and one another.

d4616e5f5efd.title: Ecosystem
d4616e5f5efd.sentence: By breaking down dead organic matter, decomposers release carbon back to the atmosphere and facilitate nutrient cycling by converting nutrients stored in dead biomass back to a form that can be readily used by plants and microbes.

d0bff160edba.title: Ecosystem
d0bff160edba.sentence: External factors—including climate—control the ecosystem's structure, but are not influenced by it.

4bfe819ec925.title: Ecosystem
4bfe819ec925.sentence: By contrast, internal factors control and are controlled by ecosystem processes; these include decomposition, the types of species present, root competition, shading, disturbance, and succession.

9955cf074f80.title: Ecosystem
9955cf074f80.sentence: Ecosystems are dynamic, subject to periodic disturbances and always in the process of recovering from past disturbances.

4f3a928b2fcb.title: Ecosystem
4f3a928b2fcb.sentence: Its capacity to absorb disturbance and reorganize, while undergoing change so as to retain essentially the same function, structure, identity, is termed its ecological resilience.

7ea9a22d2600.title: Ecosystem
7ea9a22d2600.sentence: The size of ecosystems can range up to ten orders of magnitude, from the surface layers of rocks to the surface of the planet.

ad8200aa4821.title: Ecosystem
ad8200aa4821.section: Definition > Origin and development of the term
ad8200aa4821.sentence: The term "ecosystem" was first used in 1935 in a publication by British ecologist Arthur Tansley.

b1d44ebff77f.title: Ecosystem
b1d44ebff77f.section: Definition > Origin and development of the term
b1d44ebff77f.sentence: The term was coined by Arthur Roy Clapham, who came up with the word at Tansley's request.

d84d524c01a3.title: Ecosystem
d84d524c01a3.sentence: Ecosystem goods include the "tangible, material products" of ecosystem processes such as water, food, fuel, construction material, and medicinal plants.

fd3f9c7c1d10.title: Ecosystem
fd3f9c7c1d10.sentence: These include maintenance of hydrological cycles, cleaning air and water, the maintenance of oxygen in the atmosphere, crop pollination, and opportunities for research.

85539cf7ed5c.title: Ecosystem
85539cf7ed5c.sentence: Many ecosystems become degraded through human impacts, such as soil loss, air and water pollution, habitat fragmentation, water diversion, fire suppression, and introduced species and invasive species.

39ff51047d16.title: Ecosystem
39ff51047d16.sentence: Once the original ecosystem has lost its defining features, it is considered "collapsed".

2ae4e719508e.title: Biodiversity
2ae4e719508e.sentence: Biodiversity is the variability of life on Earth.

c00c468f7db1.title: Biodiversity
c00c468f7db1.sentence: It can be measured on various levels, for example, genetic variability, species diversity, ecosystem diversity, and phylogenetic diversity.

2795e2922203.title: Biodiversity
2795e2922203.sentence: Biologists most often define biodiversity as the "totality of genes, species and ecosystems of a region".

63d57fa3fcc6.title: Biodiversity
63d57fa3fcc6.sentence: Diversity is not distributed evenly on Earth — it is greater in the tropics as a result of the warm climate and high primary productivity in the region near the equator.

2ff8f3bc5088.title: Biodiversity
2ff8f3bc5088.sentence: Tropical forest ecosystems cover less than one-fifth of Earth's terrestrial area and contain about 50% of the world's species.

04e8833c3f1d.title: Biodiversity
04e8833c3f1d.sentence: According to estimates by Mora et al. (2011), there are approximately 8.7 million terrestrial species and 2.2 million oceanic species.

557d17e0aba3.title: Biodiversity
557d17e0aba3.sentence: Human activities have led to an ongoing biodiversity loss and an accompanying loss of genetic diversity.

81e0f3a2d67a.title: Biodiversity
81e0f3a2d67a.sentence: This process is often referred to as Holocene extinction, or the sixth mass extinction.

b98ec3afd1be.title: Biodiversity
b98ec3afd1be.sentence: Destroying habitats for farming is a key reason why biodiversity is decreasing today.

b1acee7a8f18.title: Biodiversity
b1acee7a8f18.section: Role and benefits of biodiversity > Ecosystem services > Provisioning services
b1acee7a8f18.sentence: - Greater species diversity of plants increases fodder yield (synthesis of 271 experimental studies).

f70c19b66a8c.sentence: - Greater species diversity of plants (i.e. diversity within a single species) increases overall crop yield (synthesis of 575 experimental studies).

400404eba987.sentence: In 2019, a summary for policymakers of the largest, most comprehensive study to date of biodiversity and ecosystem services, the Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, was published by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).

Arthur Harris in "The Variable Desert", Scientific American: "The bare statement that the region contains a flora rich in genera and species and of diverse geographic origin or affinity is entirely inadequate as a description of its real biological diversity."

b1851de40c32.title: Biodiversity
b1851de40c32.sentence: - 1967 – Raymond F. Dasmann used the term biological diversity in reference to the richness of living nature that conservationists should protect in his book A Different Kind of Country.

89d50e9b2453.title: Ecosystem service
89d50e9b2453.sentence: Ecosystem services are the various benefits that humans derive from ecosystems.

88f2ada77f6d.title: Ecosystem service
88f2ada77f6d.sentence: The interconnected living and non-living components of the natural environment offer benefits such as pollination of crops, clean air and water, decomposition of wastes, and flood control.

540745fb90f7.title: Ecosystem service
540745fb90f7.sentence: Ecosystem services are vital for human well-being.

a23531bac204.title: Ecosystem service
a23531bac204.sentence: They provide direct and indirect benefits from nature, such as clean water, food, and climate regulation.

0cc76a1c0a64.title: Ecosystem service
0cc76a1c0a64.sentence: Ecosystem services are grouped into categories of services, which was popularized in the early 2000s by the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MA) initiative by the United Nations.

67caa13cd24f.title: Ecosystem service
67caa13cd24f.sentence: These are provisioning services, such as the production of food and water; regulating services, such as the control of climate and disease; supporting services, such as nutrient cycles and oxygen production; and cultural services, such as recreation, tourism, and spiritual gratification.

b3fd94c7500b.title: Ecosystem service
b3fd94c7500b.sentence: An example for water purification as an ecosystem service is as follows: In New York City, where the quality of drinking water had fallen below standards required by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), authorities opted to restore the polluted Catskill Watershed that had previously provided the city with the ecosystem service of water purification.

fd9121d14849.title: Ecosystem service
fd9121d14849.sentence: The cost of this investment in natural capital was estimated at $1–1.5 billion, which contrasted dramatically with the estimated $6–8 billion cost of constructing a water filtration plant plus the $300 million annual running costs.

54132b63c069.title: Ecosystem service
54132b63c069.sentence: The six major methods for valuing ecosystem services in monetary terms are:

401d4a6edb9d.title: Ecosystem service
401d4a6edb9d.sentence: - Avoided cost: Services allow society to avoid costs that would have been incurred in the absence of those services (e.g. waste treatment by wetland habitats avoids health costs)

c7059f8abdd4.title: Ecosystem service
c7059f8abdd4.sentence: - Replacement cost: Services could be replaced with human-made systems (e.g. restoration of the Catskill Watershed cost less than the construction of a water purification plant)

207a3082de19.title: Ecosystem service
207a3082de19.sentence: - Travel cost: Service demand may require travel, whose costs can reflect the implied value of the service (e.g. value of ecotourism experience is at least what a visitor is willing to pay to get there)

c33478b4649f.title: Ecosystem service
c33478b4649f.sentence: - Hedonic pricing: Service demand may be reflected in the prices people will pay for associated goods (e.g. coastal housing prices exceed that of inland homes)

3abe4b080060.title: Ecosystem service
3abe4b080060.sentence: - Contingent valuation: Service demand may be elicited by posing hypothetical scenarios that involve some valuation of alternatives (e.g. visitors willing to pay for increased access to national parks)

5d0b953c29f3.title: Ecosystem service
5d0b953c29f3.sentence: A peer-reviewed study published in 1997 estimated the value of the world's ecosystem services and natural capital to be between US$16 and $54 trillion per year, with an average of US$33 trillion per year.

0057a0738b43.title: Ecosystem service
0057a0738b43.sentence: Payments for ecosystem services (PES), also known as payments for environmental services (or benefits), are incentives offered to farmers or landowners in exchange for managing their land to provide some sort of ecological service.

d08beb59ed2d.title: Ecosystem service
d08beb59ed2d.sentence: The term environmental services was introduced in a 1970 report of the Study of Critical Environmental Problems, which listed services including insect pollination, fisheries, climate regulation and flood control.

70535e04d974.title: Ecosystem service
70535e04d974.sentence: In following years, variations of the term were used, but eventually 'ecosystem services' became the standard in scientific literature.

a17983305fcf.title: Ecosystem service
a17983305fcf.sentence: Modern ideas of ecosystem services probably began when Marsh challenged in 1864 the idea that Earth's natural resources are unbounded by pointing out changes in soil fertility in the Mediterranean.

053e8d96cd2e.title: Natural capital
053e8d96cd2e.sentence: Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, which includes geology, soils, air, water and all living organisms.

987e375ac164.title: Natural capital
987e375ac164.sentence: It is an extension of the economic notion of capital (resources which enable the production of more resources) to goods and services provided by the natural environment.

15f4ea390333.title: Natural capital
15f4ea390333.sentence: For example, a well-maintained forest or river may provide an indefinitely sustainable flow of new trees or fish, whereas over-use of those resources may lead to a permanent decline in timber availability or fish stocks.

432ed99774ea.title: Natural capital
432ed99774ea.sentence: Some natural capital assets provide people with free goods and services, often called ecosystem services.

15a63ea2de17.title: Natural capital
15a63ea2de17.sentence: All of these underpin our economy and society, and thus make human life possible.

14b40fccca84.title: Natural capital
14b40fccca84.sentence: In a traditional economic analysis of the factors of production, natural capital would usually be classified as "land" distinct from traditional "capital".

5f731ae8929c.title: Natural capital
5f731ae8929c.sentence: The historical distinction between "land" and "capital" defined "land" as naturally occurring with a fixed supply, whereas "capital", as originally defined referred only to man-made goods.

a1b18fbbc4b1.title: Natural capital
a1b18fbbc4b1.sentence: (e.g., Georgism) It is, however, misleading to view "land" as if its productive capacity is fixed, because natural capital can be improved or degraded by the actions of man over time (see Environmental degradation).

a0e8ef118882.title: Natural capital
a0e8ef118882.sentence: The term 'natural capital' was first used in 1973 by E. F. Schumacher in his book Small Is Beautiful and was developed further by Herman Daly, Robert Costanza, and other founders of the science of Ecological Economics, as part of a comprehensive critique of the shortcomings of conventional economics.

51fef308ed9d.title: Natural capital
51fef308ed9d.sentence: These ecological economic values are not currently included in calculations of national income accounts, the GDP and they have no price attributes because they exist mostly outside of the global markets.

9e8b5792bf7e.title: Natural capital
9e8b5792bf7e.sentence: According to the OECD, natural capital is "natural assets in their role of providing natural resource inputs and environmental services for economic production" and is "generally considered to comprise three principal categories: natural resources stocks, land, and ecosystems."

517c4824d838.title: Natural capital
517c4824d838.sentence: Unpriced natural capital is what we refer to when businesses or individuals exploit or abuse nature without being held accountable, which can harm ecosystems and the environment.

d639b020949f.title: Sustainability
d639b020949f.sentence: Sustainability or being sustainable is the ability to continue the same over a long period of time.

370dcd6757fb.title: Sustainability
370dcd6757fb.sentence: In modern usage it generally refers to a state in which the environment, economy, and society will continue to exist over a long period of time.

36451a91b7be.title: Sustainability
36451a91b7be.sentence: The term sustainability is derived from the Latin word sustinere.

c324cb3a56f7.title: Sustainability
c324cb3a56f7.sentence: "To sustain" can mean to maintain, support, uphold, or endure.

79619dee44d2.title: Sustainability
79619dee44d2.sentence: Sustainability is regarded as a "normative concept".

da573d7b0983.title: Sustainability
da573d7b0983.sentence: This means it is based on what people value or find desirable: "The quest for sustainability involves connecting what is known through scientific study to applications in pursuit of what people want for the future."

ba4ea205658e.title: Sustainability
ba4ea205658e.sentence: Many definitions emphasize the environmental dimension.

46428321a262.title: Sustainability
46428321a262.sentence: This can include addressing key environmental problems, such as climate change and biodiversity loss.

b263889721fc.title: Sustainability
b263889721fc.sentence: Details around the economic dimension of sustainability are controversial.

2d01bca12d46.title: Sustainability
2d01bca12d46.sentence: Scholars have discussed this under the concept of weak and strong sustainability.

e6cf74a40c90.title: Sustainability
e6cf74a40c90.sentence: It is challenging to measure sustainability as the concept is complex, contextual, and dynamic.

3551068c98e2.title: Sustainability
3551068c98e2.sentence: Indicators have been developed to cover the environment, society, or the economy but there is no fixed definition of sustainability indicators.

d896e7fa1b7b.title: Sustainability
d896e7fa1b7b.sentence: One point of criticism is that the concept is vague and only a buzzword.

011b9afbd94e.title: Sustainability
011b9afbd94e.sentence: Another is that sustainability might be an impossible goal.

eef00d3fe978.title: Sustainability
eef00d3fe978.sentence: "Sustainability is often thought of as a long-term goal (i.e. a more sustainable world), while sustainable development refers to the many processes and pathways to achieve it."

dbb6e6aa9f74.title: Sustainability
dbb6e6aa9f74.sentence: Scholars usually distinguish three different areas of sustainability.

518edfee5841.title: Sustainability
518edfee5841.sentence: These are the environmental, the social, and the economic.

c286dabc3e8b.title: Environmental degradation
c286dabc3e8b.sentence: Environmental degradation is the deterioration of the environment through depletion of resources such as quality of air, water and soil; the destruction of ecosystems; habitat destruction; the extinction of wildlife; and pollution.

a93a99c236b0.title: Environmental degradation
a93a99c236b0.sentence: The United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction defines environmental degradation as "the reduction of the capacity of the environment to meet social and ecological objectives, and needs".

79cb0c930504.title: Environmental degradation
79cb0c930504.sentence: When natural habitats are destroyed or natural resources are depleted, the environment is degraded; direct environmental degradation, such as deforestation, which is readily visible; this can be caused by more indirect process, such as the build up of plastic pollution over time or the buildup of greenhouse gases that causes tipping points in the climate system.

22bbd8c42cf7.title: Environmental degradation
22bbd8c42cf7.sentence: Since the establishment of agriculture over 11,000 years ago, humans have altered roughly 70% of the Earth's land surface, with the global biomass of vegetation being reduced by half, and terrestrial animal communities seeing a decline in biodiversity greater than 20% on average.

ed1439e7f0f0.title: Environmental degradation
ed1439e7f0f0.sentence: A 2021 study says that just 3% of the planet's terrestrial surface is ecologically and faunally intact, meaning areas with healthy populations of native animal species and little to no human footprint.

371c69b2c77b.title: Environmental degradation
371c69b2c77b.sentence: However, the scale of environmental degradation is not only determined by population growth but also by consumption patterns and resource efficiency.

0f2e861f4db3.title: Environmental degradation
0f2e861f4db3.sentence: Industrialized nations, with higher per capita consumption rates, often have a disproportionately large environmental footprint compared to less developed regions.

063b0170a40c.title: Environmental degradation
063b0170a40c.section: Biodiversity loss > Impacts of environmental degradation on women's livelihoods
063b0170a40c.sentence: Women's livelihoods, health, food and nutrition security, access to water and energy, and coping abilities are all disproportionately affected by environmental degradation.

a9c611a1b5e8.title: Biosphere
a9c611a1b5e8.sentence: The biosphere (from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos) 'life' and σφαῖρα (sphaîra) 'sphere'), also called the ecosphere (from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos) 'settlement, house' and σφαῖρα (sphaîra) 'sphere'), is the worldwide sum of all ecosystems.

3355ebb61f8f.title: Biosphere
3355ebb61f8f.sentence: It can also be termed the zone of life on the Earth.

e445b1e9c5f7.title: Biosphere
e445b1e9c5f7.sentence: The biosphere (which is technically a spherical shell) is virtually a closed system with regard to matter, with minimal inputs and outputs.

b51417aa4585.title: Biosphere
b51417aa4585.sentence: Regarding energy, it is an open system, with photosynthesis capturing solar energy at a rate of around 100 terawatts.

a6259c84a76c.title: Biosphere
a6259c84a76c.sentence: By the most general biophysiological definition, the biosphere is the global ecological system integrating all living beings and their relationships, including their interaction with the elements of the lithosphere, cryosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere.

cc1a800cee84.title: Biosphere
cc1a800cee84.sentence: Every part of the planet, from the polar ice caps to the equator, features life of some kind.

66dfa23ef791.title: Biosphere
66dfa23ef791.sentence: Life forms live in every part of the Earth's biosphere, including soil, hot springs, inside rocks at least 19 km (12 mi) deep underground, and at least 64 km (40 mi) high in the atmosphere.

67d6fe3947a8.title: Biosphere

67d6fe3947a8.sentence: The term "biosphere" was coined in 1875 by geologist Eduard Suess, who defined it as the place on Earth's surface where life dwells.

a65e3263c0bf.title: Anthropocene
a65e3263c0bf.sentence: Anthropocene is a term that has been used to refer to the period of time during which humanity has become a planetary force of change.

f76387359841.title: Anthropocene
f76387359841.sentence: Originally a proposal for a new geological epoch following the Holocene, it was rejected as such in 2024 by the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) and the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS).

a0cd8b6b4b3e.title: Anthropocene

a0cd8b6b4b3e.sentence: This result was not out of a dismissal of human impact on the planet, but rather an inability to constrain the Anthropocene in a geological context.

f885cda1de16.title: Anthropocene
f885cda1de16.sentence: Various start dates for the Anthropocene have been proposed, ranging from the beginning of the Neolithic Revolution (12,000–15,000 years ago), to as recently as the 1960s.

a7eefa01f96a.title: Anthropocene
a7eefa01f96a.sentence: The biologist Eugene F. Stoermer is credited with first coining and using the term anthropocene informally in the 1980s; Paul J. Crutzen re-invented and popularized the term.

66dfc4c84519.title: Anthropocene

66dfc4c84519.sentence: The exact rate remains controversial – perhaps 100 to 1000 times the normal background rate of extinction.

02ffbec46add.sentence: One geological symptom resulting from human activity is increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) content.

0ee125ea702b.title: Anthropocene
0ee125ea702b.section: Nature of human effects > Climate change
0ee125ea702b.sentence: Most of this increase is due to the combustion of fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and gas.

666e03e1d75a.title: Anthropocene
666e03e1d75a.sentence: The name Anthropocene is a combination of anthropo- from the Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthropos) meaning 'human' and -cene from καινός (kainós) meaning 'new' or 'recent'.

fef37b73acea.title: Anthropocene

10d1be14bcd6.sentence: In March 2024, an internal vote was held by the IUGS: After nearly 15 years of debate, the proposal to ratify the Anthropocene was defeated by a 12-to-4 margin, with 2 abstentions.

c30fcede2233.sentence: The categorisation of ecosystem services varies depending on classification system.

399710d375a2.title: Ecosystem service
399710d375a2.sentence: The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MA) groups the services into the four groups: regulating services, provisioning services, cultural services and supporting services, where the so-called supporting services are regarded as the basis for the services of the other three categories.

912a00712a56.title: Ecosystem service
912a00712a56.sentence: An ecosystem does not necessarily offer all four types of services simultaneously; but given the intricate nature of any ecosystem, it is usually assumed that humans benefit from a combination of these services.

4529018a72f6.title: Ecosystem service
4529018a72f6.sentence: In fact, some services directly affect the livelihood of neighboring human populations (such as fresh water, food or aesthetic value, etc.) while other services affect general environmental conditions by which humans are indirectly impacted (such as climate change, erosion regulation or natural hazard regulation, etc.).

e35d82066064.title: Ecosystem service
e35d82066064.sentence: To prevent double-counting in ecosystem services audits, for instance, The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity replaced Supporting Services in the MA with Habitat Services, and "ecosystem functions", defined as "a subset of the interactions between ecosystem structure and processes that underpin the capacity of an ecosystem to provide goods and services".

53d5fd13a0fa.title: Ecosystem service

3bd6467c5939.title: Ecosystem service

0b135b429253.title: Ecosystem service
