c61d95552082.sentence: In economics, utility is a measure of a certain person's satisfaction from a certain state of the world.

bf2ec900763d.title: Utility
bf2ec900763d.sentence: - In a normative context, utility refers to a goal or objective that we wish to maximize, i.e., an objective function.

d263f1e37326.title: Utility
d263f1e37326.sentence: This kind of utility bears a closer resemblance to the original utilitarian concept, developed by moral philosophers such as Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

804e775db637.title: Utility
804e775db637.sentence: - In a descriptive context, the term refers to an apparent objective function; such a function is revealed by a person's behavior, and specifically by their preferences over lotteries, which can be any quantified choice.

cef82e03f599.title: Utility
cef82e03f599.sentence: A utility function represents that ordering if it is possible to assign a real number to each alternative in such a manner that alternative a is assigned a number greater than alternative b if and only if the individual prefers alternative a to alternative b.

cd23d54cb707.title: Utility
cd23d54cb707.sentence: It was recognized that utility could not be measured or observed directly, so instead economists devised a way to infer relative utilities from observed choice.

ffe62da3e671.title: Utility
ffe62da3e671.sentence: These 'revealed preferences', as termed by Paul Samuelson, were revealed e.g. in people's willingness to pay:

fe844143d042.title: Utility
fe844143d042.sentence: Economists distinguish between total utility and marginal utility.

48c930134979.title: Utility
48c930134979.sentence: Total utility is the utility of an alternative, an entire consumption bundle or situation in life.

7756c2243413.title: Utility
7756c2243413.sentence: The rate of change of utility from changing the quantity of one good consumed is termed the marginal utility of that good.

b8fa407ed646.title: Utility
b8fa407ed646.sentence: Utility can be represented through sets of indifference curve, which are level curves of the function itself and which plot the combination of commodities that an individual would accept to maintain a given level of satisfaction.

5ebea317ba5f.title: Utility
5ebea317ba5f.sentence: Combining indifference curves with budget constraints allows for individual demand curves derivation.

c1f23af17ed5.title: Utility

254372ae85db.title: Goods
254372ae85db.sentence: In certain economic contexts, goods are anything that is good, usually in the sense that it provides welfare or utility to someone.

720de67bba36.title: Goods
720de67bba36.sentence: Economics focuses on the study of economic goods, i.e. goods that are scarce; in other words, producing the good requires expending effort or resources.

66622706c75a.title: Goods
66622706c75a.sentence: Economic goods contrast with free goods such as air, for which there is an unlimited supply.

86e620655051.title: Goods
86e620655051.sentence: Some things are useful, but not scarce enough to have monetary value, such as the Earth's atmosphere or seawater; these are referred to as free goods.

513b093d0dc3.title: Diminishing returns

6902aaaa418c.title: Goods
6902aaaa418c.sentence: For example, a microwave oven or a bicycle that is sold to a consumer is a final good or consumer good, but the components that are sold to be used in those goods are intermediate goods.

7f52675481fd.title: Goods
7f52675481fd.sentence: Durable or long-lasting goods, such as machinery, human skills, or ecosystems, which in turn are used to produce further goods, are known as capital goods.

d45ffc168160.title: Goods
d45ffc168160.sentence: Goods are commonly considered to have diminishing marginal utility, which means that consuming more gives less utility per amount consumed.

d9b5a6cf7d21.title: Goods

9c2df74a7563.title: Goods

b196ce404f74.title: Microeconomics
b196ce404f74.sentence: Microeconomics is a branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources and the interactions among these individuals and firms.

4b8e725c94cd.title: Microeconomics
4b8e725c94cd.sentence: Microeconomics focuses on the study of individual markets, sectors, or industries as opposed to the economy as a whole, which is studied in macroeconomics.

de534fa1ec17.title: Microeconomics
de534fa1ec17.sentence: While microeconomics focuses on firms and individuals, macroeconomics focuses on the overall level of economic activity, addressing issues of growth, inflation, and unemployment—and national policies related to these issues.

2020c6cb2e67.title: Microeconomics
2020c6cb2e67.sentence: One goal of microeconomics is to analyze the market mechanisms that establish relative prices among goods and services and allocate limited resources among alternative uses.

51d5d2f1a93d.title: Microeconomics
51d5d2f1a93d.sentence: Microeconomics shows conditions under which free markets lead to desirable allocations.

e6d56239f402.title: Microeconomics
e6d56239f402.sentence: It also analyzes market failure, in which markets fail to produce efficient outcomes.

d09924f08464.title: Microeconomics
d09924f08464.sentence: Microeconomic theory typically begins with the study of a single rational and utility maximizing individual.

33e8b7b5a6d7.title: Microeconomics
33e8b7b5a6d7.sentence: To economists, rationality means an individual possesses stable preferences that are both complete and transitive.

a495a4a21fa1.title: Microeconomics

0a8775e61e9b.title: Microeconomics

f471550d9abf.title: Microeconomics

b0ae02bd2c1c.title: Value (economics)
b0ae02bd2c1c.sentence: In economics, economic value or simply value is a measure of the benefit provided by a good or service to an economic agent.

3fe164b3e09f.title: Value (economics)
3fe164b3e09f.sentence: Economic value is generally measured through units of currency, and the interpretation is therefore "what is the maximum amount of money a person is willing and able to pay for a good or service?” Value for money is often expressed in comparative terms, such as "better", or "best value for money", but may also be expressed in absolute terms, such as where a deal does, or does not, offer value for money.

17c338c57269.title: Value (economics)
17c338c57269.sentence: Said another way, value is how much a desired object or condition is worth relative to other objects or conditions.

c3c23de86d99.title: Value (economics)
c3c23de86d99.sentence: Economic values are expressed as "how much" of one desirable condition or product will, or would be given up in exchange for some other desired condition or product.

d63bd30c3c6f.title: Value (economics)
d63bd30c3c6f.sentence: From this analysis came the concepts value in use and value in exchange.

cb32aae470b8.title: Value (economics)
cb32aae470b8.sentence: Value is linked to price through the mechanism of exchange.

df341ee3ae8f.title: Value (economics)
df341ee3ae8f.sentence: Value theories are a large part of the differences and disagreements between the various schools of economic theory.

283264ab83e6.title: Value (economics)
283264ab83e6.sentence: In classical economics, the labor theory of value asserts that the economic value of a commodity is determined by the total amount of socially necessary labor required to produce it.

6d8bad923688.title: Value (economics)

6d8bad923688.sentence: According to this theory, the consumer places a value on a commodity by determining the marginal utility, or additional satisfaction of one additional unit.

3646eb61bac2.title: Value (economics)

8dff9a78e3a4.title: Value (economics)
8dff9a78e3a4.sentence: As such, everything is seen as a commodity and if there is no market to set a price then there is no economic value.

e0e4adef90d7.title: Biodiversity offsetting

eb544784f48e.title: Incentive
eb544784f48e.sentence: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organization to alter their behavior to produce a desired outcome.

82da69260ebc.title: Incentive
82da69260ebc.sentence: In comparison, disincentives discourage certain actions.

6e9a6a68a035.title: Incentive
6e9a6a68a035.sentence: Incentives encourage specific behaviors or actions by persons and organizations, and are commonly employed by governments, businesses, and other organizations.

0aedb2d09323.title: Incentive
0aedb2d09323.sentence: Incentives may generally be divided into two categories: intrinsic and extrinsic.

ea417321532d.title: Incentive
ea417321532d.sentence: An intrinsic incentive arises when an individual is motivated by personal satisfaction, interest, or enjoyment in an activity, without seeking external rewards or responding to external pressure.

9994a9c49542.title: Incentive
9994a9c49542.sentence: Extrinsic incentives involve external rewards or pressures, such as monetary compensation, recognition, or the threat of punishment.

25dd1208df08.title: Incentive
25dd1208df08.sentence: Author David Callahan identifies three broad classes of incentives.

b4133da1daa3.title: Incentive
b4133da1daa3.sentence: Remunerative or financial incentives, involve material rewards.

2d2c8091b2fd.title: Incentive
2d2c8091b2fd.sentence: Moral incentives involve action being regarded as the right or admirable choice; individuals acting on moral incentives may experience self-esteem, praise, or admiration from others, while failing to act accordingly can result in guilt, condemnation, or even ostracism.

e7d9b7f7b9f5.title: Incentive
e7d9b7f7b9f5.sentence: Coercive incentives threaten, when failure to act in a specified way occurs, the use of physical or coercive force by others.

00c9e32a58b4.title: Incentive
00c9e32a58b4.sentence: A misaligned incentive arises when the goals of different parties conflict.

a3cb14cc68b1.title: Incentive
a3cb14cc68b1.sentence: This can occur within firms, but also in government, healthcare, education, and environmental policy.

f4395ecbce78.title: Incentive
f4395ecbce78.sentence: Incentives, however, can also produce unintended outcomes.

1ef8d1cab6a0.sentence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments found that, after correction for publication bias, the mean effect of financial incentives on performance is close to zero in most field settings, with modest positive effects in laboratory experiments and when incentives are framed as losses.

f0179dba6db8.title: Ceteris paribus
f0179dba6db8.sentence: Ceteris paribus (also spelled caeteris paribus) (Classical Latin pronunciation: [ˈkeːtɛ.riːs ˈpa.rɪ.bʊs]) is a Latin phrase, meaning "other things equal"; some other English translations of the phrase are "all other things being equal", "other things held constant", "all else unchanged", and "all else being equal".

0ceac174d938.title: Ceteris paribus
0ceac174d938.sentence: When using ceteris paribus in economics, one assumes that all other variables except those under immediate consideration are held constant.

a7775597f9b4.title: Ceteris paribus
a7775597f9b4.sentence: An example in economics is "If the price of milk falls, ceteris paribus, the quantity of milk demanded will rise." This means that, if other factors, such as deflation, pricing objectives, utility, and marketing methods, do not change, the decrease in the price of milk will lead to an increase in demand for it.

1af826bd99ae.title: Ceteris paribus
1af826bd99ae.sentence: The clause is often loosely translated as "holding all else constant." It does not imply that no other things will in fact change; rather, it isolates the effect of one particular change.

75e86121d63c.title: Ceteris paribus
75e86121d63c.sentence: Economist Alfred Marshall had significant effects on the popularity for the ceteris paribus clause in the 19th century.

842bf0b0147c.title: Ceteris paribus
842bf0b0147c.sentence: In breaking it up, he segregates those disturbing causes, whose wanderings happen to be inconvenient, for the time in a pound called Ceteris Paribus.

7845db31fa8e.title: Ceteris paribus
7845db31fa8e.sentence: One thing to note is that since economic variables can only be isolated in theory and not in practice, ceteris paribus can only ever highlight tendencies, not absolutes.

ab5c440668c5.title: Ceteris paribus
ab5c440668c5.sentence: The more the issue is thus narrowed, the more exactly can it be handled: but also the less closely does it correspond to real life.

7a48dc290a84.title: Ceteris paribus
7a48dc290a84.sentence: The more we apply the rule of ceteris paribus the further we distance ourselves from reality, e.g. If hydrocarbon fuels are infinite then society is sustainable.

a52d6fa7f97a.title: Ceteris paribus
a52d6fa7f97a.sentence: Amid highly connected situations, a change to any one variable will change all others.

58f4a32a8736.title: Ceteris paribus
58f4a32a8736.sentence: In this way, when these complex connections are active, it is not possible in reality to hold all other values constant.

96f5cfb8245f.title: Ceteris paribus
96f5cfb8245f.sentence: Ceteris paribus has been relevant in economics for centuries, dating back to its first traces in 1295 by Peter Olivi.

ee1ca05fa6af.title: Economic model
ee1ca05fa6af.sentence: An economic model is a theoretical construct representing economic processes by a set of variables and a set of logical and/or quantitative relationships between them.

e721d0589307.title: Economic model
e721d0589307.sentence: The economic model is a simplified, often mathematical, framework designed to illustrate complex processes.

6c15b009c87a.title: Economic model
6c15b009c87a.sentence: Simplification is particularly important for economics given the enormous complexity of economic processes.

edf9b97fd153.title: Economic model
edf9b97fd153.sentence: This complexity can be attributed to the diversity of factors that determine economic activity; these factors include: individual and cooperative decision processes, resource limitations, environmental and geographical constraints, institutional and legal requirements and purely random fluctuations.

402cd4638959.title: Economic model
402cd4638959.sentence: - Forecasting economic activity in a way in which conclusions are logically related to assumptions;

0014b2904337.title: Economic model

1b23c826a42a.title: Economic model

1e3a966f3270.title: Economic model

a3df7758eb64.title: Economic model

3b8d59dffb05.title: Economic model

429ddcd8311b.sentence: In economics, and in other social sciences, preference refers to an order by which an agent, while in search of an "optimal choice", ranks alternatives based on their respective utility.

5036931db9a2.sentence: In economics, an indifference curve connects points on a graph representing different quantities of two goods, points between which a consumer is indifferent.

392db3adef7b.title: Complementary goods

f72b9c02ec21.sentence: In economics, an ordinal utility function is a function representing the preferences of an agent on an ordinal scale.

d246c7925a7f.title: Ordinal utility

5d277a07aca4.title: Ordinal utility

d8efad334872.title: Ordinal utility

7bddfdfb5bbc.title: Positive and normative economics
7bddfdfb5bbc.sentence: In the philosophy of economics, economics is often divided into positive (or descriptive) and normative (or prescriptive) economics.

527cfcef7690.title: Positive and normative economics
527cfcef7690.sentence: Positive economics focuses on the description, quantification and explanation of economic phenomena, while normative economics discusses prescriptions for what actions individuals or societies should or should not take.

adea6cb33bd4.title: Positive and normative economics
adea6cb33bd4.sentence: Examples of positive economic statements are "the unemployment rate in France is higher than that in the United States," or "an increase in government spending would lower the unemployment rate".

f81885b46dfa.title: Positive and normative economics
f81885b46dfa.sentence: Either of these is potentially falsifiable and may be contradicted by evidence.

cb48738b9bc8.title: Positive and normative economics
cb48738b9bc8.sentence: The price of milk should be $6 a gallon to give dairy farmers a higher standard of living.

8421ae0eaa1c.title: Positive and normative economics
8421ae0eaa1c.sentence: This is a normative statement, because it reflects value judgments; this specific statement makes the judgment that the benefits of the policy outweigh its costs.

c44cdce11b1c.title: Positive and normative economics
c44cdce11b1c.sentence: John Neville Keynes's The Scope and Method of Political Economy defined positive economics as the science of "what is" as compared to normative economics, the study of "what ought to be".

107a15c4fac1.title: Positive and normative economics
107a15c4fac1.sentence: Keynes was not the first person to make the distinction between positive and normative economics but his definitions have become the standard in economics teaching.

ea6ba0da6d9c.title: Positive and normative economics

99d4aca1ed9b.title: Positive and normative economics
99d4aca1ed9b.sentence: Economics also often involves the use of objective normative analyses (such as cost–benefit analyses) that try to identify the best decision to take, given a set of assumptions about value (which may be taken from policymakers or the public).

fc40dd182149.title: Ecological economics
fc40dd182149.sentence: Ecological economists have questioned fundamental mainstream economic approaches such as cost-benefit analysis, and the separability of economic values from scientific research, contending that economics is unavoidably normative, i.e. prescriptive, rather than positive or descriptive.

cbc405118ae7.title: Trade-off
cbc405118ae7.sentence: A trade-off (or tradeoff) is a situational decision that involves diminishing or losing on quality, quantity, or property of a set or design in return for gains in other aspects.

34cc8e36f047.title: Trade-off
34cc8e36f047.sentence: In simple terms, a tradeoff is where one thing increases, and another must decrease.

f576adea191c.title: Trade-off
f576adea191c.sentence: Tradeoffs stem from limitations of many origins, including simple physics – for instance, only a certain volume of objects can fit into a given space, so a full container must remove some items to accept any more, and vessels can carry a few large items or multiple small items.

33626c790ad2.title: Expenditure minimization problem

9f848581d649.title: Hicksian demand function
9f848581d649.sentence: In microeconomics, a consumer's Hicksian demand function (or compensated demand function) represents the quantity of a good demanded when the consumer minimizes expenditure while maintaining a fixed level of utility.

1f4ee19981d3.title: Hicksian demand function
1f4ee19981d3.sentence: The Hicksian demand function illustrates how a consumer would adjust their demand for a good in response to a price change, assuming their income is adjusted (or compensated) to keep them on the same indifference curve—ensuring their utility remains unchanged.

42707c73e27b.title: Hicksian demand function
42707c73e27b.section: Hicksian demand and compensated price changes
42707c73e27b.sentence: The Hicksian demand function isolates the substitution effect by supposing the consumer is compensated with exactly enough extra income after the price rise to purchase some bundle on the same indifference curve.

17ff2e04bb69.title: Equivalent variation
17ff2e04bb69.sentence: The equivalent variation is the change in wealth, at current prices, that would have the same effect on consumer welfare as would the change in prices, with income unchanged.

98a6507fc5fd.title: Equivalent variation

adf97e7173f4.title: Compensating variation
adf97e7173f4.sentence: Whereas CV measures the welfare change in money at new prices, EV values the welfare change at the old prices, and can be thought of as the change in income that the consumer would be just willing to accept in order to forgo the price change.

b9e8b20069d8.title: Deadweight loss
b9e8b20069d8.sentence: In modern economic literature, the most common measure of a taxpayer's loss from a distortionary tax, such as a tax on bicycles, is the equivalent variation, the maximum amount that a taxpayer would be willing to forgo in a lump sum to avoid the tax.

2c53dd9111ee.title: Deadweight loss

22503a12a772.sentence: Various definitions of economics have been proposed, including attempts to define precisely "what economists do".

af174a9e8f57.title: Economics

b440000244a6.title: Definitions of economics
b440000244a6.sentence: The term economics was originally known as "political economy".

1d6a5a4805e8.title: Definitions of economics
1d6a5a4805e8.sentence: This term evolved from the French Mercantilist usage of économie politique, which expanded the notion of economy from the ancient Greek concept of household management to the national level, as the public administration of state affairs.

658b31104428.title: Definitions of economics
658b31104428.section: Definitions > Say, Carlyle, Mill, and Menger
658b31104428.sentence: In 1803, French economist Jean-Baptiste Say distinguished the subject from its public policy uses, defining it as the science of the production, distribution, and consumption of wealth.

56810ed00b21.title: Definitions of economics
56810ed00b21.sentence: Alfred Marshall provides a still widely cited definition in his textbook Principles of Economics (1890) that extends analysis beyond wealth and from the societal to the microeconomic level, creating a certain synthesis of the views of those still more sympathetic with the classical political economy (with social wealth focus) and those early adopters of the views expressed in the Marginal Revolution (with individual needs focus).

d6f01e1d95ec.title: Definitions of economics
d6f01e1d95ec.sentence: Political Economy or Economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life; it examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and with the use of the material requisites of well-being.

146bcfebd9ce.title: Definitions of economics

388b4444f860.title: Definitions of economics

d5dae2a127a9.title: Factors of production
d5dae2a127a9.sentence: In economics, factors of production, resources, or inputs are what is used in the production process to produce output—that is, goods and services.

eecfaf12b647.title: Factors of production

dfec2b14c0f2.title: Factors of production

4ac0c72b46a9.title: Factors of production

c5b413269208.title: Factors of production

b3a6da4aeee2.title: Factors of production

0247d9aada96.title: Factors of production

a6bddcaecdfd.title: Capital (economics)
a6bddcaecdfd.sentence: A typical example is the machinery used in a factory.

284e784d6c3f.title: Capital (economics)
284e784d6c3f.sentence: What distinguishes capital goods from intermediate goods (e.g., raw materials, components, energy consumed during production) is their durability and the nature of their contribution.

3248d81999ea.title: Capital (economics)

6120cee70eec.title: Capital (economics)

2d0006868d81.sentence: An economic system, or economic order, is a system of production, resource allocation and distribution of goods and services within an economy.

69d414efba6f.sentence: The scarcity problem, for example, requires answers to basic questions, such as what to produce, how to produce it and who gets what is produced.

c1dbf91a7b76.title: Economic system
c1dbf91a7b76.sentence: An economic system is a way of answering these basic questions and different economic systems answer them differently.

6dc1ed8ee1ab.title: Economic system
6dc1ed8ee1ab.sentence: Economic systems are commonly segmented by their property rights regime for the means of production and by their dominant resource allocation mechanism.

226860462138.title: Economic system
226860462138.sentence: Economies that combine private ownership with market allocation are called "market capitalism" and economies that combine private ownership with economic planning are labelled "command capitalism" or dirigisme.

a79b40f4e722.title: Diminishing returns
a79b40f4e722.sentence: In economics, diminishing returns means the decrease in marginal (incremental) output of a production process as the amount of a single factor of production is incrementally increased, holding all other factors of production equal (ceteris paribus).

4b06db386ade.title: Diminishing returns
4b06db386ade.sentence: The law of diminishing returns (also known as the law of diminishing marginal productivity) states that in a productive process, if a factor of production continues to increase—while holding all other production factors constant—at some point, a further incremental unit of input will return a lower amount of output.

e33e75fa4daf.title: Diminishing returns
e33e75fa4daf.sentence: Under diminishing returns, the output remains positive, but productivity and efficiency decrease.

13dc7aba608d.title: Diminishing returns
13dc7aba608d.sentence: Given that the capital on the floor (e.g. manufacturing machines, pre-existing technology, warehouses) is held constant, increasing from one employee to two employees is, theoretically, going to more than double production possibilities and this is called increasing returns.

581110cd1937.title: Diminishing returns
581110cd1937.sentence: If 50 people are employed, at some point, increasing the number of employees by two percent (from 50 to 51 employees) would increase output by two percent and this is called constant returns.

ee5608db8ea2.title: Diminishing returns
ee5608db8ea2.sentence: Increasing the number of employees by two percent (from 100 to 102 employees) would increase output by less than two percent and this is called "diminishing returns".

b53d6f0a1e3b.title: Diminishing returns
b53d6f0a1e3b.sentence: Thus, diminishing marginal returns imply increasing marginal costs and increasing average costs.

f84dfd77e4d1.title: Diminishing returns

51a2321b79dd.title: Diminishing returns

64f4db40237a.title: Diminishing returns

118ed1932ef2.title: Production-possibility frontier
118ed1932ef2.sentence: In microeconomics, a production-possibility frontier (PPF), production-possibility curve (PPC), or production-possibility boundary (PPB) is a graphical representation showing all the possible quantities of outputs that can be produced using all factors of production, where the given resources are fully and efficiently utilized per unit time.

cb3855b75998.title: Production-possibility frontier
cb3855b75998.sentence: A PPF illustrates several economic concepts, such as allocative efficiency, economies of scale, opportunity cost (or marginal rate of transformation), productive efficiency, and scarcity of resources (the fundamental economic problem that all societies face).

33e6fc7e6a19.title: Production-possibility frontier
33e6fc7e6a19.sentence: One good can only be produced by diverting resources from other goods, and so by producing less of them.

84c4f7246291.title: Production-possibility frontier
84c4f7246291.sentence: By doing so, it defines productive efficiency in the context of that production set: a point on the frontier indicates efficient use of the available inputs (such as points B, D and C in the graph), a point beneath the curve (such as A) indicates inefficiency, and a point beyond the curve (such as X) indicates impossibility.

256b7c738608.title: Production-possibility frontier
256b7c738608.sentence: In contrast, if the economy is operating below the curve, it is said to be operating inefficiently because it could reallocate resources in order to produce more of both goods or some resources such as labor or capital are sitting idle and could be fully employed to produce more of both goods.

b8b468c1bf1c.title: Production-possibility frontier
b8b468c1bf1c.sentence: An outward shift of the PPF results from growth of the availability of inputs, such as physical capital or labour, or from technological progress in knowledge of how to transform inputs into outputs.

7f395c376e55.title: Production-possibility frontier
7f395c376e55.sentence: In the long run, if technology improves or if the supply of factors of production increases, the economy's capacity to produce both goods increases; if this potential is realized, economic growth occurs.

9b3d6abdaae6.title: Production-possibility frontier
9b3d6abdaae6.sentence: Conversely, the PPF will shift inward if the labour force shrinks, the supply of raw materials is depleted, or a natural disaster decreases the stock of physical capital.

229ec35b979a.title: Production-possibility frontier
229ec35b979a.sentence: Conversely, a natural, military or ecological disaster might move the PPF to the left in response to a reduction in an economy's productive capability.

e1c1bd83f0b0.title: Production-possibility frontier
e1c1bd83f0b0.sentence: The shape of a PPF is commonly drawn as concave to the origin to represent increasing opportunity cost with increased output of a good.

3f95c2a702fa.title: Production-possibility frontier
3f95c2a702fa.sentence: That is, as an economy specializes more and more into one product (such as moving from point B to point D), the opportunity cost of producing that product increases, because we are using more and more resources that are less efficient in producing it.

e5a896bf5f5a.title: Production-possibility frontier

115199302620.sentence: However, an economy may achieve productive efficiency without necessarily being allocatively efficient.

69c7f05ddeeb.title: Production-possibility frontier

4777f2982276.title: Labor theory of value
4777f2982276.sentence: The labor theory of value (LTV) posits that the economic value of a good or service is determined by the total amount of socially necessary labor required to produce it.

3af831fa8dfb.title: Labor theory of value
3af831fa8dfb.sentence: The theory is usually associated with Marxism, although versions of it were originally used by classical economists like Adam Smith and David Ricardo to explain the long-run "natural price" of commodities.

186851d405a8.title: Labor theory of value
186851d405a8.sentence: The first version of the theory, associated with Adam Smith, suggests value is determined by the amount of labor a commodity can command in exchange.

da8d0a705180.title: Labor theory of value
da8d0a705180.sentence: The second version, developed by David Ricardo, argues that value is determined by the quantity of labor embodied in the production of the commodity.

610455bd5ee9.title: Labor theory of value
610455bd5ee9.sentence: Marx extended this analysis to develop his theory of surplus value, which holds that profit originates from the exploitation of workers, whose unpaid labor is appropriated by capitalists.

6f0ea6450af2.title: Margin (economics)

1ff3f688ff8b.title: Labor theory of value

286fa4cf5aa5.sentence: Institutional economics focuses on understanding the role of the evolutionary process and the role of institutions in shaping economic behavior.

60b2f4f8a341.title: Institutional economics
60b2f4f8a341.sentence: Institutional economics emphasizes a broader study of institutions and views markets as a result of the complex interaction of these various institutions (e.g. individuals, firms, states, social norms).

c5fb006c5511.title: Institutional economics
c5fb006c5511.sentence: Institutional economics focuses on learning, bounded rationality, and evolution (rather than assuming stable preferences, rationality and equilibrium).

4030c61b79d5.title: Institutional economics
4030c61b79d5.sentence: Its name and core elements trace back to a 1919 American Economic Review article by Walton H. Hamilton.

ff959ff83889.title: Institutional economics
ff959ff83889.sentence: It was a central part of American economics in the first part of the 20th century, including such famous but diverse economists as Thorstein Veblen, Wesley Mitchell, and John R. Commons.

175375e17ce8.title: Institutional economics
175375e17ce8.sentence: Thorstein Veblen (1857–1929) wrote his first and most influential book while he was at the University of Chicago, on The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899).

5faa36502200.title: Institutional economics
5faa36502200.sentence: In it he analyzed the motivation in capitalism for people to conspicuously consume their riches as a way of demonstrating success.

efb1432a26ea.title: Institutional economics
efb1432a26ea.sentence: With the new developments in the economic theory of organizations, information, property rights, and transaction costs, an attempt was made to integrate institutionalism into more recent developments in mainstream economics, under the title new institutional economics.

a306647f0e2c.title: Institutional economics
a306647f0e2c.sentence: The earlier tradition continues today as a leading heterodox approach to economics.

1932106ce3fe.title: Mixed economy
1932106ce3fe.sentence: A mixed economy is an economic system that includes both elements associated with capitalism, such as private businesses, and ones associated with socialism, such as nationalized government services.

a0734c34da7a.title: Mixed economy
a0734c34da7a.sentence: More specifically, a mixed economy may be variously defined as an economic system blending elements of a market economy with elements of a planned economy, markets with state interventionism, or private enterprise with public enterprise.

6f400fed1e61.title: Mixed economy
6f400fed1e61.sentence: The idea behind a mixed economy, as advocated by John Maynard Keynes and several others, was not to abandon the capitalist mode of production, but to retain a predominance of private ownership and control of the means of production, with profit-seeking enterprise and the accumulation of capital as its fundamental driving force.

8dd61cfee7f2.title: Mixed economy
8dd61cfee7f2.sentence: The difference from a laissez-faire capitalist system is that markets are subject to varying degrees of regulatory control and governments wield indirect macroeconomic influence through fiscal and monetary policies with a view to counteracting capitalism's history of boom and bust cycles, unemployment, and economic inequality.

7c65811fda4e.title: Mixed economy
7c65811fda4e.sentence: In this framework, varying degrees of public utilities and essential services are provided by the government, with state activity providing public goods and universal civic requirements, including education, healthcare, physical infrastructure, and management of public lands.

32919b7fc26f.title: Mixed economy
32919b7fc26f.section: Typology > Mix of free markets and state intervention
32919b7fc26f.sentence: Other examples of common government activity in this form of mixed economy include environmental protection, maintenance of employment standards, a standardized welfare system, and economic competition with antitrust laws.

5a7f25644b26.title: Mixed economy
5a7f25644b26.section: Typology > Mix of free markets and state intervention
5a7f25644b26.sentence: Most contemporary market-oriented economies fall under this category, including the economy of the United States.

f7b0eb2a2cac.title: Mixed economy
f7b0eb2a2cac.section: Typology > Mix of free markets and state intervention
f7b0eb2a2cac.sentence: The term is also used to describe the economies of countries that feature extensive welfare states, such as the Nordic model practiced by the Nordic countries, which combine free markets with an extensive welfare state.

49dc078c5089.title: Mixed economy
49dc078c5089.section: Typology > Mix of private and public enterprise
49dc078c5089.sentence: Examples include the economies of China, Norway, Singapore, and Vietnam—all of which feature large state-owned enterprise sectors operating alongside large private sectors.

45bb8098f312.title: Mixed economy
45bb8098f312.sentence: As it is unlikely that an economy will contain a perfectly even mix, mixed economies are usually noted as being skewed towards either private ownership or public ownership, toward capitalism or socialism, or a market economy or command economy in varying degrees.

69c452347eb5.title: Subjective theory of value
69c452347eb5.sentence: The subjective theory of value (STV) is an economic theory for explaining how the value of goods and services are not only established but also how they can fluctuate over time.

28792d060d7d.title: Subjective theory of value
28792d060d7d.sentence: The theory claims that the value of a good is not determined by any inherent property of the good, nor by the cumulative value of components or labor needed to produce it, but instead is determined by the individuals or entities who are buying (and/or selling) that good.

6d04c236c001.title: Subjective theory of value
6d04c236c001.sentence: The contrasting system is typically known as the labor theory of value.

15f6fce49b3c.title: Subjective theory of value
15f6fce49b3c.sentence: It is one of several theories that sprang from the marginal revolution, which was a departure from classical economics, and in particular STV departed from the labor theory of value.

1015687ed505.title: Subjective theory of value
1015687ed505.sentence: The modern version of the subjective theory of value was created independently and nearly simultaneously by William Stanley Jevons, Léon Walras, and Carl Menger in the late 19th century.

b59e35dc79fc.title: Subjective theory of value
b59e35dc79fc.sentence: Thus a good's value may increase substantially following its creation if the good is perceived as being of greater importance, or as being more desirable than before.

2bcc4412f253.title: Subjective theory of value
2bcc4412f253.sentence: There are many variables that can influence this process, including, but not limited to, changes in the age of the good, personal affinity, cultural significance, scarcity, as well as situational circumstances.

ef9a62486c34.title: Subjective theory of value
ef9a62486c34.sentence: This is often seen in the case of collectable items such as cars, vinyl records, and comic books.

6575e5387777.title: Subjective theory of value
6575e5387777.sentence: According to the subjective theory of value, by assuming that all trades between individuals are voluntary, it can be concluded that both parties to the trade subjectively perceive the goods, labour or money they receive, as being of higher value to the goods, labour or money they give away.

90dfcfa3b4fc.title: Subjective theory of value
90dfcfa3b4fc.sentence: The theory holds that one can create value simply by trading with someone who values the items higher, without necessarily modifying them.

570fadd6717b.title: Subjective theory of value
570fadd6717b.sentence: The theory has helped explain why the value of non-essential goods can be higher than essential ones, and how relatively expensive goods can have relatively low production costs.

c1b8ba073028.title: Subjective theory of value
c1b8ba073028.sentence: A combination of both labour and subjective theories can be seen in the formulations of English economist Alfred Marshall.

e235497d1849.title: Subjective theory of value
e235497d1849.sentence: He argued that prices are determined by both the objective costs of production, the supply, and the subjective utility of consumers, the demand.

7700986c2799.title: Factors of production

7700986c2799.sentence: It integrates, among other things, the first and second laws of thermodynamics to formulate more realistic economic systems that adhere to fundamental physical limitations.

c5eac6aa7759.sentence: Matter can be recycled or reused through refining or reforming, but it cannot be created or destroyed, placing an upper limit on the amount of material that can be withdrawn and used.

99b3baf74663.sentence: Integral to ecological economics is the following notion: at the maximum rates of sustainable matter and energy uptake, the only way to increase productivity would be through an increase in design intelligence.

f00456a9515d.title: Factors of production
f00456a9515d.section: Historical schools and factors > Ecological economics
f00456a9515d.sentence: This provides the basis for a core tenet of ecological economics, namely that infinite growth is impossible.

34bd5325ca4c.title: Factors of production
34bd5325ca4c.sentence: In the first half of the 20th century, some authors added the work of organization or entrepreneurship as a fourth factor of production.

337ecb34fafb.sentence: Within classical economics, Adam Smith (Wealth of Nations, Book II, Chapter 1) distinguished fixed capital from circulating capital.

6e631829f6b6.title: Capital (economics)
6e631829f6b6.sentence: The former designated physical assets not consumed in the production of a product (e.g., machines and storage facilities), while the latter referred to physical assets consumed in the process of production (e.g., raw materials and intermediate products).

197212287707.title: Capital (economics)
197212287707.sentence: Adam Smith provided the further clarification that capital is a stock.

85872c947f32.title: Capital (economics)
85872c947f32.sentence: On the other hand, constant capital refers to investment in non-human factors of production, such as plant and machinery, which Marx takes to contribute only its own replacement value to the commodities it is used to produce.

6d4dc38486c9.title: Capital (economics)
6d4dc38486c9.sentence: In Marxian theory, variable capital refers to a capitalist's investment in labor-power, seen as the only source of surplus-value.

d908dcc8bfc3.title: Capital (economics)
d908dcc8bfc3.sentence: Detailed classifications of capital that have been used in various theoretical or applied uses generally respect the following division:

1933bd179aa5.title: Capital (economics)
1933bd179aa5.sentence: - Financial capital, which represents obligations, and is liquidated as money for trade, and owned by legal entities.

e4f55c91e5cd.title: Capital (economics)
e4f55c91e5cd.sentence: - Human capital, a broad term that generally includes social, instructional and individual human talent in combination.

9955e61bf465.title: Capital (economics)
9955e61bf465.sentence: - Natural or ecological capital is the world's stock of natural resources, which includes geology, soils, air, water and all living organisms.

fa1715b0e0d4.title: Capital (economics)
fa1715b0e0d4.sentence: It is in the form of capital assets, traded in financial markets.

42626344e5f8.title: Capital (economics)
42626344e5f8.sentence: Its market value is not based on the historical accumulation of money invested but on the perception by the market of its expected revenues and of the risk entailed.

77a8a9b58705.title: Capital (economics)
77a8a9b58705.sentence: - Public capital is a blanket term that attempts to characterize physical capital that is considered infrastructure and which supports production in unclear or poorly accounted ways.

70faee75e100.title: Capital (economics)
70faee75e100.sentence: This encompasses the aggregate body of all government-owned assets that are used to promote private industry productivity, including highways, railways, airports, water treatment facilities, telecommunications, electric grids, energy utilities, municipal buildings, public hospitals and schools, police, fire protection, courts and still others.

03e8f5bc427d.title: Capital (economics)
03e8f5bc427d.sentence: Some natural capital assets provide people with free goods and services, often called ecosystem services.

9089f8d74e9e.title: Marginal utility
9089f8d74e9e.sentence: Marginalism eventually found a foothold by way of the work of three economists, Jevons in England, Menger in Austria, and Walras in Switzerland.

236386ff02cf.title: Marginal utility
236386ff02cf.sentence: William Stanley Jevons first proposed the theory in "A General Mathematical Theory of Political Economy", a paper presented in 1862 and published in 1863, followed by a series of works culminating in his book The Theory of Political Economy in 1871 that established his reputation as a leading political economist and logician of the time.

78ff629247b8.title: Marginal utility
78ff629247b8.sentence: Jevons' conception of utility was in the utilitarian tradition of Jeremy Bentham and of John Stuart Mill, but he differed from his classical predecessors in emphasizing that "value depends entirely upon utility", in particular, on "final utility upon which the theory of Economics will be found to turn." He later qualified this in deriving the result that in a model of exchange equilibrium, price ratios would be proportional not only to ratios of "final degrees of utility", but also to costs of production.

483943bac73d.title: Marginal utility
483943bac73d.sentence: Carl Menger presented the theory in Grundsätze der Volkswirtschaftslehre (translated as Principles of Economics) in 1871.

34223d35eee0.title: Marginal utility

c4c8a9c807b0.title: Marginal utility
c4c8a9c807b0.sentence: Although the Marginal Revolution flowed from the work of Jevons, Menger, and Walras, their work might have failed to enter the mainstream were it not for a second generation of economists.

ef492f2687ba.title: Absolute advantage
ef492f2687ba.sentence: In economics, the principle of absolute advantage is the ability of a party (an individual, or firm, or country) to produce a goods or service more efficiently than its competitors.

1108f02b9003.title: Absolute advantage
1108f02b9003.sentence: The Scottish economist Adam Smith first described the principle of absolute advantage in the context of international trade in 1776, using labor as the only input.

d1deea790d52.title: Absolute advantage
d1deea790d52.sentence: The concept of absolute advantage is generally attributed to the Scottish economist Adam Smith in his 1776 publication The Wealth of Nations, in which he countered mercantilist ideas.

4031ceaf61ab.title: Absolute advantage
4031ceaf61ab.sentence: Smith argued that it was impossible for all nations to become rich simultaneously by following mercantilism because the export of one nation is another nation's import and instead stated that all nations would gain simultaneously if they practiced free trade and specialized in accordance with their absolute advantage.

e32dad517db1.title: Absolute advantage
e32dad517db1.sentence: The UK is able to produce one unit of cloth with fewer hours of labor, therefore the UK has an absolute advantage in the production of cloth.

09c8ab649b3c.title: Absolute advantage
09c8ab649b3c.sentence: Therefore, Portugal has an absolute advantage in the production of wine.

b87914ea2def.title: Absolute advantage
b87914ea2def.sentence: If the two countries specialize in producing the good for which they have the absolute advantage, and if they exchange part of the good with each other, both of the two countries can end up with more of each good than they would have in the absence of trade.

407d84f31b08.title: Absolute advantage
407d84f31b08.sentence: Since absolute advantage is determined by a simple comparison of labor productiveness, it is possible for a party to have no absolute advantage in anything.

1cf0569579fb.title: Economics
1cf0569579fb.sentence: Even if one region has an absolute advantage as to the ratio of its outputs to inputs in every type of output, it may still specialise in the output in which it has a comparative advantage and thereby gain from trading with a region that lacks any absolute advantage but has a comparative advantage in producing something else.

8996c53adf09.title: Comparative advantage
8996c53adf09.sentence: Comparative advantage is an economic principle that explains why people, firms, and countries can often benefit from trade even when one party is more productive at producing every good or service.

a191a69e4588.title: Comparative advantage
a191a69e4588.sentence: The principle states that greater gains from trade arise when each participant devotes a larger share of its labor and other productive resources to the activities with the lowest opportunity cost and obtains other goods and services through trade.

6e67f4981eb6.title: Comparative advantage
6e67f4981eb6.sentence: Comparative advantage differs from absolute advantage, which concerns being more productive overall, and competitive advantage, which concerns outperforming rivals in a marketplace.

e91828e159a9.title: Comparative advantage
e91828e159a9.sentence: David Ricardo developed the classical theory of comparative advantage in 1817 to explain why countries engage in international trade even when one country's workers are more efficient at producing every single good than workers in other countries.

f021318935f3.title: Comparative advantage
f021318935f3.section: Classical theory and David Ricardo's formulation > Ricardo's example
f021318935f3.sentence: In a famous example, Ricardo considers a world economy consisting of two countries, Portugal and England, each producing two goods of identical quality.

1269ab8865db.title: Comparative advantage
1269ab8865db.section: Classical theory and David Ricardo's formulation > Socio-political context of discovery
1269ab8865db.sentence: While the mathematical formalization of comparative advantage is attributed to David Ricardo's Principles (1817) the doctrine emerged primarily as a response to the socio-political turmoil of the British Corn Laws.

dbc782a5926b.title: Comparative advantage
dbc782a5926b.section: Classical theory and David Ricardo's formulation > Socio-political context of discovery
dbc782a5926b.sentence: Following the Napoleonic Wars, the 1815 Corn Laws imposed high tariffs on imported grain to protect domestic landowners, sparking a fierce debate between the landed gentry and emerging industrial capitalists.

3385e687d98e.title: Comparative advantage
3385e687d98e.sentence: In 1930 Austrian-American economist Gottfried Haberler detached the doctrine of comparative advantage from Ricardo's labor theory of value and provided a modern opportunity cost formulation.

c60d867acbe6.title: Comparative advantage
c60d867acbe6.sentence: Haberler's innovation was to reformulate the theory of comparative advantage such that the value of good X is measured in terms of the forgone units of production of good Y rather than the labor units necessary to produce good X, as in the Ricardian formulation.

9f27b89fe615.title: Comparative advantage
9f27b89fe615.sentence: Comparative advantage is a theory about the benefits that specialization and trade would bring, rather than a strict prediction about actual behavior.

9527de0b39a1.title: Comparative advantage

226446f7fc35.sentence: According to Galbraith, nations trapped into specializing in agriculture are condemned to perpetual poverty, as agriculture is dependent on land, a finite non-increasing natural resource.

5492feeb754b.title: Production-possibility frontier
5492feeb754b.sentence: The slope of the production-possibility frontier (PPF) at any given point is called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT).

dd4d91a08282.title: Production-possibility frontier
dd4d91a08282.sentence: It measures how much of good Y is given up for one more unit of good X or vice versa.

836c70f35bef.title: Production-possibility frontier
836c70f35bef.sentence: It is also called the (marginal) "opportunity cost" of a commodity, that is, it is the opportunity cost of X in terms of Y at the margin.

13d5745b721f.title: Production-possibility frontier
13d5745b721f.sentence: If, for example, the (absolute) slope at point BB in the diagram is equal to 2, to produce one more packet of butter, the production of 2 guns must be sacrificed.

c8b6c7201602.title: Production-possibility frontier
c8b6c7201602.sentence: Pareto efficiency is achieved when the marginal rate of transformation (slope of the frontier/opportunity cost of goods) is equal to all consumers' marginal rate of substitution.

ae4cb57c50df.sentence: His theory was based on the labor theory of value, which distinguishes between exchange value and use value.

5466083a61c3.sentence: Rather than an explanation of constants, and of the basic evolution of economic life, the "marginal" technique provides at best an explanation of ephemeral, short-term variations.

e673e4473a8f.sentence: Maurice Dobb argued that prices derived through marginalism depend on the distribution of income.

5b91fa114e05.sentence: The ability of consumers to express their preferences is dependent on their spending power.

2843c31c95fc.title: Implicit cost
2843c31c95fc.sentence: In economics, an implicit cost (also called an imputed cost, implied cost or notional cost) is the opportunity cost equal to what a firm must give up in order to use a factor of production for which it already owns and thus does not pay rent.

f26e8a4ca1af.title: Implicit cost
f26e8a4ca1af.sentence: In other words, an implicit cost is any cost that results from using an asset instead of renting it out, selling it, or using it differently.

c2bf5e4d5cda.title: Implicit cost
c2bf5e4d5cda.sentence: It is the opposite of an explicit cost, which is borne directly.

71409f5b5efc.title: Implicit cost
71409f5b5efc.sentence: The term also applies to foregone income from choosing not to work.

472fc058ffd0.title: Implicit cost
472fc058ffd0.sentence: Implicit costs also represent the divergence between economic profit (total revenues minus total costs, where total costs are the sum of implicit and explicit costs) and accounting profit (total revenues minus only explicit costs).

3bfb2f346bf5.title: Economic cost
3bfb2f346bf5.sentence: Economic cost differs from accounting cost because it includes opportunity cost.

eed9f4c64c19.title: Economic cost
eed9f4c64c19.sentence: Economic cost is used mainly by economists as means to compare the prudence of one course of action with that of another.

eae57ba250e6.title: Economic cost

b062c932f1f2.title: Sunk cost
b062c932f1f2.sentence: In economics and business decision-making, a sunk cost (also known as retrospective cost) is a cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered.

6fe9cacae905.title: Sunk cost
6fe9cacae905.sentence: Sunk costs are contrasted with prospective costs, which are future costs that may be avoided if action is taken.

5c8d8752e88a.title: Sunk cost
5c8d8752e88a.sentence: According to classical economics and standard microeconomic theory, only prospective (future) costs are relevant to a rational decision.

22d8fab132b1.title: Sunk cost
22d8fab132b1.sentence: This is known as the bygones principle or the marginal principle.

82b9f41df30c.title: Sunk cost
82b9f41df30c.sentence: Thus, if a new factory was originally projected to cost $100 million, and yield $120 million in value, and after $30 million is spent on it the value projection falls to $65 million, the company should abandon the project rather than spending an additional $70 million to complete it.

bcfaed18193f.title: Sunk cost

fd63ccb716d3.title: Sunk cost
fd63ccb716d3.sentence: Even though economists argue that sunk costs are no longer relevant to future rational decision-making, people in everyday life often take previous expenditures in situations, such as repairing a car or house, into their future decisions regarding those properties.
