c339b6d96b8a.sentence: An example of a compensation principle is the Pareto criterion in which a change in states entails that such compensation is not merely feasible but required.

f192492b4344.title: Compensation principle
f192492b4344.sentence: But its use is more controversial and complex with some losers (where full compensation is feasible but not made) and in selecting among more than two feasible social states.

c196f7117e30.title: Neoclassical economics
c196f7117e30.sentence: However, many less conservative neoclassical economists instead use the compensation principle, which says that an intervention is good if the total gains are larger than the total losses, even if losers are not compensated in practice.

66ed7f599ec0.title: Economic analysis of climate change
66ed7f599ec0.sentence: According to the compensation principle, so long as those benefiting from a particular project compensate the losers, and there is still something left over, then the result is an unambiguous gain in welfare.

d512b9139558.title: Lump-sum tax
d512b9139558.sentence: A lump-sum tax is a special way of taxation, based on a fixed amount, rather than on the real circumstance of the taxed entity.

20779b990ce6.title: Lump-sum tax
20779b990ce6.sentence: In this, the entity cannot do anything to change their liability.

54d4ca4f26a6.title: Lump-sum tax
54d4ca4f26a6.sentence: Lump-sum taxation is economically efficient in that it doesn't create "deadweight loss".

61f191916953.title: Optimal tax
61f191916953.sentence: Some taxes are thought to be less distorting, such as lump-sum taxes (where individuals cannot change their behaviour to reduce their tax burden) and Pigouvian taxes, where the market consumption of a good is inefficient, and a tax brings consumption closer to the efficient level.

b31c6a4c4632.title: Lump-sum tax
b31c6a4c4632.sentence: A lump-sum tax is one of the various modes used for taxation: income, things owned (property taxes), money spent (sales taxes), miscellaneous (excise taxes), etc. It is a regressive tax, such that the lower the income is, the higher the percentage of income applicable to the tax.

b6aafbfc1981.title: Lump-sum tax
b6aafbfc1981.sentence: A lump-sum tax levied per-person is known as a "head-tax" or "poll-tax".

4ce382b6b452.title: Lump-sum tax
4ce382b6b452.sentence: In the real world, lump-sum tax is not that easily applicable because many people believe that those who have higher ability to pay should pay higher taxes (progressive tax system) and if it were to happen, people with low income would have to be charged very high amounts of money relative to their income and that would be politically unacceptable.

dcec5ae05636.title: Regressive tax
dcec5ae05636.sentence: The lump-sum tax has fallen from mainstream practice, with only one country, Switzerland, still adhering to it.

aa256317b63b.title: Welfare economics
aa256317b63b.sentence: A direct consequence of the second theorem is that a benevolent social planner could use a system of lump sum transfers to ensure that the "best" Pareto efficient allocation was supported as a competitive equilibrium for some set of prices.

f292f3e184df.title: Missing market
f292f3e184df.sentence: A missing market is a situation in microeconomics where a competitive market allowing the exchange of a commodity would be Pareto-efficient, but no such market exists.

5b74e345777e.title: Missing market
5b74e345777e.sentence: A classic example of a missing market is the case of an externality like pollution, where decision makers are not responsible for some of the consequences of their actions.

46f6787cf66f.title: Missing market
46f6787cf66f.sentence: When a factory discharges polluted water into a river, that pollution can hurt people who fish in or get their drinking water from the river downstream, but the factory owner may have no incentive to consider those consequences.

bf36f2402a54.title: Missing market
bf36f2402a54.sentence: Hence, there are not enough incentives for the formation of a pollution market.

0bae410feb6f.title: Missing market
0bae410feb6f.sentence: Again considering the pollution example, downstream residents might seek to be paid by the factory owner who pollute their water, but because of the free rider problem it may be difficult to coordinate.

1f15f700c8ac.title: Missing market
1f15f700c8ac.sentence: If the river has several factories along its banks, it may be difficult or impossible to monitor which factory is responsible for downstream pollution.

3651f0c4c603.title: Missing market
3651f0c4c603.sentence: High transaction costs might also deter market formation.

02c5ff693370.title: Missing market
02c5ff693370.sentence: Markets can also be missing if there is a failure of trust or information.

75629ad0f5f5.title: Missing market
75629ad0f5f5.sentence: The same applies to alternative automotive fuels: few filling station owners will be interested in offering the fuel until alternate-fuel cars are on the road, but people will not buy alternate-fuel cars until filling stations exist to service them.

34cb22a9fec4.title: Missing market
34cb22a9fec4.sentence: In many cases of missing markets, it may be possible for the government or another actor to create circumstances that make market exchange possible.

4b6dd53b53a4.title: Missing market
4b6dd53b53a4.sentence: In the case of pollution, one popular solution is for the government to assign property rights in order to allow Coase Bargaining.

67aecb930ff1.title: Microeconomics
67aecb930ff1.sentence: In such cases, economists may attempt to find policies that avoid waste, either directly by government control, indirectly by regulation that induces market participants to act in a manner consistent with optimal welfare, or by creating "missing markets" to enable efficient trading where none had previously existed.

459f509167dc.title: Contract curve
459f509167dc.sentence: In microeconomics, the contract curve or Pareto set is the set of points representing final allocations of two goods between two people that could occur as a result of mutually beneficial trading between those people given their initial allocations of the goods.

b8179afc6805.title: Contract curve
b8179afc6805.sentence: All the points on this locus are Pareto efficient allocations, meaning that from any one of these points there is no reallocation that could make one of the people more satisfied with his or her allocation without making the other person less satisfied.

e75f5082d5a7.title: Contract curve
e75f5082d5a7.sentence: It is drawn in the Edgeworth box diagram shown here, in which each person's allocation is measured vertically for one good and horizontally for the other good from that person's origin (point of zero allocation of both goods); one person's origin is the lower left corner of the Edgeworth box, and the other person's origin is the upper right corner of the box.

b2a5d688589d.title: Contract curve
b2a5d688589d.sentence: As with all points that are Pareto efficient, each point on the contract curve is a point of tangency between an indifference curve of one person and an indifference curve of the other person.

8bc65ca6b08f.title: Contract curve
8bc65ca6b08f.sentence: Thus, on the contract curve the marginal rate of substitution is the same for both people.

7524d92c13fb.title: Contract curve
7524d92c13fb.sentence: The analysis cannot say which particular point along the contract curve they will end up at — this depends on the two people's bargaining skills.

a6ad3497c814.title: Contract curve
a6ad3497c814.sentence: Any Walrasian equilibrium lies on the contract curve.

c02694262f9f.title: Inequity aversion
c02694262f9f.sentence: Inequity aversion (IA) is the preference for fairness and resistance to incidental inequalities.

e13350b0ec61.title: Inequity aversion
e13350b0ec61.sentence: Researchers on inequity aversion aim to explain behaviors that are not purely driven by self-interests but fairness considerations.

ccef3ea70c24.title: Inequity aversion
ccef3ea70c24.sentence: A more recent definition of inequity aversion (resistance to inequitable outcomes) was developed in 1999 by Fehr and Schmidt.

d40d5c55a90e.title: Inequity aversion
d40d5c55a90e.sentence: where α parametrizes the distaste of person i for disadvantageous inequality in the first nonstandard term, and β parametrizes the distaste of person i for advantageous inequality in the final term.

52f488e10be0.title: Inequity aversion
52f488e10be0.sentence: The partner typically vetoes the deal when low offers are made.

fbc363d0be80.title: Inequity aversion
fbc363d0be80.sentence: People consistently prefer getting nothing to receiving a small share of the pie.

0ed2c5db0ac6.title: Inequity aversion
0ed2c5db0ac6.sentence: Rejecting the offer is in effect paying to punish the dictator (called the proposer).

8da7e94d06d9.title: Inequity aversion
8da7e94d06d9.section: Human studies > Punishing unjust success and game theory
8da7e94d06d9.sentence: Without inequity aversion's rejection of injustice, stable cooperation would be harder to maintain (for instance, there would be more opportunities for successful free riders).

ddc2502a297a.title: Inequity aversion
ddc2502a297a.section: Human studies > Punishing unjust success and game theory
ddc2502a297a.sentence: Thus, individuals who free ride on the contributions of fellow group members are likely to be punished because they earn more, creating a decentralized incentive for the maintenance of cooperation.

ca63fe80fc92.title: Inequity aversion
ca63fe80fc92.sentence: An experiment on capuchin monkeys (Brosnan, S and de Waal, F) showed that the subjects would prefer receiving nothing to receiving a reward awarded inequitably in favor of a second monkey, and appeared to target their anger at the researchers responsible for the inequitable distribution of food.

adaef3f48233.title: Social welfare function
adaef3f48233.sentence: Introducing one additional axiom—the nonexistence of Dutch Books, or equivalently that social choice behaves according to the axioms of rational choice—implies that the social choice function must be the utilitarian rule—i.e., the weighting function w(u) must be equal to the utility functions of each individual.

40aca70a7573.title: Social welfare function
40aca70a7573.sentence: This result is known as Harsanyi's utilitarian theorem.

4149d98b9d8d.title: Social welfare function
4149d98b9d8d.sentence: According to Harsanyi's theorem, any non-utilitarian social choice function will be incoherent; in other words, it will agree to some bets that are unanimously opposed by every member of society.

a8fc0e906c1a.title: Social welfare function
a8fc0e906c1a.sentence: Instead of imposing rational behavior on the social utility function, we can impose a weaker criterion called independence of common scale: the relation between two utility profiles does not change if both of them are multiplied by the same constant.

63d5220b4b7a.title: Social welfare function
63d5220b4b7a.sentence: For example, the utility function should not depend on whether we measure incomes in cents or dollars.

fbdde898a4b7.title: Social welfare function
fbdde898a4b7.sentence: If the preference relation has properties 1–5, the function w must be the isoelastic function:

9755c7c42941.title: Social welfare function
9755c7c42941.sentence: - For η=0 we get the Nash bargaining solution—maximizing the product of utilities.

ab45e55e886c.title: Social welfare function
ab45e55e886c.sentence: - For η=1 we get the utilitarian welfare function—maximizing the sum of utilities.

2f5359ca23ef.title: Social welfare function
2f5359ca23ef.sentence: If we require the Pigou–Dalton principle (that inequality is not a positive good), then η in the above family must be at most 1.

d790c3932b05.title: Social choice theory
d790c3932b05.sentence: Majority rule can create cycles that violate the transitive property: Attempting to use majority rule as a social choice function creates situations where we have A better than B and B better than C, but C is also better than A.

200edab35772.title: Social choice theory
200edab35772.sentence: Condorcet's example demonstrates that democracy cannot be thought of as being the same as simple majority rule or majoritarianism; otherwise, it will be self-contradictory when three or more options are available.

68b54790a212.title: Social choice theory
68b54790a212.sentence: This contrasts with May's theorem, which shows that simple majority is the optimal voting mechanism when there are only two outcomes, and only ordinal preferences are allowed.

f804263e3774.title: Social choice theory
f804263e3774.sentence: A summary of 37 individual studies, covering a total of 265 real-world elections, large and small, found 25 instances of a Condorcet paradox for a total likelihood of 9.4%.

5afba39d668e.title: Social choice theory
5afba39d668e.sentence: But much of the research in the field assumes that those utility functions are internal to humans, lack a meaningful unit of measure and cannot be compared across different individuals.

96ace0c3d2a1.title: Social choice theory
96ace0c3d2a1.sentence: Whether this type of interpersonal utility comparison is possible or not significantly alters the available mathematical structures for social welfare functions and social choice theory.

0fb18feeacdd.title: Social choice theory
0fb18feeacdd.sentence: In one perspective, following Jeremy Bentham, utilitarians have argued that preferences and utility functions of individuals are interpersonally comparable and may therefore be added together to arrive at a measure of aggregate utility.

67b9ba126850.title: Social choice theory
67b9ba126850.sentence: Utilitarian ethics call for maximizing this aggregate.

7306da9e147a.title: Social choice theory
7306da9e147a.sentence: It has been used to defend transfers of wealth from the "rich" to the "poor" on the premise that the former do not derive as much utility as the latter from an extra unit of income.

029a5ea6736f.title: Social choice theory
029a5ea6736f.sentence: Following arguments similar to those espoused by behaviorists in psychology, Robbins argued concepts of utility were unscientific and unfalsifiable.

57586e32686a.title: Social choice theory
57586e32686a.sentence: Robbins argued that this notion is beyond positive science; that is, one cannot measure changes in the utility of someone else, nor is it required by positive theory.

131ca597ba54.title: Social choice theory
131ca597ba54.sentence: John Harsanyi agreed that perfect comparisons of mental states are not practically possible, but people can still make some comparisons thanks to their similar backgrounds, cultural experiences, and psychologies.

441f21e27938.title: Social choice theory
441f21e27938.sentence: Harsanyi and Sen thus argue that at least partial comparability of utility is possible, and social choice theory should proceed under that assumption.

cef60dbc9fef.title: Distributive justice
cef60dbc9fef.sentence: Five types of distributive norm are defined by Donelson R. Forsyth:

10bdb83a57ad.title: Distributive justice
10bdb83a57ad.sentence: - Equality: Regardless of their inputs, all group members should be given an equal share of the rewards/costs.

e427942981b7.title: Distributive justice
e427942981b7.sentence: - Equity: Members' outcomes should be based upon their inputs.

3a58fc0ade70.title: Distributive justice
3a58fc0ade70.sentence: - Power: Those with more authority, status, or control over the group should receive more than those in lower level positions.

7c36c12803f9.title: Distributive justice
7c36c12803f9.sentence: - Need: Those in greatest needs should be provided with resources needed to meet those needs.

0065e6d010de.title: Distributive justice
0065e6d010de.sentence: - Responsibility: Group members who have the most should share their resources with those who have less.

378b573b208d.title: Distributive justice
378b573b208d.sentence: Therefore, an individual who has invested a large amount of input (e.g. time, money, energy) should receive more from the group than someone who has contributed very little.

bd6da9f6fab8.title: Distributive justice
bd6da9f6fab8.sentence: Members of large groups prefer to base allocations of rewards and costs on equity.

1053d7ed3d5d.title: Distributive justice
1053d7ed3d5d.sentence: These individuals should be given more resources than those who already possess them, regardless of their input.

54dd22dcff27.title: Distributive justice
54dd22dcff27.sentence: Attention is mainly given to ways in which unchosen person circumstances affect and hinder individuals and their life opportunities.

3a7d68e89c36.title: Distributive justice
3a7d68e89c36.sentence: The main issue with egalitarian conceptions of distributive justice is the question concerning what kind of equality should be pursued.

29dc8a258dfa.title: Distributive justice
29dc8a258dfa.sentence: The principle of strict equality therefore holds that even if an unequal distribution would make everyone better off, or if an unequal distribution would make some better off but no one worse off, the strictly egalitarian distribution should be upheld.

1a53897aa68e.title: Distributive justice
1a53897aa68e.sentence: This notion of distributive justice can be critiqued because it can result in Pareto suboptimal distributions.

f78c675e3171.title: Distributive justice
f78c675e3171.sentence: This illustrates a concern for the equality of welfare, which is an ex post conception of equality as it is concerned with the equality in outcomes.

203376dce858.title: Distributive justice
203376dce858.sentence: This conception has been critiqued by those in favour of ex ante equality, that is equality in people´s prospects, which is captured by alternative conceptions of equality such as those that demand equality of opportunity.

4c16f9dbf47a.title: Distributive justice
4c16f9dbf47a.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness
4c16f9dbf47a.sentence: - the equality of people in rights and liberties;

a53549343d8d.title: Distributive justice
a53549343d8d.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness
a53549343d8d.sentence: - the equality of opportunities for all; and

b84be43376be.title: Distributive justice
b84be43376be.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness
b84be43376be.sentence: - an arrangement of economic inequalities focused on benefit maximisation for those who are least advantaged.

c7a82466fcb6.title: Distributive justice
c7a82466fcb6.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > The just 'basic structure'
c7a82466fcb6.sentence: Building a modern view on social contract theory, Rawls bases his work on an idea of justice being rooted in the basic structure, constituting the fundamental rules in society, which shape the social and economic institutions, as well as the governance.

0afc77b33383.title: Distributive justice
0afc77b33383.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > The just 'basic structure'
0afc77b33383.sentence: This basic structure is what shapes the citizens' life opportunities.

32284a4a40d8.title: Distributive justice
32284a4a40d8.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > Basic principles of a just distribution
32284a4a40d8.sentence: The first principle, the liberty principle, is the equal access to basic rights and liberties for all.

851a4943aae4.title: Distributive justice
851a4943aae4.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > Basic principles of a just distribution
851a4943aae4.sentence: The second principle, the difference principle, addresses how the arrangement of social and economic inequalities, and thus the just distribution should look.

cb38d6046752.title: Distributive justice
cb38d6046752.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > Basic principles of a just distribution
cb38d6046752.sentence: Firstly, Rawls argues that such distribution should be based on a reasonable expectation of advantage for all, but also to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged in society.

6300eab011f1.title: Distributive justice
6300eab011f1.section: Theories of distributive justice > Justice as fairness > Basic principles of a just distribution
6300eab011f1.sentence: Secondly, the offices and positions attached to this arrangement should be open to all.

b95ef8aa2cff.title: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics
b95ef8aa2cff.section: History of the fundamental theorems > Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem
b95ef8aa2cff.sentence: In their 1986 paper, "Externalities in Economies with Imperfect Information and Incomplete Markets", Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz showed that the fundamental welfare theorems do not hold if there are incomplete markets or imperfect information.

0165f36a023a.title: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics
0165f36a023a.section: History of the fundamental theorems > Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem
0165f36a023a.sentence: The paper establishes that a competitive equilibrium of an economy with asymmetric information is generically not even constrained Pareto efficient.

01d9ad452359.title: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics
01d9ad452359.section: History of the fundamental theorems > Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem
01d9ad452359.sentence: A government facing the same information constraints as the private individuals in the economy can nevertheless find Pareto-improving policy interventions.

8d85f9454962.title: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics
8d85f9454962.section: History of the fundamental theorems > Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem
8d85f9454962.sentence: Greenwald and Stiglitz noted several relevant situations, including how moral hazard may render a situation inefficient (e.g. an alcohol tax may be pareto improving as it reduces automobile accidents).

4ffde2328236.title: Equity (economics)
4ffde2328236.sentence: The concept of horizontal equity means treating people alike if they are in the same or similar economic situations—making them pay the same taxes and/or providing them with the same public services.

29b5a5367179.title: Equity (economics)
29b5a5367179.sentence: Vertical equity means treating people differently according to the differences in their income, wealth, or other measure of need or ability to pay.

ef4de7c3394a.title: Equity (economics)
ef4de7c3394a.sentence: This principle underpins many tax systems, advocating that those with comparable incomes should incur similar tax burdens.

3f82319452de.title: Equity (economics)
3f82319452de.sentence: It is related to the concept of tax neutrality or the idea that the tax system should not discriminate between similar things or people, or unduly distort behavior.

d5ec0e019bec.title: Equity (economics)
d5ec0e019bec.sentence: It is typically advocating that those who are better off should contribute more to the public coffers.

81a8dc12b9c9.title: Equity (economics)
81a8dc12b9c9.sentence: This principle supports progressive taxation, where tax rates escalate with an individual's income or wealth.

49d9fae7e87f.title: Equity (economics)
49d9fae7e87f.sentence: If the rich pay more in proportion to their income, this is known as a proportional tax; if they pay an increasing proportion, this is termed a progressive tax, sometimes associated with redistribution of wealth.

6b10dc6016f4.title: Equity (economics)
6b10dc6016f4.sentence: Progressive tax is one of the main financial tools to help decrease the inequality between income groups.

5035ecd3288f.title: Equity (economics)
5035ecd3288f.sentence: However, the practical implementation of horizontal equity is fraught with challenges, as defining what constitutes similar economic situations can be highly subjective and complex.

e1c33e8e4972.title: Equity (economics)
e1c33e8e4972.sentence: Attempting to determine vertical equity also raises the serious problems discussed earlier that are associated with interpersonal comparisons of utility.

0138fca7c034.title: Social planner
0138fca7c034.sentence: In welfare economics, a social planner is a hypothetical decision-maker who attempts to maximize some notion of social welfare.

d72f4f8eb7c7.title: Social planner
d72f4f8eb7c7.sentence: The planner is a fictional entity who chooses allocations for every agent in the economy—for example, levels of consumption and leisure—that maximize a social welfare function subject to certain constraints (e.g., a physical resource constraint, or incentive compatibility constraints).

7d4df8e8f491.title: Social planner
7d4df8e8f491.sentence: This so-called planner's problem is a mathematical constrained optimization problem.

4da31d2e41f7.title: Social planner
4da31d2e41f7.sentence: Solving the planner's problem for all possible Pareto weights (i.e., weights on each type of agent in the economy) yields all Pareto efficient allocations.

ae4acee6ae68.title: Social planner
ae4acee6ae68.section: Connection with the fundamental welfare theorems
ae4acee6ae68.sentence: However, the planner is a purely fictional entity; solving the planner's problem requires knowledge of consumers' preferences and all physical resource constraints in the economy.

4e9451441100.title: Social planner
4e9451441100.section: Connection with the fundamental welfare theorems
4e9451441100.sentence: Thus, a natural question is whether a decentralized market could implement a Pareto efficient allocation, or conversely, whether the outcomes from a decentralized market are Pareto efficient.

aabf78a22249.title: Social planner
aabf78a22249.section: Connection with the fundamental welfare theorems
aabf78a22249.sentence: The fundamental theorems of welfare economics answer these questions, under certain key assumptions.

c6c2d0c0a447.title: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model
c6c2d0c0a447.sentence: Ramsey originally formulated the model as a social planner’s problem—maximizing aggregate consumption across generations—before it was reformulated by Cass and Koopmans as a decentralized economy with a representative agent and competitive markets.

5e9841016146.title: Dynamic efficiency
5e9841016146.sentence: In economics, dynamic efficiency is achieved when an economy invests less than the return to capital; conversely, dynamic inefficiency exists when an economy invests more than the return to capital.

b2ecc821b5dd.title: Dynamic efficiency
b2ecc821b5dd.sentence: In dynamic efficiency, it is impossible to make one generation better off without making any other generation worse off.

e115a0a36482.title: Dynamic efficiency
e115a0a36482.sentence: An economy in the Solow growth model is dynamically inefficient if the savings rate exceeds the Golden Rule savings rate.

2d18aa435ac5.title: Dynamic efficiency
2d18aa435ac5.sentence: A savings rate higher than the Golden Rule savings rate implies that an economy could be better off today and tomorrow by saving less.

aa1d37b6cfe0.title: Overlapping generations model
aa1d37b6cfe0.sentence: In Diamond's version of the model, individuals tend to save more than is socially optimal, leading to dynamic inefficiency.

a5c262936729.title: Dynamic efficiency
a5c262936729.sentence: Abel, Mankiw, Summers, and Zeckhauser (1989) develop a criterion for addressing dynamic efficiency and apply this model to the United States and other OECD countries, suggesting that these countries are indeed dynamically efficient.

9fbc9db2c368.title: Dynamic efficiency
9fbc9db2c368.sentence: In relation to markets, in industrial economics, a common argument is that business concentrations or monopolies may be able to promote dynamic efficiency.

d045ae716776.title: Prioritarianism
d045ae716776.sentence: Prioritarianism, the priority view, or priority to the worst off is a perspective within ethics and political philosophy stating that "social welfare orderings should give explicit priority to the worse off".

76ea2a996cae.title: Prioritarianism
76ea2a996cae.sentence: Prioritarianism resembles utilitarianism, and is likewise a form of aggregative consequentialism.

d36765afe08f.title: Prioritarianism
d36765afe08f.sentence: While common forms of utilitarianism view the consequences of an action as having equal moral weight regardless of the person who experiences those consequences, prioritarianism dictates that the consequences of an action should be weighted differently depending on how relatively advantaged the bearer of the consequence is, ceteris paribus.

010785337bb2.title: Prioritarianism
010785337bb2.sentence: In effect, the impacts on those who are more disadvantaged are weighted heavier in the moral calculus than those who are more advantaged.

f361228d9a54.title: Prioritarianism
f361228d9a54.sentence: Prioritarianism does not accord any intrinsic value to equality of well-being across individuals and would not regard a move toward a more equal distribution of well-being as better if the worse off did not benefit.

fc3f0f6f0cc6.title: Prioritarianism
fc3f0f6f0cc6.sentence: The maximin principle ranks outcomes solely according to the well-being of the worst-off member of a society, potentially at the expense of overall good or of other members in society.

5cca2e817da6.title: Prioritarianism
5cca2e817da6.sentence: Another objection to prioritarianism concerns how much weight should be given to the well-being of the worse off.

48649e6b65a9.title: Prioritarianism
48649e6b65a9.sentence: There may be issues of arbitrariness or "sloppy intuitionism" lurking there.

3408fa4e09e9.title: Ethics of climate change
3408fa4e09e9.sentence: Prioritarianism offers one ethical justification for imploring a high discount rate; future people will be better off than we are today, benefiting people today is more valuable than benefiting future people.

e971ff5c7a41.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
e971ff5c7a41.section: Background > Axioms of voting systems > Independence
e971ff5c7a41.sentence: A standard principle of rational choice is independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA), which says that when deciding between A and B, one's opinion about a third option C should not affect their decision.

a6451927aba7.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
a6451927aba7.section: Background > Axioms of voting systems > Independence
a6451927aba7.sentence: - Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) – the social preference between candidate A and candidate B should only depend on the individual preferences between A and B.

347ea16ac6d7.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
347ea16ac6d7.section: Background > Axioms of voting systems > Independence
347ea16ac6d7.sentence: - In other words, the social preference should not change from A≻B to B≻A if voters change their preference about whether A≻C.

4bfe68380c25.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
4bfe68380c25.section: Background > Axioms of voting systems > Independence
4bfe68380c25.sentence: - This is equivalent to the claim about independence of spoiler candidates when using the standard construction of a placement function.

41348faecdf7.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
41348faecdf7.section: Interpretation and practical solutions > Rated social choice > Nonstandard spoilers
41348faecdf7.sentence: Behavioral economists have shown individual irrationality involves violations of IIA (e.g. with decoy effects), suggesting human behavior can cause IIA failures even if the voting method itself does not.

832740511c1d.title: Scitovsky paradox
832740511c1d.sentence: What Scitovsky demonstrated was it is possible that if an allocation A is deemed superior to another allocation B by the Kaldor compensation criteria, then by a subsequent set of moves by the same criteria, we can prove that B is also superior to A.

ee230d73adf9.title: Scitovsky paradox
ee230d73adf9.sentence: The paradox occurs when the gainer from the change of allocation A to allocation B can compensate the loser for making the change, but the loser could also then compensate the gainer for going back to the original position.

83952a03fe04.title: Scitovsky paradox
83952a03fe04.sentence: It is named after the Hungarian born American economist, Tibor Scitovsky.

5180dec47da0.title: Scitovsky paradox
5180dec47da0.sentence: He has therefore offered his own criterion called the “Scitovsky Double criterion”.

954cccc801cc.title: Scitovsky paradox
954cccc801cc.sentence: The Scitovsky criterion was developed by Tibor Scitovsky in his paper “A Note on Welfare Propositions in Economics”, 1941.

25aa7a628d53.title: Kaldor–Hicks efficiency
25aa7a628d53.sentence: For instance, Tibor Scitovsky demonstrated that the Kaldor criterion alone is not antisymmetric: it's possible to have a situation where an outcome A is an improvement (according to the Kaldor criterion) over outcome B, but B is also an improvement over A. The combined Kaldor–Hicks criterion does not have this problem, but it may not be transitive (given A as an improvement over B, and B over C, A is not thereby an improvement over C).

0361b6f6a502.title: Original position
0361b6f6a502.sentence: In philosophy, the original position is a hypothetical position from which members of society would consider which principles they would select for the basic structure of their society if they had no knowledge ahead of time regarding the position which they would end up occupying in that society.

f8dc5f7fc337.title: Original position
f8dc5f7fc337.sentence: The idea of having no such knowledge, because everyone is behind a veil of ignorance, represents a thought experiment often associated with the work of the American philosopher John Rawls.

a48a5f69b70f.title: Original position
a48a5f69b70f.sentence: In this "original position", the "veil of ignorance" prevents everyone from knowing their ethnicity, social status, gender, and (crucially in Rawls's formulation) their or anyone else's ideas of how to lead a good life.

1b388437dd5a.title: Original position
1b388437dd5a.sentence: Ideally, this would force participants acting rationally to adopt an "initial agreement" on the principles impartially.

6a8aea669da2.title: Original position
6a8aea669da2.sentence: The original position figures prominently in Rawls's 1971 book, A Theory of Justice.

dc49ed41c48f.title: Original position
dc49ed41c48f.sentence: He further argues that the representatives in the original position would adopt the maximin rule when evaluating alternative principles of justice.

9a8c1751649c.title: Original position
9a8c1751649c.sentence: Derived from decision theory and game theory the maximin rule directs attention to the outcome for the least advantaged position.

2338670db58c.title: Original position
2338670db58c.sentence: However, the same thought experiment had already been described earlier in social choice by William Vickrey and John Harsanyi, who independently derived proofs showing a rational observer in the original position would adopt a utilitarian framework.

3dd54492df66.title: Original position
3dd54492df66.sentence: In this respect, John Harsanyi’s analysis suggests that rational individuals, not knowing their future station but treating outcomes according to expected utility, would opt for maximizing average or total well-being.

703eb6978be5.title: Original position
703eb6978be5.sentence: In a 1987 empirical research study, Frohlich, Oppenheimer, and Eavey showed that, in a simulated original position, undergraduates at American universities agreed upon a distributive principle that maximizes the average with a specified floor constraint (a minimum for the worst-off in any given distribution) over maximizing the floor alone or the average alone.

62517e8c790c.title: Original position
62517e8c790c.sentence: While Rawls had argued that individuals in the original position would unanimously choose to maximize the welfare of the worst off, this principle of distribution was by far the least popular choice in the survey and was the preferred choice of less than 5% of participants.

724df87aa122.title: Tax wedge
724df87aa122.sentence: Put differently, the tax wedge is the difference between the price consumers pay and the value producers receive (net of tax) from a transaction.

4a85815be2f7.title: Tax wedge
4a85815be2f7.sentence: The tax effectively drives a "wedge" between the price consumers pay and the price producers receive for a product.

c71a4a6823d2.title: Tax wedge
c71a4a6823d2.sentence: After a tax is introduced, a new equilibrium is reached, where consumers pay more (P∗→Pc), suppliers receive less (P∗→Ps), and the quantity exchanged falls (Q∗→Qt).

b14a240128e0.title: Tax wedge
b14a240128e0.sentence: The difference between Pc and Ps will be equivalent to the size of the per-unit tax.

86ac5a852f0b.title: Tax wedge
86ac5a852f0b.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Deadweight loss
86ac5a852f0b.sentence: The filled-in "wedge" created by a tax actually represents the amount of deadweight loss created by the tax.

e88495d918eb.title: Tax wedge
e88495d918eb.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Deadweight loss
e88495d918eb.sentence: The deadweight loss created by the tax is equal to 12× Tax ×(Q∗−Qt), represented by the shaded triangle in the figure.

591229cfd854.title: Deadweight loss
591229cfd854.sentence: When a monopoly, as a "tax collector", charges a price in order to consolidate its power above marginal cost, it drives a "wedge" between the costs borne by the consumer and supplier.

d5d4cfbf7c40.title: Atkinson index
d5d4cfbf7c40.sentence: The Atkinson index (also known as the Atkinson measure or Atkinson inequality measure) is a measure of income inequality developed by British economist Anthony Barnes Atkinson.

98af1289ea38.title: Atkinson index
98af1289ea38.sentence: The index can be turned into a normative measure by imposing a coefficient ε to weight incomes.

724e347dfaf9.title: Atkinson index
724e347dfaf9.sentence: Greater weight can be placed on changes in a given portion of the income distribution by choosing ε, the level of "inequality aversion", appropriately.

74b98779df80.title: Atkinson index
74b98779df80.sentence: The Atkinson index becomes more sensitive to changes at the lower end of the income distribution as ε increases.

daa3dc0b3bb5.title: Atkinson index
daa3dc0b3bb5.sentence: Thus the Atkinson index gives the share of current income which could be sacrificed, without reducing social welfare, if perfect inequality were instated.

7bc8cd7e90af.title: Atkinson index
7bc8cd7e90af.sentence: The Atkinson index then varies between 0 and 1 and is a measure of the amount of social utility to be gained by complete redistribution of a given income distribution, for a given ε parameter.

c3e73795bf17.title: Atkinson index
c3e73795bf17.sentence: - The index is non-negative, and is equal to zero only if all incomes are the same: Aε(y1,…,yN)=0 iff yi=μ for all i.

4a55363f25b9.title: Atkinson index
4a55363f25b9.sentence: In this case, the welfare equivalent equally distributed income is equal to mean income, and the Atkinson index is zero.

62a6d1095d53.title: Atkinson index
62a6d1095d53.sentence: The Atkinson index with inequality aversion ε is equivalent (under a monotonic rescaling) to a generalized entropy index with parameter α=1−ε

24fc81924a53.title: Atkinson index
24fc81924a53.sentence: - The index is (non-additively) subgroup decomposable and the corresponding generalized entropy index is additively subgroup decomposable.

e1b0f345f16a.title: Atkinson index
e1b0f345f16a.sentence: Many popular indices, including Gini index, do not satisfy this property.

d2d83a3a5b56.title: Marginal cost of public funds
d2d83a3a5b56.sentence: The marginal cost of public funds (MCF) is a concept in public finance which measures the loss incurred by society in raising less revenues to finance government spending due to the distortion of resource allocation caused by taxation.

5d7d271297b3.title: Marginal cost of public funds
5d7d271297b3.sentence: Formally, it is defined as the ratio of the marginal value of a monetary unit raised by the government and the value of that marginal private monetary unit.

8a6542c91dec.title: Marginal cost of public funds
8a6542c91dec.sentence: The applications of the marginal cost of public funds include the Samuelson condition for the optimal provision of public goods and the optimal corrective taxation of externalities in public economic theory, the determination of tax-smoothing policy rules in normative public debt analysis and social cost-benefit analysis common in practical policy analysis.

37ce61b802df.title: Marginal cost of public funds
37ce61b802df.sentence: The initial statement of the MCF problem is generally attributed to Pigou (1947), who stressed the application of the cost-benefit rule to the financing of public spending.

7899ff8f11a3.title: Marginal cost of public funds
7899ff8f11a3.sentence: Practically, MCFs can be calculated based on the tax rate and the elasticities of demand and supply.

4307d5bc0383.title: Excess burden of taxation
4307d5bc0383.sentence: A common position in economics is that the costs in a cost-benefit analysis for any tax-funded project should be increased according to the marginal cost of funds, because that is close to the deadweight loss that will be experienced if the project is added to the budget, or to the deadweight loss removed if the project is removed from the budget.

d5ad76797633.title: Non-convexity (economics)
d5ad76797633.sentence: In economics, non-convexity refers to violations of the convexity assumptions of elementary economics.

d647200ff6f4.title: Non-convexity (economics)
d647200ff6f4.sentence: Basic economics textbooks concentrate on consumers with convex preferences (that do not prefer extremes to in-between values) and convex budget sets and on producers with convex production sets; for convex models, the predicted economic behavior is well understood.

2157e99be3c3.title: Non-convexity (economics)
2157e99be3c3.sentence: Convex analysis centers on convex sets and convex functions, for which it provides powerful ideas and clear results, but it is not adequate for the analysis of non-convexities, such as increasing returns to scale.

250cb9f19cda.title: Non-convexity (economics)
250cb9f19cda.sentence: When convexity assumptions are violated, then many of the good properties of competitive markets need not hold: Thus, non-convexity is associated with market failures, where supply and demand differ or where market equilibria can be inefficient.

7d739b6b8e95.title: Non-convexity (economics)
7d739b6b8e95.sentence: For example, we can imagine that, for zoos, a lion costs as much as an eagle, and further that a zoo's budget suffices for one eagle or one lion.

a02fca6f3e01.title: Non-convexity (economics)
a02fca6f3e01.sentence: Thus, the zoo-keeper's preferences are non-convex: The zoo-keeper prefers having either animal to having any strictly convex combination of both.

5761e3c28690.title: Non-convexity (economics)
5761e3c28690.sentence: Non-convex sets arise also with environmental goods (and other externalities), and with market failures, and public economics.

be8b14cfa488.title: Non-convexity (economics)
be8b14cfa488.sentence: The Shapley–Folkman lemma establishes that non-convexities are compatible with approximate equilibria in markets with many consumers; these results also apply to production economies with many small firms.

909f86b26716.title: Utility–possibility frontier
909f86b26716.sentence: In welfare economics, a utility–possibility frontier (or utility possibilities curve), is a widely used concept analogous to the better-known production–possibility frontier.

bd3dc4a4f191.title: Utility–possibility frontier
bd3dc4a4f191.sentence: The graph shows the maximum amount of one person's utility given each level of utility attained by all others in society.

d6e9d9c10c72.title: Utility–possibility frontier
d6e9d9c10c72.sentence: This means that points on the curve are, by definition, Pareto efficient, which are represented by E, F and G in the image to the right.

e1d59d0aa509.title: Utility–possibility frontier
e1d59d0aa509.sentence: Meanwhile the points that do not lie on this curve are not Pareto efficient, as shown by point H.

9f38f46d8dbe.title: Utility–possibility frontier
9f38f46d8dbe.sentence: All points on or below the utility–possibility frontier are attainable by society; all points above it are not attainable.

5bfde0b1bf0f.title: Utility–possibility frontier
5bfde0b1bf0f.sentence: The slope of the UPF is the trade-off of utilities between two individuals.

c482c8467438.title: Utility–possibility frontier
c482c8467438.sentence: The utility–possibility frontier is derived from the contract curve.

5e8ceb16d442.title: Utility–possibility frontier
5e8ceb16d442.sentence: In a competitive economy, any allocation over the utility–possibility frontier is a Pareto optimum, as the UPF is a representation of the Pareto contract curve in a different dimension (utilities rather than goods).

4e948260599d.title: Utility–possibility frontier
4e948260599d.sentence: Usually, the social welfare function, which incorporates the deservedness of the two individuals and states how society’s well-being relates to that of the two individuals, is required to maximize social welfare.

19274c0ddb8e.title: Utility–possibility frontier
19274c0ddb8e.sentence: To maximize social welfare, a point on the UPF would be chosen that also falls on the highest indifference curve for society.

0dcf9a5c5fc5.title: Welfare economics
0dcf9a5c5fc5.sentence: Such point is called "the point of bliss".

08a6b740d6eb.title: Tax wedge
08a6b740d6eb.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
08a6b740d6eb.sentence: There are two types of tax incidence or tax burden created by a tax: the statutory incidence of a tax and the economic incidence of a tax.

914818e4c416.title: Tax wedge
914818e4c416.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
914818e4c416.sentence: The economic incidence of a tax falls on the party that bears the actual cost of the tax.

f4c94ca9cf2a.title: Tax wedge
f4c94ca9cf2a.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
f4c94ca9cf2a.sentence: The statutory incidence of a tax falls on the party, producers or consumers, that has to physically send a check to the government in the amount of a tax.

c12b71dfa2f3.title: Tax wedge
c12b71dfa2f3.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
c12b71dfa2f3.sentence: The statutory incidence of the tax is irrelevant to the economic incidence of the tax.

5865241fce76.title: Tax wedge
5865241fce76.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
5865241fce76.sentence: In fact, the economic incidence is completely determined by the elasticity of supply and demand.

1961465a35f8.title: Tax wedge
1961465a35f8.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
1961465a35f8.sentence: The party with the more inelastic (steeper) curve bears more of the tax.

99d77d352e1a.title: Tax wedge
99d77d352e1a.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
99d77d352e1a.sentence: For example, consumers of tobacco products typically bear more of the tax on tobacco, because they are addicted to the product and their consumption is not strongly affected by price changes (demand is inelastic).

aa10a43c409a.title: Tax wedge
aa10a43c409a.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
aa10a43c409a.sentence: Producers bear more of the tax when supply is inelastic; for example, producers of beachfront hotels would bear more of a tax on hotels and accept lower prices for their product, because a change in price would not have a large effect on the quantity of beachfront hotels.

758e06f78e3e.title: Tax wedge
758e06f78e3e.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
758e06f78e3e.sentence: In the long run, however, supply and demand both become more elastic: consumers' preferences for a product can change (cigarette smokers can quit smoking), and suppliers can choose to reduce their investment in, or leave, the market (a hotel chain can decide to sell its beachfront properties).

3f4c25b59f31.title: Tax wedge
3f4c25b59f31.section: Implications of a tax wedge > Tax incidence
3f4c25b59f31.sentence: This means that the economic incidence on consumers and producers can change in the long run.

fecd17058faf.title: Nuisance
fecd17058faf.sentence: Nuisance (from archaic nocence, through Fr. noisance, nuisance, from Lat. nocere, "to hurt") is a common law tort.

bb1b67e6c4d9.title: Nuisance
bb1b67e6c4d9.sentence: It means something which causes offence, annoyance, trouble or injury.

093e4d4c7416.title: Nuisance
093e4d4c7416.sentence: - to describe an activity or condition that is harmful or annoying to others (e.g., indecent conduct, a rubbish heap or a smoking chimney)

f91078e6536c.title: Nuisance
f91078e6536c.sentence: A nuisance can be either public (also "common") or private.

3b0be4a2e244.title: Nuisance
3b0be4a2e244.sentence: It includes conduct that interferes with public health, safety, peace or convenience.

f15ef1108cd9.title: Nuisance
f15ef1108cd9.sentence: Private nuisance is the interference with the right of specific people.

8177cdab0ff0.title: Nuisance
8177cdab0ff0.sentence: Under the common law, persons in possession of real property (land owners, lease holders etc.) are entitled to the quiet enjoyment of their lands.

10cff532a2e8.title: Nuisance
10cff532a2e8.sentence: If a neighbour interferes with that quiet enjoyment, either by creating smells, sounds, pollution or any other hazard that extends past the boundaries of the property, the affected party may make a claim in nuisance.

43208b1a7283.title: Nuisance
43208b1a7283.sentence: Nuisance is one of the oldest causes of action known to the common law, with cases framed in nuisance going back almost to the beginning of recorded case law.

8b83812beaa9.title: Nuisance
8b83812beaa9.sentence: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the law of nuisance became difficult to administer, as competing property uses often posed a nuisance to each other, and the cost of litigation to settle the issue grew prohibitive.

e4456de3515f.title: Nuisance
e4456de3515f.sentence: As such, most jurisdictions now have a system of land use planning (e.g. zoning) that describes what activities are acceptable in a given location.

3046ce1d1507.title: Nuisance
3046ce1d1507.sentence: Similarly, modern environmental laws are an adaptation of the doctrine of nuisance to modern complex societies, in that a person's use of his property may harmfully affect another's property, or person, far from the nuisance activity, and from causes not easily integrated into historic understandings of nuisance law.

35cd44c4d69b.title: Nuisance
35cd44c4d69b.sentence: In the field of environmental science, there are a number of phenomena which are considered nuisances under the law, including most notably noise, water and light pollution.

d10e76bc335e.title: The Problem of Social Cost
d10e76bc335e.sentence: "The Problem of Social Cost" (1960) is a law review article by Ronald Coase, then a faculty member at the University of Virginia, dealing with the economic problem of externalities.

8149eb67cdd0.title: The Problem of Social Cost
8149eb67cdd0.sentence: Coase argued that if we lived in a world without transaction costs, people would bargain with one another to produce the most efficient distribution of resources, regardless of the initial allocation.

29cbb67e9fe4.title: The Problem of Social Cost
29cbb67e9fe4.sentence: Because in the real world there are costs of bargaining and information gathering, legal rules are justified to the extent of their ability to allocate rights to the most efficient right-bearer.

fe3d4a30ed54.title: The Problem of Social Cost
fe3d4a30ed54.sentence: However, many welfare-maximizing reallocations are often forgone because of the transaction costs involved in bargaining.

82c6bc9961c8.title: The Problem of Social Cost
82c6bc9961c8.sentence: For instance, the sweetmaker may have many neighbors who claim "nuisance" — some legitimate and some not, that the firm would have to sort through, and some of those neighbors who do claim nuisance may try to hold out for excessive compensation.

bf8d5c4ea569.title: The Problem of Social Cost
bf8d5c4ea569.sentence: Coase and others like him wanted a change of approach, to put the burden of proof for positive effects on a government that was intervening in the market, by analysing the costs of the action.

944f87f2b19f.title: The Problem of Social Cost
944f87f2b19f.sentence: The argument forms the basis of the Coase Theorem as labeled by George Stigler.

0d8e6e40d0d0.title: Market failure
0d8e6e40d0d0.sentence: "The Problem of Social Cost" illuminates a different path towards social optimum showing the Pigouvian tax is not the only way towards solving externalities.

59e047598b30.title: The Problem of Social Cost
59e047598b30.sentence: The article is foundational to the field of law and economics, and has become the most frequently cited work in all of legal scholarship.

ee0226fee89c.title: The Problem of Social Cost
ee0226fee89c.sentence: Along with an earlier article, “The Nature of the Firm”, "The Problem of Social Cost" was cited by the Nobel committee when Coase was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1991.

2f5abde98406.title: Strict liability
2f5abde98406.sentence: In criminal and civil law, strict liability is a standard of liability under which a person is legally responsible for the consequences flowing from an activity even in the absence of fault or criminal intent on the part of the defendant.

da8b798c2e98.title: Strict liability
da8b798c2e98.sentence: Under the strict liability law, if the defendant possesses anything that is inherently dangerous, as specified under the "ultrahazardous" definition, the defendant is then strictly liable for any damages caused by such possession, no matter how carefully the defendant is safeguarding them.

f33c81e4411c.title: Strict liability
f33c81e4411c.sentence: Other than activities specified above (like ownership of wild animals, etc), US courts have historically considered the following activities as "ultrahazardous":

d5cc03174074.title: Strict liability
d5cc03174074.sentence: - storing flammable liquids in quantity in an urban area

db5df69e3df8.title: Strict liability
db5df69e3df8.sentence: - emission of noxious fumes by a manufacturing plant located in a settled area

6bf99300546a.title: Strict liability
6bf99300546a.sentence: - locating oil wells or refineries in populated communities

72a3bdc162c0.title: Strict liability
72a3bdc162c0.sentence: It discourages reckless behaviour and needless loss by forcing potential defendants to take every possible precaution.

521486bb1607.title: Strict liability
521486bb1607.sentence: An early example of strict liability is the rule Rylands v Fletcher, where it was held that "any person who for his own purposes brings on his lands and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril, and, if he does not do so, is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape".

d5b9b09082a8.title: Environmental impact assessment
d5b9b09082a8.sentence: After an EIA, the precautionary and polluter pays principles may be applied to decide whether to reject, modify or require strict liability or insurance coverage to a project, based on predicted harms.

cff8de649e8f.title: Strict liability
cff8de649e8f.sentence: The trend toward strict liability in the United States during the mid to late 20th century nearly destroyed the small aircraft industry by the mid 1990s.

436450f56c80.title: Strict liability
436450f56c80.sentence: Production had dropped from a peak of 18,000 units per year in 1978 to under only a few hundred by 1993.

f958c6322eb6.title: The Problem of Social Cost
f958c6322eb6.sentence: The factory may be in a better position to know what measures to take to reduce harm, and can be the cheapest avoider, illustrating Coase's argument.

302534d67c4d.title: The Problem of Social Cost
302534d67c4d.sentence: Guido Calabresi in his book The Costs of Accidents (1970) argues that it is still efficient to hold companies liable that produce greater wealth.

1a9babafde21.title: The Problem of Social Cost
1a9babafde21.sentence: In the real world, where people cannot negotiate costlessly, there may be collective action problems of those who caused a nuisance, for instance by smoke emissions from a factory to many neighbouring farms, and so getting together to negotiate effectively can be difficult against a single polluter because of coordination problems.

0257f0e30e6b.title: The Problem of Social Cost
0257f0e30e6b.sentence: If it is efficient for the farmers to pay the factory to reduce its emissions, some of those farmers may hold off paying their fair share, hoping to get a free ride.

bb78e691e89b.title: Nuisance
bb78e691e89b.section: Law related to nuisance, by country > England
bb78e691e89b.sentence: Under English law, unlike US law, it is no defence that the claimant "came to the nuisance": the 1879 case of Sturges v Bridgman is still good law, and a new owner can bring a claim in nuisance for the existing activities of a neighbour.

606ba251bdd5.title: Nuisance
606ba251bdd5.section: Law related to nuisance, by country > United States
606ba251bdd5.sentence: Such limitation often became necessary as the sensibilities of urban dwellers were offended by smells of agricultural waste when they moved to rural locations.

2e34bd58a41f.title: Nuisance
2e34bd58a41f.section: Law related to nuisance, by country > United States
2e34bd58a41f.sentence: For example: many states and provinces have "right to farm" provisions, which allow any agricultural use of land zoned or historically used for agriculture.

09e5e21fbc99.title: The Problem of Social Cost
09e5e21fbc99.sentence: Coase used the example of a nuisance case named Sturges v Bridgman, where a noisy sweetmaker and a quiet doctor were neighbours and went to court to see who should have to move.

7017b132ae52.title: Nuisance
7017b132ae52.sentence: Under the common law, the only remedy for a nuisance was the payment of damages.

ca07b71bd84b.title: Nuisance
ca07b71bd84b.sentence: However, with the development of the courts of equity, the remedy of an injunction became available to prevent a defendant from repeating the activity that caused the nuisance, and specifying punishment for contempt if the defendant is in breach of such an injunction.

cfff1a3c1a50.title: Nuisance
cfff1a3c1a50.sentence: The law and economics movement has been involved in analyzing the most efficient choice of remedies given the circumstances of the nuisance.

8a0dd0e9730c.title: Nuisance
8a0dd0e9730c.sentence: Atlantic Cement Co. a cement plant interfered with a number of neighbors, yet the cost of complying with a full injunction would have been far more than a fair value of the cost to the plaintiffs of continuation.

4579a3c45288.title: Nuisance
4579a3c45288.sentence: The New York court allowed the cement plant owner to 'purchase' the injunction for a specified amount—the permanent damages.

b801ebccf68e.title: Nuisance
b801ebccf68e.sentence: In theory, the permanent damage amount should be the net present value of all future damages suffered by the plaintiff.

3cf34354fa30.title: Externality
3cf34354fa30.sentence: Pigou argued that a tax, equal to the marginal damage or marginal external cost, (later called a "Pigouvian tax") on negative externalities could be used to reduce their incidence to an efficient level.

caa42fc9923e.title: Martin Weitzman
caa42fc9923e.sentence: For example, in the case of pollution, the relative slopes of marginal costs and marginal damages must be examined (the marginal benefits are the avoidance of the marginal damages).

bc4c927b49c0.title: Martin Weitzman
bc4c927b49c0.sentence: His research showed that if the slope of marginal costs is steeper, price controls are more effective and if the relative slope of marginal damages is steeper, then quantity controls are more effective.

921efa4b9d90.title: Externality
921efa4b9d90.sentence: Pigou expanded upon Marshall's ideas and introduced the concept of "Pigovian taxes" or corrective taxes aimed at internalizing externalities by aligning private costs with social costs.

986f060960eb.title: Georgism

41b9e1d7be86.title: Georgism

9ae63fa61de0.title: Georgism

d7ae76b4e759.title: Georgism

7df8e19138a6.title: Georgism

6572c199b391.title: Risk neutral preferences
6572c199b391.sentence: In economics and finance, risk neutral preferences are preferences that are neither risk averse nor risk seeking.

f9680009ded7.title: Risk neutral preferences
f9680009ded7.sentence: A risk neutral party's decisions are not affected by the degree of uncertainty in a set of outcomes, so a risk neutral party is indifferent between choices with equal expected payoffs even if one choice is riskier.

7c3a94c83d63.title: Risk neutral preferences

b3b5ae14281f.title: Risk neutral preferences

be94132fa12e.title: Exponential discounting

8837bf3a1aed.title: Hyperbolic discounting

77cf62f485f0.title: Hyperbolic discounting
77cf62f485f0.sentence: According to hyperbolic discounting, valuations fall relatively rapidly for earlier delay periods (as in, from now to one week), but then fall more slowly for longer delay periods (for instance, more than a few days).
