6f6ffed51c38.sentence: Finally, parametric insurance may reduce transaction costs involved in writing and administering insurance policies because there is less need for actual loss assessment for payment of claims or underwriting rating requirements to determine the premium based on liabilities and extent of risk sharing.

698621494adc.title: Parametric insurance
698621494adc.sentence: The main drawback of parametric insurance policies is that they often do not cover the full basis risk of the insured.

d698322da7e7.title: Parametric insurance
d698322da7e7.sentence: Policies are based on parameters and, therefore, do not always cover the full damage that occurs.

276d94f77d02.title: Parametric insurance
276d94f77d02.section: Examples > Coral Reefs in Quintana Roo, Mexico
276d94f77d02.sentence: In response, Quintana Roo created the Coastal Management Trust Fund to purchase a parametric insurance policy for protecting and restoring the reef.

49d6237d626b.title: Parametric insurance
49d6237d626b.section: Examples > Coral Reefs in Quintana Roo, Mexico
49d6237d626b.sentence: The parametric policy has an annual maximum payout of $3.8 million and is triggered by wind speed.

966b90915ec2.title: Parametric insurance
966b90915ec2.section: Examples > Coral Reefs in Quintana Roo, Mexico
966b90915ec2.sentence: The insurance policy was triggered during Hurricane Delta in October 2020, for which the Coastal Management Trust Fund received $850,000.

bb92abcba9d1.title: Parametric insurance
bb92abcba9d1.section: Examples > Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF)
bb92abcba9d1.sentence: CCRIF is an insurance company established in 2007 that allows Caribbean and Central American countries to purchase parametric insurance products for weather catastrophes.

8e899efa93c2.title: Parametric insurance
8e899efa93c2.section: Examples > Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF)
8e899efa93c2.sentence: By pooling their risks together, each participating country is able to purchase insurance for significantly less than if they had gone through the private market.

2dc789cfcb5d.title: Sustainable finance
2dc789cfcb5d.sentence: Sustainable finance is the set of practices, standards, norms, regulations and products that pursue financial objectives while taking into account environmental, social, and governance considerations.

39f2c3d0bdf1.title: Sustainable finance
39f2c3d0bdf1.sentence: It is often used interchangeably with Environmental, Social & Governance (ESG) investing.

2e128f58ecce.title: Sustainable finance
2e128f58ecce.sentence: It is important to distinguish between ESG integration for better risk-adjusted returns and the broader field of sustainable finance that also includes impact investing, social finance and ethical investing.

bb972773ad8e.title: Sustainable finance
bb972773ad8e.sentence: The long-standing concept was promoted with the adoption of the Paris Climate Agreement, which stipulates that parties must make "finance flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development." In addition, sustainable finance has a key role to play in the European Green Deal and in other EU International agreements, and its popularity continues to grow in financial markets.

437cf033d863.title: Sustainable finance
437cf033d863.sentence: Sustainable finance has become a key cornerstone for the achievement of these goals.

3a1a8435d5df.title: Sustainable finance
3a1a8435d5df.sentence: This commitment involves 193 member states and comprises 17 goals and 169 targets.

8ab3c11cd9cc.title: Sustainable finance
8ab3c11cd9cc.sentence: In 2015, the United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda to steer the transition towards a sustainable and inclusive economy.

24c61127408e.title: Sustainable finance
24c61127408e.sentence: Their growth is consistent; GSS+ (Green, Social and Sustainability bonds and Sustainability-linked bonds) reached a volume of $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025.

84e077839608.title: Sustainable finance
84e077839608.sentence: Public finance will continue to play a key role, but a significant share of the funding will have to come from the private sector.

7a1db65df1f6.title: Sustainable finance
7a1db65df1f6.sentence: Over the past two decades, sustainable finance has developed from a niche academic topic into a recognized field of research and education.

91ea4138856d.title: Sustainable finance
91ea4138856d.sentence: Sustainable finance has become an established part of higher education in business and economics.

68d1e7ce8389.title: Environmental, social, and governance
68d1e7ce8389.sentence: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) is shorthand for an investing principle that prioritizes environmental issues, social issues, and corporate governance.

6cd4c08b6584.title: Environmental, social, and governance
6cd4c08b6584.sentence: MSCI, a global ESG rating agency, defines ESG investing as the consideration of environmental, social, and governance factors alongside financial factors in the investment decision-making process.

72e84d336c69.title: Environmental, social, and governance
72e84d336c69.sentence: The term ESG first came to prominence in a 2004 report titled "Who Cares Wins", which was a joint initiative of financial institutions at the invitation of the United Nations (UN).

0ea39cfa9a8d.title: Environmental, social, and governance
0ea39cfa9a8d.sentence: By 2023, the ESG movement had grown from a UN corporate social responsibility initiative into a global phenomenon representing more than US$30 trillion in assets under management.

a94d4e0c29c6.title: Environmental, social, and governance
a94d4e0c29c6.sentence: The issues often represent externalities, such as influences on the functioning and revenues of the company that are not exclusively affected by market mechanisms.

9d57da0c6f5a.title: Environmental, social, and governance
9d57da0c6f5a.sentence: As with all areas of ESG, the breadth of possible concerns is vast (e.g. greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity, waste management, water management) but some of the chief areas are listed below:

c8b7b3832d9c.title: Environmental, social, and governance
c8b7b3832d9c.sentence: The social dimension of ESG focuses on how companies affect employees and communities, including workplace well-being, equity, and human rights in the supply chain.

8927d78efe30.title: Environmental, social, and governance
8927d78efe30.sentence: Corporate governance refers to the structures and processes that direct and control companies.

b778763a6fa8.title: Environmental, social, and governance
b778763a6fa8.sentence: Corporate Governance in ESG includes issues from the Board of Director's view, Governance Lens watching over Corporate Behavior of the CEO, C-Suite, and employees at large includes measuring the Business ethics, anti-competitive practices, corruption, tax and providing accounting transparency for stakeholders.

7ef9d8d69be9.title: Environmental, social, and governance
7ef9d8d69be9.sentence: ESG saw outflows for the first time in 2023.

eda714e6df67.title: Environmental, social, and governance
eda714e6df67.sentence: Amid allegations of greenwashing and stricter regulations, there is a notable decrease in funds incorporating ESG-related terms into their names.

34f4151cda5f.title: Environmental, social, and governance
34f4151cda5f.sentence: An increasing number of funds in the United States are removing ESG-related terms from their names, a trend not observed in Europe.

f185347d45e7.title: Environmental, social, and governance
f185347d45e7.sentence: These areas include data quality and a lack of standardization; evolving regulation and politics; greenwashing; and variety in the definition and assessment of social good.

a245e79191bc.title: Environmental, social, and governance
a245e79191bc.sentence: This has led to accusations that ESG creates a mechanism for influencing markets and corporate behavior without democratic oversight, raising concerns about accountability and overreach.

375804c04c20.title: Environmental, social, and governance
375804c04c20.sentence: The Freshfields report concluded that not only was it permissible for investment companies to integrate ESG issues into investment analysis, but it was also arguably part of their fiduciary duty to do so.

64cbaf80698b.title: Green bond
64cbaf80698b.sentence: A green bond is a fixed-income financial instrument (bond) which is used to fund projects that have positive environmental benefits.

44b8b963b148.title: Green bond
44b8b963b148.sentence: The main difference is that the funds will be used only for positive climate change or environmental projects.

a202f313048a.title: Green bond
a202f313048a.sentence: Like normal bonds, green bonds can be issued by governments, multi-national banks or corporations and the issuing organization repays the bond and any interest.

2cefdeae0887.title: Green bond
2cefdeae0887.sentence: The categories of eligible green projects include for example: Renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention and control, environmentally sustainable management of living natural resources and land use, terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity, clean transportation, climate change adaptation.

8eefff1add9a.title: Green bond

3bbf75b0bb06.sentence: Since the 2008 financial crisis, the social finance industry has been experiencing a period of accelerated growth as shifts in investor sentiment have increased demand for ethically responsible investment alternatives by retail investors.

d40a65d6977c.title: Social finance
d40a65d6977c.sentence: Social finance, through its innovative approach to solving social problems while creating economic value, has met the need of disaffected retail investors who seek ethical investment alternatives following revelations in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis of widespread unethical business practices by mainstream corporations in pursuit of profit.

778a3ab2f3e9.title: Social finance
778a3ab2f3e9.section: Comparisons with other forms of social welfare enhancement > Comparison with corporate social responsibility
778a3ab2f3e9.sentence: Their critical analysis of the efficacy of social impact bonds concludes that social finance draws capital away from productive investment opportunities and exacerbates allocative inefficiencies caused by excessive existing government regulation.

0b109c7f05b9.title: Social finance
0b109c7f05b9.section: Comparisons with other forms of social welfare enhancement > Comparison with corporate social responsibility
0b109c7f05b9.sentence: Social theorists Jed Emerson and Alex Nicholls reaffirm these claims by suggesting that social finance provides the greater direct investment required to address various social challenges and fill the capital gap that currently exists, given that many social needs have increased in severity, complexity, and scale, while charitable donations are on the decline.

e03f89e1fc07.title: Social finance
e03f89e1fc07.sentence: The social finance industry faces several headwinds, including the struggle to produce desirable returns for investors, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect from mainstream banks, and lack of access to retail investors, an area that is believed to have perhaps the most demand.

ff0907071b6f.title: Social impact bond
ff0907071b6f.sentence: A social impact bond (SIB), also known as pay-for-success financing, pay-for-success bond (US), social benefit bond (Australia), pay-for-benefit bond (Australia), social outcomes contract (UK), social impact partnership (Europe), social impact contract (Europe), or simply a social bond, is a type of outcomes-based contracting, whereby a contractor typically attempts to effect a policy of government but does not get paid by the government unless specified goals are achieved.

dc85f4173193.title: Social impact bond
dc85f4173193.sentence: Repayment to investors is contingent upon specified social outcomes being achieved.

3ba2f6645050.title: Social impact bond
3ba2f6645050.sentence: While they operate during a fixed period of time, they do not offer a fixed rate of return.

0ef9b59e3a2d.title: Social finance
0ef9b59e3a2d.sentence: Unlike conventional bonds, however, SIBs operate on a pay-for-performance basis, in which bondholders are repaid only if the program’s outcome targets are achieved.

cb0ca2003b09.title: Social impact bond
cb0ca2003b09.sentence: The first SIB was announced in the UK on 18 March 2010 by then Justice Secretary Jack Straw, to finance a prisoner rehabilitation program at Peterborough Prison.

0aeec0e8c605.title: Social impact bond
0aeec0e8c605.sentence: The first SIB was launched by UK-based Social Finance in September 2010.

0b2efd509af9.title: Social impact bond
0b2efd509af9.sentence: As of May 2023, 23 countries use SIBs, with (as of 2022) 276 projects in place and capital raised to the value of $745m.

f17e925de40b.title: Social impact bond
f17e925de40b.sentence: This type of financing allows the government to partner with private service providers and, if necessary, private foundations or other investors willing to cover the initial costs and assume performance risk to expand promising programs, while assuring that taxpayers will not pay for the programs unless they demonstrate success in achieving the desired outcomes.

d68e76e3c6cd.title: Social impact bond
d68e76e3c6cd.sentence: Critics note that because the outcomes-based payments are dependent on governmental funds which must be budgeted, social impact bonds do not actually raise additional capital for social programs, but instead displace funding for other programs.

04cc6a175297.title: Social impact bond
04cc6a175297.sentence: Given the need to budget for a return on investment, a program evaluation, middle managers, and the expenses of designing the complex financial and contractual mechanisms, social impact bonds, according to critics, may be an expensive method of operating social programs.

9396da6d519c.title: Sustainability-linked bond
9396da6d519c.sentence: A Sustainability-linked bond (SLB) is a fixed income instrument (Bond) where its financial and/or structural characteristics are tied to predefined Sustainability/ESG objectives.

90367ffb43a5.title: Sustainability-linked bond
90367ffb43a5.sentence: The objectives are measured through predefined Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and evaluated against predefined Sustainability Performance Targets (SPTs).

b2c0138dcae8.title: Sustainability-linked bond
b2c0138dcae8.sentence: The proceeds of SLBs are intended for general purposes, and the use of proceeds is not determinative in their categorization.

96e258751281.title: Sustainability-linked bond
96e258751281.sentence: Bonds where the proceeds are used to finance or re-finance green projects, social projects or a combination of both are called Green, social and Sustainability bonds respectively, and should not be confused with SLBs.

515cd30ed248.title: Sustainability-linked bond
515cd30ed248.sentence: Italian utility Enel issued in September 2019 the first sustainability-linked bond.

9d895ac7a3c2.title: Sustainability-linked bond
9d895ac7a3c2.sentence: If this target is not met, Enel will pay an annual penalty of 25 basis points on its coupon rate.

114df2423552.title: Sustainability-linked bond
114df2423552.sentence: SLB issuance in 2020 was around $10.6 billion and $5 billion in 2019.

845217b0704c.title: Sustainability-linked bond
845217b0704c.sentence: Over 85% of SLBs were linked to environmental KPI with reducing greenhouse gas emissions being the most common type of KPI.

740a82592726.title: Climate finance
740a82592726.sentence: Financial instruments used in blue finance include blue bonds, the marine equivalent of green bonds, which raise capital specifically for ocean conservation and sustainable marine activity.

7fad7cd123c7.title: Conservation finance
7fad7cd123c7.sentence: Labelled bonds, such as green bonds (and related labels such as blue bonds), earmark proceeds for eligible environmental projects and typically follow voluntary market guidance on use of proceeds, project evaluation and selection, management of proceeds, and reporting (sometimes supported by external review).

9ba845879795.title: Conservation finance
9ba845879795.sentence: Some analyses discuss labelled bonds as one channel for mobilising private capital for nature-related objectives, including bond structures linked to sustainable forestry and fisheries and examples such as the Seychelles sovereign blue bond.

5a84979931f1.title: Green bond
5a84979931f1.sentence: Green bonds follow the Green Bond Principles stated by the International Capital Market Association (ICMA), and the proceeds from the issuance of which are to be used for the pre-specified types of projects.

012c8ab52745.title: Green bond
012c8ab52745.sentence: Issuers of green bonds usually follow standards and principles set by private-led organisations such as the International Capital Market Association (ICMA)'s Green Bond Principles or the label of the Climate bond initiative.

1eae2e5d23f6.title: Conservation finance
1eae2e5d23f6.sentence: For labelled bonds, market guidance such as the Green Bond Principles recommends core practices including defined use-of-proceeds, processes for project evaluation and selection, management of proceeds, and periodic reporting, sometimes supplemented by external review, to support investor assurance that proceeds are allocated to eligible projects.

10514a234bb4.title: Conservation finance
10514a234bb4.section: Challenges and criticism > Governance, standards and greenwashing
10514a234bb4.sentence: Market guidance for labelled instruments, including the Green Bond Principles, recommends practices such as defined use-of-proceeds, processes for project selection, management of proceeds, and periodic reporting, sometimes supplemented by external review, as mechanisms intended to reduce information asymmetries and support accountability.

c4932320bd05.title: CITES
c4932320bd05.sentence: CITES (shorter acronym for the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, also known as the Washington Convention) is a multilateral treaty to protect endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade.

1d8bdcc28933.title: CITES
1d8bdcc28933.sentence: The text of the convention was finalized at a meeting of representatives of 80 countries in Washington, D.C., United States, on 3 March 1973.

4623201b25fc.title: CITES
4623201b25fc.sentence: It entered into force after the 10th ratification by a signatory country, on 1 July 1975.

630d006b8b6f.title: CITES
630d006b8b6f.sentence: Although CITES is legally binding on the Parties, it does not take the place of national laws.

1f4d4e2992c9.title: CITES
1f4d4e2992c9.sentence: Rather it provides a framework respected by each Party, which must adopt their own domestic legislation to implement CITES at the national level.

e63962c70fd7.title: CITES
e63962c70fd7.sentence: CITES works by subjecting international trade in specimens of listed taxa to controls as they move across international borders.

571e9904d182.title: CITES
571e9904d182.sentence: CITES specimens can include a wide range of items including the whole animal/plant (whether alive or dead), or a product that contains a part or derivative of the listed taxa such as cosmetics or traditional medicines.

35c23cce2bbf.title: CITES
35c23cce2bbf.sentence: Over 40,900 species, subspecies and populations are protected under CITES.

e660f2a1834b.title: CITES
e660f2a1834b.sentence: By design, CITES regulates and monitors trade in the manner of a "negative list" such that trade in all species is permitted and unregulated unless the species in question appears on the Appendices or looks very much like one of those taxa.

6bd744e30ee8.title: CITES
6bd744e30ee8.sentence: Because the remit of the Convention covers millions of species of plants and animals, and tens of thousands of these taxa are potentially of economic value, in practice this negative list approach effectively forces CITES signatories to expend limited resources on just a select few, leaving many species to be traded with neither constraint nor review.

5427699ebb54.title: CITES
5427699ebb54.section: Shortcomings and concerns > Approach to biodiversity conservation
5427699ebb54.sentence: General limitations about the structure and philosophy of CITES include: by design and intent it focuses on trade at the species level and does not address habitat loss, ecosystem approaches to conservation, or poverty; it seeks to prevent unsustainable use rather than promote sustainable use (which generally conflicts with the Convention on Biological Diversity), although this has been changing (see Nile crocodile, African elephant, South African white rhino case studies in Hutton and Dickinson 2000).

15c8e45a97b5.title: CITES
15c8e45a97b5.section: Shortcomings and concerns > Approach to biodiversity conservation
15c8e45a97b5.sentence: It does not explicitly address market demand.

acd2300b1184.title: CITES
acd2300b1184.section: Shortcomings and concerns > Approach to biodiversity conservation
acd2300b1184.sentence: In fact, CITES listings have been demonstrated to increase financial speculation in certain markets for high value species.

af364a4f8f46.title: CITES
af364a4f8f46.sentence: As of 2002, 50% of Parties lacked one or more of the four major CITES requirements - designation of Management and Scientific Authorities; laws prohibiting the trade in violation of CITES; penalties for such trade and laws providing for the confiscation of specimens.

bd377ae0d667.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
bd377ae0d667.sentence: Integrated Conservation and Development Projects (ICDPs) are biodiversity conservation projects with rural development components.

1248af344531.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
1248af344531.sentence: These projects aim to attend to biodiversity conservation objectives through the use of socio-economic investment tools.

4a59efb06500.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
4a59efb06500.sentence: The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) first introduced ICDPs in the mid-1980s; they wanted to address some of the problems associated with the "fines and fences" (non-participatory) approach to conservation.

d5e27cfdf191.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
d5e27cfdf191.sentence: ICDPs are typically linked to a protected area, such as a national park.

eeb86b267a4e.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
eeb86b267a4e.sentence: They typically receive funding from external sources and are initiated and managed by conservation organizations and development agencies.

9b9e9f03ee02.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
9b9e9f03ee02.sentence: - Diversified local livelihood options will reduce human pressures on biodiversity, leading to improved conservation.

8721f74342b5.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
8721f74342b5.sentence: Conservation organizations have faced criticism over their relationship with the communities in which ICDPs operate; in particular, they have been criticized for designing projects with little to no input from local communities.

fe623c61d946.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
fe623c61d946.sentence: Additionally, minority ethnic groups and women are rarely accounted for in the redistribution of costs and benefits.

862dd0994bb2.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
862dd0994bb2.sentence: ICDPs have been criticized for their focus on alleviating the impact of local communities on protected areas, causing them to overlook external factors like growing market demand for forest and wildlife products, demographic pressures, and vested interests like illegal logging, mineral extraction and ranching.

5cb19dcddc35.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
5cb19dcddc35.sentence: In addition, ICDPs that are funded internationally may not be financially or economically sustainable once their external funding has been exhausted.

9e427f9dd144.title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project
9e427f9dd144.sentence: The Wildlands & Human Needs Program was initiated in 1985 by WWF, and incorporated 19 ICDPs in 12 countries in Africa and South America.

b55773f467a0.title: Ivory trade
b55773f467a0.sentence: The ivory trade is the commercial, often illegal trade in the ivory tusks of the hippopotamus, walrus, narwhal, mammoth, and most commonly, African and Asian elephants.

caaff2fc536c.title: Ivory trade
caaff2fc536c.sentence: Elephant ivory has been exported from Africa and Asia for millennia with records going back to the 14th century BCE.

53caf75dd64d.title: Ivory trade
53caf75dd64d.sentence: At the peak of the ivory trade, pre-20th century, during the colonization of Africa, around 800 to 1,000 tonnes of ivory were sent to Europe alone every year.

0ea5e876573d.title: Ivory trade
0ea5e876573d.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > 1980s poaching and illegal trade
0ea5e876573d.sentence: In 1979, the African elephant population was estimated to be around 1.3 million in 37 range states, but by 1989, only 600,000 remained.

eb40b3cc004e.title: Ivory trade
eb40b3cc004e.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > 1980s poaching and illegal trade
eb40b3cc004e.sentence: Throughout this decade, around 75,000 African elephants were killed for the ivory trade annually, worth around 1 billion dollars.

1a6439369b16.title: Ivory trade
1a6439369b16.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > 1980s poaching and illegal trade
1a6439369b16.sentence: Although many ivory traders repeatedly claimed that the problem was habitat loss, it became glaringly clear that the threat was primarily the international ivory trade.

028117d58f05.title: Ivory trade

028117d58f05.sentence: Throughout the debate which led to the 1990 ivory ban, a group of southern African countries supported Hong Kong and Japanese ivory traders to maintain trade.

2d97188e2f5b.title: Ivory trade
2d97188e2f5b.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > Southern African oppositions to the ban
2d97188e2f5b.sentence: This was stated to be because these countries claimed to have well-managed elephant populations and they needed the revenue from ivory sales to fund conservation.

cdbc6ec7a909.title: Ivory trade
cdbc6ec7a909.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > CITES debate, an attempt to control and ban
cdbc6ec7a909.sentence: Some CITES parties (member states), led by Zimbabwe, stated that wildlife had to have economic value attached to it to survive and that local communities needed to be involved.

781d8c902fc2.title: Ivory trade
781d8c902fc2.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > Renewed sales
781d8c902fc2.sentence: Using criteria that had been agreed upon at the 1989 CITES meeting, among much controversy and debate, in 1997 CITES parties agreed to allow the populations of African elephants in Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe to be "downlisted" to Appendix Two which would allow international trade in elephant parts.

d3b307ed1bfc.title: Ivory trade
d3b307ed1bfc.section: Elephant ivory > African elephant > Renewed sales
d3b307ed1bfc.sentence: Forty-nine tonnes of ivory was registered in these three countries, and Japan's assertion that it had sufficient controls in place was accepted by CITES and the ivory was sold to Japanese traders in 1997 as an "experiment".

8a421a5c1c05.title: Ivory trade
8a421a5c1c05.sentence: Ivory was formerly used to make piano keys and other decorative items because of the white color it presents when processed but the piano industry abandoned ivory as a key covering material in the 1980s in favor of other materials such as plastic.

2b6b2f2878b1.title: Ivory trade
2b6b2f2878b1.sentence: Also, synthetic ivory has been developed which can be used as an alternative material for making piano keys.

d304f171e1ab.title: Reserve design
d304f171e1ab.sentence: Reserve design is the process of planning and creating a nature reserve in a way that effectively accomplishes the goal of the reserve.

1fc27f251904.title: Reserve design
1fc27f251904.sentence: All nature reserves have a primary goal of protecting biodiversity from harmful activities and processes, both natural and anthropogenic.

c6383a492bce.title: Reserve design
c6383a492bce.sentence: These include habitat preference, migration, climate change, and public support.

f153383344e2.title: Reserve design
f153383344e2.sentence: If a reserve is put up in an area that people depend on for their livelihood the reserve often fails.

56ad583dbc61.title: Reserve design
56ad583dbc61.sentence: They continued to hunt and log within the park and eventually the park size had to be reduced [8].

c95f0aa886df.title: Reserve design
c95f0aa886df.sentence: When a reserve is too small, carnivores have increased contact with humans, resulting in higher mortality rates for the carnivore.

e9fb34673b1a.title: Reserve design
e9fb34673b1a.sentence: Reserve systems are a series of strategically placed reserves designed to connect habitats.

172d7f240a76.title: Reserve design
172d7f240a76.sentence: Studies showed that reserve networks are extremely valuable for conservation, and can help increase migration between patches up to 50%.

17794e965076.title: Reserve design
17794e965076.sentence: To be efficient and cost-effective, yet still effectively protect a wide range of organisms, nature reserves must be established in species rich geographic locations.

75141b55bd93.title: Reserve design
75141b55bd93.sentence: Biodiversity hotspots could be considered the most important places to put reserves.

6e097d8fe6cf.title: Reserve design
6e097d8fe6cf.sentence: Reserves must be designed with future habitat in mind, perhaps incorporating both the current and future ranges of the species' of concern.

54b804d387aa.title: Reserve design
54b804d387aa.sentence: 80% of observed range changes were made polewards or upward, as predicted by global climate change, at an average of 6.1 km per decade.

31fb886847f9.title: Human–wildlife conflict
31fb886847f9.sentence: Human–wildlife conflict (HWC) refers to the negative interactions between humans and wild animals, with undesirable consequences both for people and their resources on the one hand, and wildlife and their habitats on the other.

58ffc1721253.title: Human–wildlife conflict
58ffc1721253.sentence: HWC, caused by competition for natural resources between human and wildlife, influences human food security and the well-being of both humans and other animals.

9b5b4606094a.title: Human–wildlife conflict
9b5b4606094a.sentence: In many regions, the number of these conflicts has increased in recent decades as a result of human population growth and the transformation of land use.

5043d16e93cc.title: Human–wildlife conflict
5043d16e93cc.sentence: In general, the consequences of HWC include: crop destruction, reduced agricultural productivity, competition for grazing lands and water supply, livestock predation, human injury and death, damage to infrastructure, and increased risk of disease transmission among wildlife and livestock.

05d5f3a17ef8.title: Human–wildlife conflict
05d5f3a17ef8.sentence: The resulting damage to crops, infrastructure, and at times, people, can lead to the retaliatory killing of elephants by locals.

a0b47bbe23d1.title: Human–wildlife conflict
a0b47bbe23d1.sentence: For example, as a result of the human-elephant conflict in Sri Lanka each year as many as 80 people are killed by elephants and more than 230 elephants are killed by farmers.

51771816bb96.title: Human–wildlife conflict
51771816bb96.sentence: These can include health impacts, opportunity costs, and transaction costs.

4f26ba4346ba.title: Human–wildlife conflict
4f26ba4346ba.sentence: In addition, research has shown that the fear caused by the presence of predators can aggravate human-wildlife conflict more than the actual damage produced by encounters.

d6b49dccc058.title: CITES
d6b49dccc058.sentence: Each protected taxa or population is included in one of three lists called Appendices.

59791b4f7910.title: CITES
59791b4f7910.sentence: The Appendix that lists a taxon or population reflects the level of the threat posed by international trade and the CITES controls that apply.

82dbfd6274c1.title: CITES
82dbfd6274c1.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix I
82dbfd6274c1.sentence: Appendix I taxa are those that are threatened with extinction and to which the highest level of CITES protection is afforded.

09d0645215b1.title: CITES
09d0645215b1.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix I
09d0645215b1.sentence: Commercial trade in wild-sourced specimens of these taxa is not permitted and non-commercial trade is strictly controlled by requiring an import permit and export permit to be granted by the relevant Management Authorities in each country before the trade occurs.

d8de7b230387.title: CITES
d8de7b230387.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix II
d8de7b230387.sentence: Appendix II taxa are those that are not necessarily threatened with extinction, but trade must be controlled in order to avoid utilization incompatible with their survival.

6f0025a84e52.title: CITES
6f0025a84e52.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix II
6f0025a84e52.sentence: The vast majority of taxa listed under CITES are listed in Appendix II.

a2c5a4a14ed9.title: CITES
a2c5a4a14ed9.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix II
a2c5a4a14ed9.sentence: Any trade in Appendix II taxa standardly requires a CITES export permit or re-export certificate to be granted by the Management Authority of the exporting country before the trade occurs.

36e47549ec08.title: CITES
36e47549ec08.section: Regulation of trade > Appendices > Appendix III
36e47549ec08.sentence: Appendix III species are those that are protected in at least one country, and that country has asked other CITES Parties for assistance in controlling the trade.

01afab7fa255.title: CITES
01afab7fa255.section: Regulation of trade > Exemptions and special procedures > Captive bred or artificially propagated specimens
01afab7fa255.sentence: In the case of commercial trade of Appendix I taxa, captive bred or artificially propagated specimens may be traded as if they were Appendix II.

3da3e0147840.title: Human–wildlife conflict
3da3e0147840.sentence: Mitigation strategies for managing human-wildlife conflict vary significantly depending on location and type of conflict.

3b87b6d67045.title: Human–wildlife conflict
3b87b6d67045.sentence: Still, there are a variety of management techniques that are frequently employed to mitigate conflicts.

4ad3d82a4a03.title: Human–wildlife conflict
4ad3d82a4a03.sentence: Regardless of approach, the most successful solutions are those that include local communities in the planning, implementation, and maintenance.

0ff8c46b7cfc.title: Human–wildlife conflict
0ff8c46b7cfc.sentence: - Compensation: in some cases, governmental systems have been established to offer monetary compensation for losses sustained due to human-wildlife conflict.

d14207aceaf1.title: Human–wildlife conflict
d14207aceaf1.sentence: These systems hope to deter the need for retaliatory killings of animals, and to financially incentivize the co-existing of humans and wildlife.

271c05c9827e.title: Human–wildlife conflict
271c05c9827e.sentence: The success of compensation in managing human-wildlife conflict has varied greatly due to under-compensation, a lack of local participation, or a failure by the government to provide timely payments.

a9138f24ee54.title: Human–wildlife conflict
a9138f24ee54.sentence: A recent review found that 15.4% of study cases researching human-carnivore conflict used livestock-guarding dogs as a management technique, with animal losses on average 60 times lower than the norm.

091e6faa61d7.title: Human–wildlife conflict
091e6faa61d7.sentence: - Translocation of problematic animals: Relocating so-called "problem" animals from a site of conflict to a new place is a mitigation technique used in the past, although recent research has shown that this approach can have detrimental impacts on species and is largely ineffective.

99f4231ef40c.title: Conservation biology
99f4231ef40c.section: Context and trends > Threats to biodiversity
99f4231ef40c.sentence: Conservationists have claimed that not all the species can be saved, and they have to decide which their efforts should be used to protect.

e1585f7a2d72.title: Conservation biology
e1585f7a2d72.section: Context and trends > Threats to biodiversity
e1585f7a2d72.sentence: This concept is known as the Conservation Triage.

13004b09ebeb.title: Conservation biology
13004b09ebeb.section: Context and trends > Threats to biodiversity
13004b09ebeb.sentence: The extinction threat is estimated to range from 15 to 37 percent of all species by 2050, or 50 percent of all species over the next 50 years.

7457dc14c364.title: Rights of nature
7457dc14c364.section: Underpinnings and development > Critique of anthropocentric legal systems
7457dc14c364.sentence: They point out that the perspective of nature as primarily an economic resource already has degraded some ecosystems and species so significantly that now, prominent policy experts are examining "endangered species triage" strategies to decide which species will be let go, rather than re-examine the economics driving the degradation.

e13dcba241bc.title: Marxan
e13dcba241bc.sentence: MARXAN is a family of software designed to aid systematic reserve design on conservation planning.

7b3973f43a71.title: Marxan
7b3973f43a71.sentence: Marxan supports the design of cost-efficient networks that meet conservation targets for biodiversity.

769b1cd1277b.title: Marxan
769b1cd1277b.sentence: The simulated annealing algorithm attempts to minimise the total cost of the reserve system, while achieving a set of conservation goals (typically that a certain percentage of each geographical/biological feature is represented by the reserve system).

4c04d603a4c7.title: Marxan
4c04d603a4c7.sentence: Computationally, Marxan provides solutions to a conservation version of the 0-1 knapsack problem, where the objects of interest are potential reserve sites with given biological attributes.

436b1cd3ddf3.title: Marxan
436b1cd3ddf3.sentence: Marxan is the most widely used decision-support software for conservation planning globally, and has been used to build marine and terrestrial conservation systems covering approximately 5% of the Earth's surface.

60a9dafa90e6.title: Marxan
60a9dafa90e6.sentence: MARXAN is the most widely used systematic reserve planning software in the world, and has been used to create the marine reserve network on the Great Barrier Reef, in Queensland, Australia, the largest marine protected area in the world.

0c28b7ba4fbe.title: Marxan
0c28b7ba4fbe.sentence: In contrast to the algorithms conventionally used to solve conservation problems, such as heuristics or simulated annealing, the exact algorithms used here are guaranteed to find optimal solutions.

bd78aebd8ffc.title: Marxan
bd78aebd8ffc.sentence: Finally, this package has the functionality to read input data formatted for the Marxan conservation planning program, and find much cheaper solutions in a much shorter period of time than Marxan.

53fb5fa691d7.title: Paper park
53fb5fa691d7.sentence: A paper park is an area with designated environmental or conservation protection status, but with little actual implementation of environmental management or protection measures.

284de2d70e87.title: Paper park
284de2d70e87.sentence: This can stem from process or governance issues, or from weak regulations and lack of enforcement.

30449c955666.title: Paper park
30449c955666.sentence: Of the 3,449 Natura 2000 MPAs assessed, 70% faced at least one significant threat, with some sites in the Netherlands and the UK experiencing up to 12 threats.

6b77e1ac8185.title: Paper park
6b77e1ac8185.sentence: Only 0.07% of the total MPA network was free from any assessed threats, while 86% of the network was impacted by damaging fishing gear.

b5aa2c74ca1b.title: Natural resource
b5aa2c74ca1b.sentence: Natural resources are resources that are drawn from nature and used with few modifications.

983684c2a43e.title: Natural resource
983684c2a43e.sentence: On Earth, it includes sunlight, atmosphere, water, land, all minerals, along with all vegetation, and wildlife.

5039fa298007.title: Non-renewable resource

68568b0f5e93.title: Renewable resource
68568b0f5e93.sentence: A renewable resource (also known as a flow resource) is a natural resource which will replenish to replace the portion depleted by usage and consumption, either through natural reproduction or other recurring processes in a finite amount of time in a human time scale.

be37c2ce65dd.title: Renewable resource
be37c2ce65dd.sentence: When the recovery rate of resources is unlikely to ever exceed a human time scale, these are called perpetual resources.

5ec7b9c4d124.title: Non-renewable resource

f5b360bdabc6.title: Non-renewable resource

19b51e3bb3b3.sentence: Manufacturing of renewable energy devices uses non-renewable resources such as mined metals and land surface.

aecf3558ea79.title: Natural resource economics
aecf3558ea79.sentence: Natural resource economics deals with the supply, demand, and allocation of the Earth's natural resources.

87db1da0c0fa.title: Natural resource economics
87db1da0c0fa.sentence: One main objective of natural resource economics is to better understand the role of natural resources in the economy in order to develop more sustainable methods of managing those resources to ensure their availability for future generations.

208b82568aa7.title: Natural resource economics
208b82568aa7.sentence: Its focus is how to operate an economy within the ecological constraints of earth's natural resources.

72b939f1ee84.title: Natural resource economics
72b939f1ee84.sentence: The traditional curriculum of natural resource economics emphasized fisheries models, forestry models, and mineral extraction models (i.e. fish, trees, and ore).

2808be9a3eef.title: Natural resource economics
2808be9a3eef.sentence: In recent years, however, other resources, notably air, water, the global climate, and "environmental resources" in general have become increasingly important to policy-making.

16aa65198160.title: Natural resource economics

98c348ac5c0b.title: Natural resource economics
98c348ac5c0b.sentence: Traditional areas of environmental and natural resource economics include welfare theory, land/location use, pollution control, resource extraction, and non-market valuation, and also resource exhaustibility, sustainability, environmental management, and environmental policy.

3713f56cd90a.title: Environmental economics
3713f56cd90a.sentence: Natural resource economics as a subfield began when the main concern of researchers was the optimal commercial exploitation of natural resource stocks.

22f5b7e517fb.title: Exploitation of natural resources
22f5b7e517fb.sentence: The exploitation of natural resources describes using natural resources, often non-renewable or limited, for economic growth or development.

153330350b0b.title: Exploitation of natural resources
153330350b0b.sentence: Environmental degradation, human insecurity, and social conflict frequently accompany natural resource exploitation.

aa6fe32fe8e0.title: Exploitation of natural resources
aa6fe32fe8e0.sentence: The exploitation of natural resources started to emerge on an industrial scale in the 19th century as the extraction and processing of raw materials (such as in mining, steam power, and machinery) expanded much further than it had in pre-industrial areas.

e9b528d3077b.title: Exploitation of natural resources
e9b528d3077b.sentence: - Advancing technology: Increasing technological sophistication enables faster rates of natural resource extraction.

23f140132723.title: Exploitation of natural resources
23f140132723.sentence: - Overconsumption has created a high demand for natural resources, further exacerbating natural resource exploitation

0e8fddd89933.title: Exploitation of natural resources
0e8fddd89933.sentence: - Consumerism: Unsustainable consumption, driven by both population growth and materialistic ideologies, increases the demand for production and, thereby, the extraction of the natural resources needed to supply this demand.

f80bcb5392eb.title: Exploitation of natural resources
f80bcb5392eb.sentence: Foreign industries also contribute to resource exploitation, where raw materials are outsourced from developing countries, with the local communities receiving little profit from the exchange.

41ae0942639c.title: Exploitation of natural resources
41ae0942639c.sentence: According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, around 33% of the Earth's soils are presently classified as moderately to highly degraded, with projections indicating that more than 90% could face degradation by the year 2050 and thus cause significant economic consequences.

d5d2103423cc.title: Exploitation of natural resources
d5d2103423cc.sentence: To ensure sustainability, the consumption rate must remain equal to or less than the supply rate.

c78d70728823.title: Exploitation of natural resources

d0f8e219f489.title: Exploitation of natural resources

743c362dce70.title: Malthusianism
743c362dce70.sentence: Malthusianism is a theory that population growth is potentially exponential, according to the Malthusian growth model, while the growth of the food supply or other resources is linear, which eventually reduces living standards to the point of triggering a population decline.

a5ec315aa515.title: Malthusianism
a5ec315aa515.sentence: These concepts derive from the political and economic thought of the Reverend Thomas Robert Malthus, as laid out in his 1798 writings, An Essay on the Principle of Population.

f8d947c8551e.title: Malthusianism
f8d947c8551e.sentence: Malthus suggested that while technological advances could increase a society's supply of resources, such as food, and thereby improve the standard of living, the abundance of resources would enable population growth, which would eventually bring the supply of resources for each person back to its original level.

2a3ea2bce786.title: Malthusianism
2a3ea2bce786.sentence: This event, called a Malthusian catastrophe (also known as a Malthusian trap, Malthusian check, Malthusian snatch, Malthusian crisis, point of crisis, or Malthusian crunch) has been predicted to occur if population growth outpaces agricultural production, thereby causing famine or war.

13fe346fc8d4.title: Malthusianism
13fe346fc8d4.sentence: Research indicates that technological superiority and higher land productivity had significant positive effects on population density but insignificant effects on the standard of living during the time period 1–1500 AD.

57171c7bd514.title: Malthusianism
57171c7bd514.sentence: In Babylonia during the period 1800 to 1600 BC, for example, the daily wage for a common laborer was enough to buy about 15 pounds of wheat.

16f965e074bb.title: Malthusianism
16f965e074bb.sentence: In England in 1800 AD the wage was about 13 pounds of wheat.

153e9f13cbad.title: Malthusianism
153e9f13cbad.section: Theory of breakout via technology > 20th century
153e9f13cbad.sentence: After World War II, mechanized agriculture produced a dramatic increase in productivity of agriculture and the Green Revolution greatly increased crop yields, expanding the world's food supply while lowering food prices.

b4b75541ca8e.title: Malthusianism
b4b75541ca8e.section: Theory of breakout via technology > 20th century
b4b75541ca8e.sentence: However, populations of most developed countries grew slowly enough to be outpaced by gains in productivity.

0e73915d9c0f.title: Malthusianism

ad24bce25f2e.title: Malthusianism

a26c71baa905.title: Economic rent
a26c71baa905.sentence: In economics, economic rent is any payment to the owner of a factor of production in excess of the costs needed to bring that factor into production.

4a305b286239.title: Economic rent
4a305b286239.sentence: In classical economics, economic rent is any payment made (including imputed value) or benefit received for non-produced inputs such as location (land) and for assets formed by creating official privilege over natural opportunities (e.g., patents).

12717306783f.title: Economic rent
12717306783f.sentence: Economic rent is viewed as unearned revenue while economic profit is a narrower term describing surplus income earned by choosing between risk-adjusted alternatives.

39ffda799244.title: Economic rent
39ffda799244.sentence: Unlike economic profit, economic rent cannot be theoretically eliminated by competition because any actions the recipient of the income may take, such as improving the object being rented, will change the total income to contract rent.

b565cec1469a.title: Economic rent
b565cec1469a.sentence: For most other production, including agriculture and extraction, economic rent is due to a scarcity (uneven distribution) of natural resources (e.g., land, oil, or minerals).

950d9122b695.title: Economic rent
950d9122b695.sentence: The term scarcity rent refers to the price paid for the use of homogeneous land when its supply is limited in relation to demand.

15bd2e031f33.title: Economic rent
15bd2e031f33.sentence: Conversely, if land differs in fertility (i.e., productivity), the surplus that arises due to the difference between the marginal and infra-marginal land is termed differential rent.

da2a682318da.title: Economic rent
da2a682318da.sentence: For example, economic rent can be collected by a government as royalties or extraction fees for resources such as minerals, oil, and gas.

1c2de52eedea.title: Economic rent
1c2de52eedea.sentence: Observing that a tax on the unearned rent of land would not distort economic activities, Henry George proposed that publicly collected land rents (land value taxation) should be the primary (or only) source of public revenue.

4c5d2a662f79.title: Economic rent

691c5bd12b65.title: Economic rent

e0f7b06458dd.title: Economic rent

7a49f11baeb7.title: Resource curse
7a49f11baeb7.sentence: The resource curse, also known as the paradox of plenty or the poverty paradox, is the hypothesis that countries with an abundance of natural resources (such as fossil fuels and certain minerals) have lower economic growth, lower rates of democracy, or poorer development outcomes than countries with fewer natural resources.

a936cacdd046.title: Resource curse
a936cacdd046.sentence: In 1993, Richard Auty first used the term resource curse to describe how countries rich in mineral resources were unable to use that wealth to boost their economies and how, counterintuitively, these countries had lower economic growth than countries without an abundance of natural resources.

a4b021283601.title: Resource curse
a4b021283601.sentence: The idea that resources might be more of an economic curse than a blessing first emerged as early as 1711, with English publication The Spectator noting, "It is generally observed, that in countries of the greatest plenty there is the poorest living." The idea gained further traction during debates in the 1950s and the 1960s about the economic problems of low- and middle-income countries.

357caa6777c7.title: Resource curse
357caa6777c7.sentence: An influential 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong correlation between natural resource abundance and poor economic growth.

ea0884db99c5.title: Resource curse

e9ec400b8777.title: Resource curse
e9ec400b8777.sentence: Prices for some natural resources are subject to wide fluctuation; for example, crude oil prices rose from around $3 per barrel to $12/bbl in 1974 following the 1973 oil crisis and fell from $27/bbl to below $10/bbl during the 1986 glut.

33c06622fefe.title: Resource curse
33c06622fefe.sentence: When government revenues are dominated by inflows from natural resources (for example, 99.3% of Angola's exports came from just oil and diamonds in 2005), the volatility can disrupt government planning and debt service.

6df20269dc14.title: Resource curse
6df20269dc14.sentence: "Oil production generally takes place in an economic enclave, meaning it has few direct effects on the rest of the economy." Michael Ross describes how there are limited economic linkages with other industries in the economy.

4430db84b1d7.title: Resource curse

bc070879c655.title: Resource curse
bc070879c655.sentence: Even when politically stable, countries whose economies are dominated by resource extraction industries tend to be less democratic and more corrupt.

627848596d57.title: Resource curse
627848596d57.section: Other effects > Democracy and human rights
627848596d57.sentence: According to Michael Ross, "only one type of resource has been consistently correlated with less democracy and worse institutions: petroleum, which is the key variable in the vast majority of the studies that identify some type of curse." A 2014 meta-analysis confirms the negative impact of oil wealth on democratization.

219bb07b8677.title: Resource curse
219bb07b8677.sentence: Most experts believe the resource curse is not universal or inevitable but affects certain types of countries or regions under certain conditions.

266a0bd08cdf.sentence: The Hubbert curve is an approximation of the production rate of a resource over time.

005dcadd3969.sentence: It first appeared in "Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels," geologist M. King Hubbert's 1956 presentation to the American Petroleum Institute, as an idealized symmetric curve, during his tenure at the Shell Oil Company.

a635b4278c3f.title: Hubbert curve

6d50aeecbe06.title: Hubbert curve

65b230bfdb85.title: Hubbert curve
65b230bfdb85.sentence: Because of such factors, real world Hubbert curves are often not symmetrical.

2c73f26e2914.title: Hubbert curve

b4e95726ab1c.title: Hubbert curve

b71e8d1f7ead.title: Dutch disease
b71e8d1f7ead.sentence: In economics, Dutch disease is the apparent causal relationship between the increase in the economic development of a specific sector (for example, natural resources) and a decline in other sectors (like the manufacturing sector or agriculture).

208946c729ba.title: Dutch disease
208946c729ba.sentence: The term was coined in 1977 by The Economist to describe the decline of the manufacturing sector in the Netherlands after the discovery of the large Groningen gas field in 1959.

b8bfab5faccc.title: Dutch disease
b8bfab5faccc.sentence: The presumed mechanism is that while revenues increase in a growing sector (or inflows of foreign aid), the given economy's currency becomes stronger ("appreciates") compared to foreign currencies (manifested in the exchange rate).

1b7640b80c6c.title: Dutch disease
1b7640b80c6c.sentence: This results in the country's other exports becoming more expensive for other countries, while imports become cheaper, rendering those sectors less competitive.

b1f0a73b312e.title: Dutch disease

b9ba375c49a0.title: Dutch disease

5ce77577d205.title: Dutch disease

307ba9d8e8c8.title: Dutch disease

aecd774c96ab.title: Dutch disease

7c654f1972f6.title: Dutch disease

fd76e66a8876.title: Law of rent
fd76e66a8876.sentence: The law of rent states that the rent of a land site is equal to the economic advantage obtained by using the site in its most productive use, relative to the advantage obtained by using marginal (i.e., the best rent-free) land for the same purpose, given the same inputs of labor and capital.

48f778b50504.title: Law of rent

f80c2e678468.title: Law of rent

15eefa671589.title: Law of rent

a8ebdadcae37.title: Law of rent

6d059a7c64f5.title: Law of rent

a9d5acf5fdd5.title: Law of rent

184903b643ae.title: Cornucopianism
184903b643ae.sentence: The term comes from the cornucopia, the "horn of plenty" of Greek mythology, which magically supplied its owners with endless food and drink.

fd233ee1591e.title: Cornucopianism

4484f6ad595a.title: Cornucopianism
4484f6ad595a.sentence: Julian Simon was one of the best-known cornucopian thinkers in modern times, who suggested in his book, The Ultimate Resource, published in 1981, that humans have always found a way to develop and enhance resources over virtually any roadblock.

262ad50f5db4.title: Cornucopianism

3ff2b7e908b2.title: Cornucopianism

cea035e987d8.title: Cornucopianism

ceb484e43df8.title: Cornucopianism

0f0b2a99149e.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager
0f0b2a99149e.sentence: The Simon–Ehrlich wager was a 1980 scientific wager between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich, betting on a mutually agreed-on measure of natural-resource scarcity over the decade leading up to 1990.

c5201d7c8b02.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager

c64565c2ca16.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager
c64565c2ca16.sentence: In response to Ehrlich's published claim that "If I were a gambler, I would take even money that England will not exist in the year 2000", Simon offered to take that bet, or, more realistically, "to stake US$10,000... on my belief that the cost of non-government-controlled raw materials (including grain and oil) will not rise in the long run".

41c6fb14239b.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager
41c6fb14239b.sentence: Ehrlich and his colleagues picked five metals that they thought would undergo big price increases: chromium, copper, nickel, tin, and tungsten.

6718e901080b.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager
6718e901080b.sentence: Then, on paper, they bought $200 worth of each, for a total bet of $1,000, using the prices on September 29, 1980, as an index.

c4842dafbbb5.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager

89b52339b45a.title: Simon–Ehrlich wager

c7e6a7a815d4.sentence: In population ecology and economics, optimum sustainable yield is the level of effort (LOE) that maximizes the difference between total revenue and total cost.

78bb02efd867.title: Optimum sustainable yield

827a140f762d.title: Optimum sustainable yield

acd261abea10.title: Optimum sustainable yield

8ddca349810f.title: Optimum sustainable yield
8ddca349810f.sentence: In environmental science, optimum sustainable yield is the largest economical yield of a renewable resource achievable over a long time period without decreasing the ability of the population or its environment to support the continuation of this level of yield, and enables an ecosystem to have a high aesthetic value.

56b90992ca7c.title: Fish mortality
56b90992ca7c.sentence: Knowing these rates can help managers to set harvest limits to (MSY) maximum sustainable yield or (OSY) optimum sustainable yield to give the maximum benefit to the stakeholders of the resource.

fc59e968b328.title: Fishing down the food web
fc59e968b328.sentence: Fishing down the food web is the process whereby fisheries in a given ecosystem, "having depleted the large predatory fish on top of the food web, turn to increasingly smaller species, finally ending up with previously spurned small fish and invertebrates".

731adce48d42.title: Fishing down the food web
731adce48d42.sentence: The process was first demonstrated by the fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly and others in an article published in the journal Science in 1998.

68918b6fe96b.title: Fishing down the food web
68918b6fe96b.sentence: Over the last 50 years, the abundance of large predator fish, such as cod, swordfish and tuna, has dropped 90 percent.

e67dcae2714b.title: Fishing down the food web
e67dcae2714b.sentence: The model showed that over the last 50 years the mean trophic level of fish catches has declined by somewhere between 0.5 and 1.0 trophic levels.

4710aedf5a9b.title: Fishing down the food web
4710aedf5a9b.sentence: This decline applied both globally, on a worldwide scale, and more locally on a scale specific to oceans, that is, for the separate FAO subareas: the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, and the Mediterranean-Black Seas.

208fd032c07a.title: Fishing down the food web
208fd032c07a.sentence: The trophic level of fishes usually increases with their size, and fishing tends to selectively capture the larger fishes.

05fa86222bd3.title: Fishing down the food web
05fa86222bd3.sentence: Consequently, over time, small fishes start to dominate the fisheries catches, and the mean trophic level of the catches declines.

e6df520d0632.title: Fishing down the food web

594f985aa693.title: Fisheries subsidy
594f985aa693.sentence: Fisheries subsidies include direct transfers of funds, income or price support measures, tax credits, exemptions and rebates, low-interest loans and guarantees, preferential treatment and use of regulatory support mechanisms.

7f0e6ca532c4.title: Fisheries subsidy

5fa4da074fe1.title: Fisheries subsidy

08b675d708a3.title: Fisheries subsidy

1f7a25c28140.title: Fisheries subsidy

85d7ffd274cd.title: Plant genetic resources
85d7ffd274cd.sentence: Plant genetic resources describes the variability within plants that comes from human and natural selection over millennia.

9cd7d94667c4.title: Plant genetic resources
9cd7d94667c4.sentence: In the State of the World’s Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (1998) the FAO defined Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (PGRFA) as the diversity of genetic material contained in traditional varieties and modern cultivars as well as crop wild relatives and other wild plant species that can be used now or in the future for food and agriculture.

cc3e4d4c01a3.title: Plant genetic resources
cc3e4d4c01a3.sentence: The first use of plant genetic resources dates to more than 10,000 years ago, when farmers selected from the genetic variation they found in wild plants to develop their crops.

c0b63a09ab75.title: Plant genetic resources
c0b63a09ab75.sentence: Plant conservation strategies generally combine elements of conservation on farm (as part of the crop production cycle, where it continues to evolve and support farmer needs), ex situ (for example in gene banks or field collections as seed or tissue samples) or in situ (where they grow in the wild or protected areas).

3df80b1e6070.title: Plant genetic resources
3df80b1e6070.sentence: Most in situ conservation concerns crop wild relatives, an important source of genetic variation to crop breeding programs.

c81b826f26a0.title: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
c81b826f26a0.sentence: However, only about 120 cultivated species provide around 90% of food requirements and four species (maize, wheat, rice and potatoes) provide about 60% of human dietary energy for the world's population.

3924de0ae785.title: Access and Benefit Sharing Agreement
3924de0ae785.sentence: Plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage of mankind before the CBD came into force, they could be freely exchanged for plant breeding and scientific research.

afa0d1e4b640.title: Plant genetic resources
afa0d1e4b640.sentence: Article 15 of the CBD specified that countries have national sovereignty over their genetic resources, but that there should be facilitated access and benefit sharing (ABS) under mutually agreed terms and with prior informed consent.

8dbbf7d7a761.title: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
8dbbf7d7a761.sentence: The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (also known as ITPGRFA, International Seed Treaty or Plant Treaty) is a comprehensive international agreement in harmony with the Convention on Biological Diversity, which aims at guaranteeing food security through the conservation, exchange and sustainable use of the world's plant genetic resources for food and agriculture (PGRFA), the fair and equitable benefit sharing arising from its use, as well as the recognition of farmers' rights.

20724414f296.title: Plant genetic resources
20724414f296.sentence: Going further to protect national sovereignty of plant genetic resources, an instrumental piece of legislation, the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA), was adopted by the FAO in November 2001 and came into force in 2004.

20597c4c428f.title: Plant genetic resources
20597c4c428f.sentence: The ITPGRFA established several mechanisms under the Multilateral System, which grants free access and equitable use of 64 of the world’s most important crops (Annex 1 crops) for some uses (research, breeding and training for food and agriculture).

336ce8f766c3.title: Plant genetic resources
336ce8f766c3.sentence: This is facilitated by the Standard Material Transfer Agreement, a mandatory contract between providers and recipients for the exchange of germplasm under the Multilateral System.

a35df5d90ec0.title: Nagoya Protocol
a35df5d90ec0.sentence: In comparison, the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture has a multilateral access/transfer framework via the Standard Material Transfer Agreement, allowing 8500 transfers every week.

f8fcc53d3192.title: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
f8fcc53d3192.sentence: The treaty recognises farmers' rights, subject to national laws to: a) the protection of traditional knowledge relevant to plant genetic resources for food and agriculture; b) the right to equitably participate in sharing benefits arising from the utilisation of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture; and c) the right to participate in making decisions, at the national level, on matters related to the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture.

bd47137cb28d.title: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
bd47137cb28d.sentence: However, as Regine Andersen of the farmers' rights project, among others, including Olivier De Schutter, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Food, argue, the interpretation and realisation of farmers' rights is weak and is not the same across all countries.

b62ee58eaa88.title: Sustainable seafood

2fb5b6652196.title: Sustainable seafood

ad5220fbf5f4.title: Sustainable seafood

e97aeebde406.title: Sustainable seafood

780688d3c05d.title: Sustainable seafood

4d18583a7d3a.title: Shifting baseline

e4827ce1865e.title: Regional fishery body
e4827ce1865e.sentence: A regional fishery body (RFB) is a type of international organization that is part of an international fishery agreement or arrangement to cooperate on the sustainable use and conservation of marine living resources (fish and marine mammals) and/or the development of marine capture fisheries whose such capacity has been recognized by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization under the United Nations Fish Stocks Agreement.

d46940967b01.title: Regional fishery body
d46940967b01.sentence: RFABs issue non-binding recommendations only, but they are usually organised as more independent, impartial expert bodies, expected to be guided by science and sustainability rather than the immediate political and economic interests of its members.

dd15b2f28ba5.title: Regional fishery body

70d4d4897b4b.title: Regional fishery body

c9e037bfb075.title: Regional fishery body
c9e037bfb075.sentence: RFMOs exercise the prerogative to establish a diverse array of rules governing fishery management, deploying strategic tools such as catch limits (quota), technical measures, spatial and/or temporal restrictions, and overseeing monitoring, control, and surveillance activities to ensure rigorous adherence to these regulations.

e37088e15413.title: Regional fishery body

4ae950fc1dbd.title: Maximum sustainable yield
4ae950fc1dbd.sentence: In 1977, Peter Larkin wrote its epitaph, challenging the goal of maximum sustained yield on several grounds: It put populations at too much risk; it did not account for spatial variability in productivity; it did not account for species other than the focus of the fishery; it considered only the benefits, not the costs, of fishing; and it was sensitive to political pressure.

5e59997f6cbc.title: Land use

3f3bf1726d53.title: Land use

d0c69c53db81.title: Forestry

0e2d46d429c5.title: Forestry
0e2d46d429c5.sentence: Forestry is practiced in plantations and natural stands.

3a1a05a787c3.title: Forestry
3a1a05a787c3.sentence: A practitioner of forestry is a forester.

8bc139797e90.title: Forestry
8bc139797e90.sentence: Modern forestry generally embraces a broad range of concerns, in what is known as multiple-use management, including: the provision of timber, fuel wood, wildlife habitat, natural water quality management, recreation, landscape and community protection, employment, aesthetically appealing landscapes, biodiversity management, watershed management, erosion control, and preserving forests as "sinks" for carbon dioxide.

a355fd08b2e1.title: Forestry
a355fd08b2e1.sentence: The management of forests for timber production is known as silviculture.

14f5bceaee6f.title: Forestry
14f5bceaee6f.sentence: Although forestry is a broader concept, the two terms are often used synonymously.

7f8131ff5eeb.title: Forestry
7f8131ff5eeb.sentence: Forestry is an important economic segment in various industrial countries, as forests provide more than 86 million green jobs and support the livelihoods of many more people.

1e73f1120879.title: Forestry
1e73f1120879.sentence: Worldwide, an estimated 880 million people spend part of their time collecting firewood or producing charcoal, many of them women.

2e9f2b8404ce.title: Forestry
2e9f2b8404ce.sentence: Economic and policy decision-making tends to prioritise market-based benefits such as timber production which has led to recent frameworks emphasising that forest management must account for non-market ecosystem services such as cultural, social, and ecological functions which are often underrepresented.

1ef507e72e69.title: Forestry
1ef507e72e69.sentence: Some 252 million people living in forests and savannahs have incomes of less than US$1.25 per day.

48975c027846.title: Forestry
48975c027846.sentence: Logging is an inherently dangerous occupation, with a fatality rate 30x higher than all other U.S. occupations.

81ebf522d6af.title: Forest management
81ebf522d6af.sentence: Forest management is a branch of forestry concerned with overall administrative, legal, economic, and social aspects, as well as scientific and technical aspects, such as silviculture, forest protection, and regulation.

7b4d37567057.title: Forest management
7b4d37567057.sentence: This includes management for timber, aesthetics, recreation, urban values, water, wildlife, inland and nearshore fisheries, wood products, plant genetic resources, and other forest resource values.

542bfa9bf408.title: Forest management
542bfa9bf408.sentence: Management objectives can be for conservation, utilisation, or a mixture of the two.

fe3a79d95736.title: Forest management
fe3a79d95736.sentence: Techniques include timber extraction, planting and replanting of different species, building and maintenance of roads and pathways through forests, and preventing fire.

52fd576e803b.title: Forest management
52fd576e803b.sentence: Forests supply water, mitigate climate change, provide habitats for wildlife including many pollinators which are essential for sustainable food production, provide timber and fuelwood, serve as a source of non-wood forest products including food and medicine, and contribute to rural livelihoods.

f428a3e07a52.title: Forest management
f428a3e07a52.sentence: Some forests have been and are managed to obtain traditional forest products such as firewood, fiber for paper, and timber, with little thinking for other products and services.

6bbc2f0e74cb.title: Forest management
6bbc2f0e74cb.sentence: Nevertheless, as a result of the progression of environmental awareness, management of forests for multiple use is becoming more common.

f445adfe1176.title: Forest management

87304e6d8e06.title: Forest management

5e85f2178774.title: Forest management
5e85f2178774.sentence: Forest management varies in intensity from a leave alone, natural situation to a highly intensive regime with silvicultural interventions.

95b94ade725f.title: Forest management
95b94ade725f.sentence: Forest Management is generally increased in intensity to achieve either economic criteria (increased timber yields, non-timber forest products, ecosystem services) or ecological criteria (species recovery, fostering of rare species, carbon sequestration).

dae06a6e9190.title: Forest management

d21dafb2a43c.sentence: Its main traits were centralized management by professional foresters, the adherence to sustainable yield concepts with a bias towards fuelwood and timber production, artificial afforestation, and a critical view of pastoral and agricultural uses of forests.

f17d16e161aa.title: Groundwater
f17d16e161aa.sentence: Groundwater is the water present beneath Earth's surface in rock and soil pore spaces and in the fractures of rock formations.

acc2070df858.title: Groundwater
acc2070df858.sentence: About 30 percent of all readily available fresh water in the world is groundwater.

918b433f655f.title: Groundwater
918b433f655f.sentence: About 99% of the world's liquid Fresh water is groundwater.

39df7a52ae64.title: Groundwater
39df7a52ae64.sentence: The depth at which soil pore spaces or fractures and voids in rock become completely saturated with water is called the water table.

6f45b529155b.title: Groundwater
6f45b529155b.sentence: Groundwater is recharged from the surface; it may discharge from the surface naturally at springs and seeps, and can form oases or wetlands.

eb0c9e664822.title: Groundwater
eb0c9e664822.sentence: Groundwater accounts for about half of the world's drinking water, 40% of its irrigation water, and a third of water for industrial purposes.

91ee9383c0cf.title: Groundwater
91ee9383c0cf.sentence: This makes it an important resource that can act as a natural storage that can buffer against shortages of surface water, as in during times of drought.

704c40d083e2.title: Groundwater

a2ee9e7330fb.title: Groundwater

a2ee9e7330fb.sentence: In fact, there is considerable uncertainty with groundwater in different hydrogeologic contexts: the widespread presence of contaminants such as arsenic, fluoride and salinity can reduce the suitability of groundwater as a drinking water source.

9e97e78e3609.title: Water resources
9e97e78e3609.sentence: Water resources are natural resources of water that are potentially useful for humans.

9554a21374df.title: Water resources
9554a21374df.sentence: For example, they serve as a source of drinking water or irrigation water.

992ea09ad166.title: Water resources
992ea09ad166.sentence: Approximately 97% of the water on Earth is salt water, and only 3% is fresh water; slightly over two-thirds of this is frozen in glaciers and polar ice caps.

dc5887590ede.title: Water resources
dc5887590ede.sentence: The remaining unfrozen freshwater is found mainly as groundwater, with only a small fraction present above ground or in the air.

ec1f9270558a.title: Water resources
ec1f9270558a.sentence: Natural sources of fresh water include surface water, under river flow, groundwater and frozen water.

b6309fb4dba4.title: Water resources
b6309fb4dba4.sentence: There are several artificial sources of fresh water; treated wastewater (reclaimed water), atmospheric water generators and Desalinated seawater.

2612d7958412.title: Water resources
2612d7958412.sentence: Other important sources includes: rainwater harvesting systems, wells, and boreholes, artificial recharge ponds, dams and reservoirs.

ae8920c86991.title: Water resources
ae8920c86991.section: Natural sources of fresh water > Surface water
ae8920c86991.sentence: The only natural input to any surface water system is precipitation within its watershed.

55a8935d3cf5.title: Water resources
55a8935d3cf5.sentence: They include more frequent and intense heavy precipitation which affects the frequency, size and timing of floods.

a1d79eb79f28.title: Water resources
a1d79eb79f28.sentence: Also droughts can alter the total amount of freshwater and cause a decline in groundwater storage, and reduction in groundwater recharge.

c925b217e4e4.title: Water scarcity
c925b217e4e4.sentence: Water scarcity (closely related to water stress or water crisis) is the lack of any, local or economically viably transportable, sources of fresh water resources to meet the standard water demand in a region.

cafba26e70cb.title: Water scarcity
cafba26e70cb.sentence: There are two types of water scarcity.

8c168a6acae1.title: Water scarcity
8c168a6acae1.sentence: The other is economic water scarcity.

d8002eadbb90.title: Water scarcity
d8002eadbb90.sentence: There is and has always been enough physical supply of freshwater for current or near or distant future demand in a global scale.

fcef7d51ac00.title: Water scarcity
fcef7d51ac00.sentence: As such, water scarcity is caused by a mismatch between when and where people need water, and when and where it is available.

224f7b54ae0e.title: Water scarcity
224f7b54ae0e.sentence: This can happen due to an increase in the number of people in a region, changing living conditions and diets, and expansion of irrigated agriculture.

5732993f1a8b.title: Water scarcity
5732993f1a8b.sentence: Climate change (including droughts or floods), deforestation, water pollution and wasteful use of water can also mean there is not enough water.

c9b6fe1d7d15.title: Water scarcity
c9b6fe1d7d15.sentence: Half a billion people live in areas with severe water scarcity throughout the year, and around four billion people face severe water scarcity at least one month per year.

c83c7c92afb4.title: Water scarcity

a890aeb984b7.title: Water scarcity

a890aeb984b7.sentence: The main cause of water scarcity as a result of consumption is the extensive use of water in agriculture/livestock breeding and industry.

7574159fba82.title: Water scarcity

f17485c6b1b8.title: Water scarcity

c0e248280e01.title: Water scarcity

41e3fc1b31a9.title: Drainage basin
41e3fc1b31a9.sentence: A drainage basin is an area of land in which all flowing surface water converges to a single point, such as a river mouth, or flows into another body of water, such as a lake or ocean.

e89b6aea200f.title: Drainage basin
e89b6aea200f.sentence: A basin is separated from adjacent basins by a perimeter, the drainage divide, made up of a succession of elevated features, such as ridges and hills.

168339827fbb.title: Drainage basin
168339827fbb.sentence: In North America, a drainage basin is commonly called a watershed, though in other English-speaking places, "watershed" is used only in its original sense, that of the drainage divide.

19431f0b382b.title: Drainage basin

bf0d600228b9.title: Drainage basin
bf0d600228b9.sentence: Most of the water that discharges from the basin outlet originated as precipitation falling on the basin.

32d456977612.title: Drainage basin
32d456977612.sentence: Because drainage basins are coherent entities in a hydrological sense, it has become common to manage water resources on the basis of individual basins.

427a53569d1d.title: Drainage basin

0eb0ae7037e0.title: Drainage basin

d1cfd7659994.title: Drainage basin

34ea049323ce.title: Aquifer
34ea049323ce.sentence: An aquifer is an underground layer of water-bearing material consisting of permeable, porous, or fractured rock, or of unconsolidated materials (gravel, sand, or silt).

7ead039486c2.title: Aquifer
7ead039486c2.sentence: Groundwater from aquifers can be sustainably harvested by humans through the use of wells.

9bbd10f96a6c.title: Aquifer

3a2f004db5c0.title: Aquifer

3b8141703dd0.title: Aquifer

33ba61361922.title: Aquifer

b365a704e121.sentence: Overexploitation can lead to the exceeding of the practical sustained yield; i.e., more water is taken out than can be replenished.

a28c719cf781.title: Aquifer
